Oral evidence: Entrepreneurship and business , HC 728
Tuesday 27 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 27 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Liam Byrne (Chair); Dan Aldridge; Antonia Bance; Chris Bloore; Sarah Edwards; Alison Griffiths; Mr Joshua Reynolds .
Questions 3 4 - 70
Witnesses
II
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Matt Adey, Michale Moore and Chris Lewis.

Q34 Welcome to this second panel in today ’ s opening inquiry into entrepreneurship in Britain. Chris Lewis, we are going to kick off with you. Welcome back to the House of Commons. The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor report that was published this morning shows that it is getting harder for entrepreneurs to get the start-up and scale-up capital that they need. Is that your sense? Tell us what is going on and what is going wrong.

You are right. There is a continued increase in supply of entrepreneurs, but they need access to capital. We heard it earlier in the previous session. I work in industry. My full-time main job is running a venture capital trust , and we see it every day when trying to match entrepreneurs with capital. There is so much demand and we are limited in the amount of capital that we have. We would like to be able to raise more.

The biggest challenge we are currently facing is the unintended consequences of last year ’ s Budget, where the income tax credit for VCT investment by UK taxpayers was reduced from 30% to 20%. That is having a very significant impact in terms of the reduction of fundraising for this year ’ s fundraising, which runs from now until the tax year end.
Q35 How significant an impact has that tax change had?

When we first spoke to Treasury about the impact of this decision, just after last year ’ s Budget, we started to model a reduction in fundraising of 20% to 40%. Our current level of budgeting and modelling goes beyond that, so it is having a serious impact. We are perhaps one quarter of the way through the fundraising cycle so far, so it might be early days, but all the indicators, for all the VCTs that are currently open for fundraising, are that it is markedly down on last year. If the rate of fundraising does not improve, we hope that, with this Committee ’ s help and with Treasury, we will be able to revisit it together, collectively, so the Government can take action before it is too late.
Q36 Can you give us a sense of how many millions less that means flowing into equity investment in start-ups?

Let us say that the VCT industry raises £900 million a year, which is what it has done broadly for the last five years. If we go on a 50% reduction, that will have a direct follow-on impact on to the amount of investing that we do. It is already down by half for next year, and the year after, and the year after.

Because VCTs are long-term patient capital, we do several rounds of investing. When we have existing companies on our portfolio, you will appreciate that every year, or every two years, subject to milestones, we do another round of investment. The companies that we support need that continued support. Whatever cash we have from fundraising every tax year, we owe it to them to continue supporting them further with advice and capital. By doing that, there is a big imbalance, therefore, in terms of the amount of free capital or free cash that we have to invest in new businesses, which obviously reduces as a result of having reduced the amount of overall funding.
Q37 We could be talking about a half - a - billion - pound impact on early-stage venture investment.

You are looking certainly in the hundreds of millions of pounds of reduction, both into follow-on and new portfolio companies. Those new portfolio companies will not exist every year for the next few years. There is a whole—I will not say a generation — cohort of entrepreneurs we will not be able to support quite as well as the ones we have managed to support over the last 30 years.

Q38 Matt, the British Business Bank has been quite important in how it is trying to revolutionise the way in which entrepreneurs can get access to finance. Some of that is through the start-up loans and creating wider funds. I was with pension funds last week, talking to them about the fact that they like that they can invest into those funds so that you have the ability to share that finance around.

We have heard from the last panel that , in particular, if we take women and ethnic minority businesses, they are still struggling to access finance. I wondered how you are extending that support. Have you revisited whether it is doing what it needs to do? How are you changing tack to make sure that we are getting that money where it needs to go?

Thank you very much for the question and for the invitation. I will jump in straight to that challenge that you have there. There has been a significant increase in venture capital in the long term in the UK, but it has been very concentrated in male-founded businesses. The venture capital industry is notably male as well.

B eyond the building of our investment into venture capital, there are things that we are doing to try to reach those parts of the venture capital world where it does not work. For example, starting last year, we have a £ 400 million allocation to our investor pathways capital. That is pathways for the investors to get into the venture fund world. W e are looking at groups of people who are starting to get into venture capital and to become a venture capitalist , but we are selecting those people who are more diverse than the VC market is now.

T he first allocation we made was a £ 90 million allocation this summer, having met and engaged with several emerging venture capital funds. W e are happy to say that , for that £ 90 million, 57% of the people who were involved in those funds, which we are now supporting , are female . That is massively greater than would be in the general area.

We are also doing a lot in angel syndicates. We are focusing o n getting the angel finance out into the regions with our regional angel program me . We also have some money that we can actually spend , rather than lend , in helping diverse angel syndicates get up and running. T hat is helping people who do not have the funds and find it difficult to create an angel syndicate.

Q39 On that point, every year so far in this Parliament this Committee has toured around the UK to talk to businesses and start to understand what the challenges are in their locale. We heard a lot that, when people are looking for that private finance, capital and VC funds, they would have to come down south to get it. They could not get it in the regions.

When you are saying you are setting them up, are they very new? What is the size of them? What is the scope? We know that that is a problem, so it is good that you are addressing it, but what is the reality of that on the ground and how far along are you? That has been quite important to them, to feel that they did not have to come down south just to find money.

Yes, indeed. It is been known for a long time that a lot of venture capital funds and angel syndicates are London-based. There is good evidence going back several years that investors invest in businesses and start-ups that are near them. They do not want to be too far away. We do not want to be three hours away on the train or on the plane. Getting more offices of venture funds out in the regions is helpful, and that is something we try to do. We have a whole range of nations and regions funds. We have a fund, including some debt, but majority equity, in every nation or region outside of London now.
Q40 How large are they?

They vary in the regions from £ 100 million to much larger. The northern powerhouse is the biggest one, but that covers the north-west, Yorkshire and Humber , and the north-east. That is £ 600 million. The smallest ones are at the £ 100 million end.

Through those regional funds and the other finance that gets there, including start-up loans, which was mentioned on the debt side, every year the funds that flow into those regions are generating economic activity with those funds at the rate of £ 100 million at least in every nation and region. That is significant. It is not going to solve the problem completely, but it is helping.

Q41 No , d efinitely. If I was an entrepreneur, whether I am in the regions or down south, how would I know to engage with these funds? What are the mechanisms of doing that? How do you get that word out, and who do you work with?

One thing, for example, that the Committee is quite interested in is the emerging development of devolution and mayoral authorities. A lot of constituencies—around 40%—currently are not covered by one. The obvious thing is to work directly with some of the strategic teams in a mayoral authority. At the moment , that does not cover the whole of the UK. We are keen to understand how it is that an organisation such as the British Business Bank is getting that information disseminated down to entrepreneurs, wherever they might be.

There is a certain amount of information about this on our website , so people can look if they go out there, but obviously not everyone gets to our website. We have a local growth team. It is a small number, but there are one or two people in each of the nations and regions plugging themselves into those local ecosystems and drawing attention to what we can do. T heir job is to connect those clusters.
Q42 They connect in with local authorities, chambers and things like that, which are, in theory, the obvious places. You have tried to make sure that they are plugged into it.
Then you are linking them back into the British Business Bank products and how you can make use of those schemes.

Q43 I was really struck by what you were saying. In the era of AI, where I think most of us currently would probably go and ask —pick your own AI tool— for advice, are you getting an increase in people coming to you who have used AI to find you? M aybe there is even the challenge where they are using AI to fill out all the forms . M aybe that is a good thing or maybe that is a bad thing . I would be interested if you could comment on that.

I was also really struck by your comment about three hours being a bit too far to travel from London. I started my career as a credit analyst for a global multinational, and so the credit exposure that I was working on was often significantly larger than much of the debt that you would presumably be putting out. It would not have crossed my mind to not go and see an organisation , if I had concerns about it or wanted to understand more, just because it was three hours out of London. You can get from London to Newcastle in three hours on a train . I t is really not hard. I am questioning what the mindset is in the London investment community that that seems a bit too hard. Let us start with AI and then you can tell me why I am completely wrong.
I think that AI will have an impact on that. We are looking at ways that we can use AI in the bank to reach out to people who want to engage with us, and it is early days for that.
Q44 Are you seeing an uptick in applications coming in off the back of it?

In most cases, the applications go into our delivery partners that we put funding to . W e invest in venture capital so we see that. On that desire to be close to the businesses they are investing in, there is a little bit of analysis that was done a few years ago. If we look back over 10 years, where is the investor and where is the business that has been invested in? Sixty per cent of the time, the travel time was less than an hour. Eighty per cent of the time, it was less than two hours. You could see that cluster of activity. If you were near, say, Edinburgh in Scotland or Manchester, you could see that being closer. If you are in London, that is further away.
Q45 It is accepting the issue and therefore having to respond to the issue.

Yes, you need that in-person touch before you make a venture capital investment. Some funds are becoming more regional. I am sure many will be looking to open offices in Manchester at the moment , for example.

Q46 Can I come back on that? That is a remarkable statistic. It takes me longer than two hours to get back to my constituency, where Gymshark was founded. That is probably a bit of a concern . We are never going to achieve growth in every postcode or in our towns and across our country unless something changes on that. Wow. That is a bit of a blow.

You probably heard in the previous panel that we are not getting it right on female entrepreneurs and finance for ethnic minority entrepreneurs. You are an all-male panel, as we have this conversation. I know that that is not you guys ’ fault, but what are we getting wrong? Why are we apparently not getting the finance to the equally ambitious, talented and driven women and ethnic minority-led businesses in the country to help us avoid that opportunity los s that we seem to be losing . I think £ 75 billion is what we said in the previous panel. That is pretty terrifying . I could spend that £ 75 billion if I could.

This is a really serious problem that vexes our industry specifically. You heard in the last panel that really damning statistic of 2% of funding going into all-female-led investment teams. We have worked with L evel 20, which operates across private equity and venture capital, primarily private equity, on tracking where the investment teams are. It is a slightly different bit of the lens, but it goes to a point that was made earlier . If we have a group of white men who are in the main decision-making seats, it is hard to change that culture.

The position we have got to in the industry, which is not anything to boast about really, is 27% of investment professionals being women the last time we did the survey, which was at the beginning of 2025 . We are due to complete a survey at the beginning of the new calendar year. About half that number would be in the investment committees, which are where all the key decisions are taken. A slightly smaller percentage — 15% or so —are in senior investment positions. T hat is a big challenge.

You then step aside from that and look at where there is been a lot of effort . You have already heard about some of the initiatives that the BBB is doing. T he Invest in Women T askforce a couple of years ago set itself the target of not just trying to address some of the cultural points and long-standing legacy issues, which, as we can see, will take a bit more time to fix as people progress through careers, but also saying, “ Where is the capital for female-led teams and female founders? ” T hat initiative has led to BGF, BBB and others getting involved. T here are efforts being made to address it, but I do not think there is a single fix. It is going to take a lot more.

I f I might, without cheating, Chair, pull it back slightly , this is in the context of, to add to what Chris said earlier on, somewhere under a billion going into VCTs every year. Last year, there was £8 billion invested by VC in the UK. That is a subset of the overall £25 billion that was invested across the whole country in private equity and VC-backed businesses. There have been year-on-year variations, but that is growing. T o pick up one of the themes from the first panel, the entrepreneurship is growing. I was struck by the increase in the monitor figure that was shared today. A lso, we can see that in around different parts of the country.

As a final cheat , I will link into the previous question about what happens beyond the UK. I work here in London, but I live just south of Edinburgh, so I can relate to the four-hour trip from Berwick on a good day. C ulturally, it matter s that the BBB and investors are out there. Ms Bance was at an event we had in Birmingham just a couple of weeks ago . O ur industry is certainly seeing lots of opportunity beyond London in the nations and regions . W e want to encourage more of that. We are really taken by how stakeholders, whether they are parliamentarians or the different councils, the mayors and so on, are really engaging on this . T hat is very encouraging.

Equally, the mindset has to work both ways. Here in London, we have one of the most globally significant financial centres on the planet . It is No.2 in the latest Global Financial Centres Index and consistently there. T he push-pull needs to work for us to get people here, as well as going north or south-west from here as appropriate.

Q47 I agree with much of what you just said, but it is an internal problem that we have. This is not about an external challenge that we are facing about those coming here and leaving . It almost sounds like, from your answer about those who are in the room making the decisions, those people have not caught up with the times . W e are missing out on billions of potential revenue from female-led and ethnic minority-led companies, because our internal process as a country and the way in which venture capital is working in this country is not up with the times.

What was really interesting , and I would perhaps have expected you to have mentioned , was what the previous panel mentioned about the potential lack of expertise in the types of businesses that these people are setting up and how we are not in a position to fully understand their potential scale-up and profitability. I understand the question about who i s coming to this country and money, b ut this is an internal problem . T his is a cultural problem between us .
Forgive me — I in no way wish ed to suggest it was anything other than a thing in the UK that we ought to fix.
Q48 How do we change it ?

We have the largest hub of private capital expertise anywhere in the world outside the United States. We have a great starting point and that is giving us great competitive advantage. I was at an event in Cambridge last week, where there were 500 people trying to stuff themselves into the Guildhall for the new exciting opportunities that are there. I could see around the room that there were a lot of female academics, ethnic minority academics and others who are right at the forefront of all this.

We have some cultural challenges that we as an industry need to be really aware of . We need to make sure that we are not putting barriers in the way of people who wish to invest. The Invest in Women Taskforce—I hope I do not misquote that and I will correct it if I get it wrong—identified right at the outset that, if women were provided with the same opportunities in finance as male-led investment teams, we could get another £250 billion into the UK.
That is now £ 313 billion.
Q49 That was part of the Rose review and everything. That was five or six years ago and we still have not made significant progress.

May I suggest that you cannot do this by fiat or legislation ? The pressure—you are exerting it and I respect that fact—on the industry and the decision makers within it has to continue. The opportunities arise all over the country. To pick up the point I nearly missed there, about whether we are missing out on opportunities, there is no question that we are. Whether it is university spin-outs that could then become unicorns and create great wealth for huge parts of the UK or smaller businesses in neighbourhoods that you all represent, we have to do better.

Q50 Other countries legislate, and we heard an example of it in the previous panel. Canada specifically has legislated to support women and indigenous-led businesses in its country. I take your point, but Canada shows an example of where Government can lead the way and push venture capital along the way.

I take that point. You are the decision makers on that, not me. The BBB, with its pathway programme and other initiatives, is absolutely directing the capital there. We have to make sure that the demand and the opportunity is understood and then fulfilled.

Q51 We have had quite a good run around on some of the issues about regional disparities in access to finance, so I want to move on slightly , though this is very important to my region of the w est m idlands, among others. T he Prime Minister has set out a really clear ambition to reindustrialise this country . I would appreciate hearing from the panel in turn about the efforts they are making to ensure that finance reaches the manufacturing and hard tech materials and production businesses that we all hope will start up and scale in this country.

T he nations and regions fun d s , which I mentioned earlier, are not the typical London-based venture capital type of fund. We are on the second round of the midlands engine investment fund now. T hat has a debt element to it ; it has an equity element to it, but it is focused on the strengths of the regions that those funds are in. I t is not doing quite the same as a high-tech VC fund in London. It is active in a way that is suitable for the region it is in . W e have those funds in every region.

W e are trying to get that and looking at what we can do across the industrial strategy sector priorities as well. W e are bringing that dimension into our activities as well. The w est m idlands covers a wide number of those industrial strateg y priority sectors .
Q52 It covers all of them.
It covers a ll of them, as you say, but it is not just the high-tech ones. It is the others as well and we are very aware of that.

Q53 Do you think the British Business Bank is doing enough? You are operationally independent, but the steer could hardly be less strong from the Prime Minister around the need to reindustrialise. Do you feel you have adequately taken that into how you do your operations?
We have done very significant activity. I am not saying that there is not more that we could do in the future, but we are a British Business Bank. We are not just a London-based VC funder.

What is wonderful about the UK is the diversity of its economy. You very kindly joined us at the investment forum in Birmingham a couple of weeks ago. The conversations we had over the course of that afternoon had more manufacturing focus and reindustrialising as a theme than perhaps we would get in other parts of the country. If we are to emerge from this really dramatic moment in time , where we have a tech revolution coming at us full steam ahead that is going to give us great opportunities to create these businesses of the future and whole new bits of the economy that we do not even imagine yet, while also disrupting and requiring us to transform the existing businesses, we need to get the capital, entrepreneurs and ideas all in the right place on that. That will be in different forms.

For west midlands manufacturing to continue for the next 20 or 30 years, it needs to be able to adopt AI and other technologies. There is no shortage of appetite to be part of that from our industry. In other parts of the country, whether it is the OxCam corridor or wherever else, there may be more of a life sciences focus. Sometimes that is about the services that go with that and sometimes it is about the labs and the pharmaceuticals that may come from it.

Personally I am a big supporter of industrial strategies, because it lets us understand how policymakers are thinking and gives really important signals to investors. We can see—it is quite exciting—that reindustrialisation as a way of galvanising people works. My only caveat would be to say that I do not think we should be looking to recreate the 1970s or 1980s industrial economy, because the world has moved on. We should be aiming to retain and develop all the modern industries here in the UK.

I am going to take the opportunity to answer that and touch on a number of points we heard earlier. On reindustrialisation and manufacturing, it was good news in the last Budget that the Chancellor increased the investment limits that VCTs can make into heavy manufacturing businesses. That increased the gross assets test by 100%, which means it is easier to keep investing into heavy manufacturing or heavy plant and machinery type businesses. That was a win, so we are pleased with that.

In terms of reindustrialisation, there is the arrival of financial services and AI across all the regions. Just last month there were two in Manchester. There was one exit, which was an AI company sold to a Nasdaq company. There was a record series B round for a UK payments business. They all had a Manchester postcode, so that is great.

Trying to reach growth in every postcode is a fantastic goal but difficult to achieve on a checklist basis. VCTs have been investing across all the regions of the UK for a long time. In the last maybe five to 10 years, we have seen what used to be a heavy balance towards London and the south-east — maybe 75/25 to the regions —change . A couple of years ago, that reached parity. W e are broadly at 50 / 50, which is a good thing.

As p art of that, we also reach , as a result , a large r proportion of ethnic minority and female entrepreneurs. There are always some sector imbalances. We do a lot of retail and some fashion brands , so naturall y at Pembroke we have more female founders. The latest one is a company called With Nothing Underneath. It is a shirts company. You may know it , but that is one of many. The data of about 2% representation is not something that I see, in the world that I live in , in the day-to-day . We are closer to a third of female representation across the board, whether it is at founder level, at board level of the VCTs or in investment teams . A cross all the staff in our business it is more like 50 / 50. T his is something that we have been working on very hard.

The key bit for us in terms of making even better progress is what is called the age limit restriction on some of the investments that we can make. Currently, the rules say that, if a business is between seven and 10 years old, it no longer qualif ies for the VCT or EIS investment offering . That is a shame because we know that businesses in the regions —we have stats on this —take up to 40% or two years longer to reach maturity for VCT investment. A s soon as they get to the seven-year mark, all of a sudden , they are told, “ I ’ m sorry : you don’t meet the rules so we can’t invest in you ” , which is a shame.

Q54 Interest in entrepreneurship among young people is high, but few make the transition. We know that access to entrepreneurial finance is at its lowest level since 2021. Women are more likely than men to rely on close family funding. We know that this entrepreneurship is heavily dependent on family resources. What are you doing and what can we be doing to make sure that a young person ’ s financial background is not a barrier to them starting a business?

The first panel covered some of this in terms of being exposed to that education around entrepreneurship and so on. It helps people get into that start-up place. If we reach out, we can have an impact. Our start-up loans have been mentioned already. Forty per cent of those loans go to females. About 20% of businesses are female run, but our start-up loans are 40% female. It is the same with ethnic minorities ; we are getting that in. We are also looking at that from disadvantaged areas.
Q55 What i s your strategy around young people in terms of engaging with young entrepreneurs?

You mentioned earlier the way in which information is accessed and the younger people do that, so using AI and finding those opportunities. The old website does not do it for them. You need to engage with them in a different way.
Q56 It sounds like there is a bit of work to be done on youth engagement.
There is definitely some work to be done there. That will be the case for a lot of finance providers. It is not the easiest way to get in.

Formally, the industry does not run programmes or the like. When you look at the way in which venture capital firms look to find potential businesses in which to invest, they have to be , and are , ever present at or near university campuses. They are engaging with young people there. There are places such as Code B ase in Edinburgh and a lot of similar initiatives around the country where young entrepreneurs are getting help with the earliest forms of funding beyond what their families have helped them with . They will , hopefully, be put in the pipeline.

In our jargon, we call it the ticket size . Y ou are writing quite big che ques , so it is not going to be the earliest start - up person there. W e are certainly engaged in all the ecosystems and networks around universities and other places where people get involved in entrepreneurialism . I n London, famously it is in the east end . There is no lack of appetite on that.

Q57 Entrepreneurship exists across all 650 constituencies , and many of us do not have universities. There is a real issue with accessing that. We have a fantastic college, but we know that very little engagement happens with the college. I wonder whether that is part of something that you would be looking at.

It can be done. I am trying not to break myself into jail here and cause a problem. Typically, our industry will be investing in a later stage than that early-stage entrepreneur. In terms of making sure that we are part of the conversations, whether it is in Bristol, Glasgow or Leeds, we are—
Q58 Or a town.

I live in Melrose in the south of Scotland. We are 50 miles from Edinburgh. I will put my hand up and say that there is not a single venture capitalist anywhere near me in the area for young people. Equally, we are keen , and it is possible, to make the connections through the local cities. That tends to be where the agglomeration is, where the ideas can come together and where that really rich network of entrepreneurs and those with the capital can come together.

Q59 I am about to talk about high streets, and I particularly wanted to ask you, Michael Moore , about that. Y ou mentioned Melrose . It was taking me back to the Melrose Cup and the very beautiful high streets of Melrose that I was fortunate enough to visit. You have just described a picture of the types of businesses that you invest in . I am really curious about whether , directly or indirectly, your members are investing in organisations and businesses that would reach the high street , so small businesses and high street businesses.

It is a different part of investment from where we are at. The private equity part of our industry had, over the years, high-profile investments in chains of high street or retail businesses, but we are not involved at the high street level individual ly business by business. The British Business Bank, through its debt facilities, is more likely to be in that space.
Q60 Matt , is there anything you want to add to that ?

That is a very helpful answer. There is one thing I would very quickly add to that, and that is the value of community development financial institutions — CDFIs . M any of them are very local. They are a type of investor institution that we are increasingly engaging with to reach th ose local areas. For example, there is one in north Coventry.
Let us dig into one of the problems we are quite interested in.

Q61 Matt, we know that private investors and funds own a significant amount of the high street properties around the country. Constituents may think that the local authority owns every shop and decides which retailer goes into it. That is not the case across the country. What incentives do you think investors and institutions need to be able to give the flexibility in leases and fit-out costs to allow those micro-SMEs to get into our high streets more?

I suspect that a lot of that is done more through private equity in terms of buying up those retail outlets. You see that there are some planning issues around that and allocations, but it is not an area that I am particularly familiar with.

Q62 Planning issues would not necessarily stop who goes into a retail unit. We know that investors and institutions would probably rather a large multinational in a unit because they can secure a 10-year or longer lease with a smaller rent-free period than a small SME, which does not have the history, the background or all that resource. We do not need planning to change something like that. We need to put resource and incentives in place to encourage institutions and investors to accept those sorts of tenants. What do you think we as politicians or the Government can do to encourage?
That is probably out of my area of expertise.
Q63 Is there anyone who might have some thoughts on that area ?

I have a thought, but, similarly, it is a bit outside of our main focus . With some experience, the first hurdle for a landlord is the credit risk of the tenant coming in. I do not know whether it is through central Government or the BBB, but there could be some sort of collateral or loan guarantee, or lease guarantee in effect, whereby an authority or a body could back up a first-time tenant looking to open that shop without the credit rating that a big megacorp might have.
That is useful. We will move on to the Budget question.
Q64 As we are very short on time, in one sentence what would you like tomorrow? Make it big and bold, please. Matt, what would you like from the British Business Bank?
You have already had quite a good weekend, Matt.
I a m glad you said that . It is difficult for me to say more than that in the situation. We will find out tomorrow.
Q65 I t is a wish list . Think big.
You have heard about the range of activities that we are doing. We would like to do more of them.

The BBB is one of the most significant cornerstone investors in any one of the funds that we would have, from early-stage venture capital funds all the way through. We applaud this briefing that happened over the weekend that suggests that there will be a big increase in the facility. That has to be good.

We would add two quick things on to the back of that. We would like the Government to continue to focus on pension reform and on the fact that we saw last week the statistics that only 0.85% of the default scheme assets from DC pension scheme s are put into unlisted equities, of which we are a large subset. The target set out in the Mansion House c ompact was, and remains, 5%. They have got to 0.85% after three years. We think it will take an extra 10 years after 2030 at this rate. T hat goes to the domestic capital funding and domestic entrepreneurs. We need more of that.

Q66 Let us spell this out. The briefing you put out at the end of last week said that, at the current pace, it is going to take us until 2040 before we get the target level of investment in unlisted investments in the UK. It is going much too slowly.

You can think back to the ambition that the then-Chancellor, Jeremy Hunt, put, along with the City of London corporation mayor , Nick Lyons, and the previous Chancellor, Rachel Reeves, and a later Lord Mayor expanded with the accord to look at infrastructure and real estate. If we look back to that original stuff , for the UK start-ups that should become tomorrow ’ s scale-ups and the next generation ’ s great businesses for the UK, 16 times as much international pension capital is funding the UK compared to UK pension capital funds.
Q67 T he Mansion House reforms have stalled, have they not?

I am trying to be generous. We work very closely with them. It is clearly not fast enough. The idea that, instead of it taking five or six years to get to the target, it might take 15 or 20, is obviously not good. We will continue to work with the pensions industry on that.
Q68 W hat does the Chancellor need to do to speed this up ?

We have seen reform in the sense of the Pension Schemes Act in the last parliamentary Session . That is leading to a lot of consolidation. T he re is pressure in the conversations that we all have to speed up that consolidation, mak ing sure that there is the expertise available to actually get that investment delivered and that , in terms of people being told about their DC pensions for the future, they can see the diversification of returns they will get from spreading a bit of that into these businesses that are in their own backyards. W e think that there is a really strong case for saying that these are UK businesses that could go from Birmingham to be world - beaters, but they will not do it without capital.
Q69 That is an issue we are going to return to.

VCTs are genuinely, I believe, in the national interest. They fuel growth in every region with patient capital and advice. One reason they were set up is that they democratise access to the venture capital asset class. It is one of those few access points for UK retail investors into venture capital. It brings in a large amount of private investment.
Q70 W e are so short o f time . We need you to focus on the thing you want the Chancellor to say.

First, on the income tax credit cut from 30% to 20%, put it back to 30% as soon as possible. If not, work with us to keep monitoring the impact and act before it is too late. Secondly, increase and relax the age limit rules that prevent us deploying the money that we are trying to raise.

If I may be greed y , scale up reinvestment relief that allows founders to put some of the capital they have earned from a start- up back into the next generation of businesses . Then we will be firing on all cylinders.
Thank you so much to our witnesses. That has been an excellent session. You have really helped us get some excellent evidence on the record.

sessions.w: The Entrepreneurs Network; Global Entrepreneurship Monitor UK; Centre for Research in Ethnic Minority Entrepreneurship, Aston University; Lifted Ventures

segs.tx: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee
Oral evidence: Entrepreneurship and business , HC 728
Tuesday 27 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 27 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Liam Byrne (Chair); Dan Aldridge; Antonia Bance; Chris Bloore; Sarah Edwards; Alison Griffiths; Mr Joshua Reynolds .
Questions 1 - 33
Witnesses
I
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Philip Salter, Professor Mark Hart, Professor Monder Ram and Jordan Dargue.

Q1 Welcome to today ’ s session of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee as we open our inquiry into entrepreneurship in our country. We open it on the day that the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor for this year is published. Mark Hart, you are one of the lead authors of this internationally acclaimed study. Do you want to tell us what it said and give us the good and bad news for the UK?

This is the 27th year we have been publishing this report, so it is very timely that we released it this morning as you start the inquiry. In terms of the headlines, the central message is that ambition is alive and well in the UK. We are in a more entrepreneurial society than we have ever been since we started the project back in 1999.
Q2 T hat is actually quite a big assertion : t he UK is the most entrepreneurial it has been since the study started in 1999.

Since 1999, a bsolutely. W e measure that in terms of the number of people who are thinking of setting up a business in the next two or three years, the number of people who are in the first three months of doing so, the number of people who have been running a business for at least two and a half years , and established business owners as well. Our survey is not just about people who are in the process of start - up . I t is an adult population survey . W e are trying to measure the level of entrepreneurial activity in the whole population of the UK.
W e are now talking about 46% of the adult population who are involved in some of those categories that I have been talking about. This is a tremendous step change.
Q3 How big a step change is it since the study started in 1999?

We are talking about just over 16% of the adult population involved in nascent entrepreneurship and new business entrepreneurship, so the first two and a half years. That has risen from just about 8% 25 years ago.
Q4 So t he level of entrepreneurship has basically doubled in 25 years ?

Absolutely, yes. We also see that that has been driven by two groups, which is really pertinent to the subject of some of the questions that we have seen in advance, and that is young people, so 18 to 24-year-olds, and females. Female entrepreneurship has been surging, certainly in the period since 2011.
The step changes occurred at the great financial crisis and have step changed since the covid crisis. We can see reactions to those events in the UK economy and society. That is really important.
Q5 T he survey is not all good news .

It is not all good news . We can see that, yes, the headline rate of entrepreneurial activity is fine. Ambition is alive and well among many groups, but we have a problem of retaining people. They are starting up, but getting them to survive and, more importantly, grow their business is really problematic.

We see that in terms of the exits. We do a panel study where we follow some of these nascents over two years, particularly ethnic minority individuals and women. We see that very few of them get to the second or third year. They drop out. Women drop out at twice the rate of men.
Q6 Is that failure rate going up?

It is going up. We have an exit rate in the data as well. You have a bumper edition of over 100-odd bits and pieces of evidence that you can plough through in the report. Yes, the exit data is actually rising as well, so it is swings and roundabouts. We are more entrepreneurial, but we have a problem in an entrepreneurial ecosystem that sustains that level of entrepreneurial interest.
Q7 It is only about 2% of businesses that get to that million threshold.

This is another statistic, and this is not from the GEM survey. This is the ONS, HMRC, PAYE and VAT data, where I look at how many businesses get to £1 million turnover in three years. I do that because I work on the Goldman Sachs 10,000 small businesses programme and all I hear is , “Getting to the first million, getting to the first million”. I went to the HMRC data and said, “How many actually do?” It is 2% of every cohort of start - ups for the last decade and a half, of those that survived, and half of them do not. The median of the rest is £84,000, so go figure in terms of a VAT threshold.
Ye s , quite .
That is an interesting discussion point.
You have set the stage for us very nicely there.

Q8 Going back to that, how does the UK compare internationally? When it comes to people deciding to start a business, is the UK more ambitious and entrepreneurial in the number of businesses we start?

I always describe it as somewhere between the US and mainland Europe. In other words, we are more entrepreneurial , in the statistics I have shared , than France and Germany, which are our two closest comparators we use, but less so than the US , though I have to say that this year the US is showing a downturn in entrepreneurial activity. That is very clear.

One negative point is that we do not compare well to France and Germany with the support for entrepreneurs, especially for young people. T hat is a fundamental problem that we need to be thinking about. O ur student population are left to their own devices. It is all to do with individual institutions , whereas in France you have the Pépite system, with 32 hubs for student entrepreneurs. In Germany, you have the exist grant system, where you have monthly stipends for people who want to start up a business and also transfer research out of universities. We are so far behind those two comparator nations. W e are better than France and Germany at getting the start - up rates there. We are doing less well —and that is being polite —in terms of being able to support those as they get into business.

Q9 Going back to the point you were making in answer to the Chair ’ s original question about how many businesses survive, are we better or worse, beyond that three-year threshold , than the US, France and Germany?

It is pretty much the same. When we look at firm-level data, as opposed to individual population data, so the surveys, the survival rate is pretty much the same as in France and Germany. The exit rates are slightly higher, but there is no statistical significant difference between them, so they are much the same. The challenges we see in the UK are also there in France and Germany.

Q10 What is the lesson that we should be taking? Are you suggesting—and feel free to challenge back—that, even though the support that France and Germany give their young people does not manifest itself in France and Germany in greater levels of entrepreneurship, if you took our population, who are more naturally entrepreneurial, and gave them more support, we might do better ? If so , what is that support we should be giving?

I would not push back against that at all. We are light years behind what they have been doing in France and Germany—Germany since 1998 and France since 2014—where you have national and regional programmes that are geared towards young people , yes, in a university setting, and the entrepreneurial activity that we observe in GEM in the UK is more than just those out of university. It is really important that we look closely at the evaluation of those schemes . We can see that they help survival improve. That is what the evaluation of this evidence is telling me from Germany.

A point I have made is that we have to recognise that these young people need support. It is not all about this lost generation narrative . I t needs to be reset a little . A t the same time that you have this million or just under a million in the latest data, we can see that, in fact, you have other individuals who are the most entrepreneurial that they have ever been. Go figure . What is that all about? We need to understand that a little more.
Q11 What is the No. 1 thing you want to make sure we translate here?
It is not about reattaching people to the workforce or training. It is about actually supporting them on their entrepreneurial journey. We need to do that with policy intervention. It is clear.
That is a g ood framing.

Q12 Mark, the UK sits 37th on the national entrepreneurship context index, below the US, France, Germany and the OECD average. Which of the framework conditions is holding the UK back most and which countries have improved those conditions over the same period?

Entrepreneurship education at secondary and tertiary education is holding us back. We need to raise awareness of the financial initiatives that we have here. We have a plethora of funds available for small business and entrepreneurial activity, but it is awareness. This is what I come across all the time. It is understanding where to go. We need to lean into that and address that. That is one issue.

I spend a lot of time in Paris working on other programmes, such as the Goldman Sachs programme. Bpifrance is very active in that space in terms of supporting not just young entrepreneurs but the entrepreneurial stock as a whole. It is about the infrastructure, the education and awareness of the finance, not its existence. It is about the leveraging of what is there already in the UK, which is really important.

Q13 My constituency is a coastal town: Weston-super-Mare. We have some very low-funded organisations providing that sort of support. It is not good enough at all. Do you see disparities between cities and towns? Are you able to extrapolate that from your findings?

It is a UK report, but I think we have a Scottish, Northern Ireland and Welsh report. We need to look , and I can share after this session the details of that. Yes, there is huge regional disparity and local disparity. We really need to think about making sure that people can access that wherever they live and work.
Pulling that out would be really great.

Q14 Phil, I had the pleasure of attend ing the launch of your Job Creators 2026 report a few weeks ago. From that report, the number that really jumps out is that 54 of the 100 fastest-growing companies in the country have at least one foreign-born founder, and they are valued at £15 billion. From those numbers it sounds like it is quite a good place for people who want to come to the UK to start businesses, but the range of uncertainty for founders to commit to the UK i s a problem. Could you tell us about that?

It is the other side of the coin of what Mark talks about. When it comes to talent, you can either have home-grown talent or bring it in from outside. We are lucky enough to attract a lot of talent from all over the world. That equates to over half of the fastest-growing companies. Those are the most valued companies, and that is why we have such a huge figure as £15 billion.

We could attract a lot more. The reason we can get a lot of those people is that they come through our universities, and, traditionally, we have been able to keep people on after they have studied in the UK. They have gone on maybe to work in another field, become an expert and then start a business, and one of these really high-growth businesses. All businesses matter, but , for the purpose of the Job Creators report , we focus on really high-growth businesses.

There is so much uncertainty at the moment around the visa system. People in the country do not know how long they are going to stay and the Home Office needs to get back to a very large consultation that took place on that. Also, we do not really have an entrepreneur visa that is working properly. We have a visa that attracts only a few thousand. We can open that up to attract more people by giving the endorsing bodies more collateral to make decisions. We could also extend the high - potential individual visa. That currently is a fast-track visa for people who have gone to certain universities around the world. We could include business schools in that, which is not in the metric that they decided. That would include business schools such as INSEAD. World-famous business schools could come in.

There is also the cost of visas, especially for start-ups and small businesses. That is in the thousands for individuals and in the thousands for companies. When you talk about dependants as well, it becomes completely uncompetitive compared to mainland Europe. There are a lot of positives inasmuch as we are still a country that can attract these people, but we are missing a massive trick by not letting more people come in.

Q15 What is our opportunity cost then? What potentially are we losing out on as a result of that uncertainty and unfriendliness, as you would probably put it, from the Home Office and some of those procedures?

It is not people coming over and starting businesses as a solo entrepreneur. They are mixing their talent with the domestic workforce as well, so they are often starting it with entrepreneurs in the UK. They are highly mobile and the reality is that they are very susceptible to tax rates , incentive schemes to exit your business and things like that. All of whatever is announced tomorrow in the Budget will feed into how attractive we are.

Visas are one part of it, but I would extend that out to other areas, such as culture. One reason that people like to come to the UK is that it has the rule of law and is culturally a very good place to live and build a family. To build a family, you need to know how long you are going to have to stay in the country before you can get citizenship. Ultimately, why would you build a business in a country that is not even willing to say, “You are allowed to live here. You are allowed to have children here and be here for generations”?

Q16 Professor Ram, you have spent a lot of time looking at the barriers that minority communities face in particular. Based on the data that has been published this morning and some of your own work, give us a sense about the key barriers and maybe the opportunity cost that the country is running as a result .

There is a link between the comment about uncertainty and talent in diverse communities. That applies to communities in the UK. At the moment, ethnic minority businesses contribute £25 billion to the economy. That contribution could rise to £100 billion if they grew at the same rate of their white counterparts to do that.
Q17 We have a £75 billion opportunity cost here.

Yes. It is a huge opportunity that we are losing sight of because we do not recognise the talent fully in our own diverse communities. We need to have much better data on minority entrepreneurs. We have been trying to persuade Government to do this for many years. There is a real benefit to be had by simply getting a better grip on the evidence base and integrating it into various policy domains. That is very important.

The issue about access to finance has been well rehearsed in the Government ’ s small business strategy. It applies with particular force to ethnic minority communities. There has been a long-standing issue about access to finance in ethnic minority firms. We did the first major study in the UK in the year 2000 and many of the issues that we identified there still pertain, particularly in relation to the core issue of discouragement. Discouragement means that good business propositions are being wasted because people from diverse communities believe they will not be treated fairly, despite the fact that they have a decent proposition.
Q18 These are quite durable barriers.

They are absolutely barriers that can be addressed. They go with the grain of the policy pronouncement about growth in every postcode, opportunity , and integration and inclusion. It is one of those areas that have an economic and social pay-off at the same time.

Mark talked very persuasively about the role of young entrepreneurs and the NEETs agenda , and how entrepreneurship is a way of addressing NEETs. I can tell you that, for decades, minority entrepreneurs have been addressing the NEETs issue all by themselves, because they disproportionately recruit from their own community. They disproportionately recruit people who do not have qualifications and provide a real pathway for economic development and social mobility through the prism of enterprise. There is a great opportunity to be had. T his is with the grain of devolution as well. If we get to know and understand our local communities really well, we could work with the talent that is already there and enhance and leverage that.
Q19 We have problems with data, confidence and access to finance. I think that you and I have also spoken about barriers to government procurement in the past.

Procurement has been a really important public policy lever for all sorts of different policy issues. We have been talking about the importance of using the public sector procurement levers and, importantly, the corporate sector in supporting and leveraging business talent in diverse communities. The Government ’ s intervention on social value and youth enterprise recently is very much aligned to that.

We have been involved in initiatives that have helped minority entrepreneurs get into the supply chains of large corporate sectors. There is an organisation called Minority Supplier Development UK, which we set up in 2004. It is a corporate sector organisation that is providing real contractual opportunities and pathways to growth. We can do that in the public sector. There is a real critical mass of entrepreneurial talent in diverse communities who are not in the right networks, do not know the right people and do not know the informal networks that have an outsize importance in who gets contracts. This, again, is something that is very doable and we can address.

Q20 Jordan, we are quite interested , moving on from the challenges that are faced by ethnic minorities , in also, specifically, women in the business arena. T oday, the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor released a report with some good news, which is always nice, where we have a record high of nearly 15% in 2025 of women who were in their early - stage entrepreneurship journey. T he investing in women code was set up after looking into some of the challenges for women , and access to funding was cited as a barrier.

W e are aware that closing that gap between men and women could add £ 250 billion to the economy, which is absolutely enormous. From your experience, what more do you think the G overnment need to do to get the most out of that potential that , at the moment, we are losing?

That figure that you have just quoted there has actually gone up to £ 313 billion now. That is how much could be added to the UK economy if women were supported in the same way that our male counterparts are with access to direct finance. We have seen some positive movement in terms of a 65% increase in equity investment into women, but we still remain at that 2% of overall funding into female-led businesses.

We are starting to see progress, but we are mistaking activity for progress , and we need to be very careful of that. I f we start to look at activity as being progress, we do not see those outcomes and we certainly will not see that increased economic value that we have the opportunity to gain.

We are seeing more female founders enter the world of entrepreneurialism . Professor Mark Hart highlighted there that we are seeing women drop off at that two to three - year gap. T he reason that that is happening is that women are not getting access to capital at that very early stage. M y ask today is that we start to look at products that are available for female founders who are entering the entrepreneurial ecosystem that look at more than a debt focus. We have start - up loans . W e have angel investors now —we will come on to angel investing next —but we need to see more products and gateways. We are still seeing unconscious bias in the funding ecosystem, which is why we need more women to be participating and making those investment decisions.

We must have a greater focus on how we support women to angel invest as well. Thirteen per cent of the UK angel investors are women, which is good, but 11% of them are in the south - east. T hat means that there is a very small percentage of women angel investors in the rest of the regions. W e have recently launched a campaign where we are asking for the G overnment to fund and support female founders with a pound for pound co-investment fund. W e are saying that we will work to increase women angel investors across the UK . F or every pound that a women angel investor invests, we are asking for a pound of investment from central G overnment . We believe that that is the only way that we are going to move the dial from that 2% mark. I f we do not move that, we have lost a lot of economic value.

Q21 That is a really important point. Some of the announcements that we have heard from John Healey over the weekend suggest some quite chunky adds to the balance sheets of the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank. We do not yet know how that money is actually going to get diffused into funds. Presumably, this is a big opportunity to capitalise some of the initiatives that you have just mentioned.

It absolutely is. One of our concerns is that we can see money coming through the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, but that money has been deployed into growth - stage and scale - stage businesses. Venture capitalists are investing at a greater level up the ecosystem chain, which mean s we have a real big deficit in this early - stage investment ecosystem, which comes back to Professor Mark Hart ’ s report.

We are losing female founders in what we are calling the valley of death. They may get their first cheque or their first piece of investment, but , because they are not being supported in helping the businesses go at pace with funding and finance, we are losing them in the second and third years of evolution , at that very important stage where they need more capital. T he only thing that will fix that is having some of those dedicated funds, which will filter down into what we believe can be a very good private and public mechanism that will ultimately change the outcome for female founders , and we will make a huge amount of progress across all areas.
Q22 The only thing I wanted to pick up on was that you said that there need to be more or different products. Is that specifically because the types of businesses they are running are different?
Yes, a bsolutely .
Q23 Therefore, can you give an example of what it is that they need that is different from a male-founded entrepreneurial business?

We know that women make 80% of consumer decisions in the average household. We are seeing brilliant women starting fantastic businesses that are consumer-led. They are retail sector and industry-led businesses, for example, but we are not seeing dedicated funding streams for those types of businesses. We see innovation funding. We see tech-based funding. We see hard tech. We see life science and clean tech funding.

We need to see different products that are going to support more female-led businesses in those areas where we are not seeing dedicated funding streams. We are typically seeing debt for those types of businesses. Unfortunately, female-led businesses are not often in a position to take on debt at that early stage. Yes, as they grow and scale, absolutely, but we need to see more angel investment. That is what we need.
Q24 It is equity.
Yes, equity angel investment. We will see that happen more so from women if women can see that the public sector is also supporting in those key areas.
That is s uper helpful . We now have the big question. We are going to use this as a jumping-off point for anything else you want to put on our policy recommendation list.
Q25 It is the Budget tomorrow. What would you like to see in it? What one measure could encourage more people to start a business?

For me, it is all about youth enterprise. We have to get serious. It is not just, as I said earlier, about reattaching young people to the world of work or to training. It is actually thinking about their entrepreneurial journeys as well, for male and female, ethnic and non-ethnic groups. It is about having a serious look at a youth enterprise type of funding arrangement, a grant, or something like that. We need to be quite serious about that.

To date, it is all about, as I say, “Let ’ s get them into a job. Let ’ s get them into training”. We need to recognise the reality, as Monder has pointed out as well, of what young people are actually doing. In the report we look at solo entrepreneurs. There is a huge amount of high ambition there. We just need to pump-prime those young people. I want to see something really tangible tomorrow. I always like to go on the eve of Budget night and have a dream, but we really need to lean into our young people, who are the future of our entrepreneurial capability in the UK .
Q26 I think that that is more likely, if it comes at all, to come in the Milburn recommendations than the Budget. Is that something you have been putting to Alan Milburn?

I have tried to have a conversation with the Milburn review, but, as you can probably gather, to date I am quite frustrated by that, because it is all about this lost generation of NEETs. Can we just stop using the phrase NEET? There is another E that we are not actually talking about: entrepreneurship. We have ignored that completely and the evidence is staring us in the face.

Q27 This is a follow-up to build on Antonia ’ s question. You mentioned earlier that we need policy interventions. I want to press you to be specific about what the policy interventions are that you think will help entrepreneurs that you may wish to see in the Budget tomorrow.

I look at our counterparts. Money is being devoted, through policy and through universities, to young people to give them monthly stipends to run their business and translate research in their universities into businesses. There are examples out there of how we do this. I have submitted a note that gives you a page of my response to Antonia ’ s question on the Budget.
Q28 Ye s, we have that. Give us a sense about the money involved. What kinds of sums are we talking about?

We are talking about €2,000 or €1,000 monthly and access to €30,000, for example, on the exist programme in Germany. That is €30,000 in terms of capital, equipment and stuff like that, but a monthly stipend of €1,000 or €2,000.
Q29 How long is that for?

It is a year or two years, to get them established. The start-up loans in the British Business Bank are wonderful. Its original intention was for young people. That is really brilliant. Connecting it to our universities and to our education system is really important. There are wonderful programmes across the university sector, but they are not co-ordinated. That is the problem.

Q30 Jordan, I wanted to come back on something you said about the unconscious bias around this. It goes to ethnic minority businesses as well as women-led businesses. In my constituency—and I think it is probably disproportionate to cities—so much entrepreneurship is women and ethnic minorities who, for whatever reason, build businesses there. The beauty industry in and of itself has £28.3 billion of value to the UK, but it is consistently not seen as a priority area. How problematic is that bias in the UK? Are you both seeing that? I do not think we really recognise it enough.

It is very problematic, unfortunately. From an investment perspective, because there are more men in the ecosystem who are working in venture capital institutions and private equity, they are making the decisions on what gets backed. If we think about the women-led businesses, so femtech and healthtech, for example, and beauty and retail, as you have just mentioned there, unfortunately, the men aren’t understanding those businesses, so it is not often seen as something that should be a priority to back and invest in. That is why we need to see more women operating in those organisations and being a part of those investment committees.

We are not saying, “Make it all women”. We are saying, “Grow the table and make it very diverse”, so that you have lots of different skills, opinions and knowledge around sectors and industries. That is one way that we will start to see women being backed.
Let me return to Ms Bance because, Professor Ram, we would love to get your views on the Budget as well.

Q31 I wanted to stay with Professor Hart for a moment on the idea of a youth enterprise grant or a monthly stipend. A thousand euros would be three times the value of the universal credit basic allowance every month for a young person under 25. Is that really what you are suggesting? What activity requirements would you put alongside that? How do people qualify for that sort of allowance?

At the moment we see businesses coming out of our university sector and young people, which are already there. We have to do the sums on this. I do not have the Treasury spreadsheet ; I agree with that. We need to go away and do the sums to find out how much it would cost. Look at the evidence from elsewhere. See what it would actually take to do this.

You are probably thinking about 32,000 individuals in Germany who have had the benefit of this, so it is not universal. There is an entry fee, if you like, in terms of what it is they are proposing to do and actually develop. It is not available to every 20 or 21-year-old who is coming to the end of their degree. In France, for example, there are about 40,000 of these students with national enterprise status. That is the sort of scale we are talking about, but the growth ambition there is the key entry fee.

For me, it is all about not chasing the headline numbers of start-ups, but finding out where the growth ambition is. I am coming back to the female point, and the GEM data has shown this. When you control for the types of businesses that women set up, women are just as ambitious as men. Take the sector difference away from that , and that should be evidence enough to the equity, the angels and — dare I say— the VC, to say, “We can back women because they are some of the most ambitious entrepreneurs in our society ” . Look at Buy Women Built. I work with some of the most ambitious female-led businesses in the Goldman Sachs 10,000 small businesses programme . The potential is there. The financial sector needs to pay attention.
Q32 Professor Ram , what are your asks for the Budget?

Before the Budget, can I come on to something that Dan Aldridge mentioned about the kinds of businesses he was seeing in his communities ? T his hits upon a really neglected topic. There is a big concern at the moment about reviving our high streets. E specially in an area you know well, Chair, in Birmingham, which is a great example, women and minority communities gravitate towards those high streets and set up businesses.

There is one stellar example, which I want to draw your attention to : Soho Road . That is an area you will know very well. People are talking in other parts of the country and the city about the death of the high street. There is no recession in that high street. It is one of the busiest , most entrepreneurial high streets you will see. T here is a waiting list of international entrepreneurs wanting to locate there. We would call that FDI in another policy discourse , b ut we do not here. Why? T hat street provides jobs and provides different communities with a pathway to economic development. It integrates different communities and has a huge number of growth firms , which are not recogni s ed as such.

I do not think that the business support system is agile enough to integrate the policy thinking, the economic thinking and the social policy domain. It provides answers. There was a piece of research done by anthropologists a few years ago . T hey knocked on every door in a surrounding street and every business on that street . T hey found out that there ha d been businesses there for three or four decades. They spoke three or four different languages for business purposes. They contributed disproportionately to the tax base. They employed a huge number of non-family workers, again from NEET communities. W hy are we not seeing that as a resource? W e see these shopping malls as a resource and try to attract them. This is the talent that goes unrecogni s ed in our own communities.

To address Antonia ’ s point about what I would like to see in the B udget , I would start off with that : recogni s ing the talent there. We now have a system in the UK that is reasonably well developed in the Business Growth Network and the Business Growth Service . D o we know what priority they are attaching to going out and finding the female businesses or ethnic minority businesses in their patch? Is there any warrant for them to work with those businesses? Do we know how many of them they are supporting? Do we know how many of them they are facilitating to grow? W e have a mechanism there, but I am not sure how well we are utili s ing it. That is one thing.

The s econd thing is that someone needs to own this agenda. Someone needs to drive this particular agenda. If we were to look at international best practice, let u s say in Canada, for example, there is a discernible body there, integrated within G overnment, whose job it is to drive black empowerment in that particular case. We do not have a nything similar. I am not advocating a policy of separation. It is actually integration on steroids to make sure that it is integrated in every policy domain . W e need to see what works.
Q33 It sounds like quite a bold plan for growth in every postcode, as we now call it. Jordan, what are your top asks for the Budget tomorrow?

W e need to stabili s e the tax - efficient investment scheme. We do need to stabili s e that . I t would be very useful to look at enhanced tax - efficient investment schemes for women backing women. We know that there is going to be a transfer of wealth to women over the next five to 10 years, with baby - boomers transf erring and women being able to take hold of quite a lot of the household wealth. W e need to think about some tax - efficient investment schemes that are going to help women to back more women.

A s I have mentioned earlier, it would be very good to see some of the B udget aligned to how we support more women in their early - stage investment journey. I f we do that, we will absolutely see them being able to take on more capital and progress their businesses , coming back to the economic value.
That is nice and specific. Thank you.

I am going to say three things , but I will say them quickly. O n Mark ’ s point, we put out a report called Starting Out and Starting Up . T his was all about tackling the NEET challenge. C urrently , if you employ someone you get a grant of £3,000. If you start your own business — there will have to be metrics for this —and you get to a certain point, we think that you should also be able to qualify for that grant, because you could then go on to employ people.

There are other ideas. We used to have the new entrepreneurs allowance. We had the enterprise allowance before that as well. T here was a lot of mentoring involved there. Now is the time to bring something back, given where we are with 1 million youth unemployed.

The hard policy announcement I woul d like to see in the Budget is around R&D tax credits . I mention that one specifically because there is not a trade body to represent them, but they are in an absolute mess. A lot of entrepreneurs who are doing very innovative things are choosing not to apply for them because they are being hounded by HMRC with demands from previous years to give back money. T his happened for a good reason . T hey were not being properly managed and there was a lot of fraud that took place within them, but within that context we now have lots of legitimate founders and a lot of innovation that is not being undertaken .

T hat is with the backdrop of work from economists such as Van Reenen and others that show how effective they are. I n the past, I think when we doubled how generous they were, we also doubled the level of innovation . P atent quality went up 60% as well. T here is a lot of really strong evidence that they work, but they need now to be properly targeted . T here are ways of doing that in Canada. I will leave that as a tantalising thing to look into.

T he final one is something that connects a lot of what ha s been said today and is a more ambitious idea than potentially some of the things we may hear tomorrow . It is about connecting up G overnment and data. W e put out a report called The Master Key . T his is the idea of having one identifier across businesses. Currently, as a business owner —I am a small business owner myself —I have to keep telling G overnment what I am, what I am doing and who I am . T hat is annoying.

A big part of that is that there are millions of hours to be saved . We could quote that number. O n the more positive side, imagine a place where G overnment would know exactly who I was . I f I was growing fast enough and I was a female founder in Doncaster , they could target me and say, “The data is showing how amazing your business is doing . F or that reason, we are going to push you towards something ” , maybe one of the schemes that Mark i s running, or someone else. It is the underlying basis of a lot of interventions and the state capacity to act and deliver on the things we all want. It is slightly boring, but , if we get the plumbing right, the engine can really get going on the economy.

Thank you so much. The clock is slightly against us, so I am afraid we are going to have to conclude it there, but that gives us an excellent checklist against which to judge the Chancellor when he rises to his feet tomorrow afternoon. That concludes this panel.

Examination of witness
Witness: Paula Sussex CBE , Public Service Ombudsman.

Q62 A very warm welcome to the third of our three sessions and the final session for the Child Maintenance Service i nquiry. We are delighted to welcome Paula Sussex, who is the Public Service Ombudsman. I want to reflect on the complaints that you deal with in relation to the Child Maintenance Service and try to understand the patterns that you have observed and why they seem to differ in volume , in particular , from what the DWP is experiencing and reporting.

Thank you , Chair, and thank you , C ommittee. I t is perhaps helpful to say at the start that the o mbudsman comes right at the end of the process. B y definition, a parent who is complaining will have been through two stages of the complaint process and the good work that our colleagues at ICE do before they come to us. N one the less, as you say, Chair, it is remarkable that , although we observe that DWP says that CMS complaints have declined, ours have doubled over four years .

I am afraid I have no firm evidence as to what might be driving that, but we think that there is some element of complaints not being handled effectively , by definition , a nd t here is that compound of , if you have been through two stages and you then go to ICE — the i ndependent complaint examiner —if you are still not satisfied , you then come to us.

However, I should set this in the context that we are doing some wider research on the general increase in complaints across all public services. We are seeing something like a 20 % to 25% increase in complaints coming to us. O ur analysis is starting to show that there is generally — if I can describe it as this — greater persistence and greater distress, which is causing complainants to persist for longer. T he third possible reason — which is , of course , another global reason — is the pressure of the cost of living on a lot of parents and families.
Q63 Would y ou say that the Child Maintenance Service is one of the services that you have the most complaints about ?

No . A s I am sure the Committee knows, we have a health and a g overnment jurisdiction. Health is 80% of our work and g overnment is only 20%. In terms of the g overnment work, l ast year we received only 500 complaints , and that will be against a considerably larger number for the whole of our g overnment work. H owever, CMS is about one third of the complaints that we receive about all DWP services.
T hat is very interesting.
Q64 O n those statistics, what themes are coming out in the complaints regarding the CMS?

W e have recently written to the Department about a systemic investigation that I will come to in a minute. B y way of making some overarching comments, as the Committee will know very well, CMS manages an unenviable combination of high - volume and highly complex processes , so it is fair to say that it is doing some very good work in the simple cases.

On the themes that we see, I would say that there are a raft of issues about better customer service . S omething that we observe in other areas of DWP is a process that is designed and run around the customer rather than the policy or the regulations and, a t the root of it, standing in your customer ’ s shoes . That is difficult to do if you are operating something that is — as I know from my own operational experience as an accounting officer . No ne the less, when you know that your customer base is having an extraordinarily tough time —they are not in the best state— y ou have to be really rigorous about how you communicate with your customers, how you keep them up to speed and how they are understanding the rules and regulations.
