Q29 Welcome to the fifth public evidence session of the International Relations and Defence Committee of the House of Lords looking at the multilateral governance of artificial intelligence. It is being livestreamed on parliamentlive.tv, and there are people watching it. The transcript of today’s session will be sent to you, so any minor modifications or corrections that you might want to make can be delivered to us. I ask any members asking questions to declare any interest they might have that is relevant to the subject. I declare that I am a senior counsellor with the Cohen Group in Washington.

When you answer the first question, please introduce yourself to the committee and the outside world. All the initiatives that we have seen so far in AI governance have involved Western powers and China. There is an argument that only those powers with the technological advancement and knowledge should set the norms and standards for AI, and that they be adopted on a global basis. Can you comment on that and what the potential strengths and weaknesses are in the concept of the existing powers setting the rules for the future?

Good morning and thank you so much for having me. I am a research professor at the University of Cambridge, where I lead the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, which I believe is the world’s oldest research centre on AI and society. It was established about 11 years ago. I recently took up that post. Prior to that, I was living in South Africa for 18 years, working very closely with the South African Government and Governments across the African continent. Three years ago, I founded a think tank called the Global Center on AI Governance, which is headquartered in South Africa but has a mandate to work across global majority countries, supporting South-South co-operation on AI and particularly helping ‘Global South’ Governments to establish governance norms that are pertinent, applicable, relevant and suited to their own contexts and domestic priorities, while thinking about all these issues within an international context.

Chair, I will start with your question about who is setting the norms around these technologies. Of course, that is a very emerging area. We do not have many international frameworks or binding laws that constrain how AI is developed and used around the world. There are a number of problems with that. One is that countries that are not part of those arrangements and norm setting will receive norms, laws and standards that are either not useful to them or that undermine what they might be trying to do. We have seen examples of this before, with the impact of GDPR internationally. In setting a very high standard for the sharing of personal data globally, GDPR has, for example, restricted international research collaborations that have involved the sharing of genomic data.

In the longer-term view, if there are only a certain set of countries that are setting the standards and laws around such a strategically important technology, we are going to create international stability by leaving behind parts of the world that are rapidly taking up newer positions of power. We are in a multipolar world, and it is not one where a single world order is dictating how the rest of the countries might engage internationally. It is very short-sighted to think only that countries such as the US are setting standards that are applicable for everybody.

The question is also partly moot because the US is pushing for deregulation, but what we really need is stricter governance, enforcement mechanisms and institutional capacity to govern everywhere in the world, because this technology can take us in many different ways; some that might be hugely beneficial and some that might be very risky and could undermine values that we have spent the large part of the 20th century collectively building.

Q30 I was interested to read in our briefing notes t hat when South Africa held the presidency of the G20, it commissioned research that said that less than 10% of all global governance frameworks on AI have emerged from developing countries. You have just articulated why that is not a good thing. Do they themselves feel left out of this debate? What issues and agendas would they want to see as most important? Since this inquiry is looking at the role of multilateral agencies in this space, what mechanisms, structures or organisations exist for such issues and agendas from developing countries to be fed in?

I will answer that in three parts. First, what is the status of AI governance in the ‘Global South’ ? Secondly, what are the issues that ‘Global South’ Governments care about? Thirdly, what international mechanisms exist?

To answer that first question, I think that we can update those statistics. I was very involved with South Africa’s G20 presidency and there is a lot that we can discuss about how the UK’s G20 presidency can pick up some of the consensus that South Africa built.

The Global Center on AI Governance, which I lead, conducts a study called the Global Index on Responsible AI that, interestingly, is funded by the FCDO. That index measures what 138 countries around the world are doing to develop governance frameworks on AI and implement them. What we have seen over the last two years is that the ‘Global South’ has led the charge in developing AI governance frameworks. If you look at the total number of governance frameworks on responsible AI that have been published and proliferated over the last two years, over half of them come from ‘Global South’ countries. However, 78% of those frameworks are non-binding. They either do not contain any provisions to support implementation or they are not enforceable and do not provide protections for individuals or communities at risk. What they do show is positive executive intent. They show the hyperscalers that they are thinking strategically about the value of AI for their countries and that they are open to the kinds of partnerships that are flowing in, but they are not ensuring that there are safeguards in place to protect human rights, ensure democratic accountability and so forth.

We are also seeing an implementation gap in the frameworks that exist in the so-called global North vis-à-vis those that exist in the ‘Global South’ . The statistics are something like 45% of all the frameworks that exist in the ‘Global South’ are being implemented, whereas it is 65% in the global North. You have to caveat that with the fact that many of these frameworks are new, but we are also looking for whether they contain provisions that would enable implementation, such as oversight authority authorities or budget provisions that would enable budget to be put forward to support their implementation.

Where I see huge difference is in the articulation of what the risks are. This is probably the starting point for why global governance around AI is so fragmented—we do not have a shared language for what the risks are. In the global North, we are talking a lot about the existential risks of the dual-use problems associated with these advanced technologies and the frontier risks and how we get access to frontier capabilities in order to test and evaluate them. But in other parts of the world, the risks are quite different.

But, in other parts of the world, the risks are quite different—the enforcement capabilities and a l ack of institutional capacity to manage the risks that might be coming with them. I n South Africa, for example, data centres are being established, and a number of people are making complaints to the South African Human Rights Commission about human rights concerns they have with these data centres being established. T he c ommission is now overwhelmed with more cases than it is able to respond to.

There are re ally big risks around labour. It is not just about labour displacement , the impacts on job markets in terms of jobs disappearing and the shared risk —t his is a really important issue in the UK, too ; i n parts of the ‘Global South’ , it is accompanied by the new forms of labour that are occurring through the AI supply chains and value chains. For example, there is data - labelling work , where people tick , “ I am not a robot ”. F or many months on end , t heir work is just consumed with this digital micro - labour to manage and help train AI systems. T his kind of work is very badly paid. Ther e are no labour protections associated with it . There ha s been significant whistleblowing around this. Of course, if there are no labour protections , accompanied by weaker institutions that are not able to enforce protections that might exist or apply laws in new areas, it creates a real vacuum.

S ome of the other concerns are around the environmental impacts, which are unevenly distributed and very hard to attribute. There is an increase in environmental disasters, largely in the global N orth. We do not know quite how far AI is contributing to it, but that is another area that people are certainly concerned about.

Another area is public understanding of and public literacy on AI. In South Africa, w e did a study to assess what people knew and perceived about AI . We interviewed over 3 , 000 South Africans of all walks of life in their local language, and almost two - third s of South Africans did not know what AI was. T hose who did know got their information through algorithmically mediated platforms. Again, there is a democratic gap in Governments moving forward with trying to adopt AI, particularly in the public sector, and people being able to understand what is happening and being able to challenge some of those decisions. A lot of the very real risks that are being felt across the ‘Global South’ are much more immediate than some of these more hypothetical concerns about existential risks.

There is a shared set of risks around things such as AI sovereignty and the dependence on foreign tech providers, particularly for critical services — whether that is defence , national health systems or social grants. That risk is shared globally. I would think about how the UK can play an important role in supporting ‘Global South’ Governments to negotiate stronger deals and terms with the hyperscalers that come in, particularly in the absence of binding domestic frameworks.

I am happy to go into more detail on anything else I hav e spoken about , but the third question was on what international mechanisms exist . T he most important one , from a few years ago , was what UNESCO had developed . It developed the ethical framework for AI and spent time evolving ‘Global South’ countries in developing the principles and values that are articulated there. W hen it was promulgated, there was a shared sense that, “Y es, this also reflects our interests ” . T hen , UNESCO developed its readiness assessment tool , which provided countries with a mechanism for seeing where the gaps were in relation to this international standard and where their own regulatory regimes were at. O ur centre led that work in nine southern African countries. I t wa s very difficult to do it , because the questions asked referred to global indices that simply did not include those countries , such as broadband , gender - related issues or representation in Parliament . There was a range of different things , b ut we do not have adequate , globally representative evidence from all these different countries to be able to support some of those internationally led processes that are designed as one - size - fits - all.

M ore recently, we had the UN Global Dialogue . That has been importan t, I so far as it has been very deliberately inclusive of countries everywhere a nd multi-stakeholder , b ut of course there are thousands of voices all with two minutes to make a short statement, and there i s very little room to listen to one another and figure out the areas of shared concern and consensus. T he UN has a very tall task ahead of it . There will be the May dialogues, and I imagine that this big mandate will devolve into a set of thematic issues and the countries that care most about some of these thematic issues will position themselves more strongly on AI safety and security, access to compute and compute infrastructure , or talent and capabilities. I worry about how that may move forward.

China led the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization—WAICO— which was launched in Ju ly this year. W e should talk about that . It has not gone very far, certainly not far enough to say ho w influential and impactful it will be, but it was important in so far as it articulated a starting point that was relevant and pertinent to ‘Global South’ c ountries on how they could have a political voice globally . T he developmental focus in terms of AI supporting socioeconomic development was front and centre. It also articulated issues around training and capacity strengthening. It is important to see where that might go . Ten African countries have signed on to that. Ther e have been a couple of collaborative efforts since to send African diplomats to China for training. I t is important to look at what they centred their emphasis on and why that reflected the interests and priorities that were important in the ‘Global South’ .

Th e G20 was particularly valuable, a nd it is unfortunate that South Africa was not able to pass on to the US in the way that that should have unfolded. That was an important moment for South Africa to represent the broader ‘Global South’ and the broader African continent and put forward concerns around the labour impact, unequal access to compute infrastructure and the need for governance standards that reflect diverse priorities. That was important for putting some of those things on the table.

Q31 ​ ​ ​ ​ Baroness Blackstone: ​ Much of the commentary about middle-income and low-income countries and AI has focused on these countries being a battleground for Chinese and US interests. Can you comment on that and in doing so, say what the advantages and disadvantages of that are?

​ ​ Dr Rachel Adams: ​ My perspective on this is that this is a Western framing that is not how African Governments see what is happening strategically in their jurisdictions. I do not think they see themselves as a battleground for US and Chinese influence. It is important to say that the US influence is now almost solely through the companies whereas, previously, USAID had enormous influence and relevance in shaping developmental agendas across the ‘Global South’ . That now does not exist. We see the FCDO and others, such as Sida in Sweden and the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, playing important roles there. From an African perspective, it does not feel like a US-China dichotomy.

The US hyperscalers are coming in with very big offers to develop AI infrastructure and cloud computing and establish data centres. These have been hit by national constraints. In Kenya, a massive data centre build was not able to move forward because there simply was not the energy infrastructure to enable it to be established.

Certainly, those of us who work on the human rights and democratic accountability side are concerned about these hyperscalers coming in without strong negotiations and contractual terms that provide local Governments with the opportunity to leave a partnership or change a provider, should they want to. Countries should have a diverse range of foreign tech providers, where they are relying on foreign tech providers. T hat is much harder in resource - constrained environments, but it is important for issues of sovereignty, which is not solely about ownership but control , management and governance.

China has an important influence in the offer of these open - source or open-weight technologies . There are various degrees to which the technologies of Q wen and DeepSeek are completely open, but they are more accessible to African innovators , who are able to adapt them for local use . T here is a lot of work in adapting these technologies to work in local languages and work on local issues.

I am not an expert on the open - closed conversation to be able to comment on that. T he point I am trying to make is that it is a Western framing on the US and China. S trategically, if you are engaging with African countries and with ‘Global South’ countries, that is not the framing to use ; instead, you should be thinking about what the practical and helpful partnerships are that can support these countries to have their own agency and to participate, and be allies, in international co - operation on AI .

Q32 ​ ​ Lord Darroch of Kew: ​ Dr Adams, there is a compelling statistic in our papers that, in 2025, Microsoft found that 25% of the working population of the global North use AI in the workplace, but only 14% do so in the ‘Global South’ . Can you give us your judgment on how successful multilateral, international government initiatives on AI have been in spreading technological capability to low-income and middle-income countries?

​ ​ Dr Rachel Adams: ​ I think that was Microsoft’s diffusion report , and there is a lot we can talk about on whether AI diffusion is leading to equitable socioeconomic benefits and, ultimately , productivity gains in different industries. P art of the problem with these statistics is that they are modelled on formal economies and very industrialised societ ies, so they are often not rel evant to the kind s of economies we might find across the ‘Global South’ .

I ha ve been part of the AI for D evelopment initiative that the FCDO has been funding for a good number of years . It was initially founded by Canada and Sweden, and I think it has been the largest funding initiative to support AI for development and building AI capabilities across Africa, and with FCDO support it has now moved into Asia as well. It has been an important initiative. With myself and the think tank that we run in South Africa, it supported me in helping with the drafting of the African Union’s continental strategy. It has helped us to engage with the g overnments of Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Nigeria, Senegal, Morocco, Egypt and more in supporting local organisations and civil society groups to advance democratic principles, gender equality issues and issues around human rights protection and accountability in these governance frameworks. It has supported AI capacity development in, I think, 13 universities across Africa, which has supported many graduates; a lot of AI innovation for good—for social development, agriculture, health or climate change—has come out of university innovations that this funding initiative has supported.

There are so many funding initiatives now, and a lot of them are led by big tech. When I think about what has been successful or not, I ask what the initiatives are that have been led by local priorities. Canada and the UK have been very good at involving local partners and local experts in setting the priorities around what the funding should address, supporting the strengthening of local democratic institutions that are able to sustainably continue this work after funding leaves, and supporting universities that are able to train the next generation of graduates. That is more long-term thinking because a lot of funders want to support exciting innovation that rapidly scales. There have been a number of barriers to innovations scaling to the degree that we might want to see across Africa, and I can speak to that if needed, but we are not necessarily going to see quick wins. Very often the hype and the narrative is around leapfrogging and quick wins, but actually we need to be thinking about long-term institution building, the preservation of democratic values and involving local publics and citizens who are able to contribute and help to shape these debates.

Q33 You have answered to a great extent the question that I was going to ask about recent global initiatives. Rachel, I think you feel that the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance was cumbersome—that is the view that I got from you. What advice would you give those who are now going through the process of the sub-committee aspect of that dialogue in order to make sure that the ‘Global South’ has a real buy-in in the UN dialogue? The second part of my question is this: you talked about 10 African countries having signed up to China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization. Are they countries where China already has a history of trading or infrastructure support?

I shall answer the second question first because that will be quicker. I do not know enough about who those 10 countries are and I need to check them, so I do not know enough to be able to comment properly on that.

For the UN process, “cumbersome” is probably a good word. What we want to see, and this is where the UK has an opportunity, is thinking about how this credible and legitimate global process can be used to move towards actual concrete decisions, resource allocations where they are needed and accountability. How do we link up that UN process with regional organisations like the African Union or sub-regional organisations like ECOWAS, with regulators, data protection authorities and national human rights institutions that are already regionally and internationally well linked up to the UN, scientific institutions, research centres and funding mechanisms?

From my position where I sit—I have been involved in a number of these different processes, from the global summits to the OECD, from UNESCO to the UN—there are now many different multilateral arrangements that are trying to work effectively in this area, and we need to establish some kind of mechanism that links them together so that, for example, we can see what commitments were made at a global summit and whether they were echoed again in the next one. Is there a mechanism to track how far all these big commitments made by different companies and Governments are resulting in the flow of finances to the places that they are talking about? Are people getting trained, in terms of the numbers being cited? We need some kind of mechanism that makes more concrete these very grand arrangements that at the moment are still quite rhetorical and a talking shop.

The G20 is an enormous opportunity to build commitments with partners that can be carried into more inclusive institutions. It is an important set of countries being brought together that are able to carry out the commitments that are made in those fora—in the African Union or the EU, and in these other spaces. We can talk more about this, but the UK has a very big opportunity in diplomacy, and the G20 is an important space for moving some of that work forward.

Q34 Thank you for what you have been saying to us, which I have found extremely interesting, particularly about your own initiatives in Africa, and indeed we have a summary of the African Union continental AI strategy on our papers, which is very clear.

You have hinted at my question—you are saying that the FCDO is funding some of these resources—but what is the scope for the UK to take the initiative in engaging with the ‘Global South’ that would be meaningful? You made a point about China and WAICO and the different perceptions of the ‘Global South’ compared with the competition between America and China, but is there space for a country like the UK to engage in a way that addresses the needs of those countries on their own terms? China has said it wants to use AI for development to show people how to do it, but possibly in a different way from us. Is the UK credible if we try to do this? How would we do it? What resources would be required, given that we have pretty well decimated our aid budget? It seems to me it does not have to cost a lot of money but you might think differently.

The UK is already doing a lot. The AI for Development initiative that has been running for over six years on the African continent is testament to the work of the UK but also, importantly, the co-operation with Canada, Sweden and now Switzerland, which are also party to it.

Perhaps because I spent a lot of time working in institutions across the ‘Global South’ , I think that where we need to be putting effort is in supporting and strengthening the capacity of democratic institutions across the ‘Global South’ in places like South Africa, Kenya, and Nigeria, particularly where they have institutional credibility, such as competition commissions that are investigating monopolies; public protection ombudsmen that represent the voice of people where AI is being used in the delivery of public services in ways that might be less than accountable; human rights institutions; and gender equality commissions. It is important to support those organisations to do their work, and particularly for them to engage in these international processes.

Often it is the well-funded countries that are able to offer rigorous, robust, multidimensional engagement in these international fora; they are able to send teams of experts to represent them in all these different rooms. There is far less funding in ‘Global South’ countries to participate to that degree. There are experts sitting in human rights commissions, data protection officers and now energy regulators that would be valuable if they had the opportunity to represent their countries’ interests and constraints in these international fora.

Importantly, the UK needs to move forward on AI diplomacy. There is a huge gap there, not so much in terms of the need to develop international frameworks, but we need to be training the people and equipping the institutions that are already on the front line of international engagement around AI. The UK has global diplomatic muscle. It is known for its ability to be able to co-operate and deliberate on very thorny issues, where you are balancing very different interests and needs of different countries. It has done that with the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, and it is going to need to think about how it does that again. The UK should use its incredible higher education institutions and its institutional capacity, which is quite neutral, world-class and carries an international brand, in order to provide training to diplomats in ‘Global South’ countries and support the building of relationships between individuals working in different parts of the world on these issues so that, from a slightly more bottom-up perspective, we can build a shared language around what the risks are.

We are building a new programme on AI diplomacy at the University of Cambridge. The FCDO is involved in that. We want, and the UK needs, to be an anchor nation on this programme. It draws together all the international links that we have with Governments and international organisations around the world to really centre the UK and the University of Cambridge as a place that can offer training on these issues in a very prescient way.

Given what you have told us, it is perfectly reasonable to promote the University of Cambridge’s role in this. However, you mentioned Kenya, for example, where our aid budget next year will be £5 million—almost nothing—and we are currently still in the process of reducing our diplomatic service by something like 30%. So how do we do that? It seems to me everything you say is terrific but the money and the people are not there.

We already have the Chevening scholarships, which would fund people from Kenya to come to the UK and participate in a programme like that. Training and education is incredible soft power. It is not as expensive as building data centres or compute infrastructure. The University of Cambridge already has international education standards that are adopted by the majority of countries around the world, and it is time that we deliberately and decisively saw that as diplomatic power that can be used now.
Q35 You will have heard the previous witnesses answer this question: what would be your top recommendation from this committee to the British Government?

Using the G20 opportunity to address and resurface some of the shared commitments that were identified during South Africa’s G20. We have not spoken about this, but the UK has done a lot of leading work in issues that do not seem immediately strategic, like tech-facilitated gender-based violence, and these issues were really pertinent during South Africa’s G20 presidency. I would suggest resurfacing issues like that. The UK being an anchor nation for a global AI diplomacy programme is another important recommendation that feels to me like low-hanging fruit.

Thank you, Dr Adams. We are grateful to you for coming along today and being the sole representative at this particular evidence session. Thank you for the information you have given us and the views you have expressed.

Daan Jujin, Director of Research, Arq Foundation; Nick Moës, Executive Director, The Future Society .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Daan Jujin and Nick Moës .

Q29 Welcome to this fourth session of the House of Lords International Relations and Defence Committee and our investigation into the multilateral aspects of the governance of artificial intelligence. The session is being streamed live on parliamentlive.tv and there are some people who are interested enough to listen to these things. Before they ask any questions, I will ask members of the committee to declare any interests they might have. I declare that I am the senior counsellor for the Cohen Group in Washington . You will get a transcript of the session today. If you could expeditiously return that with any tiny technical changes you might want to make, that would be useful.

I will start the questioning by talking about the whole question of the European Union and Europe in general and the governance of AI. It is said that Europe is lagging behind both the United States and China on artificial intelligence. Do you accept that characterisation of the current debate? If that is the case, can the European Union and Europe in general shape the international environment in order to capture whatever standards might eventually be adopted on a global scale? Let us start off with Nick, who has just got off a plane.

I would perhaps bring more nuance to the idea that we are lagging behind across the whole stack. The US and China are clearly leading in frontier AI development and the amount of investment in compute, for example. But the EU leads in some aspects of the stack. They are the overall nuances that we have to bring out.

Also, Europe—and this applies beyond the EU—and other Governments that are neither the US nor China, do not need to be a leader in frontier AI development to be able to shape the rules for governing it. That is the second aspect that brings more nuance.

Being behind when it comes to the critical frontier AI model development itself makes international co-operation a lot more urgent. Therefore, the ability to use other parts of the stacks and other points of leverage is important and will help to shape those international standards, norms or whatever regulatory regimes may slowly emerge. Market size, industry capabilities, talent pipeline, regulatory powers and specific stacks, such as ASML or the production of lithographic machines by Zeiss or Siemens, are other technical layers of the stack where the EU is very well positioned.

From that bargaining power, there could be a stronger influence than most might expect over how to produce and develop frontier AI. This is especially true when it happens in collaboration with other Governments or so-called middle powers, such as the UK itself. I believe that the EU, the UK and their partners can build very practical arrangements that protect them now and make wider agreements on this international regime easier to reach.

I am happy to dive a bit deeper into this, but it might also be useful to get into the details a bit later. However, there are a lot of precedents that have shown the bargaining power that the EU has maintained, and I hope that we will get to that at some point in this hearing.
You are saying that the lack of any technical capability inside Europe as a whole would not inhibit the chance of determining what the international standards were?

A lack of technical capability is a mischaracterisation, because that is not the case across the stack. There are significant technical capabilities at the layer of, for example, chip design, lithographic machines and some of the elements in the chips that are key to making the data centres that eventually train the very large models. That is the same with the gas turbines that are necessary to power those data centres. The EU has quite a bit of technical capability in certain spaces that is unique worldwide and can therefore use that as leverage.

Beyond technical capabilities, and I would in fact question the premise that technical capabilities are that influential. Market access, for example, and the 450 million fairly rich consumers, relative to the rest of the world, that the EU market provides is a significant bargaining chip when setting up safety requirements, which basically makes market entry conditional on satisfying some of the safety standards that the EU may want to see shaped. That is why we have seen companies—American companies in particular—that are very interested in shaping international standards, listening and taking a cue from what the EU’s preferences are when it comes to safety and security standards. This is not done in a happy way; they perhaps feel a bit constrained by the EU preference for safety and reliability, but it is definitely occurring . We have seen companies adapting their safety frameworks globally to comply with EU rules. There is a Brussels effect here that seems to be in play.
That is interesting. Da a n, could you address the same points?

Da a n Jujin: Thank you very much. By way of background , I am the director of research at the Arq Foundation. We are a philanthropically funded think tank based in Brussels and our mission is to help Europe to prepare for transformative AI. I am very glad to be here today. It is a privilege to be able to speak.

I have a s lightly different take on this question to Nick. I agree with your characterisation that Europe is lagging behind the US and China on most parts of the AI stack, and I think that this is an important disadvantage for the EU and the UK in their ability to shape the international environment.

It is often said that in AI there is no number three, and I tend to agree with that. The US is clearly in first place, China is in second place, and for a long time no one has really come close to them. Europe in particular has relatively poor positions in multiple parts of the AI stack. For instance, when it comes to frontier models themselves, the best European model is currently roughly one and a half years behind the frontier of AI, according to Epoch AI, which is an independent AI research, monitoring and evaluation organisation. Europe does not own any of the big players in the chip design space. Those are Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, which are all American companies. Europe does not own any of the leading-edge fabs where AI chips are fabricated. All the big cloud providers are American-owned . When it comes to the physical compute on European soil, Europe hosts only 5% of that, compared to more than 70% in the US.

All that does not mean that Europe has no influence whatever. Europe has already shaped the international environment, in particular through the AI Act and the code of practice for general purpose AI signed by most leading AI developers. However, the EU has come to realise that owning the world’s leading rulebook is not sufficient to shape global AI developments, especially since this technology is becoming increasingly securitised. Together with seven other leading European AI researchers and think-tankers, I wrote a scenario called “Europe 2031” over the summer, which lays out what it could mean for Europe to get caught in an AI competition between the US and China and be left without any leverage over developments. It might be relevant at this stage for me to introduce myself, since I forgot to do so. It is of relevance. I am vice-chair of the scientific panel appointed by the European Commission to assist the Commission in how it deals with frontier AI systemic risks and the enforcement of the AI Act. This is a relevant affiliation. I am also the executive director of t he Future Society, which is a think tank that has, for the past 12 years, looked at questions of AI governance and geopolitics in the US and the EU.

That being said, to answer your questions, there are two main principles that characterise the EU’s vision on AI. The first is: h eavy is the head that wears the crown . In this race to ever more powerful AI or artificial superintelligence, the EU sees that whoever is winning that race, as far as general AI goes, poses the most risk and therefore should be faced with more safety requirements. Therefore, the regulation has different tiers. The most powerful tools that exist—frontier AI or general purpose AI with systemic risk—should face much greater scrutiny when it comes to safety requirements.

The second principle is: beware of geeks bearing gifts. This is the notion that for 15 to 20 years there has been in the EU a certain conflict with the digital platforms and tech companies and there is now a widely held belief that those digital platforms and tech companies, be they from the US or China, do not have the EU’s best interests at heart. Therefore, the strategy behind the EU’s regulatory vision has been to improve its bargaining powers vis-à-vis these companies by ensuring that there are additional requirements and means for pressure under the rule of law and the normal legislative and democratic process—nothing arbitrary—to equip society with tools to say no when these platforms or technology providers do not respect our values.

Those two principles characterise that vision. You asked also about the Brussels effect and whether this vision is spreading across the world. Again, while reminding everyone that I am appointed by the European Commission and that that therefore probably plays out in my assessment, I would say most certainly that there has been evidence that companies abroad—especially US companies but also some Chinese companies—have complied and even started lobbying for rules abroad that espouse the approach of the EU. The Brussels effect is not accidental. You have to bear in mind that the EU rules have been significantly shaped by US companies through the code of practice that Daan mentioned earlier, co-drafted with the leading industry players alongside over 1,000 stakeholders from within civil society, academia and other industries outside of that of the providers. There is still significant weight given to the voices of US companies, so it is normal that the rules, which I believe are the strongest binding rules that exist in the world right now, have been quite accepted within the industry, at least on the US side. We have seen, for example, OpenAI writing to the Governor of California to ask that the EU-led code of practice be also applicable in California and provide presumption of compliance with California.

The Brussels effect exists, as evidenced by the fact that the industry proposals we are now hearing about—frontier AI regulatory organisations or new forms of Bills in the US and across the world—from Google and Microsoft at least tend to echo and harmonise with the EU’s ideas. The companies have changed their internal governance frameworks to comply—so, compliance has taken place. The code of practice is still a voluntary tool, yet all companies have either signed it or, in the case of those who have not, including some Chinese companies and one American company, are it seems de facto applying it concretely, from what we know from the outside.

The EU rules have stren gthened Europe’s hand, so this notion of improving the bargaining power seems to be working so far. It is difficult and uncomfortable, especially with the current US Administration applying a lot of pressure. But even beyond AI, the EU digital rule and also some of the UK’s rules have been helpful in influencing the behaviour of these companies. For example, X was fined under the Digital Services Act—the platform regulation in the EU—and despite significant screaming and pressure from the US Administration and Elon Musk calling for the abolishment of the EU, in the end X paid the fine, appeared in court as per the usual process, and has modified its practices in order to maintain access to the EU market. I t will not keep spreading on its own. We definitely see the Brussels effect , with legislators in Brazi l, the UK, Korea and Japan wondering whether it is working or not. The Brussels effect works if everybody thinks that it is a good idea for it to work. Of course, with the pace at which technology is evolving, it is very important that we keep questioning whether the bar is being set high enough in terms of safety and security.
​​ ​ Daan , you took a slightly different view in your first answer . P erhaps , briefly, you could comment on the second one.

​​ ​ Thank you, Nick, for t he clear explanation . I agree with Nick that you could characterise the EU’s regulatory approach as a risk - based approach , with d ifferent tiers and levels of stringency for different kinds of models.

It c ould be informative to explain how the EU’s regulatory approach has evolved over time. T he European Commission began drafting the AI A ct all the way back in 2019. T his was three years before the launch of ChatGPT , and l arge language models wer e not really a thing back then . I n a sense , the European Commission was very prescient —already back then, i t noticed these risks from AI emerging . But b eing so early also made its job quite difficult , because over the coming years, we saw the emergence of general purpose AI models —tools, such as ChatGPT, that can be used for all kinds of different purposes. T he draft legislation that the C ommission had written before then was very use case specific. It was more focused on how different AI models were applied in different domains or jobs. Then , over time, it became clear that something was needed for these general purpose models , and the general purpose regulation was bolted on top of the AI A ct. E ventually , that was operationalised through the code of practice , which Nick mentioned.

O ver this period, we have seen a shift from this broad , use case - based regulation towards a narrower and more targeted regulation aimed at addressing larger - scale risks from AI systems which are aimed at the model layer or even at the entity developing the model. In parallel, we have seen a greater focus emerge within Brussels on competitiveness and sovereignty. When it comes to the Brussels effect, I am more sceptical than Nick. I think that we will see a full-blown Brussels effect, where many jurisdictions will adopt very similar regulation to the AI A ct. But we have already seen firms adapt their behaviour as a result of the AI A ct and the code of practice. T o give an example, the code of practice requires AI developers to watermark the text output of their models. W e have seen both OpenAI and A nthropic adopt that recently, and it is certainly not clear that they would have done that without the EU . T hat means that the AI Act will not be able to touch all of them.

I especially hope that the code of practice will form a foundation for a future foreign regulation or international g overnment and governance. The EU’s technical tools and regulatory knowledge can really play a part there. S uch roles, as the story of the AI A ct shows , have to constantly evolve as well.

Q36 I am not quite sure about this question any longer. To the extent that the EU has a common approach, or you could describe it as having some sort of agreement in relation to governance of AI, so let us assume there is a common EU approach—although I am not sure there is; that is clear from what you have been saying so far—how does that differ from the UK’s approach? There is strong alignment between the UK and the EU when it comes to goals. Both the UK and the EU have said explicitly that they want more transparency over AI developments, they want these AI systems to be safe and reliable and they want to have sovereign alternatives in order to not be fully dependent on products from the two superpowers, but their approach towards these ends has been different. The EU has a much larger market and therefore has been able to rely more on regulation—on incentivising companies to adhere to their rules and standards to enter the EU market—whereas the UK is a smaller market and is therefore focused more on building state capacity and societal resilience through investments and technical non-regulatory means. The UK’s AISI is a great example of that and a real inspiration for the rest of the world. We are also seeing the UK take other measures like the Sovereign AI Fund, the new AI Economics Institute and the newly announced AI Biosecurity Lab. These are precisely the types of interventions that are suited to the UK, given its position, and that can offer inspiration to other countries.

There is also room for more collaboration between the UK and the EU—for instance, between the UK’s AI Security Institute and the AI Office, which is sort of its counterpart at the EU level. The AI Office is looking for more evaluation expertise that the UK has plenty of, while in turn AISI is looking for better guarantees that it will retain access to these frontier models in order to test them before pre-deployment. There is room for collaboration there, and I think the upcoming G20 presidency provides an opportunity to strengthen those ties.

I do not believe the UK should try to fully become part of the EU’s regulatory orbit. I do not see much upside there, and it could come with large downsides, for instance, in the relationship between the UK and the US.

When it comes to alignment between the US approach and the UK’s approach, Daan has covered most of it. There is some greater convergence, and nothing made that clearer than the UN Security Council in September, where both Foreign Secretary Miliband and French Foreign Minister Barrot have basically alluded to not only the same risks from AI but the same approach to preventing them, so I think the convergence of goals is there.

The UK has historically led the world in international governance—in the 20th century, with maritime safety, nuclear test bans and the verification regime that came with it, and in the 21st century when it comes to financial stability and climate change. In this space the UK has done the Bletchley summit, and now the EU has come in with a complementary piece of the puzzle of international governance. The UK has provided the momentum and the impetus while the EU has provided maybe the first set of regulations.

As Daan and as I have mentioned, the UK can probably address the very specific risks that have manifested over the summer—the questions of loss of control and challenges to cyber security and resilience from agentic AI. That is something that the EU, because its law is now already a year and a half old, would have a harder time addressing, so the UK can probably do more work on that front in terms of crisis prevention. The current convergence seems like a natural way to work together on an international—or perhaps minilateral, rather than multilateral—regime to work on the more acute and most severe risks that have come up. Everything else that Daan has said I am just echoing—plus one.

Q37 There has been quite a lot of publicity for the Council of Europe’s framework convention on AI, which has been welcomed as the first legally binding international treaty on AI. Could you tell us how you assess its importance? Do you regard it as significant, or not so much?

I must admit that in preparing for this session I had to look up again what the framework convention said, which is somewhat telling. On the positive side, it is the first legally-binding international treaty and, if ratified, it will commit states to keep AI activities consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law. However, the principles that are outlined in the convention are very high-level. They are mostly aimed at current challenges from AI systems: bias and misinformation. They do not address future challenges like the loss-of-control risks that Nick just mentioned. Furthermore, there is no verification mechanism. Implementation is left to national jurisdictions. China has not signed it. The US has not ratified it and will not do so in the foreseeable future. It is a step in the right direction but it is not the end solution that we need here. If the UK were to ratify this convention then that would provide symbolic value, and it would count towards the five ratifications that are needed for the convention to enter into force, but this is really a start, not an end solution.

Regarding its significance, as Daan has mentioned, there is a problem with its scope; it does not address the foundation models, the general-purpose models or frontier AI explicitly. However, it may be significant in that it shows that rules on their own, even if they are agreed upon by many treaties, are nothing without proper enforcement. A key takeaway here is that, whatever regime either will be built domestically in the UK or has been built domestically in the EU, these rules are only as strong as their enforcement. In this case—because of the dual-use nature of this technology, the significant power that comes with it and the competitiveness gain—that enforcement will require a lot of diplomatic engagement and more pragmatic cross-border co-ordination between authorities. California has regulated on frontier AI, and that is the kind of player that the UK would probably be collaborating with to effectively enforce any rules, but unfortunately the Council of Europe’s convention does not have a credible enforcement mechanism.
So you both agree that it is not that important. But it is.
It is a symbol that countries can come together to an agreement, but it also highlights the problem of enforcement.
Field Marshal Lord Houghton has a predictable question.

I should caveat my answer by saying that I am by no means an expert in military applications of AI or defence, but I can speculate a bit. My sense is that by default, the incentives will be increasingly to adopt AI in the military regime and increasingly to cede more and more control to AI systems, because the shorter decision timelines can make better integrated decisions over time. That will enable all kinds of new forms of warfare. We are already seeing how transformative drones are in Ukraine, and AI will enable many more of these types of revolutions. That scares me, to be honest, especially because, as you said, the incentives are such that they push states to keep their progress secret and not regulate this internationally. Enforcement here may be even harder than in other domains.
Nick, have you a view on this?

As an economist by training, I take the incentives very seriously. The rationalist approach to this would be that the incentives a priori would align with what Daan said. However, having interacted a bit with the security and intelligence services in the UK, I am witnessing significant concerns—in the UK and in the US, by the way—about these incentives. So this race is by no means inevitable.

We had what was probably a similar experience with nuclear proliferation, yet we managed what was considered impossible back then: we developed the International Atomic Energy Agency and the nuclear test bans. We have a lot of tools that have addressed the dual-use nature of nuclear, both the opportunities of nuclear power but also the risk that comes with nuclear weapons. Here, the timelines are very compressed because the technology is evolving much faster than nuclear weaponry. However, the UK’s security and intelligence services are among the most sophisticated, mature and intelligent that I know of, and there has been significant progress towards this. We saw Five Eyes making its statement back in June.

I think there is an appetite on all sides because this is a new type of security threat. It is not a terrorist group using AI; it is AI escaping human control and becoming its own stand-alone entity. When you interact with these swarms, as Daan mentioned earlier, you see that they are stand-alone out-of-control intelligent agents that could conclude that basically, some humans are the enemy. That is a new type of security threat facing the security services of most countries, including the US and China, and therefore there are some incentives for collective action. That will be difficult, like all collective actions, but we already see the US and China working towards establishing reporting mechanisms for incidents that could pose national security threats. So we may have more hope than the a priori incentives would indicate there.

This dual-use nature, by the way, is definitely something we have also seen in cyber security. Despite US disengagement from multilateral fora over the past maybe 10 years, the UN and China have managed to make progress on the governance of cyber security, thanks to the UK as well. So there is a way to govern that dual-use approach and bring some order to that technology, at least on things that all Governments can agree on, such as that humans should keep control over AI agents and never have decisions completely made by agents without the intentions of the developers being taken into account.

Daan mentioned investing in that technology; there should be not only investment in that technology but concrete measures that create demand for it.

Concrete crisis prevention measures should be agreed on at the G20 and with the EU. As both Daan and I have highlighted, there is a complementarity between the EU’s regulatory context, which gives quite a lot of bargaining power, and the independent testing capabilities of the UK AI Security Institute, which are unparalleled. So my third recommendation would be, agreeing on an EU-UK operational partnership.

Thank you for all that, and for enlightening the committee. We are grateful to you for coming and giving us the benefit of your advice. We will send you a transcript of today’s proceedings. If there are any minor technical details, you might come back to us very quickly.

Oral evidence: Tourism , HC 143
Tuesday 27 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 27 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Dame Caroline Dinenage (Chair); Mr Bayo Alaba ; Gill German; Nigel Huddleston; Alison Hume; Dr Rupa Huq; Tom Rutland; Jeff Smith ; Jo Stevens .
Questions 87 - 16 4
Witnesses

I : Anthony Breach , Director of Research and Policy, Centre for Cities ; Bernard Donoghue OBE, Director, Association of Leading Visitor Attractions ; and Alistair Handyside MBE, Executive Chair, Professional Association of Self-Caterers UK .
II : Laura Citron OBE, Chief Executive Officer, London & Partners ; Joss Croft OBE, Chair, Tourism Alliance ; and Merryn Kidd , Chair, Somerset & Exmoor Local Visitor Economy Partnership .
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Anthony Breach , Bernard Donoghue and Alistair Handyside .

Q87 Welcome to this meeting of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee. Today, we are holding our second evidence session on tourism. For our first panel, I welcome Anthony Breach, director of research and policy at the Centre for Cities, Bernard Donoghue OBE, director of the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, and Alistair Handyside MBE, executive chair of the Professional Association of Self-Caterers UK. Gentlemen, thank you very much for joining us this morning. It is really good to have you all with us. Before we begin, I need to remind Members to declare any interests at the point they ask a question.

I will kick off. To start with you, Bernard, we hear lots of discussion about the Government’s proposed overnight visitor levy. There are very strong feelings both for and against it, including on this panel. What problem do you think it is attempting to solve? Will it be the most effective way of addressing that?

I think it is attempting to solve three distinct problems. The f irst is the paucity of local government finances over several decades. Local authorities have seen a failure to fund not only their statutory services properly but also the voluntary services — those non-statutory functions such as tourism and culture. This presents an opportunity for new cash to local authorities and to regional mayors.

The s econd is, I suppose, precedent, in that many countries overseas , and indeed many cities , have this model to get more money back into their own visitor economy. Some are more successful at this than others. For example, when it was proposed that Amsterdam would have a city tax scheme, all the money was to be hypothecated for the visitor economy, yet Visit Amsterdam, the tourist board, has never seen a penny. There is a difference between intention and delivery.

I suppose the t hird is that all of us in the visitor economy from who m you are going to hear today are nothing if not realists. We realise, particularly in light of tomorrow’s Budget, that the overnight visitor levy is likely to be enacted, with a push to devolution across England in particular. Particularly f rom our perspective at ALVA, we are keen to see any new proposal made as functional, efficient and effective as possible, for not only the broader economy but the visitor economy as well.
Q88 Thank you. Alistair, do you agree that those are the problems that the Government are setting out to solve through the overnight visitor levy? Do you think it will achieve that?

I broadly agree with Bernard, although I hope that questions on the method of delivery, how the money is spent and how it is collected will be asked during this session. That is where the real challenges lie.
Q89 Thank you. Anthony, do you have anything to add?

Thank you , Chair, for the question. I recognise a lot of the issues that other members of the panel have suggested. They are clearly part of the wider context for this reform. I think the core of the argument that the Government are making for this is that it is a step in the ir programme of devolution to improve both local and national economic growth. If you look internationally, we are an exceptionally centralised rich country for our size. We are by far the most centralised country in the G7, and only about 5% of our taxes are collected at local level compared to about 14% in France and 24% in Japan —both places that have a visitor levy. The implication is that tha t then means that local government has few incentives to grow its local economy. If it increases the size of its tax base, create s more jobs and increase s wages, ultimately that all flows up to Whitehall and does not increase resource for local government in particular. That adds up to quite a big national problem, as well as being an individual local problem.

Our expectation and hope is that the visitor levy is an important first step in moving towards a more typical local finance system similar to those we see in other countries. I think for the purposes of this debate and Committee, one important implication is that we need the visitor levy to be as pro-growth as possible and to provide strong incentives for mayors to support the visitor economy and increase the number of visitors in their cit ies .

Q90 That is really helpful. Bernard, I go back to you. When you set out the objectives and certain problems that you thought this levy was attempting to solve, there was not a positive economic case among them. It was all a degree of political inevitability about giving strategic local authorities this power. Apart from political support, do you see there being a positive economic case in the same way that Anthony set out, and that that could be a good reason for introducing this levy?

Yes, potentially. Tourism is the UK’s fifth biggest industry and third largest employer. It creates more jobs at all skill levels more quick ly than any other sector in this country and is the third largest employer in every UK constituency. If you were planning to organise a growth strategy for the fifth biggest industry, you would not start where we are now. We do not have a Government tourism strategy . D espite one having been written for the last two and a half years , it has not been published. There have been three examples in the last 10 months of policies emanating from N o. 10 and the Treasury affecting tourism , but they are all completely unlinked to each other and they have been created in isolation from the tourism strategy.
Q91 Which are?

First , the Treasury proposal to charge overseas visitors to enter our free national museums and collections. That has now been vetoed, wisely. The s econd is the overnight visitor levy. The t hird was the decision to cut VAT for visitor attractions over the course of the summer. Now, if you had a normal tourism strategy, they would all be elements of tha t , but we do not , so they were all determined in isolation from each other. That is no way to grow Britain’s fifth biggest industry.

Coming back to your particular points, yes, if an overnight visitor levy is introduced with care, consultation and caution, the money emanating from it, if hypothecated and reinvested back into the visitor economy, could be transformational.

Q92 Alistair, we heard a number of reasons why your fellow witnesses think that a levy could be a good idea. PASC UK opposes the levy in principle. What evidence would you need to hear to change your opinion on that?

I will again pick up a couple of things that Bernard said. We do not have a visitor economy growth strategy. We have a situation where domestic rural and coastal tourism are in significant decline, with an almost 30% reduction in overnight stays since 2022. Introducing a levy into those areas will have a disproportionately different impact than if you introduce it into cities and metro areas, where visitor economies are growing. This is why we are absolutely adamant that robust economic impact assessments must be made. If you ask the same questions of different areas, you will get different answers. For us, the No. 1 ask i s that we do not skirt this and go through too quickly, as we did in Scotland and Wales. We must have a proper, robust economic impact assessment and political analysis of this before implementation.

Q93 I refer honourable Members to my declaration in the Register of Members’ Interests. I am also a former t ourism Minister, I used to work in the sector and I go back quite a long way with pretty much all the panellists we have here today in terms of interactions. I should also declare that Alistair organised a trip with PASC for me down to the south-west in my shadow Secretary of State role earlier in the year. I am also an active member of multiple APPGs. I hope that that means I know what I am talking about here. Let me start off with my view and then come to you.

I think this is a ridiculous idea. I have yet to see any evidence whatever that you can support an industry by taxing it more. That is my point of view, but if it is going to go ahead—Bernard, I think you are right that it will be in the Budget tomorrow—we all want to make sure it is done in the most helpful or least destructive way. To that extent, there has been a debate, a consultation and lots of views and opinions about how the levy should come in, whether it should be x pounds per person per night, or a percentage levy. First, what would you like to see? What would your preferred option be?

I suppose that there are two answers to that. In our submission, we put that it should be a percentage rate so that it would be a progressive taxation, if you like. However, the easiest to administer would be a flat rate of x pounds—so, something like £4 or £5—but that would be disproportionate, according to whether you stay at Claridge’s or a T ravel I nn. Our preference would be a progressive rate.
Q94 Alistair, what is your view?

Absolutely. I keep deferring to Bernard here . It is so regressive to have a system of per person per room per place per night. Our pricing varies hugely from summer to winter. We are trying to build winter. A percentage goes down as an amount over the cost , whereas a flat rate stays up and can become enormous. For example, in Wales, it went from a 3% or 4% tax to a 20% tax. The regressive nature of a per rate is less favourable for us.

Q95 The other element is that we are talking about and focused a lot on tourism here, but the reality is that this will be imposed on all commercial accommodation types —absolutely everything. It will therefore impact not just tourism but business travel, visiting friends and relatives, carers staying overnight to look after relatives, and absolutely everything. Do any of you have a comment on this? Do you think it is right? Will it help the economy?

I do not think that you can distinguish between different constituencies or demographic types. To come back to your first point, again if you were organising the growth strategy of Britain’s fifth-biggest industry, you would acknowledge the fact that UK tourism plc at the moment is internationally uncompetitive. We are one of the most-taxed destinations in the world. This just adds to that tax base. It makes us uncompetitive. Also we have seen that , when successive Governments have added tax burdens, customers have responded. For example, we no longer have tax-free shopping. That is an act of economic self-harm. The quicker that this Government reintroduces that, the better. We have VAT at 20% . It is often argued that we should have an overnight visitor levy because so many other European countries in particular do as well, but they do not have 20% on their tourism economy. The vast majority have either 10% on their tourism economy, including accommodation, or less than that.

Q96 Or, indeed, it is a deliberate strategy to reduce over-tourism, which is exactly the point. I know some colleagues will come in on affordability and the details of the mechanics later on, so we will park some of that for the moment. Alistair, looking not so much at who will pay and the arrangements over the imposition of the admin—my colleagues will come to that—how will it really be covered? Is it possible in this day and age where we often have packaging, all-inclusive or B&B, to say which bit is the accommodation versus which is not? Will this not just cause confusion and difficulty for those administering it?

With any of these tax systems, I have great sympathy when they impact one sector more than others. If you have food and beverages, how do you separate those? I understand all those challenges. The way I would look at it is that, at the end of the day, the consumer is less worried about how something is componentised—I made up that word . They are looking for what the price is. With the CMA rulings, we have to show a final price, so it will become somewhat invisible.

We have analysed our data very closely for the last three years, and prices have not gone up by inflation. In 2028, if you in Government say to us that we must add 5% to our business costs, because that is what it will be, a nd we want to cover inflation, we will be trying to put up our prices by almost 10%. I would defy any of you in this room to find a business that can put up its prices by 10% in a year. This will end up being paid and absorbed by the businesses. This is a business tax, make no mistake. Before profit, before anybody takes any money out of it, it is a business tax. Business taxes will hit investment, jobs and local economies.

Q97 Of course, there are many arguments as well, such as in the submissions, for exemptions for very small pitches where you have tents, and those kind s of things. That creates real complexity in the implementation of a tax system there, but I know that that will all be considered. Bernard, you mentioned as well that we are already one of the highest taxed countries in the world for tourism, which I think is beyond question.

I have a question for all of you, and I will make sure Anthony has an opportunity to answer here. Bernard, you articulated that there is no clear strategy. There are different Government Departments, responsible for different things. The taxation element has the business Department involved. There is DCMS involve ment , the Cabinet Office coming in and No. 10’s views and opinions all the time. Do you think this speaks , across Governments —let us be fair—to not understanding and not prioritising tourism as the importan t industry that you have said it is?

Yes, absolutely. I will add to that. It has just been clarified for us that the overnight visitor levy would also be subject to VAT. Ultimately, you would have a tax on a tax on a tax on a payment. That makes no sense whatever.

To go a little further, I first appeared before this Select Committee 29 years ago, when DCMS and indeed the Select Committee w ere first created. In those 29 years that this Committee and its predecessor Committees have been standing, we have had 26 tourism Ministers. It is not just a case of not having joined-up g overnment; there is also a really strong case here for no corporate memory about the importance of tourism across all Government Departments.

I recognise a lot of the frustrations in the comments made by other members of the panel. You see this kind of churn not just in tourism but other policy areas as well. One thing to reflect on in the context of devolution is that this is being devolved to mayors, who will be responsible for their place, and will take a place-first approach to the implementation of this levy. I think that should help resolve some of the problems presented by members of this panel. The mayors are all very conscious of the impact of policies that they make on jobs, investment and the economy in their local area. If this becomes the single most important revenue stream to them, that will focus minds even more.

I just think this is the wrong tax at the wrong time. I appreciate that you can see support for it in metro areas, where the scale would b e dynamic, but Manchesterism does not work very well in east Devon. It really does not translate in the scale we would raise. My final worry is that I worked with Nigel as tourism Minister before, during and after covid when we were trying to move business out of London. That has been Government policy for 20 years that I have known about. We are about to give London the biggest marketing budget over all the small counties around the country. Who wins—Visit London or Visit E ast Devon? That is just to give you an example.

Q98 I just want to follow up with one question. What you have all said came across very clearly in terms of there being a big difference whether you are a city or outside cities. Let us take for the moment that this is going to happen and it works in cities. Bernard, you said it needs functionality, efficiency and effectiveness. Is there a stand-out city anywhere, not necessarily just in the UK but elsewhere, that you think does this really well? Where would you point to?

I would point to San Francisco. The re, the money is well administered. San Francisco also has a statutory registration scheme for accommodation, which is crucial. That is a first step for the implementation of something like this. If we do not know who is providing paid accommodation, we do not know who to tax. They have a statutory registration scheme , and they also go one step further: they hypothecate the money s . It is 100% ringfenced to be reinvested back into San Francisco’s culture, heritage, nature and transport. I know that the Treasury hates hypothecation and I understand all the reasons for that, but this is one of those opportunities to reinvest back into the reason that most people are in accommodation in the first place.

Q99 Good morning to you all. I declare an interest. Prior to coming to this place, I worked in hospitality. I ran, owned and consulted in businesses across the country, and in London as well specifically in terms of my operations. I now represent a coastal community, which I will come to in a second.
First, what effect would the overnight levy have on the affordability of domestic holidays, the UK’s competitiveness and visitor demand?

Thank you for that question. Our starting point on this is that it makes sense for mayors individually to choose what is right for their area. As Jo mentioned just now, it might work for a large urban area and a mayor may come to that conclusion, but it may on the other hand not work for a coastal community. The mayor will take that decision, and it is entirely appropriate that we have different responses across the country because we have these very different tourism markets. I would expect any local economic assessment to identify both the pros and cons of introducing this levy within that context.

When you look into the evidence on the elasticity of visitor trips between business trips and tourist trips , you see that tourism trips are considerably more elastic than business ones. People are more price - sensitive. It also seems to be the case that elasticit ies for domestic travel are higher than for international travel. Once people have chosen a destination abroad that they want to go to, they are pretty likely to continue to want to go there, even if there is a small increase in price. Domestic visitors again seem to be more price - sensitive. Therefore, I would expect that , especially coastal communities where cost - competitiveness is a key part of their offer, the visitor levy might not make sense in a way that it might in a larger urban area.

I entirely agree with Anthony. Anything that puts the price up, particularly in the cost of living crisis, is something that UK citizens will think sensitively about. We are now in year 5 of the cost of living crisis. Only earlier this month, we saw the lowest consumer confidence index since the end of covid. People are making really tactical decisions about how they spend their leisure pounds and leisure hours. Nowadays, particularly for visitor attractions, the competition is not between one visitor attraction and another , but the average family in the UK has a disposable leisure budget of £100 per month. That is a family of four going to a cinema once—or out to dinner, on a day trip, or having a subscription to Netflix, Amazon Prime or Disney+. Competition for the leisure pound and leisure hour has become more competitive, with people making really tactical decisions. If anything looks like it will make the price of a staycation or domestic holiday more expensive, and the ease to book abroad more engaging and enticing, people will do that. If your question is, “Do you think this will have a detrimental effect on domestic tourism?”, from a price point of view it undoubtedly will.

Thank you for your comments earlier about the differences in markets. I will not repeat that it will have a greater impact on rural and coastal areas, primarily domestic visitors and not business stays, which are much more sensitive.

I will go a bit into the technology on pricing elasticity of demand, or PED. This happens in every business, regardless of whether we are talking about hospitality. You work out how much you can put up your prices by how much it will push down demand. In a tiny business like ours, that is an argument between my wife and me. She wants prices up; I want them down , otherwise we will not fill up. Airbnb has algorithms and AI, and every bit of it is based on that argument . Up puts prices up and demand down. UK H ospitality H aven in Lichfield ha s done the work to show that for every 1% increase in price in our sort of area, rural and coastal, you get a 1. 2 5% decrease in demand. So a 5% increase in price, which I genuinely do not think we can pass on , would result in a 7.5% reduction in bookings. That is why I sa y we cannot pass this on. We will have to absorb it.

Q100 Anthony, you talked about the fact that things are very centralised in the UK economy, so how do you incentivise local government to invest, which then obviously improves the experience for visitors ? What do we do? Alistair, you talked about feasibility. I link into that SIC codes and that kind of stuff, so that a case can be made to the Treasury. You also mentioned the need for a proper impact assessment. In a roundabout way, how do local economies and councils support an industry that is important to them, where we know the re are challenges of investment and finances at local government level—touching on Bernard’s point right at the top ? What do they do? How do they try to make the case?

I think this has to be the first step in a longer journey towards fiscal devolution. We are going to hear what is in the fiscal devolution road map tomorrow with the Budget. I hope that will set out not just the visitor levy and the proposals already announced, but a longer period beyond the spending review of increased fiscal autonomy for local government. That will have to entail a closer connection between the economic base of a place and its local government across far more than just tourism. That will be across things like the industrial space, domestic property, income tax sharing and so on . That will all be really important if we want to provide a broad set o f incentives for places to help grow their local economies. We know other countries around the world have these sorts of lev ies and tax es . We know in particular that the big cities can absorb this kind of levy, and it can both provide the funding to help finance larger schemes such as the new Beatles museum being develo ped in Liverpool, and change incentives in the larger scheme to help the mayor and local government support more hotels being built, street cleaning and improvements to the visitor and residential experience in places visitors are likely to visit.

Q101 Alistair, can I come to you quickly with a slight twea k on that question ? I understand your journey. I ran businesses. It is important with regard to taxes how that can affect profitability , and y ou want to survive and thrive. If the local authority, for example, could ensure it, what is needed to earn your trust in how a visitor levy could be spent wisely so it will support and sustain your industry? Is there a case to be made for that?

Regrettably, I am not sure that there is because, like many in this room, I do not believe that we would get hypothecation or ringfencing. Without a guarantee that the money would be spent collectively and wisely, I do not really want to go forward with that. It will cost my business somewhere in the region of £20,000 a year. I think I could invest that £20,000 on extending the visitor experience better than the local council could—with respect to the local council, which is very supportive of tourism.
Thank you, I think I have veered into one of my colleague’s question s so I will end it there.

Q102 Anthony reminded us by implication that this is a permissive measure. It is a voluntary thing for areas to come into.
