If we want to give cities like Manchester—my city, where a visitor levy has worked well—the opportunity to raise a levy, is it not the right approach to have this kind of permissive measure? If rural and coastal areas do not want to take it up, that is fine. If the big cities do, that is up to them. Is that not the right approach?
I completely agree with that , personally. We are already seeing some mayors saying, “Thanks, but no thanks; this is not right for my area.”

I think it comes down to there having to be , as part of the process, robust economic impact assessments and the local council consulting with citizens in their area, rather than what has been suggested that there is a fast track to this. You need proper economic impact assessments and local consultations because you need local solutions to local challenges.

Following from that, local authorities will have different spending priorities. In addition to my day job, I chair the People’s History Museum in Manchester. We are very excited about the prospect of hypothecated funding for the culture and arts scene in Greater Manchester. We think we would be one of the beneficiaries of th at— if it is functional, effective and efficiently operated.

Q103 Good morning. I want to focus a little now on the potential impact on tourism business, which we touched on already with one of my colleague’s questions. Primarily for Bernard and Alistair, how should the Government assess the impact of the levy alongside the other tax , regulatory and employment cost pressures currently facing tourism businesses?

The first thing is to be transparent about how the current UK Government tourism strategy is being created. We have heard no news about it for several months. When I was at VisitBritain, I managed to write a UK tourism strategy in three months. This Government have had two and a half years and , apart from isolated policy proposals, we have yet to see anything comprehensive or useful .

The second thing is that the taxation burden needs to be at the heart of that, being very critically honest about our international competitiveness against countries such as Spain, Italy, France, Germany and the USA , and what the tax burden actually is and if it could be relieved at all before adding a further tax that consumers are likely to be affected by in terms of their preferences ; b usinesses will certainly be affected by it because they may not be able to transfer it on. H aving a critically honest appreciation of our international competitiveness, particularly in terms of taxation, is the first step to understanding whether this is a useful further tax step.

I think we have to look at it in the round. Most of the MPs here are very familiar with our cumulative impacts and DNA. That is what has been thrown at us since covid. This is not looked at in the round but in silos individually. It has to be looked at as part of a cumulative impact.

We do not have a visitor economy growth strategy, as Bernard has said several times. We were hoping for a domestic target. We have an international target, but not a domestic one. Domestic tourism, particularly rural and coastal, is in freefall . S o, Nigel, would you want to be the tourism Minister writing a visitor economy growth strategy with no tax changes, no regulatory changes, no budget and bringing in a visitor levy on top? That is not a gig I would want to write. As Bernard has alluded to, we should not be starting from where we are today. We should have a strategy and then, if it was part of a strategy, we might be looking at it very differently.

Q104 Going from the strategy to the ground-level impact on much smaller businesses, some of which you represent, what would collecting and reporting the levy involve in practice, particularly for micro-businesses and operators that are managing only one or two properties?

There is no detail yet, but we have the examples of Scotland and Wales , which I suggest the Committee should look at very closely, perhaps if only as a case study in learning how not to do it. We think it is likely to be quarterly . M aking T ax D igital is quarterly. That would be another burden when we are told by the Government that they want to cut the regulatory burden by 25%. T hey would have to report quarterly. You could be reporting quite small sums of money as a small business. Someone has to organise the time to collect it and remit it , and someone has to receive it and check that it is correct. You have to look at the administration costs of an extra tax. It is a whole new tax; it is not done by any currently existing system. It will have to be built, managed and checked, all of those things. We are being asked by Treasury to report on how many hours that might take and we are in the process of doing that, but it is another burden on very small businesses that already have to deal with all of that. I think we have to start treating small businesses with a bit more respect. They do not ask for a great deal but a great deal is demanded of them. It will be another administrative burden on top of the cost s to which I have already alluded.
Q105 On collection and reporting, is there an international example that works well or better than others?

No. We have looked to try to find good examples. None of them is perfect. It is a very complex tax to do. Colleagues sitting behind me will be giving evidence different from mine because it will affect their sector differently. If I was representing them I would say that; if they were representing me they would say what I have said. It is a very complex tax. It sounds dead easy: just charge the price of a cup of a coffee on a stay and we will all have lots of free money. It is much more complicated than that. You must do robust economic impact assessments, not take shortcuts or race this through legislation. It needs serious contemplation.

Q106 Would anybody like to come in on this question, maybe Bernard first? Who should be legally responsible for collecting and remitting the levy where a booking is made through an online platform : the accommodation provider or the platform?

That is a very good question. I do not think there is a lot of clarity because that happens in different ways in different countries and different municipalities. That is the kind of clarification we would love from Treasury. Rather than an overnight visitor levy being presented—this may be a crude summary—as a kind of smash-and-grab raid on the visitor economy to give local authorities free cash, a more considered approach about legal entitlement, legal insurance and who has technical responsibility is absolutely required quickly. If the legislation is going to come through, as we suspect it might , in the next couple of days, a good bulk of accommodation has already been sold for next year, so that will not be taken into account in new legislation. Anything we are talking about has to be at least two or three years in advance of that—this is not stonewalling—in order to have exactly the kind of measures and functionality in place to deliver this for the benefit of everybody.

And everybody has to build the system s to do this. If you have a complicated system by which every mayor is choosing a different rate, different exemptions and different classifications, anybody who operates on a national basis, or across two regions, has to build that into their booking systems. The administration on platforms can be absolutely enormous the more complex the system is. I am not stonewalling, but you have to give people time to build this in.
I do not have anything to add.
Q107 Do you envisage that most people would pay on arrival, which seems to be the case internationally in a lot of respects?

Pay on arrival is something we would not welcome. We do not want to get into disputes with our guests about whether they need to pay a tax. You need to put it into the whole booking process, because the CMA says it has to be that way. Therefore, if you are booking in our sectors, or in hotels where you pay, or put your credit card in at the point of booking, it would have to be included in that price at that point, but the remittance date would have to be post the date of the booking completing because, if the booking does not complete, there is no stay tax.
Q108 Presumably, there are other countries where this is applied regionally or state by state , and you can book through digital online platforms. How do they manage it?

It is very difficult. The APPG for tourism and hospitality brought over the German hotel association manager. I think he has to manage 38 or 42 different systems in different cities. Some states in Germany have said , “N o more tourist taxes until you sort it out. ” It can get to be so disparate with all the issues that follow that. Guest confusion is one of the biggest ones you need to worry about with everybody setting a different tax. Everybody setting a different tax will cause displacement issues. If Cornwall were to set 6%, you can bet your bottom dollar Devon might set 2%. You are setting people against each other as well to drive it because everybody knows displacement will drive bookings. That is what will happen.

Q109 Bernard, you were talking about the fact that there have been 26 Ministers and there is no co-ordinated approach. I totally get it. Up until a few years ago I was in that world as well, so I understand that frustration, but this is not particularly a party political issue; this is just how we have looked at the industry over a generation. That would be my perspective. You mentioned earlier corporate memory, which is a really good point. I agree with you. I do not want to be overly sensitive about this. I totally understand corporate memory. That is obviously linked to taxation approaches. What would you do differently?

Thank you for giving me the role of tourism Minister. I appreciate it enormously. It is not a flippant point that in the past 29 years we have had 26 tourism Ministers. The average tenure of a tourism Minister in DCMS is less than 14 months. A notable exception was Nigel Huddleston—this is a completely non-political point of view—who was the right Minister at the right time in the wrong crisis. Thank goodness he was there for two and a half years . B ut, in addition to no corporate memory being sustained by changing Ministers on a very regular basis, DCMS, as I think the Chair has mentioned on a number of occasions, has quite a turnover of senior civil servants, so there is no corporate memory even within the A dministration, let alone political appointees and Ministers.

A further point would be something that Chris Smith introduced almost 28 years ago when he was Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, which is a cross-departmental ministerial committee where every G overnment M inistry, including devolved A dministrations, are present and looking at tourism, so UK tourism plc. That has happened from time to time. It was resurrected under the previous Conservative G overnment to great effect, particularly in terms of crisis management, but because we have such a silo mentality within different G overnment D epartments, when you have something like tourism that is as important for transport as the Home Office, Culture, Media and Sport, Treasury and Communities and Local Government, et c , you need a consistent thought-through approach which is comprehensive and ambitious. At the moment we do not have that, as evidenced by the fact we are still waiting two years on for a tourism strategy from the Government.

I would like to go back to what was in our original submission when you called for evidence. That was a whole different look at the way tourism is valued by G overnment — the way it is recorded in the G reen B ook with businesses like mine. With displacement, you would spend the money in Essex rather than coming down to Devon, would you not, whereas you go abroad? Tax money that is spent at my place is tax revenue that the Chancellor gets. We have to start looking differently at the way we value tourism. We have to have that growth strategy and stuff has got to be within that. We should be talking here about how to grow the domestic visitor economy and not have isolated conversations about components like this. I would urge very much that we start looking at it as the fifth largest economy and the impact that changes like this can have on it. We are certainly not growth - driven.

Q110 We have touched on little bits and pieces of the San Francisco experience that flashed up earlier. Assuming it is happening tomorrow, I want to move on to how the levy revenue should be allocated and governed. If a levy is introduced, how should the proceeds be used to deliver demonstrable benefits to tourists, businesses and local communities? How do you square those factors?

Our position is that we should not have hypothecation of the visitor levy , and there are a few reasons for that. One is that, when we look abroad at how hypothecation systems work, we do not see many examples of hard hypothecation where there is a very specific commitment that the revenues must be spent on x, y or z programmes. Instead, we see more vague commitments, as Bernard mentioned, to support the visitor economy. Bernard has also said that those do not often translate into actual lending support on the ground for the visitor economy. If we are thinking about the logic of the argument s here for the visitor levy and fiscal devolution to drive growth, it is not just money coming in , which is then spent on things that improve the visitor economy; it changes the behaviour of mayors and local government to enable more activity to happen than would otherwise be the case . There need to be quite strong commitments that the mayors themselves need to make to do things they would not have done otherwise—other things that cost money but also things that do not cost money—and to be held accountable by local businesses , local residents and by national G overnment that they are doing those particular things. If we have a system of hypothecation , we risk giving mayors a bit of a smokescreen where they can say, “ Don’t worry : t he money has been hypothecated. I’m going to spend it on things that are great for the visitor economy. Don’t worry about it.” If it is unhypothecated , that puts the focus on mayors to justify why they are raising the levy in the first place.
Q111 They would have to come up with a plan.
Yes, t hat is what we would argue.
Q112 What do you think?

I would take a different view. This is an opportunity for hypothecation to work and to be tested to see that it works. Currently, culture, heritage, tourism and nature are not statutory duties and so they are the first to be shed when local authorities are looking at cutting their budgets. In addition to my day job, I chair a number of things. One of them is the London and south - east region for the National Trust. Within our region alone, we probably get two or three calls a week from a local authority saying, “Hypothetically , ”—it turns out it is not so hypothetical—“if we were to discharge ourselves of our heritage assets, our museums, collections and our green spaces, would you, National Trust, be prepared to take them on?” Of course, the answer is, “No, not without cash.” Therefore, what hypothecation does by ringfencing that money 100% to be reinvested back into those non-statutory duties, which have fallen by the wayside over the course of the past 20 years or so, is reinvest back into the reasons why most people are coming to visit different places — so culture, heritage, tourism and nature.

It can lend itself to other things like tourism infrastructure and transport. When Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester , we had good conversations about hypothecating the money in Greater Manchester for use in strategic investments, not just tactical investments, such as an equivalent of the V&A storehouse of the north, so museums and galleries could combine and have a collection centre in the north of England. Similarly, in the west country I chair Bristol Old Vic Theatre. We no longer receive any money from Bristol City Council, despite being one of the most important commissioning and producing houses in the whole of the UK. That is because culture is not a statutory duty. What this provides us with is hypothecating in order to reinvest in the very fabric and offer that entices people to travel in the first place.
Q113 Alistair, how do you view this?

I would come at it from making sure that the people who have to charge the levy, administer it and send it back have a fair say in some kind of forum in the area. Cardiff is an example. It has set up a forum which is a mixture of the accommodation providers—we are on that panel—other visitor economy partners in the city and the council. You sit down together and try to work out the best possible plan forward , but, unless that is a mandated component of any levy in the legislation, it will not happen and that spend will not be done in partnership, because the queue outside the door for that money will go round the block. The people who support this levy are those who think they can get some of the money, and those who do not support it are those who are effectively giving it away.
Q114 How tightly defined are we saying these categories should be? If you have no hypothecation at all, would it stretch to bins, policing and transport?

The strategic authorities , which are quite different from local authorities and the statutory duties are not provided by the S A s , are focused on economic matters. It is things like transport , skills and planning. In principle, we would say it is acceptable if some of the revenues are then used to support an expansion of the planning team which then facilitates the construction of more hotels or a wider visitor attraction in the area. That could be justifiable, but obviously the mayor would need to justify this to both residents and the visitors who are paying the levy. If there is a vague hypothecation requirement , the risk is that it becomes harder for local businesses and local people to enforce, as opposed to one where the mayor has to make the full case from top to bottom about how the money is raised and how it is spent.
Q115 Referring to the San Francisco experience, you said it goes entirely back into culture. Where does that stop? Currently, how do you decide?

In our submission we have laid out all the areas where we think the money could be spent well. One of the opportunities this gives us, were this to happen and were it to be hypothecated, is to think afresh about local government settlements. We would not want this money to fill the poverty gaps in local authorities. I t is still the case that the Local Government Association says that one in four local authorities in England is on the cusp of bankruptcy. This is not a solution to that. The solution to it is getting local government settlement right between central G overnment and local authorities. This is not a smash-and-grab raid to fix another D epartment’s problems.
Q116 What safeguards could you build in to stop it being taken over by adult social care , which is the biggest item of expenditure by any local authority?
You could specify how it should be spent on the face of the Bill.

To avoid what has been said, it will need to be pretty specific; otherwise, two things could happen. One is that it will just get absorbed into general council budget, but the second one that we need to be fearful of is that there are lots of councils that are really strapped and value tourism , and find some small way to support them. There are not many these days, but some do. If this comes in, I suspect that, instead of them continuing to find that budget to support tourism, it will get lost in the general mix and they will use the tourism tax to replace it. So that will not be extra money; it will still be used in the wrong way.
Q117 It would prop up other gaps.

I would argue that the fact it is going to strategic authorities rather than local authorities will mitigate most of that risk . T he SAs do not have the same statutory responsibilities or funding pressures that local authorities do. It may be the case that a strategic authority will wish to share some of the proceeds with its constituent local authorities. One can imagine, say, a large city sharing some of the proceeds of the revenue raised to help fund street cleaning, which is a service provided by the local authority beneath the strategic authority, but, given the proposals set out by the Government, I do not think there is any significant risk of proceeds from the levy being used to fund social care, certainly not in the combined authorities where the large urban areas are.

Q118 I am a London MP. In London, t here are 32 boroughs; there is the City of London. I represent two of them: the London Borough of Ealing and the London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham. They would love a bit of this rather than it just being swallowed up by the m ayor. What do you think? Should our London boroughs get a share of this?
I would argue that, if you want the outer London boroughs to benefit from the levy, it does have to go primarily to the mayor rather than the constituent boroughs.
Q119 I have one inner and one outer.

There is perhaps a case for some degree of sharing, as mentioned, between the strategic authorities and local authorities to cover some of those local services that touch on the visitor economy, but if we did it at just local authority level we would see Westminster, Camden and the City of London snaffle up the vast majority of the receipts and most of the rest of London would see very little. The fact it has been collected either entirely or primarily by the GLA means that the mayoralty can fund interventions that perhaps support tourism across the wider city region but , in particular , interventions to support the labour market and transport network that enable people across London and all Londoners working in the visitor economy, even if they work in the city centre but reside in places such as Ealing, Hammersmith and Fulham.
Q120 Does the mayor know best, or should the boroughs be given it ?

For me, some of these things still fall down very much. There are possibilities of it working in a metro context, but not a rural and coastal context. If you say that Exeter had decided to raise a visitor levy I would be in that area to pay it, but I am 20 miles from Exeter and I would see very little of it . I would be paying it but not getting any benefit. If I was a councillor outside Exeter, would I be getting any of the budget to spend on my local amenities, or whatever you choose to spend it on? I doubt it very much. People are notoriously strong on hanging on to their budgets, are they not? I think you would struggle.

One of the best estimates for London is that this could raise £150 million a year, so all local authorities within London would want a slice of that action. One of the things Sadiq Khan has said and that I think is incredibly useful and optimistic is that this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to look at using this money on a strategic basis rather than tactical interventions by local authorities. You could do something really significant, including a world-class conference centre in London, with that sort of money which no local authority itself could bear the burden of.

Q121 I am a coastal MP. I was brought up in that area. Previous to this role I was in leader ship in local government and I sat around tables having to look at those non-statutory services in a way that was very painful. I know that local government does grapple with this to try to find some kind of balance. There is a broad spend on things that matter to people beyond actual nuts-and-bolt services, so I know it is a huge issue.

As to rin g fencing these funds for the area, coming at it from a place-based perspective, there seems to be a strong argument for that. My biggest tourist town is Rhyl. If the real basics are improved—waste collection, available public toilets, street cleaning and making the place nice—it adds value to why people want to come. I believe that will have a positive impact on the businesses that operate there.

Alistair, aside from the complexities with the visitor levy as a whole—I can see the complexities in administering it—if there is good local consultation and a robust impact assessment, could there be a broad benefit for businesses that operate in that area if that general area is improved as a result of the introduction of the visitor levy?
I am going to come back to you. I do not want to pre-empt the outcome of a robust economic impact assessment and local consultation.
Q122 At a local level though if that were done .

In Wales, Cardiff — a city — voted to have one , and the three north - west counties said no because they had to go through a process and had to ask people, so I am going to reset on that. I do not think it is impossible to come up with a tourist levy or visitor tax that could be better. It is not what we are looking at , at the moment. There are so many unanswered questions on this one, but leave it to the point so it is impossible to ask that question. If I genuinely thought that the money would be spent absolutely to improve a place in a way my visitors would recognise, or believe they are spending—whether or not I am absorbing it, they will think they are spending it—the optic is that the price of the holiday has gone up because of the tax, whether or not I put up the price. They need to see a tangible benefit. While I can see the scale that Bernard talks to, in my area there is no single thing like that that you could do. You would have to have a myriad of things that the local government, to call it that, was doing that we could sell as to why this tax is in place. We cannot just impose it; they will reject it and go and stay somewhere else.

Q123 I am chair of the APPG for coastal communities. As an MP who represents a coastal community—Scarborough and Whitby—which depends on tourism, I would make the observation that we have the first rural metro mayor in York and north Yorkshire, which is an issue because we have a city, York, with five-star hotels , and, on the coast, we have a very different tourism economy. It is highly competitive and highly price-sensitive with a lot of family-run businesses. It is almost an example of what has been raised today about how in one authority we could have a very different range of tourism and competitive dynamics within that. We also assume that all mayors will take the tourist levy. In fact t hey won’t . There will be similar businesses such as caravan parks just down the road in, say, Lincolnshire that will not be having the tourism levy. There is already quite a lot in the mix. When I speak to my local businesses—I have spoken to about 30—they were all worried about this particular issue.

Looking at local flexibility and the ability to lay the tourist levy, the Government are saying that you are either in or out and it is a percentage, but would different local rates, exemptions and administrative arrangements across England create confusion and complexity for visitors and businesses operating in more than one area? Nigel, you have touched on this. Could I turn to Alistair?

In my heart, I do not want to charge children to come and stay at my business. I do not want to charge disabled people to come and stay at my business. I do not want to charge veterans and scouts and all these kinds of people. I get that, but that is putting a burden of exemptions that would then have to be at some point checked out perhaps by the visitor accommodation provider themselves. I do not want my members to have to be a judge about whether somebody is actually disabled, 14 years old, a veteran or a boy scout. You cannot put that kind of burden on hospitality providers. Exemptions sound great in principle, and my heart goes out to those, but if they are going to be administered they need to be done as they are in Scotland where you pay the tax and you reclaim it. Therefore, you are putting the whole burden and cost back into the system. This is another reason it is an imperfect tax. That is a real danger.

Regarding the other point that you alluded to, when you have a mayoral area that has both a metro and a rural context, I really doubt that the rural businesses that we represent would see as much benefit as the ones that are getting the work done in the metro part of that area. This is why it is splitting, even in this meeting, between horses for courses, for want of a better term.
I agree with Alistair. The ability for strategic authorities to opt in and opt out already makes for an uneven playing field, and that is not a good place to start from.

We would argue that having a single national framework and then mayors being able to decide whether to levy the rate and what rate to levy it at makes sense. You can adjust the degree of the tax burden and the reward relative to the needs of the local economy. We would say that it does not make much sense for that national framework to allow mayors to vary the rate by local authority. That will not only introduce more complexity, but it will also introduce a situation where mayors are incentivised to really squeeze the pips of the local authorities where there is a high demand for tourism in that area, risking wider impacts to the national economy.

To come back a little bit to something Gill said about whether there is a place-based local aspect to this, we think that that is right and that there is a behavioural impact that we think is at the core of the logic for the Government’s fiscal devolution agenda. An absolutely essential corollary to that is that, whatever revenues are raised by the levy for different mayoral areas, they should not be equalised between different mayoral areas. If a place is effectively penalised with fewer grants for levying a visitor levy, that will completely blunt the incentive to try to grow the visitor economy in that particular area. That is truly just a burden on business without any of the growth incentive side of it. We have to allow that, if the revenue is raised, if a place decides to go for it, if it decides to set a rate at whatever rate it deems acceptable, that has to be considered its money that it is raising to be used for its own purposes, not an input into a national Government grant formula.

Q124 Okay. Can I come back to Anthony briefly on that? Tourism does not really fit the mayoral boundaries. Going back to the price-sensitive, lower end of domestic tourism, which is so valued, such as the holiday parks, you have a holiday park in North Yorkshire and then just over the border there will be one that does not have the tourist levy. That seems to be unfair.

We do not quite have enough time to get into the topic of local government boundaries and the impact on local government finance. The big-picture issue is that we will have to draw boundaries somewhere. Some mayors will set the levy; some mayors will not. There will always be a live political question facing mayors on both sides of those boundaries as to what the levy should be and whether it should be levied at all.
Q125 Okay. What safeguards should apply before a scheme begins? Should legislation require a minimum implementation period, regular reviews, or indeed a sunset clause?

Yes, yes and yes. This is so complex and potentially such an opportunity that it needs adequate thought, analysis and consultation. That is not a stonewalling piece. This is so fraught with difficulties and, as you have just identified, displacement and inconsistency that this needs to be given a lot of thought and time to achieve all the political and economic goals that the Government are setting out.

It will primarily impact the businesses that serve the great British holiday: the self-catering, the holiday parks and the bed and breakfasts. It is the lower-average-cost accommodation that will be hit the hardest by this, and the people perhaps in lower-income streams who will be thinking they are paying this even if they are not. In the Wales consultation on this, the reaction of lower-income groups to these kinds of taxes is described as visceral. So be careful what you wish for.
Q126 The fact is that we have a cost of living crisis and many of the small, family-run accommodation providers are already worrying about their financial sustainability.

It is perhaps harder to justify a sunset clause. I do not know of any other tax in the UK or indeed similar systems elsewhere that have that kind of phasing out. One element where we would expect this to be pro-growth is that a percentage-based levy is a buoyant tax where revenues rise over time as the economy grows and expands. If that is set to expire at some point in the future, that will dent the ability of mayors to both borrow against that revenue and to levy that tax with the idea of spending it on projects that are actually good for the economy. Any such levy should come with not just an assessment of the impact on businesses and how they plan to spend the money but, also, what the commitments are from the mayors about their behaviour that they will change in the governance of their local economy that will be good for the visitor economy.
Q127 Thank you so much. Gentlemen, those are all the questions that we have for you. Was there anything that you were burning to share with us that we did not get round to today? Alistair?
I am going to harp on about thorough economic impact assessments and full consultations. They are an absolute must.
Q128 Thank you. Bernard?

I merely thank you for looking at tourism again. This is the fourth time that this Select Committee or its predecessor Select Committees have put pressure on the Government to take tourism more seriously. I will end by saying that tourism is not just where you grow jobs—we are very good at it—but it is also where you grow people and communities, and that needs to be factored in as well.
Q129 Brilliant. Thank you very much. Anthony?

For me, it is emphasising that this is a levy that will be right in some areas and not right in other areas, and it is appropriate that the mayors should have the power to ultimately decide whether the levy is the right levy for them in their area.
I thank all of you for coming and for all your time this morning. It has been really helpful, and we have really enjoyed speaking to you.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Laura Citron, Joss Croft and Merryn Kidd.

For our second panel I welcome Laura Citron OBE, chief executive of London & Partners , Joss Croft, chair of the Tourism Alliance , and Merryn Kidd, chair of the Somerset & Exmoor Local Visitor Economy Partnership. That is a mouthful, is it not? Thank you all very much for being with us this morning. I will pass over straightaway to Jo.
Q130 Thanks, Chair. How effectively is the current destination management system in England converting national tourism ambitions into local growth? Laura, do you want to start?

Thank you very much. The new national system, which has clear, structured layers of destination management, is the right one, but in our view it is underfunded and therefore not able to be effective because it does not have sufficient long-term funding. The structure itself was created after a very thorough review, and we support the structure.

It varies tremendously across the nation depending on size, region and other factors. For us in particular in Somerset & Exmoor, the local visitor economy partnership programme has been fantastic. It has given us an opportunity to have a seat at the table with many bigger areas, and it has forced us to work with partners that we would not have done before. The de Bois review noticed that there were so many disparate organisations working towards the same end, and that was very evident in more rural areas. We have brought together many different organisations now sitting at the table together. We are a partnership of four. That has forced us to come together to create a strategy for the same end.

The de Bois review was well timed. It produced its recommendations in September 2021. The Government response was in the following year. It is not a problem of structures; it is a problem of funding. The de Bois review recommended these different layers that we would have from a national through to a regional through to a local. That is very sensible. That was very well received by the industry. The funding has not been there to see it through to its end as well, so you have a lot of destinations. The Tourism Management Institute released a report last week. Ninety destinations across UK and Ireland had completed it. Some of the statistics within it are absolutely horrifying: 16% of destinations do not have a full-time employed person looking after that destination, and 22% of them said that they were unlikely to survive the next five years.

A lot of people often think that tourism is all to do with the marketing. The point of the LVEPs is, of course, to do with marketing, but more importantly it is to do with the management of tourism. If I give you an example, 80% of all inbound tourists who come to the UK will use an intermediary; 45% of those will use a tour operator. They need product. They need international-ready product. They need product that has commissions, that has allocations in it, and that is ready 18 months in advance. Without the people in the destination to provide that training, that business support and the training for people to understand what international tourists are looking for, you do not get sold internationally. If 45% of the business is coming through tour operators and they do not feature your programmes, you simply are not on the shelves to get sold. Without that minimal investment—and it is small investment—for the LVEPs to be able to have that business support function, it does not matter what marketing they are undertaking because, frankly, you are not going to get sold. The approach of the de Bois review was absolutely right : w e do not need another restructure. We need to make sure that these LVEPs are invested in at a base level to allow them to provide the services and support that the international trade needs to sell them.

Q131 Thank you all for your answers. I represent a seat in Wales—Cardiff East. I looked at this list of local visitor economy partnerships, destination development partnerships, destination management organisations, local authorities, VisitEngland and VisitBritain, and I thought, “How does anybody understand what each of those do, and how do they interact together?” I was quite interested particularly, Laura, in what you said about how you think the structure works really well. From your perspective—and I will ask all of you—do you think that those respective roles are clear and understood , and are they effective at the moment?

I will answer from a London perspective, but I recognise that the situation may be quite different in other parts of the country. The way that we are organised in London is that we have a growth agency as London & Partners, which is the growth agency for the Greater London economy across all sectors, of which tourism is one. We act as the local visitor economy partnership and as the convention bureau, and we operate Visit London, but we do that as part of a much broader portfolio of activity, including inward investment, innovation, small business support, London global brand and so on. We are able to look at the experience economy and tourism as one growth sector alongside frontier innovation and professional services and other sectors of the economy.

We have a very good working relationship with the team at VisitBritain and VisitEngland. They promot e the national story and we promote the London one. We are working across three areas at a London level. One is the strategy for the experience economy in London and how we convene the industry together to shape a strategy and provide insights and data that businesses use to shape their own plans. The second is that demand generation/promotion piece that Joss talked about: marketing campaigns and, importantly, selling business events internationally, which is an important part of demand in London. The third area is around developing that product that Joss has talked about—supply-side interventions. What do we want the future experience of London to be? How can we bring in the best experiences in the world and put them in this city so that it continues to be a world-class visitor destination?

Our relationship with the national agency is largely around the demand generation side. It is around collaboration on campaigns. London is a tourism gateway for the UK. We could be doing a lot more to use the visitors who come to London and encourage them to visit other parts of the UK, but we are not currently doing that systematically.

Q132 I am very glad you said that. I might chip in with a question that I was going to ask later, Laura. Next year, we have the Tour de France, which will go through Scotland, England and Wales. The year after, we have the Euros in Scotland, England and Wales. How effective are the current organisations such as VisitWales, VisitScotland, VisitBritain and VisitEngland in spreading out on a big national programme, a big event thing like that, and getting people not just to come to London but to go right across the UK? We find it very frustrating in Wales.

To come back to the first question, the structures, the good will and the partnerships and relationships are there, but there isn’t long-term, multi-year funding on a sustainable basis. There have from time to time been pots of money that have been competitive to do gateway work on joining up different destinations. We have recently run a really effective campaign jointly with Scotland where we have been encouraging visitors to London to take the train and visit Scotland as well. The results on that are really effective. It shows that it works. We have to compete for these very small pots of money and it is not multi-year, so you cannot build towards it strategically. We know that some of these events are coming years in advance, but we do not know what the funding will be in the years that they are coming, so we cannot work together as a system to plan.

Q133 By the time the funding is confirmed, you have run out of a load of time that you could have spent planning. Right, okay. Merryn, going back to my original question about the respective roles, do you think they are clear enough?

As one of the newer LVEPs, part of our piece of work over the last year and a bit has been to communicate this to our stakeholders in the area. We are very clear about what an LVEP is, but if you say that word to someone who runs a small B&B they will not know what that is. We are one of the examples. There is no full-time member of staff who is being paid to run the LVEP in Somerset & Exmoor. It is all being done out of people’s day jobs. I am a CEO of a visitor attraction. We are all giving our time to do this thing that has been imposed from on high. It has been an excellent thing for us, and we are doing the best we can with our stakeholders to communicate why it is a good thing and why we can represent them so much better now, but it is a long piece of work, and even tiny amounts of funding would enable us to employ someone to do even just the admin.

The roles are clear. We have a network of people with whom we work, and they are very happy with it. Accreditation has created this clear responsibility for us but without any funding to deliver it. I am on the fence about saying, “We are clear about the responsibilities, but we can’t deliver them.”

To talk to Laura’s point and your point about bringing people around the country, this for us is an opportunity to attract more international visitors or domestic visitors out of the cities. One thing that we were lucky enough to do, funded by VisitEngland, was to attend travel trade shows in Amsterdam. When I wanted to go with a business partner, this was not funded at all. The stand was funded by VisitEngland, which was great, but we had to pay for our own flights. I had to persuade a hotelier to come with me.
Q134 We will come to that shortly. Can you stick to the questions and try to keep answers a little bit pithier, ladies and gentlemen, please? Thank you.

In terms of the clear roles, VisitBritain’s role is to drive that demand, VisitEngland has a co-ordinating role on the product development side, and then the LVEPs are there to do the product development, the training, the business support and the engagement with businesses so that they are trade-ready. It is not just the marketing piece. It is clear to those of us who work in the industry. We heard in the previous session about Government understanding of tourism and understanding the long chain and the long tail that there is within it as well. Customers do not recognise LVEP boundaries. They come for the experiences. They come for the thematics and the destinations that they want. I do not think it matters if the international visitor understands. Of course they do not. That is not the role of the LVEPs. The role of the LVEPs is to get their businesses ready to accept these visitors and to develop products—we have heard about the international competitiveness—while making sure that the products and experiences are available and world class for our international visitors. It is clear to those of us who work in the industry. For the visitors, I am not sure it is quite so important.
Okay, I will leave it there.

Q135 Thanks for being here. You have all said that you think the structures are right. You all have, effectively, strategic roles. We heard from Jamie, who is the chief executive at Chester Zoo, last week. He described all these various roles of VisitBritain, VisitEngland, the LVEPs and the DMOs as confusing. I have heard similarly from other stakeholders. For individual operators and attractions, are those respective responsibilities clear enough to the people in the industry?

If you were to look at an individual business and where they see the value, where does the value sit in terms of that engagement? It might be the business support that they are offered through their LVEP, the training, getting them travel-trade ready and getting them international ready. It might be working with VisitBritain and the international offices that VisitBritain has. VisitBritain’s international offices are an absolute jewel in the crown , i f you are interested in the Dutch market, working with the people on territory who understand the trade, the media and the operating environment. People will understand better where they see that value most.

As someone who is both an attraction and represent ing the LVEP, the value for the attraction certainly in our area is to be able to make their voices heard louder. There is no point for me as the CEO of the Bishop’s Palace trying to advertise internationally for visitors to come to my organisation. It is the value of joining up and saying, “Hey, Somerset & Exmoor is an amazing place to be.” My role as chair of the LVEP is to communicate this to the organisations within the area and to let them know why we are there and what we can do for them, and that is time-consuming. Most of the businesses are small micro-businesses.

We operate as a social enterprise, a public-private partnership funded partly by grant and partly by businesses. For me, that is really important because if we are not doing things that businesses value they will not pay to participate. We have over 300 businesses in London that are annual paying members of London & Partners, and they really hold us accountable for what we are doing, because if they do not feel that we are adding value they are not going to renew. Additionally, some of them choose to come with us on trade missions to go and sell, particularly around business events, conventions and trade shows. Others also pay from time to time to participate in marketing campaigns. For me, that is a really important test of whether we are doing the right things, because businesses simply would not pay otherwise.

Q136 Building on what we have talked about there, the confusing structure is something that we have all dealt with for a while. You have previously said the purpose of the LVEP was appropriate, but it is not properly funded. We have these layers. As Jeff said, we have heard in previous hearings people saying, “I don’t get what VisitBritain or VisitEngland do.” They do not see the benefit. VisitEngland is primarily domestic promotion and VisitBritain international, and then there is a plethora—I think 100—of DMOs around the country. I have faced it in my area. I have Visit Worcestershire on the border, Visit Gloucestershire, Visit Warwickshire and Experience Oxfordshire all competing to try to get people to the Cotswolds. The purpose of the LVEP was to get that co-operation, get them working together and package in a more appropriate way.

However, i t all goes back to funding. The LVEPs got £4 million. We spent billions supporting the industry during the pandemic. Inbound tourism alone brings in something like £30 billion of export revenue a year, and in return the Government gave £4 million back. By the way, that was my G overnment. It has not got much better. The frustration that you are all expressing of how much the industry gives versus how much it gets in support is one that is really key.

The question that I have for you therefore is this. What is realistic in terms of a long-term funding model? What do you need from the Government and how much do you need from the Government? Is it going to have to be, Laura, your model of saying a little bit of G overnment or taxpayer money, but at the end of the day it has to be primarily commercial? What is realistic here? Sorry, there is lots in there, but you know what we are getting at.

I will start with the small. In Somerset & Exmoor, we have drawn up a menu of what we would fund if funding appeared, and it is a tiny amount. We have choices of 50 grand here and there. If it pops up, we will be ready to act. That only adds up to £200,000 a year, and that would keep us going. About £1.3 billion was put back into the economy in Somerset & Exmoor, which is a huge amount. With just a 5% raise, that would be an extra £64 million. All we need is a couple of £100,000 to keep us going. I can only speak for our area and what I would suggest. We have nothing from Somerset Council—not a penny.
Q137 Joss, is this a familiar story? If you went to the DMOs and LVEPs across the country, do you think they have their very clear ask of how they would use money effectively ready to go?

Absolutely. They are so engaged with their industries. They know exactly what there is to do. I will give a shoutout to VisitEngland. It recently launched a connected destinations fund, which is to get LVEPs working together across boundaries. I talked earlier about consumers and international visitors not necessarily recognising our authority boundaries. That is very good.

In terms of the funding, though, Nigel, I have been around for a long while. When I first joined VisitBritain in 2000 at the turn of the millennium, the funding settlement from central Government was about £35 million a year. Here we are 26 years later, and it is £18 million. If you were to take that £35 million in 2000, it would probably equate to somewhere near £200 million at the moment. Currently, it gets £18 million. It is not a problem of structures. It is not a problem of ambitions or delivery. VisitBritain delivers about 20 or 25 to 1, or in the recently cut business events growth programme 35 to one. The deliveries of the ROIs are there, but it is not getting the funding to be able to deliver that. That is on a national scale, but that could just as easily apply on a local scale as well.
Q138 Can you comment on how that compares internationally in terms of who we are competing with globally?
Tourism Australia spends more in China than VisitBritain gets as a grant in aid.

Q139 Laura, you have done particular programmes to prove that , when you make those activities and when you do that promotion , there is a really strong ROI. You have provided some evidence. Can you talk about that?

I am happy to. We have very clear ROI on the benefit of marketing campaigns in particular. On a domestic marketing campaign, we see about a 15 to 1 return and over 20 on international, but that is only the marketing part. It is important to think also about that medium to long-term growth of the sector, and that requires investing in the product side as well, otherwise you do not have anything to market later.

Q140 You said 15 to 1 ROI. You do not get that every day, do you? If you look at the successful DMOs, and indeed, unfortunately, those that have failed—even Visit Cornwall went under about a year ago—how can you incentivise, encourage and cajole commercial partners to come in? We all know that both central G overnment and local government funding is really tight, and it has to be, does it not — this mix? DMOs have different models. Some are almost entirely public and some are almost entirely commercial. What needs to be done? What is the magic formula there to get the private sector to come in here also ?

In our case, I do not want to give the impression that the private sector is a panacea. London & Partners overall has a budget of about £42 million, of which about 84% is grant. The private sector is a significant part, but let us be clear that it is still majority grant funded. That is across everything we do. Of that, we would spend as core about £3 million on the experience economy a year. This year, we have an additional £5 million for a marketing campaign. That is nearly all mayoral grant funding. It is not national funding. This is the mayor choosing to invest in what we do for the sector.

Q141 Merryn, in that context, Bernard said that there is potentially £150 million raised for London. Does that scare you as somebody who is outside London? Remember, 50% of all inbound tourism spend is spent within the M25.

They are going to come to London first. We are not under any illusions that people will fly from China directly to Somerset. That is all well and good. The job we have is then to draw them out of London as well so that they extend their stay and we all benefit from that. The sums are astronomical. We have had a lot of conversations about funding being distributed via mayoral authorities. Somerset & Exmoor, nowhere near, not a sniff of it. We feel there is a growing disparity between the regions that have these and those that do not, and we are losing out.
Q142 Do you have any comments, Joss?

You asked what incentive there is for the private sector to be investing in this. My tour operators—I have 140 of them—currently spend about £30 million per year marketing the UK as a destination because it is in their interest to sell the destination. Yes, of course they want Government to fund those demand-driving activities that they will benefit from, but they need to be able to engage with the local product. They need that internationalised trade-ready product. It is in their interest to do it. They want to sell outside London, partly because of the costs of London and partly because of the authentic experiences that you can get across the whole of the United Kingdom as well. They need those new products to keep visitors returning all the time and to keep their overseas partners interested as well. They already do invest. They just need a little bit of help. The LVEPs need to be funded to be able to provide that help to them.
Excellent. Great. Thank you very much, Chair. I look forward to seeing you all at World Travel Market next week.

Q143 I want to come back to this idea of where the locally raised revenue from the levy will end up. A lot of the evidence that we had also touched on the idea that there is no single point where visitor numbers, needs, costs and potential growth are measured. You have your LVEPs, but they are a little bit disjointed. What factors do you think should determine how this tourism growth income gets distributed between areas? The figures that we are looking at show that only 15% of visitors to London make it outside. That is a worry. If everyone is going to be jealously guarding their pot of money, how do you sort that?

Yes, you are right ; I think it is o nly 38% of international visitation into the United Kingdom goes outside London. I will talk about tour operators again. They deliver about 44% of their business outside London, so they are a key mechanism to getting people outside London. If you are looking at this and you are serious about getting business outside London, you need three things: you need the ability for people to be able to get there; you need the right product to get there; and you need the right marketing to make people aware of that access and indeed what the products and experiences are.

Events have a key role to play here. We all saw the Taylor Swift effect and the Oasis effect in driving business , and driving business again outside London. There is probably some role for central Government to look at why we constantly hold the FA Cup in London—there are plenty of other places to have it—and why we have the Euros and the ATP Finals in London. There are huge opportunities, and some funding ought to go into that. What that mechanism is, I think, is probably a bit more difficult to say. I do not think there is a clear route where you should say, “You should avoid London again.” Again, I do not think that is the case. First-time visitors will come to London. We are an island. The growth markets only have access routes into London. The opportunity is to grow London and then encourage those visitors, particularly second-time and third-time visitors, to travel outside London as well. Rather than having a formula per se, it is more around having the strategy and then the metrics within that which will drive that.
Q144 Something like rail packages. You sometimes see at mainline stations they say that you can take a train from here to Oxford or Cambridge.

In most countries in the world, you turn up to the central station and you take a trip down to Orléans, for example, or you might take it down to the Loire Valley, wherever you want to go, but you are probably not going to have to pay £250 on the day to do it. You need the ability to distribute rail fares and access to rail fares before people get here as well and make people aware of that system. There are products such as the BritRail Pass. Most visitors in most international destinations do not expect to be paying £250 for a day trip on the day itself. There are other elements as well. We do not make it easy for people with the multiplicity of ticketing that we have, and there is a lack of translation facilities on the ticketing machines or the kiosks and the ability to be able to speak those languages as well. Getting people out and making sure that people are able to purchase before they arrive to avoid some of those challenges is absolutely important.
Q145 Merryn, congratulations on having the most picturesque commute in the country. I probably have the ugliest one.
You must come to Wells sometimes . There were two points there. You asked about distribution of funding, which I would like to go back to.
Q146 It is a disadvantage for those unfashionable places.

It is a real worry for us w here we are, if the levy is imposed , and distributed and raised via mayoral authorities, what will happen to areas like ours. We do not want to miss out on that. We are already missing out on funding because of that. It seems to me that we have created this local visitor economy partnership system without any funding, and we are talking about maybe creating a new stream of funding without anywhere to distribute it. There is a natural tie-up there.

Going back to the distribution of people out of big cities , not just London, Somerset & Exmoor has about 14% of international visitors —that is all it is— so there is a growth opportunity there. They spend about 24% of the spend. We are very keen to attract more of them. We were lucky enough to show the China National Tourist Office around Wells the other week. The group that came was absolutely blown away and said, “If only we could tell everyone about it.” I t is not that the product is not there; it is that we are not showing it to the markets because we do not have the funding.
Q147 You have to work harder as a non-mayoral destination. Is there a two-tier thing going on?

Absolutely, yes, from what we see. We have wonderful neighbours in Visit West in Bristol . I t is well funded and able to deliver great activities and marketing in its region. It is kind enough often to pass visitors to us to extend their stay or in family trips and things. We are very much concerned about that disparity.

As London, we absolutely want to encourage visitors who come to London to visit other parts of the UK also , not only because it is obviously good for the UK economy but because we know that visitors who also go somewhere else have a better experience. It is good for everyone. We need partners in LVEPs that are well funded that can work with us, and VisitBritain to be funding us over the long term to work together in partnership ; and for VisitBritain to be putting out that narrative about the UK as a multi-destination place—telling people the story of the different places that they can visit as part of a single holiday. We are absolutely ready and willing and keen to partner with the rest of the UK.

Q148 As an outer London MP, there are places within London that they could go to as well. Camden is well established, but in somewhere like Southall there are any number of Indian restaurants and experiences that you could have. Those should be pushed by London & Partners a bit more. There are certain destinations that have a high visitor management cost but relatively few overnight stays—we are going to one next week— such as Blackpool, the Cotswolds and places like that. They may not have the infrastructure for overnight stays, so they are not going to get this levy, but they still need funding. How would you sort that problem?

I use the c ity of Wells, the smallest city in England, as an example. We get calls sometimes from group travel leaders who want to stay in the city, and there are not enough rooms for them, so we then have to push them towards Bath and Bristol, which, though only 20 miles away, is a whole other world. We get the majority of our money from day visitors, and we will lose out again if we do not have the infrastructure to be able to house them, which is why we want the visitor economy to be seen as part of economic growth, the infrastructure, and to get our councils involved with that as well.
Q149 Could you make a formula where the levy does end up reaching into those forgotten corners a bit?
I do not think I can solve the problem there. There is a real risk of missing out in places like the Cotswolds and smaller destinations without adequate hotel space.

Within London, the benefit of having a levy that is connected at a London level is that we have similar issues within the city. If you look at the London borough of Brent, which hosts Wembley Stadium, it has huge numbers of visitors, which comes with significant cost, but actually relatively few of them stay overnight in the borough. If you were to do a levy that was ringfenced at a borough level, it would be left with a lot of costs but would not necessarily get proportionate support for that. There are imbalances between where people spend their time and where they sleep.

Don ’ t just think about the levy. We heard earlier today about the 20% VAT, whereas it might be 9% in France. Of course, you are also paying VAT on all your food and beverage. These taxes are happening. That could be devolved down to the local destination. It is not at the moment, but there might be some opportunities moving forward to look at that.
Q150 Do you think that the London boroughs should get a share of this? Yes or no, if you like.

We have talked about the benefits of spreading that economic benefit out of London, but out of zone 1 or zone 2 as well is absolutely important. We need these destinations to be thriving and buoyant destinations to be able to attract the visitors as well. There must be some mechanism whereby those that are not funded by a levy are still having those base levels of support. If you look at somewhere like Brent, it does not necessarily have the hotel stock, but, actually, it is quite a good place to stay in order to get people into central London while you are not paying central London fees. Maybe there are other opportunities for seeing what levels of support those boroughs can receive as well.

Looking at it from a holistic view, for Somerset & Exmoor, there are places without hotels and bed nights. If we look at Exmoor where 60% of jobs are dependent on the visitor economy, we need them to have some of that benefit even though they might not have loads of hotels right there. It must be spread around a certain area. If the LVEPs were involved with this, we would be able to look at it as a whole and distribute according to the needs of the areas.

A big part of our experience economy programme is working with local councils on their growth ambitions for this sector and how we can support them. We are speaking with local authorities in London week in, week out about how they want to grow their destinations locally. We have really exciting growth opportunities in lots of outer boroughs in London to create genuinely exciting world-class destinations. Our role is not to dictate what those growth ambitions should be , but to back them by supporting them to get investors to come into the borough to build hotels and bring in new attractions and events to the borough. For us, that is an important part of that overall strategy for London, because we know that visitors want authentic local experiences. Yes, of course, they want to come into the city centre and see things like this, but they also want to go to Southall and experience different cultures and different cuisines. That is such an important part of why people come to the city.

Q151 My substantive question has been covered about as far as reaching outside London, and I am really grateful for your answers, so I am going to go straight into my follow-up question. How do we enable more of that regional tourism to take place along the lines of making it internationally bookable so that it is quite easy to see? I can go and book somewhere to stay and things to do in London. How do we spread that out across England and the rest of the UK , and make that commercially viable to do? As a follow-up to the follow-up, can we make better use of social media and AI here? For a lot of people I know, that is their first port of call when they are planning visits. I wonder if that could be part of your answer as well. Thank you, Chair.

Absolutely. We have seen in the last 12 to 18 months a really dramatic shift in the discovery and booking behaviour of consumers. To be honest, the whole industry globally is running to catch up with that. We are really keen to work in partnership with other areas on that bookability of product. We have in the past been funded by VisitBritain to do some work with Manchester, where we have been able to partner with airlines to have flights that come into one destination and then out of the other so that people can do those multi-stop trips. We have also even done it with Paris where we did a partnership with Eurostar so that visitors from the US could come into one city and out of another. That bookability, you are absolutely right, is key. I would echo everything Joss said about the cost and complexity of rail travel being a major barrier to dispersal.

In our region, it is about education for the businesses. It is about tying them up into travel-trade-ready product, which we do not have and we are not strong at. It is a new thing for a lot of people. They do not even know what I am talking about when I approach them and start saying it.

Back to where I was earlier about going to speak to travel trade buyers in Amsterdam, there were only a few businesses that we could represent at that point. When they followed up with asking about packages for people with disabilities, et c , it is a real effort for us to try to find something that will meet their needs. We have been very grateful to the LVEP programme and VisitBritain for helping us get there, but there is a lot of work to do, and if we are not funded we cannot do it.

One of the big challenges is that a lot of people assume that international visitors behave like British people do. They don ’ t. We are pretty happy as Brits travelling internationally to book Eurostar and then a Paris hotel , fine . If you wanted a two-week holiday in China, you would be using an operator, and that is how most of the world sees a trip to the UK. It is complicated. We are not seen as very friendly people. We drive on the wrong side of the road. We have our own currency. We are not seen as very welcoming. It is a big deal. It is a big investment as well. We are a very premium destination for people as well. International people use OTAs, online travel agents, or they will use more traditional tour operators. It is about making sure that businesses know how to work with these people. If 95% of all Chinese people us e an intermediary to travel to the United Kingdom and you are not engaged with those intermediaries, you are not getting sold in China. Any ambition you might have around China as a market will never be realised. It goes back to that point around having the LVEPs, the capacity, the capability and the desire to work with the travel trade that will then get them sold internationally.

You talked very briefly about AI. We are seeing that that is massively changing the way that people discover destinations and people plan for destinations. It is not the way that people are booking destinations. Nobody is handing over £1,500 to ChatGPT in order to take their holiday to the UK. That is just not how it works at the moment. Maybe at some point in the future that will be the case. We have to make sure that, in so far as we can, we have a national tourist board such as VisitWales or VisitBritain that is making people aware of these destinations, but then we need to give people the opportunity to book it, and that is where the trade comes in as well.

Q152 Good morning. I would like to ask a little bit about infrastructure investment and what potential growth that could provide to tourism. Merryn, you might in particular have things to say about this, so perhaps I will start with you. What infrastructure investment would make the greatest difference to the growth of local visitor economies?

In our area, transport. The city that I live in, Wells, does not have a railway station. There is a population of 11,000, and yet I welcome 500,000 people across the drawbridge of the Bishop’s Palace every year. They have to get to us somehow. We are trying to meet net zero targets. We are making people drive. The bus system is not good enough. They are being cut. Our local MP, Tessa Munt, does great work in trying to get bus routes put back in. The trains are expensive. The nearest train station is Castle Cary. That is where everyone goes, too, for the Glastonbury Festival, which is a few minutes away. We really struggle. I know my colleagues in Exmoor would say, “It’s not the last-mile challenge; it’s the last 25-mile challenge to get people there.” We want to be able to pass people around our own county, and it is very difficult.

Rail investment, absolutely. We heard in the earlier session about overnight visitor levies. They work best when the visitors can see what they are being taxed on and where that investment goes. That might be transportation and rail as well.

In terms of investment, there is a real challenge for private sector businesses at the moment, particularly with accommodation as well as attractions. Their operating costs have gone up massively over the past two years. We saw the increases in national minimum wage and the national insurance contributions, and now they are about to suffer an overnight visitor levy as well. That is taking money away from the system and their ability to be able to invest in it.

We heard earlier about the international price competitiveness of the United Kingdom. The World Economic Forum about two and a half or three weeks ago released its report that found that the UK was 106th out of 110 countries for price competitiveness. All the time that prices are increasing, we find that people are reducing their length of stay here. They are not staying quite as long because they have a fixed budget, and more and more of that is being taxed out at the various levels that we have. If we are not price competitive, we had better be damn sure that we are offering the right product and good enough world-class product. These high business costs are deterring businesses from investing: investing in their staff, investing in refurbs and investing in growing their businesses. Investment is absolutely intrinsically linked to that demand and to the international competitiveness, because what people look for first when they choose an international destination is whether it offers value for money. That is N o. 1. No. 2 is whether they get the welcome here.
Q153 Laura, on infrastructure investment, what is the perspective from London?

Critical. We have seen the transformational impact of the Elizabeth line on our tourism industry. That has enabled hundreds of millions of pounds of investment in the Royal Docks and in the extension of Excel, the convention centre, which then has brought significant increased spend. The other key area for us would be affordable housing because we need people to be able to work and live in London to support the sector and to work in the sector and develop careers in it.

Looking beyond more traditional infrastructure towards the infrastructure that enables the visitor economy, we see significant international investor interest in coming into London to build significant new visitor infrastructure, particularly stadiums, arenas and large-scale new immersive experiences as well as hotels. One of the benefits of being an LVEP that sits within a growth agency is that we are the inward investment agency for London. We have teams that deal with large-scale capital investors across all asset classes, and so we are able to work directly with those investors and help them to land those really large-scale investments in visitor infrastructure. For London, it is the transport and the housing and all the multi-sector infrastructure plus that really specific visitor infrastructure.

Q154 If you can divide it like this, was the most useful part of the Elizabeth line the greater connectivity to those destinations in east London, or was it the additional or better method of transport from Heathrow that made a greater impact?

I could not give you any numbers on it, but both have been game changers. A couple of weeks ago, I was at IMEX, which is one of the biggest trade shows globally for the meetings and conventions industry, and spoke to people who organise very large-scale events and choos e between global cities. I heard time and time again that that ability to get their delegates into Heathrow and then whether into the city centre or to Excel has been a game changer for London’s attractiveness.

Q155 That is helpful. My next question was going to ask about the extent to which transport and digital connectivity constrain tourism growth in urban and rural destinations. We have touched on transport a bit already, so if there is anything you want to add there please do. On digital connectivity, is there anything in particular, Merryn?

Yes, I feel I should answer this one because we really struggle in our area. I have been all around the world. I would be absolutely fine using my phone. We do not have 5G in half of Somerset. We don’t have e ven that basic level. In a large-scale tourist attraction, people want to come in. They want to be able to use their phones. They want to be able to livestream as they are walking around. They cannot do it — certainly not in the city of Wells at the moment. That is a real problem. It will be come more of a problem because people are booking much closer to the dates of experience. They wait and see what the weather is like before they book for an attraction. If they cannot do that quickly and easily because of the connectivity, we are really in trouble.

I do not have much to add other than for the visitor in terms of their digital needs , but also businesses and their digital connectivity. We have talked about the preponderance of the use of intermediaries, be that OTAs or tour operators. They all use systems. If you do not have digital broadband and the ability to connect to those systems, you will be at a huge disadvantage.
I have nothing to add to what I have said.
Q156 Finally—this is for all of you—where should Government intervene when commercially weaker destinations cannot attract private investment on their own?

Government intervention takes many forms. We had the Discover England Fund that was around product development, packaging up experiences within England and then being able to distribute them internationally. That came to an end because of the pandemic, regrettably. This new fund, the Connected Destinations Fund, to be able to get people to work across boundaries and LVEPs and to work together for considered and appropriate customer experiences across those boundaries , is an excellent idea. The funding is not massive. The funding is probably £1 million a year, which sounds like a lot of money and of course is a lot of money, but within the grand scheme of things in terms of the £30-odd billion that inbound tourists will bring it is not much money. There are opportunities for supporting and intervening when it can build towards that successful consumer proposition. Here we are. We have the LVEPs across the United Kingdom. Only 22% of them are saying that they will survive for the next five years. The industry needs those LVEPs to be sustainable, and that is where public intervention can make a serious difference.

I think t he Connected Destinations Fund is specifically for partnerships between LVEPs and mayoral strategic authorities, or has a strong leaning towards that. Once again, there is a gap for some of the destinations that need it the most. I will leave it there. You have talked about the funding that we do not have.

The proposed levy should not be a substitute for longer-term G overnment funding into tourism. I know it could be an answer, but there should be something separate to that certainly for smaller destinations.

Within London, we are already currently developing a strategy that will identify where we have the potential to grow new destinations, and that will inform where we need to be investing as a city. Different destinations would have different needs. For some of them, it might be that the barrier is last-mile transport infrastructure.
