Customers do not recognise LVEP boundaries. They come for the experiences. They come for the thematics and the destinations that they want. I do not think it matters if the international visitor understands. Of course they do not. That is not the role of the LVEPs. The role of the LVEPs is to get their businesses ready to accept these visitors and to develop products—we have heard about the international competitiveness—while making sure that the products and experiences are available and world class for our international visitors. It is clear to those of us who work in the industry. For the visitors, I am not sure it is quite so important.
Okay, I will leave it there.

Q135 Thanks for being here. You have all said that you think the structures are right. You all have, effectively, strategic roles. We heard from Jamie, who is the chief executive at Chester Zoo, last week. He described all these various roles of VisitBritain, VisitEngland, the LVEPs and the DMOs as confusing. I have heard similarly from other stakeholders. For individual operators and attractions, are those respective responsibilities clear enough to the people in the industry?

If you were to look at an individual business and where they see the value, where does the value sit in terms of that engagement? It might be the business support that they are offered through their LVEP, the training, getting them travel-trade ready and getting them international ready. It might be working with VisitBritain and the international offices that VisitBritain has. VisitBritain’s international offices are an absolute jewel in the crown , i f you are interested in the Dutch market, working with the people on territory who understand the trade, the media and the operating environment. People will understand better where they see that value most.

As someone who is both an attraction and represent ing the LVEP, the value for the attraction certainly in our area is to be able to make their voices heard louder. There is no point for me as the CEO of the Bishop’s Palace trying to advertise internationally for visitors to come to my organisation. It is the value of joining up and saying, “Hey, Somerset & Exmoor is an amazing place to be.” My role as chair of the LVEP is to communicate this to the organisations within the area and to let them know why we are there and what we can do for them, and that is time-consuming. Most of the businesses are small micro-businesses.

We operate as a social enterprise, a public-private partnership funded partly by grant and partly by businesses. For me, that is really important because if we are not doing things that businesses value they will not pay to participate. We have over 300 businesses in London that are annual paying members of London & Partners, and they really hold us accountable for what we are doing, because if they do not feel that we are adding value they are not going to renew. Additionally, some of them choose to come with us on trade missions to go and sell, particularly around business events, conventions and trade shows. Others also pay from time to time to participate in marketing campaigns. For me, that is a really important test of whether we are doing the right things, because businesses simply would not pay otherwise.

Q136 Building on what we have talked about there, the confusing structure is something that we have all dealt with for a while. You have previously said the purpose of the LVEP was appropriate, but it is not properly funded. We have these layers. As Jeff said, we have heard in previous hearings people saying, “I don’t get what VisitBritain or VisitEngland do.” They do not see the benefit. VisitEngland is primarily domestic promotion and VisitBritain international, and then there is a plethora—I think 100—of DMOs around the country. I have faced it in my area. I have Visit Worcestershire on the border, Visit Gloucestershire, Visit Warwickshire and Experience Oxfordshire all competing to try to get people to the Cotswolds. The purpose of the LVEP was to get that co-operation, get them working together and package in a more appropriate way.

However, i t all goes back to funding. The LVEPs got £4 million. We spent billions supporting the industry during the pandemic. Inbound tourism alone brings in something like £30 billion of export revenue a year, and in return the Government gave £4 million back. By the way, that was my G overnment. It has not got much better. The frustration that you are all expressing of how much the industry gives versus how much it gets in support is one that is really key.

The question that I have for you therefore is this. What is realistic in terms of a long-term funding model? What do you need from the Government and how much do you need from the Government? Is it going to have to be, Laura, your model of saying a little bit of G overnment or taxpayer money, but at the end of the day it has to be primarily commercial? What is realistic here? Sorry, there is lots in there, but you know what we are getting at.

I will start with the small. In Somerset & Exmoor, we have drawn up a menu of what we would fund if funding appeared, and it is a tiny amount. We have choices of 50 grand here and there. If it pops up, we will be ready to act. That only adds up to £200,000 a year, and that would keep us going. About £1.3 billion was put back into the economy in Somerset & Exmoor, which is a huge amount. With just a 5% raise, that would be an extra £64 million. All we need is a couple of £100,000 to keep us going. I can only speak for our area and what I would suggest. We have nothing from Somerset Council—not a penny.
Q137 Joss, is this a familiar story? If you went to the DMOs and LVEPs across the country, do you think they have their very clear ask of how they would use money effectively ready to go?

Absolutely. They are so engaged with their industries. They know exactly what there is to do. I will give a shoutout to VisitEngland. It recently launched a connected destinations fund, which is to get LVEPs working together across boundaries. I talked earlier about consumers and international visitors not necessarily recognising our authority boundaries. That is very good.

In terms of the funding, though, Nigel, I have been around for a long while. When I first joined VisitBritain in 2000 at the turn of the millennium, the funding settlement from central Government was about £35 million a year. Here we are 26 years later, and it is £18 million. If you were to take that £35 million in 2000, it would probably equate to somewhere near £200 million at the moment. Currently, it gets £18 million. It is not a problem of structures. It is not a problem of ambitions or delivery. VisitBritain delivers about 20 or 25 to 1, or in the recently cut business events growth programme 35 to one. The deliveries of the ROIs are there, but it is not getting the funding to be able to deliver that. That is on a national scale, but that could just as easily apply on a local scale as well.
Q138 Can you comment on how that compares internationally in terms of who we are competing with globally?
Tourism Australia spends more in China than VisitBritain gets as a grant in aid.

Q139 Laura, you have done particular programmes to prove that , when you make those activities and when you do that promotion , there is a really strong ROI. You have provided some evidence. Can you talk about that?

I am happy to. We have very clear ROI on the benefit of marketing campaigns in particular. On a domestic marketing campaign, we see about a 15 to 1 return and over 20 on international, but that is only the marketing part. It is important to think also about that medium to long-term growth of the sector, and that requires investing in the product side as well, otherwise you do not have anything to market later.

Q140 You said 15 to 1 ROI. You do not get that every day, do you? If you look at the successful DMOs, and indeed, unfortunately, those that have failed—even Visit Cornwall went under about a year ago—how can you incentivise, encourage and cajole commercial partners to come in? We all know that both central G overnment and local government funding is really tight, and it has to be, does it not — this mix? DMOs have different models. Some are almost entirely public and some are almost entirely commercial. What needs to be done? What is the magic formula there to get the private sector to come in here also ?

In our case, I do not want to give the impression that the private sector is a panacea. London & Partners overall has a budget of about £42 million, of which about 84% is grant. The private sector is a significant part, but let us be clear that it is still majority grant funded. That is across everything we do. Of that, we would spend as core about £3 million on the experience economy a year. This year, we have an additional £5 million for a marketing campaign. That is nearly all mayoral grant funding. It is not national funding. This is the mayor choosing to invest in what we do for the sector.

Q141 Merryn, in that context, Bernard said that there is potentially £150 million raised for London. Does that scare you as somebody who is outside London? Remember, 50% of all inbound tourism spend is spent within the M25.

They are going to come to London first. We are not under any illusions that people will fly from China directly to Somerset. That is all well and good. The job we have is then to draw them out of London as well so that they extend their stay and we all benefit from that. The sums are astronomical. We have had a lot of conversations about funding being distributed via mayoral authorities. Somerset & Exmoor, nowhere near, not a sniff of it. We feel there is a growing disparity between the regions that have these and those that do not, and we are losing out.
Q142 Do you have any comments, Joss?

You asked what incentive there is for the private sector to be investing in this. My tour operators—I have 140 of them—currently spend about £30 million per year marketing the UK as a destination because it is in their interest to sell the destination. Yes, of course they want Government to fund those demand-driving activities that they will benefit from, but they need to be able to engage with the local product. They need that internationalised trade-ready product. It is in their interest to do it. They want to sell outside London, partly because of the costs of London and partly because of the authentic experiences that you can get across the whole of the United Kingdom as well. They need those new products to keep visitors returning all the time and to keep their overseas partners interested as well. They already do invest. They just need a little bit of help. The LVEPs need to be funded to be able to provide that help to them.
Excellent. Great. Thank you very much, Chair. I look forward to seeing you all at World Travel Market next week.

Q143 I want to come back to this idea of where the locally raised revenue from the levy will end up. A lot of the evidence that we had also touched on the idea that there is no single point where visitor numbers, needs, costs and potential growth are measured. You have your LVEPs, but they are a little bit disjointed. What factors do you think should determine how this tourism growth income gets distributed between areas? The figures that we are looking at show that only 15% of visitors to London make it outside. That is a worry. If everyone is going to be jealously guarding their pot of money, how do you sort that?

Yes, you are right ; I think it is o nly 38% of international visitation into the United Kingdom goes outside London. I will talk about tour operators again. They deliver about 44% of their business outside London, so they are a key mechanism to getting people outside London. If you are looking at this and you are serious about getting business outside London, you need three things: you need the ability for people to be able to get there; you need the right product to get there; and you need the right marketing to make people aware of that access and indeed what the products and experiences are.

Events have a key role to play here. We all saw the Taylor Swift effect and the Oasis effect in driving business , and driving business again outside London. There is probably some role for central Government to look at why we constantly hold the FA Cup in London—there are plenty of other places to have it—and why we have the Euros and the ATP Finals in London. There are huge opportunities, and some funding ought to go into that. What that mechanism is, I think, is probably a bit more difficult to say. I do not think there is a clear route where you should say, “You should avoid London again.” Again, I do not think that is the case. First-time visitors will come to London. We are an island. The growth markets only have access routes into London. The opportunity is to grow London and then encourage those visitors, particularly second-time and third-time visitors, to travel outside London as well. Rather than having a formula per se, it is more around having the strategy and then the metrics within that which will drive that.
Q144 Something like rail packages. You sometimes see at mainline stations they say that you can take a train from here to Oxford or Cambridge.

In most countries in the world, you turn up to the central station and you take a trip down to Orléans, for example, or you might take it down to the Loire Valley, wherever you want to go, but you are probably not going to have to pay £250 on the day to do it. You need the ability to distribute rail fares and access to rail fares before people get here as well and make people aware of that system. There are products such as the BritRail Pass. Most visitors in most international destinations do not expect to be paying £250 for a day trip on the day itself. There are other elements as well. We do not make it easy for people with the multiplicity of ticketing that we have, and there is a lack of translation facilities on the ticketing machines or the kiosks and the ability to be able to speak those languages as well. Getting people out and making sure that people are able to purchase before they arrive to avoid some of those challenges is absolutely important.
Q145 Merryn, congratulations on having the most picturesque commute in the country. I probably have the ugliest one.
You must come to Wells sometimes . There were two points there. You asked about distribution of funding, which I would like to go back to.
Q146 It is a disadvantage for those unfashionable places.

It is a real worry for us w here we are, if the levy is imposed , and distributed and raised via mayoral authorities, what will happen to areas like ours. We do not want to miss out on that. We are already missing out on funding because of that. It seems to me that we have created this local visitor economy partnership system without any funding, and we are talking about maybe creating a new stream of funding without anywhere to distribute it. There is a natural tie-up there.

Going back to the distribution of people out of big cities , not just London, Somerset & Exmoor has about 14% of international visitors —that is all it is— so there is a growth opportunity there. They spend about 24% of the spend. We are very keen to attract more of them. We were lucky enough to show the China National Tourist Office around Wells the other week. The group that came was absolutely blown away and said, “If only we could tell everyone about it.” I t is not that the product is not there; it is that we are not showing it to the markets because we do not have the funding.
Q147 You have to work harder as a non-mayoral destination. Is there a two-tier thing going on?

Absolutely, yes, from what we see. We have wonderful neighbours in Visit West in Bristol . I t is well funded and able to deliver great activities and marketing in its region. It is kind enough often to pass visitors to us to extend their stay or in family trips and things. We are very much concerned about that disparity.

As London, we absolutely want to encourage visitors who come to London to visit other parts of the UK also , not only because it is obviously good for the UK economy but because we know that visitors who also go somewhere else have a better experience. It is good for everyone. We need partners in LVEPs that are well funded that can work with us, and VisitBritain to be funding us over the long term to work together in partnership ; and for VisitBritain to be putting out that narrative about the UK as a multi-destination place—telling people the story of the different places that they can visit as part of a single holiday. We are absolutely ready and willing and keen to partner with the rest of the UK.

Q148 As an outer London MP, there are places within London that they could go to as well. Camden is well established, but in somewhere like Southall there are any number of Indian restaurants and experiences that you could have. Those should be pushed by London & Partners a bit more. There are certain destinations that have a high visitor management cost but relatively few overnight stays—we are going to one next week— such as Blackpool, the Cotswolds and places like that. They may not have the infrastructure for overnight stays, so they are not going to get this levy, but they still need funding. How would you sort that problem?

I use the c ity of Wells, the smallest city in England, as an example. We get calls sometimes from group travel leaders who want to stay in the city, and there are not enough rooms for them, so we then have to push them towards Bath and Bristol, which, though only 20 miles away, is a whole other world. We get the majority of our money from day visitors, and we will lose out again if we do not have the infrastructure to be able to house them, which is why we want the visitor economy to be seen as part of economic growth, the infrastructure, and to get our councils involved with that as well.
Q149 Could you make a formula where the levy does end up reaching into those forgotten corners a bit?
I do not think I can solve the problem there. There is a real risk of missing out in places like the Cotswolds and smaller destinations without adequate hotel space.

Within London, the benefit of having a levy that is connected at a London level is that we have similar issues within the city. If you look at the London borough of Brent, which hosts Wembley Stadium, it has huge numbers of visitors, which comes with significant cost, but actually relatively few of them stay overnight in the borough. If you were to do a levy that was ringfenced at a borough level, it would be left with a lot of costs but would not necessarily get proportionate support for that. There are imbalances between where people spend their time and where they sleep.

Don ’ t just think about the levy. We heard earlier today about the 20% VAT, whereas it might be 9% in France. Of course, you are also paying VAT on all your food and beverage. These taxes are happening. That could be devolved down to the local destination. It is not at the moment, but there might be some opportunities moving forward to look at that.
Q150 Do you think that the London boroughs should get a share of this? Yes or no, if you like.

We have talked about the benefits of spreading that economic benefit out of London, but out of zone 1 or zone 2 as well is absolutely important. We need these destinations to be thriving and buoyant destinations to be able to attract the visitors as well. There must be some mechanism whereby those that are not funded by a levy are still having those base levels of support. If you look at somewhere like Brent, it does not necessarily have the hotel stock, but, actually, it is quite a good place to stay in order to get people into central London while you are not paying central London fees. Maybe there are other opportunities for seeing what levels of support those boroughs can receive as well.

Looking at it from a holistic view, for Somerset & Exmoor, there are places without hotels and bed nights. If we look at Exmoor where 60% of jobs are dependent on the visitor economy, we need them to have some of that benefit even though they might not have loads of hotels right there. It must be spread around a certain area. If the LVEPs were involved with this, we would be able to look at it as a whole and distribute according to the needs of the areas.

A big part of our experience economy programme is working with local councils on their growth ambitions for this sector and how we can support them. We are speaking with local authorities in London week in, week out about how they want to grow their destinations locally. We have really exciting growth opportunities in lots of outer boroughs in London to create genuinely exciting world-class destinations. Our role is not to dictate what those growth ambitions should be , but to back them by supporting them to get investors to come into the borough to build hotels and bring in new attractions and events to the borough. For us, that is an important part of that overall strategy for London, because we know that visitors want authentic local experiences. Yes, of course, they want to come into the city centre and see things like this, but they also want to go to Southall and experience different cultures and different cuisines. That is such an important part of why people come to the city.

Q151 My substantive question has been covered about as far as reaching outside London, and I am really grateful for your answers, so I am going to go straight into my follow-up question. How do we enable more of that regional tourism to take place along the lines of making it internationally bookable so that it is quite easy to see? I can go and book somewhere to stay and things to do in London. How do we spread that out across England and the rest of the UK , and make that commercially viable to do? As a follow-up to the follow-up, can we make better use of social media and AI here? For a lot of people I know, that is their first port of call when they are planning visits. I wonder if that could be part of your answer as well. Thank you, Chair.

Absolutely. We have seen in the last 12 to 18 months a really dramatic shift in the discovery and booking behaviour of consumers. To be honest, the whole industry globally is running to catch up with that. We are really keen to work in partnership with other areas on that bookability of product. We have in the past been funded by VisitBritain to do some work with Manchester, where we have been able to partner with airlines to have flights that come into one destination and then out of the other so that people can do those multi-stop trips. We have also even done it with Paris where we did a partnership with Eurostar so that visitors from the US could come into one city and out of another. That bookability, you are absolutely right, is key. I would echo everything Joss said about the cost and complexity of rail travel being a major barrier to dispersal.

In our region, it is about education for the businesses. It is about tying them up into travel-trade-ready product, which we do not have and we are not strong at. It is a new thing for a lot of people. They do not even know what I am talking about when I approach them and start saying it.

Back to where I was earlier about going to speak to travel trade buyers in Amsterdam, there were only a few businesses that we could represent at that point. When they followed up with asking about packages for people with disabilities, et c , it is a real effort for us to try to find something that will meet their needs. We have been very grateful to the LVEP programme and VisitBritain for helping us get there, but there is a lot of work to do, and if we are not funded we cannot do it.

One of the big challenges is that a lot of people assume that international visitors behave like British people do. They don ’ t. We are pretty happy as Brits travelling internationally to book Eurostar and then a Paris hotel , fine . If you wanted a two-week holiday in China, you would be using an operator, and that is how most of the world sees a trip to the UK. It is complicated. We are not seen as very friendly people. We drive on the wrong side of the road. We have our own currency. We are not seen as very welcoming. It is a big deal. It is a big investment as well. We are a very premium destination for people as well. International people use OTAs, online travel agents, or they will use more traditional tour operators. It is about making sure that businesses know how to work with these people. If 95% of all Chinese people us e an intermediary to travel to the United Kingdom and you are not engaged with those intermediaries, you are not getting sold in China. Any ambition you might have around China as a market will never be realised. It goes back to that point around having the LVEPs, the capacity, the capability and the desire to work with the travel trade that will then get them sold internationally.

You talked very briefly about AI. We are seeing that that is massively changing the way that people discover destinations and people plan for destinations. It is not the way that people are booking destinations. Nobody is handing over £1,500 to ChatGPT in order to take their holiday to the UK. That is just not how it works at the moment. Maybe at some point in the future that will be the case. We have to make sure that, in so far as we can, we have a national tourist board such as VisitWales or VisitBritain that is making people aware of these destinations, but then we need to give people the opportunity to book it, and that is where the trade comes in as well.

Q152 Good morning. I would like to ask a little bit about infrastructure investment and what potential growth that could provide to tourism. Merryn, you might in particular have things to say about this, so perhaps I will start with you. What infrastructure investment would make the greatest difference to the growth of local visitor economies?

In our area, transport. The city that I live in, Wells, does not have a railway station. There is a population of 11,000, and yet I welcome 500,000 people across the drawbridge of the Bishop’s Palace every year. They have to get to us somehow. We are trying to meet net zero targets. We are making people drive. The bus system is not good enough. They are being cut. Our local MP, Tessa Munt, does great work in trying to get bus routes put back in. The trains are expensive. The nearest train station is Castle Cary. That is where everyone goes, too, for the Glastonbury Festival, which is a few minutes away. We really struggle. I know my colleagues in Exmoor would say, “It’s not the last-mile challenge; it’s the last 25-mile challenge to get people there.” We want to be able to pass people around our own county, and it is very difficult.

Rail investment, absolutely. We heard in the earlier session about overnight visitor levies. They work best when the visitors can see what they are being taxed on and where that investment goes. That might be transportation and rail as well.

In terms of investment, there is a real challenge for private sector businesses at the moment, particularly with accommodation as well as attractions. Their operating costs have gone up massively over the past two years. We saw the increases in national minimum wage and the national insurance contributions, and now they are about to suffer an overnight visitor levy as well. That is taking money away from the system and their ability to be able to invest in it.

We heard earlier about the international price competitiveness of the United Kingdom. The World Economic Forum about two and a half or three weeks ago released its report that found that the UK was 106th out of 110 countries for price competitiveness. All the time that prices are increasing, we find that people are reducing their length of stay here. They are not staying quite as long because they have a fixed budget, and more and more of that is being taxed out at the various levels that we have. If we are not price competitive, we had better be damn sure that we are offering the right product and good enough world-class product. These high business costs are deterring businesses from investing: investing in their staff, investing in refurbs and investing in growing their businesses. Investment is absolutely intrinsically linked to that demand and to the international competitiveness, because what people look for first when they choose an international destination is whether it offers value for money. That is N o. 1. No. 2 is whether they get the welcome here.
Q153 Laura, on infrastructure investment, what is the perspective from London?

Critical. We have seen the transformational impact of the Elizabeth line on our tourism industry. That has enabled hundreds of millions of pounds of investment in the Royal Docks and in the extension of Excel, the convention centre, which then has brought significant increased spend. The other key area for us would be affordable housing because we need people to be able to work and live in London to support the sector and to work in the sector and develop careers in it.

Looking beyond more traditional infrastructure towards the infrastructure that enables the visitor economy, we see significant international investor interest in coming into London to build significant new visitor infrastructure, particularly stadiums, arenas and large-scale new immersive experiences as well as hotels. One of the benefits of being an LVEP that sits within a growth agency is that we are the inward investment agency for London. We have teams that deal with large-scale capital investors across all asset classes, and so we are able to work directly with those investors and help them to land those really large-scale investments in visitor infrastructure. For London, it is the transport and the housing and all the multi-sector infrastructure plus that really specific visitor infrastructure.

Q154 If you can divide it like this, was the most useful part of the Elizabeth line the greater connectivity to those destinations in east London, or was it the additional or better method of transport from Heathrow that made a greater impact?

I could not give you any numbers on it, but both have been game changers. A couple of weeks ago, I was at IMEX, which is one of the biggest trade shows globally for the meetings and conventions industry, and spoke to people who organise very large-scale events and choos e between global cities. I heard time and time again that that ability to get their delegates into Heathrow and then whether into the city centre or to Excel has been a game changer for London’s attractiveness.

Q155 That is helpful. My next question was going to ask about the extent to which transport and digital connectivity constrain tourism growth in urban and rural destinations. We have touched on transport a bit already, so if there is anything you want to add there please do. On digital connectivity, is there anything in particular, Merryn?

Yes, I feel I should answer this one because we really struggle in our area. I have been all around the world. I would be absolutely fine using my phone. We do not have 5G in half of Somerset. We don’t have e ven that basic level. In a large-scale tourist attraction, people want to come in. They want to be able to use their phones. They want to be able to livestream as they are walking around. They cannot do it — certainly not in the city of Wells at the moment. That is a real problem. It will be come more of a problem because people are booking much closer to the dates of experience. They wait and see what the weather is like before they book for an attraction. If they cannot do that quickly and easily because of the connectivity, we are really in trouble.

I do not have much to add other than for the visitor in terms of their digital needs , but also businesses and their digital connectivity. We have talked about the preponderance of the use of intermediaries, be that OTAs or tour operators. They all use systems. If you do not have digital broadband and the ability to connect to those systems, you will be at a huge disadvantage.
I have nothing to add to what I have said.
Q156 Finally—this is for all of you—where should Government intervene when commercially weaker destinations cannot attract private investment on their own?

Government intervention takes many forms. We had the Discover England Fund that was around product development, packaging up experiences within England and then being able to distribute them internationally. That came to an end because of the pandemic, regrettably. This new fund, the Connected Destinations Fund, to be able to get people to work across boundaries and LVEPs and to work together for considered and appropriate customer experiences across those boundaries , is an excellent idea. The funding is not massive. The funding is probably £1 million a year, which sounds like a lot of money and of course is a lot of money, but within the grand scheme of things in terms of the £30-odd billion that inbound tourists will bring it is not much money. There are opportunities for supporting and intervening when it can build towards that successful consumer proposition. Here we are. We have the LVEPs across the United Kingdom. Only 22% of them are saying that they will survive for the next five years. The industry needs those LVEPs to be sustainable, and that is where public intervention can make a serious difference.

I think t he Connected Destinations Fund is specifically for partnerships between LVEPs and mayoral strategic authorities, or has a strong leaning towards that. Once again, there is a gap for some of the destinations that need it the most. I will leave it there. You have talked about the funding that we do not have.

The proposed levy should not be a substitute for longer-term G overnment funding into tourism. I know it could be an answer, but there should be something separate to that certainly for smaller destinations.

Within London, we are already currently developing a strategy that will identify where we have the potential to grow new destinations, and that will inform where we need to be investing as a city. Different destinations would have different needs. For some of them, it might be that the barrier is last-mile transport infrastructure. For others, it might be that the public rail is not good enough. For others, it might be that they are missing an anchor attraction or some surrounding F&B. For others, it might be that the destination is fantastic but nobody knows about it and they really need a marketing push. We need to be tailored and work through with local areas what the different interventions are that will support them from the starting point that they are at and that will reach the growth ambitions that they have for their local area.

Q157 Joss, the Tourism Alliance said that , whenever we have the national visitor economy strategy , the Government should set out clearly which bodies are responsible for what and where the accountability is. Who ultimately should be accountable for delivering the Government’s ambitions for tourism?

Tourism is everyone’s business, for a start. One of the challenges that we have is that not all the levers required for a successful visitor economy sit within the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. We have heard about aviation from the Department for Transport. We have the Treasury around the taxation system, the Home Office around the visas and the ETAs, and DEFRA around some of the rural communities. We need a growth strategy that has delivery mechanisms within it, named delivery bodies across G overnment and accountability there. We would like to see some type of strategic tourism panel that sits across a lot of decision making across G overnment. We heard earlier today about the intraministerial groups, which is absent at the moment. We need to see that accountability that sits across G overnment within that growth strategy whenever it arrives. Without some of those delivery mechanisms, the targets and the proper funding, a strategy is purely a wish list. We really need to see within that funding commitments over a serious amount of time and multi-year resources. We need the timetable. We need the accountable delivery bodies. That needs to sit across G overnment as well .
Q158 Laura and Merryn, would you agree? Do you have anything to add?
Taking Laura’s example of Visit London sitting within the broader economic infrastructure, we need tourism to be treated as part of that infrastructure rather than just some marketing subject.
Q159 That seems to be a clear priority for the forthcoming strategy. What other key priorities would you like to see?

In terms of the Tourism Alliance, we would like to see various elements within it. As I say, it needs to be that cross-government approach to it. We need to try to improve , where we can , any of the understanding across officials and Ministers in terms of the importance of the visitor economy to placemaking, employment and jobs. There is a whole raft of activities within the submission that we have ma de, but a lot of it is around multi-year funding, measurable targets and named delivery bodies that will really help our sector achieve its ambitions. We have lofty ambitions, and we need to make sure that those ambitions and the opportunity are matched by the investment from Government as well. We have a £ 50 million target. That is achievable. We need to make sure that that economic benefit is spread across the whole of the United Kingdom. We need the structures and the support through the LVEPs that will enable that target to be met as well.
I second that.

Tourism was not identified as a priority sector in the modern industrial strategy. At a London level, it is one of our five priority sectors in the London growth plan . In London, we have chosen to define it as the experience economy rather than tourism, the distinction being that the experience economy includes the spend of the 9 million Londoners who, for us, are a very important audience. It also recognises that the value of the experience economy is not just in the economic benefit of the transaction itself but in the placemaking, and that the experience economy is what makes London a destination that global talent wants to be in and that global investors want to be in so that the sector has a value beyond its direct GDP. That is why we have defined it as the experience economy. In London, it is in our industrial strategy. It is one of the five priority sectors. That has made a significant difference , I think, to the commitment of the strategic authority to continue to invest in it and to our ability to convene industry and stakeholders around it.

As we have heard, this sector will always be a team sport. Nobody will ever hold all the levers. Besides all the ones that you have mentioned at national level, even within London, we might be the LVEP but we are so reliant on local councils, Transport for London, the police and , of course , industry, which is the one that delivers the product every day. We have to think about this as a team sport.
Last but not least, Alison.

Q160 Thank you, Chair. Coming off the back of the national visitor economy strategy , tourism and growth are so closely aligned, and it seems to me that with coastal destinations— I should say I am the chair of the APPG for coastal communities—some of our towns on the coast are the most attractive to visitors but the hardest to get to. Would you agree that the transport corridor issue, which has been touched on, is so important when Government are drawing up the strategy? Perhaps I could come to you first, Joss.

Yes, absolutely. We need to react to the modern-day realities. A lot of the infrastructure developments that you see around rail in terms of engineering works take place during the school holidays at exactly the time that visitors are likely to be travelling. I saw Network Rail saying that the busiest day on the English railway system is Friday, and that is because of commuters. You may see a decrease of commuters on the Friday, but it is also those leisure visitors travelling. The busiest day on the Scottish transport system is a Saturday these days. Why on earth are we having engineering works on the days when visitors want to move mostly? In some areas, it is going to be last mile, and in some areas it is going to be last 25 miles . How can technology help assist with that either in terms of managing the existing infrastructure or, looking to the future, how can it help some of those transportation issues? It absolutely has to be key.

All tourism relies on three things: means, money and motivation. Do people want to go there? Do they have the money to do it? Can they access the destination? That access to a destination is absolutely key. Most international visitors when travelling on a city break do not want to travel more than two hours from their point of entry into the country for a short break. R ealising that regional ambition and that regional economy is about making sure that we are able to encourage more direct routes into some of the regional airports, because that would facilitate access to some of these coastal and rural destinations.

For Somerset & Exmoor, we have some very well-known coastal destinations such as Weston-super-Mare, Burnham and Minehead. They are mostly popular with domestic visitors. A lot of people from the midlands choose to visit that area. They can just about make it on the train a certain distance, and then it all falls to pieces. One of the most beautiful bus routes is from Porlock through to Lynton and Lynmouth. My colleague from Visit Exmoor is sitting behind me. I believe they have to fight for it in tourist season every year to run at decent times. It is an absolutely stunning bus journey, and yet it keeps getting the threat of being cut. How are we to get people to Minehead or Lynton and Lynmouth if we do not have those bus services?
You do not need to hear from me on coastal tourism.

Could I add on that? We talked a lot about the overnight visitor levy. I mentioned it tends to work best when the visitors can see what they have actually invested in. There are examples across Europe. When you arrive at Interlaken and you go to your hotel, you will be given a little booklet. Of course, it could just as easily be a digital booklet nowadays. That allows you free travel with your bicycle on the local bus services. That free travel with your bicycle on local bus services is also available to local residents, and it is supported by the overnight visitor levy. You can see how that might help in driving some of that regional spread in a more sustainable fashion to get people out and about and to some of these destinations that are perhaps slightly more challenging to reach.

Q161 That is really helpful. Thank you very much. Thank you for your time today. You have all been brilliant. We are really grateful for all your very thorough answers to our questions. Before I let you go, was there anything that you were burning to tell us that no one thought to ask you? Joss ?

I referenced it before. The sector needs a five-year funded growth plan. It needs to be published. There needs to be accountability across G overnment. There needs to be investment in destination development and investment in marketing.
Q162 I am writing it all down.
Tourism is a key opportunity for growth. If we are looking for growth in this country, we know there are huge opportunities.
Q163 A recognition of the huge firepower of tourism to drive the growth that the Government are looking for.
Yes.
Q164 Very good. Laura, finally.
I would come back to the very first question, which is that we have made really significant progress on getting the right governance structures in place. Now we need to fund them to be effective.
Brilliant. Thank you very much, all of you.

segs.tx: Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The future of farming , HC 216
Tuesday 27 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 27 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Alistair Carmichael (Chair); Sarah Bool; Charlie Dewhirst; Helena Dollimore; Sarah Dyke; Ben Goldsborough; Terry Jermy; Josh Newbury; Henry Tufnell.
Questions 119 - 297
Witnesses
I : Stephen Morgan MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, DEFRA; Mike Rowe, Farming Director, DEFRA; Gareth Baynham-Hughes, Director of Marine and Fisheries, DEFRA.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Stephen Morgan MP, Mike Rowe and Gareth Baynham-Hughes .

Q119 Good morning, everyone, and welcome to this meeting of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee. T his morning we return to our inquiry in relation to the work of the Department and its arm’s length bodies. Welcome, Minister , to the Committee . Just for the benefit of those who are following our proceedings and for the record, I invite you all to introduce yourselves to the Committee , and I will start with you, Mike.
Good morning, I am Director General for Food and Farming in DEFRA .
I am Member of Parliament for Portsmouth South and Minister for Food, Fisheries and Farming.
Good morning, I am the d irector for Marine and Fisheries.

Q120 W e have a lot of material to cover this morning so we will just crack on. First, congratulations on your appointment , Minister. You were originally appointed as a Minister of State by Keir Starmer and then reappointed by Andy Burnham as a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State. What is the difference between the two jobs in terms of how you are able to do it?

It is a real privilege to be before the Committee today . It is my first time before the Select Committee ; indeed , the first time before a Select Committee as a Minister of this Government. It is a real privilege to be the Minister for Food, Fisheries and Farming, now appointed twice by two separate Prime Ministers. To have the opportunity to serve in Government representing a constituency that looks to the sea for its food and livelihood is a real pleasure.

I have been conscious that the Government have been working really hard on a whole range of areas including the “L and U se F ramework ” , the “F arming R oadmap ” and other initiatives, and that actually it has been a very challenging time for farmers across the country. We always say that farmers are used to dealing with change, but they do not take resilience for granted. That is why I have been really keen to get out and about across the country to engage with our fishermen and our farmers on the issues and challenges that they face. As a result of that it is very clear to me that we need to do more to support the resilience of the sector across our country.

Q121 I thank you for that . M indful of the fact that you yourself appear to have a hard stop at noon c an we maybe just keep questions and answers for everybody tight? The question was, what is the difference between being a Parliamentary Under-Secretary and a Minister of State?
E ssentially they are just different grades within the Department , are they not ? O bviously my responsibility —
Q122 Does it have an impact on how you are able to do the job?
No, I do not believe so . M y job is to listen to the sector , to act on what I am told, and to make decisions that are based on evidence before me.

Q123 I want to start this morning by looking at a few issues around fisheries. The Committee has its inquiry into fisheries and the marine environment. We have published our first report, “ R esetting the r elationship with f ishing c ommunities. ” We have had your response. Read ing it short y ou are quite happy with the relationship between the industry , the communities and the Government ?

We also work in partnership with fishing and seafood sectors. There are lots of ways that the Government already do that; I have made it a priority in my first few months in post representing Portsmouth South with a small fishing community. I am not complacent, and that is why I am really keen to engage with communities across the country, which is why I visited Newlyn, I have been up to Scotland, Fraserburgh, Peterhead and I have been to Weymouth. I have been to Grimsby to meet fishermen directly to talk to processors and others.
Q124 In our report we suggested the creation of regional management groups. That was an idea that did not find favour with you. What is your objection to them?

We already engage through regional fisheries groups, and we have certainly taken on board the feedback with regard to improved communication with the MMO; I have also spent time with the MMO in Portsmouth. There are lots of ways that the Department already engages with the fishing community. There is always more we can do, but I want to make sure that engagement is meaningful and improves outcomes to drive the agenda that we want to see, which is a thriving, sustainable fishing community.
Q125 Do you see no need for regional management plans?

There are already structures in place. There are online meetings and physical meetings. I have been very impressed by how I have seen the MMO engaging with the fishing community. There is obviously work in hand around negotiations currently . I regularly engage with the fishing community , and I have established a regular forum to meet with representative bodies . I am always keen to learn from the Committee as well.
Q126 We also suggested a sea use framework, akin to the “L and U se F ramework ” . You did not like that idea either?

I welcome the work of the APPG for fisheries and I am due to meet representatives of the APPG in the next few days. Coming into post i t strikes me that there is not a particularly clear strategy around fisheries. I will therefore use the feedback from this Committee and the APPG to set out a direction of travel to support our fisheries communities for the future.
Q127 The APPG’s plan for a thriving and sustainable UK fishing industry said that you should produce a fishing strategy within the next 12 months. Is that something you can commit to doing?

As I mentioned I have come into post and seen that there is no strategy. I am very keen to work with my Department, my officials , and the sector to think through the long-term vision for our fishing communities.
Q128 Is that a commitment to one in 12 months or not?
I am meeting with colleagues of the APPG in the coming days.
Q129 We could write th e strategy tomorrow , though it would o nly be meaningful if you produce it.
I recognise the value of a strategy, and I am keen to work through that in partnership with others.
Q130 Okay, I will take that as a no, then. I am going to look at the year-end negotiations that have started this week. Who is leading for us in them?
Priorities around fishing, for me, are obviously the negotiations with our coastal states, making sure we get the best deals through the best negotiations —
Q131 Who is leading the negotiations, Minister ?
It is D EFRA officials.
Q132 Yes, DEFRA officials , so i t is not yourself or Mike. Who will it be ?

I t w ill be Gareth from my Department. I obviously set the parameters for that and the principles for the negotiations and then hand over to officials to work through the detail with coastal states and others.
Q133 Would you anticipate getting involved at any stage?

Of course. I have obviously seen the principles for the negotiations; I cannot get into the detail of how those negotiations will proceed. My engagement with the sector has obviously been key to those negotiations, as have some of the visits that I have made to Norway and other places, to understand some of the issues and challenges.

Q134 I want to look first at the position around Northern Shelf c od. Given that there are three distinct sub-stocks , are you content that the ICES advice for a zero TAC—total allowable catch—is a sensible basis for negotiation?
I obviously cannot comment on live negotiations.

Q135 No, I am not asking you to . I am asking if you are content that that is a sensible way to negotiate. You have three distinct biological sub-stocks in the northern, the Viking and the southern areas, but they are being treated as one.
I have seen advice. It is important that, in terms of negotiations, we follow the science. T hese are obviously very much live discussions, and I will bring in Gareth on that point .

Our starting point is the science. There has been a lot of work over the last year or so with ICES—the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea—to look specifically at all the scientific questions around c od, including the sub-stock question. It has set up a tiger team. Actually the Minister is not aware that we had a letter yesterday from ICES thanking the UK scientists for their contribution on that. That gives a reasonable basis with a range of scenarios for a negotiation that will then take place for Northern Shelf c od between EU, UK and Norway. A zero TAC advice is always extremely difficult, including the risk of closing other fisheries if you cannot have any bycatch , so i t is complicated.
Q136 If you ha d a zero TAC for c od in the North s ea, what would the implications be for other whitefish species?
The implications would be severe.
It would be a j oke .

That is why consideration has to be given to other measures. There has been work throughout the year with the sector as well on additional measures such as spatial closures or other forms of closure that could provide stock protection but allow some other fisheries to continue. As the Minister says, these are live negotiations.
Q137 What is the Government’s assessment of the relative health of the three different sub-stocks?

I do not know the very latest formal assessment , obviously, as w e were part of the ICES tiger team; that does suggest there is still uncertainty around the sub-stock in the southern North s ea in particular. There are ways in which scientists are trying to understand the different recovery potentials of the sub-stocks, which are all managed as a single stock in these negotiations. Those are the things that the expert negotiators, not just from the UK but from other countries, work through. We take industry position inputs into this kind of negotiation ; for example , last week we received material from some of the Scottish whitefish producers setting out alternative ways in which you could manage this fishery.
Q138 Are you content to negotiate on the basis of it being a single entity, even though they are all different?
At the end of the day there will be a single TAC agreed for those three stocks because t hat is the way the northern shelf cod is managed.
Q139 Is that the way you view them ?
I expect it to reflect an intricate understanding of the science around the stocks.

Q140 Okay. I want to look at the imbalance between the fish that are taken as a consequence of the bilateral between the UK and Norway. Last year, Norway caught 22,581 tonnes of whitefish in UK waters. We caught 9,496 tonnes in Norwegian waters. How d id we get to that outcome?

I recognise the importance of partnership with Norway, which is why an early visit was to Norway to meet with my equivalent Minister, to make sure that we continue to get the best possible outcome for the UK fishing industry. I am aware of the concerns that you yourself have raised, Alistair.
Q141 Is that the best possible outcome, 22,000 to 9,000 ?

I am aware of the challenges around Shetland in particular, which is why I have written to you and said I am keen to come up to Shetland next month , or indeed in December. Under the current terms it is obviously a reciprocal relationship between the UK and Norway , t herefore Norwegian vessels can come into UK waters and vice versa. I am conscious of the balance and we will obviously continue to engage with stakeholders on these issues to make sure UK interests are at the heart.
Q142 This is something that is under review in this round of negotiations, is it not?
T he current arrangements will be , yes.
There was something placed in the written —
Q143 We are looking for something that is better than what we have , are we not?

There is an overall balance, as the Minister said, within the reciprocal access. For some parts of the fleet that access is working really well; for others there is the imbalance you have talked about.

Our interest s , working with the sector and with the Scottish Government, will be to find the best UK position and then to try to secure the best outcome with Norway. We met with the sector at official level yesterday, and they wrote to the Minister to follow up and to thank officials for the engagement.
Q144 What about the best position from the point of view of conservation of stocks?
All those access agreements reflect the separate total allowable catch setting process that includes taking the scientific advice as part of it.
Let us go to s aithe, s pecifically.
To s aithe, y es.

Q145 You heard me speak about the Norwegian fishing trawler, the Havstrand, which is a 70-metre refrigerated trawler that catches 787 tonnes of s aithe in one trip. Putting that into its context , that is 50% of the entire Shetland fleet catch for a whole year, and 12% of the UK quota for s aithe in the North s ea.

Bad though these statistics are, if you drill down the catch apps suggest that in fact the majority of that catch is smaller-sized s aithe, which we should really be leaving in the sea, should we not? According to ICES, s aithe is a species that is under biological pressure, so it is subject to overall TAC reductions this year. Do you think the deal that you did last year helps or hinders that?
I do not know that I have a specific answer on it ; o bviously , we are aware of the overall statistics.
Q146 There are two options here, Gareth : d oes it help or does it hinder?

I do not know that I would have phrased the question in that way. The way that we take forward the negotiations is to secure outcomes that are backed by and reflect the science, and that includes things such as catch composition and the state of the stock by year class; we have a good understanding of that. That is what goes into the overall TAC agreements, and then through the negotiations on access, that does not undermine that science.
Q147 Are you content that the bulk of that fishing effort should be in the north - north-east of UK waters, specifically around Shetland?

I am sorry, but I do not have enough information to hand about any particular pressures for that stock beyond the overall stock level. What I can say is these are all issues that we have been talking through. We had the Shetland Fishermen’s Association yesterday ; they have followed up with the Minister. All these things are exactly what goes on the table to try to get a good outcome, noting that there are more interests than just s aithe in the UK - Norway access arrangements. Overall, in these things there is access to other stocks that might be of interest to other parts of the fleet.
Q148 What are we getting from the north - north-east then?

I do not have the full details of the full arrangement. As you say, it is up to 30,000 tonnes, and there are different elements of the fleet that are interested in different parts of it. In fact , the Shetland Fishermen ’s Association ’s letter to the Minister is explicit that for some parts of the sector the agreement is working well, but they are worried about all the issues you have been raising around s aithe, large vessels, large catches, and small fish. All those are live issues in discussion.
Q149 We get something back ; we are just not sure what it is ?

It is obviously based on a prediction. It is not that we sit down and agree it with the sector, but the whole purpose of these quota and access deals in particular is to support fishing businesses in the way they want to operate the business, which is different from the science advice .
Q150 The difficulty I have here, Gareth, is you give us a response that says you are content with the engagement between the Government and the sector, and then we get outcomes such as this.

Last year the sector was not unhappy with the prospect of that agreement, and then what has happened this year is there is a change in the pattern; that is the sort of thing that you would then think about reflecting in the next negotiating position. As I say, the sector wrote to the Minister yesterday and they were specific about feeling confident they are working with officials to develop these positions that we can take into negotiations. There will be a balance ; at the end the Minister will have to agree a balance in those access arrangements.
A s I mentioned at the outset, I am very keen to engage more with the sector, which is why I have made it a priority since my appointment.
Q151 T wo final very quick questions. Fuel costs : w e are hearing of boats actually leaving active fishing because they simply cannot afford to go to sea. What are you doing to help them?

That is a message I have heard loud and clear from my visit s to Newlyn, Weymouth and other ports across the country. I absolutely recognise the pressures that the industry is under. There is obviously support for fuel via our existing tax system , and we are monitoring the situation very closely to understand the pressures that fishermen are facing.
Q152 That is stuff that was there before the current spike. What are you doing to help them with the current spike?
We are keen to continue to engage with the sector to understand the issues and challenges that they face . We are alive to some of the challenges that they are facing.
Q153 They are talking now about stopping going to sea. Do you have a hard proposal to help them , to keep them going to sea?
We have heard the message around using the coastal growth fund as an option. I am very keen —
Q154 That is not what the coastal growth fund is there for. The coastal growth fund was in place before the spike in prices.

Indeed, but the re have been call s to use that fund for this purpose. What I am saying to you, Chair, is that obviously there is existing fuel support via taxation policy. We have heard the message loud and clear from the sector and w e are looking at options for the future.

Q155 As a consequence of decisions that were taken by the previous Government and then baked in for another 12 years by this Government, our fishermen are competing with fishing industries in other European countries. We have press notices here, “Commission approves €15 million Irish state aid for fishing and agriculture companies facing increased fuel prices. ” “ Commission approves €25 million Spanish state aid for fishing companies. ” “ Commission approves €4.5 million German state aid for fishing and aquaculture companies.” These are the people who we are expected to compete against ; they are helping , so w hy are we not helping our industry?

That is another reminder why there is probably a need for a strategy to support our fishing communities. I would not want you to mischaracterise what I said earlier, Chair, in terms of not wanting a strategy, I just want to work it through with the APPG and do it in partnership with the sector.
Q156 Yes, and i n terms of pounds and pence, what is there going to be for the industry ?
Gareth, can you chip in on that question?
Sorry, Chair, could you repeat the question?
Q157 These European countries are all giving their boats help with fuel costs. We are not. Are you going to? Otherwise they might as well just tie up now. There is no point in giving them false hope.

That is not a decision for me, obviously. As the Minister says, at his request we are looking at options, not least because the sector ha s asked us to reallocate that funding. It has specifically said, “We understand there might not be new funding, can we reallocate that funding?” In its own right, that raises questions about whether that is possible.

Q158 One final question around the SPS agreement. We know that you are not going to be able to answer any questions about the SPS agreement because nobody knows what is in it; you probably are as much in the dark as we are. Can you give me some assurance that you would not sign up to an SPS agreement that would bring fisheries management issues into the field of play ?
More broadly, I welcome the Government’s reset with the European Union. I was in Paris last week at the G7 and then SIAL — the largest food and drink expo in the world — talking with industry.

Q159 I appreciate this. You are the one who has the pressure of time here, so I am trying to keep it very tight. Is there going to be a read-across between SPS and fisheries management or not? Is that something that you would be prepared to have ?

Obviously we need to protect British interests. I heard loud and clear in Paris last week the benefits an SPS agreement will bring in terms of cheaper, easier exports to other countries and the benefits it will bring our seafish industry, as I also heard loud and clear on my visit to Newlyn. I obviously cannot go into any detail about the negotiations because we have the summit coming up on 20 November.
Q160 Are there no undertakings on fisheries management then?
Do you want to add anything on SPS?
I am not worrying about our future ability to operate a sovereign fishing policy since we left the common fisheries policy.

T hat is a brief statement. We shall possibly revisit that at some point in the future. For the moment we are going on to questions around biosecurity and animal welfare. We have quite a lot to cover here. Sarah, do you want to lead our questioning on that?

Q161 Good morning. This year has been an exceptionally difficult year for farmers. We have had drought, the chaos around SFI and the worst bluetongue outbreak on record ; the south-west has been particularly badly hit. On top of the immediate costs of the bluetongue vaccination, veterinary treatment , and fallen stock, fallen stock collections in the south-west ran at three to four times the normal levels this summer, with charges of up to £35 per sheep and over £160 per cattle. Disposal is obviously a legal requirement, and it is vital for disease control.

When we are looking at this , many farmers are not only concerned with those costs that are impacting their farm businesses but also about the longer-term losses from reduced fertility and birth defects. What support will the Government provide to those farmers who have been so badly affected by outbreaks this year?

Thank you for the question, Sarah . I absolutely understand how incredibly difficult it has been for farmers across our country. I have met with the National Sheep Association and the NFU, and I have been talking directly to farmers about the challenges that they face on top of other issues around input costs, drought, wildfires, and so on. It is worth saying that as of yesterday there are 3,445 confirmed cases across the United Kingdom. It has obviously been a significant outbreak this year.

I was very keen to get on the farm, engaging in these issues early on, which is why I visited Cornwall to talk to a farmer who had been affected , alongside Tom Bradshaw, the NFU president. I absolutely recognise the real challenges that farmers have faced, and that is why I have made it a priority to work through options for further improvement. That is why we worked with industry to support the vaccine supply, reduced some admin burdens that farmers have had to face, supported on-farm veterinary support, and enhanced testing capability.

I have been to APHA and the Pirbright Institute to see directly what the scientists have been doing in terms of testing capability and, more specifically, on fall e n stock. We are working with industry on future options and monitoring the situation closely. It is worth me also saying that when we had an urgent question in the House as well, there were particular issues that were raised around maps, and we have improved the heat maps so we know where the confirmed cases are across the country. We have done a range of things based on the engagement we have had with farmers but there is always more we can do, which is why it is worth just stressing as well that I am keen to learn lessons from the outbreak this year. I have already started that process with my officials to make sure what we have learned from this year does not get repeated in future years.
Q162 Some European countries are subsidising b luetongue vaccinations. Is this something you would consider?

My understanding is that is not something that we would consider at the moment ; whether you take up the vaccine or not is obviously a decision for a farm alongside their vet. The current situation is we do not believe that there is a case for mandatory vaccination or the subsidising of vaccines. The costs are obviously between £2.50 and £3 in most cases. What is key is the communication to encourage farms to make sure that they do take up the vaccine.

Q163 T he communication is something I want to touch on because some farmers and industry representatives have argued that the Government communications were not sufficiently timely or proactive as the outbreak spread so quickly. One Devon farmer and councillor, Cheryl Cot tle -Hunkin, criticised DEFRA’s handling of communications during the emergence of cases in the south-west . S he was incredibly vocal about this, having outbreaks on her own farm , argu ing that the farmers were not adequately alerted to suspected local cases or increasing disease risks. She suggested that delays in communication left some farmers feeling they had lost the opportunity to take proactive action at an early stage. Who was ultimately responsible for getting the message across to farmers about the urgency of getting those vaccinations done?

On outbreaks such as these , DEFRA uses tried and tested approaches to work with the sector to make sure information is spread across to the relevant agencies. There are always lessons we can learn from our approach, which is why this lessons learned exercise is really important. What strikes me is that DEFRA did a number of things that were successful. There were a series of webinars that were well attended; 1,000 farmers attended one. Obviously we used various different portals and blogs to get information out to the community. I am very grateful for the work the NFU has done on communication as well. I would say it is a partnership approach ; everyone can play their part in making sure the messages get across to farmers—APHA, Pirbright, the NFU and other farming organisations , with DEFRA at the heart of all of that.

Q164 Obviously the NFU did a great job in getting the message out , but d o you think it is not down to a membership body such as the NFU to get the message out, that ultimately it is the responsibility of DEFRA and the APHA to do that job?

It is a partnership approach headed by DEFRA. That is why I am proud of some of the things the Department did in terms of the webinars and the regular communication with farmers. There is always more we can do and we will take on board the feedback we have learned from farmers this year to make sure we improve it for next year.
Q165 V accine take-up was slow at the start of the outbreak. Do you feel that that is something that we have to learn from very quickly as we face future outbreaks?

I am keen to learn any lessons but, a s I mentioned, we work ed really hard to improve the supply coming into the country, working with industry to make that happen. I am not aware of any particular challenges around vaccine currently.

Q166 I just want to move on to TB. T he previous farming Minister said in June that the Government would respond at pace to the new bovine TB control strategy for England . W hen will the Government respond to these recommendations?

Thank you for th at question. Obviously, there is the TB control strategy that came out in June of this year following extensive stakeholder engagement and co-design with the sector. We have agreed to adopt the strategy, but obviously we are looking to publish the next stage of that process, which I can confirm will be out before Christmas.

Q167 I have personal experience of TB. Two cows were culled after reacting to a TB test on my family farm this month. When the results came back after slaughter, both animals were clear of TB. This is not the first time ; it happens all the time. It has happened to my neighbouring farms, friends and family, so I know firsthand how heartbreaking this is for farming families. Bovine TB costs the taxpayer over £100 million a year in England, and healthy animals are being lost along the way. What is DEFRA doing to improve the accuracy of the testing so that cattle are not slaughtered unnecessarily? With the previous Minister admitting the SPS work was delaying cattle vaccine trials because of the capacity problems, will the 2030 target for cattle vaccination be met?

There is a lot in there, but it is worth saying that I hear your concerns. I heard that loud and clear from spending a day on a farm in Cumbria with James Robinson and working through with him a very similar experience of being in touch with the VMD and with APHA.

In terms of vaccines we are continuing to develop the cattle vaccination and skin testing. There is obviously the rollout of the badger vaccination in priority areas, and we are collecting found dead badgers as well. I might just turn to Mike to add anything further with regard to TB.

That covers it, Minister. It is obviously a devastating disease for the farms that contract it, and while it is not under my personal responsibilities, it is something that the teams working on it in the Department are trying to look at every tool in the toolbox in terms of how we can get a grip on the disease. There is work that is being done to make use of privately funded TB blood testing to support better risk-based disease management.

Longer term, our approach on a number of issues that are facing the sector is to try to think how we build long-term resilience into the farming sector so that we can be better at equipping farmers with the tools they need to manage multiple risks. Some of that can be done through peer-to-peer learning in terms of trying to get best practice to be common practice across farms.

Q168 I have seen TB testing on farm ; the inaccuracies are incredible. The calliper system has been in place for 40-odd years now. We should be doing this much better. C attle that test positive on a non-statutory test face compulsory slaughter at present . Resolved in conclusive reactors can already be kept on farm under a lifetime restriction, sold only direct to slaughter. When will the Department create an equivalent responder category for non-statutory test positives , so farmers and vets can manage these animals in a way that is best for their herd?

Thank you for that, I will certainly take those concerns back to the Department. It obviously just reminds us how important the next stage of the strategy is. It is worth noting that we are developing a new industry - g overnment strategy board to drive the recommendations from the strategy. I will certainly feed that back and take it forward in terms of the work that I am doing alongside Baroness Hayman, who is the Minister responsible for biosecurity.

Q169 Thank you. My final question is that the current guidance only allows non-statutory tests in OTF herds that have already had gamma testing, and stops further testing the moment OTF status has been regained. That means farmers cannot keep checking for hidden infection once a herd is clear. I have heard that on my own farm. We also heard that when we visited Gatcombe f arm down in Devon; they found that exact example when they were reinfected back in 2023. Will you allow these tests in OTF herds without affecting their status? How will the Government make sure the SPS agreement does not restrict this activity going forward?
I recognise those challenges. I will certainly take it back to the Department and explore the points that you raise further. Mike, do you have anything further you wanted to add to Sarah’s question ?

It is right, Minister, that that is something we can look at in the strategy. I know that there is expansion of Government-funded mandatory interferon-gamma blood testing to help try to detect infection sooner and reduce breakdown duration. I do not know enough about the issue to know if that specifically addresses your question, but it is definitely something we can pick up with the teams in DEFRA.
Yes, it would be great if you could follow that up.

Q170 It would be a lot of stuff to bring back to the Department; w e will maybe follow up in correspondence. It would be good if we could get an answer by the end of the month , d oes that seem reasonable?
I will see what we can do .

Q171 Minister, we have the current policy and we have the strategy in respect of TB. I am just worried about the SPS. I know you cannot comment on negotiations, but are you worried about the difference between what our strategy and our policy says in this country and the European rules, and the divergence between the two?

We obviously take these issues extremely seriously. Protecting biosecurity of our country is vital. That is why I work really closely with Baroness Hayman who leads on both the SPS and biosecurity issues, and those are at the forefront of our mind in the negotiations.

Q172 The EU is not permitting us to vaccinate cattle ; it has extending testing regimes. Are you worried about that in terms of combating TB, and our fight against TB to have official TB status by 2038?

Lots of things that we do are world-leading in this space, which is why I was keen to see what Pirbright and APHA are doing. We can obviously get back to you on the specifics in terms of the response that Sarah has asked for, and I am very happy to do so.

Q173 I just wanted to pick up on the consultation that was released yesterday on the CO 2 stunning of pigs. I am very much with the Government on the animal welfare agenda ; the strategy is a visionary document, but obviously to actually achieve welfare gains we need to make sure anything we do is based on robust evidence.

The statement released by DEFRA yesterday stated , M inimising distress during handling and slaughter is an important part of safeguarding pig welfare, and that both argon and electric stunning are proven to substantially reduce animal suffering. But i f you then dive into the Animal Welfare Committee’s opinion, it notes that “exposure to argon still causes vocalisations and sometimes escape attempts.” I t takes longer for pigs to lose consciousness, which could have welfare implications and would certainly have commercial impacts for abattoirs. It then goes on to say that the CCTV the Committee saw was not in the gas system itself, so it was inadequate to properly assess their welfare.

On automated electric stunning we know that in a pig stunning trial as much as one-fifth of pigs showed signs of consciousness after they had gone through the process. By that point they are hoisted up by their rear trotters, so they would have to get the pigs down, re-stun them and put them back up again, which again could have terrible welfare implications. Pigs are big beasts, so potentially that could pose a risk to staff as well, further exacerbating labour shortages that abattoirs are already facing.
