Given all that , can you, hand on heart, at this point say that the evidence base is strong enough to bring that consultation forward?

We have engaged with industry in advance of going out to public consultation. You will know that the commitment to do so is very much from our animal welfare strategy, which Baroness Hayman and the Government launched last December. It is really important that we have that engagement with industry and obviously encourage people to respond to the consultation, opened only yesterday with a deadline of December.

I am very keen to make sure we deliver on our manifesto commitments as we set out at the election, but also to work with industry around mitigating the risks and challenges. Mike, do you have anything further you wanted to add in terms of the specifics of Josh’s question?

Only that the consultation provides an opportunity for some of those issues that you have raised about argon and how suitable it might be as a replacement method. This is about gathering the evidence so that Ministers can then take decisions on the back of that consultation. We are keen to hear views about all aspects of the document that has been out.

Q174 Wr itten responses to a consultation are clearly not the same as a full industry-led trial with independent oversight, which seems to me to be what we really need. Even the Animal Welfare Committee is not saying argon or electric stunning is certainly better, there are definitely reservations there. There are clearly huge gaps in the evidence. My question is, should that not have been gathered before the consultation was released?

My understanding is the proposal would have significant improvement to pig welfare at the time of killing. As I said, we have been talking to industry and I hope those issues are teased out in the consultation period, which I encourage people to contribute to.

Q175 Lastly, I hosted a drop-in on CO 2 use for the National Pig Association just yesterday; I did not know the consultation was going to be coming out yesterday, but it was quite timely. It told me that it has had many meetings with DEFRA officials and it has raised these concerns and many others, and yet none of that seems to have had any bearing whatsoever on what is in the consultation document. It does not see any of those nuances even reflected. Will you be engaging with pig producers and abattoirs going forward ? We can see that their concerns are only going to grow louder and louder in the coming weeks. There is a lot going on in the industry and this is another thing that they feel is being heaped on them.

Yes, I absolutely understand the pressures that the sector is facing. That is why I have met with the National Pig Association early on, and why I have met with pig farmers directly on farm. I am committed to having a summit with industry, processors and others to recognise the challenges that the sector is facing and to work through what the options might be to provide further support.
Q176 Were they tell ing you that the evidence is not there ?
Not at any particular meetings I have had so far, but I will commit to seeing the sector further to get into that detail and make sure that everyone ha s contributed to the consultation.
Q177 They are telling me that there ha ve been no proper trials done in the use of argon . Are they not telling you that ?
Baroness Hayman leads on these areas, of course, but I will certainly follow up with them on the points you have raised today.
Q178 Mike, you have started the consultation but you are consulting on stuff that you have not properly trialled. Is that not putting the cart before the horse?

I have to be clear that it is not my policy area, but my understanding is that the Animal Welfare Committee report that was published in 2025 recommended, for all the reasons set out in that report, phasing out the current method s —CO 2 —and that there are other methods that the c ommittee suggested in their report. What we are trying to do now is gather information and evidence from the industry about the implications of moving from the current methods to those new methods.
Q179 What other countries are doing this ? Denmark ? The Netherlands?
I do not have that information, I am afraid.
There is no mention in the EU whatsoever, and America is only looking to move to CO 2 and is baffled that we are looking to move away from it because the evidence base is not there .

Q180 You are content to go on this? Okay, we will maybe raise this with Baroness Hayman, she is coming in later. Stephen, you mentioned your summit there. It is a fact that the pig sector is going to have too many pigs on farm between now and Christmas, they are not going to be on a contract and there is going to be no way for them to get to market. That is going to lead to a back-up of stock on farm, which in itself then becomes an animal welfare issue. Is that something that your summit is going to address?
More generally, obviously, I want to drive more profitable, productive farming.
Q181 I have given you a specific question, w e are all agreed on the general s.

That is why I am really keen to work with the sectors to drive growth in the sector. You will know from your experience that it tends to be boom and bust in the pig sector, and therefore a key point that I would want to get across in the summit is about market monitoring and forecasting, working with industry and what the options are for growth for the future.

Q182 Does that mean that you are going to be addressing the specific concern of the industry that between now and Christmas you are going to have this animal welfare problem because you are going to have too many pigs on farm that you cannot get off to slaughter?
If I am going to convene industry, I am keen to hear their views and concerns to see what Government can do to build resilience and growth in the sector.
Q183 Are you hearing it from me for the first time? Have y ou not heard this? You must have ongoing dialogue with the NPA, NFUS, N FU and others.
I mentioned I have already met with them, been on farms, talked to them . I am very happy to engage further .
Q184 Have they told you that this is their concern? If that is their concern, surely it should go on to the agenda for your summit , should it not?

The way that I operate working with the sector is to ask what issues they want to discuss with me, then we work through those. It is a partnership approach to then improve outcomes for our farming community, very much in the spirit of the “F arming R oadmap ” . I am very happy to explore issues they would such as to raise with me when we have that summit.
Q185 Are you telling me that will be on the agenda ?
I am v ery happy to discuss any issues that industry wants to talk about.
Okay.

Q186 I should refer to my wider register of interests submitted to the Committee in relation to my family connections with the industry. Just going back to Josh’s point here, it is quite well established within the industry that electrical stunning can lead to worse welfare outcomes. The use of argon and nitrogen when we have CO 2 readily available presents another issue because I would ask, which countries would you expect to import the argon or nitrogen from?
We will have to get back to you on those specific points.

Q187 Okay. I can tell you that Russia is the major producer of those gasses, and that would mean that our domestic food security is further compromised by relying on a Russian import. That in itself would seem to be the wrong way to go about it.

As the Chair just alluded to, we already have 15,000 pigs backed up on farm. The transition period in this consultation around the use of CO 2 talks about two to three years. That would require shutting down the abattoirs for a conversion. These are abattoirs that are running at full capacity trying to deal with the situation in the market as it is. Two to three years would be unworkable and would create additional welfare problems on farm because there would not be the throughput in the abattoirs to get the pigs that we are already producing. That does really need to be considered when you are looking at this. Would you agree with that?

Thank you for that. I know that you speak with real authority on these issues, having worked for the National Pig Association in the past. It is really important that as many people as possible contribute to the consultation, and I am very happy to meet any M ember on these issues to make sure that their views are fed into the consultation.

Q188 From pigs to poultry, in my circumstance. The trial of the avian influenza vaccine has just come to an end within Norfolk. We are very proud o f what our local poultry producers have been doing to work with the Animal and Plant Health Agency on that. I had a meeting with the APHA on Friday of last week to talk about this. The findings are now obviously coming to a conclusion, but one of the things that was raised with me is that the vaccine itself has to be administered through a travelling process using liquid nitrogen, which makes it quite a costly process. Will that be taken into account when recommendations are given on whether this vaccine is given approval going forward?
Thank you for that. I can give you assurance that we will certainly look at those options.

Q189 In terms of the next steps for this, obviously if we look at other counterparts around the world, Australia, for example, has had its first cases of avian influenza this summer, in August. It has done a mass rollout scheme for wild birds at a cost of around A$ 230 million , so i t is doable in terms of if the Government puts their mind to it. What do you believe is going to be the next steps for the Government in terms of AI approaching us as the season has now started?

Thank you for that. Again, these issues are for Baroness Hayman to answer, and I work really closely with her . M ore broadly on biosecurity issues , w e obviously take these issues extremely seriously and I will certainly take back your views and ideas to the Department.

Q190 In terms of moving away from Baroness Hayman’s portfolio towards yours, obviously one of the issues that we have within the poultry sector is the lack of insurance that is now available. I raised this with former Minister Daniel Zeichner in a Westminster Hall debate. There does not seem to be any action that ha s come from DEFRA since that point , in terms of the support divergence and increasing the number of insurance providers. Is this something that you are aware of at all, Minister ?

Thank you for raising this. You will know we published our “F arming R oadmap ” earlier this year and established a farming and food partnership board. There are a number of sector growth plans that we are taking forward ; there is one around horticulture and one around poultry.

I met representatives from the poultry sector at the partnership board yesterday. We want to make sure we have a really good plan to build resilience and a sustainable sector for the future. All those issues that you described around insurance and other matters will be brought out in the plan so that we can ensure growth for the sector for the future.
Q191 When you say it will be brought out in further detail, have you had any conversations with NFU Mutual, for example, on this issue , or the only other provider of insurance?

I have met with representatives of the poultry sector. I have not had that particular point raised with me directly yet, but I am very happy to follow through on those as we work out the sector growth plan for the future. Mike, do you want to chip in more broadly around support for the poultry sector?

As the Minister mentioned, we are trying to make sure the sector growth plans are industry-led. They were commissioned by the farming and food partnership board ; w e are expecting the poultry one to be submitted back to the board within the next six months. As the Minister said, these sorts of issues alongside others—we are aware that there are issues in the planning system, for example—are holding back growth in the sector. We are trying to look across the board at the systematic challenges that need to be addressed in order to enable the sector to grow, and I would expect this to feature in that plan somewhere.

Q192 Minister, I wanted to ask you about the issue of local abattoir provision, something that has been vastly eroding in recent years; in Sussex—where my constituency is—we have just one abattoir left in the entire county. At a national level we had 2,500 abattoirs in the 1970s; we now have just 200 in the whole country. It is a really big issue for local farmers because it means they have to transport animals much further for slaughter, which can have animal welfare considerations. It also impacts their ability to sell meat locally and reduce food miles when we lose abattoirs.

This week the NFU published a letter with 150 organisations saying that the sector is in crisis and needs support from Government. Given that DEFRA put a huge amount of money into supporting the farming industry in this country, is it not right that we also think about protecting this vital national infrastructure of abattoirs? Do you recognise local abattoirs and the network of them as vital national infrastructure and can you say anything about how DEFRA can support them and make sure we do not lose more abattoirs in the future?

It is an issue that has come up on the engagement that I have had through agricultural shows and visits across the country over the summer. I am aware of the coalition’s letter led by the NFU and 150 different organisations. DEFRA works really closely with an abattoir working group and a task and finish group to work through the options for the future. I have met with Susan at the FSA to look at what options can be done around regulation and visits.

It is worth saying that we have seen about a 2.5% reduction in local abattoirs across the country; I do not recognise the 10% reduction. They are hugely important to food resilience, which is why I am pleased there is work going on with industry and my officials to monitor the situation and see what further action can be taken.

Q193 Can that working group look at setting up a dedicated fund to support local abattoirs? If we are putting £2 billion a year into supporting farming in this country , it would make sense that we put a small amount of money into that local infrastructure that the farming is dependent on.

My understanding is the letter calls for a dedicated funding stream to support that. I want to look at what other measures we can take at this stage in terms of reducing some regulatory and vets ’ inspection burdens on abattoirs and then see if there is anything further we can do to deliver on the commitments we have made.

Q194 It is a really important point that the small and medium-sized abattoirs are closing at a rate that there simply will not be any left in 10 years. That is really important for the local supply chain, rare and native breeds and organic farmers. Recently—in September 2024—the Smaller Abattoir Fund was closed and has not been replaced. Will you be looking at bringing in a replacement for that? How are we going to stem these closures?
In my answer to the previous question I mentioned the support we are providing around regulatory visits and vets’ activities .
We are talking about the small abattoirs.
Indeed, and it is about how we can make that more proportionate. I will certainly take away the suggestion around additional support.
I am going to move on to questions around water and heat resilience.

Q195 Apologies, I am leading a Westminster Hall debate at 11 am so I shall ask a couple of quick questions and run away; I do not run that fast. I wanted to ask about water resilience. It has been an incredibly tough year when it comes to drought; it has been like this for a number of years now in places such as Norfolk. If you follow the news it seems we are not out of the woods yet; there is potentially more to come.

Water is obviously crucial and critical to the operations of farms. I welcome the £15 million in grants for on-farm reservoirs. The core problem—farmers tell me this all the time—is getting the necessary licences and planning permissions. I understand that this cuts across different Departments, including MHCLG, and different briefs. When can farmers expect progress on the process of getting licences and planning permissions to be made easier?

Just to echo what you have said I absolutely agree with how difficult it has been for farmers across the country this year. I heard about the value of reservoirs loud and clear on a farm visit with Tom Bradshaw to his own farm. We are obviously funding the water management grant of £15 million, the detail of which will come out next month.

There is a range of things that I am keen to do across Government. Yesterday there was a discussion at the farming and food partnership board with representatives from across Government—including MHCLG—working through some options for the future. Obviously the Prime Minister has taken this issue extremely seriously, hence the announcement in August of the additional £15 million when he was on a potato farm in Cornwall.

There is a range of things we want to do around abstractions and working with the Environment Agency and speeding up the planning process to deliver the change that we need. I mentioned there was a very healthy discussion about these issues and working with the sector at the partnership board yesterday and we have set some clear milestones to take forward further action. Mike, is there anything specific you want to add about abstraction planning or funding finance?

We are trying to take a system-wide look at the barriers, some of which might be in the planning system; hence we had colleagues from MHCLG in a meeting yesterday that the Minister referred to. We know there are issues with abstraction and if you have to have an environmental impact assessment there can be issues with the Natural England screening of that. We had both those organisations represented in the room and are trying to crack this in a group way as well as looking at the role that finance can play. Yesterday we agreed a plan of action with the sector and those other bits of Government—as I mentioned—to try to work through some things.

Smart abstraction may well be one thing—it is being trialled at the moment—but currently farmers would need to apply to the Environment Agency in order to get abstraction licences. Are there ways in which we can use technology for automatic monitoring of river levels so that we can take that out of the loop? That is one example of the changes we are looking at but we totally get the urgency. We started this work just before we experienced the extreme drought and it is something that Ministers are committed to resolving.

Obviously you want to build more reservoirs and make it easier for people to build reservoirs. The national planning policy framework—which has come out recently—is helpful; it is about prioritising food production and the work of farmers. It is a really helpful strategic document that should drive the change that we need.

Q196 I am glad you appreciate the urgency, particularly around abstraction licences. As you will be aware, last week I held a farming conference in south-west Norfolk with 70 farmers and landowners. I have numerous farmers whose abstraction licences are up for renewal next March. They need to be putting seed orders in now but they do not know if they are going to have the water available. It is risky enough; we need to de-risk where possible. Do you think the current arrangements for abstraction licences properly prioritise food production and support for farmers? You have indicated that perhaps they do not and that is what we are looking to reform.

More generally we obviously want to make it easier to build reservoirs. We want to review and update the planning guidance and remove some unnecessary barriers that exist. I have heard those messages loud and clear from parliamentarians but also on farm visits. Mike, is there anything further you want to cover in terms of those issues that Terry described?

Clearly there will always be a lead-in time for getting a reservoir from obtaining the permissions through to then building it. We obviously need to factor in any health and safety considerations with regard to the HSE aspect in this. Following the actions that we agreed yesterday with other partners around the table, we are hoping that they would see some benefit in terms of the construction of reservoirs next year. Obviously with the summer we have had, we would all prefer that to be quicker but equally this is a challenge that has been left unresolved for too long and we are trying to grip it now.

Q197 I want to continue Terry’s questions but also delve into the wider issue of the very hot summer that we have had and the impact for farmers. Just to follow up on Terry’s question, in August the Government announced £50 million of funding would be reallocated to SFI to help farmers adapt to the risk of future droughts. Can you comment on how DEFRA has ensured that this money is ring-fenced for drought resilience?

We have had £50 million allocated; when we did similar schemes before it was a slightly smaller amount and it supported about 70 reservoirs across the country. We will set up the specifics of the application opportunity when we publish it next month. This is alongside broader work the Government are doing around private investment going into the water sector to improve water management issues, which I know you are very passionate about and do lots of work on.

Just on the specifics we decided not to try to ring-fence that extra £50 million within SFI for certain drought-specific measures. At the time the windows were opened we put out communications around the actions that were available under SFI.
Q198 Why did you not ring-fence it?

Given the speed that we would have needed to try to get the changes through we would have needed system changes to enable some sort of ring-fencing for that money. We decided to prioritise opening the scheme over pausing and getting those system changes done.
Q199 Are you reconsidering that for next year?
It is one of many options that we are looking at for next year in light of the experience we have had this year.

Q200 On the broader issue of the very hot summer that we have just had we also saw a number of wildfires, which is something the Committee has been looking at. In Stourbridge particularly, farmers played a critical role in getting those wildfires under control by creating firebreaks. When thinking about this issue in my own constituency we actually asked the local council whether it is in touch with local farmers in preparedness for any wildfires and there is no such link, database or connection.

In light of all the work going on in Government about wildfire preparedness , what role does DEFRA see for farmers? Are you doing any thinking about how we can further upskill local farmers and support them in that role and the fact that they own land that can be used in response to wildfires?

I just want to pay tribute to the tremendous activity of farmers over the summer. Obviously this demonstrates again the resilience that we see from our farming sector. You will be aware that the Prime Minister hosted a wildfire summit last week on these very issues. I was able to secure the NFU representation at that important summit so that the farmers’ voices are heard in decisions around what we might do differently in the future.

More generally you mentioned the firebreaks, which was a new flexibility announced by the Environment Agency in August when the Prime Minister was in attendance. There is more work we can do around preparedness, which is why working directly with the sector is really important to learn lessons and make sure that we have a robust system for the future.
Q201 Just making sure the local council knows who the local farmers are in a situation such as that is important; you do not want to be gathering those names and phone numbers at the time.

The work of the local resilience forums is also key here. It plays more broadly into the wider work that the Government are doing around resilience and the work of partners to make sure we are more resilient to some threats and concerns.

As part of the announcements made last week following the summit, there are some new actions that we are looking to bring into our suite of environmental land management schemes that are specifically designed to help counter wildfires.
Q202 You slightly led into my next question: is the Department outside ELMs looking at other ways to support more nature-friendly farming and climate resilience?

Absolutely. The ELMs budget is £2.3 billion a year but there is also work on local nature restoration strategies and work that can be factored in from biodiversity net gain. Only yesterday it was announced that the Government have partly contributed funding to secure the Rothbury E state, for example, in order to try to get extra funding into more nature-resilient farming on important landscapes. There is a range of measures specifically on wildfires. We also made those announcements regarding new actions in ELMs last week.

We have had the starter; we have had the fish course. Now we come to the main course: sustainable farming incentive and the 2026 application window 2. Sarah, you are going to lead our questioning on this.

Q203 Minister, I am a big fan of your enthusiasm with the lists of the farms that you have been visiting and all the lists that you have done. Given that farmer confidence in DEFRA has been devastated by the shambles—as it has been said by farmers themselves—of SFI window 2, we really need to drill into some details. Can I take us back to 21 September, the day before the launch of actual window 2? What estimate did DEFRA have of the number of eligible farm businesses likely to apply compared to the budget?

Just to start by saying that obviously earlier this year we redesigned SFI based on feedback from the previous year. That was about making sure that the funding was more fairly distributed and targeted more effectively to farmers as much as possible, which is why we introduced the two windows of opportunity. The first window opened earlier this year and then obviously the second window in September. I am really keen to learn lessons from what happened this year. The system held up despite huge demand, which is why I have started conversations with the sector to see how we design the scheme for the future.
Q204 Specifically on that question , how many farms did DEFRA expect and what was the budget?
We were modelling high demand.
Q205 What does high demand mean?
Significant contribution—
Q206 What does significant mean?

Perhaps Mike can get into some detail of the modelling that was undertaken. Obviously we saw a very difficult summer for the farming community and therefore some saw this as an opportunity to support them.

Q207 If we do not get this right at the start we are going to be here talking about this for the rest of the day. Sarah has asked you a very direct question here. How many applications did you expect to receive? I do not know if either of you or neither of you knows the answer. That is the question that has been asked; unless we get the right answer to that, nothing else is going to make sense.

Our best estimates—noting that we had made some changes to the scheme compared to the previous iterations—were that we had in excess of 20,000 expiring agreements, some of which we would have expected to come into SFI. We clearly had window 1 that was open for people without an existing ELM agreement. Obviously we do not know who might have started an application the following day because of the speed at which it closed. As I think you know, for window 2 we secured 12,200 applications. Our best guess is that north of 10,000 would have potentially missed out who wanted to come in but could not.
Q208 Are you saying you were expecting 20,000?

We knew that we had in excess of 20,000 agreements expiring but we could not always guarantee—given the changes that we have made to the scheme—whether people would want to go into the new scheme noting that we had removed some actions and changed some payment rates or whether they would want to go into other schemes. Clearly what we saw over the summer was an exceptional spike in demand as a result of those applications.
Sorry for interrupting, Sarah.

Q209 That is okay because it is really important. There is a lot of expectation on farmers to be able to forward plan and part of forward planning is to know exactly whether they can or cannot get into these schemes. If there were 20,000 expiring and you said 12,200 submitted—we think it was 12,500—that means 12,500 were unable to. What was the budget and how was it going to be allocated? Basically you went in knowing that farmers would not be able to get it.

We made a number of changes to the scheme to try to make the money go as far as possible such as reducing those actions from 102 to 71; we capped agreements for the first time at 100,000; we reduced the three most popular payment rates; we brought some actions under a cap so that you are holding for a certain hectare and we removed the management payment. Against that backdrop we were not comparing like for like in terms of those old agreements.

Equally some expiring agreements are mid-tier, which are the legacy agreements that are halfway between what we would describe as SFI or higher tier, for example, and we did not know who might want to go up into higher tier versus down. This is all modelling, estimates and forecasting. We knew that the budget was going to be heavily oversubscribed hence why we made all the changes that we did to try to make it go as far as possible.

Right at the last minute we were able to secure an agreement to first put that extra £50 million in that was announced in August and then an extra £20 million and a residual £3 million. Having published that the budget would be £180 million earlier in the year when we said what date the scheme would open, we were then able to put an extra £73 million on top of that: around a 40% increase.

Clearly in light of the experience we had that was not enough because the demand was as high as it was. We knew we were going to have high demand and the budget that we had was finite, which is why we made that suite of changes in consultation with stakeholders around this time a year ago.
It took the budget to £253 million.

Q210 On that basis why did you make it first come, first served? You knew demand would be higher. DEFRA did its own survey; 60% could not get the application in on time. One farmer left a funeral to try to get the application in on time. Are you setting farmers up to fail?

I have committed to move away from first come, first served; we refined the scheme this year. You will appreciate that was before my time in the Department but I am very keen to learn lessons from this year. I have heard heartbreaking stories of the impact it has had and how stressful it has been for farmers across the country. That is why I welcome the survey that you have undertaken to capture views and concerns that we will feed into the co-design for next year.

Q211 The NFU believes that the value of the expiring agreements that we were talking about exceeds £520 million, and the budget for the 2 SFI windows in total is about £310 million. First, do you recognise those figures? Is the NFU right on that? Secondly, can you explain where that difference of £210 million has gone?

The NFU’s assumption would be that everyone in an expiring agreement would all go downwards into SFI rather than upwards in the hierarchy of schemes within the ELM suite , for example , if everyone who had an expiring mid-tier all went and looked at SFI rather than up at a higher tier. I recognise those numbers and they are in the ballpark of what our expectations were.
Q212 What is going to happen in terms of that missing £210 million? Again you are committing to having this longer-term vision and that there is funding there but there is an open gap here.

I do not accept the characterisation that there is missing money. The Department set out the full details of the spending review settlement that was secured nearly two years ago. At headline level that includes £2.3 billion for the farming budget, of which roughly £1.9 billion is for environmental land management schemes.

As per what we set out in our “ Farming Roadmap ” , over time we are seeing money that had previously been earmarked for SFI being applied to higher tier and landscape recovery. As I say , I do not recognise this notion of missing money but in our “ Farming Roadmap ” we have been publicly recognising that money within the farming budget is going to be tight. Therefore over time we expect that higher tier and landscape recovery will take a bigger share of it.

That said SFI is still the largest scheme that we have at the moment, and we estimate spend this year will be about £851 million on those legacy agreements that we already have. Clearly in window 2 and window 1 that we saw this summer, we committed £310 million; because these are three-year agreements that is a further £930 million that has been signed up to in applications that we have received.

Q213 From what I understand so far, DEFRA knew very well it was going to be completely oversubscribed. There was no sufficient funding to allow this and farmers were not given any indication. They were not told exactly when the window would open so many were staying up throughout the night. It opened at 10 am and shut just under six hours later.

Minister, I know you said you are going to learn lessons but how are you going to stop this happening again? This is numbers and banding around but how could farmers have possibly known? This is a repeat offence for the last two years of the carpet being swept away from under their feet. How could they have known that they had to be there and get through?
Obviously in terms of the design of the scheme for this year, that was set out quite early on in the year.
Q214 I do not think that detail was there earlier on in the year.

We set out the overall design of the scheme early in the year through the farming conferences that took place, obviously before my time in the Department. The date of opening window 2 was announced at least three and a half weeks in advance. Obviously in terms of the time it opened—10 o’clock that morning—that was not public knowledge because RPA needed to run some tests before going live on the funding opportunity.

Q215 Would it not have been better to tell RPA not to rush and actually to have communicated that so everyone could have planned? Even land managers did not manage to get all their applications in, God forbid a farmer trying to when they were on farm.

I have already said we are going to scrap the first-come, first-served approach. That means some trade-offs in terms of how we design the scheme for next year but we are already working in partnership with the NFU and others to design that scheme to get it right for the future. As Mike said earlier , NFU and others were involved in the design of the scheme for this year, but we need to work through what the options are for next year to make sure that people do not miss out on the opportunity.
I doubt NFU would be happy with you saying it helped with the design.

Q216 Can I just get a sense of what was happening inside the Department? You had the first window , and 25% of a much less pressured window was allocated on the first day. This fastest finger first approach should have been obvious to the Department at the end of June before you started the design for the second window. Is that a fair comment?
The only thing I snagged on there was design for the second window. As the Minister was saying , what we tried to do earlier in the year was set out the timetable for both windows.
Q217 You surely sought to learn from the experience of the first window.
Yes.

Q218 You saw what was happening, the big glut of early applications coming in, and then you have another window opening that is going to be under much greater pressure. Stephen, are you getting briefed on this?
Yes and really leaning into the lessons.
Q219 Were you getting briefed on the extent to which the window was going to be oversubscribed? You are the Minister here; Mike is the official.

We very much understood the level of demand. Lessons have to be learned for the future, as I have clearly got across today. On the day itself we were made aware of how it was going. That is why we certainly communicated that information via the DEFRA blog to make sure that applicants knew how much was being spent throughout the day.
Q220 Even these warnings—25%, 50% and 75%—were not being seen , according to the respondents to our survey.
I am very keen to see the full findings of your survey and want to make sure that feeds into the co-design of the scheme.
Q221 The decision to carry on with a first-come, first-served allocation was made by yourself in knowledge that it was going to be oversubscribed.
All the decisions around how the scheme would run this year were made before my appointment to the Department.
Q222 You were briefed. You knew that there was a problem coming down the track and you decided to carry on with it, nevertheless.
The information about how the scheme would operate had all been published.

Q223 If you knew that you had published how it was going to be done and it was apparent to you—as Mike is telling us , it should have been apparent to you—it was always an option for you to turn around and say, “Look, this isn’t going to work. We need to pause and redesign it.” Why did you not do that?

I hear the message loud and clear from farmers that they want consistency in their approach from DEFRA in the spirit of the roadmap. We understood the levels of demand, which is why I was pleased to help secure additional funding.
Q224 Even if you are wrong it is still important to be consistent.

We understood the levels of demand, which is why I was pleased to make sure we secured the additional funding of the £50 million the Prime Minister announced in August and then the £20 million, which took the overall pot to £253 million.

Q225 When farmers talk about wanting a consistent approach they just want to know that they can actually apply to a scheme and that there will be money. They would much rather have had this paused and delayed further. What is another week at this point rather than the devastation this has caused? This is now shifting farm practices. It is going to have a far longer impact because they are going to have to put land back into production, diversify and look at the intensification on farming.

I appreciate that plan was made before you came in but you are the Minister and you said earlier, “The decisions I make are based on the evidence before me.” The evidence was screaming to anyone that this was going to be a problem. Fundamentally the ministerial team and DEFRA have to go away and look at this because this cannot happen again; this is not the first time. I appreciate the scheme is changing but I have no faith that this will not be repeated in the future.

I will politely remind you that this is a scheme inherited from the previous Government that had no budget control. We have refined and improved the scheme over the years since we have been in office. You have already heard me put across the key to designing a better scheme for the future, building on what has worked and what has not. That is what I am committed to doing and working with the sector to make it happen.

Q226 At its root the problem is the budget is just not big enough, is it? You cannot account for this £210 million that has been lost because the NFU figures—which come on a freedom of information request from the Department itself—say that those people who were coming out of schemes were getting £520 million. The window envelope for SFI26 was £310 million. We have lost £210 million and we do not know where.
Mike has answered that point already.
Q227 Do you think that is going to come from future higher tier agreements?

We obviously publish the annual report on farming grant schemes , with the most recent report coming out relatively recently. You will know that we are committed to £11.8 billion over the lifetime of this Parliament with an annual budget of £2.3 billion.
Q228 Do you not think the budget needs to increase?
Obviously we are always keen to have more but we have to work within the spending envelope we are provided and the funding settlement that we are given from the Treasury colleagues.

Q229 I wish to say that this is farmers’ livelihoods here; it is not about political points. We very much try to keep the politics out of this room when we are discussing this. The Department has announced that there is a technical issues group, which will be expanded to allow farmers to report an issue up to one week after the window closes. Can I ask how many applicants are in this pool and will they be offered agreements?
You are referring to the exceptions, which we announced following the closure of the scheme. RPA is working through those as we speak.

There are two groups. One is those that requested digital support and the other is those that reported—as you mentioned—that they had some system issues. RPA is working through all those cases and contacting individual farmers. It will depend on the individual circumstances of the farm. In some respects farmers might have felt there were system issues but it might have been the system performing as it was expected to in terms of applying the rules of the scheme. That is why RPA is committed to looking at every individual case within those groups.
Q230 I appreciate you are saying RPA is looking at it but given that that money is gone, where will the money come from for that?
We are not talking about large sums of money; lower than £5 million is our best estimate but it could be lower than that. It depends on RPA working through those on a case-by-case basis.
Q231 To what extent is the extra cost of administration of SFI eating up the budget compared to basic payments?
Unlike the basic payment scheme, SFI is not and never was intended to be a universal income support payment. It is a payment for the provision of public goods.
Q232 Do you know how much it costs to administer BPS?
I do not have that information before me.
Q233 Do you know how much it costs to administer SFI?
I do not have that information before me.
Q234 Can you get us that information? It should surely be available.

I can. A key part of that information is also looking at the benefit-to-cost ratios that we get from SFI compared to BPS. BPS was generally regarded as having zero or very modest benefit-to-cost ratio and was poor value for taxpayers’ money. SFI—depending on the actions, because some deliver more for the environment than others—had benefit-to-cost ratios of up to 5:1. We need to look at the benefit we get from the scheme as well as the cost of administration.
Farmers who are playing up to the edge of the field might see things differently now.

Q235 Fundamentally the two schemes have very different objectives do they not? Basic payments was fundamentally just designed to support farmers based on the amount of land they farm whereas SFI is clearly public money for public goods.
Yes.
Q236 When you are talking about value for the taxpayer you are comparing apples and pears there, are you not?
That is correct.
Q237 You cannot really say basic payments was a poor scheme with poor value for money on a cost-benefit ratio if you are looking at very different metrics from what you are saying there.

We still apply a common economic assessment to the use of public money that looks at the public money that used to be dispersed through basic payment scheme, which is very low, and the value for public money we get through SFI. As you go upwards into higher tier and landscape recovery, those assessments get bigger. Even though there might be different schemes , we still apply a common analytical methodology to look at the value for taxpayers’ money that they deliver.

Q238 As part of that are you going to look at the number of farms that are left with no public support whatsoever? Obviously , under basic payments that was zero. Now that we have had this second window that is going to be quite a substantial number of farms.

As the Minister has mentioned there are a range of options we can look at for how we can learn the lessons from this year, scrapping first come, first served is one, and look at what we might do in terms of the scheme next year. There are some stakeholder organisations that will be calling for the actions that we offer to be those that deliver most for the environment. We will have to balance both maintaining an attractive offer and respecting what is happening in the industry.

I fully understand that farmers want certainty and planning predictability. That is why this year we tried to set out the details of the scheme as early as possible even though the budget turned out to not be enough. We are also in a highly dynamic environment; agriculture does not sit still. Three years ago, arable farmers in particular did not want to come into the scheme , so calibrations had to be made to make it more attractive. Now the arable sector is feeling a very different set of headwinds.

Again there are discussions live with stakeholders at the moment. We need to think about what is going on in the sector and look at the uptake against various actions. Do we need to restrict the number of actions and look at payment rates again and the overall cap? These are all calibrations we can make to try to learn lessons from this year as we prepare the offer for next year. I am noting there is a real pressure to get clarity on this quickly but equally I am hearing quite a lot of demand for quite fundamental change.

Q239 Just extremely quickly on a point you raised there, Mike—I would be interested in the Minister’s reply to this as well—SFI does not focus on food production; it focuses on public good for public money. Obviously , without taking into account food production, do you not think that is fundamentally flawed for the future security of our nation?

Obviously the “ Farming Roadmap ” sets out an ambition to at least maintain current levels of food production. The sector growth plans will drive that work, which is industry-led , as Mike said earlier. More broadly I want to see stronger, fairer, more sustainable funding streams for the sector. That is why I am coming in and looking at it with a fresh pair of eyes, looking at the various schemes and making sure we deliver on the commitments we have set out in the “ Farming Roadmap ” .

Just to directly address the point even further in addition to what the Minister said, we very much see SFI working in tandem with food production and not displacing it. Actually , in response to SFI24 , in some cases we had made some payment rates so generous that whole fields were put into legume fallow or herbal leys , for example. We restricted the payment rates and the amount of land for some actions to try to make sure we were not inadvertently displacing food production. It is very much a land-sharing scheme whereas with some other schemes I mentioned you might be looking more at taking land out of production and landscape recovery if planting trees or restoring people is your aim.

Q240 It could be the best administered scheme in the world; the reason we have such a dash for people going for it is that there is no profitability in farming for the production of food. The Government and previous Governments have taken the opinion that there is not going to be a basic payment system now for the production of food so our farmers are going to consistently be disappointed by any process that we put in place. Is that something that you are considering in terms of reviewing the system going forward?

Obviously we have responded to Minette Batters’ s “ Farming Profitability Review ” , which is a really important piece of work that we commissioned in Government alongside the roadmap. We are very much keen to make sure we are driving productivity and profitability in the sector, which is why these growth plans and the work of the partnership board that I mentioned earlier are vital. We need to make sure the scheme matches the overall strategic ambitions as we have set out in the roadmap.

Q241 Are we really at risk here of just producing a lot of strategies, roadmaps and plans that only do good for the forestry sector and nothing else, and not actually putting any additional funding or looking at how we can streamline processes through either regulation or tax incentives to our farming communities for the production of food?

I do not want strategies for strategy’s sake. It is really important that we set up what the strategic direction is or what we want to achieve around more profitable, productive, resilient farming practices. That is why that partnership approach is really important. I have certainly said to my officials it is really important that we use the roadmap as a framework for everything DEFRA does.
Q242 Would the Department ever consider including food in public good?
You would need a more specific proposition than that. Public goods is quite a strict economic definition.
Q243 Okay, food production: w ould the Department ever consider including food production in public good?

It is something that has wider societal benefits. The more food we can produce domestically the more it contributes to our national food security. I should confess—as I am probably displaying—I am not an economist on whether it would meet the strict definition; my instinct is probably not. That does not mean that food production is not important. In fact, in our “L and U se F ramework ” and the “ Farming Roadmap ” for the first time we committed strong wording about wanting domestic production to be at least maintained if not grown.

Q244 Sarah started by talking about the damage to DEFRA’s reputation and the standing among farmers. Imagine you were one of the farmers who did not get your application in so you do not know what you are going to do between now and the beginning of next year. You heard that at the biodiversity COP the Government announced something shy of £2 million to go into the purchase of the Rothbury E state on top of £5 million of public money that has come from the National Lottery Community Fund. How do you think you would feel?

Obviously I have heard frustrations from colleagues today and indeed from the farm visits I have done following the closure of the scheme. That is why being really clear on what our vision is around how we are supporting a profitable and productive farming sector is vital and the roadmap is a key document to drive the change we want to see in partnership with the sector.
Q245 Would you be happy to hear that £1.94 million was going into the purchase of an estate?
Obviously we want to drive good food production alongside delivering on environmental outcomes.
Q246 Is that the purpose of the Rothbury E state going forward in its new iteration?
Obviously this is a discussion for my ministerial colleague, Jenny Riddell-Carpenter, who leads on these specific issues. Mike, do you want to chip in on that specific project?

This funding did not come from the farming budget; it was elsewhere in DEFRA’s resources and was an explicit commitment made with regard to the Government’s international commitments on 30by30. An issue that we will obviously be looking at closely is how this might affect the tenants on the estate because we want to make sure again that we are consistent with commitments.
Q247 Does it go with strings attached?
I genuinely do not know the detail beneath what I have just said but it is money that is co-funded alongside other sources of —

Q248 You are putting in almost £2 million; the entire purchase is something in the region of £17 million, just so somebody can go to the biodiversity COP and have a good news announcement. It is an expensive press release at that, is it not?
To the best of my knowledge this is work that the Northumberland Wildlife Trust had had in train for a long time.

Q249 DEFRA has done very well to get £17 million; I am not denying its interest in the Rothbury E state. I am just asking whether this is a good signal to be sending at a time when farmer confidence in the Department is at an all-time low.

I would refer you back to the £11.8 billion we are putting into farming over the lifetime of this Parliament. We are very keen to understand the frustrations and concerns that the farming community have and make sure th at our schemes deliver for farmers across our country.
We will go on to countryside stewardship and landscape recovery.

Q250 We have just been talking at length about the need to make sure that publicly funded schemes deliver maximum benefits for both farmers and the environment. Do you believe that countryside stewardship, higher tier and landscape recovery are living up to those aims?

On countryside stewardship higher tier, we opened it on a new live service only last September. Prior to that there was a legacy of longstanding problems. We were reliant on paper-based application forms and have already secured 751 live higher tier agreements worth £31.8 million since we opened that service. We absolutely recognise that there is more we need to do to try to simplify countryside stewardship higher tier.

We have made commitments about wanting to move away from the invitation-only approach and have introduced a new expression of interest process to try to make it easier for more farmers to access the scheme. We have introduced some new single action agreements, for example on woodland creation or species-rich grassland, which is a way in which we hope we can ease some pressure on SFI. There is further work that we are doing. We are providing advice from the Minister right now in terms of other changes we think we can make to higher tier in order to get more people into it.

One thing I would say about higher tier is that it is very analogous to similar schemes such as the old countryside stewardship, environmental stewardship and new countryside stewardship. Sorry for the stewardship overload. Those schemes have been operating in this country since 1989; we have good experience of them. Natural England advisers have been working on them for a while. While it has only been a year since we put the new higher tier on the system , it is building on decades of practice

Landscape recovery is definitely the newest and most innovative of all the schemes that form the environmental land management suite. We currently have 56 projects in the pipeline, three of which have moved into implementation. We recognise that some complexity that we have encountered in a new innovative scheme of trying to get multiple landowners to agree to long-term actions at scale across big geographies is perhaps harder than we thought it would have been when we first had the ideas for the scheme. We are again preparing advice from Ministers on various things we can take to open up the pipeline and get more projects through to implementation. There are some due to go into implementation very soon but again Ministers have asked us for advice about what more we can do to open that up.

Q251 I really welcome a lot of those changes that you have set out to higher tier; it will enable a lot more to get in, particularly smaller farms, which was a real concern we had as a Committee a couple of years ago. When we spoke to Baroness Batters in reference to landscape recovery, she made it clear that she fears that with the way the scheme is designed we could end up with , in her words, “ d iamonds in paper crown s ” . There is a concern of large sums of money going into discrete areas and then equally valuable landscapes around that area or elsewhere in the country getting nothing whatsoever. Do you think that represents good value for the taxpayer and for nature?

I mentioned earlier that when I came into post I was very keen to understand all the schemes. I see how complicated they are. How we might do things differently is something that I have heard loud and clear from the sector. I was keen to get up to Upper Duddon in Cumbria and see what was going on there. What I saw there was a young farmer who was really ambitious and hopeful for the future as a result of that money going in.

Just to pick up on the specific points that you raised, Josh, it is a complex scheme and the governance is tricky. We are obviously investing significant amounts of public money over a significant amount of time. Working through what that looks like is absolutely a priority of mine and I welcome any feedback or concerns to feed into that process.

Q252 I will come back to landscape recovery in a minute. Just to go back to higher tier, earlier this year DEFRA announced new single focus higher tier agreements—which you mentioned—for species-rich grassland and scheduled monuments. Clearly the Department has specific objectives on those and thinks the scheme can help to reach them.

In stark contrast to what we have discussed around SFI, despite there being a budget for 1,200 agreements, from what we can see publicly it seems that only 650 expressions of interest were received between July and September. Why do you think that scheme is not attracting farmers?

I would want to check those numbers. I am not disputing them; I just do not have them before me. Some changes we announced earlier in July are still being worked through. As broadly as possible and in the right sequence we are trying to move away from that invitation-only. To date it has quite heavily been an adviser-led scheme. We are also looking to see if there are ways in which we can get external advisers to be able to help sign off applications because we are aware of resource pressures in Natural England.

The changes that we announced in July at Groundswell were very much a first step in terms of what we are trying to do to open up higher-tier stewardship. Again this was something that we discussed with a group of stakeholders within the last two weeks in terms of some other things and actions we can take. It is a work in progress.

Q253 We have heard as a Committee that a particular clause in agreements that would allow DEFRA to unilaterally withdraw funding is particularly causing concern for farmers. Understandably they do not want to make permanent changes to the way that they manage their land only to find that funding then disappears. Have you been picking that up as a concern that puts some off from expressing an interest?

That is very much an issue that has been raised with me. I have basically brought together different applicants to understand some challenges and issues as they progress their applications. It is definitely something that I am aware of and exploring with my officials.

Q254 Mike, you mentioned you are looking at where to go next. Are you looking to redeploy that money elsewhere, broaden the focus of the agreements that are available or just do another promotion drive and hope that you reach that 1,200 for the money to be spent?

What we are very much focused on is trying to simplify the schemes on an administrative basis so that we do not have a bottleneck of people wanting to get in because they are waiting for either permissions from Natural England advisers or others. The scheme is high ambition in terms of the outcomes that it is pegged to, in particular SSSI restoration where you need quite specific actions on specific landscapes. It is always going to be more involved from a delivery perspective than SFI, which is designed to be self-service. We are trying to take out any unnecessary administration so that we can make it easier without diluting the effectiveness of it.

Q255 Just going back to landscape recovery, across the 2022 - 23 rounds we understand that 56 projects entered the two-year development phase of the scheme. Based on public announcements it seems that only three have moved into the implementation phase. Why do you think so few projects have moved into that? Stephen, you alluded to some challenges of the complexity of it.

It picks up on what I was saying earlier around some barriers and challenges that the sector has faced. There are unique partnerships being established and these are things that people are signing up to that will have quite a lasting impact so working through that detail is vital. They are essentially complex agreements. As Mike says we want to make that process simpler and that is something that we are very much focusing on.

Q256 In the “ Farming Roadmap ” it mentions that DEFRA will provide information about future rounds of landscape recovery in 2026. Obviously we know that the applications have not been open at all during this Parliament. Given that we are a little over two months away from the end of the year do you intend to open the scheme for applications soon? If so do you know when?
I cannot make that commitment today. Obviously we have not announced a third round but working through the details of how the first two rounds have gone is the priority for me at the moment.

Q257 Recently I went out to the North Moor just outside Langport to meet the project team behind the Greater Sedgemoor landscape recovery project , including Damon Bridge from the RSPB, who is leading on that. They have over 4,000 acres in that scheme and are at an advanced stage of their development but they are desperate to know when they are going to receive an implementation agreement. Could I ask your Department to push on that so that we can get this project off the ground?

Bearing in mind what Josh has just said, they have said to me very explicitly that there is a real bottleneck in getting farmers to take up on this scheme because of that two-year withdrawal element. They are making a long-term commitment and need to be able to plan and one of the problems is that they are not getting all the farmers within that catchment set up. I would also like to specifically ask if we can get this project—the Greater Sedgemoor landscape recovery project —up and running. I also have another one in my patch, Adapting the Levels, which is also at a stage where I would very much like to see that up and running as well. If we can get some news on that I would be very grateful.
I will take that away, look at where we are with the applications and get in touch with the relevant stakeholders.
Q258 With delinked payments falling to just £600 in 2026 and 2027, how many farm businesses does DEFRA expect to have no environmental land management revenue agreement by the end of 2027?

I might need to come back in terms of by the end of 2027 but as of right now we have 84,000 live ELM revenue agreements in place. Clearly as part of the work that the Minister was alluding to in terms of how we recalibrate SFI, we have lots of schemes and agreements that are due to expire next year. Again we are trying to work with stakeholders to think about how far we can spread the money. Some decisions that we take over the coming months about the design of schemes for next year will have a material impact on the number of agreements by the end of 2027. That is why it is difficult to speculate.

Q259 It is something that I would really urge the Department to actually get a proper number on. If you do not know the numbers that are going to be outside the scheme I would ask what support is going to be made available to them. We need to make sure that all our farmers are being supported in the best possible way. Do you have any plans on how you would support people outside the schemes?

One of the comments I made earlier—which one of your colleagues also picked up on—was that SF I is not designed to be a universal income support payment; there will always be a finite budget for it. We would love to see as many farmers as possible adopting more nature-friendly and regenerative practices; that is very much the ambition in the roadmap. We have public money with which we will try to go as far as possible to encourage that. We know and recognise—quite honestly we set this out in the roadmap as well—that over time we expect the balance of schemes to change. At the moment , SF I is not designed to do the job that you are suggesting it is there to do.

Q260 Not all support for our farming community has to be pounds and pence; it can be a regulatory burden as well. Minister, outside these schemes is there any action that you would be planning on doing to help in terms of the regulatory framework they are working with?

Obviously what I want to do is make sure that our farmers are equipped to deliver what they need to deliver. I have a key role in making that happen with my officials and that is why lots of things we set out in the “ Farming Roadmap ” will hopefully drive productivity and profitability. We mentioned the growth sector plans and issues around water storage earlier. Looking at how we change regulations and do things differently in order to achieve profitability is absolutely a priority of mine.

This is relevant to your final point. We have commissioned the Law Commission to undertake a review of the environmental legislation that applies to agriculture. That review launched in April this year and we are expecting it to conclude in early 2028. The Law Commission is obviously leading it independently but it is planning to do a consultation on changes that we can make to simplify that suite of environmental legislation. We are on it in terms of regulation and are trying to look systematically at all the things we might need to encourage the profitable, productive, sustainable, resilient sector we want.

Q261 Just turning towards fair access and food security, one thing I would be interested to know is how will DEFRA replace the first-come, first-served aspects of the SFI system in 2027 to ensure funding reaches farms delivering the greatest environmental benefits without disadvantaging smaller farms or—more importantly—undermining domestic food production?

Obviously there are some trade-offs we need to think through as we co-design the scheme for next year. Earlier I mentioned the workshops we have been doing with the sector. I am also keen to hear from parliamentarians about what they want to see the scheme looking like for the future. There is only a finite resource for SFI but working through that detail with you to design the scheme for the future is an absolute priority.

Q262 One thing that I am slightly concerned about is that when I asked whether food would be included in a reviewed system going forward as a benefit of public payment, Mike said effectively food does not have an economic benefit. I am really concerned if that is the thought of DEFRA going forward.

I was answering your specific point about whether food is considered a public good and I was trying to give you the economic textbook answer. I have been in the Department for 26 years and I have never seen there be so much of a focus within the Department on both environmental and economic aspects of farming. We have tried to set that out in a roadmap and Ministers have talked about that being two sides of the same coin.

We have commitments made in the “L and U se F ramework ” and the “ Farming Roadmap ” around at least maintaining domestic production. We have set up the farming and food partnership board on the back of the Batters review. We are trying to get sector growth plans in as many sectors as possible starting with horticulture and poultry because they are the two where we see the biggest early opportunities but that is not where our ambition ends.

I do not necessarily agree with that characterisation that we do not take food and food production seriously. In fact, you only have to look at the hearing in front of the Public Accounts Committee last week when our permanent secretary was talking about food security being national security and the work we are doing on food resilience. I do not think it has ever been as high up the departmental agenda in my period there since 2000.

Obviously food is a key part of my portfolio. The good food cycle framework came out in July 2025, which is an area of priority for me. Obviously there are themes about resilience, affordability and healthy support for children and young people. Some good outcomes have been achieved from that strategy but we are working through what that might look like for the future.

Q263 Just moving on to a slightly different aspect within ELMs of nature markets. The “ Farming Roadmap ” envisages private nature markets playing a great role in farming farms, yet many farmers tell us that markets simply do not exist for them. We went up to the Westmorland county show to gather evidence there and Lisa Bennett—a local farmer—gave evidence to us. When I raised a question about nature markets she shrugged her shoulders and said, “I’ve never heard of this before. We are upland farmers; this is not for the likes of us. It is for large arable maybe down south, in Norfolk for example.” I would like to hear what concrete steps DEFRA is actually taking to develop these markets and how it will ensure that public funding remains available where private finance cannot take that slack.

There was a publication we put out yesterday called “ Growing Places ” that very much looks at this issue of how we can get more private finance into farming. In some respects, some farmers I have visited around the country would already benefit within their food chain from producing to a certain standard that does not necessarily need G overnment intervention or G overnment-backed schemes to enable it. There are pockets of it happening.

Something we have also committed to is setting up a working group looking at private finance to try to understand more systematically where the barriers are. The opportunities are big and we are trying to get private finance in alongside landscape recovery. Again there is much more work we need to do on this.

Q264 Is the other issue that we face with this not that it is a free market? There is no set structure for these private investors to come in and set out schemes that make sense to our farmers. I can speak to some farmers who are on the Norfolk-Suffolk border and have been involved with schemes with Nestl é , PepsiCo or other bodies such as that. You can go two miles up the road and there will not be a scheme available. Is the Department going to take any action to set out a framework of what these private finance initiatives should actually look like?

That is what this working group I mentioned will look at. Where are the pockets in which it is actually working? I recognise it is pockets; it is not widespread. What are the conditions for success where it is successful? What are the barriers where it is not working? Setting up the market in the first place is probably the biggest one. I can assure you it is something that this task and finish group is looking at.
Again, obviously the “ Farming Roadmap ” is key to unlocking that investment with that certainty and consistency we are looking to deliver over a 25-year plan essentially.

Q265 Just for you Minister, do you have full confidence that the private sector will be able to take over all the slack within the system to finance these schemes? Obviously as the processes are set out from G overnment expenditure it will decrease. On SFI it will close eventually in the hope that private finance will take over the complete slack. Do you honestly believe that will happen?

We want to work in co-operation and partnership with the private sector. The growth plans are going to be really important. They are industry-led but I am certainly keen to make sure we are engaging banks around what the opportunities are for the farming community going forward so there is a nice blend of both public and private investment.

Q266 With the current economic climate of the world do you think that there will be private companies that will wish to invest in these environmental schemes or will they just see it as a nicety that they can go without? A lot of my farmers turn around and say they are only doing this because it is greenwashing and then once they find that the economic situation is too tough for them they are going to opt out of these schemes.
We learned lessons from the work that Mike just mentioned that has been commissioned recently. I am certainly keen to hear any further thoughts and views as we work that through in more detail.
Q267 The US Secretary of State told us that these capital markets would be functioning by 2030. Is that still the Department’s view?
I do not know the answer to that. We can get back to you on those specific points.

Q268 You mentioned earlier you were happy about the EU reset and the relationship with Europe is going to be obviously a key point of discussion. Talking about financing will the SPS agreement or any deal necessitate some basic income support payments?
I cannot get into the specifics of negotiation.

Q269 What about in terms of the principle going forward? If you are going to put Europe and the UK on an even playing field, Europe is moving more towards that model again. I want to have a commitment from the Government and a recognition of what we can do.
There are no plans to do so.
Q270 I am conscious of time, but I have an important question. What is your vision for the uplands in England? What will they look like in 20 years?

As a new Minister, the uplands will be one of my priorities. I have been to Dartmo or and Cumbria to understand the complexities and challenges they face: in some cases , those are long-standing. The “L and U se F ramework ” is a key document in recognising the significance of the uplands. There are issues around grazing numbers and how the land is used; the “L and U se F ramework ” will hopefully lead to better decision making.

I am also mindful of the important work that Dr Hilary Cottam is doing in Dartmoor to set out a longer-term vision, with a place-based, community-led approach that I hope will deliver lasting change in the area. To deliver on that vision, we need a key role and strong partnership working around the funding streams we offer: that is the key message I heard on my visit to Dartmo or .

Q271 Do you view livestock farming as an issue to be managed or do you view it as central in terms of the management of upland areas? There is a distinction between the two: I appreciate you might think it is only semantic.

Grazing numbers are important—farmers raise that issues with me—but it is also important to deliver environmental outcomes. It is not a binary choice, it is nuanced. Natural England has a particular role to play around supporting farmers with their HLS agreements, but I recognise that these are contested spaces; it is vital to have a clear strategy and vision for these communities, so I welcome Dr Hilary Cottam’s work.
Q272 Before we come on to Natural England, I should declare that my father is a non-executive board member.

We have 5,400 higher-level stewardship agreements expiring in ’ 27-28, so it is important to understand whether farming or grazing is an issue to be managed, or whether it is integral to the beauty of the uplands in and of itself. How many of those agreement holders have a route into replacement schemes, and how will you prevent a funding gap for those who do not?

We want to avoid a cliff edge. I have already had conversations with Natural England; in the case of Dartmoor, some agreements will soon be expiring. We are working through those as we speak and will continue to prioritise that work. It is important that our investments in the uplands are tailored to habitat, site conditions and environmental outcomes: that is why there is more work to do, and I am committed to making that happen.

Q273 We are worried that both Natural England and the Rural Payments Agency lack the capacity to process the volume of countryside stewardship higher-tier claims that will arise when these other agreements expire.
I have raised these issues with Natural England; I work closely with that organisation, which also has new leadership.
Q274 What is DEFRA specifically doing to address that cliff edge?
Mike, do you want to answer the capacity point?

I would like to respond to your first question. I can remember when the Lake District was designated as a UNESCO world heritage site because it was a farmed landscape. We absolutely want farming to thrive throughout the country.

On the specifics of the HLS expiries, we are taking a cohort-by-cohort approach. That will vary depending in particular on whether SSSI land is associated with the agreements, and if so, the state of that SSSI. There may be some expiring HLS agreements where it makes sense to move the best part into the higher tier without elaborating the agreement. There may be others—depending on the state of the SSSI condition and the management options or practices that the agreements have historically funded— that might need a more hands-on approach and more discussion and negotiation with Natural England. Natural England is working through those cohorts to make sure there is a smooth transition; that might mean taking slightly different approaches for different groups of agreements—depending in particular on the status of the SSSI—but we are providing advice to Ministers on how that should be handled.
Q275 D o you think it is going to be fine?

It is challenging. We are dealing with long-term agreements: ideally we want similar actions to happen on multiple holdings, which brings complexity. The situation in Dartmoor is particularly complex and that often gets into the media.
Q276 You are de-stocking animals on Dartmoor at the rate of 76%.
We are guided by Natural England.

Q277 In terms of this cliff edge, if 5,500 agreements in the higher-level stewardship scheme are ending, will a 76% de-stocking rate be your blueprint in , for example , Cumbria? Is that what we should expect?

As our independent statutory nature conservation adviser, Natural England will look at the state of individual SS S Is. My understanding is that it will not provide a blanket, one-size-fits-all approach across the country; it will look at what is needed in each place and use that as a starting point.

Q278 If this is being totally led by Natural England, are you concerned by what you hear from other stakeholders with whom you presumably engage? Those stakeholders have told this Committee that they feel this policy is being done to them rather than with them, and that when Natural England shows up—if it ever does—it shows a lack of understanding and a lack of respect; the relationship is simply not there.

In answer to that question, I have been to Dartmoor and attended the Dartmoor f orum hosted by Sir Geoffrey Cox. I have also met with a number of farmers through the groups that Hilary Cottam is convening. It is important that we engage with local processes and local organisations: there are existing groups and fora that we work with in Dartmoor to deliver the commitments that we want to see delivered.

Q279 Are you saying that we should not lead with Natural England?
