If we are putting all the emphasis on Natural England to lead the process and deal with this cliff edge, we are hearing from other stakeholders that we will either end up with 76% de-stocking rates, or with local farmers on the land feeling that they are not being listened to or taken along on this process.

We are always keen to work in partnership with Natural England, respecting that it has , by statute , independent status as our nature and conservation adviser. I have also heard anecdotal evidence that on the ground, the relationship between Natural England and some landowners is very good; it works in some areas, and we want that to be common across the country. In partnership with Natural England we are looking at all the expiries and taking a chunking approach to how we treat different cohorts of agreements. We will then provide advice to Ministers on the best way forward.

Q280 I am conscious of time, but what about the social and cultural value? In terms of the landscape, you talked about how farmers play an integral role in places such as Cumbria. Are you worried that there is no emphasis on those traditional practices?

That is why Dr Hilary Cottam’s work is important in looking at a system approach to supporting important heritage—as well as habitat protection and grazing levels—and setting out a longer-term vision. Upland communities have seen converging challenges for far too long; addressing those issues in partnership, along with Hilary’s work, is really important. We will hopefully be moving on to Cumbria in the new year.
Q281 Are you worried about the loss of practices such as hefting, breaking down genetic diversity, and ancient commoning traditions? Is that something DEFRA is concerned about?

Yes, those issues are on our radar: again, it will depend on the particular area. For instance, when we talk about SSSI land—where Natural England operates within a specific regulatory framework—it is hard to give you a one-size-fits all approach, but the best outcomes we have had in agri-environment schemes over 40 years have been when we were working in partnership.

Q282 I am definitely not asking for a one-size-fits-all approach; that is not what people are telling us they want. We went to the Westmoreland show, and we have engaged with stakeholders and farmers; you heard a quote from a farmer earlier. It is definitely not the approach that is being reflected back to the Committee.
Can I quickly ask about common land: are common holders not being allowed to claim SFI or countryside stewardship for their common land?
Commoners can already apply but at the moment there are certain issues with the system: my understanding is that we are working through those issues.

Historically, the system has not provided for this, at least on the common land itself, although in-bye land can be accessible. The RPA is currently piloting an approach to see if countryside stewardship higher-tier land can be put on the system; if that works we will look to open up the scale. At the moment, you are correct that common land is not eligible for SFI, but we are trying to tackle it for the higher tier.
Q283 T hey are excluded because of a software engineering issue ?
It is a legacy issue; it is not new, and my understanding is that it is because—
Q284 It is not new but you have not fixed it until now, and that is why they are excluded ?
The RPA is on the case now, fixing it in terms of the trials and the pilot.

Q285 Before we move on, I want to go back to Henry’s point about 75 % to 76% destocking, which comes about because you have a very particular view on how Dartmoor should be managed and how it should look. That is the vision point. Surely the vision should not be coming from Natural England: it should be coming from the Department, and Natural England should then be charged with the delivery of that vision.
I completely agree.
Q286 Then why is it not happening?
That is why I have asked Marian and Tony to come to the Department to see me on these issues, and I have been to visit directly to hear concerns.
Q287 Is the vision of Dartmoor with a 75% reduction in livestock a D EFRA vision? Or have you subcontracted that vision to the arm’s length body?

Everyone recognises that as a result of overgrazing, the SSSIs in Dartmoor are not in a good state at the moment. We are working with Natural England, the land managers and the Dartmoor Land Use Management Group— chaired by Phil Stocker—to see if there are different ways in which we can tackle this problem. The accusation is often around blanket stocking rates, but I have heard the former CEO and chair of Natural England say that the biggest issue is the overwintering of sheep. At the moment, we are working with Natural England to see if there are ways in which we can reduce the overwintering of sheep without reducing overall stocking levels; there is a level of detail beneath that headline figure, which I know has some traction. We are trying to balance Natural England and its independent responsibilities with the requirements of the regulatory framework and what is best for the area.
Q288 We have now gone to a place where the Government are telling farmers in Dartmoor where they can overwinter sheep.
I meant that we want to try to reduce the overwintering of sheep on the moor because it is preventing the establishment of the flora and the fauna there.
We will be returning to this with our upcoming report on upland farming, so I will not delay the Committee further. Charlie, we are awash with DEFRA strategies.

Q289 We have the “L and U se F ramework ” , we have had the Batters r eview into farming profitability, and we have the “F arming R oadmap ” . The “L and U se F ramework ” calls for 9% of agricultural land to be focused on environmental and climate benefits, a further 5% to be used for food production while incorporating environmental benefits, and 2% to be used for housing. How does that marry up with the Batters r eview and the “F arming R oadmap ” ?

The “L and U se F ramework ” is exactly what it says on the tin : i t is an overall framework to make sure that we make better decisions based on land use across the country. There is more work to do to help deliver that. The “F arming R oadmap ” is about setting certainty and consistency for the sector over the next 25 years ; this document drives my work in the Department to deliver the outcomes that we want to see achieved.
Q290 I hope it would be your ambition to improve domestic food security by increasing domestic production.
We are always keen to make that happen.
Q291 Is that not going to be very difficult when you take 9% of land out of productive use?
That is why these strategies are important, and working through them to make sure that we make better decisions and that I give informed advice. That is my priority.

Q292 Let us take the poultry sector; it is an interesting one. We import large amounts of chicken from countries such as China and others in the Far East, which we would perhaps choose to avoid if we could produce it ourselves. There has not been a single new broiler unit approved in this country for the last two years because of problems with the planning system. We have NGOs jumping on the back of every planning application and issues with statutory consultees—such as Natural England—preventing increased domestic food security and increased food production. Supermarkets and processors will tell you that if we produced more chicken meat at home, they would be able to sell it. Minister, can I ask you to go away and work with your colleagues across the MHCLG and others to ensure that we break down these barriers? That would come at no cost to the Government and would be a real boost to the rural economy.

Thank you, Charlie: that is absolutely the spirit of the work the partnership board is doing and the growth sector plans that we are taking forward with industry. I mentioned horticulture and poultry: we are expecting those documents in the new year. They could be helpful in taking forward the growth that we need to see in poultry and other sectors.

Q293 On the planning point specifically, do you undertake to work with colleagues in the MHCLG to look at how the current system is preventing that growth? We have farmers who are unable to replace decaying buildings in order to reduce stocking densities and create better welfare, even though more emissions would be captured and it would be better for the environment. It seems barmy that farmers are not able to modernise and improve their own farms.

I completely agree. That is why that partnership approach with MHCLG and others at the partnership board working with us on the sector growth plans is absolutely vital to build the more resilient, sustainable sector that we want to see in the future.
Q294 When are we going to get a food strategy?

The good food strategy came out in July 2025: I am working through the details of that, and performance metrics are on the way. Some good things have been achieved through the good food neighbourhood scheme, which was announced relatively recently, with £10 million to support 45 local authorities across the country, the introduction of breakfast clubs and increased eligibility for free school meals. I want to make sure we get on and deliver some good, positive things working with the sector and that is why I am looking at that as we speak.
W e still do not have a date ? We have a few other questions, but I want to clear up the one on horticulture. Ben, do you want to take the lead on that?

Q295 This has already been alluded to in terms of the co-produced horticulture roadmap and plan that is coming through. Within the protected horticulture sector, there are greenhouse growers in my constituency—on the Crown Point estate in Kirby Bedon—who are facing a lot of trouble because they do not have a SIC code to allow them to access the energy intensive industry compensation scheme. They can grow 70 kilos of tomatoes in one square metre, thus increasing our food security and increasing profitability within our farming sector, but they are blocked off from help with rising energy costs. What assessments have you made, Minister, on the price that is paid through excluding this sector from the EII support schemes?

I mentioned the importance we place on the horticultural sector, which is why we are developing a sector al growth plan with it. It has been a pleasure to meet with representatives of the industry and the NFU in the last couple of weeks to work through the details of that plan, which we hope to publish early in the new year. You will know that 20% of farm gate value comes from the horticultural sector, but it uses only 2% of land, so there are huge opportunities for the sector going forward. I am aware of the challenges it is facing around labour, energy costs and so on. With specific regard to high energy costs, I recognise that this is a significant concern for the industry and we are working through that. I saw it directly in terms of the issues that were raised when I joined you in Norfolk, and when I visited Isle of Wight Tomatoes over the summer. We are continuing to look at options based on the evidence before us because I appreciate how important this is to the sector.
Q296 Will you be arguing with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade to give a SIC code to protected horticulture?

We are working through the sector growth plan in tandem with the sector, looking at the issues and challenges. We will then take that back to the partnership board, which has cross-Government representation. If there are particular asks in there, we will try to make them a success.

Q297 I would quickly add that the last time I asked this question of the former Secretary of State for DEFRA, I was told by a representative from the Department, “It’s for global trade bodies and the National Audit Office to define this.” There did not seem to be any ministerial engagement in the process. Can you, as the Minister, give assurances that you will be pushing on this issue?

These issues have been raised with me, and I am very alive to them. The sector growth plan is the vehicle for unlocking the barriers that the sector faces, and I am very much involved in the detail of that.

We have a few other questions around the wool market and the position of milking goats but , unfortunately, time is not with us; we will pursue those questions with you in correspondence, along with a number of other pieces from today. Thank you, gentlemen, for your attendance. We shall doubtless return to these and other matters in the future. For the moment, that concludes our session.

sessions.iT: State of the Fire and Rescue Services

segs.tx: Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee
Oral evidence: The State of the Fire and Rescue Services , HC 733
Tuesday 27 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 27 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Ms Abena Oppong-Asare (Chair); Sagal Abdi-Wali; Chris Curtis; Mr Will Forster; Mr Gagan Mohindra ; and Alan Strickland .
Questions 1 to 36
Witnesses

I : Jonathan Smith, London Fire Commissioner ; Simon Tuhill, Chief Fire Officer, West Midlands Fire and Rescue Service ; Kathryn Billing, Chief Fire Officer, Cornwall Fire and Rescue Service ; Jon Lacey, Chief Fire Officer, Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service .

II : Roy Wilsher, His Majesty ’ s Inspector of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services ; Phil Garrigan , Chair, National Fire Chiefs Council ; Cllr Wendy Maples, Chair, Local Government Association ’ s Fire and Rescue Authority Committee ; Steve Wright, General Secretary, Fire Brigades Union .
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Jonathan Smith, Simon Tuhill, Kathryn Billing and Jon Lacey.

Q1 Good morning and welcome to the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee. My name is Abena Oppong-Asare and I am the Chair of the Committee. This session, we are going to be looking at the state of fire and rescue services. We are very happy to have you all here because you are experts in your field so I hope you can guide us in terms of raising with the Government what we need to strengthen policy - wise. Before we start, I would be grateful if you could all introduce yourselves.
Good morning, everyone . Thank you for the opportunity. I am Jon Lacey, chief fire officer for Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service .
Good morning, everyone. I am Simon Tuhill . I am the chief fire officer for West Midlands Fire Service .
Good morning, everybody. It is a privilege to be here. My name is Kathryn Billing and I am the chief fire officer of Cornwall Fire and Rescue Service .
Good morning, everyone. I am Jonathan Smith . I am the London fire commissioner.
Can I ask Committee members to introduce themselves?
I am Alan Strickland, Member of Parliament for Newton Aycliffe and Spennymoor.
I am Chris Curtis. I am MP for Milton Keynes North and I should declare that my brother is a local firefighter in Milton Keynes.
I am Sagal Abdi-Wali. I am the MP for Holborn and St Pancras and I should declare that I am still leader of the council in Camden.
I am Will Forster, MP for Woking.
I am Gagan Mohindra, MP for South West Hertfor d shire.

Q2 First , I want to say thank you for you r service. I know it is not easy to do the work that you do. I a m going to start with a question on wildfires. I a m not sure whether you also went to the G overnment ’ s wildfire summit on Friday. If you did, it woul d be good if you could weave some of the answers through when responding.

T he wildfires took place over the summer. Can you describe the scenes that you saw as a firefighter and cover how that is impacted your work and what you woul d like to see the G overnment implement? I understand that on Friday the summit discussed the wildfire action plan . I understand that that is something that the fire service sector has been calling for. If that is the case, tell me what you woul d like to see in it.

Thank you for the question. Perhaps I will pick that one up initially. I attended the major incident wildfire in Stourbridge in the west midlands. It is fair to say that the scenes that day will stay with me for ever . I have nearly 29 years ’ service in the fire and rescue sector , and the things I saw that day were something that I have never seen before. The scene of devastation across such a wide area of a relatively urban part of the west midlands was deeply upsetting.

The firefighters were magnificent. My firefighters went above and beyond what could be reasonably expected. The incident was physically demanding for them. It was the hottest day of the year and very windy. Not only was it physically demanding —and there were firefighters who had to be treated by paramedic colleagues for heat exhaustion —but it was also psychologically really taxing.

At that incident, 20 residential properties were fully consumed and destroyed by fire, and that is something that my firefighters took really personally . We had members of staff crying at the scene because they felt they were not doing the most they could, and of course they were working in incredibly difficult conditions.

At one stage, almost every single resource in West Midlands Fire Service was deployed not just to Stourbridge, but to the nine other significant fires going on across the west midlands , including three other major incidents , and the hundreds of other fires that were taking place, even those smaller fires. T he impact on us was huge and the impact on my staff has been quite profound.

T o speak to the G overnment ’ s commitment around the wildfire action plan, the fire sector really supports that. We know that fire and rescue services are not going to be able to fix the wildfire challenge on our own. This takes a whole - of - society approach. T hat includes fire and rescue being adequately resourced and prepared to deal with wildfires, meaning that we have the right PPE for our firefighters, the right vehicles, the right equipment and indeed the right numbers of firefighters . T hat day showed , not just in the west midlands but across the whole of the country, a sector that was incredibly stretched due to the loss of firefighters over the last 15 to 20 years.

I t is not just the fire and rescue sector that can do the response part of wildfires. We also need government support around bringing together the whole of the community . T hat includes local authorities that can support with public space protection orders so that we can enforce people behaving responsibly when we are at those times of significant wildfire risk. It includes t he use of national alerts to let people know what they should and should not do. It includes l andowners, the Countryside Alliance and the National Farmers Union thinking about responsible land management, particularly in the west midlands where there is urban - rural interface . T his is not just burning in farmers ’ fields , peatland or moorland , but it is impacting on residential properties , which is something that many services are now starting to face as we go forward.

T hen there is the civic duty of the public behaving responsibly. The wildfire in Stourbridge was deemed to be caused accidentally , but over the course of the summer we had several wildfires caused by people behaving a bit more irresponsibly , with the use of disposable barbecues or careless disposal of smoking materials , or indeed deliberately.

One significant incident that happened on the 13th in Highter ’ s Heath in s outh Birmingham that resulted in the total loss of six houses was deemed to have been started deliberately. T here is a whole - society approach not just around regulation but also society having that civic duty to come together as climate change makes the role of the fire service more complex.

Q3 That is really helpful, particularly your perspective on the whole - society approach. You mentioned the national emergency alerts. As we saw for the first time last year —I believe it was in August — national emergency alerts were issued in relation to the wildfires. There was a bit of criticism , as you know , in terms of whether it met the threshold and why the alert was issued , particularly with the wildfire. Do you know whether you have done any lessons learned to see whether this was effective and is something that should be embedded in the system going forward?

The sector ’ s belief is that that message was effective. In fact, we would have advocated for it to have happened earlier. That day there were wildfires going on across the whole of the UK and major incidents declared in many fire and rescue services. That message, telling people what they should and should not do, was one of the crucial bits of public messaging that enable d us to get the hook in to speak to the public about how we would like them to behave at a time of extreme risk of wildfire.

Q4 Building on what you have mentioned so far, I am interested to hear, given the lessons from the wildfires and that climate change means we might expect more of those, how your plans and tactics might change. Is there a need for different innovative methods? I am thinking about the commitment around military air support. Different fire brigades during the summer were testing out different new bits of kit. How might we expect your approach to change and what support might you need from Government to help you do that?

F unn ily enough , back in 2022 the London Fire Brigade experienced significant challenges with wildfires , as colleagues on the panel will remember . P articularly 19 July 2022 will live long in the memory . There was 40 ° to 41 ° heat that firefighters had to operate in.

W e have had to completely overhaul our operational response to deal with these challenges. I n a bizarre way the fact that the London f ire c ommissioner is having a conversation about wildfire probably tells you where we now are. Six or seven years ago , we were not having that conversation . We had had some significant grass fires and some significant challenges previously , but nothing to what we saw back in 2022. We as an organisation , specifically the LFB , had to learn a number of lessons to make sure that we were as prepared as possibl e . O ver the last three to four years , we have overhauled our training provision . We have brought in new kit and equipment . We have different vehicles . O ur incident commanders deal with wildfire in a different way .

A s you will appreciate , we had been set up predominantly as an urban fire and rescue service . W e were still dealing with the aftermath from the Grenfell Tower inquiry and the subsequent recommendations that the LFB was having to deliver against. T o then find ourselves dealing with the incidents that we faced back in 2022 has meant we have had to re - posture ourselves as an organisation . N ow , as we approach the summer period , there is a long run - up.

Simon ’ s point is right : this is a whole - societ y approach . One thing that we now do is to write to all the local borough chief executives to talk about how we manage open green spaces and encourage people to behave in a different way when we get into the summer. T he emergency alert is something where, as a country , we have to get into that habit. In southern Europe , for example , that is a very common occurrence . T hese alerts will be sent out and it changes the way that people behav e and think about wildfire.

I f I talk parochially from the LFB ’ s perspective , we have had to completely overhaul our operational posture for the summer period. W e brought in significant numbers of firefighters over the summer period because we were anticipating significant heat . O n the hottest day of the year , which I think was 13 August , we got up to 38 °C or 39 °C . We use a system called recall to duty , so we have 2,500 firefighters who are signed up to a voluntary recall to duty. W hen we anticipate particular challenges around our operational capability , we are able to bring additional resource in. I t meant that, on that day , we crewed every single pumping appliance and every single specialist vehicle to try to maintain the position that we had in London .

I f I may go through the call figures, in July we were 40% up on the previous three-year average. In August we we re 49% up on the previous three-year average. We have done 20% more wildfires in 2026 than we did in 2022 , which is the biggest challenge to us as an organisation. W e are having to think very differently about how we posture ourselves as an organisation to deal with what is now , to use that hideous phrase , the new normal.

We are thinking about next summer now . I know that we will need additional PPE . We will need additional kit and equipment. I very much welcome the G overnment ’ s positioning on wildfire at the moment , particularly the summit , but we would need to see the resource flow in to fire and rescue services right across the country in order to deal with what is now a significant challenge. T his has been rising for some time . W e experienced it particularly in 2022 , where we lost over 40 houses in Wennington and Dagenham in particular , because the fire had spread in a way that we simply had not anticipated before.

This year we have been able to hold it in London and support the national endeavour . W e have sent 300 LFB firefighters to major incidents in England and the south of Wales. Nearly 60 vehicles have been deployed to support the national resilience effort . T hat is what this is going to take . T his is a UK issue for us to contend with. The national resilience of UK fire and rescue services has been severely tested over the summer period . We now have to think very seriously about how we make sure every fire and rescue service has the resource it needs to deal with these issues , which we know we are going to face for the foreseeable future.

Can I start by thanking you all for what you and your teams do to keep our communities safe? Mr Smith, you spoke about the national alert. Some of the feedback we had from domestic abuse charities was the concern that victims of domestic abuse may have secondary phones. The feedback I would offer is this: can we roll the pitch if we are going to send out a national alert to make sure those people are able to hide their secondary phones ? I wanted to make sure that that was on the record.

Q5 I wanted to follow up on what both Jonathan and Simon said, particularly about the increase in resources, the different vehicles and PPE. Have you identified new technology that you think should be factored into part of what the Government are looking at , which will help mitigate particularly stuff such as wildfires and other things that you are responding to?

An alternative option is a predominantly on-call fire service. Most people in Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service have day jobs and then respond by page r s to the emergencies as and when they happen. They are hugely dedicated people giving up their time to respond to emergencies every day of the week and evenings. Under normal circumstances that works quite well, but on the Dunwich fire during the summer that we experienced in Suffolk the turnaround of staff was hugely challenging.

Technology can help to a point there. As soon as we brought air assets in to the Dunwich fire, that quenched a large amount of the fire quite quickly. We had to take that at a risk of cost, because Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service already runs at a budget pressure this year, meaning that any other resources that we bring in for spate conditions, such as wildfires, floodings or coastal inundations, come at an extra cost that we then need to find through our fire authority, which of course is challenging.

In terms of the technology available, it is encouraging to hear that the RAF may well be providing us with firefighting aerial capability. The challenge there is that that may then come at a cost to local authorities to be able to fund that, which will be impossible because we are already run ning at pressure .

D rone capabilities and technology such as robotics also can play their part in wildfires and other emergencies . The challenge there is that certainly local authorities and fire authorities do not have the capital investment to bring in this technology . W e certainly do not have the capital and revenue budget to keep up with emerging technology that could be so useful to us and could prevent fatalities in the public , but also firefighter fatalities .

T he budget also comes into effect where we have seen cutbacks over recent years , and certainly over the decades , where firefighter numbers have been reduced . T hat provides its challenges . Dunwich is an example . W here we have on-call firefighters , you can only rotate them around a shift so many times before you are putting their pager down to bring them back to another fire , or to the Dunwich fire only a few hours after they just left .

We think that n ational resilience and the capability there should be looked at for investment to make sure that , when you press the button , it is not just London that is supporting but all the other fire service s. Another 14 came to assist Dunwich . J ust as Dunwich finished , we then put Suffolk firefighters across the country to Hampshire and to Wales to help them when we were already stretched , because we knew they needed that help .

T here is technology out there . It needs to be worked through carefully . S upport through capital and revenue investment will help us to embrace that , take it on board and move it forward at pace .

Q6 I wanted to come in on something that Mr Smith mentioned about being prepared for next summer. We are seeing a lot of extreme weather. It is a lot more frequent now and it is going to probably impact us in the winter as well, especially with flooding. I understand that that is not a statutory duty for the fire brigade. I wanted to understand how you are prepared for other extreme weather inciden t s, especially flooding if it is not part of your duty .

It is a key question for us. Yes, we are now anticipating warmer, wetter winters as well as longer, drier summers. The kit and equipment that we have purchased to deal with wildfires—we have these terrain support vehicles—during the summer give us a four - by - four capability to deal with wildfires and in the winter give us an enhanced flooding capability. We are looking now at our next generation of pumping appliances , which are going to need to be as multifaceted as possible. We are going to have to make sure that we are postured correctly in the summer period to deal with wildfires, but now there is what we are seeing in the autumn and winter.

There was a week in April that sums up where we are at the moment. On the Monday night, we had flash flooding in south-west London and what are referred to as spate conditions, so we had significant numbers of calls coming into the control room. We had to then think about how we were deploying our resources. At the end of that week we then got temperatures of 30 ° to 32 ° , all in the same period. In a microcosm, that gives you an understanding of some of the challenges for all fire and rescue services.

This is a global issue clearly, not just for the UK, but it is something we are having to think about very carefully in our longer-term strategic planning and when we are buying kit and equipment. There is the PPE challenge. What we are looking at next year is lightweight PPE that can be used in a wildfire scenario, but in a whole range of other rescue scenarios as well, so it is multi-purpose, because that is the nature of modern firefighting.

Last year, we went to 44 different incident types as a fire and rescue service. The role continues to expand. The risks and challenges that fire and rescue services are dealing with continue to expand. That is something we have to think about very carefully in how we plan for the future.

In Cornwall we had the first two named storms that hit us this week. For areas such as Cornwall, rurality really matters. We have dispersed communities, long travel distances and critical infrastructure vulnerabilities among our communities, and they become isolated really quickly. We have touched on wildfires and then gone more broadly into storms and flooding.

We have to look at the risks that we are facing as a fire and rescue service. They are changing significantly and quickly. The question for all of us is whether the resilience arrangements that we have in place are changing quickly enough to keep up with that pace of change. If we are serious about committing to building resilient communities, which touches on wildfires, flooding and storms—it is the whole piece—from my perspective fire and rescue services need to be seen as part of the nation ’ s resilience arrangements and critical to that infrastructure, not simply about that emergency response piece.

If we look at it at the macro level, we support nationally. We are sat there as a critical part of the UK ’ s resilience architecture. It is not just the fire piece. It is the critical national infrastructure, the support for energy resilience , and food security more broadly. We respond to the impacts of extreme weather, as we have just pointed out. If we then look at that meso level, we bring together partners through our local resilience arrangements. We connect places and communities. We strengthen resilience and we are there really often to support community cohesion. At the micro level, we work directly with individuals, the most vulnerable people and families , to safeguard and build capacity.

The value from the fire and rescue service perspective is that we operate all three of those levels. We do that simultaneously. We are trusted and respected. We are embedded nationally, but also embedded within our communities. I have 31 fire stations. They are absolutely at the heart of our communities. My firefighters are predominantly on-call. They are the people ; they are the communities. That resilience cannot rely on good will alone. It requires sustained and sustainable investment. From my perspective, the fire and rescue service is absolutely critical to the nation ’ s resilience .
Q7 I am going to move on to the fire safety risks from e-bikes and e-scooters. What are the trends you are seeing locally in the incidence of fires involving e-bikes and e-scooters?

Someone described e-bikes and e-scooters perfectly to me the other day when they said that that has become the new chip pan fire. It is lithium-ion batt eries more broadly actually, the truth be told, not just confined to e-bikes and e-scooters. It is a challenge, because we want to support green technology. We want to see that continue to evolve, but there have been very significant risks with e-bikes and e-scooters, particularly on the black market.

Regulation has a key role to play here. We are really keen to see that the secondary legislation around the Product Regulation and Metrology Act now comes forward. There is a key role, particularly when it comes to the regulation of the online marketplace. We really need to see that come through. At the moment , there are too many counterfeit products on the market.

There is still a lot of education required to make sure that people understand the dangers of self-conversion kits with bikes , and the importance of charging e-bikes and e-scooters properly. We have run a significant campaign called ChargeSafe , which is directly focused on the issue around e-bike s and e-scooter s , and particularly safe charging in HMOs and other shared accommodation , where we have e-bikes and e-scooters being stored in escape routes . We are point ing that out and working with housing providers.

It is definitely something we have to keep coming around to. Back in 2020 , the London Fire Brigade did 20 e-bike or e-scooter fires. In 2025 , we did 210 , so it has been going on an upward trajectory. A ctually this year, and we think it may well be down to some of the education that we have been doing, it has started to come down slightly , but at this moment in time we have to be relentless about it .

M y big ask is that we push forward with the secondary legislation and see that come online . I was having a conversation with the c ommissioner of the Singapore Civil Defence Force at the World Fire Congress , which was held in London about three weeks ago . I was asking him how Singapore deal s with e-bikes and e-scooters . I t is through very strict regulation . There are only certain manufacturers that people can purchase e-bikes and e-scooters from. It is very clear . T here is proper kitemarking and real strict safety standards that sit around it. T here is a huge role for education , but also a huge role in regulation as far as we are concerned.

I t is a broader question around lithium-ion batt eries , not just e-bikes and e-scooters . An other trend we have seen over the summer period is recycling sites that go up in fire where people are not discarding lithium-ion batt eries properly. T here is a whole range of challenges that come with new and emerging technology , but of course we want to see that new and emerging technology come through because , going back to our previous conversation around the impact of climate change , we know that that is the route forward. There is a whole range of measures we would want to see , not least , in the regulatory space , to see that secondary legislation come forward , which I think will then make a big difference.

Jonathan has explained that exceptionally well about the increase of e-bikes, the challenges that they face and the fatalities, sadly, that they cause. “Counterfeit” was a word that was mentioned by Jonathan there. That is why it needs to be part of a whole system approach to dealing with e-bikes and lithium-ion batt eries that are not legitimate batteries manufactured in the correct way.

For a long time, the fire service has worked with partners across the system to deal with faulty washing machines, dishwashers and a whole load of other things. That is why we need close partnership working with trading standards across the board to make sure that we are all working on this together , that whoever has the legitimate powers is able to deal with these , that the resources at the import area, such as Felixstowe port , are taken seriously , and that we have the right resources in there to prevent them entering the country in the first place.
Q8 Do you think we need to get to a kitemark standard? Mr Smith referred to that.

You look at the role that regulation can play. A lot of this is to do with education , and giving people very simple, straightforward instructions — so that they are able to recognise straightaway whether something meets a certain safety standard — is definitely something I would support. Having listened to international experiences, that seems to be the way that they have seen a significant reduction , as in the Singaporean example that I gave , in the numbers of e-bike and e-scooter fires that they were dealing with. I would certainly welcome that .
Q9 Excuse my ignorance. Are e-bikes and e-scooters a problem nationwide ?

Yes. Like Jon athan, West Midlands Fire Service responds to numerous incidents. We tragically had a fatal fire in November 2024 where a young couple and their dogs died as a result of an e-bike being charged in the hallway of their family home. We have launched a really big national campaign — “Fast . Fierce . Fatal . ” — which explicitly addresses the challenges around lithium-ion battery fires. As Jon says, they are a problem for us throughout the system. They are a problem when they cause fires in people ’ s homes, but at the end of their lives when they end up in recycling plants they are a huge issue as well. When they catch fire, we can be on site for many days. That is something where the entire UK fire and rescue service is facing a pressure.

We have talked about the changing landscapes of climate change. This is one of those weird ones where it is an impact of climate change that is not really weather - related. New technology such as that is something that the fire service is having to pick up, alongside lots of other things that we deal with now. Thirty years ago, the fire service did not really deal with cyber threats, as an example. Now my service spends hundreds of thousands of pounds protecting our systems from attack so that our systems are able to take the 999 calls and we can mobilise fire engines. That was something we never used to spend money on and now we do, and we do not get funded to do that.

Alongside the reducing budgets that we have had since 2011, we are also dealing with new threats, whether that is lithium-ion battery fires, cyber or a way more complex built environment now. There is the proliferation of houses of multiple occupation, particularly in more urban areas. Those are all emerging risks for fire and rescue services , and we are dealing with those with less money in the first place.

Q10 Before I hand over, I have one separate question. The life of someone who is fighting fire has changed significantly over the years. How much would you guess is actually spent firefighting versus spent educating and on prevention?

We operate to risk, rather than demand, as an emergency service. When you look at the percentages, even in some of London ’ s busiest stations you are looking at around 7% to 8% in terms of emergency response. When you start talking about the role that firefighters have around prevention and protection in particular, again in a heavily urban and very complicated built environment such as London, they are now spending nearly 20% of their time on prevention and protection work.

The big one is around operational training, which is always the bit that gets missed. The only way fire and rescue services can keep pace with this changing nature of risk, as Kath was alluding to, is through much more regular training. A question we were debating the other day is that, in two or three years ’ time, we will be sending firefighters to risks that we do not yet know about. We are going to have to be as agile as an organisation can be so that we can re-posture, as we have done in LFB for wildfire, for any particular challenge that comes over the horizon.

The big thing for us as an organisation is that, when you need the fire service, you need it, and you need it in numbers, as we demonstrated over the summer period. One of the thing s that came out of the wildfire summit held last week was that we have to have the ability to flex , as a sector , when the demand demands it, so in a summer period have the option to draw down on national funding to bring in additional firefighters to deal with peak demand, and then have an opportunity to do something differently when that demand is not there — for example , more prevention work, protection work, work in other areas or time available for training.

It is one of these things where we are postured for risk, as we should be. When you need the fire service, you need it there in numbers and you need them well trained, fit and able to deal with what is in front of them. At the same time, the role of the fire service continues to evolve. We have to have that agility in our training provision to make sure we can keep pace with it.

The majority—over 70% — of my service is on-call. That means that they do around about 120 hours on call a week. There is not a lot of time left in a week. They will be called when they are needed. In that context, arguably 100% of their time is dedicated to emergency response, because we will call them when we need them.

I would also add to that point that we need the ability to flex. We did not declare a major incident during the wildfire. We were very close. I had some of my on-call firefighters working in excess of 12, 18 or 20 hours, and less than six hours later they were back again. That is great, but is it resilient? Is it appropriate for us to be asking our people to work in those challenging conditions? Throughout the storms, I had over 250 firefighters out at the weekend. That is half my staff dealing with the storms. Again, it is that resilience piece. On Jonathan ’ s point, the ability to flex is important.

At the World Fire Congress, Sweden talked about its resilience model. It has people who almost commit to community service. They have different routes of how their young people are trained and educated. Some go into the public service life, but, for those who do not, when the nation needs them or the communities need them, they have the ability to call on them because they are already trained in certain roles.

I was going to reinforce Jon ’ s point around the fire service being a three-legged stool. You have response, which is the fire engines on blue lights that people classically think the fire service is about. Equally important is the prevention work that we do, often with the most vulnerable communities. The best fire is the one that we have prevent ed, because we have done the prevention work in the first place. Then there are our protection colleagues, who use the legislation to ensure building safety. It is a three-legged stool. If you take any one of those away, the fire service will fall over.

The demands on us now are so much greater that sometimes we are having to make difficult decisions about resourcing. Jon and Kath have talked about seasonal demand and temporal demand. We know that, in west midlands, we attend 50% more incidents and there is more risk in August than there is in February. We attend 70% of our incidents between 10 a m and 10 p m , and that is when almost all of our community work happens as well. By and large, fire and rescue services have quite a static model of their distribution of firefighters. Without investment in the fire service, all of us, as chief fire officers, are having to make difficult decisions around where we put our firefighters and assets.

I would like to have more firefighters available in the summer, as well as maintain the numbers in the winter. At the moment, I might have to make difficult decisions about moving my workforce around, based on the fact that our funding has not increased in line with CPI. One stat that I have written down here is that , since 2011, if our revenue budget had gone up with inflation, I would have £36 million more to run West Midlands Fire Service. My budget i s £150 million. That is a substantial loss in real-term spending power that we have had to absorb in the west midland s.

Q11 Can I follow up quickly? Jumping back on e-scooters and the fire risk, like many other places in the country, Milton Keynes has a real problem with illegal e-scooter use on many of our roads and pavements. Because of the fire risk, it creates real challenges for the police in terms of confiscating and disposing of those e-scooters, which makes it very difficult to stop people using them. Do you have any thoughts on how we can better support the police with that process, given the fire risks?

This question is interesting, because this was one of the areas that we discussed at the World Fire Congress three or four weeks ago. There is no actual silver bullet for dealing with lithium - ion battery fires, and e-bike and e-scooter fires in particular . A number of options are available. For example, in London, we work very closely with the Met police in having secure compounds. There are sensible things that you can do. You can have an external compound that is away from any life risk, and sleeping risk in particular. You make sure that you separate out the lithium-ion battery or the e-bike or e-scooter from anything else that could be combustible. Of course, those storage facilities do not exist in the numbers that we require.

There is a lot of science going into dealing with this issue of lithium-ion batt eries. There are dry powders that are now available. There are particular fire blankets that are available. We have an ultra-high - pressure lance that we can use that can penetrate a battery and flood it, in effect, to prevent it becoming a fire risk.

When we are talking to any colleagues, including housing providers—we do a lot of work here with Peabody—we recommend very safe and secure storage for e-bikes and e-scooters that is away from the living accommodation. The key thing is that it needs to be away from the living accommodation. We need to make sure that it is not compromising means of escape. We need to separate out where e-bikes and e-scooters are , and put additional mitigations in place that will stop any spread of fire.

In terms of actually resolving the issue of lithium-ion batt eries themselves, science is still playing a bit of catch-up, if I am honest with you, in terms of giving us, as a fire and rescue service, the additional measures that we need. There are things you can do. You can take sensible precautions that mean you can store these in a safe place.

The actual answer is to make sure the vehicles being used are safe themselves, hence my answer to the question before. It is around the regulation. If we have people using lithium-ion batt eries , and e-bikes and e-scooters, whether they have a kitemark or a safety standard that we would all accept, that is how we resolve this issue. That is something that we have learned from international comparisons, which is why I was keen to stress the point that we want to see that secondary legislation come forward on the PRAM Act. That is how you resolve this issue.

Q12 I have a quick question in regards to the awareness campaign and ChargeSafe. With the companies that are most likely to be users, so Deliveroo and Uber Eats, how much response have you had from them? How collaborative are they in raising that awareness?

Funnily enough, we have done a significant amount with particularly Deliveroo , actually. We have run a number of sessions at a number of fire stations in London with those who are operating in the gig economy, in particular Deliveroo, Just Eat and a number of others that are predominantly the users of these e-bikes and e-scooters. I have to say that, particularly with Deliveroo, to give it some credit, it has really stepped into this space about protecting its drivers.

A lot of this is education. It really is. It is about explaining the real dangers that come with this technology if you are using conversion kits or equipment that does not have the appropriate safety standards around it. When we do that, we have had really good engagement, particularly with companies such as Deliveroo. We have to keep that momentum going forward. That needs to be matched with the legislation keeping pace as well.
Q13 I wanted to follow up on that. Is it a matter of it being difficult to identify which is not the appropriate battery to use, or is it down to cost? I want to understand a bit more.

It is a combination of all those things , the truth be told, which is why we want to see the secondary legislation come forward, so that it is very clear what charging capability is safe to use. We always advise away from purchasing online in areas where we do not know what their safety standards are, which is another reason why we want to see the legislation come forward. There is no one thing. It is a combination of these elements that come around it, which is again why we want to see the legislation come forward.

I was going to answer Mr Curtis ’ s point. It is an area that the fire service can assist with. My understanding normally of lithium-ion batt eries is that they are relatively stable if they are just sitting on a shelf. It is when they are charged or suffer some thermal shock or impact. That is when there can be an issue with them.

The example that I mentioned before was when it was on charge overnight. As Jon said, often what happens is that people leave them on charge in their hallways, which is the worst place they can be, because that is where you would try to leave the house should there be a fire. My understanding is that they are relatively stable. It is when they are subjected to either charging or a shock that issues are cause d .

Q14 As far as I understand, the police ’ s risk assessment is that they cannot move them through their normal processes , though. That is part of the problem, because that makes it more difficult to confiscate them. Is there anything we can do about that?

Are they saying that in terms of putting them in their vehicles and moving them to a location? The key thing —and this is what we do with the Met —is a conversation between the local fire authority and Buckinghamshire police, in your case . T here are things you can do. As Simon said, as long as they have not been involved in an accident or subjected to heat, they should be relatively stable.

I f the police have concerns and are worried about how they transport this kit and equipment, it is a conversation with the local fire service to provide that reassurance and potentially some options to help them in that endeavour, because that is the biggest risk. When you see these illegal e-bikes and e-scooters on the road, as well as being dangerous from a road traffic collision perspective, we need to consider the fire risk that comes with it. T here is a key thing around partnership working there . I f there is concern, I would expect the local fire service to step in and assist.
That is really helpful.

Q15 The Government are currently reviewing the Civil Contingencies Act. How confident are you that your respective fire and rescue services and local partners are prepared to deal with either one major prolonged incident or several incidents that run concurrently?

From a London perspective and building on what Kath was saying before, this is the question for our time when it comes to the civil defence and homeland defence of the UK. I was very pleased to see that the Defence Secretary was saying the other day, supported by the Prime Minister, that we need to have a serious conversation about the resilience of this country. It does not matter whether it is wildfire, flooding, a pandemic or, heaven forbid, some sort of war scenario that we are having to plan for. There are huge challenges to the country ’ s civil and national defence, and fire and rescue, as Kath was saying before, has a critical role to play.

We are working very closely with Government at the moment at both a local level and a national level. There is a significant role for fire and rescue services to play in this civil defence and civil resilience space. We have well-trained, well-equipped and capable professional firefighters who can be deployed in a whole range of scenarios. If you look at what happened during covid for example, firefighters were driving ambulances, setting up vaccination centres, and doing body recovery and a whole range of other activity.

Getting it on to a firmer footing around what the role of the fire and rescue service is within civil defence and civil resilience is a huge opportunity, not only for us as a sector but for the country ’ s defence. If we look at the pressure that is undoubtedly going to come on the military over the next few years, we need to make sure that fire can step into that space behind the military. Often you will hear of MACA requests : military aid to the civil authority. If the military is having to think about our external posture, it then requires additional support in managing the resilience of the UK more broadly. Fire and rescue has a key role to play in supporting that.

We very much welcome the refreshing of the Civil Contingencies Act. There is a huge societal question around our civil and national defence and how we are more prepared as a country. Kath was alluding to European examples. If you listen to Scandinavian fire and rescue services , or you listen to the fire service in Poland and other places in Europe, they are really stepping into this whole civil defence space. I would very much welcome the opportunity for fire to be in there. Those are the conversations that we are having through the National Fire Chiefs Council with the Fire Brigades Union and G overnment around what more we can do .
T his is something we really have a USP as a sector to be able to step in and support. I still have three fire stations in London that have London Fire and Civil Defence Authority written on them .
That will save some money .

Some of this is a bit back to the future. When you look at the challenges that we are facing, the risks that the four of us have already discussed this morning, as well as the preparedness for any potential conflict that the UK could find itself dealing with, this is a real question of our time , and fire has a real opportunity to step into this space.
Q16 Does anyone disagree with Jonathan?

As I said, for me the fire and rescue service is right at the intersection of risk, people, place and community. More broadly we hosted the Duke of Cornwall, Prince William after Storm Goretti in Cornwall. I said to him at the time, around the Civil Contingencies Act, that that was written back in 2004. We are in a very different place in the context of risk and challenge, and complexity of that risk and challenge.

You have your cat 2 responders. You have your water and your power companies. Openreach and network providers are not even on the list, because who would have even thought that we would be living in a world where we rely so much on connectivity in our phones? So, again, what is the biggest concern of our communities? It is the fact that they lose power, water and connectivity. Those people are not necessarily required to be sat around the table or even in that cat 1 responder role.

More broadly, I think your question was around the local resilience forums. I talked about the risk becoming much more challenging. From my perspective in Cornwall—and obviously colleagues may disagree—local resilience forums work because of the strong relationships that we have and the committed people. That is what I would absolutely say, but too much of the system relies on good will. As that demand grows, we need to ensure that the arrangements that we have are absolutely sustainable, but also invested in.

There is a funny thing about preparedness, which is that the challenge is almost how you know whether it works . If nothing happens, you do not actually know whether it has worked. It is very much like prevention , and the time to invest in it is in peacetime. We tend to invest in preparedness or prevention once a crisis has happened. As we said, the challenges and risks that our nation faces, from our perspective and my perspective, absolutely require that investment now. Let us invest in peacetime. Let us ensure that the fire and rescue service is prepared to step into that resilience space.

If I may build upon your question as to whether we disagree or agree, I agree with Jonathan and Kath ’ s comments around what the fire service could and does provide for resilience and working within our resilience forums in our counties.

The challenge is that, as w e have talked a lot around , we have an amount of resource and we have to apply that to the risk that we see within our own areas of the f ire a uthority. S ometimes we have to make choices and decisions about where we put that risk . T hat can be difficult and uncomfortable because you cannot always address every risk that you have.

W ith the new risk we talk about, the civil resilience piece is growing, and it quite rightly should to protect our country and our communities . I t is a difficult choice for f ire s ervices as to where they are going to put that resource. Do we do that three-legged stool and put it into prevention and protection, response , and resilience? T hat gets to the point where we stretch ourselves too far.

Y ou will find that , across the country, fire and rescue services support their resilience forums across all our areas, and quite often chair those resilience forums on a day-to-day basis . That is an added responsibility, which we enjoy . W e know it is the right thing to do. Y ou are right : we are best placed to do that. W e have to think about the capacity of the fire and rescue service , our resource , what our statutory duty is and what we get provided funding to be able to do. W e are always keen to help , but it comes down to capacity sometimes to achieve it.
Q17 Aside from resources, what extra powers or reforms could strengthen your ability to tackle these incidents? I will turn to Simon, because I appreciate you have not commented on the first one.

I would support my three colleagues in what they say around resilience and where fire can step into that space. We would really like central Government to tell us what they actually want from the fire service and firefighters. Sometimes we think that that central government guidance is lacking.

It may surprise members of the Committee to know that in England the fire service has no statutory duty to respond to flooding. Of course we respond to flooding, we have lots of kit and equipment , and we train our firefighters to do it, but we do not get any funding to do that. I know that that is one area that was raised in the summit the other day , and there was commitment to consider that statutory duty. Wales has a statutory duty to respond to flooding and the Welsh Government provide funding to the fire service for some of its equipment. We would like that to be rolled out in England as well.
Government are absolutely the strongest when they provide clarity, consistency and capacity. That is what we would ask for.

The only thing I would add to what my colleagues have said is that there is a question around what the role of a 21st century firefighter is. W e are having lots of conversations with the Fire Brigades Union ; I know that Steve Wright is on the panel next. When the role maps that we currently operate to first came in back in 2003-04, the world was a very different place. With where we find ourselves now in 2026 and all the issues and threats that we are now dealing with as organisations, that needs to evolve as well.

We are having some excellent conversations with the FBU and the national employers. Underneath all this, there needs to be a complete overhaul of the current role map structure that fire and rescue services operate under, because the world has changed. When that first came in , in the early noughties, we were dealing with issues that were what you would call traditional from a fire and rescue perspective. That is not the world we are operating in now . In a post- c ovid, post-Grenfell, post-Manchester A rena world , we are operating in a very different space and we need the role maps to keep pace with that changing nature of the role and the organisation. That would be the big thing I woul d look to change.

One thing that has not changed , though , is the outstanding commitment of our firefighters and our staff who work within fire and rescue services , their ability to continue to step up and their desire to serve their communities. The value and the respect that the public have for our fire and rescue services has not changed. The opportunity is now to not necessarily take advantage, but recognise the incredible asset that you have, invest in it and allow it to support community and national resilience much more broadly.

Q18 The final question from me is on building safety. MPs are debating the Second Reading of the building safety Bill. If you do not know it—this is not a test—the Bill is there to make some progress on tackling unsafe buildings, particularly following Grenfell. Quite a lot of campaigners have said that it misses a lot of issues and does not make things anywhere near as safe as they need to be. Do you have any comment on that draft legislation or other building safety issues?

Is it the remediation Bill that you are referring to? We are keen to see the remediation Bill come forward, because we still have 1,600 buildings in London that have a simultaneous evacuation strategy on them because of various fire safety defects, including cladding. We very much welcome the remediation Bill, but we want to see these things accelerate.

For me, there are still far too many buildings across the whole of the UK that are unfit and unsafe. They have additional remedies in place, particularly around simultaneous evacuation . Fire and rescue services are having to take account of buildings not behaving in the way that we would expect, which cannot be right , so we want to see legislation come through.

To be fair, in the post-Grenfell world there has been a whole slew of legislation designed to improve building safety , and it is all heading in the right direction. The big ask from us is that we want to see that accelerated. All of this legislation we see as only the first part , and we will need to build on it. There are the RPEEPs—the residential personal emergency evacuation plans —which bring equity of rescue to disabled people. We see that as a very good first start but there is more that needs to be done. The same is true across a whole slew of legislation. Is it moving us in the right direction? Yes , it is, but we want to see the pace continue to increase.
Q19 How long do you think we should give landowners and landlords the chance to make their buildings safe?

It is very difficult to put a set timeframe on it, because every building is very different and no fire safety risk is exactly the same. You have to think about the type of cladding or the type of fire safety defect. For me, it has to be very, very strong legislation that put s that emphasis on the responsible person and the building owners, when they know that they have unsafe buildings, to see them remediated and to see the fire safety changes made that make those buildings safe. We want to see that happen as quickly as possible.

Next year is the 10th anniversary of the Grenfell Tower fire, which in itself is extraordinary. We have done a lot of good things around legislation to push this forward. The establishment of the Building Safety Regulator has been a very positive thing and working very closely with the BSR has been important.

This legislation is only the start. The bigger issue is the culture change within the sector and making sure that safety is at the centre of everything. When we are building new houses or looking at the built environment that we are operating in, safety — fire safety specifically, but also building safety more broadly — must cut through the culture of everyone who is involved with building moving forward. If we get that right, the legislation will keep pace with that change. It is something we have to be relentless about. A big lesson that has come from Grenfell Tower is that we have to be relentless in that space , making sure that fire ’ s voice is heard loud and clear at the table when it comes to building safety.
Q20 It is 15 months the Government are planning to give landlords. There are over 100 buildings that have yet to identify whether they have cladding.

One thing I have been thinking about—I found this really useful—is that we are looking to do a submission to the Government and we want to be helpful in terms of the work that you are doing and what to prioritise. I have heard that the secondary legislation, particularly with the lithium batteries and scooters, will help mitigate that substantially. I am hearing from you that emergency alerts are the way forward and that is something you would probably want us to recommend.

As you know, the Government did the wildfire summit on Friday. I know that you went to a summit in Singapore . I was wondering whether there are any gaps that you want to mention to us that we could put in. We could certainly follow up.

There is also the Civil Contingencies Act. I know that the Government are looking at that and I think that you are best placed to give direction, given that you chair a lot of the forums up and down the country, in terms of what you want to see on that. I know you have said that you are looking for clarity from the Government about what they want to see.

If you could give us a steer as to what you want us to say and what your sector is saying, we can certainly make those recommendations. I am not expecting you to answer that now. You can follow that up. If there is something burning that you want to flag with us now, that would be helpful.

It is that key piece around the fact that we recognise, as we have said to you today, that the complexity, challenges and risks are significant, and they are coming at us, as a nation and communities, at pace. You have four of us here today, but you have all fire and rescue services , and I am sure you will hear from the chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council later. We are always willing to step up. We are stood there saying, “We are ready but we are probably not as prepared as we should be”.
Q21 It is resources .

Yes. It is the clarity of the role of the firefighter. What is it that the Government would like us to do? If you do not want us to step into the resilience space, that is fine as well. From our perspective, we believe that we have a compelling case. We kind of do it anyway. Take advantage of the incredible, respected and trusted asset that you have at your disposal, but provide us the clarity, provide us that direction and set the expectations. Unfortunately, as you probably hear from many, we just need that capacity and investment.

The resourcing for me is the key point. Fire and rescue service s , whether they are the largest one, such as London, or one that is very reliant on on-call services , such as Kath ’ s and Jon ’ s, have been significantly underfunded for 20 years. The resourcing that we have available now to deal with these risks that we are facing is not enough to deal with the plethora of challenges that the modern fire and rescue service is now expected to deal with. We will deal with them, but they require that investment, which is why the wildfire summit and the proposals that were coming from that is a really good step forward.

There is the acknowledgement that fire and rescue services need that resource, but it will look different. For example, I will not need an air capability to deal with wildfires in London, but I will need PPE for frontline firefighters. It will be different across the board. If we are getting into a position where there is an acknowledgement that resourcing needs to come forward for UK fire and rescue services, there will also have to then be a degree of localism that comes with that. The risks and challenges in London are obviously very different from the risks and challenges that Kath will face.

Broadly speaking , the investment in fire and rescue services will have huge dividends for the UK ’ s civil resilience. That is the big thing. This is not just an ask for more resource for the sake of it. This is actually to deal with the risks that we are now faced with in order to help the country be more resilient to the types of challenges that we know we are going to face over the next five , 10 or 15 years.
That is really helpful . I know that the wildfire summit looked at PPE in terms of making sure that that was adequately resourced.

I found that really helpful. I am sure that the rest of the C ommittee did as well. You have given us a lot to raise on your behalf. If there is anything you feel that you have missed out, please liaise with our team. Thank you for your time.

Q22 Good morning. If you heard the first session and what was discussed, I guess that some of it is linked into some of the issues that you are going to raise today. Could the witnesses introduce themselves ?
I am Steve Wright , general secretary for the Fire Brigades Union. I have been in the fire service for over 25 years and worked in a couple of different services, Buckinghamshire being one.
It ’ s the best one !
It was when I was there . I am representing nearly 34,000 firefighters across the UK.
Phil Garrigan : Morning, everyone. I am Phil Garrigan , chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council and previously chief fire officer for Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service.
Hello. I am C ounci ll o r Wendy Maples . I am the chair of the f ire and rescue authority committee with the LGA. I am based in East Sussex, where I am a county, district and town councillor.
