Thank you for taking the time to see us today.

Q23 We will start off with two questions briefly to all of you , if that is all right. First, how would you describe the state of the fire and rescue service in England today? S econdly, how would you describe the resource challenge that the fire service is going to face between now and 2030 or the end of this Parliament? Steve, do you want to go first on that?

Steve Wright : It is an important question, is it not ? W hat we have seen and what you have just heard from the chief fire officers is that , over the last 20 years , there has been a severe underinvestment in funding for the fire and rescue service across the UK . In particular, England lost 10,000 firefighters from 2010 onwards, one in five of the workforce . T hat has a huge impact. It has an impact on not just firefighter safety but public safety. It means we are getting to incidents slower than we used to. We saw 10 fire stations closed in this city alone . T hat has an impact on response times , when we are responding to the array of incidents that we attend now, as you heard from the previous panel.

I joined the fire service in 2001 . T he job has changed significantly since then, but what has not kept pace is the resources that we need to respond to these incidents . If you look at the wildfires this summer , do not underestimate the conditions that firefighters were working in. I was at a fire station last night , and a fire station in Wales last week , talking about the impact of not having the right PPE, not having the right resources and limited welfare breaks during that period .

W hen firefighters were on the frontline of these wildfires , it was the same time as the world cup was taking place , when professional footballers were taking hydration breaks every 20 minutes. From the reports that we had , firefighters were on the frontline for over 20 or 30 hours . T hat has had a massive impact on the mental health of firefighters .

We had the Stourbridge incident and the Wennington fires in 2022. Firefighters respond to incidents expecting to be able to deal with what is in front of them. We get r eports from our control rooms across the UK . O ur members in those control rooms are taking 999 calls from members of the public and having to tell them that there are no resources to send to those incidents.

I am speaking from the perspective of someone who has been on the frontline, dealing with these wildfires . I have sympathy for the chief fire officers who are having to make those difficult decisions without the resources in place to deal with them.

When we talk about on-call firefighters, the impact on our control members and the impact on officers, there are just not enough resources in place . It is a tragedy that in 2026 we are really not learning the lessons of the past . As an example, wildfire was placed on the national risk register in 2013. In 2022 , we saw a whole street in We nn ington burn to the ground , and yet we are still here making the case that we need more firefighters on the frontline.

Phil Garrigan : It will be no surprise that I will reiterate some of the things that Steve just alluded to , to be fair . B oth Steve and I attended the wildfire summit in Merseyside last week . If there are any specific questions , I am sure we can f ield them.

You asked us to describe the state of fire and rescue services a s it stands . T he climate and the context in which we operate has changed significantly over the 37 years since I have been in the service. The role and responsibilit y that fire and rescue service s hold now is significantly different. The risk and demand are changing . A gain , I will not go back as far as Steve , but , if you go back 10 years , the increase in demand on the fire and rescue service has now risen by 21%.

Jonathan Smith , the c ommissioner of London , describes going to 44 different incident types over that period. That does not surprise me . It probably extends to 50 or so types of incident that we respond to across the UK fire and rescue service . Y ou have seen the number of firefighters over that same period decline by 14% . W e have 11,000 fewer firefighters than we had then.

Fast - forward into what has been a significantly busy period for the fire and rescue service over that wildfire period . Steve is absolutely right . T here were times when services were requesting resource , human resource specifically , and we were not able to facilitate those requests at times during that really peak time of activity.

As I said previously , I was the c hief of Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service. We would often co-ordinate the national response . I know about mutual aid . I am very familiar with it. I know what that looks like that . That is probably the first time that we have been unable to facilitate the demands that were placed on the fire and rescue service.

T hat is climate - related . W e talk about wildfire specifically. We have seen some really positive indications from the current Government in regard to investment in the response. I still think it requires more than that. It is workforce capability and capacity that we need to address . I would hope and suggest that, in the longer term , we see this as a really strategic solution to some of the broad er challenges facing the UK , particularly around its resilience . I t is not just wildfire or flood . It is the geopolitical threat . It is where t he fire and rescue service can step in and support communities .

T he re is one more thing that I would say before I pause . The role that we fulfil is predicated on put ting the communities that we serve first. The public always come first . E verything that we do is to protect them . T hat is really important . T he things that I am saying here and the things that I have said over the last number of years in this role are very much about ensuring that the public are protected in every eventuality . W hether that be the risk that they face in high-rise buildings or the risks that they face from wildfire or flood , it is about ensuring that the fire and rescue services are on the front foot and are equipped and capable of dealing with every eventuality in the way that the public would expect.
D oe s a nyone else want to make any points on that?

Roy Wilsher : Yes, I will chip in. As people have mentioned, it will be 45 years next month since I join ed London Fire Brigade . I have been around for a while. I now inspect fire services and police forces . W e are into our fourth round of inspection of fire services. We look very clinically at what fire service s are doing . I am pleased to report that we have seen some improvements this year. It has been quite a journey. We have seen lots of improvement in terms of leadership, culture, prevention and protection.

Strangely enough, it is the response area that needs a bit more work . W hat is behind that is the identification of risk. C hief fire officers in their community risk management plans are looking at risk much better ; they are allocating resources much better to where it is needed. In terms of resource, for everyday work it seems to manage. It is the surge capacity that is the problem. For wildfires or flooding, you need extra resource . I t is not every day of every year, although there has been a reduction . It is that ability to step up and surge, as Jonathan Smith was describing, that they link into.

U ndoubtedly, resources are tight. Resources have reduced . T he grant allocations have not kept up with pay rises . T here are fewer firefighters . T here is not enough capital investment. That is a real issue , if we are talking about new equipment for fire services. The cost of borrowing to buy that equipment is increasing without capital investment. O verall, I am pleased to say that, in our fourth round, halfway through, we have seen some really pleasing improvements.

Q24 Can I ask you a quick follow-up on your answers , please? I t would not take much to convince us of the challenging financial situation that many of our fire services have been in and that, given the extra pressures of climate change and lithium batteries, the cuts that we saw in the previous years were clearly a mistake. We still operate in a world where there is a fixed pot of money and it is never going to be enough.

Is there anything that the Government can do to help fire services —y ou are probably operating far more efficiently because of those difficult challenges — to operate more efficiently or to move resources towards the challenges that we are going to face in the future?

Phil Garrigan : Yes. I t is interesting . W e talk about reflecting the risks, and the risks are significant, but we also have to reflect the demand that is placed on the sector . Roy gave you an example of that.

F rom a financial point of view, in trying to ensure that we have the right resources to respond to the challenges that we face, there are some things that are challenging for us at this moment in time. W e welcome the multi-year funding settlement, by the way . T hat is absolutely applauded, but some of the financial implications of that , and the link to the GDP deflator , mean that the uplift in grant that the fire and rescue service will receive will not reflect the inflationary pressures that we are facing. When we talk about uplifting wildfire PPE, by way of example, the cost of the PPE will increas e with inflation ; the money that we are receiving will not.

Equally, we have inequity that exists across fire and rescue service s around governance models, which I am sure we may well touch on . S ome have the luxury of council tax flexibility. O thers have significant restrictions still built in . S ome fire and rescue service s can address the shortcomings within their services or the gaps that they perceive by increasing council tax.

T he only other financial consideration that I would make is that the fire and rescue service used to receive capital funding up until 2013. We receive no capital funding now . I n effect, we have to borrow . A s we borrow, that has an implication on revenue . W e build up the revenue , so we take it away. That means we are sometimes papering over the cracks.

W hen you look at the fire stations that the firefighters work in, many of them across the UK now are not f it for purpose. They do not have the facilities around diversity . T hey do not manage the contaminant risk that is present in the everyday life of a firefighter.

Ensuring that the grant reflects inflation, ensuring that council tax flexibility is afforded across the board, and recognising the capital challenges would be my three asks around the financial envelope.

Q25 There is one final b it from me, Steve . Y ou just mentioned contaminant risk. We know that there is plenty of evidence now that firefighters face a significantly increased risk of cancer later into their lives. We had some welcome measures from Government back in April about how they are considering that. Do they go far enough ? As a union, is there anything more that you would ask for from Government?

Steve Wright : There are three elements to DECON , our campaign to prevent the risk of cancer in firefighters. It is a personal issue for me . I t is something that I campaigned heavily on when I stood to be the general secretary a couple of years ago, having lost my father , a 30-year firefighter , to cancer . Ha ving a son in the job as well , it is about protecting the future of our firefighters .
The first element of DECON is about making sure that there is investment in every single fire and rescue service and that fire stations are adequately prepared to deal with contamination risk.

The second is — we welcomed the announcement from the Health Secretary at the time, Wes Street ing , in September — health monitoring . W e are working hard to make sure that is in place in 2027 as per the Government’s commitment . T hat will go a long way to deal with the mental issues that firefighters face, knowing that th e threat exists but that something i s in place.

T hirdly, it is about having a conversation around presumptive legislation, which is in place in many parts of the world but not here in the UK. We lag way behind many countries, the US, Canada, Australia and many parts of Europe , in that .

Those are the three areas that we really need to get investment in to make sure that firefighters are protected from what is a known risk but not necessarily in plain sight at the operational incidents that we attend.

If I may , I will just take the opportunity, as everyone has, to speak about the lack of resources and the cuts that we have seen in the fire service. This past year , w e have had to run significant campaigns to keep fire stations open. In Oxfordshire, our members were balloted for industrial action and kept open four fire stations. In Dorset and Wiltshire, we were set to see eight fire stations closed. It is not a historic issue . We cannot keep pointing to austerity as what has dropped the number of firefighters . As me and Phil have both spoken about , it is happening now . W hat you can do now is to prevent those issues that we are facing and the frontline cuts that are having an impact on our safety.

Q26 We know that there is an increased risk. There is a very real chance that that risk may continue to increase . If you look around the rest of the world, wildfire s arguably have a very big impact on cancer risk for the people who live near them. Therefore, the fire service increasingly going to these incidents could increase that risk.

When you look at the way that the Industrial Injur ies Advisory Council works, it acknowledge s that there is an increased risk, but because it does not double the risk of any illness — the numbers that I have here give a 16 % to 58% increase in cancer risk ; it is potentially a bit higher —that limits fire personnel’s ability to get compensation or access to some of those extra health protection measures that you talk about. Do we need to rethink the way the Industrial Injur ies Advisory Council works so that it can better account for places where there is an increased risk but not a doubling in risk of things such as cancer?

Steve Wright : Yes, 100% . We need to learn our lessons from other countries. We speak to firefighter unions all across the globe . In Norway , t hey have just advanced the case on presumptive legislation. It is certainly something that should be explored and looked into . As you quite clearly state, we need to consider this in how we look at things.

Q27 You talked about work capability earlier, Phil . T his is for anyone on the panel. I just wanted to understand whether staff retention is a concern at the moment in terms of keeping people in posts. We know that generally with the fire service you have people working in posts for a long time, but I am just worried about the new generation that is coming up. I hear that there are challenges.

Roy Wilsher : I can start from an inspect ion point of view. So far w e are not finding that in fire services or in the people who manage fire services. We do in policing. It is quite a big issue with constables leaving and retention there, but we have not found it in fire so far.

Phil Garrigan : Yes, I would concur with that from a whole - time perspective , for the firefighters who are employed and where that is their career. P eople referenced the on-call system in the previous panel session . W e have done some research around the on-call arrangements that are in place . T he report described the position as “ fragile ” . We often find that we are not able to field fire engines because we have a lack of available people , who work a day job and then make themselves available for the fire and rescue service out of hours. That is a real challenge for us.

There w ere 104 recommendations made with the Exact report that was commissioned to look into the on-call system and how we can strengthen that. We welcome the support from MHCLG. MHCLG ha s committed financial resourc e and individuals to work with us to explore the ways in which you can recruit more and retain people for longer . We recognise that we are operating against a societal challenge . T hat is really helpful.

Q28 It has been almost 10 years since the fire at Grenfell killed 72 people. What progress has been made to eliminate fire risk in buildings and particularly to ensure that that incident could never occur again?

Phil Garrigan : I will go first. We have made some significant progress . On the previous panel, Jonathan Smith talked through the legislative changes that have happened as a result of Grenfell and the recommendations that have followed . T he national fire chiefs have been working tirelessly in seeking to work our way through the recommendations that were applicable to either the sector more broadly or London specifically and take some of the learning from that.

T here is undoubtedly still work to be done. I would go back to Jonathan’s point around still unremediated buildings . H e referenced there being over 1,000 in London . T here are over 2,000 across England that have not yet been remediated. Self-evidently, we are 10 years on and there are still some buildings that are classified as unsafe , which we need to seek to address.

It is not singular . Y ou would accept — the Grenfell inquiry would accept this too —that t here is a system requirement in this. It is not just down to fire and rescue services and the role that they fulfil. There are a number of key partners and organisations that need to support us to collectively address the gaps that remain.

We have learned a lot . S elf-evidently, some of the biggest learning has come around the families , the survivors and those affected and how they felt during that period. We have done some extensive work on this. I really do applaud the work around the duty of candour, with the Hillsborough law and the likes, because that puts the victim, the survivor and the family at the centre of some of the decision-making for organisations. That is really important . I t is something we have sought to instil in fire and rescue services across the length and breadth of the country.

There is still work to be done. Jonathan talked about accelerating that work and doing it at pace. That is still required. We should not find ourselves , 10 years on, with un remediated buildings and people living in unsafe conditions.

Roy Wilsher : F rom an inspectorate point of view, we put specific questions into our inspections about how fire services have dealt with the recommendations that apply specifically to them. Again, there has been really good progress in terms of fire protection and safety, the competence of the officers, the work that they do and the work in fire controls on fire survival guidance , i f a number of calls come through, and the communication between the fire and the controls themselves. T he work is there.

T his is one area where retention of staff can be a problem for fire services . T hey get trained up and skilled up, but there is work in the private sector, so they might leave. There is also pressure from the Building Safety Regulator , particularly in urban areas— you hav e west midlands and London here, and I know East Sussex is dear to Wendy’s heart—where there is a lot of high-rise .

We have seen good training, good survival guidance and training on protection. It is the remediation . There are other parts of the system that really need to catch up with the work the fire service has done.

If I may, just to echo that, one thing that is a real problem is that you have councils that are also responsible for these buildings . W hile councils are very keen for the housing stock that they provide to be at the appropriate standard — at the LGA , we believe that everybody should have the right to a safe and secure home — keeping pace with that is really difficult , with councils really struggling financially.

T he other side of that is also looking at , when remediation has happened, whether the fire safety engagement assessments are at the right standard. We need to make sure that there is training in place to keep building up that workforce and that the workforce is working to a suitable standard so that we can trust that the remediation that has happened is of a quality that is appropriate to make those homes safe. It is a real challenge.

An ask from the LGA is that industry should be paying for building safety remediation. That includes also looking at how that gets paid for when assessments are done of remediation to be sure that th e remediation is of a good standard.

If I can come back to the point about the state of fire, I would make a strong argument about needing to have additional resource in terms of both revenue and capital. The LGA absolutely welcomes the multi-year settlement , but I will give you an example of the lack of capital investment . A s Roy has pointed out, I am in East Sussex . I am specifically in Lewes. Lewes has a fire station that was meant to be the gold command centre in the Lewes 2000 floods. Twenty - five years on, that fire station is still in the floodplain. E ven though there have been increased flood defences nearby, that station is likely to go under , should we have another flood. That is a massive challenge. I am talking about Lewes and East Sussex, but that is something that you see repeated nationally.

The last thing that I want ed to say was that we hold such respect and appreciation for all the hard work of our firefighters. It is remarkable what they managed to achieve this summer, but one thing that has not changed in the state of fire — I say this in a general way — is just how much of a resource they are for our communities . They are a key resource for our communities because of t he respect in which the fire service is held . That has not changed. While we have had all these other changes around extreme weather, new technologies and pressures on finances, what remains is the respect in which our fire service is held by our communities. That is a huge asset and a huge resource , if we are looking for whole - society resilience.

Steve Wright : The Grenfell Tower fire was a measure of the state of the fire and rescue service . S ystemic failures, including in the fire and rescue service, played their part. We need to listen when Andy Burnham talks about 40 years of neoliberalism and the impact of deregulation and privatisation . L essons are still not being learned after 72 people lost their lives and 300 people lost their homes.

That is why we firmly stand with the bereaved, the survivors and the residents. We attend the Grenfell Tower silent walks every year to make sure that they understand that we stand with them. There are lessons still to be learned around this.

One recommendation from the Grenfell Tower inquiry was for a c ollege of fire and rescue , which we may get into . That is an opportunity for the fire service to set national standards, to deliver a fire and rescue service fit for the future, to be resilient, to respond to the incidents that firefighters attend and to make sure firefighters are paid appropriately to deal with those .

When we talk about understanding risks that are coming down the line, it was our union that sat in a room much like this in 1999 and warned the Environment, Transport and Regional Affairs Select Committee about cladding, and yet the fire commissioner from London talks about cladding still being wrapped around some buildings , unsafe fire safety practices and failings in buildings that firefighters are having to deal with on a daily basis. That is in all parts of the UK. It is about learning those lessons , taking them forward and making sure that there is justice for those affected by the Grenfell Tower fire.

Q29 MPs are today going to be debating the Building Safety (Remediation of Unsafe Cladding etc ) Bill . E very now and again , I use the shorthand. Today is the first time that we are debating it. I t is to tackle unsafe cladding particularly , as we have not made the progress we should have in the last 10 years as a country. What amendments, if any, would you like to see in the Bill?

Phil Garrigan : To be honest , I am probably not in a position to give you that specific level of detail. I can come back to you on that and give you an indication of what would be the strongest amendments to make in that context.

M y only ask , though , would be to ensure that the r emediation Bill is moved through at pace. You asked the previous panel around time and when you would like to see unsafe cladding removed from every high-rise building as defined. There was a commitment for that to take place by 2029 . My view is that we would want to accelerate that , but , self-evidently , if we were assured that by 2029 all buildings across England were safe and remediated , that would send a strong message to the victims and survivors of Grenfell.
I would add ensur ing that there are powers to compel building owners to do the right thing.

Q30 Thank you very much for offering to come back to us , if you have anything. I suppose that turns the question around. Have the Government , in drafting the Bill , consulted you, the National Fire Chiefs Council or your respective organisations on this Bill before they published it?
Phil Garrigan : Yes, it is my understanding that they have.

Steve Wright : From the reports that we have seen and the information that we have had passed to us , i t will take a decade for this remedial work to take place . I n that next decade , with the shortages of firefighter numbers and the lack of resources available , we are going to be dealing with that threat and risk now.

We can all sit here and say that we want it done quick er and that we want you to move as fast as possible . I am sure there will be speeches to the effect that that is going to be done , but the reality is that it will not be done . O ver the next decade , firefighters and members of the public are going to be put at risk because this work is not taking place as quickly as possible. It is a known risk and we need to make sure that it is being dealt with.

Roy Wilsher : Again, as the i nspectorate , we have not been consulted , but neither were we invited to the wildfire summit or the wildfire c ongress , which is an oversight considering we have more evidence on the performance of fire services than any other organisation.
The LGA has been engaged through the joint inspection team.

Q31 I want to direct this to you, Wendy, under your LGA hat. We have heard from th is panel and the previous panel how the roles and responsibilities of the fire and rescue service have changed. We asked in the last panel about the Civil Contingenc ies Act and what changes the fire and rescue service would like to see . I understand that for the previous panel it was more about clarity.
I just wanted to hear, particularly from the LGA specifically, whether there has been any specific ask for how that could change, particularly in terms of recognising the fire and rescue service .

There are a number of different ways to come at those two questions. The roles and responsibilities have changed in effect by virtue of the fire service responding to changes in conditions. We are now working on a fire sector review, looking at roles and responsibilities and what elements of that could be included in statutory responsibilities , particularly the responsibility for flooding and new technology responses.

In terms of the Civil Contingenc ies Act, we would be really interested in, with Government and partners, having discussions about what a whole - society response and whole - society resilience would look like. We would see having partnerships and conversations with Government, the fire service and local authorities at a range of levels as absolutely instrumental to making that move forward. I am not sure whether I have answered your question.
That is really helpful, particularly on the whole - society approach, how that would look and how the service will factor into that. That is helpful, particularly around identifying the other risks.

Q32 I have a couple of questions around standards and performance. I will start with you, Steve. You mentioned in your written submission to us that the Fire and Rescue Service s Act 2004 shifted and replaced national standards with locally agreed arrangements. You expressed concerns that that has led to slow response times and basically a postcode lottery in the provision of fire services. Could you say a bit more about that and give us some examples of the variations that you think that has created?

Steve Wright : Of course, yes. T here has been a huge fragmentation of the UK fire and rescue service. W e often phrase it as a postcode lottery, which is very much what it is. Firefighters are getting paid different amounts in different parts of the country . The training , including initial training , and competenc ies are different . That exists.

N ot having national standards has meant that there is a worsening of the response and capability that we give to our communities and your constituents. When you talk about figures, we now take three minutes longer, on average , to get to primary fires, dwelling fires, than we did in the mid-1990s. That cuts across the board.

We have a bit of an issue with how this data is collected. The MHCLG figures only report back on the first appliance getting in attendance. O rdinarily , that is four firefighters on a fire engine . S afe crewing levels are five. That is what we campaign towards. We always ha d five firefighters on a fire engine when I joined the fire service.

W orse than that, in some places, the first response that is recorded is by a small fire vehicle response. It is not necessarily a fire engine that can deal with the issues that are facing them, the dangerous issues and incidents that firefighters attend. We have seen an increase in that. We have seen an increase in demand for the fire and rescue service over the last 10 years. The risks are evolving , yet resources are diminishing.

The postcode lottery exists. One prime example of that is wildfire PPE. The services that I have worked in, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire, do not have lightweight PPE to attend wildfires, yet neighbouring brigades have managed to do that. That comes to the point about the need for central g overnment funding. In the past, it was a 50 : 50 split. It is some way off that nowadays. County councils and other fire authorities are having to make tough choices on what they invest their money in. I have attended incidents across the Thames Valley where different services respond with different kit , different training , different resources available and different response standards.

This is a question of what we want from the inspectorate. An inspectorate that can inspect national standards set by a college of fire, for example, would be the way to start improving standards and not allow this continual slide that we have seen over the past 20 or so years.

Q33 Roy, do you want to come in on that? It would be good to get your view on it. Do you agree with Steve ? Have there been some benefits from different services being able to adapt and do different things?

Roy Wilsher : I agree and disagree. I agree on some things. There is not a national standard on response. That went a long time ago. A lot of it is based on risk. That probably needs to be a bit more scientific in some places because some of the standards for response are based on what the service has always had . It could be a bit more scientific.

In terms of wider standards, there are a lot of standards that have really benefited . The c ode of ethics is a classic . It is read into the standards. The culture has improved in fire and rescue services . E mbedding that core code of ethics has been one of the reasons that those standards have improved. We look at standards. Those standards are now characteri s ed as good . W e inspect, and they work pretty well.

I also agree with Steve and probably everyone else on the panel that a college of fire is vitally needed in terms of a college like the College of Paramedics. It could set the standards for training as well . T he National Fire Chiefs Council does its best to offer guidance, but if there were mandatory standards for training you would avoid that need .
I agree and disagree with Steve . T here are some standards that work very well, but they could be improved , alongside a college of fire.

Q34 J ust to pick up that point about a college of fire and rescue to develop national standards, we would be really keen to hear the witnesses’ views on, as you started off , Roy, what standards that college should push nationally , w hich elements should be set nationally and whether there are standards that are so important that they should be mandatory .

Phil Garrigan : If I may, I will comment on the broad question of standards, in the first instance. Steve is quite right . I nconsistency has developed over the last number of years. As austerity kicked in, we moved things to more local determination , probably legitimis ing the removal of some of the infrastructure that supports fire and rescue services to co-ordinate on a national scale. As a result of that, we found local solutions to national problems. M y view is that we need to find national solutions to local problems , with interpretation somewhat applied at a local level.

There is inconsistency around the standards that are applied in fire and rescue services. Roy is quite right . T he National Fire Chiefs Council, as a convening body, seek s to address that and support fire and rescue services to secur e that consistency.

The need to reverse some of the impacts of austerity is probably the reason why the recommendation sat there from Grenfell in regard to a college of fire. A college of fire gives us a legitimate way to drive standards across the board, not singularly response standards — I may come back to that in a second —but competency standards and the like.

There are a multitude of areas where we think we need to be more consistent . Y ou become more consistent by setting a standard and then applying that standard back into the sector. We have done a lot of work . T he Fire Standards Board ha s really strengthened the work that we do on a national level. The HMI review s those national standards to see whether they are applied in service. The introduction of inspectors has been fundamentally beneficial to the UK fire and rescue service . Since its introduction, I have seen fire and rescue service s improve across the board . T hat is evident in the work that Roy ha s alluded to and what he has seen.

But — there is a “ but ”— we need to see the college of fire brought to fruition . It is coming to the point where have talked about it and we have gone out to public consultation in regard to its introduction . W e need to move away from a concept into something that is more of a reality. G iven the financial predicament that the Government find themselves in, we know it will require investment to deliver exactly what we know and have been saying is required for the UK fire and rescue service . W e also need to understand its operating model, its governance, its functions and what standards fit within it.

A lot of that work has been done, and we now need to move it on to the next level , to implementation, but it takes legislative change and it needs financial investment. That is absolutely fundamental in shifting the UK fire and rescue service significantly around its professionalism and the standards that are applied .
That was really helpful.

Q35 Thank you for those answers. I quickly wanted to ask about the Government embarking on reforms to devolve more power to mayors , reorganis e local government and realign public services . W hat potential benefits and / or risks do you see for the fire and rescue service s in those reforms?

Again, it is a good question. It is a tricky question. We already have a number of different models for governance, all working towards the same standards hopefully, across counties, standalone fire services , PFCCs and deputy mayor models.

T he risk is that we either add yet another model into what is already a complex equation or decide to create something that is more uniform, when the models that are in existence, whether it is county or standalone, work in their context.

That really comes down to this whole question about risk. Assessing local risk and fire services doing that through their CRMP is absolutely critical to understanding how communities are best served. Having a broad - brushstroke model that goes across the whole piece risks missing that. At the same time, I do understand that there may be a real interest in having something that is more uniform. Uniform is not necessarily better in terms of addressing local risk. There has to be that iteration between the two.

F rom an LGA perspective, we are interested in having those conversations and in where Government are going with that, but we have to make sure that fire has a seat at the table when we are having those conversations. To give the example of East Sussex and West Sussex moving towards a mayoralty, our fire service had to invite itself along to one of those first meetings of the SBSA. It is fine now . T hat has been done, but there needed to be a little bit more foresight about that.

Roy Wilsher : W e need certainty for fire services. They were an afterthought. Every time we inspect a service , they are not quite sure . Sussex is quite settled compared to some areas. If you go to Northamptonshire, at the moment there is a police , fire and crime commission er whose term is ending, but there is no certainty about where that fire service will end up in terms of governance , if and when a mayor is coming in , or whether there will be a strategic authority. Certainty for fire services, with a bit of resource to help them change , would really benefit everyone at the moment .

Steve Wright : We welcom e the discussion around devolution and what that brings to the fire and rescue service , but we want to make sure that there is maximum democracy and democratic scrutiny. As politicians, you would all want that. Our fear is that we will lose some of that. We have mayor s in London, Greater Manchester, York and North Yorkshire who directly manage fire and rescue services.

I will make one point around PFCCs . W e welcome the move from the Government to abolish those . Looking back to the previous Government and the White Paper in 2022 , we and o ur members felt that PFCCs were an alignment of us and the police service. As firefighters, w e are always proud that, w hen we turn up at incidents, people like to see us. That is not always the case for the police . W e are a humanitarian service. That allows us to do a wide range of activities. We have had lots of discussion today about what more the fire and rescue service could do. K eeping that separate from the police is important.

F or us, it is about making sure that there is democratic scrutiny of the people who are making decisions for the fire and rescue service around budgets and cuts. If we had not had that this year, we would have seen more closures of fire stations and fewer fire engines, and we would probably be talking about even greater risk s being faced by the communities that you all represent.

Phil Garrigan : J ust very briefly, Roy has alluded to certainty. Sometimes it has felt like the fire and rescue service is a bit of an afterthought in terms of governance and the arrangements that are put in place. Wendy has alluded to the number of governance models that we have in place . It makes no sense to me, to be fair. We need some level of consistency in how fire and rescue services are governed and how they are made accountable to the people who they serve.

There have been commitments around reviewing the operating models. We know that mayoral authority coterminosity is really important in regard to how the fire and rescue service functions. “C oterminosity with who ?” is the question. You can look at it from a mayoral authority point of view . We want someone to make that commitment. “ This is what the governance looks like, and this is where you sit within it ” , rather than there being multiple different ways in which that is discharged.

When I talk about coterminosity, I talk about it from a mayoral authority point of view because that strengthens the work that we do around resilience. When we look at how the fire and rescue service can support the national resilience response through local resilience forums, that is through a mayoral authority.
I have a very quick question . Has anyone left a bag outside the room? W e cannot move, if not. I am glad that we have the fire and rescue service in the room today.
Roy Wilsher : Look for the people in uniform.
No one ha s left a bag outside the room . Have you? Do you want to quickly get your bag? I t is creating a bit of a panic. Thank you.

I just want to add to the point about the importance of democratic scrutiny. One of the key points about the college of fire and rescue is that it will provide an opportunity to create a clear leadership programme. One thing that has come up a number of times is the importance of the international research that has been done and making sure that it is shared so that you have that golden thread of research running through fire and rescue.

F or fire authorities, we need to make sure that fire authorities — people who are working in that democratic scrutiny realm — have the training and resource to understand exactly what they are scrutini s ing. The LGA is working very hard to ensure that that is in place for anybody who is on a fire authority and anybody who is in local government, regardless of which format that is in.
We have that in place. We could do with more of it. It would be fantastic to link in with the college of fire and rescue so that it happens across the piece.

Q36 I hav e one final question . I know we have gone over time. It is just directed at Roy. The i nspectorate did an annual assessment just recently, which demonstrated that more needs to be done in terms of equalities. You may remember that in May 2024 the Home Affairs Committee did a report into the fire and rescue service . I know that a lot of work has been done over the years , but c oncerns were raised about homophobia and racism. I just wanted to understand why the i nspectorate said that and what further needs to be done in this space.

Roy Wilsher : I personally issued two reports, one on value and culture , and one on misconduct and discipline , in the service. We did find—this was only back in 20 23—that a lot needed to be done. The code of ethics had not been embedded. Some of the behaviours we found, particularly on watches, w ere not appropriate for a public service. There was some lack of understanding of why diversity, equality and inclusion was important and certainly why positive action was important .

I am really pleased to say that, with really good leadership from everyone here , the LGA, the NFCC, the Fire Brigades Union and the leadership in fire services themselves , we have seen some significant improvement. What is really pleasing about this round is just how embedded that code of ethics is . We are seeing behaviours start to change. It is not everywhere. The fire services —it is the same with policing — do not represent their local communities as much as they should, but there is great effort to move that way.

People now have difficult conversations more often, which is often the start of reducing poor behaviour. The culture is more open. We are seeing better leadership in terms of communication and chief fire officers being seen. Again, it is not everywhere, but it is three years on from when I reported in 20 23 and, in 2026, while there is more work to do— there always is in this area—we have seen those improvements.
That is really helpful.

Steve Wright : I will just make one point, which is slightly separate. T here has been an improvement from the Westminster Government since 2024 . The creation of the ministerial advisory group was an important step forward, bringing together key stakeholders in the fire sector to discuss the ongoing issues.

I would just make one point to encompass everything that everyone has said today . T he Fire Brigades Union and the employers have embarked on an ambitious joint agenda about what the role of a firefighter looks like . W e are making great progress on that. It come s back to the funding and investment to do that , and to deal with the resilience issue and the threats and risks that this country faces.

There are some positives that are coming. W ith the Prime Minister , the current Secretary of State Angela Rayner and the announcements last week , w e have an opportunity — I believe it is an opportunity — over the next year or so to make the fundamental changes to fix some of the issues that we have been talk ing about for the last 10 or 15 years where the fire service has taken a downward trajectory.

Thank you for your time . Steve gave us a call to action in terms of democratic scrutiny, which is essentially what we are trying to do. Roy, you mentioned earlier that you were not consulted about the wildfires summit in terms of what the Government are doing . We will feed back and make sure that you are involved properly in the process because you have a lot of expertise to feed in.

As I said to the previous panel, we will be looking to make recommendations to the Government, particularly on some of the stuff that is impacting the fire and rescue service. T here may be some follow-up actions after this meeting. I just want to say, o n behalf of my colleagues, that I found this really insightful . I really appreciate your time and what you are doing to keep us safe . Thank you.

sessions.iT: Pensions Credit uptake  in Northern Ireland
sessions.w: Older People for Northern Ireland; Advice NI

segs.tx: Northern Ireland Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Pension c redit uptake in Northern Ireland , HC 740
Wednesday 28 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 28 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Tonia Antoniazzi (Chair); Chris Bloore; Claire Hanna; Simon Hoare; Mike Kane; Mr Paul Kohler; Katrina Murray; Gavin Robinson; David Smith; Robin Swann.
Questions 1-4 1
Witnesses
I : Siobhan Casey, Commissioner for Older People for Northern Ireland, and Kevin Higgins, Head of Policy, Advice NI .
Written evidence from witnesses:
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Siobhan Casey and Kevin Higgins.

Q1 Welcome to the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee’s session on pension credit take-up in Northern Ireland. We are joined by Siobhan Casey, the Commissioner for Older People for Northern Ireland, and virtually by Kevin Higgins, Advice NI’s head of policy. Welcome to you both.
Siobhan, we do not have time for much of a preamble, but could you outline the current picture of pension credit take-up in Northern Ireland and why it matters?

It really matters. What I think people do not understand is that receiving pension credit unlocks so many other opportunities for people. For me, though, it is also about protecting people from poverty. If we cannot reach people entitled to pension credit, that is saying a lot.

About 8% of older people in Northern Ireland are in relative poverty, and another 8% are in absolute poverty. We are seeing that, as people move from their 60s to their 70s and 80s, that is growing, and the oldest pensioners are facing the greatest financial vulnerability.

We have very low private pension rates in Northern Ireland compared with the rest of the UK. That means that people are particularly dependent on their state pension, which leaves them vulnerable to rising living costs and unexpected expenses. It is difficult to heat homes adequately and maintain a healthy diet. All those things lead to deterioration in physical and mental health, which puts pressure on public services. When public services are stretched, that makes it even harder for people, making them more vulnerable. There is growing evidence, too, of increased food insecurity among older people.

That is why getting these types of entitlements to them is really important. There is also the fact that older people are likely to live with one or more long-term health conditions or disabilities, which means that their living conditions can worsen. Many older people live on fixed incomes, so they do not have the opportunity to increase their earnings.

Why is this important? I am conscious that the Department for Communities’ analysis dates back to the early 2020s. It is looking to aggregate better data, which is really critical, but the latest trends show that we are having an increase, which is really good. We all know that the Department for Communities has a really good Make the Call campaign, and it is really trying to promote things better. However, our older population—people over 65—is increasing every year by 6,000 or 7,000. It is an ageing demographic, and we have to be aware that this is coming down the line.
Q2 Siobhan, how many eligible people are not claiming pension credit?
Kevin will probably know this, but I think the Department for Communities has said between 23,000 and 30,000 older people.
Q3 That is a lot of people. On average, how much is each person missing out on financially?
I will let Kevin speak to that one, because he will probably know the financials a bit better.
Q4 All right, Kevin, I am going to come to you. Why does it matter, how many eligible people are not claiming, and how much are they missing out on?
Thank you to the Committee for allowing me to dial in remotely. I also thank your staff for all their work to set this up.

For me, the uptake issue is so important because older people are not getting what they are entitled to. They are not getting what the law says they need to live on. To me, that cuts to the heart of it. We have people out there—we are talking here about older people—who the law says require a certain amount of money due to their needs and circumstances, and they are not getting that.

We are in the cost of living crisis that Siobhan talked about. Older people spend a lot longer in their homes—particularly older older people. If you check out the price of home heating oil in Northern Ireland, it is well over £1,000 for 900 litres of oil. That is just one example. We know that about two thirds of households in Northern Ireland rely on home heating oil. That is one example of why it is so important that every penny of money that should be coming into all households, but particularly those of older people, does come in. I welcome that the Committee is focusing on pension credit uptake, because it is an issue that needs a lot of attention.

Regarding the numbers, the estimates from the Department are admittedly dated, from 2019-20. The Department is working on updating those figures, so we expect some shift, but according to those figures, 66,000—about 72%—of those entitled are receiving it. That leaves around 28% or 26,000 pensioner households that are not getting the pension credit they are entitled to. As for amounts, it is about £1.1 million a week in unclaimed pension credit, which totals about £55 million per annum in unclaimed entitlement, which is a significant amount of money—particularly on Budget day. We are all talking about money today, so it is appropriate to talk about the money that is not coming in to older people’s households.
Q5 What is the trend in pension credit take-up in recent years? Is it getting better or worse?

It is increasing, I think in line with the promotion from the Department for Communities, and the fact that we have 6,000 or 7,000 people every year reaching 65 and coming in. The trends are going up.
Q6 Siobhan, you mentioned that, if you claim pension credit, it unlocks other packages of support. What are those other packages of support?

Things like housing benefit and cold weather payments, the free TV licence for those aged 75 and over, and help with dental, optical and hospital travel costs. Kevin will back this up: the reason a lot of people are not claiming is that they are afraid to declare—well, first, as we spoke about outside the room, Tonia, there is their pride. They do not want to go out and say they need extra support. Then you have the whole matter of declaring savings to public authorities. People are afraid to do that because it may take away from other benefits, and because they are private. The thing is, even if you are entitled to a small amount of pension credit—you declare £1 earnings for every £500 of savings—it unlocks so much more. I really do think that is the message that we need to get out.

Q7 I want to ask about pride and the reticence that it might bring, along with the use of the word “credit”. Credit suggests debt. Have you any thoughts on that? There is a presumption that older people are less keen to apply. Is there any differential in Northern Ireland between urban and rural? It has always been my take that rural communities are more resilient—if I could use that phrase—and less inclined than urban to ask for anything. I just wonder whether you have any observations on that.

I worked in Age NI for 15 and a half years before I took this job , and it would have been a constant thing that people were saying they did not want to take money in case it took away from schools or other areas of the economy. They did not realise that this was a n entitlement . It is not a favour ; it is actually an entitlement. That would have been my experience in trying to convince people : “Yes, you’re entitled to this. You worked hard for it . I t is not taking away from other key services. So it’s important that you do claim.” Kevin, do you have more information on the rural - urban split?

T hank you for the question. My sense is that, in rural Northern Ireland, there are certain issues that may make it a bit more difficult for older people to get the information and advice that they might need in order to go ahead and maximise their rights and entitlements. An example is access to services , being able to travel to get to them, and reliance on public transport. That can be difficult ; s ometimes there are issues with that. M aybe there is just one bus to a certain place and one going back in the evening. T ravel can be very difficult. In urban areas , there will be more accessible services, the likes of advice services and advice centres, where you can pop in and seek the information that you may need. There could be more resilience , I agree , in rural areas, but that resilience might mean that people are not pursuing their rights and entitlements ; they are getting by.

That takes me to some of the other issues . You are right about a lot of older people having a sense of independence . They have worked all their days ; they have paid their big stamp and their national insurance , and they want to have the respect and the dignity and the right to be able to live on the stamp and the insurance . That feeds into their being reluctant and thinking, “W hy should I have to divulge all my financial information —my bank accounts and so on? ”

I nterestingly , there is another issue, which is almost guilt. Older people are very aware of what has happened generally over th e last 10 or 15 years in terms of cuts to the social security system, particularly for working - age people . To a large extent , with the triple lock, older people have been protected , but working-age people have experienced various austerity measures , cuts , reforms , freezes and so on . O lder people are very aware of that , and I think that has fed into this as well . There is a “Well, I have enough to do me” attitude . They are seeing other people finding things a lot tighter or a lot more difficult than they are , and therefore there is a certain reluctance to come forward.

Q8 I am not going to get into the weeds of the overall welfare budget , because I think that the data points in the opposite direction to the one that you suggest , but l et me ask this very specific question of you both. A yes or no answer will suffice . In your assessment , i s there a problem with the use of the word “ credit ” ?
It is not something that has come to my attention before.

No, I don’t think so. Ve ry often what I find that people are coming through our doors about is cold, hard cash. People are struggling to pay bills , get their oil tank filled and so on. At this stage, because we are in this cost of living crisis, things like what you have mentioned are maybe less important. If we were not in the situation that we are in, things like that potentially would come to the surface and the name of things could be important , but at the moment we are in a place where it is potentially less important.

Q9 Thank you for joining us, Kevin and Siobhan. I am wondering to what extent this is a Northern Ireland problem or a UK- wide problem. Do you have any figures on the uptake in GB , or the regions of GB , compared with Northern Ireland? Is it better or worse , or do we not know?

We should know. I have not analysed the figures , but t here will be uptake figures . I know that the Government have just recently , in GB, launched a pension credit uptake campaign. I can certainly get the numbers for the Committee , but that is not something I have analysed in preparation for this meeting.
It would be great if you can write to us on that, Kevin.

Q10 Good morning, Siobhan and Kevin. You have touched on the impact on eligible pensioners who do not claim pension credit, as that unlocking mechanism opens up other avenues for support. In your assessment, how much is the low uptake of pension credit contributing to pensioner poverty and fuel poverty? Kevin, you touched briefly on the price of oil, but what about the overall impact?

I think it is definitely impacting it. There is the heating cost, but we can also look at the figures around food insecurity. Older people are the largest group going to the likes of the Trussell Trust. There is a 91% increase in those going for food support. Then there is the reduction in the winter fuel payment too, so there is certainly an impact on people.

I totally agree with that. The independent advice sector has done some benefit uptake work. The Northern Ireland Audit Office says that, in one year, there was something like £17 million generated—this is extra money in people’s pockets—during the benefit uptake campaign with the independent advice sector. It is currently estimated—although the number could be very different from this—that the unclaimed amount is about £55 million. If you do a targeted uptake campaign that generates around £15 million or £20 million, you will have a significant impact on the amount of money that is going unclaimed.

I completely agree with you: imagine the impact that that £15 million or £20 million will have on the mental health and wellbeing of older people. They will feel, “I don’t have to get 500 litres or 200 litres; I can fill the tank up. I can get proper food in the fridge. I can get taxis to go to GP and dental appointments.” It would be a fantastic boost if we could maximise the uptake for older people.

Kevin mentioned taxis, and it is about their social life too. Community transport is being used up taking people to health appointments. Particularly in rural areas, Simon, we are trying to get people to use community transport to do their shopping, to get to the hairdresser or to do whatever. That extra money gives them that bit more independence, so it is really important.
Q11 Do you have any information about the eligibility threshold? Would raising it by a few pounds bring more pensioners into eligibility?
Kevin and I did some work on that a couple of years ago. The figures for the people not meeting the threshold were quite staggering then, so I think that needs to be looked at.

Yes. The point about thresholds is very interesting. The Committee will know about the new state pension that has come in for people who retired after 2016. For those with a full contribution on the new state pension, the weekly amount is £241.30. The standard minimum guarantee in pension credit for a single person is £238—just a couple of pounds below. That speaks very clearly to your point about amounts of money. It is good that people claim their state pension, but on the downside there is scope to be able to get a top-up of pension credit. As we have touched on, that is so important for the likes of passporting.

In Northern Ireland, we have a home heating oil support scheme. No doubt, there will be other targeted schemes to help with the cost of living in the Budget, but you can bet that a lot of those schemes will require you to be on pension credit to get an entitlement. That reinforces how important it is that people get their pension credit entitlement. If they do not, they will lose out on some of the cost of living measures that will be announced, maybe in the Budget.

Q12 Good morning to you both. To follow on from Robin’s point about thresholds, about 20-odd years ago, when I was starting to help in political office, a lady came to me and we talked to her about pension credit. At that stage, £6,000 was the maximum that you were allowed as savings, and she had about £7,000. I have never forgotten her looking me in the eye and saying, “But, son, £4,000 of that is for Wilton’s , ” which was the local funeral director. That showed the sort of savings and preparations she had made—so that she wasn’t burdening anyone else. At that stage we were able to talk to her not about divesting savings, but about maybe taking a prepayment plan, so that she could invest in the funeral but also bring herself within the eligibility criteria for pension credit. Whether it is Advice NI or even the Make the Call service, do they give practical and tangible advice that would allow somebody to come within the criteria for pension credit?

Thank you for that question. There are a couple of really important aspects. It was £6,000 and my understanding is that it is now £10,000, but the point still applies. That lady could come in with £11,000 and say exactly the same thing, so it’s a fair point. In terms of thresholds, if we could shift it from £6,000 to £10,000, which was some years ago, there is a debate to be had around shifting it from £10,00 0 to £15,000 and so on, or up to £16,000. So there is a point well made there as well.

On another point, often in advice centres people come through the door, we start the calculation, and we find, as you did, Gavin, that the person has no entitlement to pension credit. For whatever reason, they are slightly under. What you have to do is not leave it there and not just park that issue. You look at the circumstances of the individual. Very often you will explore other health problems or disabilities and so on. Then it becomes a circuitous route. If you can get an entitlement to attendance allowance, not only is that a bit of additional money, but attendance allowance unlocks additional premiums within the pension credit calculation, and that will then allow you to get a successful pension credit application.

Your point is well made. You know this in constituency offices and advice centres. The case has an initial face value, but your work only starts at that point. Then it is about exploring and doing a holistic piece of work, exploring every avenue, and very often, as in the example that I gave you, you can get to a place where you can unlock the additional income that that household is entitled to. There is an issue on the savings—I agree with you, and I also agree that very often there is more than meets the eye to doing this pension credit uptake work. It is about not accepting what comes forward at face value, and unlocking the entitlement that will come after you do some hard, hard yards.

Every £500 of savings is equivalent to £1 of income. If you are out by £2,000 or £3,000, that is £6 of income. It i s about beginning to help people understand the nuances of this and the fact that even if they are not going to get the maximum amount, it will open up other opportunities, as Kevin says, for other benefits.
Q13 Siobhan, you mentioned briefly that private pension build-up is lower in Northern Ireland. Do you have any high-level data on that?
No, not here.
Q14 It rings true, but I wasn’t sure if there was data . How effective is pension credit at tackling poverty? Do you think that the level of pension credit is adequate where it is currently set?

You could always be asking for more, Claire. The challenge is getting people to receive what is there now, and then there are onward negotiations on that. In terms of recommendations, at the minute we are calculating the number of people applying. There was a report two weeks ago on planning for an ageing society. As a Department we need to look past publicity and application numbers and actually look at the successful awards and additional income. With this demographic increasing year on year by 7,000 or whatever, how are we going to do the proactive thing?

Also, at the stage of digitalisation, we have to engage people who are missing out on key support. At the minute the Department—Kevin will know about this because we have been working with the Department—are going in now, targeting specifically the 23,000 to 30,000 older people who they believe are missing out. They write a letter and send it to their homes. That type of targeting is not scattergun; it i s direct, and that i s really good. We have worked with them on the outreach letters, and will work with them on the promotion of it.

A person receiving a letter at home might still be a bit concerned. It is about Advice NI, Age NI and the commissioner’s office getting together and saying, “Look out for this. This is important to you.” That is a good proactive approach that has been adopted by the Department. The point I made earlier about the independent advice sector is also important. There needs to be support for those organisations, for accessible claim handling and capacity. People would prefer to come to Advice NI or Age NI or their local resource centre to get support. We have to be seen in the collaborative and collective approach.

The other two recommendations are that other public bodies need to be signposting as well; it is about working right across. I know they will do that. The Housing Executive and others will all be working to try to identify people; good work is being done but, because of that ageing demographic coming up, it has to get better and be more targeted. I know the Department is doing more about aggregation of proper data and analysis, which will be good.

Q15 Are those eligibility criteria and the income and savings thresholds at the right level? With the cost of living, do you think those are set at the right place to bring into the remit all those who need support?

It is a fair point. During your whole working life, you are always encouraged to save for your retirement and be responsible. To some extent, you should not be penalised for that. There is a judgment call to be made there on whether the level of savings is a bit too low and punitive. As we discussed earlier, if you raised that threshold from £10,000 to £15,000 or whatever, there is a balance to be struck in providing support to those people. It is not an awful lot of money. Older people like to have a bit put by to leave to future generations or to take care of themselves later on. There is definitely a debate now; I would support those levels increasing.

I have a couple of comments on your point, Claire, around levels. To repeat, the new state pension is £241, and the minimum guarantee of pension credit is £238. Structurally straightaway, if there are no other circumstances, that person will not be entitled to pension credit because the new state pension is those couple of pounds over. There is a systemic and structural issue there.

A bit of thought is required in terms of trends and so on. In May 2021, there were 63,450 pension credit claimants; in May 2026, there are 60,030. That has gone from roughly 63,500 to 60,000. I take Siobhan’s point that recent months have bucked the trend. There has been a slight increase in pension credit claims, but it is a downward trajectory. It is understandable, given the increased amounts in the new state pension, and the increased state retirement age. I think shortly we may get to the point where we are below 60,000 in pension credit claims for the first time ever.

There is more to the statistics; it takes a little bit of nuance. There could be a slight increase now, but the overall trend could be down. That makes it even more important that for every single household that should be getting even a little bit of pension credit, for the reasons we outlined, there should be more effort. The Department needs to put in more effort—we all do—to ensure that those households are getting every pound they are entitled to.

Q16 That helpfully leads us into the next question. Kevin, you were talking about the Department needing to do more. As you know, this Committee is Westminster-based and clearly interested in Northern Ireland, but there is obviously a wider Whitehall discussion to be had. Could you help us understand the breakdown in responsibility for the funding, promotion and delivery of pension credit between the Department for Communities in Northern Ireland, which is a devolved Department, and the Department for Work and Pensions in Westminster?

Others can correct me if I am wrong on this, but I believe that as social security is devolved to Northern Ireland, complete responsibility lies with the Department for Communities and the Minister in that Department. To me, it is very straightforward in that respect. We do not have to look over to Westminster and the DWP; we can take responsibility ourselves in Northern Ireland to do what we have to do, which in this case is to increase pension credit uptake.

There are systems and so on, and there is the issue of parity, but the fundamental point is that social security is devolved, and therefore the responsibility lies with the Department and the Minister.

Q17 To unpack that a little bit, it is devolved, but we operate the same system on exactly the same terms with the same criteria and legislation. The money is coming directly from Westminster, and the systems used are Westminster systems. To deviate from any of that, there is a cost. At the moment, while it is the Department’s responsibility, it is an English or Westminster system that is being deployed in Northern Ireland, is it not?

That is exactly right. That is why we would operate on this principle of parity, so that we can achieve the efficiencies and savings by using the same systems, and we do not build our own system here. Yes, we are devolved and independent, but the principle of parity would carry across for the vast amount of time.

One example—and you will know this well, Gavin—is the introduction of welfare reforms and universal credit. There was an intense debate about that because of the potential differential impact in Northern Ireland, particularly around the introduction of PIP. Twice as many people per head of population claimed working-age DLA at the time, so there was concern about the impact of welfare reform. We did introduce all of that, but you will remember that the Evason working group was set up, and then we put our own unique mitigations in place.

For example, our benefit cap mitigation was put in place following the Evason report recommendations. That benefit cap mitigation is worth its weight in gold now, because the Government abolished the two-child limit. So for families with children in Northern Ireland, we have the two-child cap abolished, and we have the benefit cap mitigated—it is fantastic. But you are right: we had to build an IT system to deliver our unique mitigation system, and we have to fund it. The Executive took the decision to fund it out of the block grant.

I digress a little bit there. In terms of the pension credit, yes, we tend to plough the same furrow, but the responsibility is local. In terms of uptake, we can do a lot around awareness raising and uptake campaigns, giving a little bit of funding to places like Age NI , Advice NI and the advice sector to maximise the effectiveness of uptake campaigns.

Q18 Thanks, Kevin. Before I bring you in, Siobhan, let me just put it this way. There are three things: funding, promotion and delivery. Delivery is the Department for Communities , but using Westminster systems; funding is Westminster; and promotion is the Department for Communities .

Kevin mentioned unique mitigations. I spoke earlier on about the fact that there are 660,000 leaflets going out from the Department for Work and Pensions here to promote this. That is going out to certain localities across the UK, whereas the Department for Communities is planning to do direct targeting. Sometimes the unique mitigations can even be an improvement—they might be an example.
Q19 How effective do you think the co-ordination is between the Department for Communities and the Department for Work and Pensions?
I wouldn’t be in a position , really, to understand that.

In terms of the targeted letters and so on, that data is held by the Department for Communities . That is a unique exercise, and we will be writing out to our own people here in Northern Ireland, completely separate to what the DWP are doing. They will have their database of people who may be entitled to pension credit. It is stand-alone, in terms of the data and the work that is being done.

It also speaks to the issue of us needing to be a lot smarter about data sharing. A lot of information is held in the Department for Communities , and the various benefits that are within that, and between Departments. For example, Health might be able to see that certain older people’s health problems are increasing, their health declining a little. That means, if you put your benefits hat on, there could be entitlement to attendance allowance or the severe disability premium on pension credit. The Department for Communities could be better joined up not only within the Department, but with other Departments, such as Health in particular.

As Siobhan was saying, there is real scope for targeting and being able to have a more personalised conversation, almost at an individual level: “Kevin Higgins, I think you could have an entitlement to pension credit.” That becomes a more powerful conversation than, “Oh, you might be entitled to ring this number,” which people might not engage with to a great extent. This issue around data sharing is something that we should be able to push the barriers a little to get the results we want to get.
Do you have anything to add, Siobhan?
No. I think I was saying that earlier. There is a move towards that data sharing, from what we can see from our conversations with the Department for Communities.

Q20 Paul Kohler was asking about the difference between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and whether this was a UK-wide phenomenon or just a Northern Ireland issue. Simon Hoare was asking questions about the rural and urban divide, and the support for and resilience of people in separate communities. What do you think are the main barriers to uptake in Northern Ireland that differ from Great Britain?

I do not know that they differ. The barriers are that people wrongly assume that owning a home, having savings or receiving a small occupational pension excludes them, and some think that awards will be too small to justify applying. Others fear disturbing existing benefits, as I said earlier. Many find the system confusing. The application process is quite rigorous, and you can imagine that if you are in your 70s or 80s, it might be off-putting. We talked about people feeling uncomfortable to ask. I work closely with the commissioner in Wales, and I understand from them that the same issues arise there.

Q21 Kevin, I presume you are pretty NI-based, whereas Siobhan is now engaging with people across the United Kingdom, so I will move the question on just for you, if that is okay. We talked about trust, and Simon asked about whether “credit” is the right phrase, because that implies a level of debt or some sort of burden. You have not picked that up as an issue, but do you want to expand a bit more on some of the pressures around stigma, complexity and trust in Government and whether you believe those to be significant barriers?

We would find that, and it is to be expected. Older people will not know the intricacies of the benefits system, and the starting point for many is this fear of doing something wrong and not knowing what they do not know. Obviously, there will be a fear factor, so to me the fear factor is very important, as is the complexity of the system, as I said.

When people come into advice services and we unlock entitlement, the severe disability premium additional amount on pension credit is actually £86 a week. The basic minimum is £238, but if you meet that other bit of the criteria, you can actually boost that by almost £90 or £100. For a couple who satisfy that, it is £172. There is that fear of doing something wrong, but often when we unlock that money for people, they will still look at the adviser and go, “Are you sure about this? I don’t want to be doing something wrong. I’m not sure I should be claiming this additional money at all.”

There is that almost fear of taking the step even to get advice and then, even when you present the additional money to people, they say, “Oh, I’m not sure. I don’t know about that.” There is that reticence. It is just inherent in older people that they have enough to get by —t hey ha ve the state pension and so on —b ut they could be more aware of the amount of money that they could be missing out on and that they could be deploying towards the cost of living , oil and everything else .

Perhaps we should also think about that word “credit”. P eople will have very mixed opinions about universal credit, and there are conversations about that all the time . Whether the word “ credit ” is linked to debt , I am not so sure , b ut pension credit might somehow be linked to universal credit , so perhaps there might be mixed views of that out there in the public domain . That might be a tangible point, but a piece of research could be needed just to unpick that .
Thank you very much, both.

Q22 Thank you both for coming in. There are a couple of things that I am exceptionally aware of. I think about my grandparents and how their lives were fundamentally changed when they got benefits—those days were pre pension credit. They got the support that they were entitled to compared with the generations that followed, who have had the benefit of workplace pensions investment. Certainly, that is borne out by Government statistics that pensioner poverty is most obvious in the over-75 age group. I am really interested in the targeting proposal—particularly, how you are using that to drive the take-up. Is it just going to be, “Right, we know you fit th ese criteria. How can we convince you to complete the forms?”
