How do we make those clear and bring them to the fore?” For example, my first thought when it comes to the helplines being run by Victim Support is that, surely, we want to know the questions that are being asked—we want to know what victims are phoning up and asking about, and where they are not finding their way to the right information. We need to respond to those things very quickly.

Q40 You mentioned exclusion zones, where offenders are banned from specific areas. I want to ask about restriction zones, where they are confined to specific areas. At the moment, those are only going to be used for high-risk sexual and violent offenders. Do you think they should be used more broadly for domestic abuse perpetrators?

Yes, I do think they should be used more broadly. The reason that has been set out in the way that it has could be just about operationalising it with policing and others, and how you implement it so you are not exceeding people’s expectations of what really will happen. But surely, if we want to set that out as an option, we want to know—and this is some of the data we have been asking MOJ and the Government for—the number of tags, and the number of restriction zones and exclusion zones. We are saying, “Please let us know,” which would be a way to reassure people that these options are being used and implemented.

The Government have said that they expect this to extend to other categories, but it seems really obvious. The things that the victims I speak to are doing to sort out this change in the timeline—moving house, changing jobs, not finishing a course—should shock us all. It is a huge price for them to pay, not having seen it coming and being quite taken aback and surprised by it. At the very least, we have to get the measures right and make sure there is a lot of transparency about them.

Q41 Finally, can I ask you about domestic abuse protection orders, which are supposed to be rolled out across criminal, civil and family courts from next month? How do you feel they are going? Are they making it possible to use positive requirements and make offenders fulfil certain criteria? Are they doing all they could be doing?

The DAPOs are not using positive requirements very much right now, if at all. The ability to apply from the family court is not being utilised. The way that was set out in the Domestic Abuse Act, and the ambition of that, has not been fully realised. I have not seen the final evaluation for the DAPO pilot; I think that is meant to be published fairly soon.

The Home Office is rolling out DAPOs, and I am told that most areas are gearing up to be able to apply and achieve a DAPO. But we have to remember that they are somewhat limited in what they set out to do. It is a mixed picture and has not been done in a way that has achieved the full ambition.

Some legislative changes have been needed, which I think people did not foresee, about offenders not having to give their agreement to some of those positive requirements and about age limits. I understand that that is the whole point—it is a new thing and it is needed, and we probably envisioned that we would have to make some changes. One area that has implemented them is Greater Manchester; I have spoken to that team specifically and they are very positive about what they have achieved so far.

I think this is the point: we have to know where we are in the journey. It is not a full roll-out as it was set out in the Domestic Abuse Act. I would question whether we have invested enough in the positive requirements and how you build that scaffolding around the DAPOs. I think that that has been under-resourced. Are they probably able to apply in most areas? Yes, but I think we are not nearly there yet.

Q42 What you said about the victims having to think about leaving home or changing their career was very moving. On the Probation Service and tags, there was a figure of 5,000 people being without any tags at all.

Would you agree that the Government are in a quandary, where you have to have the victims’ faith in what you are trying to do but you are also trying to carry the public with you in the decision on prison releases? We all know how much the Probation Service is under pressure, but do you agree that not setting up that phone line is unacceptable?

I do. I find that the Probation Service are really honest, willing and open, and full of people who want to do the right thing, but this has put them in a very difficult position in terms of change. Since the Sentencing Act, this had been very clear—the Government said, “We’ll stand up this line, and we’ll make sure we have the risk assessment in place and other issues sorted out”—but as we got closer, it became clear that that was not going to happen. That is a combination of probation and MOJ, and it has exposed cracks that were already in the system around release. It was already inadequate on release, full stop.

I would say that the Government have a real opportunity now to sort that out permanently once and for all. Those issues have been there for a long time, and we cannot just pretend that things will be perfect. We have to be rigorous about it, and the impact on the victim must be built in. I have had people say to me, “Nicole, people will always be released,” but it was never safely planned. You cannot then layer on an early release and more uncertainty and expect that to work without quite serious effort, attention and grip. I think we are getting slightly closer to that, but we are not quite there yet. And yet we are doing it—the releases are happening.

Q43 I have a couple of quick questions. As I am sure you will both agree, it takes immense strength for victims and survivors to report crimes of domestic abuse, controlling or coercive behaviour or sexual assaults. We know that; that is fact. Do you think that the impact of the early release scheme will mean that victims are less inclined to report? Will they think, “Well, what’s the point, if they’re going to be out after whatever sentence they may end up with?”?

I do worry about that. I worry about my own responsibility and speaking to the media so openly about these concerns, because of course you are balancing people’s confidence in systems. I want people to know—you were a police officer, so you will know—that there are lots of people who are willing to help, who are going the extra mile and all those things, but you cannot deny how the people who I have spoken to and who have spoken to the media have felt and how they have been let down.

It is a balancing act. On the whole, I obviously want people to reach out for help and support; it should be there, and it will be there in lots of cases. Over the years, it will not have been the only thing, but there have been quite a few things that have eroded the trust of victims in the criminal justice system.

I agree. For the survivors I speak to, it has eroded their trust that it is worth their while explaining what has happened to them when they have been met with constant challenges, whether that be not being believed or listened to at first, or the years that it takes to navigate the system. When you add early release on top, it is just another thing that means that they think, “Actually, why is it worth me coming forward?”.

I would add one small thing on the protection orders, which comes back to the join-up that we were talking about at the start in terms of cross-Government work. When it comes to slavery and trafficking risk orders and prevention orders, there are lessons to be learned for the Government, about the police and the Crown Prosecution Service having the awareness, about monitoring and about local forces not being able to apply for orders in their patch, which the Government are addressing with the changes they are making at the moment. The women we are trying to help with this strategy can face overlapping harms, and there are lessons to be learned from things we have tried to do in the modern slavery space that may not have worked as well as we would have liked for survivors of domestic abuse.

Q44 Following up on that, we heard in evidence to the Government before these early release decisions were made that any perpetrator of any crime being sentenced to prison time is a deterrent, no matter how long the sentence. I disagree; I think the longer the sentence, the more chance you have of thinking twice before you go and commit a crime.

Do you agree with that sentiment, or do you think that perpetrators of domestic abuse think, “Well, I’m going to get even more time off”? How much of an impact does that have on their decision making or if they are second-guessing themselves? What are your thoughts?

I do. I have heard from a lot of victims recently who, once they have got their head around what is happening about how long you would stay in custody, how long you serve your sentence in the community and how that has changed, will say things like, “I wish I had said all of what he had ever done.” In other words, “I wish I could have built the picture so that it was clearer that what he was being sentenced for was really commensurate with what happened”—he or she, depending. I understand that; I suppose the flipside is that in the Sentencing Act we have a move, or a drive, to community-based sentences and a presumption of a community-based sentence.

My immediate question is what that looks like. What is an adequate community-based sentence for someone who is a perpetrator of domestic abuse, given all those risks? We have not been able to talk enough and work enough in Government on that, because of early release overshadowing so much, but in actuality it has already started. The Sentencing Act has ensured that that will happen for some of those sentences, and that will be an emerging concern.

I often see—I am sure you do, too—the Sexual Offences Act being used to hold perpetrators of modern slavery to account. In a way, I agree with that approach, in terms of it disrupting crime taking place, but there is a reason why there is a lifetime sentence in the Modern Slavery Act. It recognises the level of horrific action that is going on behind controlling someone: trafficking, exploitation and women being raped multiple times a day.

I sit through cases that are used as best practice, when the police have done a fantastic job of identifying perpetrators and taking the victim through the criminal justice system and supporting them. I get to the end of those presentations, and when they say that the person was held to account with two years in jail, and then you add the early release scheme on top, I am shocked. It leads to survivors really questioning what justice looks like for them. That is something I hear time and time again from them. I have serious concerns about whether we are using the powers under the Modern Slavery Act—I do not think we are—and what this additional move is doing to survivors.

Q45 As we all know, when we talk about things like controlling and coercive behaviour, it can mean many things. It could mean a one-off incident or a series of incidents. I welcome the Government’s recent changes to the early release scheme, but do you think that all domestic abuse cases, regardless of the levels and regardless of whether they involve controlling and coercive behaviour or domestic rape, should be exempt from early release?

I have tried to make that case. I tried to make that case as an amendment to the Sentencing Act, to say that particular offences should be excluded. It is a little bit difficult to say that all domestic abuse perpetrators are offenders, because of some of the ways we track those cases, but I believe that they should have been excluded.

It is not for me to answer whether that is realistic for the Government, given what they knew. I do not know all the information they had in front of them about prison spaces. That is not for me to answer; it is for them to make that decision.

I definitely wanted domestic abuse-related offenders to be excluded, because of the respite alone, but that has not happened. Victims will understandably have not followed the Sentencing Act and all these changes, and they are quite shocked. They are genuinely quite shocked by this change and feel that it has come out of the blue. I have had victims say to me, “How can people in Government change what the judge said and ordered?” It just does not make sense to them, and I can see why that would be the case.
Presumably, Eleanor, you agree with those comments.
Eleanor Lyons indicated assent.
Can I take Catherine Atkinson and Preet Kaur Gill’s questions together, just so we can move on?

Q46 I want to go back to preventive orders—something I used to do a lot when I was a barrister. I am conscious that you have so many different types of orders, including non-molestation orders, sexual harm prevention orders, stalking orders or injunctions against harassment. Moving to having a universal order with domestic abuse prevention orders seems like a really positive step.

Do you think that there should be a simplification of all the orders? Do you think that more needs to be done for consistency across police forces? Should minds be applied again when there is early release, to see whether or not those kinds of preventive orders are needed for those offenders?

In respect of domestic abuse perpetrators, do you think that Drive or a perpetrator programme should have been part of the release conditions? How robust is it that markers are being put on properties, and that there is an expectation of what the police response to a call-out from that number should be to support victims further?

I think the original thinking was that the more the DAPO was developed and rolled out, the more it would almost be a natural progression to use those as opposed to other orders. It would not be for all orders , though ; w e are far from that. I n many areas , I have had people say to me , “We are likely to continue using some of these other orders until we straighten out the issues with the DAPOs . ”

It is another thing to know they exist. In police reform, we have to achieve some way for police forces to know and have at their fingertips all the right information. It does such a disservice to victims , and also to the safety of those in frontline response , if they show up to an incident at a residence or a location where they do not have all the information in front of them.

What worries me a little is that some of the improvements that we need to look at urgently will start to get kicked into the long grass — not necessarily intentionally , but because we will be so focused on police reform . W hat about the here and now? Some of these problems, as you say, are very chronic. There are some pilots and initiatives about ways to share information manually about various orders. None of that is really good enough. A lot of it comes down to the technology being used , the different methods in different forces and the lack of a uniform way of sharing those orders. That leaves it up to the victim to explain the order , to have it with them and to talk about it . T hat is just not good enough.

In relation to early release, you are right about being clear on what the role of the police is in breaches . Most people and most victims think a tag goes off if there is a breach and that somehow that activates a kind of overarching response. That is not the case, actually ; the probation officer will know about it eventually , within a time period, but a predictable action will not necessarily be taken. That needs much more clarity.

You are right that Drive is something that the Government have got behind and rolled out . That is about knowing much more about the perpetrator and offender. Surely there is much more scope to draw that a bit closer to problem - solving for some of these issues with early release. Yes, I think you are on to all the right issues and ideas there.
We are going to move on to online harms . I will bring Robbie Moore in.
Q47 Just before we move on to online harms, I want to ask a further question on the early prisoner release scheme .
I told you it was a big topic.

It has to do with understanding your perception of the erosion of trust among victims and survivors in coming forward to the national grooming gangs inquiry that we now finally have in place. It has been put to me that while there was a roll-back by the Government and those perpetrators of very serious sexual crimes, including rape, will now not be released at serving 33% of their sentence, there is still this challenge of trust being eroded. Do you feel that there may be victims and survivors who are less reluctant to come forward to provide evidence as part of that inquiry? It has certainly been put to me that that is an area of concern.

Gosh. I am not trying to cop out, but that is a bit out of my scope , given the kind s of experiences I have talking to victims , who se experience will traditionally be domestic abuse - related. There i s a real overlap there , but I do not know that I have heard specifically about the grooming gangs. I wish I could tell you more. I will try to find out a bit more and maybe bring that back to you , but I cannot recollect hearing specifically—
I only asked that as a bolt-on, because I know that domestic abuse and child sexual exploitation ha ve been heavily linked.
Yes, heavily linked.

Some of the survivors of sexual exploitation who I work with are survivors from the grooming gangs , and t he thing that they brought up is the criminalisation aspect of their exploitation, which you will know about . However, they are also consistently speaking about this credibility requirement, which I know is slightly different to the early release scheme.

I cannot stress enough how harmful it is to have, on the one side, our hopefully making progress when it comes to domestic abuse and saying, “We understand it takes time to come forward and that it is difficult, and that we should be listening to and believing you as the premise”, but then to have a different rule for survivors of sexual exploitation and saying to them, “We don’t believe you, we must question your credibility”, taking place in legislation. That is something that I am hearing consistently from those survivors. When you have multiple overlapping harms taking place, I think that will lead to long-term harm, in terms of people feeling confident about coming forward.
I am sorry to interrupt, but given that Peter has specific questions on that topic, can I go to him now? Then we will come back to you, Robbie, for online harms.

Q48 I was going to start by asking about changes to credibility under the proposed Immigration and Asylum Bill, but I think we have covered that quite extensively. So I will move past that to ask about other changes proposed in that Bill and how they interact with action on violence against women and girls.

First, on reforms to the national referral mechanism, do you feel, Eleanor, that they will be helpful in identifying potential victims? How well do you think the Home Office is currently able to identify the victims of modern slavery in the asylum system and outwith it?

There are some commitments in the action plan underpinning the VAWG strategy where I think good progress has been made in terms of the national referral mechanism. That is largely around better advocacy for child victims of exploitation and devolved decision-making pilots.

However, looking at national referral mechanism reform as a whole, I see that as harmful steps taking us backwards in our ability to identify victims of exploitation. The credibility requirements, as we have touched on, cause incredible concern among survivors. But there is also something bigger here. We rely on victims of modern slavery not being able to come forward and self-identify but being identified by a first-responder organisation. When we are cutting funding for dedicated police teams and we are not recognising the role that is going on across non-statutory responders, we are reducing our ability to identify survivors.

That does not apply across all police forces; some forces are really aware of their roles and responsibility, as are some local authorities. But increasingly in my time as commissioner, I am hearing survivors say, “I was told by a police force that I wasn’t able to be referred into the national referral mechanism”, or, “This didn’t apply to me”, only for them to find out that that was the wrong information.

I am concerned about our overall overarching approach to identifying victims of modern slavery at the moment. We see from the rising numbers that we are still identifying them in huge numbers, but I do not think that we are reaching everyone who needs our help and support.
Q49 You said you had specific concerns about the proposed changes in the Bill to the NRM. What are those concerns?

My main concerns are that the Home Office is saying that national referral mechanism reform is being delivered through the credibility requirement—clause 36 of the Immigration and Asylum Bill, part 5. They say that will make it easier to identify victims of modern slavery. I completely disagree with that premise; I do not think that it is making it easier for us to identify them. It is creating a culture of fear among survivors that they will not be believed and it is introducing a very strange precedent for this group of survivors that we are questioning their credibility and their stories when they come forward. I think that is universally doing harm at the moment.

When you say as a Government, “We are passing this law”, and it feels detached from survivors, that is not what I find when I speak to them. They are deeply concerned. I have had al-Fayed survivors get in touch with me and say, “This will actually stop women like us being recognised”, and they are already struggling to get the support they need. However, they are also coming forward to me because they are nervous about what it will mean to other women and girls being exploited at the moment.

Q50 The claim is consistently made—not by me; I am just reporting on it—that asylum seekers at risk of their asylum claim being turned down are belatedly turning to claims about modern slavery, in order either to have another go at claiming asylum or to delay any attempts to remove them from the country. Is that a legitimate complaint? Is it something that you have seen? If it is, does that undermine the position of very real victims of modern slavery in the asylum system? If that is a concern, does it need to be addressed so that we can better protect genuine victims of modern slavery?

If you are confirmed to be a victim of modern slavery by the Home Office, that does not give you any automatic right to remain in the UK. I really struggle to understand that assertion being put forward by the Government. Also, when I question the Home Office on the data behind those claims, they really struggle to provide any meaningful statistics.

The best ones they have managed are how many high-risk deportation flights are delayed after 3 pm on that day from a claim. It is a tiny percentage of those victims of the modern slavery system; I think it is less than 1% or 2% of those victims. I do not see any evidence from the Home Office to assert that claim.

The Home Affairs Committee, chaired by Dame Diana Johnson before Dame Karen Bradley, questioned the Home Office extensively on that claim. It found that there was no misuse of the system when it comes to it. The largest nationality of survivors of modern slavery are UK nationals.

Making the knee-jerk reaction across all survivors of exploitation that we “must”—which is the wording of the legislation—question their credibility if they have been exploited is going to affect all victims and their ability to come forward and speak freely about what is happening to them. Even if the Home Office was trying to address an issue, as I have outlined, the numbers are incredibly small on the evidence that we have seen. I am concerned about that part of the legislation.

Q51 I am only a guest from the Joint Committee on Human Rights , and I know that you are coming before us—perhaps this can be a taster of that session—so very briefly, do you just have a one-line response on changes to transparency and supply chain statements? That is also connected to this wider piece around protecting particularly vulnerable women.

Yes. I think the parts in the Bill are steps forward, but we need to be asking businesses to actively prevent the harm and forced labour happening in their supply chains across the world, not just report on it. The UK is hugely behind compared with our international partners in this space. That means that we are not doing enough to protect survivors at the moment.
Q52 Dame Nicole, this is obviously Eleanor’s bailiwick, but did you have anything briefly to add?
No. I thought that was very comprehensive.

Q53 Focusing on online harms, as an overview do you believe that the online platforms have effective measures in place to protect violence against women and girls? We have quite rightly heard criticism of them from the previous Safeguarding Minister.

Again, with th is strategy there were some commitments in here about specific offences. It is really positive to see those steps forward. On the one hand this space is really busy, and on the other it is less clear in terms of where we are and exactly where we are headed. There are a lot of actions and statements of intent in this action plan.

Again, it is unclear at DCMS now that DSIT has been decommissioned and the portfolio has been transferred to DCMS. I would like to see a much greater bringing together of the VAWG sector service providers to give regular on-the-ground, quick input and expertise to DCMS and Ofcom about some of the things they are seeing in the here and now—the helplines, the first ports of call.

In some ways, the strategy does point to all sorts of ways in which we strengthen prevention, such as education about digital spaces, accountability and take-down measures. The kinds of things I believe need to happen are all there in lots of ways, but we do not have clarity about who, when and how.

One thing that is genuinely missing is tuning into the helplines and services that are real ports of call. For domestic abuse in particular, where this gets difficult is around coercive and controlling behaviour. Sometimes online harm will be very obvious to some of us, but with domestic abuse it is not always so obvious because you would have to know the context of the domestic abuse and what the threats or presence online looks like. We lack a full understanding about that.

There is also a disconnect between what we expect of the police in terms of these issues and what is recorded, what really happens and what is dealt with. Frankly, that is partly because of the barriers about what they feel is achievable that are put in place for them. If you are a victim of domestic abuse and you approach the police over criminal damage, online abuse or non-fatal strangulation, some of those things will be more obvious for the police to pursue and account for. I am afraid we are missing a huge amount of online harm because it falls into the “too hard to address” category. The immediate advice to victims is “You stand down. You hide away. You get off the platform.” There is so much more to do.
A great step forward would be understanding where we have got to so far with the commitments that we do have and understanding who is taking responsibility for those actions within DCMS and when.
Q54 Do you think that the Online Safety Act has had the benefits that everyone was expecting when it comes to dealing with modern slavery and domestic abuse?

Not particularly in those areas, partly because of some of the dynamic I described. There needs to be much firmer clarity about the role of Ofcom in regard to some of these crimes and some of these areas.

I know we talk about specialist services provision, but if Ofcom says it wants to be an evidence-led regulator, we have to invest in the evidence base. Where will you get the evidence base? You get it from the places that are directly supporting victims. Those charities and services are not funded to the extent that they can provide research to Ofcom. They are providing support to people who are calling.

If we want that to happen, we have to construct that and make sure we are supporting those services well enough so that we can understand what they are hearing and add to the evidence base. Engineering that will require a much more assertive role from the Government.
Q55 Eleanor, did you have anything to add?

I will briefly add that when it comes to sexual exploitation, perpetrators are now using the internet—they have amazing ability with AI speed reach—to groom their victims online. Even in my time as commissioner, I have seen a huge increase in sexual exploitation facilitated through platforms. I do not think they are doing enough.

When I looked at adult service websites there were signs of trafficking in 60% of those ads. The adverts were not being taken down, there was nowhere for those women who were being exploited to report the harm, and there was no age verification on those websites. Survivors told me that children were contacting them online.

When I look at the third-party management on OnlyFans, there are clear conversations about trafficking, exploitation, violence and control taking place on those platforms. I do not think we or the platforms are doing enough. I have had good engagement with Ofcom; I work closely with them and welcome their collaboration, but the difficulty is that perpetrators are using the internet at far greater speed than we ever thought they would when we passed the Online Safety Act.

If we are trying to prevent harm and prevent individuals from being groomed, we need to be as forward-facing as the perpetrators. We need to understand how they are using tech to reach across society and to reach new groups of vulnerable girls. They tell me that they are being targeted while sitting in English class, whereas before—even five years ago—that was not what we were seeing.

It also means that the women I used to see being sexually exploited, who were far more visible to charities and safeguarding professionals, on the street or in certain areas or communities, are now being controlled online and are appearing in pop-up Airbnbs and brothels. That makes it harder for us to identify and reach them. I welcome the BIPs about online harms in the action plan, but they are not truly looking to the future enough to understand how this landscape has changed, even in one year.
Q56 Do you feel that additional legislation is needed to address the concerns that you have raised, or is current legislation sitting there and just not being acted on?

First of all, the Online Safety Act needs to be fully applied. I welcome Ofcom’s approach in focusing primarily on children to begin with, but we now need to look more broadly to protect all individuals online. We need to leave that door open for new legislation to understand where AI is being used in an incredibly harmful way to recruit and control very vulnerable victims. We need to have that conversation in policy making.

Q57 On online harms, the Public Accounts Committee was concerned that the Government, whether through legislation or Departments, are not able to have the agility to respond to the rapidity at which that is being perpetrated and is moving.

You mentioned Ofcom, but also the platforms. Given that perpetrators are likely to outwit new legislation as quickly as we can pass it, what should either Ofcom or the platforms themselves do to cut down this explosion of sexual exploitation, including of children, which you described and which is also vividly described in the recent threat risk assessment by the n ational centre for violence against women and girls and public protection ?
We will take Peter’s question now as well.

Q58 Very briefly, the Human Rights Committee recently looked at AI. A lot of these questions presuppose that there is an offender somewhere, even if they are behind a keyboard, but one of the risks with AI is that the black-box nature of the process means that harms can be generated without accountability necessarily landing with any one human. As we think about protecting ourselves from AI, what would be your priority for making sure that we build systems that are inherently safe for women? Sorry; I appreciate that I am asking for a brief response to a very big question.

I will try to be brief. Over the last year, we looked at the future and evolving threats, and one of the key things that came up was how perpetrators are using AI—whether it is to generate CSAM, or to target a huge range of individuals online by using fake ads or profiles to start conversations with them and then either grooming, controlling or blackmailing them. It is difficult for policymakers to understand how to respond to it when perpetrators are moving more quickly than was outlined in the strategy, but platforms need to take far greater accountability for this. The Online Safety Act is welcome, but ideally, you would not actually need this legislation.

Platforms know about a lot of the harm taking place. I have questioned them on why when there is a clear sign of a woman with no age verification—sometimes it is even listed that they are a teen—being sexually exploited, there is not somewhere for that to be reported. Is it okay that their take-down process seems to take an absolute age, when I think it should be immediate? In my mind, it is not.

This comes back to the whole-society approach in the strategy: we need everyone to play their part to stop violence against women and girls. If we look at the rising numbers of younger UK girls we are seeing being sexually exploited, part of that is being driven by the explosion of things happening online at the moment.

I am not saying that the strategy answers everything, but it does provide some clarity about the infrastructure that Government should be putting in place or intended a year ago to put in place. When I was looking at those particular sections before coming here today, I was thinking, “I don’t really know if these things are happening or not,” so how would I then know about the nimble reaction that is required?

I believe there needs to be much more time, attention and energy, so that it is clear for service providers that are seeing these trends—they will be the ones who spot the emerging trends—where that activity is sitting and how you would engage with it, because I feel it is not clear to most people. That would be a good first step.

A good recent example of progress is the National Centre for Violence Against Women and Girls and Public Protection , which was a commitment in the strategy. It is up and running and is going from strength to strength. It is equipping police forces with some of this information at much greater pace, and that needs to be built upon.

Where perpetrators have been learning in online spaces about how to carry out drug-facilitated sexual assaults, the national centre has been working with the National Crime Agency, and there has been much more join-up and clarity. Those who care and want to see change need to know what their vehicles are for making that change. That is a good example, but we need to see so much more of these commitments built on, and it must be clear for us how to address those.

In terms of the platforms themselves, I hope Ofcom can help make it clear to us, as users, which platforms we should feel confident in and which we should not. I hope the public will increasingly vote with their feet or their fingers.
Thank you. I refer you to the valedictory speech that Jonathan Hall made last week in this building, in which he talked about quite a lot of this, so I think we have a lot of people on our side.
We have kept you a long time because we have extra Committee members here, but we have a few final questions from Matt Bishop about information sharing with immigration services.

Q59 The VAWG strategy committed to requiring the police to seek a domestic abuse victim’s consent before sharing their information with immigration enforcement. Do you know whether that is happening? If it is, how is it working?

It is not happening, as far as I understand. It was a really celebrated notion. In shorthand, we call it the firewall—the idea that information about you would not be passed along to immigration services. It is absolutely clear: many police leaders have talked to me about this, and they would like to see it.

I have asked the Home Office about how often information is aiding any kind of immigration enforcement when it is passed along, and it is not often. All it is doing is protecting perpetrators, because it means that migrant survivors are very worried to come forward. They are told a lot of misinformation, and they obviously have huge support needs. It plays straight into the hands of the perpetrator, as you know.

The disappointment in the language of that commitment was this idea of asking for consent. Picture yourself in that situation—you can quite easily, as a former police officer. If you ask in a certain way, “Are you sure you’ve had consent?” maybe the victim will feel they have to give consent for information to be passed along. That needs clarity.

Again, we are about a year on, and I do not think we have achieved what that commitment set out to do, which is for everyone to understand how that consent would be obtained and operationalising that. It is, frankly, a great frustration for many, many people that that commitment has not been acted upon yet.
Do you have anything to add, Eleanor?
I completely agree with Nicole on this area. We have pushed in many bits of legislation and not managed to get it passed, but it is something that I think stops us identifying very vulnerable women.
Q60 My last question is, are there any other areas where immigration policy is not aligned with the VAWG strategy?

I think, unfortunately, there are. When you speak to survivors, they tell you that perpetrators who are controlling and exploiting them use immigration policy as a means to stop them coming forward. They say, “If you come forward, you’re not going to be believed. You’re going to be deported. You’re going to be held to account by the Government.” Sadly, when we have rhetoric coming from Government and policymakers that echoes that threat, I think it leads to real harm and stops us being able to identify victims who really do need our support.

That is something I hear day in, day out. We have kept you longer than even we were expecting, but I think you can see the level of interest in this area across many Committees. Certainly for the Home Affairs Committee, there is much more we want to do on this, and there are questions that we need to put to the Prime Minister and the Home Secretary in due course. Thank you once again to our witnesses. This is something that we will be working on and taking forward.
Backbench Business Committee
Representations : Backbench Debates
Tuesday 27 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 27 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Bob Blackman (Chair); Mary Glindon ; Alison Hume ; J amie Stone ; Martin Vickers .
Questions 1-3
Representations made
I : Patricia Ferguson .
Patricia Ferguson made representations.

Q1 Welcome to this meeting of the Backbench Business Committee, where we will be considering applications from colleagues for debates in the Chamber and Westminster Hall. The first application is from Patricia Ferguson for a three-hour debate in the Chamber on fixed-link connectivity in Scotland’s islands. Patricia, please present your case.

Thank you very much. I think it is fair to say that this is a very interesting subject, not to say fascinating to those of us on the Scottish Affairs Committee. It was first brought to our attention last year when we visit ed Unst to look at the spaceport at SaxaVord. We were quite surprised, I think it is fair to say, that there was such enthusiasm for the idea of fixed links, in this case tunnels, to connect some of Scotland’s islands.

The more we have looked into it , the more we have visited the islands and the more we have listened to the case, the more compelling the idea of providing more fixed links to Scotland’s islands seems to us—or at least the idea of considering them — because at the moment there are what have been described to us as intolerable limitations on the lives of people living on the islands, and on businesses too.

The ability to connect with both the mainland and other islands is very important for the islanders, but ferries have proven to be difficult in recent years. Even when the ferries are working, when things are going well, weather is a huge factor, and the distance and geography are also difficult. We think this debate request is very timely, not only because we have published our report but because there are now specific proposals for fixed links in the Shetland Islands. Just last month, Shetland secured £23 million from the Scottish Government to develop its plan for inter-island tunnels, so there is a real prospect that this major project will go ahead. It seems a timely point for the House to take stock of these developments.

Transport is devolved to the Scottish Government. We know that, so there is understandably not a lot of opportunity to debate these issues in the Commons . However, they cannot just be viewed as devolved in this context, because the ability to commute around the islands also affects our security and our industry . I t affects the culture and the nature of the people of the islands, and their ability to live the kind of life that the rest of us take for granted. It is also very important in terms of the economy.

To get to Unst, we had to travel quite some distance by minibus over a number of hours, but we also had to take three ferries. Now, if you have a doctor’s appointment or if you want to go to the cinema with your family, it need s a lot of planning if you live o n the islands.

Our Committee visited the Faroe Islands . T here are a number of tunnels connecting the islands, and they have seen a halt in depopulation. They have seen the opportunity for people to get to the main city and to services very easily. Their theory is that everyone in the Faroe Islands lives in the same city, and that no one should have a commute of more than an hour to get to anything they need.

This seems to us to be a really exciting and very interesting issue to take up. O ur report is quite a good one, if I may say so myself, and it bear s further discussion among colleagues in the Chamber. The level of support we have had for our request for a debate indicate s that there is cross-party support , too. I am very happy to answer any questions.

Q2 Thank you for proposing this debate. As a Committee, we have a rather large waiting list for the Chamber. You allude d to wanting it in a timely fashion . Would you consider taking a Westminster Hall debate to get it further up the list , or are you looking to wait for the Chamber?

My understanding is that it might not be until perhaps January or February , which would be absolutely fine . W e would prefer to have it in the Chamber , if possible, rather than in Westminster Hall , because we think it needs to be looked at quite critically by colleagues from across the House . We think we can attract more people to do that if the debate is held in the Chamber. But if it needs to be Westminster Hall, obviously we would understand.

Q3 W hat do you hope to achieve by the debate? The reason I ask is that, as you rightly point out, transport is a devolved matter. While we could have a strong debate and reach cross-party agreement , it will presumably still be the Scottish Government who have to decide what to do on this. Am I correct in that assumption?

The Committee’s feeling is that the UK Government will have to be involve d, too. The cost of a fixed link , a subsea tunnel, is very high. It is immense, so we think the UK Government would have to be involved , but we think the UK Government should want to be involved because of the impact on our security.

Consider getting to SaxaVord, where our spaceport is likely to be and where we will launch our satellites. If you think about the Government’s economic rationale for a lot of the ir work and the Prime Minister’s ambition to have opportunity in every postcode, that should not exclude the islands. The islands should be part of that agenda.

We think it is about more than just transport to or from the islands. It is also about the way of life on the islands, it is about giving people opportunity, and it is about ensuring that people can live and work on the islands.

At the moment, if you are building a house, you might have to arrange for builders to come from another part of the country, and you would certainly have to arrange for supplies to come. That might mean factoring in a three-day stay for the lorry driver. The cost of everything is so much higher for people on the islands, and we do not think that is particularly fair.

Also, if you want to give birth to a baby, you just can’t on some of the islands. You have to go to Glasgow for two weeks before the birth , and t he health board will give you £60 a night. I challenge anyone to find a hotel in Glasgow for £60 a night. You might have to have children looked after. Your partner would want to come, presumably. Life is just that bit harder, and it does not need to be like that, it seems to us.

We think the UK Government would have to be involved in some way. The model used in the Faroes was that the Faroe Islands Government had loans that were underwritten by the Danish Government. That is one model. We are not prescriptive about that, but we think it is something that bears wider debate.

Thank you very much , Patricia . Any other questions? The Clerks will be in touch with you in due course. I f you are interested in having a Westminster Hall debate on the subject, that does not prevent you from coming back and asking for a Chamber debate in the future.
Thank you. Thank you for your time.
That completes the public business of the Committee. The Committee will now go into private session to consider the application and the allocation of time.
