segs.tx: Environmental Audit Committee
Oral evidence: Prospects for UNFCCC COP31, HC 745
Monday 26 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 26 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Environmental Audit Committee m embers present: Mr Toby Perkins (Chair); Barry Gardiner; Sarah Gibson; Sojan Joseph; Dr Roz Savage; John Whitby.
Energy Security and Net Zero Committee member present: Bill Esterson.
Questions 24 - 42
Witnesses

I I : Tania Kumar, Policy Director, Energy Transition, Confederation of British Industry; Kim O’Dowd, UK Campaign Lead, Methane and Energy Transition, Environmental Investigation Agency; and Pelin Zorlu, Head of Climate and Energy, Chatham House.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Tania Kumar, Kim O’Dowd and Pelin Zorlu.

Q24 For those in the Public Gallery who joined towards the end of the last panel, you are very welcome. We are holding an Environmental Audit Committee hearing on the COP31 negotiations. We just heard from the Ambassador of the Republic of Türkiye and the Australian High Commissioner; their nations are the two host nations of COP31.

We are about to start our second panel, which will consist of a number of UK-based organisations that support us with both the international and UK context to these discussions. I will ask our three panellists to introduce themselves and the organisations they represent and briefly say where they see the COP31 negotiations as we head into them, having heard what our international visitors just said.

Thank you very much for having me. My name is Kim O’Dowd. I am a campaign lead at the Environmental Investigation Agency. I work specifically on methane from the energy sector and the energy transition. More widely, my organisation works on a range of issues, from forest and wildlife protection to oceans and plastics. In the climate team, we focus on the regulations, governance frameworks and financial mechanisms that drive mitigation, particularly for super-pollutants and the energy transition.

On where the COP31 negotiations are going, I think that we are lacking a bit of visibility on how the next COP interacts with the wide variety of other initiatives that are happening in parallel to the UNFCCC. You mentioned earlier the road map that the Brazilian Presidency led, and that is one, but there was also, for example, the conference in Santa Marta on transitioning away from fossil fuels that is being picked up; it will be held again in Tuvalu in 2027 with a pre - conference in Ireland. That has driven significant momentum on the issue of energy transition.

That is just one, and there are other initiatives—such as the global methane pledge or the global cooling pledge—that are happening, and it is not very clear how those interact. A bit more clarity on that would be interesting to hear.

Thank you for inviting me. My name is Pelin Zorlu. I am a senior research fellow and climate and energy lead at Chatham House , which is an international affairs think - tank. I am based in its e nvironment and s ociety c entre, where we work on a range of issues including climate, energy, natural resources, innovation and futures.

In answer to your question, we don’t expect any landmark decisions this year; negotiations are expected to be at a more technical level. However, there are certain benchmarks for success, and the UK can be very helpful in securing them. The first one is protecting the fundamentals. This year, we will kick off the next global stocktake, which will conclude in two years’ time. Science has been the backbone of this process. Unfortunately, recent Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change progress has stalled due to blocking from a number of countries, which means that the best available science may not feed into the next global stocktake.

The science is not ambiguous. You will have seen UNEP’s latest report on overshooting 1.5° C . This is likely to undermine the process and the IPCC as an institution, so I would fully recommend that the Australia n and Turkish COP Presidency, as well as the UK, unblock this going into the discussion. We do not want this to toxify the overall discussion, so it is really important that they work behind the scenes and unblock this issue going forward.

The other thing is upgrading and elevating the importance of adaptation and resilience going forward, as a red thread across multiple P residencies. This is too important to be treated as a secondary issue, as we are seeing more and more the impacts of climate change. Sierra Leone and the UK are now co-facilitating the adaptation agenda at COP31, so this is a really great opportunity to elevate the issue.

Third ly , electrification is a flagship initiative that the COP31 Presidency announced. We need to really position electrification as key to energy security and ensure that we do not avoid talking about transitioning away from fossil fuels. The tough discussions need to find a way of docking into the global stocktake process as well.

Finally—the Ambassador and the High Commissioner touched on this, as did your questions—we need a clear endgame. Australia and Türkiye have been working brilliantly together , but I think there are lots of questions around whether they have a clear endgame political strategy in place and who i s going to bring whom if the discussions become difficult.

As th e Ambassador and the High Commissioner alluded to , both countries have very strong regional economic security ties with different groups, and they will be really well placed to unblock issues, but we really need that transparency. Even the perception of a lack of transparency can derail discussions in these negotiations, so I would strongly encourage the UK to also support progress in these areas.

Thank you very much for having me. I am Tania Kumar, the e nergy t ransition director at the Confederation of British Industry , one of the UK's leading business groups. I cover every single sector of the economy across the UK British business community. That means not just those directly involved in delivering our energy, but all the manufacturers across our communities and those that are involved in sustainability, waste, supermarkets—you name it—looking at the entirety of our energy transition.

To your question, thinking about what we have heard from the Ambassador and the High Commissioner and what we will be looking at as a business community, the context is really important, and both ambassadors reflected on that. It has been a critical year across the globe. If we look at what has happened in the middle east and the closure of the strait of Hormuz, we have been reminded of the second global energy shock in five years.

The last one was quite localised to Europe. That has also given a new aspect to what we are looking at during this summit. It will be all-pervasive in the negotiations at the talks, most notably across the business community globally when it thinks about how it delivers the transition, but also for our households and communities regarding how we have this discussion with the public all over the globe.

The second bit reflected on the opportunities, and the green industrialisation story must be key. There are two truths to hold here, and delivering a transition is extremely difficult. We are talking about something that has not been undertaken before. There is the question of how we, as part of the negotiations, think about how and where there is room for that and what the set-up is for the UNFCCC process to engage in those topics, because it was designed for an emission-reductions process. The UNEP report is extremely startling, but it is also another moment where we have to look at the science and how we deliver against that.

The third important area, which many people have repeatedly reflected on, is the UK’s role in climate diplomacy. I also think foreign diplomacy should be included when it comes to these issues, and not just across energy, but also when we think about the CBD COP. It is a very pivotal role for us as the UK. At the end of the year we will be taking on the G20 presidency. Looking ahead to what comes out of COP, there is the question of how we tackle some of these issues. We have an incredibly important role to bring both the Global North and Global South together in those areas, not least because thereafter we also have the G7 presidency as well. It is a really pivotal moment for the UK, as the world will turn to us to help navigate what have been very controversial topics. Building that consensus and retaining it is, for us, not just a COP process. We should instead now be thinking about this as a three or four-year process that is under way.

Q25 We have already seen lots of changes in the diplomatic relations between various countries in recent months. A s you touched on, it is going to be a very important year . Pelin , what is driving climate diplomacy in 2026, including the trend towards negotiating outside the UNFC C C process?

A s you will know, in the past 15 or 20 years , climate diplomacy has evolv ed from primarily being in the domain of environmental policymaking and now heavily intersects with economic policy, energy and national security and trade and industrial policy. W e are seeing examples of that at various levels : unilateral , bilateral and plurilateral . There is the EU ’s CBAM, and South Korea recently announced a very significant green transformation package on a par with the US A’s Inflation Reduction Act. W e have also been seeing this prominently in the critical minerals discussions within the G7 , G20 and l ots of sectoral coalitions , such as the UK - led just energy transition partnerships. T here has been a lot of change in terms of what climate diplomacy means now and it very much intersects with all those aspects.

The second point is specifically on the energy sid e. A s my colleague mentioned, this is the second fossil fuel - related energy shock s ince 2022 , with Russia ’ s invasion of Ukraine and now the Iran crisis and the closure of the s trait of Hormuz. W e are again seeing energy and economic security becoming the driving forces for the clean energy transition , as countries see the deployment of renewables and the infrastructure around them— including EVs , solar PV and so on— as a way of maintaining their strategic autonomy as well as energy security.

That has been gaining momentum e ven though s outh - east Asia was not directly impacted by Russia ’ s invasion of Ukraine ; however, they were feeling the impact of the international oil and gas markets and have been building their resilience in that direction anyway. I think Pakistan avoided $12 billion in the aftermath of the Russia-Ukraine crisis in imported fossil fuel bills. That is the second trend that we are seeing.

Finally, going forward, as we overshoot 1.5 ° C, which hopefully will be temporary, climate-related risks—those related to food, water and other related infrastructure—as well as the threat from actors who may weaponise emerging vulnerabilities, will also become salient. In that regard, I really welcome the Foreign Secretary’s announcement at UNGA about mobilising funding for climate security and working in partnership with other countries.

Kim O’Dowd : More and more, we are seeing an acceptance of two-tier multilateralism. That concept has not just been invented; we have been talking about it for a long time, but it was emphasised by the last Brazil COP presidency, which talked about two tiers. There is one tier, which is the UNFCCC, and that is about consensus, signal giving and negotiation outcome. There is then a second tier that is more about the coalition of the willing, and that is focused on implementation.

In these discussions, it is very important to remember—my colleague touched on this earlier—what the UNFCCC and COP are actually meant to do, and what the Paris agreement is meant to do. It is a temperature target, nationally determined contributions and a financial accountability mechanism. However, it is not necessarily the place to discuss how we are going to transition away from fossil fuels, how we are going to mitigate specific greenhouse gases, or how we are going reduce emissions in a specific sector.

It is a positive sign that we are accepting that we might need to have other means to accelerate implementation, rather than just focusing on the UNFCCC. Initiatives such as the UK near-zero methane marketplace, which was launched at COP30, are a very positive sign to accelerate the reduction of methane emissions in the fossil fuel supply chain, as well as initiatives on cooling or, as I mentioned earlier, the Santa Marta conference. I think those are a certain novelty in the current geopolitical climate context that I think are interesting, and we should pay attention to them.
Q26 How are the positions of the EU, the UK and the major polluting countries crystallising as COP31 approaches, particularly around fossil fuels? What coalitions are evident?

Pelin Zorlu : That is a bit of a hot potato. There is a very strong rationale for the UK and the EU to work together in this space, as they have been on the same page in their directions of travel. There are interesting and really impactful projects, such as the UK’s North sea grid project, which involves building joint infrastructure and harnessing not only offshore wind potential but interconnections. There are lots of areas where there is a huge amount of co-operation.

On their relationship with other countries, what we have been saying is that energy geopolitics has very much been shaped by the US-China geopolitical rivalry, and climate action and clean energy deployment has been very much embedded within that, as the US has become the world’s largest LNG supplier and China has become the world’s largest clean energy supplier—it is very much within that.

However, that very much suggests a zero-sum game, and I think we should avoid that sort of world. It is about the role of not only developed countries but emerging middle powers, whoever you consider those to be—it is an ambiguous concept at the moment that is still evolving. Working with countries like Brazil and India, as well as China, is consequential for the economies of both the UK and the EU, and the economies of those countries. The fact that most of the emissions will come from these emerging countries will have an impact on how quickly we bend the curve and also on how long we stay above 1.5 ° C. But because the growth will come primarily from those countries, that offers a great opportunity for the UK and the EU to work with them and expand the opportunities around green industrialisation and clean energy transition.
Q27 Thank you for mentioning the dynamic between the US and China. How far does international climate finance reduction among key donors drive climate diplomacy?
Finance has been a difficult issue in the context of COP negotiations. Obviously, we have an agreement, which was quite difficult to land, but it landed with NCQG.

Personally, I always thought that we need private sector finance; public sector finance is not nearly sufficient to get us where we need to get to. It has always been about how countries can create the enabling environment and give the right policy incentives, both to drive investment domestically and to create markets for their own products where they have comparative advantages internationally.

The economics of the clean technologies make it much easier now, but obviously there is a big division between some of the developing countries’ emerging markets in terms of accessing capital. It is much more expensive for them to access capital; for them, the cost of capital is a lot higher.

In that regard, the UK’s initiative on the EMDE taskforce is really valuable, as it leverages the expertise in the City of London and works with key emerging markets to reduce barriers, or the perception of barriers, and reduce the cost of capital. I think that is how we will be able to do it. The countries will then be able to tap into their own public and private financial resources, as well as being able to attract foreign direct investment and other forms of support.

Obviously, we need to continue talking about the quantity—how much money countries need to continue committing to new financial assistance—but it is important that we move beyond the discussion about just the quantity of finance and discuss where this finance is going, and consider whether we have the right financial architecture to support countries with the different issues that they need to tackle.

Let me give an example. If you are a Global South country and want to get support to transition away from fossil fuels, you currently have so many points of access: the Green Climate Fund; the Global Environment Facility or GEF; bilateral agreements; and the private sector and so on. This is not organised in a coherent way that enables a country to go from point A to point Z. The sequencing to ensure that countries have first access to support, to get staff to work on this issue and then develop the plans, the policy and the regulatory frameworks to work on the transition, and then get support to unlock private sector finance to invest in projects, is not done at the moment. It is very important that we fix that, because it will not only accelerate mitigation but make the money that we have more efficient and cost efficient; it will considerably reduce the administrative burden.

I am not necessarily talking about creating a new fund for each issue that we need to tackle—absolutely not; there is a big fund fatigue. It is about looking at what funds we currently have and ensuring that they are connected and talking to each other, so that we give countries a credible and structured architecture.
I think this topic is not necessarily talked about enough in the spaces that we go to and it is something that the UK could also bring into the different spaces that it engages with.
I am pleased to say that we have been joined today by the Chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, Bill Esterson. Bill, you are very welcome. May I invite you to ask a question?

Q28 Chair, thank you for inviting me to join you today. This cuts across some of the work that my Committee has been doing. You probably are aware of some of the reports we have published. We are about to publish a report on international climate finance, which is very timely with COP coming up. It will be published in time for COP as well. I am reflecting on the answers to the questions about the role of the private sector in climate finance. Tania, do you think the business community’s role in climate diplomacy is about climate finance, or is it wider than that?

First and foremost, I should reflect that the UK set the precedents for increasing involvement of the private sector since COP26. That has been something that we need to draw on because that is where we had cross-party consensus. I do not want that to be missed from this Committee or the work of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee. It is increasingly important.
There are threefold areas where the business community gets involved.
Q29 Sorry to interrupt you, but are you saying that you think business should be involved in rebuilding the broken political consensus?

Absolutely, and that is exactly what we are doing. We at the CBI have done that quite proactively. The first bit where I see the role of businesses in climate finance specifically is the aspects of the green growth opportunity. CBI Economics and the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit have done work talking about those opportunities. The £108 billion that many will have heard about has contributed in the last year. We have been taking that internationally. In fact, I will speak about that with many international counterparts when I go to Antalya at the end of next week. That is the first opportunity for us.

I am not just talking about the way we have collaborated with Governments to create stable policy frameworks, such as the contracts for difference for offshore wind. I cannot tell you how many different delegations consistently talk about the value of the CFD. How has that been constructed? How did we create the LCCC? How has the LCCC expanded into other forms of technology? The regulated asset base model for Sizewell is heralded in nuclear and has built a lot of coalitions globally. The role of nuclear in energy systems has been a big focus for many countries that have not looked at that to date. That is one area.

The second bit that is incredibly important is how that finance is used to build new technologies and make the proof case for them. It is not easy to do that. Coming back to my colleague’s point, where do businesses sit outside this two-tier multilateral process? We are not in the negotiation rooms, but we are helping our negotiating teams to show what the art of the possible is on financing some of these projects. However, it has to be a whole system. Where does private capital fit into the road map? It has to allocate risk appropriately. There is not a role for the private sector all the time; you need the multilateral development banks to be involved. How do we assess that risk across various different countries? Where do you need the private sector to play a role in demonstrating that this can be an investable, bankable project?

A lot of our businesses in the UK are leading some of those coalitions. We have companies like SSE, National Grid and Octopus all at the front and helm of the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance. They will be going to COP in Antalya to talk about how we are electrifying in the UK, how we are treating blockers on grid investment and reflecting on recent announcements such as GB Grid and what the role of the private sector is.

In conclusion, we have a fundamental role, and increasingly so because of the pressures that many Governments are facing at the moment to fund these transitions. We are sitting around those tables with international policymakers alongside the UK Government to demonstrate the strength and leadership that we are able to show.

Q30 You have demonstrated a role there for business in this country , in leadership and in sharing good practice. Perhaps I can turn to you, Kim O’Dowd : w hat is the equivalent in your part of the forest, so to speak, in the environmental agencies?

We absolutely see a role for private finance. Coming back to the point I made earlier, it is very important to talk about sequencing. Private finance will not happen if we do not have a strong basis to de-risk investment, and one way of d oing so , for example, is having strong regulatory frameworks. It is very important to think about what the sequencing looks like and to accompany countries all along that sequence.

First, for example, a country probably needs grants for enabling activities—capacity building, policy development, training and so on —and th at will help it build its regulatory framework. Then the country will probably need help in accessing private sector investment. There are instruments that exist , notably the Green Climate Fund —GCF—which had the P rivate S ector F acility , whose role was to help countries access private sector finance. Ensuring that countries continue accessing th at and are aware of the various instruments that exist is extremely important. I would emphasise the need not to take the problem in the wrong order , but as a sequenced pathway.
Q31 Beyond finance and business, what is the role of environmental groups in taking climate diplomacy forward?

I hope it continues to be a very important one. I think we have expertise that we can share with the negotiators, and we need to have a continued role in the negotiations. On what we were talking about earlier, in the current geopolitical context we are seeing a shift towards more fragmentation, which is not necessarily a bad thing; it just means that there are more points of entry to interact with the negotiations. The UNFCCC continues to be one. However, we also have coalitions of the willing, for example, that often have secretariats hosted in think - tanks or NGOs, which I think is a very positive thing, because it is an easy way of tapping into the expertise of NGOs and civil society groups. We are seeing, for example, in the context of the Santa Marta conference, that they have again appointed NGOs and think - tanks as—I think the name is—“godmothers”, who are going to help build the position of the conference and give expertise on various issues, be it finance, trade and so on . T hat is a very positive outcome.

The only risk I might see, though, is that because we are increasing the points of entry to negotiations, smaller NGOs, and even certain G lobal S outh and developing countries, might have more difficulty attending some of those spaces. T hat is a risk we need to be conscious of, and we need to ensure that civil society is present in any space.

We are really grateful to our panellists for the detail we are getting, but I am conscious that we have quite a bit to get through, so could I ask panellists to be a little more succinct in their answers?
They were very good answers, I thought , Chair.
Indeed.

Q32 Following on from that, how do you respond to the priorities and approaches laid out just now by the A mbassador and the High C ommissioner? They talked about what their priorities were, and you have mentioned some of them to a certain extent. Where, if anywhere, do you think the gaps were in their approach? T hat question is to all of you.

I will be brief. One point mentioned earlier was methane. It is great to see methane on the agenda, but it is very important that we continue talking about energy sector methane as well as agriculture methane, especially in the context of the energy crisis. Methane in the energy sector is just a waste of gas: you let it leak into the atmosphere when it could be captured and reused. In fact, the International Energy Agency found that around 200 bcm of gas is wasted every year just through leaks and vents, which is equivalent to twice what Qatar exports every year. In the current context, it is key that we continue to put methane in the energy sector at the forefront of the agenda. The UK is doing that, so I would say that that is great and should continue.

The other thing is that agriculture remains a topic that is not sufficiently addressed. It is on the agenda for this year, but not in the context of mitigation. We seriously need to start talking about mitigation in the agriculture sector. I know that it is difficult—I am very aware—but that does not mean that we should not do it. It is also difficult to transition away from fossil fuels, but we are doing it, so we need to start talking about agriculture. For that, we need to create spaces to talk about agriculture in terms of policies and not just research and development, which is often the case today. I will focus on that , but I have more if you need it.

I mentioned some of the things that I think would serve as benchmarks, but there perhaps needs to be more clarity on how electrification and TAFF will somehow connect, or not connect, and if not, what the pathway is to ensure that it remains a priority.

I would also love to see a TAFF road map or plan from Türkiye and Australia, obviously, but also from the UK. I think that that is just the way forward: for all countries to come and put forward how they are going to go about this. There is also science; the importance of science in the global stocktake process needs to come up as an early issue to resolve.

The first quick point is that the difficulty with the UNFCCC process is that whoever has the Presidency often announces new initiatives. As both my colleagues reflected on, we still have the targets of trebling renewables and doubling energy efficiency. I agree with the point about electrification.

We have more and more alliances. From a business community perspective, consolidation is really important, so that it does not just become about many people signing up to lots of different initiatives, essentially. The UK business community is working with the UK Government on really identifying which alliances we are part of and where we can coalition-build and bring some of those alliances together. That includes reflecting on how Brazil progresses its Presidency and how we look ahead to Ethiopia, for example.

Secondly, adaptation and resilience continues to be the poor cousin of the UNFCCC and COP process. Globally, that has ignited us. Again, to the spaces, because we are so focused on the emissions reduction targets and 1.5°C, a new space has now been created. Because of that overshoot, what are the consequences, how do we adapt, and how do we come together to talk more about adaptation and resilience?
Q33 So that is about consolidation, in a way, rather than the exciting, new, shiny things, which is a good sign.

My next question is really aimed at Ms O’Dowd. Beyond CO 2 , we have mentioned methane and other super-pollutants. In terms of tackling these super-pollutants , are F-gases equally important, or is methane the part that you are most concerned about ?

No, that is equally important. If my colleagues heard me, they would not be happy if I said it was not. It is just that I specialise in methane, but my organisation does a lot of work on F-gases and HFCs. That is extremely important, so thank you for asking the question.

That should also be a key priority for the Presidency, especially in the context where we have just gone through the hottest year we have ever experienced, with record heat in many, many countries. The conversation around cooling is going to be big, but you cannot cool at the expense of the planet. We need to have important conversations about how we ensure that we give people access to cooling—not just AC, but through things like buildings—and also talk about the acceleration of the Montreal protocol on reducing HFCs. That needs to be an essential part of the discussions.

We would love to see the UK develop a cooling action plan. That would notably consolidate some of the work that you have done in the EAC on this topic. We should remember that it is an important part of the climate discussion, but also of the adaptation discussion.

The UK is the co-chair of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition , which is a UN programme working on super-pollutants. It has been great at leading on methane, and I really salute the work of DESNZ colleagues on this. But the UK also has to remember that the CCAC is not just about methane; it also covers F-gases and nitrous oxide. I know that we said that we do not want new initiatives, but it would be great to put it more clearly on the agenda.
This Committee shares that concern.

Q34 You have just given us some of your views on the COP31 Presidency priorities. Seeing as Ms Zorlu has already mentioned breaching 1.5 °C probably three times in the last half hour, should there be and will there be a focus at this COP on getting back to 1.5 °C ?

This is very much the framing question of the latest letter from the Presidency: how do we progress the implementation of the goals of the Paris agreement, which basically stipulates that we aim for 1.5 °C ? There are different aspects to it. On the mitigation side, it is obviously about transitioning away from fossil fuel, and it is also about electrification, finance, and adaptation and resilience. That is very much going to be the framing discussion at COP31, I imagine.
Q35 Is it accepted that we have gone past the original target?

The latest UNEP report basically said that we will be breaching 1.5 °C in the next three years, at least temporarily. That does not mean that the goals of the Paris agreement are no longer valid or that we should not pursue that. Every fraction of a degree that we avoid or reduce by has a huge impact on the planet and livelihoods.
Q36 What are the UK’s specific priorities for COP31?

I will focus on the topics that we particularly work on in my own organisation. I already mentioned methane; maintaining the leadership the UK had on methane in the energy sector is particularly important. It led the last COP declaration on methane from the fossil fuel sector and is working towards a near-zero methane marketplace. It would be great to see some announcements about any progress or any new signatories that the UK might have worked with. That would be very important.

In terms of methane and other super-pollutants, there is again a key question around finance. There is still a big lack of financial assistance for super-pollutants. At the last COP, an initiative was created called the super-pollutant country action accelerator, which is led by the Climate and Clean Air Coalition. It is a mechanism to support countries in developing plans and regulations to reduce super-pollutants, and it mirrors the approach of the Montreal protocol and the multilateral fund—one of the key reasons that the Montreal protocol was so successful was that financial mechanism. Supporting that mechanism for super-pollutants would be very important, especially as the UK is the co-chair of the CCAC. We would like to see a new financial commitment towards the accelerator.

Also on super-pollutants, the UK signed the Belém declaration on fertilisers last year, and we would like to see the UK recommit to that and explain how it is planning on implementing the declaration. Finally, something on cooling would be key because it is the only big topic that has not been broached.
Q37 Any other UK priorities?

I will add two quick ones. One is definitely electrification. The UK is leading another initiative called Electrify Now, bringing together a consortium of countries to demonstrate practically what economies and policymakers need to do to electrify an economy. That is twofold. There has been so much focus on the energy sector and power. Reflecting on the UK’s progress on its own carbon budgets, a lot of it has been delivered by the power sector, but we need to talk about the demand side to that. There is a huge piece that we need to discuss on electrification of demand .

Another topic to bring to the COP discussions is industrial decarbonisation. That is the biggest question here around the energy transition not being a deindustrialisation, which we are contending with domestically in the UK. When we head to Antalya, the Budget will have just taken place, so we will be looking at the raft of domestic measures that come out and how we can demonstrate that we are reconciling how you actually deliver these transitions practically and deliver the economic opportunities that we at the CBI have been able to identify, essentially.

The UK is held in very high regard in these negotiations and is seen as an honest broker and a coalition builder. Given the geopolitical shift in allies, that is a very good role for the UK to continue to play. The UK has led lots of initiatives: some of the acronyms that I mentioned but also Electrify Now. Prioritising which ones are the highest-impact ones and working in partnership with some of the key countries in this way is really important, while protecting the fundamentals of the process that we definitely need to maintain multilaterally.
Q38 When do you think we can expect to see a written ministerial statement outlining these priorities for the UK? It is not really a question for you, but when do you think we will see one?
I am hoping before we go to Antalya in the next week or so.
Bill Esterson has a final question to follow up there.
Q39 Kim O’Dowd, you have been asked, and have said quite a lot, about “me-thane” or “meth-ane”.
Sorry, I am French, so I do not pronounce it “me-thane”.

It is fine, as long as we all know what we are talking about. On the one hand, we have very high numbers of people who rely on burning methane: the heating industry relies on it in the UK, and that is true across the world. On the other hand, we have emissions that are uncontrolled. What is your sense of how achievable it is to put those two together while we reduce our usage of methane, given that it is very hard to see how we can move particularly quickly away from using it? How viable is biomethane? How viable is it to collect and use some of these other sources that your analysis clearly points to as being very worrying?

I am not a biomethane expert, necessarily. We have looked a little bit into it. It is a valuable option if it does not drive the production, for example, of manure. We have seen cases, notably in California, where because farmers can make money by producing biomethane, they will just expand their herd sizes to collect more manure to produce more biomethane. There has been an investigation by colleagues from Friends of the Earth USA on this. We need to put in some guardrails to ensure that we are not replacing one problem with another.

However, if we manage to produce biomethane in a sustainable way, we need to ensure that it does not leak, which is currently not looked into as much. There is more and more conversation about methanation of the energy sector, but biomethane leaks almost as much as fossil fuels. Countries have not really developed any regulations yet in terms of monitoring, reporting and verifying emissions in this sector, so that is one thing that countries could prioritise. Then, as for the fossil fuel sector, they could do leak detection, repair, and avoid venting and flaring. As we move towards this potentially valuable solution for waste and agriculture by way of reducing methane emissions, we need to ensure that it does not leak, basically. That is one important point .

If you mean gas as just the fuel that we extract from the ground, and how that fits into methane remediation, methane is the sprint and the general transition is the marathon. We need to do both hand in hand. Obviously, we want gas to be used less, but we know that it is still going to be there for a few years, so we need to urgently reduce the emissions associated with the production and consumption of that gas.

Q40 On the point about biomethane, I noticed that France is one of several countries where there are greater incentives for farmers, in particular, to collect biomethane. Is that something you would advocate more widely?

Again, it depends how it is produced. If there are guardrails, that does not mean that it is incentivising the extension of herd sizes, which is something that can happen. But in the context of the current herd sizes, then, yes, I think it is a valuable solution.
Q41 So with the right safeguards. Pelin, your organisation will have carried out some analysis on methane and these tensions. What is your take?

I have not been involved, but recently my colleagues published a paper on biofuels. That basically made the case that not all biofuels are equal. Whether they are sustainable and economical really depends on the country context.

As a side note, on the back of Hormuz we have seen some of the mandates for the mixing of biofuel with diesel being brought forward. That creates a tension between food security and energy prices. It can also lead to further degradation of primary forests, for example in south-east Asia. It is basically about being very clear about where it is good and useful—it depends on the country context—and where it should be avoided.

Q42 Can I push you a little bit beyond “it depends” for a moment? You mentioned the strait of Hormuz and the very severe energy security concerns it brings. What is Chatham House’s analysis of how viable biomethane or other biofuels might be as alternatives to improve our energy security?
That is not really my area of expertise, but I am very happy to give further evidence through my colleagues on that.
Thank you very much, Ms O’Dowd, Ms Zorlu and Ms Kumar, for the excellent evidence that you have provided. It is incredibly helpful. We will have a short break before we start the final panel.

Wednesday 21 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Bradley (The Chair) ; Lord Barber of Chittlehampton; Lord Faulkner of Worcester; Baroness Hollins; Lord Johnson of Marylebone; Lord Mohammed of Tinsley; Lord Mott; Baroness Pidgeon; Baroness Redfern; Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson; Baroness Watkins of Tavistock.
Evidence Session No. 2 Heard in Public Questions 26 – 3 7
Witnesses

Eavan Mckay, Policy and Public Affairs Manager, National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC); Jessica Ford, Policy and Research Manager, Action for Children; Nicola Smith, Senior Policy Adviser, Barnardo’s.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Eavan Mckay, Jessica Ford and Nicola Smith.

Q26 Good morning to the three of you. We have Eavan Mc k ay from NSPCC, Jessica Ford from Action for Children and Nicola Smith from Barnardo’s. Thank you very much for coming this morning and giving us your time for this second session into our inquiry into looked-after children. This is an oral session that is recorded and is livestreamed on the parliamentary website ; you will receive a transcript from today’s session for your correction if necessary.

W ould you briefly introduce yourselves more fully , in terms of your roles, the roles of the organisations you represent and your particular interest in this inquiry, which may seem self-evident ? Thank you very much. I will start with Eavan.

Hello, everyone , and thank you for having me. I am the policy and public affairs manager at the NSPCC. The NSPCC is the UK’s leading child protection charity. We provide services, programmes and practice frameworks that professionals use and deliver to prevent abuse and neglect. We also operate Childline and the NSPCC Helpline. As our name suggests, we have a major focus on prevention, so I will probably talk a lot from that perspective today. We also commission and conduct research, using that evidence from practice to inform policy and system reform. Thank you for having me.

Morning, everyone. I am the policy and research manager at Action for Children. I lead on children’s social care policy with a focus on the care system and child protection. Action for Children is a voluntary sector provider of children’s services in England and across the UK. Our services span the full spectrum of the system, from preventative early help through to care placements and support for children who are leaving care. We do not have statutory child protection roles like the NSPCC do es , but we run many edge-of-care-related services.

I am a senior policy adviser for children in and leaving care at Barnardo’s. Barnardo’s is one of the oldest children’s charities ; much like Action for Children, we are a service delivery partner in the children’s social care system and our work spans the entire care system. We offer a lot of early intervention and edge-of-care work. We are also one of the largest voluntary fostering and adoption agencies. We still operate a small number of residential care homes and we offer services for young people when they leave care. We span the whole of the children’s social care system.
Thank you very much for those introductions. We will move straight on into questioning with Baroness Shawcross -Wolfson .

Q27 Thank you so much for being here with us this morning. I want to start with a big picture question. Our committee has already heard a lot about the extensive issues in the children’s social care system and the challenges faced by children in care. We have also heard about the very poor outcomes regarding educational attainment, mental health difficulties and employment for care-experienced children.

Could you tell us what you think the hallmarks of a good social care system for children in care would look like? What should the system be targeting? What are the benchmarks? What does good look like for this cohort of children?

The simple way of viewing this is that these are children of the state: the state becomes their parent and , as their parent , we should want the very best for them. We should have the same aspirations and ideas for these children as parents up and down the country have for their own children.

In terms of how that looks, we really need to address the record numbers of children in the care system. While some children will always need to enter children’s social care and that will always be important, we also need to think that perhaps some children are entering the system because we are not doing enough to support their families earlier on. Can we do more to make sure that all children who can safely stay with their birth families do stay with them? A good social care system would definitely do that.

A s I said, w hen it comes to the children who enter the care system , we are trying to do the same for them as any parent would do for their own children. In that sense, we need to make sure that they are in the right homes, with the right love, with the right care, for the right amount of time and with the right amount of support and opportunities that we would expect . This ensures they are able to participate and achieve in education at similar rates to children who are not in the care system.

W hen those children become young people and move into adulthood, we must support them at that stage, just as many parents do. When their children get to 18 and they go off to university, their parents are on the end of the phone to support them ; w e need to do the same for children in the care system. We need to give them that support and what they need to move into adulthood, so that they do not face higher rates of homelessness, higher rates of entry into the criminal justice system or higher rates of suicide and things like that. That is the overall vision as I see it.

I reall y agree with what Nicola said. Broadly speaking, we are on the right track with the reform programme. The Families First model spans the entire spectrum of the system. Obviously, we are looking at providing better support for children to remain safely within their families and whole family support.

From there we move into the kinship space for children who are unable to remain with their families, where there is much better support for kinship arrangements and crucially that they are sustainable over time. We must ensure kinship carers have what they need, so they are not doing this in the face of total adversity because they are committed to caring for the child, but that it actually works for the whole family in that situation.

For children who need to go into care, the Families First model prioritises fostering for the majority of children. However, crucially—this is a really key message that I want to land today—there must be recognition within that that fostering cannot work for all children. It works for the majority but not all. For those children who need to go into residential care, we need to do a lot more thinking about what that care looks like. These are largely children with high and complex needs who need a lot of therapeutic input. For me, that part of the system needs to be much more squarely focused on therapeutic care and outcomes.

Equally, that Families First model needs to go beyond that, so we are thinking about how children can return home. We need a lot more post-removal support for families. Where children go into care and the prospect is that they will remain there for some time, we cannot say, “Okay, job done ; they ’ ve gone into care . W e know they ’ re safe and we know they ’ re getting the support they need” . There needs to be continuity of work with the family. This would ensure that , for cases where reunification is appropriate, it becomes possible because the work has been done with the family. Eavan and I work on reunification policy a lot together and I am sure she will say more about that this morning.

As I said, we are on the right track , broadly speaking . It is just that we are at the very start of this process and we are essentially unpicking large-scale system dysfunction. The system has been designed for younger children and for harms within the home. However, I am sure the committee has heard from the DfE that we now have an ageing cohort within care. We are looking at adolescence a lot now, and in that space we are talking about extra-familial harms — harms outside the home. How do we get good outcomes for those children in a system that was not really designed for them? We need far more specialist expertise in adolescence, alongside professionals who are on the front foot of emerging teenage trends.

Another crucial thing for me —this comes back to what Nicola was saying — is that we need to look much more holistically at outcomes , p articularly for children in care . W e need to look not just at their experience of care, which is largely where Ofsted’s focus is, but at what their life looks like outside of that. What does it look like at school or in relationships with their existing community? We then build up a picture that allows us to look at the child’s journey over time, rather than just looking at a snapshot in time, which is what the current system and data in it largely do. We need to look at the trajectory: where have they moved on to from a starting point? We are quite good at doing this in the education space but are not there yet with children’s social care. Moving away from that snapshot in time is a key point.

An ideal system, achieving better outcomes , would be much better at capturing subjective experiences, and this is really hard to do well. I know that Ofsted and the DfE are trying, but in a lot of cases it is a bit of an add-on. It is a bit of, “Oh, let ’ s go and talk to some children and some parents and carers” , and then you get into a whole issue around inclusivity, representativeness, and the accessibility of those opportunities to engage with those children and families and carers , p articularly where there are complex needs or there are communication needs ; or you may have a child in an out-of-area placement where the local authority is being inspected and actually that child is now out of that local authority area. It needs to be a very focused effort where what we refer to in the sector as participation is recognised a specialist skill and is not just an add-on. It is not just about having a board of children and young people who meet quarterly. We need to be a bit more upfront about how tricky it can be to obtain that qualitative, child-centred data. In a system at the start of immense reform, that data can quite easily get left behind because it is very hard to do well, and in all honesty we struggle with it in the sector as well.

I agree with everything that has been said so far. A system that works well and is delivering good outcomes for children is going to be one that is focused on prevention at every stage of the child’s journey. Jess set some of that out just now. At the moment, we are in the process of delivering wide-scale children’s social care reform, and there is a lot of hope and optimism in terms of the ideas behind that reform of building a more preventative system.

Earlier this year our charities , together with the Children’s Society and the NCB , jointly release d the Children’s Services Funding Alliance report, which we have done for the past —I cannot even remember how many years now .
Yes, I think it has been five years.

That report showcased what we have seen over previous years : c urrently 80% of children’s social care funding is being spent on late-stage intervention and crisis support. There has been around a 40% reduction in early support funding for those early preventative services over a 10-year period. That is really concerning.

We have these reforms that are really focused on this Families First model that is investing in preventative earlier support. However, it is going to take time for those to filter through the system for us to actually see the impact of those reforms and for that to impact the number of children who are reaching crisis point. We need to be realistic about how long that will take and talk about the level of investment required so we can really see those changes come through into the system.

I would also say that neglect is a really illustrative example of where the system does not work in a preventative way and is not targeting harm early enough. In 2024 , we produced research where we spoke to local authorities about neglect and multi-agency professionals, including social workers, told us that often they feel very confident in spotting the signs of neglect but , because of the way the system is structured , often those incidents do not reach that threshold of intervention. Essentially, they are told that they need to wait for that harm to escalate before support can be put in place. That is really wrong for children and families because we are allowing them to stay in harmful situations for a protracted period of time. It is also really awful for the system , because we are allowing families to get to a crisis point that requires late r- stage intervention, skew ing the funding and creat ing awful situations for those children and families. That is a really good example of where there should be more focus: the current reform programme does not have a specific focus on particular harms, such as neglect, or how it is going to tackle that through greater investment and greater workforce upskilling.

One of the things we have talked about is looking at the definition of neglect. At the moment, the definition stipulates that neglect needs to be assessed as persistent. That is really difficult for a practitioner to observe , because it is often a cumulative harm ; there is a kind of drip-drip effect in terms of the harm that is building for that child. The definition is wrong to say that support cannot be given until it reaches that point of persistence because we are losing opportunities for early support to be in place .

Jess also mentioned other areas that I would absolutely echo. The preventative model and this idea of working with families in a holistic way is really honing the belief that I think we all have that , wherever possible , children should stay with their families if the support can be in place to allow that to happen safely . Those principles really need to be applied at every single point in the system. There is a lot of focus on how we can prevent children entering care, and that is absolutely right but , as Jess mentioned, what can we do to say when a child could safely return home ? H ow can we make sure that is possible?

At the moment, when children return home—this quite often happens in an unplanned way, or even if they are supported to return home in a planned way—local authorities are telling us that they struggle to provide and sustain long term support. We produced joint research with Action for Children in 2024 showing that local authorities want to provide more support to families before and after a child returns home , but they simply do not have the resources to do so.

This is a real problem because essentially what is happening is that children and families reach this cliff edge where they return home, the support is then cut off and of course the problems that resulted in them going into care in the first place could well resurface . T hat return home then breaks down and they return to care. We know that that is happening from the data we have: return - to - care rates are really high and that is worrying.

There is also a really good economic case for the Government to pay more attention to this. We commissioned P rofessor Lisa Holmes to do some research on this issue. We know that the Government are spending around £300 million per year —I will make sure I get the exact figure—on return homes that break down. We also know that , if they were to invest in longer - term support for reunification, that would cost about £67 million. The difference is really stark. That preventative approach needs to be looked at throughout the whole system.

Thank you so much . T hose were incredibly rich answers and I know my colleagues are very keen we start digging in . W e have some great material here about what good looks like , but I want to come back to you on one point , Jessica: it sounded like as we do not necessarily have a very clear idea of what good looks like for children with very complex needs. Is that fair?

Yes, that is fair. Part of the issue is that we do not always really know what we mean when we talk about complex needs. For me, there are three categories. First, complex needs that are inherent in the child are things to do with health and learning needs. Secondly, complex risks are about harms within the child’s direct environment, whether that is a harm to them or by them. Thirdly, children in complex situations is about their environment and structural issues, such as poor-quality housing, pressures that the family are facing, poverty and all those kinds of things. Those definitions need unpicking a little, but key to that , once you have understood those definitions, is to apply them to the cohort of children who we have in care.

We talk about how care entries have stabilised but , when you look below that data , we know that they have dropped significantly for under - nines and particularly under - fives, whereas the adolescent cohort has increased, particularly at 16 - plus. You have to be careful with the data because there are significant kinds of influencing factors —for example, unaccompanied asylum - seeking children are included within the care cohort. However, we know that a lot of this adolescent rise is about extra - familial harms . Over time , we have become much better at identifying those harms, but the care system’s service response to them is not good enough yet.

There is a really critical point to make here about the current drive towards fostering. We wholly support it ; it is absolutely the right thing to do and , as a provider of fostering places, we will be part of that attempt to grow places and diversify the foster carer market. However, we have to recognise that , for a lot of that cohort, the foster sector is probably not going to able to meet that sort of need. This is why I am keen for the committee to take away a key point around the importance of looking at children’s homes and not minimising the role that they play within that fostering debate , p articularly where we are talking about complex needs.

Whether we are talking about complex needs or complex risks, where there are high needs—they are not adolescents and it is due to neurodiversity, autism, health needs, all those sorts of things that we are all very familiar with—we must recognise that the children’s home sector has a key role to play. It will always have a key role to play, but there is a lot of discussion around having a therapeutic sector . M y sense is that there are a lot of providers that are not actually delivering genuinely therapeutic care and that is really critical in this complex needs space. W hat needs to go before that is really understanding the cohort and understanding what we are all talking about when we say complex needs.

Q28 I want to come back to the general description Jessica Ford made of the system, when you said “ l arge-scale system dysfunction” . Could you help us understand whether there was there a particular policy change that contributed to this concerning state of affairs arising or whether it was just a general drift over time? Have there been any one or two specific policy changes that have inadvertently worsened the state of the system?

I have not thought about that before ; t hat is a really interesting question. I believe that there has been drift over time. We also have to be a bit careful about what we mean by dysfunction as well. I know there is a lot of media interest and public discourse around deprivation of liberty orders , the rise in the use of unregistered homes , high costs and all of that. Sometimes that type of conversation masks the reality of what is going on in the system and particularly on this high costs point. As I was previously implying, the care requirements for a lot of the children who are in the cohort now will have high costs. That is what the requirement is and we need to make the distinction between what is a justified high cost and what is not. In order to do that, we need better data and I know that the DfE is working on that. It is wanting to develop a dashboard where you are able to do like-for-like comparisons across different placement types. T he dysfunction has certainly emerged over time.

In the care system, the market has been left to do what it wants. I do not think there is enough national oversight of what the market looks like, such as the inherent risks in it . The ability to shape the market as you would want for the current cohort of children just has not existed and we are now doing that very late. The market reforms that have been proposed are very comprehensive and they will get us to a better place, but obviously that does not do anything for the children currently in the system.

In your remarks, your description of the dynamics within the age groups of the children in care was interesting. I have not seen that in the briefing material that we have had so far — that the younger group populations are stable or falling, and adolescent children are increasing as a proportion of the overall mix. You also said that the percentage of unaccompanied asylum-seeking children was a growing and important part of that story. Could you help us understand the dynamics of what is going on in the older population and the extent to which unaccompanied asylum-seeking children are a part of it?

Obviously you get fluctuations over time of unaccompanied asylum-seeking children entering the care cohort, and that tends largely to affect the adolescent cohort. We have perhaps in the past made some assumptions about the extent to which that is driving those increases in the older cohort and given less focus to the non-UASC cohort and the extra-familial harms that are having am impact there. Certainly when we do our Children’s Services Funding Alliance report , there will always be a line in there as a caveat that UASC are included within the data. It can tend to affect the proportion of what type of care is being used so , over time, how unaccompanied asylum-seeking children are coming into the system will then affect the split across the different care types.
Could you just give us a sense of the proportions? I am not sure I have a grip on that.
Some 9% of children in the care system are currently unaccompanied asylum-seeking children.
How has that changed over time?

In terms of the percentage, I am not completely sure. I can say that, if you look at the increase of children in care over the last 10 years, the number who are unaccompanied asylum seekers is comparatively small. There are definitely bigger issues at play. If you look only over the last one or two years, a lot of the increase in children in care came from the unaccompanied asylum-seeking children.
We can follow up with the committee on the data , if that is helpful .
I was going to ask you to do that, please.

Q29 I have a question on s ocial worker instability. I see that 24% of young people experience three or more different social workers in one year. Do we have difficulties in recruitment in certain areas ? I t just seems quite a lot for a child to have three social workers in a year .

There are definitely difficulties in recruitment and retention; that is absolutely agreed. I would separate it into a couple of different issues within the context of the current reform programme at the moment. For example, we are really supportive of the new family help model that is trying to address the fact that we need fewer assessments and fewer handovers of care. There needs to be less unnecessary thresholds that determine who is working with a family and what type of support they receive. We strongly support the idea of having a more streamlined system , one of the effects of which could be having fewer social workers or fewer workers who work with a family , so that they have more consistency. That is really helpful.

I will let others talk about retention issues, but one thing that we have thought about in relation to that change is that we know that we need prevention across the whole system, as I talked about at the beginning. Actually in some local areas we have spoken to there are real issues around skills and expertise. For example, previously, early targeted help and early help workers might have been delivered through non-social workers. That new model now—the Government have just consulted on this—will mean that it will all be delivered through S ection 17 ; this should mean that there is social work oversight but essentially there could be non-social workers holding those cases.

We have heard from local authorities that that could place additional pressures on those workers due to a lack of confidence or a lack of skills and they are worried that that could potentially hamper retention as well. That definitely should not be happening ; t hat is not the ideal system for a child or for a family. We want consistency of care. We want it to be relationship-based and trauma-informed. We know from the evidence that , actually , it is far more effective when they have consistency of workers—consistency of relationships—who can really get to know the child’s lived experience and all the pressures on a family. That new model is not what we want.
No, b ecause a child would feel more detached would they not? You will not be able to build relationships and build their confidence if this is what happen s in certain areas.

I am not sure if the DfE mentioned to you that there is an enduring relationships strategy now, which is all premised on this idea that we need to get better at recognising the importance of continuous trusted relationships. That strategy is 0 more focused on children’s relationships with friends, family and members of their existing community. The principle obviously applies across the system ; h owever, the ability to deliver that is very difficult in the face of workforce issues not only because it is the workforce that facilitate that process of finding those relationships — maintaining them and nurturing them —but because those relationships are also directly with the workforce. The issues with social workers around recruitment and retention are replicated across the system.

In local authorities, alongside the social work teams, you also have leaving care teams. There are figures within those teams called personal advisers who work with care leavers in that transition out of care. That role is very variable across different areas, and the case load is very variable. Some of the capabilities around really understanding all the different challenges and risks around that transition to independence and leaving care are not always fully understood. I am not sure that the expertise is necessarily always there across all those life domains. That is how they are referred to. You are looking at health and well-being, relationships, social security, finances, housing and all of that. We need to have a system where those teams and personal advisers really know what those challenges are and what support is available locally, regionally and nationally for those young people to tap into. A s with social work, what meaningful work can you really do when you have a high case load?

I think we are going to get on to a conversation about residential care, but I would say within this context that the residential care workforce also needs a lot of attention. The DfE ha s recently commissioned a residential workforce review that is looking across training, CPD, qualifications et cetera, and I am quite hopeful that is going to support this. Hopefully we can get more into that in the later questions.

Q30 Indeed, and that is going to be the area I am going to ask you about. Thank you very much for coming to see us this morning. Two of you have experience working for organisations that run residential care homes. Can you tell us a little your experience ? H ow extensive is your coverage? How much more would you like to do? Why is it so much more expensive to put children into residential care than to have them in foster homes , and numbers are going in the other direction ? Jessica, you said that you strongly favoured fostering but the numbers are coming down . I would like to get a sense of why you think that is.

In a market where you do not have enough foster placements , a lot of those placements ultimately end up being inappropriate to the child matched to them. You hear a lot about instability in placement, placement moves and out - of - area moves. When you see children eventually going into children’s homes, they have bounced through several foster placements. To be honest, a lot of the time, those placements were probably never likely to work because they were not adequately matched , w hether that is due to the carer’s skills and ability to meet the needs, or whether actually maybe it was not the child’s preference to go into a foster placement in the first place . W e hear about that. When you add that together with rising complex needs, you start to see many more children going into children’s homes.

Our view as a voluntary sector provider is that we definitely need a much more mixed market in the residential space , if we are going to adequately meet needs and if we are going to do very careful matching of the child to the home not only in what the home can offer but in matching to the children who are already in the home and making sure that all those peer groups are going to work. The voluntary sector—I am sure Nicola will tell you about this as well—is doing a lot of this specialist provision and we need to properly recognise the role that the voluntary sector is playing in that space.

All the work that the Government are doing around the market needs to really recognise that when we talk about a diversified market, a mixed market and reducing private sector dominance. We need to really think about what we need to do to unblock voluntary sector growth so that we can play a bigger role in this. I have mentioned previously that, in our view at Action for Children, we need to really understand what we mean by therapeutic care. We need to make sure that residential homes are genuinely offering that, ensuring that there is an evidence-based psychologically informed practice model understood by the workforce in practical terms. Everyone who is in the home needs to know what they are driving at.
How many homes do you have?
We have a residential growth programme at the moment, so we are in the process of planning and registration. I think currently it is around 15, but I can confirm that. We are across the UK as well.
It would be helpful to have a similar figure from Barnardo’s too, please.

I believe it is about 10 across the market, but I can also check that figure. There is definitely a lot that Jessica said that I would agree with. Going back to Lord Johnson’s question about how we ended up here, and this sense of market drift that has happened, it feels very much like the residential care market was ignored for a certain amount of time and that there was not a lot of focus on it.

We are seeing more and more older children entering care, more and more children with complex needs entering care, and at the same time we are seeing a reduction in foster carers. We have lost just over 7,000 foster carers from the foster care market in the last four years. This is resulting in much greater pressure on residential care homes to be able to take children often , as Jessica said , because foster placements have broken down.

We also know from research Ofsted did a couple of years ago, where it looked at children’s care plans, that only 50% of children in residential care had residential care on their care plan. One - third of them had fostering on their care plan. Clearly the residential care market is taking some children . P art of your question was why there is growth in residential care; it is because we have not had those foster carers coming through the system. We have had a reduction in foster carers and an increase in children entering care, and that has put pressure on residential care.
What do you think the role of the regional care co - operatives is going to be?

The role of the regional care co - operatives has the potential as a system to help improve some local authority practice in commissioning services. At the moment, every local authority does it on their own. When it comes down to things that you need to do, such as sufficiency planning, working out how many foster carers you need and what types of foster carers, you are doing it on an individual basis. If you put everybody together, you are going to be able to grow those skills and understanding. You are also going to be able to commission at a much bigger level. This should hopefully mean that , if you are a local authority that needs only one or two residential placements, by placing with other local authorities you can block commission rather than spot purchasing, and spot purchasing at a relatively last minute. It has potential.

However, I have some nervousness around regional care co - operatives. One of the things that might happen is, once you start commissioning at a regional level, you are going to encourage people who can provide at a regional level and those are the bigger providers. We know that there are some very small providers out there currently that might operate in only one town or one city. They do a very good job but they are very small and they could end up pushed out in a regional commissioning market, which could result in fewer providers rather than more. We are a bit concerned about that point.

The other point I am concerned about takes very much from our experience of when they did a regionalisation programme in adoption. This is the idea that we could split the care system. I know we have talked a lot on this panel this morning about the importance of prevention and things such as reunification. However, under regional care co - operatives, those co - operatives are going to take the care bit, the fostering bit and the residential care bit , b ut family help, family support, advocacy and independent visitors are all going to stay with the local authority. In that situation, are we going to end up splitting the care system a little more and preventing a system that could look like a continual journey for a child who, for instance, enters care, but where reunification with some family support is on the agenda? Could we end up splitting all that because different people are doing different things in different places and they are not talking to each other?

It is possible that we could get round those issues with the regional care co - operative programme, but it will need a careful rollout. We need to be learning from the pilots and really investigating what is going on there. It cannot be seen as a panacea, and there are some concerns around it.

I encourage the committee not to look at residential care in isolation. When we look at this, we need to appreciate that the pressures on the residential care market are influenced by these wider pressures on children’s social care in general. Yes, we need to look at market reform, and this is all really important—Nicola and Jess are speaking to that—but we need to continually assess that support up stream. We need to ask whether families are receiving that support before needs escalate , because the placement pressures are not just a market issue but a reflection of the wider pressures on the system.

Nicola’s point about them sitting in different places is important because the legal status of a child—whether they are in care, or in pre-proceedings on the edge of care—should not determine the amount of support a family receive to enable the possibility of them either staying at home or returning home. Too often, we think about children as being either in care or out of care, when the reality is that families’ needs do not disappear because of that child’s legal status. If we think about it in that way, it is really dangerous from a child protection point of view.

The recent awful case of the death of baby Victoria Marten showed that. Previous children had been taken into care ; Victoria was going to be taken into care and the presumption was then that the risk was removed. However, risk is not removed because a child is taken into care. For example, that child may return home or, as in the case of Victoria, her previous siblings had been taken into care but she was an unborn child and the risk remained there. Working with families in the longer term and having a commitment and understanding that in many instances it is right to work with families in the longer term, not to close cases early and not to stop that support when a child enters the care system, is the right way to go.

Going back to reunification, I would be happy to find the case studies and submit those to the committee . W e really saw through the research the NSPCC and Action for Children did together , where local authorities — Coventry was a good example — really committed to investing in this idea that they would work with a family for as long as was necessary and that they would not close cases , that that was the right thing to do , The level of support needs might drop down potentially and it might become less intrusive but , if those relationships were good, if that support was collaborative and if that family had a good relationship, it was really important to keep that support going to allow the possibility of return homes and to secure the likelihood of those return homes being stable. It is important for us to not have this clear distinction between in care and out of care because that is not the child’s experience.

Q31 I just wanted to ask quickly—to really try to understand this residential market— whether you have any data on how many homes there are in the charity-run, not-for-profit, local authority and privately run sectors? We have seen a lot about the privately run sector in the news. Over 20 to 30 years the trend was for local authorities to either pass their home to others to manage or close them because they had so many children coming into foster care. The shift in the cohort you have described to us would suggest they need those homes now and of course they are not there; hence the private sector set in. Is there any data available?

I cannot give you numbers , but I can give you percentages. Some 80% of the residential care market—as you might call it—is now run by the private sector. Something that we have not included that I would like to emphasise is that many private homes are very good. They run very good provision for children and meet their needs , but the growth of the private sector has also resulted in a real geographical problem with residential care. We now have four times as many children’s homes in the north-west as in London. There are not more children in care in the north-west; it means that children end up being cared for very far from home, which is one way that we do not meet their needs.

One reason is that we have become so reliant on the private sector, which buys homes where property is cheap.
