That is why it has bought a lot of property in the north-west but that is not necessarily where the children need the homes. I very much agree with Jess that we need to diversify the market. We need to bring back local authority and voluntary sector provision to ensure—going back to the very first question— that we have the homes that children need where they need them , so that we do not end up with a lot of homes in the north-west and not very many in London.
Did you say that 80% of children are in private homes?
No , I said that the private sector runs 80% of the residential care market.
When you say the market , do you mean spaces for children or local authority spending decisions? They are slightly different.
I mean the actual residential care homes themselves ; 80% of all our residential care homes are run by the private sector .
You may not have this but , if you have , it would be very interesting to see: is there a level of analysis under that in terms of spaces for children —not just homes but their sizes?
Ofsted does this annually.
How about spending? It would be interesting to see if there was a disproportionate number of children versus spend.
I am not sure whether spending data exists .
That may have been included in the CMA work , but it would have been a one-off.
We can pick that up.
Can we look at that? If you have more information , please send it in.

Q32 I am very interested in this housing issue. We have Section 108 on new housing developments and we usually look for a school or health provision , but I do not think we have routinely looked at whether we should ensure that Section 108 is used for a children’s home as well. As we are about to build several new towns and some big developments , would that be useful?
I am going to put my cards on the table and say that my understanding of housing legislation is not great.

If Barnardo’s or NSPCC, for example, wanted to deliver more care homes, and if we could take this away as a committee , would it be helpful if they were significantly cheaper for you to go into in expensive areas? I hear exactly what you have said.

We are going to come on to talk about fostering but we need a world that includes the housing element, which has often been missing from this conversation. For instance , in fostering, if all you build is a lot of one-bedroom flats , you are not going to have a lot of people with a spare room. I do not know exactly how to do that because I do not know housing , but I would like a situation where the housing and planning positions of local authorities took into account, for instance, building homes that are big enough such that people could have a spare room and that we do build residential care homes.
That would be really helpful because it is something we really can take away.
Can we move on to the next section? I am not trying to shut you down , but I am sure you will get an opportunity to add to another question.

Q33 I have learned a lot in the last half hour or so; this is really impressive. I want to ask about one particular bit of the market that we heard about from the DfE last week that is clearly an issue: the use of unregistered children’s homes. What extra risks does this regular, routine use of unregistered children’s homes pose to the children and society?

What the risks boil down to is the issues about the safety and suitability of the property itself , for the child. That equally applies to the staff around safety, vetting and all that sort of thing. The risk of harm and exploitation increases because these places are flying under the radar and the staff are not necessarily skilled to identify or manage that risk.

Just to reference a previous discussion , it is not just about being able to get a children’s home in a local authority where you know there are children who need children’s homes; it is about what goes around the placement and what integrated support is available across multi-agency partners. There is isolation in both a service and social sense. Crucially—I know I keep coming back to this point on residential care—there is a lack of meaningful therapeutic input.

On unregistered, the current approach is a bit carrot and stick. I am not sure if you are aware of the Ofsted proposed reforms to ILACS and SCCIF, the inspection frameworks. They are proposing what they are calling a limiting criterion , where local authorities will not be able to get above a certain judgment if they are seen to be using unregistered provision. While we support that really focused approach , there are risks around unintended consequences. You could end up in a situation where you have local authorities that are actually being very careful about their use of unregistered provision but a child may go into a registered placement that is actually far less able to meet the needs than the unregistered provision. The unregistered placement may be a well-known, trusted provider currently going through a registration process. It is a very nuanced issue and I am conscious that the media interest in it does not always fully represent that.

That limiting criterion approach needs to be very careful. You need to be looking at the quality of oversight the local authority has and the extent to which it is proactively addressing its use. It needs to be going to these unregistered providers and making sure they are getting registered or replacing that provision entirely. That oversight of the use of it is very different in different local authorities.

I can imagine at least two categories of unregistered homes. One is an unregistered home getting children funded through it and the other is on track to registration fairly soon but might be a provider that is already providing registered care homes. You would probably—at least I would—have more faith in the latter than the former. My understanding from the conversation that we had with the DfE is that , technically , an unregistered home is illegal. What should we do about that?

We have come to the view in Action for Children that there needs to be a temporary registration system for situations that I am describing , where you are in the planning process and on the map with Ofsted , which understands who the provider is and the quality that we are talking about. It is just a case of opening a new setting ; the type of support that is going to be provided in the setting is very similar to the existing footprint and all that sort of thing. There is such a gulf between that and a setting that has just popped up out of nowhere , with no track record. It is unhelpful to talk about unregistered provision without making those distinctions.

It is very important , because obviously Barnardo’s has been providing homes for 100 years , but that is a different thing from a fly-by-night, suddenly existing children’s home taking state funding. Where the state is funding children, Ofsted should presumably be inspecting that home.

Yes , and Ofsted is doing work to get a better handle on where unregistered is springing up. There is definitely no want of ambition or enthusiasm to address that. My understanding is that it is a capacity problem.

I was going to ask if that is essentially a capacity problem because it has been recognised for some time. You may not know but what is being done about that capacity problem to speed up the process of registration?
Do you mean specifically on unregistered or generally speaking?
On unregistered.

There is certainly work under way to look at registration as a whole. There is a big backlog on registration, whether it is on trying to tackle unregistered settings or not . There is a prioritisation process where , if you are funded to open a setting through the capital investment programme or are opening in a geographical area of shortage , you are fast-tracked. I would argue—possibly Nicola as well—that there should also be a fast-track for voluntary sector provision where you are a trusted provider.
Yes.

There are a few other measures that could be considered on this point. We have an issue where it would help a lot if we were able to transfer registered managers between settings within our own footprint. Currently you have to go back through the whole registration process for that registered manager to move to a new setting. Things like that could be quite easily picked up. As I said , I do not think Ofsted is unaware of these issues and is not tackling them; it is a capacity issue around churning through these registration processes.

I can see that that potentially is a soluble problem. We could do away with the unregistered category , because we would have that temporary registration setting. Where there was already an organisation such as yours with a track record , you could fast-track , as you could in certain other circumstances. You might think of the few that are left, "Well, do we really want those?"

It goes back to everything that we have just talked about —having enough places and residential care . W e will get on to fostering. Look at the number of children who were subject to deprivation of liberty orders and the number who ended up in unregistered. The Children’s Commissioner did research on this and found young people living in caravan parks, holiday homes and things like that.

There is certainly a part of the unregistered market that is being used at present simply because there is nowhere else for that child to go , and we need to solve that problem. There is definitely an issue with unregistered provision that is on the road to registration , but there is certainly provision being used at present—small amounts , but no amount is right—where children are being placed in provision that they simply should not be in .

When we talk about the backlog and the time it takes for registration , I do not have a sense of whether we are talking about months or years here. From your experience, if you were opening a new home how long would it take you to get registration through from start to finish?

We find it is really variable across different local areas. Registration can happen within 12 weeks if everything is in place, all the paperwork is sorted, you have a registered manager, workforce and all your DBS stuff sorted and there are no planning issues to resolve. Planning issues can hold things up for any amount of time really.
When you say planning do you mean the building planning process?
Yes. It sits with the local authority. You often have to go through a process of changing the use of the property.
Then it is not an Ofsted capacity issue; it is a planning department capacity issue, so it is the two together.
Yes. Ofsted would tell you that there are frequently planning issues that are holding up registration processes.

Q34 Could I ask what your assessment of the DfE ’ s plans for foster care is? On the face of it they are very exciting. In particular I am interested in kinship foster care, which our previous evidence has suggested is not funded properly if you really want that stability.

I would be incredibly positive. I have worked at Barnardo ’ s for a very long time and for pretty much all that time I have been calling for a national foster care campaign. Last week the Government actually launched a national foster care campaign. There is a lot in this strategy to be very positive about.

As I mentioned at the start, Barnardo ’ s is a foster care agency that recruits foster carers. We know that within society there remain a lot of myths about who can be a foster carer; for example , that you have to be married and own your own home. As one voluntary agency trying to dispel these myths we do the best we can. Is it not nice to get the whole engine of government behind a national conversation about what foster care is ? F oster care changes; it is not the same. You do not have to be a foster carer full time; you can do short break care.

At Barnardo ’ s we offer really quite unusual foster care placements. We do remand foster care for young people who would otherwise enter the criminal justice system, for example. We do not think a national conversation has happened in this way before so it is very positive.

I am very pleased with other ways that the Minister has really started to listen to some things foster carers have been telling us for years, particularly around what it is like to be a foster carer in the system. He is looking at things such as the concept of delegated authority—a posh term for being able to sign the form so that your child can go on a school trip—to make that the default and make it a lot easier to create a family environment. We are saying to foster carers, "You ’ re really key; you ’ re part of the team around the child and deserve to be in the room”. Too often they have been excluded in the past. This is all really good stuff.

Where could it perhaps go a little better? This comes back to the previous question around housing. Housing and foster care is definitely an issue that we know happens. When it comes down to why we—as Barnardo ’ s—struggle to get foster carers, frequently it is because adult children are staying at home longer; the Covid pandemic and people working from home mean spare rooms are often used as offices nowadays and people generally are struggling with the housing market.

I know the Education Committee did its inquiries and talked about whether we could join up housing so that we do not just build one-bedroom flats , because that is not going to give us a spare room. It feels like housing is a bit missing from the foster care strategy; there is not a lot on it.

The other element that we would really like to look at is that it is great to get 10,000 foster carers in but we have to keep them there and make sure that retention is as important as recruitment. There are some things that we could do on the central government level just to really say as a country how important we think foster carers are. For example, we could give foster carers a national exemption to council tax to show that we think foster carers are really important.

That is a great example. I have spoken to foster carers who say, “Nobody understands what it is like for our finances when a child we have worked with really well is either going back home or leaving us because they are perhaps going to higher education and then we have no income for three months”. You cannot guarantee the right child next week; I fully understand that but is there something about continuity of income for a period? I am not talking about for ever.

There is certainly something about allowances generally and looking at the whole system of allowances. There is significant local authority variation in the whole system of allowances, which makes it very difficult to be able to say what the system is. Certainly as a voluntary sector organisation that provides foster carers on behalf of local authorities there is significant variation in the whole allowance system that could be given a little more attention in terms of that.
I am aware of time. Does anybody else want to say anything and pick up the kinship?

Can I add something? I will pass to Jess as well. I will not be long because I know there will probably be more to say on the recruitment and retention. I would just really urge the committee and Government to look at the fact that we also really welcome this recognition of the vital role of kinship carers and the investment and focus on getting more foster carers. We would really want them to apply the same principles to ensuring there is adequate support for children returning home to their families as well.

We are looking at kinship care because we are recognising that outcomes can be improved and that it might be right for a child to stay within that wider family network if possible. We have not had that same level of focus when it comes to actually supporting the family to see if that return home could be possible. I would really echo that point.

Our research showed us that over half of local authorities do not have a policy or strategy for reunification and how they can prioritise that. There is no national strategy or guidance on reunification so we do not know how local authorities are going to be incentivised to pick that up as an area that they can focus on , in terms of practice improvement without that national direction.

We have seen some good examples of good practice but on a national level it is not looking good , because we know that one in five children who return home then actually return back into care within a year. Something is going quite badly wrong there. We really welcome this focus on kinship care and getting more foster carers. With kinship in particular we would say there is lots of learning and we want those principles to be applied to reunification as well.

The only other thing I would add for fostering—I will let Jess come in on the retention and recruitment point—is that there is some really interesting learning around and we need to focus on what we want the role of foster carers to be. Of course bringing them in and recruiting and retaining them is the first part of that. There is some really interesting evidence internationally. Again it links to the points that I am making on reunification about how foster carers can actually work more collaboratively with birth parents, play that supportive role of modelling parenting, help build that relationship , and how that can really support those return homes when they are possible and safe to do so — that mentoring role. That is something I would encourage the committee to look at. I am happy to submit some international evidence that I referenced.

I will do quickfire. For the 10,000 places ambition it is really vital that it is a diverse pool of carers. Recruiting lots of the same people is not going to help to the extent that the Government need it to. As Nicola said retention is really key. We have good retention as an independent fostering agency almost solely because we offer wraparound support for foster carers. We are talking about short break, respite care at weekends, therapeutic input, all that sort of thing.

To Nicola ’ s point on financial support , we have a commitment around inflation-linked national minimum allowances, which is great. The consensus in the sector is that it still does not cover the cost of caring. We also have the fees, which are skills-based and are the opposite of the allowances. We do not have any standardisation of that across the country so that varies hugely. I am not sure if DfE spoke to you about the Staying Put scheme, which is the stay-on scheme for foster children beyond 18. There is no baseline for allowances in staying put at all so that needs looking at.

The organisation Kinship is the key player in this space. It has done a lot of work on the prevalence of poverty among kinship families, which I implied in an earlier comment. From its research it learned that it is financial issues that can often deter kinship arrangements. What the Government want to do is get as many kinship arrangements as possible to sit outside the formal care system, ie not within the fostering space. There is a new piloting programme—Kinship Zones—where financial support among other things is being piloted for kinship arrangements outside foster care. That is brilliant and is showing us a lot about what financial support can do to support the stability of kinship arrangements.

The consequence of it—this is obviously inherent in piloting things—is that we now have a huge discrepancy between kinship carers within the pilot who are having non-means-tested allowances at the same level as foster carers , versus the rest of the country who are on means-tested allowances. The pilot is due to run for three years. With the Government being so committed to kinship it feels like a bit of a gap and that we could be doing something in the meantime.

My final point is that paid employment leave for kinship carers is something that Kinship is also really pushing. That would be on the same level as adoption leave. It is about that moment when the child arrives, settling them, routines, bonding, working through trauma and all that sort of thing. There is nothing in the system for that at the moment. It is being looked at; there is a parental leave review ongoing and we are hoping to see that as an outcome.
O n staying put, d id you say there is a scheme?
Yes.
Is that a g overnment-backed scheme?

Yes. It is what it sounds like: you can stay put until 21. There is some discussion around the age — as to whether it goes up to 25 or not. As you would expect it is very popular. In some local authorities you can be paid quite adequately through the allowance for it , but in others you are not.
Is it not standard across the counties?
No.
The Chair: That is very helpful. I had not heard of that.

Q35 I am just going to comment on what you said, Nicola : i n Sheffield in the past we have tried to have a rebate scheme for foster carers getting council tax back on certain bands. It has been signed off by the finance officers but never got through the b udget so it will be interesting if we can get it as a national scheme.

My question is on a separate note. You have all raised it today and the previous panel that gave evidence last week talked about the growing complex needs of our young people. The obvious question that flows from that is : is our training and development of staff adequate?

I am thinking about two different things in relation to that question. There are the expertise, training and skills as you say, but then there is also the system, the resource and what is in place to allow them to harness that expertise and skills and put them in place to support children and families. We have this system or landscape now where practitioners are increasingly working families with multiple interacting challenges and harms and they interact with other challenges, whether it be poverty, domestic abuse or mental health issues. We have to think about how well-skilled professionals are to work with that picture.

From an NSPCC perspective we would think about, “Okay, well, looking at the whole picture, how well is the workforce equipped at the moment to respond to specific groups of children and specific types of harm?” There are a couple of things that I would bring out on that point. I have talked about neglect and I will have to talk about it again , I am afraid , because it is really important in that we know the system at the moment is not responding to neglect in the way that it needs to. In the research that we did , we spoke to multi-agency professionals who told us that they are essentially often being told by their superiors above that they have to wait for it to escalate to a later point before they can have that intervention in place. That is not right for children or the system.

I talked about changing the definition so that it considers removing the persistence point to make it easier for professionals to access support earlier. There is also something there about recognising the contextual stresses on families. Scotland—in its definition of neglect—recognises poverty as a contextual system stress that can overload parents and be a contributory risk factor. It does not mean that there is a direct correlation between poverty and neglect; they are completely different things and neglect can happen in any home but it means that poverty can work to overload parents to make parenting more challenging. Most importantly , poverty can influence the likelihood of other risk factors such as poor parental mental health or stressors , and we know from evidence that those things can increase the likelihood of neglect. That is the first thing that I would raise in terms of a harm that we do not think is being tackled well in the system and that there needs to be more skills, upskilling and training around. That could be done through a national neglect strategy in the first instance and by looking at that definition.

The other area and group of children that I would point out is babies and infants. NSPCC feels really strongly that the system needs to do far more to ensure there is specialist understanding of child development, attachment and infant mental health to assess the lived experience of babies and infants. Babies and infants represent 34% of serious case reviews—when a child is seriously harmed or killed as a result of abuse and neglect—which is really stark. It is persistent over time; it has not reduced.

We are seeing over the long term that the system is not responding to better protect babies and infants in the way that it needs to. We know that babies and the youngest children cannot verbally disclose harm in the way that older children can. Practitioners really need that confidence to identify risk through professional judgment, observation and understanding of babies ’ lived experience and expertise.

We can see that through serious case reviews; we know what is going wrong. In the murder of Star Hobson, for example, it was identified that practitioners over-relied on what the adults were telling them about Star ’ s experience; they were not doing a good job of assessing risk and actually bringing to life the lived experience of Star, which had horrific consequences. That feels like a really crucial area that we want more to be done on.

I would highlight the children ’ s social care response to child sexual abuse. There were a number of reviews, including the independent inquiry into child sexual abuse and the Casey review, which have consistently found that practitioners are often—again in a similar way to babies and infants but in a different context—overly reliant on children verbally disclosing abuse.

In intrafamilial child sexual abuse , there is a lot of shame and a challenge for that verbal disclosure to come through the system , and professionals need to not be reliant on that . They need to really have that professional curiosity and those skills in observation and analysis of patterns , and to understand those behavioural indicators. All the evidence shows us that there are real, persistent challenges around the skills and expertise to be able to do that within the system. I would point to those two areas in the first instance.

I have also mentioned—but will say it again in this context—that there are definitely some questions around the workforce ’ s capability in the context of the roll-out of the f amily h elp reforms. As I said , we are very supportive of the principle of the reforms. From speaking to local authorities about that implementation , there are two things I would mention now. First, the scale and timescale of reforms are placing a lot of pressure on local authorities. There is a lot of concern about when the money is going to run out and whether they are going to be able to implement in the time that has been given to actually allow the impact of the preventative measures to come through.

Secondly—this is very important when we look at prevention across the whole system—with this new f amily h elp model , it is very welcome that more children will be getting the level of Section 17 support that was in place before for a child who reached Section 17. That support should now be in place for those children who were previously identified as e arly h elp and it should be more streamlined, comprehensive and robust. That is really welcome.

What we have concerns about from speaking to local authorities is actually that in lots of areas what they are doing to deliver f amily h elp is just combining the e arly h elp and Section 17 support. What that means—if the new introduction that the Government just consulted on goes ahead in terms of all that support being then delivered under Section 17—is it could actually risk that threshold going up and that old - school e arly h elp support not being in place because it has been removed. For this to work and be preventative across the whole system, not just shifting thresholds, we also need that investment in the true e arly h elp support services as well as the f amily h elp ones that are being rolled out at the moment.

Q36 Building on the question that my colleague asked, I understand all that you have said about identifying child abuse and all that , but I do not want to focus on that. One of you talked earlier about Ofsted needing to inspect the whole life of the child, not just the home, and I agree with that; it is important. There is a real challenge for all the professionals involved to do two things that are in tension. One is to have the highest possible expectations of this young person and the other is to deal with the complex and very challenging needs.

I wonder if there is a skill set, training programme or set of developments that can help people maintain those two things, which are often almost daily in tension for many of these people. If you lower the expectations you never get the outcomes in the long run. If you do not acknowledge the needs you cannot get the improvement going. Do any of you have schemes for doing that?

I cannot speak to schemes and I will let others come in , but local authorities need the space and commitment of long-term funding and investment in children ’ s social care that is not just tied to programmes of reforms to really be able to invest in workforce development and skill sets.
I agree with that but do you know of schemes or people who have developed the ability to do what I just described?

I certainly cannot think of a specific scheme. When we look at Ofsted this is definitely something where it very much can come down to individual inspectors and approaches. The new framework for inspection that Ofsted recently consulted on aims to do this. We are very much keen to look at the starting point of the child and be able to get an understanding of some early groundwork that we have put in to help progress.

To give you an actual real-life example, we had a child in one home who had very severe autism and many behavioural issues and difficulties interacting with services. When we took them in, the home managed to work with the child , who had never used a knife and fork or sat at a table before and get them to sit down and have a meal. That is not attending school or the higher outcomes and things we absolutely want , but i t is very important that the inspection regime recognises that progress and is able to acknowledge the very good work the providers have done , because it is the foundation for the next stage on.

At the moment as Barnardo ’ s we find it very dependent upon the inspector and how the inspection ends up going. The current framework very much starts talking and looks far more to embed the experiences of children and young people within the inspection framework. It should maybe help but it is very much going to be about individual inspectors. To answer your question , I do not know of a scheme that has been able to achieve that.

Q37 We have talked a little about Ofsted in different ways with unregistered homes in the workforce and the new inspection framework. What other priorities should Ofsted bring to the table in its inspection regulation work?

I am happy to lead on this. We feel really positive about the new inspection regime , particularly in respect of the proposed evaluation areas and the new approach to grading and reporting. It could bring a much more consistent, thorough and nuanced approach to how quality is assessed, reported and communicated.

Obviously the proof is in the pudding. There are issues around having meaningful buy-in from local authorities and providers. We see this in the education space , where the effect of not securing the buy-in of the target of the inspection is quite serious. We are at a really critical point with Ofsted now in how it is inspecting where we can start doing some stuff much better.

To secure buy-in from those being inspected—local authorities and providers—they need to be seen to be really accurately and sensitively reflecting the quality of care and representing context in a sufficiently nuanced way. Context is all about the factors that are influencing how those services and that care are being delivered: things that are both within the local authority or provider ’ s control and those that are not. We need to be serious about what those things are that are not within their control.

To Nicola ’ s earlier point we need to see much more consistency of inspections across both place and time so that people feel confident that they are getting fair treatment in a sense. They need to know that they will have the same level of assessment and there will be the same expectations when they are next inspected.

Related to that point about needing buy-in, we need to get to a place where Ofsted has a relationship of both oversight and support so providers and local authorities are supported to go on this process of continuous learning and improvement. Some of this is about the accessibility of the inspectors. In an ideal world you would have the same inspector showing up over a period of time. They would be available between inspections to have meaningful discussions about quite basic things such as what the distinctions are between the different grades, what they mean in practical terms, what they can do better next time to get to that grade and remove some of that slightly opaque process.

Equally there need to be feedback mechanisms. When I speak to the operational directors who oversee all our provision at Action for Children they tell me that the feedback mechanism must sit outside the formal complaints process. There is no confidence that using the formal complaints process is not going to affect you in your relationship with the inspector and potentially the outcomes there.

I have talked about this point around assessing outcomes relative to starting points, looking at the journey and trajectory and looking holistically at the child ’ s life beyond the setting and specific care that they are receiving in the local authority. Within that there is something about not making comparisons between what are essentially non-equivalent cohorts by Ofsted.

Another key point that we raised in our response to the Ofsted consultation is around the voice of children, parents and carers. I mentioned this earlier in the session. There needs to be a lot of proactivity on Ofsted ’ s part about how this is done, offering different modes of engagement at different points inside and outside the inspection processes. Ofsted needs to think about all those different groups it needs to reach and not just go for those that are most available for the discussions.

My final point is quite specific. There is a new evaluation area on enduring relationships. This goes back to what I was saying earlier around DfE really wanting the whole sector to focus on building and maintaining continuous trusted relationships for children. That is really welcome; the new evaluation area is really overdue. At the moment I would say it is framed quite squarely on what the local authority or provider is doing to support the child to build and maintain relationships with family, friends and their community.

What we as a provider find—particularly in the children ’ s home space—is that there is a lack of clarity around how those relationships can continue with the workforce within the placement. When a child leaves a placement—whether that is due to breakdown or because they move out of the system—what does good look like in that situation? How can we navigate all the issues around consent and risk for some relationships to continue with the workforce?

There is something that you hear quite commonly in the sector around children who have left a children ’ s home being invited back for Sunday lunch every week. In practical terms that is quite hard to do in some settings, particularly where the relationship sits with a particular member of the workforce in the home. Some of the solution is about seeing it as an organisational responsibility. There is a gap where there is guidance needed to support that process so that settings feel really confident to do it, obviously where the child has the preference to continue those relationships. That new enduring relationships evaluation area is really positive but that is a really crucial missing part of it.

Can I just come in with a couple of extra points? I agree with most of that and this time I will not repeat what has been said. One thing that we have found in the past is that Ofsted kept a little aside from the general direction of children ’ s social care reform. We introduced a new framework for children ’ s social care in England but we did not update the Ofsted inspection regime to go with it. That has changed because we have just had a consultation, which we are very pleased about as you will gather.

Going forward, as we have a government reform programme we have to make sure that as we learn from things such as the f amilies f irst for c hildren p athfinder from regional care co - operatives we are continually having conversations with Ofsted and enabling it to update its inspection regime, which cannot sit entirely independently. For a long while there was a certain sense of, “The Government are telling us to do that but Ofsted ’ s telling us to do something different”, and that has an impact.

The other element that I want to bring in—just to add a little to what Jess said about the involvement of children and young people—is thinking about the involvement of children and young people in the actual inspections themselves. We ourselves run what we call the Young Inspectors Programme , where we get some children and young people from our own services to go to inspect our services for us and talk to the children and staff. We find that incredibly rich in terms of what they are able to tell us. Our young inspectors do about 10 inspections a year and are able to give us a really different perspective than what we might get from an Ofsted inspector. I wonder if Ofsted could do something similar.

I will be very quick because I am aware of the time. W e responded to the consultation that has been mentioned and really felt it was a very welcome focus on children ’ s experiences and the stable relationship element that Jess pointed out. There are just three areas—I will be very quick—that we pointed to that could be further strengthened.

There was much greater emphasis on assessing how well the system was bringing in and listening to children ’ s voices, which we were very pleased to see. I want to go back to the point that I raised earlier about the unique vulnerability of babies and infants. When we cannot bring in the voice of babies and infants in the same way as we can for older children, what that inspection framework needs to include is a really clear assessment of how skilled professionals are at bringing in the voices of those who are less visible through the observation and supervision mechanisms that can do that. That is the first point I would raise.

The second point is around how the system is working to prevent harm from escalating and whether we are responding early enough. There were some elements that we included in our consultation response about strengthening that area of the framework.

Thirdly, this links to what Nicola said about how we need real join-up between these different changes, the Ofsted inspection framework and the wider expectations in f amily h elp. We were really pleased that in the f amily h elp guidance there is—not enough , because I would call for national guidance or a strategy—reference to how f amily h elp teams should be supporting and working around supporting reunification. We need to look at how the Ofsted inspection framework can examine the quality of reunification planning and pre- and post-support and how well that support is working with the f amily h elp teams to deliver it at different points in the system.

This is a small point that builds on what Nicola said, which I thought was very important. I have seen this in the school inspection work since Ofsted was invented in 1992. When you change the way the system works and what it is expecting , you need to change the Ofsted inspection framework but also invest in the inspector ’ s skills; otherwise they are looking for the wrong thing.

We are a little worried. The Ofsted inspection regime includes a lot more things such as the enduring relationships and talking to children and young people. It is all really positive but it also still includes a data scorecard that is basically how many placement moves you have had and so on. Could we get some inspectors who go, “Oh, I recognise that; that ’ s what I am going to focus on”?
What if the Ofsted inspectors do not know what good or bad look like in the new system or cannot find them?

Can I thank you immensely for the time and the amount of information you have given us this morning? I was going to ask you a question about priorities , but you have laid out very clearly where you think the priorities should be. If there are any other matters that you do not feel we have covered , please write in to us. A huge thank you for your time this morning. All the committee would agree it was a very helpful session and we will certainly keep in touch going forward. I will close the session.

sessions.w: Osman Koray Ertas (Turkish Embassy); Jay Weatherill (Australian High Commission)

Environmental Audit Committee m embers present: Mr Toby Perkins (Chair); Barry Gardiner; Sarah Gibson; Sojan Joseph; Dr Roz Savage; John Whitby.
Energy Security and Net Zero Committee member present: Bill Esterson.

Witnesses
I : Osman Koray Ertaş, Ambassador of the Republic of Türkiye to the United Kingdom; and Jay Weatherill, Australian High Commissioner to the United Kingdom.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Osman Koray Ertaş and Jay Weatherill.

Q1 Welcome, everyone, to this special meeting of the Environmental Audit Committee ahead of the forthcoming series of COP31 panel events. We are pleased to have strong panels with us today, the first of which features the Ambassador of the Republic of Türkiye and the Australian High Commissioner to the United Kingdom. Gentlemen, I invite you to introduce yourselves, and I thank you for your attendance. We will start with you, Your Excellency, Mr Weatherill.
My name is Jay Weatherill. I am Australia’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom.
I am Osman Koray Ertaş , the Ambassador of Türkiye to London.
Q2 Thank you for coming to see us. You both want to set the scene briefly before we head into the questions ahead of COP31. We will start with you, Ambassador Ertaş .

Thank you very much, hon. Chair and distinguished Members. It is a great pleasure for me to be here with my distinguished colleague. With Australia, I think we have come up with an innovative approach to COP processes, which is vital at a time when multilateralism is being challenged in a dramatic way, in many senses. Over the past 10 years, after we ratified the Paris agreement, and for about three decades before that, we have made a lot of commitments. We now have strong acquis, so the important thing is implementation—it is time to implement what we have committed to. Geopolitics is getting tougher, and we are losing public support in some countries, so we have to lead COP in such a way as to have public support and to focus on implementation and, as much as possible, on consensus, bringing together the different interests of different parties. We look forward to working with the UK and the UK Parliament, as it is a leading country on climate issues. We look forward to hosting some of you in Antalya.

Thank you, Chair and Committee members. Thank you for the invitation to speak to the Committee. It is a great pleasure to be here alongside my colleague, the Turkish Ambassador. We are really honoured to lead the COP31 negotiations alongside Türkiye as the host and president. We share the view for ambitious and practical outcomes in line with the Paris agreement.

Australia comes to the role after undergoing a pretty major clean energy transformation. In just six years, we have doubled the share of renewables in our electricity mix to almost 50%, with a goal of 82% by 2030. One in three Australian households now has rooftop solar. In my former role as Premier of South Australia, I was also co-chair of the Climate Group ’s States and Regions Alliance , and I saw at first hand how Governments, together with business, sub-national government and communities, can work together to accelerate the transition and seize the economic opportunities that exist.

We are interested in COP31 having the same focus on practical delivery, partnership and inclusion, particularly for the Pacific region. We think the UK will be an important partner for us in sharing that climate objective. We are delighted that Prime Minister Burnham plans to attend COP31, building on the UK’s continued international climate leadership, and that Foreign Secretary Miliband is strongly engaged on climate issues in his new role. By working together, we think we can confront the global challenge of climate change and seize the economic opportunities. That is the promise of COP31, and we are very keen to realise it.

Q3 Thank you very much. Ambassador Ertaş , this approach, with two nations combining to lead the COP negotiations, is without precedent. Can you explain, from Türkiye’s perspective, how this came about and how you anticipate the two countries working together to host and co-lead these important negotiations?

Australia is leading the pre-COP arrangements, the preparations and the negotiations. We are serving as the COP31 President, and obviously we lead the Action Agenda, which is a vital portion of the larger conference, as you all know.

As a matter of fact, it is an effort to bring different countries with different interests to the same table in their shared interests. Being two nations in different parts of the world, with different interests, challenges and development levels, means that we are bringing different aspects to the fore. Australia being in a different part of the world is quite helpful for the voice of the Pacific islands to be heard. We recently concluded the pre-COP summit in Tuvalu and Fiji. This is the second time that has happened, as they hosted a similar summit a decade ago. Türkiye sits on the Mediterranean basin, which is quite a stressful region in terms of the climate challenge. We bring different challenges, but we serve the same objective.

From day one, not only at the official and governmental level but at the societal level, we have been working in very close contact. Our youth champions and younger leaders on the climate agenda are actively engaging with one another. We have been working since January, and the official meetings started in February in Istanbul. There have been some critical benchmarks in Bonn, at London Climate Action Week and in New York. At all those events, we managed to get away from our differences and focus on issues of consensus and compatibility. So far, it has been working quite well from our perspective.

Q4 You reflect on the different contexts that your nations face, in terms of your geographical position and the challenges. It is right to reflect on the recent appalling floods in Türkiye . Our hearts go out to your compatriots who are dealing with that; we send them our sympathy.

At previous COPs, we have seen the host nation drive an agenda around a particular area. Last year, it was deforestation. You rightly identified the important case of the Pacific islands, which were a strong part of Australia’s push. I will ask you for your perspective first, Ambassador Ertaş , and then I will go to the High Commissioner. Do you feel there have been tensions in that relationship, or are you entirely comfortable with where these negotiations will be starting from?

Osman Koray Ertaş : They are going very positively. Obviously, things will be clearer as we get closer to the summit—we are very much closer—but up until now, when we had the stocktake, things had gone pretty smoothly. Also, the pre-COP event in Tuvalu and Fiji was an important alignment. We hope we will continue to carry the flag from our forebears, and we will pass the baton to the next country to host the summit. Overall, as I say, it is a positive engagement that is yielding positive results.

This is also enabling us to talk to different continents and cultures at the same time. Türkiye has its own special connections with different geographies, including the middle east, Africa, the Caucasus, the Black sea and the Balkans. Similarly, Australia, as my colleague would attest, has specific connections and ties with different regions, especially in Asia and the larger western world. Being different but connected parties is helping us to convey the same message to different geographies, cultures and interests.

Q5 I invite you to respond, High Commissioner. Obviously, we are all conscious of the discussions at COP30 about where it would be hosted. Ultimately, we have this unprecedented arrangement of Türkiye being the host and Australia being president of negotiations. Are you comfortable that the issues that Australia raised at COP30—the reasons why it wanted to be the host nation—will be adequately covered? Are you comfortable with where the negotiations are at the moment?

Yes, we are. Because it is an innovative arrangement, we have spent a lot of time making sure that we are aligned. We are aligned on the fundamentals: a shared commitment to multilateralism, strong COP31 outcomes and advancing the objectives of the Paris agreement. Those fundamental alignments are important. Türkiye has accommodated the specific matters that we wanted to advance—in particular, our focus on the Pacific nations and being a voice for the Pacific in international relations.

Ultimately, the success of all this depends on making sure that we bring to the table as many interests as we possibly can. In a sense, Australia and Türkiye having to resolve and find common ground on these matters is a precondition to our being able to do that across all the countries that will attend this conference—it has been a good starting point. Our differences in geography, interests and levels of influence have proven to be a strength rather than a challenge, and that will help us as we move into the negotiations.

Q6 In his third letter to parties, the Turkish Presidency concluded: “ The challenges before us are considerable, but so are the opportunities. ” From your perspective, High Commissioner, what are the key challenges to delivering the practical, inclusive and ambitious outcomes that led us all here?

The context is tricky, of course. We have a challenging environment internationally, including global energy shocks. On energy security, economic resilience and climate action, we are having to grapple with a different world from the one we had a little while ago, with all these weather conditions: the record-breaking heatwaves, the floods in Nepal, the wildfires and a supercharged El Niño . All those things are concentrating minds. Also, the middle east is making sure that energy transition is a powerful issue. It could not be more urgent, but things are making it harder to do.

These are big challenges, but electrification and clean energy represent opportunities to grapple with some of the emerging challenges. Energy independence is becoming a significant matter in the considerations of many nations. In that regard, pursuing electrification and renewable energy provides an opportunity, not just a challenge. Also, on a broader level, at a time when there is pressure on multilateral institutions, actually demonstrating that they can work would send a powerful message to the world. This is quintessentially an issue that requires international co-operation to resolve. We must make this multinational arrangement work, and if we can demonstrate that it can work on this very challenging issue, it may form a pattern for a lot of other challenges.
Q7 Your Excellency, Ambassador Ertaş, how far do you feel that discussions in the lead-up to COP have been driven by this year’s global energy disruption?

This is certainly a fundamental issue. We need to convince public opinion in our respective countries, and international actors, that green transition is not a rival of energy independence and energy security. Those two major issues support each other. Once we lose public opinion, Governments lose steam and do not focus on these issues any more. We are trying to build on the existing consensus that we have agreed upon in the last five years, and we are trying to implement more.

One major issue is the lack of funding and finance. One of our priorities, in our six Action Agenda items, is to identify the needs of countries, transform them into bankable projects and link them to available finance mechanisms at both the national and international level. The world is becoming more conflictual and volatile. We should not let the climate agenda be on the back burner rather than the front seat. On our end, as a country that is a net energy importer and sits in a very volatile part of the world, we continue to underline the importance of a green transition, eventually reaching net zero, and transforming our economy and energy systems with a specific and special emphasis on electrification.

Q8 The UK’s Foreign Secretary recently said that climate and nature loss represent an urgent national security issue. Indeed, I think he shared with many international partners the UK Government’s findings on the national security threat posed by climate and nature loss. Do you agree with that? To what extent will that drive the discussions we have in Antalya ?

As a matter of fact, the COP31 President, who is also our Minister of Environment and Urban isation, made a similar remark. We are understandably investing a lot in the defence industry; as NATO countries, there are benchmarks and objectives that we all want to achieve. In the meantime, climate challenges are also national security issues. Unfortunately, we have seen that quite clearly in recent years: the recent floods in Istanbul and Nepal, and even the wildfires in Wales, which are unexpected in this country. We also have to invest heavily in our climate security and climate change objectives.

We certainly share the Foreign Secretary’s analysis. Speaking as a voice for the Pacific island nations, this represents an existential threat to them. It has pretty substantial implications for the movement of peoples in our region, which itself creates pressures and strains that have national security implications. We share the Foreign Secretary’s analysis.

Q9 Could you both elaborate on what you feel is coming out of the CBD COP in Yerevan at the moment, in terms of the strides made on nature loss? How ought that to feed into COP31? Perhaps you could reflect on your hopes and expectations for the CBD COP outcomes transitioning into COP31, on the issues of nature loss and ecological collapse, as our Foreign Secretary spoke about.

We have established 10 priority items for our summit, and one of the items is to do with the Rio convention synergies. We value these linkages between the three Rio conventions , and obviously the event in Armenia is quite critical in that regard. We are fully on board in support of their ambitions , both on the desertification and biodiversity agendas. There will be strong connections between us and the other Rio convention efforts and objectives.
I support the Turkish A mbassador ’ s observations.
Q10 Thank you both for joining us. Ambassador, you have already outlined one of your objectives . For both of you, what are your key objectives from COP31 ?

We have identified 10 priority items and six global goals. Th o se six global goals are tangible and measurable. The first priority is electrification and the clean energy transition. We have offered parties an ambitious electrification target of 35% by 2035. That is to increase electricity ’s share of global final energy consumption to 35%.

The second priority is about zero waste and methane reduction. We aim to reduce the projected increase in global municipal waste generation by at least 50% by 2035. That will also support our efforts to reduce methane emissions and promote a circular economy.

The third objective is to do with climate resilient cities. We aim to reduce energy use intensity in buildings by at least 25% by 2035. We have designed some specific proposals and projects , which we offered to parties.

Fourthly, we are focusing on green industrialisation as an important theme. We aim to increase the global circular material use rate to at least 15% by 2035. We believe that countries should not have to choose between decarbonisation and deindustrialisation , and if we can achieve the green transition , it will support economic growth, employment and competitiveness , and we will continue to have strong public backing for our policies.

The fifth priority is to do with youth and education. We want climate awareness and the concrete objective is to integrate climate education into our national curricula by 2030 and achieve climate action education for all by 2035.

The sixth and final priority , which is tangible, is about finance. We plan to initiate a climate implementation bridge. This is not a new fund but an effort to bring together countries ’ needs on the green transition, convert them into bankable projects and link with available finance sources. That has been developed in co - operation with UNDP.

On all these six pillars , we have worked with international organisations . For example, on electrification , we worked quite closely with IRENA and the International Energy Agency . On zero waste and food security , we have been working with the FAO . On climate awareness , we are working with UNESCO. In addition to the six pillars , there will also be a focus on food security , on oceans and seas and on resilient health systems. This is the overall focus of the Action Agenda . As I say, there will be complementary and supporting initiatives that will allow parties to achieve these objectives.

We share and support Türkiye ’s ambitions in that regard. Australia ’ s ambitions are very much focused on implementation. We want practical measures that accelerate the delivery of the Paris agreement and the four broad priorities that are accelerating the global clean energy transition : improving access to finance , facilitating investment , growing the global green industry and elevating Pacific priorities. On clean energy, we see electrification backed by modern grids, energy storage and investment as fundamental. It is climate policy, but it is also increasingly sound economic and energy security policy. We want COP31 to deliver outcomes that help countries access climate finance and attract investment to strengthen resilience and build modern, low-emissions industries.

For the Pacific, that includes access to predictable, non-debt-creating finance. The Pacific Resilience Facility is a practical example of Pacific leadership. It emerged from the Pacific nations themselves. We are proud to support it and very grateful for the UK’s contribution of £10 million to that facility.

Australia and Pacific island countries have also agreed on an access to climate finance for SIDS and LDCs statement and action plan, which was launched at the pre-COP. That plan sets out a collective vision to improve the way vulnerable communities can access that climate finance. UK support and leadership in that area have been critical in advancing those objectives.
Q11 You have mentioned finance and leadership. Is there anything else that either of you feels that the UK could be doing to support you arriving at what is in those objectives?

The UK is a critical partner, especially o n the finance pillar, not only because London is the second most important financial centre in the world but because of the UK’ s expertise in turning targets into bankable projects. So we are working very closely, both at g overnmental level and with the financial institutions here , to try to offer these instruments to countries, especially in the least developed world. There are some financial mechanisms , such as the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facilit y . If we can achieve this together with the LDC T echnology Bank, and the UN in Istanbul , we will continue to bring fresh capital to some bankable projects in the least develop ed countries.

The UK will be quite active in three or four events during C OP . One is about methane reduction. Another has to do with deforestation. We will also co-chair an event on green industrialisation. Al l th o se things are fundamental to the larger climate agenda. And this thing is not a one - off effort. Once Türkiye h ands over the P residency , we will continue to follow these priorities and continue to work together with the UK. On a national level , I was planning to use some figures if you have any questions on what we are doing nationally, but we will do the first offshore wind tender in Türkiye , and on this also we are working quite closely with UK partners, both official partners and on the business side.
W e look forward to our ongoing co - operation with the UK in having this green transition and agenda success.

T he UK could assist us , in our role of heading the negotiations , to finalise the rules to transition the long - standing a daptation f und from the Kyoto p rotocol to the Paris a greement . On a daptation finance , we are focused on cutting red tape and helping existing climate finance deliver greater impact and reach communities when and where it is needed. For the Pacific, adaptation and resilience are immediate challenges , and t he new Pacific R esilience F acility is a Pacific - driven initiative that is about creating that fast, predictable , non-debt - creating finance for the likes of water security projects, disaster preparedness, resilient agriculture, early warning systems and nature - based solutions. The UK has made a contribution to that , but it could also make a contribution to the rules that allow it to be accessed and it would assist us in our negotiations if it supported us in that.

Q12 That is very helpful; it is good to know where we should be pushing. In terms of the ongoing Presidency, how are you working with the Brazilian COP30 Presidency and any other previous presidencies to ensure that continuity?

From early on, beginning in January, we established close contact with the team that is delivering on the Brazilian COP. We strongly support its priorities, especially on deliverables. There are certain agenda items that the Brazilian Presidency is still monitoring, and it will update the conference parties in Antalya, especially about transitioning away from fossil fuels. As you will remember, Brazil has worked on a road map for transitioning away from fossil fuels following discussions at COP30 and we look forward to hearing where they are on that.

Obviously, Brazil’s position as a sizeable middle power that has connections with different geographies is valuable for us. As a nation that is part of the larger European reality and also has strong connections with the Global South, Türkiye will continue to have strong bonds to bring different parties together at the table.
I think we have both been assisted by the previous COP arrangement. We draw on the knowledge of people who have hosted COP to maintain that continuity and learn how to conduct our roles.
Q13 Following the previous COP, the Brazilian Presidency promised road maps on both transitioning away from fossil fuels and deforestation. Will those road maps be produced before COP31?

What was achieved at the Brazilian COP will be specifically followed by us as well. There were six different axes at the outcome of the Brazilian COP and our priorities perfectly fit in the decisions on the six different axes. Obviously, transitioning away is one of the most difficult topics; many countries are having reservations on that, but we will continue to bring together the interests and the concerns of different parties.

We acknowledge that every country has different starting points and needs, especially in the field of energy, so we will try to somehow respond as much as we can to the different needs of different parties. For sure, we will continue to work with Brazil to deliver these commitments.
Q14 I appreciate that the transition away from fossil fuels is going to be difficult, but deforestation did not figure in your list of priorities. Is there a reason for that?

Deforestation is also an important agenda item for us. Obviously, the letter from the COP31 President is not an exhaustive list. We tried to continue with what the Brazilian COP Presidency did and there will be specific events in Antalya focusing on deforestation. It is a fundamental issue for our agenda item as well.

I suppose there is a challenge in transitioning away from fossil fuels, but it is probably worth remembering that before Paris, the world was heading towards 4 °C warming and now we are projected to reach 2.6 °C . That is still not enough, but it is an achievement.

In relation to the road maps committed to during the Brazilian Presidency, the expectation is that they will be published before COP31. We are looking forward to that. We do not have direct control over the release of those, but that is our expectation and we are certainly looking forward to it.

Q15 The Turkish Presidency’s third letter to parties highlights the importance of tackling methane emissions, but focuses only on waste. Why are even more significant sources of methane such as fossil fuels or even livestock not mentioned?

We should have a holistic approach on methane reduction—not only the food waste, but also major emitters on the methane side. Zero waste is much more than a waste management policy at our end. It is a vision that encourages us to rethink how we produce, consume and use our limited resources.

Globally, around one third of the food produced today is lost or wasted. It accounts for an estimated 8% to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. The specific focus on zero waste does not mean we are not focusing on the vital part of methane emissions. As a matter of fact, the UK is leading a debate on this subject in Antalya with our strong support. On a national level, this zero waste initiative has gained momentum, beginning in 2017, and it has been an emblematic example of how green transition can be achieved in a particular context, where you can start from scratch, from zero, all the way to modern limits. Today, for example, the waste recovery rate in Türkiye is about 37%. It was only about 10% when the project started. We have achieved almost $8 billion for our economy with these efforts. More than 600 million trees, for example, have been saved, and our objective is to get this waste recovery rate to 60% by 2035, in less than 10 years.

We are also focusing on the seas and oceans. We have already removed more than 375 tonnes of marine litter from our seas. This will be a specific focus on our end, but obviously we will continue to give due priority to other sources of methane emissions.

At pre-COP, our Minister for Climate Change announced that Australia would support Türkiye ’s zero waste and methane reduction target, reducing global waste generation by 50% by 2035. Within Australia, our safeguard mechanism incentivises emissions reductions, including methane emissions, so about three quarters of the methane emissions from the resources sector are currently covered by that safeguard mechanism.

Q16 On your priority of supporting climate-resilient cities, I presume this partly looks at the construction industry itself, which is a high emitter. Are there specific parts of the construction industry that you would be looking at, for example, such as the production of cement, which is a particularly high emitter? Are there other elements that you are looking at?

Yes, there are major sectors that are major emitters, including cement, as you say. There is the aluminium sector as well. We will have a specific focus on these sectors, nationally, in our policy to achieve net zero by 2053. As you might remember, we had a terrible earthquake more than three years ago—one of the largest earthquakes in mankind’s history. After the earthquake, the Government was able to build more than 450,000 units—homes—in the larger earthquake regions. While rebuilding, we paid the utmost attention to having climate-resilient buildings and tried to decrease the energy use intensity in those buildings.

We will continue on a national level to do similar projects in different parts of Türkiye . The city of Istanbul is unfortunately located on an earthquake fault line. We have ambitious plans to have this urban change in Istanbul and in other major cities that are vulnerable to disasters. This is a priority item nationally for us as well. We also want it to be embraced internationally by different partners.

I think this might fall within the global goal on adaptation, which includes the creation of a technical taskforce to look at a whole range of evidence that can advance that agenda. The national adaptation plans will remain a key focus; I think 93 of those have been submitted to date. We support those discussions on strengthening national adaptation planning and implementation.

Q17 High C ommissioner, in concluding the Fiji pre-COP , Minister Tabuya said that the key goals for Antalya were getting finance to the people who need it and “putting the ocean in its rightful place” at the centre of the climate agenda. That ties in very much with the Turkish Presiden cy saying that you would amplify the voices of vulnerable communities, of developing nations and of the Pacific islanders.

I welcome what has happened with the host country agreement—the funding arrangements that have been agreed—but how will you facilitate the voice of the Pacific nations and the indigenous communities? Look at what happened at pre-COP: the Australian Minister said that he expected 50 leaders from across the world to attend; in the end it was 14. Only two of those were from outside the Pacific region, and they were from the So uth China sea and the Indian ocean, so there was not the appetite to reflect the ambition at pre-COP. How are we going to turbocharge that when it comes to COP itself?

In the way we think of pre-COP, the fact that it happened was a significant moment. It did elevate the voices of Pacific island nations , and they were grateful for that. Each of those leaders—true, they were largely the leaders in that region—appreciated the international focus on their part of the world. It also allowed them to elevate a range of initiatives that might have been lost in a broader international conference, and I think they appreciated that. If you go through the remarks from each of the nations, you can see that they found it gave them a way of talking about their particular needs that would have otherwise been difficult to get on the international agenda.

Q18 The SIDS have long been a very powerful voice, often amplified in a coalition with one of the other major countries such as India or China. It is not as if they have not had a voice at COP, but sometimes their objectives have not actually been realised in terms of the agenda.

I think, in terms of their objectives, they put the question of finance front and centre. The Pacific Resilience Facility is a substantial achievement. It now has pledges in the order of $210 million.
Q19 You launched a specific action fund in Australia, didn’t you?
Yes.

I think that is a great initiative, but you will know that $5 billion of the funds that were pledged have not yet been disbursed and of course the Pacific island states, and small island states in general, are concerned that people are pledging money but it does not seem to be coming through and getting to where it is needed. How can we turbocharge that?

I think that is because the rules about how to access that funding have proved difficult or oppressive to gaining access to the funding on a certain basis. The idea of the Pacific Resilience Facility is that it is designed in a different way, which means that the criteria and the rules for accessing it, and the ease with which it can be implemented, are different and more beneficial for Pacific island nations. I think that is what they have appreciated: something that works instead of somebody making a grand gesture about something that is not practical from their perspective. In that regard, although we did not have leader representation, having the UK special representative for climate, Rachel Kyte, there was an important element of that whole equation.
Rachel will be with us later this afternoon. I am sure I will press her on some of the same issues.

I am sure she will be able to answer in far greater detail than I have been able to do. A few other things emerged at pre-COP, such as the Taku Pakasoa agreement on strength in unity, which confirmed support for science-based action to triple renewable energy and double energy efficiency, and to transition a lot of those Pacific island nations away from fossil fuels, on which they heavily rely and which are themselves quite precarious, especially given international interruptions.

Q20 I am delighted to hear you say that, but you will not be surprised if I ask you this. Australia has announced a considerable ambition for 2035, but you have also announced that you are expanding fossil fuels. Do you think that sits easily with what you have just said about encouraging other nations to move away from expanding fossil fuels and to move more quickly towards renewables?

We are reducing our reliance on fossil fuels. We have quite ambitious renewable energy targets. I think I mentioned in my opening remarks that there has been a substantial increase in the take-up of renewable energy.
Q21 In September last year, you announced the new position from Australia, which was certainly an improvement. It is an ambitious goal—is it to have a 65% reduction by 2035?

That’s right. It is heading towards net zero, of course, for 2050. There is also an 82% reduction along the pathway. We have a pathway that is realistic when you look at what has been achieved in the last five years. The evidence is in what we have been doing and what we have achieved. We fully accept that it involves a transition, which means that there will still be the use of fossil fuels, especially gas as a transitional fuel, as we move to a renewable energy future.

Q22 Turning to Ambassador Ertaş, I welcomed what you said from the P residency about amplifying the voice of vulnerable communities, particularly youth , within the teams. When I was at the CBD convention last week, I had the privilege of meeting the Global Youth Biodiversity Network. I wonder what energy you, as the host country, are putting in to ensur ing that youth are properly represented in Antalya, and how you are going to amplify their voices in the way the P residency suggests.

First of all, it is unfortunate that only two countries from outside the region attended the conference. That is why we have to continue to work hard for their voices to be heard on the other side of the world.

We have included oceans and seas among our 10 priority items. There will be a specific day—17 November—that will focus on oceans and seas, and there will be a couple of new initiatives as well. Obviously , we have to build on the existing ones, such as the fund spearheaded by Australia. The first one is the regional and international co-operation for oceans initiative, which we have designed with the UN E nvironment P rogramme. Our objective is to enhance the climate adaptation capacity of marine and coastal areas, support coastal resilience through technological and innovative approaches and, more importantly, mobilise climate finance.

The second initiative is a marine litter action platform. It is something we have started to do on a national level, and our objective is to contribute to emissions reduction by connecting identified needs with best practices and sources of finance to scale efforts and to reduce marine litter. Finally, we will have a high-level dialogue on Antarctic messages to strengthen the role and visibility of Antarctica in climate research, recognising its critical role and vulnerability to climate change.
On youth and education, we want to translate climate commitments into child and youth-responsive policies.

Q23 My question is not about policies for young people, but about giving a voice to young people at COP and in the negotiations. We will be deciding things that will be far more pertinent to their future than mine , certainly—you are a much younger man —so it seems important that we involve them in the decision making in a way that has not always happened in the past. That is what I was seeking from you.

We have a UN youth c hampion, as you know, and we are trying to use that instrument quite prominently in order for the youth to have their say in the whole system and particularly in the negotiations. We want to strengthen the participation of youth in the decision making— that is one of the objectives that we have clearly declared—and we continue to work with institutions such as UNICEF, for example, on that front.

Thank you very much indeed, Ambassador Ertaş and High Commissioner Weatherill. We are very grateful to both of you for your evidence today and would like to take this opportunity to wish both of your nations well in the COP31 negotiations. We will be following your leadership with great interest and hoping that the COP31 negotiations are the success that we all hope and need them to be.

sessions.iT: UK Envoy for Complex Consular Detentions
sessions.w: The Rt Hon Alistair Burt (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office)

segs.tx: Foreign Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: UK Envoy for Complex Consular Detentions, HC 744
Monday 26 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 26 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Emily Thornberry (Chair); Alex Ballinger; Aphra Brandreth; Dan Carden; Edward Morello; Sir John Whittingdale.
Questions 1-4 0
Witness
I : The Rt Hon Alistair Burt, UK Envoy for Complex Consular Detentions, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office .
Examination of witness
Witness: The Rt Hon Alistair Burt.

Q1 Welcome to today’s Foreign Affairs Committee sitting. We are hearing from the right hon. Alistair Burt, the Government’s first ever envoy for complex consular detentions. It is a role that this Committee and our predecessor Committee called for and, it would probably be fair to say, campaigned for, so we are pleased to see you today.

For those watching the session, I should make it clear that the witness will not be able to discuss individual cases in any depth. Instead, we will ask more general questions about the newly created role, its remit and how it relates to existing Government structures for supporting those who are detained overseas, and I will start with that.

We are pleased to see you in the Committee. We called for the role to be created on several occasions, as did our predecessor Committee, which Dan was part of as well. Will you set out what you see your new role to be?
