To reiterate a lot of what Laurie said about how some of that joined - up working is not happening , w e know that not all local authorities in Wales have data - sharing agreements with DWP, for example . I f that was done more effectively, we know that people would be accessing more of the support they are entitled to. I think the C y nn a l pilot will be a key test of th e attitude that you are referring to .

W e commissioned expert legal advice earlier this year that showed that Welsh G overnment do have the power, under devolved powers, to introduce a trial payment for Wales , b ut the risk is that DWP and HMRC treat the Cynnal payment as an income and then families lose out on some of th e money that should be coming to them.

I think that it is a good example . I f UK G overnment were able to facilitate that pilot happening, a lot of learning c ould come from these schemes about what works to tackle child poverty . W e have seen in Scotland that the introduction of the Scottish c hild p ayment ha s had a real impact on driving down rates of child poverty there . T here is a lot we can learn from that.

Just to add my voice to some of this , o ne interesting thing I found when I have spoken to various civil servants in the Welsh Government in recent months is they often had a different view on precisely what is the power of Wales to do things like the Cynnal . That does not seem like a very healthy set - up for effective policymaking if the policymakers do not know what the powers ar e, for which there should be co - ordination.

I also add my voice t o the idea that there should be more effective data-sharing between G overnments and even within G overnments. Often UK G overnment D epartments do not share data with each other in the most timely manner , and they wi ll say they have good reasons for that . I do not want to make an overall judgment , but that is definitely a pattern that we see all the time .
We will return to t he lack of data or the lack of coherent and joined-up data. Thank you for highlighting that .

Q12 I think we have agreed that we all need to work better togethe r. I just want to focus on the UK G overnment strategy separately. I am interested to hear what you think are the key barriers that may prevent Wales from achieving the ambitions of the UK G overnment’s child poverty strategy.

I t depends on what you define as the ambitions in that strategy. O ur opinion of that strategy is that it is not sufficiently ambitious, given all the levers that are at the disposal of the UK G overnment. While we welcome d the decision as part of th e strategy to lift the two-child benefit cap, we know that that on its own is not likely to be sufficient to tackle child povert y. F orecasts by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation show that , over the coming years , child poverty rates are likely to creep back up without further action. I think that is important to know.

It is probably also important to note that the Welsh Government ha ve their own child poverty strategy , and they have a legal duty since the Children and Families (Wales) Measure 2010 to have a strategy to eradicate child poverty. There will be different priorities . W e know that the new Welsh Government are committed to developing a new Welsh child poverty strategy and ha ve particular policies in this area . It is one of their priorities in G overnment, which take s us back to th e question of how well these different strategies work together .

T here is also a point about often UK G overnment policies undermin e efforts in Wales to tackle child poverty. W e heard earlier that although housing is a devolved area, local housing allowance is not, and that is a huge driver of poverty for families in the private rented sector.

Q13 It might have been a bit un fair of me not to outline the themes of the UK Government child p over ty strategy , just so we are all talking about the same things . The main three themes they were looking at w ere boosting family incomes, driving down the cost of essentials and strengthening local support, such as the Pride in Place p rogramme and things like that . T h ey are the strategy themes there. I will come to the same main question for Laurie, please.

On realising the ambitions, we have talked about some of the things already. We mentioned that there is a focus in that on getting people back into work, but a lot of families living in Wales are unable to work, whether it is because they have caring responsibilities or health or disability needs so they ca n not get into work . W e ca n not just focus on work being a route out of poverty because that is not going to work for a number of our families.

Working in silos, as we may have already mentioned, is another barrier that we need to overcome. T here is a lack of indicators and milestones set out . I know that the Welsh Government are now looking at what th e measures and targets could be in the Welsh strategy, but it is unclear what they are in the UK strategy at the minute.

I have v ery similar points , to be honest. On t he depth of poverty that we are seeing and experiencing , trying to lift 32% of children out of relative poverty and deep poverty is a big target , so we would welcome some aligned measures between both strategies. Also the social security system , which we have already talked about , i s not sufficient at the moment to be able to afford those families what they need to not be in relative poverty.

I have mentioned earlier that we have a lack of data and information about families , particularly those with no recourse to public funds , and so they are not even experiencing that safety net — they are unable to access universal credit, child tax credits and so on. We have a very hidden group of children in those families experiencing poverty , and they are more likely to experience deep poverty and homelessness. I do not think we can see child poverty strategies as homogenous; we have to see them as layered.

We gave examples earlier, such as t he Bevan and Barnardo’s reports that found the likelihood of nought to four-year-olds being in poverty within families is far higher than for other age groups. We need to have nuanced, addressed and targeted poverty strategies that are aligned with clear measures around those groups , and the targeted indicators and drivers for change that we really need to see.

In some sense , the challenge is the same in Wales and the rest of the UK. It is just a question of what happens to incomes in general and the fact that the really fast ways of achieving reductions in poverty through the benefit system are also the most costly.

Earnings and employment of course have to be taken seriously as a lever , but I agree that there are challenges. To add an example, there have been policies in the past where , through the benefit system , with tightened conditionality, the UK Government have tried to get more parents into work , but they have got into low-earning or part-time jobs that do not help with long-term career progression . T hat is not going to provide a huge amount of help for families in getting them out of poverty in the long term.

Thinking about the wider ambitions, clearly there are some areas where the Welsh Government have more responsibility for local services or education and health than the UK Government. It will be a question of whether the policy priorities are aligned and whether they are talking to each other and making sure the policies do not undermine each other.

On the indicators point, I think that the UK Government have quite a good range of indicators broadly , in that they are looking not just at incomes but at spending on core essentials and that kind of thing, but it is not disaggregated very much. It is not zooming in on Wales — it cannot because the survey data you need for that is just not large enough in Wales. More evidence would be valuable to answer these big questions of which particular groups in Wales and in the rest of the UK are struggling .

Also , the joined-up working thing is important. Another example I recall from the English case was when the removal of the two-child limit was announced. It was announced quite late , so local councils in England were not able to adjust their own support schemes to take account of it , and some families would have seen lower council tax support because of the UK Government increasing their benefits, which probably was not anyone’s intention. There is a matter of policy announcements happening in a timely manner and the data being shared in a timely manner. That kind of thing could easily happen between the UK and Welsh Governments if policy intentions are not communicated well and the data is not shared. These policies can be designed in tandem.
We will move on to the issues in rural Wales .

Q14 Thank you all for appearing before us this afternoon. Ms Jones, f ollowing on from the UK Government strategy, do you think there are any particular challenges for rural Wales in benefiting from the UK Government strategy?

Yes, definitely. One thing has been alluded to already. For us it is it is not just about the communities that we consider purely rural. We have been doing a lot of work this year with communities in Caerphilly borough . M any of those communities are as cut off from services as those areas that are considered more traditionally rural . One issue that comes up when we talk to families all over the country in rural, post-industrial and coastal areas is transport —that is a consistent theme.

We know that access to public transport provision has fallen . R eliable, accessible bus routes and bus services are really key . T hat has an impact on people’s ability to access employment opportunities and training opportunities, or just to go back an d forth from services or childcare settings , increas ing a family’s likelihood of living in poverty. We know that a third of low-income households in Wales do not have access to a car, and if you are living in a rural area, that makes life much harder. It makes a family’s ability to access support, increase their income or manage costs much harder.

Q15 Ms Crawley, do you have anything to add about the challenges that more rural areas face? I think it is important that we are clear a bout what we mean by rural areas. I suggest that access and transport , or the lack of public transport , might be a helpful definition in that regard, but are there any other specific issues that you have identified for rural areas benefiting from the UK Government strategy?

Barnardo’s in Wales is a town and city-based charity working with families, but when we have worked in rural areas we often see them as quite cut off. For example, in Merthyr v alley communities, if a third of people have no access to a car , they are relying on bus routes . For access to schools and education , i f you live more than three miles away from a school, you can potentially get access to home-to-school transport , but if you live less than three miles away, you do not have that funding support. You could be walking your child to school or ensuring that your child gets to school by walking over five miles a day , and that is putting a strain on time and ability to work — access to transport, access to education.

There is also the oil issue. Rurality often means having oil containers for heating. It is much more expensive, more difficult, much more costly to fill up. We have certain communities living with that issue as well , and no great solution to it at all. That is what we have seen generally, but mostly we are working with town or city communities.
Q16 Thank you. N early 73% of the households I represent are off-grid, so I very much hear your concern about the heating oil situation. Ms Ryall , is there anything you would like to add?

Action for Children in Wales supports a number of families who live in rural communities in north, south and west Wales. Last year, Action for Children took part in the Welsh Government lived experience exercise to get the voices of children and young people. In some of the themes that came from that, families living in rural communities raised exactly the things we have been talking about today—challenges with transport, accessibility of services.

Lack of opportunities for children and young people in those rural areas means they are much more isolated, which affects their emotional wellbeing. They do not have the experience of even leaving their community area , and unfortunately that sometimes can build a generational sense of, “There is nothing out there for me , so we’ll stay where we are”. There are lots of issues throughout rural areas that we need to consider.

From my perspective, one important thing to consider is that the broad income poverty statistics do not take account of lots of the differences in costs between rural and urban areas and the benefit system does not take account of these differences in costs either. Those main levers , and some of the main indicators , are not going to shed light on all of these issues. We all still aware of them because we are talking about them , and that is good, but it is important to bear in mind that there are not loads of indicators that will help us very easily track progress in this over time, which is a bit of a shame. I think there should be a focus on trying to make sure the survey data is there to try to measure the prevalence of these difficulties and test if policies going forward are helpful in addressing them.

I am conscious of time and we have a lot more questions to get through. Your answers are comprehensive , but if the point has already been made , you are more than welcome to reference it and say I have made that point. That would be very helpful.

Q17 On that note, I definitely want to emphasise the importance of transport. Brecon used to have a direct service to Cardiff, which meant that it was easier for local residents to be connected with employment opportunities all the way to Cardiff. Going the other way, it made it easier for tourists to get to Brecon, and clearly tourism is one of our major industries , so that has had a disastrous knock-on impact.

My question is for Tom. What are the distinct economic challenges in rural Wales that we should consider when talking about child poverty? I fully agreed with Sarah when she mentioned the importance of heating oil and LPG , because those prices are going through the roof at the moment.

I do not have a huge amount of detail on this point. Looking at broad patterns in the labour market, it seems that rural pay versus urban pay is a significant factor here. The difference between employment rates in rural and urban areas does not seem great , but the rural jobs are lower paid. That interacts with transport and there is less opportunity for people to migrate within Wales to higher - paid jobs. Beyond that, it is a matter of thinking carefully about what extra costs faced in rural areas might be missed by the system as it is , and what the optimal policy levers are to target them. I do not have a huge amount to add beyond that.

Q18 F orgive me, Mr Wernham, but I am coming back to you on something you mentioned in answer to my question , about how the statistics—please tell me if I am misquoting you—perhaps do not always reflect the differences between the challenges that an urban household and a rural one may have. Is it correct to conclude that the way that we currently measure poverty and the statistics we currently use fail to truly appreciate and give us a proper idea of rural poverty, however we may wish to define rural?

Essentially , statistics are headlining income poverty. They only take account of costs in so far as you have families of different sizes and differences in housing costs. They do not take account of any of the other different costs at all, so they will be very much blind to that aspect. Maybe one area has higher housing costs than another , but because it has better public services, people will want to want to live there. In general, the after - housing - cost measures of poverty are better at predicting deprivation. You need to be a bit careful when comparing areas. Sometimes there can be other things going on, like in that example.

B eyond that, we have our material deprivation indicators and those sorts of things, which should indirectly take account of these different costs in that , even if they are not explicitly asking about the transport and types of heating available — if these things are eating up families’ budgets, that might make them more likely to be unable to afford essentials. We have the statistics there that should be getting at these things. Whether they are really optimally getting some of these specific rural factors—maybe not.

I am not an expert in what those specific factors are so I cannot be definitive on that , but I have made the point several times now that we have really small sample sizes , so even with the best measures in the world, we are asking so few people in Wales — in urban Wales and rural Wales — that the measures bounce about year to year and it is really hard to rigorously keep track.

Q19 On that specific point, the Committee received some evidence last week that touched on the inadequacy of the survey data from Wales just because of the small samples. How useful would it be if, for example, a G overnment body of some sort—I will not name which one—decided , “L et’s get a better baseline understanding here and actually invest in more extensive survey data ” ? How helpful would that be?

More data will always be helpful as long as it is designed in a sensible way. If your goal is to just boost the sample size for income measures or deprivation measures, you would want to make sure you are asking the same questions so you can combine those measures. By all means , ask additional questions to find out Wales-specific information , but you do not want land up with a different survey that is asking questions in a different way so you cannot pull it together. That is important.

Another point is that , with surveys in general, we have seen big drops in response rates in recent years. It is not just about the numbers of people you survey but whether they are representative of the population. We have reasons to think that has got worse even at a UK level. We have not studied specifically what the situation is in Wales but I would not be surprised if we also had concerns about representativeness there. Partly you can get around that by re-weighting the data, which we do, but that is not going to solve all of this problem , especially when you have very low proportions of people answering the survey. Thinking about how you make sure you reach everybody with a survey and how you incentivise people to answer and to give accurate answers is also important.

Q20 T his question is about intergovernmental working . You have already touched on this, so if you have already answered, obviously do not repeat your answer . The question is about the importance of the co-operation between the UK Government, the Welsh Government and local government in ending child poverty. Do you think that those three layers are committed to working in partnership? You have already touched on tha t with the Cynnal payment. Do you think the Cynnal payment might be the first test of such intergovernmental working? Ms Crawley, you started on this, so can I start with you?

Yes, the Cynnal payment is definitely the test bed for us. If we can get DWP and Welsh Government and others working together , and we can get that devolution and devolved powers , that would be fantastic, but they are only suggesting £10 —that is quite small. It will support many families, but it is probably not enough. We have already talked about the benefits system, the social security system , being part of the big driver for getting families out of poverty. I think it is a good start, but it needs to go much further.

My thing is around local authorities understanding their own data — understanding the poverty levels of single - parent households or of larger families , and looking at services that can be targeted towards those communities. We have had certain programmes—Flying Start, Families First, Communities First—for quite a long time. They are supporting families with these issues, but they are not putting money directly in their pockets , when t hat is what they need. I would advocate for a better and greater understanding at a local level —with powers and changes that are devolve d— and at Westminster level.

The Welsh Government have the power to introduce that payment. What they do not have is the power to legislate to give it a longer-term basis — as Scotland did , having fu rther devolution of powers over social security.

What is needed from DWP and HMRC in the short term, just with that pilot, is to agree not to treat that £10 a week as additional income for those families, and to make sure that that pilot is able to operate effectively and that we can see what difference it might make. As Sarah says, it is only a £10 a week pilot, whereas the full child payment in Scotland is just over £28 a week, which per child can obviously make a big difference to families’ experiences. We definitely want to see that full programme and roll out for the longer term. We want to see further devolution of powers over social security to give that a legislative long-term basis and potentially the additional funding that comes with that devolution as well.

C an I add one quick thing to build on what Mabli said about longer-term support ? That is really key . A number of the measures that are in place at the moment provide crisis support , when what we need to be looking at is how we can support families in a much longer-term approach, rather than at the point when they are in crisis and then we are providing crisis grants or discretionary assistance funds. Action for Children continues to provide crisis grants for families, even though they already have access to the discretionary assistance fund, for example. It is that longer-term need that is key.

Q21 I know we have touched on the point about co-operation between Governments quite a lot already , but you may have further points to add . T here are two elements to this question . H ow does having two child poverty strategies — for Wales and at the UK level — influence the degree of co-operation and co-ordination between the two Governments? How could it, or should it, strengthen that co-operation in future?

I think having separate strategies across UK Government and Welsh Government is not a bad thing on its own, but a lot more join-up is needed. We see that there is some crossover across the two areas, but how is the Welsh Government strategy influencing the UK Government strategy, and what kind of consistent measures are there around that? Mabli might have a better answer than me on that one.

I do not know if it is a better answer, but I think you would naturally expect to have two different strategies because the Governments have different responsibilities and powers over different areas. Likewise, some local authorities will have their own anti-poverty strategies for the areas that they are responsible for. In general, our sense is that some of the weaknesses in those child poverty strategies at both th e UK Government and Welsh Government levels in the past have been very similar , in that current strategies from both Governments lack milestones and targets, which is something that we want to see.

Going back to Laurie’s point about how often the programmes or policies put in place are more about dealing with mitigating the impacts of poverty rather than really tackling the root causes, that is something that we would like to see a lot more of from both Governments.

Q22 It is interesting that you say that , because we said right at the start that child poverty has remained pretty constant for the last 20 years or so in Wales. I think that there are similar figures from across the UK. Ultimately, are we ever going to solve this with the types of systems we have now? While helping people in need at the current time is obviously clearly important, are we always going to rely on redistributive policies or do we actually, as you just mentioned, need to get to these root causes? Some of them have been mentioned , including transport and infrastructure. We have talked about jobs , economy and services.

It feels sometimes that we entrench poverty rather than providing services and support to get people out of it. I am probably being quite simplistic there , but it just feels like we are never going to solve this , because although so much great work is being done , the situation has not , as we said, changed in 20-odd years.

I t is a good question. When we are talking about what drives poverty, it is the dual issue of people’s incomes not being sufficient to meet their costs. That is ultimately what is behind the fact that those child poverty levels have not shifted ; people’s incomes, whether from work or the social security system, have not really kept pace with how much costs have gone up. I think if we want to tackle the root causes of poverty, that is where the work needs to focus.

That can be through things that are in the UK Government’s hands, such as the social security system or overall powers of the labour market and the economy, but there is a lot that the Welsh Government can do as well. Housing costs are obviously a huge driver of poverty. The Welsh Government have a lot of powers over housing. They have powers over things such as childcare, which is why we have advocated for more funded childcare hours universally to enable more parents to take up work or more hours of work. There is a very clear link between the number of parents in a household , the number of hours they work and the likelihood of the children in the household living in poverty.
Things need to happen at different levels , but from our perspective , we definitely always need to keep those core drivers in mind.

Q23 The hon. Member for North Dorset talked about turf warfare . Could we talk a little bit more about that ? We have UK Government agencies , like jobcentres , and we have Welsh Government agencies and local authority action. Can we have some real-world examples of where these agencies are helping or hindering in addressing and bringing down child poverty across the country?

From our experience, there are some good examples of where local authorities are providing a single point of access for our families , for example . That single point of access will link into a range of support systems to be able to bring families to one point of contact to say, “This is all the support you are entitled to, this is where you can get it from, and we can help you with that”. That is where it is working really well.

For other families, it is a bit of a postcode lottery because local authorities do not always do that consistently. Then families do not know where they can access support, how they can access it or who they need to speak to, and it becomes a complicated system of application forms and criteria that they do not really understand. Something that is working well is when local authorities have a single point of access that links into all those different areas across Governments, and it is easy to give that information to families.

Q24 You have skills advisers in England. That is done by Careers Wales, but I do not know how. Is there another concrete example of agencies helping or hindering in meeting their objectives ? I do not know whether it is helpful to focus on more specifics. I appreciate your point there about local authorities and single points of access.

In Wales , as a charity we do not support parents directly to get into employment, training or skills. We leave that to existing organisations and parties. That does not mean that we do not direct and signpost them, but we do not do that directly as a charity.

Q25 Do you mind if I change the topic slightly , because I do not think we have talked about education? I was wondering about the impact of education. We have seen the shocking results from PISA schools in Wales. Compared with England , Welsh children are two years behind on science and consistently performing worse. Can you comment on whether you think that has had an impact on a higher child poverty rate in Wales , as opposed to other parts of the UK?

Can I reverse the question? For me, the impact of child poverty is affecting the educational attainment rates for children across Wales, rather than it being the other way around. As I mentioned right at the beginning of the Committee, for children who are living in poor home conditions , with families who cannot afford to put food on the table , heat their home or have bedding or a bed to sleep in at night, that will impact not only on their emotional wellbeing but on their ability to engage well with education and achieve what they potentially could achieve if they had all that support in place and a reasonable standard of living. For me, it is about poverty impacting on education.

Q26 After housing costs, 38% of children in London were living in relatively low-income households in 2022-23 to 2024-25 , but the quality of education in London has gone up. How would you reconcile those figures?

I think it is difficult to compare London and Wales. For a start, they are very different geographical areas . T here are lots of things there. W ithout understanding that dataset completely, I do not know if I can answer that question . Tom, do you have anything to add.

I have done some research in this area that is relevant to this question. We can think of the potential causal direction in both ways. Poor education today might lead to lower earnings in the future, and poverty rates going forward when they grow up.

As for t he other way around, we have, broadly speaking, stark correlations with poorer children doing worse educationally than richer children. The best way to close that gap is not clear. One example we have looked at is the two-child limit , where we were able to evaluate the effect on early educational attainment of the two-child limit. The way the policy was designed meant you could get quite a convincing group who were affected and a group who were not, who were otherwise very similar. Even though the two-child limit drastically reduced children’s family incomes, it did not seem to move the dial on of their early educational test scores at all. That does not rule out effects down the line, but that is one point. That does not mean that there are no interactions between poverty and educational attainment, but closing that gap might be a question of improving access to services and other things, rather than just giving cash income.

Whe re we looked at Sure Start centres in England, they were shown to have quite strong effects on educational outcomes by comparison. To some extent, if that finding is borne out as we look at other outcomes, it does make the job a little bit harder. Do you want to support living standards now or do you want to close some of those longer-term inequalities with more targeted measures, through services and so on? But yes, it is a question where there is ongoing research to do on the causal connection between income and these wider outcomes.

Q27 Can I follow up on Henry Tufnell’s question ? F orgive me, but I am a little confused. Maybe you can help me. Mr Tufnell asked you a question , and you said no. You reversed the question — poverty is feeding into lower educational attainment. The poverty figures show, as Mr Tufnell has pointed out, that London is higher up in the poverty figures than Wales when housing costs are taken into account , and yet London’s educational attainment, notwithstanding that data, is markedly higher than that of Wales. Either Mr Tufnell was asking the question in the right order or your contention, Ms Ryall, is not passing my logic test.

I think the witnesses have already answered the question in the way they wanted to present the ir evidence . If they wanted to reverse the question and say that you cannot compare London and Wales, I think we accept that that is their evidence.

It will manifest itself with some nuance, but if poverty is poverty, and if the lack of a bed, a lack of bedding, a lack of a hot meal in th e evening and so on has a broadly similar impact on an individual , irrespective of where they are living, there must be some correlation, surely, as Mr Tufnell appeared to be driving us towards. You get into this sort of spiral that lower educational attainment feeds into less opportunity for well-paid economic activity. It also reduces the attractiveness for entrepreneurs, investors and job creators to look at a particular area because of the educational attainment. The two are inextricably linked, are they not, irrespective of which end of the telescope you might be looking from ?
That is a fair point, but I still stand by my original point that the poverty does affect children’s educational attainment.

You are not taking into account some other dynamic factors of rurality: lack of access to services in general, educational materials , as well as the opportunities and schools that they might have in London. There are other dynamic factors at play within that position.
Okay, that is a fair comment.

You cannot just compare London and Wales and say that one has higher poverty but also higher education. There are lots of other factors at play in access to services, the quality of the schools and those sorts of things. Where we have been able to do research on the two-child limit t hat isolate s the effect of income while holding everything else constant, i t tells us that maybe if you just give poorer families more money and do nothing else, i t will not necessarily move the dial on these gaps. However, it does not mean that you should not target resources at poorer families in other ways to try to close these gaps.
Absolutely. But let us just tease out—
I am conscious of time, Simon, and we do need to move on.
I just think you are asking us to accept , on the face of it , what you believe to be true , without necessarily having it fully interrogated.

Let us move away from London and look at the figures for the north-wes t. They are—a gain, after housing —identical to Wales, at 32 %. In t he south-west of England , t he part of the country that I am lucky enough to represent — in Dorset —the figure i s 21% . There is clearly a differential between that and Wales. In the north-east , where there will be very similar demographics , geographies , access points and everything else compared with Wales, the figure is sitting at 30%, much closer to the Welsh figure of 32%. Yet educational attainment is better in England than it is in Wales , so there must be something else that is playing into that.
Okay, you have made your point, Simon. Thank you very much.
It was more of a question than a point.
I know, but I am conscious that education is not an issue that we are covering today. We are looking at child poverty —although I accept the links with education.

Q28 You mentioned at the beginning that the data being used here is after housing costs. Can you explain the housing costs and other pressures on Welsh families from rurality, deprivation, deindustrialisation for decades and so on , and that falling housing costs are not a true reflection of the challenges facing our children and young people ? H ow can they can succeed educationally in those communities ? Please provide evidence if you have any .

I think it is important to note that there is a belief that the lower child poverty rates in Scotland and Northern Ireland are in part due to lower housing costs in those parts of the UK, whereas in England and Wales we generally have higher housing costs , and there is a very clear link there with that as a driver of poverty. Members will know that those higher high housing costs apply across the country. P ressures around the supply of social housing, affordable housing and the private rented sector apply all over the country. There is a really clear link there with families’ experiences.

The point about the different measures of poverty is an important one. There is no single measure of poverty that is perfect and that can give you a complete picture of children’s and families’ experiences on its own. What we would recommend, particularly as the Welsh Government develop their new child poverty strategy, is to look at including measures and targets across a range of different measures of poverty. Taken together, they can provide a more complete picture of incomes and costs, material deprivation and depth of poverty, and that is needed to give a more complete picture.
Q29 This is a very quick question. Laurie, you mentioned that there is one local authority that has a single point of access. Which local authority is that?
Cardiff.
Thanks.
I like that answer.

Q30 Over the summer, the Committee was fortunate enough to sit down down with Young Farmers members and were able to speak to teenagers and young people about the impact of rural poverty and so on. Obviously, the voices of children and young people are extremely important. Do you have any good examples of where children and young people have been able to influence you and share their experience , and then see a policy change following the intervention?

Action for Children has young ambassadors who support us. They are from across Wales, but also from across the UK. We have young ambassadors from every nation who can share their experiences with us and share the experiences of other young people and that influences policy change in Action for Children. We give them the space to be able to speak to councillors, MPs and MSs where possible , so that they can directly influence decision making there as well. We also have a young person in our Headlands school who attends the Welsh Youth Parliament. They are able to influence from that perspective, which is a really good opportunity for them , and they feel really valued and heard within that, which is really helpful.

We have also seen that young people are often engaged in consultations and they share their experiences. I think it is important to note that when children share their experiences, they often feel quite vulnerable in that, even if it is just writing it down, because they can be embarrassed, as I mentioned earlier, or it just brings up feelings of trauma that they are having to relive. They do not always hear back from those consultations about what actually happened following that: “What has my voice led to? What changes has it led to? What impact has it had?” We talk about consultation fatigue as well, which is a real thing. I think we mentioned earlier the lack of uptake in surveys and I suppose we do not want to risk doing the same thing to our children and families , and then having them not willing to engage so that we cannot hear what their voices are saying.

I will give you a quick example of where we have raised children and young people’s voices—young carers in Newport. We run a Newport young carers service. The education maintenance allowance was doubled with their voices going directly to the Senedd to say, “We need more money to be able to access our education, to travel to school, to get the books we need and the resources we need”. That is a direct example of young people saying what they need, how they need access to it and what will make a big difference and change. We are trying to do that all the time.

W are speaking about policy changes and practice changes as well , and also directly influencing organisations like ours. How do we direct our services? How do we direct our resources? What do we choose to do that could make a bigger difference? We are always listening to children and young people to try to do that. We are also working with local authorities and commissioners to say where is the feedback that we are getting? What could we do differently with this service? How could we make it more accessible to children and young people? We are always working within that sort of environment, a more dynamic environment of feedback.

We also deliver the child poverty fund through Barnardo’s. Whether we want to see that data or not, what it is absolutely telling us is the levels of poverty and deprivation people are experiencing. One of the things was a lack of opportunities that people, children and young people, experience when they are living in relative poverty and deep poverty.

I just want to give you a quick example. In the last year, we have supported 1,450 children and young people in Wales with a spend of over £126,000 . It is about that sticking plaster — do they need utilities payments, suitable clothing, winter coats? But the one thing I wanted to focus on was that 30% of that spend was for what we called the “ winter wonder offer ”. That was children and young people saying, “I would like a present. I would like th at this year.” That could be a toy, an experience, that they were not going to have access to otherwise.

We have been able to give children and young people some treat s over the festive period , and we have done the same over the summer period as well , because friends might be getting access to days out and trips out and things that you would hope all children and young people want to experience. They do not hav e access to that. It has been charities like Barnardo’s that have stepped in and really given those opportunities. That is where we hear it most and directly from individuals. What do you need, what would you like and what could you have? We can support that.
Q31 You mentioned one example of the impact on a Government decision. Have any other decisions come from young people?

Baby bundles. Although it is postcode related in deprivation , and it is through the Flying Start programme, on average it costs about £500-plus for parents to bring their baby home from hospital and have just the items that they need to ensure that baby is safe, well and supported. We have influenced that through work with families and the Bevan Foundatio n, as I referenced previously, and we now have baby bundles being implemented within Wales, which is fantastic. Again, it is a start for families bringing their children home.

There are particular cases where parents are incredibly anxious about bringing their child home. We have assisted with parenting skills through our Parent Factor programme , and we have the Baby and Me service , where we support families to try to stay together through changes in their parenting ability. That is actually preventing children from being removed, going into care and actually costing an awful lot more money and having poorer life chances. We are always trying to ensure that we can maximise the opportunities for families to stay safely together. Baby bundles are just one small part of that, but they are also reducing and removing stress and anxiety at a very difficult time —a stressful time — for families.

I am mindful of time but let me give one example. We have developed a young carer ID card and app for our young carers in north Wales. That came from young people telling us it is really difficult when they are having a difficult morning with caring responsibilities. They do not always want to tell people what has happened. W e have developed an app that links directly into the school so they can contact the school and say, “We are having a bad morning .” T hat change has made a real difference to the lives of young carers — that communication.

We have also worked with young people around our Jay review, which is around the criminal exploitation of children. Young people’s voices were instrumental in that inquiry , and obviously there have been some changes as a result of the Crime and Policing Act as well.

Q32 I think we have discussed quite a bit the inadequacies of the data available to us. My final question is this: do you believe , from the evidence and the data that we currently have, that we have a reliable and effective picture of the situation facing people in poverty in Wales at all? Is it the case that we have a firmer grasp of the levels of poverty in rural areas versus urban areas , or are there deficiencies across the board?

I do not want to repeat the points that have been made about the quality of some of that data and how it has actually reduced over time. It would be good to improve that data and improve some of the sample sizes in Wales, particularly to allow us to go a bit more in depth for different groups , who is more likely to experience poverty and what that looks like for them.

However, in general , that should not be seen as a barrier to putting policies in place now, because we do know enough about some of the larger groups that are most likely to be impacted by child poverty. That is going back to the larger familie s— those with three or more children — and particularly households with a child under five in the household. There is a very clear link with the likelihood of the children in that household living in poverty, and current policies are not designed to support families with younger children. There is a clear gap there where the data is showing something, but the policies are not responding to it.
Thank you.
Q33 Are there any specific gaps that you would recommend are addressed as a priority?

Families subject to no recourse to public funds is an obvious gap that has been referenced already. We also do not tend to be able to do demographic breakdowns of ethnicity in Wales due to the sample sizes that we have. However, the evidence there is shows that there is a higher risk for households from ethnic minorities to be living in poverty. There are definitely gaps there that could be addressed.

We need to better understand the impact of some of the measures that are already in place. For example, we have Healthy Start vouchers, and we know that there is a good take-up of them and that they are having an impact, b ut what does that mean longer term? What impact are they having? Do they improve the lives of families in the longer term?

It is a very big picture. We can get big-picture ideas of which groups are struggling by looking over a long time period, combining data and thinking about commonalities with the rest of the UK. Really, the gap is because we have small sample sizes , and trying to measure how Wales is diverging and how that is being affected by policies starts to become a bit of a hopeless task. Even though we have some big picture facts we are confident about, trying to precisely measure how things are changing in Wales for different groups becomes very difficult with the data landscape as it is at the moment.

Q34 To finish, we have talked a lot about data today , and a lot of our inquiries seem to find that data is poor across the board. I wonder, though, if we could end on a positive note. Is there anything, with the data that is out there at the moment, that has enabled you, in your organisations or your knowledge, to make sure there is a more effective policy design or delivery? Is there anything you can think of? Mabli , you are nodding .

Following on from my previous point about the link between having a child under five in the household and the risk of child poverty, and the work we did with Barnardo’s on that, I think that has helped us advocate for new policies around increasing access to funded childcare, a child payment for the youngest children, and more support targeted at those families. That is an example from us.

Thank you, Mabli. If no one has anything else to add, I will bring this session to a close. Thank you very much for your time this afternoon. You have given us some in-depth answers , and I am sure we will be using those answers to build on as we go forward in our inquiry into child poverty in Wales and how we can mitigate against it. Thank you all very much .

sessions.iT: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
sessions.w: Alex Weir (Baringa); Marc Hedin (Aurora Energy Research)

segs.tx: Environment and Climate Change Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
Wednesday 21 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Sheehan (The Chair); Lord Ashcombe; Baroness Coffey; Lord Jay of Ewelme; Lord Lennie; Baroness McIntosh of Pickering; Baroness Rafferty; Lord Rooker; Lord Trees; Baroness Whitaker.
Evidence Session No. 4 Heard in Public Questions 37 - 4 6
Witnesses
Alex Weir, Director and Energy Policy Expert, Baringa; Marc Hedin, Head of Research, Aurora Energy Research .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Alex Weir and Marc Hedin.
Q37 Thank you, and welcome to the second panel session of the day. Our two witnesses are with us. Before I move to the first question, I will ask each of you to briefly introduce yourselves.
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for having me here today. I am head of research at Aurora Energy Research, a power market analytics company.
I am a director at Baringa Partners, which is a management consultancy with a big focus on energy consulting. It is very nice to be here.
Excellent. The second panel today will be focusing on market mechanisms and the cost effectiveness of technology portfolios.

Q38 Thank you very much for being with us today. We have heard, not least in the last session, that different technologies are on a different state of readiness for responding to Dunkelflaute events, whether lasting days or lasting weeks. You might want to say a bit about that, but in particular could you say something about the relative cost effectiveness of different technologies? That is an issue on which we particularly want to focus. Finally, could you say whether some technologies have benefits other than stopping the lights going out when Dunkelflaute is with us? Who would like to go first on that? You both look eager.

I will start with small framing point opening statement, if I may . Dunkelflaute is the right place to start because we are building a system that is quite wind heavy, but I also reflect on the fact that it is probably the wrong place to stop. Weather affects all technologies on the system, not just wind and solar. We know that gas plants lose output in hot weather. This happened this summer during the heatwave. Nuclear de-rates when cooling water warms, and there are interconnector fails. One event that came quite close to breaking Britain in the last decade was during the Beast from the East, when a cold snap stressed the gas network. That was not a wind drought. Therefore, we would encourage the committee to ask for a resilience assessment across all types of weather—heat, cold, drought, storm, not just wind drought—especially as our climate is changing and therefore the risk might differ tomorrow compared to today.

To address the first question, we have run a whole-system comparison of two scenarios, one where we honour the firm, low-carbon capacity commitment from 2021, investing a lot in CCS, in additional nuclear, in BECCS and hydrogen and so on, and one that is more a cost-conscious scenario to understand what the impact was on both. We know that that cost-conscious scenario still does include some nuclea r and , some CCS, but it also has a bit more long-duration energy storage, as was mentioned in the previous panel, and more renewables, and it also maintains, which is important, a large unabated gas fleet and adds some gas and diesel peakers as well to ensure that we can address scarcity events appropriately. The difference between the two is about £80 billion over the 2040s in total system cost. That is a reduction of average system cost by about 10% in the 2040s.

The downside to having a lower-cost system is a bit more emissions. We are talking about an extra 6.1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year during the 2040s. Put the two together, removing that last slice of emissions from the power system costs roughly £1,300 per tonne, so the question is whether decarbonising the last percentage of the power system is the best available use of money. This money problem is important because the deeper problem is that by decarbonising peaking capacity we are risking adding enormous system costs, which would in turn slow down the pace of electrification, and it makes the electricity we want people to switch to more expensive relative to gas and petrol. That disincentivises exactly the fuel switching and uptake of electric vehicles and heat pumps that we would like. This is particularly important because electrification of society is materially more meaningful to decarbonising the British economy than decarbonising the last few percentage points from power generation. Electrification probably brings more value for money when thinking about emission reductions.

I agree very much with everything you have just said. We have very similar results in our core cost-effective scenario. It is also around 6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions per year in the 2040s from the power system, which is, as you said, a relatively small proportion of the overall emissions in the economy at the time. The broader point I was going to make is that you need to look at the whole energy system, not focusing too narrowly on the electricity system in terms of decarbonisation.

On the specific point around different technologies, the same applies when you look at technology: you need to look at the technology in the context of the system in which it is deployed. There is no single silver-bullet technology that is better than all others. The marginal value of all technologies decreases as you deploy more of them; that is true of gas, nuclear, wind, solar and storage. When you add an extra megawatt of a technology that is already widely deployed in the system, it is essentially competing with the other units of the same technology. A layered approach is what you need, and what we have. At the moment, a lot of short-duration storage is the most cost-effective thing to be added to the system, because there are still a lot of short-term price spreads within a day that can be captured by short-duration batteries, which helps reduce the amount of gas turn-up that is needed in the short term.

As we build out more intermittent renewable generation, we will need to add longer-duration storage, which is what you are already seeing happening with more four-hour batteries, for example, and longer-duration batteries coming forward. The need for ultra-long-duration storage arises only when you reach very high penetration of renewables and are trying to drive out those last few tonnes of carbon emissions. Those technologies have a role to play, but it is in that tail scenario rather than something that would be cost effective to deploy at scale today.

I have one other question. In the last session, one of our witnesses said that we need to follow up on all technologies. Do you think that is right, or do you think some technologies are so unlikely to be part of the final mix that we need not continue with them?

As was discussed in the previous panel, there is a lot of uncertainty as to when technologies are regarded as proven technically but also proven economically. When technologies are proven both technically and economically, it would be great to implement them in the system. Because there is so much uncertainty as to what that timeline looks like, there is great value in keeping optionality in your system. The gas fleet is appropriate for rare events—perhaps a couple of periods a year of deep and long renewable shortfalls—until we have something that is as cost effective and as technically proven. Many of the technologies discussed in this committee are, to some extent, unproven, even if there are prospects for them, and we can be quite optimistic about them. When we think about the reliability of a system, a reliability assessment is quite difficult to make of technologies that are partly unproven and do not have a history of operations in the system.

I agree. To be a bit sharper about it, I do not think we should say we need everything all at once. I am not sure that is the point that the previous witness was making, but the point about optionality and research and development across a range of technologies is important. However, that does not mean we should be racing to deploy everything at very large scale as fast as we can. That is the recipe for a very expensive system that may not deliver the outcomes we need. There are certain technologies where there has been a lot of research and development already and the costs are not coming down. They look like a relatively unlikely prospect of delivering value in the UK system.

Every power system is different. The natural resources, the demand profiles, the weather patterns and the climates of different countries vary. What is suitable for one country is not necessarily suitable for another. Take floating offshore wind: the UK has quite a lot of sites for fixed-bottom offshore wind, whereas countries such as Japan have very deep waters very close to shore, and floating wind might be the only viable offshore wind solution. There can be value in the UK developing technologies from a commercial and export potential. That does not mean we have to deploy them all at scale in the UK.

Q39 Thank you very much for coming in. Following on from that, I would like to modify my brief her. W hat is the value—particularly the relative value—of investing in firm generation technologies that contribute to improving base load, obviously nuclear, but also particularly tidal and wave, to reduce the amount of flexible generation or storage required in the future?

Nuclear is not the same as wave, and it is not the same as tidal. They each have very different characteristics. Nuclear is a true base-load technology: it should run at a capacity factor of 90% or more. While it is technically capable of flexing its output, that is usually not economically sensible because the vast majority of the costs are in building the asset, and when you build a very expensive asset you want to use it as much as possible so the costs come down. Some advanced nuclear technologies can flex their electricity output by diverting some of the heat from the reactor into a heat store—and either use that heat or use that heat to generate electricity—but the core technology is base load.
Wind and tidal are not base load; they are intermittent, tidal with a fairly high predictability. Wave has much less flexibility and is much more correlated with wind output.

The answer will therefore differ between those technologies. You need to look at them all from a system perspective. It is not just about adding more nuclear capacity to the same system. You would be adjusting what other capacity is built. With more nuclear, you would need some less flexible generation and less storage. You would also need less renewable capacity, because adding nuclear will otherwise simply curtail more renewables.

A system with no nuclear capacity that is very heavily dependent on wind and solar will almost certainly be lower cost with some nuclear capacity. Conversely, a system such as France, with huge nuclear capacity, would be unlikely to find more nuclear cost effective. More renewables would be more cost effective there. Tidal may offer some benefits depending on cost, but it is at the moment still an expensive technology that is still intermittent. It may reduce the amount of very long-duration storage needed, but it will not reduce—
The Chair : Intermittent, but predictable.
It is predictable, but still intermittent. There are times when it is generating nothing, so you still need flexible generation or storage to fill those gaps.
The tide is twice a day, but waves are all the time.

The tide goes twice a day, but the tidal range changes a great deal from spring tide to neap tide. There is a monthly pattern, and you would still need flexible generation and storage to manage that gap. It would reduce the need for very long-duration storage beyond the month, but that is still a very long duration. Wave energy, related to the height of the waves, varies significantly with the amount of wind there is. From the time I first started in the energy field in 2009, when I visited the Pelamis wave snake in Scotland in deployment, to today, the costs are still very far from being cost effective. I personally see very little prospect of wave power at scale being a cost-effective option for the UK.

To continue on wave, if I may, is it not the case that the contracts for difference system makes it difficult for wave to compete, because other forms of marine energy, and certainly wind and solar, are more scaled up, but wave has not had that innovation push from either the private sector or the public sector?

The contracts for difference scheme is not primarily designed for demonstration projects. Other forms of innovation and deployment funding are better suited to those pre-commercial technologies, because it is very hard to raise capital for large-scale deployment of technologies at that technology readiness level. There are separate pots and separate clearing prices for wave—certainly for tidal energy — in the CfD scheme, so they are not having to compete head to head with wind and solar.

We heard in the previous session also that we are looking at Dunkelflaute events and how to mitigate the effects of those. When the wind does not blow, we also do not have waves, and we are in the doldrums.
Tide, so not quite.
We are talking about wave here.
I think you have covered it, but just finally to nail the point: wave energy is not ring-fenced between contracts for difference .
I am sorry, I did not quite catch that.
Wave energy bids are not ring-fenced within contracts for difference. That is the point — it is automatic. That is for the record, as it were.

Q40 Welcome. First of all, we are currently 50% self-sufficient in energy, and it is forecast that we are going to become 90% dependent on imports. Do we have a timescale for that? I know it is dependent on being less r elian t on oil and gas reserves in the North Sea, but what timescale are we looking at?
I am sorry. I am not sure I quite got the question.
We are currently 50% self-sufficient in energy. We are going to become 90% dependent on imports. Is that in 10 years—
I think we need references.
The reference is in the footnotes from an article by one of the bidders in the North Sea scale. It would be good to have it on the record, but you could write to us if you do not have the timescale.
If you do not recognise those figures, please do say so.
You do not think we are going to be 90% dependent on imports of energy in the next 10 years?
I am not familiar with that report. I presume you are talking about all energy, not just electricity.
Yes. As we become less dependent on oil and gas from the North Sea, we are going to become more dependent on imports.
Of oil and gas .
Oil and gas is not my specialist area.

Indeed. That is fair enough. Thank you. I can send you the article; it is very interesting. What, to you, are the cost and energy—and the environmental—implications of importing a greater proportion of our energy in times of high demand and low supply, compared to investing in low-carbon dispatchable power?

Interconnections in the power sector are extremely valuable for most of the year. They help the system be more optimal and more cost effective. They are probably least valuable in exactly the hours that this inquiry is about. The reason is correlation. A Dunkelflaute event does not stop at the Channel. It may sit over north-west Europe and therefore apply pressure on all neighbouring systems at the same time. The one interesting exception is probably Norway, because Norwegian hydro is stored rather than weather dependent, and is therefore far less correlated with wind. However, it is not unlimited, and exports from Norway to the UK are increasingly subject to Norwegian politics and water levels. Norway has become a lot more cautious about exporting into high European prices, because it is already a highly electrified country and does not want to risk high-price contagion to Norway during those critical hours in the UK or elsewhere in Europe.

Does it not help that we are also exporting energy to Norway at certain times? It is a two-way process. I understand we are looking at an interconnector with Germany, which may bring other opportunities but also issues.

For most of the time it is very helpful because, as I mentioned, there is some correlation and there is a risk that a Dunkelflaute goes far beyond the British Isles. However, on many days there is decorrelation and, as my colleague mentioned, all systems are different; they react in ever so slightly different ways. It makes sense sometimes, when there is surplus in Great Britain, to export to Norway for them to refill their reservoir, or to Germany or to France, and vice versa, because it helps to optimise all power systems.

However, if the discussion is specifically about reliability and Dunkelflaute events, I would take some perspective from saying that interconnectors can truly provide reliable back-up in those moments. That is already a reality when you look at the de-rating factors of interconnectors in the capacity mechanism, which are in the 50% to 70% range depending on the interconnector. These already reflect that today. It is not guaranteed that they will be available at all the critical hours.

I agree with all that. I have only a couple of points to add. One of the valuable things around interconnectors is that peaks can occur at different times in different markets, so there is still some capacity and reliability benefit, even if there is a broader Dunkelflaute event.

On the broader point about imported energy as a whole, the availability of gas during prolonged high-demand periods is increasingly under scrutiny. The Government have a consultation out at the moment on gas import capacity, which is focused on the system’s ability to provide the flow rate of the gas, including the imports coming through, rather than necessarily the amount of stored energy that we have access to.

One of the big changes with the expansion of liquefied natural gas and the sources of that is that boats can come in every day, providing quite a high volume of energy, but the key is the ability to maintain peak flow through the whole system. Although that might be seen as import dependence and negative from a security of supply perspective, it does provide diversification, where a Dunkelflaute event here is very unlikely to be correlated with events in other parts of the world that would slow down or interrupt the rate of arrival of LNG. It is important to think about the whole system.
I have one last question. Within the portfolio, interconnectors have a role to play, but they will not be a game-changer in the long term.

I think they are a game-changer from a cost and stability of the system perspective because, for most of the year, most of the time, they are hugely beneficial, as Marc was saying. They are not the silver bullet to ensuring security of supply during Dunkelflaute events.

Imports and interconnectors are linked to international co ‑ operation, and maybe there is a wider point to be made. We were discussing earlier about low-carbon firm capacity and how to decarbonise the remaining percentage of the system that helps tackle Dunkelflaute, for instance. We do not necessarily need to assume that everything has to be solved domestically. That is a fair point, and that is why we discussed interconnectors. That can apply to carbon reduction as well, because carbon does not stop at the border. There might be international co ‑ operation that might be helpful for carbon removals, rather than investing in domestic projects that might not be as cost effective, especially when you compare the pounds per tonne removed of a domestic project with some removal programmes elsewhere.

Q41 Good morning. Thank you for coming. It is an interesting discussion. May I follow up on one point from the last discussion? That 90% figure was mentioned in the first panel today. I did not quite understand it, but I did not feel it was appropriate to come in with a supplementary.

I have a second point about Norway. If the extra water coming into the N orth Atlantic from what was Greenland and the Arctic changes the Gulf Stream and causes the Norwegian coast to freeze, we are in real trouble in terms of interconnectors, because they would be in a very different situation from now. That is not my question, it is just a comment, but it does concern people, given the way things are changing in the Atlantic.

On the issue, the current market mechanisms do not reward the low-carbon assets that are only needed rarely, such as hydrogen storage and retained gas. It is a challenge, in a way, that they become a strategic reserve. In your view, are the existing market mechanisms appropriate for delivering the technologies required at the scale required? If we think about the value of a strategic reserve, could you give your view about how it would be funded—private or public—and whether those controlling a strategic reserve would be able to operate in other markets while holding the reserve? Would that grant them economic flexibility?

On the comment about Norway, I will not respond in detail, but the important point is that we are probably not factoring in sufficiently security of supply assessments, and the risk of dramatic changes to weather patterns resulting from events that are still considered unlikely to happen in the next 30 years, but not vanishingly unlikely. There is a broader point about the risk of major changes in weather patterns that is probably not being considered today.

On the point about market mechanisms, the blunt answer is no, they are probably not appropriate today, but that is widely recognised and there is a lot of work under way. The Government, NESO and Ofgem have been looking at the changes that are needed. One example is the cap and floor scheme for long-duration energy storage, of which phase 1 is in progress. There have also been proposals around changes to the capacity market scheme, the CfD scheme and the way markets operate, as part of the review of electricity market arrangements—the REMA process—that DESNZ ran for about three years, concluding last year.

My broader point around market arrangements is the proliferation of individual policies to tackle specific perceived issues with the way investment signals and dispatch signals work in the market, but they are generally not joined up and frequently send conflicting signals. One of the speakers in the previous session made the point that the CfD scheme does not necessarily factor in the implications for system reliability, which then has to be picked up through the capacity market scheme.

These schemes run in isolation and often optimise for a single metric—strike price in the CfD scheme, or the capacity market clearing price in the capacity market, which is an annual availability payment on a de-rated capacity—rather than factoring in the broader system costs. The other underlying point is the way our wholesale market, balancing mechanism and ancillary services mechanisms work , is also not always aligned with sending the optimal signals for dispatch, investment, stability and carbon.

My view is that there are important changes that are being considered. Some of the ones not taken forward under REMA will probably have to be looked at again by the Government. My broader concern is that these mechanisms do not talk to each other sufficiently at the moment.

One other important point to mention is that the strategic spatial energy plan being developed by NESO is an attempt to look across the whole energy system and provide a view on the overall best mixture of different assets—where they should be and when they should come online—to deliver the lowest-cost system while meeting the Government’s climate targets. That is a valuable piece of work. The question is whether the mechanisms are in place for the Government to implement that plan. That is where I see a gap at the moment.
You described a classic silo effect, and that could be highly damaging and probably dangerous if it continues.

Yes. There is a lot of awareness of the issues, and there are bespoke interventions to try to address them. From a danger perspective, the issue of security of supply is very well recognised and understood. The risk is primarily around cost, where the mechanisms are not delivering the most cost-effective mix of technologies and are not sending the right signals for how those should be operated across the system.

To add to that, our original assessment earlier was that probably the most cost effective and realistic thing in terms of timing—in the next 20 to 25 years—to tackle Dunkelflaute events is to maintain a gas fleet on the system and potentially add some peakers. It is a fleet of assets that would run very little. The timing here is important. The CCGT fleet, for instance, in GB is currently around 29 gigawatts, and the bulk of it is set to retire in the late 2030s and early 2040s. It is therefore important to ensure there is a mechanism to maintain that fleet online. As was mentioned in a previous panel—not today, but earlier in the month— on the cost of refurbishment versus new build versus some of the new low-carbon firm capacity options discussed in this committee, maintaining that fleet on the system is by far the most cost-efficient thing we can do.

At the moment, it does not need a dramatic rethink of the system. The capacity market is a perfectly fine instrument for doing that job in many respects, but it may need some adjustment to remain fit for purpose, and that specific purpose, in the next 10 years. Something else that would potentially be helpful for this challenge is policy clarity on the role of gas capacity in the system beyond 2030, because that would go a long way to reducing the cost of capital for new peaking generation. The policy risk is currently considered very high, which translates into higher debt and equity costs. Providing that clarity would also reduce those costs.
That is i nteresting. Thank you.
To follow up , the Government are currently reviewing the integration of low-carbon technologies into the capacity market. What would you like to see come out of that review?

They are eligible to participate in the capacity market already. The issue is that technologies that are not receiving a separate form of support, such as the CfD or legacy renewables obligation, are often not competitive with unabated thermal technologies, particularly peaking plants, which are relatively low cost to build, and the capacity market pays a capacity payment.

My view is that we need to be quite careful about creating a separate capacity market for low-carbon technology. There is a risk that that leads to much higher system costs and creates yet another separate mechanism, which goes to my point about these mechanisms not being joined up. There may be some issues with how de-rating factors are set in the capacity market, or implicit advantages for lower-capex technologies over higher-capex technologies, so there may be some tweaks that you could make to the rules. However, I would be very cautious about creating a completely separate market for low-carbon technologies.

I agree. Creating more markets creates more distortions to the market and suboptimal behaviour in dispatch and potentially in investment decisions. Keeping the capacity market technology-agnostic seems to be the right way forward. It can be adjusted. As I mentioned, it might require some, probably minor, adjustment to remain fit for purpose in the 2030s, but I would stick with the capacity market that we currently have.

The UK Energy Research Centre said in written evidence—and I think that this was also mentioned by the Hydrogen Energy Association — “ F uture storage assets are unlikely to be financed solely to provide energy during rare multi-week droughts . T heir commercial viability should account for their ability to generate value throughout the year ” . Therefore, we can spend some money, store these things, and use them as firm energy sources as well as to provide the energy to fill gaps during the Dunkelflaute. Would that be viable cost effectively?

That is already the case. Long-duration energy storage has a very high de-rating factor in the capacity market, which shows that it is considered quite heavy for stress events, but it also cycles along the year. Long-duration batteries — six to eight hours, for example — would be expected to help optimise the system day in, day out, ensure lower system costs and contribute to a number of ancillary services. There is a lot of value for the system beyond just responding to those stress events. However, there are currently some limitations that we discussed in some of the previous panels around long-duration storage with respect to Dunkelflaute events. If you have an event lasting three to four days and assets that can only store energy for 10 to 12 hours, they obviously cannot, on their own, respond to that entire event.
We were talking about ultra-long-duration storage. That s hould be possible , yes ? I mean, f or example, compressed air or hydrogen.

For ultra-long-duration storage, can it, and should it, operate in the market outside of extreme Dunkelflaute events? If it is storing a very costly fuel, it often will not respond unless prices are very high. From a commercial perspective, it could be open to doing so, but ultra-long-duration storage can choose very carefully which periods to operate in.

Q42 As I understand it, these salt caverns the UK is blessed with are numerous and can store vast volumes. We are currently paying wind power generation to be turned off. If, instead of doing that, we can use it to either compress air or produce hydrogen and store it continuously, then it is effectively free energy available for firm power generation or to fill gaps, even very long-duration gaps. Is that possible?
It is certainly possible, and people are looking at doing exactly that. I would be cautious about describing it as free energy or that it is necessarily the most cost-effective solution.
We would save the curtailment cost, would we not? At the moment, we are paying people not to generate that energy.
Most of the curtailment costs come from paying for gas to turn up in the south, where the generation is needed.
Is the cost coming from the gas?

Most of the cost is coming from the gas. The most cost-effective solution today is to reinforce the transmission network so you do not have that grid-related curtailment, which is what the plan is to do. There is a distinction between grid constraints and economic curtailment, the term for when there is genuinely more renewable energy generation than demand in the country at that point in time. That is nothing to do with grid constraints; that is when there is genuinely surplus wind power, where storage is, to some extent, a cost-effective solution.
Co-location is important.

Co-location can be important, but if the network is there, then co-location is not necessarily the right answer.
