The issue is more around how frequently you get events of oversupply and whether it is cost effective to build high-capex infrastructure to capture and store energy that is only used very rarely. For ultra-long-duration storage, the critical factor is cost of the capex of the infrastructure to store the energy. Salt caverns are very cheap from a storage cost per kilowatt-hour, but the cost of building the infrastructure to convert the surplus electricity into hydrogen, if it is only being used very rarely—or relatively rarely because periods of oversupply are rare—makes it extremely expensive.

On the point about oversupply, when we think of it in terms of energy volume in terawatt hours, a lot of that volume will be spread across many small, frequent events, for which you do not necessarily need ultra-long-duration storage. The current battery fleet is well designed—or you could add some batteries to it—and a four to six-hour duration is probably sufficient to capture a lot of that oversupply when it arises. There may be an event or two a year when you have a longer period of excess supply.
What I am hearing —please correct me—is t hat you do not think the risk of Dunkelflaute is that high .

I do not think that is what I said. I do think the risk is high, in the sense that it will definitely occur, and the more wind we have in the system, the greater the depth of the event in terms of gigawatt hours and terawatt hours involved. Per year, there will probably be two quite significant events—long duration, in excess of 24 hours—when renewable generation will be under around 20% of its long-term annual output. That is two events a year, which is quite important. The more important question is how we address that and, crucially, how timely that solution can be, because many of the solutions explored have limitations, both in terms of whether they can cope with such a long-duration event and whether they can be delivered on time, when we have a system that will be very wind intensive. As soon as 2030 or 2035, we will have a lot more wind in the system than we currently have. A lot of that wind has been procured and will be delivered. It is about planning for that system.

It is planning for something that will help us fulfil the clean power action plan in the timeframe the Government have set out. What we are trying to do in this inquiry is to see how far along the Government are in their thinking on how they will address these issues. That is the point of the inquiry, and it is about looking at the low-carbon energy technologies that will fill that gap. I will come to Baroness Rafferty for a final question.

Q43 Thank you both for your very helpful contributions. You have already outlined, in part, some of the responses to my question, which is about the short and medium-term key policy gaps that might exist and need to be tackled to address and improve resilience to Dunkelflaute. I think that is the first time that I have pronounced that; possibly correct, possibly incorrect, it depends if it has an umlaut. Does it have an umlaut?
No.

It is au, not ü . Okay, good. I know we have just been talking about some of those issues, and Lord Rooker’s question focused on market mechanisms. Is there anything else you would like to add and amplify so that we can focus on some of these gaps?

I am conscious I did not respond to Lord Rooker’s question about strategic reserve, and that is a point worth bringing up. Some countries have strategic reserves and some do not, and there is a legitimate debate about what is effective and what is not. A strategic reserve sounds like a very sensible thing to have. Reserves are often sensible measures to take against rare events, but the care needed is that the reserve does not negatively affect investment in assets outside the reserve, because that can make the problem worse. I would caution policymakers to not think that a reserve is a silver bullet. There may be a case for a reserve at some point to tackle those very rare but very deep events where assets are unlikely to be commercially viable in the market and so would not be built. However, it would need to be strongly ring-fenced from the rest of the market, because if that reserve is also playing in the market, it will be cannibalising the revenues of other assets built in the market, leading to fewer of those, which requires more reserve, in a reinforcing process.

There is also a risk that if it is playing in the market, it may have been depleted by the time you need it for the one-in-30-year extreme, prolonged Dunkelflaute event. There may be a case for a strategic reserve, but I do not think there is a case right now, and it would need to be considered very carefully to ensure it does not negatively impact the rest of the market.

I have three points. I do not know if they are necessarily new, but they summarise what we have said to date. The first point is that it would be very useful to commission a broader resilience assessment, and I think that goes to your point, Chair. The system is changing. It will be more renewable - heavy and therefore more climate sensitive. We are also introducing a number of technologies that are yet partly unproven in terms of historical performance. The climate itself is changing, so the occurrence and severity of Dunkelflaute events may change in the future.

As was mentioned in this panel and the previous one, there are also gaps in policy design. For instance, allocation rounds are done first, then we think of storage next, and they are not necessarily joined up. It is probably something that the SSEP could consider, in a changing climate and a changing system , how that original assessment should be undertaken.

The second point is to clarify the long-term role of unabated gas, and do it soon. If a small amount of unabated gas is permitted in the long run, the Dunkelflaute problem becomes far more manageable and considerably cheaper to manage. If it is not, the costs can escalate quite steeply. We mentioned around £80 billion of additional system costs in the 2040s to remove roughly 60 million pounds of carbon, broadly 1.4% of the total emissions allowed in the upcoming carbon budgets to 2050. It is a very modest amount of emissions. Either answer is workable; it is more the absence of an answer that is doing damage, because operators planning closures will always assume the worst. If we lose the fleet, it will be quite difficult to get it back on its feet because it takes years to order a turbine and so on.

The third point is to be willing to look beyond the power sector and even beyond our borders for the last few tonnes. A cheaper power system that is nearly clean will cut much more emissions than an expensive one that is perfectly clean, because people only switch to electricity when electricity is the cheaper option. If we want to decarbonise, electrification is the way forward, and to ensure electrification we need a competitive electricity system.

Q44 Thank you. I have a final question for you. Martin Lambert from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies mentioned last week that he thought the carbon price should be raised to around £150 to £200 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent, to incentivise greater investment in carbon capture technology. The higher the cost of emitting carbon, the greater the business case for capturing and storing it instead. Could I have your views on his suggestion?

I think that CCS has a huge role to play in decarbonising the British economy, particularly in industries where there are processes that are extremely difficult to decarbonise with electricity otherwise. For instance, electric furnaces cannot reach the right temperatures for steel and cement. A higher carbon price would incentivise investment in those areas. However, for the power system, we need to be careful of potentially perverse outcomes, because adding more cost in the power system to technologies that will be marginal and that will be setting the price makes electricity more expensive. Therefore, it will make that critical electrification to the grander scheme of decarbonisation more difficult. I would be wary of adding additional costs to the power system for the sake of decarbonising the last percentage of the system.

I completely agree. From an economist’s perspective, carbon prices are a very efficient tool, but they are not applied universally across the economy. The risk of raising the carbon price and applying it to power, but not to gas used in heating, for example, would disincentivise electrification and probably lead to increased emissions overall. There is also the point about international competitiveness. It would probably be harmful for the UK to raise its carbon prices unilaterally, as that would simply cause offshoring of emissions. Any change would need to be done in concert with the EU and with a strong carbon border adjustment mechanism in place. We need to be wary of acting unilaterally.
If you could just indulge us a little bit longer, Baroness Rafferty has a question.

Q45 It is probably a daft question. In thinking about Dunkelflaute and its broader geographical footprint, to what extent are meteorologists involved in these discussions? The energy sector is one thing, and you both mentioned the lack of joined-up policy. Is there close collaboration in considering prediction of these events and understanding broader weather patterns? How do meteorologists and the weather people input into all this?
I think that you had someone from the Met Office in the first session or the second session.
We did.
Did we? I am sorry. I was not here.
It was someone who is currently seconded to NESO. The answer is: very closely.
Good. I am sorry. My apologies.

Q46 I have one final question. The Government are currently assessing the trade-offs between cost and system benefits of different technological options. What would you like to see come out of that? Do you understand, first of all, what the Government are doing in terms of assessing those cost - benefits?
At the risk of repeating myself—
Is it unclear to you? I am not putting words in your mouth at all.
It is unclear to me what the outcome will be. I do not know exactly what decision the cost-benefit analysis is leading to.
It would help the industry with this whole issue and other issues, would it not?

As part of that broader discussion on cost-benefit, again at the risk of repeating myself, there is already a lot that is being discussed in the media and the public domain about the cost of electricity in this country, which is harming the rate of electrification. I strongly believe that a higher pace of electrification in this country is the way forward. It is quite important to reflect on what can actually make the system cheaper. The system will get decarbonised whatever we do. We are procuring a huge amount of renewable energy that will displace gas and other fossil fuels. Over the past 20 years, we have removed all coal from the system and are now introducing more and more renewables. We just need to make sure that the system we are designing is fit for purpose and supports an economy that will become increasingly electrified, especially, as some of the questions pointed to, given the fact that domestic oil and gas supplies are dwindling, whatever we do. In the near future, it will be far more secure for the system to be more electrified than less.

We have a plethora of technologies that we are trying to understand in terms of what they can deliver and how much they will cost. How do we compare them? You must do this daily. Can you help us? I do not mean now, as we are out of time, but could you write to the committee so that we can understand a little better how these technologies compare in the ways that I have asked for? It is a difficult thing to do, I understand, but if you c ould do your best it would be helpful.

I am sure we can send you something. The one point I would make is the one I made at the beginning: it is not about looking at individual technologies. It is about running whole energy system models and varying the technology mix.
Indeed. That is a message we are hearing loudly and clearly.

The numbers I communicated earlier about the £80 billion difference in system costs between two scenarios were based on such analyses. We looked at one system where essentially we are building more low-carbon firm capacity and one where we build a lot less, where anything that has not been committed so far is not necessarily built. That gap comes from there. We were not analysing one single technology but looking at a whole-system approach, because that is the only way to understand the outcomes.
It is an important issue. We very much appreciate you sharing your knowledge with us. With that, I bring the public session to a close. Thank you very much indeed .

Uncorrected oral evidence: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
Wednesday 21 October 2026
10 am
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Sheehan (The Chair); Lord Ashcombe; Baroness Coffey; Lord Jay of Ewelme; Lord Lennie; Baroness McIntosh of Pickering; Baroness Rafferty; Lord Rooker; Lord Trees; Baroness Whitaker.
Evidence Session No. 3 Heard in Public Questions 31 - 3 6
Witnesses
Nick Smailes, Special Projects Director, t he Faraday Institution; Andy McNeill, Senior Policy Consultant, Energy Storage Association.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Nick Smailes and Andy McNeill .

Q31 Good morning and welcome to the Lords Committee on the Environment and Climate Change. Today is the third session of the committee’s inquiry into Dunkelflaute weather events and the challenges they present to the Government’s ambition to deliver the clean power action plan by 2030. Today we have divided the session into two panels. The first will focus on long-duration energy storage solutions and the second on market mechanisms and the cost effectiveness of technology portfolios.

Before we start, I remind everyone that the session is webcast live on Parliament TV and a transcript will be taken and made public. Witnesses will have an opportunity to review the transcript and, if necessary, make very minor amendments. Members are reminded that they should declare any relevant interests the first time they speak, and this applies to all witnesses. I will take the opportunity here to say that I am a director of Peers for the Planet.
I am very pleased to welcome our first panel this morning. I will ask each of you to introduce yourselves.

Good morning, Chair, and good morning, committee members. I am a senior policy consultant with the Energy Storage Association. I will give a brief introduction as to what the Energy Storage Association is so that that is available to everyone. We are a member-supported trade association. As the name suggests, we are focused on advocacy and progressing the opportunities and the potential for energy storage in the UK. We have more than 40 members currently and, more pertinent and relevant to this context, a number of those have a specific interest in long - and longer-duration energy storage. That includes technology developers such as In v inity , Offgrid Energy Labs and Storelectric that are working on novel battery technologies and compressed-air energy storage, which we will touch on in the session. We work with academics at Durham and Keele Universities and a number of other organisations, such as the British Geological Survey . It is a broad church of members focused on progressing the agenda for long-duration energy storage.

Lastly , in this introduction, it would be remiss of me not to acknowledge the relationship we have with the Long Duration Energy Storage Council. It is through its kind introduction that we are joining you today with this opportunity to offer evidence to the committee. Thank you.
Excellent. Thank you for taking the time to be with us today.

Good morning, Chair. Good morning, committee. Thank you for inviting me. I am director of special projects at t he Faraday Institution. The Faraday Institution is the UK’s leading battery science research organisation. We fund research into batteries in academia. We also have an early-stage commercialisation capability where we take the discoveries from our science and seek to accelerate them to market. We are funded through the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade . We started in 2017 out of industrial strategy. We have done three years’ analysis into ultra-long - duration energy storage requirements for batteries . and I look forward to sharing more of that with you during the session.

Q32 Excellent, thank you both very much. The evidence that we have received so far has emphasised the need for a diverse portfolio of low-carbon storage and dispatchable power solutions beyond 2030 to address Dunkelflaute risks. What is the added value of long-duration energy storage technologies such as pumped hydro, compressed air or ultra-long-duration batteries compared with low-carbon dispatchable power?
Apologies in advance if I keep looking at my notes. It is a broad subject and I am keen to make sure that I do not miss the opportunity to share our perspective.

I would like to focus on two elements in relation to this question. One is an obvious one , and I am sure that it is well known to the committee, but I will mention it briefly. That is security of supply and energy security, particularly with low-carbon dispatchable generation, in particular that that is fuelled by fossil fuels. With domestic production in decline, notwithstanding this morning’s announcement on the green light for Jackdaw, we are on a one-way street to increasing import dependence for fossil fuels by the middle of the next decade. I will talk periodically about 2035 as an anchor point. I appreciate that others have different anchor points. I choose that one because that is the end of the system operators’ current 10-year forecast. It also happens to be the timeframe within which we can realistically think about making changes to the outcome when it comes to capitally intensive storage development.

By the middle of the next decade, we are estimated to be around 80% dependent on fossil fuel imports — natural gas. Given the challenges that we are living through today , and did back in 2022, everything that we can do to try to break that dependence on imported primary energy is valuable. I appreciate that low-carbon dispatchable power has other technologies in its armoury, including, for example, hydrogen to power. We will maybe touch briefly on hydrogen to power and its relative merits as we go through the technology section of the conversation.

The main point about adding value that I want to bring to the committee’s attention—apologies to those who already see this—is that if we look at the mid-2030s, give or take the current forecasts, we anticipate that we would require about 29 or 30 terawatt hours of generation output from unabated — at the moment — gas-fired generation. That is not a massive amount against a backcloth of, by that point in time, over 300 terawatt hours; it is still a marginal supply. However, the point that I want to make in relation to that is that at the same time we are forecasting to be curtailing increasing quantities of renewable generation. Again, to use the system operators’ most recent numbers, by 2035 , curtailment—they forecast what is called economic curtailment. For the committee’s benefit, that is when the system is long; we are generating more electricity than we can consume. It is not a locational issue ; it is an energy balance issue. That economic curtailment is forecast to rise from not very much today, a couple of hundred gigawatt hours today, to something approaching 50 terawatt hours.
Why is that set to increase so much?

It increases primarily because of the increasing penetration of intermittent renewable generation on to the grid. As we deliver the already committed and likely future committed offshore wind, onshore wind and solar, the installed capacity grows so much greater than the average use.
So grid capacity is the limiting factor there?

No, not in this instance. Curtailment has two limbs and they are both important because the solutions are different. I will briefly close on economic curtailment . N early 50 terawatt hours —t hat is electricity that could be made available to the consumer and to the market but is not because there is not enough demand at that point in time.

To take your point, Chair, on what is called congestion-related curtailment, that is when there is demand on the system but we cannot get the electricity from A to B. That is what we are experiencing primarily today, and the committee will be aware that in 2025 almost 10 terawatt hours of electricity were curtailed due to congestion. In simple terms, that is about the equivalent to the output from our largest operating nuclear plant for the whole year. We basically turned that off for a whole year because we could not get electricity from A to B.

That will in part be resolved by the Great Grid Upgrade , but at extraordinary cost. The recent NAO report suggested that by the end of the next decade we could be spending well over £150 billion on grid upgrades if we follow the current trajectory, but it will never be fully resolved. Although NESO does not forecast congestion-related curtailment, there are well-known and well-renowned industry experts out there who do. They are forecasting that congestion-related curtailment could also be up to around 50 terawatt hours by the middle of the next decade. Therefore, you could be looking at 100 terawatt hours of electricity generation lost to the system. It could have been generated, the assets were there, they were installed and operating, but the turbine blades were locked or the breakers were open.

That speaks to the as yet underexplored value of long-duration energy storage. If we can store that energy, and not even all of it, in theory we could displace all that unabated gas from the system in 2035. The system on an annualised basis is long in energy. The problem that we have is a temporal one where we cannot supply the electrons at the time that the customer needs them. That is obviously where storage comes in.

This is a gross simplification and I am not trying to suggest that the answer is to retire all the gas generators and replace them all with storage assets, because there are challenges, particularly in the context of this inquiry, on extended-duration events where there may be a significant call on those assets.
That is the focus of this inquiry, indeed.

Yes. The point is that there is an asset that at the moment is being viewed increasingly in the public domain as a problem, which is curtailment. I am personally concerned that that will become a poison pill that affects the continued progressive implementation of renewable electricity generation, because there will be too much emphasis on why we are paying wind farm operators not to operate.
In some ways that it is a good problem to have. We have this free energy — clean energy, green energy — and we just need to know how to absorb it usefully, how to harness it sensibly.

Exactly. We will come on to cost competitive ness later on. If you take a simplified view of the world and say that those electrons are free at the point of supply—that is overly simplified because there could be other use cases for them, industrial growth , and so on— most energy storage technologies would compete reasonably well with unabated gas if they are being supplied by electricity that otherwise would not have been produced. It change s the dynamic in the energy system and it makes it very important that we get after harvesting those and removing that opportunity cost.
Thank you. Do you have anything to add?

I was going to talk about batteries in particular. We agree with you that a diverse portfolio will be required from 2030. We think that batteries over 100 hours of storage can play a very significant role. Unlike combined - cycle gas turbines with carbon capture and storage, 3 terawatt hours of ultra-long-duration energy storage could absorb and use the surplus energy that you have just been discussing with Andy.

Some of these ultra-long-duration energy storage solutions technologies are nascent. What is the potential to scale them up to the tens of terawatt hours that we will need, that we are told that we will need, should a Dunkelflaute event extend for a week or two?

We are funding research now. We have started research programmes in novel technologies, aluminium and iron in particular. We think that they can reach very low costs, which could compete with unabated gas and all the low-carbon technologies. Your next question is about timing, but we think that the research will take another five to seven years. That will get us to a large - scale demonstrator in megawatt hours. The scale-up to gigawatt hours would then take two to three years, so these things would be available in the second half of the 2030s. They are much easier to make than lithium - ion and sodium - ion and we think that we could mass-make them in the UK, design and manufacture in the UK. We believe that they could be deployed in terawatt hours by 2050.

Time is already slipping away. The committee would be very interested to hear more about the state of readiness and the timeframes involved in some of these technologies. We have talked about compressed air and liquid air, and these mechanical sources of energy would be of real interest to us , as opposed to stuff that we have to burn.

Q33 To some extent you have asked — and answered — the question that I was due to ask. The Government, we understand, launched a funding scheme for ultra- long- duration storage projects in September 2026, which is quite late. Could you put a bit more flesh on what you have indicated? To what extent is battery technology a question of scaling up the technology we have currently, a lot of which is lithium - ion and so on, or to what extent are these newer technologies the only way to satisfy the scale that we will need? To what extent are they likely to be deliverable within the time course that we have?

Lithium - ion and sodium - ion will not deliver the economics for ultra-long-duration energy storage because ultra-long-duration energy storage assets will be cycled very infrequently ; o ur modelling is eight to 10 times a year, so they have to be very cheap. Our target is £11 per kilowatt hour to £15 per kilowatt hour , installed. The only chemistries or technologies that will do that are aluminium and iron, and we have done a lot of research on that. The electrolyte has to be aqueous—it has to be water—to reach those costs.

There has been a significant amount of research globally into aluminium and iron , but nothing like lithium - ion and sodium - ion because those have been driven by the electric vehicle market. Aluminium and iron will not be inside a car ever because you cannot get the power out of them. However, they are, in theory, much simpler chemistries to scale than lithium and sodium, because things do not have to be exact, you do not need dry rooms, and you do not need gigafactories anything like what you see in China. Aqueous aluminium, we think, can be manufactured very similarly to lead acid, which we already manufacture at scale in this country, and iron - air will look more like a chemical plant. We have been manufacturing chemical plants in this country for decades and are quite good at it, so we think that we can scale this and reach mass market within 10 years.

Before we move on from the second question on battery technology—and I defer to Nick on the art of the possible and the efforts towards that—from an Energy Storage Association perspective of our members, we have much more of a view on the here and now and what alternative battery chemistries can do to help transition the system in the period while we are pursuing transformational breakthroughs in technology, cost and scalability. The issue here is not having technology to store energy. We can store as much energy as we want. It is a question of cost and, to a second extent, it is a question of land use and how much land you need to host the infrastructure.

Th ere are mature technologies available today , such as flow batteries, redox flow batteries, including those using vanadium and other electrolytes, and other alternative battery technologies such as zinc and zinc gel. We have members who are working in both those areas. They are available now to the market in ability to scale. They are unlikely to achieve ultra-long duration, but every megawatt hour or gigawatt hour flow batteries you put on the front end of an event—because a Dunkelflaute does not start as a Dunkelflaute ; it starts as a supply-demand gap. It is just how long it will run for, so the more you reserve your ultra-long-duration technologies for those low-frequency, high-impact use cases , the better.

If we can be harvesting that otherwise curtailed electricity in the short term and storing it in technologies that are ready, we should be doing that. Obviously, we are doing that; the UK is doing that. It has an internationally distinctive cap and floor scheme for long-duration energy storage. However, the decisions that have been made on the technologies that have been awarded or are minded to be awarded licences in that scheme are very narrow. It is 99% pumped storage hydro and lithium - ion batteries.

That has sent a bit of a chilling effect through the alternative battery sector, inasmuch as : is the UK interested in this technology to the point where we are talking to members who are concerned about whether they should continue with manufacturing activities in the UK, where they are manufacturing already in the UK, and other companies that are declining the opportunity or the option to enter the UK market because they are concerned that what the UK is looking for is lithium and pumped storage hydro ? It is an issue that we are discussing with regulators and with government, but the point that I want to make is that there are battery technologies available in the interim while Nick and the people working with him are working hard on delivering a step change in cost and performance for the future.
Can I follow up on something you have just said? You said that we can store as much as we like; the limitations are economics and land use. What are the land use limitations?

In principle there are none. There is enough land in the UK to host whatever storage technologies we need, but there is competition for that land, whether it is agriculture, whether it is residential. We are already taking land out of rural use for the purposes of renewable generation. We have to be mindful about how much pressure we put on particularly relatively scarce, high-quality farmland , and so on, and the natural environment.
A lot of the storage would be underground, as we talked about in this context. Would battery systems occupy a lot of land?

We will maybe come to that in the balance of the conversation. There are some technologies, things that are storing energy vector in bulk—compressed air, natural gas ; compressed air being the most obvious example. They will go underground. Most of the other technologies are likely to be located on the surface.
Before we go further, we have Lord Lennie and Baroness McIntosh.

Can either or both of you give me a rough cost comparison between the storage solution, iron and aluminium batteries, and the flow batteries? Are you talking ridiculous costs or are you talking modest costs?

For the iron - air and aluminium batteries that we are talking about, the target is £11 to £15 per kilowatt hour , installed. That is a capital cost, and that is everything. That includes the land, the service roads, the concrete, all the electrics. It does not include the grid connection. The energy density, the amount of energy you can put per square metre on a site, is ever so important to the overall cost. At that cost, they compete with unabated gas. A vanadium battery, I am afraid, has a very low energy density. You cannot get very much energy because you have a great big stor e but the store takes up a lot of space. Their cost is well north of £100 per kilowatt hour , installed. Unfortunately, there is not enough vanadium in the world to deliver all the storage that we are talking about in terawatt hours. Zinc is possible but we do not believe that it can reach the £11 to £15 per kilowatt hour.

The last thing that I would say is that on the ultra-long-duration storage batteries we are trying to deliver security of supply to the system. For the unabated gas that currently delivers security of supply, we are trying to replace that at the same or lower cost. The fact that you can store energy and make it available to the system — very cheap energy ; free energy, in effect , possibly — gives you multiple savings for the UK. It is £3 billion a year that we are talking about in our modelling. It is replacing security.

The land use framework said that 10% of agricultural land, prime agricultural land, potentially could be taken out of use. A much bigger issue is that there is a revolt in the countryside against these, particularly the battery storage units that are being built on the back of people’s homes. They have been told that they have to evacuate in the event of a fire. Why can these not be built adjacent to factories? I honestly believe that there will be a riot in the countryside if this persists.

I live in the countryside and I do not want to see batteries built beside my house. We believe that these batteries, first, need to be built very close to where the offshore wind makes landfall, because this is firming up wind generation. It is turning wind into something closer to baseload.
There are solar farms as well, to be fair.
It would sit beside solar farms but—
That is a different issue altogether. We are not going to discuss solar farms.

The majority of these, the mega sites we call them, would potentially sit on sites that are currently marked for gas turbines, for CCGTs. You might have heard me say aqueous. We believe that iron - air and aqueous aluminium will be significantly safer and not prone to thermal runaway like lithium - ion and sodium - ion.
We are not talking about lithium - ion batteries here.
There are safety aspects.
These will be different. These will be safer than lithium, which is what I think the public are worried about.

Q34 I know, Mr Smailes, that you have been working on this for some time — energy systems capital. We have heard about the length of time that it will take to get the solution that everybody is aiming for. There is another, and you have started going into this, about compressed - air and liquid - air energy storage in the UK. I remember being a bright new MP 15 years ago or whatever and being told that it was the future then. I want to get a sense of how much storage capacity these technologies are expected to contribute. The briefing says by 2040, but I would like to know by 2030 and 2040.

If we talk specifically about compressed and liquid air, these are effectively proven technologies. There is not a lot of technology risk left. We know how to compress air, we know how to liquefy it, so they are ready and available for use. Their footprint in the UK currently is pretty modest. One very positive thing, despite my critical remarks in relation to the technology diversit y, or lack of it , in the cap and floor window 1 minded - to list , is that there is one compressed - air storage project in there. It is relatively modest in scale , 15 megawatts generation capacity, but it has a 30-hour duration. It is demonstrating that you can quite readily scale that technology to deliver over longer durations, so there is some sign of progress in relation to compressed air.

Compressed air works in two contexts. You either put it in tanks on the ground and then it is a bit like any other form of surface storage, a battery or whatever, or, in the case of this project, which is with Storelectric on Teesside, you put it in a salt cavern—these happen to be existing salt caverns—where you have a much bigger tank that you can operate. Compressed air in particular has a potential to scale under the tip of the iceberg, if you like.
What do you think will happen, though, with liquid air as well?

On liquid air there were projects that bid into the cap and floor window 1 ; they were not successful. There is a company that many of you may be aware of, High v iew, that is currently building, outside of the cap and floor scheme, a commercial-scale facility at Carrington in Manchester. That will, I hope, come online relatively imminently. It is not a member of ours so I cannot speak authoritatively, but it is making progress. I think that is a 50-megawatt to 300-megawatt hour facility, so it is at meaningful scale. It is not necessarily grid scale, but it is getting there. The potential is there.

The UK is lagging, I would say, internationally in many respects in progressing diverse technologies. We are very much focused on pumped storage hydro and lithium - ion at the moment, but there are compressed air and liquid air projects, particularly in China. China over the past 24 months has commissioned a large amount of liquid - air and compressed - air storage.
Coming back to the UK, what do you think the likely share of the capacity will be — 1% , 5%?
By 2030, it will be a fraction because there simply is not the project pipeline to deliver it.

By 2040, depending on the actions of policymakers, both technologies have the potential to scale beyond their current projected capacities. I would have to go and look up the exact numbers to see what NESO is forecasting for 2030 and 2040, but they are still forecast to be peripheral technologies. If you bear with me briefly on compressed air, the distinctive factor with compressed air is its ability to utilise underground storage. We are currently using a fraction of the salt cavern storage potential that the UK has. Salt caverns are very good for storing energy — much better than depleted oil and gas reservoirs, for example.
Are they located well around the country?
They are , unfortunately , concentrated—
In Yorkshire and the north-east?

Yorkshire, Cheshire and Dorset. They are available in shallow water offshore, but that obviously complicates development. I think that we should increasingly be looking at our salt cavern capability as a strategic asset and then deciding what would be the best use of that between natural gas, biomethane, compressed air and hydrogen.
If compressed - air storage is competing with hydrogen storage, which is the more dense energy solution?

The pecking order, if you like, is that you would start with natural gas. I mention that not to do a deep dive on biomethane, but I think that biomethane is one of the neglected opportunities for ultra-long-duration energy storage. We are used to storing natural gas. We can produce biomethane domestically. If we store it instead of using it to fuel my gas hob or my gas boiler at home, which can be electrified, that is a strategic national resource.

Natural gas is four to five times more energy dense than hydrogen, much easier to use in terms of transportation and end-use case. Compressed air is much less energy dense than hydrogen, because you are not combusting, you are not releasing chemical energy ; you are just releasing potential energy in the form of pressure. It is, give or take, in the region of 10 to 15 times less energy dense than the equivalent amount of hydrogen.

That might lead you to ask : why do we not put hydrogen in these tanks ? The challenge is that you have to look beyond that and largely look at round-trip efficiency — how much electricity you have to use to generate the hydrogen to generate the power. With the best will in the world, the current round-trip efficiency for hydrogen is in the high 30 s in terms of percentage , whereby for compressed air it is mid 60% and climbing.
You have answered my question. Thank you very much.

Q35 I would like to turn to water and what have you. What is the potential for the new pumped hydro and the pumped thermal electric storage in the UK and what are the barriers and delivery timescales? I am very interested in the amount of land that these will take up, because , as you mentioned earlier, there is a lot of pressure on space, particularly in the south.

The UK has a relatively proud history of pumped storage hydro but we have not built any for 40 years. The big success story from the cap and floor window 1 , which is intended to facilitate the next wave of long-duration energy storage development—I will just check my notes —t hree projects in cap and floor window 1 , over 50% of the generation capacity and the storage capacity have been allocated to three pumped storage hydro projects. They are obviously geographically constrained. You can build conventional pumped storage hydro only where you have enough of a height difference and you can have freshwater storage at the top and the bottom. Those projects are all reasonably mature.

We do not follow the pumped hydro storage sector closely because there is another trade association there, the British Hydropower Association, which does a very good job there. The potential is there; in fact, we are banking on it. In order to deliver long-duration energy storage requirements for the middle of the next decade, those projects need to be delivered. There will be risks associated with delivering any large capital project. I would hazard a guess that those three projects alone will cost somewhere between £4 billion and £5 billion.
When will they be ready?

They are currently slated to come on — one is 2030 and the other two are 2033. Typically, the lead time from final investment decision to commissioning on a pumped storage hydro project could be anywhere between five and 10 years. The civil engineering project is on a colossal scale. But the developers are committed to delivering those, and some of those are serious companies, such as SSE, which has the largest of those projects in Coire Glas .
I would like to briefly mention other forms of pumped storage hydro. You may be familiar with high-density pumped storage hydro.

Before you do, it seems from the notes in the briefing we have that the amount of power it will produce over any length of time is still pretty modest. We are spending huge amounts of money and it is still 10 years away, which seems to be the magic number that keeps coming back at the moment — whatever we do, whatever the cost. They are trying to get us there in 2030. It seems that we are some distance away.

The reason that that timeline has kept moving out has not been to do with project pipeline or project definition ; it has largely been to do with revenue certainty. In a rapidly changing energy market, without the cap and floor scheme there was not a policy landscape in which these projects made any sense commercially.
That is definitely a key barrier to it?

That was a key barrier. The cap and floor scheme has been designed and implemented. I have to say that it has not yet been proven, because it will be proven when projects take final investment decisions. I think that the earliest, realistically, will be the middle of next year for projects in window 1 taking final investment decision. The quantities are modest in the grand scheme. Pumped storage hydro is not the solution to Dunkelflaute , but it is part of the armoury that reduces the load on ultra-long-duration technologies by managing those higher-frequency, lower-impact events at the front end of the supply-demand gap distribution curve. Because it is a mature technology, it is reasonably energy efficient. You are looking at typically around 80% round-trip efficiency.

The reason that I want ed to very briefly mention high-density pumped storage hydro is because it is a slightly different prospect. It is an area the UK Government have invested in through their L o DES scheme with a company called RheEnergise down on the Dorset coast, which has a demonstrator running now successfully. The key benefit of high-density pumped storage hydro is that it uses a high-density fluid. The fluid is two and a half times the density of water, so you need 40% of the height difference to get the same amount of energy output. It opens up a much broader range of geographies for the deployment of that technology.
What is the liquid being used?
It is a proprietary fluid that is blended using weighting agents to be stable so that they do not settle out. I know of them, but I do not work directly with them.
Can you comment on pumped thermal?

Pumped thermal , I would say , is in its infancy in the UK in particular ; in fact , perhaps globally. It is an exciting technology because of its ability to scale and its ability to generate efficiency, but we have had limited traction in the UK. There is one company — again , supported by the LoDES scheme — SynchroStor , which appears to have done some great work on de-risking some of the core technology at the middle of the concept, but it has not got any traction at any great scale. There were no pumped thermal projects bid into cap and floor window 1 , which by definition means that none of them was sufficiently technologically mature.
So 10 years is probably well out there in this case.

Yes and no. It all comes down to application of effort. If the incentives are there, if the drivers are there to drive the level of technological innovation and development, stuff can be done very quickly. Again, the science and engineering is well known, it is just applying it in a slightly different manner.
Going back to land use, this is underground, am I right, rather than primarily above ground?
Pumped heat?
Yes.
Most of the technology platforms that are in existence at the moment would be above ground.
A space stealer.
Yes and no, but we need space. I do not think that we should be—I may have set the hare running by talking about land use competition. Apologies if I have.
Not at all.

We will have to use space. What we have to do is use the space that we have created. We have to reuse brownfield sites. Nick was talking about repurposing as we retire gas-fired generation, just the same way as we have retired coal-fired generation. It will be cheaper to build on green fields, it always is, but we need to have the courage of our convictions on planning to make sure that we recycle brownfield land and grid connections so that we do not proliferate the system with unnecessary grid connections and so on.
Keep it pragmatic.

Q36 If you were the Secretary of State, what are the primary policy gaps that need to be addressed to accelerate the deployment of long-duration energy storage technology? In order, what are the things that need to be addressed?

In terms of the batteries, they will not be allowed to generate or to optimise their revenues from participating in the market because they will be used primarily in a way that is consistent with optimising system security. That has two implications. First, that asset will have to be controlled by the system operator because it is a national asset. It needs to be there for security and it needs to be there to minimise system costs, and that will require an operational reform.

Secondly, because this asset is not necessarily being used to maximise revenue and return on investment, because the regime will be about security of supply rather than optimising profit, investors will find this a very risky asset and therefore there will need to be payments to eliminate that risk, much as we do with nuclear and reserved generation today. Those would be the two for ultra-long-duration energy storage batteries. Over to you, Andy.

Thanks for giving me a break. I will just give the highlights of them and if there is any additional information on the details I am happy to cover that. The first one that I mentioned briefly already is to improve demand signalling for long-duration and ultra-long-duration energy storage. Everyone at the moment is trying to answer the question for themselves. Nick and his team have spent an extraordinary amount of time and work trying to do this. There are consultants; there are bodies around. We would like to see a centralised view on what the actual demand is for long-duration and ultra-long-duration energy storage and the asset that will best serve the system. That is one.

A second one links to your introductory remarks, Chair. You said that we need diversity, we need everything. I think that we need to be encouraging diversity. It is too early to be picking winners in this space, because we have not done this for so long. If I look at the cap and floor scheme and the capacity market that currently exists, we should be further developing those to make sure that we do not squeeze out promising technologies before they have had a chance to develop and mature. At the moment, it does feel like we are falling back on the trusted or proven technologies around hydro and batteries.

A tangential point to that is that we would also like to see a second round of the LoDES scheme — longer-duration energy storage. It was a grant-funded scheme that ran 2022 to 2024. It was valuable in developing some of these technologies such as high-density hydro and vanadium flow - battery technology, getting to the point where they could bid at a commercial scale for something like a cap and floor licence. When you are looking at grid-scale development, there is a big difference between having a technology demonstrator and having a commercial project. That difference in implementation is hundreds of millions of pounds, but even in speculative capital it is tens of millions of pounds to get to the point where you can compete. That would be a related point.

Maybe the bigger policy ask would be on better integrating public procurement across four key areas. Long-duration energy storage we have spoken about a lot, but linked to that are related processes around the allocation round process for renewable energy generation. At the moment energy storage is the tail-end Charlie. We are trying to mop up after the renewable generations come on the system. We need to get ahead of that so that we do not have this curtailment challenge.

On the transmission and distribution network investment plan process, at the moment there is too much emphasis on grid reinforcement to move peak volumes around the system with pylons and cables. If we are smarter with the way we use storage, we can minimise the need. That £150 billion to the end of the next decade maybe does not need to be as much if we are smarter about how and where we deploy those storage assets.
The last part of that is the capacity market. In terms of policy, that is a real opportunity for government to get better joined-up thinking.
Just briefly, were you referring to contracts for difference? How do you think that should be improved?

That was a great set-up. Thank you for that question. That lets me make another point very briefly, which is that the contract for difference process has now matured. It has been running for many years. Perhaps it is time to put a bit more challenge back on to the developer side of that equation. Linking it to storage would be to ask them to take responsibility for shaping or firming some of their delivery.

At the moment the developer simply generates whatever it generates and the system operators try to work out how to balance it. If we can get to a place where we start shaping some of that, as Nick was describing , at the point of generation, perhaps evolving the CfD process to introduce an element of shaping requirements , a s a developer, you then have to put some emphasis on storage. I do not mean to just turn that all on immediately, but that could be a ratchet mechanism over time that , as the generation technology matures and the market matures, to get the revenue certainty that they get from a CfD they have to work a bit harder.
Finally, presumably this would help with intermittency.
Absolutely, 100%. If we can manage intermittency at the point of generation—it is called shaping or firming—there is less requirement to do that balancing further down the value chain.
Thank you, that is very helpful.

Can I ask a quick question about pumped storage? Presumably, our current pumped storage is operating from time to time all the time to help balance the grid. I live in highland Scotland. You will know that we have dams everywhere, but we get only something like 5% of our electricity from current hydro. I cannot believe that the environmental damage that would happen with some of these schemes— Earba is a beautiful place; I do not know whether you know it —
Yes, I do.
—would make any difference to provide the scale that we will need in the future. Is that a fair point?

It is a point. I do not necessarily agree with it. I also live in the Highlands. I do not live too far from Cruachan , where one of the original pumped storage hydro schemes was. It comes back to needing everything. We genuinely do need everything. I agree with the point that when you look at the total capacity that those three projects will deliver, it is about 88 gigawatt hours of storage capacity. If you are looking at terawatt hours, I appreciate that that feels like a drop in the ocean, but I go back to my earlier point that we need technologies that are better suited to addressing the front end of the distribution of supply-demand gaps so that you can minimise the amount of investment that you need to put into that “break glass in case of emergency” ultra-long duration. That is maybe where I would agree but differ slightly.
There is an environmental cost.

We have to come to a close here; we are well over time. Thank you very much for your generosity with your time and for taking the time to be with us today. Thank you very much. We will finish the first panel.

Witnesses: Chris McDonald MP , Alexandra Jones, Kanishka Narayan MP , Ollie Ilott, Baroness Lloyd of Effra and Sarah Connolly.

Welcome to today’s meeting of the Science and Technology Committee. This is our second session on the machinery of g overnment changes that were announced before the summer recess. Today , we will be looking at ministerial responsibilities and what the changes mean for the future of science, innovation and technology policy and decision making. We are very pleased to be joined today by Nigel Huddleston from the Digital, Culture, Media and Sports Committee : this is an early example of how we will be working across C ommittees , and I am sure the Departments will be working across Departments as well. We are very pleased to have Ministers and officials from each of the three Departments most affected by the abolition of D S IT ; m any thanks for joining us today and demonstrating that the abolition of D S IT will not lead to less scrutiny of science and technology.

Before we start our main session , I want to turn briefly to the provision of information to our C ommittee by Departments. Since the machinery of g overnment changes, responses to correspondence and reports from our C ommittees have been regularly delayed beyond agreed deadlines. This is something that the Committee does not expect to become routine. Can you commit to underlining to your respective teams the importance of timely engagement with this Committee ? I see all the Ministers are nodding, which is great ; I will accept that , and thank you very much for that .
Could each of you introduce yoursel ves in response to the first question presented to you ? T he first question from our C ommittee is from George Freeman.

Q56 Morning , all. As a veteran of a few g overnment machinery changes, may I thank you for your time this morning ? We have heard quite a lot of concerns in previous hearings about just the damage and the risk of disruption, leav ing aside everything else. As you know, in the last two years we have been very focused on applauding the Government’s announced increase of funding and the focus on industrial strategy , and have been focused on how this actually plays out across G overnment. You will have seen our report, “ Flying Blind : Innovation, Growth and the Regions ” , asking which money is being allocated to which geographies and which sectors , so that we can track delivery.

I want to ask about three things this morning: first , the disruption, secondly , the budgets, and thirdly , the political vision and delivery leadership. I am going to focus on Minister McDonald and Director General Jones . Minister, with the vision, the aim and the political side of this , t here is no perfect structure, but can you update us on what the rationale was for getting rid of the Department that , in its creation, had sent a signal that we were putting science, innovation and technology at the heart of Government? In particular, how is the delivery governance run? You have two Ministers in Cabinet, a Secretary of State for DBIST and a focused AI Minister. That can be a strength and potentially a cause of some clash. I am keen to hear from you the vision and then the political implementation, and then perhaps I will come to you , Alex, on the money .

Thank you very much, George. You are right : you have been through a few machinery of g overnment changes yourself as well , and you would probably agree with me that the civil service is incredibly adept at following those instructions. Of course it comes with some cost, as any restructure does. It is very important to set out the rationale for it, as you say.

To my mind, in any sense—you will forgive me, I am an engineer and I come to it from an engineering perspective—form always follows function . Y ou have to adapt the form of g overnment to the function that you want it to carry out. We are fortunate in that the Prime Minister has given a very clear objective; in fact , he gave that objective very directly to me when he appointed me to the job. What he said to me was that he wanted to put science back in the service of industry. That is a really strong focus on the application and commercialisation of science. I know that this is something that you wrestled with when you were Science Minister too; we recognise that the UK punches well above its weight in terms of curiosity-driven research, basic science, but that much of that science is commercialised overseas.

Despite the fact that the Prime Minister gave me that objective, I was very clear in a speech that I gave early on to the Universit ie s UK conference that that does not in any way diminish the work that we are doing on curiosity-driven research. That is quite clear , and t he funding remains for that ; it is protected. What we need to ensure is that those results bear fruit in the UK economy for the advantage of people in this country. Really , it is about ensuring that that end-to-end pipeline of commercialisation works. I have a bit of experience of this ; this is the job that I used to do in industry. It is hard, it is very difficult to do, but we have the best advantage in the UK because we have such a strong fundamental science base.

That is the overriding objective. There are many things we need to do, but there are two things that it strike s me that we need to do to be successful at that. The f irst , as I have said, is to really strengthen the pipeline of scientific discovery, but we also need to expand the industrialisation capability . T hat downstream science activity happens in collaboration between Government and industry , and a lot of the activity happens in industry as well. We have seen a decline in industrial research floor space in the UK over a long period of time. Much of that is associated with the fact that we have had a decline in large industrial UK headquartered firms , so t here is a structural aspect there. Government need s to help to commercialise the science, but also to intervene in such a way as to encourage firms to invest in industrialisation capacity. The support we have had for many Governments over many years around the Catapult n etwork is an excellent example of that.

Q57 I have two quick supplementaries on that. First, I support science in the service of the economy but I hear concerns, including one we had from Sir Paul Nurse and CaSE and others, that this is a relegation of the importance of b lue s ky. As you know, quite a lot of scientific progress is accidental and not planned. Can you reassure us that the core science budgets are not going to get top-sliced with defence, AI, and all sorts of other priorities?
Secondly, in Cabinet, who is really in charge and how do those tensions get mediated? Is there a Cabinet Committee ? W here does the clutch of Government really sort those tensions?

I will answer the first part of your question; I might defer to Kanishka on the Cabinet side, as obviously he sits there. I am very grateful that you have asked that question , as in every opportunity I have I am keen to provide reassurance around discovery science. As I said, I did it in my initial speech to Universities UK and am very happy to do it here as well. The Secretary of State also said the same to the Business , Innovation, Science and Trade Committee yesterday. This is not a diminishment of scientific discovery, but it is about ensuring that we capture as much of that scientific discovery as possible in the UK. We are clearly not going to catch all of it : there are spill-over effects that benefit the rest of the world . T hat is fine , and we should be really proud of that.

At the moment , the drop-out rate of companies that are spin-outs of universities or that manage to get early-stage funding and then depart from the UK economy is a loss of economic activity for the UK, so it is how we deal with that. Aside from the high-level machinery of g overnment change, even within my brief the bringing together of both the science and the investment portfolios actually gives a much clearer direction to the investment side that the investment activity is not really about just passively responding to the very many inquiries that we get for investment in the UK , but about directing our investment strategy towards commercialising science as well.

Q58 In which case the tension could go the other way . W e have heard people saying, “Look, we are really worried, there is a big focus on AI, defence, and growth.” Minister Narayan, you are in Cabinet alongside the Secretary of State . C an you reassure us on how those tensions get mediated, and who protects basic science?

Thank you for the question. The Chair asked us for a brief introduction, so I am the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, sitting across the O ffice for the Prime Minister and Cabinet, as well as BIST , the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Department.

I noticed with interest your observation , born of experience, that either this can be a great thing , in terms of having two representations for the voice of science and technology at the Cabinet table, or it can be a challenging thing. I am very determined to make it a great thing. The way it is working at the moment is that I am a Minister of State in the Business Department, so the Business Secretary and I are precisely aligned in having mediated questions of how different sectors in the science and technology landscape are engaged . W here there are trade-offs , those are made internally in the Department. We then represent that at the Cabinet table.

You will know that , regardless of the more recent machinery of g overnment changes, there are clearly trade-offs across different sectors . F or example , you talked about defence relative to science, so those are mediated there. The National Economic Council and the National Security Council engage on areas where there are also trade-offs involved on both economic and security aspects. The fundamental thing I would say is that , whether it is in the realm of AI or indeed in defence or in science, the task that we are focused on, both in the BIST Department and specifically on AI through the OPMC, is to make sure that we are getting the biggest upside from basic science right across those areas as well.
Q59 Can you give us an example of a trade-off that you are pleased has been well managed?

Let me give you one specific thing, and it is clearly in the realm of AI. Historically, I have been incredibly keen that data assets right across different parts of Government be used in a way that support s British science, British technology and British firms. By being able to co-ordinate across Departments through the Prime Minister’s AI t ask f orce, working closely with the Ministry of Defence, we were able to be the first country to prioritise working with Ukraine on securing real-time battlefield data. We are t he only country so far to have be en able to do so for British technology firms , doing fundamental pieces of innovation but also then commercialising that. To me, that is a pace and a prioritisation of progress that is distinct and is born out of the structure that I have described.

Q60 Alex, you are a veteran of these changes as well . Can I ask you about the budget and the allocations? W e have heard a lot of early announcements of the £86 billion, the record funding in four years. I observed as Minister that we made a record announcement in 2021 and it took about three years to work through the system, which is my first point. We have all heard big announcements on extra funding for AI, data and defence. Can you explain whether , and how , that is not going to reduce UKRI’s core research budget, and if there is extra money? When are we likely to hear what those allocations are? We are going into a B udget next week. We are flying blind as well at the moment , and we do not know what has been allocated where . T his could lead to some quite big changes, and cuts in what we had thought w ere the budget s . Can you reassure us?

As you know, we published t he UKRI s trategy and set up all the allocations of the budgets, and we are working through actually implementing much of that. Some of the announcements you have seen on AI have absolutely been part of UKRI’s budget. T here are three buckets: discovery research, Government priorities and scale-ups, and it has been looking at how you allocate from those Government priorities and scale-ups to make sure we are investing in AI and other technologies. Those have been met within budgets.

All Departments are contributing towards defence , and we are working through the details of that now. As you know, much of UKRI’s research also contributes to defence. It continues to be the case that about half of UKRI’s budget, if you include talent and infrastructure, is going towards discovery research, and that is something that, as the Minister has said, we are really committed to do ing . One of the opportunities of the machinery of g overnment change is to just make sure we continue to have those conversations across G overnment, but also in the Department for growth and a D epartment that is thinking about resilience, to make sure that, as discoveries come through — we do not know where they will come from — we are able to make the most of them.

Q61 To be clear, your Department gave us very clear information last year : UKRI’s budget on bl ue s ky was £14 billion, on g rowth was £7 billion, on s overeign m issions was £8 billion and on t alent i nfrastructure was £7 billion. Do those numbers still hold, or are they likely to change in light of these announcements ? W hen will we know?

The machinery of g overnment has not changed those budgets. We are working through the commitment across all Departments to contribute towards defence ; we are working through those details, absolutely, and we will be able to update on that more in the weeks ahead. The machinery of g overnment change has not changed the way we are allocating UKRI’s budgets. It has enabled us to make sure we are bringing that together, particularly on the second and third buckets with, as the Minister said, some of the investments, the scale-ups and the trade, and thinking about that in the round.
Q62 This is m y last question . W e see local g overnment reorganisation s , we know their costs and we know that the benefits are questionable. What is the cost of this reorganisation?

We do not know yet. Departments are absorbing the costs within their administrative budgets, as is always the case, so we are working through that. It is also being assessed by the GIAA to make sure we are doing this in the correct way, so we will not know that as yet but we are working through it, and it will be absorbed by admin budgets in the usual way.
Chair, the scene is set.
Q63 O n that last point, you say you are working through the costs. Will they be published? Will we get a figure to say that this machinery of g overnment change costs x , y or z ?

I would need to come back to you on the details of that, but we will certainly be publishing d epartmental budgets in the usual way. We are sorting all of those out now, so let me come back to you on the full detail . W e are definitely planning to evaluate it and look at the implications.
Kit has a very quick question.

Q64 I need to declare my interest, if I may : I am chair of the a ll -p arty parliamentary g roup for l ife s ciences, and I chair an artificial intelligence company focused on public protection and national security, building sovereign capability.

When you publish the numbers, are you able to tell us what each of the Departments is going to be spending less on as a result? Obviously if they are absorbing it, it means they are having to find that cost from elsewhere.
They will be absorbing it in the administrative costs rather than the wider issues.
The administrative costs come out of the CDEL in each Department .
A very good point.

Q65 There will have to be an allocation from other budgets or you will have to fire people. The money just does not appear from nowhere. If it is spent on this, it means it is not being spent on something else or being returned to the Treasury.

It does not tend to come from CDEL . I n the m ai n , it comes from the RDEL side of things. We will absolutely be reallocating resource, which is always something that Departments do. It will not be coming from some of those budgets, for example the R&D budgets. It will not be at a cost of investing in some of those major programme s . I t will be within the administrative budgets. We will be reallocating resource s in the way we always would , to make sure we respond .
Q66 Can you not tell us where you are reallocating it from ?
We would not normally go into that level of detail. We will definitely have the details of the budgets.
Could you, this time?

Let me come back to you on that. We would not normally go into the detail of exactly who is working on which issue. What we will absolutely do is be setting out what the priorities are, where there are any changes in those priorities, and any implications for the wider programmes.
Q67 If y ou get a very strong message from the Committee that we want to know how much this has cost , could you tell us?
Understood.

In evidence to our previous hearing , we heard from experts in Government and in the industry that they were concerned at the cost s of reorganisation in terms of money, attention and effectiveness. This Committee wants to know what those costs are.
Understood. We are working through them. Let me see ; w e can write back to you with some more detail on what we can tell you by when , and how we will do that.
G reat.

Q68 It is a pleasure to join you this morning , and t hank you also for joining our Committee yesterday. I should start off by referring members to my declaration of interest s and highlight the fact that I am a former employee of Google , a shareholder in Google and a former DCMS Minister. That means that I have been through a few MOG changes myself.

Given the fragmentation of responsibilities now, I want to focus on how we actually ensure co-ordination, in particular when it comes to policy development and policymaking . Minister McDonald , you gave a very good explanation and rationale for the changes. Forgive my cynicism here , but are the machinery of g overnment changes and the changes of responsibility truly a well-thought-out restructuring of G overnment responsibilities based on policy development and in the interest of stakeholders —o r did this really all happen because Lisa Na ndy kicked off and wanted a bigger Department ?
I guess you are allowed to be cynical, if you wish.
Duty of care , maybe.

Actually I was quite clear in my previous answer : t he machinery of g overnment changes have orientated around solving a long-standing issue in the British science and innovation space. Fundamentally, it is one of the reasons why I am sat here. The Prime Minister wants to ensure that we commercialise more UK science. I have spent my career commercialising science.

We bring those two things together. Pulling out AI particularly puts the UK in an incredibly strong position compared with our G7 and G20 counterparts, with AI at the Cabinet table bringing together science, investment and trade in the same space. It is all about alignment of science policy , and a t the top level we are aligning to the industrial strategy and the defence industrial strategy. It is driven very much by that single focus. I have certainly reflected that in all the conversations that I have had , and the officials have taken that on board.

Q69 I get that, but I remember having very similar discussions about the creation of D S IT , in terms of the need for the Government focus on that. It seems now that we have made these changes with a very similar rationale and arguments to why we created D S IT in the first place. What ha s fundamentally changed here?

As I was saying, it is this ability to now manage the end-to-end pipeline of scientific discovery through to commercialisation. I view this from the point of view of an industrialist, essentially: how can we make the best use of the science that is developed in UK universities ?

You know and understand wel l this long-standing issue around commercialisation. Where we have had a focus on scale-up of a spin-out from a university, generally when we tried to tackle this problem in the past we thought, “How can we take that very small company and make it into a small or a medium-sized company?” Actually, if you are managing the end-to-end pipeline, what I want to see and what we need to see is some of those dozens of companies that will be multibillion - turnover companies built on British science over the next 10 years, listed on the London stock exchange and headquartered here in Britain. We have to take that end-to-end approach. That is what the formation of the new Department and the alignment of the responsibilities in my portfolio enable us to do now.
Q70 We all get the purpose and the broad intent ; t he devil is always in the detail in these areas, and as I say, various G overnments have gone through them.

Another point I want to raise , before I come on to some particular issues with the DCMS side of things, is about the engagement with important players , both domestically and overseas in multiple sectors. The feedback you must be getting, and that we are all hearing from some of those stakeholders, is that they do not know where their primary contact point is now within Government: is it in the Cabinet Office, in B usiness or in DCMS? If they do not know , that causes difficulties for stakeholder engagement and that all-important engagement with industry. How can we resolve that? Are you going to be crystal clear about who owns the relationship with key industry players?

The short answer to that is, of course, yes. I can , and of course do , understand that as the machinery of g overnment change is happening, that leads to a realignment of relationships between key stakeholders and contacts in Government, and that takes a little time to work through.

Hopefully , I can provide you with some reassurance that we actually have that very well mapped. Another thing — Kanishka might want to come in on this —is that in the tech sector particularly , the corporations that we are talking about are large corporations that do not necessarily have, need or want a single point of interaction with Government . T hey want to interact in different places. Kanishka, you deal with these businesses all the time ; you may wish to comment.

Yes, that is right. Lead responsibility for the technology sector is in the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. I have worked in technology, have been a civil servant and am now back here . E very single instance of the structure of g overnment has businesses, including technology businesses , saying they speak to the Treasury on matters that are critical, not least on fiscal and regulatory levers. Historically , they spoke to the Department for Business and Trade , because trade and business are critical. They spoke to DSIT in historic instances , and they speak to application layer relationship holders in each of the individual Departments as well.

Some of these challenges are perennial challenges that you will be very familiar with. We have now made it very clear that in the specific realm of AI it is now so fundamental that it is a strategic question . I t is now so mainstream in terms of application and the risks are so material that we felt, specifically on the question of AI, t hat t he strategy and vision ought to be in the O ffice for the Prime Minister.

I would point out one other thing. Subsequent to the changes we made on AI specifically, the United States has now announced a very comparable taskforce across G overnment. I was speaking to G7 counterparts yesterday and a number of them are now doing exactly the same : locating a taskforce-based structure in the O ffice for the P rime M inister. We have tried to be ahead of the curve and to elevate the importance, while continuing to map efficiency of engagement.

Q71 Baroness Lloyd and Director General Connolly, can I come to you now about DCMS in particular? DCMS is now responsible in some parts, again, for digital transformation, digital infrastructure, cyber - security, digital inclusion and online harms , but t he DCMS budget is tiny compared with the £ 1.3 trillion of Government expenditure. The discretionary spend is tiny. How can you make sure that you have the clout and the resources to do all the things you are expected to do , and to co-ordinate effectively with other Government Departments now?
I am the Minister for Space, Cyber and Regulatory Reform ; I sit in both BIST and DCMS , and I work very closely with other DCMS colleagues.

To build on the points that my fellow Ministers have made on your question of co-ordination, there are existing formal mechanisms of g overnment to co-ordinate policy — Cabinet C ommittees, the National Security Council and so on — and formal mechanisms that you are very familiar with for discerning collective decision making and collective responsibility.

Other than that, we spend a lot of time talking to one another. I spend a great deal of time with the colleagues I am sitting next to now. The Department’s teams are well plugged in. For example, the cyber team, which was in DSIT , has transferred over to DCMS .
