As I understand it, UKRI, ARIA and OLS are now in BIST , AI strategy is in the Cabinet Office and data is in DCMS. Who is coordinating on AI drug discovery and the health data where all three will meet?

The Office for Life Sciences sits across both Health and the Business Department. It always has ; t he difference with the machinery of government change is that as a Minister in both Departments I now have direct oversight over the full life sciences supply chain, from drug discovery all the way through to application in the NHS.
Q129 The plan is that OLS will co-ordinate between the three?
Correct.
Q130 Okay. The OLS then has M HR A and NICE on regulatory speed, and they still sit in the Department of Health.
Yes.
Q131 Do they come under you as well?

No ; p art of OLS was always in the Department of Health. Obviously, they have quite different functions. The companies that the Office for Life Sciences interacts with for the purposes of drug deployment would interact with MHRA and NICE. OLS can help them to manage that pipeline. The MHRA and NICE sit with other Health Ministers. That is an important difference of accountability , actually , because my job is to work with the industry. There is a division of responsibilities there that makes sure that the MHRA and NICE are approving the use of the drugs with a separate Minister. That is quite wise.
Q132 How will it improve? Sorry, but just explain to us in practical terms how the changes will lead to a greater and swifter throughput of drugs from molecule into patient.

There are two things , actually. One is the work that we are doing generally in improving that pipeline. We have reduced the number of days to a clinical trial. Some of that is in response to requests from life sciences companies, but it is also a reflection of the nature of international competition in drug introductions. Clearly, another significant change in the industry has been the most favoured nation status rules that were brought in by the Trump A dministration, which will lead to an increase in drugs prices in the UK. That is clearly a challenge for us, but it is also an opportunity to make sure that when it comes to the additional value that the life sciences companies get, there is a quid pro quo in terms of additional value for us too.

We have been so successful at keeping drug prices at a really low level for such a long period of time, but we have to acknowledge that there have been trade-offs for that. It can mean later introduction of drugs into the UK. It can mean companies considering where they invest as well. As a result of the prices increasing, it is an opportunity for us to attract additional investment. We have managed to do that , and we have a strong pipeline of investment now.

Reducing the number of days to clinical trial and the overall drug introduction times makes us a more attractive place for drug introductions. I have said that our ambition is to be the best place to invest in Europe and the third best in the world. If you look at No. 1 and No. 2 , the USA and China, we have some advantages over China as well because we have such a trusted and secure pathway for drug introductions. That is an additional advantage we have.

Q133 Do you have transparency yet on what the cost is going to be of the increase in drugs? We have asked before in this Committee , and we have never really had an indication of what the cost is going to be. You obviously seem to know what it is.

I do not have the figure in front of me now, but over the period of the spending review there are estimates of what that will cost the NHS. The trade-off for that is around investment and greater introduction of drugs. The challenge within Government is that the costs will be felt in the Department of Health but the value will be felt elsewhere. One of the conversations I have had with the Secretary of State for Health is about how we can align incentives among the officials working in the Department of Health, so that they can make the right decisions on a value rather than a cost basis. You would appreciate that is challenging in any organisation, but it is particularly challenging in Government.
Q134 We have previously had a Minister specifically for life sciences. You are obviously doing life sciences , alongside lots of other stuff.
Patrick did as well. Patrick Vallance covered science and life sciences. I also have investment—

Previously, we have had a dedicated Minister just for life sciences. Do you think that in this wider need for co-ordination there would be value in having a specific Minister? You do not feel overloaded already, do you?
I do not , because it is all about prioritisation.
You have lots of time to co-ordinate with lots of other people.

It is all about prioritisation , really. This is the point about bringing the science and investment briefs together : t here can be a refocusing of the investment and science briefs so that the science is delivering value, and it is delivering value particularly on life sciences both through health outcomes and through investment at the same time. Clearly they are huge briefs, but we have a team and then it is about prioritising within that.

Q135 When w e had Liz Kendall in front of us as Secretary of State , w e questioned her on the cuts to the STFC. She said sitting at this table that there would be no cuts to the STFC. Yet a number of us, such as Freddie and I, who have constituency interests related to this, are seeing big cuts to some primary drivers of basic UK science. What is the latest on that organisation and that drama that it is turning into?

Chair, you asked for very brief answers , but this question is worthy of a slightly fuller answer, if you will allow me, because there are staff concerned with this as well and I want to make sure that they hear this.

If you think of the words that the previous Secretary of State said to you, de facto they are true ; t he STFC budget increased, but we have to acknowledge that costs have increased as well. The costs are inflationary costs, staff costs and so on. If you look at this restructuring that is happening within STFC, which includes withdrawing funding from certain facilities and cancelling certain investments, it is important that we think about what is happening, why it is happening and how it is happening. I will just very briefly touch on those points.

There is a cutback in funding for some facilities such as the Boulby underground laboratory , which is fairly near me. Equally, STFC is prioritising keeping open its core interdisciplinary facilities such as the Diamond light source , including half a billion pounds of additional investment there. As to why, I have explained that al though the budget has gone up the costs have gone up, but actually that , for me , is not the real reason. The fundamental problem was a lack of good financial control.

Q136 We went through all this before. Given the foundational nature of the functions of the S T F C to UK science and the alarm across the community, we do not understand why , in the same way that the Departments are absorbing the machinery of government costs, they cannot absorb these overruns and keep the laser facility at Harwell, for example, open and functioning.

UKRI has allocated an additional £135 million, I think, to support STFC through this transition over the period of the spending review. However, the important point is that STFC needs to have good financial management. That is the important point. The Public Accounts Committee actually just yesterday rightly pointed out that the overruns in STFC’s budget and that lack of appropriate financial control should have been picked up earlier by UKRI. I will accept that, but we would all agree it should have good financial control.

We all agree. The issue is that that is historic, but we face a current problem, which is that basic physics and capability are going to be eroded at a time when we are at the limits of human discovery.

Q137 I have some questions on this as well. My constituency is on the border of Harwell, so I have a particular interest in this. The previous Secretary of State for DSIT told us that where cuts fall is a matter for UKRI and STFC, not the Government. As you have implied, that is despite the critical importance of the facilities at Harwell. Do you take the same view?

Yes, I do. S T FC needs to have financial control and live within its budget. It is right that that prioritisation is done by the science community, and it has been. S T FC has used its own expert panels, and if you had the Astronomer Royal here I am sure she would have said the same ­ —

Q138 Sorry to interrupt , but we are short on time. What conversations have you had with Cabinet colleagues, for example the Secretaries of State for Health and Defence, around what the impacts of closing those facilities may be for their Departments, given the important work they do?
The conversations I have had, particularly with the Secretary of State for Business, are exactly as I have outlined. There is—
I was specifically asking about Defence and Health.
I have had no conversations with the Secretary of State for Defence or the Secretary of State for Health.
Q139 Even though the Diamond is involved in maintaining our nuclear deterrence?
As I have mentioned, the Diamond facility, ISIS and Muon are remaining open.
Q140 Will you have a conversation with the Secretary of State for Defence, then?

I would like to just finish the question, if I could. You raised this with the Business Secretary this week as well in the House, of course. The Diamond, ISIS and Muon facilities are remaining open. They are remaining open and they are being invested in: half a billion pounds in Diamond. A lot of concern was raised around Jodrell Bank, so I asked whether there were any particular issues around Defence, not with the Secretary of State for Defence but with my effective opposite number in the MOD. We received no concerns from the MOD on that either. No concerns have been raised by the MOD.

Q141 I was not asking about Jodrell Bank, which is a much smaller facility than the three at Harwell. I will move on. As I mentioned last week at oral questions, I have received information that further cuts are being required at Harwell, beyond the cuts that have already been announced for STFC. Can you comment now, on the record, as to the level of shortfall that is required?
Are you referring to the UKRI restructuring or to additional efforts on STFC?
Q142 Additional shortfall at Diamond, Isis and the Central Laser Facility.

There are two things going on. It is possible that there is a conflation ; t hat would be completely understandable because they are both happening at the same time. Last week, on Wednesday afternoon, STFC confirmed with its staff the prioritisation, which you are fully aware of, and how it affects these facilities. On Tuesday, UKRI separately launched its voluntary severance scheme with its staff as part of the UKRI restructuring. I appreciate that both those things coming together in the same week could lead to a conflation. However, the STFC plan remains unchanged. It is a plan to put STFC on a sound financial footing—

Q143 I am speaking specifically about information I have received that there is at least a £100 million shortfall in addition to the cuts that have already been announced, and that people involved have been asked to sign confidentiality agreements.
There might be a conflation there between the UKRI scheme and the STFC announcement.
Q144 Can you come back to us to confirm that?
Yes, I can. I suspect that is what it is , because they both affect Harwell. There will be a reduction of staffing in Harwell because—
Q145 On a staff call, staff were informed that if there is a facility to be closed, it will be the ISIS Neutron and Muon facility. Is that correct?
You have already heard from me that STFC has made a commitment to keeping the Diamond light source , ISIS and the Central Laser Facility operational. I am not—
That was said on a staff call.
Maybe you could give me further information about that in writing and I could look at it, but I have a commitment to those facilities that I have just described staying open.
Q146 On the record, you are committing to those three facilities at Harwell staying open over the next six months and through until 2028, when those gates are passed through?

I will tell you quite explicitly and clearly that the STFC plan is intended to keep the Diamond light source , ISIS, Muon Source and the Central Laser F acility open and financially sustainable, which they have not been. That is the current plan.
Q147 Intended?
Yes, that is right. It is the intention of the plan to do exactly that.
Q148 Okay. Will you commit to finding additional funds if the shortfall that I have outlined is true? Come what may, will you keep those open?

I am not going to commit to finding additional funds for a hypothetical shortfall that I have not heard about previously , but i f you provide me with further information about that, I will endeavour to validate it and give you an answer one way or another.

Q149 I would just like to say that the concerns you have expressed now about the financial practices at STFC were identified by this Committee at the beginning of this year, in our hearing. I am glad to see them now acknowledged. What I have not heard is a plan to address that financial best practice . M aybe you could write to us. [Interruption.] I am not going to ask you to answer now , I am afraid.
I just wanted to say t hank you —that was all I wanted to say . Yes, I will write back to you on that.
Yes, we raised that at that time and I am not sure we received such a positive response from the Ministers concerned. I appreciate that we are over time. We have two more questions to ask .

Q150 I have a very quick question. I should declare my interests: I chair the all-party parliamentary group for the polar regions, advise the Astra Carta sustainability initiative and advise a quantum fund, Firgun, a British charity in quantum biology, and a life science fund. None of those are relevant to this, but I wanted just to make sure I had declared them.

I want to ask Minister McDonald about how AI is transforming the way science is done. The traditional model is short-term funding : scientists reveal a bit more of the answer , then ask for more money , then we give them a bit more money and then they reveal a bit more. AI is going to reveal huge amounts of answers at pace, so science will become a very different activity. I am not asking you to give us the whole answer to this , but when I was Minister for UKRI, it was struggling with basic digitalisation, let alone AI-empowered research allocations. Are there any plans for turning UKRI from a pretty clunky, old-fashioned analogue research administration body to an AI-enabled funder that can fund properly in the global race?

Yes, this is a really great question. It also goes back a bit to what I have just said to Freddie about the voluntary severance scheme that UKRI launched last week. That is the product of exactly the kind of thing you are talking about — a massive transformation in the organisation, and one that we really feel the pressure to do at pace. If you think about the implications of AI in the field of science, I was so sad, actually ; I heard a leading physicist say just over the summer that the opportunity for human discovery in physics and mathematics is probably gone now. It is great because it means we are progressing in those areas, but it is also slightly sad to feel that. As a scientist, your role is going to be really quite different now.

Q151 I understand. My question really is about UKRI, which is trying, but it is still basically a pretty analogue bureaucratic machine for allocating money. Are you confident that it is modernising at pace to deal with this new world?

Yes. I am confident it is modernising at pace, but we cannot get away from the fact that this is a real race to do this. In the time it takes us to produce a plan, the technology has moved on even further. If you talk about that specific area of grant allocation that you have just mentioned, AI has the potential to completely break the whole method for grant allocation—
Q152 Sorry, Minister McDonald, but we need to come to an answer. Are you looking to provide a plan?

The short answer is yes ; we are working on it. Again, this is something we could explore much more here. We could maybe bring UKRI along as well and have much more detailed discussions about this because it is not just science discovery, but as you say, the allocation of funds element of this.
I know time is short. We would welcome your plans because it is going to have a major implication for the way science is done and the way we allocate money.
Yes, that is a very good point.
It has the potential to erode British competitive advantage unless we move really fast on this , too.

Q153 For the sake of time, I am just going to pivot that question. It is a question for Chris and for Kanishka. AI is still in a developmental stage. Obviously, we are looking at quantum and neuromorphic computing, both of which have UK advantages that are included in AI tech and innovation, but many of them are still within the research lab at this point. How are you co-ordinating our current AI plans plus our R&D spend to make sure that we are at the forefront of quantum, neuromorphic and these other AI developments, so that we do not repeat the mistakes of the past in terms of our power and weight?
There are two things : t here is the applications bit you have mentioned , but there is also the industry itself. Do you want to do the industry bit?

No, I am talking about the basic research that feeds into these further developments in quantum and neuromorphic, which are all within the AI space. I am trying to understand how it sits between Kanishka’s, “I do AI,” and your role of, “I am UK R&D,” particularly that blue-sk y research funding into our amazing universities. How is that being co-ordinated across?

You are right. If we go back to the discussions around STFC or whatever, there is investment in new capability there, clearly. If you look at quantum, for instance, you will be familiar with the ProQure programme and what we are doing at the quantum centre. The reason I made the point about the industry versus the applications is that actually some of that new fundamental science is coming from the application side and from industrial companies.

I could pick an area such as life sciences or engineering biology — the use of artificial intelligence for molecule discovery, let us say. When we are all supporting research in molecule discovery or a new dementia treatment, using brain cell analysis on a slide or whatever, that is a really practical example. That is all AI - enabled. It is using and developing AI technology at the same time.
You are not quite getting my question.
Oh, I am sorry about that.
My question is about those core bases that provide the basic science and research. AI is not “T ick, done, it has been discovered. ”
No, exactly.

Q154 I am not asking about AI applications. I am asking about the further research and development in the further extensions of how AI works. That is not all coming from industry, particularly when you are looking at really exciting areas such as quantum and neuromorphic. Just to add into that, quantum is the nearest one: we are talking about Q-Day within the next five years. The way we keep quantum within the UK also links to another bit of what your Department is doing, which is the manufacturing strategy. The way we make that investment sticky is to have a quantum manufacturing strategy.

I am trying to understand how you and Kanishka are working together in this wider economic, social and exciting role from basic through to regulatory, through to application, but also through to manufacturing around AI. We keep getting the answer that Kanishka does AI. I get that, but he is not necessarily doing these other bits, which from my perspective sit with you and other Ministers in whatever the Department is now called.
Yes, maybe I understand the question a bit better now. I am saying that essentially the research is multidisciplinary.
Q155 Research into AI is multidisciplinary?
No, because it is not just about research into AI. If someone is—
Q156 That was the question about AI in research. This is a different question. This is about research in AI.

What I am saying is that some research in AI that is driving new development in AI is being done in a multidisciplinary team that is focused on an application. The application need is then causing the AI development to happen. It is set up as a multidisciplinary team, essentially.

Just to add to what Chris has said, there are three ways in which we are trying to work very closely together on the intersection of some technologies you have described in AI. First, as Chris says, there is the AI for science strategy. That was a joint strategy with me and the Science Minister at the time, focused both on applying AI to science and crucially on the science of AI in some part. What Chris is saying about multidisciplinary teams shaping where AI is going , in the light of need being designed up front , is really critical.
Q157 That is in Minister McDonald’s Department?

AI for science is a strategy that at the time the science Minister Lord Vallance and I wrote together. I do AI for science. Chris does a series of areas of application, including life sciences and quantum. Secondly, specifically in the quantum and neuromorphic computing areas you described, Emily, which are really critical, a lot of that is really focused on one bit of AI, which is developing the next generation of computer chips. It is extremely important , because that is where a lot of our focus has been. It is not the only thing that quantum is relevant for, but it is one important area.

We are trying to fund across the portfolio, all the way from ARIA, supporting really future-oriented, high-risk support for aspects of next generation compute, through to procurement that we are doing. My hope is that when we build a heterogeneous compute cluster on AI, that effectively is a pathway to what we are trying to do on an advance market commitment on quantum as well. We are trying to make sure that right across the financing and procurement landscape, we are tightly tied up on compute specifically as it relates to quantum and neuromorphic computing developments. Those are things that we are working on.

Finally, when we are focused on areas of AI and trying to do plans, for example, the AI hardware plan, we are trying to look at the entire pipeline and say, “How do we support both PhDs, postgraduates at the earliest stages, and teams in the research lab on where the future of these technologies goes?” You cannot really answer that question centrally, especially on AI, if you do not take the future of quantum being an important part of that seriously as well. My expectation is that with the work we are doing on those functional blocks of PhD support, for example, when they are thinking about chip engineering and electrical engineering, they end up ultimately, in some small part at least—a growing part—becoming quantum-adjacent PhDs as well.
Q158 Within that stack , you are the one who will be looking at manufacturing , then, rather than BIST?
I am a BIST Minister as well. Advanced manufacturing is not my specific area.

Advanced manufacturing and digital and tech are two separate strands —w ell, they are two strands in the industrial strategy . I should not say they are separate ; o f course, there is a massive overlap between the two. Hopefully, that generates the end-to-end approach. Yes, the industry is there, the applications are with me, and then the r eindustrialisation Minister owns the industrial strategy.
Q159 Great. Thank you very much, Emily, that was a really important question. To further clarify, the funding is all with you, Minister McDonald?
Yes. All UKRI funding flows through me.

Q160 Okay, the funding for what we have talked about is with you. W e have kept you over time ; w e are very grateful for that. I have just two — hopefully brief — questions of clarification , because we have talked about devolution and science and innovation but we did not mention the Department for devolution, which is the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Are you working with that Department on the devolution of science and innovation? Who is the key Minister there?

Yes, in short. In fact, I attended a cross-Whitehall Ministers of State meeting just yesterday where we discussed this. Actually, the co-ordination is being done through No. 10 North, and there will be more information around this in the Prime Minister’s “Rewiring the State” speech.
Q161 Is there a Minister responsible for the devolution of innovation in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government?
I am the Minister responsible for the devolution of innovation.

Q162 Okay. Finally, Baroness Lloyd, we have mentioned previously that the “State of Digital Government Review” said that there were £45 billion in unrealised savings and productivity benefits from the digitisation of public services. Do you still stand by that figure, given the machinery of government changes and your responsibilities there? Are you looking at new work to identify the current overall savings?
The £45 billion figure was an estimate of long-term productivity gains. It was not a one-off figure for savings.
Yes. We wrote to you about that.

We shared the methodology with you last year. In terms of practical steps forward, the Department is focusing on the implementation of the road map and blueprint for a modern digital Government. That is how we will prioritise the areas for digitisation, the areas where the public sector can really transform. Those are costed. There are initiatives that set out what the potential benefits are going to be. There are quarterly updates on those initiatives, which I think you have seen.
Q163 Yes. They do not represent all the savings or all the programmes that are across Government. It sounds to me like you are not using that £45 billion figure as a target.
As I understand it, that figure was never a target or a cashable savings figure. That was never what it was intended to describe.
Right. Thank you very much.

I am very grateful for your attendance. It has been a really good session. We have gone beyond simply the machinery of government changes ; a s could be expected, we have looked deep into some responsibilities, how they have evolved and how they will impact our economic growth, security, safety and so on. I am really grateful to the Committee , but particularly to our witnesses. It shows that scrutiny of science and technology in the new Government is going to be just as detailed and intensive as this incredibly important subject requires.

sessions.iT: Equality at work: flexible working and disability
sessions.w: Business Disability Forum; Trades Union Congress (TUC)

segs.tx: Women and Equalities Committee
Oral evidence: Equality at work: flexible working and disability, HC 177
Wednesday 21 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 21 October 2026.
Watch the meeting
Members present: Olivia Bailey (Chair); Alex Brewer; Kevin McKenna; Richard Quigley; Rachel Taylor; Nadia Whittome.
Questions 76 - 98
Witnesses
I : Angela Matthews, Director of Public Policy and Research, Business Disability Forum; and Daisy Goodall, Policy Officer (young workers), Trade s Union Congress (TUC).
Written evidence from witnesses:
Business Disability Forum [ FWD0090 ]
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Angela Matthews and Daisy Goodall .

Good afternoon and welcome to the Women and Equalities Committee. Today we are holding a session for our inquiry into equality at work, flexible working and disability, in the context of a stubbornly high disability employment gap . W e are pleased to be hearing from a fantastic panel today with expertise in trade unions, workers and business. Thank you so much, Daisy Goodall, p olicy o fficer at the Trade s Union Congress , and Angela Mat t hews, d irector of p ublic p olicy and r esearch at the Business Disability Forum . W e are grateful to you both for coming today and sharing your thoughts with us. I will hand straight over to Rachel, who will kick us off.

Q76 I am going to come to you first, Angela. You previously emphasised that some businesses report reaching the limit of flexibility in terms of what they can offer their workforce. What types and size s of businesses are telling us that ?

Angela Matthews : BDF predominantly works with very large employers w hose workforces rang e from ten thousand to hundreds of thousands of employees . What we see — and what our members tell us — is that over the course of the past two, five, or 10 years, wh ile they have been providing a lot of redeployment or flexible working as a reasonable adjustment, they get to a point where , for example , they have too many people in office-based or desk-based roles and not enough people on the frontline. The reasonable adjustments duty in the Equality Act is about how things are right now: w hat is this person’s job, this individual’s barriers, and what can you do right now? However, some employers get to the point where they have m ade so many adjustments and introduced so muc h flexibility that it changes the shape of their organisation, and that prompts a restructuring activity.

T his affects organisations most whe re there are front-facing roles, for example, across the NHS, police, and retail, and back-office roles. I t can happen in a couple of ways. For example, someone might be returning to work and need adjusted duties for a short amount of time ; when they are fully recovered, they go back to their initial role. However, if a flexible working request has been made under flexible working rights, th at is seen as more permanent : there is not the idea that you will go back to your role after a certain amount of time. Our m embers are struggling to keep the shape of their organisation s intact while making adjustments, redeploying people either permanently or temporarily, and agreeing flexible working requests.
Q77 Do you think there is more they could do to organise their working patterns and practi ce s in ways that are more inclusive of disabled people?

Angela Matthews : M any employers struggle to find the time to retrain someone, and that is particularly the case in smaller organisations . A lot of the time the law allow s an employer to look at an individual and say, “O kay, is there an existing vacancy where we can redeploy you , which matches your current skills and our current vacancies? ” They can look at flexible working or a c hange of roles, adjusted duties, job carving, and the skills the individual has that they need now. A lot of organisations could get better at dealing with th at skills gap. W here is the space for retraining and upskilling people so that there is a broader range of roles for redeploying people when their current role is no longer doable?

I want to feed back some points that were made at a roundtable with union reps from all different sectors, including education, health and social care, police, retail, seafarers and hospitality. There was a real consensus in the room that employers do not always consult ; sometimes there is a lack of creative thinking in finding s olutions to flexible working requests. There were examples where multiple staff members ha d requests for part-time work rejected with no investigation into whether two members of staff would consider a job share. They said that employers often fail to provide evidence when rejecting a request, and that th e eight business reasons allow employers to use vague reasoning. We still have a poor culture around flexible working . T he examples you used , Angela, were strong. If the job is location-based and you have to be in one place, what about thinking more creatively about the hours that you work? If you are on the shop floor, could you have more empowerment over your roster and shift patterns? It is about empowering employers to feel that they can come to creative solutions.
Q78 That is helpful. Staying with Daisy , how s hould Government policies strike the right balance between encouraging flexible working where possible , and requiring it through legislation?

T hat is a good question ; I can go into more detail later about the legislative requirements that the TUC is calling for . We have some good examples of unions negotiating better flexible collective working agreements than the legislation, but there is evidence that stronger legislation is needed, particularly in certain sectors with less unionised work. There are a couple of examples : first, in 2021 we carried out a survey of over 1,700 reps investigat ing the impact of the pandemic on flexible working . T he results indicated that some employers only offered home working when it was effectively mandated by Government guidance ; 33% of reps —particularly those in the private sector— told us they thought home working would get harder to access post-pandemic. That shows that employers could offer flexible working when it is mandated but then decided to take it away. That is strong evidence.

Secondly, the evidence around gender pay ga p reporting shows that voluntary approaches can be difficult and do not always work. T here was sustained Government action to encourage and promot e a voluntary approach to the gender pay gap , but it was largely ineffective: 280 employers signed up to the scheme, but only five employers published th eir data. H owever , w hen mandatory reporting was introduced, there was almost 100% compliance; more than 10,000 employers reported the gender pay gap in their first year . This shows that when something is voluntary, employers do not sign up and do not have that drive to get involved but when it is mandated we see really good practice .

Angela Matthews : I agree. One of the tangible things that our members say — particularly with regard to the flexible working provisions of the Employment Rights Act and identifying a reasonable refusal — is that they would like the Government to allow them to consider the sustainability of the arrangement . In the Equality Act , f or example, t he reasonable adjustments request is about what can be done now and we regularly review that , but t hat provision is not in the ERA. Employers said they wanted an addition to the reasonableness section of the ERA so that they can say, “T his is doable now, but within our five-year strategy, we have plans that look like this, so it ’s not going to work in four years’ time. ” For example, if an employer identifie s that their business plan over the next couple of years will include structural or organisation changes, and a flexible working request w ill not fit within that, they would like to be allowed to include that strategic question as a reasonable refusal.

We absolutely recognise that there is a place for mandating such measures. We speak to many employers that want to do the right thing, but they do not know where all the guidance is , and they cannot keep up with w hat they can and cannot do. At some level, we have to let businesses be businesses : principles come from the Government but we should let businesses do their thing .

Q79 That brings me on to my next question about the academic witnesses we have seen who argue that clearer guidance on implementing flexible working across sectors and roles could encourage wider adoption by employers. Do you agree , and if so, what is the best way to produce that guidance?

Angela Matthews : V ery large businesses have many different types of roles . I t is common for our members to be able to say to postholders in some roles across their business, “Y ou can work in whatever way you want; the output is what matters . ” Bu t in other areas of the business there is no flex : “W e have to deliver in this way, to this time, with this outcome .” Often it is not about whether an employer is offering flexible working ; it is about the fact that with specific roles across very large organisations, there is more flex for that business to be operational in the way that it needs to be. Government mandates should recognise that it is not a case of whether employers are flexible or not ; it is about them looking at occupations across the whole organisation.

That said, I completely agree with what you have said about part-time flexing . M any disabled people tell us that their career s stopped when they reduced their hours or went part time . We have therefore been asking our members to voluntarily audit roles across their organisation s to show how they decide what is full-time only, what can be flexed and how , so that they can be the most inclusive employer s possible.

T here is still a widespread lack of flexible working , as we have noted for the purpose of the Committee . S ince the pandemic and the April 2024 changes to legislation , there has only been a change of three percentage points in the number of employees who have access to any form of good - quality flexible working [1] . Y ou touched on the impact on individuals when they do not get flexible working : the TUC has found that 20% of people left a job due to lack of flexible working , and this rises to 27% of disabled workers. We need to be working with employers but also mandating where needed to make sure that people have the ability to enter the job market and stay in the job market.

I also want to make a point about the impact on the individual . W hen someone return s to work after a period of ill health , their earnings can remain unaffected if they go back to their previous employer. However, if that connection is severed , the individual faces what we call a cost of j ob loss penalty , which can be about 15% of their earnings ; if they are out of work for two years or more it can be a 25% reduction in earnings. That means they find it difficult to return to work and their wages and stability of employment suffer , as does their long-term health , which has k nock-on effects for the economy. H ow can we maximise people’s performance using flexible working , rather than seeing it as a perk?
Q80 Are there case studies showing how it could be done in more challenging scenarios ? W ould that encourage more businesses to take it up ?

Angela Matthews : Yes. W e have a forum where employers swap stories about what works and what does not . T he perception can be , “F lexible working is not right for this role ,” without thinking about it further . I am not saying that is not the case. I completely agree with Daisy . W e see layers of disadvantage when someone is coming to the point where they need to ask their employer for a flexible working arrangement . Employers tell us th is is the part they struggle with the most. Usually , a line manager receiv es th e request but to get something structural and organisational signed off requires a journey up through the organisation. The line manager is waiting, and the employee is frustrated because they are not getting an answer . We see many managers — both at line manager and mid-manager level — who are up for this because they need their teams functioning, working and get ting the job done.

As Daisy said , at the end of the day there is a human behind this and when it goes up through the many layers , the conversation can easily become only about the cost, the risk to business, and the disruption . We see all this terminology in the reasonableness element of the ERA, and we forget that there is an employee who , as Daisy said , might have a disability, might be caring for their parents, might also be a parent themselves and is overwhelmed and at risk of burnout. They are trying to hold down their job and make work work for them. When our employers get together and swap stories about what works and what does not , that is usually the conversation, including how you get leaders on board.

Q81 Daisy , we have heard evidence that most disabled workers who need Equality Act reasonable adjustments do not have their needs fully met. What does the TUC’s research suggest is driving that? Is it a lack of awareness and understanding or is it th at employers are disregarding the law?

Q82 T hat is a good question. We know that disabled people experience a prevalence of poor treatment and discrimination in the workplace . I want to talk about the long waits they face to get reasonable adjustments and the rejection that is common , and then touch on A ccess to W ork , if that is helpful.

We know there are significant barrie rs. TUC research into accessing reasonable adjustments found that six in 10 disabled workers did not make a request at all because of the f ear of rejection and poor treatment. To better understand this , we surveyed 1,000 disabled workers and asked them to share their experiences. Over half, 55% , who put in a request had only some , or none, of their needed adjustments implemented . Some 19% of th ose said that their employer had not provided any reason for refusal. W hen we looked at the reasons given, the examples included that t he request was impractical, there was a financial cost, or the employer doubted its effectiveness . A ll th e se reasons undermine the legal obligations that employers have under the Equality Act. There were some shocking examples of employers saying that the person was not disabled enough or that they needed to wait for further diagnosis. One employer even s aid that they did not want the person to have different furniture to other people in a shared office. Therefore, we can see that d isabled people face awful experiences in the workplace and these are grounded in wider poor experiences. Some 49% of disabled workers experience d bullying or harassment in the past year and 16% left work due to that disability - related mistreatment. C omplaints are not dealt with appropriately ; almost a quarter are ignored entirely , and all this puts people off from claiming the adjustments that they deserve and need in order to work effectively.

If it is helpful , we can talk about A ccess to W ork , which can also be a barrier. T he National Audit Office carries out reviews that reinforce the need for employers to meet the cost of providing those reasonable adjustments . T he NAO sampled Access to Work cases and found that 40% of the support funded should have been provided by the employer, employee, or NHS , but was instead provided by the A ccess to W ork programme . It found that employers failed to make adjustments in 18% of cases . Public funding is being used when th e dut y to provide reasonable adjustments should be kicking in .

W e also know that the scheme is not reaching the disabled people who need it. S pending has nearly doubled in the past five years but it only reaches 1% of working disabled people . T he TUC has further recommendations around A ccess to W ork, but I want to make a quick point about the EHRC : it d esperately need s funding for enforcement action . If people are not getting their adjustments and employers are skirting their le gal obligations , then the EHRC needs to kick in. When it opened in 2007 , it had a budget of £ 70 million and over 500 staff , which has been reduced to around £ 17 million and 200 staff . I t cannot fulfil its current obligations , let alone take on the new responsibilities that are desperately need ed . We need to ensure sufficient funding and allow the EHRC to take on first-instance cases where proceedings have begun — or are first heard — on the failure of employers to put reasonable adjustments in place. We need ringfenced resources to conduct a targeted enforcement of workers’ rights around reasonable adjustments . A s you mentioned, guidance on the EHRC is important to boost employer confidence in using the positive action provisions in the Equality Act. The three key points are the treatment of disabled workers , the fact that they do not feel confident at work , and enforcement mechanisms .
Q83 I s it your view that clarity and understanding could be improved by updated guidance alone , or do you think there need s to be changes to the law?

W e definitely think there should be legal changes . W e welcome the changes made to the ERA — including the reasonableness test and the statutory process that employers need to follow before rejecting a request — which w ill create a clear and thorough process. We still have concerns about the eight business reasons and the low compensation award at tribunal , which make it easy for employers to reject requests . W ith flexible working requests we generally ask members to go down a reasonable adjustment route ; if the request is related to their disability, they have stronger proactive rights . We are also calling for a default right to flexible working rather than the right to request , grounded in the fact that requests are rejected and people face poor treatment , as I have set out . T hat , and the advertising duty , which I know we will talk about later, are the key TUC call s at the moment .

Q84 Angela , currently 82% of disabled people are having to wait between four and 12 months for their adjustments ; there have been calls for a more stringent process for reasonable adjustments, including a two-week deadline for employers to respond to requests in a pr e scribed way . Do you agree that this is needed , and do you believe that the impact on businesses w ill be proportionate?

Angela Matthews : W e agree that adjustments need to be implemented quicke r, and I completely identify and agree with all the stats that Daisy has shared. Our research shows that out of nearly 2,000 disabled employees, one in eight will wait over a year to get the adjustments they have requested ; t hat has to change. With regard to the two-week turnaround time , we are supportive of making anything quicker . H owever, we need to unpack what is meant by two weeks and a decision . As part of our research we carry out T he G reat B ig W orkplace A djustments S urvey with disabled employees and managers who are implementing adjustments . Th e survey shows that it is procuring the adjustment and provision that takes time, not the decision. For example , many of the em ployers and managers who contributed are still using A ccess to W ork . As Daisy said , if A ccess to W ork is taking between three and 12 months to get support in place at the moment , it needs to change before we impose a two-week turnaround time on employers.

It also depends very much on the adjustment. Many of our employers have large organisations and keep a lot of adjustments in stock . If you have the kit that someone needs in your organisation now , then two weeks is too long ; it should be sorted today , because the Equality Act says that the deadline is when you know. However, if the adjustment need ed is a job coach or training , that is going to take way over two weeks. We need to be clear in what we are saying to employers and not penalise those who are making a lot of adjustments that — by the ir nature — take longer than two weeks to implement. W e are behind t he principle of using whatever works to speed up adjustments as long as it is pragmatic.

I agree that there are barriers to this . I want to flag one of the TUC’s calls around A ccess to W ork that speaks to one of your points. If disabled job seekers who are entitled to A ccess to W ork were to get in - principle indicative award s, that would support employers to move more quickly in accepting adjustments and putting them in place. It would skip the massive delay process and make Access to Work more efficient.

I also want to raise where the two-week time frame comes from. It is proposed in the Disability Employment Charter ; it is good to flag th e many signatories to this charter from all types of sectors , including l ocal councils, NHS trusts, charities ranging from small to those such as Amnesty International, businesses of varying sizes , and consultancy services. Th ere is a lot of groundwork within the employer sector ; as you say, it is just about thinking of the practicalities of roll-out .

Q85 I have one final question. U nfortunately , many of the public conversations around disability in the mainstream media make a distinction between so-called genuine disabled people who have genuine needs and those who are undeserving of support. How far do you think these wider cultural messages shape what happens in the workplace? Do they mean that people with fluctuating or hidden conditions , or conditions that are less widely understood are less likely to ask for flexible working and reasonable adjustments in the first place?

T hat is a good point. Th e law is strong around fluctuating conditions , so you are right that this is more of a perception issue. T he Equality Act is specific about fluctuating conditions: it is about the impact of the impairment and how that affects the person’s ability to work and live.

Energy impairments are a good example : there is a lot of employer disbelief around the impact of th e se conditions . A report by Chronic Illness Inclusion stated that the widespread notion that fatigue is not real stands firmly in the way of disability equality at work. T he TUC carried out research into long covid that speaks to the experience of people with fluctuating conditions in the workplace . I want to raise what employers put in place and what they did not because it is instructive as to their understanding of what people with fluctuating conditions need. We asked our respondents — people with long covid — what workplace adjustments they had asked for and what employers had put in place . More p eople got a phased return to work than had asked for it , which is interesting because it shows that employers expected a linear recovery , even though long covid recovery is not linear . O nly 32% of respondents were able to return to work on their first attempt ; t hey needed more long-standing flexible working and adjustments than they were offered.

In all the remaining categories , fewer workers received a change than had asked for it . T hese were mostly around genuine forms of flexibility to support fluctuations in their symptoms, such as longer and more frequent breaks, permanent home working, and other changes to hours. Those requests were more likely to be turned down , which shows the culture around energy impairments in particular . O nly half the number of requests to make physical changes to enable the person to do their job were granted . Those in cluded improvements to ventilation ; people with long covid wanted to reduce their vulnerability to repeated infections , which would obviously make them feel more unwell. These issues had a serious impact on people’s longer-term health , so it is important to understand the types of adjustments that employers are offering and maybe the types that they are not offering.

Angela Matthews : In terms of whether the narrative or rhetoric out there influence s what disabled employees ask fo r , t he biggest impact is on what leaders think . T hey hear t he media narrative and the response to political rhetoric and , for example the Fonagy review into ADHD, autism, and neurodiversity . We h ave a lived experience forum at BDF where we test how disabled employees in work today feel about societal perceptions . Many forum members f eel that what their employer hears has an impact on how they are treated .

I do not have evidence that it stops a representative number of disabled employees from asking for support. I spoke to a disabled professional who said , “I have to ask because I need it and I can ’t work without it .” B ut the y feel that the response is impacted by what is going on beyond their organisation .

As I said, leaders hear it too , as do boards and investors , so it has a real impact on decisions about supported employment schemes or schemes for disabled people. I f there is such a bad rep in the media and in society , why would leaders think , “H ey , this is a great thing to do , it’s g reat for my reputation and my investors are going to love it. ” I c ompletely agree that it has an impact , mostly on decision makers.

Q86 Y ou mentioned supported work . It seems to be a great way of taking the fear out of employing someone with additional needs or additional requirements . W hat do you think we could do to encourage businesses to take on more supported internship s and those easy routes in ? F rom experience , everyone who does that says, “Oh, why haven’t I done this before? I t’s such an easy win.”

Angela Matthews : I have just come from a panel this morning talking about how employers can do more supported internships ; BDF led that conference because our members say there is a lot of jargon around supported work. Wh at is a supported internship ? What is P athways to W ork , or Access to Work? The schemes have lovely , engaging names , local authorities lead with them and they are well structured , but businesses are not keeping up to date with all these different names for different things . It is also hard when a business is in a business plan cycle ; it is taking on p rocurement contracts and saying, “T his is our recruitment partner for the next four years ,” then we come along and say , “Have you thought about supported internships and partnering with someone ?” I t does not always fit , or speak in a business language .

T o answer your question , we have to avoid talking in riddles. On our BDF panel this morning we talked about needing to get to a place where this is just another way of recruiting people to fulfil the jobs that need to be done in the business. It is not just about language; all these schemes run in different ways , have different structures and are based in different places . C onnect to W ork is a great programme for l ocal authorities . S ome are led by the not-for-profit sector ; with others you can partner directly with further ed ucation institutions. There are so many different ways of doing this , employers cannot keep up , and t hey certainly do not know w hat is best for their organisation .

I would add a couple of tangible things that employers can do to ease th e confusion. We are calling for employers to use reasonable adjustment passports ; that is a way of formalising what you need in the workplace whether you are on a placement , an employee , or a worker . It mean s your adjustments travel with you if you change line manager and so on , and it is a good way of embedding a positive culture .

A nother key way of addressing the confusion and lack of clarity is to have equality reps in the workplace . We welcome the stronger rights for equality reps that have been brought in by the Governmen t; they will embed good practice , ensure that employers can meet legislative requirements , monitor any unintended consequences , and ensure that new and existing rights are understood and implemented . T hey can help with the E q I A s and with understanding equality law changes . Before I worked for the TUC, I worked within a union that worked with the NHS ; t he equality reps there were brilliant for supporting with the E q I A s . They are a good way of ensuring that you remain compliant while dealing with lots of different legislation.

Q87 Kevin McKenna : I would like to move on and look at potential duties and obligations on employers beyond reasonable adjustments . Daisy, I know the TUC has asked for a legal duty on employers to advertise flexible working options . H ave trade unions taken steps to encourage this on a voluntary basis so you can see what might be possible ? I f you have , what have the impacts been ? T he other question is : has there been any resistance from employers ?

Daisy Goodall : Yes . W e are calling on this legal duty to publish flexible working options in job adverts , and for workers to then take up that advertised flexibility from day one . T here is support for employers so , if they cannot accommodate that , they can transparen tly set out the reasons for it. I will set out the current landscape as you have asked , and we have some TUC polling of HR managers that speaks to acceptance levels within the field .

W e already know that there is an issue with advertising in its current form . T oo many jobs are not advertise d a s flexible and we know that 58% of disabled workers — in terms of TUC polling at least —were unlikely to apply for a job if they d id not know if it could fit around their condition . Only a third of disabled respondents are likely to ask for flexible working in the first few days of a job . That shows the advertising duty would do a lot in mak ing sure that people who otherwise would not request it are actually able to access it . I f jobs advertise flexible working , they attract up to 30% more applicants . T hat is really positive .

L ooking at the current landscape , there i s some research from T imewise that showed that only about 30% of jobs currently are advertised with flexible working options included . It is better in unionised workplaces . O ur equality audit that we do every couple of years showed that already 62% of reps from the public sector and 44% from the private sector display ed flexible working options in job adverts . T hat is really good to hear . There has already been quite a lot of take - up in both those sectors .

W e have also set up some practical steps around it but I will leave that for now and focus on the polling . It is really important because it is of HR managers , so th e employer side of it . I t was conducted for the TUC by YouGov and show ed that employers we re willing to advertise flexible working arrangements in job adverts . Some 59 % of over 900 HR managers polled said that it would be easy to include specific infor mation about the types of hours- based flexible working arrangements available in each job advert , or that they already d id this . It rose to 62% of HR managers when asked about home or remote working . There was a lot of acceptance with people saying it would be easy to do and identify what they were going to advertise .

T here is interest in how this impacts on smaller businesses . A gain , we looked at HR managers for businesses of one to 249 employees and 59 % said it would be easy to include specific info rmation about the hours- based flexibility they could offer , or that they already d id this , and 63 % said it would be easy to identify that before advertising or that they already d id this , and 75 % said that about home or remote working . W e are not asking for a massive culture shift . W e are not asking for a big change . I t is something that employers seem ready to take on and it is something that would really help . The time when the worker requests flexibility is when we know that discrimination kick s in .

I will finish with an example of one company that ha s already done this and the impact on it. Zurich is the first company in the UK to advertise all vacancies with the option of part-time , full-time , job share , or flexible working . T his led to a 66% boost in applications . O ne in four of the new hires chose to work part time , so there was a big impact on its workforce . It also use s gender-neutral language in its job adverts and , as a result of both changes , it saw a 16 % rise in women applying for jobs and a 20 % jump when look ing at management roles . T hat is really helping with diversity and inclusion , and it is not complicated to enforce this duty . I t will be done through the EHRC and a ll our policies are around that .

Angela Mathews : I do not disagree with that at all . It is a question ; it is not disagreeing . I n terms of being pragmatic , there is a difference between a job advert and a job description . F orgive me , I do not know what the TUC are asking for i n terms of wh at you are saying . I agree with Daisy 100 % that t his is not a huge shift for employers , if we think about what a good job description should have in it , but it takes me to a place that is about better inclusive guidance from the EHRC . D oes it need to go all the way to being mandated through legislation ? I do not have any evidence for or against that , but a lot of disabled people tell us that job adverts are to o long . T hey feel like, even when they are applying for a job that is not about rea ding and writing or is desk- based , they have to read a lot to understand what they need to be , what they are applying for , and what they are going to need to do in the job . I do not disagree at all , s ubject to detail and practicalities .

T o come back to your question on employers ’ duties beyond reasonable adjustments : of the 1 , 480 disabled employees we spoke to in our research who have a disability and adjustments in place , only 19 % s aid their adjustments remove d all barriers that they experience in the workplace . J ust 19 %. T hat is to your point . W hat else should employers be doing ? A s I said earlier , reasonable adjustments are about an individual , an individual’s barriers , and what is being experienced right now in the job they are doing .

I f you think about your workplace it is not just your job that you experience , it is getting to the building and around the building . I t is socialising . I t is eating . I t is moving around from the entrance and the length you have to walk every day . I t is the perception that leaders have of disability , let alone disabled people . I t is how your policies are structured . A ll these things create disadvantage and barriers that the reasonable adjustments duty does not touch . T hat is why this number of just 19 % of disabled employees say ing that adjustments are removing all barriers in the workplace for them is haunting.

T he other thing to mention is health and safety legislation , which requires employers to provide a safe working environment. When we think about disabled employees , what safe means is very different . I t mean s making sure I do not fall flat on my face when I am moving around my work place — am I safe because of my body and my disability when moving around and doing my job , and so on? W hat we see is that the EDI and workplace adjustments agenda —f or want of a better phrase — has focused almost with exclusive , razor - sharp vision only on the Equality Act . E mployers , even our sector , miss a lot of really good stuff that they already have a responsibility to fulfil under the H ealth and S afety at W ork A ct . W e even get to working conditions when we look through that health and safety lens , which go es into what impacts the need for flexible working . I f we look at the stressors that the Health and Safety Executive talks about , do you have autonomy over how you work ? T his is what we are talking about : flexibility . T here is a lot more that employers can and should be doing and be aware of in terms of legislation and statutory guidance that necessarily has to reach beyond adjustments , because reasonable adjustments for an individual in a specific role only go so far to make work doable for disabled people .

Daisy Goodall : Can I come really briefly back to a point ? T he TUC policy is that flexibility would be advertised and the n the worker would have the opportunity to take up that advertised flexibility . T o speak to your point about the length of job adverts , which is a good one , there was some really interesting research from T imewise, one of our partners . It said that often flexibility is actually more important than salary when people are looking for a job . N ine out of 10 people are looking for that flexibility. Despite the length , if that is the real key thing that people are looking for , then it is really important that employers include it .

T o speak to your point about how far we mandate , the TUC has set out that all roles should be deemed suitable for flexible working unless it can be shown that the unavailability of flexible working is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim . Th erefore , it mirrors the objective justification of the Equality Act . To answer your question, t hat is how we propose fo r it to work .

Angela Mathews : T he devil is in the detail in terms of whether an employer ha s to do that up front . I am not saying th at th ey should not , but when you are getting employers with hundreds and hundreds of thousands of roles , maybe the answer is yes . A re we expecting them to do this flexibility equality analysis on every role before they advertise it ?
P robably , yes .

Angela Mathews : Whether or not it is in the advert , t he detail should be in the job description , because that is what an individual is going to be performance measured and assessed by . F or me it is all about the job description ; it is golden. I am less worried about the job advert . W e know there is a lot of improvement that needs to be made when writing an inclusive job description , so I agree with you .

Daisy Goodall : J ust one quick point : a collective agreement around flexible working will reduce the number of requests that are coming in , which will support employers when they make those decisions . L ots of unionised workplaces have collective agreements already and if your policies are really strong around flexible working , paid carers ’ leave, disability leave, and so on , then you are going to have a much easier time doing that analysis when you are looking at a big job pool .
Q88 Kevin McKenna : S ome of what you have been saying is almost in the old nudge unit style : s lightly changing language has a big impact on the employer as well as the employee .

M oving back to mandating , if you are saying th at o utside the scope of reasonable adjustments there are vast element s of things that are not covered and, a s Daisy was saying , there are some jobs where flexible working is not possible at all , is it worth flipping everything on its head , making it so that all jobs are advertised as flexible by default ? Is it worth m ak ing that a legal requirement a nd then making employers have to say , “Right, there’s this small set that ar en’t; we just can’t do anything about that , ” t o make sure that you have simplified things and evened out the demand across the board ? Y ou are not making a few jobs with a small set of demands that have to be flexible ; you are making it every job by default . H ave you thought about that ? Do you think that would be proportionate on employers ?

Angela Mathews : I t depends on what flexible means . I will talk about my own team : I am a stroke survivor . I work with a million adjustments , and without those adjustments I would not be in a job . O ne t hing that is non-negotiable is being able to work across Westminster , travel ling in whatever way I need to , to be in person and come to these things . I t is non-negotiable . Y ou could say , as a flexible working request I am going to ask for my role to be carved so that someone else in my team does the in-person stuff and I can stay at home to preserve my energy , or stay in the office and do the other elements of the role . H owever, we are a tiny team . T here is me and H amish , who is behind me . W hat is flexible and reasonable would be different if we were a team of 10.

O rganisations change a lot , so it might be that in the same team over the course of five years you move between one and nine people . W e have other roles in our organisation . We are a small to medium organisation where our advice service is a phone line available to members 9 am to 5 pm . Y ou have to be on that phone between those times. If I ask to work between 7 am until 3 pm, the answer is , “N o , sorry , you can’t because we would not be covered . W e are a small team .” F lexibility is sometimes about times and sometimes a bout , as has already been said by a colleague , fluctuating conditions . I need to work like this when I feel like this , but I need to work like th at when I feel like that .

T he biggest issue is knowing , at the point of a job advert , what we mean by flex in a role . A s an example , I might have started my day at 12 pm tod ay but then I might work until 11 pm . T hat is flexibility . O ther s who have flexible working arrangements start from 6 am and work until 11 am . T hey then have a few hours off and work from 3 pm until 7 pm . T hat is fine for a person whose job is purely desk-based and involves data auditing. However, if they did my job , that would not be okay . I t is about what we mean by flexibility at the point that we are asking employers to write t he job description in a flexibility-by-default way .” Daisy , what do you think ?

Daisy Goodall : O bviously , the TUC holds that flexibility should be the norm and we agree that there should be a default right to flexible working . A s I was saying with the job adverts , flexible working legislation would reflect that objective justification that we have in the Equality Act . M ost disabled people should already receive flexibility at work via reasonable adjustments but the reason this is so important is because of the discrimination and the stigma around flexible working , as I mention ed earlier . I f there were stronger rights for flexible working , then it would become more normalised and there would be less stigma around it .

W hen we are talking about disabled workers and the requests they are putting in for flexibility and the discussions they are having at work , it is important to highlight that polling has shown that 34 % of disabled workers do not want to talk about their health with their manager , including their disability or long-term health condition , and 20 % had not disclosed at all because they we re worried about negative repercussions : losing their job, unfair treatment , and so on . Stronger rights for flexible working would benefit disabled workers hugely even though it would not necessarily be aimed at them . We welcome the changes in the ERA around reasonableness and the duty to consult .

I also want to flag a bit of research that we have done around th e eight business reasons that remain . T he TUC and Flex for All partners asked members of the public to send in responses to the previous Government consultation on flexible working in 2021 and 87 % of almost 6 , 000 respondents felt the business reasons meant employers could turn down requests too easily . U nions agree with that f rom their experience , s o replacing these with criteria for rejection , mirroring the objective justification in t he Equality Act , would be a fairer process . That is what we are calling for .

The response to our flexible working consultation outlines how we think the legislation could be improved , including a right to accompaniment and a right to appeal that employers often already have in place but it empowers workers through the process as well . W e are trying to break down those barriers that disabled workers feel when they request flexibility.

Q89 Richard Quigley : W elcome , both . S orry I was a little late ; democracy was calling . We have seen employers on this drive to mandate people going back to the office . You might be l ucky enough to have a flexible arrangement such as all from home or half and half . W hat is the evidence to support that mandat e to be back in the office ?

Daisy Goodall : I nterestingly , lots of the research shows it is more likely to come from senior leaders than l ine managers . A CIPD survey found that 40 % of employers said there was pressure for their employees to come into the office more , and 56 % of those said it came from senior leaders . We see that t rend across the different employment sectors .

T he things that employers t alk about when mandating time in the office are things such as improve d collaboration , enhancing engagement and connection , and boosting productivity and support for new employees . T hese are all really hard to measure and unions have told the TUC that these mandates often do not have evidence around those desired outcomes . I n fact , we have some really good research from the FDA that shows m embers felt the blanket increase in mandated office time , which was introduced in 2023 , had not led to any of those desired outcomes in productivity or support for younger employees . M anagers felt they were forced to micromanage their teams and waste time doing so.

There is some evidence that is really key ; it is supported by P rospect union and P ublic F irst research . I t showed that employers that did not offer remote working were the least likely to think it improved productivity . T hat is really interesting because it shows that it is not based on evidence ; it is based on a lack of trust or bias . I f you reverse it, it shows that employers that offer remote working think that it boost s productivity . T hey talk about a perception gap and they say that it actually stunts a business’s ability to maximise productivity of hybrid work .

University of Birmingham research found that 71 % of line managers thought home working was a performance - enhancing tool , which is another really strong piece of research . E ssentially , back-to-office mandates are often rooted in negative perceptions of hybrid working, despite the wealth of evidence that home working has a lot of benefits . T hinking back to the disabled workers we have been discussing , their experiences of discrimination and reluctance to put in place arrangements may be part of the reason for the mandate and not seeing how that could impact different parts of your workforce . T his also ties in and reinforces our calls for stronger rights to flexible working and the duty around advertising .

Chair : Can I jump in super quickly ? You are b oth being so brilliantly thorough in all your answers and it is so helpful for us . I am just conscious of time , so as we go through the last few questions, could you keep the answers very short? Thank you so much.
Yes, of course.
Daisy Goodall : Yes , absolutely .

Q90 Richard Quigley : Your answers are fantastically in-depth and v ery well answered . T hank you both very much . Y ou mentioned there is an impact on disabled workers . A re you able to measure what that impact is ? W hat steps should be taken to avoid the negative impacts of mandating for disabled workers ?
Daisy Goodall : I n terms of getting th e data that you asked for , what is it specifically th at you wanted , because I have some stats ?

Q91 Richard Quigley : You have quite a lot of stats around what happens in general terms when going back to the office and the productivity of those who are still allowed flexible work ing. I s there a specific set of data for people with disabilities if they are mandated to go back to the office , or otherwise ?

Daisy Goodall : Yes . The best I have here is t he W ork F oundation , which is a really good body that we use a lot for its evidence . It did a study in 2022 that found 65 % of disable d workers wanted to work remotely and 10 % did not want to. T hat empowerment to make choices around the types of flexible working they had to manage their conditions was preferable to the mandates . Obviously, that show s that 90% express ed a desire to carry on working remotely or hybrid ly . It is really strong evidence that they are able to manage their conditions a lot better when they have access to choices .

I t is i mportant to say that there was a lot of uptick in mental health among respondents to our survey from working hybridly ; often reasonable adjustments and control over their working hours were needed to make that happen . T here are detriments to these mandates , especially for disabled workers . In the FDA study I referenced earlier, about 60% of respondents reported that office time mandates meant that disabled respondents experienced more negative impacts than their non-disabled colleagues . S o me 32% of disabled respondents said the mandate had significantly worsened their productivity and it was 80% for non-disabled respondents. Further, 45% of disabled respondents said that it had significantly worse ned their work-life balance and it was 34% for non-disabled participants , so there was quite a big difference there as well . I deally , people need to be empowered to make choices about these things and to have reasonable adjustments , because that is the way they are going to be more productive at work .

Angela Mathews : I will not repeat the good stuff Daisy has said , but we also see in our research that there is no doubt that there are benefits to working from home , or working in a hybrid way , not just for disabled people but for many people with lots of different life circumstances, backgrounds , and situations . I a gree with that 100%.

Return-to-office mandates get a bad name by default . T he reason for wanting people together is sometimes not evidence-based , and it is not always wrong . I spoke to a business leader a couple of months ago who was still trying to get 60% of time in the office back . T his person said to me , “I s it bad that we just want our people to be together ?” I am not saying that there are no other ways to bring people together but leaders we have spoken to sometimes feel that they are somehow being , by default , non-inclusive , or doing something wrong or bad by wanting people back to the office . W e see very few employers that are demanding their workforce come back every day . A lot offer flexibility with at least one day a week in the office and p eople can choose . S ome organisations have been so open about how people choose that they have seen flexible working requests go down because they have left it to employees to choose . A s a disabled person myself , I do not think i t i s right that disabled people c an work from home . I nclusion is about , “O kay , how can we get you to the office ?” I f it does not work , or it is not what you want , or it is going to be easier for you to stay at home , then that is different , but to not bother is another issue .
Richard Quigley : It just lets people off the hook , effectively.
Angela Mathews : Absolutely . It is also not good for disabled people to not be in the workplace and for organisations to say , “L et ’ s keep the disabled people at home because it ’ s too hard .”

I will be quick ; I have noted what you said . W e also hear a lot of well-meaning reasons for people wanting their workforce back in the office . A couple of our members said , “I t ’ s just easier to look after our employees when they ’ re all together .” I dug a little more on that and they said t hey had had a couple of situations where people ha d been on T eams meetings and witnessed someone have a heart attack . That is really traumatic . T hey said that when people are all together , we can see if someone is not doing okay and check in more . T here are different reasons for those mandates happening , but I would agree with Daisy that, f or the most part , we hear that some of those mandates are coming from leadership . A lot of the time the manager does not know it is going to happen before it does .

Q92 Richard Quigley : D o you think the Government should take steps to test the validity of return - to - office mandates ? I am not advocating th at th e Government should interfere . One-word answers are sufficient, if you wish.
