Witnesses: Vanessa Willems and Yann Faivre.

Q32 Welcome to our second panel of witnesses on our first day of our inquiry into the UK and the Sahel. Our witnesses are joining us virtually and I would like both Vanessa and Yann to introduce themselves for the purpose of the record. Vanessa, let us will start with you .

Hello, and thank you so much for this invitation. My name is Vanessa Willems. I am the A dvocacy and P olicy A dviser for FONGA, the forum at regional level for w est and c entral Africa. It is n ice to meet you.

Hello . It is nice to meet you. Thank you for your invitation. I am Yann Faivre. I am the E xecutive D irector for the Danish Refugee Council for w est Africa, n orth Africa and Latin America. I am based in Dakar for several years. This is where we have our regional operations.

Q33 Thank you. I will begin, Vanessa, by asking you about the fact that humanitarian access is increasingly constrained by both insecurity and Government - imposed restrictions. Of these, what do you believe presents the greatest practical obstacle to delivering assistance in central Sahel?

Thank you for this question. My answer is it depends on what country we are talking about. Recently , we have received a report from two organisations that are members of the forum, and they documented over 200 incidents that took place in 2025 of impeding access on the ground. What we see is that in Burkina Faso, for example, it is mostly security that is impeding humanitarian access, whereas in a country like Niger it is bureaucratic and administrative impediments that are the primary cause of challenges that actors on the ground are facing to access people in need. In Mali the balance is a bit more even between the two category types of incidents. Would you like me to go into more details on this?
Q34 You have touched on some specifics . I f you are able to give us a general impression of the situation, that would be helpful.

Okay, thank you. So, what incidents are we talking about? If you are talking about Burkina Faso, for example, a recent example that we faced in 2026 is the Banque des Dépôts du Trésor ; a rough translation would be treasury bank. We have been asked by the authorities to put the money meant to support the humanitarian response projects within the treasury bank. What we see is that this measure, which is not necessarily at odds with humanitarian principles, the way and rapidity that it was implemented led to significant challenges for the humanitarian actors on the ground. For example, we did not have access to liquidity quickly enough . W e did not see our payments being done quickly enough so that slowed down the purchase of different items . W e did not see the payments to humanitarian staff taking place quickly enough, so that led to other significant challenges. All that slowed down the humanitarian response.

In a context like Niger, the challenges we are facing are more like the authorisation to access the gr ants that are delivered by the authorities. They are either slowed down or for the most part there are delays in providing those authorisations, but sometimes we are also facing refusal. That is national NGOs that report those challenges, and it is with the exemptions for customs and so o n . The administrative process is too slow and the documents that need to be provided by the authorities are too slow. That also leads to some challenges for them justifying their expenses with the donors.

In Mali, a recent example that has taken our attention has been the 10% tax that the authorities wanted to impose on the humanitarian response. It required a lot of conversation between the authorities and the humanitarian community, and it led to an exemption that was provided by the authorities a few months back.

I think what those examples tell us is that within the speech of the authorities we are witnessing an increase in their desire to express their sovereignty. They want to have more leadership and oversight on the humanitarian response, and they want the humanitarian response to be more aligned with their national priorities. To be very clear, NGOs on the ground do not have any issues with s overeignty of state. We respect that , b ut the way the reforms are taken and being implemented, the measures that are being adopted, can lead to significant operational challenges on the ground, just as I described with the BDT, as we call it, the treasury bank.

This also teaches us something very important : t hat dialogue is key to keep the trust between the actors. We need a sustained dialogue. We need to build trust with those actors and be solution - oriented. We need to be supported in building that trust and dialogue space. Y ou may ask what this mean s for an actor such as the UK . I think the way you can support us is by helping us to create that space.

To give you a very specific example that will be coming very soon on the table, you may be aware that the authorities of the central Sahel, AES authorities, hosted a humanitarian forum back in August 2026. During that forum, they took a resolution to develop a humanitarian policy. As humanitarian actors, we see this humanitarian policy for the AES countries as an opportunity to engage and dialogue with them. We see this as an opportunity to put measures in the policy that could, for example, facilitate cross-border humanitarian responses.

W e also see it is equally important that we are part of the discussions and that we are being consulted in the process to set up those policies so we can raise any concerns or suggestions to make sure that the humanitarian response is as fluid and effective as possible. More generally speaking, humanitarian diplomacy is definitely a way that an actor such as the UK could support us on the field. We need your support to keep the dialogue with the authorities to help resolve solutions.

There are maybe four points I could share with you about the way the humanitarian diplomacy should be conducted, and this is based on a recent experience. First, what we see is that when you mention diplomacy conducted by diplomatic actors, it is co-ordinated. It is more efficient when it is co-ordinated among them. A recent example of that would be in Chad, where the authorities also decided to put on the table — or they floated around, let ’s say it that way — t his idea of putting a tax on the humanitarian response. We received strong support from the donors; they put down on paper their position on that and shared it with the authorities. They co-ordinated among themselves what their responses would be and that was extremely helpful.

Another point that we have in mind is humanitarian diplomacy is the most effective when it is co-ordinated, discussed and grounded in the operational realities of the field actors. W hat does it mean? It means that before your representatives go on to the field and engage with the authorities, you could have conversations, pre-briefings, with the NGOs that are operating on the ground, and receive reports from us to support your engagement with the authorities.

The third thing that we have witnessed and observed is that humanitarian diplomacy is also most efficient when it is driven and guided by humanitarian principles. The fourth point to keep in mind with humanitarian diplomacy is that it is helpful to have diplomatic actors supporting us, but we have to keep in mind that the vast majority of access issues are resourced by humanitarian actors operating themselves on the ground; their direct engagement with different actors direct on the ground. What we need to do is keep investing in the collective capacity to do so , supporting the forums at country level. Thank you so much for that question. Please let me know if I need to clarify any points.

Q35 The only point I wanted to raise is in terms of diplomatic actors in the wider setting . A re there other actors, such as Russia and China, for example, who might want different outcomes, and therefore their diplomatic actions with the host Governments might be different from ours?

It is an interesting question. W hen an actor such as the FONGA reach out to different diplomatic actors across the world to support, we do assess how they can be supportive. I do not have a specific response about China or Russia, but we have identified other stakeholders across the region where we need their support ; f or example, Turkey. We do know that they are selling drones —they are probably not the only ones— to the authorities across the three central S a h e l countries . Those drones are then used after for military purposes, but they represent an increasing challenge for our teams on the ground. We are worried about the incidents that they can represent against the humanitarian community, although it is collateral damage and they are never a direct target . W e are worried about that.

We are worried as well for the impact it can have, obviously, on the protection of civilians. Y ou mentioned diplomacy and engagement with stakeholders such as Turkey . I t is essential to make sure that they are aware of the risk that when they sell those warfare instruments to the authorities, they make sure that they put everything in place to safeguard the protection of the civilians and the aid workers on the ground. I know it is not exactly the stakeholder you were aiming for, but it is just to say that when we engage and we look at support, we also look at a different set of stakeholders, not just European ones.

We also look at the diplomatic actors within the region. An interesting lesson we took away from the political transition in Niger back in 2023 was the influence on access that actors such as ECOWAS or even Togo or Benin had on our capacity to respond on the ground. W e do try to have engagement directly with them. Our relationship today I would not say is as strong as we have with actors such as the UK or the European Union, but we are definitely building those relationships with them. I think that is also where you could have a role, to help us build those relationships and promoting IHL and the importance of humanitarian access with them as well. Thank you.

Q36 Thank you. Yann, can I ask you how the UK can ensure that its security and counter-terrorism partnerships in the Sahel do not undermine perceptions of humanitarian neutrality or put aid workers at greater risk?

Thank you for this question . I t is quite a big question. Those activities are definitely very sensitive to the context in which we are operating. I would say that definitely we can connect the implementation of some stabilisation plan s and the counter-violence, counter-terrorist activities in some areas, and the difference we feel from the population or even from the authorities or their groups, the way they see and accept us and the way they consider humanitarian workers. I t can definitely under some circumstances put at risk the humanitarian workers or the totality of our programme in some cases.

T o answer your question, the key point here is really to ensure that those programmes are made in a way that preserve the neutrality and independence of the humanitarian workers and humanitarian action in general. There is a clear need for co-ordination from those programmes with the humanitarian actors to be able to assess the risk that one is generating for the other. Although they are necessary in some context s and can be part of a global solution, there is a need to make sure that the three operations can be implemented conjunctly , otherwise to consider that maybe those activities be implemented in a more sequential manner.
Q37 Can I start with you, Vanessa, and then come to Yann? In the context of funding cuts to the Sahel, what programmes or interventions are most critical to protect from further cuts?

Thank you for that question . I t is a tough one. I think it is not so much about what one you should protect; it is more about what approach you should adopt to keep supporting the humanitarian response in - country. One guiding principle that we should have in mind is that the response must be a needs-based response. H ow do we define the needs? We need to have assessments that are conducted in an independent manner on the ground to assess those needs, but also in a way that includes the communities that are directly impacted by the conflict or the climate change that resolve any humanitarian needs. We need them to be involved in identifying the needs, prioritising the needs and ideally into the design of the response as well.

I think that is the key principle to have in mind when you think about what should be preserved. It is an approach. What you need as well is to make sure that the funding that you provide allows flexibility for the response, for the very simple fact that the needs we assess today might not be the exact same as the needs that we will find on the ground tomorrow. When you have a displacement of thousands of people from one day to the next, the needs are obviously changing from one day to the next. So, we need a flexible funding mechanism.

We also need to have a funding mechanism that allows a multi-sector response and a multi-year response so we can address also some of the causes of the humanitarian needs and build the resilience of the population for tomorrow. Yann, maybe you have some elements you would like to share on this as well .

Yes. You highlighted the principles to be respected in general. I have a couple of points of a more specific dimension. T he cuts, of course , have been impacting the very vulnerable population, and the most at-risk groups in society. In addition to all the principles that Vanessa just shared, I would say that there is certainly an importance for us, and for the UK as well, to focus on the IDPs, particularly in remote and insecure areas , and to keep focusing on the host communities . T here is a particular issue in Sahel, if we speak about central Sahel or Chad, where we are having IDPs and refugees in host communities that are potentially poorer than the people th ey host. It is very much the case in Chad , and that could generate further destabilisation around the initial area of crisis.

Women, girls and children are being extremely affected because, of course, some programmes in some areas were totally cut. I am speaking in particular about the GBV, the gender-based violence programming , that has been totally forgotten in some areas. T hey need to be kept at the centre of attention as well. It is definitely p eople with disabilities and older people who are usually the most vulnerable. Finally, there is a particular look and intention to keep on the question of the returnees and people going back to communities. We have seen in some countries in Sahel in particular some precipitation — some high speed in some returnees returning not really in a sustainable way. T here is some attention to be paid there as well.

Q38 Thank you. How are the reductions in international aid affecting local society organisations in the S a h e l to deliver services and respond to communities ’ needs? What impact do the aid cuts have on the work you are doing? Vanessa, do you want to take that one?
I do not know if I want to start or if Yann wants to start with the impact it had on the—
I can start with the impact it had on our organisation. I do not know if you want to share some elements that are common with the other humanitarian organisation s in the region.

The impact has been extremely important and is still important. We feel it. We have been reducing our workforce worldwide in the last three years by 25%. In some areas, we have been cutting down the activities, not on the bas is of the end of the needs or achieved sustainability, but just on the basis of the reduction of the funds or even sometimes the disappearance of those funds.

T he impact has been very important. It has been very important for communities where we sudden ly had to leave them on their own in some areas of the continent. We had to close down offices because the access was pretty much connected to the proximity and then to give up in some geographies in Burkina Fas o in particular and in Mali as well. We have been at the same time preparing ourselves to make sure that we could have a strong impact and continue to accompany the key popula tion that we were engaged with in the past few years . We did engage a lot in a localisation agenda. We hear very often that the local isation is going with cost reduction and so on.

Finally, what we saw mainly that was of great interest — we were already involved in localisation before for some local acceptance and local context analysis dimensions —is that since the cuts we were going faster on some sustainability agenda s with the local actors than we would go without. W e have been working a lot on creating spaces for local actors; not spaces of funding only but making sure that they were participating more obviously to the humanitarian agenda , to the programming and the design of our interventions.

You certainly heard about the S a h e l r egional f und that we created in the region, created in collaboration with FCDO. This fund is now serving some windows of funding exclusively reserved for local actors in central S a h e l and Chad. Local organisations are members of the board, piloting and participating in the co-ordination of the fund.

That is some of the impacts that the cuts have had . There has been what we used to call the prioritisation . I am not very comfortable with speaking about prioritisation because the message is always the same : that w e have been getting done what was not a priority , which is not the case. We have been making prioritisation among choices that we did before that were already priorities because the region is extremely sensitive, weak and exposed to conflict or climate change or displacement. We work also on the migration agenda at Dakar.

W e have to make choices among elements that were of equal priorities, and the choices were very much driven by the way that the funding is now, for a big part, addressed to the humanitarian community. We have already targeted geographies, very narrow targeting of geographies, so some choices have been made more on this basis rather than on a needs bas is that Vanessa was putting forward a few minutes ago. That is mainly how the funds have been impacting the work of DR C and how DR C is supporting its targeted beneficiaries in Niger.

Beyond what you just said as well, what came to my mind while you were talking was the impact in the protection sector and the local, community-based organisations that are engaged in the response. What was interesting to note shortly after the massive and abrupt cut that took place in 2025 is that local organisations that had been trained and empowered to provide a humanitarian response to address the protection needs, including of women and girls on the field, were, i n the first time, still capable to provide that response. W hat was strongly impacted quite quickly was the referral mechanism towards the protection services provided by other stakeholders on the ground.

A year down the road, the picture is evolving slightly. I heard reports of a women and girls - led organisation in countries such as Burkina Faso being particularly impacted by the funding cuts and in a more difficult position to provide their response. Overall, if you look at the protection sector, a recent note that was published by the regional protection working group that is based in Dakar identified a severe reduction of the amount of human itarian workers that a re engaged in the humanitarian response.

I am trying to look at the number for central S a h e l. What we have seen is that they had 310 organisations supporting the response in 2024, and this came down to 232 in 2025. That is a reduction by nearly a quarter of the amount of stakeholders providing a protection response within a single year. That is indeed a dreadful impact that we have witnessed on the field.
Q39 Yann, how effective is the S a h e l r egional f und at meeting both the medium and longer-term humanitarian needs in the region?

I think on the S a h e l r egional f und , and it is not only my voice bringing it, I would say that we had a lot of involvement from the FONGA with us. The S a h e l r egional f und is led by a collective of civil NGOs and INGOs together, under the presidency of one of them. The feedback we have from the assessments and the partners is that the efficiency of the S a h e l r egional f und is at a high level, that the delays in dealing with some calls and problems, the reactivity in terms of some emerging crisis—I am having in mind the cholera warning in Chad not such a long time ago —t he way the good donorship principles that were particularly committed to at the Grand Bargain are respected.

So, generally I would say that we see the S a h e l r egional f und as extremely efficient in the way it takes care and responds to the needs of the partners, international and national. I see a Sa h e l r egional f und that is extremely effective in the trust buil ding , as Vanessa was mentioning, with the authorities in this part of the world. There is a co-ownership from the different Government s we see in Niger and Burkina . W e are very often extremely surprised to see the interest that those Administrations are positioning on the S a h e l r egional f und.

The efficiency in terms of immediate financial numbers is that the S a h e l r egional f und is functioning with only 12% management costs , which is extremely limited in the industry, so the part of the funding going directly for implementation is high. The efficiency can be considered as definitely there as well. There is also a secondary effect in terms of efficiency of the S a h e l r egional f und. The secondary effect is to enrich and bring more diversity in the segment of the pooled funds. The fact that in some areas you have more than one pooled fund operating, and that it generates some competition, some common interests, some exchanges and some joint rounding processes , make the performance increase.

In terms of indirect efficiency, I would keep in mind that this S a h e l r egional f und being—not such a new player because it has existed for four or five years— a new architectur al bridge in the funding landscape generates a lot of benefits on other sides as well.

Q40 Thank you, Yann . T hat chimes with what we have heard : 90% of beneficiaries report satisfaction with assistance received through the S a h e l r egional f und. Are there any lessons that you think the FCDO could draw from this model of delivery?

Yes, the 90% is, as you said, very high and we are extremely satisfied with that. I will say that there are certainly some good lessons that the FCDO can take, and I am sure that the team in Dakar took note of some of them . The SRF is providing real evidence that locally led action can be scaled responsibly when accompanied by strong governance and appropriate risk sharing. So, that is the demonstration that we can do.

The SRF is demonstrating that early implication of local actors in the funding mechanism is possible, and that actually it can provide a lot of contextual relevance. It provides sustainability in the concept. It gives us a meaningful voice to most of those local actors that are finding in the SRF a very interesting and original space and forum to express themselves.

Q41 Thank you. You moved on to where I was going to move the conversation, so well done, which is around the 25% of the fund that supports local partners. In context such as the S a h e l, this is obviously important because they have a reach beyond many of the larger international NGOs.

Vanessa, I will ask you this question . H ow meaningful do you think that that transfer of power is in practice? In t he use of the fund to support local actors, are you seeing any practice-based examples of where that funding is able to use grassroots voices , be more locally designed , be more responsive , and have better reach?

Thank you. We see the SRF as an essential tool to meet the engagement of the Grand Bargain, but also to meet the engagement of Tom Fletcher within the Humanitarian Reset, where he says that the response should be as local as possible and as international as needed. A tool such as the SRF provides the opportunity for fixing the money, the way it goes. It helps local actors to have not only a word to say within the governance, the way the fund is identifying the needs, setting the priorities and designing the response, but it also helps them beyond that to build their own capacities to provide the mentoring that they need to keep responding.

Beyond the 25%, I think one element that is important is the second person support costs that are cascaded to the national partners on the ground. This is essential , because we tend to think that because we go local it is going to be cheaper, but the reality on the field is that local organisations also need support costs. They need to have offices, access to internet, a security management framework to satisfy the security of their own staff, and so on. I think this system is essential.

The beauty of it as well, beyond the main envelope, is the catalytic envelopes that are available and that allow funding for NGO forums on the ground, and the collective engagement that they have, but also the way it provides funding for innovation, such as the b arometer, for example. It is a project that was led from the regional level and is a tool that allows us to assess the progress that we have made on the localisation agenda since the Grand Bargain was adopted in 2016.
Thank you. I am just going to look to the Chair. We have two more questions, and I am conscious of the importance of 21 and 22.
Yes. Can you shorten them?

Q42 Yes. Just quick answer these, because we have some other important questions to ask. I am going to jump straight to 20. The fund operates across Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and Chad, but displacement, food insecurity and conflict often cross national borders. How effectively does the regional model address these cross-border challenges?

Just a small additional element to your previous question, indeed 25% of the SRF is dedicated to the local window and can be accessed directly by local actors, but the international window is as well aiming at consortia that have national partners inside, so they can bring some organisation s that are a little bit less strong , to benefit from some experience and start to build that capacity. If you put it all together, it is almost a third of the SRF that ends up being operationalised by local actors. I t is 25% directly plus the indirect part through international consortia of 31%.

Coming back to your question on how it operates, it was really a key element when the SRF was born. A t the time the sum was created five years ago , that called for a regional response to a regional crisis. At the end, we could set up only some country-based reforms that were looking at the crisis one by one. So, we thought that having a regional solution would be compl e menting those country-based fund s and enabl ing some cross-border activities. It also enables some more agility as well, an evolution of the funding from one country to the other, depending on the evolution of the crisis, taking into consideration the fact that the access in S a h e l has never been totally lost. There are some areas that are not accessible at certain times, but some of those are and we want those that were not accessible before to be coming back . The SRF proved to be a good tool as well for consorti a to manage that and to be able to focus in another area while an area was not accessible. The SRF has been enhancing this regional approach, while having a regional fund management you need, so that the SRF is managed at the regional level, taking into account regional code, but at the same time is totally embedded in the national context and requirements , so the very local particularities are taken into account and consolidated at regional level .

What is very interesting is that the SRF promotes regional advocacy, which is in many countries of the region the only way to realise some advocacy. The SRF, through its regional co-ordination, generates some spaces as well for lessons learnt with international and national actors cross-border from one region—
Thank you, Yann. I am s orry to cut you off. That is interesting and it is a helpful response. I am just conscious that Tracy has a couple of important questions for you as well.
To conclude our session, Tracy has some questions on women, girls and children.
Q43 How effectively are humanitarian development programmes addressing the underlying economic causes of gender-based violence ? Can I come to Yann first on this?

Yes, of course. As I mentioned previously, the funding cuts have been seen in some regions in Sahel , impacting gender-based violence programmes. Women and girls are among the most vulnerable and most at risk according to our protection risk assessment, and that is what we need to focus on. I think a geographic approach with the remaining funds is not always taking care of all the needs all across the board. To be very honest, there are some regions today in Sahel where women and girls who are at risk are not benefitting from the support they should be benefitting from and that they were benefitting from before.

There have been some forgotten elements in the so-called prioritisation exercise that we had to do to utilise things elsewhere. So, the impact is huge. The support to women - led organisations is probably less visible in Sahel today than it is in some other regions of the world. We know all too well that the conditions of women and girls —and the global indicators of the HEI index I will show you if you like—living in Sahel are among the most difficult currently , and for years, in the region. So, that is a key issue for us.

We keep them systematically at the heart of the protection risk analysis that we implement locally. When it comes to the Sahel gender-based violence, we keep programmes as very important in the areas where we publish the code. W e have some protection activities around the region where we monitor the cases of people denied their rights or who are victims of violence. We do not do protection monitoring alone ; we usually do it systematically with some response attached through individual protection assistance that we provide.

So, all women and girls that we meet along our programmes that are victims of gender-based violence or other type of rights denial, we endeavour to do this positively, but definitely it is not enough.

J ust to complete a quick point o n the response provided by Yann, the protection monitoring system is one of the severe impacts that we have seen from the funding cuts last year. The monitoring system is clearly jeopardised, and we have increas ing difficulty in monitoring the needs i n the field. So, if an investment needs to be made and something needs to be protected, it is this monitoring system as well , because without that it is difficult to provide a good response to the needs of the women and girls i n the field.

Q44 Thank you. Just on that, Vanessa, how should international donors balance pursuing long-term progress on gender equality with supporting initiatives such as girls’ education that may have greater political acceptance?
That might be more for Yann.

We can do both. I can start, Vanessa, if you want to compl e ment. T hat is a real key issue. The fact that we have an assistance that is getting widely reduced is bringing us most of all to consider and to declare that life - saving is essential. It is true that life - saving is essential and we want to keep all the life - saving elements as a priority and use the funds we have for that. That is very sensitive when it comes to girls and women, and you highlight the access to education, but even before , all the conditions before access to education, the life - saving activities are not fully responding to all the root causes of those issues — economic, social, safety, physical challenges that are concerned.

I would connect that with the previous question , thinking that there is a need for keeping a long-term activity and priority connected to the immediate humanitarian funding when it comes to those protection activities, particularly of this target population.

Q45 Thank you. Just to further that a little bit, how are the funding cuts and restrictions on civic space affecting local civic society organisations’ ability to support women and girls, particularly where they are in rural and conflict - affected communities?
The question is for me?
Whoever feels most appropriate to answer is fine.

I can share with you — and I am sure, Vanessa, you have that in mind as well — that last week we had communicated for Burkina Faso only the list of 10 local organisations that are closing down due to the funding cuts. We have a lot of small organisations that were extremely instrumental in the way we were answering some of those issues, and women’s organisation s are one of those organisations that are usually served by this funding, that are closing, losing their premises and losing dynamics. T his is where it is directly affected.

A second way of direct implication on this programming is the fact that we have much less frontline staff than we used to have, so in some communities those programmes might not be considered as programmes of use or priority one. We have much less frontline staff and volunteers from our partners as well going from village to village , s o our identification c apacity is certainly less than it used to be.
Vanessa, is there anything you wanted to add to that question?
Not to that question, thank you.

Q46 Finally, to you both, could disengaging from development co-operation and response to human rights violations further restrict opportunities for civil society and women’s organisations? I will come to Vanessa first on this one.
I am s orry, could you repeat the question because I did not understand it ?

Okay . C ould disengaging from development co-operation and response to human rights violations further restrict the opportunities for civil society and women’s organisations? So, stepping away from certain organisations, how would that land? What would that look like on the ground for women’s organisations?
If we further disengaged, financially and supportive?
Yes, in response to human rights violations .
I do not have any other evidence than what Yann has already shared. I do not know if you do , Yann .

I f I understood the question, if the idea is to see how we address human rights violation s and what response we can bring across our programming in central Sahel , I would say that most of them, when they are identified and are taken in charge by the teams of DRC or the partners of DRC or the partners of the Sahel r egional f und , are dealt with by the authorities . T hat is usually the way it goes. Basically, I know that very often the question of human rights is needed to be dealt with at a central level, and we need a central commitment, but when it comes to individual cases, most of the time we deal with it with the local authorities at the very local level where the violation occurred, and the response is very often provided by the technical services from the region.
I do not know if it responds to your question, but that is the way it takes place in most of our activities.
Thank you very much.

I thank you both, Yann and Vanessa, for your time this afternoon in contributing to our inquiry into the UK and the Sahel . I am concluding this evidence session and drawing our meeting to a formal close.

sessions.iT: Trade in a turbulent world: how should the UK deploy its trade instruments?
sessions.w: Maxwell Green (Make UK)

segs.tx: International Agreements Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Trade in a turbulent world: how should the UK deploy its trade instruments ?
Tuesday 20 Octob er 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair) ; Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Lord Boateng; Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury; Lord German; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord McDonald of Salford; Lord Stevenson of Balmacara ; Baroness Verma.
Evidence Session No. 8 Heard in Public Questions 70 – 7 6
Witness
Maxwell Green, Senior Policy Manager, Make UK.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witness
Maxwell Green .

Q70 ​​ The Chair: Thank you very much, everyone. I am extremely pleased to welcome Maxwell Green, a senior policy manager at Make UK. Sadly, our other witness, Fionnuala Horrocks - Burns , from DHL, was unable to join us on account of her travel difficulties. We are sorry to miss her but very grateful to Maxwell for being here.

We have a variety of different themes to ask you about. When I came to a Make UK seminar, which is what led me to suggest that you come and talk to our committee, a number of your members gave very practical examples of how uncertainty and the tariff volatility we have seen over the last year or so has affected them, and other issues that were more practically applied to them.

To give you a bit of background, we have done a lot of research into the high-level FTAs, MoUs and so on, but sometimes that does not reach down to the reality of someone trying to sell their spectacles from the UK to India and all the different problems that are created around that with customs blockages, digital certification and so on. So, if you could be as practical as possible in giving examples, that would be enormously helpful. Lord Anderson, could you start with the first topic and question?

In retrospect, the period after the Second World War appears as a golden age in international trade practice, with greater emphasis on developing countries and greater consensus. Now, the pattern is more protectionism and so on. Given this darkening international context, can you give us any signs of hope?

That is a good first question. There has definitely been a lot of instability and volatility in the global marketplace over the last five to 10 years. Time after time we have had issues around readjusting to life after leaving the EU. We have had issues with the conflicts in the Middle East, US tariffs and, most recently, the conflict in Iran. However, businesses are very resilient to some of these changes. For example, over the first half of this year trade was down by only 5%, despite all the issues in the Middle East. That is after a huge increase in exports last year, so in fact it is sitting way above where it should be when you look at two years ago.

When you look at the detail and where this is coming and going, there is a lot of volatility in individual markets, as you would imagine. That is mostly down to trade diversion. For example, in the first half of this year, we saw US exports dip by 38%. But at the same time, Chinese exports increased by 30%. Germany, the Netherland and Hong Kong were all up as well—Hong Kong by almost double compared to last year.

On the other side, when you look at importing to the UK, we are seeing huge increases in British businesses importing from the rest of the world— imports from the US are up by 11%, China is up by 7.5%, Germany is up by 9%, Switzerland is up by 93%, which is almost double, and Canada is up by 88%.

Therefore, although there are signs that it is slowing down, we are seeing that manufacturers are resilient. In our last manufacturing outlook survey, we found that the share of UK manufacturers exporting increased by 8%. That is aligned with the increased confidence that they are seeing. Export output remains positive, but overall output by the sector is slightly down at the moment and has slowed. I guess the moral of the story is that we are seeing certain signs that it is stable and certain signs that it is going down slightly.

At the same time, businesses have had to adapt to a lot of things over the last few years, and that does not come cost-free. SMEs and other businesses have had to adapt to shocks in oil prices, energy prices and input prices. We have adjusted, we are resilient and we have a positive outlook for the next few years.
In that context, what is your perspective on the service sector?
I am not an expert on the service sector, so I might leave that question and maybe come back to you, if that is okay. I am focused predominantly on goods trade.

Q71 In your own view, which sectors do you think therefore have done really well, and where do you feel the policies that are currently around us are deterring other sectors within manufacturing and development?

It is important to put it in the context of the global environment. Every country is struggling with trade and exports at the moment, so we need to compare those to other countries. Even though, for example, overall automotive sector exports have decreased slightly, they have not decreased as much as other areas. What really helped was the US EPD. For the automotive sector and the beef sector, with exports to the US as our largest single trading market, having that comparative advantage against other markets really helped to boost those exports up, specifically in 2025. I know that I just said that US exports are down this year, but they are so much further above where they should be. It really depends on FTAs and other trade tools that we are focusing on. The US EPD is one example where those sectors are doing very well. Aluminium products are up 14% to the US and steel is up 9%.

There are definitely sectors where we are seeing a lot more growth. In the industrial strategy sectors we have been focusing on over the last few years, we expect those areas to also do well and be more of a priority when it comes to future trade tools.

Q72 I am very interested in what you said about the resilience of the trade groups you represent at Make UK. You spoke about automotive, steel and the industries that have benefited from the EPD. The EDP is not an FTA; it is an understanding, but it is not legally binding. Can you elaborate on the sorts of agreements, whether binding or non-binding, that your members have done well out of? You mentioned the US partnership agreement, but what about others, and other sectors that you represent?

UK manufacturers generally favour binding agreements because they provide long-term certainty and they can look at investment opportunities much further into the future. However, as we all know, there is increasingly a fast-moving global environment and, in the time that it takes to start, negotiate and implement an FTA, things have moved on.

All agreements play a really important part, but I cannot overstate the importance of binding FTAs. For example, they open up market access on a much wider scale. Our members are very excited about the opportunities brought about by the new India FTA, which has just come into force, in a wide range of sectors. Straightaway, we are already seeing tariff reductions on alcohol, medical devices, aerospace and others, and it is also an agreement that will get better over time. Each year, we will have more market access on a range of products.

CPTPP is obviously quite a useful agreement that we are looking into. It opens up some of the fast-growing markets in Asia. The best thing about it is that it keeps developing and expanding. We are on the ground floor of that. We are looking forward to the inclusion, potentially, of Indonesia and the Philippines in that agreement.

We have a big focus on the Australia and New Zealand FTAs, which were the first FTAs that came into force after the UK left the European Union. What is great about Australia is that it was incredibly quick to negotiate, which was a big relief for manufacturers. The India FTA took four and a half years from the start of negotiations to implementation earlier this year; Australia took three. We hope that agreements such as the CPTPP will also be that quick. It took the UK three and a half years from the start but it will get faster as the accession process becomes more familiar to the bloc.

On other agreements that we could into, because obviously FTAs are not the answer to everything, we had the negotiations to update the UK-Canada FTA a few years ago, which stalled on the issue of food standards but there is an opportunity to use more sector-specific agreements. For example, if we cannot get across the line because there is a red line on food standards, we can look at critical minerals or an agreement specifically on energy, which could be quite useful with everything going on in the Middle East. With Canada, as with Australia, we are very similar partners, so it would, I hope, be a lot quicker to negotiate agreements than it would with somewhere such as India or even the GCC.
Can you comment on what exactly does well with Australia and New Zealand, given that you are involved with production and goods? Is transport a problem? What sort of goods do you export?

I can definitely get you a list of the trade stats and what products we are exporting lots of, so that you can draw down into the details. But the UK and Australia markets are very similar, which is probably why they are doing quite well.
When we looked at the recent facts, physical exports—manufactured goods exports—to Australia were down since we signed the deal.
Yes, if you look at the overall picture—
Yes, services were up but goods were down—not by much; maybe by a few per cent. I do not know whether any colleagues remember that. I was surprised by it. Why is that the case?

Obviously, there are certain sectors that are doing much better. Overall, it is looking quite flat, but there are definitely sectors that are looking a lot more positive. I cannot give you the details of why it is down overall. I think that we have a lot of work to do around the implementation of the deals, which has gone a lot better since those Australia and New Zealand deals were signed.

It is doing a lot better going the other way. Products coming from Australia and New Zealand into the UK are up quite substantially. Those inputs will go into our manufacturing to then re-export somewhere else. It is not just a one-way ticket. It is not just exporting to Australia; we also need to focus on the imports.

When you talk about these lags—you mentioned one with the US two years ago and one with Australia—to what extent do we have to factor in the world economic situation during and post Covid when supply chains were getting back to normal?
Could you repeat the question in a slightly different way? I am not sure I fully understand.

You spoke about dips in trade post 2021. To what extent were they to be expected after the Covid shutdown not only here but of supply chains the world over, as well as the recent wars that you mentioned?

Manufacturers obviously have a lag and there are things they would need to adapt to. For example, with the issues in eastern Europe over the last few years, we have had to adapt to different supply chains and move our imports from Ukraine and Russia, which were a large supplier of raw materials. We had to find new partners to bring those in. There were also domestic issues with energy prices, where we will have a lag because of the fact that it takes a while to sink in for manufacturers and for them to adapt to those changes. It is obvious that we will have some kind of push. We are seeing that at the moment with the US bringing in more protectionist policies with its tariffs last year. We saw a huge surge in exports to the US, due mostly to the fact that the UK had a much lower tariff than other markets. Now that the effects of the tariffs are starting to sink in for manufacturers, the US is starting to look at different supplies domestically instead of overseas. It has taken a bit of time but it will slowly filter into the trade statistics and what is happening.

Q73 You have spoken very well about the various trade agreements that have been signed and the different types of trade agreements that benefit your members. But behind all that, presumably there is an overarching question about what the trade policy does. What are the Government setting out as being the objectives? I am interested in your thoughts on the relationship between the two. In particular, have you any ideas that we could take on about how that trade policy itself could change and which would benefit?

The policy that is being created and implemented is of course fantastic. We think that the market access matters a lot. Whether it is an FTA or a sector agreement, it is massively helpful. But if businesses are not aware or able to understand what these things are and we also have lower competitiveness than our competitors in Europe or North America, they cannot fully be utilised. Therefore, there are some areas where we think that policy could be used to help exports grow.

The first would be around improving FTA utilisation by trying to work with industry and the Government collaboratively to try to increase the awareness of FTAs and other trade tools. A lot of businesses are still unaware of some of the advantages that they have or there is complexity with customs or the documentation.

We also think that the guidance that they get from the Government is fantastic, but it comes too late; upon entry into force. If we had it six or three months before—we are of course aware that it will come into force on that date, or soon—businesses can start to look at exporting from day one and that may that may help with the lag that you have after signing an FTA, which takes a while to fully come into effect.
Another big barrier to export support is access to finance. That is why we are very supportive of UK Export Finance and, potentially, looking at increasing its lending capacity as well.
In conclusion, signing an agreement should be viewed as the start of the implementation process rather than the end of it.

We also think we need to look not just at trade policy but also domestic policy, because they are very interlinked. We cannot look at trade policy through a single lens. Trade agreements improve market access, but if domestic policy does not support manufacturing and the competitors to manufacturing, they will not be able to take advantage of those opportunities. For example, the UK has the highest energy industrial energy price in the G7, caused by a lot of external and internal factors. The UK funds environmental and social levies through electricity bills rather than general taxation, adding around 20% to the costs of electricity for manufacturers. That increase in energy prices for manufacturers hurts competition, which has led to the UK having, on average, 46% higher energy industrial energy costs than advanced economies. We believe those costs should be funded through general taxation to reduce energy bills and support industry.
Although trade agreements can create opportunities abroad, we need to make sure that businesses remain competitive at home so that we can remain competitive abroad as well.

Stability and predictability is one of the most important things for manufacturers. You can look at the higher tariffs that the US has put on its market, but businesses need predictability and stability so that we can get that long-term investment and plan, going forward. What we find that is really good with that is free trade agreements, because they are on paper and binding and in 10 to 20 years’ time we can look at some of the areas that businesses can invest in.

There are other unilateral measures that the UK could follow. A review of the global tariff would be helpful. Without importing, a lot of businesses cannot export. Obviously, the UK does not produce everything in the world; it cannot, because of climate and other factors. So, looking again at the global tariff will help us to potentially make inputs more competitive and lead to more competitive exports.

The last thing—sorry, I know that this is a lot—is a more general point about increasing diversification. We can use all the trade tools at our disposal, such as FTAs, non-binding agreements and sector-specific agreements, to try to increase diversification not just in exporting but also importing. Obviously, agreements such as the CPTPP are vital to that, as they will keep on expanding. The UK must keep an active role in looking at other markets and issues that we could be addressing not necessarily through FTAs but through sector-specific agreements, et cetera.

Q74 You mentioned earlier the lag in information reaching manufacturers and businesses. Do you think that is because discussions across Whitehall departments is not consistent? As an organisation, perhaps you know better who works well with you and who does not. Maybe that is where the difficulties lie and the lag can be dramatically reduced if all the departments are aligned.

I am not entirely sure if that is the reason. The lag comes because awareness of the FTAs and new trade agreements is not fully known. Whether that is a problem within the Civil Service and linking up, I am not too sure. There is an opportunity to produce sector-specific market access guides. I know that DBIST and Defra have already started looking at this. If a market is really important for food exports, for example, they might want to bring Defra in. I am not sure about the politics and interactions between government departments, but there is definitely an opportunity for them to work closer together on sector-specific agreements of FTAs that will benefit a sector.

Q75 I do not suppose your members wake up in the morning saying, “I wonder what’s happened to the World Trade Organization. I wonder how it’s getting on”. Yet we have to have some basis for understanding how we are all going to work together in this world. We have had in our evidence a total sense that although the WTO has enormous difficulties and big problems, we could not live without it. So, if you were to explain to your members as they wake up in the morning that this really is an important issue, what would you think they would want, given that you have already said that businesses are looking at certainty, stability and predictability? What does the WTO bring to that table and what would you say to your members if you were trying to convince them that it was a good idea, or a bad idea, to work with it?

It is no secret that the WTO has come under scrutiny and threat. However, historically, and I know that we and our members know this, it has helped to bring smaller countries into the trade environment, given regular rules across that trade environment and reduced barriers. So, although it is important to note that in the public eye the WTO does not look like it is doing what it should be doing, there are a lot of behind-the-scenes forums, meetings and working groups happening. It does a lot more behind the scenes and maybe it is a case of bringing that out and seeing what it is doing in these working groups towards creating common trade rules or reducing common trade barriers across global markets.

In what it does now, do you think people say, “This is really helpful to us; we need to make sure it remains in place”? Do you have any examples of what you think your members will want to ensure is not just retained but also promoted? It might not be a headline about the whole organisation and how you reform it and get agreement. That might be beyond the reach of your reply. But in the undergrowth that you have talked about, there are an awful lot of things going on. What is it that people value and what tools do they use that are good for your manufacturers?

The most important thing that the WTO does is create certainty through shared trading rules. Stability is the most important part for our members when it comes to international trade. Even if there is a huge tariff, as long as we know what is going to happen, the WTO can help to regulate and push a norm across all member states.

There is a wonderful report that we got from the International Chamber of Commerce and Oxford Economics, which says that if we dissolve the WTO, that would “lower GDP for developing countries as a group by 5.1% by 2030”. That is a hard issue to try to get people to understand. What message do you give to the people who are going to be at the sharp end of trade about this body that is based in Geneva and has all this background? How would you say to them, “This is what really matters here” and on how they help us?

Even developing countries have huge potential in the future to have more of an impact on world trade, and we can increase the sourcing opportunities. I do not have a straightforward answer to how we promote that message. Potentially, it is just making sure that the WTO is a lot more publicly visible in what it is doing, especially when it comes to producing regular rules around trade that we can look at and say, “This is improving stability across the global trade market”. I am sorry that I cannot give you a straightforward answer.
No, that is very helpful.
I just want to know whether the WTO is accessible to the end user—your companies—as it could be? Is it seen as distant? Could they be more—

There is definitely more that it can do. There is definitely more that everyone can do to be more transparent, right? The WTO is a fantastic organisation but there is definitely more that it can do to try to promote to everyone what it is doing.
More than 20 years ago, when dinosaurs ruled the earth—
You were there?

Q76 I was there. In about 2002, I attended a conference of the International Chamber of Commerce at the Belfast International Convention Centre. One of the things that struck me then, and indeed subsequently in other jobs I have done, was a sense that other countries—Italy is a prime example—do rather better than us at promoting small and medium-size enterprises in the manufacturing sector, which are often represented in chambers of commerce, internationally and making them more aware of international opportunity arising from trade agreements and the like. I wonder whether in your experience and that of Make UK, you can give us some examples of best practice internationally that you think our Government would benefit from hearing about, learning from and, indeed, implementing?

I mentioned the UK-Australia FTA earlier. Australia has done fantastically when it comes to promoting their free trade agreement with the UK. We have already seen that with the huge increase in exports over the last few years. They have a fantastic website that looks at everything you could possibly want to know about Australia-UK trade, which manufacturers, or anyone, can go to and see what the opportunities are. To be fair to the UK Civil Service and DBIST, they have been really good at trying to look at export guides too. What we are missing though, when looking at import, is guidance for manufacturers to import from these markets as well. They have started doing small sections, but there is so much more that we can be doing.

The EU also has a very good online system where businesses can look at specific markets and opportunities that they could have. When a business is looking to export, there are so many options out there and so many different FTAs. Which FTA would be more useful for them? What are they making? The EU has sector-specific guides to each market. It even looks at the UK and says, “In the UK, they consume a lot of this”. Something such as that would help businesses to decide which market is best for them.

Within the CPTPP, the Canadians are very good at separating the benefits of an FTA bilaterally from the benefits you get under the CPTPP. I know that DBIST has also done that, but the Canadians are a lot more in-depth, shall we say. We could learn from that to try to get a little bit more clarity if we want to export to Canada or Mexico under the CPTPP or bilaterally. Which route do we take? Do we take the CPTPP or bilateral route? It is important because the tariff might be the same but the other procedures and provisions could be—

If I am a specialist cheesemaker, are there specific websites I can go to that will help me to understand the geography of UK trade agreements, so as to get a better handle on how I can get my cheese into that market? For example, perhaps I have a small farm in rural England or Scotland or wherever and I want to get my cheese into one of the markets that we have recently opened up. This committee has heard on previous occasions that there have been issues, oddly enough around cheese specifically, in some of these agreements.

At the moment, there is not a specific market guide. There is a DBIST “ask a question” function where you can ask a question online and DBIST will get back to you. However, that is obviously a case of having to ask questions instead of just having it in front of you straightaway. There is definitely more work to do to try to bring the opportunities that we might not even see yet to the front.

Something else worth mentioning that is kind of along the same lines, but not completely, is that a lot of guides look at highlighting sectors that already do well in a market. For example, there is a market access guide on Canada, which is a very big importer of cars and has a big car sector. But we need to be looking at sectors that have been growing massively over the last 10 years but are still at that lower level, because that is a future opportunity that we can look at. It would be good to focus more on the sectors that are up and coming rather than those that are already established, because they already have established trade.

For example, for the UK-GCC deal, we looked at products and, quite rightly, at reducing tariffs on products that we already had a large trade flow with. If we had looked at other products that were maybe 10 years away from being huge, they might not have got the tariff reduction that they needed and would not continue to grow as fast as the others, because they would not have tariff reduction or the provisions to help them to export. That is similar to your question but not focusing on emerging trends and consumption in different international markets.

Are there any other questions or comments from my colleagues? No. Maxwell, thank you very much indeed. That was enormously helpful. If you have any follow-up comments, please send them in. I think there were some follow-up comments asked of you. We would be grateful to get them. We have a few more weeks before we close our inquiry. Make UK is a very important group in how you represent your members, so any more information you can send us would be extremely well received. Thank you very much for coming and spending your time with us this afternoon.

2 pm
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair) ; Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Lord Boateng; Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury; Lord German; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord McDonald of Salford; Lord Stevenson of Balmacara ; Baroness Verma.
Evidence Session No. 7 Heard in Public Questions 61 – 69
Witness es
Tom Wills, Director, Trade Justice Movement; Rosa Crawford, Head of International, Trades Union Congress; Amrita Saha, Research Fellow, Institute of Development Studies .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witness es
Tom Wills, Rosa Crawford and Amrita Saha .

Q61 ​​ The Chair: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to our continuing inquiry “Trade in a turbulent world”. I am extremely pleased to be joined today by three people who I think will allow us to look at trade and trade opportunities from a slightly different angle from the simply commercial one: Rosa Crawford, the head of international at the Trades Union Congress; Tom Wills, the director of the Trade Justice Movement; and Amrita Saha, who is a senior fellow at the Institute of Development Studies. Thank you very much indeed, all three of you, for coming.

I think we have a full complement of the International Agreements Committee. Maybe we are waiting for one more member to join us online, but this is a great opportunity for us all to inquire from you your views on the work that we are doing. Not every question has to be answered by everyone but, please, if you feel that something has not been said, do say so. We have a list of questions which I think you have been sent, but I hope you will give us the opportunity to ask supplementary questions as well. With that, are we ready to start? Lord McDonald, maybe you can ask the first question.

Thank you, Lord Chair. For the purposes of my question, let us assume that the Government have a trade policy. My question is to all three of you. From your perspective, what have been the principal strengths and weaknesses of the Government’s trade policy in the areas of labour, development and the environment to date, and what do you think could be improved? I ask that to Rosa first.

Thanks very much for the question and thank you very much for the opportunity to give evidence. As TUC, we very much welcomed the approach flagged in the trade strategy, where the Government said it would “seek strong labour provisions” with trading partners and engage with those trading partners to hold the UK Government to those commitments. It is fundamentally important to trade unions that we have strong, enforceable labour commitments in trade agreements to make sure that we have fair trade and that countries are not gaining an unfair advantage on the basis of exploitation of workers.

With the UK-EU negotiations and the reset that the Government launched, we very much see that approach put into action, where the Government have a trading partner in the EU that upholds very high standards on workers’ rights. With the UK-EU agreement, we got a path-breaking commitment—what was called the level playing field commitment—whereby both parties agreed that they would hold workers’ rights to the level they were at in 2020 and not regress from those, and that if they did regress there would be a sanctions mechanism levied. That is a very welcome approach that was a result of trade union lobbying, I should say, on the UK and EU side for many years. That agreement being in place was a huge step forward. The fact that the UK Government are now in the process of building a closer relationship with the EU is very welcome to the TUC, because the Government have been clear that the closer relationship would be founded on mutual high standards of workers’ rights, and we want the UK to commit to implement any improvement made in the EU. That has been a very welcome approach.

In the UK’s trade agreement with Switzerland, the labour provision was also subject to dispute settlement. That has shown that the Government are also able to implement a sanctions mechanism for labour commitments with a non-EU trading partner.

It has also been very welcome that the Government have engaged closely with trade unions in their approach towards trade negotiations and trade policy, which is an important break from the past, and we are involved in the UK Government’s Trade and Sustainable Development Domestic Advisory Group for the UK-EU, and in the Trade and Labour Forum.

It should be said that UK trade unions have not yet been consulted on the text of trade negotiations, and that is somewhere where we think the Government should go further so that we can fully inform the negotiations with the needs of working people. We also want there to be a role for Parliament, because we know that you have not been consulted on the text of trade negotiations either, so we want that increased scrutiny as well.

I will just pick up on some areas where we think there is not enough consistency, though, with the approach flagged in the trade strategy about seeking high standards of labour protection. The Government have concluded trade agreements with partners where we have concerns, in particular the Gulf states and Vietnam, which is one of the CPTPP countries where trade unions are banned. In Vietnam, independent trade unions are banned and, in half of the Gulf states, independent trade unions are banned. We are concerned that in both those trade agreements—CPTPP and the Gulf states agreement—there is no effective enforcement for the labour clause. I also mention that we are concerned about trade agreements with India and South Korea, where there is also widespread repression of labour rights. So we think the Government can do more to actually put their commitments into practice.

I then just flag that, while we have really very much welcomed the approach with the steel strategy, we have some concerns that good jobs are being undermined by the tariff-free quota that has been set, particularly for India, South Korea and Vietnam, because that is allowing too many cheap imports to come in. That also undermines good jobs, so we think there are some areas for improvement there.

We also have concerns about investor-state dispute settlement undermining the Government’s ability to act in the public interest and to do things like improve workers’ rights and bring public services back into national ownership, because, of course, members of the committee will know that ISDS allows for Governments to be sued by companies for actions like renationalising public services. Indeed, the Government are subject to three ISDS cases currently that I am sure we will come on to. We want ISDS written out of all trade agreements and the commitment made, as Australia has done, that there would be no ISDS in future trade agreements.

There are areas we want to improve. As I say, there is much better engagement from this Government than the previous Government with trade unions, so we are hoping that we can do more to make that commitment in the trade strategy around high labour standards a reality.
Thank you. I understand why you concentrated on labour, but I point the other two panellists to development and the environment, and go to Amrita next.

Thank you very much for having me here. On development, based on our work at the Institute of Development Studies and University of Sussex, I would like to talk specifically about how the UK has provided support strengthening developing countries’ participation in trade. This has been through the UK’s trade and investment advocacy fund, which has been running since 2011. It specifically provides trade and investment negotiation support to developing countries. As we know, it can be really challenging to negotiate effectively due to costs—practical, resource-based operational costs. Many developing countries struggle to play a full role, and many have bare-bones operations in Geneva at the WTO. Our research suggests that the negotiations window of the trade and investment advocacy fund has been effective and has proven good value for money. It has been unique in addressing the imbalance of resources and the imbalance in the influence between developed and developing countries. It has worked on developing countries’ capacity to negotiate and has been most effective in helping to solidify negotiating positions.

We all know that negotiating outcomes are inevitably the product of multiple factors, but very specific contributions can be tracked down to negotiating texts that have either maintained or advanced the interests of developing countries. This is good, and we would advocate for this support to continue.

Secondly, UK trade policy has improved market access or, in many cases, provided continuity. The UK’s unilateral preferential market access scheme, the DCTS—the Developing Countries Trading Scheme—has made it easier and cheaper since 2023 for developing countries to export to the UK. The objective has been to stimulate trade but with a vision to promote growth, support economic transformation and help reduce poverty. The DCTS can support developing-country exports; however, it can also lower costs for UK businesses. Our research has found early positive signs that DCTS is succeeding in encouraging developing countries to make greater use of these trade preferences, and this translates into higher tariff savings. Post-Brexit free trade agreements and economic partnership agreements are also preserving preferential access.

My third point is that UK trade policies and programmes certainly articulate very strong commitments to inclusion and gender equality. The UK supports the International Trade Centre’s programme SheTrades, which works with women entrepreneurs. This is a very strong and powerful case. Export credit arrangements—for example, UK Export Finance—explicitly link its sustainability strategy to positive impacts in developing markets. There is the UK-New Zealand FTA as well as the UK-India FTA, which is focused on trade and development and labour provisions.

T hat is the positive story, but we find that there is a lack of coherence. There is no effective integration of inclusion and sustainability goals. What do I mean by that? You look at these ambitions often in trade agreements, but are they very closely linked with trade and development programmes that sometimes run in the same countries? That remains an open question. Sometimes short-term commercial interests can dominate; LDCs receiving enough sufficient priority, as well as the issue of LDC graduation, is an important one. More fundamentally, I argue that commitments alone do not demonstrate improvements in development goals or, for that matter, inclusive growth. We need to think very carefully about how funded implementation and meaningful participation by business organisations and worker organisations can go side by side with evaluating distribution outcomes. Where are the gains and where are the losses, and how can we really connect these trade preferences that are being utilised with very targeted interventions in a context where aid has gone down—where there are aid cuts? How do we make sure that the support that the UK does provide is targeted to our preference users?

Thanks for the invitation to appear today. Similarly to my fellow panellists, I say that the positive has been rhetoric and the area for improvement has been delivery. In the trade strategy released last year, again as a result of advocacy from charities, trade unions and members of the Trade Justice Movement, the Government recognised—explicitly for the first time—that trade does not exist as a set of commercial relationships in some kind of vacuum, but rather has important consequences on labour rights, emissions and international relations.

There are a couple of quotes to pick out from the trade strategy that particularly reflected our analysis. The Government said that trade “can—absent safeguards—blow away important protections regarding the environment, working conditions or product standards”. They recognised that, alongside free trade, we need a shared set of fundamental social and environmental standards if we are not going to see trade being used as a kind of engine for pushing rights and standards protections down. Another quote is that “Trade policy is one expression of the UK’s international agenda”, and the strategy links to environmental protections, labour rights, corporate accountability and human rights. All of that is very positive. We are yet to see how that very strong and mature analysis actually impacts or shapes what appears in UK trade agreements.

Since the trade strategy was published, as Rosa said, we have had flagship free trade agreements announced with India and with the Gulf Cooperation Council. With India, there was a labour chapter, an environment chapter and various provisions, but none of them was actually subject to the dispute settlement provisions within the trade agreements. Essentially, they are second-class citizens within the structure of the trade agreement and are, to all intents and purposes, not enforceable. They are warm words. They perhaps express a direction of travel, but they do not actually have any utility for Governments or for campaigners looking to protect rights or the environment.

In the case of the GCC agreement, while we have not yet seen the full text, the Government have released chapter-by-chapter summaries and, in the “General collaboration and sustainable development” chapter, while again, there are bits of language covering labour rights, environmental protections and climate action, none of that is subject to the dispute settlement provisions. What is more, it also seems to not apply at all to the United Arab Emirates, which demonstrates this extraordinary position where the UK is, on one side, saying that it understands that trade policy is an expression of the UK’s international agenda on protecting labour rights but yet, when it comes down to it, it is content not to apply even the weakest labour provisions to a country where 88% of the population are migrant workers operating in the kafala system.
There are some really concerning disconnects between rhetoric and delivery that hopefully the Government will be able to make good on in the next trade policy steps that they take.
That is a very helpful introduction.

Q62 You have all emphasised the difference between aspiration and achievement. Is it your view that the agenda—the international climate for the areas that you and ourselves are all concerned about—has darkened in recent years?

We work through the International Trade Union Confederation, which we are a member of, and with trade unions in global South countries, around the multilateral trade environment and the WTO in particular. We know that there are really existential challenges facing the WTO. Obviously, the US has been blocking the appellate body for a number of years. Then, more recently, the Trump Administration have posed really severe threats as well.

We know that there is severe reform needed from the WTO and we think there is potential through that body. We talk to global South partners and we ask them, “Do you just want no WTO?” They say no—that there needs to be a global framework, but it has to be a framework that is founded on the principle of fair trade. That means, for the trade union movement, that labour standards need to be embedded within WTO rules. They have not been since the organisation was founded over 30 years ago. That has meant that you have members like China—it is not the only member, but it is one of the most significant members—where independent trade unions are also banned. That means they also gain an unfair competitive advantage because one of the ways that they can hold down prices is that workers are not legally able to strike for better pay or conditions. For us, you need to have binding labour rights commitments within WTO rules. We also need to see more flexibilities allowed for global South countries to be able to invest in decent jobs. That means flexibilities around the subsidy rules, around the TRIPS rules and around technology transfer and the rules around special and differential treatment for developing countries. Global South countries have not been allowed to invest in the industries that they need—the clean industries as well—to have decent jobs. They need the flexibility that global North countries have essentially been able to have, because of power asymmetries.

There are other improvements we want as well, including a trade and decent work working group set up at the ILO, which involves trade unions.
