We have historically been shut out of negotiations at the WTO, which has meant that there have not been enough initiatives to promote decent work. The e-commerce moratorium was a big issue at the last WTO ministerial. We want an end to that moratorium so that global South countries in particular can collect the revenue that is often very much needed for the public purse from digital transactions. On the issue of public health, which is obviously not just a workers’ issue but does affect workers, we want an extension of the suspension of the IP rules that were applied on the Covid vaccines to other vaccines for life-saving medicines, because we need that as an issue of public health concern.

Reforms are needed, and obviously we need to get over the block on the appellate body. The UK Government have shown a leadership role in the WTO; at the last ministerial it was taking a leadership role. We would like to see the UK Government using that leadership role to press for those changes that the global union movement is calling for around the multilateral trading system and unblock the appellate body so that we can actually make it function again.
We want to move on to the next question, but we can have two quick follow-ups from Sandy and Donald.
Is it your view then that the failure of the March ministerial is capable of being remedied and is likely to be remedied?

As I say, there is potential, and we have the UK Government showing that they want to be a progressi ve actor in the trade space. We have heard from Tom as well about the intentions of the UK Government; they want to work with like-minded partners like Canada or Norway or other EU countries that also want to be progressive actors in this space. But it requires concerted action and action together because such a severe challenge is being faced.

I want to follow-up on that. I do a lot of work across the global South, and one of the issues that countries there are now becoming alive to is that, although trade can be all things to all people, if they are not allowed to develop the skill set and processing within their own countries, that conversation still goes nowhere. I want to know whether you think that there is enough work being done to help being supportive in-country, in the global South—not just for workers but for the skill sets and frameworks, where we need to move the dial for them to become much more self-sufficient in processing and developing their own product.

Thank you for the question; it is critical. I was talking about the UK’s preferential tariff scheme, which is the Developing Countries Trading Scheme, and how the UK has facilitated market access. But your point is well taken: market access is not market participation. If investments in productive capacity are absent, countries will not be able to utilise those preferences. The reality is that we can talk about improvement in aggregate utilisation of preferences through trade agreements and trade preference schemes, but the reality is that the distributional outcomes of such liberalisation are rarely uniform. When you look across products at country level and unpack that, there is much greater variation.

Think, for example, about textiles and garments. Of course there is a concentration; they are heavily imported under the trade preference scheme, for instance, with Bangladesh. There are also close links with what is happening in the UK with east Midlands businesses. It improves competitive sourcing. However, to expand the possibility to utilise those preferences requires investments and targeted support in building productive capacity in developing countries. We can further preferences and make them available but, unless those trade agreements are matched by meaningful support and targeted assistance at a time when aid cuts are quite severe, the gap and the disconnect will remain. The challenge and goal for development policy in trade right now is how we address that disconnect. How do we make sure that we get the bang for our buck that is available through development co-operation?
We will move on to the next question. There will be plenty of opportunities for everyone to speak.

Q63 Perhaps drawing on the first question, which I do not think we have had a very full discussion about, and the inclusion of environmental provisions, I would like to ask you, Amrita and Rosa, whether you are familiar with the agreement that the European Union has reached with Mercosur. The hottest issue was the commitments that the Brazilian Government accepted on the environment. For reasons that some members of this committee, including myself and the then Minister for Trade, found completely incomprehensible, we have made no attempt to reach an agreement with Mercosur ourselves. But my question to you is: are the provisions in the EU-Mercosur agreement on the environment the sort of thing that you think ought to be in a UK-Mercosur agreement, if there were one?

That is quite a specific question. More generally, what should be the UK’s priorities in reforming and strengthening the rules-based international trading system in these different areas—development, the environment, labour and so on. This is bound to be a hot subject in the years ahead. What do you think we should be aiming for, in generalities?
I would like to answer the second, more general, question, if that is okay. I am sure my colleagues will want to come in on the first part of your question.

In thinking about the global trading system, I start with the point that that is not just the WTO; it is spread into a series of interconnected agreements and that is at different levels. Strengthening the global trading system as such requires building and defending coherence and co-ordination. Trade agreements need feet on the ground and we have to be at the table to ensure that co-operation turns them into opportunities. So, in thinking about the WTO specifically, the UK should certainly prioritise a fair rules-based trading system. That requires, as my colleagues have pointed out, effective WTO dispute settlement.

Through the Trade Advocacy Fund, the UK is already helping developing countries, and it is really important that we continue that, because negotiating on an equal footing can make the system fairer and also helps the system to run more smoothly. Helping developing-country negotiating partners to conduct the right kind of analysis and have informed stances can avert the case where they just say no.

Secondly, the UK should make development a substantive part of the WTO reform, we argue, and this is with commitments matched by resources. While developing countries need a voice in negotiations, talking about productive capacity has to be matched by the capacity to implement agreements. One thing which is really critical in this is the appropriate balance of support at Geneva and country levels. Often we find that Geneva-focused support is economically efficient, but the trade-off is that it can exacerbate a capacity imbalance between Geneva and national capitals, and that could lead to negotiated agreements failing to reflect domestic needs and political realities.

My third point is really just a reality check. This was a question from before, about the ongoing lack of progress. The likely future geopolitical directions could limit what engagement at the WTO could achieve. We should of course continue to take part, not least because the opportunity costs of not doing so are very high. Given the challenging context, it is also a chance for us to think what could be done with a constrained budget by spending where it counts, to ensure that the UK continues to exert lasting influence. We should see if support may be better directed at specific negotiations alongside the WTO. This could be the AfCFTA or with ASEAN countries, and this has been done in previous trade advocacy fund programming. Identifying very specific areas of support, combined with supporting developing countries at the WTO, is quite important because the opportunity for impact might be much greater sometimes in these cases.

If I might build on that last point that Amrita made, we think it is very important that the Government have increased the funding around Aid for Trade and increased that support at the WTO level for trade union or covenant capacity in influencing those negotiations. For us also, as Amrita says, country-level capacity building and capacity building for trade unions specifically is something we want the Government to have a fund to support, which we had under the previous Labour Government. Up to 2010, the Government were funding trade unions to do capacity building, including in the area around influencing trade negotiations. That funding was cut in 2010 by the coalition Government and has not yet been restored. We are engaging with the Government about possibilities for restoring that funding, albeit we know it is a difficult financial climate, but it is not a large amount of money and it actually creates a huge outcome. Increasing union capacity to influence trade negotiations means that you can have the concerns and the needs of workers, who are going to be affected by this agreement, adequately affected in the agreement.

As the TUC, we have done self-funded projects with unions to build capacity that have had a real impact. For example, in Cameroon, on the AfCFTA, we funded a project which increased their capacity to influence negotiations. That has meant that labour considerations and the needs of workers in Cameroon have been factored into negotiations to a much greater extent than they would have been if trade unions had not had that capacity support.

We would like the Government to direct support also to trade union capacity building in their aid spend as a way to reinforce the role of workers, to have their voices heard and to influence the multilateral trading rules. I covered quite a lot of the multilateral trading asks in the previous question, so I might not go into those. I can touch on Mercosur, but I want to give Tom some space.
The two of you who have replied so far have suffered from complete brain fog about Mercosur.
I can come in on Mercosur if that is—
I know Tom wants to come in; maybe he could be more specific on that.

I shall be brief. I am not going to pretend to be an expert on the environmental provisions of the EU-Mercosur agreement. However, it is worth reflecting on the strategic wisdom of focusing on this kind of free trade agreement beyond all other approaches to trade policy, which the UK has essentially followed for the last six years. The EU put, I think, more than 25 years into negotiating with Mercosur, with a huge amount of political capital and a huge amount of controversy. The UK has its agreement with India that is set to add 0.13% to GDP by 2035. With the GCC, the figures are even less impressive. The disconnect between the political and media noise around FTAs and the actual economic advantage of them is colossal. Putting a huge amount of political capital and perhaps years of negotiating capacity into an agreement with Mercosur, which is likely to deliver pretty unimpressive economic returns, probably is not the most strategic thing we could do.

But you are aware, I am sure, that Mercosur countries comprise a very substantial proportion of the remaining rainforest. One competitor in Sunday’s election will probably chop a lot more of it down and one has said he will preserve it. My question really is: is it part of Britain’s interest? It is really rather difficult to think it is not in Britain’s interest to have an agreement with Mercosur. These are countries of extraordinarily important industrial capacity as well. What sorts of environmental conditions are the ones the EU has negotiated broadly okay, if implemented?
I am not in a position to comment on that, I am afraid.
No ne of you knows. You are just waiting to be hit by a negotiation, and then you will work out whether the EU provisions are any good.

David, we do want to move on. If any of you have any thoughts post this meeting, we are not completing our inquiry for another month or so, so we would be grateful maybe for you to feed that in. It is a reasonable point in terms of your objectives and Britain’s trade objectives.

I just have a quick supplementary question for Rosa. Do you have a figure of the relevance of unions to our exports? I do not know how many union members there are in this country. I would have thought that a lot of them would be public sector rather than manufacturing, private sector and potentially some services. Do you have a figure that would help me understand the relevance of unions in the export discussions?

I do not have a specific figure, although I can check and write to the committee, but our manufacturing sector is one of the most unionised sectors in the country. Our second-largest affiliate, Unite, represents manufacturing unions and is one of the unions that have kept very strong union recognition. So exports are incredibly important to union members—exports such as steel, automotives, ceramics. These are all areas where obviously the EU is an absolutely critical market. As I say, that closer relationship with the EU—removing more barriers to trade—is important. We very much welcome the SPS agreement currently being negotiated, but sectors such as pharmaceuticals, automotive and chemicals are still facing a lot of barriers to trade, and those are very unionised sectors.

For us, the EU is the critical relationship and the other trade agreements, as Tom has said, do not really make a huge difference in terms of our export market. That is why we really hope that, after the summit with the EU in November, we can move on and have a more expansive agreement. That is very important for the union movement.

Thank you for that; it was a well-made second point. If you could give us a rough figure—I do not know how you would want to do it; percentage terms?—it would be quite interesting to see that. That is all, because it helps us think about who is being represented in these discussions.
I am happy to write.

Q64 I have two questions, but I should first declare my interest as outlined in the R egister of Lords’ I nterests . I am a senior independent non-executive director of the Ghana International Bank, which is a major provider of trade finance.

The first question is to you, Ms Saha. Perhaps you could answer it in the context of our upcoming leadership of the G20. Is the UK giving sufficient weight to development objectives in its trade policy, and how could trade instruments be used more effectively to support developing countries while at the same time advancing the UK’s interests? While we are talking about the EU, I am sure you would agree with me that the EU’s economic partnership agreements with Africa and the developing world have not been an unalloyed success in promoting development.

I will put the second question out there while you are answering that, so that your two colleagues can think about it. Is there evidence to indicate that the department for business and trade, the FCDO, Treasury and the relevant public finance institutions are in fact working any more closely together in this area of trade and development than they used to? There is precious little evidence in the past, actually, that they have worked effectively together. What can we do to create a new institutional framework that might bring trade development and investment together?
The Chair : Sorry to ask, but can you keep your answers quite condensed at this stage, because I am quite keen to get through all the questions? Thank you.

That is a complex question, but UK trade policy has improved and in many cases provided continuity in market access for developing-country partners. Thinking back to my example of trade preferences, the unilateral preference scheme of the UK is DCTS. As I said, the evidence is that there is greater use of preferential tariffs, and this translates to higher tariff savings. You mentioned the EU and the EPAs—the economic partnership agreements. In many cases the UK has continued or rolled over the agreements, and continuity is definitely a good starting point.
But if they were faulty in the first place, how do they assist?

I was going to add that there are also instances in which there is a good basis for deeper co-operation. For example, the CARIFORUM-UK EPA already includes services, intellectual property and procurement. While starting from the point of continuity is good, having the basis for deeper co-operation is promising. However, I qualify that by saying that the distributional consequences of such liberalisation need to be unpacked. In this sense, there needs to be greater operational weight to development. That is really critical because, unless you are connecting evidence generation with accountability, there is a gap.

Actually, the UK did make some headway on this. A lot of us will remember the Independent Commission for Aid Impact review of UK’s Aid for Trade. As a response to that, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office announced the evidence innovation programme. Unfortunately, that programme was cancelled after one year of being in operation. It was meant to provide independent evidence informing the distributional consequences, both ex ante and ex post, of several trade agreements. What would be the agenda going forward? That is an important one on how we take that evidence generation. Your point about how the FCDO works together with different departments is an important one. That is exactly what this programme was set out to do in response to the ICAI review, which pointed out these gaps, as you have rightly pointed to.

In my assessment, the UK does give development meaningful recognition in its trade policy. But is there sufficient weight to ensuring that those commitments translate to economic outcomes? That is an open question, in a context where we are seeing some risks. The UK has cut overseas development assistance substantively, so bilateral trade aid to Africa has fallen back to 1970s levels. That might make several African Governments less well disposed to the UK. That is a risk to consider. On balance, yes, the UK is seeking out agreements with so-called middle powers, but what is going to happen with least developed countries? That is also a very important risk to think about, because this might work against development objectives.

On its own outside the EU, yes, the UK is small and less important in a sense in the overall scheme of things, but it is difficult to advance interests either in trade or development without being seen as in collaboration with the EU. However, it is important that we connect trade agreements with funded implementation, with links made to complementary policies; investment agreements are a low-hanging fruit. That is something that we can do even with not too many resources. A programme which can generate evidence consistently, working with the FCDO, and providing links across different departments would speak to your question about how we make those institutional links. A strategy such as that would support UK interests by strengthening trade institutions and reducing uncertainty, which would speak for commercial interests, but which would also have development impact.
Thank you very much. Tom, do you want to speak? No? Rosa? Any comments? Briefly would be helpful.

I will briefly come in on economic partnership agreements. I absolutely agree on that point that the EU economic partnership agreements have not been a success. The TUC is still a member of the European TUC, and we were a member when the EU was negotiating a number of these agreements. The ETUC has made joint statements with global South partners being very concerned about these agreements because they allow for more imports from global North countries, which undermine domestic industries, and they do not have enforceable commitments around labour and social standards.

We were very concerned when, under the previous Government, the EU EPAs were rolled over. We, as the TUC, wrote a number of joint positions with trade unions in global South countries such as Kenya against these rollover EPAs. We want unilateral trade preferences to these countries that are receiving EPAs, so that they can have preferential access to the UK market, conditional on upholding fundamental labour standards. We would not want them to have to open up their markets, because obviously there are historical imbalances which mean that their industries are at an unfair disadvantage.

Chairman, I wonder whether, with your permission, I could ask this. I would rather like to hear from Mr Wills in response. A fundamental weakness of traditional preferential trade arrangements is the assumption that removing tariffs will necessarily and automatically generate exports and improved livelihoods. Now, I am the grandson of a woman who farmed cassava and a man who farmed cocoa in the eastern region of Ghana. A Ghanaian agriculturalist, a Gambian food processor and a Kenyan textile manufacturer face immediate obstacles of inadequate electricity and transport, high costs of finance, difficulties meeting international sanitary and technical standards—some of which are set up as obstructors, actually, to trade—insufficient cold chain and storage facilities, and limited access to digital technology. How would, and how could, the UK introduce sector-specific development compacts that would work alongside trade agreements to address some of these issues? Without it, it is very difficult to see how that agriculturalist in rural Ghana, or anywhere else in Africa, or any of the other groups I have mentioned, would in fact benefit. Do you have any insights on this, Tom Wills?

I completely agree with the spirit of the question. We need to be designing trade and development policies that reflect the realities of the supply chains that you are mentioning. We also need to make sure that the trade policies that we do have in place—EPAs, free trade agreements and rules at the WTO—protect the policy space of countries to pursue their own development pathways. We are now almost 30 years after the publication of Ha-Joon Chang’s Kicking Away t he Ladder . We understand that the development pathways that have been successful for countries have not been free trade pathways, but have been where you are able to put up tariff barriers and are able to support and pick the winners in local industries. Now we are seeing—over the last, I guess, five or six years—an increasing trend in the global North towards industrial policy as well. Absolutely, I see those as two parts of the same coin in economic development.

Q65 Earlier this year, we had evidence given to us by the then Secretary of State on these matters, Peter Kyle, and he confirmed to us—I quote him—that “w e are entering a period where we are moving not just to FTAs, but to other forms of negotiations, agreements and MoUs ”. All three of you so far have been referring to different types of agreements. Can you explain your position about whether you think that really matters—that the Government go after one and not a different one? Against the background of that, from what you have seen so far from the Government in these two years, have they got that balance right? Perhaps we can start with Tom this time.

We are absolutely seeing a shift away from these traditional comprehensive, all-singing, all-dancing free trade agreements towards different types of trade instruments. I guess there are two things to say on that trend. One is that, where agreements do contain binding provisions on tariffs or quotas or standards, our position is that they should also contain equivalent binding provisions on labour and environmental standards. That is a core precept of everything that we argue for. Ultimately, it is the way of delivering trade that is sustainable, resilient and values-driven.

There is also a democratic deficit that we are at risk of here. As we move away from the processes, which in our view were inadequate, of understanding, scrutinising and approving free trade agreements, we are moving into a bit of a Wild West. The UK in the last few years has finalised 16 critical minerals agreements with partners around the world. We finalised three separate agreements with Trump’s America. None of those is a binding traditional free trade agreement. They are all interesting, important, and potentially deeply consequential to our economy and our society, but none has had any kind of scrutiny from parliamentarians. They have not been subject to debate, amendment, approval or any vote. That seems a huge democratic problem.

I guess the clearest indication of why that is a problem is the UK-US pharmaceutical agreement from last December. That was agreed with Trump, as committee members will know. It entailed the NHS making changes to the prices that we were willing to pay for US medicines and, according to some very credible academic analysis, could lead to 229,000 excess deaths by 2035. That is more than in the whole Covid pandemic in the UK. It was never subject to any kind of parliamentary discussion or debate. What we are now seeing over the last couple of weeks is six parliamentary committee chairs in the Commons writing to the Government and the NAO. The NAO has started its own investigation into that agreement. It has taken 11 months, but we are starting to develop some slightly ad hoc processes to hold the Government to account for this. That is obviously not a sustainable model for how we should be scrutinising agreements going forward. We need to update our democratic processes to ensure that, where there are relevant agreements, they are properly scrutinised by parliamentarians.

Thank you. We are very interested in what you said on the US pharma deal particularly and could not agree with you more about the other points. We would be keen to hear any follow-up thoughts you have on that. Rosa?

The TUC shares the concerns that TJM has outlined about the lack of scrutiny around the UK-US agreements, and also the critical minerals agreements. For us, the UK-US agreement has created a lot of uncertainty for the unions in the manufacturing sectors that we were talking about earlier. In particular, the pharmaceuticals agreement not having a legally binding nature means that there is a lot of uncertainty for the members about what that commitment means. There is uncertainty in other sectors as well.

It is quite a worrying trend to be going into this area of non-binding and non-legally binding agreements. We want legally binding commitments, particularly when it comes to labour standards but not just in that area. We are concerned that the critical minerals agreements have not been focusing on the often appalling labour rights conditions in the mineral extraction sectors. They also do not consider the issue that we were looking at earlier about value addition; we want that factored in, and them being made legally binding and subject to trade union scrutiny.

I should say, to go back to the earlier point about the UK-EU negotiations, that is a completely different approach that the Government are taking. Obviously, we anticipate legislation in Parliament to give legal effect to what is agreed at the UK-EU summit and any future agreement that is made with the EU. That has been a very comprehensive approach and, as I say, an approach that involves trade unions as well as businesses and other stakeholders. It is our most important trading partner. That has been a very welcome approach that we, as TUC, want the Government to be building on more rather than non-binding agreements, which have created more uncertainty, with no strong commitments on labour rights.

It seems to me that you are saying that the trade unions have not, with this Government, been able to make any headway in the discussions that they have been having on non-binding or indeed binding commitments? Is that true, or have you had a way in—feeding the sample into the process?

We do engage, as the TUC, with the Government, and that has been welcomed; the Government have been open to that engagement. We have a seat on the Trade and Labour Forum, which is consulted on trade policy. We also have a seat on the Trade and Sustainable Development Domestic Advisory Group that considers non-EU trade agreements, so there is engagement on non-EU trade policy. But we want the Government to go further and take more steps because we are not getting the labour provisions we want in the critical minerals agreement. We are not getting the binding and certainty that we want to see in a UK-US trade agreement, and we do have trade agreements with partners such as Gulf states that are abusing fundamental labour rights. We do need to go further but there has been engagement, just to be clear.

I will just add something very briefly, if that is okay. The form of agreement does matter. It is quite important, and my view aligns with my colleagues’—it affects certainty, enforcement and accountability. I also argue that legal status alone does not necessarily determine the effectiveness of an agreement. We can see that a binding FTA can contain provisions with limited enforcement. There is the UK-New Zealand gender chapter, as well as the UK-India development chapter, which exclude the general dispute settlement. Maybe the important question to think about is: how could we use the right mix of agreements, which essentially speak to international trade being—sorry, I am not going to divert from the topic—about honest mutual gain? As a general principle, the UK should adopt a “do no harm” policy, and work with trading partners to really think about the consequences of our domestic policy for foreign countries.

Q66 Picking up on your mention of the democratic deficit, I believe that you and Rosa Crawford have a concern about trade and investment rules constraining government’s ability to oversee labour and environmental standards. How well do current UK trade agreements strike the balance between promoting trade and investment on the one hand and preserving government ability to regulate in the public interest on the other? I think you are probably going to be a little bit critical, so what is the way forward?

It will not surprise you to hear me say that the balance is currently struck extremely poorly. That is particularly relevant when it comes to the UK’s 80 agreements that contain investor-state dispute settlement. Rosa mentioned earlier that ISDS offers investors an avenue to sue their host state for compensation if they are able to convince the tribunal of three private lawyers that public policy decisions made by that state have unfairly damaged the value of their investment. Our position as the Trade Justice Movement is that, in privileging the protections given to investors to continue to make a profit over the freedoms afforded to democratic Governments to enact policies in the public interest, ISDS really strikes that balance poorly.

The UK takes a case-by-case basis position on ISDS, which is a frustration given that the arguments in favour of ISDS now seem remarkably defunct. The arguments in favour of ISDS that have been put forward by government officials and Ministers in recent years rotate around two key points. One is that it encourages foreign direct investment. That might seem to make logical sense—an investment agreement leads to investment—but actually it is not backed up by any academic analysis. The most exhaustive academic analysis—one of 74 separate studies—produced in 2022 found that the impact of ISDS on foreign direct investment was so small as to be considered zero. There is no upside.

However, the UK also argued for years that it had never been sued and therefore was only a beneficiary of the ISDS system. That again is now a defunct argument. Over the last 18 months, the UK now faces three ISDS lawsuits, which between them perfectly demonstrate the absurdity and anti-democratic nature of this system. One is from the investors behind the proposed coal mine in west Cumbria. That had its permissions rejected in the High Court. The investors have come back saying that they were unfairly treated, asking for £300 million from the Government in compensation for a mine that does not exist and never had permissions to go ahead.

We are facing an ISDS case from a Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, one of the richest men in Russia. He is contesting the sanctions that were placed on him after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We do not know how much he is suing the UK state for, but he has a separate claim against Luxembourg for $16 billion, which is more than his entire net worth and half of that country’s national expenditure. That has actually caused the EU to take Fridman off the sanctions list. The threat of an ISDS claim has led to this extraordinary situation in which the EU has rewritten its whole sanctions policy, which demonstrates the power that this system gives to investors over, ultimately, national security policy in the EU.
The third case is a threatened case being brought by the Chinese steel company Jingye relating to the bringing of the Scunthorpe steelworks into public control. That is reportedly £1 billion—

Sorry, I am going to interrupt and ask a supplementary question as I am quite interested in this, because investors need to be protected or they will not make investments. ISDS works both ways. Vodafone in India is a very good example of where a country came out of the ISDS process and then behaved in its own way according to the assets of a corporate entity. Are you suggesting we should not give protections to investors? If you do not have property rights and the rule of law, then you cannot have a good investment climate, which means you cannot have a good, strong economy. My question to you is: is the ISDS structural process different from normal compensation? If the Government take my house, I should be given compensation. If they take my company because they change the law or decide not to pay a subsidy, then there is clearly financial redress—there is a contract. Are you seriously saying that we should not do that? Maybe, if there is a confusion over the terms, could you clarify why ISDS is different from a normal commercial compensation claim, to which most companies would be entitled, and the Government are being sued all the time? Maybe you could help us understand that.

We are not saying that investors should not have protection. Investors are able to access protection through domestic legal means. They may take out political risk insurance. They may access state-to-state dispute settlement mechanisms. What ISDS provides is this extraordinary additional power for investors over the freedom of states to operate in the democratic interest.

Sorry, I do not want to dominate this conversation. We are not prohibited from exercising our democratic interests. We are prohibited from confiscating someone’s assets because the politicians want to do it. All these laws are to protect the investors from a contract undertaken by a Government, like a treaty, which then the Government change and have to pay compensation—unless there is something specifically different with ISDS, which may be the case.

ISDS provides extraordinarily broad protections. It is not simply something that applies to, for instance, direct expropriation of assets. ISDS treaties contain national treatment provisions—fair and equitable treatment provisions. Over the years, we have seen those provisions interpreted extremely broadly by tribunals, leading to some absurd outcomes. For instance, $80 billion of public money has been paid out to fossil fuel companies over the last 10 years. We are not suggesting that investors should not have some degree of protection, but it is clear that at this point the balance has been struck completely in the wrong direction.

Increasingly where states do strike agreements, the majority of those exclude ISDS, because states are starting to wake up to the danger of ISDS for their public policy. Over the last 10 years, 300 ISDS agreements have been terminated by states, including by the UK, which withdrew from the Energy Charter Treaty on the basis that—this is a quote from the Minister at the time—“Re maining a member would not support our transition to cleaner, cheaper energy, and could even penalise us for our world-leading efforts to deliver net zero ”. That is a quote from a Conservative Minister from three or four years ago, understanding that the protections given to energy companies in that case were not compatible with the kinds of policy decisions that the UK wanted to take.
Thank you very much. That is helpful. Do you want to go next, Rosa? We are coming to the end of our session so if we can—
I think the Chairman has done all the supplementaries.

I will just add that, on the UK’s relationship with the EU, we do feel that the right to regulate is protected because there are specific carve-outs in that agreement. But with the other trade and investment agreements—the ones that Tom has mentioned, and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership—we are very concerned about ISDS being present because of the threats that Tom has described, where it has undermined abilities for the Government to move away from high-carbon industries, to have an active industrial policy and to pursue foreign policy objectives. In the past, ISDS has been used to challenge the renationalisation of public services and also increases in the minimum wage, so we see it as a privileged route to justice which is not available to any domestic investor, worker or any other entity, and which has been used in a very dangerous way, as Tom has outlined.

I just want to focus on the CPTTP, because the Government are currently reviewing that agreement in the light of the potential accession of a number of new members, including Indonesia and the Philippines. We want the Government to use that opportunity also to review the ISDS clause in that agreement, because Australia and New Zealand wrote out the ISDS commitments for themselves in that agreement so they were not bound by it. Australia has now committed to not include ISDS in any future trade agreement. We want the UK Government to take the same approach as Australia and New Zealand, negotiate side-letters with other CPTPP members and write themselves out of these ISDS commitments which are posing such a critical threat to workers, to industries and to public services. We do see an opportunity around ISDS and look forward to engaging with the Government on that.
So write ourselves out totally?
Of all the ISDS clauses that we are bound by.
Baroness Lawlor has a supplementary question.

Q67 It is a very interesting session. I would like just to pick up on something Rosa Crawford said. Might I ask you to think about pushing for what unions want, in respect of Lord Johnson’s question about the proportion of the workforce in unions in this country who would be involved in, if you like, the production of tradable goods, given that only 22.4% of the UK workforce, I think, is in a trade union and most of them are in the public sector, which does not make productive goods?

What is at discussion here is really, to my mind: why should certain members of the UK workforce—really rather privileged trade union manufacturing members—push for certain rights in developing countries which may mitigate against working people, many of whom will not belong to unions in parts of the world which we have been discussing, where there are no water supplies or that cannot properly meet the requirements of trade agreements? Much more useful emphasis for the trade union movement there would be to concentrate on providing help and practical support—electrification, digitisation, all these things matter. Requiring Governments to impose it as part of a trade treaty will mitigate against the very people whom we want to help. Could you take that on board when you are writing in in respect of Lord Johnson’s supplementary?

Thank you. We do not have too much time. Did you want to just briefly answer that point, which some people may be considering in the sense of: is it right to have trade deals that include anything other than very straightforward commercial terms? That is what has been presented to us. Your three agendas are obviously a substantial expansion on that, using trade as a policy to pursue ambitions. But in 30 seconds, do you want to come back to Baroness Lawlor on her comments?

It is fundamental to trade that there is a level playing field and you do not allow unfair advantage to be gained by abuse of labour rights, as well as other unfair trade practices, such as unfair subsidies. For us, it is integral to a fair and well-functioning trade system that you do have binding and enforceable labour rights. It is not an either/or in terms of interests of the workers in the UK and interests of workers in developing countries, if that was the suggestion. Workers internationally obviously want protection for their fundamental rights. That is why we work closely with global South trade union partners. For us it is about manufacturing, but well-functioning public services are also fundamental to a well-functioning economy, so public sector unions’ perspectives are also important in this as well. The connection is there between protection for labour rights and well-functioning trade policy on economic criteria as well.

But this is to prefer unionised labour over non-unionised labour, perhaps at the expense of non-unionised labour for the workforce who cannot or do not want to belong to unions. If you skew trade deals in the interests of one sector, you will see emerging an aristocracy of labour which collars government and is no more than a vested-interest arm of government. That is a great danger to the real emergence of prosperity and support for people who want to make a go of entrepreneurial activities and be part of a labour market.
This is quite a big topic. So that everyone is aware, we have heard from a cross-section of entities; we are hearing from you.
David, did you want to ask a supplementary?
Could I ask one short one on an already answered question?
Maybe when you answer it, just weave in a bit about the legitimacy of the unions to have such a strong voice in trade policy.

Q68 I may not have caught it right, Rosa, but I got the impression that what you were saying about the CPTPP was that those clever Australians and New Zealanders had signed up to certain provisions and had now managed to opt out of them, and that was a jolly good thing and we ought to do the same. But the Government spend their life telling us that the CPTPP is a great and wonderful thing, because it provides a level playing field right across not only trade in goods but quite a lot of trade in services. If you are going to have a opt-out when you feel like it, there is not going to be much there, is there?
All trade negotiations and trade agreements are a product of negotiations—
Yes, but we signed up to this one.

It is a live agreement. It is under review, in a session of future trading partners that might join CPTPP, so there are opportunities to change the terms of it, as Australia and New Zealand have done, and we are engaging with the Government on the possibilities for that. We think there are possibilities in the future to change the agreement.

On the question about trade unions and all workers, we stand for the rights of all workers, whether you are unionised or not unionised. There are fundamental rights that we want all workers to have and protections we want all workers to have. Obviously, we hope more workers will join trade unions, but we do not make a distinction about whether you are a union member or non-union member. We will fight for your rights for dignity and decent pay.
Maybe in your written response you could take some of Baroness Lawlor’s comments. That would be very helpful.
I would be very happy to.
P eople may ask, “Why should the Trades Union Congress have an overweighted place at the table?” Obviously, your feed-in is very relevant.

Chair, this is getting a bit out of hand in terms of what we are trying to debate. The points made have been extremely well made. They can be amplified in comments, but we have not decided any of this, and it is not actually germane to what we want to say to the Government about their future prospects.

Thank you for that point as well. Baroness Lawlor is entitled to her question on this. It is not unreasonable, in my view, to hear about the different types of trade policy you can enter into, which is why having these three here is a good thing. We have heard only from commercial entities so far, which is why we were very keen to have a different view on how trade policy can be expanded. There is also an assumption that could be made that fundamentally free trade deals are a good thing that should be pursued at all costs, and your input in that is very relevant, because there are costs to other sections of the economy and on to the partners we are doing trade deals with. That has been very helpful.
Are there any other final points?

Q69 Only this, I suppose: would you agree with me that there are some good examples at a municipal level in economic development in which chambers of commerce, trade unions and local authorities have come together to share good practice around economic development that has benefited both North and South? I saw one example of this myself in the link between Durban and Leeds. It promoted local economies in Leeds and in Durban. We ought to be more innovative in our thinking in this area and not get tied into patterns of thought, and sometimes institutionalised conflict, that do not actually put the interests of poor people and the delivery of the SDGs first. Do you see some sense in that? Can you share any observations in relation to it?

I do not know about the example that you shared, but I absolutely see international trade as an engine for growth and for development, if it is done on a basis of shared standards and dignity for workers—absolutely. One of the reflections that we have about the last five or six years of UK trade policy has been the focus on signature of trade agreements and less focus on how those trade agreements actually are used by businesses operating in the UK and in partner countries.

I have a very good example of exactly that kind of municipal-level engagement in the North with the South. Just last week, our regional secretary of the northern region of the TUC was on the Government’s trade delegation to India, where northern mayors met our trade union sister centres in India, and talked about exactly that sustainable growth and sustainable investment from UK businesses in India and Indian businesses in the north of England. That is a really good example of unions, employers and politicians getting together, North and South. As the TUC, we are very hopeful that we can continue with that engagement with other global South partners.

That is a very good point, because there are clear emerging examples of such co-operation. The UK supported what was called Supporting Indian Trade in Africa, which was a triangular co-operation programme—so the UK with India in Africa. It essentially had that bottom-up approach that you have rightly explained. I very much align with my colleagues today: trade can be an engine of growth and development. While of course we are talking about trade policy, which is very macro, connecting it up to the micro and meso levels is really powerful in ensuring that trade brings benefits which are more inclusive.

Wonderful. Thank you very much indeed, Amrita, Rosa and Tom. I am very grateful to have had you with us. That was a very full and varied conversation which I think we are going to find enormously useful. Please do send in your written thoughts as well, not just on the questions that were asked, but other thoughts that you think might allow us to get to a good conclusion about working out how we should pursue Britain’s best interests in trade.

sessions.iT: Legislative Scrutiny: Immigration and Asylum Bill
sessions.w: JUSTICE; Ronan Toal (Garden Court Chambers)

segs.tx: Joint Committee on Human Rights
Uncorrected o ral evidence: Legislative Scrutiny: Immigration and Asylum Bill, HC 556
Wednesday 21 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Alex Sobel (Chair); Baroness Chakrabarti; Tom Gordon; Baroness Hamwee; Afzal Khan; Baroness Maclean of Redditch ; Lord Murray of Blidworth; Lord Rook; Euan Stainbank ; Peter Swallow; Sir Desmond Swayne.
Also present: Tony Vaughan .
Questions 1 0 – 20
Witnesses
Zoe Bantleman, Legal Director, JUSTICE; Ronan Toal, Barrister, Garden Court Chambers .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Zoe Bantleman and Ronan Toal.

Q10 I would like to welcome our second panel, Ronan Toal of Garden Court Chambers and Zoe Bantleman of JUSTICE. I will start with the first question, which is regarding the interpretation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Clauses 18 to 20 of the Bill amend the way in which the courts and tribunals must interpret and apply Article 8 in the context of immigration, asylum and deportation cases. Is there a problem with the way the domestic courts and tribunals are currently applying Article 8 in these types of cases? If so, is there a need to give a clear steer in the legislation?

No, there is not a problem with the way that the tribunal currently interprets and applies Article 8. We have had Section 117A, Part 5A of the 2002 Act , for some years now and it has probably been one of the most heavily litigated pieces of legislation that we have. Most of the key provisions in that part of the Act have been to the Supreme Court at least once. Litigation of that kind is good for no one apart from lawyers. It would be great to have these amendments to Section 117 or to Part 5A from the point of view of being a lawyer keen to take points of law to court, but, in terms of deciding applications and appeals in accordance with the UK’s Article 8 obligations, it will be disastrous.

At the moment we have a tribunal of highly experienced , highly qualified lawyers who have been very carefully selected for the positions that they occupy. By and large, they make properly reasoned decisions of very high quality. They conscientiously address the factual and legal issues that are before them. They make decisions of the highest quality. If the decisions are not of the highest quality, whoever is unhappy with them can appeal to the Upper Tribunal and thereafter. There is a huge body of guidance in the form of domestic and Strasbourg jurisprudence to help those decision-makers . I simply do not see that it is a constructive thing to do to further amend Part 5A.

There is a very recent case in the Court of Appeal called IA v Secretary of State, which looked at a lot of the issues that the Bill addresses, in particular what family life is. It was a very comprehensive consideration of Strasbourg jurisprudence on that very subject. If anyone wants to know how Strasbourg interprets Article 8 family life, one need do not much more than look at this case called IA and, if one wanted to go further, the Strasbourg jurisprudence that it refers to.

A very important thing that the Court of Appeal did, having reviewed the Strasbourg jurisprudence and set out its own views on Article 8, was to say, “I n our judgment it is undesirable to lay down hard and fast rules as to how the additional elements of dependency test should be applied ”. That was the aspect that it was looking at, but I would say that that applies equally to the whole of Article 8.

If a lawyer or a barrister is given a chance to talk, they like nothing more than to talk about cases that they have been involved in, but I would like to talk briefly about the most famous case in my career. The most well-known case that I have been involved in was about a couple who said that it would breach Article 8 to remove the Venezuelan half of the couple who was with a British citizen. The Home Office had decided that they were not a genuine couple and that they were claiming to be a couple for the purpose of establishing a claim to stay in the United Kingdom. If what the couple said was true, which was that they had been together in a relationship for many years, the Venezuelan man would have been allowed to stay. It was Home Office policy at the time that, if somebody had been in a relationship of more than two years’ duration, they would not normally be removed .

The key issue in the case was whether this couple were truly a couple as they claimed. In the way that such cases are typically done , you have to provide evidence first to the Home Office and then, if unsuccessful, to the tribunal to show that you are a genuine couple. It is a bit like that programme, “Mr and Mrs ”, where each person is asked questions about their relationship and they compare the answers. In this case, in order to demonstrate that they were a genuine couple committed to each other, they talked about how one thing that they loved doing together was looking after this cat that they had bought. They talked about the cat. As is typical in these cases, they brought along loads of witnesses, people who knew them and were able to say, “This is a genuine couple ”. These people, their witnesses, also talked about the cat.

The tribunal, absolutely properly, allowed the appeal and found that they were a genuine couple. Having made that finding, the judge made some comments about pets and how important pets are. He referred to a Canadian Supreme Court case about pets. The Home Office did not like this decision. It appealed to the Upper Tribunal. The Upper Tribunal found that the First-tier Tribunal had made a perfectly proper decision, was entitled to find that they were a genuine couple and did find that they were a genuine couple. With the benefit of hindsight, the judge unwisely included in her decision a little joke at the end saying that that means that the cat is not going to have to get used to chasing Venezuelan mice, because the couple will be able to stay and the cat as well.

There was some sort of conduit from the tribunal to the Daily Telegraph , so that somebody in that paper got hold of this decision, or rather it was presented to them. They wrote this grotesque article about how Article 8 allows a couple to stay in the UK because they own a cat. It was shocking to see something so grossly misrepresented by the Daily Telegraph .

What was even more shocking was, quite a long time after that, to see the then-Home Secretary, Theresa May, addressing the conference of her party saying, “You will never believe what Article 8 entitles people to do. It entitles people to stay in the United Kingdom because they have a relationship with a cat ”. That was advanced by the then-Home Secretary as the preface to the plans to withdraw from the ECHR.

That seems to me to be a template for what has been going on now with a lot of these issues with Article 8 in particular but with immigration more generally. What goes on in the decision-making process is grossly, outrageously misrepresented by the press for various mischievous reasons. Then politicians feel that they need to act upon that.

We are straying a little, and Baroness May is still a serving member of the Lords, so we will try to move on. Maybe Zoe can come in. Your testimony also reminded me of the US film “Green Card” a little, but I will move on to Zoe’s response.

I agree with Ronan’s comments entirely. Judges are applying the law carefully. Last November, in that case of IA that Ronan has already mentioned, the Court of Appeal said that UK courts have universally demonstrated their willingness to follow Strasbourg. The share of human rights appeals allowed by the tribunal has fallen every year, from 53% in 2022 to 2023, to 44% last year, so it is quite difficult to see how this narrative of domestic judges being overly generous holds any water. When judges do get it wrong, as Ronan said—and we are all human—the appeal system corrects it. That is what it is there for.

The other infamous case, other than Ronan’s cat case, is the chicken nuggets case. In that unreported case, it was already overturned by the Upper Tribunal by the time the papers reported on it. As the former Attorney ‑ General Lord Hermer told this committee last year on 2 April, that is why we have appeal courts. Where is the problem? It is not the law. I completely agree with Ronan. It is sensationalisation of both the law and human suffering. What was the chicken nuggets case really about? It was about a young boy with emotional dysregulation and sensory difficulties.

The other problem that we have is, again, not the law. It is initial decision-making. Last quarter, more than half of human rights appeals ended with either the appeal being allowed or the Home Office withdrawing its decision. Only half of the sampled asylum decisions met the Home Office’s own quality standard.

Is change needed? No, not like this. The Government can clarify the law, but it needs to stay within what Strasbourg allows. The Bill removes the flexibility that keeps the current scheme compliant with the European Convention on Human Rights. Reopening a 12-year-old framework will only tie us up in litigation, as Ronan said, for another 12 years. That money and time of the Government, all of us lawyers and civil society would be better spent getting decisions right the first time and dealing with other problems in the justice system.

Crucially, people at the sharpest end of these changes in law and policy are going to face legal uncertainty caused by these changes in this Bill. It is going to take years for it to be clarified and in that time erroneous decisions might be made . We need to remember the people at the heart of what is at stake.

Q11 Ronan, I wondered whether you could explain a little bit more to this committee, not all of whom are lawyers, as to what the Court of Appeal was talking about when it was saying why it was undesirable to try to codify Article 8. Some people might think that, if you just create a longer list of tick-box elements, it might avoid appeals being allowed on an erroneous basis. I would be interested to hear what your analysis is as to why they are saying that codification is not something that needs to be taken to the next level.

The Strasbourg court loves repeating certain phrases and you see them recurring in many of its cases. On this subject, the Strasbourg court repeatedly says about the question of whether there is family life that it “ is essentially a question of fact depending upon the real existence in practice of close personal ties ”. That is it. It is a question of fact. Each family situation is unique and to arrive at a decision as to whether there is family life depends upon the very unique circumstances of each particular family.

The Strasbourg court gives indications or statements of principle as to the way in which that factual investigation might be conducted . The danger is of principles solidifying into rules that must be applied by the decision-maker . That is a particular danger that we would have if the amendments to Part 5A are enacted . They have the flavour of quite prescriptive descriptions of the ingredients of family life and, absent those ingredients, it is unlikely that one will have family life. They are numerous .

Going back to the discussion about replacing the First-tier Tribunal with the new system of not legally qualified decision-makers , the likelihood is that such decision-makers will place even more reliance than maybe qualified professional immigration judges would upon a single piece of legislation that seems to set out a code for deciding whether there is family life. What the Strasbourg court intends to be general principles that give guidance as to how to assess a particular set of facts will be ossified into a set of rules.

One particularly troubling feature of the rules set out in the amendments to Part 5A is that they are, virtually without exception, rules that tell you why there is not family life. They do not guide a judge to a conclusion that there is family life. They look very much like rules as to why there is unlikely to be family life in a particular situation.

In the replacement of the tribunal, I would expect that a very substantial proportion of appellants will be unrepresented, because lawyers doing this work are so few and far between and legal aid is even more scarce. It is available only in exceptional cases. You have to make a special application to get legal aid for an Article 8 case. The likelihood is that many appellants will be unrepresented and will be having their cases decided by non-professional judges, whose primary source of reference is likely to be Part 5A as amended. They will see there a whole list of factors that tell against a finding of family life being in existence.

That is why, as a general matter, it is a bad idea. If one looks at the actual substance of the provisions, they would be directing judges to make errors of law, but that may be something we come on to.

Q12 One of the bugbears of this committee over a period has been the fact that First-tier Tribunal decisions are not published, which of course has led to the fact that a lot of the reasoning of the First-tier Tribunal has been the subject of reporting that cannot be immediately verified. Lord Alton, a former member of this committee, and I laid amendments to the last immigration Bill in an attempt to require the court service to publish judgments. That was rejected by the Government. I would very briefly ask for your views, Mr Toal and Ms Bantleman, as to whether they should be published .

In fact, I believe that they now are being published . There is a pilot where certain judges’ decisions are routinely published . As I understand it, the intention is that they should generally be published. I actually think that it is undesirable on the whole that tribunal decisions as a matter of course should be published , because they contain a lot of very personal, sensitive information.
Obviously I mean published in anonymised form.
Not necessarily, no.
No, I am saying that that was the provision in our amendment.

To be honest, I am not sure what practice has been adopted as to anonymisation and whether they are routinely anonymised. From my point of view, it is undesirable that the rule for non-anonymised first-tier decisions should be for publication because of the confidentiality and sensitivity of the information that they contain.
Thank you, Mr Toal. I do not agree with you, but I hear your answer.

There is a careful balance to be struck and of course open justice is a relevant principle here. If they are published, one thing that I would encourage the committee to consider is that judicial independence and the safety of judges will be all the more important if they are targeted, because their names are unlikely to be anonymised, even if the parties’ names are anonymised.

A lot of judges have been receiving advice from the police about what steps they need to take to protect their safety. In the chicken nuggets case mentioned, I think that that judge has had numerous visits from the police and been advised about all kinds of precautions that she should be taking to protect her safety. Judges feel and are advised by the police that they are endangered by a lot of the reporting that has taken place.
The names of Upper Tribunal and Court of Appeal judges are regularly published .
It is not quite so controversial, or so hotly and vehemently—
Presumably it is because they are not the fact-finders .
We are straying slightly, so we will move on to the next section, which is on the definition of family life and risk of discrimination.

Q13 Clause 18 of the Bill, as we have just been discussing, sets out the definition of family life for the purpose of applying Article 8 of the ECHR. I presume the Government’s intention here is to deal with certain high-profile cases. The one I am thinking of may be sub judice so I am not going to mention it, but I am sure we will all know what that involves. In your opinion, will this new definition change the way the courts interpret and apply Article 8 and, if so, how? You have obviously touched on this already, but what about in terms of this specific aspect?

In part, the question is whether a fixed definition of what family life is, and the relevant matters to be considered being fixed in statute, fixes the complexity of human life that courts are going to have to consider—Ms Finch in the previous session covered this— but also how the courts understand family life, and how the Strasbourg court has understood family life. Our answer is that the Bill goes further than Strasbourg case law in ways that will hurt children the most , in our opinion .

J ust turning back to IA and to Mr Vaughan’s earlier question to Mr T oa l, the C ourt of A ppeal confirmed that family life is normally the core family and that adults need to show some dependence beyond normal emotional ties. We do not dispute that definition , which was set out c arefully by the Court of Appeal, but t he court was clear that it is undesirable , as Mr Toal has said, to lay down hard and fast rules because dependency may take many forms. Those were the words of the Court of Appeal because every case turns on its facts .

C lause 18 does exactly what the court warned against. It lists the kinds of dependency that will not count : financial dependence, emotional reliance and illness , unless someone needs constant care alone. The Court of Appeal said the opposite . F inancial dependency and disability both play a part in that. No one has to show complete dependence on another person.

The bigger change is not contained in the Bill as introduced. It is through amendments 44 and 45. Now, every parent, even one living with their own child , must produce evidence of a genuine and subsisting relationship before the law recognises family life. If they have only recently moved back together, that can count against them.

It is completely different from the Strasbourg starting point, which is that the bond between a parent and a child exists from birth absent exceptional circumstances. Think of a parent who has only just moved back to the home because of illness, a stay in hospital, a family court order or release from detention. The Government’s own supplementary human rights memorandum says that , if a test is failed , A rticle 8 generally is not engaged. The child’s interest , their family life , is not even considered . It is children who are likely to bear the cost .

O n the Government’s own figures in t he revised impact assessment, two - thirds of first - time in - country A rticle 8 grants involve a child who is British or has lived here for seven years. This is not codification. It is narrowing what is currently good law, including good law from Strasbourg . It is being done without a proper assessment of the rights of children . W here is our children’s rights impact assessment?

I would add a few s pecific points that are wrong or risk going wrong. First of all, the requirement of cohabitation is not a requirement imposed by Strasbourg jurisprudence . A case called Kroon v The Netherlands found that there was family life between a couple who had never lived together for years and years.

Secondly, it confines family life to children under the age of 18 living with their parents. In fact , the Strasbourg court and the domestic courts have recognised that family life between children and parents continues beyond the age of 18 , a t least for as long as the children are living at home or while the children are studying away or in prison but are likely to come home. In essence, i mposing a rule that family life finishes at 18 is wrong.

Article 8 also recognises and protects family life as it may develop. It is not just currently existing family life but family life as it is to be allowed to progress. There is a case called Cılız v T he Netherlands, which was about an estranged husband trying to litigate to establish a right of contact with his child. It was accepted that he had family life protected by Article 8 with his child, even though he had had little dealings with the child for a long time. H is right to litigate his contact with the child was protected by Article 8 .

Strasbourg jurisprudence recognises a whole range of family relationships that get no mention at all in the schedule. F or example, what about the relationship between siblings, especially where one or both of the siblings is under the age of 18 ? S urely there is family life between them , and s urely that is a profoundly important aspect of family life . It is potentially the longest - lived family relationship that one will have , y et that gets no mention.

T here is a case called Mar ck x v Belgium, one of the early family life cases, which recognised that family life includes at least the ties between near relatives, such as grandparents and grandchildren, because of the considerable part they may play in family life. In another case called Boyle v T he United Kingdom, an uncle was found to have family life with his nephew in spite of the fact that they had never lived together because of the role played by the uncle in his nephew’s life. T here is another case called Nazarenko v Russia, which recognised that the relationship between a child and the child’s foster carer fell within the scope of family life.

B y setting out in a piece of legislation all these fairly strict - looking rules and narrowly defining family life, there is a very significant risk that judges and , even more so , whoever is to replace the judges will be led astray and fail to find family life where they should find it.

Mr To al , may I ask a quick clarificatory follow - up ? The question was not so much about your opinion on these changes but whether you thought these changes will have a serious impact on how the courts interpret it. F rom what you have said, I take it that you think the courts will interpret and apply it in a significantly different way to how they are at the moment. Is that correct?
That is correct. I am sorry not to have directly said so , but that is the real risk. The approach to family life will be changed .
You think there will be material impact in the way that the courts interpret it.
I do. Very definitely , there will be a material impact.

Q14 Before I ask my question, can I just simply say this? I agree with you in the sense that the family relationship does not stop at 18. I have one who is over 40 and has brought another young one at two. I enjoy both of them.
Are there any groups of people who would be particularly affected by the proposed definition of family life? If so, does this clause run the risk of unfairly discriminating against certain people?

Zoe Bantleman : Ronan has already done some of the work of answering this question in his previous response. These clauses are going to fall the hardest on those with the least voice. Children, the young adults at home who Ronan already mentioned and people facing legally unqualified adjudicators , likely without a lawyer in many cases, will all be groping around in the dark with out any legal help or assistance with severe consequences of getting it wrong : exposure to the hostile environment, losing regular status, familial separation and other harms.

O n the discrimination point , one needs only to look at the Government’s equality impact assessment because it accepts that “ children may be significantly affected by the package ” . It accepts that the new family definition is “ more likely to affect disabled applicants ”, that people over 60 may face more refusals, that women , who are 83% of lone parents , may be more affected and that the impact may fall more often on particular nationalities.

It even says that a child in the UK sponsoring a parent will carry significant responsibility that, in the words of the Home Office , “ may cause additional pressure and anxiety ” . As a starting point, you need only look at the impact assessment.

Q15 We recently did an inquiry on the Northern Ireland l egacy Bill. W e have had the remaining stages just in the last two days. One of the committee’s recommendations for changes to that Bill was around the status of next of kin, particularly where a close family member had deceased. T hat was under the aegis of the European C onvention on Human Rights. The same thing applies here.

How important is family life and family connection when people come from war - torn countries and their nearest relative may be a fairly distant relative, an aunt , uncle or grandparent ? Zoe, do you have a view on that in terms of family life?

Zoe Bantleman : It is well set out in Strasbourg jurisprudence . Again, our domestic courts are following and applying that as well as they can and being corrected when they get it wrong. T here is no need to unnecessarily foreclose the definition of family life.

Parliamentarians, brilliant as they may be, have no crystal ball to look into the future and imagine every future family’s circumstances , to write them down and then to ensure that they have written them down and understood the elements of dependency that they may have. There could be unimaginable future families , separated by wars and other things that we cannot imagine now , who would have dependency and who a court would find to have family life , which, indeed, the ordinary British citizen would accept as well.

Q16 Clause 19 amends the public interest considerations that decision - makers must consider when assessing Article 8 claims. It would be helpful to hear from you about th ose proposed considerations and whether they are compatible with the balancing exercise required by Article 8.

Zoe Bantleman : The principle in law is simple. Parliament can tell judges what to weigh, but it cannot tell them to stop weighing. It cannot tell them to close their eyes to relevant matters in the balancing exercise.

Section 117 B already says that only little weight should be given , for example, to family life formed at a time when someone was here unlawfully. The Supreme Court , in a case called Rhuppiah , said that that kind of provision cannot put decision - makers in a straitjacket. There has to be some room for the exceptional case, and that room is what keeps the current law, the current legislative framework in Part 5 A, compatible with the European Convention on Human Rights.

What Clause 19 attempts to do, in my view, is to narrow that room , to take it away in two places. The first is the “ little weight ” provision, which becomes a “ no weight ” provision for family life that is formed when a person is here without leave or during an undefined serious breach of conditions. The Government’s own explanatory notes call this a starting point and say that courts can still depart from it . T here is a question here . I t is a bit of a conundrum. Does it bind courts and tribunals , and is it therefore incompatible with Strasbourg jurisprudence , or does it not bind courts ? Is it only a starting point?

The second place where it narrows the room is in the provisions for children. A child can be found unable to leave the UK if and only if — this is the phrase the Bill uses — they would get no education at all , they would face very significant obstacles or they would suffer harm that is very significant and long-lasting . T hat applies even where the parents have no convictions. It is important for this public interest point to make that point.

It implies that serious adverse effects to children that are not long-lasting but are still serious, however short-lived, are fine. That sits relatively uneasily with the statutory obligation on the Secretary of State to consider the best interests of children and to safeguard and promote their welfare and the Supreme Court’s warning in the case of Zoumbas that children must not be blamed for their parents’ conduct.

I would ask the committee to probe the Government on this point. In its human rights memorandum , it says that decision-makers carry the ability to carry out an individual proportionality assessment. Its impact assessment calls the child test “ non-exhaustive ”, but the Bill says “ if and only if ” and “ no weight ” . The text of the Bill should more clearly reflect the non-exhaustive nature of the principles that it is trying to outline or the factors it wants courts to consider, if we want to uphold clarity and legal certainty. These are , of course, key components of the rule of law.

Q17 Clause 20 amends the test for assessing Article 8 in the context of deportation cases. It removes the current sentencing threshold and provides that deportation will be disproportionate only in exceptional circumstances. A ny and all criminal offences under the sentencing threshold are very serious , but, in your view , is it proportionate to apply an exceptional circumstances framework to people who have not committed sufficiently serious crimes to be above the sentencing threshold at the moment?

Zoe Bantleman : One way that we can conceive of today’s deportation scheme , set out in S ection 117 C, is that it is graded by seriousness, which is exactly what the Strasbourg court expects. Someone sentenced between one and four years must meet one of the statutory exceptions. Someone sentenced to four years or more must in addition show exceptional circumstances.

Strasbourg has already accepted, when it looked at this in 2020 , that that framework is compatible with the European Convention on Human Rights. The bar is already very high . “ Unduly harsh ” means more than the ordinary pain of separation. The Supreme Court has described it as “ elevated ”, “ severe ” or “ bleak ”, and very few people meet it. It is also important to make that point. Only 0.73%, so less than 1% , of foreign national offenders have won deportation appeals on human rights grounds according to the Bonavero Institute’s report last year. There are more lottery millionaires each year than foreign offenders who win on Article 8 alone.

The M inister told the Bill Committee on 15 October that just over 1,000 foreign offender deportation appeals were allowed on human rights grounds between April 2016 and November 2021, 70% of which were solely on Article 8. That works out at about 125 per year on average during that time.

Clause 20 removes the grading that we have on the basis of seriousness. It drops the 12-month threshold altogether so that the toughest tests for deportation apply to someone who has never been sent to prison. Conducive deportation does not even require a conviction for a criminal offence.

It further adds another hurdle , which I cannot quite wrap my head around. I do not know whether Ronan —because he is more intelligent than me — can. E ven if you meet one of the exceptions outlined in the new Clause 20, you must still show that the public interest does not justify deportation. Previously, the exceptions told us how the public interest was to be applied . If you met one of those exceptions, that meant your human rights would be breached . Now , it is not enough to meet one of the exceptions. You must also somehow show that the public interest does not justify your deportation.
