You want to get that towards 10% and 15%; that would still leave us as an outlier but nevertheless it would be less of an unbelievable outlier than we currently are. If we do some of what the Government are proposing plus some things that we are proposing , you will get into that bracket and go from 5% to 10% , and ideally to 15%.

We need to be clarifying what fiscal devolution is. If you put 10 of us in a room you will get 12 different answers. Absolutely co-produce that with local government in particular; that is critically important. We need to make sure that we do not forget about modernising council tax because that is a big chunk of fiscal devolution, which happens today but is not fit for purpose.

The Budget next week is a stepping stone but not the answer on fiscal devolution. Some things we have talked about—shares of income tax , and business rates—are positive moves forward but there is a huge place where we can go further in thinking about actual true devolution.

We have not talked at all about the future of motoring taxes. That is something where the levies on people—both nationally and locally—are incredibly complicated at the moment depending on where you are parking versus who you are registering your car with. There are multiple different examples of where we can think about where the incidence of the tax is and how we avoid overtaxing and be in a situation where we are designing that sensibly. The thing that was most attractive from what Rachel Reeves said when she announced this was that it is a road map. The sense of a journey on this will not be answered by what we get next week; it will be the service station on the way to our journey.
Thanks to the panel, particularly for the quickfire answers to the final question. With that , the meeting is now concluded.

Oral evidence: The work of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade , HC 685
Tuesday 20 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 20 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Liam Byrne (Chair); Dan Aldridge; Antonia Bance; Chris Bloore; Sarah Edwards; Charlie Maynard; Mr Joshua Reynolds .
Questions 1 - 103
Witnesses
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Jonathan Reynolds and Amanda Brooks.

Q1 Welcome to today ’ s session. I am delighted that we are able to welcome the Secretary of State to the Committee, along with Amanda Brooks. Thank you very much indeed for joining us this afternoon. We are about to kick off our work plan for 2027 with our big business conference in the House of Commons on Monday, followed by a national road trip and a big nationwide survey to understand exactly what it is that b usiness, t rade u nion s and c onsumer a ssociations want us to have a look at over the course of 2027.

W e are very pleased to be able to kick off that process by asking you about your priorities. Welcome back to the best job in G overnment. Welcome back to the best C ommittee in Parliament. You have been out for a bit. You have come back to a D epartment that covers most of the domestic economy. Give us a sense of the vision and priorities that you have brought back to the D epartment.

Thank you, Chair. It is lovely to be with you, colleagues. As well as being two of the last few Business Secretaries, I was a member of this Committee as well, you might remember, in a previous guise. Thank you for that work you are kicking off, which is really important. This is the best job in Government. The role of this Select Committee is really important within that.

It may be worth pausing for a second to comment on the fact that it is a genuinely new Department. I know that, having done the DBT job before, people might see it in that way, but this is something new for people who are aficionados of how we have structured the B usiness D epartment in the UK in recent years. T he fact that we now have a D epartment of 8,500 people with an annual budget of circa £17 billion a year is a real , significant change in terms of the strength of these issues within G overnment . It is a privilege to come back to be in charge of them.

We cover a lot . I will give you our four public objectives, and I have not spoken of these before ; I am revealing them to the C ommittee in the proper way. The first is to lead on place-based reindustrialisation, using the industrial strategy as the mechanism for that. The second is how we make sure we have better lives and vibrant local economies , and that markets work for citizens . T hat is everything from our work on making work pay to our SME policy , to how competition law works in the UK and all the rest of the things the D epartment does.

The third — again , a reference to the new D epartment structure here —is that science, innovation and technology have to be at the heart of growth . W e have to embrace technology to do that. T he fourth is that we have always had, you might remember, a commitment to an open, connected trading economy. I would add the words “ secure ” and “ resilient ” to that, reflecting the world that we are in. T here are a lot of things, but you have to put it down into those four headings for the fundamental objectives of this D epartment.

Q2 You have managed to join and restructure the Department just ahead of the Budget. You will know that business is screaming about the cost of doing business. What have you asked the Chancellor to prioritise?

I am not going to shock you all by telling you what may or may not be in the Budget, or what I would want to be in it. I would look at the public comments of the Chancellor that you have just referenced — the reference to the cost of doing business and the need for breathing space for business. I endorse those words entirely.

There has to be acknowledgement that there is no answer to all the things we , as parliamentarians , and our constituents want to see as priorities for the state and for the Government unless we have a stronger economy than we have had in quite a few years since the financial crisis. The last set of GDP figures is very encouraging, but it is sustained economic growth that will do that. There has to be a reflection that business is the only way to do that. What the Chancellor has said has been significant in that.
Q3 Does that mean we are going to see help to reduce energy costs for business?

No specifics, I ’ m afraid, but as you know, Chair, I have made addressing the UK ’ s industrial electricity costs one of the thing s that I think are fundamental to the success of so many parts of the economy. I am very proud that BICS is being launched this year. That is a significant scheme for 10,000 manufacturing businesses. I will always make the case that that has to have been one of the issues we were right to address when we formed the Government in 2024.
Q4 Is it fair to say that energy costs were top of the list that you asked the Chancellor to act on?

I cannot tell you what was in that letter. I think that it is true to say that, if you g o t any collection of businesses, big and small, in this room and asked them, they would reference energy costs.
Q5 You are not deaf to that.
Yes.

Q6 You have the chance to integrate science and technology spend with real power now that that has moved into your Department. Hitherto, that has been a little disjointed from the industrial strategy. Will the Industrial Strategy Advisory Council now become effectively a reindustrialisation strategy council?

The mirror to the success of the industrial strategy was that it gave not just the Department but a whole range of other Government Departments a proper analytical tool as to where the opportunities lay. We have seen that. I thought that we saw, to differing extents, quite a few of the Government Departments respond to that. What was f ormer ly DSIT and UKRI were part of that.

The spend split for UKRI ’ s budget, which is broadly a third on what we might call curiosity or knowledge-led research and two thirds more applied to the priorities of the industrial strategy, is right. That work had already begun. I think that that is acknowledged.

The premise of reindustrialisation will use the industrial strategy as the tool to do that. I would add into that, as well as the IS-8 sectors, acknowledgement of foundational industries, which reflects existing work in the Department. There is a particular story to address that everyone here will be familiar with, which is how we take our success in those sectors and have more stories of brilliant British innovation resulting in commercialisation, scale-up and significant employment in the UK. I imagine that every single Member of Parliament here has heard too many stories of , “This brilliant idea originated in the UK, but we did not get the economic and commercial benefits of it . ” I now think that this Department is ideally placed to play a role in correcting that.

Q7 We will have more things to say on that tomorrow when we publish the Government response to our investing in the UK report, which was, I am afraid to say, produced under the last Administration, but quite disappointing. Do you think that the lever of science and technology spend is going to be easier to apply to the industrial strategy sectors now that it is within your Department?

There is obviously more coherence from having it in one Department. I am trying to say that I believe the work that needed to happen had already begun. Our job is to make sure that that is followed through.

To be specific, UKRI had already shifted around £9 billion of funding to focus on the industrial strategy eight sectors, so that pivot had already been taking place in the way that the Secretary of State has referred to. As part of that, around £4.5 billion is supporting innovative firms in those sectors. I t is fair to say that the changes were already happening . H ow we bring those conversations together going forward as we work, including with the Industrial Strategy Advisory Council, wh ich you have just mentioned, is going to be really important.
Q8 Is it still the intention to put the Industrial Strategy Advisory Council on a statutory basis?

Yes, I would still want and expect that to happen. As you will know, Chair, parliamentary time is under pressure, and there are a great many priorities to address. In my former life as Chief Whip it is something I have experienced a great deal of. We are still committed to putting the Industrial Strategy Advisory Council on a statutory footing.

Q9 Let me cover off a couple of bits of topical news before we dig into some of the questions about reindustrialisation. We have published the Government reply on Royal Mail today. In that reply, you said that you are open to Ofcom proposing new statutory powers to help it grip Royal Mail ’ s performance, which continues to disappoint the nation. Can you confirm today that you will look favourably on any Ofcom proposals to take or seek new powers to ensure that Christmas deliveries are safe and Royal Mail begins delivering what the nation expects?

Yes. It is a straightforward answer . I am not satisfied ; I am not happy with the performance. I think that you say in your letter, quite rightly, that there is some statistical improvement, but it is not the level of service people expect. I know for parliamentarians —we have had this in oral questions on Thursday and in other correspondence with M embers of P arliament —that it is one of the most significant issues they are facing.

W e have tried — and done, I believe — some significant things for the long-term future of Royal Mail. I want a successful, prosperous Royal Mail . You can think about how we worked pragmatically in terms of the ownership bid that came in prior to the election . W e have recognised the need for regulatory reform in terms of the USO, which Ofcom lead s on but has significant public interest. We negotiated , as part of the takeover, no dividends being paid until performance levels had improved. W e do not run the business day to day , and y ou would not expect M inisters to do that, but I believe we have put in place some of the things that are necessary for success.

I am going to have Royal Mail and the union in for a conversation about this. I need to respond to what MPs are being told. Royal Mail is a really important institution and business , and I know that it has significant ramifications when it is not hitting the levels of service. I can promise you, Chair, whether it is work ing with Ofcom, or with any part , any key player or any stakeholder in this, we will do what we can to make sure that Royal Mail is the service it needs to be.

Q10 Welcome, Secretary of State. Just going on your answer there, Ofcom says it has reliability a s a top priorit y , but Royal Mail has not met its first and second class standards for nearly a decade. We had Ofcom in the House of Commons as a group of MPs just last week. Ofcom has said that it does not foresee requesting any new powers from Government to deal with this crisis. If that is the answer from Ofcom, do you have faith that Ofcom is fit for purpose if it foresees not requesting any additional powers from Government?

All I can say is that Ofcom is a very important regulator. If it told me that it believed it needed more in its toolkit around this issue, of course we would respond openly, transparently and pragmatically to that request. I have followed the day-to-day running of Royal Mail pretty closely, as you would expect. I know how the union feels about parts of this. I know and believe that there was a chance for a significant improvement in both the morale and the industrial relations in the business from the new owners coming in. I think we would all recognise that things had got quite difficult before then.

An improvement in service will not just come about. It has to be , “What is the business plan to do that? What is the embrace of innovation and technology? How can there be a continuity of people working for the business?” There has been a significant turnover. All this has to be addressed. If Ofcom needed something else, of course we would be open to that.

Q11 We have also published today the letter from the head of the FRC confirming that the FRC will take oversight of the audit investigation into failures at Manchester City ’ s auditor. She has also confirmed that she does not have the powers to effectively investigate or prosecute directors who are not members of the accounting profession. Does this not underline exactly why audit and accounting reform is essential? W ill you revisit the decision to bring that legislation back to the House so that we do not have the kind s of accounting scandals such as the one we have heard about at Manchester City again?

My interest in audit reform goes back to being a member of this Committee, when some of these issues were there. I believe that there is a package of measures within there that I would like to see enacted. In these Departments there are so many priorities we have that, when we bid into the legislative Sessions , there will be tension on priorities in terms of those bids that have to go in. There simply is not enough time to do everything. You try to think creatively as to how you can fit different measures into different Bills or what you can put together to do it.

I recognise the case that you are making. There has been no reduction or lack of commitment from the Government in terms of this agenda. We are still committed to it. It is a matter of finding the right way and the right space to legislate.
Q12 You would agree that the Manchester City case underlines the necessity of audit reform in our country .

I would not link the two things together. I am talking about the broad issue of audit reform. We are all familiar with that. In relation to Manchester City, I know there is a lot of interest in this, but I am not involved in any of the football-related aspects of this. These are two separate things to the trade and investment relationships that we hold in the Department.
Q13 You would say that the case for audit reform is an imperative in and of itself.

The case is recognised. I am not aware of any significant opposition in Parliament. I know that some changes have happened in the absence of primary legislation, going back to the original Kingman proposals. Parts of that have been enacted ; I recognise that. In terms of the wider principles of making sure that there is the regulatory oversight of directors and those parts of it, yes, the case is still there.

Q14 I should probably declare an interest that I am an Aston Villa season ticket holder and a member of the football APPG. Secretary of State, you met the chairman of Manchester City in September to discuss UAE investment before the commission ’ s findings were made public. Can I ask whether the Manchester City case was discussed at that meeting? If so, was it raised with you that the UAE might retaliate against the guilty verdict by withdrawing investments such as the Oxford-Cambridge corridor?

I will declare that I am a Sunderland fan, which as a Manchester MP is a particularly helpful construct , as a non-threatening football brand. I moved to Manchester when I was 18 in 1998 and I love Manchester. I am so proud to be an MP for the city. I am so proud of the regeneration of the city. There is an identity among the Greater Manchester MPs that reflects the incredible story . Let us be clear : we do not have enough stories of post-industrial regeneration and success in the north of England. Manchester stands out for that.

I know some of the leading people from the UAE . I am our T rade M inister ; y ou would expect that. I n terms of that meeting — and indeed , I can tell you , any meeting — no one has ever asked me to get involved in the Manchester City sporting case, separate to our trade and investment relationships.

Q15 That is good to know, because I suspect you would agree that there should be no geopolitical interference in our national game and that people will want to hear that from G overnment moving forward.

Absolutely, Chris. I would go further and say that the Premier League itself is one of our most important traded exports. It has tremendous coverage around the world. I know that there is interest in it, shall we say. I can tell you, to be frank, that not even any constituent—and we like our football in Greater Manchester—has ever asked me to get involved in it. I deal with the trade and investment side.

We all, as Labour MPs, have a manifesto commitment to the trade deal with the GCC. The UAE is our biggest trading partner within the GCC, so you would expect those relationships to exist. In fact, we are just waiting for the signature on the GCC deal, which is an important one. I can tell you that I have never been asked to get involved, and nor would I, in the football side of this case.
Thank you for clearing that up.
Mr Joshua Reynolds: Secretary of State, welcome back. I hope you are receiving post in my name, as I am for you — and in the name of the Member for High Wycombe as well, surprisingly.
Well done for sorting the pharmacy issue out — I can say that.

Q16 Mr Joshua Reynolds: The Defence Secretary has said that the Ministry of Defence will play a central role in the UK ’ s reindustrialisation. The Chancellor has said that reindustrialisation is an opportunity to support the NEETs crisis. Your Minister for Reindustrialisation has said that reindustrialisation is maximising tradable sectors in every part of the country through innovation. What does that actually mean?

For me, reindustrialisation is based on the industrial strategy and the IS-8. As I say, I would add the foundational sectors into that. There is always an ongoing debate in the UK about where the line sits between services and manufacturing. In many cases, that is artificial. Take an iconic manufacturer such as Rolls-Royce. It generates quite a lot of revenue from services alongside that from the products that it produces.

Let us be clear and remember. What are the IS-8? They are the sectors that the data tells us represent both our strengths and our greatest opportunities. The commitment to reindustrialisation recognises that there are some specific things required in policy terms to support those sectors.

I n the context of what you were just asking, defence is one of those IS — industrial strategy — sectors. T hat fits very much with what the Secretary of State for Defence has spoken about , and indeed the current Chancellor. If you look at some of the challenges that we have on NEETs at the moment, this week we have seen the publication of a number of jobs plans reflecting on the different opportunities in those sectors, which will enable future employment opportunities. They are making some big commitments. W e know that these sectors, on average, pay about £8,000 more than employment in other sectors. T here is a really important link between all those different issues, as you rightly say.
Q17 Mr Joshua Reynolds: The IS-8 include financial services and the creative industries. Is reindustrialisation the IS-8 , and therefore is part of reindustrialisation creative industries?

The core of this is the IS-8. Of those IS-8, five are perhaps considered traditional manufacturing. Three would be services. Can you make anything in the UK without support from the financial services sector? Can you export anything without access to insurance? Can you run your business without access to professional and business services?

This is probably something this Committee has looked at, Chair. The UK has a history of producing a new document and a new economic theory and basis every year. That has to stop. The Prime Minister ’ s commitment to reindustrialisation is absolutely the right one, but we should build on the empirical tools that we have, and that is the industrial strategy.

Q18 Mr Joshua Reynolds: Finally on that, the chief exec of Make UK urged the Government, when it comes to the definition of reindustrialisation, to put some flesh on the buzzwords. Do you understand why Make UK might think that reindustrialisation is just a buzzword?

I always listen to Make UK because they are very wise people. That is a fair point and I would add to it. I think that we would all want to consider, across Government and Parliament, what the metrics and KPIs we would want to use for that are. I know that there are a lot of colleagues who want a straightforward jobs-based KPI. Perhaps this C ommittee might be able to assist in that. We might ask the Industrial Strategy Advisory Council for its wider observations. I think that it is quite helpful to bring into account things such as the degree of business investment that is going in. Perhaps we might want to consider some of our exports as part of that. It is not just about the definition; it is what we are measuring going forward.
Q19 That is very helpful, Secretary of State. You are telling us that we do need to put some tighter definitions on what reindustrialisation needs to deliver in terms of hard outcomes.
I think that we all would want to know what we are measuring. What are we agreeing on? What do we disagree on? What do we want to see more of? That helps policy in Parliament and in Government .
We will certainly offer you the benefit of our advice on that.

Q20 Thank you, Secretary of State. The Resolution Foundation found that more than half of UK postcode areas saw falling living standards during the last Parliament. How are you and your Department going to drive growth in every postcode with that in mind?

That is the central challenge for the UK, not just for the Department or the Government but Parliament. Every other challenge, whether it is public services or political fragmentation, comes from the fact that we saw for the first time, and we have seen since the financial crisis, I would argue, an end to what I would call the classic British working class story. My parents only wanted one thing, which is that my sister and I have more opportunities than the y did . We are all familiar with th e challenge that comes from that. We put into account not just the performance of the economy but things such as the housing market . T hat tells us where we are at.

H ow do we do that? Going back to those four objectives , we need to know where our strengths lie, where we need to drive investment and where policy has to support that. That is the industrial strategy. We need vibrant, dynamic markets. That is everything . T he Prime Minister ’ s recent announcement that we will move on non-competes is significant because you are taking a major ask from the tech sector that is , essentially , classic employment policy . T his D epartment now represents both of those things and we can make that activity what we need it to be.

O ur plan to make work pay is perhaps more contentious in some quarters . I think we would all recognise , when we are talking about growth in every postcode , that there have been times in British history where the overall national economy has grown but people have not felt it, either in their locality or because of the job they do . It is essentially a class-based assessment as part of that.

We have to put science and innovation at the heart of our economic policy and embrace technology. T hat is harder than people sometimes accept , because technology disrupts. There are political challenges for all of us in that . W e have to remain an open, outward-facing economy —t he UK has always been a trading nation — whil e recognising that we are not living in the late 19 90s in terms of free trade and WTO rounds. We have a very different trading situation. We have to think about our national resilience within that, whil e remaining open and outward-facing to the world .

Q21 One thing that always concerns me as a Member representing a coastal town is whether we are being measured, because we only act on what we measure. Is the Department assessing whether living standards are improving in those postcodes and whether there is the improvement that we hope to see in those postcodes such as mine in Weston - super - Mare?

It has to be not just measured but felt. People do not always feel national statistics, and we have to recognise that. I t is what Amanda has just said about why the IS-8 sectors are so important. That is because they pay wages that people feel and can appreciate.

The whole Government take into account economic statistics. That is not just a matter for the new BIST Department. The Prime Minister himself has made it clear — and those different elements of the policy menu add up to a recognition of it— that people not only need to be told the country is doing well, but they need to feel it.
Q22 Do we have metrics to see the actual growth in postcodes, but also the feeling? That would be really helpful.
You mean breaking down GDP growth on a granular level . I do not know whether the country has that, to be frank.

We can break it down at regional level, but probably not down to the point of every postcode. U nlike Bhutan, which has an excellent focus on tracking happiness in its economy, we do not have that level of detail at the granular level you are talking about.

We do, though, track, across multiple different ways in which the Department ’ s interventions work, what is happening in places . We know that over half of UKRI spend is outside London and the s outh -east , so increasingly spread. There is the work that the Prime Minister has announced to amplify that through local innovation partnerships, but also what we do on trade deals . W e have always tracked what the impact is on regions of the country and, indeed, the devolved nations. W e look at that , but, as you say, at what level of granularity ? W hat you are challenging us to is a whole new level.

Even within local authority levels, we have North Somerset c ouncil, which is largely far more affluent than my constituency, where the deprivation actually lies. That has massaged the statistics quite significantly. Even if not postcode, constituency level would be really good to be able to identify whether people are feeling the benefit.
Q23 You are identifying a constraint . It is quite difficult for the Prime Minister to prove we are delivering growth in every postcode.

I really want to stress that it is not just a slogan. I can honestly tell you that I think of the decisions we make through the lens of making sure that prosperity is genuinely a UK-wide thing. When, for instance, we had the issues around the rescue of Harland & Wolff, it really mattered to me that one of those shipyards is on the Western Isles and there is not a lot of intervention, historically, from national Government in a place such as the Western Isles. That made it important. If you look at the recent investment we made in the SaxaVord spaceport in the Shetland Islands, again that is thinking about how you make sure that this is relevant to every bit of the UK.

Q24 The Committee is quite interested in the focus that the Government have on procurement as being a means to spread some of that money that the Government have at their disposal. It is said to be worth about £395 billion in 2024-25. With the “ B uy British” agenda being quite a key policy, we heard on this Committee that we had not quite established what British meant and we were waiting for a paper to tell us how we defined that and whether that was a British company or a company that had British workers , etc .

I was wondering about how you thought, when it comes to the Government ’ s procurement, a British company can compete when we know that it is incredibly expensive at the moment to be a business, to produce products and to compete against potential bids from other countries. I will get on to how that interacts with the EU. How do you see that working? It is not necessarily going to be the cheapest option, but it might be for the country, economically, the one that spreads around the most social value and wealth.

“Buy British” is focusing on jobs and growth in the UK. There would be many people, I would assume, who would attempt a sophisticated definition of that. If you are asking about a non-UK shareholder based in the UK, that is British jobs and growth to me. A Nissan would be a great example of that. T hat focus is in line with our international commitments, so not some sort of return to pre-war protectionism and turning our back on an open and connected , outward - facing , internationalist trading posture.

T here are different definitions that exist . I f you looked at the sovereign AI UK nexus test , I think it covers where your HQ is, your R&D presence and whether you could become a category leader in the UK. The definition is less important than recognising what we are trying to do. T here is a problem to fix here, which is that many brilliant , innovative British firms tell us at times that cracking our own procurement domestic market is harder than some of the overseas ones. T here is a problem to fix as part of that.

T hat agenda covers the changes the Cabinet Office has made to social value. In some of the big inward investment decisions we are currently working on, we are looking at, for instance, how advance market commitments could work , so there is a guarantee to procure part of that investment from domestic firms. W hat is the quantum programme , Amanda ?
It is ProQure.

It is a specific initiative in the quantum space to recognise the brilliance we have there and how we want that to be part of investment decisions in the future. “Buy British” , to me, is a focus on making sure that we are getting the benefits of jobs and growth in the UK.

There are other actions that we have been taking to make it easier for businesses to plan ahead. For example, publishing the pipeline of what steel requirements we are likely to require enables businesses to plan , think ahead and bid accordingly. It is the transparency around those procurement pipelines and new guidance on how we are going to utilise national security exemptions in areas such as AI.

Q25 When we talk to defence contractors or health contractors, which are the two turbochargers of the £385 billion that the country spends on Government procurement each year , they consistently tell us that they cannot see the demand signal in their sectors.
That is n oted .
Q26 What are you going to do about that?
As I say, it is happening in some sectors. If it needs to happen in others, that is something that we can talk to colleagues about.

That is not a new problem. Thinking back to my previous tenure, I could honestly say that the Secretaries of State for Health and for Defence recognised the problem, took it seriously and put initiatives in place. I would not say that the problem is fixed, but it goes back to the point in answer to Sarah ’ s question, which is , “What is this about?” It is about fixing a problem. It is about fixing a problem where we are not linking opportunities from British procurement to the brilliant innovation and start-up sectors that we have . W e have to fix that.

Q27 If we then look at how we are obliged under our trading relationship with the EU to allow for treaty state suppliers to bid into our procurement system, is that not at odds with our “ B uy British” agenda? We know that we are still ironing out some of the challenges around the Made in Europe agenda. Ultimately, we are trying to achieve the same ends, which is to protect ourselves from the Chinese imports, but we do not seem to be working very closely together on doing that. We seem to be cutting each other off, rather than looking at the benefit on both sides of that. How compatible is that?
That is a good segue. A desire to see British firms benefit in some way to a greater degree from British procurement is a different issue from the Made in Europe agenda .

Q28 That is not how the French see it . French officials will say to us, often quietly, “You want a ‘ B uy British ’ strategy on the one hand, but on the other hand you want to be part of Made in Europe —and t hat sounds like wanting your cake and eating it. ”

It might be how they want to present it, but they are two different things. I will give you an example. If you look at our automotive subsidies, a very significant proportion of those go to European manufacturers. We are not reverting to protectionism by wanting to solve this problem that is, quite rightly, given to us by our own firms, which is how we can play a role in what the state and other Government Departments are doing.

On Made in Europe, I am very proud that the Government have simultaneously sought to improve the trading relationship with Europe, which is in all our interests, and do work around the rest of the world to maximise opportunities there. It is absolutely the case that we should work together with the EU on that agenda. We are trying to manage the same problems. We are trying to make sure that we are in the strongest possible position. If you look at, for instance, the integrated nature of automotive supply chains across the EU, it is to the detriment of both the EU and the UK if we are not continuing what we have in that. That is the basis of the discussions that we are having with the EU. The case to work closely together is a strong one.

Q29 Is that moving in a more positive direction ? At the moment some of the drafts suggest it is assembled in Europe , and therefore we are excluded from that, because their interpretation is EU rather than Europe . We also have some semantic problems here . T here is some room , perhaps , to help define that . D oes that feel like that is going in the right direction to protect our car industry , so that we can still trade with the EU and keep our British jobs , while also acknowledging that it is a much more challenging situation ?

Made in Europe is a priority not just for this Department but for every Secretary of State because of the significance of what it would represent. You will know that it is a thread running through lots of different items of European legislation. The Industrial Accelerator Act is the obvious first example of that.

We want not only to fix this problem to the benefit of the EU and ourselves, but to do so in a way that provides for the greatest degree of certainty for business going forward. If it covers lots of different aspects, how we do that in a way that gives people reassurance that we are not going to face these unnecessary trade barriers is very important. There is a lot of work going on on this. It is a very significant priority for Government. I have a lot of confidence in the argument that it is in our interests, but also in the EU ’ s interest, to work closely together on this.

Q30 I will return to steel, but I want to touch briefly on steel and public procurement. We are all, I think, very proud of PPN 022 and the impact it is beginning to have on the procurement of British - produced steel. There are still some oddities, such as the fact that DfE require s EAF steel in its procurement. A t the moment , that cannot be made in the United Kingdom, and perhaps DfE ought to get with the programme on that point. I wanted to ask specifically whether you thought , Secretary of State, all publicly supported projects should be subject to public procurement note 022. We have seen some significant public supported projects — I think of Net Zero Teesside, for example, which has decided to procure its steel and have it fabricated elsewhere in the world.

I am also very proud that this G overnment have gripped steel . Frankly , it was not always easy to even get on the agenda in previous P arliaments, especially when you look at what has happened around the world, especially in Europe, and how the C ap E x need requir es the state and the G overnment to show an interest in this. Obviously with any procurement we want to see the benefits in the UK, but that is subject to our international commitments and the free and open tendering system that we would have.

On steel in particular, this issue comes up a lot . W here the UK makes something, it is , in the main , used for domestic demand. The problem for the UK is that we have not been making enough of a range of products and the more we would make, the more would be in domestic procurement choices. That means everything , so not just the more dramatic interventions we have had to make in some parts of our steel industry but also the overall business environment.

T he key thing for steel is the expanded supercharger policy . We have ended the incredibly disadvantageous position domestic steelmakers were in, in terms of very heavy electricity use and how we compared on that. To me, the success comes from some quite dramatic things that we have had to do , such as recalling P arliament to preserve our domestic steel industry, but we are improving the business environment through energy and the changes to procurement in terms of social value. Trade defence is obviously a part of that .
We will come back to that.
Where we have the business case to make something in the UK, it will , in the main , feature in domestic procurement.
Q31 Where public money is being spent not in traditional public procurement, should those projects use British-made steel?

My instinct would be that I would expect them to. If you have a specific case where that has not happened, I would be interested in what the business decisions were that had led to that outcome. All this is part of our wider commitment to our WTO commitments and our posture as an outward-facing trading nation. In terms of certain areas of cost, particularly because we have had to put trade defence in to deal with the structural overcapacity in steel, which is a feature of the world economy , I would be interested in what decisions had led to a non-British-based choice for procurement.
We will come back to you on steel safeguards. We just want to pursue this point about devolution .

Q32 Forty per cent of constituencies are outside of mayoral areas, mine being one of them, although I am slightly on the cusp because I am a non-voting constituent of the West Midlands Combined Authority, but Staffordshire as a whole is not. On this Committee we are quite concerned about how the Government are going to direct resource and funds, and particularly how it is that you and your Department are going to make sure that these areas do not miss out. A lot of the support has been directed through the established mayoral authorities, and that leav es places such as Staffordshire without clarity.

There have been some really good announcements around local share of income tax and the visitor economy levy , and talk about this relationship with vocational skills. The Lichfield and Tamworth chamber of commerce and the Staffordshire chamber of commerce are quite keen to know where we are going with this and how quickly we can get that mayoral authority in place. Business really wants to crack on. How do you see the fact that this this timeframe is not in your gift, but you still have to support all these mayoral authorities with some policy changes that really make a meaningful difference?

When we published the industrial strategy, there were some tools in there that applied to mayoral authorities , and there were ones that were available to local authorities to try to reflect that balance. The truth is that we have just been to India on a very successful trade mission with seven of the northern mayors. It was originally their trip. I went to support them, with some other Secretaries of State. The fact is that, if your area do es not have one of these mayors, you are going to be at a disadvantage. Let us be honest: you are not on that plane. Going back to that India trip, there were areas that are in that stage. The chair of the Cheshire authority came with us to India, reflecting that it want s to start doing that kind of work until it has the mayoral arrangements in place.

We stand ready to support any area doing that work. We are also strongly committed to the Government ’ s devolution agenda more widely . T here are some things you cannot devolve from this D epartment, such as trade policy or employment law. I t is more in the innovation and potential R&D space . W e are also looking at how we can potentially even second staff to certain authorities in parts of the country to build up what they will need in terms of economic and business policy experience.

W hen you talk to businesses, they tend to like the mayoral model for engagement, because it is neither too big to be relevant to them, nor so small that it does not get the quality of engagement that they need on those areas. T here is quite strong business demand for this model going forward. A s areas are on this path, we will absolutely seek to work with them.

I t is also worth saying that certainly we recognise, and I think colleagues recognise, that, even where areas have a mayor, there are different stages. T here are different places in terms of different capacities. Greater Manchester and the west midlands are obviously very established as a tier. W e want to support not just more places to go on this journey but areas that already have a mayor . Do they have what they need in terms of economic capacity to do the things they want to do and be the partner to us at that sub-regional level ?

Q33 Could I ask that we hear some more from the Department about the specific ways that non-mayoral areas are going to receive that additional support? Even if some of those things are not now — hopefully they are next week — it would be really good for that to be well signposted. Otherwise, all the announcements that so far have come out of the Government have always been around that nexus of a mayoral authority.

I hear that and I am sensitive to that. To quote the godfather of Greater Manchester devolution, he used to always say , “Never go to Government with a begging bowl. Always go with an offer . ” I would say to parts of the country, “Come to us with an offer. What do you want to do? What do you want your local economy to be? If we can support that, we are here to do that. Tell us what you need. Tell us the relationships that you have . ”
Q34 Can I check whether the machinery of government changes and the budget recalibration is all now complete?
It is not quite.
It is not fully complete. These things are a bit more complicated. Amanda is perhaps the best person to talk about it.
Q35 Do you know what your budget is now?

Broadly, yes. We are still working through the final details of staff particularly and which Department they are going to. We need to go through the Cabinet Office standard operating processes for that.
Q36 What do you think your budget is now?
It is a round £17 billion.
Q37 That is DEL.
That is both RDEL and CDEL combined. The split is £2 billion RDEL and £15 billion CDEL.
Q38 That does not sound like it includes UKRI.
It include s UKRI, yes.

Q39 We are about to go through this period now where you have a budget, a 10-year plan, which is allegedly sometime before Christmas , and then a comprehensive spending review , where, again , the timing is unclear. At this stage, what fraction of that £17 billion do you think will be devolved by this time next year?

I would not want to put a figure on that. We are deeply committed to this. We have an ask from some of the mayoral authorities. We have to look at what the right functions, rather than some kind of envelope of money, are to do that. T he obvious space, and the Prime Minister ha s talked about this, is around the late-stage innovations, so the model of local innovation partnerships is a key part of that. We have also taken some of our existing programmes , such as the DRIVE 35 programme , which is the very significant R&D automotive programme, and given two significant pots of money to the west midlands and the north-east to work on supply chains. W e are looking at how we can do this.

T aking the commitment we have to it, we have to also make sure that this money is spent on the things that we currently spend it on. T he success of d evolution, where it has had successes, has been in improving outcomes, but it is a process ; i t is not an end in itself . A s parliamentarians and as a G overnment, we want to do this. We want to push money down to that level, but we have to make sure that we are not in a situation where we are losing something that is very good in the UK.

Q40 You are describing the classic sector-spaces tension, which has bedevilled devolution for at least the 25 years that I have worked on it. Are you able to give us a rough sense of what kind of fraction you think could be devolved?
No , I would not do that at this stage.
Q41 When do you think that begins to get clearer? Is it a 10-year plan timetable? Is it the comprehensive spending review?

The “ Rewiring the State ” White Paper is a significant part of that. That leads into the 10-year plan. Going back to the different stages devolution is at in different parts of the country, it is also about giving people the capacity that they need to make these decisions.

Q42 When a pioneering Chief Secretary first proposed the idea of total place, there were some pretty powerful constraints. There was basically a public services agreement that helped to corral exactly what it was that a local area could spend on. Do you imagine that that kind of approach to intergovernment al relations might be one of the ways in which you can ensure that your objectives are hit, but you none the less achieve the devolution by default objective that the Prime Minister set out?
I have always been a fan of that pioneering former Chief Secretary ’ s work on that particular area and others.
He was the future once.

C onditionality is sensitive in this new era of devolution. E veryone has an interest in making sure that this is a success. We have to recognise that, if you look at the spending review period, the total R&D budget is £ 59 billion. That is absolutely core to our economic success. I definitely think some parts of that can be spent at this level in a better way. Glasgow, Manchester and Birmingham led on an earlier trial of this, maybe under the former Conservative G overnment . T here has been work in this area .

W e know what is good , but we recognise that we have to do this in a way that delivers what we all want : more power and insight into local economies, building on our strengths, particularly on R&D. I t is something we absolutely cannot afford to do in anything other than a very excellent way.
Q43 It sounds like the process for managing that tension is still work ahead of you.

There is some genuinely groundbreaking and exciting work going on between the mayoral authorities and a Department like mine, as we work to pace and work out exactly how we can do this in the best way for everyone ’ s objectives.

To provide some examples of things that are already under way , the Office for Investment now has people embedded with mayoral strategic authorities, helping them to build investable propositions that will bring inward investment into those areas. On business support, there are 30 growth hubs operating around the country.

If you have a situation where we are not quite clear about the metrics for judging the success of reindustrialisation, we are not quite clear about the metrics for judging whether growth is being delivered in every postcode and we do not have the fractions of your budget that may be devolved, we can see a policy problem looming that we look forward to scrutinising over the months ahead.

Q44 Secretary of State , I am sure you will be aware that many small businesses are saying that their costs continue to increase. I suspect that, like everybody around this table, you spend time with small businesses on your high street. I am definitely going to plug The Lounge, which is a lovely cocktail and gin place in Astwood Bank, run by Louise and Karl, who I met last week. They shared with me their concerns about how long they can keep taking on these extra costs to keep their businesses going. You mentioned at the start of this meeting that you may not be willing or able to share some of the measures in the Budget. The Prime Minister has expressed how important it is to him to support small businesses. Do you expect those pressures to ease post Budget?

I can absolutely say that I, the Prime Minister and the Chancellor would endorse entirely the case you have made for the centrality of small business to the economy and a sense of local prosperity. If the Prime Minister himself were here, he would acknowledge that, with regard to his record in Manchester, which is one of economic growth and prosperity, a big sense of how people feel about that is that it is a wonderful place to be in the city centre. There are the bars, the restaurants and the feeling of people coming together and enjoying that shared space.

I have always been sensitive to the well-established sense a lot of smaller businesses have, which is that it is the bigger corporates that get to engage with G overnment. We have always been reflective on that. The SME strategy and small business plan was absolutely a part of that.

Without talking about this Budget, looking back to other Budgets, it is important to say that we had worked on things such as the doubling of employment allowance in opposition , recognising there would be costs coming from a higher minimum wage and perhaps from employment rights , with the impact of that on some businesses.

The agenda that became the small business plan was an attempt from this Department to recognise the levers that we have that would be most effective for those businesses. Tax is very significant, but we have to leave that to the Chancellor. The Commercial Payments Bill will make the UK the best jurisdiction of any major economy to be a small business in, in terms of payment from bigger businesses. The permanently lower multiplier on business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure was a part of that.
Q45 Can I come back on that? Do you think—I will try for a third time—that perhaps the threshold for small business rate relief might get raised to a more appropriate level?

I am afraid that I am too savvy a man to come before the Select Committee and speculate on the Budget. The s e are pressures that you are quite rightly identifying, Chris. The question for someone like me is what the best ways to relieve those pressures are. What are the things that get to the most businesses? I understand why that is.

B y the way, something that does not quite get the attention it deserves is the increase in capacity and the changes to the British Business Bank. I am sure I will not be the only parliamentarian where my personal Facebook account gives me endless adverts for the growth guarantee scheme, which is great. We have tried, with the levers we have in this D epartment, to put in place the things that would make the biggest difference, notwithstanding the recognition that issues of national insurance, VAT and so forth will always be paramount to how people feel the pressures of that.

We also, for the leisure and hospitality industry, work with DCMS on licensing changes and any attempt to rel iev e the pressure on those businesses. I absolutely recognise the case that you are making. W hen we talk about growth in every postcode, what is present in every postcode ? I t is small business. T hat is why they are so central to economic policy.

Q46 Mr Joshua Reynolds: T he British Independent Retailers Association told the Committee that small firms are operating on the lowest profit margin that they have ever worked on. An FSB report from August this year found that less than 18% of small firms expected to grow in the next year, while 31% said they were going to shrink, sell up or close. Just under 90% of firms reported higher operating costs than a year ago. Hospitality has seen some of the largest falls in payroll numbers , and retail recorded its lowest ever four-quarter average for employment levels in 2025. That is a pretty bleak picture when it comes to the confidence that businesses are having, especially in retail. What are you going to do to make sure that we fix that in the short term?

Those are all organisations that I have a great deal of respect for, but if you ask anyone how they feel right now, you are not going to be able to separate out wider policy from the fact that what we have seen in the strait of Hormuz between the US and Iran will have economic consequences for the UK in terms of inflation, industrial costs, energy and supply costs. If you are asking for what those figures tell you right now, that reflects a pretty obvious and difficult situation, which even a country such as ours only has so many ways to mitigate.

What are we committed to in the short term? On all the areas that we have access to, whether that is payment terms, employment law, access to finance or licensing with other Departments, we are seeking to relieve those pressures. I know what they will ask for more than anything else, and it is reflected in the question about the Budget. I can tell you that that sentiment is represented to the Treasury, but people will have to wait until the B udget to see what the Chancellor ’ s proposals are.

Q47 Mr Joshua Reynolds: As a Liberal Democrat MP, I do not go anywhere without my 2024 Labour party manifesto. On pages 28 and 29 of that manifesto, it said that Labour will replace the business rates system. We are over two years into a Labour Government. When are you going to replace the business rates system, as you promised?

That is a question for the Treasury. I have always felt that there are inequities in our business rate system. You are more than familiar with the incidence of the tax and where it falls in terms of disproportionate impact on certain sectors. I absolutely recognise and still support the case for wholesale reform, but on any questions of taxation you are going to have to wait until the Chancellor speaks.

Q48 Mr Joshua Reynolds: When I asked your predecessor that same question in July, he pretty much gave me the exact same answer. His opening words were, “ As you know, that is an HMT decision , ” which is pretty much your same words. Is that not part of the problem ? Even with the machinery of government changes that this Government have introduced, the issues that affect businesses most, whether that is business rates or energy costs, are not the responsibility of the Secretary of State for Business but other Secretaries of State .
Your D epartment has expanded, but could we expand it a little further and have a business tax policy as well?

If you wish to put proposals to Government, Chair, I would be very interested in receiving them. Everything that affects businesses cannot be in one Department. I am tempted by the proposal, but it is not possible. If you ask some businesses what the biggest issue facing them right now is, they would probably say extended producer responsibility, which is a DEFRA policy. Some would cite perhaps the emissions trading scheme, which is a DESNZ policy. Others might talk about transport connections in their area. The ZEV mandate for the automotive industry is a Department for Transport lead.

I have always thought that we do quite a lot in this expanded Department, and some of those levers are hugely important. Also, you have to be, and I want to be, that kind of shop steward and voice of business within Government. People come to us on a whole range of things, partly because I find that an enjoyable part of the job. I like being out there. I like being accessible to people. I have at times even had colleagues say to me, “You are just the voice of business . ” You are like, “That is exactly what I am seeking to be as the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade . ” We do that.

For a Chancellor, what they are doing in their Budget affects every aspect of the state and G overnment , so you are going to have to have that distinction there . I do not think you could ever move taxation policy for business into the B usiness D epartment. That would not quite be coherent , but it is an interesting suggestion.

Q49 I am very interested in the focus that the Government have on high streets. It is important to all of us around the table . Tamworth has a very pedestrianised high street area . Y ou have visited it and shopped on it, so you have that claim to fame. Y ou will be happy to know that Tamworth was recently touted as being one of the happiest places in the UK. G oing on the positive vibe in that sort of line, I met two young, small entrepreneurs last week, one called Harry, who owns a coffee shop, Crave, and the other, Kai, who started a vintage fashion store called Stay Tidy. T hey are fantastic. T hey are encapsulating some of the positive potential for young people to go out there.

I wondered whether you could comment on how your strategy is going to start to steward some of the funds and policy decisions into areas such as Tamworth . A £ 300 million - ish pot has been announced. How might that be used to help councils to incentivise this, giving cheaper rents or bringing some of these derelict buildings back into ownership so we can get not just young entrepreneurs but all entrepreneurs into those derelict spaces and inject some life back into these places that mean so much to people?

I remember our trip to Tamworth market. It is one of my favourite ever anecdotes. I will not share it with the Committee because it is incredibly amusing but probably not appropriate for this session.
Maybe in writing .

There is a wide range of goods and services available in Tamworth and I can endorse that. That is all I will say at this stage. On e of the happiest places — absolutely. For people who may not know the geography of eastern Greater Manchester, my constituency is a collection of towns, each with a very strong identit y . They are historically market towns based around wide-scale manufacturing in or close to the town centre, people getting paid in cash weekly and walking through. It has been a hard transition for us. There is no doubt about it, but it is a story that is familiar all across the UK.

When I talk about how people feel about prosperity, the high street and the town centre is a disproportionate part of that. Even if you have great employers on an industrial estate nearby, if you do not see and feel them in the same way, that is a significant part of it. In terms of different bits of Government , I always think of MHCLG as place - based ; BIST you think of as business - based. The two things coming together is the key to the success of that.

To be fair to the previous Government, there were some interesting things put on the statute book that are now coming into effect, such as high street auctions to make sure that derelict properties come back into use. That is a big issue in both Hyde and Stalybridge for me. You have to look at things such as how the business rates system works. Those will be the fundamentals in an area. I think the fund that you are talking about is an MHCLG fund, so it is not directly within there.
It is, yes.

Where I have seen successful regeneration of high streets, you sometimes need a little bit of public money to do some of the anchor things. One in Greater Manchester that is often cited i s Altrincham, where the food hall brought prosperity back to the wider town centre. We had—I do not know whether the new Department has continued, because it was changed in the time I was not there—the joint MHCLG-DBT high streets unit.
We do not have that, no.
That changed.
Q50 That is what I was hoping that you might say — that we have a joint unit that brings together these two really important Departments on this.
We had a joint unit. I believe that that has changed. I would totally agree, because people, and not just MPs, want the coherence between those two parts of Government .

It is fair to say that we still work together incredibly closely. Partly this reflects the creation of No. 10 North, where BIST, MHCLG and the Treasury are all together working on local growth in different ways. We are working really closely with MHCLG at the moment on the development of a new high street strategy. Please do not worry that because there is not a joint unit we are not spending time together. We absolutely work together.
Q51 W hen is that out, Amanda? When is that high street strategy out?
I believe later in the year.
Q52 Before Christmas, perhaps, in the winter.
I would hope so, she said carefully.

Q53 T his C ommittee has taken a real interest in the impact of the steel safeguards imposed earlier in the year. Yesterday, we spent some time with a number of people from the downstream steel industry. I spoke to a supplier and a processor of high-spec aerospace-grade metals from the east of England who were talking to me about the difficulties with c ategories 14 and 27 . T hey need approved supply because they service aerospace and defence. They are not able to source it within the safeguards without extortionate costs, so they are just about to move their work to an approved mill and machinists in India.

I spoke to people from a company from the south-west, again in aerospace and defence. They said to me that the annual four-year cost of the additional cost would be £600,000 in tariff payments, and that would send them under. They were also considering moving production ab r oad.

I spoke to people from a company based in my own constituency , who spoke to me about the difficulty that both aluminised and galvanised material were in the same category, c ategory 4, and that one was not replaceable for the other in their area of work, which was replacement exhausts for the automotive industry . T he quota was being taken up by one, leaving little space for the other. I spoke to fabricators , who spoke about the difficulty of not having an exemption for fabricated products, as they do in the similar regime in Canada.

Secretary of State, would you accept that , while the policy intent of the steel safeguards was sound, and something that we all support around this table, the execution of the design of the tariffs and the quotas has been poor ? They desperately need more detail and granularity , f or example using commodity codes within the categories, perhaps at the 10-digit level, rather than the level that exists at the moment, and we need that exemption for fabrication . G iven that, when will we be reviewing the safeguards ? W ill you commit to listen to the downstream industry and make some changes?
There is a lot there , and there is a letter coming to you setting out what was a really alarming set of evidence that we heard yesterday.

I am sensitive to that. Let me just put some information that I think is useful, and then I will come back specifically on your request at the end, Antonia. Thank you for recognising why we need to do this, because this is about more than steel. On that point of a resilient economy, people based in the UK have to know that, when we are facing structural overcapacity, we will defend the UK ’ s position. If we do not do that, why would you be based here for the long term, particularly when the European agenda is definitely tilting to a more trade defence-based posture?

If you take steel imports as a whole, three quarters or 75% of steel products in the UK by value , and over half by volume , fall outside the measures ’ scope. I know that people are concerned, but let us recognise that the majority of products are falling beyond the scope of the trade defence measures.

Obviously we do not want to put tariffs or trade defence measures on products that you cannot source from the UK. It is true to say, in how you implement a measure such as this, because of the nature of the identification of the eight-digit SIC codes, that there will be some products caught up in that because of the characterisation. I hear your call for more specificity in that. You have to balance that against what is enforceable and how customs operate s within there. T he policy intent is clearly not to increase the cost of products you cannot purchase in the UK. If, in some cases, more products that can be bought in the UK were bought in the UK, that would leave more space in the quotas for products to be imported that we do not produce, because of the nature of that.

In relation to your request for a review, we are committed to reviewing these measures. You cannot, to be frank, do that too quickly, because , when you are doing trade defence measures, people will obviously import . T hey will stockpile in advance of that, but that is just rational human behaviour. You have to see these measures working through.

W ill I commit to working with this C ommittee, with the evidence you have just given there and what you have heard from evidence sessions and the downstream users , to make sure that we have this in the best place it can be? Yes, I am more than happy to give that commitment. I would ask the C ommittee to recognise that there will be some cases, because of the way this is done, where we perhaps cannot get an absolute assurance that absolutely everything can be separated into domestic production and imports . I t is not quite as easy as doing it in that way, but we are, in terms of the intent of the policy, seeking that outcome.

Q54 T here were further tweaks made to this policy after it was published, as the D epartment was in receipt of new information . I absolutely take the point about the full review . We are just now seeing the implications of the safeguards after the stockpiling period and the run-through period has finished. Are you in a position to commit to making tweaks if new evidence comes forward at this point about what is and is not made in the UK and what is and is not available? I would suggest that, given that HMRC is able to differentiate, it ought to be possible for the quotas to differentiate in the more granular way that I have set out.

This was in my absence from the Department. You are right to say that, following feedback, I believe the quotas were increased in order to mitigate some of the adverse consequences that you are describing. There is pushback on the other side on that, in terms of what that means for domestic steel producers. You are always seeking a balance between these two crucial aspects of the industry. I believe that further changes would come after a review of how the trade measures are operating. Amanda, you would have been more familiar with this in my absence.

We are barely a quarter into the new regime, so just beginning to see data coming through. The Secretary of State has already said, absolutely correctly, that the commitment has always been there for a 12-month review. Absolutely, if there is evidence that comes forward or a change in circumstances more generally that means that we need to reconsider, the Department would want to have the opportunity to do that and to advise the Secretary of State accordingly.
We will take t hat . Thank you very much.

Q55 T he EU steel market is 125 million tonnes of production of steel a year. The UK steel market is 2.5 million, so it is 50 times smaller. Through this set of regulation, essentially we are condemning our downstream fabricators to have to buy from an incredibly small market. As you are very aware, in many cases there simply are no producers, or there is one producer, which in effect is now a monopoly, so it can sell to a UK producer or it can sell to the US. We hear d lots of instances yesterday where the steel producers were selling to US customers rather than UK customers. There is no legal obligation for them to sell to UK customers.

This looks like it is heading for hundreds and thousands of jobs being lost in the downstream sector because we are determined to stay outside of the EU steel single market. We are massively going to lose out across all our manufacturing heartlands, which is what your Prime Minister, and my Prime Minister, is looking to reindustrialise. We are heading in exactly the opposite direction. Is that fair?

No, I do not think that it is, but it is a fair question to ask what the impact will be. On our relationship to the EU, I am confident of a resolution to the UK-EU steel issue. We are not determined to stay out of that. It was one of the first topics of conversation I had with Commissioner Šefčovič because it is so important to us.

Without intervention from the Government in terms of ownership and trade defence measures, the UK would be the first major economy to not have a steel industry. That is what we were heading towards. There is absolutely no doubt about that. It was a decision for someone sitting in my chair to make. Was I willing to do that? The answer was no, to be clear.

The impact on downstream users is something that is acutely felt. As I say, in my absence, to be fair to the former Secretary of State, mitigations were put in place in terms of some of the quotas around that. We have to acknowledge that where you have, in the global economy, deliberate structural overcapacity in some sectors, of course there is a short-term dividend to that. You are getting something below market value. That is attractive if you are a purchaser of that product. I am afraid that, as parliamentarians, we need to extrapolate out what the logical conclusion of that is. It is dependence in the long term in a way that is not in our long-term strategic interest.

Q56 I am not arguing that . I am arguing that we are outside of a market that is 50 times bigger than our own—the European Union market—and that is why we are being stuffed, rather than, “Yes, let ’ s stay dependent on China . ”

If your desire is for closer co - operation with the European Union, I would share that. Europe has interesting lessons for us in terms of the level of EU production that meets EU demand, which is much greater , even in this world of global overcapacity in world markets in steel. It is doing some things that we could replicate as part of that . We are seeking to resolve the problems around steel that resulted in the EU ’ s trade defence measures causing us some significant problems.

Q57 We are negotiating now an SPS agreement for agriculture, which is essentially a single market for agricultural products. Would a good result be a single market for steel, à la SPS for agriculture?

In all these matters with the EU, you need to make a distinction between trade defence measures and what might be called single market alignment, which would be a different ask. It is helpful conceptually to keep those in different places.

At the UK-EU reset, so the summit that is coming up in November, there is a core set of things you will be familiar with there. SPS is one of them. ETS is one of them. Electricity co-operation is one of them. Then you have a whole range of additional issues that are not part of that but are reasonable . I t is worth the conversation at the same time because they are UK-EU issues. T hink of Made in Europe, steel and the rules of origin, which is an outstanding matter from the TCA. Because of the nature of that conversation, you touch into those things . I t is all part of the Go vernment ’ s desire to build a closer relationship with the EU, based not just on what we would see as being in our interest, but what i s in the EU interest as well.
Q58 T here is an ambition for deeper alignment on this .

I do not think that we are in a position where we w ould be able to announce a definitive solution by the summit, given the times that we are on . I want to tell you that this is a live and active part, as well as the wider summit agenda that you will be familiar with.

Q59 In the roundtable w e heard from various different downstream suppliers . One thing that they found quite disjoint ed was that the steel strategy that was released is all about supporting British Steel. W e are back to what I was asking you about earlier. T he Department for Education, in its procurement requirements, is asking for EAF steel because of the carbon targets that it is trying to meet. Y ou cannot do that because we cannot do it , s o we are going to be importing that steel from elsewhere to meet that target.

H ow is the steel strategy fitting into what the G overnment is then putting out as procurement? A re you aware of some of these mismatches? A re you going to review that and correct it so that we can get a steel strategy that supports our recently renationalised British Steel?

I will look at that. In Scunthorpe, we need a transition plan, which will likely be to electric arc furnaces. At Port Talbot we are in that process of industrial transformation. Those are perhaps the two high-profile examples of UK-based steel production ’ s transformation. We have other electric arc furnaces in the UK. It is important to stress , because we have this big need to transition the blast furnaces to low-carbon technology , w e should not forget that there are parts of the steel industry that have already made this journey. It is important to stress that.

I t might be that there are particular products the DfE is trying to procure that relate to that. As I am not familiar with its procurement requests, let me take that away and perhaps come back to you to give you a definitive answer on what the balance is between those things.

Q60 Alongside steel, automotive is a real sector of concern, a s is defence. We have been pressing the Government, along with two other Committees now, to set out their definition of sovereign capabilities. We do not think that you can have an economic security strategy unless you have specified the sovereign capabilities the country is trying to grow and defend.

It was really heartening to see th e fourth priority that you have set out today about secure and resilient trade. As the M O D begins to issue packages of procurement included in th e £285 billion of defence spending that it now has earmarked, do you think the Government are going to be able to move towards a better definition of the sovereign capabilities that we need to grow and defend for the future?

I can see why those Committees have that interest. I will ask Amanda because she will be familiar with work in my absence. Whether you could definitively do that without a degree of flexibility that might be required in some decisions is a genuinely interesting debate.

If we look at, say, Speciality Steel UK where we have had to get involved in issues of ownership, a function you will be familiar with that SSUK is the sovereign capability provider of is ammunition, so missile and ammunition casings. Is it the case that we could not buy that from a friendly country? No, that exists. Is it in our interest to potentially keep that capability in the UK? Yes. You perhaps need an index of where that lies. It would seem to me that the key thing would be a consistency across all Government Departments.

Q61 Our NATO allies such as Canada have set that out as the cornerstone of their rearmament strategy. There are short lists that have been issued by two or three different Government Departments . C ommittees are struggling with tessellat ing lists from different parts of Whitehall to say, “How do you send a coherent, consistent demand signal to UK plc that these are the things that we absolutely are going to grow and defend i n this country ?” so that we are not in a reactive policy frame when, for example, we have to suddenly come here on a Saturday to renationalise British S teel. W e are interested in whether your ambitions for resilience will take you to a place where we get a better definition of these capabilities for the years to come.

That is a genuinely interesting challenge to Government. There would be, knowing other Government Departments, genuinely different, good - faith views on what constituted sovereign capability. To take the example of British Steel, there had to be some pragmatism in that. We were facing a bill of £1.5 billion to make 7,000 people unemployed in a way that was completely beyond our control, in a way that was unacceptable to the UK. That was a key part of that decision.

When I look at critical minerals, our critical minerals strategy is a really good example of that need for resilience and sovereign capability. It does not say we can be self-sufficient. That is not realistic. It recognises that we can decrease our dependency on some other countries and set criteria for how exposed to other markets we should be. That is a very good example. I honestly cannot tell you whether other Government Departments think our approach on critical minerals is the right model to follow.

Q62 Jonathan Black , who you will know was the deputy national security adviser , recently left Government and wrote in the FT that, when he looks back over his time in G overnment, he now observes that there are a lack of cross-Whitehall mechanisms for creating integrated strategy. Is that a problem that you are pointing at here?

It would be churlish not to recognise that there is a fair challenge there that come s from someone with serious experience of the system. It goes to the heart of the integrated nature of dual-use technology, the modern economy and the changes to trade, which now involve much greater geopolitical threats . Y ou link it all together and there is, I suppose, at times a danger that , although things have been dealt with for years in a certain way, that is just not the right approach to do it.
