The NSC brings together core economic and security functions of the state. I would not want people to think that there are things in how the UK operates that do not take that into account and do not balance off the different factors , in terms of trade-offs between investment and security and how you make that coherent together. Could it be better , giving an example of this? T hat is a fair challenge, definitely.

One area we have been grappling with on this inside the D epartment, but I think it very much aligns with how you are describing it, Secretary of State, is on frontier and emerging technologies and what we think are the areas where sovereign capability will be really important. How we have thought about this, in partnership with colleagues from other Departments —this is not BIST alone—has been around dual-use technologies that provide the opportunity to drive growth but also strengthen our security and resilience. In the context of the choices that we have made around quantum, semiconductors, engineering biology and other frontier tech that we are investing in as a country through BIST, those are some of the considerations that we have been reflecting on.
Having a manufacturing industry is pretty core to that , and automotive is core to manufacturing.

Q63 Has the EU asked you to put tariffs on Chinese EVs as a condition of UK participation in the Made in Europe schemes? Given the market distortion of Chinese state subsidy of EVs, should we not just do it anyway?

The stories that have been in the press relate to an agreement between France and Germany rather than a negotiation with the UK, although it is of direct relevance to us. At the minute I can tell you, Committee, that the UK ’ s position has not changed, which is that we keep this under close review. Some people hear that and say, “Close review means we might be about to change it , ” or they hear close review and think we are not going to change it.

My point on this is that, if you take the UK automotive industry, 60% of what we make goes to the EU, 20% goes to the rest of the world and 20% stays domestic. In other words, we are an export-led industry where the single most important country by market share is our own. You factor those two things together. That means that different parts of our sector will have different views on this. You will know that, under our post-Brexit Trade Remedies Authority system, businesses can go themselves directly to the TRA. No automotive producer has done that.

That is the position. We keep it under close review. When I talk about “under close review”, the changes in the market are what we are looking at. I look at the significant increase in imports into the UK of Chinese EVs in the last 12 months, and that is part of it. I am balancing our own interests in terms of being an outward-facing economy with our own domestic market. As soon as there is or is not news in this area, I will, of course, share it with the Committee.

Referencing a quote I gave to Th e Guardian fairly recently, I want to make it clear that I want to work with European partners because we are facing the same pressures. If we make a decision on any element of trade defence, it is because I deem that to be in the interests of the UK. What other countries do impacts on that because of trade diversion. If one country puts up significant trade defence measures, you can expect some of those products to come in a disproportionate sense to your markets. What goes on in other countries is important, but I hold to, “We make a decision based on the best interests of the UK . ” That involves working with other partners, but that is the basis upon which any decision is made.

Q64 Help us decode this. Lord Sarwar went on the record to say that Britain and the European Union must “ work together and act in lockstep ” to tackle Chinese dominance in the automotive sector. Chancellor Merz and President Macron have issued an incredibly ambitious set of proposals for trade defence.

We are trying to understand whether the UK G overnment are going to act in lockstep with the Macron-Merz initiative . If they do not, how on earth do we think we are going to draw closer to the European Union when DG T RADE is really clear with us that it is not going to allow any kind of backdoor for over - subsidised Chinese goods to come into the European Union through Britain?

On that point, let us be clear that goods could not come into the single market through Britain. We do not have a significant Chinese OEM in the UK at this stage. If you were assembling Chinese components on a model similar, let us say, to how Nissan began in the north-east of England, you would not qualify under the TCA, under the rules of origin, for that. This is about market share in the UK rather than products coming from the rest of the world into the UK and then into the single market. Trade is a fairly complex area. I look at some things in the press and I do not think they have quite thought through how trade works and how trade agreements interact with each other.
Q65 To be clear, your argument is that the TCA is effect ively a locked door against over-subsidised Chinese goods coming into the EU from Britain.

It is not true to say that Chinese products come into the UK to enter the single market. That is not how the interaction of these trade relationships works. Of course we both face a similar problem, which is the tremendous increase in Chinese automotive exports. We are actor agnostic in terms of trade policy, but China is the country that has an industrial policy that is more significant than any other, has a size and scale , and as I am always keen to say to colleagues, involves a great deal of innovation. This is not just about cost. There is a lot of R&D and innovation going on in China as part of that. We would want to work with colleagues around that.

In terms of some of the press stories about the Franco-German agreement, that is all about the detail. That has not been perhaps surfaced to the degree to which we would be able to definitively say that that is what the ask is of the UK. Yes, Anas is right to say that we have to work with like - minded countries on a similar set of problems, but I am also pointing out that perhaps the interests of the EU as a whole for its automotive sector might at times be slightly different from how we see it in the UK. That is just a fact of where our industry is orientated and where it is.
Q66 Will shared trade defence against Chinese over-subsidisation be one of the issues explored in the summit on 20 November?
I am certainly willing to talk, and have been talking, to European colleagues about a shared set of problems and how we resolve those.
Q67 Staying on the topic of automotive, are we likely to have good news on the ZEV mandate flexibilities coming soon?

We certainly had good automotive news in the last month, including £850 million of investment from Bentley and McLaren. It was a delight to go and inspect the McLaren cars and have a drive around the track in one of them. We have also seen some indicative news from Nissan that is predicated on the ZEV mandate. Y ou will know that the Department for Transport owns the ZEV mandate. We have shown before, as a G overnment , a willingness to be pragmatic based on what other countries have done and where the consumer is. Y ou will have to wait for the formal response to that consultation, which I believe is before Christmas.
The consultation is due to close this week. Once the consultation is closed, the Department for Transport will go through the normal processes and then respond.
Q68 We have a cliff edge coming on EV batteries at the end of the year. Are we confident that everybody is on top of that problem and they are going to solve it by 1 January ?

There is an awful lot of engagement going on between the UK, our Ministers and indeed commissioners, but also across the sector, with European and UK auto manufacturers, and indeed with EU member states. There is lots of activity pushing towards a conclusion.

It is important you mentioned rules of origin because it is sometimes assumed to be part of the wider Made in Europe trade defence conversation. It is a distinct issue, as you know, left over from the TCA. What are we seeking to do? We are seeking to recognise that it is in the interests of both member states of the EU and the UK to continue the very efficient supply chains that are geographic Europe ‑ wide. That is the nature of that industry. I do not think it is in our or their interest to add further trade frictions to that, especially when the big challenge is competition from the rest of the world.
I want to move on to artificial intelligence and a couple of questions on trade. B efore we get there, I want to close off some questions on employment rights .

Q69 On guaranteed hours, we heard from USDAW in June its evidence to the Committee stating that the low - hours threshold should be set at 48 hours and that any lower threshold than that would make workers worse off than they are now. The consultation says that the Government’s preference is for eight to 20 hours as the threshold. This preference was set out by the previous Secretary of State. Do you have a similar take on what the threshold should be and do you refute USDAW’s evidence?

If you have a consultation, you have to be willing to listen to the consultation responses. That is the premise of a consultation. What are we trying to do here? We are trying to put in place a framework that gives a person who is currently on a zero-hours contract, and who is working a consistent and regular number of hours each week, the option, if they choose to exercise that right, to a contract that reflects those hours.

The key piece of evidence that we are looking for is, “Is there a point in the economy where people are routinely working more hours than they are contracted for?” That has to be the guiding principle. I would say that 48 is very high. Most people working on a full-time contract are probably working full-time hours in the main.

I know USDAW very well. I am a member of USDAW myself, I should say. Like I do with all submissions to consultations, I will look very closely at the case that it is making. Again, I have no hesitation in saying that we have always sought to implement this significant package of measures in a way that works not just with unions but with business as well.

Most businesses would have a different view when you talk to them about the low-hours threshold, but the objective is clear. It is about finding the right level at which to set the low-hours threshold that will give the maximum effective implementation of the policy.
Q70 You do not think there will be distortionary impacts. If it were set at 20 hours, would there be a bump of people whose contracts suddenly turn out to be set just above that?

This is the case that, if you do not cover every single worker, there will be some people who are disproportionately getting additional hours as part of that. Nobody originally envisaged the low-hours threshold to be as high as that, but we are talking about a consultation. It is a serious consultation. We will listen to the case being made. I have had that conversation several times; I will look at the point being made. As I say, I doubt many people who are not already on full-time contracts are routinely working more hours than a full-time contract has, but we shall see.

Q71 I will move on to employment status. Many of us were very glad to see the long-awaited employment status consultation. Many of us hoped that it might go a little further. Might we see action on employment status in this Parliament?
I am sure you listened to my well-received speech at the Labour party conference, Antonia, where I referenced this directly.
I did.

This is a complex area. The space that needs the most attention is the line between what is currently classified as a limb (b) worker and self-employed. That is the space where—it is not just delivery, but all kinds of things, for instance hairdressing—you are seeing a lot of distortion in the labour market.

I have a very clear idea of how to fix that, in terms of substitution clauses, how they are used in contracts, what the assumptions should be at employment tribunal and where the burden of proof should lie to change that. That is a priority for me.

This is a question that I get quite a lot, so I have to make this clear. What I am talking about here are the areas within my control on employment rights, so access to the minimum wage, holiday pay and all those things. This is different from the tax question. That is quite complicated. The public do not always understand that there are three employment statuses in the UK, effectively, in terms of your employment rights, but there are two in terms of tax.

I will need to legislate for those changes. It is subject to a third Session Bill. Again, this is an area where, frankly, it is not just in the interests of the 1 million or so workers who would be in that space. Businesses themselves ask for a level playing field, quite rightly, in some of these sectors. They are asking for that clarity in the law to be put in place.

Q72 There is one final question from me on employment rights. This Committee is very much looking forward to visiting Amazon’s Coventry warehouse in the coming weeks. As new access powers come into force, companies like Amazon are prepared to spend millions on union-busting activity, including using AI to surveil their own employees. Do you have confidence that the penalty level set out for breach of access rights is set at a level that is enough to deter any company from bad behaviour?

The safeguards to access are an important part of the package. Nobody has anything to fear from those. Some of the most productive and successful parts of the British economy are areas with significant union density. We could look at automotive or aerospace, for instance, as good examples of that. The regime that has been put in place is effective and will be proportionate to what is required. This is a significant part of the plan to make work pay.
I am going to move us on to artificial intelligence, which is now a major new part of your Department’s responsibility.

Q73 O n 12 October, the AI Minister set out the Government’s plans for managing the risks of AI. A lot remains unclear. This is a fast-paced and moveable feast. One of the things that I am keenly aware of is that it has been well over a year since the Government’s SME digital adoption taskforce published its final report. This really matters to constituencies like mine in Weston-super-Mare. We do not have the infrastructure of cities and we rely on volunteers and support services. When AI is used by lots of people in the sectors that dominate our economy, whether that is in retail, health or social care, it is often shallow adoption. Micro-businesses do not have the time to do that.
When are businesses in Weston-super-Mare and across the country going to start seeing the benefits of this taskforce and get a sense of the tangible progress that has been made?

First of all, let me pay tribute to the AI Minister, whose work you referenced there. This is one of the most challenging subject areas in any developed economy. He is doing an absolutely terrific job both on engagement with the public and parliamentarians and on the policy agenda.

Some of the most exciting examples of the adoption of AI have come to me from small businesses telling me about them. I appreciate that we would not say we are at a point where the adoption of these capabilities is as widespread as we want it to be. The SME digital adoption taskforce is a key part of that. The objective is to deliver this by 2035. An update was published earlier in the year. I would be more than happy to write to the Committee and tell you exactly where that is at.

This goes to the heart of the balance that we are seeking to strike, Chair. When people see or hear alarming things about AI on television or in the media, they want to know that we are doing the right things to keep them safe. I think that we are. At the same time, we have to be open to a transformative technology. In some of the recent GDP figures, we are starting to see—it is not definitive—that the sectors that are doing best are the ones that are perhaps most exposed to AI adoption. We have to seek to use this to the benefit of the UK.

It goes across a whole range of things, frankly. If you think about the pressures on small business owners, whether that is on time, the people they employ or the capacities they have, there are functions using AI that can add a whole range of things to make people’s lives easier. That has to be something that we are excited by.

Q74 One of the things that I noticed was that four of the 10 recommendations were not implemented, and some of those seem really important. One of the top lines was appointing a Minister to be accountable for SME digital and AI adoption. We have the fantastic Kanishka Narayan, but having that in the portfolio is really important.

We also do not have a replacement for the European Digital Economy and Society Index in terms of that fast-paced data that we need to be able to monitor SME AI adoption. It is really important. Could we get a reflection back, at some point, from the Department on that as a tool? To my point earlier, we only act on what we measure, and we are not measuring SME adoption at that local level. That is really important.
That is very constructive and very helpful.

Q75 We heard evidence only last week about frontier AI and where that could be going. We have heard concerned warnings. We recently did a trip to India. Through their lens, AI was very much mission-driven. It was very clear where they wanted it to be deployed across Government and the economy. That helps us to identify what types of AI we would like to see and which we can put in the category of, “We are not so sure about this”.

Some of the panellists who were in front of us last week profiteer from flooding social media feeds with far-right hate and all kinds of things. They are the same people who would quite like us not to regulate AI. I just wondered whether you have thoughts about this and whether you are pushing on how to put in amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill to deal with some of this, so that we do not have these huge multinationals running away with AI while we are left to pick up the pieces.

There is a lot to that. First of all, we cannot envisage every single use of AI that we will see in our lifetimes. Technology is moving so fast. The applications are so vast. It is an incredibly significant general purpose technology. We have to acknowledge that we are already seeing some terrific things. Cancer is being diagnosed more quickly because of AI. We have talked about small business adoption as part of that.

There is a tension here, Sarah. First of all, there is the question of regulation. Historically, it would be true to say that the UK’s strength is in regulating the application and use of a technology in the sectors that it is in—that is a strength—rather than attempting to do a general purpose regulatory effort on things that we might not fully understand the implications of. You are talking about the C yber S ecurity Bill. That is a great example. We will strengthen that Bill in the legislative process to protect critical national infrastructure. First of all, that is what good regulation looks like. Where is technology being used? How will we ensure that people are safe as part of that?

The wider question on the regulation of AI has to recognise that the frontier models are being created by US firms. To an extent, China has open-weight models that lag slightly behind, but we can see where that will go over time. It is no use to anyone to have a regulatory system with no cards to play in terms of market participants. It would be very easy to get to that point. Keeping people safe at the minute is about retaining access to those frontier models, not just for the AI Security Institute but for our security services. When a capability is created, we have to know what it will mean for the UK. We have to have access to it to keep the UK safe. In Parliament, we have to reflect that there are some tensions there, but that is what we need to do.

We should have some confidence in what has already been set up, such as the AI Security Institute, and the capabilities of our security services. Where we need to strengthen the law in areas to keep critical parts of the UK safe, that is what successful regulation looks like.

Q76 We have an opportunity with the Bill that is coming back to us. As you have already stated in this session, “if parliamentary time allows” is the classic phrase. Where are those other opportunities? Yes, we need to regulate for its application, but I do not know whether we have always been clear about quite what we would like that application to be. We should try to be ahead of this and not be led by very wealthy global corporates.

You have to use—I can tell you this, as Chief Whip—the parliamentary opportunities that you have. The C yber S ecurity Bill is a good example of a piece of legislation already under way that we can add those amendments to. There will be more in this space. The third Session has not been decided yet.

This Committee—I really mean this, Chair—could give us a really interesting perspective. In a parliamentary system like ours, we all support and believe in the checks and balances and routes that we take on legislation, but how can we make sure that we keep up to date with the technology? We talk a lot about—I have had this as Chief Whip—Henry VIII powers, but we may need some areas where we give ourselves, with appropriate safeguards, the ability to regulate.

Q77 I am conscious that over the course of the 19th century there was not one Factory Act; there were 20 Factory Acts as technology and its perils began to change. Some of those Acts were pretty hard fought and quite time-consuming in coming. The AI Minister has said that you will look at amending the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill. That is at Report stage in the Lords. Either you are going to accept some Back-Bench amendments in the Lords or lay Government amendments of your own. The only latitude that the Commons then has is to amend the amendments. Is that basically what the AI Minister means when he says that parliamentarians will be engaged in getting reform done this year?
To your point on the many Factory Acts, we had the factories here. It is different.
We have AI here too.

We do, but it is not quite the same. We led on industry. We could lead on regulation. This is not quite the same picture. We are affected by industry, but the frontier models are US-based. We have to recognise that that is what makes this a much more significant political, regulatory and policy challenge.

I will defer to Amanda if she knows better, but I believe that is what Kanishka is intending in terms of the amendments. I know it is at Report stage in the Lords, but you have to take the parliamentary opportunities that you have. This is not an opportunity to pass up.

Q78 You accept that the only chance that the Commons has to table amendments is, in effect, by amending Government amendments or Lords Back-Bench amendments. That is the legislative opportunity for the Commons this quarter.
I accept that it is more limited, but I still think it is the right vehicle to take.
Q79 Are the Government going to introduce mandatory AI incident reporting?

I would defer to Kanishka’s speech on this. I would not want to prejudge his work. I do not have it in front of me, Chair, but the premise of the amendments that the Government will table are the things that he identified in his speech.
Q80 Is it going to include legislation to clarify liability for harm by AI agents?
I would have to write you on that. I will clarify that for you.
Q81 What about laws to embed, through statute, evaluators in AI companies?

The core of the proposals that we are seeking to look at both domestically and internationally, in terms of the Prime Minister’s stated intentions for our presidency of the G20, are around the standards and safeguards in the testing space, which is where we saw the Hugging Face incident.
Q82 That could include at least the embedding of independent evaluators.

The test would be, “What retains access to frontier models?” There is no point having a regulatory regime that results in us losing access to the things that we need access to in order to keep the UK safe.
Q83 That sounds like it is still moot. Peter Kyle decided not to put the AI Security Institute on a statutory footing. Has that policy position now changed?
I do not believe it has, but I am not sure what the argument would be for changing something that is working very well.
Q84 Is there an argument to introduce laws that could seek a mandatory slowdown in the capabilities of frontier models?
We are not in a position to be able to do that unilaterally domestically.

Q85 The Cyber Bill has been years in the making and these feel like rather last-minute amendments. While we have been sitting here, we have seen that the AI Minister has tabled some amendments and DCMS is looking to table amendments to this based on external factors and external events that have caused real concern and worry not just to the UK but to the global community.

How can we make sure that we are keeping cyber - secure and cyber-aware when we cannot even get the Bill through without feeling like we have to keep adding extra bits on to it? What is going to happen when we pass the Bill? Are we going to have to open up something else?

I would push back quite strongly on that, Dan, because I would not call them last-minute amendments. I would reference the fact that the technology is moving so fast that nimbleness is required in Government to use the vehicles in our parliamentary system to do the things that we need to do. As we look at the challenges today, they are different even from the ones six or nine months ago. The challenge for all of us, as parliamentarians, is how we give ourselves the tools that we need at the pace that we need, given the pace of technological change.

Q86 That is all fine and we can capture that in this Bill, but what happens when we pass it? I was working on informing this Bill when I was at the British Computer Society before I came into this place, and for years in actuality. Once you pass the Bill and it becomes an Act, we lose the opportunity to add anything else to it. When external factors come in and hit us, what is our vehicle?

If we need further legislative changes, we have the legislative process. This goes to the heart of the conversation that we were having. What might we need to consider in future? What do we believe are the appropriate powers for Government and Parliament to move at pace as challenges change? To be frank, this is one of the underweighted elements of the debate. Based on how quickly technology is changing, it would be reasonable to expect the situation to change over the traditional timeframe of the passage of an Act of Parliament.

Again, much of this is not about domestic activity alone; it is about international co-operation. You have to recognise that that is a key part of it. We should have some confidence in the institutions that we put in place, like the AI Security Institute, and ensure that they retain access. I go back to the original challenge. It is a misconception to think that domestic activity alone is the answer to this.
Q87 We may need enabling safety and security legislation for AI that allows Ministers to implement safety laws at the speed with which the technology is changing.

If we look at our aspirations for some of the regulatory powers or some of the sandboxing powers that we want in order to develop great British businesses in the UK, there is a difficult question as to what is the right balance in the powers that we give to Government. This is the so-called Henry VIII argument, where you use secondary legislation to change measures in primary legislation on the statute book. It is something that, as parliamentarians, none of us likes. We are very sensitive when we put those into things. We might just need an honest conversation in Parliament about how we do that going forward.

I am not in any way suggesting that we move away from the correct and traditional approach, which is to have an Act of Parliament that seeks to do something specific, then have a Second Reading on the principles and go through the detailed stages. There will be proposals, as any Government would have, for the third Session of this Parliament, but we have to talk about this question of technological change versus the legislative process.

That is certainly something that we were considering when it came to the EU, for example. This was going to be the proposal that the EU reform Bill was going to take. Mr Maynard, I am keen to move on to trade and the EU.

Q88 I will stick with this for a moment, if it is okay. Government and Parliament’s job is to keep our citizens safe. You note that US and China is where a lot of the development is happening. What is already happening with all these breakouts is impacting citizens. At the speed of action with which this is happening, it could increase a hundredfold very quickly indeed.

I am nervous about this “no cards to play” realistic perspective. It sounds very defeatist. The UK is a G7 nation. We have to play our role here domestically and internationally as a convening force. I am not at all suggesting it is easy, but we have to find ways to stand up to these very large hyperscalers and to have control over this rather than ceding control entirely to them. You do not seem to see it that way.

No, I would push back strongly on that, Charlie. It is not that we have no cards to play. We have some cards to play. Some countries do not have cards to play. We are the third most significant tech nation in the world. Every other country would want to be us other than the people who are one and two. We have some cards to play.

It is about being clear-eyed. We are keeping the British public safe. I do sometimes hear, not necessarily from parliamentarians but in the wider political argument, proposals that I can see might gain some populist support, but they would not keep the British public safe because they would effectively result in us losing the access that we currently have, which is the fundamental thing that we need to retain right now.

Q89 If I may, Chair, let us say AISI says, “That model is unsatisfactory. We do not think you should release it, Anthropic , ” for example, but Anthropic goes ahead and does it. What are we going to do about it? Is the answer that we cannot do anything about it and we have to live with that or do we have a plan?

If I may, with all due respect, that perspective is where we are having problems with public opinion and discussing this as parliamentarians. You cannot take a model and somehow say, “That is entirely safe and could never be used for nefarious ends . ” It does not work like that. It is knowing its capabilities and preparing the British state—it could be our public services, security services or businesses—to make sure that we are aware of and prepared for that. There is this sense that things come to the AI Security Institute and it says, “That’s a green light. That’s not . ” I am afraid it will never be as straightforward as that.

Q90 Models have been taken down by the companies themselves. That is already happening. Some of the hyperscalers have said, “We are not going to release this model . ” Decisions are already being taken on existing models to say, “That is too dangerous to come out . ” Let us say that we have a difference of opinion with the hyperscaler. That is already happening.
Therefore, the key thing is making sure that we have, using British expertise, access to those models, knowledge and a feedback loop—
Q91 I get that. What happens if they do it anyway?

Given the relationship that we have and the role that we play, it would never be as binary as that, to be clear. What we cannot do—this is a challenge to all parliamentarians—is implement measures that effectively lose the things that are fundamental to keeping the UK safe.
I am keen to move us on to the EU and trade in our final 10 minutes.

Q92 Mr Joshua Reynolds: On 12 October, the Prime Minister said, when it comes to our deal with the European Union, “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough . ” He said last month that we could look at what George Osborne has said about the customs union; that the Government could look at what we as Liberal Democrats said at our conference about the single market; or that the Government could “go all the way”, which I can only assume means rejoining the European Union. Where are the Government on the European Union?

You have just outlined what the Prime Minister has said and how he is going to give a speech about this. If we are producing a 10-year plan, given what we have just talked about in this session, it is impossible not to have some reference to the European Union, because what the European Union does, as we have talked about, whether it is steel tariffs or Made in Europe, has significant consequences for us. He wants to have that conversation. He wants to acknowledge that.

For my part, perhaps the more productive part of the conversation is not about some of the models that you have outlined, with no disrespect to Lib Dem policy, but about the shared challenges. We have a US that is adopting a very different and more assertive trade policy than at any point since the war. We have multilateral institutions such as the WTO that are in a very weakened state because of the geopolitical pressures and tensions that go into that. We have global overcapacity in steel, as we have discussed. We have challenges around climate. The better question is, “How can we work with and have influence over the European continent in meeting these challenges?”

Q93 Mr Joshua Reynolds: You say we need to have the conversation. When it comes to the European Union, I am not necessarily sure that there is anything that has not been said in the last decade. All of the thinking that can be thought has been done on this. Everyone has a different opinion. What is the Government’s opinion?

Again, I would have to disagree respectfully on that because what we do not know is the future direction of Europe. There are some very strong political currents in Europe. There is an evolving policy agenda that reacts to, for instance, the trade shock from China. We do not quite know where that will go, but we know it will affect us. One of the things that I very much admire about the Prime Minister is that you cannot say he dodges the big issues. He confronts them head on. That is his style. He is right to do so. We have to have this conversation. Again, I would steer you towards how we address these shared challenges.

With reference to the earlier conversation with Charlie, do not discount what we are working on for the UK-EU summit and its significance for us and the EU. On SPS, we do not have a policy akin to North America, Canada and the US. Our SPS policy is broadly aligned to the EU. Removing some of those trading frictions would be a massive deal for small business, farmers and fishermen. Let us recognise that we already have a significant degree of ambition. What the Prime Minister has done is talk perhaps in warmer and more good faith terms about what he is seeking from the European Union, and we will see whether the EU responds to that.

Q94 Mr Joshua Reynolds: We know what different options could look like. We have TCA, TCA plus customs union, Swiss deal and EEA region. We know what many of those different options are. They have been modelled. We know what we would have to give and what we would have to take as a result. Is there a sense within your Department or a sense from the Prime Minister of what you want to achieve and which of those options or models best aligns with the work that you are doing?
We want a closer economic relationship with the European Union.
Q95 Mr Joshua Reynolds: Does that look like the Swiss model or the EEA model?

The Prime Minister will set out those options. I am not going to pre-empt a Prime Minister’s speech, but we have shown that we have a nexus of interests that are intertwined come what may. The Prime Minister wants to start the conversation on how we work together to resolve some of those.
Q96 The Prime Minister said that we may look to “go all the way” to rejoin, but for now the red lines exist of no single market, no customs union and no rejoin. Is that an accurate statement?

We have a manifesto commitment on those. Those were his words, which you are repeating to me, on the Floor of the Commons, but he has made it very clear that, when he is looking to this 10-year plan, he wants to recognise that what the EU does will have consequences for us, and he wants to take out uncertainty by talking about what the long-term stable relationship with the EU might be. He wants to set out the options on that. That is what he is going to do as part of that. At the same time, we are working every day on our trade relationship with the EU and with the rest of the world. The UK-EU summit is a big part of that coming up.
Q97 For now, those three red lines are bright red and standing sharp.

I am not going to pre-empt the Prime Minister’s speech. You are going to have to wait a few weeks until the UK-EU summit. In terms of what we are negotiating right now, it is consistent with those red lines, yes.
Q98 We have a couple of moments when this will get clearer. One is the Prime Minister’s speech around 20 November and then there is the 10-year plan as well.
I would look to the speech that he is seeking to give imminently in or around the summit.
Q99 Notwithstanding that, are there still plans afoot to open negotiations to join together with Mercosur?

The obvious trade priority after the success that we have had with India, the Gulf, South Korea and Switzerland would probably be Mercosur because of the EU deal. You would not want, for instance, trade disadvantage, particularly on things such as whisky exports, as part of that. I do not have imminent news to share in relation to that. There are some other specific challenges between us, including some of the recent statements from Argentina. As ever, we are still seeking to expand the range of our trade agreements.
Q100 As a full member of CPTPP, is there action that we can take to try to accelerate the EU-CPTPP alliance?

This is really the potential super trade deal. There are already formal dialogues in place between the EU and CPTPP members. Given our role, our geography and our membership of the CPTPP, we have a role to play. It is not a direct leadership role, but we are an important bridge between those two agreements.

Q101 The final thing that we just wanted to put to you, before we close, is around the Post Office Horizon victims. This is something we remain acutely concerned about. We have a total of 1,800 claims that have still not been settled. About 447 of those claims are not recognised as fully formed claims lodged with the Department.

In January this year, the ambition was expressed to us that these claims would all be settled by the summer. There are still 1,800 outstanding. As you have come back into the Department, what are the instructions that you have given to your officials as to the deadline by which you want to see justice finally delivered?

As you will know from our previous conversations about this, Chair, I have always made this a priority both as shadow Secretary of State , supporting the significant legislative changes that the Conservative Government did at the end in terms of getting justice for people , and , when we came in, by launching the appeal scheme and getting money out the door. We have paid out £1.7 billion and 87% of all applicants have been paid. Like you, I look very closely at the figures. I believe I have them in my pack.

This has been a story. Nothing will ever compensate for the level of injustice that people have suffered. I want to say that unequivocally. From where we were pre-election to where we are now in terms of getting money out the door, we should recognise that a great deal has happened.

I have looked at some of the figures for the different schemes. When I ask for information on this from the Department, where there are outstanding applications, they come from very specific circumstances where applicants themselves need more time to get that application in because of the incredibly difficult burden that they have experienced as part of this. There are a few issues where it is about people being able to evidence what they believe their loss is. If there is any specific case where this Committee or any parliamentarian for a constituent thinks that somehow these schemes, which are multifaceted and have considerable coverage, are not judging a case on its merits or giving people what they feel they need, we will take a look at that.

A lot of money has gone out the door. Frankly, I would not want to put a timescale on the end of that because, in a way, I fear that could lead to a greater injustice where people do miss out on the compensation schemes. A great deal of progress has been made.

Q102 We welcome that answer, but, none the less, when we look at the HSSA scheme, for example, 573 claims have been received, 100 offers have been made and 26 total claims have been settled. Only 5% of the claims that have been filed have actually been settled. We cannot justify a situation where 1,800 claims are still to be settled, notwithstanding the progress that has been made. It is a significant achievement to have paid out £1.7 billion over the last couple of years, but we will not leave this issue until every single one of these claims is paid.

I would not want you to leave it and nor would I leave it. We set up HSSA because of people’s experience of the pre - existing scheme and the sense that it had not met everybody’s needs. I recognise that HSSA is the one that perhaps has the biggest discrepancy between claims and offers made, but, looking down the group litigation order, there are a handful of claims still to settle. The same is true of the Horizon convictions redress scheme.

I promise you, Chair, that I will keep all these schemes under close review in order to do that. Where cases have yet to be settled, there tend to be some very specific circumstances. It is the applicant who we are thinking of. It is the claimant who we are thinking of. I know there have been conversations about deadlines or when certain schemes should be closed. I have always said that I fear that that would operate in a way that does not give people the redress that they need.
Q103 The observation that we have often made is that supplying legal advice up front could expedite a number of these issues and alleviate a lot of the grief that applicants have gone through.

I have shown a personal willingness to adjust schemes, introduce new schemes and add awards that allow people to get redress in an expedited way, if that is what they want, or go through a longer process, if they want a more significant detailed assessment of their loss. We will always consider that and we will always try to make this work as best it can, recognising that we will never be able to answer fully the incredibly horrendous experience that many people have had as a victim of this injustice.

That is an issue to which we will return. Thank you very much indeed to both of you for the evidence that you have supplied this afternoon. It has been a wide-ranging discussion. I wish you very good luck in your new role.
Thank you.
We look forward to working closely with your Department and offering you and your colleagues the best of our advice on achieving your goals.
