Witness es : Michael Shanks MP and Dan Micklethwaite.

Q207 Welcome to this morning ’ s session of the Energy Security and Net Zero C ommittee. We are talking about energy resilience, a very topical discussion given today ’ s announcement. Welcome to Minister Michael Shanks and to Dan Micklethwaite from the Department.

Minister, you have a big announcement today . I know you have a statement to give in the House later, but we will undoubtedly be pursuing it here because of the topic being absolutely relevant to what you ha ve announced. Can you tell us to start with how today ’ s announcement to approve Jackdaw will contribute to the UK ’ s energy resilience?

G ood morning, Chair. It i s good to be with you again on a really important topic. What we a re announcing today is that the Energy Secretary has given her agreement and the NSTA has given its consent to the Jackdaw project to proceed.

It is a gas project in the North s ea, which is an already licensed field, and M embers will recall it was consented previously by the previous G overnment . T hat ended up in the courts, and we have been responding to that since and have come to the decision today. It is important for a number of reasons. F irst, it does strengthen our energy security. It i s important for me to say we have a diverse range of supplies of gas at the moment from the continental shelf on our own side , from Norway and from other imports, but undoubtedly a project like this helps strengthen that energy security . Of course because the court allowed the project to continue its development while awaiting consent, it will be able to bring that gas on to the system in the UK this winter, which is important.
We estimate that it will make up 6% of our gas at its peak. So it i s important from that point of view, but we ha ve also —
Q208 Can I just interrupt you there ? I t will , at peak , be 6% of the entire gas demand for the UK . H ave we got that right?
Yes, so 5% of domestic production, and around 6% at its peak over the lifespan of 11 years . That is what we estimate from the project.
Q209 Six per cent of production, not of demand ?

It i s expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6%, which is what I said in my initial answer, but you a re right to clarify it. At its peak it will be 5% of domestic gas production. It is estimated to have a lifespan of around 11 years.
Q210 H ow much of our demand will that comprise?
Do you mean of this particular project ?
Q211 How much of UK gas use will be produced — will be contributed to — by Jackdaw at peak?

I do not have the number that way round , but our domestic production at the moment i s 42% of overall. Overall , 42% of our gas supply comes from UK continental shelves , so it will contribute to that. I don ’ t have the figure — the reverse — for Jack daw .
Q212 So will t he 6% figure increase that from 42% , or will it maintain it at around the 42% level?
Well, it wi ll increase production.
It wi ll increase that.
Yes.
Q213 So production will go from 42% to 48% — is that a reasonable assumption to make?

No, because clearly the fields are changing at all times, so we will see fields that will reduce . O f course , the exact numbers change all the time, so the live numbers change depending on what i s extracted at any given moment.
Thank you for engaging with the figures .
W e are doing the numbers early on.
Yes, y ou might find some of those questions reappear during the day, I dare say.
C an you tell us how the e nergy w ealth f und will operate? In the press release, there i s a reference to it contributing to the energy transition, for example.

P artly that is about recognising that we a re really clear that the long-term future of this country does not lie in oil and gas . A lthough gas remains important in the short term, we have to start building much more quickly the infrastructure that gets us away from fossil fuels. That is absolutely central to our long-term resilience as a country.

W hat we ha ve announced today is that we wi ll set up an energy wealth fund, which is about funding the transition. It will be capitalised initially with £2 billion up front and will be added to with revenues from the Jackdaw field as those come in. However, it is about funding the infrastructure that we need to get us off fossil fuels.

What we ha ve already been doing as a G overnment to date is bringing in private investment alongside public investment through the National Wealth Fund and Great British Energy . T his is about increasing that and making sure that we are in a position where, although we need gas in the short term, we a re building our way out of that need for gas in the long term.

Q214 O ne of the concerns raised with us , and I know with you , has been around the impact on communities and on workers — over a lot of years , in fact. Is part of the role of this fund to invest in those communities most affected ? H ow will that operate?

W e do two things on that. We have always said the transition has to bring the communities with us. The workers who are powering the country right now in the North s ea , and who have done for 60 years , do an incredibly important job , but they are also the workers who will help us build the projects of the future . It is in our own interest to make sure the transition puts them right at the heart of it. We a re doing that through the North s ea f uture p lan .

I think I ha ve spoken to this C ommittee before about the North s ea job s service , which will be in place early next year to support workers into new careers, but this is also a really important part of that. The more we invest in the infrastructure here in Britain, the more we can keep the jobs and crucially the supply chain, which is where most of the jobs in oil and gas are. We can keep those in the UK, keep workers employed and keep investment in communities, but also build the infrastructure we need for the future.
Q215 Thank you. Before I move over to Melanie Onn , how will this announcement improve the national security elements of our energy supply and energy security?

I want to say first of all that clearly domestic production from the UK continental shelf is important in an uncertain world. If we can get it from the North s ea, that does provide benefits to us. However, I also want to be really clear that in the long-term picture, it is relatively marginal overall . We will not stop being a net importer of fossil fuels because of this decision.

This is the argument I ha ve made previously. Our long-term trend for more than two decades now has been to import more. That i s not going to change. Our long-term answer to that security and resilience point is to break away from fossil fuels so that we have energy sovereignty here in the UK. That i s going to come from renewables and from nuclear. It i s not going to come from oil and gas .

Q216 Good m orning, Minister. I was listening intently to the Secretary of State on the “ Today ” program me . The first thing that she said in response to Nick Robinson ’ s question was, “T his will not bring down bills. ” I wonder why, when the cost of living is such a critical issue for this G overnment, constituents up and down the country should support this decision if it doesn ’ t help them and it doesn’t help towards decarbonisation .

We have been very clear that new oil and gas does not take a penny off bills and any argument that suggests it does is simply wrong. We trade as an international commodity what comes off the North s ea and we pay the price. We a re always going to be a price taker , which i s why we a re saying that our long-term future does not lie in oil and gas .

But it does do other things . I think we need to be really clear that the vast majority of British homes are heated by gas , so while we have to electrify the economy and move away from gas for home heating , that i s not going to happen overnight . Therefore, our supply does matter and if we can get it from the continental shelf that is important — that i s the judgment the Energy Secretary has made on this particular project . It also is important for jobs and it is important as a source of revenue , which we a re going to fund into the transition.

I a m not going to cut across anything the Chancellor might say about wider support for consumers, but I would say that it is important that we invest now in building the things that get us off fossil fuels in the long term . P eople ’ s bills have gone up because of our exposure to fossil fuels . We have to do that piece that breaks us from th at, but this is really important for our short-term energy security.

Q217 Thanks very much. Just a question or two on energy security. We ha ve heard reports of recent attacks , or potential attacks, on the UK ’ s energy infrastructure. What steps have you been taking as a D epartment to increase awareness and resilience within the system following the reports of what we ha ve seen from Russian submarines and, indeed, cyber threats as well?
The most important responsibility I have as Energy Minister is the resilience and security of the system. I wi ll ask Dan to add to some of this.

The steps that we ha ve been taking are , first, to continue to look at the G overnment ’ s risk assessment to make sure we have those risks fully up to date. There is a public version of that risk register. There is a version kept at a classified level to make sure we are really considering each of those risks in turn. We wi ll be bringing forward an energy resilience strategy later this year, which picks up on many of the points that have been raised by this C ommittee and others to make sure that we continue to have as robust a system as possible.

There is legislation going through Parliament at the moment on cyber - security, which continues to be a really important risk that we a re looking at . A cross G overnment, in each D epartment that has a responsibility for security, there is a very active conversation about making sure we are as resilient as possible and we a re also preparing the public so that they have resilience in this situation as well. Dan might want to add more.

Ye s , that i s absolutely right . We do ongoing monitoring of risks as well as the structural, cyclical approach to that through the n ational s ecurity r isk a ssessment. We do that on a tactical basis as well with our security partners and energy partners.

There i s already a strong regulatory framework in place for cyber - resilience. That i s going to be strengthened through the c yber -s ecurity and r esilience Bill, and we have an energy cyber - security strategy about going further and faster on that as well. Again, we talk tactically to the industry about that on specific information as and when we have it.

We ha ve quite strong resilience plans already for a wide range of disruption scenarios that are, if you like, cause-agnostic — we have those already. As the M inister said on the e nergy r esilience s trategy, we will take that further and think about how we can set clear energy resilience policy statements across a range of areas consistent with our cyber - security plans, our critical e nergy plans and our physical plans.
We look forward to reading the e nergy r esilience s trategy when it is published .

Q218 I know the session is mainly about energy resilience, but part of that, obviously, is today’s J ackdaw decision, which I welcome as a practical step in energy security, but also as a signal that we are in the North s ea today, tomorrow and for many years to come as that bas e is wound down. I think, as the Chair said, the most important part of this announcement today is th e £2 billion fund to help the transition from one industry to another.

Can you give us any more clarity on that and on how you will be engaging with the Scottish Government, for example ? Will this fund be restricted to the no rth -e ast? We know that jobs and supply chains are not just in Aberdeen — they a re all across the UK —so h ow will this £2 billion be felt in communities like mine and in others?

It i s really important . T he first thing I would say is that we shouldn ’ t think about this as just £2 billion for the transition . T his is on top of what we ha ve capitali s ed into Great British Energy , which is entirely about driving forward the transition but with the G overnment owning a stake in those projects , and the National Wealth Fund , which has clean energy as one of its driving missions . This is £2 billion on top of that existing investment and it is to make sure that we ca pitalise investment into clean energy projects that are creating jobs and actually retaining jobs and retaining the supply chain. The vast majority of the oil and gas jobs are in the supply chain. We need those jobs for the clean energy sectors we have to build.

Decisions about what that will be spent on will be made on the basis of individual projects, but it is fair to assume that given the number of projects that are already in Scotland and the potential for additional projects — the pipeline of offshore wind and other technologies is much greater in Scotland , and the supply chains are in Scotland — the vast majority of this will probably end up being spent in Scotland .

The benefits of this — I think you ha ve made this point before — are in every single postcode across the country in supply chain jobs and in manufacturing . I t ties into the wider Government strategy around re-industrialisation, not just investing in projects, but making sure those projects are built in Britain with the jobs that go with it.

Q219 I see the First Minister of Scotland, Jo h n Swinney, has welcomed this through gritted teeth, saying that it provides some certainty in the north - east . Have you had any chat with the Scottish Government or spoken to them about how this £2 billion might benefit Scotland?

I haven ’ t specifically yet, as we ha ve only announced it today. C ertainty is one thing I could not say about the SNP ’ s energy strategy. I have no idea from one day to the next whether they a re in favour of oil and gas or not . I don ’ t think we ha ve seen very much clarity on that . However, I will say that, on delivering on the clean energy future that we need , we have a very good collaboration with the Scottish Government Energy Minister ; i t i s important that we work together where we can on things . B ut we do need to move at pace on things like consenting , which is the responsibility of the Scottish Government , to make sure we are delivering the projects that the people of Scotland expect us to build together.

Q220 Let ’ s move on to the wider theme of this session , which is m eant to be about resilience and how the energy infrastructure of the country is protected. Apart from what you ha ve said to the C hair, what further steps do you need to take to future-proof the energy system from cyber - attacks and p hysical attacks?

There are a number of things. O ne of the things I did not say before that I think is important is I a m now chairing a group of senior chief executives in industry because the G overnment, of course, operate none of this infrastructure directly. It is in the hands of individual organisations and we ha ve to make sure that resilience, particularly cyber - resilience , is taken seriously in every single part of every single organisation.

One of the things we ha ve been driving that forward on is making sure that we ha ve the industry-led technical knowledge that i s necessary, so that people have sufficient training at all levels of organisations. We are looking at whether we need to review legislation and whether we ha ve the right powers to be able to do more in that space , and we a re also looking at all sorts of national emergency planning and cyber - resilience planning . A ll of these things are live processes we a re working through .

B uilding resilience at every single level of the energy system is what we see a s absolutely crucial . It i s one thing for company boards to say it i s important ; it i s another thing for the person operating the terminal to see it as their absolute priority . W e a re driving that forward at the moment as well.

To add to that, the industry and the D epartment work really closely with the National Protective Security Authority and the National Cyber Security Centre as well, which regularly brief and work quite closely with the industry on the steps they need to take .

B ringing it back to something the Minister said before about the energy transition, that of course is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to ensure that what we are building is resilient by design, which is far more efficient than retrofitting or trying to patch up the system that may be in place right now. There is just a big opportunity with the transition to strengthen things as we build them.
Q221 You anticipated my next question, Dan, which you can answer possibly . H ow well is this understood across G overnment and other parts of G overnment?

I would say very well. It i s something that the G overnment take incredibly seriously , n ot just because of the wider external environment but because of how important the energy system is to households and to the rest of the country’s critical national infrastructure as well. It is understood very well and we work quite closely with the rest of the D epartment to make sure, as they a re developing their policies, that they take security and resilience as a fundamental requirement of that.

Q222 Just one last question in passing. The re is a concern about cyber - security but also physical security . W e ha ve heard reports of unidentified lights, possibly drones, around North Sea structures and infrastructure. With out giving something away, what practical steps are you taking to make sure the physical infrastructure is protected?

Again , physical resilience and security are hugely important. I would say that although we take these threats very seriously and they are developing at all times , we have a very good success rate in protecting that infrastructure . B ut clearly the threat landscape is always changing so we have to stay on top of that.

On drones in particular, we ha ve been working with industry to make sure they have appropriate guidance o n what steps they can take . D rones are obviously becoming much more prevalent than ever before and people can get their hands on drones in a way that they couldn ’ t before. We a re exploring whether we do need to go further in that area, looking at the National Security Act to take any additional powers through that , including looking at whether we need more restrictions on flying and other aspects. We keep all of this under review.

Again it goes back to the point around bringing industry with us on this . Ofgem has taken security and resilience very seriously to make sure that the companies it regulates are investing in their physical and cyber - resilience to make sure it is as robust as it needs to be.

On the previous point, I think this is something that i s taken seriously right across G overnment. Dan Jarvis is the S ecurity M inister who is chairing a number of ministerial groups to make sure every single bit of G overnment is focused on critical national infrastructure but also , as I said before, on domestic resilience, to make sure we as a country are prepared. We are a bit of an outlier as a country in how much we bring people with us on their own personal resilience. That is going to be important, not just for security but for responding to storms and other events , so that people have a bit of personal resilience as well.
Q223 First, when can we expect the e nergy r esilience s trategy?
We ha ve said later this year.
Q224 Okay, later this year —a s late as 31 December 2026?
That is as late as we could go in the year, so hopefully by then, yes.

Q225 Thank you . O n physical attacks, I was at a breakfast meeting bringing together the industry on flex ibility . T he argument is very clear : i t i s much easier to attack one big central power station, for example, or an installation, than hundreds and thousands of little installations. I n the forthcoming e nergy i ndependence Bill, will there be a reflection on how we should increase the flexibility markets, recogni s ing that lots of energy is now going to be created in a decentrali s ed way and that , in many ways , that is the best way of physically protecting it ? How are the G overnment thinking about this?

I completely agree with yo u. You tempt me to reveal what is in the e nergy i ndependence Bill , which I will not do at this stage , but we will see it soon. Y ou a re right about both decentrali s ation of energy infrastructure and flexibility , and we see that as critical . That is partly why we a re investing in the first long duration energy storage in 40 years. It i s why we a re seeing more battery and shorter duration storage deployment, so that we ha ve that flexibility in the system. We also see much more deployment of the ability of consumers to make use of flexibility in terms of time - of - use tariffs that benefit the system as well as consumers.

On t he broader point , from a resilience point of view, I think is absolutely clear , as Dan said earlier , that w e have a once - in - a - generation chance to build a decentrali s ed system that reduces the risk to individual parts of the system , because it is decentrali s ed right across the country in tens of thousands of pieces of infrastructure. There are complexities in doing that but I would look to Ukraine as a really good example . Ukraine is building back from attacks on energy infrastructure by building the exact decentrali s ed energy system that we a re building, partly to decarboni s e but partly because it is much more difficult to attack the individual parts and have a wider impact on the system.
It is about strength by design . T hat i s another reason why we see it as a hugely important aspect of what the energy system looks like in future .
Q226 In terms of oversight, should the strategy seek to shift the burden of resilience from central G overnment to local government?

We want it to be a partnership , and it is at the moment . Resilience absolutely has to sit with central G overnment and local government in partnership, because the levers that we both have — the local knowledge and the local levels of trust in responding to incidents — ha ve to sit with both. It is one of the things the Prime Minister has been very clear on : strengthening the devolution agenda and that partnership with local government at all levels.

It i s also some of the work we ha ve been doing on Storm Arwen . T he report that came after that was partly around how the G overnment respond to major incidents, a storm in that case, but it would apply to other things. Rehearsing some of this , and building the training and the support that local resilience forums have , are really important part s of this as well, but it has to be about both.
Q227 S hifting to extreme weather events , then, t o what extent will the e nergy r esilience s trategy actually talk about extreme weather events and resilience? Can you go into a bit more detail?

I can ’ t go into the detail on something we have not published yet, but it is about our general sense of resilience in the energy system, which is responding to a whole series of things. Storms and extreme weather events are going to become much more frequent. We saw the summer heatwaves having a real impact on gas generators being able to generate, for example. There are widespread impacts that we have to take into consideration. That will all be part of it. However, our response, and I suppose what the strategy is about, is focusing on the overall resilience of the system and the further steps we ha ve to take , whether we are responding to storms or threat actors .

Q228 Okay ; I will ask the next question about the strategy . You might say that you can ’ t tell me because the strategy is not published , but I will try anyway . Should the UK be prioriti s ing the domestic manufacturing of components , with the subsequent ly increased cost , to reduce supply chain dependencies ?

I think this is really important . I can say what the G overnment ’ s position on this is because we ha ve been clear on it for two and a half years . We have to build supply chains much more in the UK. That is a security and an economic imperative , and it is a view shared across Europe as well about domestic supply chains in Europe.

It i s really important because in an uncertain worl d, relying on supply chains from other parts of the world makes it more difficult for us to maintain our resilience. Obviously the more we manufacture in the UK , the more economic benefit we a re getting from that . B ut also the transition to clean power is not just happening in Britain ; it is happening right across the globe and there is competition for supply chains . I f we can build and manufacture more of this in Britain, we have more of a chance of getting it quickly on to the system to help us deliver the outcomes we want to see. F rom a security point of view, it i s important but actually it i s about the economic opportunity of the clean power transition.

Just to build on that, if I may , w e have very good information on the supply chain and c ritical inputs to critical national infrastructure, working with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade . As the Minister said, having clear policies in place to boost domestic supply chains is really important. I draw attention to the c lean e nergy s upply c hain f und, which was £1 billion to support companies with high growth potential to develop those domestic supply chains, and the c lean i ndustry b onus, which was also to reward the supply chain development of investment projects in the UK.

Clearly, there i s only so far you can go, and we work very closely with industry on what stockpiles and reserves they have of critical components . We are talking to them about standardisation of components as well to make it easier to move components around should we need to do that.

Q229 S lightly moving away from that, industry always tell us that the problem is that energy is too expensive. T he first thing for business needs to be that our energy price — our electricity price in particular — will have to come down. T here is still no clear evidence that the G overnment are really working hard on making sure that energy prices are coming down . O therwise , we can talk about wanting to bring manufacturing back into this country, but it w ill not happen if energy is so expensive.

You a re not going to get any argument from me or anyone else in G overnment when you say that energy prices are too high. We ha ve been very clear on that —they are far too high. The Prime Minister has set out the ambition that we will equali s e with the European average on energy prices to deal with that competitive issue that you raise, but it i s not go ing to happen overnight.

T he challenge is that the G overnment is investing significant amounts of money to bring down the costs of crucial industries , but we have to fundamentally break the link with gas if we a re go ing bring down prices for everyone and in the long term. We are doing that in parallel , with investments to support targeted industries with electricity costs , and in the meanwhile, building the clean power system that breaks that link and gets bills down for everyone . That, in the long run, is the thing that will help deliver domestic manufacturing.

I would just say, though, on the cost point, there is always a trade-off here , and w e a re really clear about this . W e want to see domestic supply chains wherever possible , and we a re doing everything we can to support those domestic supply chains, but we also have to tackle affordability. That is a tension, clearly, because it is more expensive to build things here than elsewhere. However, there is a social benefit that G overnments for far too long have not calculated about domestic procurement that we have to shift. If we manufacture things in Britain, we have a more resilient supply chain, first of all, but we also create jobs, which creates additional tax receipts , and we deal with some of the fundamental issues in this country about us just being agnostic about industrial policy for far too long.
There are social benefits of saying we want to build things here in Britain, and there are energy security arguments for why those supply chains being here leads to a more resilient system.
Thank you. We a re going to move on. I would love to explore that further , so p erhaps we wi ll get you back yet again to probe into that answer.
I can ’ t say no.
We may come back to it.

Q230 Minister, you ha ve said on several occasions that gas will remain part of the energy mix up to and beyond 2050, so can I ask a few questions about gas security? The National Energy System O perator — N E SO — has said that it has identified an emerging risk to gas supply security in the unlikely event of the loss of the single largest piece of gas infrastructure in the system. What is the single largest piece of gas infrastructure in the system , and what is the threat to it?

Each year we do an assessment, something called N1, which is essentially an assessment of whether the gas system can cope if the biggest single piece of infrastructure was — in an extremely unlikely scenario I should say — no longer available. F or example , that could be an LNG terminal — Milford Haven would be an example of an LNG terminal.

The second part of the test is it has to be a one -in- 20 demand day — the coldest winter day that the UK could expect in 20 years. A combination of things has to occur at the same time —that is the resilience test we have. In all likelihood , t he system never has to reach that point , but the whole point is that it should be resilient , so we should be able to . W e should have sufficient redundancy in the system to meet that test every single year . T he Secretary of State has to be able to be assured that that is the case every year.
Q231 That is a given then, that we are secure in that respect — guaranteed?
E very year we have to assess all the available evidence for the year ahead and make that assessment . We have to be assured that is the case, or take actions to make sure we can meet that.

Q232 Where does the gas grid fit into this, because 23 million homes are dependant on the gas grid . Can you confirm the gas grid will remain part of our critical national infrastructure well beyond 2050?

Mich ae l Shanks: It will remain important until the last customer has been disconnected. We are working—on a domestic and industrial level—to move customers away from gas, but that will not happen overnight. The transmission network and the distribution network that go into streets and homes will remain important.

We do have a challenge that we are working through at the moment that we need to work with industry on around how we continue to invest in that gas grid while we will see customers disconnecting. That will be quite piecemeal; customers will disconnect as they choose to take on other technologies. That is a challenge for us as a country, but the gas network is hugely resilient. It has been invested in and upgraded much more recently than the electricity network, and we need to maintain that while moving people off it as quickly as we can.

Q233 There are a lot of people with off-grid homes dependent upon LNG and there seems to be some confusion in the Government as to what the policy is towards LNG. Do you support the promotion of liquid gas as an alternative fuel for housing into the indefinite future?

We have been agnostic around exactly what choices individual consumers should make. We are not legislating to ban people from making their own choices, but we do want to make it affordable and accessible for people to choose technologies that help us decarbonise. That is important and we will continue to do that.

Off-grid households are not off the electricity grid. Yes, they are off the gas grid but they do have access to electricity and so some of the electrification technologies—be it solar, batteries or heat pumps—are available. I do not have the exact number in front of me but we can share it with the Committee . W e have seen an uptick in investment in that from off-grid households since the situation in the m iddle e ast has developed , because the economics of it have become much clearer for people.

Q234 Electricity still remains, as you accept, far too expensive but if there is to be investment by the liquid gas industry in LNG for households then it needs to have a clear signal that the Government recognise in the long term that this is a worthwhile investment, including investment in biogas. At the moment that has not been forthcoming, which is causing a stuttering in that industry, unlike what is happening on the c ontinent. Can you clearly say today that there is a strong long-term future in the Government’s eyes for the LNG industry?

I can say what I have said already, which is that households will make choices about the technologies that they want to use in their own homes and their own circumstances. We said in the w arm h omes p lan that we would not choose individual technologies — that the Government would say households should choose — but that we would incentivise heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and others.

I am interested in developments in biogas and other things , but the Government obviously have to weigh up the investment cost of doing that versus the long-term trajectory we want to be on as a country. I am not for or against these things. There is often a sense that one individual thing will solve the whole issue , but the truth is that we will need a whole range of things and they will be different in every part of the country.

On the devolution agenda, that is why the Government’s commitment to devolve the entirety of the w arm h omes p lan is so important because choices will be made in individual parts of the country that will be different. It is right and proper that those are made by local decision makers.

Q235 Indecision by Government is inhibiting investment in a whole lot of different areas including—I mentioned last time we had a session—the Rough system, the storage facility. There has been no clear decision on that ; there has been no clear decision on the future of LNG. You have put forward today what I think is a very welcome decision on the new gasfield but that has been delayed far too long. What are you doing to bring different parts of your Department together to deliver a strong lead in all these areas and stop the indecision?

I am not aware there is a specific decision we have not made on biogas in front of me. If there is something I am not aware of , I will go back and look at it. I get the general point is about steers from Government; I hear that regularly from industry. I cannot always give a running steer on things but I do not think there are any specific decisions that are in front of me. We did respond to consultation on the gas system and transition, which asked a number of searching questions that, in all honesty, we should have been looking at a decade ago or more on what the gas system—which has been in transition for a long time—looks like and how we maintain that investment now and build for the future.

On storage, Rough is a commercial decision for Centrica. They have asked the Government for a particular mechanism and we will respond to that, but storage plays a much smaller role in the British system than it does for our European neighbours because we have a diverse range of supplies, not least the pipeline from Norway and our own continental shelf, as well as the LNG import terminal. Storage plays a fundamentally different role.

Q236 Thank you, we will move on. Before we move on to Matt Western, you were talking about customers who are off the gas grid but on the electricity grid. Does that suggest that there will be special support for those customers to enable them to electrify their homes for heat and power?

Not specifically at the moment , but one of the things around devolving the w arm h omes p lan is that we will look at how that funding could be used in specific parts of the country that have a significantly higher number of off-grid gas households. We have already provided increased support for the deployment of heat pumps, solar panels and other technologies so those households can take that up. We have seen an uptick in that already.
Q237 On biogas, do you have a target in mind — a sense of how much biogas you are expecting to be on the system as a proportion of our total gas supply in the coming years?
I do not have a figure to hand, no.
Thank you. We are joined by Matt Western, the Chair of the JCNSS, as a welcome guest on the Committee today. Matt, over to you.

Q238 Thanks, Chair. Good morning, Minister. I want to touch on offshore security. In terms of the power generation cables coming ashore, how many cables do we have coming in, as a risk or vulnerability, and what percentage of our electricity is coming typically—either in winter or summer , or on average—from those cables, whether that be from other countries or from our arrays?

I do not have the exact numbers to hand, forgive me, but I can absolutely send them to you. The interconnectors between the c ontinent and us are hugely important. We use the interconnectors and have done for a long time to ensure that we are able to balance electricity. The import and export across help both Europe and the UK so that remains hugely important. We have the generation capacity in the UK to meet that demand as well, but the interconnectors play an important part.
Q239 That would be very useful to know if you want to come back in writing, because we are tight for time.
Dan, very helpfully, has pointed out we do have those figures — 10 GW .
For the electricity interconnectors , it is 10—
What about the p ercentage —n ot total gigawatts ?
We would have to come back on the percentage.
It is another one of th o se questions where the answer will fluctuate hour by hour.
Give me an average, or for winter or summer.
Yes, we can share that.

Q240 Sadly on one of my days off, I went to visit an interconnector, which was interesting. NESO and Nat ional Grid are headquartered in my constituency so I take an interest in this stuff. How would you assess the security and vulnerability of those sites?

First, we have not had an attack directly on that infrastructure. We obviously continue to monitor this closely. The former Defence Secretary, now the Chancellor, made a very clear statement recently about Russian activity on top of subsea infrastructure , so we are aware that there is a level of interest in this. We obviously take as many proactive steps as we can to mitigate that risk.

Part of w hat I said earlier around bringing industry around the table is that interconnectors are a good example of where private industry manages the sites but we obviously have an interest in making sure their security arrangements are as robust as possible. We continue to keep all of that under review, and the cyber - security risk comes into that as well.

Q241 One of the things we discovered with data cables is that there is a concentration of vulnerability. Is that something that concerns you? How many interconnector sites do we have around the country?
I can name five of them , but I want to check there are not more than five . W e have a number of sites and we want to see more interconnections.
Q242 Fewer than 10 ?
Yes.
But they are geographically distributed across the North sea so they are not all concentrated, in terms of electricity cables and gas pipelines.
Q243 On power cables, what is the assessment of the risk of vulnerability to a state wishing to sever those cables? What is your assessment of that?

Dan might want to come in on this. I am always cautious about going too far into hypotheticals on particular pieces of infrastructure, but clearly in the Baltic s ea there have been incidents involving cables. As I said earlier, we have obviously seen some interest in our subsea infrastructure. We recognise that it is a risk and it is on the risk register on that basis, but equally we think we have sufficient measures in place to tackle it. Importantly, even if we were to lose a single interconnector , we have redundancy built into the system.

Those security of supply standards that are built in for electricity and gas do take account of loss of assets. We talked about gas a moment ago and it is the same for electricity. Because we have that distribution—as your colleague mentioned earlier—we can absorb the loss of some of these things, which do occasionally go on outage for maintenance reasons anyway.
Q244 How many gas pipes come into the UK?

Our key pipeline with Norway is an important piece of infrastructure and it is joint with the Norwegians. I was meeting the Norwegian Energy Minister a few weeks ago in Norway to talk about this. We take the security of that very seriously.
There are a number of gas pipelines.
There are a number of other pipelines.
And t wo interconnectors as well, to the Netherlands and Belgium.

Q245 On the Hamburg d eclaration, how well co-ordinated do you think any response would be, given that there is this European network we are part of? How well co-ordinated is that? How developed is it and how do you see that in the future?

It is well developed but we want it to go further. The Hamburg d eclaration was an important moment. I have at tended the NSEC—the group of North Sea countries—twice now. It is an important group of Ministers who meet , but the official engagement between those countries on a more regular basis is important. We are also doing much more exercising between countries to make sure we are prepared to respond to incidents.

Dan might want to say more about this , but I was in Lithuania more than a year ago now to see some of the work that DESNZ is doing there on sharing our expertise, but also learning from the Baltic states’ response to where there have been incidents as well. It is an ongoing piece of work but we recognise even closer collaboration across the North s ea countries is absolutely crucial .
Q246 Minister, you have already talked quite a bit about cyber - security. What lessons should the UK learn from the recent cyber - attack on Poland’s energy grid?

We are still working on some of the lessons from that but it was an important moment for us to recognise how real the threat is. We explored that in some detail with the security taskforce that I chair to make sure companies are aware of the risks.

One of the key lessons—I mentioned it in one of my earlier answers—is that it has to be embedded throughout a whole organisation because some of the real risks that were identified were actually from practices that were quite straightforward to resolve but were not acted on. Standardisation of passwords is an example that we all know about. Some are probably still guilty of not taking password security as seriously as we could. There are some straightforward operational things we learned that we should improve on.

There are wider lessons that we are learning and we have good engagement with the Polish G overnment on this. There are obviously security conversations that we have at a more classified level on detail.

Q247 You have mentioned the e nergy s ector c yber -s ecurity s trategy, the c yber -s ecurity and r esilience Bill, and we also have Ofgem and DESNZ’s consultation on r eshaping c yber r egulation. How do these all interact with each other , and a re we in danger of having a mishmash of things happening ? Is it clear who is ultimately in charge of each?

Dan wants to come in on this, which will be useful. We are aware of that, which is why the work that Dan Jarvis is leading in the Cabinet Office is about cross- G overnment resilience and bringing all these strategies together. Crucially—and I always say this—strategies are only useful if they are actually implemented . That is the important piece of work. It is not just about having risks on a risk register and mitigations on the risk register, but whether those are being implemented and whether we are following up and making sure that action is dealing with the risk. That is the practical work going on across G overnment as well.

If we start with the c yber a ssessment f ramework under the Network and Information Systems Regulations , t hat is basically the regulatory basis for cyber - resilience in the UK. That is split into oil and upstream gas, for which DESNZ is the named competent authority, and downstream gas and electricity, which is shared between DESNZ and Ofgem—but Ofgem take up the regulatory role there whereas we do the regulatory for oil and upstream gas. Those are the things that set the basic profile that industry needs to reach , and if they reach the basic profile they will be resilient to quite a lot of the incidents that we are seeing. There is then also a timetable for them to get to the enhanced standard, which further strengthens them to more sophisticated levels of attack.

What the c yber -s ecurity and r esilience Bill do es is extend the scope of that regulation to a wider set of entities, including the supply chain, that provide critical services, including IT services, to the energy sector —because y ou are only as strong as your weakest link in the supply chain. It also increases the enforcement powers for Government. That is how they fit together , but we have clearly defined responsibilities for who is responsible for regulating what.

Q248 On extending the responsibility to the supply chain , one of the issues that we have discussed in the Committee is the issue of overseas supply chain s, so how will the Bill apply extending those responsibilities?

On the supply chain , we obviously make decisions on a case - by - case basis. We have talked in the Committee before about one particular decision that we made. It is important that those are on an individual basis and those assessments are always made on particular projects . The supply chain is crucial to this but, equally, the balance we have to strike is about making sure resilience is everyone’s responsibility . S ecurity should be everyone’s responsibility, but there are key actors who have a particular responsibility, which is what these strategies are trying to get at. Collectively , the system has to work towards the same aims and that is the general steer that we give right across the energy sector.
Q249 Will the Bill in any way change how you make those individual decisions?
Not on specific decisions about whether—
Q250 It will not change the factors you are looking at in any way?
No, and we think we do have a sufficient lever to be able to make those decisions at the moment ,, so we are not looking at that again.

Q251 Coming on to the increasing threat from AI, can you explain what you are doing to prepare for cyber - security attacks involving AI? Obviously it can be used defensively as well, so how are you doing that? Does it matter that we do not have any of the top AI models in the world? It is very dominated by America and China , with France having Mistral as well. Could you explain what we are doing to prepare, how we are using it defensively, and whether you are concerned about our ability to do that given the way the AI market is going ?

It is hugely important , and a live discussion on the sovereign capability that we have in the UK is going on right across G overnment. Kanishka Narayan ’s appointment as a Cabinet Minister looking at AI is an important statement of how crucial we see that across G overnment.

You are absolutely right to recognise that there is an increased threat from the capabilities people have by being able to use AI, but there is a real opportunity for the energy system there as well, including for flexibility as we were talking about earlier. If we can run a smarter system with AI , there are benefits that come from that.

We are doing a number of things. Ofgem published guidance in May on the safe us e of AI within the energy system. We do want to see much more innovation in this space , so we do not want energy companies to be resistant to the opportunities that might come from it, but it has to be deployed in a safe way. We are obviously looking much more at the security aspects o f how we can make sure we are protecting infrastructure from the use of AI as a form of attack.
There are opportunities for the industry to use AI to identify their own weaknesses so they can strengthen their own systems. We are encouraging them to do that as well.
We are working with the AI Security Institute, which has an extraordinary amount of experience and insight into this , to make sure we are doing everything we can as well.
Q252 Have we actually seen material evidence of increasing use of AI in cyber - attacks on our energy infrastructure, or is it still a theoretical risk?

I probably do not want to be drawn on individual instances that do or do not occur. The resilience of our system is such that any attempts have not been successful but I want to be careful not to go too far into it. We recognise generally that AI significantly increases capabilities of people who might not otherwise have that capability.

Q253 You talked about the use of AI both offensively and defensively when it comes to cyber - attacks, but the data centres to run it also create a great demand on the system. We are limited to what we can provide in electricity supply. I asked the Secretary of State last week about how we ensure that the demand is not being taken up with things that do not further our national interest. Are you concerned that the demand that AI is creating is a threat to our energy resilience?

No, I do not characterise it as a threat but it is a serious issue. The sheer amount of demand is something we are looking at. We should not see data centres as not providing any benefit to the country. Having sovereign compute in the UK is hugely important for us—
Q254 To be clear, I am not saying it does not provide anything ; I am saying that in some instances it may be—

I totally understand the point, and you are right. I have been at this Committee before talking about the generation connections queue. The demand queue is becoming increasingly difficult because of the proliferation of data centres in that queue. We will have to manage that and we have announced some measures to do so. There is a balance to be struck. There is actually an opportunity : if we deploy data centres strategically on the system , we will soak up some of the excess electricity we are currently generating that cannot be used in the system. That is good for affordability for everyone because they become a customer for that electricity, and it can reduce restraints if done strategically.

We are working with the industry to look at whether data centres could be much more flexible in their use of electricity. At the moment it is very much an “always on” model, but are there AI models that do not require that firm power all the time so we could then make use of excess power at specific times of the day. We are open to that, but we also see AI as crucial for our economic growth and, therefore, we will make sure that we have the electricity that is necessary and work through the processes to get those on the system where appropriate.
Q255 M y colleagues have covered quite a lot of the questions I had about the Jackdaw decision , so I will move on to talk about the role of nuclear in energy resilience.

Obviously nuclear energy gives us domestic baseload, but a lot of our nuclear generation is coming towards the end of its life. Minister, are you confident that nuclear regulators are able to take into account strategic factors such as energy resilience and security of supply when they are discharging their functions, whether that is to do with new build nuclear or indeed the end of life of existing power stations?

Last week, I chaired the n uclear r egulation d elivery g roup, which is the implementation panel that is moving forward on the Fingleton recommendations to make sure we are implementing those as quickly as possible. One of those recommendations was about making sure nuclear regulation can take a basket of factors into consideration. Nuclear safety and security will always be the overriding consideration for nuclear regulation , and w e are not suggesting at all that we should move from that , but there are a number of other factors — energy security being a crucial one — that we need to take into account .

I will not sit here and say that we are in the strongest place we c ould have been , because we will see a significant amount of nuclear decommissioning before we have brought on the fleet that we need for the future , and that is because of decades of indecision on nuclear. I think the last time we took a decision on a nuclear power station that is currently generating I was not even born, and that demonstrates the fact that as a country we have been asleep at the wheel on making decisions we need to make. We are now making up for that and the n uclear r egulatory t askforce is all about making sure we can build safely, but much more quickly.
Q256 Are you confident that the Fingleton r eview will be implemented in a timely way? Are you confident that the Department is working at the pace necessary to make up for those years of inaction?

I am. I have given very specific steers on this. One is to make sure that we have the outcome in mind throughout. I do not want us to become too wedded to individual ways of implementing things if we can find faster ways of achieving the same outcome. I have given that steer clearly. We had Sizewell C presenting at the implementation panel about the innovation they are doing to make decisions faster — that is not in Fingleton, but is actually important .

T here are opportunities to go further but we are also preparing to introduce the n uclear r egulation Bill early next year to make sure that where we need to legislate , we will legislate. Our aim is to keep that Bill as focused as possible so that we can get it through P arliament as quickly as possible , hopefully, and into implementation. I have also been clear that we should be trying to do what we can without legislation to achieve the outcomes we want to achieve.
Q257 Do you think the industry is as confident as you are in the pace of the Department?

There will always be arguments that we can go faster on things. I do not think it is only for the Department; I think it is for regulators to work together. I am confident from the conversation s I have had right across the regulatory landscape that people are seized of the ambitions we have to recognise how we will get there. That always requires people to move out of their comfort zones and the proof will be in the pudding. It is one thing to say everyone is supportive of it; it is another thing when we get into implementation. That is partly why I have been very clear that people will have to move from what might be entrenched positions to get to the shared outcome we all want. That is for Government and regulators , but it is also for industry as well to be part of that conversation. The crucial thing is to bring all of that together in how we deliver these projects.

We have a huge opportunity with the SMR programme at Gwyndod , which I am visiting tomorrow, to make sure that in the Government-backed programme — the first - of - a - kind fleet of SMRs — we are building those in a different way and putting the Fingleton principles into practice as we are building right now.

Q258 Do you think the regulators are fully onboard with that and have moved to a position where they are taking risk-based decisions based on strategic factors and current scientific evidence, and on the full range of safety factors that are very strong in the nuclear industry?

There definitely is a shifting of culture but there is a lot more to do. Culture will be key to this. It is one thing to implement new regulation or new guidance, but we all know it is the decision making itself, and the culture of that decision making, that will actually shape whether we feel any difference at the end of it. All of the regulators recognise that but changing culture is difficult. My very clear view on this is that we absolutely have to implement all the recommendations in as practical a way as possible so that they can get on with delivery, but then I want to see progress on culture shift as well so that people are meeting the spirit and the outcome that is intended from that review.
Q259 How are you learning from other places, such as France, which have a strong safety culture but have delivered far more nuclear energy than we have?

That is o ne of the key things I asked . W e always assume that we have to reinvent the wheel — it is true across the energy industry. Countries are struggling with the same things but they have also found ways through a lot of it. Part of why we said we wanted to work more closely with the US on this is that we very much share the same safety standards, but if a project should be approved by a regulator in the States , it should be approved by a regulator in the UK if we believe in that. There are lessons to learn from that .

A bout France, you are absolutely right . There are still people unconvinced by nuclear power. The last few months have demonstrated very much that France has weathered the impact of the closure of the s trait of Hormuz far better than we have, and it is because their nuclear fleet has responded and kept bills low. That is the opportunity we could have had if we had been building nuclear over the past two or more decades.

Q260 To ensure the country’s future resilience , we do have to continue to build out a clean power system that works with a mix of energy. We have had a long consultation about that, which has confirmed that is the case. It was due to be included in the e nergy i ndependence Bill we expected to see earlier this year , but t hat has been delayed again. Earlier in this session you said we would see it soon. Will we see it before Christmas or after Rosebank?
I will not be drawn on the Rosebank decision, which is another regulatory decision for the Secretary of State, but you will see the Bill before Christmas.
That is good to hear.
Or 31 December.
Q261 Christmas 2026?
I hope you will see the Bill much sooner than that but—
We should have been clear on the specification of the year.
P arliamentary timetabling is not in my brief, I am afraid, but you will see the Bill soon.

Q262 But you anticipate it will be by the end of this year and that is what you are working towards. To secure all of these projects and deliver greater, broader independence of our energy, do you think within that Bill we will see—and are you working to ensure it is included—the r eformed n ational p ricing policy giv ing some certainty to developers, especially ahead of AR8?

While I do not want to get into the details of the Bill, we have already confirmed that the r eformed n ational p ricing package will be legislated for where necessary. Some of it does not require legislation , but we will legislate on that. I think transmission charging is the point that you are particularly focusing on as part of that. We have said to industry we wanted to see if there was a more permanent solution we could implement to TNUoS volatility before AR8. We have not been able to find what that mechanism is, and Ofgem has worked to see if that is possible, but we have been clear we want to find an enduring solution before AR9.

On AR8 , the timeline is already under way and the bids will be going in in the coming weeks and months. We have not been able to resolve it for then , but we are absolutely committed to dealing with the long-term volatility in TNUoS .

Reformed n ational p ricing requires two things. One is absolutely a reform to transmission charging, but still with a recognition that we need a signal about where to build things most efficiently in the country so that we bring down the cost of transmission. That is important. The second bit of that is the s trategic s patial e nergy p lan, which is about us setting out where future infrastructure should broadly be built to make sure that we are building the cheapest system.

Q263 Yes, which is what I was coming on to, because th e s trategic spatial e nergy p lan also has the pathway for grid connections post-2030. Are you worried about delays impacting on existing projects in the planning pipeline?

If I am candid with the Committee, I am worried about connections reform. It has been an extremely difficult and frustrating process and continues to be. I do not backtrack at all from what I have said previously about how important it was. The queue was completely unmanageable and we have cleared out a lot, but I am acutely aware that it is having a real, live impact on projects right now and that risks investment confidence. I want to be honest about that. It is a huge frustration for me and much of what we have talked about today genuinely keeps me up at night, but the connections process is a genuine concern. We are doing—

Q264 If you cannot deliver these projects—there is no point in building them if we cannot get them connected , because they will not provide the energy —c an we say that we are delivering resilience and energy security for the country?

Yes, we can. I completely agree with you : i f we cannot connect these projects , and connect them in such a way that does not create additional constraints , then we are not benefiting consumers in the way we should be. I do not think that means the absence of that makes the system any less resilient. We are connecting a huge number of projects all the time, but not as many as I would like.

This goes a long way back to the approach we took to how projects could connect to the system. Even in the dying days of the last Government, the connections queue stood at 400 GW and it somehow got to more than 700 GW before we came into g overnment. It was a completely unmanageable but foreseeable problem that they should have done something about. We are now grappling with that and I regret that it is as difficult as it is.

On the s trategic s patial e nergy p lan, the Secretary of State now has the pathways and we will consider them in detail, and then there will be a consultation early next year from NESO on it. We have been clear that that process is not about creating a black and white plan of what projects can and cannot go forward ; it is about saying that we need a coherent way of building the transmission system for the future instead of patching it up to where ad hoc renewables projects were built over the past 20 years. We should not have done that. We now have to build back a better system .

I share the absolute concern and I want to assure the Committee that , for me, the concern is translated into very firm action from the Department bringing NESO, Ofgem and the transmission owners together to find a way through this as quickly as possible. It is not pain free and I will be honest in saying it is not about to become any easier. It is a difficult process and we are doing everything we can, but it will remain difficult.
Thank you very much indeed. Minister, Director, thank you for your evidence this morning. That is the end of our session.

Oral evidence: National Audit Office Annual Report , HC 735
Tuesday 20 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 20 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Clive Efford (Chair); Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown; John Glen; Sarah Olney; and Chris Vince.
Questions 1 to 36
Witnesses

I : Gareth Davies, Comptroller and Auditor General, National Audit Office ; Dame Fiona Reynolds DBE , Chair, National Audit Office ; and Rebecca Sheeran, Chief Operating Officer, National Audit Office .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Gareth Davies, Dame Fiona Reynolds and Rebecca Sheeran.
Welcome to this meeting of the Public Accounts Commission on the National Audit Office Annual Report and accounts for 2025-26. I ask the witnesses to introduce themselves for the record.
I am Fiona Reynolds. I am chair of the board of the National Audit Office.
I am Gareth Davies. I am the Comptroller and Auditor General.
I am Rebecca Sheeran. I am the chief operating officer.

Q1 You are all very welcome. We are informal here, so we will be using first names if that is okay. You came in under budget by around £2 million, split evenly between spending less than forecast and receiving more income than forecast. What were the main drivers of each?

It is worth taking expenditure and income separately. We were slightly under on expenditure. It was not staff costs; actually, staff costs came in slightly over budget but very close to budget. We were under in our cash costs, particularly the spending on firms for specialist audit advice.

That mainly relates to the train operating companies. As you will remember, that was our big new chunk of audit work in the year. We had estimated a fairly prudent amount for specialist advice on those audits. It was the first year we had undertaken them. We were not quite sure what it would take but we could see that there were areas that required specialist advice, such as leasing the rolling stock, allocation of fare revenue and so on. As it turned out, we needed less of that advice in practice than we had expected. That is the bulk of the difference. There were other, smaller underspends, but that is the most significant one.

On income, we underestimated the income at the year end for three main reasons. First, an audit that we had expected to be funded out of the grant that you award the NAO, the parliamentary funding, was actually funded from a fee. That was the Infected Blood Compensation Authority. That came in as income that we had not budgeted for. We also did slightly better than expected renting out the spare space in our building, at about £0.2 million, and the rest was the timing of audit work at the year end.

Our accounting policy is that we recognise income from fee-paying audits according to the amount of the audit that is complete at the year end, and slightly more of that was complete than expected. That partly led to the achievement of our target on signing off opinions before the summer recess, which I will come to later. Those are the main reasons for the variances against budget.

Q2 You received the supplementary estimate of £1.2 million last year, but you have come in under budget by £2 million. In hindsight, why did you not manage the extra costs within your existing budget?

It is really the same explanation, because at the time we asked for the supplementary, that was when we were taking on the new train operating company audits, if you remember, which had not been in our original budget. We needed the expenditure, so had we not asked for the supplementary, we would have been well over on our expenditure budget. But as you say, as it turned out, the income overshoot would have covered it, but we could not—did not—expect that at the time we asked for the money, and we would have been pretty reckless to assume that that would happen.

As you know, the one thing that the NAO cannot do is to overspend in a way that triggers an excess vote. Particularly given that we have a role in policing that system across the rest of Government, it would not be good for our credibility to be the one on the list with an excess vote. We have to be prudent in estimating the cost of the audit work. It was the right thing to do at the time, but as you say, as it turned out, the income actually covered the additional expenditure that we needed.

Q3 You mentioned the rail nationalisation, of Avanti. What impact has that had on your audit resources? Does it give you an insight into what you can expect from other additional burdens that will be placed on the National Audit Office as we go forwards?

We certainly learned a lot from the first year of auditing the train operating companies, the first wave that came into public ownership. We audited seven of them in the year we are talking about, in 2025-26. The teams did a great job of preparing for that. We treated it as a major additional chunk of work in a new sector. We spent a lot of time talking to the previous auditors, to make sure that we understood what we were inheriting, and then getting to know the businesses in the way that we have to when planning audit work.

All that planning paid off, because it meant that we were not surprised by any of the audit issues that came up in the first year of auditing the train operating companies. All seven were signed off before the planned date, before the summer recess—a great achievement from the team involved. We also have three more: as you mentioned, Avanti is one; and we have Chiltern and Great Western coming in this year. We will build on that experience.

We are not expecting major differences, although we can never assume anything as an auditor, but we were pleasantly surprised by the consistency of the accounting treatment and the issues across all the train operating companies. They were not as different as we had been expecting. All that means that we have been able to build that into our budget for the current year.
Q4 Going forward, are you confident—having had a good run at all this—that you have the resources to deal with the additional pressures without having to seek a supplementary estimate this year?

This year, we are pretty confident about that. Rebecca might be able to give an update on the figures. All our projections are quite tight this year—we are certainly not going to have plenty of room—but they are within the bounds that we should be able to manage both on income and expenditure for the rest of the year. I don’t know if you want to add to that, Rebecca.

Yes, just to say that at this point, we are essentially at the mid-point in the year and have just conducted a detailed mid-year review. Our forecast is that we will be in line with our budget this year. I should say that the contrast with last year, when we sought the supplementary estimate, was because partway through the year, there was a change in the number of those train operating companies that we were expected to audit within the year. We are not in that position this year. We have clarity about the new work, so at this time we are not expecting a supplementary estimate.

Q5 Good afternoon, team. Can I start with an issue that is probably one of the most important that the PAC and the NAO have to deal with: devolution in local government? I want to talk about the establishment of the Local Audit Office and its role in all of that. Will it free up your resources as it takes over more of that work?

I strongly welcome the creation of the Local Audit Office. There has been an unacceptably poor situation in local government audit, as the Committee knows . I t remains urgent to tackle that, so that local taxpayers have properly audited council accounts. It is just a basic requirement, and that is before we talk about devolution. With devolution on top of that, there is a significant issue now about credible audit arrangements to allow proper scrutiny of local spending. If significant amounts of what is currently central spending are going to be devolved, which they are, the system of accountability needs to be able to deal with that.

The chair of the new body, the Local Audit Office, has been appointed: Bill Butler. He and I have met several times. He has been a guest at our board meeting, and we have had really constructive discussions about how we advise the Government on policy making on this issue, to make sure that there is a joined-up audit framework that delivers the accountability that Parliament expects but that respects local decision making and local accountability , too. T hat has to be quite different from anything we have had befor e, g iven the scale of devolution that the Government are contemplating .

W e need something m ore robust than existed even under the Audit Commission, because Parliament needs to be confident that the framework for devolution and responsibilities are clear, that people are not pointing at each other when something goes wrong, and that the importance of local accountability is properly respected. I think that means quite a big role for the Local Audit Office, auditing not just councils but also the accounts of the mayoral strategic authorities.

It also means a significant role for the NAO in helping the Public Accounts Committee understand how well the devolution framework is delivering value for money for taxpayers. That does not mean second-guessing local decisions, but it does mean being able to understand how the money is being spent and what difference that makes to value for money. Crucially, it means understanding the different approaches that are being taken to the same issue around the country. The whole point of devolution is that you are expecting more innovation and better-targeted solutions because of knowledge of local circumstances. Is that how this is playing out? Is the evidence demonstrating that local decision making means better value for money? T hat is a question in which Parliament has a legitimate interest.

Devolution does not cover everything that the Government spend, of course, but it covers significant amounts. In those areas, our work shifts from central Government audit to looking at how the devolution framework is delivering. That means working closely with the Local Audit Office to understand what its audits are showing, and giving the PAC national reports that allow you to understand how well the framework is developing.

Overall, I do not think that means a shift of resources from us to the Local Audit Office , but us doing a different programme of work in the future. As you know, our VFM work is very selective, and it will remain so even with devolution.

Q6 The critical question in all of that is that the devolution from central Government to local government means that there will be a shift in auditing from you to local government auditors. Given the history of local government audit, do you think there will be sufficient capacity to do all that work?

It will take time for that capacity to build. I am very confident that, with the early appointment of Bill Butler, for example—somebody who knows local audit very well—you will have people with a good understanding making the decisions about that future regime. However, realistically, it is going to take years to develop the kind of capacity that we are talking about, because it is not just about making sure that council audits are timelier and more robust; it means an audit regime around the mayoral strategic authorities.

As we know, there have been cases where there have been questions about individual mayoral spending decisions and without a satisfactory answer about how they are being held to account. That really does need solving. It is going to take time for that local capability to be built. There is a clear plan to do that, but it will take years.

There are two points for Parliament. First, what is the end state that we are aiming at? That is where the early discussions that we are having and we are trying to have with officials are proving helpful. And then, what about the interim between now and three years’ time, which is probably as early as you could expect mature arrangements to be in place? We might need some transitional work and perhaps more work from the NAO in the meantime, because I do not think that we can wait for three years or more for that gap to be filled. We are going to need something in the interim.

Q7 The bigger the mayoral combined authority, the bigger the problem, potentially, when something goes wrong—look at Birmingham, for example. I believe you have powers to carry out an investigation when something goes wrong with one of these authorities. Would you like to let us know how you intend to use that power and in what circumstances?

Birmingham is a council rather than a strategic authority, and we do not have any powers to audit councils. My point about the robustness of the local audit regime is that it absolutely needs to be able to tackle the issues that a council such as Birmingham has been facing for a long time and, to be honest, give a more satisfactory answer to local taxpayers than we have had so far.

On the west midlands mayoral strategic authority, the NAO was given powers when the Audit Commission was abolished, but only as a way of looking at thematic areas of expenditure across the system, not to scrutinise individual authorities. In fact, that is specifically excluded, which is why the NAO could not go into Tees Valley when there was a big clamour for that a few years ago. We could not do that under our existing powers and it would have to be a special measure to make that possible.

We have listed what we think the powers will need to be for the NAO and the LAO to put in place that effective joined-up audit framework that I was describing. Part of that is us having clearer access powers to individual strategic authorities. I do not think it needs to be for councils specifically, because the LAO must be the body to do that.

However, if we are going to do the comparative analysis for PAC that I was describing on how well a transport service is being delivered through devolved systems and what the value for money evidence is there, we need clear access powers to produce a report like that. Those are not clear enough at the moment, and we have suggested that to the team in MHCLG looking at the requirements of the devolution framework.

Q8 On accountability, you are accountable to Parliament through us for the role that you play. Where will the LAO fit in, and where will be the democratic oversight of the LAO? Do you have an understanding of that?

Constitutionally, it is an arm’s length body of MHCLG. It is a ministerial body in that sense, so it is accountable to the Secretary of State for that Department, who also appoints the board, agrees the budget and so on.
Q9 Will there be a mechanism of public accountability such as we have here?

Clearly, the Public Accounts Committee will be able to take evidence from the senior people at the Local Audit Office. In fact, I think you have a session on whole of Government accounts in December, and the plan is for Bill Butler to be a witness. There is that route into parliamentary accountability. It illustrates the point that it is a Government body and not independent of Government in the way that the NAO is. That is why Parliament will have to be satisfied that the whole system provides adequate assurance, from central decision to local implementation.

Q10 I have a question on financial impact. I am not fussed whether the Comptroller and Auditor General , Rebecca or Fiona answers—I will ask and you decide. Your financial impact has fallen from £53 per pound spent to £24 per pound spent. What caused the lower result this year?
