Fair question. Those are the two highest figures in the NAO’s history, just to put that in context. Had they been the other way round, of course, that would have been an easier story to tell, but it kind of makes the point that these figures are lumpy almost by design.

The way this works is that, where we have evidence that our work has either accelerated a decision or created the drive for a new approach that has saved money, we measure from the first year in which that takes effect. It is therefore quite a lagging indicator, because we need to actually see that happening before we put it in the list of impacts.

In the first year, there may be two years from the beginning of that impact to catch up on, so there will be quite a lumpy impact in that first year, and then, in some cases, there is an annual run-on until that finishes. Sometimes, these are genuine one-offs that just feature in one year. My point is that that gives a lumpy profile. We would not expect this to be a smooth measure every year.

We increased our target from 10:1 to 15:1 because our new strategy is predicated on making a bigger impact, so we thought that that was putting our money where our mouth is. It has also been helpful in concentrating the minds of our teams doing the planning of the work.

That is not the only factor when we plan our work. Clearly, the PAC’s interest is a huge factor, and there are other reasons why we might want to give wide coverage to Government spending. But it is really important that, where our work has genuinely created pressure for improvement—together with the PAC’s impacts, obviously—we try to measure the scale of that, so that Parliament has an accurate picture of what difference all this is making. The NAO costs taxpayers, so it is right that they have a measure of the difference that it makes.
Q11 You anticipated my next question, which was about that increase from £10 to £15. The question following on from that is: is £15 still adequate, or could you increase that further?

We ask ourselves that frequently, and the board challenges us on the same question. I suppose the care that we are taking here is that, first, that is quite a substantial increase in the target, and we wanted to give it a bit of time to see what difference it made.

I do not want to get into the territory of perverse incentives here, because it is obviously great to do work that saves taxpayers money, but Parliament needs assurance on lots of other things as well. Systemic areas of improvement, such as digital transformation and the kind of issues that PAC was discussing yesterday on digital ID, are the levers that will change value for money on a huge scale across every Department, and it can be harder to pin down individual savings when we are doing that thematic work. I do not want to drive out that work because people are chasing a cash figure with every study. It is about getting the balance right. Obviously, the PAC’s view on that is very influential as well.

I would just add that the board did think about this very carefully. It is important for us to be able to show improved financial impacts, but as you know, we are just as keen to show impacts on other areas of public policy in delivering value for money. Creating a mixed portfolio in which we can track impacts across different kinds of outcomes is therefore really important to us.

I am sure that, in future, the board will keep as close an eye on that as we do. In fact, a member of the board sits on a panel that, once a year, looks at overall value for money in terms of financial impact achievements. So we are staying close to it, but it is not the only thing that we are trying to do.

Q12 Speaking as a former maths teacher, have you considered using moving averages, because that would avoid the peaks and troughs? I take what you said, looking at the graph there. If you say that you have gone from £53 to £24, it does not look very good, but you are right in saying that, before that, it was £17. Across the five or six-year period that we are looking at overall, a moving average would give you something that would probably be a bit more reasonable.
We have discussed doing exactly that, actually, so I think that we should take that away.

Q13 Turning now to staff numbers, you have 73 more members of staff this year, and, if we look back over the past five years, you have gone from 882 to 1,101, which is just under a 25% increase. Obviously, the body of work that you have to evaluate has increased—I imagine you would say that—but there are also new trends in terms of tools, AI and so on. Could you explain that figure and when we might see it level off or potentially be reduced?

Sure. I will start, and Rebecca will come in . As you say, there were quite a few things going on over that longer period , with an increase in the number and the complexity of audits. The balance sheets of Government Departments are significantly more complex, particularly post-pandemic, but lots of other financial instruments have also been creeping into Government over that time, so that has had an impact.

Auditing standards have been driven up across the profession, for the big firms and for us. We are subject to the same inspection regime as the big four, and we have worked really hard to ensure that our quality is at least on a par with theirs. All of that has required that kind of investment in audit resource.

On the question of the direction it takes, the Commission approved our estimate for the current financial year back in April. Those of you who were there for that will remember that our bid for the current year was essentially flat—a small real-terms reduction, actually. The recent growth that you have pointed to has already levelled off in this current year.

We are forecasting a similar picture for next year, partly because we are now generating some of the investment we need through productivity improvements driven by the investments in our audit technology that you mentioned. We are in the foothills of applying AI tools in our financial audit and value-for-money work. We are already seeing some productivity benefit from that but, as you will remember from when we discussed the estimate, we have a three-year programme for delivering more through that. As I say, we have already levelled off for that reason. Of course, the big firms are investing billions in AI, and—
Q14 You are probably not able to do that.

We will never be able to do that . T he investment we have made so far will not cut it on its own ; I suppose that is the point. Although we are seeing some early benefits from the investments we have made, there is much more to come on modernising our audit in line with practice in the rest of the private sector. This is an ongoing issue. We are going to come back with our estimate in the early part of 20 27 to explain how we are taking that forward.

Q15 May I pursue that a little further? If you were in an optimal situation where you could bring forward more investment into years one and two, do you think you would do that to secure better outcomes further down the period ? Is the accounting profile you have to work with inhibiting optimal investment?

That is a great question. To some extent — but only to some extent , because money is only one of the capacities that we are dealing with here. There is the change capacity of the organisation itself. I give credit to our staff ; a cross the board, they have absorbed methodology change, technology change, real performance improvement pressure and quality improvements, and they have done a great job in responding to that.

It has involved working differently for all of us, right through the organisation . AI means that there is more of that to come —w e have just rolled out Copilot to the entire organisation. Everyone has been traine d and w e are now implementing that . W e have more specific audit tools coming through. In the meantime, w e are trying to judge how quickly the organisation can absorb that change and produce high-quality work. I think the answer is t o some extent, but I would not like to try to spend a very large amount of money in one year and expect to be able to demonstrate value for money as a result.

To reinforce that point, a small amount of the headcount growth that you cited in the last year was actually to build up some of our digital capability to deliver our digital strategy, and also to ensure that we were investing proportionately in cyber-security and information security, which the Comm ission has asked us about in the past. Earlier this month, our first chief digital and information officer joined us to help augment those skills, so that we can pursue the opportunities that, as Gareth says, are increasingly available to us.

Q16 This year, you have had 19 members of staff leave, with an average exit package of £57,000. The previous year, it was eight, with an average of £30,000. That might just be because it is more senior people who are being let go. Is that what has happened? How do you look at it from a value - for - money point of view?

T his year, for the first time in a number of years, we ran a voluntary exit scheme, and 17 exit packages were agreed. This was very much as we were coming to the end of the first year of the delivery of our new strategy, and it was to make sure we have the skills mix that we need to deliver that strategy. It also helped us manage our overall cost base. We had not run a scheme of that nature for some time. The numbers in previous years were more ad hoc agreements relating to unique circumstances.
The payback on that is less than a year.

Q17 On the staff turnover, you were below target this year, as you were last year. Would you like to explain to us what is going on there? You told us last year that too low a staff turnover could create budgetary pressures and blockages and obviously prevent promotion opportunities. Please address that.

That is a continuing situation. It is a better problem to have than the opposite. A few years ago, as the private sector was gearing up to come out of the pandemic, we had the opposite, but it is a problem for us if turnover is too far below our assumptions for exactly the reasons that you highlight: opportunities come up too slowly, and that creates a build-up of frustration.

Q18 It could also paint a picture of an organisation in which people are settled in a role, are going through the motions, are not being challenged and do not aspire to the sort of up-and-out culture that exists elsewhere. How do you ensure that that does not happen and that you maintain high-performance levels?

Partly through the scheme that Rebecca described, and partly through performance management. We have a big focus on high-quality performance management. Obviously, a voluntary exit scheme is one thing, and day-to-day good management of performance to make sure we are getting what we need out of our colleagues is another. Learning and development is the third leg.
Q19 How would you evidence the effectiveness of that to us?

We have a caseload of active performance management cases at any one time. It would not be appropriate to talk about that in this setting but, if you are interested in more detail, we can provide that out of the public session.

We take that really seriously. We have changed our performance management arrangements so that we have a clearer allocation of management responsibility. That is coming through this year. We also have a lot of training for people to make sure they are good at handling difficult cases. Our HR team has done a great job in modernising our processes around that and making sure that we are not in the position that you describe.

The results of our work show that we are not a coasting organisation. We are improving in all our core areas and making a really big impact, and that is down to the performance of all the individuals in the organisation. The evidence suggests we are making a good job of that, but you are right that it is more difficult when we do not have healthy levels of natural turnover. We are always looking at how to manage that.

The impact of the strategy has been huge, in terms of a culture change in the organisation, because every single member of staff is now really aware that their job is not just to produce a piece of work, to complete an audit, to do a value-for-money study or to play a part in a study; it is actually to promote more impactful outcomes themselves.

In the last two or three years, I have seen huge amounts of energy unleashed internally, with staff feeling incredibly motivated by this much stronger focus on impact, which plays into the HR processes, performance management and all the rest of it. People are working really hard and in a really focused way to deliver impacts and outcomes that are more stretching than simply doing a job.
Thank you very much.

Q20 May I follow up on John’s questions? “AI efficiency” can sometimes be a euphemism for shedding staff, particularly at the lower levels. On the other hand, you might need fewer staff at the lower levels—planning the audit, or whatever it happens to be—but at least as many, or possibly more, at the higher levels. Is that what is happening in your organisation?

Not yet. There has been a very slight impact on our entry-level recruitment, but it is not significant. We are in conversation with the big firms in the same sort of business as us, and it is very interesting to hear their reflections on the same question. They are saying, “ We are not actually backing away from graduate recruitment and school leaver recruitment. We think those people will be doing different things in the future, and we are emphasising digital skills from the outset, not just accountancy training.” It is changing the way in which people are trained, and their early career experience will be different. In my day, I remember standing by the photocopier, thinking, “Why did I do all of that studying at university to stand by the photocopier?” That kind of work is now disappearing from audits, so junior staff are getting earlier engagement with some of the more judgmental bits of the work.

I think all professions are grappling with this question: how do we make sure that people get first-hand experience of the nuts and bolts of this job, so that they can make good judgments when they become managers? That just means a different way of training them and giving them early work experience. In numbers terms, we are actually continuing with 55 graduate recruits this year, which is similar to last year—it has not affected that number yet.

Q21 Despite significant investment in technology and, as we have said, higher staff numbers, you again failed to hit your target of certifying 70% of audits before the summer recess. Do you want to comment on why?
In summer 2025, which is the period covered by this Report, we did not. That was a step up from the previous year, but we hit some barriers in that summer to hitting the target.

We redoubled our efforts and, since we published this annual report and accounts, we have had the summer recess for 2026, and I am pleased to say that we actually achieved 70% this year. With this long haul back to having a timely set of accounts, from the disruption caused by the pandemic, we are getting close to where we want to be.

It is not just 70% by this summer; we are also expecting to have more than 90% finished by the end of this month, which is a big step forward from previous years. Our target next year will be 70% by the summer and 100% by the end of October. To me, that has the accountability framework for accounts into the right position for central Government, and I will be very pleased if we are in that position this time next year.

Again, I just want to pay tribute to the staff who delivered that. That is a lot of really complex work all done by the summer recess, less than four months after the year end to which these accounts relate, and that is a real achievement. There were Departments that were pre-recess for the first time in several years, including DEFRA and DESNZ, and the MOD recovered from the severe problems that it had the previous year, which were linked to the Afghan resettlement scheme and missing provisions. The MOD was on time and unqualified this year, which was a significant achievement for that Department.

This really matters. We are talking about a lot of public money being properly accounted for, on time. Apart from anything else, it frees up the finance teams in those organisations to do what they should be doing: adding value to the financial planning of that Department, not still completing the accounts months and months after the year ends. All ways around that is real progress.
Q22 You said that you are on target for 90% at the end of October, so not complete. When are you hoping to have all those 2025-26 audits complete?

Soon after the end of October. The purpose of setting this firm deadline at the end of October for everything, which will be next year’s target, is that it is a deliberate message to the small number that have drifted on towards the end of the calendar year. In some cases, they will have got used to a particular rhythm, and in a small organisation that takes some resource to shift. We are now working with them to say, “Okay, this is now the expectation, and Treasury is also taking the same line.” What does that mean for every organisation? It means moving its audit committee dates and releasing some resource to get this thing done in a more timely way. I will be very pleased if we hit those deadlines for next summer.

Q23 A positive is that 83% of your value for money reports met internal standards, which is significantly higher than the 70% target, and higher than the corresponding scores for financial audit, as we have discussed. The question on my sheet asks why do MPs and senior officials—though not necessarily this MP, by the way—routinely score the quality of your value for money work lower than financial audit?

Obviously, we are asking those questions to MPs as a whole, not just the ones who engage with our work directly through PAC and other Committees. Actually, the numbers are not bad—it is not as if they are poor. Of course, what they mean by “quality” is very different to the technical assessments of quality that we are measuring through the rest of our processes. Those are different angles on the quality question —all of them valid. That is why we have them all in here as performance indicators.

We want to drive that up for MPs as a whole. We are trying to increase awareness of our work. We have a fortnightly newsletter to MPs, which is increasingly well used. We are also targeting researchers and MPs offices because we know how busy MPs are and how difficult it is to get through a typical MP’s inbox. We are working hard with the staff side as well to make sure that they pick things out from the rest of the spam that they are otherwise engaging with and say, “Actually, this one is worth highlighting.” We use this to challenge ourselves and ask how we can drive these numbers up and get better results.
Q24 So you do not feel that, as was suggested, value for money and quality standards are lower compared to financial audits, just that it is the perception?
No.

Q25 This will be my last question. The proportion of your expenditure on financial audits has increased compared with last year, meaning proportionally less is now spent on value for money work. Is there a risk of financial audit work becoming too much of a focus?

It is important to bear in mind some of the things Gareth said earlier about how our financial audit portfolio has grown over a number of years. That is really the driver of the increase in the headcount and expenditure there. To put some numbers around that, back in 2017-18, we certified 370 accounts. In the year that we are looking at now, that number is 413. Within that there is quite a variation and some of those are quite significant endeavours. It is not that the expenditure on value for money has gone down; it is the proportions. However, we are keen to make sure that we continue to invest in our value for money work. In the current year we have particularly put resources aside to modernise our reporting and how it looks on our website as an example of that continued investment.

Q26 Apologies for my late arrival. On risk reporting, you changed the number of principal risks that you report against this year. It was previously 24 and is now nine. That is to align with the strategy. However, does that mean that there is a lower level of detail in your risk management processes?

It certainly does not mean that there is a lower level of detail in our overall risk management processes. What it does mean is that the way we are looking at risk is a bit more focused at the executive team and board level. As well as making sure that our risk framework aligned with our strategy, we also refreshed our framework to make sure we were in line with best practice.

We adopted a framework whereby we categorise the principal risks, those that we think have the greatest impact on our strategic performance and reputation. Underneath that there are a series of component risks, broadly the same number that we had before, which feed into that. That is supported by a rigorous bottom-up risk assessment process with business owners throughout the business so that we are looking at a comprehensive picture at the executive team.
Q27 This year you have rated the risks of poor service delivery and a failure to deliver impact as areas of concern above the target level in your risk rating. Why is that?

In terms of impact, this was partly a response to the strategy and the fact that we have upped our ambition in terms of the impact that we are looking to achieve, specifically the ambitions that we have set to positively influence productivity, resilience and financial management in government.

We do not want to be complacent. We have been using that to challenge ourselves, and the board have very much been challenging us by asking if we are doing as much of that as the strategy indicates that we should. In response we have a new parliamentary engagement plan and have also refreshed our communications road map. We also think very deeply about the impact that we are looking to achieve at the point at which we are commissioning our VFM programmes.

In terms of service delivery, this connects back principally to making sure that we are achieving those ambitions that Gareth has already spoken about in terms of improving the timeliness of our financial audit work. This year, we have met the 70% target pre-recess, but it will be a continued focus in the coming years.
Q28 So you are expecting to see the risk analysis of your failure to deliver impact improve with your new approach to engaging MPs through our inboxes?
It should do. The poor service delivery one has already improved; we should be reporting an improved position in next year’s Annual Report and accounts.

Q29 Fantastic. In last year’s Report you highlighted sickness absence, mental health and wellbeing as principal risks to the National Audit Office, but they do not feature this year as principal risks of concern. What has changed?

Partly, they are risks that would now sit as component risks and would feed into PR2: “Failure to maintain an open and inclusive culture that supports engaged, motivated and high-performing people and teams”.
You are doing very well on that this year.

It is all the things that Gareth has spoken about, such as the focus on performance management and our wellbeing strategy. Our sickness absence has continued to fall almost month on month. We are now down at, I think, about 5.2 days per FTE, which is a very strong position and an indication of an organisation that is thriving, rather than one that is perhaps stagnant.

Q30 Before we finish, Gareth, several people have approached me about the future accountability of Governments for inquiries and the recommendations of those inquiries. I know that you may have had a number of conversations with people.

I declare my interest: I am chair of the all-party parliamentary group on haemophilia and contaminated blood. The duty of candour, accountability, and Sir Brian Langstaff’s report are dear to my heart. The suggestion has been that the National Audit Office is the place where that should sit: it should hold the Government to account for how they respond to inquiry recommendations. Do you have any advice, or a view on that debate?

As you say, we have been approached by Government on exactly that point: the strong level of dissatisfaction in Parliament about the rigour with which public inquiry recommendations are followed up, and whether they have been implemented in the way that was intended when the recommendations were made.

The most recent example is the Thirlwall inquiry into the Lucy Letby case—that appalling set of circumstances up in Cheshire. The judge in that case made a specific recommendation that the NAO should follow up NHS-related inquiries because they were so concerned that previous recommendations had not been implemented at the trust in question and could have helped to prevent the terrible events there. I therefore completely understand the seriousness of the issue and the public interest in improving the position.

The point that I have made to Government is that that needs to be really carefully thought through, because the NAO cannot become part of the Government’s own system for managing those risks. We can stand outside that system and audit it, as we do with other areas of public expenditure. Getting the design of that right is absolutely crucial. I do not think that at the moment Government have a reliable system for monitoring the implementation of public inquiry recommendations. That problem needs to be fixed first, then it would be legitimate to ask if the NAO can provide assurance to Parliament on whether that system is working effectively. I am obviously prepared to engage on that.

We have a strong sense that we must not allow our mission to creep, and must absolutely hold on to our mission to support Parliament in scrutinising public expenditure. That is what the NAO is for. You can make a case that this is a legitimate extension of that but it needs to be carefully grounded in the governance structure that I have mentioned so that we are not being drawn into something of which we should be independent.

Of course, you can be so pure that you are ineffective—I am aware of that risk as well—but those are the issues that we have suggested that we work through with Government before they are taken any further. It is crucial to be clear where the parliamentary audience for that question is, because otherwise we cannot deliver our mission of supporting Parliament and helping to make Government more accountable.

Q31 It strikes me, when I look at the recommendations of those inquiries, that they are not just about the financial trail or value for money. There are things that go beyond that, which are not the responsibility of the National Audit Office.

P articularly if they are issues of clinical practice, for example, which are more for a specialist inspectorate than for the NAO. However, that makes the point that if the question is about whether the Government Department responsible can evidence that these recommendations have been satisfactorily implemented . T he evidence base for that would be the reports of inspectorates saying, “Yes, we ’re satisfied that clinical practice has changed in the way intended. Here’s the evidence.” We will be reporting one layer up from that: “D oes the Government have the evidence to show that these recommendations have been satisfactorily implemented? ” At the moment, I have not seen a framework in place to deliver that evidence base. In that case, that would be something the NAO could add value to. What we cannot do is go in and give a properly informed judgment on whether clinical practice has changed in every NHS trust in the country.

Q32 I declare an interest in the Infected Blood Compensation Authority, because I was the Minister responsible for passing the legislation to set it up. I t was set up remotely from any Government Department, at the insistence and request of many victims. However, the point that the Chair makes is a reasonable one.

We have legislated with the expectation of certain outcomes and then, because it is so independent of the Department of Health or the Cabinet Office or whatever, we are, two years later, in a situation where, as parliamentarians, we apparently cannot achieve any accountability. I think what you are saying is that it is quite delicate and difficult for you to insert yourself into that audit process if the entity is remote from any one Department and just dependent on legislation. Is that correct?

Not quite. First, we are the auditor of the Infected Blood Compensation Authority, and we qualified its accounts in the first year because the estimate of the liability was patchy. That has improved significantly for this summer ; it is in a much better position . So the f inancial audit is clear.

We did actually report on its performance in implementing its responsibilities for paying compensation, as part of the report that the Public Accounts Committee took as a basis for two separate evidence sessions earlier this year—a really successful week, I think, for the Committee. One session had witnesses from IBCA itself, the Post Office, the military veterans scheme and the Windrush scheme, so we had four schemes accountable to Parliament for their performance in paying compensation. It was informed by a session with representatives of the victims in each case beforehand.

The existing framework can cope with holding public bodies to account, including independent public bodies of that kind. This is more the technical question of the public inquiry that gave rise to that: have its recommendations all been satisfactorily implemented?

Q33 Is it not a matter for the Government of the day to discern what they think is the appropriate response to an inquiry ? How could you possibly be holding them to account for that? It is, in a sense, the Government’s judgment—you might dispute it, whichever Government it is—but you are there to audit what they have said they will do with the report.

The proposal would be that we would not get involved in how the Government should respond to an inquiry. It would be to take the agreed action plan once the Government had responded and ask, “H ave the Government done what they said they would do? ”

Exactly. We are going to be discussing this later this year, so this is actually a really helpful input. We are talking, as much as anything, I think, about a third line of defence, meaning that we are not actually involved in the mechanics of the rights and wrongs of particular recommendations, but in whether they have been implemented. If we were to consider this the right thing to do, we would be extremely careful about the terms and conditions of any engagement. We do think, however, that it is something important for us to consider.

Q34 In something like that, there was an iterative process through statutory instruments, after conversations with the victims, on changing the parameters of the scheme to reflect the needs of different cohorts. To have a coherent single point of reference to audit would be quite challenging until the scheme is fully embedded, which has only happened relatively recently.

It is. I understand the impetus behind this: it is very frustrating to see public inquiry recommendations that could have headed off subsequent problems and were not implemented. I understand the frustration, but this discussion has illustrated the complexity of it.

The C&AG was kind enough to mention the PAC inquiry into this matter. Among the four groups that we had in front of us and a lot of the other witnesses, the feeling was very much that Government Departments that caused the injury in the first place should not be setting up a scheme to compensate the victims.

We have not had a response from the Government yet, but in the hearing we heard that there should be some form of independent standing body so that when the next scandal comes along—you mentioned one that has come along, C&AG—it is there to draw on all the experience from previous schemes that went wrong and to produce some common standards across the new schemes. It would try to resolve the thing as quickly and as litigation-free as possible so that victims can get their compensation quickly and fairly.

It is not just about compensation; it is about justice, which encompasses a wider range of issues, although compensation is at the heart of it. That is absolutely right. That is my understanding of where we need to get to. What happens is that the Government accept the recommendations of inquiries, but no one holds them to account for doing anything about that and for how they are followed through and implemented.

There needs to be an independent body—the equivalent to a body like the NAO—that has the responsibility and can hold the Government to account. It would literally pick up responsibility for the inquiry’s recommendations being taken forward, independently of Government. That is where I think we need to go. I know that others disagree and think it should be the Select Committees, but I am not convinced that they have the resources to do that.

Q35 It would be possible, once the standing committee had established the terms of an inquiry and the Government had accepted the terms—the Government always have to accept them, because they have to pay in the end—for you to become the auditor of that scheme, Gareth. I do not want to put work in your way, but these are going to be fairly large matters, because the Government will deal with small matters in another way.

We do audit all the compensation schemes, so that is definitely covered. As this discussion shows, this is a question for the Government, really. How does the Government demonstrate that it has a grip on the public inquiry recommendations that it has agreed to implement? How is it accountable to Parliament for doing that? We could help with the debate because we have some practical experience, but in the end it is for Parliament and the Government to come to a view. How do we make sure we have better accountability than we currently do for acting on these recommendations?
The issue in this case is: how can you be accountable for the delivery of something that you are asked to hand off to an independent entity?

Q36 Well, as chair of the APPG, I might question just how independent IBCA is, given some of the things that are in the path of dealing with the claims that are currently waiting to be finalised. We will not go down that rabbit hole right now. Thank you very much for your answers. I think this debate is going to be very important, so I appreciate you giving your time to answer our questions.

Before we conclude, Dame Fiona, this is your last Annual Report and accounts session with the Commission as chair of the NAO board. Looking back on your six years as chair, how do you think the relationship between the NAO and Parliament has evolved, if at all?

Thank you for the opportunity to speak briefly. It has been six fascinating and quite tumultuous years. I came in when covid was in full spate. We have had the Brexit settlement since then, and we have seen a huge churn in Prime Ministers and the permanent secretaries with whom we deal quite regularly. There have also been global uncertainties affecting how people feel about public expenditure.

Through that period, we have built an ever stronger, ever more purposeful and ever more effective NAO, and I am really proud of that. I am particularly proud of our strategy. When I came in it was very clear that the role of chair of the NAO is unusual: it is very strategic in focus, but fortunately I love strategy so that has suited me well. Actually, the strategy that we are discussing the first year of today is very different. We call it “Trust, Value, Impact”.

It is about using every ounce of our energy not only to audit and to do a series of studies on Government expenditure but to help the Government to do a better job. I think we have demonstrated, in many ways, how that has liberated the organisation’s potential and actually has begun to lead—we are being deliberately modest about what we have done so far in setting ambitious objectives—to our two strategic outcomes of greater productivity and resilience in public services, and improved financial management in Government. I think both of those are absolutely critical to our role.

Briefly, on audit, I think we have seen real improvements in quality—on which you have challenged and tested us each year—through wise investment in people, in technology and in culture change. We are never going to be complacent about audit quality but we are increasingly confident that we can hold to that level of sustained quality. There has been an interesting—for me—creative shift between audit as a compliance tool, where you simply have to do it, to using audit as a way of improving insight and analysis of where the money goes in order to do a better job. I think that is a really interesting development and there is more to come.

Bringing in the train operating companies is a good example of that. We are not just auditing the TOCs; we are drawing insights and learning from across different companies in order to demonstrate how they could collectively be more effective and do a better job. Of course, we have talked today about the Local Audit Office and improving audit at the local level, which has been an absolutely shaming gap in recent years. Now at last, though it will take time, we can see real improvements.

On value for money, we have had similar heart-searching discussions about making best use of our capabilities in those areas. There has been an ever more strategic approach to the value for money studies that we do. We are obviously very keen to ensure that the Public Accounts Committee has the reports that it needs and values from us, but it has been exciting to see the development of more cross-Government studies and whole-system approaches. I was particularly taken by the asylum report, which I think is a model for future systems that cross departmental boundaries. They are quite difficult for Government to track but we can really be helpful in that respect.

We are just beginning our new studies of particular initiatives of Government Departments, for example the one on the Ministry of Justice’s use of AI to ensure that the records that need to be produced in court are both present and correct. That is a wonderful example of a very helpful tool that I think will really benefit Departments. In all those areas we have made real progress. Of course, there is also now the new approach to the scrutiny of sensitive defence expenditure, which I think is a major step forward.

You asked me to speak about challenges for the future and since we have already discussed them today I can be very brief. One is clearly AI. We are determined—internally, and in our audit of Government Departments, as well as in our value for money studies—to watch both the potential of and the need for clear guardrails on AI. I am not saying anything original or new there. It is a vital tool—one that is completely with us and impossible to ignore—but it has to be carefully managed and observed. A second challenge is devolution. We spoke about that at some length this afternoon. It is potentially huge, and we can play a very helpful role in terms of both the devolution framework and our work with the Local Audit Office. Devolution will not work unless we can assess whether it is working. There will be huge questions about postcode lotteries and different outcomes in different parts of the country, but we are well placed to support the Local Audit Office, as well as doing our own work to ensure that the parliamentary accountability is clear and well judged.

Finally, a personal plea from me: I hope that we are entering a slightly more stable period, simply because some of the issues that we know are really important long-term issues have been squeezed out by short-term crises. There is an opportunity to use our expertise, and our good and strong strategy to move forward on important issues such as climate change, food security, public health and social care—there are so many areas. Taking a longer-term view is going to be really important.

That is my tuppence-worth as I approach the end of a job that I have really enjoyed. I am hugely grateful to my board, to Gareth and the executive team, and in fact to all the staff at the NAO. They are an amazing bunch of very committed, very bright, very dedicated people. We are extremely lucky to have them working so hard to ensure that Parliament has the assurances that it needs. Thank you.

Thank you. I think you are with us on one more occasion, when we will say a fond farewell and thank you for everything you have done, but certainly, as you have just set out, the NAO has moved forwards considerably under your chairpersonship.
It is a collective progress but thank you.
I am sure it is, but thank you for what you have done. It is a pleasure to have worked with you. That concludes today’s evidence session. Thank you all for coming along this afternoon.

sessions.w: Markos Zachariadis (University of Manchester); Hilary J. Allen (American University Washington College of Law)

segs.tx: Financial Services Regulation Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Regulatory sandboxes in financial services
Wednesday 21 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Noakes (The Chair); Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted; Lord Davies of Brixton; Baroness Donaghy; Lord Griffiths of Fforestfach; Lord Hill of Oareford; Lord Hollick; Lord Lilley; Lord Sharkey; Lord Turnbull; Lord Vaux of Harrowden.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 - 11
Witnesses

Professor Markos Zachariadis, Professor and Chair in Financial Technology and Information Systems, University of Manchester; Professor Hilary Allen, Professor of Law, American University Washington College of Law.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Professor Markos Zachariadis and Professor Hilary Allen.

Q1 The Chair: Welcome to today’s meeting, which is the first oral session as part of the committee’s inquiry into regulatory sandboxes. Thank you to Professor Allen and Professor Zachariadis for attending. The session is open to the public. It is broadcast live and is subsequently accessible via the parliamentary website. A verbatim transcript will be taken of the evidence and will be put on the parliamentary website.

Before we get going, I need to declare my interests, which are that I hold investments in a number of listed financial services companies that could be affected by regulatory sandboxes. I invite colleagues, the first time that they speak in this inquiry, to declare any interests themselves.
Could I ask each of you to introduce yourselves? We will be going directly into questions after that. Professor Zachariadis, could you just introduce yourself to the committee for the record?

Yes. It is a pleasure to be here. I am an academic. I work at the University of Manchester at the moment. My full title is professor in financial technology and information systems, but my background by training is in the economics of innovation. I did my PhD at the London School of Economics a couple of decades ago. Since then, I have worked at different universities, including the University of Cambridge, Warwick Business School, and now the University of Manchester at the Alliance Manchester Business School.

In terms of my research, I should also give you a bit of a perspective on why I am doing what I am doing. I have always researched the economics of innovation, and of data innovation in particular, within financial services. That is the single thing that I have been looking at. Within that, we aim to understand a bit more the role of technology in changing business models and operational models at the firm level, the overall market architecture at the industry level, and the benefits that we get in terms of productivity, but also consumer welfare and so forth, at the economy level.

I have done multiple studies that have looked at many different technologies. Regulatory sandboxes are one of the devices that I have been looking at carefully, because they are very closely aligned with technological development in the sector. We have a minor research paper out called “ FinTech Regulatory Sandboxes: When Regulation Meets Innovation ” , which touches upon many of the questions that have been shared in advance of this particular hearing. That is my introduction.
The Chair: Thank you. Professor Allen, could you just introduce yourself for the committee?

Yes, sure. I very much appreciate the opportunity to be here. I am a professor of law at the American University Washington College of Law in the United States. I have been looking at financial regulation globally for my entire academic career, with a particular focus in the last decade on the regulation of fintech. As part of that, I have authored four papers on regulatory sandboxes, which I believe you have access to, and I look forward to your questions.

The Chair: Thank you very much. If we could start with a general background question, could each of you outline what you see as the role of a regulatory sandbox in the context of financial services? What are they for?

One could put a definition on them, even though I have to say that definitions have been evolving, because the role of the different sandboxes that we have observed around the world has changed. Even in some cases, their initial intention has been quite different. By and large, a regulatory sandbox is a controlled environment in which firms, particularly financial technology firms, but also incumbent financial institutions and payment infrastructures, can test innovative financial products, services, technologies, or even business models with near real or simulated users, under the supervision of financial regulators. That is the broader definition, if you like.
I mentioned that there are different kinds of sandboxes. I do not know whether you want me to go into those now.
The Chair: Yes, why not.

One of the reasons that we did the paper that we co-authored with colleagues from the University of Manchester at that time is that regulatory sandboxes tend to do two things as devices. The first is to act as learning devices, which are then used by regulators, but also by the firms that participated within the sandbox, to learn more about the regulation as well as how to regulate.

They also act as regulatory devices. A stricter definition of the purpose or aim of the regulatory sandbox is , basically, to make sure that the firms that are part of the regulatory sandbox cohort comply with the existing regulations. It is about making sure that there is control and that existing regulations are being imposed on newly founded firms, which often do not necessarily have enough knowledge to do so. There is a lot more to it, but perhaps I can pass on to Professor Allen.

I agree that these regulatory sandboxes vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction . They have been adopted all over the world at this point, following the FCA’s lead. There is an implicit justification that is rarely stated for them, but is very much an important part of the appeal, which is as a signalling device. It is supposed to signal that a jurisdiction is , in essence, open to fintech business. There is that signalling aspect, but the more stated goals—and this is a riff on what you have just heard—are, first, an opportunity for regulatory learning about new technologies, and, secondly, a way of reducing regulatory barriers to entry in order to allow fintech firms to thrive. Those are the two more common stated justifications for adopting sandboxes.
The Chair: Excellent, that is a good background.

Q2 I am interested in how the effects of these sandboxes are to be evaluated and measured. I am particularly interested in the absence of any counterfactuals. How is it that the operators decide whether the outcomes are beneficial? When it comes to outcomes, I am also interested in how they are divided . Who typically benefits from these? There is also the question of whether these things are intrinsically unfair.

I am happy to take this question because it segues into a lot of the concerns that I have over the business model. I should say that I have been looking at these business models since , basically, their inception. My concerns about them have deepened over time, for the reasons that you have articulated. Basically, when we are judging the these sandboxes, the empirical literature on this generally focuses on whether the innovators have been able to access financing and to patent things.

If you look at the FCA’s early report card for its sandbox, it was really also focused on how the innovators are experiencing these sandboxes. I do not think that that should be our metric of judging the success of these sandboxes. We should be judging them, first of all, on whether that innovation is broadly socially beneficial. There is a broad conversation to be had about whether fintech innovation is beneficial for the public at least.

I should concede here that most of my experience on this issue is restricted to the United States, but most of the fintech business models that we see are really more about avoiding regulation as their secret sauce rather than technological innovation. A lot of those products are quite predatory in many respects, so I do not think that we should assume that fintech innovation is necessarily socially beneficial.

As I said up front, the other thing that these are supposed to do is to inform regulatory learning. There are a number of reasons why that goal is circumscribed . One is that sandboxes put regulators in a really unusual position of being a cheerleader , in essence, for the firms that they have picked to participate in the sandbox. First of all, that is conducive to cognitive capture. It is not surprising if regulators come to identify more with their firms than anything else. It also prevents important regulatory knowledge sharing among other jurisdictions , because there is this sense of wanting “our sandbox firm” to do better than other sandbox firms.

I could go on, but the things that we should be judging these sandboxes on are how they are improving regulatory learning and at what cost, because they are very expensive to deploy, as well as whether the public is benefiting from this fintech innovation. Instead, they are largely judged from the perspective of the innovators themselves.

I would agree. If you look at the FCA’s original sandbox, which was launched a few years back, in 2016, the aims were to reduce the time and cost of bringing innovation and innovative financial products to market, to facilitate access to finance for innovative firms, which is very important for innovation to flourish, and to enable more products.

Perhaps the most important pillar for that would be the last one, which would be to improve consumer outcomes by encouraging beneficial innovation and competition. Sadly, for the last pillar, we do not have enough information that this has been done at least in the way that people thought that it would.

We do have some information. There is existing research. There is one paper in particular that was done by some colleagues at the Bank for International Settlements and published in a finance journal a couple of years ago. Sadly, we wanted to do something very similar , but they beat us to it. That paper showed that firms that participated within the regulatory sandbox enjoyed better access to finance because of the signal effect that Professor Allen mentioned. These firms had adequate access to how to meet regulatory standards and comply with regulation. The fact that they were part of the regulatory sandbox signalled to investors that they could be more confident with their investment.

There is a bit of correlation, although they had access only to the information that the FCA published online, which included the fintechs that took part in the regulatory sandbox, and not the ones that applied but did not get accepted. There is a sample selection bias, which, as per the economics literature, can skew your results.

From the way that they did the research and similar pieces around the world in different sandboxes, it is fair to say that participating in the regulatory sandbox does increase access to finance for those firms, hence the innovative solutions being out there a bit quicker.

Of course, consumer welfare and benefits for consumers have not been assessed adequately. As an economist, but also as a researcher, it is quite a tricky thing to do. Nevertheless, that does not mean that we should not take future steps in trying to assess that, not just for regulatory sandboxes but for fintech innovation in general and those regulations that seem to be a bit more relaxed for new and innovative solutions coming to the market.
I am just curious as to why there are no agreed metrics for measuring the success of these things, which have been around for a long time.

There are metrics. Competition, for example, is one thing that one can try to assess. Particularly when it comes to the fintech space, we are trying to do something similar, not for the regulatory sandboxes but for regulations that encourage more innovation, such as open banking, open finance, or open data within financial services. There is a lack of data that we can access to try to establish that. The FCA sits on this data and I have urged it before to share a bit more with us in a safe way, so that we can do some of the independent studies that would try to measure these things. That has not happened yet. We are constantly in conversation with the FCA and would love to collaborate with it in order to do this research and assessment.
I imagine that these processes are quite expensive. Does that not create an obvious bias against very small firms wanting to take advantage of them?

Running the regulatory sandbox is expensive. For those who take part, there is the potential for some residual benefits, but, for those who do not, that could be unfair or skewed to the benefit of the ones who do. That is one argument that people have mentioned before, but I am not sure it is strong enough to say that we should not have any regulatory sandbox at all. It might be a good argument to tell the regulator to perhaps be more transparent in the way that it then publishes the benefits for those firms that take part in the regulatory sandbox, so that other firms can learn from it. There is definitely room for improvement, but not necessarily to justify that there should not be any regulatory sandbox at all. That would be a bit far-fetched.

Q3 AI is becoming increasingly important in helping consumers understand financial products, find and locate suppliers, and possibly make a choice between one supplier and another. To what extent can sandboxes help to decide on how best that should be regulated ? You made a comment, Professor Allen, about avoiding regulation. It is fair to say that AI is rather shy of being regulated , so how does the sandbox help us to solve that problem?

One of the challenges with a sandbox is that it is supposed to be a temporary thing. There is a period within which there is less risk of enforcement and some of the regulatory barriers to entry are brought down. That is supposed to be a finite period for the participants to learn how to operate in a regulated environment, and for the regulators to learn how to regulate going forward. That is the idea.

Some experience with the Canadian securities regulators is very important to acknowledge here. The challenge is that often, when you get to the end of that temporary period, the firm is in no better position to comply with regulation than it was before. The regulator is then faced with a very difficult decision: “Do we extend indefinitely the exemptions that we gave or do we shut the business down?”

You probably will not be surprised to hear that what happened in Canada, with a lot of the dispensations that were given to crypto firms, is that they were allowed to continue on their exemptive basis indefinitely, because the regulators did not want to shut them down. That is problematic for a number of reasons, one of which is that, because the conditions within a sandbox are bespoke to the individual firm, you have different firms operating in different legal environments in perpetuity.

Generally speaking, I am very concerned about the sandbox being the way in which AI regulation is formulated . I would say that you can live without sandboxes quite easily, and I think you should, for a number of reasons. First, when you have a sandbox out there, what it says to firms is, “ Don’t bother trying to comply with the laws. We have acknowledged that the laws aren’t right for you. Come on in; the water’s fine ”. If the decision is that the laws are not fit for purpose, that can be done through waivers and things that apply across the board, and then you avoid the issue of picking winners.

I am very concerned about sandboxes being the space in which AI regulation is negotiated , in large part because there is no public participation in that space. This is a bespoke negotiation , in essence, between the firm and the regulator. The firm often touts its superior technological expertise and says, “You don’t really know what’s going on here. Let me tell you how we should be regulated ”, and the public has no voice in that process. This is a phenomenon that I am quite concerned about .
The example that you have given in Canada is that , in essence, something that possibly should be regulated is, in fact, being whitewashed , because it is allowed to continue.

Yes, because it is very difficult to put regulators in a position where, in essence, they have to perform as executioner for a business model that is not able to comply with the full panoply of regulations, and it is not surprising that they chose not to perform that role as executioner.
Do you share those concerns, Professor Zachariadis?

I do. They are all valid. Having said that, there is still a way for regulatory sandboxes to exist within that context. One can develop certain safeguards, but also a framework that will ensure that the expectations for having relaxed regulations in perpetuity, for example, would not exist. It would also make sure that there is the right environment for organisations to test their products, but within existing regulatory frameworks, so that they do not have issues or challenges in complying with future regulation when they take their products to market.

There are a few things that one can do to accommodate that. My concern is mostly around the nature of artificial intelligence as a technology that is qualitatively quite different from other innovations. Regulatory sandboxes tend to be quite contextual, so you try your products based on a very particular number of users. Artificial intelligence, particularly GenAI, relies more on open systems, where a lot of data comes from different sources, basically, which cannot necessarily be controlled within the regulatory sandbox environment. In that case, maybe different techniques should be implemented to be able to understand how AI can be utilised within financial services in a more rigorous but also safer way.
Q4 I ought to declare an interest as chairman of ICE Futures Europe and an adviser to Santander and Visa Europe, which could, theoretically, pop into a sandbox one day.

In 2016, we start with the FCA doing the first sandbox, and then a number of jurisdictions have followed suit. Do you see any patterns or trends in different jurisdictions across the world that are worth bringing to our attention?

Something that I already mentioned was that, implicitly, a lot of these jurisdictions have been adopting regulatory sandboxes as a signalling device to say, “We are welcoming fintech businesses ”. A challenge with that is that, as more jurisdictions opt into it, that delivers diminishing marginal returns. Some of the reporting that has been done at the international level suggests a little bit of buyer’s remorse.

While this is not true of the UK, there was, in many jurisdictions , a failure to appreciate how expensive these regulatory sandboxes are to adopt. It was thought of as, “We can just say that we will have a sandbox, and that will be enough to attract new business”, but they are, in fact, quite expensive to implement, because the “je ne sais quoi” of these is a lot of regulatory handholding. Some of the research that has been done says that, if you do not have that regulatory handholding, the firms are less likely to succeed. It is not just the dispensations from law that help, but that guidance, which is expensive.

We have definitely seen some buyer’s remorse. We have definitely seen diminishing marginal returns as more and more jurisdictions have tried to deploy sandboxes. The UK, as first mover in this space, is somewhat immune from those concerns, but fintech sandboxes had lost some of their lustre around the world. The previous question was about AI, and we are seeing a resurgence of interest in regulatory sandboxes being the solution for many of the AI issues, so it is time for a second round in that regard.

What we have witnessed is, in some cases, the development of regulatory sandboxes, particularly towards giving access to data. A natural following device would be the digital sandboxes that even the FCA has experimented with. That is giving access to consumer data coming from synthetic databases. That is one of the trends that we have identified, and that has been used as a vehicle by different regulators around the world as well.

The other thing is the openness and realisation that, of course, the financial system is an international system by default. You cannot really isolate a particular economy or system by itself, because there are a lot of international markets that big players within a particular economy want to be part of, such as financial markets and payment infrastructures.

We have seen a shift towards more international communication and trying to develop standards and innovations that are , basically, on a par with other countries and financial markets, and that dialogue is a very positive development. Some of these have managed to creep into regulatory sandboxes and become a bit more dominant as solutions or discussions.

I have a specific question for Professor Allen. You obviously do not like sandboxes, but what is your view of how one should—or perhaps you do not think that one should—encourage regulatory innovation? How does one get regulators to think differently about their job? Do you think that there are better ways of doing it than the sandbox?

I do, yes. A lot of the research has shown that, even if you are just trying to prioritise the innovating firms, the benefits come from that bespoke guidance rather than the regulatory dispensations. You can avoid much of the deregulatory effect and still preserve a lot of the regulatory learning by having regulators simply offer guidance to people. A term that you often hear, and one that the FCA uses, is “innovation hub ”. That kind of format, rather than a sandbox, achieves a lot of the goals without those negative possibilities of having firms locked in perpetuity into less regulated environments.

It may be that, through this process, regulators discover that there are regulations that do not work for a particular business model. I do not think that you should assume that all business models are valuable, but, if they do decide that that business model is so valuable that it should be allowed to flourish, and that there is some regulation that needs to be pared back in order to let that happen, they can issue a broad-based waiver rather than having bespoke waivers that favour the firms that are able to get into the sandbox.

I should note that a real challenge or problem with these sandboxes is that there are rarely any formal criteria for who will be accepted into the sandbox. You might have some high-level thoughts or criteria expressed, but, generally speaking , it is quite discretionary. Given that, as we have seen from the empirical research, admission to these sandboxes is very beneficial for the firms themselves and, therefore, exclusionary for firms that are not selected, broad-based waiver criteria are the way to go if it is concluded that regulation needs to be changed. As a regulator, you can figure out whether that regulation needs to be changed from your conversations with industry through an innovation hub.

Q5 What I am missing here are success stories. It has been around a decade. In that decade, has there been anyone who went into a sandbox and developed something that was very successful—lots of other people copied it; the regulator thought that some of the changes that they made were worth while —and who can say, “Look at me now. I’m a household name”? Where are these people who have been through this process, benefited from it, and demonstrated this idea that, by starting small and experimentally, you can go on to greater things? I have not heard of any case where we can now say, “Do you remember them 10 years ago? They were just a tiddly little company, and now they are this ”. Are there any?

To be fully transparent, in the research that we have done, we have not focused on one particular case study that went through the regulatory sandbox and observed it over time. My understanding is that, even if you look at only the UK FCA regulatory sandbox, there are quite a few big fintechs that are now quite reputable and that a lot of people use. Whether that can be attributed to them going through the regulatory sandbox is the question.

If we knew 100% for sure that that can be attributed to their experience that they received through the regulatory sandbox, and that the FCA perhaps changed or adapted regulations over time to be able to encourage this innovation, we would be much more confident and positive about the sandboxes, but that is a big question. How do we measure that? What kind of information and data are out there and can be used as research to prove that correlation and relationship?
Professor Allen, are you aware of anyone who says, “My first great break was the sandbox, and it went on from there”?

I am not. Quite a number of firms using the FCA sandbox are already established financial institutions, so it is not just new start-ups that are participating, but a lot of established financial institutions as well.

I want to also pick up on one of the points already raised. Sandboxes are challenging in an environment where cross-border operations are really the sine qua non of financial services. There have been attempts to create cross-border fintech sandboxes under the auspices of the Global Financial Innovation Network—GFIN—of which the FCA is a part. It tried, once, to run a global sandbox. One or two firms got through.

Ultimately, the challenge was harmonisation. Even within a global sandbox, you had to get multiple regulators to sign off on the firm and the conditions under which it would operate, which is just hard . That is the same challenge that you face with any kind of firm trying to operate cross-border, so I do not think that regulatory sandboxes really alleviate that challenge. There are limitations to what these sandboxes can achieve.

Q6 I started off with a triangle of concern. It is now an octagon. You have dealt with or mentioned some of the issues. Initially, my biggest concern is a lack of transparency, which, in a sense, you have both referenced, and then a lack of a public position in this, to which I could add a lack of parliamentary position. In this untransparent process, another is law modification, whether that comes about by individual or blanket waivers, or by law changes, possibly without going through the usual channels. A broadly cast waiver is one way of changing the law, if you can set it aside.

How do we deal with this? Transparency is meant to be disinfectant. How can we cope with this? What modifications can we make while not embedding model preferences? You mentioned patents in some jurisdictions . We do not have business model patents in Europe, but there could be other IP issues that are then embedded, in essence, in legislation, which just seems to end with an oxymoron. What would be your solutions?

It is for the FCA to think about this and to establish a framework of transparency that can share more information about the process and the lessons learned. I was looking for a report last night, and the only thing that I could find from the FCA was the lessons learned report that is already a decade or so old.

There needs to be a more systematic sharing of information and insight as to what is happening within the sandbox and what things other firms within the UK ecosystem, being a fintech or an incumbent financial institution that wants to experiment with new innovation, can learn from. That is one thing.

I am not sure how far you can go. I understand the concept of transparency, but I also respect what you mentioned around IP. There are a few things that the regulator cannot necessarily share because they relate, for example, to consumer behaviour or particular consumer information. These are data and information that cannot necessarily be shared with the public, even though we, as researchers, would like to have more access to data to be able to assess and understand the effectiveness of many of the things that the FCA does, or that regulators and policymakers put on the table, including existing regulations such as open banking. Again, there might be a way to try to establish more transparency within that context.

If you will humour me, I might answer your question at a 30,000-feet—sorry, I should use the metric system ; at a very high level. So much of what we are seeing right now is really a response to a societal conviction that we should never do anything to impede innovation. That is a paradox in many regards, because we are told that innovation is inevitable, and that there is nothing that regulation can do about it, but also that innovation is so valuable and fragile that regulation should never take any steps to impede it.

That is the ecosystem in which you have agencies such as the FCA trying to figure out what to do about fintech innovation. It is this real fear of never being, in any way, an impediment to that innovation, and so you get the result that you have articulated, where you have things being done informally and quickly in order to always accommodate innovation.

That often peels away laws that were passed , often by Parliament, and that had a decidedly harm-protective function. There is a very big conversation to be had , which goes far beyond sandboxes, about the degree to which long-standing legal precedents established by Parliament and the courts should be peeled away in order to accommodate innovation. If you have that reflexive fear of doing anything that could get in the way of innovation—to be clear, not all innovation is good, or good for the public—you are going to end up with suboptimal outcomes.

Q7 I am still suffering from a lack of concrete examples of sandboxes, how they have been used , and what the outcome is. I hear two slightly different things. One is that they are there to help the regulators learn how to regulate some innovative process. Both today and in our background research, we have heard that regulators are using it to learn how to regulate this new thing.

That seems to be broken down into two things. First, should they change the rules to make it possible if there is an infringement or a conflict between this new process and the existing rules? The second is this business about learning how to regulate some new thing. That is a bit odd to me, and I would like someone to explain it a bit more. What do they have to learn other than what the rules should be?

The second thing that we have had referenced today and previously is that it is helping new businesses comply. That seems to me to be more of a concierge service. In our earlier research, we said that regulators should not just say, “ We’re not there to help. Those are the rules. If you break them, we will put you in jail” or the equivalent, but that they should say, “These rules are for this purpose. If you do this, it will comply with them. If you do that, it won’t ”. That does not seem to me to need a sandbox. That is a concierge. Can you guide me?

That concierge that you mentioned was also mentioned before with the innovation hubs. The FCA calls them innovation pathways. There is a type of concierge service, in some ways, for new ideas to go there and approach particular agents that the FCA would then assign to that organisation. They would then be in discussion on how that particular innovation can comply. That is one thing to do.

The regulatory sandbox is probably a bit more systematic in the way that the FCA will use the sandbox as a learning device, which is what you referred to before, to understand a bit more how new technological developments might affect financial services overall through products and services, but also through modifications in the overall industry architecture, which is something that one of the latest papers pointed out.

We have seen a gradual shift to a new kind of architecture within financial services that we did not have before, which is more modular, because of new technologies such as application programming interfaces and communication of data between agents, but also institutions.

These are deeper discussions or reflections that the FCA develops through conversations that it has with innovative firms, fintechs and other institutions that want to innovate and experiment with new technologies . Over time, it develops new ideas that would then potentially lead to new regulation. That does not happen automatically. It is not that, through a particular cohort in the regulatory sandbox, the FCA says, “We are now going to do this ”, but it gradually builds the intelligence through this dialogue that it is establishing with the fintechs or the organisations that are part of the sandbox in a systematic way that helps them reflect.

As a regulatory device, which was mentioned before in the categorisation that we had in our paper, it also helps fintechs or other organisations comply. Some of the regulations are not necessarily prescriptive, where you do one, two, three, and then you are done , but more descriptive. New technologies might be closer to complying with a set of rules or a bit further out, so the FCA helps them or nudges them into a particular direction.

It goes without saying that a regulatory sandbox is not always the most effective mechanism that one should adopt. In the last few years, we have seen the introduction of other mechanisms, which is something that we have not discussed. We have seen regulatory tech sprints, for instance, which the FCA has used. Another is challenges. The regulator might come up with a challenge and invite industry and universities to collaborate to come up with a solution.

These are also very effective mechanisms for a regulator to get that kind of intelligence and understand future use cases and how new technologies can be used , as well as business models and ideas that it can get from industry and universities. I had the opportunity to participate in but also assess, through the Bank for International Settlements, where I worked as a consultant for a while, some of these challenges. These could also be effective mechanisms. We are not saying that regulatory sandboxes are completely rubbish , but there are vehicles and mechanisms that regulators can use.

I have two reflections on your comment. The first is with regard to concierge services. Providing concierge services to firms in a world of plentiful resources is a good thing to do, but it is often a resource question. There should be more interrogation of whether this is the best use of regulatory funding and whether the public could benefit more from a different allocation of resources.

Secondly, I wanted to respond to your question about what regulators need to learn about their laws in the context of new technological innovations. The issue here is application. Good law is flexible and can accommodate changes in the world, but it is sometimes not entirely clear how pre-existing laws will apply to a new technology . That is often interpreted as a reason to get rid of the pre-existing laws, which is often a mistake. Law is often developed through analogy, and what the regulators can learn from this is where the analogies lie between what they are used to regulating and how this has changed.

If you will humour me once again, there is a broader issue here about the degree of legal certainty that innovators tend to demand. They think that they should be provided an absolutely clear roadmap of what the law is. That is unrealistic. Law has always been susceptible to interpretation and evolution, and there have been plenty of examples of innovation that have worked quite well and flourished in an environment of some legal uncertainty. In fact, there has been a lot of innovation that has flourished in response to legal requirements. In other words, “The law says you have to do this. You figure out the way to do it with your new technology ”.

While there is scope for regulators to be speaking to firms to learn how to apply existing laws to their technologies, that should not automatically default to those laws being peeled away, waived or repealed in order to accommodate those new technologies .

Q8 I almost feel like being a little flippant, but, if, as Lord Lilley suggests, it may be a concierge service, my first instinct was, “Why don’t we privatise it?” That is being slightly flippant. You are both at the cutting edge of research and so on , and you both know quite a lot about the UK system. Is there anything that we can learn from what is happening in the rest of the world, particularly the US, that could improve our system?

I do not think that there are necessarily good things for you to learn from the US approach. Sandboxes have never really taken off in the United States. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau proposed one at one point, but it was really set up more as a deregulatory mechanism than anything else. That happened at the end of the first Trump Administration and was abandoned by the Biden Administration.

We have seen individual states try to come up with fintech sandboxes. Arizona was the first. It has had very little uptake, in recognition of an issue that we have already talked about, which is that you want a big market for your services and, if you are restricted to operating within just one state, that is not a big enough market to really justify the investment. In that sense, there are no regulatory sandbox lessons to draw from the United States.
If I could just interrupt you there, what can we learn from the fact that sandboxes have not taken off in the US?
