That is a great question, because most of the funding in fintech is happening in the United States. What that tells you is that you do not need a sandbox. If your goal is to further the fintech industry, and I am not suggesting that it should be, fintech has flourished in the United States without regulatory sandboxes.

This is where I was heading. There have been plenty of other accommodations, particularly under this second Trump Administration. All kinds of financial regulations are being rolled back to accommodate different fintech industries, particularly the crypto industries. I do not think that that is advisable, but, again, I would note that that investment in all these fintech businesses really was at its zenith during the Biden Administration, so I do not think that you necessarily have to provide these regulatory dispensations in order to encourage the growth of the industry.

If regulatory sandboxes were just about increasing funding and entry to fintech organisations, yes, I would agree. It is not just about the fintechs, but also for the regulators to learn. Down the line, while it might be a slightly bigger investment in terms of putting together a regulatory sandbox, one could argue that, in theory at least, during the process of the sandbox, the knowledge that regulators pass on to fintech firms reduces the cost of future non-compliant firms. This clarity would reduce the workload of agents within the regulator who would have to deal with that particular firm in the future. More clarity and information, and reducing information asymmetries, would potentially be good.

I do not have data that can assess whether regulatory sandboxes are a good investment . Looking at different countries, they have been funded through different means, such as the industry or the European Development Bank, or different sources that do not necessarily rely on the regulators, so it was a much easier idea to pitch.

I will just revert to what lessons can be learned from different countries. One could perhaps spin that around and highlight a few things that can be done to improve regulatory sandboxes in the UK, and I made a short list here. One thing that we touched upon before was transparency. More transparency would be very beneficial , so that we understand a bit more the reflections from the regulators through the regulatory sandbox.

Other firms that do not participate at that moment in time can also benefit from more transparency in terms of the outcomes and how they benefit consumers in the end, which is the ultimate aim of any regulator. In that context, independent evaluators such as academics need access to more data, means and resources to be able to assess those aims and whether they have been met .

One thing that was alluded to through the discussion around AI would also potentially be sandboxes targeted at a particular technology, or more thematic sandboxes on particular use cases that benefit the public, for instance. That could be another way forward to improve the existing regulatory sandbox model. I do not know whether that helps, but those are some extra thoughts.

Q9 Thank you for all this. People need financial services, which are , by and large, provided through a market, but it is quite a strange market because of the inevitable and massive asymmetry of information between those providing the service and those receiving it. Because of that, we have a regulator. If it was not for the asymmetry, perhaps we would not need a regulator, but we do.

It seems to me that, from our discussions on sandboxes, it is perceived as a service to providers. They have a product, they want to produce it, and they want authorisation. Financial services regulators tend to end up seeing their clients as the providers, whereas, in truth, their clients should be the consumers. Is there a way of recasting sandboxes with the explicit aim of providing more information and more substance to consumers’ interests rather than those of the providers?

To be clear, the FCA has always said that one of the goals of its sandbox is to promote financial inclusion by creating more financial services products for traditionally excluded consumers, so there has definitely always been a consumer benefit justification for the sandbox. As we have seen and have discussed, it is very hard to quantify that and to see whether that is really what is happening. You end up with something that appears very much to benefit the innovators, and then assumptions that that innovation will trickle down benefits to consumers.

I am not sure that there is a way of reorienting sandboxes to be truly more consumer-focused . If you think of the whole goal of the sandbox as being to work with the firms themselves, that is an environment in which you would naturally expect the regulator to develop a relationship with the providers. As you said, that is what tends to happen.

Those risks of what we call cognitive capture, or identifying with the industry, are much higher in a sandbox where, as a regulator, you have, in essence, chosen a product that you want to see succeed, and so you become a cheerleader for that product and, ultimately, that is how you measure the success. I do not know how you could make a sandbox more explicitly consumer friendly, largely for the reasons that we have discussed. How do you quantify the benefits of that regulation for the public?

Again, I speak more from the US perspective here, but we have seen that many of the things that have been billed as democratising finance or promoting financial inclusion have been quite predatory in the United States. Extending credit to people who already were overextended, or facilitating gambling by people who did not have money to lose, make up a lot of the financial products that are being marketed as financial innovation, so I am sceptical on that front.

I will just point to what I mentioned before about transparency. You are right. It is a bit misleading to look at a regulatory sandbox and think that this is a service just for the providers that take part in it. We should see it largely as a way for the regulators to understand a bit more about innovation and technology, new developments in terms of business models, and how these can, in the end, benefit consumers effectively. That is the missing link there, to make it a bit more obvious.
Q10 I should start by declaring an interest. I hold shares in Fidelity National Information Services, Inc., which provides technology to financial services companies around the world.

I am struck a bit by a contradiction in what I am hearing here. I am hearing that there is very little evidence about how effective sandboxes are in terms of innovation, competition, and even their impact on regulation, and yet, at the same time, we are seeing that the concept has been taken global. Most regulators now have sandboxes, but what has driven their proliferation, given that there is so little evidence as to their impact?

I do not think that there is no benefit at all. In theory, you can look at things that go through sandboxes and think about the benefits that they then deliver to consumers, but also competition. Having more successful fintech organisations that predominantly go through sandboxes is a good thing in terms of competition, because they can offer cheaper, faster, and more consumer-friendly products that benefit customers. Overall, they impose more competitive pressure on incumbent organisations to then be more competitive and user friendly.

We have seen that a lot in the UK through the fintech revolution that started about 15 years ago. You do not need to have academic evidence to look at your banking application and see how it has evolved over the years. I would like to think that this is largely through the pressure that a lot of the incumbent organisations felt from innovative firms such as Monzo and Revolut, which flourished because of the UK fintech innovation ecosystem.

I would just say that regulatory sandboxes have not been successful everywhere. There are countries where a regulatory sandbox exists and is then shut down, because they could not really identify a concrete connection to further investment in fintech or the flourishing of innovation. One of these countries happens to be Greece, where I come from. They did a sandbox for a year. There was no resource to support it. There was no evidence that attributed anything to it in terms of fintech innovation and competition, so they shut it down because the money ran out.

I am sure that, if we look at the data, there will be more countries that went through the process. Regulators look at one another. They see a regulator innovating, and the FCA is at the forefront. It did that regulatory sandbox a few years ago, and then others picked up on it. There is no doubt about that. That also happens in any innovative firm. That is why we see the flourishing of sandboxes.

There is also benefit for the regulators, not just the organisations going through it. While we do not necessarily have a million papers assessing and proving that, using econometric models followed by undisputed results, one could, in theory, line up a lot of arguments for why a regulatory sandbox should exist, so I would not shut it down completely. I would not say that there is zero evidence, that they have done more bad than good, or that they ate the FCA’s money where the opportunity cost dictates that they should be doing something else. We are not entirely sure about that. I would not go as far as arguing that.

I agree with a lot of that. Under Occam’s razor, the simplest answer is often the correct one. Regulators emulated each other, in large part because this seemed like an easy win-win. It was a way of signalling to the world that you were an innovative jurisdiction , but there was often no appreciation of how expensive it would be to operate, and so we saw some buyer’s remorse and some countries shutting them down. Other jurisdictions , I am sure, have found some things to like and keep about them.

Q11 I have no financial interest in this study. I am a graduate of English language and literature, so I have an interest in encouraging accessibility, particularly of language, and the elimination of exclusivity. It seems to me that this topic is at the pinnacle of exclusivity and opacity, and really a bit of a con. Like Lord Lilley, I am trying still to get to the bottom of it.

Both of you have said that a bit more transparency and evidence from the regulators about this subject might be helpful. You might vary a bit on whether sandboxes are important or worth working on, but what happens if the emperor has no clothes, which is why the regulator may not be willing to give this so-called evidence? What happens if it is just a defence mechanism to impress politicians that the regulator is cutting-edge ?

As a fellow English literature graduate, I have used the emperor’s new clothes as an analogy many times when speaking about this sector. The key thing to realise about that story is that the reason why people go along with these things does not necessarily have to be venal. It is that crowd mentality and the desire not to seem stupid.

There is no data supporting the very widespread narratives about many fintech products and their benefits. Once you start interrogating a lot of these products, it really does fall apart, but it requires people to be willing to go out on a limb and question the conventional orthodoxy.

You alluded up front to including people. The narratives about financial inclusion, and democratising finance and accessibility, have been spun so thickly that, when you challenge these products, you are often accused, as I have been, of wanting to cut consumers off from choice and from the tools that they need to build a better future for themselves, and so trying to say that the emperor has no clothes is a very challenging position to be in.

There are different versions of that story, but, if you go back to the one from Hans Christian Andersen, the courtiers never admitted that the emperor had no clothes, even once the child called it out, because it was just too hard to admit that they had been wrong for so long. There is a lot of truth in that parable, and I perhaps have gone very off topic, but I do not think that it is necessarily venal that the regulators are going along with this story.

My answer might be shorter, but there is a discussion to be had . The FCA will have no reason to not supply further information and evidence if it is asked to. Going back to the overall discussion around innovation, particularly fintech innovation, I do not think that anybody is saying that there is no innovation out there or that it does not do anything for the public.

I would not go as far as saying that, in the end, innovation is bad, but, across many industries, there are examples where what we think of as innovation did not have any positive effects for the public at all. For instance, social media is a multi- billion dollar industry right now, but I do not see any benefit that it brings to the public. It might be the other way around, with so many hours being lost in doomscrolling through social media that it reduces productivity. That is an example that one could think about.

In fintech, I do not see any particular examples that could be so damaging, apart from, of course, creating a new monopoly and then skewing prices to the benefit of providers rather than consumers. The FCA would definitely be open to discussion and then to providing more data and transparency if it was asked to.

I would like to thank both of you very much for coming to this first evidence session. You have set us up extremely well for the remaining stages of our inquiry, and many of your comments have been very thought-provoking. Thank you very much for joining us.

Witnesses

I : Professor Jenny Gibson , Professor of Neurodiversity and Developmental Psychology at University of Cambridge ; Neil Leitch OBE , CEO at Early Years Alliance ; Richard Waite , Founder and Digital Pedagogy Consultant at Waite.EYTS .

II : Dr Mhairi Aitken , Director and Co-founder at Our AI Collective CIC ; Professor Sandra Leaton Gray , Professor of Education Futures at UCL Institute of Education ; Meg Moss , Head of Public Affairs & Advocacy at National Counselling and Psychotherapy Society (NCPS) ; and Professor Sarah-Jayne Blakemore , Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Neuroscience at University of Cambridge .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Professor Jenny Gibson , Neil Leitch , and Richard Waite .

Q81 Good morning and welcome to this oral evidence session of the Education Select Committee. This morning, we are taking evidence on our inquiry into AI and edtech , thinking about the role and the impact of AI and edtech on the early years phase of education.
I thank our witnesses very much to for being here with us this morning. Can I ask each of you to introduce yourselves to the Committee , please, starting with Neil Leitch?

I am Neil Leitch , the c hief e xecutive of an organisation called the Early Years Alliance . We represent around 18,000 members and supporters, predominantly nursery groups and pre-school s, but some child minders as well.

The one thing that I would say is fairly unique about us as a membership organisation is that we also operate 28 settings exclusively in areas of deprivation , so I would like to think that we witness at first hand some of the wonders and the challenges of early years.

Hi everyone, I am Jenny Gibson , Professor of Neurodiversity and Developmental Psychology at the University of Cambridge. My expertise is in early childhood, particularly focusing on early language and communication development and children ’ s social and emotional wellbeing.

My name is Richard Waite . I am an early years digital pedagogy and digital safeguarding consultant. My background is that I have been NNEB trained since 1986 , so I have just under 40 years ’ experience in early years, and I have gone from working in settings as management to support office for a large nursery group , and now I support nurseries as an adviser .

Q82 Thank you all very much indeed. I am going to begin our questioning this morning. First of all, could you describe the overall impact that AI and educational technology is currently having on the early years sector? Neil, I might start with you if that is okay.

From our perspective, particularly post-pandemic, we started to see more and more children arrive in our settings with social and emotional development delays. When you speak to providers and managers, they particularly quote AI and edt ech as being one of the problems that they have. What is interesting is that, still to this day , we experience that. To put it bluntly, I wish I had £1 for every manager that ha s said to me that they had to spend their day pacifying staff who had been kicked, bitten, hair pulled, and so on , by children who are not socially and emotionally developed.

I will be very quick with this, but to put it into a very practical position, f rom January through to September we have recorded 43 accidents of staff in our 28 nurseries ; 19 of those incidents related to children biting, kicking, throwing objects, scratching, pulling hair of staff, and so on. That is not even child on child. That is on adults. I would say that the big concern we have is basically child development , and children’s ability to socialise because of AI, edtech and, dare I say, sedentary lifestyles.
Thank you. Professor Gibson ?

We have done some research in our research centre recently looking at the impact of AI - enabled toys . This is where there is a generative AI chatbot embedded in something that is cuddly looking , designed for children and marketed to under-fives. We were quite concerned about these kinds of developments, and we did some research that looked at the interactions of these toys with young children, and we sought parents ’ views and educator views as well.

Particularly for the early years sector, people working as nursery practitioners or others in the sector told us that they were quite concerned about impacts of generative AI. They felt they did not have the knowledge and skills they needed, and they did not necessarily know where to turn for support or advice. On the educator side, there is a lot of uncertainty and quite a bit of worry.

On the parent and child side of things, we are seeing that it is ubiquitous . There is so much quick development in this area. From what we saw in this very initial study, very little research has been done on the impacts of generative AI on young children ’ s development that sits outside the tech development sector. We lack evidence of what impacts on child development. From the observational work that we have done so far, we did see that generative AI toy interactions were not particularly well calibrated to what we know is good and important for young children ’ s development. We have big social change happening and at the moment we do not necessarily have the evidence to know what exactly the impact is on children.
Thank you very much. Richard, what are you seeing at the moment?

At the moment—thinking about day-to-day and boots on the ground—among the staff concerns that Neil has spoken about, i t is the struggle with staffing, recruitment and getting the right type of staffing, these kinds of issues. Technology in early years has already been seen as an issue because most early years people, if you say the word “ technology ” , they immediately jump to the conclusion that you are going to talk about screen time.

If I am trying to deliver a workshop on technology, n ine out of 10 people will not come to my workshop because they do not realise what I am actually talking about. They will think I am going to talk to them about tablets or whatever , s o that is an issue and a big concern because screen time is across the media, social media, parent groups all talking about it.

It puts pressures on nurseries because they are thinking about that and now AI has impacted more. It ha s added to the mix. You not only have screen time, but you also have AI. Because of recent events in early years — even looking at cyber-security — there is this massive cloud of information that nurseries were just not prepared for. A nursery manager or an educator does not go in having knowledge about AI, cyber-security and screen time. When a manager is coming into a nursery at 7.30 in the morning and they have staff that have called in sick, the chef is not turning up—all these issues coming in—the last thing they are probably going to think about is AI, cyber-security and screen time.

Q83 Thank you very much. You have talked about the influence of AI from outside the setting. What types of educational technology are currently being used in early years settings? Is there any framework for that in terms of decision making and procurement in the early years , or any evidence base that underpins it that you are aware of? Again, I will start with Neil.
I am not sure there is a framework. It is very much an “ introduce and test later ” sort of approach that we are seeing at this point in time.

Within early years settings, I would say that i t is used at the moment predominantly for administration , and i t is fair to say that many educators value that. The problem that we have is it does not articulate any nuance whatsoever in terms of sensitivity. We are starting to see generated reports for example, that are very clinical. They do not basically take into account the nuance of a child ’ s personal attributes, and so on.

The other thing that we are starting to see is a plethora of AI generated correspondence from parents, whether that be complaints or otherwise. It ha s just meant a massive overload for early years educators. The response that they give, unlike maybe 10 years ago, which was to sit down and talk with a parent, now becomes a legal document predominantly generated by AI. T hat is where I would say it is generally being used.

That is not to say that we have not used it particularly within our settings to support speech and language, for example. There are some good products, but there are some awful products as well. I find it really interesting — to give an example — that if you were developing a piece of medical equipment for a hospital, i t would be assumed that you would understand the consequences of that machine failing or the clinical steps that need to be taken subsequently. However, when it comes to edtech , for example, nothing. We just take it for granted that it is in the best interest s of a child.

There are some very good manufacturers and producers of edtech equipment, so this is not about everybody, but we are also seeing a plethora of poorly constructed equipment being produced with no consideration for a child ’ s social and emotional development . That is a big concern , s o what we are seeing is educators reluctant to use ki t at this time. To take Richard ’ s point, their support and training is almost non-existent. They are very, very fearful. When you are fearful, you avoid. That is what has happening at this particular point in time.
Thank you. Professor Gibson ?

I do not know of any frameworks in place around edtech governance. Obviously , though , we do have a lot of regulation around child protection and child support . I do think that early years ’ educators know what i s good for children in terms of social and emotional development because of the professional training that many early years sector people have.

We perhaps need to do a bit of confidence building that actually you know what i s good for children in terms of their social development, the things that you might do with them, and then apply that to technology to say, “I s this supporting the human back and forth interactions that children need to develop and grow? ” I think e arly years educators do have that set of expertise, and I think support for them to translate that into practice with edtech is interesting.

I have seen technology mainly applied for planning sessions and things like that . From my observation, it is more educator facing than child facing. I have seen things like Alexa being used in nurseries , and I think i t is interesting that, because of the ubiquitous nature of these kinds of technologies, it is not always easy to disentangle whether or not this has a generative AI component . I think in some cases, people are using AI unawares.

I think technology as a whole in the sector because people have become scared of the idea that it is screen time . W hen I worked in the last chain, I was supporting 310 nurs eri es and I was looking at integrating technology tools into nursery settings , from coding devices to digital microscopes, all these sorts of things. This is where there is a gap in the understanding that there are non-digital as well as digital tech resources.

The word “ edtech ” may work in schools , but I think in early years I prefer the term “ digital pedagogy ” because if you put “ pedagogy ” in there, sometimes there is more of an interest in, “O kay, digital pedagogy is to help with that ” , because then we are making sure the pedagogy is there. “ Ed t ech ” does not really tell you that there is learning from such resources.

I support and work with a few companies that produce some very good non-digital plus digital tools, but due to the lack of knowledge and the fear in settings , the ir choice is, “We just will not bother. We will not get it in because the hassle of having to learn it and just figuring it all out, it is just too much for the sector at the moment , ” so most of the time they are staying away.

D igital pedagogy was introduced in the “ Birth to 5 Matters: non ‑ statutory guidance for the EYFS ” , 2nd edition . I was actually on the working group for that . There was a need to put that in there because, as Neil said earlier, you cannot put the genie back in the bottle. We are in a digital age . C hildren are exposed to technology every day , from washing machines to microwaves and mobile phones. We cannot put it back , so w e have to better prepare them for the future that they are facing.

Q84 Thank you. Finally from me, before I pass on to other members : d o you think that the Government have fully grasped the scale of the impacts of this technology on the early years sector , and what further action do you think the Government should take to support the sector in navigating these very significant changes that you have all articulated really well? I will start with Neil.

I do not think they have. I find it really interesting that , when we are looking at safeguarding, i f there is a physical connection, the Government are always very quick to respond. I understand that, whether that is about safer sleeping practices, eating, and so on. However, there is nothing when it comes to the emotional safeguarding of children that is in place.

I come back to the point, Chair, that our staff are greatly concerned that t here is no support whatsoever. They do n’ t know how to deal with AI. They do n’ t know how to deal with the consequences when things go wrong. F or example, I am amazed and appalled — this is not necessarily just in early years, but it moves into maybe further education —at t he number of educators who do n’ t understand the pressures that children are being placed under from external influences . T heir response , predominantly in the school environment , has been to exclude whatever it happens to be rather than understand. They are almost ignorant of what has led to this.

I am appalled by people who constantly say our children are less resilient; they are living in a different world. The Government need to ensure that educators are supported in not just understanding IT, but understanding children who are on the end of it, because that is not the case as it stands.

M y view is that there could be more understanding and integration across sectors. The distinction between health and education in the early years is somewhat arbitrary . S ervices that support children and babies from a very young age, including social services, health visiting and so on, are part of that early education landscape because children are learning , and the home learning environment is very important and that might sit outside traditional educational settings.

It is important to encourage joint working and thinking , and I guess cross-sector responsibility as well. T op-down government regulation is not going to solve this. It is about taking some ownership as well as being part of those professions , and parents and families have all got a part to play.

Thinking about government regulation, I do think psychological safety should be an important part of product safety standards. I think t here needs to be more exploration of that, particularly thinking about toys that are coming in with generative AI capabilities. One of the biggest risks there is th e friendship-affirming nature of interactions that generative AI has , which might be acting at a time when children are particularly developmentally vulnerable , so I think product regulation with a view to safety is important in this early years picture.

The other thing I want to say is that I am glad we are here talking about the early years. It is often missing from these conversations , so I think keeping this sector part of conversations about educational technology is really important too.

I want to share a survey T apestry th at did this year , which found that 46% of workplaces are using AI, 31% have AI guidance, but only 21% of settings have training. Training and CPD is the big thing for me ; i t has been a big thing for a long time . I have been in and out of nurseries for over three decades. I see the lack of support in terms of training and development for educators : w e have apprentices coming in who are supposedly going to be our future educators who have had no training in their apprenticeship on AI , edtech or digital pedagogy , or cyber-security . So where do they get it from?

If they are doing their level twos, level threes or their apprenticeships and none of those three things is being discussed , they are being thrown into the lion ’ s den, basically, of all this with information overload . W here is the support ? A 30-minute webinar or a staff meeting at the end of the day , when you are absolutely drained from running around after how ever many hundred s of children ? I think t hey need some space; something needs to be done to allow educators to get proper support and training , and for the leaders as well . M anagers and owners also need training.
Thank you very much. I am going to go to Peter Swallow next.

Q85 Professor Gibson, in your earlier answers, you identified your concerns about young people and young children ’ s learning and development. C ould you set out in a little bit more detail what specifically you are concerned about ? Is it their communication and language skills, their social and emotional development? What specific risks are there to young children ’ s development from AI and edtech ?

Thanks for the question. O ne of the things that parents seemed excited about in our research is that , unlike some perceptions of screen time as being quite passive edtech , generative AI gives this possibility of a back-and-forth conversation. We have done a lot of work over the years in developmental psychology showing that those back-and-forth interactions are really the essence of young children ’ s development. Those early social relationships and bonds are the basis of later language and cognitive development , s o they are absolutely critical.

What i s worrying , when you are replacing a human in those interactive relationships , is that you are potentially missing that sensitivity. If you have , let ’ s say, a generative AI toy that will always tell you that you are right or tell you that it is a friend and you can tell it secrets, i t is really quite worrying in terms of what the disruption in those reciprocal human relationships could be.

T hat is not to say that i t would be impossible to produce a product that was more positive in terms of those relationships and interactions, but at the moment I think they are not at the heart of this development. What if we had products that supported perhaps bringing the adult into those interactions ? W e have seen some research — for example, from the University of Sheffield — where digital parenting interventions can really support parents in that back and forth with their child and supports their early language development. If we had AI products that could support that in a sensitive way, I would be really positive about it , but at the moment, we are not seeing products that are well calibrated to th e social need that children have.

Q86 W ithout wanting to put words into your mouth, if I can summarise , the advantages that we might see in communication and language development come at a potential cost to social and emotional development ; is that essentially what you are saying?
I think i t would be premature to talk about any advantages yet. I have not seen a product that really convinces me of that, but potentially yes.

Q87 Mr Leitch , you mentioned that you were very concerned about children ’ s emotional development as well. What safeguards would you like to see put in place to make sure that we are protecting very young children from these risks?

I think that if we have product development and we have a body that regulate s that product development, then exactly the same should apply for edtech and AI. Those organisations should be accountable to a learned body that understands the impact of their product. That would be at least a starting point.

I also think it is really important to understand that our educators are not completely led by AI as well. If I could just give a very quick example —i t goes back a couple of years, but please bear with me. We had a mother come into one of our nurser ies to collect her child, around 4 pm , and she was inebriated. She told the manager that that morning her partner of many, many years had walked out and told her that he had two children by another woman.

The manager recognised that this was not the normal practice of this particular woman. I took that scenario last night and I typed it into AI and said, “W hat should the educator do? ” It came back with the most insensitive, inhumane process that individuals should follow, including involving the police and other agencies, and so on. What the manager did was she took the child, she took the mother, she went home with them in the evening and she sat there until 6 o ’ clock in the morning, until the mother came round basically, because she knew it was a one-off incident.
My concern is that if we follow AI and technology to the letter or if educators do, and they lose the human touch . Product development should also understand that element when it is being designed.

Q88 Thank you. Mr Waite, you mentioned that you have seen some really concerning uses of edtech and edtech tools and also some really exciting ones. What do you see as the greatest potential for these technologies to support positive development and improve outcomes?

For early years, I think a bit like screen time , where there is a limit , I think we absolutely have to have a limit on it. To be fair, I do not particularly want to see AI generated toys in nursery settings , because the value of our educators and what they deliver to the children and that personal human contact is the most essential thing. I do not want children in nurseries sitting there talking to a cuddly teddy bear telling them that they are great.

I think the parents at home need a bit of support in terms of understanding if they are buying these things that they need to really check. D o not buy something from an online catalogue, basically, if you have not properly checked it out. There are some good resources out there that I have looked at, but few and far between , so I do not want that.

On technology, I support the f orest s chool approach. I support all types of nurseries. I still believe in the three I ’ s — intent, implementation, and impact. What is the intent? If you are bringing a resource — and it could be sand , water or Play-Doh — why are you bringing that into a learning experience today? E ducators need to think about that first. How are you going to deliver it? Twenty children around a Bee-Bot is not going to happen, is it? With a Bee-Bot only one person can use it at any one time. Therefore, how do you implement it?

Groups of children in an enabling environment —w hat i s the environment to introduce these things? Then the impact is what is left — the observations, the assessment, and the next steps for the child . My view is do not bring edtech into — I do not even like edtech , sorry — but do not bring digital resources into nursery just for the sake of it, just because it looks good on your brochure or whatever. W hat are you doing with it ?

When I deliver learning experiences, I use the STEAM approach : science, technology, engineering, arts, and maths . I t makes the educator think about what the resource is. Think about the education first and then how the resource support s it . Technology is a tool, just like sand, water, and Play-Doh , as far as I am concerned. Once it is treated and respected in that way and not seen as something scary, i t can have real benefits.

Q89 When members of this Committee visited Estonia, and early years setting s in Estonia, we saw exactly that. We saw children being introduced to technology through hands-on play-based activities, often without screens, and with practitioners actively guiding the learning, including one-to-one interactions. That seems to me exactly what you are talking about, but it also seems to me that you are suggesting that in many settings in the UK we are very far from that at the moment. Is that fair?

I think we are really far away from it. We are really far away , because we are still at a phase where people are scared of it. People are worried about bringing it in and about what the consequences might be. T hey are seeing things on the news . T hey are seeing things on social media .

T he Government have brought out screen time guidance for parents. They have also brought out screen time guidance for settings. Yet last week BBC n ews was again going on about screens . Sometimes it is almost like parent bashing and when the parents are being bashed, they are coming in and bashing the educators , saying things like, “W e do n’ t want this in here. We have just seen it on the news. It is really bad . ” I think this is the issue. We have to change the narrative. The narrative needs to change, and I think we need help from the Government to change that narrative.
Q90 Mr Leitch, a re your members looking at what i s going on in Estonia and elsewhere and learning from how they are applying technology with a pedagogical underpinning in early year settings?

I would suggest that they are not. I would suggest , alongside Richard ’ s comments, that at the moment fear overtakes everything else . Obviously screen time is incredibly prominent, and so on, so they are avoiding learning elsewhere and even the use of technology beyond administration. A s I have alluded to previously , i t is used within administration b ut I think they are incredibly fearful about engagement with children.

O ne interesting thing came up in speaking to La u rence Taylor, who is the counter terrorism commissioner . We were talking about why it was th at early years educators are reluctant. He said it is because there is a plethora of AI and technology that is absolutely awful. He quoted, for example that it is legal in this country for a child to play a game that simulates the shootings in Christchurch. We can do that. I think that speaks volumes about the protection that we have for children at this time. Therefore educators are nervous, nervous, nervous.

Q91 Professor Gibson, a final question f rom me. The reception baseline assessment can involve young children interacting with digital technology shortly after starting school , b ut , as we have heard, there is this very real fear, including , as Mr Waite alluded to , coming from parents who are concerned about the amount of edtech and technology in the classroom, sometimes seeming to counter all of the very real concerns that we have been talking about this morning. How should the Government balance the educational benefits of using technology in assessment with these concerns about limiting the use of screen time, limiting the exposure to harmful forms of technology?

A great question. I do not know of any evidence to support what that balance should be. I think you can think about general principles of what we want children to learn —t hose skills of critical appraisal, human connection and what has been called 21st century skills — working in teams, collaborating, and of course not being frightened of technology and being able to critically appraise it.

I do think it is important that children are exposed to technologies and they have those conversations about when, how, and how much and does it have a mind and what can it do and what can it not do . It has to be part of a broader approach to pedagogy that involves dialogue and helping children and also educators to build that critical skill.

In international examples , in Hong Kong they have an interesting implementation of AI literacy through games and engagement with these kinds of things associated with pedagogical goals around the technology itself. I think we absolutely do need that tech to be there , b ut as Richard said it needs to be used in that intentional way.
Thank you very much.
Q92 Can I ask a supplementary question, particularly on the reception baseline test ?

I have heard examples in recent weeks of a parent saying to me, “ I told my son to say, ‘ I am not going to do it because we do n’t do screens in our house ’ ”. Another parent said, “My child just does not know how to do anything on a screen because I have kept them away from it . ” D o you think there is a contradiction at the moment between the Government ’ s purposeful introduction of screen-based baseline testing in reception and the messages that parents and educators in the early years are receiving about children ’ s interaction with screens?

I do not think so. It is important that technology is a part of our processes. Maybe my colleagues might disagree with me on that , b ut I do not think it is unreasonable. Those data are really important for understanding educational added value and the trajectories of young children going through , and understanding educational achievement in this country. T hat is really important , so that is the value of that data .

We also have to think about the counterfactual in terms of getting children to perhaps sit pen and paper tests or activities and the feasibility of that , so I would be cautious . The message around screen time is very hard to nuance, because people tend to see it as an all ‑ or ‑ nothing issue , b ut when it’s interactive and used purposefully, certain technologies do have a place in the early years and can play a positive role .

Of course, if there are children who perhaps have not been exposed to technologies , that is a pedagogical question for teachers and local authorities administering those tests. We might want to think about how we support settings and support children to take it , b ut I certainly would not be throwing it out yet.

Despite the fact that I said that , particularly throughout the pandemic, when parents were trying to hold down jobs and also support their children and so on, it should be no surprise that they reach ed for technology , screens , and so on . What I think has started to happen is that the messaging — not just from the Government but from elsewhere — has started to make the parents feel like they are awful in many instances. They have almost gone from a binary position of , “Y es, you can access , ” to , “N o, you can ’ t , ” and that is incredibly unhelpful. We should learn to understand the pressures .

I spoke earlier about the pressures o n young children living in a different world. That is exactly the same for parents. I was asked by the chief executive of one of our largest supermarkets a little while ago — a few years ago , actually, to be fair — if I would talk to their annual conference on early years , and I said, “W hat about? ” He said, “H ow we can get more parents, mums predominantly, back into the working environment ? ” I said that it was odd, but that I would speak to them. I spoke to 42 parents — all mums . E very single one of them said that they were rushed back to work . T hey felt under pressure . T hey talked about how they were the ones getting up at 5.30, 6 o ’ clock in the morning, making the packed lunches for the children or whatever it happen ed to be, doing a full day ’ s job, coming back in the evening and still preparing the meal. They said they would spend an hour, perhaps no more, with their child, predominantly in the bath , and they would buy them more sweets and more toys.

That is a long-winded way of saying that we really have to understand the pressures on parents . A s well as supporting children within early years settings, it is probably more important that we support parents at home to understand the benefits and the risks, because it is here. But they are under pressure.
Thank you. In the interests of time, I am going to move us on to Mark now .

Q93 A couple of questions from me about inclusion and closing development gaps with AI and edtech . Understandably, you will know that we focused a lot in our previous inquiries on SEND and improving SEND provision. Obviously, it is a big focus for the DFE as well. There is very limited evidence out there that states that AI and edtech can be used to close these development gaps , b ut what written evidence we have been able to find is quite optimistic about it. H ow optimistic should we be that we can use AI and edtech to close development gaps, particularly for children with SEND or additional learning needs? What sort of opportunities should we be looking for to make sure we take advantage of this? I am h appy to start with anyone, but I was drawn to Professor Gibson.

I think there is a lot of hype out there, to be honest , and I think the evidence is yet to catch up with it. At some point I started to get quite frustrated. I would go to conferences and they would say, “Oh, we are really worried about AI, except for autistic children , ” based on nothing more than an intuition quite often that this might be helpful. Personally , I would want to see a lot more in terms of well-constructed trials of products that are devised in collaboration with children and families affected by SEND.

What I am optimistic about—if we fantasise a bit more—is profiling and developments if we are perhaps having conversations around the case that provision should be needs led and not diagnosis led. However, it is quite hard to get a nuanced perspective on individual needs , particularly with waiting times being what they are and the complexity of integrating information from different sources for children with additional needs.

I think that AI tools can help with profiling and understanding children ’ s needs , so I am quite optimistic from that point of view, but I would stress that collaborative bit with members of the community, particularly parents and children , being consulted and integrated into part of this development. I think we are a long way off from off-the-shelf products that will be help ful .
Q94 Mr Leitch , is there any cause to be optimistic that we can improve inclusion in early years?

I need to be hanging on to hope. I feel we should b ecause it is an unknown position at the moment that perhaps there is hope. I would say this. I do not think it is AI and edtech that is driving SEND inclusion. It is , frankly , policy ; it is the Government ’ s prioritising of SEND that is driving it, as well as Ofsted looking at it from an inspection position. It is much more of a defensive position for why there is inclusion rather than edtech driving that.

I was in China with the Department for Business and Trade just a few weeks ago , and I saw some really good edtech products that, i f used correctly, if monitored, would be supportive of children who have additional needs.
Q95 Any that come to mind right now? Any that we should be aware of?

They didn ’ t brand them . I t was all very secretive to say the least, but they impressed me. Children with an educator would go through a routine and , effectively , it would identify , “Y ou are pushing this child way beyond what they are capable of at this moment in time . ” Or alternatively, “W hy are you wasting this child ’ s time having to go through routines when actually they want to get on to the next bit? They are curious, they are adventurous , ” and so on . I suppose that is where I would hold the hope.
Q96 T hank you very much . Mr Waite, is there a nything in your working experience that would show some optimism ?

The term “ assistive technology ” has been around for a long time and there are companies and resources around. I am thinking about large push buttons for children who cannot use a keyboard, a special mouse, a trackball mouse on that side of helping certain children with special educational needs .

M y experience is of a child in my nursery who had profound difficulties . W hen we spoke to the physios and all the people who supported him at a TAC — team around the child — meeting, it was sai d that he would get good support if he had a tablet in the nursery setting. When I went to the IT department and said, “Can I have a tablet for this child ? ” t hey went, “What?” and went straight to the CEO saying, “Mr W aite is requesting a tablet in the nursery setting”. I had to explain to the earl y years department that the reason the professional had requested that he have it was that would support his needs in the nursery setting.

Once I pushed my case forward, we did actually get some funding from the local authority to purchase it, and it was a huge benefit to this particular child. It allowed him to engage with the other children, and allowed him to feel part of the nursery setting . I t was important. This is where we have to look at the positives of such things as screen time. Children with various neurodivergence s can also benefit.

I have the experience of a child who sometimes cannot handle the nursery classroom. He gets really frustrated, puts his hands over his ears. We take him out. We have an interactive screen . There is a bubble popping game that he likes. He just taps it and the bubble pops, and he laughs and he kind of regulates his behaviour and then we can ask , “A re you ready to go back into the room? ” He says, “ Absolutely , ” and he is fine. Therefore, that is how we use it in the right way. We can use it, but I think early year s settings do not know how to use edtech or digital right now . T his is where the CPD and the support is severely needed.
Thank you. In the interest s of time, I will leave it there.
Thank you very much, Mark. Manuela.

Q97 We know that developmental and educational attainment gaps emerge before many children even start primary school , and we heard at the beginning of the meeting about school readiness and the lack of being ready for school. I n your opinion, what role, if any, could AI and educational technology play in narrowing these gaps during the early years , or is there a risk that they will have an adverse and harmful effect? I am going to start with Mr Leitch , please.

I would say avoid it. I think the most important part of a child ’ s development is their social and emotional development. All the evidence points to the fact that children who are not socially and emotionally developed will struggle to learn. F or me , that would be the foundation . S ocial and emotional development is very much about hands-on attachment, engagement, physical engagement, confidence, and so on. I am not sure that I would want a robot or an AI bot to do something similar . I think to get it right further down the line, secure children right at the beginning, and that is about , dare I say it, the avoidance of AI and edtech .

I have a less pessimistic view. T here is a role in supporting parents for technologies here. We do not always have to have technologies are child facing in early years . For p arents, child minders, others who are engaging with children, having recommend ation s for activities based on your child ’ s preferences and your families ’ priorities can be really helpful. It is about knowing what i s good for children, which is, of course, those important relationships that we need to nurture, but I think well-design ed tec hnology can support that.

One of the concerns I have is that everyone has some generalisation that technology is replacing play and there are lots of people having face-offs, play versus technology . I have a big concern about that because technology is n’ t replacing play . I t can be used to enhance it. In terms of school readiness , as you know there are concerns about that name anyway . W hat I am thinking is that if we us e the STEAM approach — I do not say STEM because I believe that art has a real place to play in early years. I know the universities might not agree . T hey prefer STEM . I think you can do coding and other things, critical thinking, learning experiences at nursery level using — there are other devices —a B ee -B ot or something like that to programme. There is a wireless microscope where children can go into the garden and film a plant and what the deeper details of a plant look like. That is exploration and investigation. Who does not want children to have good exploration and investigation and critical thinking ? W e do not need to wait for them to go into schools to be taught critical thinking , exploration and investigation. It is about the intent.

If the technology is used in the right way and it is the right technology , i t absolutely does have a place , and it can be seen by children as play. I am not saying for one minute that we are trying to replace edtech with standard play resources, right? As I said, Play-Doh, Lego, Bricks, whatever , you name it , t hese are all tools and we use tools to help children learn and develop , and t echnology is just one of those . W e are just not using it properly. As I say, a poor workman blames his tool s . We are blaming technology for failings in how it is used in nurseries. It is not the fault of technology; it is the actual lack of training and development.

I want to be absolutely clear that I was not suggesting that throughout the entire early years from nought to five that we avoid edtech . I am suggesting that the earliest point of a child ’ s life , where they are developing attachment, social emotional development, is the point where it is critical to touch, and so on. I find it interesting that , even in the DFE ’ s own research, when p arents were asked , “W hat i s the most important thing that you find that you want from earl y years setting s ? ” Number one priority is staff qualit y . That is people. Number two , k ind, friendly and supportive staff, and so on. They are the things that parents want : k ind, gentle, thoughtful educators.

If I had a child growing up at this time , and I was putting him into an early years setting, that is the quality I would want right at the beginning , rather than wanting my child to be the brightest spark in the world.

Q98 Thank you. That takes me to my next question because , as you said, early years encompasses children from birth to the age of five. Are there particular ages or stages of development where the use of AI , an attack is more appropriate or where the risks are greater to the child? I am thinking, for example, in the development of fine motor skills, where children learn through using pencils, drawing with certain tools rather than sw ip ing on a screen. D o you have a view on that, Professor Gibson?

It is all about having a balanced play diet for young children in the early years. They need to get out . T hey need to get dirty . T hey need to be picking up sticks, so they are learning that pencil grip without even knowing it, drawing in the sand, and squidging the Play-Doh. All of that is incredibly important.

Appropriate tech materials can work really well for younger children if they are in balance. That is the nuance that we really need to get. I am not talking about watching short form videos on YouTube, for example. I definitely would not recommend that. I t is about finding the things that children can learn, explore and engage with , and bringing in the parents or caregivers as well.

That said, I think we do need to be careful of that very early period in babyhood, in th ose first critical months of life where that parent-child bonding is particularly important. If anything is disruptive in that period, I would be very, very wary of it. I do n’ t know of any tech product that I would recommend at the moment for a child that age. I would definitely say let ’ s protect early childhood until we absolutely know what might be helpful or harmful. I do think it is a matter of understanding what i s good for children, providing a variety of experiences in their earliest years.
Thank you. Any other comments?

I agree. Obviously, at the youngest age, I have already said I do n’ t really want AI in settings with children at the moment. T he main one at present is smart speakers. W hen you think of what technology is, it basically is cause and effect. Like a pair of scissors is a form of technology. It is scissors that help you cut paper . I n its simplest form, for babies, we have had Fisher-Price . O ther brands are available, but we have had Fisher-Price cause - and - effect toys in nursery settings for a long time . There has been a drive to remove these and w e have gone through a phase of nurseries not wanting plastic fantastic . Th ey want all wooden and natural looking things. But cause - and - effect toys ha ve been around for quite a long time. T hey are just getting a bit more advanced.

I think in pre-school probably I would not expect toddlers to be doing coding , a lthough they can do very basic coding with the right resource; I have done it. If we are getting them ready, as you said, in terms of moving to the next level , when they are going into primary, certain things like coding and certain toys will do that , and maths . When I say the STEAM approach , if you have science, technology, engineering, arts and maths in your thinking when you are doing learning experiences, you can pretty much cover quite a few bases off without thinking, “O h, we need technology , ” or “W e need this . ” It is part of the bigger framework, which is why I like STEAM.
I will g o to Jodie. Thank you.

Q99 We have covered a range of applications of AI from emotional regulation, potentially improving communication, profiling and of course admin , b ut what choices do early years providers actually have about whether or how they adopt AI and educational technology?
Unfortunately, you addressed that to me first of all.
You reacted first.

Okay. I think they have limited choices. In terms of administration, it is fairly straightforward. F or example, we train all of our staff on the use of C opilot. We use software, management software that integrates AI in terms of producing development reports, and so on . But we focus predominantly, I suppose, on ensuring that those reports are appropriate , so w e do n’ t just take them as read. They are monitored , vetted, and so on.

When it comes to products, I come back to the point that we feel that we are incredibly limited in knowledge of what is good, bad, and indifferent. I am afraid we tend to avoid it at this point in time.

To support that, I would recommend, if it were possible, that we would have some sort of product labelling regulation that would help educators to make choices. Failing that, guidelines, and principles about what to look out for in terms of privacy policies, features, and guidance on how to appraise possible risks and benefits.

So in my experience, I developed what I called a brilliant basic s list. T he brilliant basic s list was a set of resources for the nursery group that I was with that I would recommend that supported various children ’ s development, particularly under the EYFS. I would have the resource, the intention that supports , where it can be supplied and then a small example of how that resource can be used. That is the thing , because you can put a certain toy in front of educators and they have no idea where to start because they need training . T hey need to know what that resource does . T hey need time to play.

W hen I say to educators, “P lay with it , ” they look at me like, “W hat do you mean? ” T hey have to play with it, understand it, so that they are able to come up with the right intention and how they are going to implement it. I think that is important. There are companies out there that do —as Neil said before — really good resources, but the nurseries do n’ t really know how to get access to that, where to track it.

U nfortunately, nurseries will go on to online catalogues, and they will buy resources because they are cheap, because we have to factor in budgets and infrastructure. There is not a lot of money in early years to get these things in sometimes . T he cost of them can be quite high . T hat is another setback. So the re is the hesitancy around technology as a whole in the sector and then obviously the hesitancy because actually there is a cost implication , and when the budgets are so tight people wonder, “C an I get that? ” and the answer is, “ Not really. If I get that, what happens to provisions or something else? ” So there is a budget implication and then there is training. B udget, hesitancy and training are the three concerns that make it difficult.
Q100 Y ou have covered most of the second part of my question as well, but do you perceive that there are safety risks without the training, the guidance, and the support ?

Yes, there are definitely safety risks. A few were picked up. We have things that can profile children . T here are privacy risks . T here are confidentiality risks. I mentioned earlier the example of a child confiding something to a toy . P erhaps they are experiencing some maltreatment at home or something like that . I f that is confided to a toy, what does that mean for our safeguarding practices? I think there certainly are risks and we need to be able to appraise them properly.

We tend to minimise that risk in our own settings by using restricted brands. So where we do use edtech , we will use well-known brands. We will also look to whether that organisation has intelligent, informed individuals who understand child development, very young children ’ s development, and so on. That does not secure the position because we are still fairly ignorant, but it just gives us a little bit of confidence that at least we are not dealing with a completely unknown quantity. But that is not the best way to do things, I would suggest.

Yes, safeguarding is always a big thing . With AI definitely, there are safeguarding concerns because there is a lack of awareness in the sector around it. W hen something is not statutory, when it is not something that is required, nurseries generally will opt out of it because it is seems like a “ good to have ” . I t might be in the “B irth to F ive ”. I t might be in something else . I t might be in a really good book, but it is good to have because they are focusing on what Ofsted is going to come and look at, what someone else is going to come and look at, and whether they are going to be judged on that?

T here does not seem to be any need to be concentrating on AI or cyber-security . R ight now , for me, cyber-security in early years is massive b ecause there is no awareness of it. As I said, with AI having smart speakers in a nursery is a massive safeguarding issue. It is a listening device . W e know it is . B ut nurseries will happily go and purchase them online and put them in the nursery without putting the right policies and things in place to safeguard themselves.

Q101 J ust a little bit more on safeguarding. Mr Leitch , you said at the beginning that the Government are all over physical safeguarding, but there is no support for emotional safeguarding . What specific risks do you think the increasing use of AI and edtech presents for young children rather than for the staff ? Do you think the current arrangements are adequate to manage this risk?

The biggest risks are not within early years settings, actually; they are within homes. As I have alluded to, we see the end result of that where basically there is a misuse of AI and technology. I come back to the point that alongside training and guidance for educators, a lot of the things that we do in an early years setting we share with parents, whether that be good nutrition , sleep practice —w hatever it happens to be. What I do not see at this point in time is any support being given by educators to parents who are struggling, basically, with AI and edtech.

The first point is that this should be part of an educator’s formal training. They should understand the risks associated with AI and the benefits associated with AI and edtech. At the moment, it is completely absent. I would integrate it into the formal training programmes and expectations of early years educators. That would be a starting point. Perhaps then we could do what we do with parents who are struggling to have their children eat vegetables or whatever: we share that good practice. At the moment, our educators are not really in a position to do that, other than saying avoid screen time.
It is a big ask for early years educators to be—

It is, but do you know what? That is why we are grossly underfunded, dare I say. I am not going to take the opportunity of making that case, but the reality is they are one of the most trusted people in a family’s life. They are not just their child’s educator. They are their nutritionist , their health visitor , their benefits guidance. They are even, dare I say, their relationship counsellors, and so on. Because of the new entitlements, more and more children are coming into early years settings. They are in a wonderful place to support parents. That is why they need better status, better recognition, and more money.

Q102 Thank you. Mr Waite, just this week it has come up in my office about schools moving to faceless marketing, so taking all their children’s faces off all their marketing materials, because they are worried about the use of AI and those children being visible online. I wonder if you could talk a little bit about how you think parents can be given confidence that information collected about their children, and perhaps also images, is used appropriately. Do you think there is a reason for concern around that?

Yes. I think the main thing is parent partnership, and the relationship between nursery and parent is essential. We are talking about photographs and safeguarding and things like that. Online safety again is something that not only do our educators need to be aware of, but as settings we need to make parents more aware of it. We all know in September that just went all the parents took a picture of the children in a new school uniform outside the front door, with a door number, car registration plate and everything like that. It is making them more aware of what they do. Some nurseries are now really conscious about blocking out faces because of AI fake applications that can do horrible things. There are really not nice people out there who will do horrible things with it. For me, that is a real shame because when you are maybe looking at a photograph of your child on a learning journal or something, you would have liked to have seen their face or heard their voice or just get a real sense of it. Unfortunately, because of the world we are in, all that has been taken away a little bit.
Q103 Those pictures can still be shared with parents privately, can’t they? There can be private access to images that are not out there.

Yes. If you are using learning journal platforms and they are pretty secure, parents can get those photographs. I think it is where nurseries want to share good practice or advertise what they do. They might put a learning experience on Instagram—a forest school might want to show you what they did in the forest—and sometimes just seeing the child’s hand is allowed . I am hearing people saying, “We are just going to show hands , ” or, “We are just going to show this , ” and for me that is the state we are in. That is quite sad. We have to come up with a system where we can still do some of those old things but just make it safer . That is a tough one because it is so easy to manipulate things.
Q104 Professor Gibson, do you have anything more you would like to add on safeguarding?

I think there are risks around poorly trained or poorly guardrailed generative AI models. There have been some quite high-profile cases of toys that have a generative AI component marketed to children and then being found to be able to talk about things that children should not be talking about. In my experience, you have to work quite hard to get that conversation out. The risk might not be as much as it has been blown up to be in some outlets, but it is definitely real; it is definitely there. In particular, if we do not have any regulation around what those guardrails should be, I think the risk could get bigger as we see products coming in from all over the world.

Thank you. I think in the interests of time I am going to bring this session to a close. Thank you very much. It has been a fascinating session for us this morning and lots of food for thought for the Committee. If we can change over the panels as quickly as we can, that would be appreciated. Thank you very much for being with us this morning.
Examination of Witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Mhairi Aitken, Professor Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Professor Sandra Leaton Gray and Meg Moss.
[This evidence was taken by video conference]

Q105 Welcome back for our second panel in our evidence session on AI and edtech, where we are considering AI and edtech in the early years. Can I invite our second panel of witnesses to introduce themselves to us, please, starting with Professor Leaton Gray? Thank you.

I am Professor of Education Futures at UCL. I carry out research into social and ethical implications of technology and AI, going as far as biometrics and 6G and quantum infrastructural settings. I am very interested in the long-term consequences of AI development and related standards setting. I did an Office for AI secondment from UCL in 2022 to 2023. I am a member of the College of Experts for DCMS and BIST, and I am the author of two books on digital childhoods.

I am Meg Moss , head of public affairs and adv ocacy at the National Counselling and Psychotherapy Society. I have been working for a number of years across a few different strands of AI, especially from a therapeutic perspective, the impact that it is having therapeutically on practitioners as well as young people and adults. I have also been working around regulation for a number of years. I am interested in a variety of AI issues, so things around liability and harms, safeguarding, and what is happening in the broader landscape as well.

Good morning. I am Mhairi Aitken. I am a co-founder and director at Our AI Collective. Our AI Collective is a community interest company that is focused on putting public voices and public interests at the heart of AI. For the last six years my research has focused particularly on children’s relationships with AI and, more broadly, digital technologies. In particular, it has involved child-centred approaches, which engage with children and young people to understand what their real experiences with digital technologies are. Previously, I led the children and AI programme at the Alan Turing Institute, which is the national institute for AI and data science. I also held the children’s AI summit in 2025. I am very interested in children and young people’s experiences and relationships with digital technologies, particularly AI.

I am Sarah-Jayne Blakemore , Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Neuroscience at Cambridge. I am sorry I cannot be there in person, but I have meetings here either side of this. I have run a lab for the last 22 years—initially at UCL, now in Cambridge—on the development of the adolescent brain, adolescent mind and adolescent mental health, with a particular focus on social brain development. I have an interest in things like the effects of social media on adolescent development and now AI.

Q106 Thank you all for being with us this morning. I will begin our questioning. How would you describe the overall impact that AI and educational technology is currently having on children and young people’s learning? I will start with you, Professor Leaton Gray.

I think it is hard for us to know exactly what the impact is. It is a very underfunded area. We are spending about—this is back of an envelope figures that would not pass the Treasury sniff test—£3.50 a head on rolling out tech solutions, usually to improve things like teacher workload efficiency and so on, in comparison with spending about 72p per head on evaluating the impact of what we are doing. There is an element of the reverse order to what we might have wanted to do, but events have overtaken us.

To give it some broader context, globally companies are spending about $26 million per hour for all kinds of AI development and so on. We know about the rapid pace of those developments. It is leaving us really exposed. What we are seeing is very small-scale studies, often testbed type studies, that are looking at one product with a limited sample of people and so on. That is better than nothing, but of course versions change very quickly and methodologies change very quickly in this field. It is just trying to plug the dam with a finger, really, and hoping that what has been described as the tsunami of AI is not going to overtake us even more rapidly than we fear.

I completely agree that we do not really know how AI affects learning. The problem is that, as you have probably heard many times before from researchers, good quality research takes months or years, whereas AI advances far, far quicker than that. There is an inherent problem at the moment in trying to understand how current forms of AI are influencing learning. By the time we know that, the AI will have moved on to some other form that is impossible to predict at the moment.

I think about this a lot, and in the context of social media . I think what we need to do is turn to research where we know something that might be relevant, even indirectly relevant, for AI. For example, and I can talk about this in more detail later if you are interested , but just to summarise, we know quite a lot about how the human brain develops in childhood and adolescence. We know that the brain is highly plastic during childhood and adolescence, which means that it is particularly good at incorporating environmental input into the way it develops. It is particularly sensitive to the environment and environmental experience, in childhood and adolescence. Of course, the environment includes many things, including digital interactions, AI and social media, so we can assume that social media and AI are influencing the way the brain develops if a child uses those things. We know quite a lot about that and quite a lot about how that might occur. We know quite a lot about how children and adolescents learn and what is necessary for learning. This relates back to the neuroplasticity. We know about their developmental needs, like what kinds of environmental input are important at different ages and stages of development.

That brings me to my last point, which is on social development. Like I mentioned, our main focus in my lab is on the development of the social brain and social cognition and social behaviour, particularly in adolescents, although social interaction is hugely important in childhood as well. We know that it is important for children and young people to engage in social interactions with real life people. We do not know what happens to development if those real life people are replaced by digital forms like AI bots.

I do not have too much to add to that, but there is some tangential research that I am aware of around AI assistance reducing persistence and hurting independent performance, and we can extrapolate from that the impact that that would have . That was Carnegie Mellon University and Oxford University, along with MIT and UCLA. Persistence is foundational to skill acquisition. We see that it is perhaps improving performance in the short term, but the negative effects are emerging after just 10 minutes of use, according to that study. That is maybe not directly speaking to what is actually happening to young people, but we can see that people are looking at what is actually happening to persistence and learning and the things that make knowledge sticky, that effort that we have to put into learning things.

There was a really interesting piece of work on the impact of AI on creativity in young people. For Safer Internet Day research in February this year, they spoke to eight to 17-year-olds, and 49% of them said that AI was making young people their age less creative. That is foundational to learning. Creativity is such an important part of young people’s brain development. I have nothing more to add to that, but yes, there is some interesting research going on.
I have a few points to add to what everybody has already said. I will try not to repeat.

I guess the first thing to say is it is important to remember that children and young people are an incredibly diverse group. It could not possibly be a more diverse group. It includes so many different experiences, identities and needs within that group, and experiences of digital technologies and experiences of AI are very different depending on children’s backgrounds, their identities, whether they have additional support needs, and whether they have access to digital technologies. There are so many different factors that shape or change the ways that they experience the technologies and what the impacts of those technologies are. I think that it is important to remember that we do not think of children and young people as a homogenous group.

When we think about the impacts of AI within education, it is also important to recognise that children and young people are interacting or experiencing AI in many parts of their lives , so the impacts within education cannot neatly be separated from the ways they are also experiencing or interacting with digital technologies and AI outside of formal education settings. That includes exposure to AI-generated content, misinformation, disinformation, and the challenge that that presents for critical thinking, for having the ability to reliably identify what is real and what is potentially AI generated.
