The utilities would be open to it, but there are not a lot of citizens or consumers who consider it to be a relevant enough question at this time, at least, to really engage themselves with. Again, in my view, we in the Netherlands are at a turning point where we are facing a lot of challenges that are quite severe.

Q153 One of the things I was struck by when I was looking at the map of the areas that the water companies cover was that some seem considerably larger than others. You mentioned Vitens. It seems to cover a huge chunk of the country, whereas others are relatively small. Do you see any kind of advantage or disadvantage in the size of those companies within the Netherlands? Does that have a bearing on their performance , or are they different factors altogether?

No, other factors are much more relevant, such as water sources; whether they are surface water or groundwater companies really impacts tariffs. Some areas have easier access to water than others. These factors are much more determinant in the performance of the utilities. In the case of Vitens , a managing board and a board of directors became big in the 1990s. There was the threat of privatisation , and the idea was that if it grew, it would be more difficult to take over. That is one of the reasons why Vitens is relatively big .

It is also quite problematic for Vitens because although it is a large company, its service provision system consists of hundreds of smaller systems that are not very well connected. That leads to a lot of difficulties because it is not able to actually ensure that the water is going to the systems where it is most needed. Y ou need to distinguish the size of the company from, in the end, the provision of water services, water supplies , and infrastructure . The infrastructural system is crucial, perhaps more than the size of the company.

Q154 I wanted to come on to the infrastructure because you mentioned that, similar to the UK, the Netherlands has a lot of ageing infrastructure. A lot of investment will be needed in the coming decade or two. Obviously, the difference with your system is that you do not have private shareholders who can put in equity ; i t has to come from the local authorities. How effectively have those companies been able to invest , and what is the forward view?

Like in France, the companies do not receive any funding from the local authorities. The companies are completely self-financing. They fund their investments through loans, which they then have to pay off through the revenue generated from the tariffs. Apart from the tariffs, they have no other source of income. The Dutch water utilities are able to source relatively favourable loans because they are a monopoly for water supply, for which there is always going to be demand. They are semi-public, which means that the odds that a water utility is going to go bankrupt or default on a loan are very small. That means that banks are quite happy to provide the loans for investment. Again, it means the tariff is going to increase. It has increased substantially over the past four years. I assume it will continue to increase in the coming years. T hat is the way it is.

Q155 We are interested in the role of the Dutch water bank, which was obviously set up in the wake of devastating flooding in the Netherlands. It seems to have played a crucial role in providing stable, low-interest finance. We have also heard that the bank has expanded its operations massively , and there is some concern that it is not providing enough finance now for its original objective of securing the country’s water supplies. Is its role diminishing? What will its role be in this future investment?

The Netherlands Water Bank was initially established by the water boards, not by the water supply companies, for water security and water safety issues. In principle, it has a mandate to lend to entities which have a public purpose. Water supply companies have access to the Netherlands Water Bank, and some utilities also have loans with it . However at the moment, the Netherlands Water Bank ’s main source of loans is in social housing. It has moved beyond the water sector.

For the water utilities, it is not such a problem because the private banks are also quite interested in lending money to the water utilities. Most water utilities will have loans with multiple banks because they want to spread their loans over multiple providers and keep contacts in case they need to have quick access to loans, and so on . I personally do not think that the Netherlands Water Bank ’s development is damaging for the water utilities. The water utilities in the Netherlands are still able to access the funding that they need quite easily .

Q156 Do those private banks demand a higher return on their investment? Is there a concern about water companies perhaps taking on too much debt, which is very much the case with many of ours in the UK?
I f I am not mistaken, there are limits to the loans that they are able to take. I do not think there is a concern at the moment of utilities taking on too much debt.

Q157 Is there a concern that if there are limits on the amount of debt they can take on — as you mentioned, local authorities do not put money in — there are potentially some big investment requirements coming up ? Is there then a concern that that will fall on tariffs because that is the only other option you have?

It is going to fall on tariffs. The question is how to deal with keeping the tariffs more affordable. In the Netherlands, we have never subsidised tariffs ; i t is not something that we have ever done. Instead, the social security system provides benefits or allowances that can support low-income families in covering higher costs for certain basic services. The support for low-income households to deal with higher tariffs would come from a different source than from the water utilities. The tariffs, by law, need to reflect the cost of production ; t hey need to reflect the cost of provision. They are allowed to make a small profit, which sometimes goes to the shareholders , and sometimes is reinvested in the system . They need to reflect the real costs of providing services.

Q158 Lastly, I want to ask you about the research you have done on public ownership more broadly : the studies you have looked into outside the Netherlands. What kind of lessons do you think we can draw from the work you have done looking overseas? Nobody has a perfect system , but it seems that there are very good features of lots of different systems that we need to bring into ours.

I f it is a public utility, it is important to look at it in the broader governance structure. The Netherlands has the Water Supply Act, which is crucial. The fact that there are multiple shareholders is crucial. There is a lot of shared collaboration between the water utilities. Although we have 10 water utilities, we only have four water quality laboratories because most of these laboratories are co-owned by different utilities. In my view, i t is that broader structure that makes a water utility provide an enabling environment and a situation in which it can perform well.

I f I look at the cases that I have studied abroad, they often try to reform the utility, perhaps change its ownership, or make it into a private company owned by a public shareholder rather than a direct public utility. I am not so convinced that that is enough. You need to think more about the broader governance structure and the enabling environment in which that operates. If you do not address that, then changing the ownership has little impact.
Q159 Marine , you wanted to come back in.

Yes, thank you. If time allows, I just wanted to add something regarding funding of our water sector. A fourth of our water bills funds water agencies and all the money that is collected within a river basin can be used and then redistributed to local government to help them fund investments. Local government s can use revenues from water bills, subsidies, concessional loans from water agencies, and funding from the European Union and other local governments to help them fund their investments. This was a quick add-on that I find useful : having an agency at the scale of a river basin that can give priority in terms of investment and orientate the action of local government s by bringing additional funds to issues that are seen as most urgent and relevant within a river basin.
That is interesting , but I will hand back to the Chair in the interest s of time.

Marine and Klaas, thank you so much for joining us in our little Committee Eurovision homage. We appreciate your attendance. There is a lot more that we could discuss , but unfortunately time is against us today . T hank you for your attendance and co-operation .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: David Henderson, Professor David Hall, Professor Ewan McGaughey and Professor David Saal .

Good morning, everyon e. T hank you again for your attendance. We are up against it a bit for time, but I am sure we will manage to ventilate all the issues. Can I just invite you all to say a few words of introduction?
My name is David Henderson. I am the c hief e xecutive o fficer of Water UK, which represents all the water companies in the United Kingdom.
Welcome back.

I am David Saal. I am a professor of economics at Loughborough University. I fell into water and sewage in 1999 when I started working with David Parker on privatisation of various industries . I have been working on it since, doing cost assessment modelling, regulatory work and so on .
There are so many ways we could take that introduction , but we are going to be disciplined.
My name is Ewan McGaughey. I am a professor of law at King’s College London and a research associate at the Centre for Business Research at the University of Cambridge.
And th e third of our triumvirate of Davids .

Yes , another David, I am afraid. I am a visiting professor at the Public Services International Research Unit at the University of Greenwich . I have been researching this stuff for some decades now.
We are going to be looking now at some issues with privatisation and the potential for a reformed water sector. Sarah, you are going to lead our questioning o n this.

Q160 The IWC report published in July 2025 sets out a comprehensive vision of the water industry and what it could look like . It is proposing reforms to tackle the issues of the water sector. What problems will the c ommission’s proposal s solve? W hat issues do you think are going to remain unaddressed? I will start with the first of Davids.

I t is a very good report. I should say that , in representing all the water companies across the United Kingdom, I represent the state-owned Scottish Water and Northern Ireland Water, the not-for-profit in Wales, as well as the private companies in England. It is very clear that the challenges are the same. Climate change does not discriminate against ownership model. The changing needs of businesses — especially data centres, some of which can use a hell of a lot of water when it comes to high temperatures — do not discriminate against ownership model ; nor does population growth. We are seeing that in all four nations of the United Kingdom.

Sir Jon Cunliffe has identified that there is no correlation between ownership and performance. It is a view backed up by the OECD in Paris, when it look s across Europe as well as the rest of the western world. Cunliffe has identified that , regardless of ownership model, there are three crucial ingredients . First, there must be clear strategies set by the Government of the day ; t he Government need to be clear about the trade-offs — what they want, broadly understanding the cost impact. Secondly, you need strong regulation, so you are able to implement that strategy , enforce it and m ake sure that the water companies are delivering. Th irdly, in order for the water companies to deliver, they need the money. It does not matter whether that money comes from water bill payers or from taxpayers, but it has to come.

We see challenges in the financing, whether it be privatel y or publicly owned . I thought it was very interesting hearing some of the financing challenges in France and the Netherlands that you heard earlier, where we have state-owned companies insufficiently invested in their infrastructure. That is what Cunliffe has set out to reform. There are 88 recommendations in total. It is an excellent report ; i t has now been with the Government for 15 months — 15 months tomorrow, to be exact. I t is very necessary for them to get on and deliver that report. If they do, it is going to deliver the transformation to the sector that the whole country wants to see and rightly deserves.

I will say what I agree with , and then the “ b ut ”. T he regulatory model is not fit for purpose , p articularly Ofwat’s modelling and approach to things. I agree with that. There is a great need for better public control and more local control. The idea of having more catchment management and some sort of public representatives is very good. Catchment areas are very good.

Let me just go back a little in history because this will be relevant. T here was a great report from the advisory board somewhere in the Aston l ibrary when I was there as a research fellow. When the RWAs were created in 1974 , the engineers and experts were saying, “W e need 10 to 15 entities for water basin management. We need 50 operating units. Economies of scale , how we run things and how we do things is so different if it is a city or a small place and so forth. ” I do not know who did it — I never found it out — but , l oosely, the politicians got hold of it and said , “ Ten is a good number ,” and t hey merged everything up to 10 units.

That system was never economically rational. The W A SCs were not based on any economic rationality. Most of the systems we have talked about today — I know about Japan, Germany and the Netherlands , and I have written on two of those countries — organically develop and merge. They are not forced together like that. When we come to Cunliffe , I absolutely agree that we should go to catchment management and think about it that way. However, t hat means that the way O fwat has been assessing costs would need to fundamentally change. What drives and what will be needed will be different in different catchment areas : different ways to treat sludge, different ways to get the water. We heard about surface versus groundwater and so on before.

The other issue , which I do not have enough time to go into this session, was a comment before about two periods post O fwat . T here was the first period up to 1995 , when there was basically no incentive to do anything because the price caps were set by the Government to make sure privatisation was successful. Ian Byatt came in and tightened them, and then my own research shows that the RCV values were completely overvalued. If the prices of companies went below that, that was just reflecting the true value the investors had put into the companies.

Skipping ahead to the most important thing from 2015 to 2025, T ot E x is an expenditure that needs to be funded. It is not a cost. From conversations with Alan Sutherland at WICS a long time ago, the regulator is responsible for making sure there is enough money. That is not a cost. The whole idea is Cunliffe is saying we need to do more thinking about how capital is invested, breaking up O p E x a bit. I do not have what he said down exactly in my head . What is missing in Cunliffe is what structure that needs to be . I t does not mean you have to break up the companies, but it is how you assess them.

Secondly, it is the way that O fwat assesses. O fwat was not a bad regulator because it did too much econometrics — I would say that , I do econometrics — but because of the way it did it. The goal post 2015 was driving competition, which really has not happened. Sorry, that was a bit long.
That wa s great. Thank you very much indeed.

I agree with a lot of what Dave has just said. The essential question that Cunliffe could not answer — because he was not asked — was the ownership question. We are going to hear a lot today , and we have heard a lot from the water industry , about how what matters is good regulation and about how ownership does not really matter , if at all. There are at least four reasons why that is clearly mistaken.

First, if you have private owners, then they are paying shareholders. If you do not have private ownership, you do not have to pay. A bout £ 85 billion —I think £ 85.2 billion last time Dave checked — since privatisation has gone to shareholders. That is money that could be reinvested in the system but is not.

The second big disadvantage of having private ownership is a higher cost of borrowing. If you are publicly owned, you can access the lowest cost of borrowing , close to the Bank of England base rate, the Public Works Loan Board. I f you are a private or mutual entity , because non-profits are still private, then you are going to have to access the private bond markets. The amount that has been returned to banks and other bondholders since privatisation is now in excess of the amount that has been returned to shareholders. I just did some figures myself in a short report last year , and o n the figures that I came up with , Thames Water had returned over £ 13 billion since privatisation to bondholders , w hereas to shareholders it is a little over £ 10 billion. The second point is higher borrowing costs.

The third reason why ownership really matter s and why it is not just about good regulation is that if you have public ownership , you can set public purposes in a statute , w hereas the purposes of a privatised water company are going to be oriented towards returns to capital.

Fourthly, and this is so vital , is that when you have a privatised water system , you have a permanent lobby group trying to ga me the regulatory structure , trying to make sure that the regulators are not doing the job of regulating — turning a blind eye to the pollution, the leaks, and the billions and billions that are shipped overseas. Those are the main things that obviously Cunliffe was not asked to deal with and that really matter . T his is why this Committee is a great opportunity.

To cut it short, agreeing with much of what Ewan said and one or two of the interesting points that David Sa a l made, the elimination of public ownership from his terms of reference was a really serious error. That is h ighlighted by Marine Colon’s initial statement about France, which is very simply, “L ocal authorities are responsible. ” They are responsible for the service, setting out plans and making sure decisions are taken in accordance with those plans . T hey are also responsible for deciding how the system is operated, including the potential for concessions and otherwise .

T hat cannot be said here. Even that first part cannot be said. Local authorities are responsible for nothing in the system at the moment. That is the result of a couple of major decisions made in previous decades. One was the decision that David Sa a l referred to , of the creation of the regional W A SCs in 1974. Again, as he says, it was not done o n the grounds of economic rationale but environmental rationale. That is a difference from the Dutch system , where the regional companies were developed on an ad hoc basis. That decision in 1974 effectively created multi-municipal entities that were still governed by the municipalities.

The second decision, which was briefly referred to by David Owen earlier, is perhaps a more serious one, which was that in 1984, water responsibility in the UK was nationalised. People a sk , “S hould we nationalise the water system or not? ” That was done in 1984. It was done by the Thatcher Government. That effectively t ook away the remaining responsibilities and powers of local authorities on the regional water authorities.

Since then, that has been the crying gap in the entire system that is very noticeable at the local level. I notice it on occasions whe n I am asked to comment on radio programmes on local problems. There are local councillors articulating the concerns of local people, desperately frustrated that they have no power to do anything about them at all. That has to be the most fundamental thing that should be rectified in the system : public responsibility, which implies public ownership of the system , to take decisions.

Can I just put down a marker here before you carry on? N ationalisation did not happen in Scotland. Water remained under the control of the regional councils, which themselves were then reorganised in about 1996 . I t was only then, with the creation of Scottish Water in 2002, that you had that process of nationalisation. Are there lessons that we might draw from that? Bear in mind, I do not want to start a hare running here but just put down the marker.

Q161 J ust to your point and to David’s point there , i n Somerset, we have quite a unique situation. We have the Somerset Rivers Authority , which was set up after the floods in 2013-14. It brings together water, flood and land management partners together at a catchment level. Do you think those existing partnerships , such as that particular model around the Somerset Rivers Authority, which I do not believe has ever done its job in becoming an authority, could be the start of a model for regional planning that perhaps the c ommission envisages, rather than setting up new organisations? T hat is t o David and David, Saal and Hall —o nly because you mentioned that.

T he first thing I would say is that we should go back to lessons learned . It is like how , as a parent , you do not want to make the mistakes that your parents made ; you want to fix them with your kids, right? T here was a great paper when I first started doing privatisation work , by Hunt and L y nk, which basically said that there was a loss when , at privatisation, flood management and other activities —I forget exactly what they were— were hived off from the water authorities and put into what was the National Rivers Authority. What I want to get after is that one of the things that really matters here is that water is different and sewage is different because it has so much non-priced merit goods or whatever around it . P eople may or may not be willing to pay for the environment , and we have to make decisions around that.

Yes , is the answer : the Somerset b oard could be a way forward . However, what I really picked up from Cunliffe, which I have been reading and thinking about more in the last couple of weeks — I wonder why —is how there is such a multiplicity of organisations responsible. You have to be careful because you need separate agents. One of the benefits of privatisation is you had a separate economic regulator . Y ou had an entity other than the regional water authority that was responsible for drinking water quality and environmental management. On the other hand, you need advocates. There is some balance between bringing together an d understanding and capacity, because you need capacity to know what is going on , to plan and to think, but there is also a need for agents.

One thing I pick ed up in Cunliffe was a very contradictory statement in there about how the water regulator should be merged, meaning Ofwat , but it also should be independent . T hat will not happen if it is in the same entity. So y es, but the devil i s in the details on how you do it.

I go back to my previous statement and say, yes, that is indeed possible, but the key first step is to give local authorities responsibility for the system. You phrased it as an intensely local question . T hat seems to me to clarify an important reason why these responsibilities should be devolved back to the local level, which they are in virtually every other major country in Europe and North America.

I would like to j ust carry on a bit on one or two points . O ne of the frustrations I came across over the lack of local authority responsibility was following a presentation by somebody of precisely a catchment area plan for the Eden Valley in Cumbria . I t was a very eloquent presentation of a beautifully prepared plan , with discussion with landowners, farmers and so on. S he said , “T hat was great , we we re very happy with it , we press - released it and then we did n’ t know who to show it to get it actioned .” T hat can be repeated here in many local conditions.

Again , just to comment on multiple responsibilities, I am not sure if it is necessarily inefficient . France has an astonishing range of local bodies . T he clean - up it did on the Seine involved I do not know how many local authorities , sewage authorities and water authorities but it was effective and it worked . It does that planning in managing its rivers as well . M aybe multiple authorities can work , but that issue of local responsibility is key.

Q162 I will move on because I know we are pushed for time . T he People’s Commission on the Water S ector stated that public ownership could save the public over £ 22 billion over five years because this is the return on capital allowed by Ofwat for private operators to distribute to shareholders, banks and other lenders. Supporters of the private sector often point to its role in innovation, finding efficiencies and growing productivity . T o what extent have these aspects improved in the water sector since 1989 ? C ould any gains be threatened by reforming the system?

I am very happy to describe the benefits that have come since 1989 . I would argue , and some of your earlier witnesses agreed , that we have seen a transformation specifically in terms of waste water treatment. We used to have almost no treatment of sewage before 1989 in large parts of the country , now we have tertiary treatment in almost all the major urban areas . T hat has radically reduced the amount of ammonia and phosphates entering our rivers and streams : 80 % or 70% reductions or so. We have also seen the quality of our bathing waters increase six or sevenfold in terms of those that are rated good or excellent . T his was not the case back in 1989.

Drinking water was always pretty good but is now around the world ’ s very best . T hat was not the case back in 1989 . Unfortunately, w e used to hav e cryptosporidium incidents , which can be very dangerous, happening almost every year . N ow they are happening about every decade. There have been improvements . T hat is not to say there is not a lot more to do ; there definitely is. We know that the people rightly need to have a far better performing sector , which is why C unliffe’s report is so important .

We are all in on t he catchment - based area that has just been discussed . I t is an excellent model for enabling people on the ground who understand their areas best to identify what needs to happen, work with farmers, house builders, the highways agency and local authorities , and then allocat e the funds in the most efficient way. It would also be cheaper if you had nature - based solutions being used more often than the concrete and steel we are forced to build because of very prescriptive legislations , which actually is not a good use of funds. T here can be a lot done there.

There was a discussion earlier about dividends, and it is not true to say that the public sector does not extract dividends. In Northern Ireland, the water company is forced to pay dividends to its owner, the Northern Ireland Government. In my home state of Victoria, the state g overnment own all the water companies and extract billions of dollars over time from their water companies, as the case in New South Wales. The returns on the investment , as it were, the return on equity measure , are far higher t han the privately owned companies here in England and Wales.

Dividends can be paid whether you are privately owned or publicly owned ; it is a question of whether that is being used to finance the investment . T hat £ 22 billion you mention ed is the return being paid . If we had it separately paid by the taxpayer for example, we would be paying a return to the people who lent us the money , or taxes would need to rise , or we would need to inflict spending cuts elsewhere to fund it. The funds have to flow from somewhere .

Y ou see benefits and disbenefits from different models. It is important that you identify what is needed . T hat strategy is the first recommendation of his 88, and it is the most important . Government need to be clear about what they want, then the regulation can flow , then the funding needs to flow .

Q163 Greenpeace has stated that , “ England’s 35 - year experiment with privatised water has faile d,” and s hareholder returns have been prioritised over public service . Surfers Against Sewage similarly argued that th e review , “U tterly fails to prioritise public benefit over private profit .” W hat do you say to those?

A s I say, I am not sure what Greenpeace thinks about leakage falling by about 43%, 80% reductions in ammonia, and very large reductions in phosphates in our rivers and seas. They are the consequence of very large investment. Those are facts independently verified. The state of our environment is better. It is not as good as it should be , t hat much is very clea r; i t needs much more investment. Climate change is putting huge pressure on our network. That is true across the whole of the United Kingdom. It is going to need very large investment. As we just heard, the same is true in the Netherlands and France.

Climate change is putting huge pressure across the whole world. That is going to require a stronger and bigger system, more able to withstand those torrential downpours of rain, and then enable us to provide water when we have not had any rain . I n some parts of the country , th e most recent drought we are currently experiencing has lasted 60 or 70 days. We need very large investment. It can come from bill payers or taxpayers , but i t need s to come.

I agree with hardly any of that . First, there is the idea that we need tax rises or spending cuts to finance water improvement . N o , if we had a public system , we would have about a third more of our bills going into infrastructure spending . I t would not be going in the returns on capital that you mentioned . Ofwat sets in the price reviews a limit on returns on capital , which is £ 22.04 7 billion in the current price review period . B y the way , in the last price review period it was about £ 11 billion . T he amount that shareholders and banks can get out of our water system has almost doubled in the last five years.

The other thing is this fantasy story that everything is hunky-dory and that our water system has improved . J ust some quick statistics : we have the seventh worst surface water quality in Europe , w e have the fif th worst bathing water quality in Europe — this is in England — and we have the sixt h highest bills . Y ou can find that in the Eu rEau report on drinking water in Europe statistics . I t is untenable to suggest that things are getting better .

I will just give you one more example . Ofwat also sets targets for pollution reduction and leak reduction . I n PR19 it set a pollution reduction target of 30% for Thames W ater . B y the way , that means that 70% of the statutory duty to make sure that all sewage goes through secondary treatment is not being touched by Ofwat . It is just saying , “D o 30% of your statutory obligations .” Thames W ater not only could not reduce the pollution by 30% , but pollution incidents went up by 53.6%. It had a leak reduction target of 20.4% , and it did not get anywhere close : it reduced leaks by 13.2% .

A nice comparison with this is Cambodia . In 1993, t he capital Phnom Pen h had 72% of its water being leaked and it got that down to 8% in 12 years . If Cambodia can do it and Phnom Penh can do it , there is no reason why London could not do it if we did not have the disastrous system we have at the moment .

T here is not a decision that says nationalisation or private is better . T he experience for many consumers has not been perceived as good or has not been good in the UK , but some issues boil down to what David Hall said before about the current system : there is just not any local public voice . I f you have a problem with a stream near you , how do you get that through ? E ven Cunliffe’s idea that the Birmingham mayor where I live in Solihull is going to be my representative or somethin g is just not going to work .

I t is also about the incentives and what you value . I agree with David Henderson about the Government and / or the catchment authority . I emphasise again that you have to assess costs at catchment level, integrated, not at company level , if you are going to do that . Y ou have to set priorities ; you need to get local voice to that , and then you need to set the incentives right .

I will give you two examples . L eakage came up . I cannot find them any more , but I remember years ago I did a paper on water leakage and incentives and efficiency , and w e found a couple of quotes at the time that Ofwat was telling companies “N o, no, no, do less . Y ou ’ re doing too much on water leakage .”

T he second example is from when I was working with Anglia n Water . I did its cost modelling for the 2019 price review . W e developed some beautiful models that took into account that it was an absolute leader on per capita consumption and leakage. There was nothing in Ofwat’s modelling directly in the econometrics that took that into account . If the incentives are not being set properly —it could be that the statements say , “W e want this ,” but it ’ s not being followed through — there is a problem.

With regard to the whole dividend debate and so forth, I had data that was consistent until 2015, and regulatory capital values definitely were higher than any investment that went in . T hey are not a true measure of value . T here definitely were issues in the beginning with excess funding . E ven if private companies are steward s, I will just say it, my perception from working with Anglia n Water closely for about three or four years — I no longer do —was that the people there cared and wanted to do something about the environment . T he ones I was interfacing with did, but if the incentives and the system are not supporting that, you are going to have a problem . I t is all about getting that right .

Q164 Clearly , we have some differing views around the table . However, t he stark reality is that it is estimated that over £300 billion - worth of investment is needed over the next 25 years to reach the Government goals and improve future water security . O n that basis, is it the private sector or the public sector ? W hich is better equipped to really raise that money at the scale that is required , invest over that timeframe and bring value to our customers ?

If we agree that it is £300 billion , and that is the estimate of the National Audit Office , then that money would need to be found either by the taxpayer , if it were owned by the state , or by a bill payer . That would be slowly paid over time , just like a mortgage is, which is being first paid up front by the investors . If the state can be very clear —
We would still have bill payers in a nationalised system .

T hat is right . J ust like a bank provides the funding for the house up front if you have a mortgage , and then the mortgage holder slowly repays the price of that acquisition of the house over time , here in England and Wales we have investors putting in the money up front and it is slowly recouped over time through the bill. Yes, the bill payers ultimately pay. A s in Northern Ireland , you could have no bill payers and instead just have the taxpayer. If the taxpayer is prepared to find that £300 billion over 25 years and is very clear on how that is going to be funded , then of course that would be able to work.

W e have a lot of people standing in th e queue for scarce resources: people who need money for defence , health or education . A cross the world , we see Ministers generally prioritising expenditure from those quarters rather than water . Ministers frankly prefer to cut ribbons on submarines than sewers. That is true across the world , and I go to many international conferences . There are not that many votes in sparkling clean sewers , compared with sparkling clean schools and hospitals . However, if the Government can absolutely be certain they are going to find that £300 billion , then of course they would be able to do so and facilitate all that investment. It is just that experience suggests it is a difficult thing to do.
Q165 Ewan, y ou might have a different point on that , and then I will come to David Hall .

Just very briefly , because a lot of the work comes from David’s figures , t here has been £85 billion since privatisation to shareholders and more than that to bondholders. If you add that together, that is £170 billion . If you want to finance £300 billion in spending , then it is probably going to be a lot easier to do that if you are not paying the people David Henderson represents.

I have just a couple of points . F irst , another bit of research we did was to answer the question , how much equity have private shareholders actually invested in the system since privatisation ? E quity is the additional thing , if you like, that private companies had . T he answer , we found shocking , but in real terms it is minus £5 billion —m inus £5 billion . T he actual equity on the books at the moment is £5 billion less in current price terms than it was at the start.
Q166 On that basis, does that fundamentally weaken the argument for the private ownership of assets?

Yes , hugely , because the only additional thing that you are hoping to bring is that . F or example , private equity funds , for sure , have billions or trillions of dollars available but that adds nothing unless they actually invest it in the systems . S imply buying the systems from the previous owner does not inject any money into the system . W e must have equity investment , and we have had less than zero . T hat undermines any idea that the private sector is being innovative.

I have a q uick supplementary point . In David Hen der son’s initial statement he referred to treatment , but typically the advances claimed by the private sector under privatisation are advances driven by EU regulation s. T hey are actually achievements of public regulation and law rather than the particular operator that happens to have had to implement them.

There is possibly a case with Scottish Water . S ome PF I treatment plants were put in because Scotland was late , but my understanding — I am not sure if I am correct on this —is that Scotland i s moving away from those PFIs because they are actually relatively expensive . It ha s been trying to do that.

I wanted to change the debate . If we are talking about catchment, we want to talk about public interest and we need to do the right thing, like the point befor e. W hat really matters is we need a plan of where we are going and what environmental and drinking water issues we care about , which really satisfies people’s needs and the environment . T h en we need to decide, what is the best outcome for consumers and the environment ?

T hat goes back to the public interest and how y ou get that i n but also , what is the cost of capital? You often talk about a weighted average cost of capital , which is the various ways you can do it. I am aware that we have had examples . C ompanies such as Scottish Water , and apparently Welsh Water, used retained earnings . They make a profit and it goes back into investment. They also use deb t. T hat debt could be private or public . Scotland borrows money from the T reasury , Anglian Water and Severn Trent borrow money privatel y. T here is equity investment, and we can have injections into the model . S omebody’s comment earlier today that there was no equity actually ingested in privatisation , and they just bought the company , is true . However, you could get equity investment and of course you get public injection , which is very common in America and Japa n. T he national Government actually gives grants to build capital.

I am not a financial economist , but the right way to do this is not what is the cheapest, but what is the best , lowest - risk way to do that ? M y pension fund is in trouble with Thames Water because it want s risk - free assets . USS owns a lot of Thames Water . W e want to track those kinds of investors , and we need to think about that . W e need to move forward and find the cheapest way. I am not sure if saying public or private is the best way of doing it.

I would like to just add a footnote, which is actually really important not just for water but for energy and transport. If we want to get more investment into the water system, then potentially there needs to be borrowing, and water companies might go into debt for borrowing. If water companies are taken into public ownership, our current fiscal rules under the charter for budget responsibility say that a publicly owned water company ’s debt counts as part of the national debt. We are the only country in Europe that does this. All other countries under the E uropean s ystem of a ccounts say that when you are adding up national debt, if you have publicly owned companies, including water, energy and transport, their borrowing does not add to the national debt.

One of the big reasons why the former Chancellor , Rachel Ree ve s, did not want to look at public ownership of Thames Water and putting it into special administration was a concern that it would add to the national debt. Some £2 trillion - worth of assets under management wrote to the Treasury saying , “P lease change the charter for budget responsibility accounting rules so that we take out public corporations that are market actors from the calculation of national debt, ” but it was never replied to. It is so important to understand that we are unique in artificially inflating our national debt under our own accounting figures, unlike the European s ystem of a ccounts an d the United Nations s ystem of a ccounts .
Q167 I want to move on to dividends because , historically , excessive dividends have undermined the financial stability of the sector . H as this problem been resolve d with Ofwat’s new powers ?

I did a quick calculation on that just yesterday because it looke d like a question that was going to come up. T he ones I looked at w ere Seve r n Trent and United Utilities, which have been mentioned as potentially okay companies because they are listed and so on. I j ust looked at what has happened over the last two years, in ’ 24-25 and ’ 25-26. Looking at the level of the group companies, which are the ones listed, which effectively comprise largely the water and sewage operations, each of them ha s paid out over £ 700 million in dividends in those two years. United Utilities paid out £ 712 million and Severn Trent paid out £ 727 million . T hat is just in the last two years. It is a matter of judgment whether you regard that as being a controlled level of dividend payments.

There is a nother thing that is illuminating in the annual reports . T hey both say more or less the same thing , but I will give you United Utilities’ one : “ Our dividend policy is to grow annually in line with CPIH inflation. ” In other words, the shareholders of United Utilities have a single lock . United Utilities proudly say s it is a commitment it has maintained since 2010. The idea that equity capital is somehow risk capital would seem to no longer apply if the companies are guaranteeing CPIH linking of dividend payments. We need to ask the simple economic question : how on earth can they do that economically? T hey can do that economically only if they have a regulatory system they can rely on to allow them to generate the revenue sufficient to cover all that.

T here are six companies that have paid no dividend in the last year, and five the year before that. The shareholders of Thames Water have not received a dividend for quite some time. The shareholder in Northern Ireland, the Northern Ireland Government , received a dividend. The d ividend there is running at about 2%. It is quite a bit higher than for the six companies not paying any dividend at all.

Dividends are a function of return , and return is set by the regulator , be it the utility regulator of Northern Ireland or Ofwat in England and Wales . W e can argue about whether the return is being set at the right level and whether the incentives are in the right place . W e have been very open in saying that t he system in England and Wales is broken and that the Government should get on and fix it . Cunliffe has set out a very clear set of recommendations for fixing it , starting with strategy, then strengthening regulation , and then enabling financing to flow.

The question of dividends is actually immaterial to ownership. You can have a publicly owned system that is taking dividends or you can have a privately owned system. In the case of some privately owned operators, they are not taking any dividend at all and have not for some time. The dividends situation is a bit more complicated than it may appear on face value.

Q168 Quite rightly , some water companies should not be taking dividends, particularly in the case of Thames Water. Do you think there should be some licence conditions attached to those dividends? P erhaps minimum and maximum dividends just to keep more money in the system for investment?

There are at the moment. O fwat has introduced rules to cap dividends and block them if certain criteria are satisfied , such as g earing levels, and for some companies that has affected their ability to pay dividends. There are rules and it is up to Of wat to set them wherever it wishes. If it wishes to set different rules, it is totally able to do so. This is a question for independent regulators looking at the factors before them.
I am not going to try to comment on whether the current system is right to deal with this . T here are people who are better qualified on that around the table.

There is a second issue related to thi s: is the state of the finances of the companies currently worse because , in an earlier time, excess dividends were taken out ? I will not work with the T ot E x -based data after 2015 , because it is inconsistent with the earlier data. In s ome analysis I have done from , I believe , 1991 to 2015, there were excess dividends. There was a combination of interest rates g etting low, so of course you moved to debt financing , and t here were high profits being made . There was a previous comment about the price caps being too high right after privatisation.

Is it excess dividend that was taking those profits out? Should more have been retained? Almost certainly. You have a problem where maybe the finances were not as good as they should have been in the past , even if the companies are not doing it any more. Let us remember that , if you have equity investors , or Government bond investors or whoever, they do not just give you your money : you need to give them a return, right? D ividends are not inherently evil , and n or is it bad that they are being paid, but there is a correct amount. We have to think about what we do about the problem we cannot do anything about , which is perhaps the financial state of the companies because of the pas t. H ow do we make sure we do not get there again ?

Q169 This is m y final question, Chair . This Committee proposed that a much clearer, more easily imposed regime for special administration could incentivise much better performance. Do you think that this could be enough to improve the outcomes in the water sector?

T he existing special administration regime works pretty well. There are other special administration regimes in lots of other sectors. Of course, R ailtrack was put into special administration. It cost £ 70 million for about one year , and t hen it was passed on to N etwork R ail, which of course is now the publicly owned rail operator. Bulb E nergy was put into special administration and transferred to the private sector. The system that we have at the moment has not been tested. That is the problem. It is not the existing system.

Let us imagine that the Government bite the bullet, which they definitely should , and put Thames water into a special administration. We can do that for two reasons. First , it is effectively insolvent because Ofwat has not been enforcing the anti-pollution duties. Secondly, the licence could be withdrawn for poor performance. We could talk about at least four or five other water companies around England fulfilling the same criteria : too much pollution, too many leaks , or both.

What would happen then is that the special administrator is appointed by the court, but ultimately the Government are selecting them. The special administrator would look around for a potential bidder. Y ou might have private bidders but just as easily, for instance, the M ayor of London could set up a publicly owned company, perhaps organised with local councils, and it could also bid for Thames W ater. The argument I have been making, which is increasingly widely shared, is that the shareholders have obviously done such a terrible job that they are entitled to zero compensation . T he creditors should not be due anything at all because of the state of the infrastructure , the bill that has been run up for repairs, and the excessive returns of capital.

David Henderson is not mentioning that although there are restrictions on dividends, there are massive returns of capital to bondholders. B asically Elliott, Apollo and Silver P oint are the American funds that are in control of Thames W ater. If a public body bid zero — the special administrator is entitled to choose —but said , “W e ’ re going to fulfil the statutory duties better, ” then the special administrator will be entitled to transfer the assets to a public body for zero compensation to the polluters that had done so much damage already.

Q170 We really need to get moving on, but I want to just tease out one point : let’s stop talking about this as an exercise in corporate finance and look at it from the customer perspective. As David Saal said , there is nothing inherently evil about dividends ; w e live in a capitalist economy . But the concern that a lot of customers have is that dividends represent money being taken out of the industry that should be there for service improvement.

David Henderson , w e have raised the example of no dividends being paid out of Thames W ater, but Thames W ater is a very particular structure now, where if anybody owns it — nobody seems to want to admit to being the ultimate controller — it is owned by its own creditors . I ts own creditors now lend it more money , and we believe there to be fairly significant rates of return. There is not a great deal of transparency here. By that route, money comes out of the industry that should be put into service. That is the objection that most customers would see to the current set-up.

David Henderson : I understand that objection , but in the case of Thames W ater, the company has been very clear that those interest rates are not being funded by bills . Ofwat sets the cost of debt, and that is the limit of interest that can be paid by a company through water bills to any financing it receives. Companies that borrow at higher rates need to fund that themselves, and that is the case for Thames.
Q171 It is not going to get cheap money because o f its credit rating and balance sheet, is it ?

That is right . T here need s to be a resolution, and some time has now passed since the company got into the issues that it is now facing . It need s to be resolved, but it is ultimately a matter for Government to decide which way they wish to go.
We could debate Thames Water for the rest of the day , but Henry, you wanted to come in.

Q172 I just have a question for David Henderson . We have seen the excellent report set out by Cu nliffe. With the supervisory model of the regulation, there is an added cost to the companies in terms of the interference and , effectively , how to please the individual teams from Ofwat . With that model, when we talk about the sums involved in terms of the level of investment in the infrastructure, should a movement perhaps have happened towards a catchment model based on a planning investment and driving through a competitive procurement process , whereby you can have multiple different actors involved, be they private companies, state actors or local businesses ?

You are right, and Cu nliffe points to bot h. He says that we should have regional system planning , which is how you allocate resources at the local catchment level that are going to best effect change in the environment , bringing together all the actors in that catchment : f armers, house builders , highways agencies and water companies. That is about the local environment and how you want that best changed , considering all the costs that are associated .

Cu n liffe’s idea about supervision , if you read his report in the way that the industr y and many campaigners would, is that we need to have more company - by - company assessments : t eams of engineers going into companies , understanding the condition of their assets , l ooking at the area and its topography, geology , urban density and use r s of that water , understanding the assets and the condition they should be in , and then setting the allowances accordingly.

If you did that , you could then strip away this extremely complicated series upon series of unbelievably difficult - to - understand , technically rich , jargon - filled , acronym - dr enched econometric models that teams of economists in Canary Wharf , which is the head office of Ofwat , have dreamed up . They cause so much cost and expense for companies, analysts , investors and even Ofwat , which is why it continues to grow. It has more than 100 people working for it after the Government said they were going to abolish it. This is an animal that is feeding on itself .

Cunliffe looked at that and said it has been tested to destruction and it should stop . I n its place, instead of models that are a figment of imagination in Ofwat’s eyes , which is the notional company that bears no resemblance to the real world , we should have real assessments made by real engineers , not economists , of what each company needs. If we did that, we would have a much, much better system and the cost of enforcing and implementing and monitoring it would be far cheaper . I n fact, it provides a model for many other sectors. Instead of having modelling being done where you try to pitch one company against this fantasy idea called the notional company, you instead look at each individual company on its own merits and independently assess what it needs.
David, in a minute or less.

I would like to agree and completely disagree with what David sai d because , f irst , your question was about supervision . Ofwat’s modelling is not the problem . Read the SIP R report that I was involved in . I then parted company with SIP R and Ofwat because I said the modelling they were going to do — this is about 2013 — was completely inappropriate and I did not understand what they were doing. When I worked with Angl ian Wa ter for the first time and got to know their engineers and had the kind of engagement that would happen with supervision, I understood what drove costs.

You need to have some method to evaluate companies at catchment area, not company level, and econometric or D E A modelling, which all these countries use — the Netherlands and Denmark do that , for example . You need the modelling , but you also need a regulator that understands and is engaged with the compan y. S upervision is positive and worth the effort , because right now I do not know what they are modelling . A s an academic expert in water modelling , I would not even use the data that they use —t hat is how bad the modelling is.

I just want to emphasise that the issue is not about the modelling . I nteraction with the companies through a supervisory process could really be positive because you get that understanding of what really drives costs , moving away from this battle all the time.
I am in charge of time control here as if I were a West Highlander . Terry, you are going to lead some questioning on public control and other approaches.

Q173 I j ust have a couple of quick questions , starting with public opinion , because it is fair to say that water management and ownership are very much a hot topic at the moment , and we feel that as MPs . T he Westminster Hall debate on water recently was the most attended debate ever, which is quite telling . I wonder, given your experience and awareness of the industry, whether there is evidence or a view about what the public want to happen in terms of public ownership ? I am really careful because we talk about public control and public ownership and they are very different things, but in terms of public ownership, what do the public want? David , d are we assume?

The first part of the answer to the question has to be referenced to what the polls show, which has been consistent on a two-yearly basis now for some years . U p to 82% say they want public ownership, and only 9% say they want to keep private ownership. Not only have those figures be en constant over about 10 years now, but they are also astonishingly cross-party. Who m ever people voted for, the figures come out pretty much the same. In fact, there is a slightly higher percentage of Lib Dem voters who want public ownership than Labour voters, and so on. Also , going back to privatisation itself, it was never popular ; t he poll that was taken in July 1989 showed that 79% were opposed to privatisation.

That does not answer the other implicit question behind what you are saying, which is , what does public ownership mean to the public? First , we should be quite confident that they understand what public ownership broadly means . I t does not mean a regulator who is not even accountable to a Minister deciding what to do for them , who is a bit tougher with the companies that he or she meets on a regular basis. That barely counts as public control if the regulator itself is not under any kind of public accountability. Also , there is sufficient folk memory and awareness of what can happen elsewhere in distant countries such as Scotland , that actually local public ownership seems to be what would make sense.

Going back to earlier questions about the boundary definitions, there are really quite interesting points being raised about using catchment areas rather than river basins, for example, or letting local authorities work it out ad hoc in the Netherlands way. There were strong environmental reasons for the original structure, so I suspect we should keep that original structure. It makes sense ; it is one stable element. Then w e can simply identify the groups of local councils and say, “P lease work out how you would assemble yourselves to create a governing body for this region, with how ever many of you from which parties, bodies or whatever. ” Clearly, the Dutch can manage to do it, so I suspect we can manage to do it.
Q174 Ewan , is it so bad we do not really mind what model we use?

No, it really matter s. Y es, as David said, the last two YouGov polls said that 82% of the British public support public ownership — by the way, that has been rising —and 8% support privatisation ; t here are a few people who do not know . But the rest of the world knows as well ; t hat is the other thing. Some 80 % to 90% of the OECD has water in public ownership, and you can see a more detailed analysis in the EurEau document. Sometimes it is national ownership ; s ometimes it is more local ownership .

At the moment, the water industry just ha s scare tactics . T here is this narrative that started with the Social Market Foundation report in 2018 that it would cost £ 90 billion to take water into public ownership. Then it was £ 144 billion in a recent paper by Frontier Economics reported in The Telegraph a few weeks ago . J ust in the last week or two, the water industry has commissioned another think - tank , called Public First , to say it is £ 105 billio n. However, t he reality is — this is also what people know — that those figures are insanely and dishonestly inflated, using what we call regulatory capital value, which is far beyond even market value of companies .

J ust to give you an idea of how wrong this £ 105 billion figure is, at privatisation in 1989, there was £ 5.24 billion raised when the water companies were sold —t hat comes from a Bank of England paper called “ Operation of m onetary p olicy .” I f you plug those figures in, what does £ 5.24 billion in 1989 translate into in today’s money? It is £ 14.42 billion under the Bank of England inflation calculator. Moody’s calculated that it would cost £ 14.5 billion in 2019 to take water into public ownership . T he report I have done suggests that if you take the worst companies into special administration and do not bail out the banks in America that have been running the water companies into the ground, you get a few water companies into public ownership for zero . I f you take the whole sector into public ownership, it will probably cost in the region of £ 12 billion. These are very, very rough estimates because we do not have the ac tual true cost of repairs for the water companies to make sure that all sewage goes through secondary treatment and to re pair the leaks sufficiently.

One of the things that this Committee could really do, and that I really urge, is you could tell Ofwat or put pressure on it to make sure that it find s out what is required to make sure that all sewage is subject to secondary treatment. I did an FOI with Ofwat and it did not get back to me, but it will probably get back to you, if you give it a go.
Q175 You are taking us into territory that we are about to come to in a later section, so maybe just keep that for the moment.

Y ou asked whether public or private is better . I will answer that , but I just wanted to say two things. The answer to what Ewan has said is that it is very important that the Committee takes on board that the RC V s are not representative of value . T hat goes beyond what we can discuss here , and I could provide some paper s from my perspective .

The other thing is I want to correct how David interpreted my comments about the RWAs , and this goes to accountability . The RWAs were created at 10 , and the logic of that was for river basin management and transferring water between rivers and managing. Operation unit wise, there is no justification for that because there is no interconnection in many systems. A sewage system , by definition , has only one plant . I f we had done 50 operating systems , there would be much better local accountability because they would be closer to that. I do not know if that is efficient or not , but there would be better accountability and possibly more efficien cy.

As far as w hat the public really want , I am going to answer that honestly and a little for myself . I want the water to come in, I want it to be clean , I want it to have proper pressure. That has definitely gotten better ; when I moved here , I would not have drunk the water if I had known what it was like , which I found out later when I started d oing water . T he public want the sewage to go away, but after it is gone t hey then want vaguely a better environment. There is a tension there, because if that means that £ 100 billion is going to go here and it is going to come out of the NHS, that opinion will change pretty quickly.

T he public want better trust in the system, which Cunliffe talks about a lot. They want more public accountability. T hat means more local public control, which is down to c atchment area. They want to be paying a fair price for that. What it boils down to is they want more public control , but i f they are told that tuition fees are going to go up to £ 11,000 as a result , and they are balancing all those public interest things, they would go for what is the best and cheapest way to do this. That is a financing question, not a public or private question.

I agree. When confronted with the price of what people want, sometimes their decision about how much they really want it tend s to change. You will be familiar with all the constituents you meet having competing and sometimes contradictory expectations of parliamentarians to do a lot with not very much.

T here has been some discussion about the £ 105 billion. That was an estimate put out by Paul Johnson. He is a highly respected economist who used to run the Institute for Fiscal Studies. He has looked at two components, really : h ow much would you have to compensate the shareholders , and h ow much would you have to compensate the debt holders? T hey are legally enforceable contracts. A lot of estimates can fly around , but n one of us ultimately knows. It would be for court to determine. I would suggest that if the Government were to try to unilaterally break a binding legal contract between a lender of money and the recipient of that money, there would be some potential risk to the creditworthiness of the country as a whole. Other countries have tried this , and they have received pretty swift reactions from the agencies , and they have been negative . It has made the cost of their ability to borrow much, much higher .

T his is all obviously a matter of opinio n. I t would finally be for the court to determine , but the risk is not zero. There would be a dispute . I n fact , Professor Mc Gaughey has talked about the fact that this would result in some litigation . A nyone who can guarantee how litigation is going to end is being rather foolish . T hese are serious investors with serious money at stake and they have choices ; they do not have to put their money here . T hat is just as true for the investors in the water industry as it is those for who invest in the country by lending to our E xchequer.

We are really confusing cost and cost of ownership , and I am not even sure of what . W ho owns a company ? E quity owns the company . Y ou could , in principle , change ownership — again , I am not a financial economist ; this is just common sense here — by buying the equity and giving a fair return to that . T he debt does not necessarily have to be paid off . Y ou could just take it on board . Y ou have to pay it initially , but you could restructure it gradually over time because the Government ha ve debt of 100% of GDP roughly . Th e issue of ownership is distinct . T hat debt is not really a cost of ownership because that could be taken and gradually adjusted over time. I do not get that argument .
Q176 If you are going to readjust it , then you have taken ownership o f it.
No, but you have take n ownership, you pay off the old debt holders and then you can restructure with cheaper debt.
It is a matter of simple contract.

Could I just correct what David Henderson has said ? T hat is a misunderstanding of how the law works in two respects . F irst , the process of special administration does not leave the court to decide what the figure is for compensation , if any, to creditors or shareholders. T he special administration procedure sets up a process . I f there is going to be any challenge to the special administrator’s discretion — let us say, for instance, as I said , that we have a private bidder that is offering a few billion and a public bidder that says , “W e ’ re going to fulfil statutory duties ” —a s long as the special administrator acts within the law and follows the rules , then there is not going to be a court deciding what the compensation, if any, would be.

Then you have a second situation if you bring water companies into public ownership through an A ct of P arliament . T hat is not ultimately going to be decided by a court, it is going to be decided by P arliamen t. It is true that P arliament would not want to deprive people of their property in a way that violated the European C onvention —
That would scare the markets .

N o, that is a really important myth to dispel . As I mentioned, m arkets at the moment want to have borrowing by independent market actor, publicly owned corporations, including water companies. Obviously , if you nationalise for no compensation , Venezuelan style, that is going to scare people , but nobody i s really talking about that, are they? W e are talking about fair compensation , taking into account the repair costs that are needed and the amount that has already been returned in capital to the polluters in charge of water companies.

Q177 I am just going to move on to my next question if I may, as I am conscious of time . David Hall , I was struck by the contribution from the cha p from the Netherlands earlier , when he was talking about how , essentially , in mayoral elections there, water is so good , or perhaps so boring , that it is not an election issue ; i t does not even register. Then we have suggestions in this country about mayors having more say in water . A re we risking politicising water if we have more control and oversight?

No , w ater could not become a more political issue here than it is today without any form of public ownership . T he reason for simply adding mayors to the list of district councils , county councils and unitary authorities is that some parts of the countries are governed under a mayoral system at local level . B asically , you throw into the pot all the public authorities in a given region and that will include one or two mayors ; i t is that simple . T here is not any particular magic about a mayor as opposed to a county council , in that sense .
Q178 Is there a deficit for those areas that do not have a mayor?

That depends on your view of the mayoral system compared with the other systems . T here is a long-standing debate on that. It does not matter in terms of the principle of developing a structure of public authorities taking responsibility and forming the entities.

Q179 The last point I wanted to make was around different models. We have not spok en too much about mutuals and community interest companies today, which are somewhere in between private and public , with not-for-profits. To what extent do you think these approaches could deliver more public control and better outcomes? Is it worth looking at as part of it?

Sorry, can I say something on that because I feel quite strongly about what has been said about mutuals in this current context, which is based on a lot of errors . That includes the simple and all too common error of treating Welsh Water as though it was a mutual, which it is not. It is just a not-for-profit company accountable to no one, as people have already said. It also treats John Lewis as a mutual, which it is, but it is a workers’ co-op, not a customer co-op . T hat does not give any confidence for the rest of the conclusions.

Th irdly, there is really very little evidence for mutuals having a very strong public accountability system. If you look at Nationwide b ank, for example, about 520 people turn up at the annual meeting. It is not a very powerful force. Mutuals are not used very much at all around the world. The biggest water mutual in the world, by common consent, is in the city of Santa Cruz in Bolivia, which covers 900,000 households — or at least 50% of them , because the poorest ones are not covered by the mutual. So t here is not any international evidence to support that .

We know what is likely to happen , because that was what was done with Network Rail originally. Originally , it was set up as a not-for-profit entity , to be precise . It always relied on a 100% Government guarantee to be able to borrow any money at all. Select C ommittees consistently criticised the mutual because its management processes were incredibly obscure and subject to cronyism. In the end, it was taken into full public ownership, including the debt being taken on to the public books.

I just want to add one thing about that a s well, because that happened in 2014. I am sure t he Treasury was very up front to avoid any accusations of a cover-up as to how much debt was involved. In real terms of money today, it was £ 72 billion. I had not realised how high it was, but that is pretty close to the total debt of all the water companies now. That was taken on to the public books. During 2014, the yield on 10-year gilts fell from 3% to 2.2%. In other words, it did not go up ; it actually came down. Reviews of the year sai d, “I t ’ s been another great year for gilts ,” and so on. That potential thing is another scaremongering issue. I am sorry, but I just thought I would add that to the mutuals question.
Q180 That is really useful; I appreciate that. Professor McGaughey , d o you have any views on mutuals?
Professor McGaughey : Just that there is a higher cost of capital because they are not public . T hey cannot borrow from the Public Works Loan Board .

I would j ust like to touch on governance because this has come up . I f you look at Berlin, it was privatised and then taken back into public ownership in 2013 . T he way it is run is that half the board is chosen or elected by the workforce , who of course know most about how the water industry works ; they are the experts . T he other half is chosen by the city council . Paris was taken back into public ownership in 2009 . There is representation mostly f rom Paris city council representatives , and then some workers and people who are chosen in consultation with consumer and environmental groups . T hat is the sort of stakeholder model that we could have .

A ctually , the existing law that we have now because of the Water ( Special Measures ) Act 2025 says that Ofwat has the power to change governance . W e could already have worker representation and local authority or mayoral representation . I agree that until you complete the map of mayors around England you probably want local representation , but it is going to be easier if mayors are doing it eventually .
Those of us without a mayor feel a bit left out .

In t he first part of your question , you said something about politicising . I just wanted to respond to that first . W e need to realise that we are the exception . If we take all those big Netherlands companies, I doubt they add up to Severn Trent . I do not know if that is right . T hey may have regional authorities , but they are small . M ost municipalities in most countries have some kind of local control , which in a way make s it political , but it also leads to what I mentioned before about organic solutions .

I know Pamplona very well . T here are 15 municipalities around it . T hey decided to form a quango that does waste, water and sewage . T hat was their solution . I know some Japanese utilitie s that have completely outsourced their municipal control. In t he French model, we said that there is a choice going on , but there is public control . It is political because they can change their mind if it is not working . Y ou also get these other perverse incentives .

T he entire debate here is that the rivers are not safe . I am seriously working on a project right now about measuring the cost of improving sewage quality in Japan . O ne of the research questions is , w hy do the companies go beyond their requirements ? It is a little different from what we talk about . W e are hypothesising that it might be because the mayors are competing with each other for votes . I am not saying that is what they are doing , but it is about accountability . It can still be run by the private sector if it is contracted out because all through Japan it is contracted out in many ways .

Any model can be made to work . T his is C unliffe ’s conclusion and it is the conclusion of the OECD . As he set out, w hat is critical for any model to work is having a clear strategy, strong regulation and then the money. It is true that Berlin moved to a municipal model , and it cost the city there over a €1 billion. In France , in the example in Paris , a licence expired , so there was no cost. If we are to move any company into a mutual , then you need to consider what the cost would be for the acquisition , and then of course the financing cost for the ongoing operations and the capital programme after that. Of course , as I said, any model can be made to work if you have those three ingredients that C unliffe identified in the right place.
In Berlin , they were better off in a few years , even after having compensated the shareholders.
W e are going to move on now to some questions about opportunities, costs and risks of public ownership.

Q181 I t has been very clear today that there is no perfect model we can adopt . J ust looking at this purely pragmatically , because you always have to end up following the money , if you are trying to set out a case for public ownership , what evidence do you have that it is actually better in terms of better outcomes? Ewan, y ou mentioned at one point that , on one metric , we are the seventh worst comparatively , but I assume the other six above us also had a more public form of ownership . W hat quantified evidence can you give us?
There are those beneath as well.

Yes, I have done various things on this. Let us take it point by point on the economics. First , on price, there have been two bi g comparative studies of private and public provision of water within the same country. One was in France about 15 years ago, which was a 100% sample. It covered everything . It concluded that , ceteris paribus, private water ended up being charged 16% more than public.

A m ore recent one was done by Cornell in the USA on , effectively , the 50% of the population covered by the largest water authorities, which is pretty good as a sample. It actually found figures so embarrassing that it quote s only the numbers rather than the percentage, but it found th at private water, other things being equal , is 59% more expensive than public water. It also tried to look at, does tough regulation make a difference? It found that in relation to private concessions, no. In relation to public concessions, it found it was a non-question because the view in the USA, which is also broadly the view in practice in Europe, is that if you have public ownership, you do not need a regulator. The public authority is the regulator on behalf of the public , with the accountable mechanism and the ownership relationship giving them the power. That is one interesting dimension.

In terms of efficiency, there are a number of comparative studies being done around the world , n ot only in the water sector but in others ; I am sure David Saa l knows many of these as well. It is fair to say that the broad conclusion of most of them is that there is no significant difference. There was one very detailed econometric study by Bel and Warner about 10 years ago that claimed that conclusion very firmly . It is really quite firmly established . They are equally efficient.

In terms of investment and price, Scotland is a shining example .
