I t is not quite as easy to compare surface body water quality in one country with another. The population density matters hugely.

As I am sure this Committee knows all too well, t he other thing about cost is that it sadly costs a lot more to build the equivalent piece of infrastructure in this country than in just about any other country in the worl d. W e see that in aviation , transport , housing and energy , and the same is sadly true in water . With t he cost of materials and the planning process, it takes years and years and years to build reservoirs. It is shameful that we have not built a single reservoir in more than 35 year s.

That is not for want of trying. We have sought again and again to build reservoirs that have been rejected by the last Government and by regulators . F inally , once we get the approval to build these reservoirs so that we can cope with the pressures of climate change , then the games begin with the planning authorities or the environmental impact assessments . I t takes so much longer and ends up costing a fortune more than it should.

There are complicated reasons why the average bill in England might be more than the average bill in France or Germany. It is interesting tha t , despite all those planning obstacles I just mentioned, we do not have the very highest bills actually . It is despite that actually. T he companies are bending over backwards to try to be as efficient as possible . W hy? Because it is in their owners ’ interests . T hey have no interest in running inefficient operations . I f anything , Ofwat has squeezed down the allowances provided to companies too much , which is why bills fell since 2010 for the following 14 years , down by a fifth according to real terms , which is why the maintenance of our assets is not anywhere near where it should be .

W e are right to look at Scotland. Scotland’s regulator took a very different approach . It consistently enabled just - above inflation investments to maintain the quality of the assets. It actually looked at the assets and established what was needed , as opposed to Ofwat , which looked at these backward - looking models. That is not specific to having a privately or publicly owned company ; t hat is about the quality of the regulation . Sir Jon Cunliffe’s report spends a lot of time looking at what good - quality regulation i s . That is a crucial ingredient . As he found, it is true no matter what ownership model you have.

Can I just do a hopefully quick follow - u p on a related point ? I agree o n natural monopoly . Th ese are natural monopolies . I really want to make the point that what went wrong after 2015 and with the cost modelling is that Ofwat was pushing for competition . I have heard senior people in the industry , in compan y, say to me , “T hey should stop messing around with competition and just focus on the job of doing the natural monopoly .” T he missing part of that is it also has externalities , public goods, merit goods, and all these types of things . T hat makes it much more difficult to bring the competition in.

I agree with t he comments on Scotland , but that also brings out what has been wrong here . I have had conversations with Alan Sutherland at WICS about what it did. He said , “W e want T ot E x because that ’ s what I have to fund .” H e then thought through what t he company need ed . There was a more supervisory process with Government and the company , in effect, because it is such a small , flat regulatory system . T hey came to an agreement and funded it.

Down here , we just started regulating T o t E x , which does not make economic sense because it is CapEx plus OpEx. One builds capital stock ; one i s gone . S econdly , we build cost models to do that and we try to drive competition . W hen you put that all togethe r, the natural monopoly arguments push you towards more public control , and then implementation of the competition regime has created big problems basically , because I do not know what the incentives are.
I could ask you a million questions more , but unfortunately time will not allow.
I have been reviewing the areas we had hop e d to cover and actually , gentlemen, you have basically covered it all quite organically without us having to be too prescriptive in our approach.

Can I thank you for your attendance ? Can I thank you , in particular , for the way in which you have handled your differences ? N one of this is easy, none of it is straightforward. If there was a simple solution , we would have found it by now , but being able to take something of public significance and concern and manage differences well is worth doing. Thank you for your attendance and indeed the way in which you have presented your evidence. For today , almost half an hour later than I should have done , I am going to conclude proceedings.

Members present: Alistair Carmichael (Chair); Sarah Bool; Sarah Dyke; Terry Jermy; Josh Newbury; Henry Tufnell.

Witnesses

I : Dr David Lloyd Owen , Managing Director, Envisager; Hugh Goldsmith, Visiting Professor, College of Europe and former head of Water and Waste Management Division, European Investment Bank ; John Abraham, Chief Operating Officer for Industrial Water and Energy, Veolia .
II : Dr Marine Colon, researcher, AgroParisTech and UMR G-EAU research unit , France; Professor Klaas Schwartz, Professor Water Services Governance, IHE Delft, Netherlands.

III : David Henderson, CEO , Water UK; Professor David Hall, Visiting Professor, University of Greenwich, London, Public Services International Research Unit; Professor Ewan McGaughey, Professor of Law, King ’ s College London; Professor David Saal, Professor of Microeconomics, Loughborough University.
Written evidence submitted by witnesses:
- Dr David Lloyd Owen, Managing Director, Envisager
- Dr David Lloyd Owen, Managing Director, Envisager
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr David Lloyd Owen , Hugh Goldsmith and John Abraham .

Good morning and welcome to this meeting of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee. This morning, w e return to our ongoing inquiry into the reform of the water sector , and we shall be dealing with questions around ownership of companies within the sector. We have three panels, so we are going to try to keep a good pace. F or the benefit of those who are following our proceedings and for our own official record, I invite our witnesses to introduce thems elves to the Committee .

G ood morning, everybody. I am Hugh Goldsmith. I am currently visiting professor at the College of Europe in Bruges, where I teach i nfrastructure , e conomics and f inance . B efore that, I was head of the w ater and w aste m anagement d ivision at the European Investment Bank.

Good morning. My name is John Abraham. I am the c hief o perating o fficer for i ndustrial w ater and e nergy at Veolia, covering the UK and Nordics. I am a civil engineer and a fellow of the Institute of Civil Engineers and the Chartered Institute of Environmental Managers. I have spent nearly 40 years in water , waste water and energy, across design and build operations and maintenance . M y responsibilities include several major PFI contracts for Scottish W ater, Northern Ireland W ater and the Ministry of Defence. I will say more about Veolia later on.
My name is David Lloyd Owen. I have been following the water sector since the late 1980s, first as an equity analyst, and for the last three decades as an independent consultant.

Q119 T hank you all for your attendance. David, you said your experience goes back to the 1980s . T hat is a timely prompt because that is where— back in the mists of time — I want to start : b elieve it or not, I was still an undergraduate in 1989. I want to ask a question of David and Hugh ; John, feel free to chip in if you feel moved . What were the problems with t he logic of privatisation as it was carried out in 198 9 ? What questions were being posed at that point, i f privatisation was the answer ?

When you look at privatisation per se, it was well expressed quite recently by Roch Cheroux, the new head of D ŵ r Cymru, or Welsh Water : it is not necessarily the management model that matters, it is the regulatory model . There has definitely been a clear and present failure in regulation for the last 15 years , arguably for the last 20 years.

Y our question was about what problem pri vatisation was going to solv e. T he White Paper in the mid- ’ 80s was clear that the objective was to provide benefits to the consumer. The benefits that were going to flow from privatisation included more efficiency, more innovation, and access to private finance. It was also couched in terms not only of customers becoming shareholders but of employees becoming shareholders and therefore interested in benefiting from the profitability of the company. That clearly took place in the context of the wider privatisation process.

Q120 Some of this would be driven by outcomes for customers — efficiency savings and the rest of it —and s ome was a political project around share ownership, which was part of the political zeitgeist at the time. Let us park the politics ; w e can do that. From the perspective of outcomes for customers, the drive for efficiency from the private sector suggests that there were inefficiencies. Were these problems somehow an inherent part of being in the public sector?

I am not aware of what the specific inefficiencies were. I worked with the water authorities prior to privatisation ; I worked with the water companies and the regulator after privatisation. The first thing that happened with the new water companies was that they started to look at ways of using all their assets more efficiently. For instance, t hey looked at voluntary redundancies to reduce staff numbers ; t hey were clearly driven by an efficiency agenda in those early years. I was not aware of specific issues around efficiency.

The other thing that is important to state is that they were borrowing from the Treasury or the Public Works Loans Board , and the ir finances count ed on public sector borrowing. One of the big motivations was to take the investment off the public sector balance sheet.
Q121 John, you can b ring in the private p erspective.

In 1989 I started working in the UK water industry , and I remember fierce competition for funding at the time . Do we spend money on our railways, roads, public buildings, hospitals or water? Water got pushed to the end of the queue all the time and did not get funded. On the other hand, I remember going to what they used to call a treatment palace in the n orth - w est. There was a lot of over-design , and no real focus on building efficient, fit-for-purpose solutions . So t here was a big drive to get more efficiency in design and construction.

The other element was that t he whole of Europe was thinking about urban wastewater treatment Acts and trying to clean up. Primary treatment was the main source of treatment at the time ; t here was no secondary treatment — t hat came in in the ’ 90s , and the UK were the first adopters. We were far ahead of the game in terms of secondary treatment ; w e built the next generation of treatment plants very early in the process. P rivatisation of the industry allowed funding to be focused on th ree drivers : quality, g rowth and performance.

Q122 This is a familiar tension : e verything is important until there is a crisis in the NHS , and that is where the money goes. David, you spoke earlier about regulatory failure. How much of what has happened subsequently is a consequence of regulatory failure as opposed to ownership?

It is an essential factor . T he regulatory history can be broken down to events in two crucial phases. Under Ian Byatt from 1989 to 2000 , and during his final AMP3 period in 2005, there was an emphasis on increasing investment in infrastructure and its maintenance first . Post that, the regulator moved to what some would tritely call a cheap and nasty approach , whereby cost to customer overruled everything .
Just keep the bills low.

That is right. In terms of operating spending and maintenance, it remained static for 25 years , even though £200 b illio n of new assets were brought in. U ltimately that meant a lot of new assets were simply not managed or operated : t hey were allowed to stagnate.

Q123 S ome studies show that the growth in value among water companies has been mainly funded by debt, not equity. With the benefit of 40-year hindsight, to what extent do es that tell us something about the logic behind the initial decision in the 1980s? This is an easy question for the academics.
It is clear that all the investment in the water industry was being funded by debt because when they were privatised they were debt-free. All the debt was paid off.
Q124 The debt was taken on to the public books ; i n fact, they were given a bit of a sweetener , of £1.5 billion, were they not?

They were given a £1.5 b illio n green dowry. The companies started life with working capital from the Government , and they were debt-free. No equity was paid into the companies ; t he purchase price from the people who bought shares went to the Government. It was a transaction about the future value of shares , not an investment in assets. The companies started life with a clean balance sheet ; therefore it was always going to be more attractive to fund all their investment through debt . D ebt funding is the standard way that infrastructure assets are funded all over Europe : y ou borrow to invest.

W hen the first regulatory review came out , it gave a regulated capital value that showed significant regulatory equity in the system ; but that was created by the particular regulatory model — the indexed RCV — that was being used. There appeared to be equity in the companies even though equity had not been paid in for investment. Debt funding was always going to be the main game for financing actual physical investments.
Q125 This sounds like an accounting trick just to magic capital out of nowhere , or is that a misunderstanding?

The RCV — regulatory capital valu e— model was developed in the Treasury by Ian Byatt ; w hen he was working in the Treasury there was something called the Byatt r eport , which p resented a way of making infrastructure assets attractive to private capital . One o f the things it does is to take inflation risk away from investors —in effect, passing it on to consumers — because consumer bills go up by RPI e very year , less any efficiency gains , and the assets inflate by RPI . I f that is all debt funded , your equity value goes up over time , but cash is not being paid in to build real assets . If you were dealing with a greenfield project , you would do it on project finance : debt comes in, there is a slice of equity that comes in from the investors , and that is all capital that goes into building the project , taking on risk in delivering it , and the operations . In this case , that was not how the model worked .

A t privatisation the credit rating agencies gave the sector two As , the second highest possible sovereign debt rating . O fwat made clear in its next two periodic reviews that it was perfectly happy to have a triple B rating . O ne of the consequences was that the cost of capital — the coupon — rose , as did the debt ; t he more debt the water companies have taken on , the more expensive servicing that debt has been .

There is an interesting contrast between this and Scottish Water . Scottish Water has as much debt in terms of its regulated capital value as the sector in England and Wales : however , the interest it pays is materially lower and that has an impact on its costs .

Q126 It has an impact on its stability. K eeping the focus firmly on customer outcomes, how would you characterise the broad trends in England since 1989 in 30 seconds or less ? I am thinking about pollution, leakages, consumption, investment and customer service in the round .

I have been drinking water from Thames Wate r for a round eight decades ; the quality of drinking water has not changed dramatically . There has been an improvement from 99 % to 99.3% . The big improvement has been in in waste water treatment , as John mentioned. T he introduction of European environmental regulations has driven much of the investment in the sector : the long-term objec tive of the w ater f ramework d irective is to improve the ecological quality of water bodies . The drivers are towards environmental quality. There are people who are suffering from sewer flooding in their basements , but those numbers have gone down . O fwat keeps various performance measures , and there have been improvements . T he big impact has been around the environmental improvement of waste water treatment , and that is where the big investment has gone .
Q127 You are saying that that was driven by the w ater f ramework d irective .

First , there was the u rban w aste w ater t reatment d irective , then the n i trates d irective and others — there is a whole web of directives govern ing environmental activities . Since 2000 — in Europe anyway — there is the w ater f ramework d irective , and that got translated into the UK . T he aim is to achieve the long-term benefit of making all rivers of good ecological quality for fish and for our grandchildren to swim in without the risk of something nasty happening to them .

Q128 We touched earlier on the grand vision of a share - owning democracy in the 1980s: there would be employee share owners and a wider public share ownership. Yet i n 2026, very few water companies are even publicly listed. My final question on this for the moment is, what impact has that had, and is it where we should be looking for change?

I would say that the water industry has evolved in many ways . There was the multi-utility phase , where United Utilities was created as a combined water and energy utility in the n orth -e ast . Welsh Water tried to do the same thing in its link with S WALEC ; that got turned into Hyder , which got into financial difficulties . There were strategic investors such as Veolia , Suez , and FCC ; RWE — the German multi-utility —was an owner for a while . T he 1999 price review — where the share price dropped below the capital value — was a critical moment for the industry . S ince then it has been financialised : in the latter period, the major investors have been financial investors seeking to extract cash from the business and increase leverage .
Q129 It was a watershed moment for the industry , in terms of the way that the focus shifted from customer service to financial management .

O wnership is only part of the story . During the first third of the privatisation story , a huge amount of capital was put in to b uild secondary treatment — real , fundamental , basic treatment — to clean up our rivers and improve our drinking water . We build things in the water industry really well ; t he CapEx deli very is very good value for money .

The problem now is how we are operating in maintaining the assets that we have spent the last 38 years building . The same people are operating the same assets the same way because there is an operational monopoly within a monopoly organisation . My company, Veolia , is the biggest water company in the world : it look s after water for 110 million people . If you get on the Eurostar and go to Paris, we are producing water for 4 million people there. Yet there is no market in the UK : I cannot deliver my world - class operational and maintenance services across England and Wales . I have some market in Scotland and Northern Ireland and the Ministry of Defence , but I have no market in England and Wales because it is operated and maintained by the same people the same way . Th at is where the problem is ; not the ownership , which can be detached as a PFI is run .
We will call that a good - quality elevator pitch . W e are going to move on to look at the experience elsewhere in the UK . Henry , you are going to lead the questioning .
Q130 T o crack on about Welsh W ater , is it attractive to bondholders and can it attract debt at a competitive level ?

I t is a mixed story . Originally, we called it Gwaith Cymru, the Welsh wa y . T he key element to Welsh W ater — the Glas Cymru model — was that it was not for profit , therefore any surplus was either put into customer rebates or discretionary spending.

Unfortunately, the actual performance of Welsh W ater —on all the publicly available metrics— has not been a great success . I would classify the 10 water PLCs as follows. Wessex and Northumbri a are owned by international utilities ; they generally outperform the rest of the sector . The following three— Severn Trent, United Utilities and Pen n on — are still market listed and perform on average . Welsh W ater is below average . Finally there are the four private equity companies ; they are dramatically below average, especially in the case of Thames. That is key. One has to have no sentimentality about ownership models : private equity has no other purpose than asset stripping .

In the case of Welsh W ater , there is no doubt that the finances have dramatically improved . W hen it was brought out of S WALEC , its d ebt was 93% of equity : it was a highly leveraged company . T hese days the debt is 53% , and it is the least leveraged of all the water companies , so that side has undoubtedly been a success.

We had a n honest moment last week when the new chief executive of Welsh Water spoke to the Financial Times . H e previously ran Sydney Water, so he has a lot of experience in a state-owned compan y run on private sector lines . He said that, unfortunately, he believes that the Glas Cymru model is not delivering any specific advantage and is entirely dependent on the regulatory environment .

Q131 The gearing is below average , at 62.8% ; the c redit rating is going down , so it has gone from A minus to triple B , with debt servicing costs equating to 25% of bills . With that financial situation, how will it get the money to pay for infrastructure?

It is the best rated company in the sector . One of the things you need to bear in mind is that the headline figures for debt are the lowest ratings ; its overall debt is A minus to A . Anglian is the only other company that has an A rating on its senior debt , but debt rating is clearly one of the biggest challenges for the sector overall .

There is a regulatory issue h ere: in the early 2000s , there was no ceiling on debt , which allowed Macquarie to gear Thames W ater for up to 95% of its equity through various investment vehicles . That w as a real issue for the private equity - owned companies . N ow Ofwat says 65% should be the ceiling , and 55% gearing is desirable , so it is being brought down ; but it is also evident that a lot of the gearing shot up after the 2008 financial crisis , when the cost of capital was historically low . We have now returned to normal levels , and the water sector is not equipped to finance those things without a profound impact on its profitability .

Before the creation of Glas Cymru and the not-for-profit model, EIB was the biggest lender to Welsh Water, and subsequently it has been a major lender up until the UK left the EU and EIB lending became difficult to access. I checked online last night for information about the EIB’s lending — I want to make it clear that I retired from the EIB in 2021 , so I am speaking on a personal basis . T he figure I found online was £780 million ; it has been lending amortising loans .

T he difference in many countries is that people borrow and pay it back like a mortgage . They do not take on long - term bonds that rely on their ability to refinance . T hat is what has caused the big problem for Thames right now : it cannot pay its maturing loans . Welsh Water took on a significant debt from the EIB , and I noticed that Tideway t unnel also took on long - term amortising loans . Once you have l ost access to that source of finance —it is still the biggest source of water sector finance in Europe and possibly the world — then your national infrastructure bank should potentially be stepping in .

I n the Scandinavian countries , municipally owned companies largely run all the water services . T hey could not separately access the levels of finance they need , so they have set up a communal credit bank . Austria also has a credit bank . P ublic sector banks can channel the necessary funding for that investment . Welsh Water was doing that before and after it went into a not-for-profit model , but I do not know what the attitude of the National Wealth Fund is now to wards financing the water sector .

Q132 What about accountability within the governance structure ? Glas Cymru as the holding company could have up to 200 unpaid members t o hold the Welsh Water b oard to account ; it has 47. Who are these people? It is not representative ; there is no one from the Welsh Government , no elected individuals from consumer bodies , and no local authority involvement . We are owned by bondholders in Luxembourg and then run by these 47 people who answer to no one .

I was a member of Glas Cymru for 11 years . T he selection is somewhat arbitrary : members are invited to apply , but as you say there is no actual representative mandate . T he idea is to act as a proxy , a quasi-shareholder . They turn up twice a year to meetings and ask interesting questions , and that is as far as it goes . T here is no other form of representation .

Q133 In terms of interesting questions , leakage increased by 15% from 2019-20 . The company has not met its target to reduce per capita consumption , and for three consecutive years it has been one of the worst performers in the sector for supply interruptions. Major missed targets remain. P resumably the interesting questions that are being asked do not pertain to performance because performance has been going south . D o you think that is a problem?

W hen I was first involved with Glas Cymru , I was an idealist : I thought it would be a n exemplar for the rest of the sector . I am afraid that the reality has been a disappointment . There is a crucial issue here that does not apply to England : the 1999 devolution settlement meant that under Ofwat’s blessing , it report s directly to the Senedd , the Welsh Government . Y ou cannot apply that model in England , because there is no regional devolution .

F or example , Kelda — Yorkshire Water in those days —also wished to become a mutual ; Ofwat overruled that because it did not have the devolutionary element . It e ventually got swallowed up by private equity , which was not in anybody’s interest .

A fter the 1999 price review , the regulator effectively cut bills , and that was what pushed the share value below the regulatory asset or capital value . Se veral companies went to Ofwat to effectively de- privatise themselves. There was the Kelda proposal ; Anglian and Southern Water had proposals. Some wanted to become friendly societies. The idea was to move to a model where the assets were owned by the public sector ; t he water companies would then take on the staff and operate the assets , moving much closer to the French model. That was being proposed by the industry itself. Ofwa t opposed th at until the proposal from Welsh Water ; the reason , of course , was that it was perceived as being part of the devolutionary settlement. That was what the Welsh people wanted, therefore there was a way that they could create a not-for-profit model in Wales.
Regarding t he actual governance structure, I agree with you. I have worked for a company limited by guarantee : it is a strange governance structure. You wonder who it is accountable to.
Q134 H ow do you think the Scottish model compares in terms of that accountability ?

I am not familiar with the exact governance model in Scotland . M y understanding is that it is publicly owned — therefore there is public accountability — but I am not sure whether local as well as national Government are involved on the board.

Historically , t he previous stage was in 1904 , when the water sector was being taken out of private ownership and the Metropolitan Water Board was formed . There you had r epresentatives from local g overnment plus the Thames Conservat ors , people who were democratically accountable for the area where the services were provided .

I n terms of that governance element , Scotland also has a different regulatory system , where the price settlement seems to be negotiated , rather than the confrontational version , where companies want this and Ofwat says that and ultimately the Competition and Markets Authority makes a judgment.

T he big difference in Scotland i s that it counts as public sector borrowing . I f you are trying to ensure that , as the French say , l ’eau doit payer l’eau— water should pay for itself — there is this principle of full cost reco ver y. If people are generally willing to pay for it , then you want a structure that it is not on the public sector balance sheet but can none the less be publicly owned . T here are many examples of that .

Scottish Water started off as 11 entities in the 1990s , which merged into four . They became Scottish Water in 2002, whereas England and Wales were merged into their current state in 1974 . So there has been quite a bit of catching up on the rationalisation of Scottish Water. It has adopted the Ofw at model , in that it has an external regulator , but with a different relationship : it is indeed state owned and state funded for debt , but the company is run as a quasi public - private entity — in other words , it is supposed to generate a profit and so on . When you look at the actual performance metrics , by its own admission it outperform s the English and Welsh companies on certain metrics but underperform s on others .

Y ou have to bear in mind that Scotland has a completely different relationship with its water resources . I t is a mixed picture: w estern Scotland has an embarrassment of riches , but e astern Scotland is as vulnerable as s outhern England when it comes to reservoirs and droughts . Scotland is not necessarily a paragon : it exhibits both the joys and the miseries of being in the public sector as compared with the private sector .

Q135 Veolia deal with Welsh Water and Scottish Water . O ur colleagues in the Scottish Liberal Democrats found overflow data for 12 sewer assets managed by PFI , nine of which are run by Veolia . There were 513 spills in 2023 across the se assets. In terms of the workings of the public - private partnership model, h ow can that be? I n Wales, Veolia has a contract with Welsh Water for the Five Fords waste water treatment works , and in Herefordshire —

I do not think we have any operations in Wales . We have Seafield , which is the catchment in the Almond Valley in Edinburgh , where there is a rigorous compliance regime . W e face severe fines every time we breach our licence, but that has not happened because o ur standards are higher than those required by the regulator s.

There are various spills arising from storms, which are fully licen s ed. Three or four weeks ago in Seafield, we had a once in 300 years storm: we dealt with it very well . W e work well with Scottish Water all the time . We have a lot of data that proves that where you almost ringfence a catchment and you have a PFI like we have with Almond Valley , Seafield and Esk , AVSE , which I think y ou want me to talk about later on , the performance is strong , efficiency is high and there is value for money . W e have invested a lot of money into that plant : i t is the biggest waste water treatment plant in Scotland . We produce 108% of the energy that the plant requires, and it is t he only one in the whole of the UK that is a net export er of energ y . We will hand it back to Scottish Water in less than three years’ time , so the concession is coming to an end . W e are proud of the performance of Seafield , but I can take that data away and look at it.
Q136 O ur friends at the Liberal Democrats identified 165 spillage events in Seafield in 2023 , and long-standing complaints from local residents about smells from the plant . I s that a success?

If you are familiar with the plant , it is near Portobello Beach , in a very built-up area ; it is the largest treatment plant in Scotland , so there is not zero smell coming from the plant . At certain times when the wind is blowing in a certain direction , there can be a very mild odour , and there are local residents who are unhappy with th at. I t is a well-documented and understood issue around the Portobello and Leith area . B ut if you compare the performance of our PFIs to other major plants in England and Wales , such as Bec k ton and Crossnes s , there is a positive difference .
Q137 Is this a blueprint that other parts of the UK should be looking at ?

England and Wales are already working with Ofwa t on what it call s direct procuremen t for customers, or DPC. T hey are looking at major investments similar to the Thames Tideway t unnel . F or example, Anglian Water is looking at a PPP model for desalination plants to ringfence the supply of drinking water from the sea . It is looking for separate finances, and Ofwat is pushing forward the direct procurement model .

Q138 David, picking up on your point about the relationship between the company and the regulator in Scotland , you contrasted Scottish Water —which is regulated by the Government body SEPA — with more adversarial relationship s in the rest of the countr y . That might be a way of saying that it is a bit cosy in Scotland. R elationship s south of the border ha ve produced a remarkable range of metrics against which performance is assessed. How does that compare to the situation in Scotland? Is it the same or is it different?

O ne of the things you need to appreciate about Scottish W ater is that it has faced a catching - up exercise since 2002 : you could argue that England and Wales had a 10 to 13-year head start. In practical terms, the key element to date is that the regulator has been much more amenable to increased costs and spending than in the case of England and Wales. W ith the current price review period up to 2030, that has now levelled out. The cheap and nasty model in England and Wales has been superseded . I would argue that the relationship between the regulator and the company in Scotland has been an exemplar for England and Wales , in that it has been more consistent and less confrontational about spending ; there has been an acknowledgment about the challenges it faced and the fact that it had to deal with them.

T he debate about regulation and the conclusions from the IWC review have raised an issue about what happened , and what went on, with regulation . On e of the most interesting interventions was from Professor Stephen Littlechild— the author of the English model — who went on to be the electricity regulator . H e made a submission to one of the regulatory hearings — I cannot remember exactly which one— where he said that the model ha d failed . I think he described it as purgatory, with the regulator trying to outguess the companies in a five-year cycle that then just starts again. U ltimately , when people do not agree, they go to the Competition and Markets Authority for a decision . H e argued in favour of the Scottish model because it is closer to the negotiated outcome that you get in some American regulatory systems .
The third section of this tutorial will look at the ownership and management of water outside the UK . Terry, you are going to lead the questioning on that.

Q139 We have already touched on some examples of ownership models around the world , and the C ommittee has received a significant amount of evidence and examples of direct public ownership, delegated private management and something in between . W hat approaches do you feel might work best for England , and what are their advantages or disadvantages ?
The Glas Cymru model can be used as a template. While acknowledging its shortcomings , t here is a lot to be said in favour of bringing in a sense of stakeholder participation .
That is t he governance point you w ere making with Henry .

That is right. The Prime Minister’s al lusion the other day to increased state investment in the sector is a way forward. Looking at this retrospectively , things such as private equity simply should not be allowed . Companies should either be owned by a sympathetic utility, as is t he case in Northumbria and in Wessex : t heir parent companies operate other utility companies and understand them. Welsh Water is flawed, but it is a way forward . And t he listed model is still appropriate. The crucial thing is to eliminate private equity from the sector , alongside reinstating a sense of public p articipation.

I forget the exact year , but until the mid-1980s you had local council representatives on each of the water authorities. There used to be about 50 members on the board, and that was then cut down to 11; I think they were removed in 198 4 . T hat element of accountability is important : apart from anything else, it relates to the p rocess of r ebuilding trust in the companies . W e have to appreciate that w e have lost that trust.

My g reatest analogy here is the drought of 1976 versus ’ 95. In the 1976 drought, people stoically accepted standpipes. In ’95, a friend of mine was working for Yorkshire Water when it mentioned that it might have to use standpipes. He went to a garage, took out his Yorkshire Water company cre dit card , and the person n ext to him spat in his face. I do not think people realise just how fundamental , how crucial , t hat element of public understanding — stoicism, fortitude, whatever you prefer to call it —is for a utility . When it was lost, it was damning .

I absolutely second what David has sai d. W hat are the objectives of this change ? R ebuilding public trust has to be a fundamental par t. T here are many ownership models out there. You still get listed companies that are publicly owned ; Acea— t he utility that supplies energy and water to Rome — is listed on the stock exchange, but it is 51% owned by the municipality of Rome. H aving been through this learning experience in the UK, t he challenge now is what we should do next . P ublic ownership, or something like it, is probably what the public is expecting. That seems to be the zeitgeist . T he question is, how do we get there?

An example that no one has mentioned is Northern Ireland . I went there when it was looking for a large EIB loan to fund two projects, including Alpha, a project to build new drinking water plants t o supply about half of the drinking water in the region . At the time , they were called PFI - type projects ; they were both DBFOs . T he company that delivered on Alph a —I think it was Kelda— did an amazing job . I t found a way to redesign and rethink the way the project was going to be delivered , which cut the cost down from £156 million to £ 110 million . It was done as private finance : the EIB lent about 40% of the money , a Dutch bank lent another proportion and then there was some equity . T he project was built, it worked , and the performance was outsourced to the private sector ; at a certain point Kelda decided it wanted to withdraw from operating its non-core business , and it sold the equity to Northern Ireland Water . S o it remains a private company — a project finance special purpose vehicle — but it is now owned by Northern Ireland Water , which has been able to achieve synergies through integrating it with other parts of it s operations . S o that is another way in which you can make that transition : the public sector can purchase equity .

We have to get away from the idea that there is a perfect model , or that , “This is what they do there, so it’s what we have to do here.” These things evolve over time . Y ou can try to learn lessons and see what could be done better , but I absolutely mirror what both John and David have said : y ou cannot look at ownership in isolation . You have to look at ownership, governance, finance and affordability as a package ; these things have outcomes , ultimately , in terms of consumer tariffs and consumer perception that their opinions have an influence on the performance of the companies .

Q140 A s a C ommittee , our task is to tease out those different ownership models and their advantages or disadvantages ; fortunately we do not have to make a decision . W ithin the models we have looked at, there are clear trends about how different models serve different purposes, whether that is being better for the environment or better for customers . A re there any particular trends that the Committee should be particularly aware of? For instance, which model is better if we wanted to get strong environmental improvements, or is it not as clear as that?

T here is no particular model that gives you particular outcomes. A lot of academic research has look ed at public ownership versus private ownership ; t here are certainly cases where you have a badly performing public sector and you can get big improvements. To go back to what John said, I have dealt with private water companies around the world, especially the French ones, and they are good at their business. If you package it as, “W ill you operate these sewage plants for us, and will you design, build, finance and operate, or will you just design, build, and operate ,” and you transfer risk through good contracts, th e responsibility is then on a company that is good at doing that. That is separate from the ownership of the company . G lobally, the dominant model is publicly owned, and then financing tools that give you what you need : long-term , low-cost finance that can feed into lower tariffs for consumers .

We are neutral as to whether it is nationalised or privatised . We do not bring capital , we save it . W e are focused on operational and maintenance efficiencies at scale , and that is the opportunity we get in places such as France and around the world.

There is nothing to stop the English and Welsh WASCs from taking a catchment and putting out an international tender to get the world ’ s finest operators and maintainers to come and tender over a 10 or 15-year concession period . T hey can do that, but they just don’t— nobody does. The only concessions we have are where the companies are nationalised . We have three PFIs in Scotland and one of the other PFIs that Hugh referred to . T here was Project Alpha and Project Omega — Alpha was water, Omega was waste water , and we run Omega now . W e look after all the sludges and b io resources in Northern Ireland and five major waste water treatment plants , and have done for the last 20 - odd years . T his is within Engl ish and Welsh capabilities ; t hey would have to get Ofwat and regulator approval , but we do not understand why we do not have comparative models and we do not just operate and maintain everything the same way .

T he conversation needs to turn to the Cunliffe r eview recommendations , and the comments we made on alternative operation and maintenance models , where people have clear black - and - white specifications of what the expectations are in particular catchments. I f you breach those expectations , you are instantly fined , as you are in a PFI ; t here is not some big , three-year court case , where the E nvironment A gency brings a CEO to court ; there are instant penalties for failure, which drives regulatory compliance . It is more about th e next tier of how you deliver the service s , and the c ustomer service s , for the people of England and Wales .
C onsistency is key .

It is about having alternative models; it is not one size fit s all . In England and Wales , everything is delivered the same way ; as Albert Einstein said, “ Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.” W e are doing things the same way we always have ; the model needs to evolve, and we need to bring private experts into the operation and maintenance arena , as we have with the CapEx arena . Lo ok at how the CapEx industry has evolved throughout privatisation ; you will remember the big process contracts in the ’ 90s, design and build , and the disputes . T he water industry has developed some world - leading alliances . I am a founder member of the @ o ne Alliance in Anglia Water ; it is held up by the Treasury as one of the best major capital framework deli very references . W e work well in creating the assets ; why can we not turn to all the international and global experts to operate and maintain th ose assets for efficiency and for performance ?

Q141 I am conscious of time ; I will ask one more quick question . David, you spoke powerfully about regulatory failure . I t is fair to say that few countries have privatised the sector to the same extent as England . O ne of the countries the Committee looked at was Chile , which is obviously a different context entirel y. C an any lessons be learned from elsewhere in the world around how a fully privatised system could be better regulated ?

W e have to restrict ourselves to OECD countries because they are comparable . O ne of the most useful comparators is Singapore ; water is state owned , and it has a problem: people use bottled water because they do not trust such excellent water to be so cheap . Their model has been that, although things are state owned , if the private sector can come in with something more efficient , then they are open to that. A lot of major projects such as desalination, water reuse and so on are operated by private sector companies , and the overall result has been a remarkably high quality of service .

Then there is the Scandinavian model — in Denmark , for example . Danish water costs a great deal more than British , but that means , f irst, that the water and waste water industry is entirely self-financin g: there is no debt . S econdly , the cost of the service has forced demand management into the public imagination . T he average water consumption in Denmark is roughly 100 litres per capita per day , against 142 in England and Wales . It has created something thoroughly beneficial .

Then you have hybrid models such as in Germany : roughly 25 % to 35% of the population is managed by the private sector , but the assets are held by the state . A gain , the re are very high expectations of efficiency, service, deli very and cost . T hat is certainly worth looking at . T he tricky thing about Germany is that — if memory serves me right — it has around 6,500 utilities . A s someone pointed out when I was at the IWA conference in Glasgow last week , the smaller the utility , the more it become s a princeling ; transparency and data sharing are poor, but delivery tends to be excellent.

T h e outcome for the consumer at the end of the day is an important point on which to end. G entlemen, th ose are all the questions we have for you at the moment . T hank you for your attendance . W e will move on without any pause . Our next witnesses will join us online — technology permitting — and we will have a further panel after wards, back at the table . T hank you for your attendance . Y ou are welcome to remain or to leave , as you choose.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Marine Colon and Professor Klaas Schwartz.

Good morning. Welcome to the Committee. Thank you very much indeed for joining us. For the benefit of those who are following our proceedings and for our own records, can I invite you to introduce yourselves to the Committee? Marine, we will start with you .

Thank you and good morning, ladies and gentlemen. First, I would like to thank you for giving me the opportunity to contribute to your Committee’s work. I am currently a lecturer at AgroParisTech, which is a higher education institution that trains engineers in the fields of life sciences and the environment. I am also a researcher in public management and deputy head of the joint research unit called G -EAU , which gathers 100 researchers on different water matters. I am in charge of the annual survey on concession contracts in the water sector in France for the French Biodiversity Agency. Before being an academic for the last 10 years, I was and still am a state water engineer , but I used to work for the Ministry of Agriculture as a consultant to support local government s in the management of their water and sewage utilities in rural areas.

Good morning, everyone. My name is Klaas Schwartz. I am a professor of water services governance at the IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in Delft in the Netherlands. I am also a professor of water services governance at the University of Amsterdam, focusing mainly on governance and management issues in relation to water services provision.
Marine , we will start with you for a few questions, if we may.

Q142 Welcome, Marine . It is lovely to have you with us online. We want to look particularly at the French model. We know that France uses a leasing or concessionary model for many of its water resources. Can you explain how that works and set out some of the advantages and disadvantages of this approach?

I will start by explaining the broad picture so that you can understand where the lease contract s fit in. First, the main difference and characterisation of the French model is that local government s are responsible for delivering the water and sewage services. They own the water systems and take all decisions regarding investment . They have to look for funds to invest according to their long - term planning, and they organise operation and maintenance , which means they decide whether to create their own public water operator or go for a lease contract. We call them concession contracts nowadays, according to the EU directive.

That contract is signed between the local government and a private operator. They agree on the duration of the contract and they agree on commitments that should be met to deal with the core issues and challenges that characterise this territory . This allows the private company to bill directly to the water users. With this money, it pay s for its operation and maintenance costs. If there is a little investment that is included in the contract, it also use s this money to fund these investments. Most investments that are included in these contracts today are replacements of worn-out pumps, for instance — everything that is turning engines in treatment plants. There could also be bigger investments, which are less used today, but it is still a possibility; for instance, in Nîmes, close to Montpellier where we are, the city contracted with Veolia to add biogas to the generator in the waste water treatment plant. This is the kind of element that can be agreed on.

The French model has around 22,000 water and sewage utilities ; i t is a lot. More than half are operated by public authorities , and they deliver water to half the population. This means that, compared with English and Welsh standards, our utilities are very small. We have only a few utilities that look like a standard English utility , around Paris , obviously . I am talking about Eau de Paris, S EDIF, and SIAAP . The situation may look like the situation in England before the Water Act in 1973.

In France, 31% of water services are operated by private operators , but the regulation is very different from the one that you have talked about so far. We do not have a central regulator like Ofwat. The regulation is made when there is a private operator through the contracts. As mentioned earlier, if performance is not met, operators are fined. There are penalties included in the contract. There are some incentive mechanisms to make sure that the operators deliver what is expected during the duration of the contract. The state still has a role : to check that the drinking water quality and the effluents released in the environment meet the standards set by the state. A n important thing to think about regarding the French system is the huge responsibility of the local government s.

Q143 In terms of advantages, there are so many smaller utilities, which means it is individualised and very personalised for the area. Do you see that as a benefit to the system , or do you think there should be more central regulation and larger organisations involved?

There was an attempt at the end of the ’ 90s to bring in a central, big regulator. The project has now been abandoned . At that time, there was a crisis of mistrust due to a lack of transparency about the management of water utilities. This has been overcome by setting up a platform where water utilities have to share data about their systems and performance : main performance indicators.

The main drawback of our system is that, as you pointed out, all these small water systems lack capacity in terms of expertise and in terms of financial capacity to face the current challenges that we face with climate change. The state has been trying to merge these small services . There has been a drive and we have dramatically reduced the number of water and sewage utilities over the past 10 years. There is still a long way to go to reach a size where it becomes more comfortable to tackle the current issue we are facing.

Q144 L ooking back at the contracts, you said that if you need to maintain a performance level, there will be fines. Do you think private sector involvement has generally improved service levels, efficiency and investment?
Are you talking only about the private operators or the public operators as well ?
I do not mind. You can address both if you want.

In terms of performance, we are doing quite well. Among the thousands of water and sewage utilities, I am not saying we are meeting targets perfectly everywhere . There are some issues in some places. We have very good public operators and less good public operators. There is a great diversity of situations.

The main lessons that we can get from the French experience is , first , that we have to have a strong public sector where local authorities are able to really understand the main challenges that need to be addressed by the operators , set the right targets and so on . It is important to build this capacity within our local government s and authorities to improve and make sure that you can take advantage of a very good firm that is very experienced and can deliver. If you do not understand its work, or draft proper terms of reference , you will not get the best it can offer. T he capacity of our local government s is key. Local authorities must be able to drive their operations.

In terms of investment, we have an issue of under - investment. We are quite worried at the moment in the sector because the pace of replacing old pipes is not good enough. We know we are going to have to handle a lot of investments to adapt to climate change. The way we fund investments only through water tariffs is seen today as leading to a situation where water tariffs are going to increase dramatically. The model really depends on the volume of water that is sold because , as was said earlier, only water can fund water in France, which means only water bills can fund investments in the water sector. Since we know that we are going to have to reduce the amount of water sold, we are in a tricky situation and we are looking for a new model to fund our water systems.

Q145 Excellent, that was about to be my next question , so y ou have already answered that. We are having a big debate and asking questions here in the UK about how to fund things, with that under - investment.

It has been mentioned that there are many cases where private contracts have been ended in France and the local authority has taken over control of the operations, such as Paris and Montpellier. What was the driver behind the taking back of those contracts?

The root cause comes from the ’ 90s , when there was a big crisis of mistrust towards the model of concession contracts. P rice s were going up very rapidly because there was a lot of investment to be made, as was said earlier, regarding sanitation to meet the standards set by the European Union ; that was a great driver , and w e could clean our rivers , but it is very costly. At the same time, utilities and local government relied on the private sector to bring money and expertise in the treatment and so on . At the same time, there has been a lack of transparency in the management and some cases of political corruption that you might have heard of. All this has created a lot of resentment regarding this model of involving the private operator. There has been a growing idea that we should move away from this model and trust more in the ability of the public sector to manage itself.

This is one of the roots of many decisions to go towards building a public ownership of the operator , but i t is not the only reason. It is not only the moral idea that it is not right to make money from the water business ; t here is also something else. A t a time when water issues are so sensitive , there is a will by many big cities to keep control of the whole water cycle and to not think about water services as a separate topic from urban planning and other local public services or issues , so that they could also use water and sewage services as a way to develop sound local development policy for water-resilient territories. That is also a very strong driver.
Q146 Just very practically , in terms of if a local authority such as Montpellier is taking back control, what steps need to be take n in reality? What has to be done?

In France, the f irst step is a political decision. Often it is during local election campaigns that a mayor is elected . The Montpellier mayor won on a programme that included the remunicipalisations. That was the first step.

Then it was about creating a small enterprise in Montpellier at that time. In Montpellier, a 25-year contract with Veolia was ending. The issue was to find the right people — the head of the Régie— to recruit the employees, build an organogram , fund offices, equipment and so on .

As I am sure you are aware, t he issue of human resource management is key. In the case of France, it is interesting that we have a law that protects all employees of local public services. If there is a change, if a new operator takes over, whether public or private, the new operator must offer positions to the employees working in the utility so they can keep their jobs . This not only protects workers but also helps guarantee the continuity of service.

For instance, i n the case of Montpellier, the head of the water production plant chose to follow the Régie and not work for Veolia any more. It was very nice for the Régie to rely on this high-level expertise to guarantee that once it takes over, it will have the expert from the water treatment production plant with it . That is something that is tricky.

Then at the end of the day, you get a Régie that looks like a small enterprise , with people coming from the ex-private operator and employees coming from other types of organisations. The challenge is to make all these people work together with common values.

I n Montpellier and in other cases, it is a great opportunity to involve citizens. In Montpellier , citizens have been involved throughout the process leading to the decision to create a Régie and to choose the type of Régie that should be created. O n the governance board of the Régie now, there are seats for the citizens.

Lastly, if the Régie is not ready to handle all the activities on the first day of operations, there is also the opportunity to outsource some activities to the previous operators. T his is what happened in Paris and Montpellier. I n Montpellier, the billing system and the call centre were managed by Veolia for the first years of operations until the Régie felt confident enough and developed its own system.

Q147 I have a quick final question because I am conscious we need to move on to the Netherlands next. D oes the evidence suggest that this public control has led to better outcomes? Or is it too soon to tell?

It is a tricky question because , to my knowledge, there is not yet really a study, and we should do it in France. It will be interesting. What I can tell you is that, in the case of Montpellier, for instance, the regime has been in place for more than 10 years , and is performing almost at the same level as before, under Veolia . It is able to invest a lot ; a new water production plant has been delivered recently to secure the supply in Montpellier.

Often, the worry with public operators is whether they can innovate and keep a high level of expertise. In Montpellier, it won an EU-funded research and development project to develop a mobile unit to develop waste water reuse to flush out the networks , and for diverse uses in the city. It is evidence that the public sector can also go towards innovation.
We are going to move on to some questions regarding the Netherlands experience.

Q148 Morning, Professor Schwar t z and H artelijk dank for taking time to be with us this morning. We are really interested as a C ommittee to look at the example from the Netherlands , because you have relatively large regional water companies, which is similar to the system we have in the UK, but different . In the Netherlands they are owned by local authorities , and in the UK we do not have any involvement with councils in water. T o begin with , could you give us an overview of how the Dutch model works, and what you see as the benefits and drawbacks of that system?

The Dutch model is currently more or less enshrined in the Dutch Water Supply Act , which dictates that water utilities are essentially organised as private companies , but the shares have to be owned by public entities. Historically , because we came from a situation of having municipal water utilities, it means that for these private companies that provide water services, the shares are owned by either municipalities or provinces. The Water Supply Act also dictates that these companies have a security of supply that they must guarantee and have a duty of care for the infrastructure they own and use to provide services. T hey are private companies but owned by local government shareholders, so the idea is that they combine a degree of autonomy for the water utility to make decisions that are in the best interest of securing suppl y and maintaining the infrastructure, while having the shareholders be local government means that they are going to particularly focus on the level of services that are being provided to the consumers and on the tariffs not being too high.

Q149 That Act of Parliament sets the rules for the whole system ; everybody knows what they are working to. I s there a feeling that that is a bit restrictive? Does that restrict innovation , or do people feel that it is a safety net that they want to keep in place?

Until recently, it is a model that has worked very nicely in the Netherlands. We of course also went through the 1990s with questions about efficiency. That is still a question that remains . O n the one hand, the advantage of the model is that it create s a distance between the public shareholders and a water utility, which basically operates relatively autonomously. On the other hand , the disadvantage is that you have a model in which you have shareholders that are at arm’s length , and a utility that operates relatively autonomously. A lot depends on how the utility fills that role.

The challenges for the Netherlands will especially come in the near future. The challenges facing the sector with droughts , such as we had last year and for the previous four or five years, are highly problematic. Newly emerging contaminants are problematic. We are also at a stage where a lot of the infrastructure and investment from 50 years ago needs to be replaced. This is something that is just developing. The big question is how the model will fare under these pressures , because one of the things that is going to happen is that the tariffs are going to increase. In 2022, we paid €1.90 per cubic metre. This year it is up to €2.70 and it is likely to increase further in the future given the challenges we are facing.

Q150 That was going to be my next question : what is the public perception of the cost and levels of bills? Is that a big part of political debate in the Netherlands at the moment? Are people very dissatisfied with those charges? Do they feel that it is an important, necessary investment?

C onsumer trust was also referred to earlier . Dutch consumers of water supply services have a great deal of trust in water utilities. If you go out on the street and ask people, “ How much do you pay for water? ” I do not think anyone could actually tell you what tariff they pay. I work in a water institute. If I ask my colleagues, it is unlikely that they will actually know how much they pay.

The tariff is also relatively low because other services are much more expensive: electricity and gas. In comparison , water is not something that consumers think about, other than that they want to be able to open their tap at any given moment of the day and the water that comes out needs to be good quality and potable. T he water utilities understand that the trust of the consumer is extremely important , so t hey are also investing in maintaining that trust.

Q151 Public trust in the UK is in a very different place with most of our water companies. We are very keen to get your insights on that. I want to ask you about the fact that local authorities play such a big role in the water system. I know from being a member of a local council previously that anything that the council touches can potentially become a point of political debate. Is there any politicisation of that system in the Netherlands? Is it a feature of local election campaigns , as Dr Colon was referring to in France? Or is this something that, as you said, everyone trusts is being dealt with well and they just leave it alone and focus on other issues?

One major difference is that in the Netherlands we have regional water utilities. Marine was talking about situations where one municipality decides. If you have one Government shareholder, it is easier to politicise decisions about water utilities. In our case , for example, if I look at a utility such as Vitens, it has five provinces and 92 municipalities as its shareholders. None of these shareholders has a majority. First, t here would always need to be a coalition of municipalities that argues for a certain position. Second, the question is : what would you gain? What would you win? T he level of service being provided at the moment is quite good. The tariffs are considered acceptable by the consumers. They rate water services at 7.9, which is relatively high for public services. If you were to politicise it, there is not that much to gain by doing that. It is also perhaps important that our mayors are not elected ; they are selected and recruited by the municipal councils.

Q152 That is interesting. One thing we are looking at quite intently at the moment in the UK is public involvement. A recent bit of legislation passed by our Government mandated customer panels to empower customers and give them more of a direct say, or at least be able to lift the lid on what is going on in their water company. How much direct public involvement is there in the Dutch water system? Again, is that something people are just not clamouring for?

No, it is very little. In some cases, utilities have tried, following customer service councils in England and Wales, to establish a customer council, but they could not find people who were interested in dedicating their time to be part of such a council . The utilities would be open to it, but there are not a lot of citizens or consumers who consider it to be a relevant enough question at this time, at least, to really engage themselves with. Again, in my view, we in the Netherlands are at a turning point where we are facing a lot of challenges that are quite severe.

Q153 One of the things I was struck by when I was looking at the map of the areas that the water companies cover was that some seem considerably larger than others. You mentioned Vitens. It seems to cover a huge chunk of the country, whereas others are relatively small. Do you see any kind of advantage or disadvantage in the size of those companies within the Netherlands? Does that have a bearing on their performance , or are they different factors altogether?

No, other factors are much more relevant, such as water sources; whether they are surface water or groundwater companies really impacts tariffs. Some areas have easier access to water than others. These factors are much more determinant in the performance of the utilities. In the case of Vitens , a managing board and a board of directors became big in the 1990s. There was the threat of privatisation , and the idea was that if it grew, it would be more difficult to take over. That is one of the reasons why Vitens is relatively big .

It is also quite problematic for Vitens because although it is a large company, its service provision system consists of hundreds of smaller systems that are not very well connected. That leads to a lot of difficulties because it is not able to actually ensure that the water is going to the systems where it is most needed. Y ou need to distinguish the size of the company from, in the end, the provision of water services, water supplies , and infrastructure . The infrastructural system is crucial, perhaps more than the size of the company.

Q154 I wanted to come on to the infrastructure because you mentioned that, similar to the UK, the Netherlands has a lot of ageing infrastructure. A lot of investment will be needed in the coming decade or two. Obviously, the difference with your system is that you do not have private shareholders who can put in equity ; i t has to come from the local authorities. How effectively have those companies been able to invest , and what is the forward view?

Like in France, the companies do not receive any funding from the local authorities. The companies are completely self-financing. They fund their investments through loans, which they then have to pay off through the revenue generated from the tariffs. Apart from the tariffs, they have no other source of income. The Dutch water utilities are able to source relatively favourable loans because they are a monopoly for water supply, for which there is always going to be demand. They are semi-public, which means that the odds that a water utility is going to go bankrupt or default on a loan are very small. That means that banks are quite happy to provide the loans for investment. Again, it means the tariff is going to increase. It has increased substantially over the past four years. I assume it will continue to increase in the coming years. T hat is the way it is.

Q155 We are interested in the role of the Dutch water bank, which was obviously set up in the wake of devastating flooding in the Netherlands. It seems to have played a crucial role in providing stable, low-interest finance. We have also heard that the bank has expanded its operations massively , and there is some concern that it is not providing enough finance now for its original objective of securing the country’s water supplies. Is its role diminishing? What will its role be in this future investment?

The Netherlands Water Bank was initially established by the water boards, not by the water supply companies, for water security and water safety issues. In principle, it has a mandate to lend to entities which have a public purpose. Water supply companies have access to the Netherlands Water Bank, and some utilities also have loans with it . However at the moment, the Netherlands Water Bank ’s main source of loans is in social housing. It has moved beyond the water sector.

For the water utilities, it is not such a problem because the private banks are also quite interested in lending money to the water utilities. Most water utilities will have loans with multiple banks because they want to spread their loans over multiple providers and keep contacts in case they need to have quick access to loans, and so on . I personally do not think that the Netherlands Water Bank ’s development is damaging for the water utilities. The water utilities in the Netherlands are still able to access the funding that they need quite easily .

Q156 Do those private banks demand a higher return on their investment? Is there a concern about water companies perhaps taking on too much debt, which is very much the case with many of ours in the UK?
I f I am not mistaken, there are limits to the loans that they are able to take. I do not think there is a concern at the moment of utilities taking on too much debt.

Q157 Is there a concern that if there are limits on the amount of debt they can take on — as you mentioned, local authorities do not put money in — there are potentially some big investment requirements coming up ? Is there then a concern that that will fall on tariffs because that is the only other option you have?

It is going to fall on tariffs. The question is how to deal with keeping the tariffs more affordable. In the Netherlands, we have never subsidised tariffs ; i t is not something that we have ever done. Instead, the social security system provides benefits or allowances that can support low-income families in covering higher costs for certain basic services. The support for low-income households to deal with higher tariffs would come from a different source than from the water utilities. The tariffs, by law, need to reflect the cost of production ; t hey need to reflect the cost of provision. They are allowed to make a small profit, which sometimes goes to the shareholders , and sometimes is reinvested in the system . They need to reflect the real costs of providing services.

Q158 Lastly, I want to ask you about the research you have done on public ownership more broadly : the studies you have looked into outside the Netherlands. What kind of lessons do you think we can draw from the work you have done looking overseas? Nobody has a perfect system , but it seems that there are very good features of lots of different systems that we need to bring into ours.

I f it is a public utility, it is important to look at it in the broader governance structure. The Netherlands has the Water Supply Act, which is crucial. The fact that there are multiple shareholders is crucial. There is a lot of shared collaboration between the water utilities. Although we have 10 water utilities, we only have four water quality laboratories because most of these laboratories are co-owned by different utilities. In my view, i t is that broader structure that makes a water utility provide an enabling environment and a situation in which it can perform well.

I f I look at the cases that I have studied abroad, they often try to reform the utility, perhaps change its ownership, or make it into a private company owned by a public shareholder rather than a direct public utility. I am not so convinced that that is enough. You need to think more about the broader governance structure and the enabling environment in which that operates. If you do not address that, then changing the ownership has little impact.
Q159 Marine , you wanted to come back in.

Yes, thank you. If time allows, I just wanted to add something regarding funding of our water sector. A fourth of our water bills funds water agencies and all the money that is collected within a river basin can be used and then redistributed to local government to help them fund investments. Local government s can use revenues from water bills, subsidies, concessional loans from water agencies, and funding from the European Union and other local governments to help them fund their investments. This was a quick add-on that I find useful : having an agency at the scale of a river basin that can give priority in terms of investment and orientate the action of local government s by bringing additional funds to issues that are seen as most urgent and relevant within a river basin.
That is interesting , but I will hand back to the Chair in the interest s of time.

Marine and Klaas, thank you so much for joining us in our little Committee Eurovision homage. We appreciate your attendance. There is a lot more that we could discuss , but unfortunately time is against us today . T hank you for your attendance and co-operation .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: David Henderson, Professor David Hall, Professor Ewan McGaughey and Professor David Saal .

Good morning, everyon e. T hank you again for your attendance. We are up against it a bit for time, but I am sure we will manage to ventilate all the issues. Can I just invite you all to say a few words of introduction?
My name is David Henderson. I am the c hief e xecutive o fficer of Water UK, which represents all the water companies in the United Kingdom.
Welcome back.

I am David Saal. I am a professor of economics at Loughborough University. I fell into water and sewage in 1999 when I started working with David Parker on privatisation of various industries . I have been working on it since, doing cost assessment modelling, regulatory work and so on .
There are so many ways we could take that introduction , but we are going to be disciplined.
My name is Ewan McGaughey. I am a professor of law at King’s College London and a research associate at the Centre for Business Research at the University of Cambridge.
And th e third of our triumvirate of Davids .

Yes , another David, I am afraid. I am a visiting professor at the Public Services International Research Unit at the University of Greenwich . I have been researching this stuff for some decades now.
We are going to be looking now at some issues with privatisation and the potential for a reformed water sector. Sarah, you are going to lead our questioning o n this.

Q160 The IWC report published in July 2025 sets out a comprehensive vision of the water industry and what it could look like . It is proposing reforms to tackle the issues of the water sector. What problems will the c ommission’s proposal s solve? W hat issues do you think are going to remain unaddressed? I will start with the first of Davids.

I t is a very good report. I should say that , in representing all the water companies across the United Kingdom, I represent the state-owned Scottish Water and Northern Ireland Water, the not-for-profit in Wales, as well as the private companies in England. It is very clear that the challenges are the same. Climate change does not discriminate against ownership model. The changing needs of businesses — especially data centres, some of which can use a hell of a lot of water when it comes to high temperatures — do not discriminate against ownership model ; nor does population growth. We are seeing that in all four nations of the United Kingdom.

Sir Jon Cunliffe has identified that there is no correlation between ownership and performance. It is a view backed up by the OECD in Paris, when it look s across Europe as well as the rest of the western world. Cunliffe has identified that , regardless of ownership model, there are three crucial ingredients .
