The challenge internally is quite clearly set, which is how we can go as fast as we can without doing something stupid that will expose us to legal action. A lot of what we do is a quite court-intensive , legal process and does not move at a very exciting pace.

We always have in mind “more haste, less speed”. Sometimes it is right to take the extra few months, and sometimes we are being too cautious. We do quite a lot of challenge to ourselves on those decisions. Sometimes we have to take the timing extension, and sometimes we absolutely should not and we should press ahead.
It is a live issue that we are conscious of.

Q75 Returning to the issue of media literacy, the Online Information Advisory Committee note on threats to elections recommended that Ofcom commission research on the most effective media literacy strategies for under-18s, which is particularly important given the proposals to extend the right to vote to 16 and 17-year-olds. Are you taking that advice?

We are very much thinking about that at the moment. The Online Information Advisory Committee is turning out to be a very good thing from our perspective. We have really good people. It is properly independent. It is giving us really thoughtful advice and, I hope, also informing the public debate a bit. Yes, we are thinking about how we can take that and the other recommendations forward.
Q76 Okay. What specific impact has the Online Information Advisory Committee had on your approach to misinformation and disinformation?

It has given us a proper expert view on that landscape that we had in part before but not as fully as we now have it. It has given us information on how these threats emerge and develop online. It validated some of the things that we are doing, such as our crisis response protocol, which is all about controlling things in a crisis before they get worse. It is also helpful to others, in underlining how difficult these issues are to address, by bringing in things like media literacy, prominence and the availability of trusted news alongside the regulatory aspects. It is not just what you do not like and you regulate to try to remove; it is also about what you do like and making sure that it gets sufficient airtime, prominence and attention from viewers and listeners.

I would add the whole question of possible electoral interference through misinformation, which falls short of where the legal bar is, but what can we do? Conversations with the Electoral Commission are ongoing to work out whether there are pre-emptive things that we can do and learn.

Given that we are about to see in a couple of countries around the world some highly contested elections in places such as Israel and the midterms in the States, we are going to see a huge amount of learning on how this plays out in that social world. While we are not covering misinformation and disinformation in the Act, this will go up the agenda, and the Committee is very helpful in helping us keep abreast of that.
Q77 Are you able to share anything at all from those discussions at the moment?
Not just yet, but that is the learning that I would like to come back to after the elections.

Q78 Moving on to the telecoms network, we are switching off the 2G network, the first mobile network in this country, which still hosts critical services and telecare devices. When you came before my Committee, I expressed concerns that there would be similar cases to what happened when the fixed-line network was switched off and Ofcom issued a fine to Virgin Media of £24 million because it did not offer the proper support. How confident are you that this switch-off will happen without affecting vulnerable customers?
I can give some perspective on it from the sidelines as well.

I am very happy to answer that. On 2G, the three mobile network operators have timescales that range from the back end of 2029 and the beginning of 2030, so it is a few years away. 3G has been switched off without incident.

You are absolutely right that 2G, although it is an older technology, is more likely to be used for telecare as well as some critical national infrastructure. The Government developed a voluntary concordat with the industry earlier this year, which is really helpful, underlining that it must make sure that the right information is provided sufficiently far in advance and that it must deal with vulnerable customers carefully. Ofcom’s rules will also be there as a backstop if we feel that people are not doing what they should do.

Q79 Okay. There was also a voluntary concordat or agreement for the switch-off of the fixed-line network. You had to fine companies in the end after the fact. What are you doing now to make sure that does not happen? The year 2029 is only a couple of years away.

It is only a couple of years away. The difference is that the concordat is in place now before the transition starts, whereas before it was not. The concordat was in place in February this year on the fixed—the PSTN. To be honest, Ofcom had already done a lot of work with the industry on the switching off of the fixed line —the PSTN.
Q80 My point is that those were voluntary measures, and this is also a voluntary measure. What are you doing?

It is a mix, actually. The same rules that we enforced against with Virgin Media O2 on PSTN can be applied to 2G. We have statutory guidance here that needs to be followed by operators, and we will absolutely use that if we think we need to. It is also very helpful that the Government have assembled the industry and that partnership.

Q81 I don’t think you’re quite getting my point. T h e fine happened when there was concern that vulnerable customers had died. It was after the fact. We do not want to get to that point. What data are you collecting? What are you observing? What are you watching? What measures are you taking? I do not want you to be fin ing after people have died or critical services go down.

No, and we do not either. That particular episode against which we fined happened a few years ago, of course. The incident was, I believe, in the autumn of 2023, as I recall, because it takes a while then to run the enforcement through. We did a lot around that time. We had already done a lot, to be honest, and made clear to the industry what our rules were. It is a shame that—
Q82 What are you doing now to make sure those rules are being followed?

I am sorry if I am not being clear enough. I was trying to explain that we are doing exactly what we always do with these transitions. 2G is no different from PSTN. We are absolutely clear with the industry that it needs to follow our rules.
Q83 With PSTN, people died.

Well, to be honest, n o coroner has decided that the PSTN switch-off was relevant. That has not been ascertained in a court. We fined them for not having followed the careful processes that they needed to with vulnerable customers. We certainly did and w e are doing the same now. We are absolutely clear with the industry, as the Government are, that as they switch off 2G—eventually, we do need to migrate away from these old technologies—they look after vulnerable customers and critical national infrastructure.
Q84 You are not doing anything differently from what you did with PSTN.

No, we are doing a lot differently. There is a lot that we did before, actually, which was to be clear that the rules were there. It is very regrettable that that company did not follow them on that occasion. Sometimes that happens. The other thing that has happened this time that is very helpful is that the Government have been much quicker to get the industry around the table and sign up to these things, and to get this discussed and debated. The preparations should be better. The communication should be better. We will be there as the regulator, as the back stop, if not.
Q85 Do we have a list of vulnerable customers? Do we have a list of critical national infrastructure that is vulnerable?

The Government are absolutely looking at the critical national infrastructure. It is their job to look across the Whitehall system and pull that together. When it comes to customers, that is a job for the companies. They need to work out where they are, as they do for any telecare customer. They need to be taking many steps to make sure that they are as sure as they can be where those customers are.

Q86 This is one of the things that failed last time, and I do not get any sense of confidence that it is not going to fail again this time and you will be issuing fines after the fact. I do not get a sense of confidence on that.

I would say two things having been in the telecoms situation before. First, I would not underestimate the pain of the learning that people went through last time. Organisations that made comfortable operational promises have found out that did not work. There is a difference this time around because it is not the first time, and we have learn ed .

Secondly, I am afraid to say that nobody can guarantee zero individual outcomes. It is just not possible with millions. The point is: do we have a really robust process, and do companies take it seriously? If they do, they should be able to mitigate it. There will not be a possibility of some ghastly accident in the middle of nowhere, but we want to focus on the total outcome for the country, and that has to be better as a result of the process that Melanie and her team are going through. I know that the telecoms industry understands it a lot better than it did the first time it came around this.
Q87 Okay. There is an improvement in telecoms sector understanding.
Yes, comprehension of the challenge.

Q88 Can I ask one more question? 2G and 3G are being switched off because of the roll-out of 4G and 5G. When Ofcom measures the quality of service of 4G and 5G, I have to say it does not reflect my experience and that of my constituents, which is the very patchy service across the country. Less capacity appears in the network. Are you looking at how you better measure the quality of service on 4G and 5G networks to reflect consumer experience?

Yes, we absolutely are. Eighteen months ago, we completely overhauled our website because it told you whether you had coverage, but not whether that coverage was good enough and the signal strength was strong enough to use your phone or device how you wanted to at home or at work.

The data is a lot better. We use crowdsourced data, so it reflects the public’s view and not just the projections of the mobile network operators. But i t is not perfect ; i t never will be completely perfect. There are ways that people can use our website to tell us if we are missing something at a local level.

The really important thing is also that we then get the actions going that will improve signal strength at a local level. We have seen in the last few years very significant investment. The coverage is now in quite a good place, but we need to deal with trains. The Government are on to that. Ofcom has made millimetre-wave spectrum available for very high-demand areas like train stations and football stadiums. That is another thing that needs to be sorted out.

Ultimately, a lot of the local issues are about not enough masts being available to deliver the power, and that is a lot of the time about planning permissions from local authorities. We published in June a rather revealing set of charts that showed that, for example, in Richmond, still three quarters of planning permissions for masts are refused. Glasgow, Cardiff, Belfast and Edinburgh—I do not know why it is in the devolved Administrations—are coming up the league table, doing a smarter job now and getting the numbers up as well.

I know it is really hard for local authorities ; I used to run the Department for Communities and Local Government. Those decisions locally are going to be needed now to drive coverage in the places where people do not have it.

Q89 If I want better coverage in Northumberland or when I go to watch my football team, Newcastle United, at St James’ Park and I can never communicate with anyone, you are saying that that is an issue down to approval of planning permission.

I would hope that at St James’ Park the mobile network operators O2, EE and Vodafone now, or will, make use of the millimetre-wave spectrum we have made available. That should make a real difference. If you have a part of the city or a rural area where there is a hill and the mast does not reach around the geography, it is probably going to need another one. Unless that is consented by the local authority, there is very little that can be done to improve the situation for customers.

The one other gleam of light here, though, is that satellite is increasingly coming forward. There was a story recently about the European Union thinking about this. We have already done this in the UK via Ofcom. We have already supported all three of the mobile network operators in being able to partner with satellite companies so that you can get direct calls using satellite technology on your phone. That will really help for some very remote areas.
Q90 Thank you for that. That is useful. I know that that includes Starlink as one of the satellite companies, which raises issues of sovereignty and reliability, but they are not for this Committee.
Actually, the mobile network operators are not all using Starlink. They are using a variety of providers. I agree with you that Starlink is extremely dominant globally.

Q91 Dame Melanie, you said in a letter to BT about the proposed acquisition of TalkTalk that the situation posed an “ unacceptable risk to consumers ” . Obviously, it also represents a huge concentration in the market where BT already has quite substantial market power. Can you explain what you meant by “unacceptable risk to consumers”? Which is more concerning : the service disruption, or the risk of a less competitive UK marketplace?

Look, i n the end, we were glad to see that a commercial solution had been found to save the TalkTalk business because it had been in trouble for a while with declining customers, it was heavily loaded with debt and was struggling to find a buyer for the two parts of the business. That had been going on for some time.

The risk that the Government decided to intervene over was that it was going to go into an unmanaged liquidation, and that would have had unmanageable consequences for customers, including 55,000 telecare users and a bunch of other vulnerable customers, as well as some critical national infrastructure — not to mention the connectivity of many other hundreds of thousands of people who would have had to switch network quickly. At that scale, that would have been extremely difficult. That is why the Government decided to intervene.

The CMA is now looking at the competition issues. The deadline for it to do that was last night. The Secretary of State will then need to consider that. That was what she was weighing up. Normally, obviously, a deal like this would go through a much longer competition assessment, and there would be issues, as you described. I do not want to go into too much detail on that because it is a statutory process and we are not the decision taker at Ofcom. It was that public interest, and in particular the impact on customers, connectivity and the economy, that lay behind her decision to intervene.
Q92 Moving to a different topic, Sir Ian, you will recall the concerns raised about Ofcom’s approach to complaints from reality TV participants.
I do indeed, yes.
Q93 At your pre-appointment hearing, you said it would make sense to look again at the broadcasting code in light of those. What have you done to progress those discussions?

The best thing to say is that you learn and evolve these codes in the light of experience and as issues arise. We are currently close to getting the Channel 4 report on “Married at First Sight”. We also have something that we cannot talk about in detail: privacy issues raised by one contestant, which is a separate process. At the end of that, we will wait to see what Channel 4 suggests it does on the particular issue, and then that will be a precursor to saying, “Do we need to step back and think more broadly?” I would not want to preclude thoughts on that. That is another live issue.

We are waiting for Channel 4’s two independent reports into what happened. We need to hear from it first. I hope it will get that out soon. These things usually take longer than companies realise, but it has taken a while. We have not been waiting during that time. We have been looking at our guidance in the light of what we already know so that we can come out very quickly if we need to. We are not going to wait for a long time —
Take years.

— and launch some huge process of consultation. We have guidance on how reality TV should be run and how contestants should be treated. We have strengthened that quite a lot in recent years because it is becoming an ever more popular format and it comes with risks. We will see what has gone on here when we have the full picture, but we already have quite a lot of information that we are building so that we can strengthen the guidance if we need to.

Q94 Okay. It seems pretty clear that it will need strengthening. If you look at the current code, some research ers from Aston University said that “ a production can be found to be compliant with the code and yet serious foreseen harm can still occur ” . What do you think you can do to strengthen the code to make sure it addresses that?

We are looking into that. It is a risky format, and there is a decision that broadcasters have to make about what level of risk they are taking. Our guidance is there to make sure that thinking and risk assessment are done rigorously. As I say, we are looking at that right now.

The intent of the code is quite clearly to protect people. The question is, i f evidence suggests that it is not, we would like to understand the gap between the intent and outcome before we start figuring out what to do.
Q95 Okay. When is the report on Channel 4 due?
Any day now. Channel 4 is running th o se two investigations. They are independent. We are expecting them pretty soon. We are pushing it quite hard to get them over the line now.
Q96 You must have some thoughts already, though, about what you can do to strengthen the code.

Yes, we absolutely have, and that is what I am trying to reassure you on , I hope . We have not been putting our feet up and waiting for the reports so that we can read them and start to opine. We have been thinking now. We have been having discussions with Channel 4 already. We have a pretty good indication of what we think we might want to do here. We will come out pretty quickly —certainly as quickly as we can — after Channel 4’s reports are published.

Q97 That research also talked about how retraumatising it can be for a participant to be told, “We’re not taking any action,” even though they suffered harm. What more can you do to support complainants in those sorts of cases when you do not pursue a case?

If people want to come to us, they can. In this case, we have had a complaint from a participant, so we are considering that at the moment. We certainly have not dismissed it. It is an ongoing inquiry for us. Look, w e would always do everything we can to treat people in that situation with great respect, kindness and thought, recognising that sometimes, as you say, going through these processes can in itself be retraumatising. It is an important part of our job to be really thoughtful about that.
Q98 Okay. You are thinking about it, but I am not getting any sense of what might actually happen here.
Is there something specific that you would suggest?
Q99 No, that is what I am asking you to do.

Okay. We are looking very hard at the current code , which was obviously intended to do something. There is some difficulty in having zero impact if things go through a process and it does not get ruled in somebody’s favour. The question is what support is around that person. I am not sure that is our job to do, but it is an issue that we need to think about.

There are essentially two things here for Ofcom. One is whether we need to strengthen our guidance. We are looking at that right now. We will not delay on it. Secondly, what will our view be on this programme? Sometimes we decide that , even though somebody is really upset by the way they have been depicted in a programme , it does not fall foul of our rules. I am not saying that that is the case here. We are looking into it. It is a live investigation. We always treat complainants really carefully. Sometimes we do not uphold their complaints; sometimes we do.

Q100 Isn’t one of the complications the fact that not all productions are in-house and , therefore , there are independent production companies involved? What is the stepping stone in terms of the expectations for the requirement? Is it on the broadcaster, or is it that the broadcaster adheres to those guidelines with all the independent production companies, some of them perhaps overseas as well?

It is absolutely clear that the accountability is with the broadcaster, with the licensee who has the licence to broadcast in the UK. If it commissions out, which is a very good thing for the wider creative economy rather than it all being in-house, it needs to manage that supply chain very carefully.
That was very clearly my experience at Channel 4. There was a very clear enforcement process from the channel to the commissioners to the production companies.

Q101 Thank you very much. I know that you have been very patient with us and we have kept you here quite a long time. I want to sweep up on a few little questions about the broadcasting Green Paper— "W atch this S pace ” . I want your take on it. One thing that came out of it for me is this issue around prominence and whether you are comfortable being placed in the position of judging which news sources are trustworthy.

It is a bit of a hot potato. We discussed that earlier. The industry has certainly had some very strong views on this. There are some who would say, “Keep it very simple . M ake it just about the PSBs,” and others who say, “Absolutely not.”

Some of our non-regulated media outlets—what we would have called print outlets back in the day—are very clear that they should be included as well. We do not want Ofcom to be left having to determine this from first principles. It is important that Government and Parliament, if we go down this route, decide what sorts of rules they want to apply here and make some of those big policy choices, because there are lots of different ways that you could cut this depending on what you are trying to achieve.

Q102 More broadly, YouTube describes itself as a video-sharing platform, so it is not a broadcaster nor a social media company in its eyes. How do you view it? Can you regulate it effectively under the current regime, or is more regulation needed?

It is kind of everything. It is almost in its own special, extremely successful category. It is very much where children now find news and entertainment, increasingly replacing the TV in the home on a large screen.

As we have said before at Ofcom, it is very relevant for this prominence question of how our traditional broadcasters find their viewers. It is incredibly relevant to that. It is almost like a smart TV in that respect, but it is not actually a smart TV, so it is not part of the Media Act prominence regime. It has an algorithm. It has some qualities that are very much about social media.

There will be a question about a social media ban. In the end, again, it is a really good example of how Ofcom can look across the brief. It is owned by Alphabet, so it sits alongside Google with its huge power on the infrastructure side as well as on the search side , and as one of the main AI frontier investors and developers. You have to see it from multiple different routes. It provides a great service to many of us a lot of the time, but it has risks. We need to think about the contribution that it needs to play to protect the creative economy and the public service ecology that we all hold very dear.
Q103 My question was: do you think that you have the powers to regulate it effectively under the current regime —

Not on the media side ; n o, not really, which is why we have called for an extension of the prominence principles to YouTube. We have the power to regulate it on the social media side under the Online Safety Act, but it is more on the media side where there are some gaps that we think you need to fill.
Q104 What is the message coming back from DCMS on that?
This is very much part of the Green Paper, and about prominence on YouTube as well as on social media. That is a very active conversation.

Q105 When it comes to the media that we see in our own areas, there is a really delicate ecosystem of print, digital, broadcast and community outlets right across the UK. As the BBC expands its online services quite incrementally and supposedly brings advertising into some of its podcasts, to what extent does Ofcom have a role to analyse the cumulative effect on those community outlets and commercial news publishers as well? Do you have the powers that you need to be able to analyse any collective harm, particularly because this BBC competition review has never been conducted?

We have the powers to do that. That is part of the licence fee arrangement, and it is baked in then to the operating framework that defines how we do our regulation. We do a lot of work in this area, for example when the BBC is introducing new radio stations. We get a lot of noise from the industry about where it is using its market power in a way that is inappropriate. It is quite an active part of our work.
Q106 Do you have the capacity to be able to continue to look at all this despite everything else swirling around you?
Yes. Over the next years and months, the BBC is going to have to cut some services because of the budgetary challenges that it faces.
I was going to say that.

That is likely to be a slightly different question for Ofcom: whether it is still able to fulfil its operating licence. That is what we are expecting to be a bigger part of our work over the next period.

Q107 When it comes to BBC Radio, this year the BBC replaced its annual spending breakdowns for individual radio services with an aggregate “listen” figure. Is that something that concerns you? It makes it harder for Parliament and licence fee payers to scrutinise how the BBC is allocating its radio budget. Is that something that has come across your radar?
It has not come across my radar. I am happy to take that one away. Our BBC annual report will be coming out quite soon. I am not familiar with that.

Q108 In terms of the ability for the public to scrutinise where the licence fees go ; o kay, thank you. Was there anything that we did not ask you that you were burning to tell us in the last two hours?
You did not say anything about spectrum. That is maybe the only one.
We managed to get a bit of satellite in there for you. It is an important part of our work, especially for growth.

Speaking as a multiregulator, for the Committee, it is a real challenge to get all this breadth of topic back. I completely understand. If you think we have not covered stuff, we are super happy to pick up things either when they arise or in the light of my review on social media. We could take it as an ongoing relationship. One thing I am really keen to do is make sure we have transparency and clarity about what we are doing, particularly on the question about speed and urgency. We have clocked that.
Q109 The comment that I most regularly make about Ofcom when it comes to online safety is that we think it has the teeth. It is a question of whether it has the stomach to be able to do this.
There is lots of stomach this side of the table.
Excellent. Thank you for your time today. We could have had you here all day and still never exhausted you.
A nd it would have been fun.
I am not sure that is exactly how you would want to spend your day. With all that in mind, thank you very much for your time.

Q1 Welcome to this meeting of the Backbench Business Committee, where we will be considering applications for debates in the Chamber and Westminster Hall. The first request is from Peter Swallow, and it is for a debate in the Chamber on International Men’s Day 2026. Peter, please present your case.
Thank you, Chair, for inviting me. I am on two Select Committees, and it is very strange being on this side of the horseshoe.

On 19 November, the UK will join over 80 countries in marking International Men’s Day. Last year saw the 10th annual House of Commons debate to mark that important occasion. I have come before you today to pitch that we continue that well-worn tradition, because the reality is that many of the challenges affecting men and boys in this country have not gone away. Those challenges include, in healthcare, the implementation of the men’s health strategy and the ongoing mental health crisis, which affects so many young boys and men; and in education, the importance of male role models in the face of often toxic social media influencers, and the attainment gaps that white working-class boys in particular face .

More positively, in business, we are seeing the effects of implementing day one paternity leave, which came into force in April, and we can scrutinise the ongoing Government review of parental leave. More broadly, we can look at the role that men play in addressing violence against women and girls. There is an opportunity here to have a positive conversation about the role that men play in building strong families and prosperous and resilient communities, while also reflecting on many of the real challenges. I hope you will grant this debate, so that we can continue what I think has been a really healthy and helpful tradition of spending a little bit of parliamentary time focusing on these really important issues.
Thank you very much.

Q2 Thank you, Peter. The Committee has very little time allocated in the Chamber. Would you consider a Westminster Hall debate so that you could have your debate as close as possible to 19 November, or are you committed to the Chamber?

I of course accept the tensions that the Committee faces. I am sure you are used to people coming before you and saying, “I really want that Chamber debate, because I think that this is a very important issue and I would not want to see it sidelined.” But I recognise the challenges on your time, so if that is the Committee’s decision, of course I would understand. However, I do hope that we can get as many Members as possible to participate in this debate, especially on the back of last year’s very successful and well-attended debate.

Q3 International Men’s Day is 19 November, which would be the Thursday. That could coincide with when we have time to allocate. Would you want the debate on that day, or are there other events going on that might preclude the debate from happening that day?

I am just checking what I proposed in the application. Ideally, that would be the perfect day to do it, hopefully in the first debate of the day. If not, I appreciate those limitations. A Tuesday would also work in Westminster Hall, but my hope would definitely be for the stars to align and for it to fall on that date.

We do not yet know from the Leader of the House whether we will get that day in the Chamber, but we do know that we will have Westminster Hall that day, so that is why we are asking the question. Any other questions, colleagues? Okay, thank you very much, Peter. The Clerks will be in touch with you in due course.
Thank you very much.
Iqbal Mohamed made representations.
Q4 The second—and last—application is from Iqbal Mohamed, for a debate in the Chamber on the safety of frontier AI. Iqbal, over to you.
Thank you, Chair, and thank you to the Backbench Business Committee for inviting me to share my reasons for applying for this debate.

Whether we want to or not, we cannot get away from AI. It is everywhere: on our screens, in our newspapers and on our feeds. In my mind, it is one of the greatest opportunities that humanity has ever had, but also one of the greatest risks.

I was the first Member of the House of Commons to secure a debate on AI safety, in Westminster Hall in December 2025. AI is moving at such a pace. In other policy areas, months or years might be enough time for Parliament to develop what society needs, but I think that we need to move a lot faster when it comes to AI.

The risks of AI are technical, societal and humanitarian. We have heard from the chief executives of those companies that there are existential risks to humanity from AI—between 10% and 25%. We have heard from Bill Gates that he expects AI to replace around 40% of all jobs in society. The risks are therefore not just technical or related to safety; they are societal and humanitarian as well. I attended an AI APPG evidence session yesterday evening that looked at AI machine-driven vehicles—robotaxis—and their potential impact on our society when we have 300,000 private hire drivers.

This is such a broad topic, and it demands real attention and time in the Chamber—and Members’ focus—so that we can work together towards delivering a regime, a regulatory framework, that does not impede the benefits and economic opportunities but also does not put our country or wider humanity at risk.

Just to add, I spent 25 years in pharmaceuticals—I am a regulatory compliance expert in the whole supply chain, from research to the marketing authorisation of pharmaceuticals—and I believe that the principles of pharma regulation could be applied to AI.
Thank you. I spent 12 years in regulatory compliance for BT, so I know about the markets .

Q5 Thank you for bringing your application, Iqbal. You may have heard from the previous applicant’s pitch that there is quite a long waiting list for the Chamber. You have indicated that you want the debate to be there, but I would just suggest that sometimes time in the Chamber can be curtailed by urgent questions and statements. Would you consider a debate in Westminster Hall?

Whatever is possible, I will accept. This is an important topic, and as long as parliamentarians have an opportunity to discuss it with the appropriate amount of time, that is definitely progress. Having had a debate in Westminster Hall last year, and given the speed at which AI is moving, I think that this demands more elevated attention. Having a debate in the main Chamber would hopefully give it that attention among parliamentarians, but also among the public and the media.
So you would be happy to have it in Westminster Hall if it meant that you got it sooner?
If that is the only option available, then absolutely; it is better than not having it.
Q6 Would you be happy with a Tuesday or Thursday?
Whichever day is available. I guess that Tuesday would be preferable, because more parliamentarians are normally on the estate.
Q7 Just so that you are clear, if it is a Tuesday, we have to allocate it when the appropriate Department is answering debates, so which Department would you expect to answer this one?
It is DCMS now, I believe, with digital. I know that we have an AI Minister, but I do not know which Department he attaches himself to.
I thought that it was the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, or whatever they called it last week.
DSIT is gone now.
It is combined, now.
You might get the best of both worlds. Okay, thank you, Iqbal. The Clerks will be in touch with you in due course.
Thank you very much. I really appreciate it.
That concludes the public business of the Committee. The Committee will now retire in private to consider the applications and the allocation of time.

sessions.w: Stephanie Ayres (UKspace); Robert Atchison (ClearSpace UK); Elizabeth Seward (Supersharp)

segs.tx: Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy
O ral evidence: Space resilience , HC 572
Monday 19 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Matt Western (T he Chair) ; Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom ; Lord Boateng; Liam Byrne; Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi; Lord Godson; Lord Jack of Courance; Baroness Kidron; Helen Maguire; Lord Sedwill; Lord Tunnicliffe; Baroness Tyler of Enfield ; Lord Watts.
Evidence Session No. 2 Heard in Public Questions 9 - 12
Witnesses
Stephanie Ayres, Head of Policy, UKspace; Robert Atchison, Managing Director, ClearSpace UK; Elizabeth Seward, CEO, Supersharp .
Examination of witnesses
Stephanie Ayres, Robert Atchison and Elizabeth Seward .
Q9 Order, order. We return to our inquiry with our second panel today, as part of our session on space resilience. Can I ask the panellists to introduce themselves?

Good afternoon. I am Elizabeth Seward. I am the CEO of Supersharp. We are a spin-out company from the University of Cambridge. We are now 38 people and we build thermal infrared space telescopes. My background, though, is working for BAE Systems and Airbus Defence and Space.
I am Stephanie Ayres. I am the head of policy at the UKspace trade association.
Robert A t ch i son: I am Robert Atchison, managing director of ClearSpace and previously space instructor in UK Space Command.

Terrific. Thank you for being patient. We are running slightly over, so if you can give us as distilled and concise answers as possible, that would be very helpful as always. I will kick off by looking at the threat, which we covered earlier. We talked about the UK Space Strategy , which was published on 8 September. How did you read it in terms of the ambition within it and what it is committed to? You heard some of the responses that we just heard; what are your observations? Perhaps, Elizabeth, you could start.

Thank you. It was very welcome. It was a very well-rounded piece of work. It included civil and defence together, not quite for the first time but certainly in the most coherent way that we have seen. From a personal perspective, it put earth observation back as a priority, after it had been dropped in the one before. That is something we have a significant reliance on, so that was very good to see.

It is a strategy, and as such, it sets out what we want to do, but it does not have the implementation alongside it setting out how we get there and how we do it, so there is definitely more work to be done. I see it as a good grounding and a good step 1, but we have to keep going on how we now deliver that and in what timescales.

It has budgets assigned—you heard from the previous panel the comparisons to Germany—which are not significantly more than we were already spending. A lot of that is going to Skynet and the upgrade of our military communication system. But still, it is very welcome that we are going in the right direction.
By mentioning Germany, do you think that we are not very ambitious?
Nobody is matching Germany. Some €35 billion for its space programme is a significant investment. We have around £7 billion, so we are very far behind that.
How does that compare to France?

That is a good question. I do not have that figure to hand. Steph might do, when we get to her. But I believe that France is still spending more than us. We are not spending much of that money until 2030 onwards. At the minute, we are still doing the small programmes and the step-by-step approach, when we just need to be going faster. We have a lot of capability in the country that we could be using and delivering on for the national good.
Is that frustrating for you as a start-up?

Yes. As a start-up, we are still on the path to commercialisation. Our first two satellites launch next year. We have got there through excellent support from the UK Space Agency and the grant funding. We are hitting that commercialisation gap and are now looking to sell them and to target government contracts here and abroad. But the pots of money we are looking at will not emerge for another three or four years, whereas we will be ready in the next six months.
We will come back to that. Stephanie?

We also welcome the strategy, because it is the first time that they have tried to cohere across government departments. They have recognised that it is not just a scientific endeavour but also a fundamental enabler of national security, economic growth and functioning in a modern society. The Government are right to seek a more strategically focused approach and recognise the importance of sovereign capabilities.

However, the UK has many of the ingredients, but I am less confident about the delivery. There was not much in there about the detail of how it is going to be delivered. We need to remember that this was a strategy for spending £7.8 billion that had already been identified, allocated and secured; it was not a strategy going beyond 2030. A lot of the money was going to be spent between 2030 and 2035, but other nations are making their plans into 2040, and , actually, we are, but through the ESA lens, which is a different thing. The French have their own national space budget which is a little bit in excess of ours, but they spend the same again through ESA, whereas we do not; our £7.8 billion also covers our ESA contribution.
So they spend double what we do?

Yes, we used to be fourth in ESA spending and now we are fifth, so we are going in the wrong direction with our ESA spending. But, as I said, this particular strategy looks at the money that has been allocated and for this spending review. Going forward, we would expect the MoD and the UK Space Agency to work together to look to secure more funding, along the lines of our peer nations, to deliver the strategy. I would also like to see more resilience planning in a future strategy. This one does not sufficiently cover that.
Do you think their priorities are clear, from the strategy?

I think the priority for now is clear, which is to put us on a footing towards another place. As far as that goes, the strategy is successful. To Will’s point, which he made earlier, the clear and present dangers are now slightly different and will evolve. I would like to see the strategy evolve to meet that. I would also like to see other government departments brought into the strategy. Currently, Defra, DESNZ et cetera are not represented; it is merely a strategy for the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade and the MoD.

What I would say from my view, and I would echo everything that has already been said, is that I see the green shoots of grand strategy and the UK returning to that in its viewpoint going past 2035, as Stephanie said. We have clear KPIs to 2030. At ClearSpace UK, I have the privilege of holding the UK’s active debris removal contract and we are going to de-orbit two satellites, with the launch scheduled for 2029 from SaxaVord, which gives the UK, as one nation in the world, a full circle of capability: launch, operate, de-orbit and potentially refuel as well, noting that there is a dependency on wider architecture.

The space strategy is welcome in that it brings the national, defence and severe space weather strategies together into one, which I know, from a coherence and command-and-control perspective, from my previous life in the military, is critical at the start of any operation. But linking to national resilience, and what that looks like, is so multifaceted, and I would just say, based on my previous life, that our potential adversary states, such as Russia, train their military to operate without space. They accept that from the word go. Having served in Afghanistan and places such as that, I know that we were heavily reliant on unencrypted GPS. There was encrypted GPS for other things, but when we come to these operations, we either have an assumption that we track—we assume—or we follow through and say that we are going to fight for space and whatever that means.
That is very interesting, thank you. Baroness Tyler?

Q10 I would like to pursue the issue of government support and involvement. Can you say whether you feel that the investment—clearly, we have heard that it is not on the same scale as a number of other countries—and the reforms in the space industry, which are set out in the strategy, give you confidence that the UK will be able to build a sufficient space resilience and capability, both civilian and military? In answering, could you reflect briefly on the point that came across very strongly in the first panel about an overreliance on the US and whether you feel that we should be pivoting our investment more towards Europe and the UK industry.

Shall I kick off? I will pick up on a question asked of the previous panel, which was whether we could retrofit all our assets. The UK does not have very many sovereign satellites that it owns and controls. We have four military communication satellites in the Skynet system. We now have, I think, three earth observation satellites. Potentially there are one or two classified ones, although I am not sure that there are. We have a handful, or potentially two handfuls, of satellites. We really do not have very much infrastructure to secure or retrofit. That also means that we do not have very much to rely on if we lose access to everything else.

Mr Marshall made a good point, that numbers count. That is very true, and we in the UK do not have them. But it is not just numbers, it is also mixing data sources, different actors and different types of data. Planet has optical systems, such as what you would take on your iPhone camera. There is radar available, which we can build in the UK and have done at the Airbus site in Portsmouth but do not today. My company is building thermal infrared. Those are the three layers that you need for earth observation. Then we have communications and GPS—the timing and navigation system. We have access to many of these things through our allies and we have the ability to buy them commercially, but the UK does not have a resilience plan and strategy for which ones we need to employ at which time and where we can get priority access to.

Resilience is all about, as Rob said, what do we need to be able to rely on and who owns that. Who owns that capability and delivery? What level of service do we need, both operationally and if there is some sort of problem? What is the minimum at which we can operate successfully? Those are the questions that we have not yet asked ourselves as a nation and the ones that you will have the challenge of answering in your report. We are here to help you do that.

Do I think we as a country can do it? Absolutely; we have some world-leading capability in this country. We have amazing large-scale satellite manufacturing at the Airbus plants. We have small companies that are growing, such as ClearSpace with its new contract and others around the country. We are really good at university spin-outs , building new technologies and doing R&D. We are not very good at getting those to commercialisation and supporting them through scale, and we do not have very many government contracts to actually use this amazing tech that we produce.

I would like to build on what Liz said. I am going to call for what we called for in our submission, along with an audit. We think that for the industry we need to have a national space resilience exercise: an industrial preparedness programme. It needs to be connected through the Cabinet Office, Defence and DBIST, along with trade bodies and other relevant associations. It should have four elements.

First, there should be some national dependency mapping, such as Liz described. We need to identify our critical services and their dependencies on space. We have to remember that all of our critical national infrastructure, including the grid et cetera, absolutely relies on space-enabled services. They have to be mapped.

Secondly, we need to map the vulnerabilities and alternative provisions, including second and third-order dependencies. We have all sorts of international allies and partners in that mix that we need to be aware of. They are probably good, but we need to establish that. We need to do scenario-based war-gaming where we look at the loss of PNT or SATCOM or earth observation or ground infrastructure or spectrum and the data integrity, but we need to look at them under different durations and different threat conditions, because something that goes out for a couple of hours is very different to something that goes out for weeks and might need to have a spacecraft put up to replace it.

The third thing we need is industrial mobilisation planning. We need to establish what industry can deliver in 72 hours, in 30 days, in six months, and beyond, including supply chains, personnel, launch capacity and manufacturing. Commercial operators need pre-agreed arrangements covering prioritisation, compensation, liability et cetera. The first time we use these integrated things should not be during a crisis.

Fourthly, we need the investment feedback. Where do we have gaps? What do we need to invest in? To your point about the US versus the EU, where do we go to get the help? We do not want to replicate what the United States and Europe are doing. That would be unaffordable and unnecessary. Instead, we should be identifying where the UK needs genuine autonomy and where it can develop distinctive capabilities that make us indispensable to those allies. That is a very strategic thing for us. We do not want to be replicating capabilities that lie elsewhere.

On the numbers, in the things that we are looking at here, NSpOC, our National Space Operations Centre, tracks around 811 UK assets in space all the time. Of those, 640-something are OneWeb satellites, of which we own only 16%. Eutelsat and the French own the rest. The challenge of us auditing what we have in space and working out what to do with it is not as big as it may sound. The challenge is going to come when we try to work out what to do about that. That is Rob’s job: to repair, replenish and remove.
I know that time is pressing now but would you like to add anything?
No.
Are you sure?
Yes, I will wrap it into another answer.
Okay. In a word, or a sentence, can any of you say whether it would be helpful for the Government to be more interventionist in this area?
Yes.
That is three yeses. Thank you very much.

Q11 I fear there might be some overlap but I want to carry on with this theme of developing resilient capabilities. How can the Government ensure that UK-based companies are best able to contribute to developing UK sovereign capability in space? That is open to all three of you to answer. We know that the Government need to help, but what is the best way that they can help?

One really positive thing is the Technology and Growth Alliance that has just been stood up, which seeks to take IP that has, in essence, been put on the shelf by the Ministry of Defence. This is where previous pounds have been spent and the IP has got to a technology-readiness level and we are now seeking to commercialise it. Those pathways and that help are really important, particularly for the SMEs that spin out of it. I am very privileged to be able to say that I have an anchor contract from the UK Space Agency to go and do active debris removal, but we are keenly aware that that is more than a contract; it is about establishing an industrial base from which we can grow and then work with, for example, Elizabeth and others to put those sensors on there.

To answer a previous question, the one thing that I would add about how we do this, is that we as the United Kingdom should be quite selective in what we say our strengths and weaknesses are. With my military hat on, there is always space for deception. We as a nation, as Elizabeth said, will never, nor should we, be replicating, but we can divert other people’s attention to areas that we want them to look at, which gives us freedom. That could be the industrial base, but it could also be from a strategic perspective. The UK’s overseas territories are a great asset that we do not make full use of.
Do you want to add anything, Stephanie?

I would just say that the UK Space Agency has a very good Unlocking Space programme through which it intervenes and helps other government departments, for example, recognise and use space. But there are a number of things that we, as the industry, ask the Government for, such as predictable pipelines, access to defence procurement, which is very problematic for small space companies, more targeted scale-up finance and the protection of international market access. The EU Space Act and the Made in Europe efforts are really damaging us and we need the Government to lean into that.

We also need some strategic supplier assessment. There are some companies that the Government have put in the strategy as being worth around £10 million or able to make £10 million. That might be a bit of a blunt instrument. There may be companies that need to be helped because of their strategic capabilities rather than their ability to get to £10 million necessarily. Those are the sorts of interventions that the industry would like to see.

I would say procurement and purchasing services, hardware or technologies. We do relatively well on grant funding, although I will note that the UK Space Agency grant funding programmes are always hugely oversubscribed, which is often presented as, “Isn’t this fantastic?” but actually it means that there are far more companies that could be doing great things if we had more funding to do so. One of the consequences of that is that the matched-funding contributions keep going up, so as a small company you get only 60% to 80% of the grant. Everything has now dropped to about 70%, so you have to find that extra 30%, which means you have to find investors and many of those investors are not British. So we lose control of the companies at much earlier stages. Then, when you get to a certain level and are ready for commercialisation, those procurement contracts either do not materialise or take a very long time, and as a small company with salaries to pay and a runway that you can see the end of, it is a very different situation than if you are a large systems integrator and it is just another project that gets delayed by a year. This slowdown of defence spending, with all the reviews we have been doing, has had a huge impact on many of the space companies.

We know that the Government are looking to develop partnerships to ensure that they have reliable access to critical space-based services in the event of a crisis. Where should they be looking for these partnerships and how should they be looking for them?

Again, when it comes to resilience, having that proliferated set of partnerships is also useful. From my side in earth observation, we are seeing a very strong push towards the High North and the Canada-Norway-UK alliance. Certainly, as a company we have been having conversations with other companies that link into the government strategy. There is also Japan, Australia, New Zealand and the other Five Eyes nations. The US is still a strong partner because it has such a wealth of knowledge and capability that we should not discount it at this stage. But it should not be the only one. It is about spreading who we are working with and how.

I just want to add one thing on cyber in case we do not come back to it. I know that we talked a lot about cyber attacks in space, with satellites and on ground infrastructure, but there are also cyber attacks on companies. I have talked to colleagues running small companies and we have had a significant number of cyber attacks on my company and also on others, because space is seen as so critical. This is something we work with Cyber Essentials Plus on, and there is some government support, but that would also be a useful area for greater support for critical industries. Because of the way in which the attacks are happening and becoming so sophisticated, we have to have a constant monitoring of who we are talking to and what we are talking about. It is quite draining and takes a lot of effort away from what we should really be doing.

Q12 I am afraid we are nearing time and are going to cease to be quorate. In the final minute, with apologies to colleagues who will not be able to come in, can I ask you, when it comes to SMEs—given that your business background is that you started as a start-up or spin-out from a university or research programme—just in two points, what could the Government be doing and what can we encourage them to do to ensure that this great innovation culture that we have actually becomes commercialised in the UK?

More, smaller and faster contracts for small companies with a higher-risk appetite, and a lower barrier to entry; and more support, which is increasingly massively but needs to be faster, for defence and how small companies can access defence contracts.
I would echo that, but I would also say the continuity of those grants and that funding—no stopping and starting for reviews et cetera.

Using the Government to champion us overseas, through the DBIST and giving us the exploitation route out of the United Kingdom and championing what is best. Finally, the overheads are often what kills SMEs, and security is a big part of that, so having an infrastructure area where the likes of us can go and work from and, in essence, pay for access, where clearances are sponsored, and it is in a useful location not—
So a cyber secure and physically secure space?
Exactly that.

There were other points that we wanted to raise with you. Perhaps we can put them in writing and you can respond. Sorry that we have had to cut the time. We were planning to finish at 6 pm, but we are unable to run over because we are going to cease to be quorate and the committee has to be quorate. Thank you for your time and for the information you shared with us. That concludes our second panel and today’s session. Order, order.

sessions.w: Dr Julia Balm (Freeman Air and Space Institute (School of Security Studies, King’s College London)); Jessie Hamill-Stewart (National Composites Centre); Will Marshall (Planet)

segs.tx: Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy
O ral evidence: Space resilience , HC 572
Monday 19 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Matt Western (T he Chair) ; Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom ; Lord Boateng; Liam Byrne; Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi; Lord Godson; Lord Jack of Courance ; Baroness Kidron; Helen Maguire; Lord Sedwill; Lord Tunnicliffe; Baroness Tyler of Enfield; Lord Watts.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 - 8
Witnesses

Dr Julia Balm, Co-Director, Freeman Air and Space Institute , School of Security Studies, King’s College London; Jessie Hamill-Stewart, Program Manager, Space, Cyber Security and Space Domain Awareness, National Composites Centre; Will Marshall, Founder and CEO, Planet UK .
Examination of witnesses
Dr Julia Balm, Jessie Hamill-Stewart and Will Marshall .
Q1 Today we are holding our first session on our inquiry into space resilience. Can I welcome our witnesses today and ask you to introduce yourselves?
I am Dr Julia Balm. I am the co-director and a research associate at the Freeman Air and Space Institute at King’s College London, within the War Studies department.

Hi everyone, my name is Jessie Hamill- Stewart and I am a PhD researcher at the University of Bath and the University of Bristol, where I look at cyber security and space. For the past two years, I have been building the CySpace Connected Capability Network , which is a network that brings together cyber security and space professionals all across the UK.
Hi, I am Will and I am the co-founder and CEO of Planet, which is a satellite company.

Q2 Thank you very much. Will, I understand you have to leave at 5 pm, so we will try to keep our questions pithy and if you could also keep your answers relatively concise that would be helpful, so that we can get through as much as possible by then.

Perhaps I could just start with an overview about the threat picture. We have had several strategies in recent years. I am interested to hear your views on how you see the threat picture. Also, in the light of the recent space strategy that was published in early September, what is your take on its objectives and commitments in addressing those threats? Will, can I start with you?

Maybe I can start with a tiny bit of background first on what we do, so that you have some context. Planet launches and operates fleets of earth imaging satellites. We have launched about 700 satellites, second only to SpaceX in the number of satellites launched, and we manage these large, proliferated fleets, which do earth imaging. They have a range of uses, from sustainability—we help to track deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon every day, and help Scotland to monitor its environmental regulations—through to security, where we are the main source of data for Ukraine today, for example, enabling them to monitor threats coming from Russia, plan their drone flights and all sorts of things such as that. We have a team on the ground there. I recently came back from there. Other examples include NATO monitoring and finding hybrid Russian warfare activities in the Baltics.

Space data and satellites are of course critical to national security and their resilience is key, so obviously this panel is an important matter. The way we approach resilience, just to give a sense of how we tackle it, is anchored on three things. One is proliferated architectures. Prior to Planet, it used to be that you would have a few satellites, but we were the first to build a satellite constellation of over 100. We maintain over 200 in orbit, and they are resilient. At the beginning of the Ukraine war, the Viasat system got jammed very quickly, but Starlink was operable. Some of the individual earth imaging satellites got dazzled, but our system of hundreds of satellites was resilient and has continued to operate every time, every day, throughout the war.

Our second piece is working closely with national Governments on specific threats to our fleet. We work with US Cyber Command and get intelligence from it about what threats could be happening, especially state threats.

The third level is being able to rapidly reconstitute satellites. We have rapid launches. We were meant to have another launch today but it just got postponed due to weather in the Cape. Generally, we are launching about four or five times per year; typically, around 50 new satellites per year.

Iterating those capabilities, we can build about 40 satellites per week. It is the most prolific system, alongside SpaceX’s Starlink, in being able to build satellites very quickly, about 40 per week, such that we can reconstitute those satellites very quickly in the event of something more catastrophic.

That is how we tackle it. We also try to be good actors in the broader field. Some of my work at NASA was on orbital space debris and we were the first to do open standards of publishing satellite positions so that we could co-ordinate and ensure that there were no collisions between satellites by keeping the satellites really low so that they do not create long-term space debris.

Why am I saying all these things? Primarily, because when the UK faces questions of space resilience, it needs to move into these kinds of directions: proliferating fleets. One of the ways to do that is to do hybrid capabilities—a mix of tapping commercial systems and building sovereign systems. That can be done very quickly, as we have done with Ukraine. For example, Ukraine asked us to build and operate some satellites directly for its sovereign ownership, as well as tapping our data feeds, and we were able to put its first satellite into space two months after the contract. We just did something very similar for Sweden. So now you can get sovereignty—control of the satellites—and speed, whereas you used to have to choose one or the other. I believe the UK could tap these sorts of ways of tracking and having more resilient systems by leaning into proliferated architectures and that that is very affordable these days, as Ukraine has proved.
The numbers count.
Absolutely, the numbers count, yes.
The UK Space Strategy —do you have a brief response on that?

The biggest missing piece in that is: where is the urgency? There are all the right kinds of direction, but what is the timeline? A lot of countries are grappling with the question of sovereignty. What does sovereign mean? It means, or should mean, having the systems that you need when you need them. But at the minute, the UK is on a course to build systems that are very long. For example, the ISTARI programme is building systems that may take until 2035 to build. Systems that are fully national and sovereign but give their capabilities seven years too late are not sovereign at all; they are just stupid. Honestly, that is what is going to happen on the present course.
I want to move on to your colleagues on the panel but, just before that, you said that it took how many months to deliver for Sweden?
For Sweden, it was four months from a contract to a first sovereign satellite, which means it was owned and will be operated by Sweden.
Very interesting. Jessie?

That was very interesting. From my perspective, the focus is on the cyber security of space infrastructure. You are probably aware of the cyber attacks that impacted M&S and Jaguar Land Rover and the impact on the individual companies as well as the knock-on effects. There was a cost of £2 billion to the UK economy from the Jaguar Land Rover attack.

Cyber attacks are becoming more of a reality, and this is for infrastructure outside of space. We can see that they are affecting companies. M&S could not deliver online orders for a very long time. Why am I talking about this on a space resilience panel? It is because what you may not realise is that space infrastructure—a lot of what we have just heard about—is just as vulnerable to cyber attacks . You often think about space infrastructure on the ground and satellites up there in space. You might think about the user segment and launch as well. All these different parts of space systems have clear and very worrying vulnerabilities and it is becoming easier and easier for cyber attacks to be conducted against space systems. That is partly because they are becoming more accessible—the number of organisations that are able to develop satellite systems is growing enormously and has been for the last five to 15 years—but also because cyber attacks are becoming easier with tools such as AI, which I can say more on later.

Essentially, we are encountering a situation in which our space systems are becoming more vulnerable, there are more of them, they are becoming more open and more people are learning about space because they are doing things in space. That means that if they learn about the technical system, they can also learn about how to attack it and the vulnerabilities. We are getting to a situation in which we are seeing more and more cyber threats affect critical infrastructure and , in particular, space infrastructure. If we see more cyber attacks affect the space infrastructure on which we all rely, it could become very concerning.

One of the things that really worries me about cyber threats is that they exploit unknown vulnerabilities. You do not know where your adversary will target or where, specifically, they will come in. Where is the weak point within your organisation? Nobody really knows that, which is why it is such a tricky point to tackle. The mysterious nature of the beginning of cyber attacks and the way in which they could impact space systems is a worry.
Do you think the government space strategy addresses that?
I agree with the point about urgency. This is a much bigger problem than the space strategy depicts. There are some nice—
I understand that. But you do not see any evidence in the space strategy per se that makes you think, “They get it, across government”?

There are some aspects. In the space strategy, there is a recognition of the multidimensional threat to space systems and that cyber attacks do not exist by themselves as a threat to space but that space weather is a concern, and debris and all these different threats. There is recognition of that.

There is also a willingness to tackle the threat collectively. That is good. Space is vast and our dependence on space is vast; therefore all the organisations that are dependent on space should be included. When you are thinking about threats to space, I include the supply chain in that as well. That is good.

The thing that it is missing is championing what the UK is saying and doing specifically about the cyber security of space. I may be wrong here, but when I looked up “cyber” in the UK Space Strategy , I think that it came up six times—no more than ten times. That is quite worrying for me, from my cyber background, because I know that cyber security is one of the major threats against space systems, especially when it comes to the ground, which is extremely vulnerable. I can go more into that later.
I am just conscious of time, I am sorry. If you could move on very quickly, I want to bring in Julia as well.

Of course, sorry. My last line on this point about the national space strategy is that other countries are better articulating what they are doing about cyber security and space, and therefore demonstrating how seriously they take the issue of securing space.
Such as?

Which countries? If you look to France, it has a Space Cybersecurity Center . They have central infrastructure that fosters collaboration, which articulates very clearly that France is a country that has infrastructure dedicated to space cyber security. We have bits and pieces distributed all around different organisations in the UK, but they do not come together in one central infrastructure. CySpace plays a role in that, but that is a network, not a central government infrastructure. Another country is Germany, which very clearly states its guidance for securing space systems. I mean that in a very literal sense based on what is available online. If you look it up, it has pages and pages dedicated to space cyber security.
We could talk about this the rest of the afternoon, I am sure, but we will move on to Julia.

I will echo a lot of what has been said already. I will start with the broad threat landscape picture and then go into the NSS and how that tackles it. Generally, the greatest vulnerability we are facing at the moment is that our increased dependence on space systems is not necessarily matched with enough investment or urgency and that we do not necessarily have enough response options at this given time. The pinpoint for that is both in day-to-day services and when it comes to defence. I will unpack that later.

Statistically, 18% of the UK’s GDP depends on satellite services. We know that one lost day of space systems would cost £1.4 billion. The National Preparedness Commission estimated that space underpins approximately £450 billion of wider economic activity. We know that we depend heavily on space and we are only growing in that.

We have approximately 12,000 operational satellites in orbit. The estimate is that that will increase to approximately 60,000 by 2030. We are talking about proliferation both on a horizontal and vertical level. But when we are discussing vulnerability, we are looking at the loss of those space systems. As was mentioned earlier, how do we measure those cascading effects across not only the space sector but all the sectors that space impacts? A disruption to a satellite service can propagate and affect several sectors simultaneously. The key questions we are trying to poke at now are: are we designing space systems to withstand disruption for either a short period of time or a period of time that is incredibly relevant—say, when are under attack—or for a longer period of time ? Do we have enough contingencies to also allow for continued access to that space service, whether provided by ourselves or by our allies? That is the threat picture that I would paint.

Moving on to the space strategy and how we have addressed that, I would begin by saying that there is a real question of accountability. When we look at space and how a new domain sits across multiple departments, it is really hard to place that responsibility and who is accountable for, say, when a service goes down or is lost. Obviously, we have DBIST , the MoD and even the National Armaments Director Group all trying to work together on the defence elements, but then we are talking about the cascading effects across other departments that are not necessarily waving a space flag or even a defence protect-and-defend flag or mission. That dispersed responsibility can be a strength, but in some ways it is something we have to focus on for cohesivity. In the national space strategy, there is that “one government” approach that is being pitched. Following through and seeing that being implemented would be great, but it is incredibly difficult for a domain such as space, which has the challenges of classification issues, to be able to share that information in a timely manner—we say at “the speed of relevance”—within the UK, but also to our allies, in order to be effective at reconstituting.

Q3 Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi: Let us move on to hostile activity in space. Mr Marshall, if I can start off with your good self, to what extent are adversaries able and willing to disrupt space-based infrastructure that the UK is heavily reliant on? In answering the question, could you point to some evidence of what we have seen to date?

Obviously, Ukraine again serves as the best example, which is where very few bespoke satellite systems were taken out or jammed by the Russians. I think that the same would happen for UK capabilities in a situation such as that. In this increasingly hybrid world in which we are living with Russia—hybrid does not do it justice—Russia will take action on systems if they think that they are supporting Ukraine. At Planet, the whole company and me personally are on Russia’s bad actors list and we are constantly trying to ensure that we are resilient against its attacks. The UK cannot assume that it is going to be. That is why I emphasised the proliferative nature of this.

The OneWeb system is a good example of how you get a proliferated system, but we do not have that in the ISR space. In fact, in the ISR domain the UK mainly relies on the US, which is not always there, but the commercial systems can be ready to provide that very quickly. The most important aspect is leaning into these next-generation capabilities, which are by their very nature more resilient and which the UK has not really leant into as yet .

Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi: I fully hear the point that you have made just now, and previously on sovereign capabilities. We have seen the devastating impact that Starlink being slowed down and restricted for Ukraine has had.
If I can move on to your good self, Ms Hamill-Stewart, what do you think of space-based infrastructure and the threat of disruption to that?

We are already seeing attacks on military ground infrastructure. You will be aware of the RAF Fairford incident and other intrusions that we are seeing into ground defence infrastructure in the UK. Granted it is not space yet, but it might be space next.

The Ukraine example that my colleague mentioned is a really good one. It makes me think about the cyber attack against Viasat, which took place just before Russia invaded Ukraine back in 2022. They specifically targeted Viasat’s KA-SAT network to disrupt the communications of the Ukrainian military, because they knew that that is what the Ukrainian military were using to communicate. It put Ukraine on the back foot just before Russia invaded.
Pre-emptively .

Yes, pre-emptively, and with a political motivation. What is even more worrying about that case is that it ended up having wide implications as well. If you are not already aware of them, it ended up impacting thousands of European satellite internet broadband users as well, including critical infrastructure.

Cyber attacks such as that demonstrate that not only is space infrastructure vulnerable but, as the UK becomes more and more involved in these military conflicts, we are already seeing evidence of the UK’s defence and military being targeted in this way—physical access as well as cyber attacks . Why do we worry about physical access when it comes to space? We worry because the ground infrastructure is that central controlling and monitoring aspect of the entire constellation and the other dependent services. The importance of the ground infrastructure of space systems cannot be underestimated. It also happens to be the most physically accessible. If you know where it is, you know where to find it and how to potentially try to target it.

Other things the UK is doing at the moment potentially demonstrate vulnerabilities that could be exploited. One of those that is very well known is the disruption of NATS. If you were trying to get a flight in the last few weeks, you will have been affected because of the air traffic control architecture being disrupted by a tiny—minute—error, which resulted in many flights being disrupted. Somebody told me that Heathrow Airport was chock-a-block with passengers. This is disruption, and cyber attacks on space are especially concerning because when it comes to space, as was mentioned, it has all those dependent industries that could be affected. Airports could also be affected by disruption to space because aeroplanes need GPS to take off and land accurately. But it is most worrying because cyber attacks , especially to space, can demonstrate an approach by a nation state—an adversarial nation state—to try to undermine trust in things working well.

Space is extremely important. We cannot afford for it to be disrupted just to demonstrate what people can do. One of the reasons for that is all the dependent sectors. The finance sector needs the timing that is provided by space services, for example. We are at a critical point where we are extremely dependent on space but are also demonstrating these key vulnerabilities in military architecture, which could then be transferrable to the space domain, which worries me quite a lot.
Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi: Dr Balm, gi ven what we have just heard, what sort of hostile threats in space should we be most concerned about, both sub-threshold and in the event of conflict?

It is incredibly important to look at the effects of low-cost agitation, such as spoofing and jamming, and how that can have an outsized effect in the space domain. Certain actors can employ agitation tactics more easily than others. I point to the fact that there are nuclear weapon states and non-nuclear weapon states in space and our space infrastructure is inherently linked to our nuclear infrastructure as well, with C2. The ability to escalate and de-escalate is quite distinct.

I point also to a couple of threats that I am currently watching from the last week or so. On 15 October, Russia’s satellite Kosmos 2612 adjusted its orbital inclination to follow an ICEYE satellite, ICEYE-X36, at approximately 26 metres away from it, which if you know the space domain is incredibly close. This manoeuvring into or across low earth orbit into a coplanar orbit is something that we do not usually see because it is extremely expensive to use fuel on such a manoeuvre.
