But this has happened recently and it could be a signal of som e intention from Russia, or it could amount to something related to a kinetic attack or even an electronic attack.

On Sunday, just yesterday, there was an attempted arson of a SpaceX Starlink base in Lithuania, which mimicked what we saw a couple of weeks ago in Bulgaria and Poland. We talked about space-based infrastructure being under attack, but it is really important to look at the links alongside ground-based segments, where it might be that those low-cost agitation tactics of burning a building that contains those receivers are a way to gain an outsized impact.
Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi: Mr Marshall, if I can come to you, what do you think we should be most concerned about in terms of hostile threats in space?

Again, you would have to look at all the systems that the UK relies on and which are most vulnerable to this. At present, the UK is completely reliant on the US for a lot of its intelligence services. The US just turned some of those systems off for Ukraine. It has done that multiple times. The reliance on just that partnership is extreme in the intelligence domain, which is one of the key things that SpaceX is doing, and which is why 80% of Ukraine’s satellite imagery comes from Planet. We have been there every single day for them. The way in which it is different to the Starlink situation is that we work directly with Ukraine. Our contract is with the Ukraine Government, not with the US Government as is the case with Starlink. You have to choose your partners wisely, have systems that are proliferated and have ways of working with multiple actors so that you are resilient. That is possible.

Most of all, you have to invest in systems that are sovereign. I cannot identify the specific ones that are most vulnerable right this second. We could go and do some research and come back to you on what I think are the most vulnerable systems but, generally, the UK has got almost no proliferated architectures that it could leverage today, even though they are readily available from companies that could provide that.

Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi: That would be very interesting. Please do send that information through. Lastly, may I come back to you, Ms Hamill-Stewart, on how much risk comes from potential cyber attacks aimed at satellite infrastructure?

A lot. You can look at the potential implications. There have been a number of attacks, which I included in a research paper I wrote quite a few years ago, and there were attacks that were intercepted where attackers were making their way through ground infrastructure to the important admin management section.

There are many ways in which cyber risks can escalate. If you are worried about satellites in particular, let us take it out of the defence context, and think about a university spin-off or individual organisation that maybe has a CubeSat. There are just a few students. It is a small company. It does not have loads of governance to manage its cyber security. It gets intercepted and an attacker somehow manages to gain control of its satellite. That is something that you really want to worry about, because then they could, in a really worst-case scenario, crash it or collide it with another satellite. Then there are the implications of debris, as Will knows very well.

The cyber risks might sound like they are virtual and a bit science fiction, but there are two points on that. First, they can be cyber physical, and cyber physical threats have been a well-known topic area for many decades. Stuxnet, used in an attack on a nuclear plant many years ago, is one example. But there are also physical implications, such as gradually changing the controls or coming in and understanding how the infrastructure works, which gives you the information to then come back and conduct a stronger attack later.

At the moment , attackers, especially nation state-level attackers, probably have the capabilities to do more disruption than they are doing right now. Therefore, it is something to worry about, because they probably have those capabilities but are just not doing it yet. They have not decided to do it yet.

The other thing I would mention here is that hundreds of cyber attacks on space infrastructure are being reported through platforms such as the CSIS, about which I can provide more information at a later time . Ther e are threats such as ransomware. All these cyber attacks that we are seeing on terrestrial infrastructure—physical attacks on ground stations, for example—are also impacting space. This worries us, because we need it.
Just in the waning seconds of your presence, Mr Marshall—
I have a few more minutes, so do not worry too much.

Q4 M uch like the peace talks, you can stop the clocks so we can beat the deadline. You have flagged up the dangers of Ukraine, the Baltics and so on—Russia being the obvious thing—but could you, and indeed your colleagues, just reflect a little more on who the other threats are, and from where? Who are the dark horses? I have just been in Japan and heard about the impact on it from China and so on. I would just like you to reflect in a little more detail on your latest assessment of those dangers.

I would jump first to China, but also the increasing collaboration with Iran and other countries that might have lower-risk thresholds to take action against systems. At least China has a lot to depend on in space, whereas Iran has very little, so maybe they could use one another and work together in partnership in a way that is pretty destructive .

The West is generally more dependent on its space assets than other countries. Russia, pushed into a corner, may do extreme things such as have been reported about the nuclear weapon capabilities it has. Something such as that going off in space would be extraordinarily destructive for the entire space sector and all the economic and security systems that are dependent on that.

But, actually, I would take this question rather in the direction that Jessie was talking about with cyber. The threats that we are going to see come down the line are going to be primarily AI-enabled cyber threats that exploit vulnerabilities we did not even know were there, just like we are seeing on conventional systems. We are already seeing AI hack out of our containment systems during testing. This is a threat to space and everything else. Just give me a couple of seconds to tell you that the systems that are hacking out, such as Hugging Face, are now co-ordinating between hundreds of agents, and one of the other things they are doing is specialising. Those agents are specialising so that they can pass things off. Co-ordination and specialisation is exactly what distinguished humans from the rest of the animal kingdom and led to our dominance over them. We are at a point where, in the last two years, we sit in Silicon Valley, in the middle of the AI triangle between Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and we feel in the middle of that—and space has a role to play, by the way, because we can provide satellite data that will up-level AI systems to have physical-world understanding. That can be very helpful for security—but where are we going next?

In the last two years, we have seen 1,000x improvement in the capabilities of LLMs—large language models—that have gone from just being able to roughly say a few sentences to being able, literally a couple of weeks ago, to do Fields Medal-level mathematics overnight. We are going to get another 1,000x in the next two years. We have no idea how to control that, and there are narrow risks to do with cyber threats that we are seeing today—the ability of AI systems to build bioweapons—and we have got to stop them. But we have actually got a more generic control risk that people are just not understanding in the political debate. Everything about AI is about, “Are we going to lose jobs? Are there threats to our cyber security?”, and things like that, but we are facing a much bigger moment. We are facing an existential moment of whether or not we are going to give over control. Alan Turing said that we will inevitably lose control, especially when they start co-ordinating, which is exactly the moment we are at. That was in 1952.

I just say this because space, like every other domain, is going to be attacked by these systems. I would expect that we will see more Hugging Faces that make Hugging Face look like a walk in the park. They could attack our space infrastructure, but they could attack any infrastructure if we do not get a handle on managing AI risk. This Parliament and this country can do stuff about that. The UK’s AI Security Institute can be part of a verification system. We, with our satellite data, can be tracking all of those data centres, to know where to put those on-ground inspections. It is possible to verify AI treaties.

We need clear guardrails, and we need to then actually slow down the pace of development if we are going to be wise with this technology. At the present clip, there is no way we are going to be wise, and we will see open-source technologies doing hacks soon that will shock the world, based on Chinese systems. Those could attack space infrastructure; they could attack any infrastructure. That should be priorities Nos. 1, 2 and 3 for this Parliament until we get it fixed. At the minute there is some sense that we cannot slow down, but it is absolutely necessary to do that. It is the only way to be wise, and the Overton window is changing on that very rapidly. It would have been inconceivable to think about any sort of controls on AI just six months ago in the United States, but that has changed very rapidly. You wait. A few weeks or months from now, we are going to see events that will change the Overton window again, such that it becomes possible to really talk about proper controls on AI.

I agree with Jessie that that is the primary vector you need to be thinking about. Forget nation states; Russia and China are going to be small fry compared with cyber threats because of AI capabilities far more powerful than anything we have dealt with before. That is the trumping consideration for this and every other committee in this House.
Thank you for that. Lord Boateng wanted to come in.
Lord Jack of Courance : On that bombshell.
On that bombshell. Sorry.
Yes. I will just return you to the more mundane and prosaic—
I suppose we can.

Q5 It is about an area on which your company is well placed to assist us with. You are headquartered in the United States, you have satellite manufacturing operations in Germany, and you have an office here in London. In the light of that, what is your take on the risks that we should be concerned about to supply chains for the assembly and deployment of satellites? While the sovereign state is of significance, do you see potential for closer co-operation between the UK and the EU in this area? Can we continue to rely on the United States in the way we do and to the extent we have in the past, given where the US is on so many issues at the moment ? You referred yourself to the experience you have had in Ukraine. Can you help us with that?

First, the UK should definitely be working in close collaboration with the EU, its most natural partner on security matters, given the geography. Space is definitely part of that. The UK should really lean into those systems that it could share.
In preference to the US.

It should do both ways. The US and Europe have a huge amount of alignment, especially against emerging threats between Russia, China, Iran and North Korea. We should actually work more with the US. We have already rid our supply chains of any components that are from China or anything like that, but our components come from all over Europe and all over the US. We assemble the satellites both in California and in Germany. Those systems are dependent on supply chains, but those are not the vulnerabilities. The vulnerabilities are: how does the system work and is it vulnerable in space? Are those systems there when you need them? Yes, in that context, the UK should be strong partners with other countries. Again, let us distinguish between the work with other countries. Ukraine lost Starlink because it was getting it via the United States Government. It did not lose Planet because we are working directly with Ukraine. The UK can take a lesson from that.
Where do you see the threats to that?
To our operations?
Yes.
Again, I refer back to the cyber threat—that is the biggest one that we face today, because those things are going to emerge so fast.

But you are headquartered in the US. Suppose the US took a view that they did not actually much like what you were doing. You are subject to regulation there. Could they not make life extremely difficult for you, as they have done through the banking sector and in a number of other ways?

It is a very good question. That is why we have started building up more capacities here in Europe, so that we can provide capabilities to European countries that are independent. We do that with manufacturing; we have ground stations here in the UK and in other countries in Europe; and we have mission control systems here in Europe. What we just did with Sweden, for example, was to build and launch the satellite and then transition it to their control. This is not subject to the US at all. By the way, most of our satellites are not subject to shutter control because they are just lower resolution than the cap. But the point is that you can have your own sovereign systems that are not under the jurisdiction. They are national systems under national jurisdiction.
Does our space strategy sufficiently recognise that?
It moves in that direction, but slowly.
In other words, it does not.

No, it does not, with the necessary urgency. Again, this can happen really fast . The way the US changed the space sector was that NASA started putting 20% of the budget towards new players, 20% of the launch budget—
Why have you gone to Germany? You have gone to Germany to manufacture. Is that because Germany has done a similar thing?

We have been in Germany for 10 years, after we acquired a small company there called RapidEye , and we have our mission control systems there, so we had a technical base to build on. Also, I hate to say it, but they are in the EU and we want to go after EU business; if you are outside the EU, you have a much smaller probability of that. It is still in trade discussions. We obviously are going to put our biggest eggs in the biggest baskets, but we wanted to have an independent capacity to build, launch and operate our satellites. It is not to spite the US that we are continuing to do that. We actually just doubled our manufacturing capacities in the United States as well. There is so much demand from so many countries to have sovereign eyes. When you realise that the US may be backing out and saying, “Hey, you take more ownership”, the first thing you want is more and better eyes on what is going on so you can understand your threat environment, which primarily Europe has relied on the US for, and to be able to more accurately use the systems that you have. Satellites have given Ukraine an information advantage, against a conventional disadvantage. We can provide that very quickly to the UK and the rest of Europe.

Dr Balm, I wonder if you can help us with this. This is a defence-related question where you have done so much interesting work. How can we better protect ourselves in the UK in our ground-based infrastructure and assets, both sub-threshold and in possible times of war?

That is a great question. To tack on to exactly what Will was saying, I think it is important to look at the long pedigree of data-sharing agreements between the UK and the US that have historically existed and continue to exist. The post-Brexit strategy is for the UK to retain its strategic autonomy, but also those transatlantic and European partnerships and how they plug in. My answer to that would actually be that what is really key is diversity as our resilience strategy—that we make sure that we are able to reconstitute our assets, because we have got so many alliance structures bilaterally and multilaterally. There is the brilliant Kensington T reaty between the UK and Germany, and hopefully an MoU is coming out in early 2027 with that. We have got these strong partnerships that allow us to reconstitute our assets relatively quickly.

I guess a short answer on that is that we really have to embed ourselves within these allied structures. We have NATO; there is the “NATO first” posture that was announced with the strategic defence review. But we must make sure that we are at the table when something like the EU Space Act is written, and also for the next EU developments, when the EU Commission is tasking defence developments in Europe. We should be at the table for those conversations to make sure that we are involved in those security architectures.

If I can press you on your knowledge of our ground-based infrastructure—where we launch things from, where we hold important technology—to what extent, in your view, is that safe, given what we have seen in recent times: that non-state actors or people operating on behalf of states can create enormous damage in ways that, quite frankly, we did not anticipate?

On the loss of access to our spaceports, the one that we are investing in with the national space strategy is Sax aV ord , which would allow us to reach polar orbits. One of the key risks is that we are no longer really able to reach equatorial orbits with a high-density payload. A really heavy payload would have to be launched through key allies like the US, where Falcon 9 provided us the ability to launch. There is Taiki. We were also planning on Juno and Oberon being launched with Falcon 9, but they are no longer accepting delivery slots post 2028. Losing our ability to access key slots is important. Now, we will be able to access with Sax aV ord a certain amount of space infrastructure, but it will not fully reconstitute. The other option is Ariane 6, but that cost is not similar to Falcon. It is actually far more expensive. It is not a reusable rocket—
And it does not have the capacity.
No, there really is no alternative at the moment .

Q6 I am now going to move on to the UK’s favourite topic: weather—but space weather. The N ational R isk R egister has said that the risk of severe space weather is between 5% and 25%, and that there would be a significant impact. I wondered if you agreed with that assessment and if you could perhaps describe to us what that impact would look like.

There is some context I can provide. The sun is active for periods of 11 years at a time, and we are currently situated right in the middle of that 11-year cycle. That will be ending by the end of the decade. Because it is so active, it means it is really unpredictable , so the timeline that we get for knowing that there is going to be a geomagnetic storm or radio interference can be from some data released weeks, hours or even 30 minutes before. When it comes to radio frequency interference, we do not really know the impact until it happens.

The event that you are citing would be similar to the Carrington event, which was in 1859 and was the most intense geomagnetic storm on record. We have not faced anything similar to that. Obviously, we did not have a satellite in orbit in 1859, so the effects would be really serious today. The problem now, as I mentioned, is that we are in this active solar flare cycle, and we struggle to be able to attribute whether there is a natural threat or a manmade threat. Say, for example, there is interference in a satellite which impacts atmosphere and atmospheric drag. Can we attribute that necessarily to something that was a hostile activity with hostile intent, or was that something natural? We are seeing that up until the end of 2030.

I guess what I wanted to understand a little bit further is the difference between what might happen from space weather and something hostile. You said there could be some similarities. Could you perhaps explain what some of the differences might be as well, and just expand on that slightly?

I can just give something brief and then I will pass it on. Essentially, it allows for a degree of ambiguity , actually, because it is a similar thing to what happened with Starlink, which was already mentioned by Will, when the loss of service happened in Ukraine. There is a degree of plausible deniability to say, “Oh, well, this is something that we could not predict and had no control over. It was actually a natural impact”. It is hard to verify that. It is like those locks that you put on your baggage when you go to travel, and it dings with a little pop-up when the TSA has opened the lock. We do not have anything on a satellite currently that announces that you have been intentionally jammed or directly attacked, because it is impossible really to dictate whether or not that was a natural impact. I do not know if anybody else wants to speak.

I would only say that these things are far from academic. During this solar maximum, part of the challenge was that the academic literature in this area did not predict how big it was going to be. It ended up being more than twice as active as the normal 11-year period. They have this 11 - year period of activities, but this one went up almost twice as much and no one really predicted that. People were operating their satellites too low because it excites the upper atmosphere and increases drag. I have colleagues that lost two-thirds of their satellites. Two satellite companies lost two-thirds of their satellites in the first year because their propulsion system was not able to keep them above it fast enough, so they got pulled down. It is great that satellites are operating really low because it means they are naturally clearing from a space debris standpoint. It also increases resolution for a given telescope or what have you. A lot of earth imaging systems operate quite low. If you do not predict it, you can really lose fleets of satellites very quickly. None of that was intentional—except if you ascribe free will to the sun. It had a big effect.
Further to that point, what can your company do, or what can the UK do, to mitigate against the risks to satellites from adverse space weather?

The first thing is doing slightly better at the modelling. Since then, we have actually updated some models that do perhaps predict these higher events. The second thing is radiation hardening. For the nuclear weapons potential threat, we really should be leaning at eventually having radiation hardening of commercial systems. Ukraine is fully dependent on very commercial systems. It is not just that they are dependent on space; it is mainly that they are dependent on commercial space. As I said, we are 80% of the imagery being provided for them, and there is something similar with Starlink on the comms side. Those systems are not radiation hardened like the GPS systems against a potential nuclear blast. It is actually not that hard —i t is an R&D project — but it is hard to expect the companies to just do that on their own for a hypothetical event that is a geopolitical thing . The country should come in and say, “We will help you with your R&D and share some knowhow on how to do that, so you can integrate that into your systems so that they are less vulnerable at a system level to those radiation events”. That would help both the natural events and things like a nuke explosion in space.
With that, I had better go. Thank you so much. I will leave a few cards here if anyone needs to contact me.
Thank you.

I will just mention something on the point there regarding whether it is a space weather event or whether it is a cyber event . F rom the cyber perspective it is much less humiliating to say , “W e do not know the source of this problem ”. As has been alluded to, the implications of a cyber event can look very similar to space weather. From a cyber perspective, you will often see in the news that companies have encountered some kind of issue, but you will not as often s ee , “We know that it was a cyber attack . This vulnerability was exploited”. Actually , access to that information about cyber attacks that happen is in itself a major issue.

Q7 Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom : Can I come back to the 5% to 25% chance of a solar flare? The Carrington event, which you mentioned, Dr Balm, was originally classified as a one-in-100-year event, until someone in government realised that it had happened more than 100 years ago —s o they reclassified it as a one -in-200-year event. Does the same sort of magical thinking apply to the 5% to 25% chance of there being serious damage from adverse space weather in the risk register? What is that figure based on? It is a wide range in itself, but is it accurate?

I just briefly caution against adding probability to catastrophe. W e need to be quite hesitant about putting percentages behind things like the Carrington event and the Kessler syndrome—quantifying the red line in which we are no longer able to operate in space. Once you have put a number on that, we can walk ourselves close to it. Or once you have quantified or put a statistic next to the Carrington event, then we can relax ourselves and relax our defences against it. I caution against that .

It is very similar actually to deterrence. Y ou do not recognise the structure of deterrence until t here is a failure. It is very similar in the sense that we have to experience failures, readjust ourselves, and make sure that we have a degree of risk baked into our portfolios to be able to adapt to them.

I would build on that and say that I agree. In trying to put a figure on it and to say when it will happen , any meteorologist will tell you that you cannot predict when a major space weather event will happen. It is hard to predict. Whether it is a space weather event or a cyber attack , whether it has come through the supply chain or it was an error, the impact will be the same because of our dependence on space. Resilience comes from having plans in place and expecting these major catastrophes to happen. What are we going to do when that constellation is knocked out? What are we going to do when we lose GPS or an equivalent or Skynet? Having those resilience plans is really important . You have to expect these attacks to happen.

What are we going to do when it comes to cyber attacks ? Are we going to wait for a major cyber attack to happen against Skynet? It would be better to prepare for it and have plans in place that include mapping out those dependent sectors and which sector —manufacturing sectors and wider—will struggle if we see a disruption to space. In the Jaguar Land Rover attack, there was manufacturing that was stopped. People did not have work because they could not keep the processes going because of the cyber attack . Those knock-on effects on the economy are really significant .

One of the ways in which you can be resilient is by recognising that there are lots of capabilities in the UK, in academia especially, which does not get mentioned enough in the context of cyber in the U K Space Strategy. There are a lot of capabilities in the UK, in cyber and in space, which could be leveraged and applied to the defence domain or could be pivoted into space and applied to helping to secure space and also help with the radiation hardening and other aspects that we have just heard about. But there needs to be more support directly from the Government for individual companies to gain things such as security clearance and understand what space even is. This could help to grow the space cyber and space security ecosystem in the UK. That is well needed.
Perhaps you could write to us as a committee to cover the point you just raised and elaborate on that point about how we can use academia more.

Q8 I just have a really quick question, because you have answered most of what we were going to cover in this section. We have heard from you about distributed approaches to satellites and all the changes we ought to make, potentially in the future, on cyber space and all the rest of it. But, just briefly, how vulnerable is the existing estate, if you like, of satellites? Can they be retrofitted to have any of the resilience capabilities you have been describing?

I am glad that you have mentioned that, because one of the elephants in the room is the fact that when you talk about securing space, especially from the cyber perspective, and you talk about AI and the mechanisms being added to satellites today and hardening them more for weather events, this completely disregards all of the thousands of satellites that are already up there in orbit—travelling sometimes at thousands of miles per hour—that you would have to be very clever to gain physical access to and to retrofit any kind of measures on to. One of the big vulnerabilities of space, and satellites in particular, is that you cannot walk around a satellite in the same way as you would a water treatment centre. You cannot check for blinking lights and you definitely cannot add lots of things on to them. Even with the satellites that are being developed and deployed now there are limits. They cannot be extremely heavy. That is why there are discussions about, for example, orbital data centres and how they would be deployed, because currently there is still a limit on the compute that can exist on satellites in space.

There are many vulnerable satellites already, and the threats and risks we are discussing in this room today will no doubt change in another 10 or 15 years. It could be that AI evolves in this major way, which I agree with Will on, or it could be another threat that emerges. Threats always emerge.

For satellites that are being deployed or developed now, there are more abilities to upload software and do more with them but, for the satellites that are already up there in orbit, you just have to try to detect. It goes back to the point about resilience—what are you going to do when they are disrupted?— rather than trying to rely on the measures that you adopted to ensure you had done everything you could to stop them from being intercepted. At the end of the day, we cannot stop a space weather event from affecting them, so having the resilience in place and knowing how society would continue without critical space systems is a really important aspect of this conversation.

Might I just quickly add, and this goes back to the first question about looking at the space strategy? One of the four key technology areas that was identified there was in-orbit assembly and manufacturing. We are some years away from manufacturing as a component, but one large component of ISAM is rendezvous and proximity operations—RPO—which allows us not to necessarily walk around satellites but be able to adjust and update them. There is development of gas stations in orbit, but manufacturing moving into orbit is a natural development and it was a good step in the right direction to see that recognised in the space strategy.

I can see that it should be possible from now on, noting the physical limitations, to be able to put satellites up that cover all our requirements and have the ability to have software et cetera updated and are therefore designed to be more resilient. Recognising the limits on that, how big a task would it be to either retrofit, update or replace the functions that we already rely upon for satellites that we have been putting up there for decades? It seems to me that we can put up Gucci new ones that work very well and are more resilient. But what about the old ones? How big a task would it be to replace them or retrofit them? Is it even conceivable?

As has been mentioned, we are not there yet with this technology. Think about the scale of satellites, then think about how many satellites there are, and then you have to position them and get to each one. It is not like going up to a car parked in a car park; it is like going around the UK and trying to find your car. Where each satellite is positioned, randomly—
To cut to the chase, it is inconceivable?
The academic mind would say that to retrospectively fit measures on to all the satellites is not entirely inconceivable but extremely challenging.

And therefore presumably extremely costly. What I am trying to get to is : we can talk about what we should do in the future, but we have an existing estate that we have to consider on which we are completely dependent. Your earlier points about war-gaming, resilience and what happens when they are knocked out were really well made, because if we cannot do anything about them, that dependence will continue for the foreseeable future. Is that correct?
Absolutely.

On costs, it was announced that £7.8 billion was attached to the space strategy, but much of that was already pre-committed funds packaged within it. That is a relatively modest budget. If we compare ourselves to where Germany is, it announced €35 billion to be spent by that 2030 deadline. The lion’s share of investment in the UK will be spent between 2030 and 2035. To some degree, there is an assumption that we will have this large booming industry that will be able to deliver between 2030 and 2035 and will be able to be kept up until 2030, when that delivery is made.

A great deal is going to happen between 2030 and 2035, it would seem, across almost everything for which this committee has oversight responsibility. Clearly, it is going to be a golden period. Can I just quickly ask, with the machinery of government changes, mergers and all that, how well are we set up, institutionally, to deliver this?

It is difficult. There has been a move with the “one government” approach, but I struggle to identify the right person to go to either within the Government or even MoD Main Building. The seats do not remain hot for long, to put it kindly. It is something that has been changing around quite a bit.

There has been a lot of positive direction when we look at the National Armaments Director Group and how Rupert Pearce has a space background, coming from Inmarsat. There have been movements in the right direction, but being able to see them pay off will take a slightly longer time. I am optimistic about the “one government” approach and its cohesivity, but I would cite that the UK Space Agency moved back into the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology in April, then got moved into DBIST shortly after, and now there is a co-director model. That has all happened within a relatively small timeframe in which there have been reshuffles of key people and positions within that organisation itself—and that is just the UK Space Agency.

There are positive steps in the right direction when we talk about cohesivity, but it is an incredibly difficult task to actually deliver on. Much of the space sector in the UK is either backed by mavericks or it is personality-based, where somebody really cares about a specific type of development in the domain and carries it forward.
That is really helpful .

I would echo that. One of the exercises that CySpace did last year was that we went around and did a capability-mapping exercise looking at different capabilities all around the UK, from down in Cheltenham all the way up to Scotland and Northern Ireland. In each of those regions we looked at what their capabilities are and what we have in order to deliver space, space security and space cyber in that specific region. One of the problems that kept on coming up again and again was the fragmentation and lack of clear guidance. I am not necessarily asking you to create a set of requirements specific to space but just to provide a cohesive clear idea of what space security is and what is needed to ensure it, and also guidance for how companies can participate in the space system. In order to deliver this, you need more manpower, as it were, or womanpower, but you also need it not just within government; you need to have that collaboration.

If I look at cyber security in space and the current collaboration, it is not extensive. From what I see across government and industry, the information flow is not extensive. Therefore, mechanisms are needed that allow industry to support this.

There are capabilities and there are certain barriers that get in the way of, for example, smaller companies engaging and supporting such strategies. One of those is security clearances and adhering to the different security standards in defence. If you lower those barriers and make it easier for companies to work with the Government to help to deliver on the strategy and these suggestions we are making, then you will realise that we have significantly more capacity than you might think, rather than relying solely on the brilliant UK Space Agency team alone. It needs to be a collaborative effort, and that comes with more funding, probably, to incentivise people to work together, but also more infrastructure. I am sure we will hear more of that in a second in relation to the trade bodies. We have capacity, but there needs to be more collaboration as well.
That is great. Thank you very much.

I just want to revisit the previous point about the systems that are out there and, as Lord Sedwill said, may have been up there for decades. We have legacy systems and computing software that runs half of all government departments. These are satellites, or networks of satellites, that are more vulnerable to attack. Has an audit been done by the Government to establish what that legacy estate looks like and what needs to be done to update or upgrade it to make it more secure? Does either of you have a feel for that?

I do not have that, but I would be happy to try to find it. This demonstrates one of the barriers of collaborating with and gaining data from the Government. I would need to be cleared to a certain level even to have that conversation.
It is like doing an audit of what is out there and understanding where the dependencies are and so on.
I am happy to include that when I write back about the academia. I will do as much as I can to understand whether an audit has taken place.
Thank you in advance for that. Thank you both, and thanks to Will in his absence for his participation as well. We really appreciate it. It has been an excellent session and very informative.

sessions.iT: Border security and irregular migration: The work of the Border Security Command
sessions.w: Duncan Capps CBE (Home Office); Rob Jones (National Crime Agency)

segs.tx: Home Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Border security and irregular migration: The work of the Border Security Command , HC 720
Wednesday 21 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 21 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Dame Karen Bradley (Chair); Mr Paul Kohler; Ben Maguire; Robbie Moore; Margaret Mullane; Dr Peter Prinsley.
Questions 1- 68
Witnesses
I : Duncan Capps CBE , Interim Border Security Commander, Home Office and Rob Jones, Director General (Operations), National Crime Agency .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Duncan Capps and Rob Jones.
I welcome our witnesses to our Home Affairs Committee one-off sitting on border security and irregular migration. We are grateful to have our two witnesses. Will you introduce yourselves?
I am Duncan Capps. I am the border security commander in the Home Office.
I am Rob Jones, director-general of operations in the National Crime Agency.

Thank you. W e are really pleased you could come. This is a topic of great interest to the public. There have been some very high-profile stories over the summer, which we are keen to explore. We are also keen to find out what has been done and to understand the general situation. We will kick off questions with Ben Maguire.

Q1 We all welcome the fall in the small boat numbers in recent months. As a Committee, we have been looking at that closely. What evidence is there that it has been driven by enforcement activity or policy changes, rather than by external factors beyond our control?

It is worth stating where we are in terms of those numbers. Year on year, compared with this point last year: last year we had just under 37,000 arrivals last year, and this year to date we have had under 21,000, so 16,000 fewer individual migrants have arrived. In terms of boats that have arrived, we have had 305, which compares with 600 boats that had arrived at this point last year. In terms of migrants, that is a 43% reduction, while in terms of boats, it is a 49.8% reduction, or almost 50%. That means that with migrant arrivals, we are at the lowest point that we have had since 2020. I anticipate that by the end of the year—with a little touching of wood—we will come in below 2019, so we will have the lowest numbers really since the big phenomenon of small boats began.

To your question, the Border Security Command has now been in existence for two years, and the Government’s intent was to bring together all the various systems and to look across the whole of Government, particularly with international partners, to address what I know you all understand is a very complicated and complex problem. The idea was to try to put in priorities for where the Government were, to bring in the resources and to bring law enforcement, Departments and other Government agencies into that fight and really cohere the work with international partners.

We break down what we do broadly into three areas. First, those things that attract migrants to the UK—you will be aware of some of the initiatives that have been placed, that the Home Secretary has done, to try to make things less attractive to people who would seek to come here illegally. That includes our organised immigration crime taskforce, Operation Lockstream, under Deputy Chief Constable Wendy Gunney. That has had some great effect on illegal working and some of the pull factors.

The upstream piece is where we work with international partners. That is very much about how we deal with stability in those countries from where people seek to come here, working with those Governments and those along the routes to try to stop migrants making the journeys in the first place. We are very much trying to interdict the supply chains, where the boats, the equipment and the facilitation take place.

We then get into the work that happens in the near borders, principally with France, but also with Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. In that regard, what we are trying to do is obviously to stop the migrants coming across, really digging into the facilitators, the illegal criminal gangs and the small boats equipment.

I will let Rob talk about some of the detail, but I offer that we have had huge success now in terms of working with partners to reduce the flow of migrants into Europe in the first place. We have had great success in terms of reducing the supply of equipment and boats, and particularly with our work with France and near-border partners, of being able to do that last line of defence on the beaches. The French have had a 60% success rate in stopping boat events this year. Put those combinations of factors together and that is why we have seen, month on month this year, a pretty steady and progressive erosion of migrants’ ability to come across.

Q2 Is that something new that we have been doing though? As a Committee, we have been hearing about lots of those measures for the past two and a half years. Why has that suddenly led to a change in numbers now?

I have been involved in this since December 2022, when I started setting up the small boats operational command , and I think that this is now the coming together and bedding-in of all those measures, with some of those upstream relationships now really starting to bear fruit. The resourcing, training and expertise of the people who have been involved in that take time. It is one thing setting out a policy and putting resource into it, but it takes time for some of those things to take place. Rob, you probably ought to comment.

Thank you, Duncan. To focus on that point about why we are convinced that it is because of something that we have done and not just other environmental factors, we have done everything that Duncan has said, and we have made this the main effort for the NCA. We have built a response that focuses on five key areas: social media, high-value targets, equipment, criminal finance, and the movers and shakers in northern France. Those people all now face unbearable pressure day in, day out. That makes them desperate; it makes them change their business model. We have seen an adaptation because of that pressure, and what you have seen this summer—we will get on to some of this later, I am sure—is that pressure being exhibited in them changing their behaviour.

There are key indicators of our progress. At any one time, we have around 100 operations running. Those operations use the full suite of tactics available for national security threats. It was not always like that with organised immigration crime. There has been a clear demand signal to the system in the UK that this is an effort right across HMG, and the policy and influencing around that system by the BSC is really helpful. We have a laser-like focus on the operations. We have targeted known suppliers of equipment, and then, after that, that equipment has no longer appeared in crossings. That is point one.

Point two is that we have seen people finding it much harder to bring together the package of engine, boat, lifejacket and migrant at the same time and place in northern France. We have intervened with European partners on multiple occasions, as a direct result of UK intelligence, to prevent what we call a “go kit”—a car with all that equipment—from getting to migrants. We know that crossings would have happened if we had not dealt with that. All those things build up the pressure. We also had a record year last year in terms of seizures of equipment.

We do not just do that; obviously, we are seeking to bring people to justice as well. But, as we know, an awful lot of that criminality is based overseas. That is why, in the upstream effort, we have come away from France and gone further and further upstream, with covert tactics to confront this, to empower the goal-line defence in France and Belgium. By the time people have got that far, it is very hard to stop them. We are working way away from that now, at scale, to disrupt them and prevent them from getting to France. Those factors coming together have contributed to that drop.

Q3 What success looks like is obviously how many crossings there are, but do you have specific KPIs in other areas, particularly on reducing gang activity—you also mentioned the seizure of equipment—other than literally just the number of crossings being made across the channel?

Absolutely. We also track seizures of equipment, disruptions overseas and arrests; we track a whole range of different indicators. There is always a lag from the activity that we undertake, because this is a movement that is dynamic across all the routes. A very strong year last year set us up for what we have seen this summer, and, as the weather deteriorates, we are working really hard to make sure that we are in the strongest position we can be in for next year. It is therefore not just about one factor; it is about monitoring all of those and making sure that there is pressure on all of them .

Sometimes, arrests are not the most effective way of stopping crossings; sometimes, taking disruptive action overseas is much more effective. Arresting somebody and getting them imprisoned overseas is good—we need to hold them to account—but driving down the numbers and getting people off the water is the ultimate bottom line for us. We don’t want to contest organised immigration crime in the English channel; we want to do it at a time and place of our choice, which means ports and airports, and we need to get migrants off that route. So, sometimes, it is better to disrupt them way away from the UK, even though that might not result in an arrest.

Q4 To build on that, I want to discuss the role of the Border Security Command a little more. As has rightly been touched on, one of the reasons for setting it up was to improve inter-agency co-operation. How do you feel co-operation has improved since the command was set up? Do you feel that it is of a status that needs more improvement since your involvement commenced?

Without being patronising, that is a very good question. We are two years into this journey, post election and the setting up of this organisation, which you will be aware pulled together some of the existing organisations, including mine. If you recall, my predecessor appeared before you this time last year, when the Maritime Command, the Small Boats Operation Command and Home Office Intelligence were pulled into Border Security Command, making it just under 3,000 people. That brought a really key operational intelligence focus to that.

I would offer that, two years into this, with the relationships, systems and convening authority of this appointment—you will be aware that it is enshrined in the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act , but does not require that—everyone understands how they can play their role, whether that is the organisations for which Rob has responsibility, the Crown Prosecution Service or the Foreig n and Commonwealth Office . I think it has taken time for all that to pivot in, so I think the system is working really well.

However, we should be really clear that if we get to the end of this year below 25,000 arrivals, that is still 25,000 arrivals too many. I am not quoting the Home Secretary, but we are relentless. Everyone gets up every morning wanting to drive that down to a level where it is no longer significant, so there is always more to be done in that regard.

I think it was helpful that we managed to sign the deal for the next three years with France, which has given certainty in that space, and it is good to be able to coalesce around. I think that the direction from the previous Prime Minister, as well as this Prime Minister’s laser focus—you will be aware that he visited us in the summer—is helping. There is still more to do, but it is in a good place now.

As Rob said, what we have to do is certainly not claim victory now, and none of us are. We have to make sure that we set the conditions now to stop those people who would seek to travel to the north of France next year and make those crossings.

Q5 Just to press you, you said that there is still more to do, so are there any areas of the inter-agency co-operation that is lacking at the moment on which you would like to see more emphasis and focus?

I certainly would not single anyone out; I think everyone is really behind this. In a lot of cases, some of the initiatives that we have put in—let’s take our work upstream with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office and our taskforces that deal with the main routes up through the west of Europe, central Europe and the Balkans. Some of that work and those relationships, as well as the rationalisation of the footprint that Rob, the Home Office and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office have to make sure that we are all pulling in the right direction, is going to continue to yield real benefit. As Rob said, we need to do as much of that upstream as we can.

There is still more to be done in some of the work that we are doing within the UK to address the pull factors, but I am confident we are getting there. Based on a year’s-worth of experience dealing with immigration crime in the UK and illegal working, we can now be more focused on the things that pull migrants to want to come here illegally, and making it really difficult for them to do that. I would say those are some of the areas we can really work into.

There are areas where we have taken very direct action in relation to illegal migration, and we are quite advanced in those areas, but there are other important areas that are catching up in priority.

Criminal finance, cash-based economy, the grey economy and the high street—all those things are relevant to illegal migration, because you do not want someone to think that they are going to come work for cash in a vape shop in the UK. That has spun up our Operation Machinize and our work with the NPCC on really pressurising what could be seen as a pull factor, and it is really important to make sure that the lies told overseas about coming to the UK—that you can melt away and work with impunity—are confronted and that people are arrested.

That is coming up to the level of activity that we have in the more direct areas of chasing facilitators and people who are involved in this directly. The informal value transfer system—the hawaladar s—is really important to us, but it is really difficult to deal with. It is hidden from regulation and the reporting regime that we get with suspicious activity reports from banks.

All of these areas are catching up with the higher priority areas, and we need all of those to be flat out to squeeze this. With the help of Duncan and the convening power that we have across Whitehall, that is exactly what we are doing. Everybody is at the table, and that is the important thing.

The other benefit that I have seen is the legislation that came through. I have talked before about acts preparatory and going early to disrupt organised crime at its earliest possible stage, and we are now starting to use that. The business model that I described was largely legal. Ubiquitous social media is not illegal to run. The equipment is not illegal to possess. Using hawaladars is not illegal, unless we can prove a link to criminality.

We now have section 13 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 that allows us to seize equipment, which is brilliant. You have seen some of that recently, with 25 vessels seized in the UK under that legislation. That would have been 25 vessels with at least 79 people in. Criminalising that business model with the new legislation has been important, as well. That is another benefit of what the Border Security Command has helped with.

Q6 You touched on what I want to get on to next. Obviously, the statutory responsibilities of Border Security Command are much broader than just dealing with illegal migration and small boats issues, although that has rightly been given huge attention. That has predominantly been the key focus. Is that justified and what are the implications for other areas of work that you are also mandated to focus on, where less attention may be afforded?

You are right. The intention for Border Security Command was that it would be a system leader across all illegal immigration into the United Kingdom but, as you say, to start with, the clear and present focus for us was illegal migration by small boat and the facilitation around it. You will recall in the summer, when we talked about the common travel area and some other threats, that we are interested in that. I am sure we will come later to displacement.

If we are successful in the small boats area, is there a demand that has to be satisfied by other ways to get into the United Kingdom? We are very interested in those things. I also have a remit for wider national border security. You will be aware that I have the only law enforcement maritime capability in the UK. That was involved in the boarding of the MV Smyrtos. We facilitated that using our cutters. We still maintain a persistent presence in that.

I oversee the joint maritime security centre. We work very closely on national resilience and critical national infrastructure. That work is still going. We are concerned about the common travel area. We are concerned about clandestine entry into the UK, and we keep that as a plate that is spinning, working with Border Force, NCA and other regional police forces.

The focus at the moment is definitely on small boats, but it cannot be at the expense of not keeping an eye on those things. Because you and Parliament would not thank me if we fixed the small boat problem and all that happens is we get people displaced into other dangerous modes of entry. We all remember the awful situation at Purfleet where people died in a container. I don’t know if you have any thoughts on that, Rob.

I have just a couple of points. The most egregious breach of the border remains small boats. That creates community tension and problems across society. We have got to deal with it, and we will be relentless in pursuing that. At the same time, there are other breaches of the border in relation to drugs, firearms and other issues. Be assured, we are looking at where displacement might go for organised immigration crime.

At the same time, we must concurrently be alive to the way those threats are developing, as well. We have to maintain our response against other smuggling methods. We have prioritised small boats. Specialists who understand smuggling and global networks and are experts in drugs are now tackling small boats. We are backfilling and developing other people to ensure we retain the level of expertise we need to tackle drugs. You cannot pivot towards one threat without there being an opportunity cost or consequence.

That is what we seek to mitigate with the ongoing work around resourcing where we have had an uplift in resources. We are holding the line, but this is challenging. The national security threat, the National Crime Agency’s remit around a range of threats, from child sexual abuse through to OIC and drugs and firearms—none of that has gone away. We are pursuing that concurrently while we get after this.

To offer one other thought, this organisation is a little like an athlete: it is now match-fit and getting better. I came in from the military, and when I first got here, I was surprised by the communication and slight stovepiping in some cases. I am not saying that we are completely out of that, but it is so much better, in terms of co-operation, understanding, clear prioritisation, and the link between Parliament making policy or Ministers making directions for resources to be allocated and actually being able to pull levers to make things happen. Those techniques and relationships will endure and are good for all these threats, and you can now pivot into those in a more dynamic way than you could before.

Q7 That takes me nicely on to my question on funding and its prioritisation. How do you as an organisation decide whether the interventions funded by the Border Security Command are value for money? On prioritisation, what areas of spending are you most confident represent good value for money?

Part of the compact to set up the Border Security Command was that it would act as the system leader, so it would run the strategy and plan by allocating funding to the various endeavours. Obviously, there is the core funding that sets up my organisation, but this year, there is £290 million being focused through organisations that have a role, including the NCA, agencies and the CPS.

We covered a little of this in our first statutory report, which was published in the summer, and we will deal with a lot more of it in our report next year. We work through my system leadership board, which all the director-general level representatives are on, and we monitor the progress in all those areas. Of course, when we come to the end of what is essentially our first proper year of doing that, that ongoing assessment process and bids for what will go on in future will hopefully allow us to identify the things that are having the greatest effect, which we will want to double down on and continue to fund, and the areas where we perhaps have not had as much success, so that we can pivot that funding. That process is pretty dynamic.

Obviously, one of the major parts is the funding that we channel through the National Crime Agency to establish the pivot that Rob talked about and the upstream network for us to work together on this. Rob, do you want to talk about measures of effectiveness in your area?

To make sure that we are providing real value for the money invested in us, as we go from year to year and as we plan for future interventions, we look at what works and try to double down on it. That is connected to the funding, as the easiest answer to your question is that the Home Office pay on results.
Q8 What has not worked? In your time in this role, have there been any interventions that you have deemed not value for money and stopped?

We have not been through a full cycle yet, so it is probably too early in the gestation of the BSC to identify anything that has been genuinely unsuccessful. If I had to give an example, the work we did to pull together some of the recommendations on work in the UK under Lockstream has perhaps been focused against criminality more generally. Coming into the next year, we will focus that on organised immigration crime much more specifically, rather than on a more general part. I would not say that it has not been effective, as it has been very successful in addressing wider criminality, but given my clear main effort, we will pivot it much more towards what we see as the pull factors for small boat migrants coming to the UK. As you would guess, that is a lower-cost part of the area around people looking to come and work illegally here.

Q9 On the opposite side of this—maybe this will build on the answer you just gave—if more funding was to be awarded for you to make additional interventions, on whatever you deemed fit, to meet the objectives, where would that funding be allocated to give value for money? Would it be specifically to address the pull factors you mentioned?

You might want to touch on this later, but as you will be aware, post the one in, one out deal, the Home Secretary has pulled together all the work that was already happening under a small boats taskforce. That looks at deterrence, potential returns and that element of the issue, so that we can start to build in consequence when people jump the queue and come here illegally. That is an area that I expect the Home Secretary will want to resource using funding from BSC.

As Rob said, it is about addressing these things upstream, with partners in the countries that they come from, and capacity building. Critically, it is about doing that as the whole of Government, so that when we negotiate with those countries, we bring in all the equities cross-Government, not just organised immigration crime. There is a compact here: do they want things from us? Yes, they do. We need to wrap in those in a way that perhaps did not happen before.

If we can stop people wanting to leave their countries, we can stop the facilitators exploiting them to cross borders, and, critically, we can stop the supply chain. That is far more effective because when people get to the north of France — many of you have been there —broadly, t hey will keep trying until they are either successful or die , and that causes all sorts of problems. I would offer that the work we have done with France in the n ew d eal, and particularly with the flexibility to look at what we have learned over the last three years and before to focus on the things that are successful —t hat is a core part of that, but it is only holding the ground.

On your point around where we are at and what works, it is quite early because we have gone from the build and the uplift to then assessing where we can best place resources. W ithin the envelope we have, we are constantly looking at whether we can redeploy and get behind something that ha s had a tangible impact . A cross the areas that I talked about — the five key areas that we operate against — the work on criminal finance for OIC is interesting , because the narrative around following the money and organised crime holds good, s o there is impact . B ut on the money and the way the money flows work in relation to organised immigration crime, it is a much smaller pot of money and it is much more organic. T he system, because it is based on trust, is harder to penetrate and disrupt. That does not mean that y ou should no t do it ; i t i s about finding the right place to target it.

T hose are the areas that are catching up with other elements that we do , a nd when we get through next year, we will be in a much better place to get behind what we think is most effective. All of those areas are productive — I see benefit in all of them. If there was a wider effort, it would be upstream. On t he big issues that draw people to the UK — that push people to the UK — some of those are beyond the NCA in terms of dealing with them. We are tackling the organised crime, but in dealing with the causes of this and making sure that the UK is not an attractive target for smuggling gangs, the price is an efficient and effective system that we support by undermining the organised crime. You need to keep looking further and further away from the UK for the causes of this and try to tackle it as far away from France as you can , a s Duncan said.

One further point, which goes back to your previous point, is that communications and perception is an area that we are doing quite a lot in but can do more. As Rob said, this is unlike most other crimes, which try and stay under the radar. This is overt: it is on TikTok and all of these other apps. It is about working with those companies to try to put deterrence into this—not just in northern France but in the countries where people are coming from. That is an area we have developed this year and I think we can do more.

We are working with the French now in the camps to try to have communications with them. We do dialogue under a thing called Op Asper, where we try and explain the realities of what it means. We are trying to drive down people risking their lives. I think that there i s a big piece we can do there to try and bring some truth to the perception of it. You saw some of the work that we did with the French for the first time, using some imagery to show people that might come that the reality is not what they think —p articularly if you come from the Horn of Africa, you are going to go through countries and be exploited and so on . I think that is one area that we can do a lot more in: working with our ambassadors and high commissioners in those countrie s. It is one of the areas I want to develop next year.
Q10 Have you assessed h ow many attempts, on average, it takes for someone to get across in a small boat?

Y es. On average , I think it is not quite double figure s, but seven or eight. I cannot verify that, but you will be aware that since last year , we have a very strong debriefing presence now in Manston. M ost of the anecdotal evidence is that people try a number of times to get over.

Q11 There must be a point where it becomes not economically viable f or people to do it . W hen we were in France last year, we were told that if it got to more than three attempts, people would just stop trying. Are you saying that it is still more than that?

I think it is more than that. There are a lot of people in the camps at the moment, which is bad in one respect because a lot of people are there , b ut it also represents the fact that the French are making it very difficult, particularly in the Dunkirk / Calais area , to get across . T o take your logic , y ou are right that t here is a moment — from a criminal perspective , if w e look at the business model —w here it stops being particularly viable . Part of our strategy is to drive it to a point where it is not worth the criminal gangs doing this, because the cost of getting the boat and the engine, as well as the risk of them being interdicted and jailed, is so much that they stop being in this business.
Q12 You said that there are a lot of people in the camps at the moment. Can you give us an estimate?
Under 4,000, but close to 4,000, in the two camps between Calais and Dunkirk. I think the French estimate at the moment is that there are almost 3,800 people between those two camps.
Q13 What was it previously?

In my experience from when I previously did the job in SBOC, it was broadly about 2,000 between them. Our understanding from our French partners, who we work with closely, is that it is almost double what we would normally expect.
Q14 What is your estimate of the average amount of time that somebody would be in a camp before they either get across or give up?

I cannot give you an accurate answer to that, but it can be quite a long time. Broadly, the poorer the nationality, the longer they tend to stay in the camps. It can be a period of months, if not longer, that they are living in what, as you have seen, are exceptionally unsanitary and difficult conditions.
Dreadful conditions, yes.
I am sorry that I cannot answer accurately.
Q15 Do you have any intelligence on the make-up of those 3,800? Are they predominantly single men or is it mixed with families?

In terms of gender, it is predominantly single men. There are some females and some families, but it is 90% single men coming over on small boats. In terms of nationalities, as you would expect, it is those that we most frequently see: those from Eritrea, Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia and Afghanistan. The number from Afghanistan is slightly higher. Those who are slightly more wealthy will tend to come in more quickly, will take less time on the routes from their original countries and will broadly try to cross more quickly.

Q16 We have had many presentations at this Select Committee, and the message—from, I think, Rob and your predecessor—was always that organised crime is very good at adapting, and that that is not going to change any time soon. I agree with the Chair that this is a massive issue in our constituencies. As well as the cost, it is the faith and trust, isn’t it? It is rolling on. As organised crime keeps changing, which it is good at doing, what is the biggest challenge now for you?

My initial response is they do adapt, but we are thinking about their next move, and we are thinking about that now. I do not want to telegraph where we go next, because I want to be ahead and waiting when they change. The symptom we see is a higher number of attempts. That is grit in the business model—that is really good. The fact that there are more migrants in northern France is not a good thing—it shows the intent is high—but it shows that they are struggling to make the crossing. The fact that events have plummeted by something in the region of 50% and the fact about the number of times people are successful are important facts for communities that understandably feel threatened by this.

The assurance I can give is that we have seen the business model starting to shake, and we are actively working to understand where it goes next, if it does displace, to get ahead of it and be waiting. There are not an infinite number of possibilities for the small boats model. You have seen attempts to use larger vessels. You have seen attempts to evade the French patrols by going out of the areas where the French have very tight control. You have seen them try Belgium. The thing about small boats is that they depend on specialist equipment, on a just-in-time logistics model, and on people being able to bring all that together at the right time and in the right place. That is its vulnerability.

The strength of the model is that it was low cost, but we are increasing the cost because we are increasing the risk. We are increasing the cost to OCGs not just financially. Up till now, they have tried to absorb a lot of that, but they cannot do that forever, because they are driven by profit. We have also increased the cost to them in terms of risk. It is more likely than ever that you are going to get arrested. It is more likely than ever that your equipment is going to be seized. Every time that happens, they need to go again.

People will continue to attempt organised immigration crime and people smuggling. Attempting them in the English channel is getting riskier and riskier for everybody involved. We just need to continue and stay flat out until that viability is no longer there.

This is a very good question. The things that have worried me most this year have been the increasing size of the boats and the increasing occupancy. You will have seen that this year we had a boat with 230 people in it—extraordinary. It ought to be put on the record that it is only a matter of time until we have a mass casualty event in the channel. It is extraordinary that that has not happened so far. You will be aware that my officers were involved in a rescue with the French in French waters, on one of the western launches, where we rescued 168 people. None of them drowned—quite an extraordinary thing. That worries me.

You will probably want to do in a bit of detail the displacement into Belgium and down to the western beaches, particularly Normandy. That represents the fact that they are finding it more difficult to launch around Dunkirk and Calais; it is not impossible, but more difficult. The displacement into Belgium was a real fear of mine at the beginning of the year. We set up a taskforce with the Belgians to address that. Not only have we pretty much shut down that route, but we have increased co-operation between France and Belgium and Belgium and the Netherlands, noting that the Belgians have far more permissive use of number-plate and facial recognition. That has had the bigger effect of making it much more difficult for the boats and the engines to be moved from broadly where they were being stored—in the Venlo area around the border with Germany and the Netherlands—in time, as Rob said, with a ready pack. That has made it much more difficult and is one of the contributing factors, so that co-operation has been effective.

Again, on the western launch, it is much more difficult for the criminal gangs to operate in that part of France. It is a very long way. They have to get the migrants to move down there. They have to move the boats and the engines. As you can imagine, we are working very closely with the French to deal with that.

One thing that has made a big difference this year is the French changing their on-water maritime posture. They have physically interdicted 15 boats on the water. Their view, which I share, is that that has had not just a direct effect but a deterrent effect. We have seen boats giving up rather than being stopped by the French. Principally, that has addressed the taxi boat methodology when there are fewer people in the boat when they go and pick people up. That is one of the other displacements that was difficult.

At the risk of going on, there are a lot of things. We think about it and we work very closely with the French because most of it is in that space, but you will understand that the difficulty is that it is France. We have to work with the French in the way they do it, while offering every bit of support and intelligence that we can.
Q17 That brings me to my next question. The displacement of where the boats are launching from leads us to attempts in other areas outside Kent. How have you responded to that?

Let me start with the Dieppe area launches. We have had four of the larger boats, which we think was a criminal gang in that area. Three of those made their way up successfully and came across, and the other was the one that we rescued. We then had three boats, larger ones again, that launched from the old D-Day beaches in Normandy. The first one launched on the 6 th and entered UK waters on the 7 th . We picked it up with the French coastguard and it was intercepted by the RNLI. The reason for that is we obviously patrol Border Security Command assets in the short straits, because that is where the vast majority come across. You will be aware that the two RNLI vessels that picked up those migrants came into Eastney marina. There was then a public disorder incident and the police had to try to put a cordon around it.
We have some questions about that later.

That was all very difficult, and I share your concerns about how we deal with that. The short answer to your question is that there were two further ones—one that we moved by sea to Dover and one that was brought ashore at Gosport. There is no intention for us to set up a reception facility in that south coast area around Portsmouth. My absolute aim over this next two or three months, working with French partners, is to shut that route down for lots of very good reasons, not least that it is nearly 60 nautical miles. If people try that in the winter, we are going to have loss of life, and it really, really concerns me—not just that, but the reception is much more difficult, with the issues of the RNLI, which you might want to talk about, and the problems that we had bringing people ashore in Portsmouth, which is not well set up for it. It is probably my No. 1 concern at the moment, and it is the one that I am working hardest on.
Q18 How are they getting the migrants from those camps? France is a big country, and it is not easy to move people—

That is a seven-hour train journey from Paris. I go down there. The French p réfet m aritime —the senior officer who runs it—is based out of Cherbourg, so we go out there quite a lot. We believe they are moving down either by van, facilitated by the OCGs, or using public transport.
So it is taking hours and hours.
Just tha t . There are no camps in that area, and the French are very, very keen that that does not develop in the same way as it has in the north.
Q19 How much are migrants now being charged on average for passage?
We did some investigations into that, and it has broadly come down. It is over €1,000 but under €2,000.
That is a lot lower than we were hearing last year.

Yes, and depending on the nationality, they are price-sensitive. The OCGs will charge more for those who they think can pay, who will broadly get perhaps a better service. If you are coming from Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia, you will be packed into enormous boats. As Rob said, the average occupancy this year is 69. Those who have been following this for a long time will remember that it used to be a few people in a boat, and the average is now almost 70.
Q20 How much do the boats cost them?
We do not know that.
They can expect to pay in the region of £14,000 or potentially more.
Q21 And they expect that once the boat is gone, it is lost.
It is, yes.
It is one use.
Q22 So you need to make sure that they are losing enough boats that it is no longer economically viable.

Absolutely, and that is what we seek to do. On the way it is priced, that figure is a symptom of OCGs trying to maintain the business model by less events, because they are so vulnerable and they have less access to equipment, and pushing them into bigger arrivals with larger boats.
Q23 I guess if you can put 200 migrants on a boat and make €200,000 from that crossing, it is economically viable. If you cannot do that and you are losing enough boats, it is not.

The migrant numbers reducing is a good thing, but the most stark one is that we are at pretty much half the number of boats that came over last year, and we pretty much directly attribute that to the work we are doing.

Q24 First, I think you should be congratulated on what you have been doing. It is a huge triumph that you have managed to bring this situation so much more under control.
