As you said, the job is not done, but you are making an enormous difference. We are very grateful to you and your teams for doing that, and I think the country is grateful to you.

I want to ask about the intelligence that this whole thing depends upon. Is there more that you could do, or more that we could help you to do, with your intelligence so that you can take pre-emptive action? I am thinking particularly of increasing uncertainty in various parts of the world. We were hearing yesterday in another meeting about the terribly deteriorating situation in Yemen. I am expecting that you may improve the situation from some countries, but there will be other countries where things deteriorate. My question is about how you look at things further upstream and whether there is intelligence that we could assist you to resource.

Thank you. In tackling organised crime, the target I would have is 100% coverage. I am never going to get that, but I am as close to that as I can get with the access we have to everything that is available in the UK. In terms of upstream intelligence and our relationship with the intelligence community in the UK, that is a very helpful element of what we do. The SOC mission is supported and avowed by that community as a priority for them as well. I am very grateful for that support, and we benefit from it.

In the key areas where we work, we are looking to maximise all the intelligence collection that we can upstream, and we are doing that with UK partners and overseas partners. We have a large presence in Europol, which accesses European intelligence. We have more joint investigations running in Europol on this than we have had before. We have more intelligence collection. In short, we have a well - resourced intelligence effort in the key areas where we are working. We do have support from colleagues across the UK system . It is a priority for them , and we are benefiting from it.

B ringing H ome O ffice intelligence into Border Security Command and pivoting that organisation ’ s efforts to focus on organised immigration crime and small boats ha ve been very effective. Rob alluded to working with international partners. This is not just a UK problem ; it is a worldwide problem . It is destabilising : the countries that are losing their people do n’t want to lose their brightest and best . And no one wants to pay facilitators , who are in some cases poly- criminal and doing bad things with the money that they are getting from this. There is a shared zone of interest in that , and a ctually we do a lot of reciprocal work, both on the law enforcement side and on the prevention side , with those partners.

I do think we have moved now into a space where we are better able to share intelligence , in a way we couldn’t, and— even if it ’s not intelligence — information, awareness and some of the debriefing stuff we do . We can track all the way back through the migrant journey , using the taskforce approach. W hat we are trying to do, as Rob said, is make this much more , not haphazard, but intelligence led and really focused , using all the sources we have, including the powers to look at magnetic media , phones and open - source intelligence, which is a massive area because all this is happening in plain sight , all the way through those journeys. So it is an improving picture, but one that we need to keep working on .

Q25 One thing that sometimes concerns people is the idea that people pitch up in this country without any identity documents whatever and there doesn’t seem to be a simple way for us to identify who they are. Of course, there are worries that some of them may have criminal intent or criminal backgrounds . P eople are a bit worried about that. Obviously, many people coming here are people of good intent, who are genuinely seeking asylum , and those people should be supported , but in among them are these unidentified individuals . What more can we do about that?
T he story there probably starts with Manston and the reception c ommittee to fix identity , so perhaps Duncan, you want to take that question.

As you set it out is correct. A lot of them will , if they have travel or identity documents, get rid of them before they come through the system . In almost all cases —it’s 99% of those who arrive by small boat — they are seeking to gain asylum in this country. So in most cases , they are compliant ; they want to portray a story that allows them to do that. It is broadly our belief that most people who would seek ill , on the terrorist side of things , will not come by small boat , because th ose who do are all biometrically enrolled : they all go through facial recognitio n; they all go through fingerprints.

But your point about those who might have criminal records or seek to do bad things in this country is our concern. The Home Secretary has been really clear that we need to have zero tolerance of that. So identifying those people , through all the ways we can , monitoring them and making sure we use intelligence to stop that and to deal with it as firmly as we can if it happens is absolutely part of what she has now directed us to be able to do. You will be aware that we have counter-terrorism officers embedded with our teams at Manston and Western Jet Foil .

Q26 I want to ask a separate question, about the equipment and boats that we have to rescue people who are at sea . Our rescue service is a volunteer service, which is a bit different from some other countries ’. We have th e RNLI. Are the boats that the RNLI have to fish people out of the water and out of these fragile rubber boats the correct vessels, or do we need to invest in better vessels to do that?

I t is worth being really clear here that 98% of rescue s of small boat migrants are done by Border Security Command , by the m aritime and s mall b oats o rganisation. To be really clear, o nly 2% of rescue s of small boats are done by the RNLI . They do an amazing job , b ut should not be pulled into this unless they have to be.

I arrived in this role at the end of 2022 , and we had just established the contract for crew transfer vessels. Essentially, these are the vessels that are normally used to take crews out to the wind farms. We have adapted those to be able to rescue small boat migrants. No boat , apart from a lifeboat , is designed to do rescues . In most cases , there is a mayday and somebody will go and assist, but of course you need a boat that can actually do that. These have been designed or modified specifically to be able to come alongside small boats and rescue them. The high-profile incidents on the Normandy launches into Portsmouth were RNLI, because they cover that area. We now have a plan in place to stop them having to do that. I deal very closely with RNLI—the chief executive is a personal friend of mine. We are also procuring an additional crew transfer vessel to allow us to do that.

The reason that that was set up was twofold. First, it was to be able to ensure that we can fulfil our safety of life at sea responsibilities—as a signatory of the maritime conventions, we have to do that. Secondly, it was to provide control for people coming into the United Kingdom.

Q27 It would be great if the message that rescuing these individuals in the sea is not the work of the RNLI could be more widely dispersed. As you know, we have had a terrible situation of RNLI people being vilified by some people who would wish us ill.

It is worth being really clear to the Committee that it has been absolutely appalling. Peter Sparkes , the chief executive, is a personal friend. We served together: he was Royal Navy and I was Army. The abuse that his people, and their families and children, have had is extraordinary.

I have to be honest with you: it is the same abuse that my staff get. You will be aware of the protests that routinely happen outside Manston and Western Jet Foil. So-called auditors film it. I will not give the names of the people who have done it, but you will have seen that. It is absolutely extraordinary.

These people are hugely proud of what they do; their role is to save life at sea and control the borders of this country, which they do with incredible professionalism and humanity—you have seen them in action—and they have been subject to the same kind of abuse.

I am hugely grateful that we have the RNLI as partners. They particularly assist us when the seas are really bad and in the worst rescue conditions, because they are the experts in that, working with the Maritime and Coastguard Agency. We work very closely with them.

Q28 Could you set out what the auditors are? On our trips and in meetings with parliamentarians from around the rest of the world, we have heard the view that in the UK you get arrested for free speech, and that we are an authoritarian state. Could you set that out so that there is a factual, on-the-record position of what these people are?

Yes, 100%. As you can imagine, having spent nearly 40 years serving my country, I believe that free speech and the right to democratic representation are a core part of what we are. We have absolutely no difficulty with people who protest, but violent protest is obviously more difficult. What we tend to get is a lot of people who film our activities. The so-called auditors often post those videos, live or subsequently, on various social media channels—YouTube or whatever. Thay can be quite antagonistic. We do not stop them doing that, because they are on public property and it is not for us to do that, but a lot of time they are filming our officers and their cars, and there is some intimidation involved in some of that. We don’t stop them doing it. The police are exceptionally good around Dover—as you might imagine, we work very closely with them—and it is only stopped if there is criminality. But the act of filming and communicating is not illegal and is allowed to continue.
Q29 Would you like some rules to be changed to make it illegal to make films of people who are engaged in this life-saving activity?

As you might imagine, I would be cautious about calling for legislation. The police have been very good at putting containment areas around our key facilities—particularly at Dover—where we are doing safety of life at sea and you have very vulnerable people. They respond to that pretty sensitively and quite dynamically. If this continues—the debate around this is not a sensible one; it can be very febrile—we need to be very cautious about where it leads.

Q30 I just wondered how it happened that the boats arrived outside Kent and seemed to catch everybody out. Following on from what Peter said earlier, the public want to know whether all those people who arrived in those boats, which you were not aware of, have been security checked, and whether all checks have been sorted.

I think what you are describing are the two incidents that happened in September at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe, when we did not intercept the boats on the water. To put it in perspective, I took over this role in December 2022 . We had one boat in August last year that we did not intercept on the water and met on the beach. And we had those two, one that came into Samphire Hoe and one that came into Folkstone, both of which were met on the beach by the police. In that time, we had 2,316 small boat arrivals, so that represents less than 0.1% of arrivals. We always seek to interdict on the water. It wasn’t that we did not detect those, but they were detected too late for us to mobilise one of the crew transfer vessels and other assets to actually meet them on the water. They were intercepted—
Q31 So that the public can understand that, why were they detected so late?

It was an extremely busy day on the water and the surveillance conditions were really difficult. We have a networked system of surveillance and intelligence. We map them with the Coastguard coming off the beach. We have crewed surveillance aircraft and drones, and then we have coastal surveillance towers. That all comes together and networks into a system that then queues the assets. It was a particularly busy day, with multiple rescues going on. The boat was identified about 4 km off the beach, and it was too late by that stage to get a crew transfer vessel to meet it. It was met on the beach by law enforcement, immediately then supported by our officers. In one case there were five people on one boat, and the other one on the subsequent day had 21. I will not go into detail.

There are a couple of procedural issues that we identified in terms of the notifications that came off the system. I am confident that any errors that happened have been identified. We should be really clear: it wasn’t that they were not detected. They just were not controlled on the water. It represents an exceptionally small number. That is why, with a lot of people saying we are acting as a taxi service, we intercept them on the water, because we do not want them getting to the beach. Some of you who have been around this a long time will recall that when this started off, people would get on to the beaches and then get into the hinterland of the UK with none of the checks that we have discussed today. I am not blasé , but I am very focused.

Q32 I know you’re not. Would you say that there is an issue with messaging for the public? There is a public perception, obviously fanned, I feel, by certain sections of the media, but it is not what it appears, is it?

I think people genuinely think that most small boats arrive here on the coast, people disappear, and we do not intercept them. However, the reality, as I have said, is that in the last four years we have had 2,316, and there have only been three that we have not met on the water—and one last year was a person on a jet ski. [1]
Q33 I apologise for being late—I was at the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee. How do you liaise with the media? Do you suggest they come with you to see what is happening?

I have been very keen to open our doors and show people more of what we do. It slightly plays to the humanity of what we are trying to do, the efforts that we are making and the protection we are trying to put in there. There will be people that you never persuade, but there will be those that perhaps just do not know and could be informed. We have worked with the French this year. You will have seen some of the quite difficult coverage. People’s perception would be that we are overrun, not that we are nearly 50% down.

I would like to do more. We have been able to do more. We have been able to publicise more the work that we are doing. For the people that would like to understand this better, there is more that we can do. There are very sensible journalists out there that have covered this in a very straight way and have been honest and involved when the Home Secretary went out to deal with this. A lot of them are very good. There is a story, but they are very honest. There are others for whom it is always a story. You might imagine that for my people it is pretty difficult at times. I am not looking for sympathy, but we would like it to be a more even story.
Q34 Do you invite politicians—MPs?

The all-party parliamentary group and all the local MPs are invited to operations. We are always happy to have any MPs, county councils, and all the people involved in it. As you know, Sir, we are inspected and audited a great deal—rightly so, because it is such a sensitive operation. But I would be very happy to show anyone around our facilities, have those conversations and do those briefings.

On the organised crime element and what we can do with the media, we have briefed in great detail our strategic approach. We have briefed the Crime Reporters Association. We engage as much as we can. Obviously, sometimes we have to wait before we tell the story. But it is a really important point. We see the legitimate public interest and understand it. We completely understand the need to get the truth of the way the UK is tackling this out there. We will do our best to address that.
We need not to avoid the difficult conversations that we are having here. We need to confront this, because it is something that most people in this country are concerned about.
Q35 I want to move on to international co-operation on enforcement. What type of international co-operation has been most effective in reducing small boat crossings?
I will start with pre-planned operations on organised crime, and then, Duncan, you may want to come in on the taskforces.

We have developed our presence in Europol. We work in operational taskforces and in joint investigation teams on judicialised investigations with partners. That has resulted in a number of successes in Europe, particularly Germany, where we have had large days of action, with hundreds of officers out on the ground, to seize equipment that is on its way to France. The way this model works is that there is a lay-up point before materials are called down. Targeting that with European colleagues has worked and has had an impact on crossings. That is an important part of what we do.

As well as co-operating in Europe with judicialised investigations, we have bilateral relationships in all the source countries for migrants, and will target facilitators in those countries, as well as money launderers and the controlling minds. We do that at a scale that we have never done before. That is important to us. We are dealing with the equipment and the supply of equipment in Europe, with the middlemen in France, and with colleagues in OLTIM in France and with other French units, as well as bilaterally in some of the source countries. We have spoken publicly about work in Iraq and elsewhere to try to stem the flow.
That is the high-level view of that. It is difficult to go into specific operations that are still running. Many are running today and will come to fruition. We will talk about those when we can.

Q36 Can I mention one specific measure, which I put to the Home Secretary? I would be interested to hear your thoughts on the UK rejoining the Eurodac system, which is the data-sharing system with other European countries. As far as I understand it, we are essentially going blind when asylum seekers and refugees come to this country. We do not have any of that data sharing any more. That is something the Home Secretary seemed to intimate would be a helpful measure. Is that something you would see as a helpful step?

Yes, completely. I welcome more access to European data and access to Eurodac. You are absolutely right. We absolutely welcome real-time alerts, more biometric data and all those things to make this as efficient as it can be.

Riffing on Rob’s point, despite the fact that we are out of the structures of the European Union, we work every day to try to bring those things closer. It is in the European Union’s interest for us to work as a partner. Those borders of France are the European borders—and the criminality and everything that goes with it.

Your question is a really interesting one. I have been involved in the past, in my military career, with a lot of upstream work and capacity building. What is innovative in what we have done here is that, rather than have just country-specific stuff, we have tried to link up those countries and those areas where we see the broad migrant roots.

We essentially have three major, and one slightly more minor, taskforces. One basically comes out of north-east Africa, through Italy and the central Mediterranean. One comes through Iraq, Turkey, Syria, Iran and Kuwait. The final one is through the western part of Europe and the Balkans. Then we have a slight side piece, which works in Vietnam and those countries there—you might remember that, a couple of years ago, there was a large influx of Vietnamese, who are broadly being trafficked into quite unpleasant stuff in the United Kingdom.

Rather than look at those as individual, isolated countries, we work across that entire route not only to deal with the causes of people leaving in the first place—working with the security agents and Government organisations to interdict those—but to get in the supply of boats and equipment. That allows us to share that in a way that is not restricted by the boundaries of those countries. That is joint piece of work that we do with the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office; the NCA, as the law enforcement lead for all operations in overseas jurisdictions; and other partners across Government. That has been has been effective in interdicting boats and equipment. It is also a vehicle through which we share information and intelligence, which they are very interested in.

That does not just help us with channel crossings; those facilitators are trying to get people across the Mediterranean to other countries. We focus on the countries that have equities—France into Morocco; Italy into Libya. Working with them in a partnership has been really innovative and effective.

T o bring back to life the point about what we are doing upstream and to build on Duncan ’ s point, we have 160 international liaison officers in over 50 countries now supporting all those taskforces and working with the equivalents of the NCA on law enforcement. F or all those people, wherever they are, illegal migration is a top priority now .

Q37 I will follow up very quickly ; I know we are getting short of tim e. You touched on the co - operation on the various routes that migrants come through. How are we checking that the funding we provide to other nations, particularly to countries like Iraq that have a history of human rights abuses , is being used correctly and for the reasons we provided it in the first place?

That is a really good question. We always work through high commissioners and embassies under Foreig n, Commonwealth and Development Office auspices. We make sure that we accord with all their processes and assurances. But there is a tension here : some of the countries that people are leaving are the ones that potentially have questionable pasts. We have to be pragmatic about that whil e making sure that we adhere to our rules of law and our values and standards. The short answer to your question is that it is all done through the Foreign , Commonwealth and Development Office in accordance with their platform and their assurances.

Q38 I echo Peter Prinsley’s comments and congratulate you. Rob, we have met many times; Duncan, I think this is the first time. Many of us on the Committee were very sceptical. To halve the number this year is phenomenally good. I know we should not get overexcited, but it is hugely impressive, so thank you.
Turning to something that perhaps was not such a great success—although it was a pilot, and that is the point of pilots—can you tell us about one in, one out and why it ended?

I would slightly push back on the idea that it was not a success. I would say that it was. I t was the first bilateral agreement that we made with any country within Europe after leaving the EU . W e managed to return 1 , 631 il legal entrants to the United Kingdom, all of whom were from countries that we would have had difficulty returning to otherwise.

We facilitate d safe and legal routes. We work ed closely with UNHCR and other agencies to do that. We got a great education programme in place. Did it scale to the level that I would have liked it to? No, but it absolutely proved that we can make these things work. As an exemplar of how it could be done in the future, it was very successful. I would like to take it as a model in the future and potentially be able to do something else with it.
Q39 T hat is really interesting and v ery positive. W hy did it end? Why is it not being continued?

It was always intended to be a pilot, as you know. It was meant to run for a year from the summer of last year to the summer of this year. The Home Secretary negotiated with Minister Nuñez, her counterpart in France, to extend it un til the beginning of this month to get us through what is, as you well know, traditionally the peak season , b ut the French were not willing to extend it . It was always intended to be a pilot. We will have a couple of flights this month and then that process will finish.

G oing back to the EU piece, the French position was that they see their border as the edge of the European border, not just the French border, and that an arrangement for returns should be with the European Union, not just France.
Q40 I will come to that in a moment, b ut before I do, do you think that it was a deterrent at the size it was, or did it need to be bigger to be a deterrent?

It i s very interesting. I was n o t convinced to start with that i t would be a deterrent, but I think it has been . T he UNHCR process ed up to 10,000 applications on our behalf, regardless of the fact that we only accepted just over 1 , 400 —I think the number in to this country was 1,496 . But that meant that there were 10,000 or so migrants who had applied through a safe and legal process who did not cross during that period because they had their applications in place. Therefore, rather than being a deterrent just because you had the return to France, it also served as a process that stopped people making their crossings by small boat.
Q41 Do you agree, Rob?

I do. Obviously, you were concerned that organised crime would just allow them to constantly traverse the channel. That did not play out. There were attempts to do that, but the vast majority of those removals stuck. That is important. It is one to watch in the future because the ability to return people quickly is helpful to our undermining of the business.
Q42 Do you know what happened to them once they were in France? Did they stay in France?

I went on one of the return flights, which returned 45 people. They were processed through Paris-Charles de Gaulle. The French then put them into a holding centre, gave them details and they were then supported to resettle into France.

Interestingly, and slightly counter to the narrative, I was very surprised that the mood on the plane was generally very positive and the people were thanking the escorts as they went back into France. That is very counterintuitive, but a tribute to the way that they had been treated. I know that there has been some slightly negative press around how they were treated and the way that it was done, but that was not my experience.
Q43 How do you account for them wanting to leave France in the first place and paying good money to do so, and then being happy to return?

It is a very interesting conundrum. Some of them come from countries where they are not treated well by law enforcement. I think that they were slightly surprised that, notwithstanding the fact they were put into immigration retention centres and returned to France, it was done to them in a humane and decent way.
But they are also sold a lie.
Q44 I wondered about that

Resetting that is important. The best antidote is sunlight and making sure that people understand just how hard it is going to be if you run the gauntlet of the English channel, end up here having entered illegally, and then realise—
Q45 That the streets are not paved with gold.
Exactly.
Q46 Can we do more to get that message out?

One of the questions earlier was: what more could we do in the future? One of the areas is communications, both online and in the countries of origin. It is one of the big things that we want to expand into and which we are resourcing now to get that message out. The FCDO will help us with that.
Q47 One of the issues is returning people who are over here and whose application fails. What are the numbers like on that at the moment?

It is really difficult. You find that our “frequent flyers” who come over mostly by small boat are from countries that we do not have returns agreements with. Since the beginning of the small boats phenomenon in 2018, we have broadly returned about 5% of those who have arrived here; the number is under 7,000. Operation Hillmore, the one in, one out deal, made a big difference because it allowed us to return Afghans, Iranians, Yemenis and Somalians in a way that we could not do before.

However, you are absolutely right that one of the things that I would like to see, and that the Home Secretary is absolutely focused on, is being able to do more returns to those countries from which most of the people arriving illegally originally come. You will have seen the work she is trying to do with Eritrea and some of the others.
Q48 And do the return hubs have a role to play?

I think they almost certainly do. You will be aware that the Home Secretary publicly announced that she had set up a small boats returns taskforce. That will be looking at all those options and working with partners to see what else we can do after learning from the Hillmore experience. Is there is a role in that to give me all of the tools we can possibly have to continue the good work that we have done?

Q49 Of course, we used to have tools under the EU and the Dublin agreement, and now we have the successor: the EU pact on migration and asylum. Would being within that have a role to play and would that be useful?

Rob talked about Eurodac and the sharing of information. We would very much like to be part of that, however we can make that work. If we were part of a European returns agreement, that would not be unhelpful to us. However, there might be other ways that we can do it. You will be aware of the work that we are trying to do with the Calais group and partners to try and facilitate some of that.
That was a hugely diplomatic answer. Well done, that was good.
Q50 You see a role for safe and legal routes?

That is a personal view. I have slightly crossed the Rubicon. I was not sure that they were useful. However, if we accept that migration is a worldwide problem and that there will always be people who would seek to come to this country and that they are not all bad people, part of that could be safe and legal routes. We have safe and legal routes but the focus on the one that we did for the small boats deal was effective not only because of the returns but particularly because of the deterrent. My sense from that was that a lot of people did not want to cross to here by small boats. They would like to come here, but that allowed us to process their applications in France, to do their biometrics and to do all the checks that Rob was talking about in advance so that we were not having to do that when they arrived here. Speaking from a personal point of view, I think that is potentially something we would look at in the future.
Q51 Is the small boats returns task force part of your organisation, BSC?
It sits at the moment under Dan Hobbs in migration, borders and international, but I am intimately involved in it and my teams are in it.
Q52 What is it doing in addition that was not being done before?

It is looking at all the potential options that we could have above and beyond those things that we are doing, such as returns hubs, returns to more difficult countries. It will bring in immigration enforcement and all that work because, as you might imagine, the Home Secretary is very keen, after Op Hillmore, to be able to put something in place that will achieve some of the effects that we wanted from that, as obviously we cannot continue it.

Q53 So if you were designing policy, there would be upstream work, first, to communicate that the streets are not paved with gold and to give them a reason not to leave their home country, there would be communications that we need to improve, and in an ideal world there would be some form of safe and legal route so that someone who is a genuine asylum seeker could make an application without having to get on a small boat.
Working with partners.
Would you have zero tolerance on people arriving by irregular means?

That is a difficult question for me, isn’t it? I personally think, having listened to the Home Secretary and the Prime Minister, that it is not British to jump the queue. Some of the people who are jumping the queue are the youngest and the fittest, not necessarily the most deserving. My personal view is that we adhere to the rule of law in this country and one reason, ma’am, that people are not happy in this country is that people are seen to be getting away with it and there is not consequence. Part of that is about consequence. In a perfect world, yes, you would like a situation where you have policies in place that would mean that if you came in illegally there were consequences and you could deal with that.

Q54 We have heard, in international examples, that some countries have sanctions on migrants who break the conditions of their being an asylum seeker. For example, we heard that in Sweden if an asylum seeker is found working illegally, that is considered when their decision is finally made. Would that help you?

Again, I am moving into a policy formulation area, but I think it comes under the area of consequence. If you break the rules, there has to be a consequence for that, otherwise it does not form a deterrent. Part of what you laid out, which is our strategy, is the deterrent effect that, if you do break those rules, there is consequence in that: either return, not being able to work or whatever it might be.

Q55 It strikes me that working illegally is one of the big problems because people come here and they may be in debt bondage. We have heard takeaway companies telling us that prices will go up if they cannot employ people who have arrived by irregular means, but they are breaking the law. It is against the law to employ those people.

Just to reassure you, part of the really significant work that we do with immigration enforcement criminal finance and investigation is to try to get into those companies and stop them employing people illegally.
Q56 Are you involved in that?
Yes, I am.

So that comes under your brief as well. We will finish with some questions on public disorder and small boat arrivals. I know that you touched on it earlier, but we are keen to explore it before we finish.

Q57 I will go back to some of the issues that Peter Prinsley raised earlier about the protests and public disorder on the south coast prompted by the small boat arrivals. What challenges does that create for ensuring that those travelling by small boat are intercepted and processed safely and securely?

I laid some of that out earlier, sir. First, there is the danger of their crossing, which is such an enormously long journey. Through our work with the French coastguard we actually get pretty good early warning that they are arriving. You can imagine that although we saw it as a possible scenario, we saw it as unlikely just because of the sheer distance they were crossing.

The first boat that arrived on 6th into 7th September was unexpected and the response was the best we could put together at the time. My team went down there to do the landside response, supported by Border Force. You will be aware that that came under the coastguard’s responsibility because the RNLI worked with them—they were tasked to do it. The marina they were taken into was the one that they were allocated, which, as it turned out, was less secure or unsecure and not where you would want to do it. You will be aware that there was a protest that turned violent. I commend the Hampshire and Isle of Wight police for being incredibly professional in terms of what they did there. It allowed us to remove those migrants.

We subsequently had two more. The second arrival was intercepted by the RNLI. Because the sea was incredibly smooth and there were only 49 young men on the boat, all of whom were fit enough, we cross-decked them from the RNLI vessels into one of my cutters, a law enforcement vessel—it is a 42-metre, grey funnel boat. We moved that up to Dover, where we disembarked them at Western Jet Foil in the way that we normally would.

That is not particularly easy. If you have people who are obviously suffering medical problems or children, that would be difficult. We have to do it in circumstances. The final arrival, because it was night and it was a significant number, we brought into the site in Gosport, which was secured by the police. We then moved them by road to Western Jet Foil, and then on to Manston for onward processing.

Q58 You touched earlier on the fact that only about 2% of cases are dealt with by the RNLI. You mentioned that one of the arrivals was transferred to one of the Border Force vessels. Why did that not happen in the first place? Why did RNLI come in and get involved at that point?

To be clear, we have the boats that operate in the short straits that are principally there to intercept migrant boats. The cutters, of which there are four, are coastal patrol vessels whose job is law enforcement, interdicting drugs and dealing with criminality. They are supported by some smaller coastal patrol vessels. Their function is not to do rescues, and they are not suitable for it because they have high freeboard and they are not designed to be able to do that.

But because we had it down there—it berths at Portsmouth—we were able to transfer the migrants to it, because of the difficulty that we had seen the first time with public disorder. We worked with the local chief constable down there, Alexis Boon . We thought that was the least-risk option, to move them by sea, but that is not a standard response for us to be able to do that, and we cannot always guarantee that we will be able to do it.
Q59 So why was it that the RNLI picked them up in that ? Who should have been picking them up? You said your cutters should not, so who should have been picking them up?
We patrol the short straits principally, where the majority of the risk is.
Q60 Your cutters would not, so who should have been there? You mentioned the coastguard.

Yes; but bear in mind, the thing that people do not actually realise that the coastguard in this country does not have its own boats. The coastguard works under the Department for Transport, but it does not have its own boats, which is why we have set the operation up in the short straits. The coastguard, if there is a mayday or an emergency will task any vessel that happens to be there or the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, which in this case was what responded to the vessels coming across.

They were in the right place. To put it into perspective, it is a seven-hour steaming for a boat to come from Dover to that area, so they could not be on task—and that day I think we had 500 arrivals in the short straits. They were occupied with that. The RNLI responded to that as it would to any other.
Q61 If that happens again, presumably the RNLI will be called into action again.
No, because we have an operational contingency in place where we will look to do those rescues.
Q62 Is that a new contingency that you did not have in place at the time?
That is correct.
Q63 How long did the crossing take?

The best part of two days. I think by the time they got to Dover they had been on the water for about 40 hours. By the time they were intercepted it was 30 hours. It is extraordinary. I can see what you are thinking: if that happened at this time of year, as the temperatures go down. Bear in mind that a lot of those people will have fuel burns from when the petrol mixes with the salt water in the bottom. I really do worry about this.

Q64 May I ask one more question? Sorry, I know we are running out of time. We touched again earlier on the protest, and also on people interfering with the rescue of small vessels. Could you tell us a bit more? It is obvious that that is hampering operations. You mentioned the contingency to stop the RNLI having to step in, but what contingencies have you put in place for this?

There are two questions. The first is about where the RNLI brought the migrant boat ashore at Eastney marina. You saw protesters in the water and at the tents that were rapidly set up to try to process the migrants, interfering with all of that. There were a number of arrests. That was really difficult.

Q65 Can we be clear that that is a potential impact on public safety? You cannot identify who the migrants are, and they could potentially just disappear. You would not know who they were, and the public are in danger because of that.

Yes , 100% . I do not need to say to you that there are safeguarding issues and vulnerable people. That is where we do the immediate lifesaving: getting people into dry clothing so that no one gets hypothermia, and making sure that no one is suffering from secondary drowning. All of that was really difficult because of the violence. You might remember that some of the people who were in the water were subsequently rescued by the RNLI, towards whom they were being violent. It was extraordinary.

For the second landing, we moved them by sea, so there was not an issue. The third one was at night. We could not do that and cross-deck, so the police put in a very significant operation to protect the site where we brought the migrants ashore, to allow us to do the initial triage and medical support and then move them out by boat. However, I will seek to avoid having to do that in the future by making sure that I have a Border Security Command vessel in that area to do those interceptions if we need to, while all the time trying to stop them in the first place.
That was my next question.
Obviously, it is about cutting it off at source. To be clear, the French want to shut this down as much as we do, for various obvious reasons. That is my main effort over this winter period.

Q66 To conclude, because I am conscious that we will suddenly hear some bells and Parliament will start again: from the public’s point of view, is it better for you to intercept these boats and process the individuals . They are going to arrive anyway , and w e do not want them arriving without you having the chance to deal with them and potentially identify the criminals and others who are there.

It is just that—and, of course, to make sure, because we are a humane country , that people do not die. We broadly have an incredible record for saving life when you look at the number of people who come across.

I agree with all of that. It is vital that you fix identity and get to them, and you can only do that if you intercept them and bring them back. It is an interception, and a consequence of that is that you save life. All of that is positive.
Q67 To conclude on the gangs, you must know who the gangs are, where they are from and what work is being done to tackle them. Is there work being done diplomatically with their source countries?

Yes, there is. We have talked before about the over-representation of Iraqi Kurds and Afghans in this. There are some now who have come in to this from sub-Saharan Africa, and we are working on all of those to break the links that they have to Europe and to prevent them from moving people to Europe. They are getting arrested and disrupted at a scale that we have never done before.
Q68 Duncan, do you have anything to add?
I just want to say how much I appreciate the work of Rob and his team ; I pay tribute to that.

We do appreciate that you are working in both the public and national interest, and we are very grateful for it. I recognise the frustration that people feel when they see th o se pictures, and particularly when they see things online , so i t is very good that you have set out that there is some misinformation out there , as well as why you do the work you do . Thank you very much for your time. I will conclude the session before the bells ring.

[1] Following the evidence session, Duncan Capps provided the following clarification: Further to my evidence at HASC, I just wanted to clarify a remark I made about the 2025 uncontrolled landing being a man on a jetski. An abandoned jetski was initially linked to the report of an uncontrolled landing on 6 September 2025 at Kinsgdown, but that subsequent investigations ruled this out as a Channel crossing attempt. This was what I had in mind when I made my jetski comment, but I confirm that the actual uncontrolled landing involved 5 people in a small boat, all of whom were successfully recovered on the day.

sessions.iT: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement
sessions.w: Department for Transport; Department for Transport; Department for Transport; Civil Aviation Authority

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement , HC 482
Wednesday 21 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 21 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Transport Committee m embers present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Steff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Daniel Francis; Alex Mayer .
Environmental Audit Committee member present: Mr Toby Perkins.
Questions 624 – 7 79
Witnesses

I : Keir Mather MP, Minister for Aviation, Department for Transport; Hannah Newell, Director for Heathrow Expansion, Department for Transport; Martin Gilmour, Deputy Director for Heathrow Expansion, Department for Transport; Tim Johnson, Interim Executive Director for Consumers, Markets and Communications, Civil Aviation Authority.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Department for Transport
– Civil Aviation Authority
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Keir Mather MP, Hannah Newell, Martin Gilmour and Tim Johnson .

Q624 Welcome to this morning’s evidence session. This is the seventh and final oral session in our scrutiny of the Government’s draft Heathrow expansion national policy statement. I would like to welcome Toby Perkins MP, who is joining us as a guest from the Environmental Audit Committee, which he chairs. Could I please ask our witnesses to introduce themselves, starting with the Minister?
Good morning, Chair. My name is Keir Mather, and I am the Aviation Minister at the Department for Transport.
Tim Johnson. I am the consumers and markets director at the Civil Aviation Authority.
Good morning. I am Hannah Newell, director for Heathrow expansion at the Department for Transport.
Morning. I am Martin Gilmour, deputy director for Heathrow expansion at the Department for Transport.

Q625 Thank you very much, and welcome. The draft Heathrow expansion NPS opens with the statement that “ The Government is committed to harnessing the opportunities Heathrow expansion creates ” and the second chapter is devoted to demonstrating what is termed a “clear need” for this development. However, the Secretary of State has reportedly said that the Prime Minister is “open-minded”. Is the Government as committed to this policy as it was in June?

Thank you, Chair. May I very briefly—I remember your encouragement for me to focus on brevity—thank all the members of the Committee for your continued scrutiny of the HENPS? I look forward to considering the recommendations that you put forward alongside the more than 27,000 responses that we have had through the consultation.

You are of course right to say, Chair, that the Prime Minister has emphasised the importance of the consultation process and of considering the views of different voices. We have been clear throughout the national policy statement review that we are going to carefully consider the views that we receive through the consultation alongside this Committee’s recommendations before we set out the next steps in relation to the HENPS.

As Aviation Minister, I of course realise that any decision that relates to a third runway at Heathrow will be absolutely consequential for the UK economy more broadly, but it is obviously normal for a new Prime Minister to want to look at the detail of what is a very large privately financed project. At the same, I fundamentally recognise that air connectivity plays an incredibly important role. Heathrow airport, as our international hub airport, plays a critical role within that. The needs case of the HENPS sets out the potential benefits of expanding Heathrow, and that they are significant, but ultimately the Government also have the four tests that would need to be met in order to facilitate expansion. That is exactly where we are in the process.
Q626 The Prime Minister has said that he thinks this is principally “a matter for London and Londoners.” How will that be factored into the Department’s analysis of the consultation?

I think the Prime Minister was rightly reflecting on the fact that community impacts that might arise from any planning decision in relation to Heathrow expansion would be especially felt by communities in London. I would hazard a guess that a significant portion of the consultation responses will be from affected parties in London, whether that be local residents or local businesses. That is why the HENPS itself puts a very strong focus on mitigating community impact and placemaking. The four tests have an especial impact in a London context. That is also why we sought the views of affected communities throughout the process. I went to Heathrow myself and met with the community groups most affected. I think the Prime Minister was speaking to the fact that this is a decision of enormous consequence for London.

At the same time, it is important to reflect on the fact that the Prime Minister also recognised the central importance of Heathrow to UK economic growth and resilience, and its status as an international hub airport in contest with the likes of Charles de Gaulle and Schiphol.

I think those two things can be true at the same time. Of course, this is a matter for London and it is of enormous consequence to London; at the same time, this is a national question and we have had a range of national answers to it through the consultation.

Q627 I think your Department’s own figures say that 900,000 people will experience more noise with expansion than without. Obviously, some of those are outside London, particularly to the west. If the decision will be primarily for Londoners, could the Mayor of London have a veto?
No, that is not the case. The Mayor of London has been—
Okay, fine.
I can go into that if you would like; otherwise, I will keep shtum.
Q628 Given what the Prime Minister said, if this is a project that is supposedly to benefit the whole of the UK economy, as you have just suggested, why should the decision be primarily for London?

It is not a case of it being primarily for London. It especially relates to London because of the community impacts I spoke about, but also, as you say, compliance with the four tests, including the ones about specific local impacts of air pollution and noise, and the economic and job creation benefits that could accrue from an expanded Heathrow airport.

In terms of the mayor’s role, he has submitted a representation through the consultation. He can have involvement in the DCO process, particularly through the examination phase. In terms of what the mayor is responsible for, any potential promoter of Heathrow expansion would have to work extremely closely with TfL, which the Mayor of London chairs. There are many ways in which the views of the Mayor of London, and of TfL especially, will be incredibly consequential to how any process around Heathrow expansion might unfold.
Thank you. We will move on to aviation policy.

Q629 On “for London and Londoners” first, Keir, how will that manifest itself democratically? There is a vote planned, isn’t there? Is it just going to be for London MPs? Surely, MPs from Hull and Edinburgh should let our London colleagues make the decision if it is for London and Londoners.

I can certainly allay your concerns on that point. Any vote on designation on a revised HENPS would require a vote in Parliament, which of course everybody would be fully entitled to vote in, and I would encourage them to take part.
Q630 So not just London MPs. Okay.
No, certainly not.

Q631 In an ideal world, we would be considering this proposal within the context of an up-to-date aviation framework for the UK. The current framework we have in the UK dates back to 2013, which was pre-covid, and our understanding of the climate emergency was different back then as well. Should updating the policy framework for aviation in the UK not have been the starting point before looking at Heathrow? Surely Heathrow has to fit into an up-to-date policy framework.

Hannah and Martin can speak to the especial reasons why Heathrow expansion needs a designated process through its own policy statement. I do not agree with the broader thrust of the question, about the fact that Heathrow expansion is being considered in a context where we do not have a general strategy for how aviation policy in the country is conducted.
Q632 Where can I find that strategy?
I think you can see it in the actions of the Government. We are facilitating—
Q633 So it is in the clouds somewhere; I have to piece it together myself. There is not a document?

It is not in one document, but it is in statute, for example. We have passed the SAF mandate and created the RCM, which is a world-leading way in which to pursue sustainable aviation fuel. We have consented expansion at Luton and Gatwick. We are doing some of the everyday fixes that the Prime Minister talked about around aviation policy to make the travelling experience better for passengers. We are pursuing a lot of work through the Department on aviation decarbonisation, and we are reviewing the jet zero strategy.

That principle of facilitating growth in our aviation sector, but doing it in a way that meets the UK’s legally binding carbon commitments and making sure that all the ancillary benefits of jobs growth, reindustrialisation and pushing more power out into local communities, which the Prime Minister has talked about, are facilitated through our aviation policy, does constitute an aviation strategy. It is a fair challenge to say that it is not contained in one document. I recall that when the Secretary of State gave evidence to this Committee—I think it was almost a year ago—she said that if there is a call from the sector to produce a consolidated strategy for aviation, that is certainly something that she will consider. In the meantime, we are advancing those priorities through a lot of different avenues.

The only thing that I would add to what the Minister said is that Heathrow is a nationally significant piece of infrastructure, so it is subject to the Planning Act 2008. That is why we need a national policy statement to take forward any expansion. The previous airports national policy statement only applied to Heathrow, and one of the reasons why we have renamed the HENPS for this post review is to clarify that it only applies at Heathrow. In terms of capacity elsewhere, that is subject to the making best use framework, a policy framework that was introduced in 2018. Since that was put out, we have seen applications come forward, some of which the Minister has mentioned. That is where that sits in the aviation strategy ecosystem that the Minister explained.

Q634 Some people who live next to other airports and already feel the impact of noise, air pollution and all those things are a bit befuddled that we are spending so much time on this airport when they are living next to one that causes them just as much discomfort, inconvenience and so on. They wonder why, as a Committee, we are looking at Heathrow but not their airport, whether it is Gatwick or elsewhere. It feels like we are missing something, because this is a national policy statement and was a chance to look at all aviation as a system in the UK—I know it is bigger than just the UK. Instead, in a national policy statement, we are just looking at one airport. It is not even just a London policy statement, going back to this “London and Londoners” thing.

In the consultation, we asked whether we should review that making best use framework—should it be updated, and if we were to update it, what should it cover?—recognising that that applies to the airports outside of London and the south-east.

It is a fair challenge to ask how we are working across the piece, and you are right to say that there is all this attention on Heathrow airport, and if you live near Edinburgh airport or Glasgow airport, for example, and have concerns about air and noise pollution, you might wonder what the Government are doing in that space. I would say that a lot of the ancillary policy questions that affect Heathrow expansion are national, and we are advancing work on them.

If you take airspace modernisation and the refresh of CAP 1616, which is going to allow for quieter, more efficient journeys that will hopefully reduce noise for local communities, there is an impact of that. The fact of the matter is, though, that at the same time, Heathrow airport has been operating at almost 95% capacity for, I think, two decades now, and the rest of the London airport system, I believe, is scheduled to be at full capacity by the mid-2040s. This is a pressing question for us to consider on a national basis because of Heathrow’s value not only as our international hub airport and the resilience that gives, including to airports like Edinburgh that facilitate connections in for longer-haul connectivity, but because of the enormous amount of air freight that is moved through Heathrow—I think that 24% of the value of imported goods to the United Kingdom move through that single airport. So it is of national consequence, but you are right to say that our aviation policy needs to serve the whole United Kingdom.

Q635 Yes, but a lot of that value is gold that goes backwards and forwards—it is an interesting area, but I do not understand why we have to do that quite so much. In terms of airspace modernisation, I do not speak for Edinburgh, but they would say that the focus on Heathrow is delaying the modernisation of airspace right across the UK because it is soaking up all that capacity.

You touched on modelling of air passenger numbers up to 2040. One of the challenges is that we do not have a long-term predictor of demand for air travel, particularly beyond 2050. Is that a concern, when we look at the economic benefits of this?

You are right that the model runs to about 2054. That runs for one year of the airport being at full capacity once all the capacity is increased. In the economic appraisal we extrapolated those benefits out to a full 60-year appraisal period, and that is in line—
Q636 But Heathrow said last week that it might not reach full capacity until 2059, so we are getting pushed further into that really uncertain period.

I understand. What I would say is that that is in line with the standard approach that is taken in transport appraisal. Obviously, the model is an ongoing focus for the Department. We continue work on it to keep it up to date, but that is the approach that we have taken for the HENPS.
Q637 Do you think that standard is good enough for this project, though?
We have conducted the economic appraisal—
Q638 Because in all sorts of ways it is getting special treatment, isn’t it?

We have done it in line with standard transport appraisal guidance. We have used the peer reviewer that I know the Committee has seen previously to look at the work that we have done and the work that Frontier have done, and I think it is as it needs to be for the purposes of the HENPS.
Q639 Keir, overall, how compelling do you think the economic case is for expansion?

It is worth saying that the research that has already been conducted shows that if expansion does proceed it can create economic growth right across the country. It is obviously right to acknowledge that the economic case is less when compared with the 2018 ANPS. We can talk about the range of factors as to why that is the case, such as planning increases at other UK airports and reduction in the number of business passengers.

However, separate analysis carried out by the Department for Transport shows that the cumulative benefits of the scheme could create between £39 billion and £52 billion-worth of benefits for UK passengers and the wider economy, and a lot of that growth can be centred on areas outside of London and the south-east of England. I think it was Dr Laird who said in the evidence that he provided to you that that is still high in terms of rate of return for a mature economy that is already very well connected.

In terms of meeting the expectation that Heathrow is critical to economic growth, but also that the benefits of that growth are accrued across the United Kingdom, the case for it is there, but I also will not say to the Committee that it compares in the same way as it did in 2018, because it does not.
By a factor of 10.

I also reflect on the fact that it is about economic growth, but also economic resilience. It is about the comparative disadvantage of having not expanded the airport compared with where we are now with the capacity constraints that we might see. Through that air freight piece, but also through the question of international connectivity through a hub airport, I think it is critically important that we reflect on what the resilience impacts may or may not be of not expanding Heathrow airport in that context. Whereas other countries have moved far ahead to cement their status with their international hub airports, whether that be in France, Germany or Turkey, we are in a position where Heathrow is at 95% capacity, and we need to think about those broader questions in that context. It is a resilience question as much as it is a growth question.

Q640 But Heathrow choose to operate at 95%. They could operate at 80% if they wanted to. That is just where they are. This comes back to a point that we have talked about previously: how much capacity do you think we should reserve for resilience? I am going to stop the Chair quoting the point she often quotes, that we just need an extra runway with no extra flights to give us the resilience we need at the airport. How much capacity should we reserve at the airport just for resilience—or should we use 95% of capacity again?
It is a good question. We need to facilitate Heathrow expansion so that we can build resilience in—
Q641 They are going to want to use all the capacity, aren’t they?

That would be the argument. Resilience is critically important. The argument that you would make in the context of expansion is that facilitating growth in a sustainable way through a phased approach could be the way in which that expansion happens.

There is also a broad piece around making the existing footprint of the airport work better, perhaps through terminal modernisation. The HENPS reflects the fact that if expansion goes ahead, it will need to be facilitated in a phased way through an increase in those things that facilitate resilience, whether that be surface access schemes or terminal expansion or how you get passengers through the airport. I am not sure if I am landing exactly on what your question is, but that resilience has to be baked in across the process.
That is fine; I know it is not easy.

Q642 Can I pick up a couple of points? First, on the aviation strategy, or lack of, you talked about environmental groups and communities near other airports, but the concern about the lack of an aviation strategy that we heard was principally from people in the aviation sector themselves. For instance, where is the strategy for the place of aviation in facilitating freight or domestic connectivity? On domestic connectivity, we found a lot of support for the idea of getting more flights from the regions to Heathrow, but nothing on the mechanism of how that would happen—apologies, because this may come up in later questions.

On economic growth around the country, y our own Department ’ s figures showed that a lot of the growth around Heathrow and west London would be at the cost of some of our UK regions. Many of the regional airports are not in great financial shape and are worried about losing business. They are very reticent about going on the record, but they are not coming four-square behind Heathrow airport’s expansion this time around like they were eight years ago.

Those are all fair challenges. From the perspective of regional aviation, there are a number of regional airports that are behind Heathrow expansion because of the greater benefit that it could accrue to them by facilitating connectivity to that hub airport. Hannah may want to speak in a moment about what the HENPS specifically includes to facilitate growth in regional aviation. You are right to say that, in some of the modelling, forecasted long-haul connectivity does decrease at certain airports. In a lot of the Prime Minister’s comments, he reflected on the fact that regional aviation is central to the success of our aviation sector in the UK, and that we need to reflect on that as we go through this process.

I recently met with the trade organisation representing small airports, and they set out some of those same concerns about connectivity to airports and the fact that the cost stack is increasing due to international and domestic factors, which make the cost of doing business challenging for them. They raised air freight in that context. We know the impact that East Midlands airport and a number of other airports have on our freight resilience and connectivity. If there is a consistent call for an air freight strategy or a way in which we look in one consolidated way at aviation strategy across the United Kingdom, I would be very keen to hear those calls from the sector. In the meantime, we will carry on working through all the policy questions that we deal with on a daily basis, but it is my responsibility to serve the best interests of UK aviation. If the Committee wishes to reflect on how we could go further through the HENPS, whether in relation to m aking best use or those broader questions, we would be very glad to hear that feedback.
Q643 Are you suggesting that it might have been better to have the aviation strategy put in place before the proposal for a runway 3 at Heathrow?

No, that is not quite what I am suggesting. Whether it is in aviation decarbonisation through the creation of a framework to facilitate SAF production in the UK or consenting to airport expansion at Gatwick, Luton or London City, the Government are getting on with the job of supporting UK aviation. The question remains, however. If there is a call for a strategy that addresses all these questions in the round, that is an appeal I would be very keen to hear, because we want to be as responsive as possible in meeting the needs of the sector.

Q644 Minister, your own Department’s analysis, even now that it is updated, has a negative net present value for Heathrow expansion. Why do you think expansion is a good idea if society does not benefit from it overall?

It is a very fair challenge. I think I set out in my previous answer to Scott how some of those economic benefits accrue in ways that have perhaps not been reflected in some of the analysis that we have seen, in terms of Heathrow expansion potentially generating tens of billions of pounds of economic value, and that value being accrued in areas outside of London and the south-east of England. You are also right to challenge me on the net present value. I would say that that does not account for all the anticipated impacts and benefits that Heathrow expansion could bring. That is why the Department commissioned that extra analysis from Frontier Economics, which looked at key impacts that sit outside of the NPV calculation. It found positive GDP benefits in all modelled scenarios and indicated that those benefits could support growth across the country. It is also worth saying that freight benefits that could result from an expanded Heathrow are not fully included in any of the appraisal or modelling undertaken. In 2024, that represented £216 billion-worth of imports and exports to and from the United Kingdom. There are ways in which the NPV does not account for the entire potential benefit of an expanded Heathrow, but it is a fair challenge to raise. I do not know if we want to add anything else on that front.

The only thing I would add to what the Minister has said is that in providing an application for development consent, any promoter would have to demonstrate that their application met the economic growth test, which would also seek to address that. The work we have done at this stage—the economic appraisal and the spatial computable general equilibrium modelling by Frontier—looked at the scheme level and the case for the HENPS. At application stage the promoter would have to demonstrate that what it was doing met all those requirements.

Q645 The difficulty for us as a Committee is that we started this process six weeks ago with one set of figures. A supplementary piece of evidence has now been given to us with a different set of figures. Even that supplementary written evidence accepts that the revision will mean that further results will be presented in chapters 9 and 10, on the technology development scenario and the scenarios and sensitivities analysis, but those results are not yet available—the Government will produce them in due course. Combined with that, we have the issues around the welfare analysis in the HEAR, and the GDP comes from the Frontier model. Why did we not try to look at those in a combined way and combine some of those aspects? The difficulty we currently have is with the level of information that we have and that not being combined. What is the rationale behind that and how do you propose to bring it forward?

In terms of the technical issue, I know that the Committee has had a letter from my colleague at the Department. That was about the modelling at Gatwick and a scenario that the modelling produced, and which had not previously been seen, regarding the constraint on runway and terminal capacity. Because of that, the HEAR did not capture all the ensuing, expected passenger benefits. We have now corrected that and written to the Committee with an update on it. The punchline is that that will increase the benefits from expansion but not our overall conclusions. Regarding whether we can combine the work of the S-CGE modelling and the economic case, as I said they look at slightly different things. The S-CGE modelling looks at the impact of an intervention such as expansion on the wider economy—at what business, investment and trade opportunities arise. The economic case does the pure benefits versus costs: how do you stack them up? We are looking at whether we can bring those two together and combine them in the way that you have suggested. That is a complicated process because it involves the risk of double counting, so we want to do it in the most analytically robust way. We are working on that and hope to provide an update on it alongside the final HENPS.

Q646 I hear what you say on the written evidence, but on the two aspects I referred to, the supplementary piece of written evidence, HEN0088, “Updated figures will be published alongside the Government’s consultation response.” So you are accepting that this will continue to move and we will receive those after we have made our comments on that.

In the inquiry we have heard about potential economic and business benefits, and particularly about losing the international competitiveness of having a hub airport. I think there are some compelling arguments on that point, but we have struggled to find figures. Do you have figures that you can produce to us on that aspect?
On which aspect, sorry?

We have heard consistently that, other than growth, one issue is the competitiveness with Schiphol and Charles de Gaulle, but no one has really been able to produce any figures to evidence that. Do you plan to produce figures in due course about why we would lose our competitiveness as a hub airport if we do not have a third runway?

I think the way that that manifests itself in the work of the economic appraisal report—the HEAR—is in what we forecast to happen in terms of capacity and where we expect that capacity go. Underpinning the work of the appraisal report are assumptions made about traffic that routes through Heathrow and otherwise would not have done so, or traffic that routes through other airports. I think that is how that is addressed through the economic appraisal report. Martin, do you agree?
Yes, that is correct.

Q647 Lastly, chapter 2 of the HENPS talks about the potential economic and strategic benefits of Heathrow expansion but not the environmental and welfare costs. Why does it not comment on those and what is your position on that?
As in, why is the NPV not included in the HENPS?
Yes.

The reason is that we see the HENPS and the HEAR as two documents that sit alongside each other. There is lots of information in the HEAR. What we sought to do in the HENPS is the planning framework, so it summarises the strategic case and the needs argument. The HEAR should be seen alongside it. In the HENPS we also set out elements like the economic growth test and the other tests that we would expect any application to meet.
Q648 Is that the same reason why the NPS does not set out the net present value?

What we tried to do is use the existing ANPS and update it for ease of comparison. The figures in the HENPS use the same figures for comparison as the ANPS, rather than introduce new ones, but as Hannah said, those figures are in supplementary documentation, setting out the whole case for the NPV and what is included. Obviously, those environmental disbenefits do form part of the NPV, and they are set out line by line in that supplementary documentation.

Q649 I have one question of clarification. I am looking at the detailed figures for your economic case, in appendix B of the letter of 24 September. Table 2 shows the number of displaced passengers versus new passengers, and it shows that if runway 3 goes ahead, up until 2050 the vast majority of new passengers at Heathrow are displaced—in other words, taking a journey to or from Heathrow as opposed to another airport. Is that correct?

It is right that we model the whole system. We do not just look at airports; we look at the movement of different passengers between them. I would have to look at what specific level of displacement versus new passengers is on that, but it is also modelling the cost, so some passengers who can afford to—

Q650 This is just the passengers. It says: “Additional Heathrow passengers with expansion under the central current trends scenario, no cost pass-through case, compared with no expansion.” For example, in 2045 the business share will be 94% displaced and 6% new passengers, and the leisure share—which is the vast majority of Heathrow passengers—will be 87% displaced and 13% new passengers. That suggests that an awful lot of passengers using runway 3 would have otherwise been going in and out of other UK airports.

People want to fly from Heathrow. That places a big demand on it, and people are willing to do that. People’s preferences and choices of where they fly is an important part of the model, and that is why we see a lot of demand at Heathrow. On the specific displacement figures, we would have to come back to you.

The other element is that this is as the system fills up over time. By the 2050s, the system is more full, but in the period where the system is less full, you do see more displacement. It is about the longer-term case as well as the medium-term impact.
I suspect Scott is going to pick up on why passengers make the choices they make.

Q651 Martin, you made a comment about people wanting to fly from Heathrow. Surely people want to fly from their local airport. There is nothing special about the coffee at Heathrow that makes me want to go via Heathrow. What do you mean when you say that people want to fly from Heathrow? If I live in Edinburgh, surely that fact does not hold true.

What I am saying is that when you provide capacity at Heathrow, it fills up very quickly. Because of the routes, connections and access that it provides, that is a factor, among many other variables, that is accounted for in the model.

Q652 But does that not become circular? If you had an aviation strategy, maybe destinations to and from those other airports would flex depending on what is happening at Heathrow. These decisions are not in isolation from each other.

They are not in isolation, but this process is happening concurrently with the expansion in capacity at other London airports, which will facilitate greater connectivity from them. We are operating in a context where, by the mid-2040s, London airport capacity will be more full, and Heathrow expansion could be one means of facilitating a greater ability to deal with that in a more resilient way. But that is not to say that that would disadvantage the ability to fly from Gatwick, Luton or wherever else. People also choose to fly from Heathrow because of its connectivity to routes that otherwise are not served by London airports, which is an important factor in the context of this conversation.

Q653 To explore that a little more, there is an interesting difference in passenger choice between those who are using Heathrow to fly out of the UK and those who are attempting to get in. As someone living in the north, lots of my journeys overseas have been from Heathrow or Gatwick, but that is because that was the only choice available to me. Is there a difference between the choices that UK passengers are forced to make when they are going on their holidays overseas, and the choices of passengers flying into the UK, who might prefer to get to London as their holiday destination? Has there been any assessment of how much this is satisfying the demands of overseas passengers versus UK-based passengers?

We may have to come back to you on that one. It goes back to the point that I made, although probably not very well. This is about the system growth over that period, and the growth in demand that we expect to see over that appraisal period. When we look at the breakdown of the model, we see long haul growing out of destinations other than London over that period as well. By the time you get to the 2050s, you are seeing growth elsewhere. To go back to the point, there is a nearer-term impact that I think is what the letter is getting to, but I am very happy to come back on those points in more detail.

A resounding theme coming from the Committee, which I will be certain to take way and reflect on, is whether we need one approach for looking at some of these questions in the round. I would just say that—quite jealously, as a northern MP—I share your sentiment and I would like to see better long-haul connectivity from the likes of Manchester. They have expansive plans to facilitate that, and the Department for Transport also has a responsibility, alongside considering these questions, to think about how best we can facilitate that.

In my view, however, that does not change the overall calculus that Heathrow serves—and will continue to serve—as the UK’s international hub airport, with connectivity to certain parts of the globe that could not otherwise be efficiently or effectively served from other airports. Therefore, we need to think about these specific questions in that context. I would like to see long-haul connectivity increasing at a broader range of airports across the United Kingdom, and I will reflect on how we can do that in a more joined-up way.
