But that is the basis upon which the DCO application would be approved. You would have to set out a credible path for meeting those targets in any case before you began, even if phasing meant that X or Y project came online at a different time.
And also for managing the impacts of that construction-based traffic, as you mentioned.
Surface access has been a major issue for many of the aviation industry witnesses that we have had. Daniel, are you done on question 18?
Yes, although I could have carried on with the Piccadilly line and the Elizabeth line, et cetera.
Q744 There is a requirement for promoters to set out a credible plan for future rail enhancements. What does that credible plan actually look like?

As we have discussed, the targets that overlay it provide a tangible basis upon which to design the respective schemes. In terms of what comes in the HENPS now and what would come through the DCO application, we have to be cognisant of the fact that phased delivery of airport expansion, and the concurrent impacts on the number of passengers travelling to the airport, will require different rail schemes from different parts of the country to the airport that are delivered at different times.

Therefore, it is not wise to be too prescriptive in saying that X or Y scheme must be delivered through the HENPS. It is better to have a top-level way of linking the public transport targets with when ex pansion is likely to occur , in a way that mitigates the impact on the SRN, both through construction and through greater access. It is deliberately flexible to allow promoters to explore a range of schemes, but ultimately, it has to be done in the context of meeting quite stretching targets.

Q745 The HENPS and the strategic vision refer to rail surface access to the west and south, but they obviously stop short of explicitly promoting or requiring either. Why did the Government not consider it necessary, given everything we have talked about regarding our climate obligations and the public transport mode share targets? Why didn’t the Government see it as necessary to include that within these documents?

I suppose that returns to quite a fundamental question about h ow the process is designed, which also came out of the multi-promoter question . That is about whether being more prescriptive leads to more specificity in the meeting of targets. With that, you lay out exactly where you are going to go over time. Alternatively, does more flexibility allow for more diversity of approach in how a potential promoter might bring schemes forward, and for greater flex about how you might do it over time, given that this is a major infrastructure project that will have implications for things like carbon budgets on a multi-decade basis?

The HENPS, as currently constituted, has more of an emphasis on flexibility to allow the range of options to be explored. We have spoken a lot today about affordability, deliverability and not setting expectations that cannot be met. The risk of being too prescriptive is that you stumble into exactly that sort of jeopardy. That is why we have taken this more flexible approach to the surface access and multi-promoter question s.

Q746 Tim, the CAA’s surface access policy currently prevents Heathrow from fully funding any rail schemes that have beneficiaries beyond airport users, but of course if there were to be southern or western access, that would obviously benefit others. Given what the Minister said about these schemes having to be privately financed and that there will not be any taxpayer support, who will ultimately pay? Will this be sorted out before the DCO process?

We have an established policy, and we will consult on potential changes to that. As I said, I think the policy will need to take account of any requirements set during the planning process. Our starting point is our statutory duties and thinking about the interests of consumers, but we recognise that this is an issue that will need to be resolved. We will be consulting shortly on that surface access policy.

Q747 We have had a few bits of evidence that raise concerns about there not being limits, meaningful failure points or an objective basis for determining what becomes an unacceptable impact. In the first instance, I would like to hear your view about how a developer or an application might fail these tests, and how you propose to respond to that feedback.
I certainly take that feedback on board. If there are concerns about compliance with either of the tests, with regard to it not being sufficiently tangible, I would be very glad to hear them.

I will take them both in turn. With the air quality test—of not producing air quality impacts that result in new breaches, or that make existing breaches of legal obligations on air quality materially worse—I think that is a pretty tangible, firm and measurable basis upon which to measure compliance with that test. Similarly, noise is compared with a 2024 baseline, which is measurable.
As I say, I would be very keen to hear more about where we can go further.
Q748 Okay, it is measurable, but what happens if there is a breach? What is the enforcement?
The tests are fundamental to consenting to a proposed expansion—
Q749 What if they are breached after the fact?

Within the HENPS, there are a number of mitigation measures that need to be met. There are also safeguards in place in terms of compliance and how to have retroactive compliance assured if a promoter does not meet the obligation. I do not know whether there is anything—
Q750 Assured? So some sort of scheme that would compensate and pay out?

I think the detailed monitoring, enforcement and compliance need to be worked through. At this stage, we are setting out that we would want to see modelling and projections that you can meet that test over the life of the scheme, and hopefully that gives confidence that it has passed the test. However, in order to provide confidence and trust in that process, you would then need to set out, as part of the DCO, how it will be monitored and tracked over time. In the event that it is breached because the modelling was wrong, you would need corrective action.
Q751 That is very helpful, because we can’t predict the future, can we? This all becomes a little meaningless if there is no real enforcement or consequence.

I don’t want to drag us back to CNGI—I want to take us back there purposefully and productively. How would you answer the charge that, as long as the mitigation hierarchy has been applied, the tests are really not very meaningful?
I would disagree, because I have been at repeated pains to say that approval of the project is contingent on the four tests. It would be quite hard to see how they are meaningless.
Q752 But the presumption in favour means it is unlikely that the residual impacts will ever outweigh the need for this classification.

The mitigation refers to residual impacts, so after you have done everything to mitigate, compensate and reduce—that all still applies in terms of the hierarchy. In the event that there are still residual impacts, such as additional traffic or anything else, it is then that you are weighing up whether the strategic national need outweighs what is left at the end after you have done all of that hierarchy of interventions.

Q753 I do not want to repeat your own words back to you, but the possibility of filling in some more information—some clarity—might be worth seizing here. Just to reinforce that, on your answer to the question of where this sits, whether it is in DCO conditions or in the HENPS itself, both promoters and communities would be reassured to have expectations more clearly signposted. You sound like you have committed to doing that. Is that a fair assessment of your response?

Those sorts of sentiments have come out as part of the consultation process. Of course, they have been raised by you today and may form part of the Committee’s recommendations. I am very happy to take them away, reflect on them and think about how we might address them.

Q754 It seems likely that, over the next decade, we are going to improve our air quality standards and move them closer to the WHO guidelines. As part of this process, we can assess the airport plans against the existing legislation, which is quite dated, or we could choose to think about how that will improve over the coming years. Do you think it is right to go for that legal minimum, rather than move towards something that we know will protect health much more?

It is an interesting debate. I think the test has been set as it is because it gives us criteria to work off, which gives you an ability to form a clear and objective assessment about whether the test is likely to be met in a way which is established, which has legal precedent, which is measurable and which is ultimately enforceable. The purpose of the test is, of course, to achieve the objective you set out, which is to protect public health over time, but we need to do that in a way that ensures, to the greatest extent possible, that compliance can be linked to, if that makes sense.

Q755 Yes, but it is dated. In terms of public health, I think the HENPS says that it is acceptable for some of the improvements in air quality around Heathrow to be unwound—for air quality to get worse. That is not acceptable, is it?

I think the wording says that, while a worsening of air quality is not on its own a reason to refuse development consent at that stage, you still need to pass the test and show that, first, you have reduced it as far as possible and, secondly, not resulted in any new breaches or made existing breaches worse. It is not saying that there will be no change in air quality, but it is setting a limit for what we think would be acceptable.
Q756 These improvements have been hard fought, and despite the legislation being a bit out of date, it was much welcomed. It is not great that air quality is going to get worse, is it?

The air quality test in the HENPS has been updated to reflect the Environment Act 2021 and new requirements around particulate matter. We would consider that it has been updated to reflect current standards on air quality.

Q757 There is still a lot of uncertainty about the health impacts of ultrafine particles. Do you think those are adequately assessed within the process, or are you hoping and looking for more from the people who are bidding to undertake this work?

We know that it is an area of increasing concern. We talked earlier about non- CO 2 impacts. This is another area where there is not yet scientific consensus about the impact and how you can mitigate that.

Q758 It is not about the consensus, is it? What about the operators? Can we expect them to have looked at the evidence and to show that their plans meet the best evidence base possible in terms of protecting people from these particles?
I would expect them to do that as part of the process, yes.

Q759 The draft HENPS requires “significant adverse impacts” from noise on health and quality of life to be avoided by limiting or reducing overall aircraft noise, but that throws under the bus those tens of thousands of people who do not currently live underneath the immediate landing or take-off paths but will do under runway 3. You are using 2024 as an acceptable baseline, despite the ANAS and ANNE studies suggesting that people are more annoyed by aviation noise than was originally understood, and at lower levels. Why was 2024 an acceptable baseline?

I think 2024 was chosen as the baseline year because it was the most recent data available at the time, and it is considered to be a reasonable but challenging baseline year, given expected technological improvements coming down the track.

It is also worth saying that the ANAS and ANNE studies were considered as part of the draft HENPS, with modelling undertaken at these levels as a sensitivity test. We are trying to factor that work into noise considerations, and that applies as much to those who could be newly overflown as those who are in the noise envelope of Heathrow currently.
Q760 You rely on aircraft being technologically better and reducing the noise emissions. Should the HENPS have a backstop if the forecast noise reductions are not achieved?

The test is there, in a sense, to serve as a baseline upon which approval would be granted. In response to Steff’s question, we set out how you would re-achieve compliance if it were not met under a theoretical scenario.

Through the work the UK does at the International Civil Aviation Organisation, we have a strong expectation that technological improvements will reduce the noise impacts of aviation by between 0.1 dB and 0.2 dB per year. We based our assessments on noise impacts on the lower end of that expectation. We are trying to be as rigorous as possible. That is why the 2024 baseline year is quite a challenging target, but one that is measurable.

Q761 We are never going to get to the point of having glider passenger aircraft—certainly not for long haul—so there will never be no noise impact, particularly for those living within 4 or 5 miles of the airport underneath the direct paths that cannot be varied. The DCO for Gatwick’s runway project provided funding for residents at three levels, starting from 54 dB equivalent, yet the HENPS requires funding from the much louder 57 dB equivalent. Why did not you use the same approach for Heathrow as for Gatwick? Noise is noise, whichever airport you live close to.

I think the answer to that is that the threshold for Gatwick was developed through the DCO process and reflects the circumstances of that project. Mitigation measures are decided on a case-by-case basis. We have proposed a threshold. It will then be for the applicant to come forward with their proposals for how they would mitigate it, to be resolved through the DCO process.
Q762 Is it too late to change things so that the figure in the DCO is equivalent to the Gatwick figure?
We are consulting on the noise test. If people think that level is not right, we will listen to that as part of it.

Q763 The DFT obviously thought that 54 dB was appropriate for Gatwick. Why should you have to live in a louder environment before you are entitled to any insulation just because you live near Heathrow?
If the Committee wishes to reflect on that in its recommendations, I will certainly take it away and review it as part of our process.
Q764 Okay. Certainly, Gatwick airport thought that provision would be fair as well.

This is nothing to do with runway 3, but I have just written to both the CAA and you, Minister, about the inordinately slow roll-out of noise insulation. Thousands of people are eligible for it but less than 200 have actually got the noise insulation works that they are entitled to under previous expansions at Heathrow. Given how slow the process is, partly because of Heathrow’s own foot-dragging and partly because of CAA rules on what the airport can and cannot spend on mitigation, what confidence can the public have that requirements and commitments made during the process for runway 3 expansion will be enforced and delivered, given that they are not being enforced and delivered at the moment?

I will turn to Tim in a moment, but I believe it was through the 2018 ANPS that it was required to pay £3,000 for noise compensation. Taking off my HENPS hat for a moment, if west London MPs have concerns about the speed at which that is being rolled out, that is a very live concern for me. When I went to Heathrow airport and met with community groups, something they consistently raised was that you learn to live with noise, but it has a lifelong impact on your ability to live a happy and fulfilled life. I can certainly take that away.

What I would say, in terms of the draft HENPS and how it encourages a potential promoter to go further in terms of community compensation and statutory blight, is that the Secretary of State expects that compensation requirements go much further and that you have a comprehensive package of support for affected communities. If the Committee’s view and the view of respondents is that the existing level, which has been carried over from the previous ANPS for ease in order to have that conversation, does not go far enough, I would be very glad to hear it, because we want to make sure that a potential promoter does not just meet the bare minimum, but goes a lot further.

I cannot predetermine the Committee’s work, but it would be interesting to look at that through two lenses: the question of the actual amount, and the speed and the expectation by which roll-out of any potential mitigation and compensation scheme might occur.

Q765 I think that normal people who are not immediately affected would assume that the mitigation would be in place before the flights started rolling in, yet we have had terminal 5 with us for 25 years and we are not even now seeing the conditions that were imposed as part of its planning application.

Tim, Heathrow Airport Ltd tell me that they are constrained in meeting their current requirements for noise mitigation, free bus travel and other sustainability and environmental delivery by CAA rules about what they can and cannot spend money on. How would you ensure that the future regulatory model will not compromise delivery of the commitments and mitigations that the local community has been led to expect and is being told will all be fine under any expansion?

We understand that this is a really important issue for local communities. Through our price control process, we set an envelope for Heathrow. It is absolutely a matter for them to make sure that they make these schemes available within that envelope, but we will also challenge Heathrow on what they propose to spend. You will be aware that in the current two-runway configuration, they spend roughly £10 million a year. That is the allocation. They proposed a fivefold increase in that, and we did not feel they had sufficiently justified that in their initial application. We have not made final decisions on that. We recognise that it is an important issue.

Q766 Part of the noise insulation spend is going to be cut in the next period because Heathrow did not spend up to their required amount under the previous period. It sounds like you are going to be responsible for even less money being spent on noise insulation than in the last period.

We are not reducing the amount. Their current budget allocation for it is £10 million a year. They have proposed a fivefold increase to £50 million a year. We are in the process of reviewing that. Their initial justification was not clear. We have final decisions coming up on that in the next couple of months. We do recognise that it is an important issue, and we would expect to hold Heathrow to account to make sure that they make these schemes available so that it is easy for the public to take them up.

Q767 Minister, you touched on accountability and enforceability. Stakeholders, including MPs, community organisations and local authorities, find it really difficult to get any sense of anybody being interested in enforcing the conditions that are there. Are you proposing anything different or more beefed up as part of any decision on a third runway, so that affected communities will get what the decisions say they are entitled to?
As Martin said earlier, this is an area that we are thinking through at the moment. It has been a theme of the consultation responses.
We would be happy to discuss it with you.
I know it has been a theme of the evidence that you have heard as well. It is certainly an issue that we are thinking through.

When I went to Heathrow airport as part of the consultation process and met with the leadership at Hillingdon council and with local community groups, I heard of a whole range of ancillary issues that have been created by the operation of Heathrow airport. We all acknowledge that the airport is critical to UK air connectivity and provides thousands of good local jobs and everything else, but there are negative externalities that have occurred as a result of it that go beyond noise and air pollution. You think about issues to do with community degradation, antisocial behaviour, crime—those are all things that I take very seriously as Aviation Minister. Separate to this process, I would like to reassure you, in terms of working productively with CISHA and the airport to get round the table with community groups and address some of those problems, that is something that I am interested in facilitating as Aviation Minister.
CISHA, which was not even engaging with MPs and I did not even know about until six months ago.
If there is space to go further, we must go further.

Q768 A lot further. Can I talk about fixing figures for community compensation? In the Gatwick DCO, there is an amount per home. Our predecessor Committee recommended against fixing figures for any kind of compensation because they need to be assessed subject to need, particularly for noise insulation, and of course prices change. Why has the HENPS doubled down on stating fixed figures at this stage?

The HENPS has carried over the figure from the 2018 ANPS. It is worth saying that any compensation package would have to receive scrutiny as part of a planning proposal, and therefore there is space for analysis of different options there. In terms of whether you want to be prescriptive with a particular figure, I am happy to consider that as part of the Committee’s reflections and our review going forward.

Q769 Tim, when we were discussing the slow progress of insulating homes and so on, you seemed to be saying that that is an affordability issue for the airport, so it has to be managed over time. But every time I go to Heathrow airport, there is something new getting built. As the regulator, are you saying that expanding car parks and so on—I am putting words in your mouth—is more important than providing insulation to these homes?
No, we are not saying that. We are saying that there is a range of requirements—
Q770 So where does this sit in the priorities for you?

As with any expenditure that Heathrow wish to pass onto consumers, our job is to make sure it is justified, proportionate and efficient. In their initial submission for the current price control on the two-runway operation, we did not feel that the justification was significant. Similarly, we have pushed back and asked them to provide additional justification on many other areas that they have put forward. We apply the same level of scrutiny across the board. Heathrow clearly invests a lot of money every year, and we need to make sure, on behalf of consumers, that that is—
Which consumers? Who are your consumers?
Q771 Apologies, but are you saying that you do not think it is good value for Heathrow to spend money on providing insulation to homes? I do not want to put words in your mouth.

We are not saying that at all. All we are saying is that if Heathrow want to pass some costs on to consumers, whether it is for insulation, new car parks or a new terminal, they need to demonstrate the case for doing so with some evidence and demonstrate how they are going to incur those costs efficiently.
Q772 What if Heathrow does not want to spend the money but the local authorities or local communities think the money should be spent?

Ultimately, Heathrow has to put forward the plan. They can use a range of evidence. As we have seen in Gatwick, I would imagine that out of the DCO process there may be some requirements around this, and I would expect Heathrow to factor those into their case, and in the DCO process—this goes for any other promoter that gets a DCO—would need to say, “Look, here’s the planning condition. This is what it requires us to do, and this is how we are going to deliver that outcome efficiently.”
Q773 But if you don’t think it is efficient, it will not go ahead. That is the challenge, I guess.

We say, “We understand that you need to deliver an outcome that has been specified, and the question is how you do so efficiently.” It would not be for us to say, “There is a planning condition”—if there is one, or another legal requirement—“and you don’t need to meet that.” We take that as an input; it is how we deliver that.

Q774 Where does the cost—the health cost, say, or the local congestion cost—fit into the negative side of the net present value calculation? Are they all taken into account, or are there other factors, such as the health cost or the congestion cost, that either have not or have not sufficiently been incorporated into that plus-and-minus calculation that has led to the NPV?

Those externalities are taken into account in the NPV, as calculated in the HEAR and the supporting work. The full detail of that is set out in the economic appraisal report. Just to delineate the process, as Tim said, the HEAR sets out the NPV of doing the thing—the case for expansion and expansion as a whole. In the course of submitting their application, they would set out the things that they would do, including in relation to noise and those things. Once those are determined, the CAA would not debate the toss on whether they should do it; it is in the efficient delivery of it that the CAA would take a role and a view. That is the basis of the negotiation—if there is any—that is happening between the airport and the regulator.

Q775 As a general observation, the CAA’s core role is safety and the economy, and local economic welfare, local health and so on are either not the CAA’s responsibility or elsewhere, which is why it comes back to Government and what they require in the HENPS and the subsequent DCO.

However, there might be a broader question to answer there, while respecting the independence of the CAA, about how the DFT might better facilitate conversations on that matter, and that theme came out through the community consultation I did.
Q776 It is not just conversations, but teeth.
Exactly. I will happily take that away and think about how we can do better.

Q777 The Committee has heard evidence that the Longford conservation area will be demolished if expansion goes ahead, and about the case of a vibrating barn. Does the HENPS provide any additional protection in terms of dealing with risks to heritage, beyond what exists in planning law already?

There are sections in the HENPS on heritage. I think we would want to come back to you on the specific detail of what those requirements are. Yes, heritage is important, but I would want to double check the specific detail of how far that goes in relation to current planning law.
Q778 If you found out that it was basically the same, do you think there would be any case for having something more specific, given that we know almost precisely what is likely to be lost?
Would that be better placed for conditions placed as part of a DCO proposal in respect of a specific scheme put forward for delivery, perhaps?
Martin Gilmour indicated assent.

Q779 Thank you very much. We will produce our report on the draft HENPS by 26 November, as you have requested. That is a tall order, and I would like to thank all the Transport Committee team—the core team and the additional support we have had—for all the work they have done and will be doing in very short order. Minister, could you set out the next steps for the Government after 26 November?

Absolutely. May I reiterate my genuinely heartfelt thanks for all the work the Committee has done to move so quickly on this matter? We will consider the 27,000 responses we have had to this consultation, analysis and the Committee’s recommendations very closely before we set out our response and our next steps. I reconfirm to the Committee that any amended HENPS would be published, laid in Parliament and subject to a vote prior to having legal effect. As I say, at this stage in the process, we will carefully consider the responses and then set out our next steps in due course.

Thank you. Thank you very much to all of you for your evidence and the time you have spent preparing for today. If there is anything you did not get a chance to cover, or to cover adequately, please feel free to write to us—you did make a couple of references to that in your answers. That concludes today’s meeting.

Watch t he meeting
Members present: Emily Thornberry (Chair); Fleur Anderson; Alex Ballinger; Aphra Brandreth; Richard Foord; Abtisam Mohamed; Edward Morello; Sir John Whittingdale.
Questions 1-5 3
Witnesses

I : Catherine Belton MBE, Author and investigative journalist, The Washington Post, John Lough, Senior Research Fellow and Head of Foreign Policy, New Eurasian Strategies Centre, and Dr Ruth Deyermond, Senior Lecturer in Post-Soviet Security, King’s College London .

I I : Dr Nigel Gould-Davies, Senior Fellow, International Institute for Strategic Studies, Craig Kennedy, Associate, Davis Center for Russia and Eurasian Studies, Harvard University, and Isaac Levi, Europe-Russia Policy and Energy Analysis Team Lead, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Catherine Belton, John Lough and Dr Ruth Deyermond.

Q1 Welcome to the Foreign Affairs Committee’s first oral evidence session in our new inquiry on Russia. We will hear from two panels today, the first focusing on Russian domestic politics and society, and the second on the Russian economy. Can I ask the witnesses to introduce themselves?
Hi. I am Catherine Belton. I am the author of “Putin’s People” and I am a reporter with the Washington Post writing about Russia.
I am Ruth Deyermond. I am a senior lecturer in post-Soviet security in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, and I work primarily on Russian foreign policy.
I am John Lough. I am the head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, which is a think-tank that was founded a couple of years ago with seed funding from Mikhail Khodorkovsky.

Q2 Thank you all for coming. Let me start at the most general level, and then we will come down into more specifics. People watching this session may never have been to Russia, or may have been but many years ago, so will you paint a picture of what Russia is like these days and how it may have changed recently for ordinary Russian people?

The picture in Russia has changed a great deal, especially this year, when Ukraine was able finally to bring the war home to many Russians. Before then, Russian society had become increasingly militarised. Of course, there were a great many ordinary Russians agreeing and volunteering to go and serve in the war because they were being given massive payouts by the state to risk their lives on the frontline, and many wives were encouraging their husbands to go there so they could get the money, but life in the biggest Russian cities, despite sanctions, was pretty much going on as usual. The restaurants were still full; people were bustling around going shopping. Yes, perhaps you would not be able to buy the latest Louis Vuitton handbag because of sanctions, but goods were coming in via routes through Turkey, India, and Kazakhstan and central Asia, and if you closed your eyes and shut out the Kremlin propaganda, you could really try to pretend that life was the same as before the war.

This year, that has really not been the case, because you have Ukrainian drone attacks reaching ever deeper into Russia—to Moscow—and hitting oil refineries. People have really felt the impact of strikes, too, on Wildberries, the Russian e-commerce giant.
Q3 That is their equivalent of Amazon, isn’t it?

Yes. People have really been feeling the strain on their pocketbooks as well. As I said, in previous years, restaurants and shops had been bustling; this year, there has been a record amount of restaurant closures, and shops are shutting down. That is because the Russian budget is coming under increasing strain. The Kremlin had to impose a massive tax hike at the beginning of this year, and it is forcing a lot of normal consumer companies out of business.

So people are feeling it now. It is a much bleaker situation. Everywhere, you would see patriotic posters and advertising for people to sign up for the war, but there is not the same enthusiasm for this any more. You see this in the opinion polls. In a poll in August, 66% of people believed that things were only going to get worse. That was a level that we had not seen since the years of the Soviet collapse.
Q4 That is very interesting, and really helpful and comprehensive, but is there anything that you want to add, Ruth?

If we are looking at the very big picture for people who are not as familiar with Russia, just to give some context to the picture that Catherine painted, we are over 25 years into Putin’s presidency now, so we have really two generations of adults who have grown up with an authoritarian Russian Government.
Q5 Has there been a period when there has not been an authoritarian Russian Government?

The 1990s were different, partly because it was chaotic and the political centre was weak, but there was pluralism, there was media pluralism, there was civil society to a degree, and that really went—
Q6 And that was a change from forever, in terms of Russian history—just so we get the broad sweep.
Yes, precisely. There was this brief window when you did not have a highly authoritarian Government, although the Yeltsin presidency in the 1990s certainly was very far from an ideal democratic one.

The degree of authoritarianism that Putin brought to the presidency has slowly expanded. Initially, there was a big wave of authoritarian crackdowns on media and political dissent in the noughties during the second Chechen war, and it has grown much worse, of course, since the start of the full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022.

The reason I mention this is that Russia now has at least two generations of people who have known nothing but Putin’s presidency, and that, I think, makes it very difficult for people to conceive of a world where Russia looks different and behaves differently.
Q7 John, is there anything else?

To build on what Ruth said, 30 years ago I was working in Moscow as a NATO official, and I struggle to recall how, in that world, in which there were obviously tensions between NATO and Russia because of NATO enlargement but Russia was co-operating with NATO, it seemed that Russia was trying to build a relationship, particularly with Europe, that would solidify some of the positive changes that had taken place with the collapse of the Soviet Union. Instead, we have seen this re-emergence of what I can only really describe as muscle memory. Russia now finds itself in a posture—the notion that confrontation is natural, “The west is our enemy”, “Britain only wishes us ill”; all this sort of thing—with which I think a good deal of society feels actually quite comfortable. People have really very easily fallen into line.

One must also say that there is a high degree of repression in Russian society at the moment. You have people being sent to jail for 12 years for a Facebook post or something that supposedly maligned the Russian army, or for giving $10 to the Ukrainian army or something like that. This is a really very nasty, very repressive system, and it was difficult to imagine 30 years ago that Russia could turn so quickly back in that direction.

Q8 Thank you. That takes us to the next question: how resilient do we believe Putin’s regime is? We hear that it is renewing itself, but how is that going? To what extent does Britain’s approach to Russia reflect an understanding of what Putinism is? Is it anything? Is it an ideological project, or is it simply a response to the actions of the Russian state? Does it hang together as an ideology? Is it renewing? How resilient is it?

First, it has proved over the last five years, while facing this hurricane of sanctions under various pressures of war, that it is in fact very resilient. It certainly has a strong ideological content to what it is doing at the moment, which is proving to be quite effective in motivating the ruling class.
Q9 Could you explain what the ideology is?

The ideology is one of Russia having a distinctive place in the world; feeling that the world is governed in an unjust way by a group of western countries that have simply got too big for their boots; and that there is a chance now to re-engineer the global system to the advantage of countries such as Russia. What goes hand in hand with that is the notion that Russia should have certain rights in Europe. It should have the right to establish a zone of influence on its borders—a buffer zone, if you like—or what a former Russian President called a zone of privileged interests on Russia’s borders.

It has now embarked on that project in a very serious way. In my view, there is no reason to believe that at the point at which the war in Ukraine comes to an end—though I do not see that happening any time soon, at least as long as Putin is in power—Russia’s appetite is going to stop there, assuming it holds on to those territories it has already seized, and maybe even extends its influence further into Ukraine.

There is a very coherent worldview here, that is, of course, allied to a notion of how Russia should be governed. That is on a strongly centralised model, which has been substantially refined over the past 25 years. As Ruth said, in the ‘90s there was certainly pluralism in Russia. If you looked at the way the regions of Russia interacted with the federal centre, it was very different. We have moved far away from that model, which might have been some sort of embryonic parliamentary system, to something that is heavily centralised, autocratic and very much in the Russian tradition.

To maintain that system requires preserving an enemy, and we are currently the enemy, or part of the so-called collective west. I am sure you will want to talk about this in more detail, but the UK is definitely singled out as playing a particular role.

Q10 I have heard you speak about this before. Forgive me if I have got it wrong but, essentially, the focus has historically been America although is obviously not now. We are now enemy No. 1 in terms of Russia’s focus. The rhetoric certainly focuses on the UK, is that correct?

The rhetoric has focused in recent years, particularly since the start of the big war in Ukraine, very heavily on the UK. I would say that Germany is now starting to compete for that attention, as the No. 1 hostile actor.

In the case of Britain, you have to understand that this history goes back hundreds of years. For the most part, our relations with Russia have been difficult, confrontational and indeed adversarial on occasions. We are seen as being a civilisational other, if I can put it that way, with our tradition of liberal democratic values, and things that simply contradict so much of what Russia thinks about the world and how the world and societies should operate.

For that reason, there has historically been a significant degree of antagonism. There have, of course, been moments when the Russian elites have indulged in some Anglophilia. I think Britain is admired in certain ways. There is the tradition of Peter the Great, and all that sort of thing. It goes back a long, long way. There is an expression in Russian that implies that the English woman is always doing bad things in Russia—Anglichanka gadit—and every time anything goes wrong these days—
It’s the women! I know you didn’t make up the phrase, but we just want to be clear about this.
I shall explain. Because England—Angliya—is a female noun in Russian, it goes from that.
Oh, I see. It is not English women.

It is not pointing at English women as such; that needs to be made clear. To this day, when things go wrong in Russia, very often the finger is pointed at Britain, which must be the malign actor that has somehow brought it about.
Q11 Is there anything you want to add, Ruth?

Just a couple of things on Putinism as an ideological project. In addition to what John said, which I entirely agree with, it is important to recognise that Putinism taps into a wider and much older ideology of Russia as a bearer of a distinct civilisation and as having a unique role in the world that is radically different from, but perhaps in a similar style to, the idea of American exceptionalism.

That is also deeply and intimately connected to the idea of Russia as a great power—not just Russia as a state that happens to be a great power at any given moment, but Russia as a state that is destined to be a great power. Being a great power is essential to Russian national identity and, as one Russian official said recently, if Russia is not a great power, Russia is nothing and does not exist as a state. That obviously has implications for Russian foreign policy. It also has implications for the way that the Russian Government understands the immediate past.

To go back to the 1990s, this was a period when Russia was not by any measure a great power, except for the continued possession of nuclear weapons and the fact that it has a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. By most measures, Russia is still not a great power, but the responsibility for that failure to be a great power clearly cannot be anything to do with Russia itself; it must be the fault of external malign actors who want to bring Russia down. There is the narrative about Russia’s immediate past and the end of the Soviet Union, as you can see in Putin’s recent speech to the Valdai Club, but the way that they talk about the 1990s and later is always in terms of Russia having been betrayed by the west or Russian naivety leading to Russia being undermined by a malign west—historically, as you said, particularly the United States, but now particularly the UK.

I just want to go to the point about the resilience of this system and how much the Russian elites have united behind what John described as a very coherent worldview that they are seeking to redraw the global security map to redraw global trade. The war in Ukraine is to some degree an opportunity to do that, because it can gain various leverages. At the outset of the Ukraine invasion, Putin wanted the west to give Russia various concessions, including the return of NATO to its 1997 borders. These were the discussions before he went ahead with the invasion, and this is what he is seeking to entice the west into rehashing as part of the discussions over peace in Ukraine and so on. These are his ultimate objectives.

Of course, most of the Russia elite have lined up behind Putin’s war, even though many of them were shocked at the invasion. They did not know or believe that it was going to happen, and they did not think that Putin was going to rip off the mask in such a deliberate way. Every other incursion or interference that he had had in foreign countries before that had always been done with a measure of plausible deniability. Whether it was the Salisbury poisonings or the death of Alexander Litvinenko , there was always an excuse or a reason why it was not actually the Kremlin’s hand, but here you had missiles killing Ukrainian civilians and so on. Most of Russia’s elite will line up behind the Kremlin agenda, but only if they perceive that the Kremlin is winning, so it very much depends on the moment.

Earlier this year, in April, we began to see Putin’s ratings plummeting to lows not seen since the start of the war. We had signs of fissures within the Kremlin elite. There was Sergei Kiriyenko, who was the first—

Sorry to cut across you. We have so many ideas coming out at the moment, which I think will spark a lot of other questions, so we will come back to what is happening in relation to the Opposition and the strength of Putin in the face of that. Shall we start with the Duma elections? Fleur, perhaps you could ask some questions on that.

Q12 I am Fleur Anderson, the MP for Putney. I have a couple of questions, so that we can understand the State Duma elections, which happened from 18 to 20 September, a little bit more. I will start with you, Ruth. What do the election results signal about the confidence of the Putin regime’s control of the Russian political system? What should external observers read into the election results? Beyond the crazy numbers, which we are obviously very envious of, what should we be considering when we look at them?

I do not think the Duma elections tell us that anything radically different has occurred, because in many respects, Duma elections have looked the same for a very long time. Some of the attempts to control the nature of the elections—to control the outcome—have been certainly interesting and potentially significant. I am thinking particularly of the fact that Yabloko , the only anti-war liberal party in Russia, was blocked from standing in these elections, which tells us something potentially about anxiety around creating a space for opposition to express itself electorally. Yabloko has been around since the 1990s, so the fact that this party was not allowed to stand for the Duma elections now is noteworthy. Beyond that, I will defer to my colleagues.
Q13 John, do you want to add to that? Also, what is the significance of 60 new deputies who fought in Ukraine now entering the State Duma?

First of all, I would not dignify this spectacle that calls itself the Duma elections by describing it as real elections. We know that the Kremlin was always going to manage this process, and it did succeed in managing it quite effectively. But as Ruth was saying, having to take one party off the ballot at a very late stage was embarrassing, because the Yabloko party was expected to probably get about 1% to 1.5% of the vote and therefore just be a convenient decoration for the authorities, who could then say, “Well, look, we give people this choice of a liberal party with democratic views, and our society just doesn’t buy it.” Then, suddenly, the internal polling was showing that the party—which had a 43-word programme, by the way—was actually probably going to do rather better, because its message was that the war in Ukraine needed to be ended; it was running on a peace ticket. That, in itself, is very interesting and suggests that the Kremlin, as always, is worried about how to manage certain attitudes in society.

Beyond that, we have this combination of the United Russia party and then these loyal parties, the Communists among them, who are all basically aligned on foreign policy and the war and so on, but on what one calls domestic policy, they have some slightly different emphases when it comes to the economy and how resources should be distributed.

You refer correctly to one of the most interesting elements of this spectacle, which was the encouragement of war veterans to run. Some of these people have been specially schooled and put through programmes to prepare them for Parliament and then roles in government. There are now well over 40—maybe nearly 50—of these people, who, it has to be said, have varying degrees of experience of the war in Ukraine. Some have just been there for a few weekends in a drone unit far from the front, and others have been on the front. Some, indeed, are accused of war crimes. It is a mixed bag. When the first Duma session took place after the election, there was something like a 20-minute standing ovation for these people, which indicates that they are receiving a certain status.

Putin has been trying to encourage the notion that a new elite is being established in Russia—these deeply patriotic people who are going to play a role in shaping the country’s future. We could see on that first occasion with these people in their military uniforms, standing up in the Parliament, that this process is well under way. Where exactly it is going to lead, and whether those people are going to become a problem remains to be seen. Probably those in Parliament will be less so, but the networks around them—the war veterans, particularly those people who have been accusing Putin of being weak in his conduct of the war—are likely to play some sort of role in Russian political life, simply because of the number of veterans coming back with all their PTSD and the lack of access to adequate services for people who have been seriously physically injured. We know from the experience of Afghanistan that these groups can become very well organised and often criminalised and will present a challenge for the authorities.

Q14 We are going to continue with some more questions about the opposition and the Duma, but I have two other more general questions first. Catherine, as a Committee we have done a report on disinformation in which we talked about Russia and looked more into this. What is the strongest evidence we have that Russian disinformation efforts targeted the Brexit referendum here? Has that targeting increased, evolved and changed with social media and AI and what should we know about that?

I am afraid that I have not researched Kremlin disinformation efforts on the Brexit referendum. I was writing my book at that time, and I was not looking deeply into this. However, we have seen how this whole ecosystem has evolved in the Kremlin, and I have been lucky enough to have access to some intelligence materials which show the role of Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy head of the Kremlin administration, and his role in directing various political strategists in concocting a whole machinery of disinformation and seeking to undermine western support for Ukraine in France, Germany, Spain and the UK. We have seen documents on the orders that have been given. This is almost the second front in Russia’s war against Ukraine. It is almost as important as the military battle itself, because if you have undermined western support for Ukraine, then the battle is won. They have poured huge resources into this—it is so important for them.

As I was starting to say before, the strength of the cohesion around the Putin regime depends first on how the war is going in Ukraine, but secondly, how the west is reacting and how the west is doing in comparison. Earlier this year there was a great deal of concern because not only were Ukrainian missiles hitting targets deep into Russia, but Trump was starting to praise Zelensky for the deep strike campaign. He was basically saying, “Yes, it is an escalation, but this is an escalation that might bring an end to the war.” Putin was no longer enjoying such cosy relations with the American President, and Europe had been showing this remarkable degree of unity that no one really expected and was continuing to funnel huge amounts of money to support Ukraine’s war. However, in a matter of months the Kremlin and the entire Putin elite seem to have changed their view because they see that the winds are again changing and the disinformation campaigns that have been going on since the start of the war are having an impact.

We can see the rise of the AfD in Germany, which parrots Kremlin talking points. Its representatives recently travelled to Moscow. They are talking about reopening the Russian gas pipeline, Nord Stream. Russian disinformation stokes the fears in Germany that they are going to face an energy crisis by winter and that they are going to run out of gas supplies and that they need cheap gas. We saw how many voters in east Germany really buy into that, which was one of the reasons for the success of AfD there, as well as this fear that somehow Europe is going to be pulled into war. The disinformation networks very ably stoke that.

Putin and most of the Russian elite are looking at Europe. They see the riots in France, as well as the rise of Marine Le Pen and the fact that she was saying, “Well, we can’t afford to give any more assistance to Ukraine.” They then think, “Okay, this war has been very difficult. No one expected it to go on as long as it has—it has now gone on for longer than world war two.” Earlier this year, the members of the Russian elite who I was speaking to just had their head in their hands, saying, “We don’t see any good way out of this.”

However, it has flipped 180 ° in a matter of six months, because they see that unity in the west is now crumbling. Some of that is due to the disinformation campaigns, but it is also obviously due to our own political problems, which they leverage for their own needs.

Q15 Can I ask a follow-up on this? We heard about the Ukrainians attacking data centres in Russia, and that it was having an impact on the number of right-wing bots and the traffic on X in the United States. I am sure that Members, who are used to having a certain amount of nonsense on their social media, have found that there has been a decline in it. Is this part of a fight-back? Are you able to answer questions like that? Where is this coming from? Is this a co-incidence?
No, I am afraid that some of the reporting on the diminishing activity of Kremlin bots was perhaps exaggerated or misreported.
It is misinformation on disinformation.

Yes. There had been a very narrow look at a few days around the attack, but there is always a big spike in Kremlin bot activity on Putin’s birthday, which is 9 October. The data centre attacks were straight after that, so there was a very natural dip.

There is a very good tracker of Kremlin bot activity called Antibot4Navalny , and it showed over a longer period of time that, in fact, the bot activity has not really diminished from the average. It is just that there had been a spike a few days before because it was Putin’s birthday. I am afraid that the Kremlin bot activity is not dependent on those data centres being hit.

Q16 I would like a very quick answer to my next question please, Ruth or John, if either of you have more evidence about that Russian disinformation. In general, what would you say are the most common misconceptions that western policymakers have about Russia today? Is there anything you would like to say to us and to Parliament about misconceptions that we have about Russia that we should know about? Just in a brief answer, before we move on.

A couple of things quickly. One misconception is that Russia is simultaneously both a great power and vulnerable to collapse, but I do not think neither of those things is true. There is an anxiety about what is going to happen to Russia that drives broader western thinking—I am afraid that you could see it in the Biden Administration—and that includes western thinking about the war in Ukraine, as well as wider approaches to Russia.

Beyond that, there is a more general assumption that is much more evident in some other European countries—perhaps, above all, in Germany—that once the war is over, Russia can return to being some kind of relatively normal international actor with whom the UK and other states can do business to a degree. I think that fails to recognise the extent to which the Russian political elite, which includes not just Putin but the people around him—and, to a degree, Russia more generally—see the west as an existential threat to Russia. That is not something that is going to change, unless there is a radical change in regime type in Russia.

Q17 May I return to the question of the stability of the Putin regime and the opposition? With the fall of the Soviet Union, we saw the colour revolutions sweep through a lot of former Soviet countries, but in Russia there has never seemed to be any concerted attempt to change the nature of the regime. After Boris Nemtsov’s death and after Alexei Navalny’s death, there was a brief flurry and then it all disappeared and went quiet again. Is it that there isn’t any great feeling that this is an unrepresentative, wicked regime that people would like to remove, or is it that the opposition exists but it is simply not possible to organise? To what extent do you think that there is a groundswell against Putin within Russia itself? John, why don’t we start with you?

Those are big questions. First, the elites, by and large, are not happy with the way Putin has got Russia into the war in Ukraine, a war that he can’t really win satisfactorily on his terms. My view is that, as a result of what he has created in Ukraine, we are going to have a smouldering situation there probably for decades. So this is a real mess. And, of course, he has then complicated their lives and the running of their businesses because of sanctions, which are probably going to hang around in some form for a very long time.

As far as Russian society is concerned, we have to keep it in mind that it is atomised and the authorities have done a great deal to ensure that it stays that way. So you don’t have the type of horizontal linkages in society that you have in, for example, Ukraine. This is what makes Ukraine’s example so fascinating. If Russia were allowed to develop in a less autocratic, top-down-driven model, you would probably see many of those things appearing in Russia. In fact, we were starting to see, in the noughty years, as volunteer networks and other things were forming and with the way charities were working, that it was not dissimilar. But, for historical reasons, Ukraine is much more advanced in that respect.

There is no real opposition, joined-up opposition, to the current regime. The authorities will do everything to keep it that way. So at what point might change come in Russia? It is going to be driven by the elites. Society may be instrumentalised for that purpose, but change is not going to come from below. We have to be very clear in our understanding of that. The question then arises: are there ways in which we could incentivise parts of the Russian elite to think differently about their interests, in such a way that the interests of the state could then be somehow moderated? We are only at a very early stage of trying to understand that particular puzzle, but it seems to me that is where change in Russia is going to come from.

Russia is a country where change can happen very suddenly. This regime has many strengths, but it also has clear vulnerabilities, and the biggest vulnerability is Putin’s heath and his ability to run the system currently. But it is also brittle in the sense that because rule has been so heavily centralised, it is not good at crisis management. If it has two or three crises to manage simultaneously, that is when it starts making serious mistakes. The laws of biology are, of course, working against Putin and those of his closest associates who are well into their 70s, and it seems to me that we are going to see, certainly over the next decade, some probably quite fundamental change in Russia.

Q18 You mentioned Putin’s health. He is 74 years old; he is not going to live forever. Does he have a plan for succession? Are there heirs apparent? What do you think the dynamics might be if something were to happen to Putin?

I will speak briefly. We can see some of the manoeuvring already within the Russian elite. I mentioned Sergey Kiriyenko, the first deputy head of the Kremlin Administration. Before the Duma elections is really when you see some of the tension coming to the fore, in the infighting that arises in the Russian elite at times of tension. For instance, earlier this year—over the summer, when they thought the war was not going their way—there was an ally of Kiriyenko and others who were somehow popping up and speaking freely publicly. There was a former Kremlin lawyer called Ilya Remeslo , who went viral for daring to say that Putin was a war criminal and a thief, and should go to jail. This was somebody who used to work for Sergey Kiriyenko in the Administration.

Observers who were watching then were saying that it was a real bunfight within the Russian elite over Russia’s direction. There was rising discontent over the prolonged war. In an interview, Remeslo said that half the Kremlin Administration were not behind Putin’s war and thought that it had gone on for too long, and they had hoped for a negotiated settlement through Trump, so that they would be able to walk away with Donbas, and have their cake and eat it. Obviously, when that did not happen, the tensions came to the fore. You could see Kiriyenko fighting against hardliners in the FSB.

It was also partly a battle over internet restrictions, which the hardliners and the FSB had been behind, but which caused a lot of disgruntlement in the Russian elite, because they are used to a very digital society and suddenly they could not access basic services, conduct phone calls over WhatsApp, or anything like that.

You could see the manoeuvring, and in some ways Kiriyenko is continuing it. He has his own faction in the Duma elections; it is a political party called New People. One quite prominent political commentator was saying, “Well, you know what? In some ways, it doesn’t matter how much the Kremlin ruling party win in this upcoming vote, because this might be the last Duma election for Putin.” It is a six-year term; according to normal Russian life standards, Putin might not be around at the end of this Duma. Then, it does not matter whether United Russia is behind Putin or not. Maybe Kiriyenko would seek to scoop up those votes and bring United Russia to join his party, New People.

Kiriyenko is really the front man for a more progressive, technocratic wing in the Kremlin that would like a more pragmatic relationship with the west. I do not think they would ever give up this idea of great power competition, but they might want a return to Russia’s integration with the west, as long as they can continue to compete, and they might be more willing to make some concessions on Ukraine than hardliners in the FSB, who still want the war to be prosecuted ever more toughly.
Q19 I can see some scepticism on Ruth’s face; maybe you would like to share your view.

A little bit of scepticism, as it relates to foreign policy. It is important to recognise that since the start of the war, and it was actually happening before, everything about the Russian state has been geared towards war. The economy has been re-geared to prioritise war, as have the structures of the state. The penal system is very taken up with prosecuting people who have the temerity to object. Even the education system—five-year-olds are being educated to be warriors, right? They are being dressed up in little uniforms, given little toy guns and taught about the great patriotic war—the second world war—and they also have visits from veterans of the war in Ukraine. This is a state that has been re-geared for existential war, including existential war with the west.

Although there might be some changes—in fact, I am sure there would be some changes—and possibly a desire to kind of pull back a little from the war in Ukraine, I am afraid that I do not think you will see anything really fundamental changing until you have a change of regime type in Russia.
Q20 Can anything be read into the Wagner mutiny—the Prigozhin attempt at a coup? Is something like that possible in the future, or was that very much a one-off?

It certainly sets a precedent. It shows it is possible. We do not see where that challenge would come from currently. Looking forward, if Putin’s authority in office weakens because of his health and his inability to carry out his duties as before—the way he manages all these different factions and interests is a job of manual control, and it is fair to assume that he would probably not do it as well in his late 70s as he did 25 years ago—then that can open up opportunities, because systems this kind can weaken very dramatically at that point.

The view in my institute, the NEST Centre, is that when Putin goes—and that is assuming he either dies in office or is unable to carry out his duties—we are probably going to see a period of collective leadership akin to what happened at the end of Stalin’s rule. Similarly, just as it took three or four years for the next Soviet leader to emerge unchallenged, we could see something of that kind.

If you put that into the mix and fast-forward a little bit, the generation of people who are likely to be the players in that configuration will have grown up in somewhat different circumstances. I do not think that they will necessarily have the same obsession with the idea that the collapse of the Soviet Union was the greatest trauma or this sense that Russia was mistreated in the 1990s, which is what Putin demonstrates. He comes back to that again and again—that Russia was deceived and that western countries took advantage of Russia’s weakness. I think they will be imbued with something else.

Q21 Can I come back to your answer, John, about where the opposition lies? You s aid it was most likely to be the elites. D o y ou not see the efforts of people like Open Russia to try and promote some kind of popular movement—democracy, in whatever form it might emerge—as a realistic future for Russia any time in the foreseeable future?

Not for now, although I would like to think that if it is possible to preserve Ukraine’s independence and for Ukraine to develop successfully as an independent democratic country—and Ukrainians would most certainly be capable of doing that if they were not being attacked by their neighbour—we would see a very important example being set. In this case, the fact that Russians in many cases think that Ukrainians are the same as Russians—which of course they absolutely are not, but this is in the Russian mindset—could have an enormous impact on Russian society as a whole and give encouragement to those parts of the elite that think that Russia needs to be governed on a different model and that the whole Russian state needs to be reorganised. We could potentially see some very dramatic change, but if it were to happen, it would take place over decades rather than five or six years.

Q22 Are you suggesting that if there is a succession resulting from Putin’s removal—for one reason or another—and the elites step in, then their attitude towards the west might be different because they might not have the same experience and knowledge of what went before? Are you suggesting there might be a willingness to reach an accommodation , which Putin clearly is unwilling to even consider?

There might be, but a lot will depend on what western countries can offer and how they can possibly incentivise some of those groups to change their behaviour. Let’s face it, there are others who are invested in confrontation, making money out of it and see their futures in that paradigm. That does not mean to say that it is all going to be stable and will go forward in the form that we see it today. It will be challenged and will undergo some significant change.

Q23 I am interested in the attitude of ordinary Russians. Dr Deyermond, you were talking about the militaristic society. I remember the “Mr Nobody Against Putin” movie, which was the most extraordinary exposure of the way in which children are being brainwashed. Do you think that has had an effect, and that the vast majority of young people and ordinary people in Russian buy into the idea that they are defending the motherland and it is under threat from these wicked western countries? Is there that sort of popular support for what Putin is doing?

I will be very careful in my answer because, of course, it is difficult to get clear evidence. Given the nature of Russian authoritarianism, it is difficult to say this with a high degree of confidence. Certainly, one thing you can see that has transmitted itself, at least in my experience, through the generations, away from the generations that remember and resent the Soviet collapse, is, as John was saying, a deeply conspiratorial attitude to the west—the idea that the west is engaged in a whole succession of conspiracies against Russia. Those conspiracies range from the large scale—trying to bring down the Russian economy in the 1990s—to the really trivial.

I will quickly give an example. A couple of years ago—or slightly more, now—a group of Russian students who I taught were absolutely convinced that when Hillary Clinton gave Sergei Lavrov a reset button to mark Obama’s reset and accidentally misspelled the Russian word for “reset”, that was not an accident; it was a deliberate conspiracy to humiliate Russia by showing that the west did not care about Russian. You find those kinds of attitudes quite often in my experience. That view of the west as engaged in a large-scale, ongoing conspiracy against Russia is going to take a lot of work to overcome. In that regard, the UK and other western countries should be reinvesting in Russian-oriented free media. Clearly, the BBC World Service is vital, even more so given the Trump Administration’s cuts to similar programmes in the US. If the UK and other western states want to see even the beginnings of a different kind of Russia, that has to start with things such as addressing disinformation and making clear, accurate information available to Russians through media.

Q24 That is something I have a great deal of sympathy with. Catherine, you have done an enormous amount to expose the corruption and the way in which the Putin regime operates. Do you think that what you have revealed in your publications has reached into Russia? Are people aware of the kind of things that you managed to uncover? I know that they have waged a campaign to try to shut you down, but to what extent are people becoming aware of the reality of the Putin regime?

I do not think people in Russia, to a great degree, really care about corruption in the elite. It is, by and large, expected that the Tsar of Russia should live in a palace. As long as they are buying into the Kremlin propaganda—that Russia is trying to reassert its rightful role on the world stage; that the west has been acting against Russian interests and is trying to tear apart the country and break it up; that their feelings as a great power are somehow being attacked—then most of them do not really care about corruption at the top of the Kremlin, but again it depends. Most Russians are starting to feel that the war is now dragging on, and that the losses to the economy and to society are becoming too great. We see the fall in ratings for Putin, despite the outstanding result in the Duma election, which, of course, was rigged. So yes, the corruption allegations can have some impact, but they are not as important as the overall direction of the economy.

Going back to John’s point about ways to incentivise groups in the Russian elite to take a more accommodating stance towards the west in future, I still disagree with my colleague Ruth because there is still a significant element within the Russian elite who made their fortunes in the 1990s and remember different relations with the west and how that was. We have also seen an increasingly vocal stance from those groups this year, including from some who are close to Putin.

The chief economist of one of Russia’s biggest state banks, VEB, gave a presentation in which he said that Russia cannot win a war of attrition with the west. Therefore, if the west is to change the stance of Russian elites, it has to continue to show unity and show that it continues to be able to fund Ukraine and is not going to diverge from that goal. We also had German Gref, who is a very close ally of Putin indeed and is the head of Russia’s biggest state bank, Sberbank, allow himself to publicly dare to say, “ But, a ctually, everyone wants this war to end as soon as possible. That is all we want.” That was earlier this summer.

I therefore think that that group still exists, but the only time they are willing to put their heads above the parapet is when things do not look to be going well for the regime. Also, in September 2022, when Putin was forced to withdraw from regions such as Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and so on, there were Russian billionaires who were sort of whispering then. Of course, they would not say it publicly, but privately they were saying, “If there are further military losses like this, we are going to see a palace coup. Something will happen. Putin’s legitimacy and standing will not be able to withstand it.” Again, it is all dependent on the outer environment and how they consider Putin to be doing in this wider war.

Q25 I would like to touch on media freedoms. Dr Deyermond, you referenced the importance of the west perhaps being able to support people in Russia in receiving more independent news. How do you think that might work when Russia controls the media coming in and there are various restrictions there?
Of course, that was also the case in the Soviet period, and the impact of western media was enormous at certain points in the Soviet Union.

Obviously it is difficult, because the Russian Government took steps to limit access to a free internet and therefore the availability of alternative news sources and information sources. States continue to try to promote freely available Russian-language information for that reason. I do not have technical expertise on this, so I do not know what the good workarounds would be for the restrictions, but it is something that we need to be focused on because it is critically important. Sorry, that was a rather vague answer.

Q26 That’s fine. This one is perhaps for you, John. I recently read a report by Amnesty that came out in September, which referenced how individuals from low-income countries were being trafficked into Russia on the promise of jobs, but then being used on the frontline in Ukraine. What does it tell us about the capacity of the Russian army, for it to be moving in that direction? Do you think that that is a central strategy or perhaps an individual regime in Russia operating in that way?

It tells us, first, that the Russian army is short of soldiers —particularly, good soldiers. They need to recruit people who can operate drones and more complicated systems, rather than what one might call simply cannon fodder. Recruiting enough soldiers appears to be an increasing problem for them because of the very serious losses that they are sustaining. You are absolutely right that there have been stories of people who have essentially been trafficked to the frontline. The Indian Government had to intercede at one point and liberate a large number of Indians who found themselves effectively in captivity in Russia. There are supposedly representatives of up to 40 countries who have been fighting with the Russian army—notably, of course, there is a large North Korean contingent, which in itself is absolutely fascinating.

As long as the war continues in this form, I would expect to see the Russian authorities do absolutely everything to keep the numbers up, including going after foreign citizens, who can be tricked in some cases. It is also a money-making mechanism for the people responsible for recruiting. These people are just numbers at the end of the day, and the fact that they have had no military training or cannot speak Russian is probably irrelevant.
Q27 You referenced earlier the fact that the regime is very repressive and that individuals go to prison for the smallest of things. What are the conditions like for prisoners in Russia?
For prisoners generally?
Generally—the human rights conditions for prisoners.

All the accounts that we read of people who have been in the system indicate that human rights are violated on a truly massive scale. The Russian prison system is not somewhere you are going to end up and enjoy good health—let me put it that way. It may not be as bad as it was in the 1930s—people are not going to die of starvation—but at the same time it is a pretty brutal environment.
Q28 Catherine, when we implement sanctions in relation to human rights violations, do you think they make a difference, or will Russia continue to do as it pleases?

I am afraid that the ones committing the human rights violations come from the most hardline group, and I am not sure they really care about having access to their properties in France or wherever. They will seek to redraw global maps and re-establish themselves in Dubai, Istanbul and other places where the sanctions do not hit. Of course, it is an annoyance, but I do not think it will change the behaviour of that particular faction of the Russian elite.

Q29 This is my final question. Dr Deyermond, do Russians see international human rights legislation as beneath them? Do they have their own standards of what they perceive to be human rights? Do they think, “We are not responsible for anything that the west and others hold us to account for. We will continue to operate as we please”?

The Russian state, certainly since the start of Putin’s presidency, has seen international human rights discourse and standards as really a cover for hypocrisy—as a set of ideas that the west use in order to con everybody while advancing their own national interests. This was something that developed particularly during the US presidency of George W. Bush. The Russian view was that the language of democracy and human rights in the west was really just being used to advance US national interests and absolutely nothing else. That is still something that you see, and it is now embedded in Russian governmental attitudes towards human rights.

One of the other things that the Russian Government do—this is partly to push back against western human rights pressure, but also to generate broader confusion or uncertainty about it—is to mirror the western language of human rights back against the west. For example, the US State Department used to issue an annual human rights report detailing human rights violations around the world. It always used to talk a lot about Russia, so the Russian Government started to produce their human rights report, in which they set out all the violations of human rights in the UK, the US and elsewhere. That is, I think, designed to cause global uncertainty around the legitimacy of human rights challenges in Russia.

If I may very quickly come back to the issue of media, the engagement with media and the need to ensure that there is free and widespread access to fair reporting as it relates to Russia also needs to be thought about in relation to the global south—the global majority. At the moment, Russia really is making the running in these places. It is telling a very strong story about western hypocrisy, western human rights violations and how resisting the west in Ukraine is really resisting western colonialism, which understandably lands very powerfully in the states that live with a legacy of western colonialism. Therefore, by extension, all the things that the west is saying about human rights violations and war crimes in Ukraine and in Russia are all western lies. The UK needs to be doing more to target that narrative as well.

Q30 On Russia’s attempts to put across its own narrative and, against that, to stop news and information coming from the west, I know that a lot has happened in terms of their attempts to close down internet access, VPNs and so on. Can you say a little more about Russia’s attempts to control information and ensure that western reporting does not reach its citizens?
And what we can do to counter that, which is the other side of the coin.
I would defer to one of my colleagues on that because it is not my particular area.

Again, I cannot claim to have expertise in this area, but that is clear in the slowing of YouTube and in the fact that having VPN access that works is effectively a precondition for being able to read western media in Russia these days. The VPN channels are regularly being challenged, but there still seem to be ways of getting around that.
