To add to that, on the potential way of fixing the price cap, there are two options. One would be to verify that the price actually paid was below the price cap. Currently, the price cap level is about half the global market price. That would be via bank statements and invoices. However, if instead the desire is to scrap the price cap and say that this is a policy that is not effective at reducing Russia’s export earnings, the UK could use the leverage, as Craig has recommended previously, to tax the use of a unique UK maritime service. A tax of about 5% or 10% on the use of UK insurance to transport oil could generate between £100 million and £300 million every month, and that could be used for the reconstruction of Ukraine, for example. I think th at is one of the cases where the UK does have leverage.

Let me, lastly , touch on the refining loophole: at the end of this year, the UK will finally implement a ban on the import of jet fuel and diesel from refineries using Russian crude oil. The UK does have leverage here. We are a big market that th o se refineries want access to. At the beginning of the year, the US put pressure on India to stop buying from Russia, and some of the big refineries actually did. Jamnagar, which is the world’s largest refinery, buys 9% of all Russian seaborne crude oil, which is significant for one refinery alone.

There are only four refineries that we have identified globally, in Turkey, India or Georgia, that buy from Russia. They buy around £700 million-worth of Russian crude oil every month. By saying, “You ’re interacting with sanctioned shadow tankers and buying from Russia, so we do n’t want to do business with you,” the UK and EU could cut off a significant amount of Russia’s revenue —w e estimate £400 million in tax revenues every month.

Perhaps I can briefly add a couple of points. As my colleagues have suggested, if the question is , “W hat more can we do on sanctions ?” it is as much as anything about better enforcement of what is there already. Th at is particularly true of the oil price cap, where the so-called attestation fraud that Isaac referred to is rampant. There are ways that we can try to do better there to ensure that it is not violated systematically in the way that it currently is, including by using our near - monopoly on maritime insurance services.

A second, UK-specific point—an old chestnut, I know, but it is important not to forget it—is our overseas territories and the continued un transparency of the beneficial ownership registries there . A long-planned and committed reform keeps being rolled back. There is reason to believe that there is a great deal of Russian money there that warrants scrutiny.

A third point—something that we cannot do on our own, but only with our European partners—is to think more carefully, concertedly and creatively about where our China policy fits into all this, because China is, in NATO parlance, the “decisive enabler” of Russia’s war in Ukraine. It provides a huge and continuous flow of dual-capable war resources that Russia cannot make for itself. We need to try to incorporate that more systematically into our China relationship.

Finally—again, this is something to work on with our European partners—there is the use of Russia’s frozen assets. As we have already heard, Russia is hugely increasing its own financial commitments to the war next year, and Ukraine is suffering a severe and growing funding gap as a consequence of the escalation of Russia’s attacks on critical infrastructure. The best way to address this is to use the aggressor’s money directly and make it available to the victim—that is the only sanction that simultaneously hurts the aggressor and helps the victim. Most of that money is locked in continental Europe, but we have some, so we should find a way together to make that happen. That is $300 billion, which really would be a gamechanger.

Q47 You have gone through a whole scale of things I was going to ask you about, which is very convenient for me. I just have one more question. Last week, I met a Chinese delegation. We talked about their technology exchange with Russia and the dual-use things that you talked about, Nigel, and as you might expect they were very clear in denying that anything like that was happening. For the record, what sorts of technologies and equipment are being used to enable Russia in their war? What measures could we, as the UK or with our allies, put in place to try to interdict that?

There are all sorts of components, particularly those used in UAVs, or drones, including some of the essential things, such as brush magnets and things like that—you would have to speak to an engineer, which I am not. To add an intriguing detail, a couple of months ago, it was publicly reported that a Chinese company had taken out an equity stake in a Russian drone manufacturer directly. When that was made public, that detail was expunged from the share record, but the further you look, the more evidence you will find. There is a deep and dense relationship—their relationship with North Korea is even closer, but we do not really have any relationship with that country, so it is all about China.

What do we do about it? That is probably a longer, larger discussion for another occasion but, briefly, the goal of such a conversation or engagement, which again has to be with our European partners, is not to do what we seem to be doing currently, where all our leaders beat a path to Beijing’s door, there is maybe 10 or 15 minutes about Russia’s war in Ukraine and the rest of it is all about trade investment with us. Can we link those two together? Can we in some way make China think more carefully about the consequences of its decisions? If China is the decisive enabler of Russia’s war against Ukraine, given that that war has profound and long-term implications for the security of all of Europe and that Europe as a whole, including us, is a fundamental trade and investment partner of China, has it really thought through where its essentially unalloyed and deepening support for Russia might lead? We should force it to think harder about its choices and the implications.

While it is absolutely essential to have those conversations, at the end of the day, the area where you have the greatest leverage is the area in which you have a dominant role in the global trading infrastructure: oil and oil exports. Everybody has limited resources; focusing them on what more can be done to constrain oil exports and the value of them gets you the best bang for your buck—the greatest return on your investment of administrative resources.

Q48 That is hugely helpful. In the short time we have left, I will turn to another aspect: manpower and labour. We understand that Russia continues to lose more than 1,000 casualties a day in Ukraine, such that its estimated loss is now 1.4 million. At the same time, a lot of its younger people have been trying to escape attempts to call them up for service. How is that impacting on the labour supply? To what extent will Russia be able to sustain the losses that it is currently incurring?

That is an excellent question. If we look in the round at all the ways that the war is causing trouble for Russia, there are two points. One is the prospect of a financial crisis, as Craig touched on. The second is the labour aspect. Russia now suffers by a long way the most severe labour shortage in its history . That is a consequence of both the huge increase in demand for labour to be sent to the front—and to die in very large numbers—and the huge increase in demand for labour in the military factories, which are now working round the clock, three shifts day and night.

The other blade of the pair of scissors is the enormous losses on the battlefield, as well as those who have left Russia and continue to do so as mobilisation rumours once again resurge. As long as the Kremlin wants to avoid forcing people to fight instead of paying them very well to fight, that means that financial incentives have to increase. It also means that it is the citizens themselves who decide whether to fight, and it is increasingly those in the greatest financial need who are doing so—that is, frankly, the halt and the lame and, sadly, the alcoholic and the drug addicted. It is not only a problem of quantity, but a problem of quality.

There is growing evidence that, this year, Russia’s capacity to replace the numbers being lost on the battlefield is steadily declining. It is not at the critical point where it will have to impose an open second force mobilisation, after the one in September 2022 that I mentioned, but it is clear that elements of a so-called hidden or covert mobilisation are taking place at the margins. People are being given offers they cannot refuse. People who have chronic debt burdens, for example, are being told, “Well, you can go to prison for a long time or you can go to the front.” They are trying to import people from other parts of the world to fight, often under false pretences—I think this came up in the first session. They are told there is a job at a military factory. They arrive and are told, “Here’s a gun—you’re off to the front.” That is the thing to watch.

Finally, military recruitment is part of the overall labour market. That means that wages are rising far beyond productivity. That is stoking inflation, which is eroding the living standards of ordinary Russians. I think the very first question we were asked in the session was, how is the Russian economy doing? Briefly, the economy as a whole is now stagnant. The only part of it that is sustaining growth is the defence industrial complex. Others are finding that their real wages are beginning to fall.

The labour issue and the financial issue are very directly linked. We are seeing credit continuing to expand, with 40% of it now going into the arms industry. These are soft credits from Russian banks that will not get repaid by the industries themselves. They will eventually need to be assumed by the state. That will be a big post-war problem for it to deal with. They are borrowing this money not to invest in capital goods—that is why we are seeing a steep decline in capital investments—but to pay higher wages and to cover losses. We are seeing an expanding credit bubble, a lot of it being driven by labour shortages, without that credit going into fundamental productivity. That is a huge issue. They are debating it in Russia. They know it is a problem. But it also leaves a big post-hostilities restructuring of debt to deal with.

I come back to the question about the EU, the UK in particular, and the US. People often think that, when it comes to credit markets and reopening global credit markets to Russia, that is a US call. I worked for two of the US’s largest investment banks for over 20 years, based here in London. London is where all these decisions ultimately get funnelled through and all this investment into Russia gets channelled through. If the UK continues to have sanctions on the access of Russia to western credit markets, then, even if the US lifts them, you are not going to see a big rush of American money going in. The UK actually has a huge amount of leverage over Russia’s ability to re-access western credit markets. I promise you that it is one of the first things that Russia will be demanding in negotiations, because it will be critical for it to try to accelerate the restructuring of its problems so that it can accelerate rearmament post conflict.

Q49 I have got the impression this morning that, while there is chronic corruption in Russia, that seems to be something that people expect and tolerate. I suppose the real question is: does it add to economic insecurity, or is it that, because it seems so much a part of the system, it doesn’t?

The question that came up about civil society is connected with this and is incredibly important. In fact, it has been the primary focus of my scholarly research: why is it that civil society failed to congeal effectively and demand more rights from an overbearing state in Russia?

If we look at the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is actually a very instructive period, because Russia was following many of the same patterns that western Europe had followed on its way to a more liberal order 50, 100 or 150 years earlier, depending on which country you are looking at.
Oh, you’re looking at serfdom, which was abolished in 1868?

Well, 1861—sorry! That was off the back of the loss in the Crimean war, which was a huge wake-up call. Russia stopped short. It could have kept on fighting, but it realised that it had overburdened itself with debt and the technocrats advised the Tsar, “Don’t keep fighting, because our situation will only get worse. We are up against a west that, while not fully committed to this, is committed enough and has enough of an industrial advantage over us.” Russia then embarked on massive reforms following that.

The same thing happened after the loss in the Russo-Japanese war: massive reforms. It is the one period in which we actually have a parliamentary moment in Russia, for about eight years. Then the first world war comes along and the rest is history. We could go on and on .
Q50 Is that what happened before the 1990s?

Yes. Again, Gorbachev comes here to London in July 1991. He is asking for a further handout from George Bush and Helmut Kohl for debt, because the Russian deficit has ballooned: there is too much spending on the military, and the Government are not willing to demand that the population work for slave wages because they are afraid that, if they do, there will be an uprising. It is a very similar situation to today.

I could go on, but finally we said, “We are not seeing enough progress on reforms.” Within four months, the Soviet Union has defaulted on its foreign debt. Three days later, the Belovezha accords, which disband the Soviet Union, get signed. Debt is therefore really important to watch.

We then have those moments when the old regime has been rejected and you have civil society trying to reassert itself. However, Russia has the resource curse, which comes back, and the leadership has realised that, if you can simply control a few key rents from key natural resource extraction areas, you can have a great deal of financial control without a lot of accountability to the broader population.

That will be the interesting question going forward, post this conflict. Isaac talked about the decline in the contribution to the budget from the oil and gas sector and from natural resources. We can change that: we can provide technology, welcome Gazprom and everyone else back into our markets and provide them with credit. That number will then go way up again, because we will breathe new life, as we have in the past, into the rent-generating natural resources part of the Russian economy. That will enable its authoritarianism to stay alive for longer.

I will just make a point on debt, because it is really important and often misunderstood. There are many observers who say—and the Kremlin is happy to repeat this—that Russia’s overall debt-to-GDP ratio is enviably low, on paper, compared with any European country. It is only about 20% of GDP. That might lead one to think that Russian public finances are in a healthy state, but that is just a number; it is a statistic. What really matters is the annual repayments that a state needs to make in order to satisfy those debt requirements.

Now—this is an astonishing fact—Russia pays more servicing its debt every year than Germany does , and as a percentage of GDP, it is even higher. The real burden—the flow of costs for Russia—is higher than it is for many European countries, including Germany.

Nigel had brought up an incredibly important point. To help you understand, the German bund has a 3% to 4% yield. That is how much is costs the German Government to borrow. Guess how much it costs the Russian Government to borrow on the 10-year right now? It is almost 17%. It is incredibly expensive funding.

Not only that, but Germany has pretty much the entire global debt marketplace to appeal to; they have a very broad addressable market. Russia only has a tiny domestic market. I have seen plenty of economists, and even Vladimir Putin, talk about Russia’s strong debt-to-GDP ratio and say, “We’re just fine.” He mentioned it in Vladivostok at the beginning of September but then went on to talk about the problems they have.
Q51 As far as the individual is concerned, I think your evidence earlier was that individuals face consumer debt at a higher level.

Certainly, consumer debt is very expensive. Again, if you are looking for signs of a system under stress, which could lead to a critical event where you get a cascading effect, we saw the single-A bond index in Russia move from 19% to 24% just over the course of September. There was a 5% increase for single-A corporates—so investment-grade corporates borrowing in the Russian bond market.

Those are very unusual upward spikes, and it has to do with the whole problem of the debt bubble now reading across into the broader financial system and everyone slowly starting to realise, “Oh my goodness. There is so much more unfunded debt that the Government have.” They are going to have to bail out the regions and all the bad debt on the arms manufacturers. When you add it all up, the total amount of potential liability that the state has is double what the official treasury bond market would suggest. Markets are starting to recognise that in Russia and they are pushing up borrowing costs. That is the sort of thing that causes knock-on effects.

To make the comparison once again and show what an expensive war this is for Russia to fight, during world war two the interest rate in Britain was 3% and in America I think it was 2.75%. The Russian state has to pay vastly higher rates year after year.

Q52 We have another question about the confiscation of assets , but you made it clear at the beginning of your evidence that the way the Russians are pushing forward on this war is that they are not confiscating assets in the way that most war economies normally do. I will not cover that.

They are confiscating foreign corporate assets at a growing rate, actually. They are confiscating some of their own, but in the past two months there has been a spate of confiscations from the western companies that have unwisely stayed in Russia.
Q53 Oh, really? Could you give us some examples?
I think it was Auchan—the big French retailer. There are others I can send to you; it can be easily checked.
If you can think of them later, do send us a note because that would be interesting. Unless anyone has any further questions—

May I make one last comment? I will be quick . In terms of summarising the UK’s leverage and the things it can do, oil is a huge finance resource for the Russian state budget, especially the fossil fuel type.

I want to briefly touch on the shadow fleet, which has built up over time. Five hundred and sixty vessels have left western ownership or insurance to start moving away from connections to those sanctioning jurisdictions. I believe it was at the beginning of last week that France detained a falsely flagged Russian shadow tanker off the coast of India. They have now detained five; the UK has detained one.
We have given assistance to others.

Yes. The other area is the Russian flag registry has become the largest flag registry for all the Russian shadow fleet. The UK could sanction that as well; the EU has done so. Working with those false flags— those flags in small island states—that are facilitating the huge network that is required to transport Russian fossil fuels, would be a big win.

If you have any further thoughts on that, please send us a note because—subject to what the Committee thinks—I think it would probably be a good idea for us to write to the Foreign Office before we finish our inquiry to highlight the things that we think the Government should be doing on sanctions now. We will never get a proper response because they always say they cannot discuss it, but it is important that we nudge them.
Thank you for your time. I am sorry it has been so cold in here, but your evidence has been incredibly interesting. Thank you very much indeed.

Members present: Baroness Hayter of Kentish Town (The Chair); Lord Barber of Ainsdale; Lord Best; Lord Camoys ; Baroness Carberry of Muswell Hill; Lord Fuller; Baroness Harding of Winscombe; Lord Udny-Lister ; Baroness Valentine.

Witnesses
Rt Hon. Wes Streeting MP, Secretary of State for Defence ; Rupert Pearce, National Armaments Director, Ministry of Defence; Ben White, Director , Industrial Strategy, Ministry of Defence.

Examination of w itness es
Wes Streeting, Rupert Pearce and Ben White.

Q98 Good morning and welcome to the Industry and Regulators Committee. My name is Dianne Hayter , the Chair. I will introduce my colleagues later on . This is being broadcast and a Hansard report will be made. You will have a chance to check that in case there is anything that we have misunderstood from what you have said. Could you introduce yourself, Secretary of State, and your colleagues? Then we will go straight into questions, if we may.
I am the Secretary of State for Defence.
I am the national armaments director.
I am the director for the defence industrial strategy.

The Chair : Can I thank all three of you for your time today? We know how busy you are. The armaments director has been in position for a year now ; other people are more recent in their job. We appreciate very much you coming here. We are not looking for, as I am sure you have been advised, the quantum of defence expenditure. We are looking at what the SDR suggested 16 months ago now as a new relationship between government and industry.

I am not sure, Secretary of State, whether you had a chance to see the Bayeux T apestry . If you had, you would have seen panel 32, which is William ordering the felling of trees, the building of boats and the gathering of arms. I do not know whether nobody told Harold or whether they did not respond, but there are some similarities now with how we respond to threats, which you yourself, I think in Liverpool, said are the most dangerous you have known in your lifetime.

We are focused on the relationship between government and industry. In the light of what we are hearing — that there may be a delay, maybe for a year, until knowing what the expenditure is going to be — we are interested in how you provide the sort of environment where defence companies can respond to the demands of the current threat under the SDR.

Good morning. Thank you, Chair, for inviting me to appear before your committee and for the focus on this particular area , which is extremely important. My overall priority, which is an easy one to set and much harder to deliver, is to make sure that we are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat those who would do us harm. That means strengthening our capability, our defence industrial base and our alliances.

The industrial piece sits across all those things, providing the capabilities we need and working with allies to develop those capabilities where we can. In an environment where NATO asks us to be ready to potentially fight and win a war, we need to make sure that we have not just the defence industrial base that we need now to meet our requirements, but also a wider industrial base that we would need in warfighting to sustain our warfighting machine and see us to victory. That is the context in which we see this.

There is a big opportunity, as we do those things, to support the key planks of the Prime Minister’s overarching political agenda, which is to re-industrialise our country, backing Britain by buying British and providing opportunities, particularly for the next generation and those million or so young people who find themselves not in education, employment or training. Fundamentally, we have to keep our eyes on our core business of defence, but there is also an opportunity for the Ministry of Defence to be both a ministry for growth and a ministry of opportunity. We want to make sure that we are supporting the Government’s wider objectives.

Thinking about that central challenge of the money and to what degree we have certainty, people can judge this Government, or the Labour Governments we have had since the general election, on their record so far. When we came in, defence spending was 2.3% of GDP. By next year it is set to be 2.7%, so we are well on our way to the 3% and 3.5% milestones, with 3.5% by 2035 being our NATO commitment.

In a way, the debate about defence spending and what we will see at the Budget and the spending review is a helpful one for me, as Defence Secretary going into Budget and SR negotiations. I am never going to complain about people saying that my department needs more money. I wholeheartedly agree with that and I think the Chancellor agrees with that. It is also important because it helps the public to hear the case over and over again of why investing more in defence in the current threat environment is important, because the public support is there, but we should not take it for granted.

There is, though, an overstatement of uncertainty. We know, for example, that, at the Budget, the Chancellor will provide the £4.7 billion shortfall that arose out of the DIP negotiations undertaken by my predecessors. I pay particular tribute to Dan Jarvis for the heavy lifting he did to get the DIP over the line. We also know that, at next year’s spending review, whenever the spending review is, the Chancellor intends to set out the pathway to 3.5%, and we can make some educated guesses in the meantime.

There is plenty for us to go at now in terms of the money we already have. There is a degree of certainty about an upward trajectory, which I think industry welcomes and the department is working on the basis of . One thing that is very different in this role compared to my last one is that, when I was the Health Secretary, I was under pressure all the time to demonstrate value for money, harder efficiency and productivity improvement, and to get my department to balance its books. The challenge at health was, “Isn’t your answer, Labour, just throwing more money at the NHS?” The only challenge I now get as Defence Secretary is, “Why won’t you throw more money at defence?” That is important. We need to spend more, but I also have responsibility to my colleagues across government and to the taxpayer to make sure that that money is well spent.

The Chair : That is an interesting phrase. I think you said that there is an overemphasis on uncertainty. We have met a lot of people in the industry who are feeling that uncertainty, but perhaps I could ask Lord Udny-Lister to take that forward.

Q99 Lord Udny-Lister : My question is about confidence and the signals you are going to give to industry. I suppose it starts off with, “When will the defence and investment strategy be published?” Can you give us an indication of a date? Even without that date, can you tell us that it will give the signals to industry that will enable it to tool up, prepare and have confidence to invest money in developing products and services for the defence industry? It is the signalling that I am particularly interested in.

W e are now a year on from the publication of the defence industrial strategy and it covers the delivery across regional growth, industrial resilience, skills, SME access, innovation, procurement reform and partnership with industry and allies. There was £773 million worth of funding attached to it, including £250 million for five defence growth deals, which are having a real impact, and £182 million for defence skills programmes. There is a lot there in terms of clarity and direction.

We will have just shy of £300 billion spent over the next four years. There are clear demand signals within that. We have the defence investment summit coming up before the end of this year. That is a great opportunity for this country to demonstrate the extent to which we are investing more and open for business, and, more than that, open for a real partnership with industry. This cannot just be a classic transactional relationship. Indeed, we have come in for some criticism over the years for being too transactional.

This is about making sure that we are clear with the order book, as we will be, about investable opportunities. It is also important that we are not just going out to tender with commissions for particular projects or platforms but going out, in the spirit of the integrated force design model we are working to, with our requirements over the next decade and working with industry from design right through to procurement and then delivery. Industry partners can help us to determine what it is that we need, whether those are exquisite offers, designed specifically to meet our needs, or right through the spectrum to off-the-shelf.

To your question, I do not want to sound complacent. I appreciate that there is more we can be doing. There is more clarity to come, but I do not think that we are in a bad place in terms of the money that is available and the demand signal that has been sent out, through the defence investment strategy and the defence investment plan. Through the mechanisms we have set up, such as the Defence Industrial Joint Council, there is a genuine commitment at every level of the department, ministerial and official, to work in partnership with industry in order to meet our requirements and build a stronger defence industrial base for the country.
Do we have a date for the summit?
Off the top of my head, I cannot remember what I am doing next week at the moment .
It is 1 December.
It is 1 December.
The Chair : Thank you very much. I think you heard it here first, in that case.

Rupert Pearce : To provide further comfort on the delivery, the defence investment plan was clearly higher level. It looked across 10 years, with more detail in the first and less in the second five. There is a real sense of long-term direction in terms of our military strategy. We clearly did not want to provide too much public detail about exactly what we are doing every week, every month, every quarter, because a lot of it is highly classified. We are now turning that defence investment plan into a delivery plan with industry.

We have already started to share the fruits of our work in a much more detailed, granular way, looking over the next six quarters and beyond. Industry is leaning in and engaging with us. It is very much a collaborative exercise, which is what this is all about, turning from a transactional relationship to one that is a true relationship, with industry bringing good ideas, investment and the capabilities to us to help us move out of the gate quickly. That is where we are today. That will start to be shared more broadly as we go forward. We are actively moving out on the ambitions of the DIP right now.

Q100 Good morning. Perhaps I could pick up on your answer there, Mr Pearce, about the delivery plan and focus in on some of the procurement processes that we have heard a lot about during this inquiry. In particular, we have heard over and over again anxieties about pace and speed of contract processes. In some cases we have heard about it taking six or seven years even to get to contract. Is the delivery plan addressing this and how is that particular issue going to be dealt with, so that we can speed up processes that, at the moment , do not appear to be commensurate with the threats of modern warfare?

I completely agree with your concern and accept that something has to change within defence, and fast. It is very much part of what we are looking to support and achieve through the rolling out of the DIP, but it is being dealt with partly through other means. Inherent in the defence industrial strategy is working with industry to speed up and simplify our procurement processes. Indeed, it is called out in the SDR as something fundamental that has to shift.

The requirement for that to change has only got greater. The SDR, remember, assumed that we had 10 years to deliver this transformation. By the autumn of last year, the prognosis was that we had only five years. We have to accomplish a lot more change at the front end of this programme to result in capabilities arriving in time.

We are doing a lot here. If I look forward, we need to procure in more ambitious and well-calibrated ways. We have a tendency to over ‑ procure and to design for the exquisite, as opposed to the good enough. In some areas we want to be exquisite still, because it is a key capability to overcome our adversary. In other areas, good enough is, by definition, good enough and that is what we need to procure for.

We also need to think about ways in which we develop our capabilities in increments. We need to be more modular in the way we design capabilities so that we can have a baseline capability and then spiral develop from that over time, managing the risk inherent in long-term procurements in cleverer ways. That has become especially true given the amount that we are now procuring in software, not hardware. So many more things we are buying now are systems, or systems of systems, and we need to think about the implications for that as well.

That is why the two most profound things changing inside defence are that, as the Secretary of State just said, we are moving to an integrated force model, so we start to look across all of our domains and front-line commands to procure for them, and, at the same time, instead of being given requirements by the front-line commands, we are now given problem sets. That gives us the design authority in my group to think about how we solve those problems. At one stroke, we get much more room for manoeuvre in terms of how we procure and we are able to work with industry, innovators and our allies to think about how we can design the solution. The pace of that solution has become one of the key value criteria in the way we procure. The whole mindset and philosophy of procurement is changing.

I will then pivot very quickly to talk about some of the very practical things we are doing. We are trying to simplify our procurement and take layers out of it. We are trying to engage much earlier with industry in inviting it in to figure out how we can solve these problems. Above all, we are trying to stratify our procurement. Yes, those big platforms require a lot more planning and design, but why take the same approach for everything? If we stratify our procurement and develop proper commercial pathways for different types of procurement, we can really shorten things dramatically.

We have done that in terms of procurement for Ukraine and the story of Commercial X. Commercial X has made over 1,000 procurements in the last three years and its average pace from genesis to contract is 50 days. That is the kind of thing we need to be looking at. We need to take that model, amplify it, deepen it, resource it properly and do more like that. There are a lot of good green shoots going on. We are looking to take our big platforms down from an average of the six years you called out to two. We are looking to take our systems down from three years average to one and everything else to three months. We have metrics to track that and the team are working very hard to get there.

I can say, because I have not been around long enough to take personal credit for it, that, on major platforms, that has already come down from six years to just under five years since the publication of the SDR. There is definitely more to go at, but it shows that words are being matched by action, which I found reassuring in my early weeks in office.
All that is very reassuring. Thank you. Can we look forward to a report in due course on how successful you have been in speeding up procurement in all the different segments?

Absolutely, yes. I am a devotee of, “You can’t manage what you can’t measure”. We need the measurements and ambitious targets, and then we track ourselves against them. This is very much the way we report on the objectives of the SDR. A nice thing about the SDR and the defence industrial strategy for me is that they come with hard metrics of performance. We can build a lot more into our reporting, which we would be very happy to bring back to you.
A love of targets is another big difference between this department and my last one.
The Chair : It is a big culture change you are ahead of.

The cultural change is almost the biggest shift. Naturally, in the environment in which we have been living for the last 20 or 30 years, there is very strong risk aversion. There is a focus on inputs, not outcomes, and a love of process, sometimes for the sake of process. It is a comfort blanket. It is a place of psychological safety. It is entirely understandable and normal.

If we are going to accomplish change in my group—national armaments—we have to find new places of psychological safety that are commensurate with what we face, which is the need for speed, the need to deliver transformation in our armed forces, the need to dramatically strengthen and deepen the capabilities of our supply base so it becomes a national strategic asset, and the need to innovate at pace. We could build great capabilities but if they are out of date in six months we have achieved nothing. Those things require a change of mindset.

The key for us as leaders is to create a working environment where people feel inspired and empowered to behave differently. We know we can achieve that because, when we lifted the system from them to support Ukraine, because Ukraine was willing to take more risk, we operated at an incredible pace. That is something we are phenomenally proud about. The people have the capabilities to do this. We have to provide a system in which they can flourish.
The Chair : Sometimes you need some political cover.

Q101 Lord Camoys : I was very keen to ask about the lessons from things such as Commercial X. Witnesses to our inquiry have identified both Commercial X and Taskforce Kindred as examples where contracts have been placed quickly by the MoD and innovation has been encouraged. Minister, given that the MoD has shown it can do this—we talked about culture—how can you change the culture? How do you go about that so that the MoD is more willing to move quickly, to accept greater risk, and to move away from process and more into delivering outcomes? How do you actually go about that?

As the Chair just alluded to, part of it is about providing not just political direction but political cover for a willingness to hold risk. Part of it is accepting this environment, where the nature of warfare is changing at a pace we have simply not seen before, if you think about where the war in Ukraine is today versus where it was at the start and the way in which the Ukrainians are innovating at a rate of knots. You have to be prepared to fail and to fail faster, to learn and then move on and adapt.

I am afraid that, in our world, “failure” is not a word we are comfortable with. Failure is often used to drive political embarrassment, Urgent Questions and parliamentary scrutiny, and sometimes with good reason. We do not aspire to fail, but, in a world in which our success relies on us being able to not just out-produce but out-innovate our enemies, part of a culture of innovation is accepting that, for every great idea you have, there are plenty of failures and setbacks you have to go through in order to arrive at that ultimate success.

Being comfortable with that as Ministers is important. We have a particular asset in the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard, who absolutely gets this and has been a driving force and a champion for the defence reform that was put through by John Healey. The NAD group gives the MoD an institutional set-up and framework that is the best chance of dealing with those problems that the Ministry of Defence has been plagued with over the years around procurement, value for money and productivity.

Part of the challenge is making sure that we take everyone with us. The other opportunity we have is a very forward-leaning, modernising set of defence chiefs. They are absolutely critical for driving the culture change that Rupert mentioned. In a world in which you are handing over problem sets rather than issuing requirements and trying to do that across the armed forces, that is a big shift and not one that everyone will be comfortable with. Sometimes, in this phase, it will involve saying to people, “We didn’t ask you for the specific requirement. We asked you for the problem”. That is a shift in culture behaviour. Initially people might encounter that as bureaucracy. Actually, it is the path to bulldozing the bureaucracy, waste and efficiency duplication that is holding us back.
The Chair : I would like to bring in Baroness Harding. I do not know whether you know, but she had to do some of this culture change when she was driving the vaccine initiative at the time of covid.
I remember very well.

Q102 To be fair, I was testing, not vaccines, but it was the same thing. When we started this inquiry, I think I actually said in the committee that I thought I knew literally nothing about defence procurement. With each session, I feel like I am going back six years to covid procurement. It feels to me that there are an awful lot of parallels.

I wanted to press you a bit more. I completely understand and agree about this important shift in culture. Secretary of State, you have talked clearly about what you are doing within the department. I wanted to push you on whether, to achieve this culture shift in the MoD, you need greater political direction and air cover from the very top of the office, from the centre of government. What do you need from the Prime Minister to create that shift in the country to allow the MoD to get some stuff wrong and spend some money not wisely in order to shift the culture to innovate as you are describing? What do you need from the top of the office?

With this Prime Minister, I am struck by his willingness to run into really big , hard things. We have seen that domestically with social care. We are seeing it internationally on AI and the way in which he is going about that, trying to do so through multilateralism, which has slightly gone out of fashion in the world, to put it mildly. His level of intellectual curiosity about things is a strength, and communication is one of his superpowers. In terms of helping the country to understand and to walk through some of this, I do not think we could ask for a better champion who instinctively understands where defence fits in his overall vision for re-industrialisation and spreading opportunity, as well as growth, across the country.

The other big asset we have is the Chancellor. The Treasury as an institution is one I have come to know and love in my previous experience in government. For reasons I understand on the fiscal side of the Treasury’s responsibility, with an abundance of caution and learning from examples of waste, inefficiency and white elephants that government has seen over the years, it can ironically sometimes lend itself to thinking that more regulation, process, scrutiny and sign-off is the answer. It can slow us down and work against growth, value for money and productivity certainly.

Building a high-trust environment with the Treasury is really important . That helps with the Chancellor because he has done my job before. That can be a double-edged sword when people know the department well and can see through flannel. That is a good thing.

My impression is that the DIP process, difficult though it was for everyone involved, means that the Treasury and the Ministry of Defence are working from the same number sets, the same set of assumptions, the same agreed plans and the same understanding of the challenges. Therefore that is a good ground for us to speed things up. That is not an event; that is a process. We are going to have to continue. Just as the Treasury challenges us on value for money, doing what we say we will and delivering to time and to budget, we will also have to do a bit of upward management to the Treasury to make sure that we are operating in a high-trust as well as a high-performance environment.

I do not doubt our Prime Minister’s communication skills at all, as you set out. This is not a party political point. It was quite striking that defence was not mentioned in his party conference speech. Do you need him to make a big strategic statement in order to help give your officials more air cover to change the way they work, take more risks and innovate, as you describe?

In defence of the conference speech, it was about the vision for the condition of Britain. It was a vision for the kind of Britain we want to be here at home. There is no doubt in my mind that he understands and is concerned about the threat environment that we are operating in, is concerned about the risks that we and our allies are carrying, and is engaged internationally. The fact that he did two and a half hours in the Commons yesterday with an international update the first day back should provide reassurance that he is focused appropriately on both foreign and domestic, and the links between the two.

What is the prize for us as a Government ? We want the public to understand the threat environment. We want to build national resilience and we need the country to play its part. We want people to be alert, but not alarmed. We also want people to see security as the essential precondition for hope and opportunity. The reason why the Prime Minister is uniquely placed to do this is that you need someone who is able to tell that compelling story and can marry hope and opportunity on one hand with the backdrop of threat, uncertainty and risk on the other.

We have to bridge those two. We cannot afford to be just about hope and opportunity, without also focusing on risks and insecurity. I think that you will see, in the coming weeks and months, the Prime Minister bridging those two things, particularly as he is engaged in international fora as well. That is a good opportunity for him to get that message across.

Baroness Harding, if it gives you comfort, I feel that I very much do have air cover for the change programme that the national armaments group is engaged in and I am leading. I find the Ministers enormously supportive of the process of change and actually asking how they can do more to support. There are a whole series of decisions around how we orchestrate our procurement, because we have to move at pace, and I see a lot of support for that.

It is grounded in the SDR. The SDR calls out this necessity for change and doing things differently, including the cultural shift. The defence industrial strategy articulates that, and so does the defence investment plan. Once the DFIS—the defence, finance and investment strategy—comes out, it will talk about another piece, which is about making sure that no UK defence company struggles for growth because of lack of access to capital. We want the UK to be the best place in Europe, if not the world, for a defence company to establish itself. I see enormous passion throughout the ministerial group and among the quad to do that. Yes, I see that air cover.

Look at my background. I am not a defence careerist. I am not a civil servant. I come out of industry. I ran a space services company and I was a venture capitalist. That is a very strong statement of intent about the nature of the kinds of behaviour we need to start to infuse in our procurement engine.

Q103 My questions are all about the SMEs—the small and medium- sized enterprises. We have heard a lot from them. It is not only that they bring innovation, new ideas, entrepreneurial spirit and all that, but the large defence contractors depend upon them to scale up and do a lot more, and they face incredible barriers. I know you set aside £2.5 billion between now and 2028 for the SMEs, but here are some examples of things that they face: a brand-new start-up being asked for three years of audited accounts, a procurement document that managed to pass the 1,000 pages mark for an SME to deal with, security clearances that take more than six months for the individuals concerned.

Can I put some specifics that you might like to react to and see whether you are able to comply with these ideas? Could we have a single front door, so that there is somewhere for SMEs to go where they know their queries and issues are going to be discussed directly? It may be that the Defence Office for Small Business Growth gets expanded and does that job. Could we have a single standard contract for smaller SMEs, instead of these incredibly lengthy and difficult contracts? Could we have payment terms that do not wait until delivery before you get your money, requiring these SMEs to borrow to pay the staff, with banks very reluctant to lend when there is only a single purchaser? These are all difficult issues. Can we get to the specifics and help the SMEs to flourish?

That is a great challenge. There is no doubt in my mind about the fact that we need to do much more to support SMEs to engage in opportunities that will come through the defence investment plan. We do not start from a bad place, but we do not start from a place that I think any of us would be happy or comfortable with. There is a lot more to go at.

Instinctively, I think the Defence Office for Small Business Growth is and should be the front door. It was established back in January this year, so it is still nascent. There is an opportunity, and actually a responsibility on us, as well as looking at what we can do to remove barriers in defence processes and drive up SME spend, to continually engage with the SME sector to see how that is working, as we are still in the early stages. The website, the contact centre and the guidance services are specifically designed to improve access and reduce confusion. The proof of the pudding will be in the eating: how do SMEs feel that that is going? How easy do they find it to engage?

Similarly, I absolutely take your challenge on payment terms in terms of making sure that we pay readily and on time for work that is being undertaken, but also recognising that, if we are dealing with our primes and, for all sorts of reasons we are all familiar with, a well-laid timescale does not quite go to plan, there is a big difference between a BAE or a Leonardo adjusting and reprofiling, and an SME, which is standing up the workforce and getting ready to do the work, being told, “We’re not going to be with you for another three months”.

Making sure that we are agile, responsive and supportive, and recognising the support that will be required where those sorts of things happen, goes back to what I said earlier about being a good partner. That is not just about being a strategic partner in terms of setting our overall strategy and thinking about procurement. It is also about how we work effectively on contract design and delivery.

In terms of the single standard contract, it is of course instinctively appealing to me, but I am a politician and I like simplicity. I will turn to Rupert to talk through how in practice that is doable.

I am going to bounce that on to Ben in a second, having said that, because he is in charge of it. You are looking for facts. We deal with over 12,000 SMEs today. We do £5 billion a year of business with SMEs today, albeit only 25% of that number is direct, so a lot of them come through the primes. I want to change that. The extra £2.5 billion target by the middle of 2028 is actually growing our business by 50% with SMEs, so it is a very big ambition. That , in itself, has to drive a change of behaviour.

You have obviously seen and read the SME action plan. That is a holistic plan looking across all the things you are talking about: making access to capital easier and addressing payment terms, both direct and indirect. Actually, we pay SMEs very quickly. Sometimes what happens is that it goes into the primes and then the primes pay them slowly. That is what we have to address by setting expectations of standards with primes, without which they will cease to be primes.

We are looking to standardise contracts wherever we can and get rid of longevity. We now have a single front door, but we are not set up for 12,000 companies to come through that door at once. Somehow we have to digitalise that engagement as well, probably working through ecosystems and communities that bring SMEs to us.

I will hand off to Ben to talk about some of the granularity, because there are a lot of facts here that are moving in the right direction, When I meet with SMEs—and I would call out particularly the recent SME round table at Farnborough, which I attended with Min DRI—I see a complete change of tone now. There is much more trust, transparency and engagement. SMEs are coming up with ideas. We are taking those ideas and running with them.

For example, one reason why SMEs struggle to engage on the larger programmes is that they are very large and often require a lot of skillsets they do not have. They might be able to deal with one piece of the procurement, so they are forced to sit behind the primes that put together the front piece. If we procure in more modular ways, we give SMEs a chance to bid direct with us for the module. Better still, why do we not have a dating agency for SMEs to come together and collaborate in coalitions that can bid against a prime? Those are things I warmly encourage and endorse and we are looking to get after, but you cannot get there without the dialogue changing and without creating forums for SMEs to meet you and talk about their specific issues. Then we can start to fix them.

The Defence Office for Small Business Growth is the front door. It started only in January, as the Secretary of State said. At the moment it is concentrating on those cross-cutting issues that we have identified affect all SMEs. That is the most powerful and impactful thing it can do immediately. As we scale it up, it will be able to receive more of these requests and deal with companies.

Dealing with 12,000 companies is a challenge, so we are still working through how we provide a level of service that is proportionate and achievable. A standard contract is a really good suggestion. One of our accelerated commercial pathways is specifically for SMEs, trying to make it easy for SMEs to work with us, taking all the best practice that we have and applying it, removing any barriers that we find along the way and that becoming a standardised approach for how to contract with SMEs. It does slightly depend on what type of product or service they offer as to which contracting route we would choose, but that exists now. It has been launched.

On payment terms—I hope you will find this comforting—we pay 94.6% of our contracts within five days and 99.9% within 30 days. In terms of making sure that they have access to funding and smoothing that financing situation for SMEs, we are definitely playing our part.

The final area I will allude to, which is a fertile area for SMEs, is innovation. Remember that, on one side, we have procurement of the solutions we know we want to adopt, but, as a separate exercise, we are also fostering a lot of innovation, including early-stage innovation. UK Defence Innovation has £400 million a year to put into mid-stage TRL—technology readiness level—opportunities. It is constantly horizon scanning for new ideas and capabilities. This is a very fertile area for SMEs to jump on board. The money we have now allows us to bring their technology forward without it costing them an arm and a leg, and without them having to bet the company on getting a contract at the end of it.

If you look at a competition we ran recently called Project Brakestop , which is looking for a mid-range cruise missile, we deliberately created an environment for lots of innovation by not over-specifying what we needed, leaving room for manoeuvre for companies to come up with clever ideas or different ways of solving the problem. Over 20—I think 24—companies applied, only one of them a defence prime, so there were lots of SMEs. Most of them we had never heard of. One was a Formula 1 engineering company. Go figure. When you think about it, a missile is not so different from a Formula 1 car.

Every single one of those companies got funded to the next level and went away having learned something and, I hope, wanting to come back and have another go, even though they did not win. We got down to five. Next phase we got down to three. Within six months, we had three functioning cruise missiles at very low cost that did what they said on the tin. Two of those companies were brand new SME suppliers, so it is a really exciting way to foster innovation in the UK.

The Secretary of State talked about failure. Did we fail with those 20 companies we decided not to procure from? I do not think so. We all learned a lot. They learned a lot. They will be back. It is a really exciting way to foster innovation. The key was to put those SMEs in contact with front-line commands and their rapid capability offices, so we can rapidly prototype and iterate with people who really know what the problem is and live that problem on the battlefield. We can then get to minimum viable product and product-market fit, making that entity far more fundable because it has a development customer alongside it.

These are the kinds of models that I find incredibly exciting for rapidly growing SME communities in the UK and their technology, without them having to bet the farm or put themselves at risk. What emerges is a company that then scales super fast , with us waiting to deliver the contract and the venture capitalists very eager to come in and fund those kinds of companies because of where we have taken them.
That was reassuring. Many thanks.

Q104 Good morning. We have talked a lot this morning about developing a new relationship between the MoD and the defence industry, so more of a partnership relationship and less a narrow transactional way of doing business. Are there risks in that , in terms of what some might call potentially a more cosy relations hip? Earlier this year, the National Audit Office produced a report that pointed to what the Public Accounts Committee estimated could be as much as £1.5 billion worth of fraud. What are the safeguards that can be put in place to guard against those risks as the relationship is changed in the way that we have all talked about seeing as desirable?

This is a risk we need to be alive to. It is not just a risk of cosiness or, worse still, fraud and corruption. It is also how you get the balance right between competition and the innovation and value for money that competition inspires, and, at the same time, taking into account social and economic value, the benefits of backing Britain by buying British, and the fact that sometimes there will be potential tensions between those two things.

This is why, in setting out the intent to buy British, we also have to be prepared, in some cases, to defend going to open competition or UK competition. We sometimes, as I encountered in my first few months in this office, need to be willing to look colleagues in the eye, who are rightly banging the drum for their constituency interests, or look industrial partners in the eye and say, “I hear your case for a direct award, but in this particular instance we judge it not to be of benefit”, and be prepared to field the occasional brickbat if work is going elsewhere. We have a really good track record in MoD of spending in Britain, but also spending outside London and the south-east, so we have a good story to tell.

In that spirit of going out with problem sets rather than specific requirements, it is about encouraging industry to work together. That in itself helps to drive innovation and competitiveness. It is about working with trade union partners, who also have a important stake in this and recognise some of the direct choices and trade-offs that we face.

We are going to have to keep a sharp eye on this. As we set out the framework around buying British and publish the new guidelines around measuring social value, we need to make sure that we have a degree of independent and impartial rules and frameworks that can help us steer through those choices and trade-offs, so we are not leaving too much to individual discretion. That is where some of the risk comes in. There have to be checks and balances.

I can assure you that there is no cosiness at all. It does not stop it being a businesslike relationship. There is no cosiness. Cosiness to me means that we wave things through; we accept mediocrity; we wait for them to catch up. That is absolutely not the case. If you want to be a successful partner of defence going forward, you are going to have to be really good . You are going to have to be on your mettle. You are going to have to invest in skills, jobs, young people and apprenticeships.

With the benefit that comes from us leaning into a relationship-based approach to wanting our supply chain to be strong, vibrant and capable comes a responsibility for industry to step up to our expectations of it. I will never use the term “cosy” when I am talking about my relationship with industrial partners. I would not expect them to say the same back. They want us to have a sharper edge, to move at pace and to have more consistent behaviours that allow them to invest. I am trying to change national armaments to do that. In return, from them I want professionalism, a commitment to productivity and a commitment to excellence. We talked about primes. I want them to prove to me that they are fostering their SME communities in the right way. Otherwise, they have no business being a prime, for example. It is a very businesslike relationship, with shared goals.

We cannot get away from two things. The first is that a strong and vibrant defence industrial base in this country is an absolutely essential prerequisite of our deterrence and ability to fight and win. It is really vital .

We cannot get away from something I totally agree with. It is one of the reasons I took this job. If we are going to be spending 2.5%, let alone 3.5%, of GDP on defence, we are honour ‑ bound to do that in a way that delivers jobs, growth and capabilities into this economy and grows the great British companies of tomorrow. Of course we need to do that, but, in seeking those two objectives, the last thing we are going to let slip is standards.

We have been given very specific fraud targets by the Treasury and we are organising around that to meet that challenge. Part of that is around bid rigging. We are working very closely with the Competition and Markets Authority, which has been incredibly helpful in supporting defence.

I will talk about the Defence Industrial Joint Council briefly. That is our mechanism to build this strategic partnership. There are 21 members of that. It is primes, mid-tier, SMEs, academia, trade associations and trade unions, so it is not one group favoured over another. Where we work very closely with the primes, it is specifically to manage risk, performance, productivity and resilience, and not preferred bidder status or helping them with business development.

That is all about engagement with the defence sector. We are very open to business with adjacent sectors as well. We know that we have to have serious conversations with the automotive industry, for example, and we have begun that process.

The Public Accounts Committee, I think, made a recommendation that consideration should be given to putting a clear plan in place to recover funds that have been lost to fraud and economic crime, and a proposal too that a senior individual should be appointed at two-star level, predominantly focused on this issue of safeguarding against economic crime and fraud. Is that a proposal that is still under consideration?
It is being actioned.
In response to all those directions a fraud strategy is being put together by the department and will be published in due course.
The Chair : The PAC will be pleased that its report is being implemented. That will be good news.

Q105 Our national defence is predicated on certain critical raw materials, not all of which are sourced from our allies, certain unique production processes, which are not always located at home, and certain robust supply chains, which are not always controlled here within the UK. Have the Government and your department mapped all these critical vulnerabilities? What can you share about the mitigations you have in place to address these single points of failure?

You are absolutely right to identify this risk. The defence supply chain capability programme is embedding resilience across planning, acquisition and decision-making, and trying to improve our visibility of end-to-end supply chains. We are addressing strategic dependencies through critical minerals analysis and supply chain mapping, as you described, and looking at this not just in terms of our own sovereign capability, but particularly surfacing this conversation with our NATO allies as well. I think that we are all concerned about the same supply chain resilience around critical minerals, semiconductors, batteries, energetics and our overall industrial capacity. If you think, across our alliance, we have considerable breadth and depth, but there are still challenges.

The defence industry warning, advisory and reporting point gives us a single point of engagement for reporting and managing security incidents. This is something we are suitably concerned about and focused on, not just domestically, but also with our NATO partners.

To amplify that a little, we are in the vanguard of looking at our supply chain several layers down. We have built a digital twin of our supply chain, which we continue to evolve, and infused that with real-time data from our suppliers. We are beginning to get a level of common visibility that allows us, both systemically and on a case-by-case basis, to get after those areas of fragility.

Where you have a systemic problem, that might be something government looks to fix. Where you see fragility in a particular supply chain, you might go after the prime or group of SMEs. Without the visibility, it is difficult to do that. We are really investing in the digital side to help us do this better. It takes you to all sorts of strange places. It is the old, “For want of a nail, the battle was lost”. Your supply chain is only as strong as its weakest link. We have to take this very seriously, because resilience and staying power is everything in terms of our deterrence and our ability to fight and to win. This is a very key thing.

Critical minerals is just one vector for that. We look at the 28 critical minerals that we have identified as critical to defence, and we are looking at each of them in terms of our supply, the consistency of that supply, the quality and our ability to control it. Fortunately, this is an area where we are not alone. We can work with our allies. Countries such as Australia and Canada I would call out as having particular strengths in critical minerals, and of course the United States. We are not bad , actually, but we need to look at this holistically with our allies and work together to ensure that we have mutual resilience.

We ourselves have some interesting critical minerals. You probably saw that the National Wealth Fund recently made an investment in an asset called Tungsten West. That was about to disappear from the UK and we stopped that. We turned it around and now we are investors in it. We are making commitments towards offtake of tungsten, which is clearly an absolutely critical mineral in terms of the defence sector. It is a journey, but we have made some very important first steps towards a much more muscular supply chain strategy.

I am pleased that you used the word “offtake” there. It is the first time, I think, in this inquiry we have heard that. That is most encouraging, because it gives that sense of some pipeline, which small businesses, or large businesses, are interested in. We are an industry committee and the Secretary of State has mentioned strategic dependencies. Are there any ways in which we can help the conversation, or do you feel you have it all in hand?

One thing that I am concerned about always is the tendency to siloed working. It is endemic in the British state. The longer I spend in government, the more I understand why that is the case, because often coherence can mean slowing down, and people just want to crack on. We need to make sure that we cohere more effectively, but also do not lose momentum.

To that challenge, and building on Rupert’s point, there is a risk that silo thinking leads the Ministry of Defence, and the conversation we are having around our defence industrial base, to think solely in terms of precisely that: our defence industry. In a warfighting context, we should not be neutral or agnostic about the current and medium-term strengths of our steel industry, automotives and a whole number of other parts of our industrial base, which we would normally think of as not being defence-related, but, in a war context, would be both relevant and needed, in terms of switching into supporting our productive capacity and sustaining a war effort.

That is the great thing about this inquiry. The role that your committee and the Commons BIST Committee can play is to look right across our industrial base, and right across industry, and think about this in terms of sovereign capability, in the way that we conventionally do, but I would really like people to be thinking about sovereign capability in a warfighting context. If you make warfighting the strategic objective and focus, it inspires a whole different set of choices.

This broadens out to the wider global economic context at the moment . On the one hand, you have a whole bunch of NATO allies that are absolutely focused on spending more and working more effectively together, because we can see the threat environment. That is not to say it is all perfect or easy, but there is absolute agreement on that in a defence warfighting context. If you switch into the economic lens, you have “Made in Europe” and “America First”. If we are not careful, healthy competition starts to look like self-defeating rivalry.

I keep coming back to this point. I say this internally in the department. I am saying it much more frequently publicly as well. NATO tells us that we ought to be ready to fight and win a war by 2030, not because we want one and not because we are saying it is definitely going to happen, but we can see a scenario in which that becomes more plausible and likely than we would and should be comfortable with. If we accept that premise, that has to reflect through all the choices we make and the way we behave. Here in the UK and across the NATO alliance, we are taking that seriously to slightly different degrees in different contexts. I would like all of us to think really seriously about that challenge and apply it, not just in terms of what the Ministry of Defence is doing, but in how we are thinking about industrial strategy across the board.
The Chair : If our transport does not go, everything else stops.

I used to think about this. A good innovation under the previous Government was the NSC for resilience, which I attended as the Health Secretary. It was great because it played a whole number of domestic departments that would not normally attend the National Security Council into that conversation about resilience. It is really valuable . I used to think a lot about the challenges in the NHS today set against what we would do if there was a major disaster and how the NHS would cope. We should be thinking about that across health, education and logistics in particular . Y ou can see the challenge.

As I am sure your colleagues back in the office know, the House of Lords is doing a short-term inquir y on resilience , which must be reporting fairly soon . I am sure they will have spoken to your people about that .

Wider society is definitely an issue for us. It is very important that wider society is resilient because, if you look at the lessons from Ukraine, we know that war does not just happen on the front line . Our adversaries will reach into and try to degrade our society. Look at attacks on our GPS system, for example . E xquisite timing is woven through so many of our critical national infrastructure systems. We have to look at that as well.

W e are quite unusual , in that we war - game with industry. We do industry war games that look at the changing role of industry from the onset of war through the logistics of getting our capabilities on to the battlefield and then supporting them . That has thrown up some really interesting areas that we need to get after to strengthen our interworking with industry.

You can see what has happened in the supermarkets . T hey are losing all their stock. If you know Lord Robertson, he keeps asking us whether we have water , wind-up radios and wind-up torches at home. The message is clear.

Q106 If you will forgive me, Secretary of State, I want to move away from th e big - picture account that you gave of the state of the world and what we are facing , and go back to the phrase that you have used a few times, “Buy British ”.

N obody can argue against boosting sovereign capability , our own capacity and employment. I n light of the replies to Lord Fuller’s question about critical supplies, could you give us a sense of how practically the department is going to go about finding the balance between boosting UK companies via procurement, particularly down the supply chain, and looking to companies elsewhere , from which we can, frankly, procure more timely and superior supplies , components and equipment? How practically is that balance going to be struck?

U ltimately , this come s down to questions of judgment . I n any procurement , we have to balance a whole range of considerations. You mentioned timeliness . We also have to balance value for money, effectiveness, social impact, economic impact and the opportunity costs that arise from different choices.

It is not a choice between military capability and British industry. B ack to the previous conversation that we were having around resilience , I see buying British not as a protectionist stance but as a means of broadening and deepening our defence industrial base, which is going to be critical for warfighting.

I do not think there is necessarily a tension between buying British and working in partnership with allies . With programmes such as GCA P , there is plenty of work to go around . E ven if every NATO member could afford to double its defence spending tomorrow , we would not be able to spend it because every country is facing similar challenges in terms of the breadth and depth of its defence industrial base.

It is about building overall UK sovereign capability and national resilience while also thinking about that same challenge at a NATO level. How do we make sure that our allies across the alliance are strong and that their defence industrial base will be able to sustain the warfighting machine ? T he danger, especially with integrated supply chains , as we have, is that we think, “L et ’s not worry too much about it because we buy from Germany and they’re all right ” .

It is like the aero plane analogy. We saw this during the pandemic quite literally with masks. Y ou put your own oxygen mask on before helping others. We should be under no illusions that , if we were in a warfighting scenario, that is exactly how our NATO allies would behave. They would be thinking about themselves first, perfectly legitimately, and then thinking about others alongside that , but as a slightly second - order issue. That is the way in which we have to think about this strategically.

Q107 This is probably for Mr Pearce because it is a quite specific procurement and supply chain question. The Government ha ve set out an intention to enable always - on procurement or an always - on pipeline of munitions, including via a set of new munitions factories. This is another covid PTSD moment for me because I am deeply worried that , as a country , we have not remembered that we need to have always - on vaccine production and always - on diagnostics. That is because it is really quite hard to maintain always - on in peacetime.

I want to explore how you are setting up that capability. What types of contract are you offering those factories ? How are you going to enable it to be viable for them and for their supply chains to be genuinely always on?

Baroness, you have hit the nail on the head. It is not easy. You have to be quite selective about it. I would add another concern in defence, which is that many of the models for the delivery of munitions capabilities are changing.

Look at drones, for example, which is one of the things that we would like to be able to procure on an always - on basis. If you look at what is happening on the battlefield, the competitiveness of a drone changes about every four to six weeks. There are measures and countermeasures. Twenty kilometres back from the front-line in Ukraine , there are a lot of software engineers engaged forward in supporting the efficacy of a munition. That is a completely different model that we are not used to. I cannot go out there and buy 5 million drones, put them in a factory and hope that they will be competitive a year from now.

The whole way that we procure and stockpile is subject to change. We have to evolve with these new models, which involve a lot of pac y innovation with in a capability , and pull industry into a new relationship with defence. That has to be built into the way we procure always - on as well. It is a huge challenge.

Put another way, I might want to buy 10,000 drones of a particular type a year for my own purposes, for training and operational purposes , but I want to know that my partner can 10x or 100x production at the flick of a switch when I find myself on a glidepath to war. These are huge challenges that industry and defence have to solve together.

T o some extent, my life is made easier because, as you know, we are very proud to support Ukraine. We provide over £3 billion worth of support to Ukraine a year, much of it in the form of the provision of armaments . In the short term, an always-on capability is easier for me to procure because I am able to procure for my own operational need and I procure for Ukraine.

Look at this amazing success story of Thales in Belfast with LMM, the medium-range missile that is proving itself to be a really capable missile and a kinetic effect on the battlefield . M ost notably , it is able to support Ukraine in going after the new jet-powered Sh a heds and protecting the citizens of Ukraine ’s cities . T hat is something where we have taken up production by orders of magnitude , and the nature of the requirements and the purchasing from the Middle East and from Ukraine now is sufficient that we do not have to worry too much about always-on. There is just a big draw of capacity there.

W e supplement that with an always-on capability that is our daily bread, if you like, for training purposes. That is where we are going to go.
