We have half a dozen weapons capabilities, including CAM M , ASRA A M, LLM and NLAW, where we have got to always-on relationship s. W e are buying in modest amounts , supplemented in each case by demand from Ukraine. That is the best that we can do for the moment.

Q108 As you have probably gathered, there were some technical glitches getting me online . I see that I am now huge on camera , so a pologies for that. M y question relates to government defence growth deals. Those are to support infrastructure, workforce and industrial development for the defence sector in some areas. I wanted to ask two related questions.

First, what are the plans for areas with important defence industries but without those defence growth deals? C onnected to that, how will the Government ensure that regional and local defence industries have sufficient skilled staff?

Thank you very much for that question, Baroness Valentine. I n terms of what we are doing so far, we should not see the five growth deals that we have at the moment as the summit of our ambition. They have worked and are working well to bring together a whole range of partners in place s to build on existing defence industrial strengths with a view to deepening what they can do. We are seeing that happen already.

In terms of defence skills, we have the money for the five defence technical excellence colleges in England, which are helping to improve the quality of teaching and the offer , specifically for defence skills, but those have broader application across other parts of industry. They definitely offer a real advantage in terms of industry partnership s , work placement opportunities and future career progression. I would like to see more of those.

It is deeply frustrating, to put it mildly, that we have the funding available to support two defence excellence technical colleges in Scotland, but the myopic politics of the Scottish Government means that it is not being spent. T he money is there and the opportunities could be there for people, young people in particular, in Scotland. T o the SNP, its separatist agenda is more important than providing skills, jobs and opportunities to the people of Scotland. T hat is intolerable.

That is why the Scottish Secretary has announced that , if the Scottish Government continue to drag their heels, we are just going to spend the money and create that provision without them. If they want to have a constitutional row about that, I think the people of Scotland would prefer us to focus on opportunities for young people in particular in Scotland rather than the usual constitutional obsessions of the SNP.

There is lots to go at and lots that is being done. B eyond those areas , to your challenge, that do not yet have defence growth deals, we are thinking all the time about what more we can do, even from a really good starting point on defence expenditure outside London and the south-east, to spread opportunity and growth in every postcode, to coin a phrase.

The one area where Luke Pollard , at ministerial level, and the MoD generally are most exercised is the north-east of England. We have a really great story to tell overall in terms of where defence expenditure goes, but , if I look at where our money is currently going, MoD expenditure per person is £70 in the north-east of England compared to £1,130 in the south-west. If I look at the number of direct jobs supported by MoD expenditure, it is 900 in the north-east and 36,700 in the south-west of England.

E ven in the MoD , where we have a really good story to tell about driving industry, growth, jobs and opportunities across the length and breadth of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, we have an Achilles heel in the north-east, where we have big employment challenges as well. I am keen to lean in and do more where we can.

Can I just follow up on the skills question ? Y ou we re talking there about the south-west . W e heard from Plymouth, but it seemed to me that the skills that you will require in Plymouth eventually are way beyond anything that is likely to come locally, both immediately locally and in the wider region. How do you join those two things up?

There are a few ways of doing that. T o build on the point I was just making around the north-east, one is to support new growth and new opportunities across the country as well as building on existing successes.

Secondly, we need to make mobility in our country easier. One thing that is constraining UK growth at the moment is that people cannot access the jobs and opportunities where they are . T hat comes from a combination of housing pressure and transport costs. There are just so many constraints on the labour market . I f we can start going hard at those mobility challenges, we will be in a much stronger place.

S ince you cited Plymouth, Luke would not forgive me if I did not mention Team Plymouth in particular. One of the strengths of that approach —there is more to do, and more for my department to do—is that you have the right partners around the table to look at housing supply, the skills offer, the transport links and the way in which Plymouth can pull in people from across the region.

Finally, as we meet those skills challenges, we really have to be much more muscular about growing our own. The Home Secretary regularly complains about the extent to which Cabinet M inisters come to her asking for visas to get skilled workers into the country . I regret to confess to the committee that I have barely been in this job for three months and I have already been at it myself , in terms of the skills shortages that we have had in Scotland. That was necessary and right to fill an immediate skills gap that presented a real delivery challenge for us as a country, but it is not acceptable at a time when we have 1 million young people in this country who are not in education or employment.

A big part of what we are doing in terms of defence skills should be growing our own, not just backing British industry but also backing British talent, recognising that we are not the only ones in this race. I used to think about this a lot in the health context. It is all very well taking a short- term ist view that we can just pull the immigration lever and import some workers from elsewhere, be very grateful to them for being here and the contribution that they make, and it will save us some money because we do not have to bother training people and we are just taking someone else’s skilled workers. In a global environment in which the competition for these types of skills and this type of labour is becoming fierce r , we should not assume that we can continue to pull the immigration lever and, I would also argue, nor should we morally .

I agree with everything that the Secretary of State just said, but I would add one further thing . W e are looking to publish a defence jobs plan shortly. I will ask Ben to talk about that in more detail, but that is the nexus between government, industry and, of course , trade unions to get ahead of these plans for growth. If w e are to be successful, we need to have the right skilled people in the right place at the right time . T his is something that we are looking at holistically across government, trade unions and industry.
We are just agreeing with No. 10 and BIST when we can publish our defence jobs plan . It should be coming out imminently.

The other thing that I would like to mention is that, underneath the skills work and the growth deals work, we also have regional defence and security clusters all around the country . Those work very closely with our UK defence innovation teams . T hey also play a role in local communit ies, identifying and feeding back to us what skills are missing and how we need to feed into things such as the defence technical excellence colleges to plug those skills gaps. That has all gone into our jobs plan and that should be coming out soon.

We will be reporting on this mix annually . Y ou have probably seen our regional plans that have come out. We have nearly 500,000 jobs in the defence industry in the UK and 25,000 apprenticeships . Some 70% of that is outside London and the south-east . A s the Secretary of State said, we have had a good start, but we now have to calibrate that to our ambitions as well.

Can I just push a little bit on the quantity that we are talking about here ? I t does seem to me that, realistically , if you are going to gear up within the sort of timescales we are talking about, you are going to have to pull every lever that there is . You think that you are going to train people up into these jobs to satisfy the numbers that you are talking about. Does the jobs plan suggest that that is possible?

Yes . T he heart of the defence jobs plan is exactly addressing that demand for an additional , just to put it in context, 53,000 workers in priority occupations by 2035 and supporting around 50,000 opportunities for young people annually by 2035 . T here is a big requirement and therefore a big ambition. It is going to require sustained focus . That mean s we have to be realistic about where we are versus where we need to be , and the bridge between those two things.
You had some figures in front of you . B eing Welsh, did you have Wales there as well as the north - east?

I most certainly do . I gave you , first of all , expenditure per person with UK industry . I n Wales , the figure is £340 and the number of direct jobs supported is 4,900 . It is nowhere near as bad as where we are in the north - east of England, but there is certainly more that we could be doing .

Northern Ireland, for very obvious and visible reasons , is well known for its defence industry. T he numbers there , on a per capita basis , do not look nearly as impressive as those striking images that we often see as ships come alongside . It is £140 per person in Northern Ireland and 1,000 jobs supported .

I t comes back to my point , really . There is a really good story to tell . W ith the Prime Minister’s emphasis on growth in every postcode , t here are lots of government departments that would love to have this starting point, but the MoD would be the first to say that there is absolutely no room for complacency . W e want to make sure that we are genuinely spreading opportunity across the country at a time when we are investing more in defence.

Q109 Lord Camoys : Western intelligence agencies have warned that Russia is stepping up efforts to target Europe’s defence industry, including its senior executives. A Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger , chief executive of R heinmetall , was uncovered in 2024 . J ust in September , a man was charged in connection with alleged plans to sabotage drone manufacturing sites in Swindon. Keeping defence capacity available depends on defence companies being protected from physical attacks and cyberattack s .

Secretary of State, can you assure the committee that the Government are able to give defence businesses, large and small, the guidance, support and protection that they need in order to keep themselves safe and their operations secure? Without revealing anything sensitive, can you let us know what you are doing to address the unique threats that defence companies are currently facing?

Yes . R ecognising , as you do , the classification challenges of open discussion in this particular forum , this is something we are very concerned about. My problem with the term “ hybrid threats ” is that it does not accurately convey to the public just how serious the threats that we are talking about are . This is s abotage, targeted assassination and what is in effect state-backed terrorism in some cases . W e should see it in that context.

Of course , this is something that concerns industry. W ith the attributions that have been made against Russia in particular by some of our friends in Europe, we can see a pattern emerging of targeting those companies that have played a particular role in supporting our friends in Ukraine.

With that in mind, we have been providing appropriate classified briefing s to senior security-cl e ared industry personnel to inform them of the threat environment and to help identify risks and vulnerabilities, map those and set out what they can do to deter, defend and mitigate those risks. T his is an evolving environment . I t comes back to the theme that has run throughout this committee, encouragingly, which is that this has to be part of the whole national security and resilience picture. It is not just about government and conventional defence. This is now a challenge for all of us.
Q110 I have a few supplementar y questions, and my colleague s might also . You have a very hard stop.
That is because I foolishly agreed to do the House of Commons Defence Committee on the same day as your committee , which can only be described as masochistic.
We also want you to be able, at the end, to say whether there is anything that you would like to leave in front of us. There are a few questions.

One is about regulation . W e have heard that some of the regulation is a bit out of date. It was probably apocryphal, but we heard about some autonomous marine vehicles having to have a lifejacket on board.
It does not surprise me . T his is the British state that we are talking about.
How are we dealing with all these different regulations that might slow things down?

A large part of our focus is about taking back control , sovereign capability and improving democratic accountability and our ability to respond as politicians when the public complain, rather than hide behind regulators and say that it is some unelected quango’s fault.

There is a big drive across government on deregulation and improving how , as a state, we become much more agile, innovative, flexible and responsive, which is really important not only on the growth and opportunity side of the Government’s ledger but on the defence and security side. The Chancellor has recommitted to reducing the administrative burden of regulation on business by 25% by the end of the Parliament. We are still routinely receiving reports of regulatory frictions, which led to the Regulatory Innovation Office adopting defence technology as a focus area.

You can understand why , in a defence context , you do not just take off all the regulatory oversight and constraints, because we are talking about lethal capability, but , at the same time, throughout our Armed Forces and our industry, people are ch a mping at the bit to push the frontier of innovation .

T here is still more to do. I met one Royal Marine who was developing underwater drone technology . He was testing it in a pond in his back garden because the regulatory hurdles to test in other environments were too high. He just took the risk himself and did it at home. I applaud his ingenuity , drive for innovation and entrepreneurial spirit, but there should be the same can-do approach in his workplace.

Lots has been done. The Government have the right intention, ambition and spirit, but there is still more to do and more to go at. In the spirit of industrial partnership that we keep coming back to , this has to be a two-way conversation. Where industry tells us that pointless regulation is getting in the way, where our Armed Forces tell us that regulatory handcuffs are getting in the way , and where we agree that they are pointless and not serving their purpose , or the risk calculus is in the wrong place and we are not getting the balance right, we are really keen to act.

I see a lot of support from government towards that and from regulators as well, which is very encouraging. I would probably call out test and evaluation as an area where we can do more . I t is very expensive for SMEs to take their wares off to Canada or somewhere to do the testing. I am thinking particularly about areas such as maritime autonomy or even aviation autonomy , where we can do more. We talked about somebody doing something in their pond at home. T he MCA is working with d efence to lighten the load and allow us to do more in our coastal waters to test out d efence autonomy. I t is a journey, but things are getting better, and there is now very much a constructive relationship with regulators.

As part of the defence industrial strategy, we have committed to running a series of regulatory sprints. We started with autonomous systems. That has reported now . I t was commissioned in February and reported in May . T hat work is now being implemented by the Uncrewed Systems Centre and the single services , which are in particular looking at things such as software assurance .

T he really big opportunity here is the regulating for growth Bill because it contains sandboxing arrangements, which would mean that you could do testing. If you placed it in an area of operation and put a box around it, the regulations that meant lifejackets had to be in place would be lifted.

There are two things. There is the regulation and there are the testing facilities. You have particularly mentioned SMEs. T hey need access to that. I gather that there are difficulties around not being able to turn off GPS and things like that, which are problematic. You are on it, are you?

We are on that . A s Ben has eloquently said, the Defence Industr ial Joint Council is where industry to defence come together to look at these issues. This is wh ere the practicalities of these working groups are so powerful. In a vacuum, we are not going to get to half of the practical problems that industry faces, but , if we bring industry to the table, we are in a much better position to do that.

I have a small question . A couple of times you have mentioned sovereignty and buying British. I understand from some companies that they are not absolutely certain about what you mean by a British company. I do not know whether some definition is awaited . Does it mean that the company is headquartered or owned here , that the manufacturing happens here , or that the IP belongs here ? Is there a definition or are you coming up with one?

There is a definition and i t is being e volved in conjunction with industry . A nother DIJC joint initiative is to define sovereignty or, in essence, to define Britishness. It is focused more on the location of IP, jobs, skills and growth potential as opposed to pure ownership. It is more practical . H ow do British people benefit from a business? I t may matter less who owns it ultimately , if they have a job in a town where they have great prospects. Ben, do you want to add a little bit on that?

We have been running consultations with hundreds of companies in the UK , facilitated by ADS and Ma ke UK, under the auspices of the Defence Industrial Joint Council in order to make sure that the definition that comes out has the intended consequences. The current legal definition of a British company is that it has an address in the UK. That is not sufficient for our purposes.

We are a bit more ambitious than that. From my perspective , politically, what I really care about and what I am really getting at when I say “ B ack Britain by buying British ” is whether the jobs , growth and opportunities are felt by people here in Britain whose taxes are paying for this . That is the thing that I care about more than anything else in terms of how we define buying British . T here are other important equities, but for me those are the most important ones , where we have a lot to go at.

That is about honouring the moral opportunity and obligation that we have to provide jobs , opportunities and growth for our people, but , for me, it is also about not being remotely complacent about taxpayer support for increased defence spending. It is high at the moment . Long may that continue. It is necessary. P eople can see the unstable and uncertain world that we are in, but I do not take it for granted. The more that people see the money that they are putting into defence as taxpayers being translated in to not just capability but jobs and opportunities, the better.
F inally, as I know from my previous life as the Health and Social Care Secretary, it makes life much easier with the Treasury if you are a ministry for growth and not just a ministry demanding more.
It is resilience as well.
Yes, you are a bsolutely right .
Now that you know what we are asking about and the follow-up to the SDR, is there anything that we have not asked you on which you would like to leave us a closing statement?

I will say a few final things . I made this point throughout the session, but we have to see the defence industrial base here in Britain and the collective defence industrial base of NATO members as a key part of warfighting and winning, not just as providing the means to others in a transactional sense. It is about the broad industrial base and the productive capacity that we have to win. It is about out-innovating and out-producing our enemies. There is a danger if that is not seen as being as absolutely integral to the defence of the realm as the Army, the Navy, the Air Force and so on. That is the first thing that I would say.

The second thing that I would say is that we have an absolutely outstanding Minister in this area, Luke Pollard. In terms of appearing before your committee and responding to evidence , he would relish the opportunity . S ince I am new in post and the C hair was persistent, I have gladly accepted your invitation to come this morning. Min DRI would also have relished the opportunity and would be very happy to appear in future.
Thank you. I am glad you did give way to a little bit of persuasion. It is important. I know he is very good on the detail, but hearing your tone is also extraordinarily important to us.

Can I t hank you and your two colleagues ? This is the final oral session before we write our report, which will land on your desk before too long. Thank you very much for that . T hat ends this session of the committee.

Oral evidence: M ission G overnment , HC 116
Tuesday 20 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 20 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Simon Hoare (Chair); Richard Baker; Markus Campbell-Savours; Sam Carling; Lauren Edwards; Peter Lamb; John Lamont .
Questions 45 - 109
Witness
I : Rt Hon. Darren Jones MP, formerly Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister.
Examination of witness
Witness: Rt Hon. Darren Jones MP .

Q45 Good morning , colleagues . I am very pleased that the r ight h on . Darren Jones, Member of Parliament, has kindly agreed to join us voluntarily under no compulsion whatsoever . Mr Jones, h aving served as the Prime Minister’s Chief Secretary and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, we thought it useful to hear your fresh thoughts, reflections and suggestions on your time —the good, the bad and the ugly as it were— in the Cabinet Office. It would be remiss of me not to put on record in public this Committee ’s thanks for how you engaged with us , the time you spent with us and indeed what you did within the Department when you were a Minister . Sometimes politics is not terribly good at saying thank you , so o n behalf of the Committee , thank you.

I want to take us back to the heady days — before the gilt came off the gingerbread — of m ission g overnment. You will remember there was a g reat fanfare. Pat McFadden was your predecessor and there were issues that you inherited. Not a day went by without us hearing at least four times from Ministers about mission-led government and how it would shake everything up, the silos would be broken and the way of doing g overnment would be recast. When did mission government get its death certificate? Nobody talks about it anymore and it does not seem to be the underpinning mindset of , “ Le t’ s change things around and make things better. ”

The missions for the incoming Labour Government were a set of political priorities that came through the manifesto process in opposition coming into g overnment, which were then attempted to be translated into changing the way Government worked in order to focus on delivering those outcomes. It was essentially an exercise of prioritisation and trying to get the system to tackle some big challenges that maybe it had not for a long time.

Certainly in the first year or so when I was Chief Secretary to the Treasury we were trying to embed mission structures into Government. We had these mission boards that brought Departments together . In the spending review that I led I asked mission boards to submit their own spending bids alongside the Departments so we could see how we could pool budgets to come together.

In practice it did not work for a number of reasons. First , the money we assigned to missions ended up going to Departments anyway because we were told mission boards could not be constitutionally accountable to Parliament in the same way Departments are. Once the Departments got the money, the Departments decided how to spend the money and so collaboration was not as easy as it maybe should have been if it had gone to the mission board.

Cross- d epartmental working is also just very hard. C onstitutional norms and a tendency to protect the way the system works eventually stopped it from being effective. Wit h Andy Burnham’s team , he has a different set of priorities and has clearly set those out . He has decided that the missions will continue and still be delivered under the bonnet by the Government — NHS waiting lists coming down, more police officers in our community, the clean energy mission going for economic growth at the top of the league table — but the political focus has changed with a new administration.

Q46 Let us just pause there for a moment because there was a growing sense that the orthodox high priests of the Treasury suddenly saw mission boards as being effectively a challenge to their total authority . No longer would Treasury be able to play one Department off against the other because of a cross- d epartmental approach to policy delivery. What you seem to be saying now is it was just accountability. At that time d id any Minister say, “ We want to try and do something new here so let ’ s create a way for mission boards to have that line of democratic accountability through Parliament , ” or was it just a metaphorical shrug of the shoulders and simply going, “ Oh , okay, well, it was a good idea but it ’ s fallen at the first fence ” ?

O ther current and former Ministers might think differently , but my sense of it is it was a classic example of the system saying, “ Well , you can ’ t do that because of constitutional norms .” Therefore the mission boards continued as technically Cabinet S ub -C ommittees in their status, which have decision-making power but the money still sat with the Departments in their normal structure . As we all know if you do not have money in the spending review to do something you are probably not going to get around to doing it.

Q47 That is an understandable answer but I am sure you understand that it is also a disappointing one . Here are a fresh-faced Government coming in, after 14 years in opposition, master of all they surveyed in terms of a parliamentary majority , and the working presumption a t that time was a belief that Keir Starmer would be Prime Minister for at least two terms. Does that just speak to a surprising lack of small - r radicalism within the early days of that Government and to the wider assessment of Keir Starmer ? I am not asking anybody to speak ill of the metaphorical dead but of a rather unambitious, non-creative technocrat who just tried to make the status quo work rather than create anything new.

I would not personally pin it on Keir Starmer or quite frankly any Minister . When I was in the Cabinet Office I spent a lot of my time trying to get the system to focus less on process and more on delivery of outcomes because there is a lot of process : meetings, slide decks, groups. You just think , “ What is actually changing in the real world as a consequence of all this activity? ” I had to do a lot of work in terms of the incentive and accountability structure for senior civil servants but also seek absolute clarity on what they were being measured against in terms of real-world change.

I have two observations. First, w hat happened initially in response to mission boards was a lot of process. A lot of people worked very hard ; there were mission board s and lots of data, slide decks and people talking but it did not actually deal with the fundamental constitutional barriers to radical change of the state. My second point is that the civil service is reluctant to change. Ministers who have an average lifespan of maybe two years or so can only achieve so much in that time period . The incentives and accountability structures to make sure that senior civil service is delivering the political priorities of the Government of the day is an area where we have to do much more work. I started some in Government but I know that there is much more to be done.

Q48 We will all take the point about the rapidity of ministerial churn. I j ust want to go back to the assertion of some basic points . There was m assive parliamentary majority, decimated serried ranks of O pposition in Parliament and t he belief that Keir Starmer would be Prime Minister for 10 years . It was a personal goal of the Prime Minister to deliver change, do things differently and so on . How surprised or worried should this Committee be? Against that backdrop the civil service was still reticent to pick up that ball and run with it to help Ministers deliver a fundamental resculpting of how the state delivers service, monitors progress and makes things better for Mr and Mrs Smith of 32 Acacia Avenue.

The Committee should be worried about it ; I am worried about it . In practice, a Minister sets a political direction but then relies on the civil service to implement and deliver it. The trouble is, especially when you are very busy as a Minister —the Prime Minister’s d iary is obviously the busiest of al l— there is not sufficient pressure on the detail or accountability elsewhere for how this is being performed. If there is a reluctance to deliver change you have to push really hard for it to happen.

I remember when I was Chief Secretary of the Treasury and it was my construct to get the mission boards to submit their own spending bids and bring the mission boards together in a meeting chaired by myself as Chief Secretary of the Treasury and Pat McFadden as CDL for them to explain what their bids were. The Treasury would have been quite happy not to do any of those things and just do the d epartmental approach that i t ha s always done. This is why I say accountability for performance of the senior civil service matters so much because there are too many opportunities for the system to not deliver what Ministers have asked for. You can only have so many things where you call them in every single week to say, “ How are you going? ” There is a whole load of other stuff that just does not happen.

Certainly in the senior civil service — particularly Cabinet Secretary level — there is very little accountability. There is a big debate for us in Parliament about how the Government can improve accountability within g overnment. I had started some work and they were making some progress , which is good. Also in Parliament I do not think the current set - up for holding senior civil servants to account in Parliament is sufficient, especially because they have become very political as a group.

Q49 Finally from me before I bring in Mr Lamb, we saw the appointment of Sir Chris Wormald and many were surprised that he achieved the senior role of Cabinet Secretary . We had the destabilisation of Sue — now Baroness — Gr a y . Those are t wo people who arguably were there to help or shoulder some burden for the Prime Minister in terms of driving forward that implementation. Hindsight being a wonderful thing , w hat is your assessment of the either singular or cumulative impact of those two characters in post and the manner of their leaving in terms of helping the Government get up to speed as quickly as it needed to?
I am going to be conscious not to provide comment on individuals , certainly where there have been employment tribunals and others involved.
I do not think there have been tribunals .

There were settlements , and as a consequence of settlements I suspect there was a commitment not to bring anything to a tribunal. I am just not going to go into that space with your permission but thank you for the invitation.
Damn.

At the centre of Government there are the Prime Minister , the Prime Minister’s Chief of Staff , the Prime Minister’s PPS, the Cabinet Secretary and the Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister or the First Secretary , whichever title you want to give them , plus probably the Chancellor , although they are always slightly separate. That is basically the key team for driving things forward. This is probably a reflection of the fact that my role was new as Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister but I found that there were often conflicting views about who had what authority to do what. It was n ot just political disagreement but constitutional disagreement.

For example , I had to explain to the new Cabinet Secretary how my role worked , why it was constructed in that way and why being a Minister specifically inside the No. 10 business unit — not just being CDL in the Cabinet Office— was different and important . I had to explain why it meant that officials from the Cabinet Secretary downwards were accountable to me as a Minister in No. 10 as well as to the Prime Minister . The Cabinet Secretary d id not really like that , but that is how it had been constructed.
Q50 Our understanding was that effectively when you spoke, it was as if the Prime Minister had spoken.

Yes. I would deputise for him predominantly on domestic policy. We had David Lammy as Deputy Prime Minister who did a lot of the foreign policy interactions with him alongside the Foreign Secretary . The Cabinet handbook has not been updated since David Cameron and there was nothing written down as to how these roles should operate and interact with each other.
Do not forget, Mr McFadden told us that the Cabinet m anual was totally irrelevant and we did not even need to worry our pretty little heads about it.
You should write down how some things work because if you do not write it down people have different interpretations.
Exactly. It is open to interpretation.
Q51 Just in the spirit of freestyling, the accountability —
We are annoying the C lerks today. We have torn up the script, Darren. We are r if fing ; w e are like an acapella group.

The accountability point is an incredibly important one that a lot of members here are probably going to want to explore. Just as the conversation around constitutional norms is sailing off into the distance and having brought it up again, some thing that this Committee is increasingly concerned about — at the very least I am increasingly concerned about — is that the more that we look at the systems of accountability of Government the more clear it is that we are still very reliant on the good chaps principle and that there would not be a lot of protection were a Government to come in that did not honour a lot of those principles.

That being the case , I guess the question is how far the constitution should really have inhibited a Government that came in. At what level were you finding that people were saying that constitutional norms would be breached and that you could not do things in the structure? As far as we can see really, if the Government just wants to get on with it the only person who could really intervene would be the Cabinet Secretary saying, “ We ’ re just not going to do that. ” Within the current system it is entirely feasible to remove a Cabinet Secretary who does not do those things in order to progress those areas.

I would be told all the time that there were things I could not do because of the constitution and I would often reply with, “ The constitution is unwritten so if I decide to do something , it changes ; therefore why can ’t I do it? ” I am a fan of an unwritten constitution because in theory it provides flexibility, albeit within the norms of how we should expect Government to work , their accountability to Parliament , the role of civil servants and how that differs from Ministers .

To give you one example, when I was at the Treasury I realised that the Treasury acts more like a bank than a f inance d epartment. It negotiates with each Department how much money it is going to give it for what particular things and then it says, “ Now you , Department , are broadly accountable to Parliament for the money I ’ ve given you. ” I wanted to know how they are spending the money , h ow that align s with their KPIs and whether we can spot problems earlier before they become multi-billion-pound problems . The Treasury has this system called OSCA R—Online System for Central Accounting and Reporting— where each month a Department uploads an Excel spreadsheet. Basically it shows how much they are spending against how much they were given to try to manage overall spending levels.

The quality of the data around how much is being spent on the primary care system , the SEND system or whatever it might be just was not there. I said, “ Well , can ’t we just integrate the finance systems? Let ’ s plug them together so that we can see how the money’s being spent against the priorities that are set by the Government. ” I was told, “ Well , you can ’ t do that because constitutionally the Departments are accountable to Parliament , not to the Treasury . ” I had to push and push and push in order to get a pilot to look at how you might integrate the technology. When I left the Treasury I was suddenly told it had become deprioritised so I had to go back and say, “ No , you need to reprioritise it. ” Heaven knows where it is now ; I do not have the foggiest idea.

The idea that civil servants can say to you, “ Well , we interpret the constitution and we are telling you, the democratically elected Ministers , that this is not possible, ” is not sufficient. It is important to have that check and balance because you cannot have Ministers who also just ignore what Parliament expects of them in terms of how they should behave. You need that internal check and balance but i f officials are going to play that role — certainly at the senior civil service and Cabinet Secretary level — they must be more accountable to Parliament than they already are.
Q52 When you said to them , “ The constitution is an evolving document, change it, ” what was the response?

They did not really have an answer because I do not think anyone ha s said that to them before. In practice how did I do it? I had to get the Cabinet Secretary to write a letter to every other Permanent Secretary to say that the Prime Minister and the Chancellor and I had said this was going to happen. I had to make sure the money was in the spending review for it to happen and I tabled a written ministerial statement here so that it was on the public record and no one could get rid of it. That was my greatest hope : that it meant that constitutionally, I was allowed to have integrated financial reporting across Government. It is just ba r my.

Of course we should see how money is being spent across Government in a more granular way and us e technology to better spot problems. We spend enormous amounts of money ; we cannot rely on a monthly Excel spreadsheet being uploaded to an IT system. I hope that project continues ; I need to check with new Treasury Ministers b ut the fact it was so difficult for something that is really not very controversial paints an example of the problem that needs to be fixed.
Q53 If they did not have a counter answer and you still had to do all these other things , presumably the default position was to ignore you if they did not want to do any thing .
Yes.

Q54 Coming back to the Cabinet m anual , of course t hat was first drafted in the run-up to the 2010 general election. Speaking to people involved in the drafting it was always intended to be a living document that belonged to the Prime Minister rather than the civil service. You have alluded to this already but do you feel it would have been easier to enable some changes to have happened i f an updated version of the Cabinet m anual had been produced that set out that these were the things that were going to happen?

Yes. There is quite a lot in it and a lot probably would not change very much to be honest. For the role of the Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister , the way the system knew how to interact with me and what authority I had or did not have from the Prime Minister was based on an email . We would ask the Prime Minister’s principal Private Secretary to write an email to people. The trouble with that is that when new people come in , they do not have the email in their inbox so y ou have to try to find it and resend it .

It would be much better just to put it in the Cabinet m anual and say, “ You have to read that when you are coming into your role. ” That is really important because w hen a document is owned by the Prime Minister , the Prime Minister is so busy and w hat that actually means is it is owned by the Cabinet Secretary . The Cabinet Secretary and his or her team do all the detailed work around tha t . It might go to the Prime Minister for final approval in the box. The idea that the Prime Minister is going to be able to get into the weeds of the Cabinet m anual or the pay bands for the senior civil service in the context of civil service reform is for the birds. That is why again there is an accountability gap. If officials are leading that work —albeit with oversight from the Prime Minister — who is doing the detailed accountability of what is going in it and how it works ? There are gaps there that need to be filled.

Q55 I f this is the document that is essentially going to set out how civil servants are going to try to deliver on the Government’s own commitments, perhaps in the run-up to taking control or change of administration, people will be spending more time thinking about what type of Cabinet manual they want to produce in order to ensure the outcomes from the process they are trying to put into place.

At the end of the day , if the Prime Minister tells the system that something is happening , they will do it. Getting to that point can often be quite difficult for the rest of us , essentially. If you can come in with an update to the Cabinet m anual changing the structure or the ministerial roles and the Prime Minister just says to the system, “ This is how it’s going to work, ” they will do that. More often than not you do not have that very clear agreed direction at the start ; it tends to bumble a bit as you try to figure it out.
Q56 We are already moving in this direction but d o we need to delegate more power from the Prime Minister to Ministers for oversight of the civil service within their Departments?
Yes.
Q57 How would you see that working?

My successor — the First Secretary of State — is the obvious person to whom the Prime Minister would delegate a lot of detailed policy work ; that happens already. Because t he Prime Minister is the Minister for the C ivil S ervice and the Cabinet Secretary is very clear that she reports only to the Prime Minister and that she is in charge of civil service reform , y ou need much more ministerial buy-in. It would make sense for the First Secretary of State — with an d on behalf of the Prime Minister — to be the Minister who is accountable for that.

Take the example recently in the news — it is for the Government to confirm whether this is the case or not —where i t was reported that the Cabinet Secretary was asking for legislation to be drafted for the next session to give her the statutory authority to direct other Permanent Secretaries . I do not necessarily disagree with the principle of that but I do not think the person who receives all that power should be drafting their own Bill . They are not going to be able to come to the House of Commons and present the bill, nor is the Prime Minister

Q58 The Cabinet Secretary’s ends are welcome. My view is she does not need legislation to do it. What needs to be done is a proper restoration of Cabinet c ommittees that take decisions , ha ve the full effect of Cabinet responsibility, become g overnment policy and Permanent Secretaries have to discharge it. That does not require legislation ; that is just the ordinary operation of things on the proviso that Cabinet committees have their recognised status. Am I wrong in that?

No, that is an answer to the question. As an extension of that , some work that I ha d started was to introduce — for the first time, amazingly — performance-related pay for the whole senior civil service. When I came into the Cabinet Office, there were some Departments that did not have KPIs at all. It is remarkable really. You need to have proper KPIs, incentives and a ccountability, and then when that flows through the system it will work. This is perfectly common in lots of businesses and other organisations . It is the case in some Departments , but from the centre of Government downwards this is new so it is important that we get it right.

To finish answering your question, if there is legislation a Minister has to be responsible for that legislation ; who is that Minister ? If you say the Prime Minister is the lead Minister for civil service reform, does that mean the Prime Minister is going to come and answer questions at this Committee on civil service reform or present a Bill for second reading in the floor of the House? No. You have to have someone such as the First Secretary of State who has oversight of the detail and you do not just leave it to officials who put papers in front of the Prime Minister who says, “ Well , that looks okay. Thanks so much. ”
Peter Lamb : I will relinquish time to enable other people to come back in , but I would like to remain on the list if possible.
Q59 Of course. Do you think that system is created by evolutionary accident or engineered design?
Both.
That suggests that I would agree with both serendipity and Machiavellian planning.
I find it remarkable — as I said just now — that there were no clear KPIs .
Q60 Which Departments did not have the KPIs?

I cannot remember the complete list now but there were Departments that did not have them. Some did and they sorted it out themselves. When I had to recreate the No. 10 D elivery U nit — a fantastic team of direct ministerial appointments and civil servants — I tasked the team with building a dashboard that translated Prime Minister’s priorities into key data and metric points that were shared across everybody . We would give Permanent Secretaries a RAG rating — green, amber or red — and they would have to report every month.

When it got to the point that I was told Permanent Secretaries were coming over to 70 Whitehall to ask, “ Why is it that I ’ ve been given an amber-green as opposed to a green ?” I thought, “ Hurrah , we ’ re making some progress because actually they really care about this accountability framework. ” I do not know whether it existed in the past and then just got dropped between A dministrations , but that needs to be a permanent function with clear lines of accountability to Parliament.
Q61 A yes or no answer if you can : w ill the creation of the o ffice of the Prime Minister make a difference?
Will it make a difference t o what ?
Q62 Will it make a difference to d oing stuff and d riving change ?

Yes, i f it is done properly . These were plans that I started to pull together when I was in g overnment. I have said to you before I tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed. My main frustration was that there was too much in the Cabinet Office but also No. 10 as a business unit was a sealed unit ; i t did not work with Cabinet Office people. You would have political appointees and some civil servants in No. 10 doing communications but not meeting with the Government Communications Service, or policy people not meeting with the secretariats to try to think what we are going to drive forward.

I was not allowed to abolish the Cabinet Office ; instead I just said, “ Well , you must meet with each other every week and have a shared work plan. ” That helped but there was still a sense that No. 10 is different to the Cabinet Office. In my world t he idea of the o ffice of Prime Minister and Cabinet was to basically try to abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward.

Q63 We have a huge number of consultants and people with a business background who were brought into Government to whip it into shape and that has been going on for decades. What you have described there is how some very basic business feedback accountability measures have not been implemented in vast swathes of Whitehall. Why do you think that is ? When various parties have been in g overnment we have made a conscious effort to bring in basic business expertise and it has not filtered through .

I do not know is the short answer but I am amazed that it was not. If I had to try to guess what the answer is it would be that Ministers are more focused on their political priorities than basic management and leadership within the civil service . I understand that really . As a p olitical Minister I did not really feel I should be involved in performance management and civil service bonus changes and KPIs ; I should be focused on delivering other things. If you do not have a politician pushing it and no one else is calling for it, I suppose it is easier just not to have it.

This is my point on accountability of senior civil servants to Parliament and within the whole civil service : y ou need to reward people for doing brilliant work. You also need to hold people to account if they are not performing. Who is doing that? If you are not doing it to each other in the civil service and there is no real hard wire into Parliament, is it not just comfortable to come to work every day ? No doubt you do good work and provide the public service that you have come into the civil service to provide but there is just not enough drive and performance culture in that.

Q64 What you have described is understandable in one way ; people do not get into politics to make sure the civil service runs effectively. What you have described there is that if somebody is not taking that role on in the way that they should and maybe does not have the resources and the backing that they need throughout Whitehall, it actually has a really adverse impact on a Government’s ability to be able to achieve what it wants from a policy point of view because nobody is driving that through. Would you agree?

Yes . That is important not just in terms of public service delivery or the political priorities of the Government of the day but also bread-and-butter functions such as the Government Communication Service. I spent a fair amount of my time working with David Dinsmore, the former Permanent Secretary for Government c omms , because we realised that the state was failing to interact with the public. There are apparently 7,000 officials —a remarkable number—across Government in the Government c omms s ervice spending hundreds of millions of pounds a year, if not more.

Our assessment was that we were engaging with roughly 2% of the public. Government have so many different brands, Departments, campaigns or functions that the public do not really know whether the Government are doing something good or not because they are confused by the branding and we do not put it in front of their face because we are not using the system very well. That is a problem for our democracy. It is not even a party political issue ; it is just something that needs to work more effectively. If you do not have someone driving that change through, you just carry on doing what you have always been doing and do not rise to the challenge.

Q65 Just going back to t he concept of mission g overnment , i t has been a concept in public administration circles for some decades. As somebody a little outside at the time, given what we know about Whitehall around siloed working and the dominance of the Treasury , it seem s that there was maybe an underestimation in opposition about the scale of the challenge. Would you agree with that assessment? With the benefit of hindsight, what would you do differently to try to address those constitutional barriers and siloed ways of working so that you could be more effective as an incoming Government?

The theory of missions feels fine to me because it is essentially a framing of priorities, which any Government have to do. From the Treasury perspective , in the first year we h a d gone through annual budget setting so Departments did not have long-term budget settlement ; the Treasury’s mechanisms for holding Departments to account had not really been used properly for a number of years ; the delivery unit did not exist as I was saying just now and KPIs and performance were not in place . The architecture to deliver priorities had basically fallen away and there was a repair job really to be done to rebuild the machine in order to then deliver priorities. I suppose we would not have known that in opposition ; you only know it really once you get to the inside and see how it works.
Q66 Is there anything that you would have done differently with hindsight?

The work that is already happening will mean that for this and future Governments it should be easier . If they want to call their priorities missions, I am totally fine with that and Governments should not say that cross- d epartmental working is so difficult therefore they are not going to tackle a particular problem. I do not mind Governments using that framing or taking it forward in that way but you just have to keep your foot on the pedal about making sure the machine is able to deliver it.

Q67 Just a final question fr om me . Something that we have found as a Committee is that the willingness of Departments to share data is often an obstacle to the Government being able to achieve their goals. Is that something that you would also recognise and how do you think we can approach tackling that challenge?

Yes . Quite frankly, i t is maddening. When I did the first spending review, which was just to carry us over a year until we did the multi-year spending review, I spent far too much of my time as Chief Secretary of the Treasury talking to Cabinet colleagues on the other side of the table about whose data was right . They would present data ; I would have data from my officials ; the Treasury would say , “ Well , our data is right, obviously, Minister ,” and then you would end up talking about the interpretation of the data . I said to them, “ Look , before we do the next spending review, I do not want to do that again. We have to have an agreed set of data. If we do not know something, that ’ s fine, but just be clear with us that we don ’ t know something .”

In the Cabinet Office , in the main multi-year spending review, we use the joint data analytics teams to do a lot of Sherpa or prepping work before the ministerial meetings to say, “ Well , actually, okay, Department, this is your data ; Treasury, this is your data ; let us independently look at it in the Cabinet Office and say whether we think that is right and what the gaps are and present it in a unified way, ” and that helped quite a lot.

There is a tendency not to want to share data across Governments but I do not really understand why because we are all trying to achieve the same thing . Actually , with the dashboards that the team built for me in the delivery unit — where we had agreed what the data was, what the data source was and how we would interpret it — we shared that across Government and everybody was okay with it . Maybe there is just a cultural reluctance to do it but actually in practice when it happens it seems fine , so I would encourage them to do it more.

Q68 Can I just raise a bugbear question ? I would really value your thoughts on this. The Prime Minister or the Chief Whip picks up the phone to some hopeful B ackbencher and says , “ I want you to go and be the j unior Minister in the Department of Paperclips . ” “Oh, t hank you , Prime Minister ; what a great honour, ” and off they go. Nobody ever thinks to ask what that new Minister’s skill set is , their experience of managing people, identifying routes to deliver change , monitoring the staging posts going forward and that they know how to handle and where the boundaries are, apart from reading the ministerial code with regard to civil servants . They are terrified that their rise up the greasy pole might be temporary because they may be accused of bullying if they are too bombastic , that gets them a black mark and their name becomes too hot to handle and so on . In essence the question is that politicians often default to a criticism of the system and/or the civil servants , but we do not do enough training of politicians on how to be good and effective, monitoring change and delivering dynamics, do we? There is work to be done there, is there not?

There are two areas where I would agree and they are slightly different. For Ministers in particular , I find it very odd that there is no mentoring, training or anything really. In opposition , we had some sessions from the Institute for Government, which were very useful. In g overnment it does not exist. One reason I announced the recreation of the n ational s chool of g overnment was that I thought civil servants needed better access to training than the outsourced contracts that we had inherited were providing . I also said I want ed the n ational s chool of g overnment to have a track for Ministers where you can bring Ministers together and think about how Government and t he system works and things such as project management skills .

Q69 It is not bringing Ministers in because they are busy being Ministers in that half-hour diary slot — 8.30 am through to whenever — it is identifying people who are going to be Ministers early and getting them trained up so they can hit the ground running.

Training at work is important . I do not disagree with the idea that you give Members of Parliament access to more insights and support about what it is like to be in Governmen t. I still find it slightly mad that one minute I was Shadow Chief Secretary to the Treasury , which essentially just required me to be good in the TV studios, and the next I was given paperwork and having to make billion-pound decisions and you just get asked , “ Well , which one do you think is the right answer? ” “Well, that one?” It is remarkable really.
Close your eyes and say , “ Oh , that one. ”

Exactly . “ What do you think? ” It is remarkable . When I was at the Cabinet Office I used to do what I call ed delivery lunches, when I would bring junior Ministers in from across different Departments at different levels just to give them 45 minutes or an hour to ask them, “ How are you doing? How is it going? What are the problems? ” Actually what was interesting was that a lot of the feedback from those conversations was quite similar across Departments. It was still mostly about prioritisation , KPIs and accountability .

Private office staff are the most wonderful civil servants. They work extremely hard for their Ministers , so I do not want this to sound like a criticism of them but many Ministers would say, “ I do not have people in the private office who do project management for me . These are my priorities. These are the people responsible for delivering them. I am going to get them in every week. I am going to keep track of it and we are going to let you know how it ’ s going. ” Some Ministers would be setting up their own project management tools and just doing it themselves . There is definitely much more that can be done on training , mentoring and support for Ministers .

In the United States, the JFK School of Government will put on a session for newly elected members of Congress for a couple of days when they will say , “ This is what we think the latest thinking is in terms of geopolitics or the financial position of Government or public services .” It just brings everybody up to a level that then means they can go off having thought about it in a consistent way. In our system we do not have very much of that at all, either in Parliament or Government, and it is an easy win for us to do more of that.

Q70 Only about a year before you came into office, the Independent Review of Governance and Accountability in the Civil Service led by Lord Maude had been published . That found that the arrangements for governance and accountability of the civil service are unclear, opaque and incomplete , as you have described. It described an avoidable level of tension and frustration between Ministers and civil servants and made some quite poor recommendations. Was that still on the agenda when you came into office or has that quietly disappeared?

I do not know is the answer. When I was at the Treasury, no. When I was at the Cabinet Office I got on with what I thought needed to be done but it certainly was not with reference to that report . I could not tell you who — at an official level — is responsible for implementing the findings of that report. Presumably it is the Cabinet Secretary a s the head of the civil service but I never saw anything come through my box that made reference to the report or changes being made to accountability and governance of the civil service.
Q71 Does that describe to you an institutional resistance to reform within the civil service, certainly at a senior leadership level?

Maybe. I do not know . The fact that it was not something that we were given as an ongoing set of reforms that we needed to be cited on suggests to me that it may not have been completed and therefore just maybe dropped between administrations.

Q72 How can that be resolved? Lord Maude clearly found general agreement that these issues need to be addressed . How are we going to break the logjam in terms of ensuring there is actual proper reform and accountability in the civil service?

One problem is that you are not allowed to see the advice that is given to previous Ministers ; it is all boxed off . If you ask the same question , officials have to write it up again ; t hey are not allowed to just show you what they advised last time, which was an issue not just in this space but in other areas of policy. For example, for illegal migrants on small boats , y ou might ask the question, “ Well , what advice did you give to former Ministers about the range of options that were available? ” “ We can ’ t show you that because constitutionally we are not allowed to and therefore we have to write it all up again and it is going to take us some time to work it through. ” There must be a better answer to that.
Q73 What does , “We are not allowed to do that,” mean constitutionally to the lay person? That just does not make any sense.

I actually do not know. There is a rule somewhere — although I do not know where it is ; maybe the Committee could help me find it — that says you are not allowed to see the advice given to former Ministers . I can see that you would not be allowed to see the thoughts or answers of former Ministers , the ministerial readout box; t hat is fine. Surely if an official has written up a factual assessment of a policy area you should just be able to access that and give it to new Ministers .
You are such a revolutionary, Darren.
Q74 How does that inter act with freedom of information?
It is ministerial advice - e xempt.
It would seem to me interesting , Chair, to find out all these rules , which are often pointed to—
Are they conventions?
O r conventions , and find out what the justification i s.
They are not written down ; t hat is the problem.

You will have to stop me from going down a rabbit hole here . If you are going to try to transform the way the civil service works using technology, for example, for policy advice, using AI you would be able to do a very quick and efficient job of pulling together information from a knowledge management system quite quickly and then the civil servant would check whether it meets the political considerations and speed the whole thing up. If the AI is not allowed to access documents from the pa s t, how on earth are you going to use it in order to be able to provide policy advice? You will not have a knowledge management system for it to be able to access.
This would be an interesting question to put to civil service at a future session actually in terms of how AI and its use in terms of driving efficiency will work .
We have both the First Secretary and the Cabinet Secretary due to be before us.

Q75 We can pursue that there. Just a final question from me in terms of how this context related to delivery of the missions. We did a question around the Mission Delivery Unit, which was created in the Cabinet Office and had a substantial staff including a Permanent Secretary-level appointment leader, but it only lasted a year. Why was that? Was that because of some issues we have talked about today in terms of e ffectively driving the missions with other considerations as well?

The Mission Delivery Unit has essentially become the No. 10 D elivery U nit. There is a delivery unit that exists. My reflection of the No. 10 D elivery U nit is that the prioritisation , metrics and integration with other Departments are much better. Under the Mission Delivery Unit you would have lots of meetings , s lide decks and data presentations but i t was not hardwired to the cultural incentives for officials to move more quickly. It is not that the Mission Delivery Unit was a failure ; i t is just that in many ways we have upgraded it and named it the No. 10 D elivery U nit instead.
Q76 Was t hat more effective ?

Yes . I am a huge advocate for the delivery unit team. They are still fairly small . We only really got around to doing it in the second year once I ha d come in. They are very good at not just doing the data analytics and accountability but going out and trying to really understand the supply chain. I was always very conscious of, “ Okay , if this data is true, show me which schools in different constituencies across the country are now experiencing something different that is more positive. How do we know that? ” They would be very good at working their way through all the way through to the end user and reflecting that back.

Let us t ake one example of NHS performance. We had a metric for reducing waiting lists, which is obviously important. The delivery unit did some work and realised that the biggest frustration for patients across the country in terms of their appointments was getting a letter in the post after the appointment happened. We we re spending enormous amounts of money sending out letters for no purpose whatsoever. It is actually quite an easy thing to fix. You would suddenly improve the sentiment of patients very effectively but y ou would not have known that had the delivery unit not really dived into the actual customer order journey and what the customer experience of the public service was .

Q77 Just on some of those points you made, Darren, about civil service resistance to change in general terms and having to constantly chase and prod to make sure things are happening from the Minister’s side, project management skills is a really helpful point. Where do you think that best fits, bearing in mind Minister’s capacity? Is it something that spads or private offices should do more of?

My hope for the n ational s chool of g overnment is that it provides training to everyone because I would not want to make a false distinction between roles. Ministers should have a particular set of training opportunities, and No. 10 should make it clear that Ministers are expected to do it. Sometimes Ministers might decide that actually other things are more important than going to training; they need to be told it is almost mandatory training, such as you would have in the real world.

Equally for special advisers. One of the things we have tried to improve is the HR system for special advisers; I did not think they got treated very well. They should get the opportunities for training and support because their jobs are very intense and they only really have their own community to support each other. Then, of course, for officials, especially in private offices where they are supporting Ministers to deliver on their priorities.

Q78 In terms of actually operating that and doing the project management, are you telling civil servants to please get on with priority X and then having to constantly ask every week, “Oh, how is that going?” If Ministers do not have the time who should be doing more of that? Should it be the private office, the special adviser, or someone else?

If there are clear priorities, either p rime m inisterial priority or Secretary of State priority, that should be integrated into the team supporting Ministers, so the private offices. You will often be attached to a director general or if you are a Secretary of State to a permanent secretary, so they should also be a part of it and, of course, special advisers as well.

I was always trying to encourage Whitehall to use technology more effectively. I just desperately did not want printed out slide decks, so that if I want ed a change or I ha d to ask a question I ha d to wait a week for it to come back. Using interactive data and dashboards is a really useful way to make sure that you make that process much easier. The No. 10 D elivery U nit dashboard is a great example of that. Anyone can just log in and see. You can interpret the data and see the feedback from different parts of g overnment; you can see where you are in terms of your target delivery. In many ways it feels just a routine part of checking how things are going as opposed to it being too rigid or too process driven.

Q79 On a separate note I also want to ask about arm’s length bodies. I am reminded of that statement from Keir when he went to the Liaison Committee—I think it was—where he described them as sometimes a thicket of reasons you cannot do something. Are Ministers and Government generally finding that arm’s length bodies have too much responsibility and that is getting in the way of them doing things? If so, would you say there is a general attitude of trying to resolve that, or is that becoming a bit insurmountable?

I never really experienced arm’s length bodies getting in the way of my work, but that is because I did not really have many of them at the Treasury, in the Cabinet Office or No. 10; it might feel different to different Departments. My direct experience of arm’s length bodies is how difficult it is to get rid of them, often because they are established in primary legislation.

Then there are often issues about them getting paid better than civil service equivalents who work in Departments, and if you start trying to restructure the teams it becomes quite complicated and expensive from an HR perspective. They are very hard to get rid of. You would have to check but I am pretty sure every Government ha ve done a review of ALBs and tried to reduce the number, but the outcome has been more of them, not less.
Could we then have the arm’s length body for the removal of arm’s length bodies?
There you are. I am not against them in principle, but I find it odd that where we did want to get rid of some, apparently it was so difficult to do.

Q80 I am trying to get at the levers Ministers have available to them to implement priorities more generally, and whether that is one of the avenues by which there is institutional resistance. As a C ommittee we have found significant accountability problems with some arm’s length bodies that we have looked at, going back to that again. There was the inquiry into the ONS, of course, which hopefully is now on the right track but took a while, and more recently the Charity Commission as well. I am just trying to get at how we deal with the accountability problem there in terms of being able to deliver ministerial priorities?

It is the right question. If I was still being a Minister, the way I would hold an arm’s length body to account is I would have to physically bring it in and tell it I wanted something to happen and then say, “I am going to see you in two weeks.” The trouble with that is there are only so many days in the week; you cannot do that for everything.

The drive to want to reintegrate arm’s length bodies into the Department so that you are attached to the civil service performance management framework and have direct lines into Ministers is the right answer. There has obviously been a tendency to create arm’s length bodies for lots of things. I believe the view is right when people say that you should not create them unless it is absolutely essential , and that there are more that could be integrated.
Q81 Should they all have the ability to take ministerial direction?
Yes, although I am trying to think of an example. I suppose the OBR, for example, would not necessarily agree with what the C hancellor of the day was saying to it .
The OBR and the statistics authority exempted.
Yes.
Q82 But Natural England, the Environment Agency, Homes England, Highways England?

Yes, you are right, there are clearly some where you would want the independent check and balance, although even those can sometimes be infuriating; best not to get me started on those ones either. That might be the exception as opposed to the norm.

Q83 I turn back to the general issue on accountability. Thinking about structures, where I have seen things go very badly wrong has tended to be where the people who are ultimately held account for a decision are not the same people who are involved in making that decision or seeing it through, which very much seem s to be the current arrangement with Ministers, civil servants and policies. One thing that would, of course, empower Ministers would be if they were to have more direct control. We have talked about that briefly on instructing people but ultimately, when someone fails, the powers around hiring or firing, pay and progression lay with the civil service.

My question is, where do you feel that should end? Particularly, where you have Ministers potentially only being around for a short bit of time, how do we ensure that in that window they still have the ability to leave a mark on someone’s career path if they fail to deliver?

It is a tricky question; I buy the argument that you have to be careful not to politicise the civil service and, at senior levels of the civil service, it is actually quite political so I should use my definitions carefully. If Ministers can just say, “I ’ m firing all of you and I ’ m bringing in my own people,” I am not sure that is a system that I would support in this country.

If Ministers set out their political priorities for which they have a democratic mandate and there is clear accountability for the civil service for delivering it, if they are not good enough they either need to go somewhere else or get more training or leave. I am not sure anybody really leaves the civil service ever for performance reasons. I once asked how many people had been fired for performance issues and was told it was one person. Maybe everybody is doing a brilliant job, but just in any organisation that percentage does not feel quite right. I would still fall into the much stronger lines of accountability, including to Parliament, as opposed to politicians having the right to just fire or hire officials at a whim ; that would be the wrong direction.
Q84 Accountability means coming in and answering questions , it does not mean there is an actual end consequence. What negative impact is there for failure to deliver as a civil servant?

Very little, at the moment ; I once referred to it as the sideways shuffle. If someone is deemed to not be very good they just get found a job somewhere else in the civil service. If that is a more appropriate job for them in their skill set, then that is totally fine. Actually it seemed to me that often you were just moving people around and no one ever leaves.

In theory you want accountability through the civil service, but also ultimate accountability in the Cabinet Secretary and the permanent secretary group. If your senior leaders are on the hook to Parliament for their performance they will drive a culture of incentives, but also of accountability through the system. If they are not on the hook because they say, “Oh well, the Minister’s responsible and he ’ s going to be off in a bit anyway,” there is no incentive to drive because you do not have any skin in the game. That is why you need performance management much more widely through the civil service, but for the Permanent Secretaries and the Cabinet Secretary in particular, much stronger accountability in Parliament.
Q85 It still requires some consequence. In this case, is it reputational damage by virtue of being made to look silly in front of Parliament?

It is ultimately for Ministers. It will be for the Prime Minister to say whether he or she has confidence in the Cabinet Secretary of the day and for Secretaries of State and their permanent secretaries. One of the things I had to change is that where Departments had KPIs, the Secretary of State had not been involved in setting them, which I thought was odd. There were lots of KPIs about good financial management and running the Department well and those types of things, which was totally fine, but they did not have the political priorities of the Secretary of State in their KPIs.

I have changed that now. Interestingly, the way that was implemented was that we had to tell the Cabinet Secretary what our political priorities were, and the Cabinet Secretary then dealt with the KPI setting for the permanent secretaries. It was still slightly distanced from the Ministers. So you are right, once you have set out what the priorities are and how you are going to measure them, there ought to be incentives for doing a good job. I am totally fine with using the bonus pot that we have for rewarding and promoting people who show effective delivery and giving them more responsibility.

You are right, there also need to be consequences for poor performance, but linked to that a proper system that supports people, such as you would expect in any workplace. If someone is not able to do the job very well you do not immediately fire them, you try to figure out why and give them training or support. If that still does not work tell them, “Well look, I am sorry, this role is not for you.” That just does not exist in the civil service right now.

Q86 I t is interesting that in local government, failure to undertake the direct instruction of council could constitute gross misconduct, which would be immediate dismissal. We have noticed that local government in general seems to be a bit better at delivery than central Government do these days.

Moving on, we briefly touched on questions around Treasury.
