One question that came up from one of your predecessors when he was at this Committee, Lord Maud, and was discussed by various different groups of people at the time, was that he previously talked about splitting the Treasury as a means of having a body that is capable of doing the economic end of things but does not necessarily have control over what Departments do in quite the same way. His proposal was you would actually move the payroll financing Department side out of the Treasury and put it somewhere else. What are your views on Treasury influences across the wider civil service?

The Treasury gets quite a lot of flak, and a lot of the time it is probably not fair. The Treasury could operate differently in Government, as I said earlier ; more like a finance department than a bank. It could use the levers it has more effectively on holding Departments to account for their own performance, but that should be integrated with No. 10 and the Cabinet Office, which currently it is not, very effectively.

Should the Treasury be split? I tend to say no. I can see an argument for moving the public spending teams together with the Cabinet Office teams on delivery and performance so that you are looking at money as well as outcomes and outputs.

As a former Chief Secretary to the Treasury I worry about that, though. There is always a demand for more spending across Government. Prime Ministers and No. 10 staff would often quite like it if there was just more money to solve a problem. The Treasury gets flak because it is the only Department that has to say no to everybody, but that role is really important . That is why I tend to land on not agreeing with splitting the Treasury. If you put public spending control outside of the Treasury you might just start to see, “Oh okay, well we can re-profile this, or we can find you a bit more money here or there.” That might happen a bit more, and the way the Treasury works in controlling public spending is a really important way for the system to work.

Q87 Sometimes the objections are less about the overall amount of money and more about the processes involved. For instance, Departments that are able to make significant savings or wish to re-prioritise money that has already been allocated to them—I accept that some movements have already been made to approve this—would benefit from having greater control over the money that was already allocated to them as to what they do with it.

Yes, that is right. We did something called P roject R eset, which I started at the Treasury and completed when I was at the Cabinet Office, which was trying to take out unnecessary approval points. I was amazed when I was at the Treasury how many committees you needed to get through to get approval to spend money. To take the health example, you might have a hospital, an integrated care board, NHS England, the Department for Health, then the Treasury and the Cabinet Office and, if it was politically important enough, No. 10. They would often have to keep going through this process time after time. It is no wonder nothing happens.

In Project Reset we basically went through the stack of approvals and said, “Well, which ones can we take out and give Departments more authority for their own decisions in return for more accountability for what was happening?” That has been and is being implemented, and we have seen much more efficient delivery as a consequence of it, where months and months have been saved in the process. The bit that has not quite flown through yet is the extra accountability that I would want in return for the extra delegation, and that goes back to the integrated finance system point that I was making earlier.

Q88 Turning back to missions, do you feel some of the success is around how they are developed? It feels as though a lot of the missions that were developed for this Government came out of a process that was in part about trying to win an election, natur ally, and what the Labour p arty thought the biggest issues in defining the subsequent election may well end up being if they could deliver on them. That might not necessarily be the best approach for getting buy-in from civil servants, whereas some of the things that we look at, such as the moonshot and covid, you could very easily see civil servant buy-in to those processes. Do you feel that a clearer process of involving the whole system in developing those priorities would deliver a better outcome?

Maybe ; I was not really involved in setting them up so I cannot speak with much authority. If you can get Pat McFadden to come, for example, I am sure he would have views, having started that whole process as CDL in the first year.

You are right, they were a political construct of prioritisation. Some were not really cross-Departmental: health just needs to get on with the elective waiting list in health; there is a little cross-Departmental working on planning and financing on the clean power mission, but really DESNZ just need s to get on with it; the Home Office really just needs to get on with getting more police officers in the community. Where the mission structures worked quite well was on things such as violence against women and girls, which really was a cross-Departmental problem and you needed different Ministers who were brought into the same mission as a team to really push stuff through Government. It was still hard in many ways, but in those instances that kind of mission structure worked quite well.

In many ways the missions continue, they are just called different things. Andy Burnham’s team have set up taskforces on some of their priorities; we obviously have Cabinet subcommittees, although I do not know whether they have changed actually, I have not looked, but it is basically just a vehicle for getting people to work together across Government on the priorities of the day.

Q89 It was very much billed as being the way in which the whole of Government would operate post-election. Was that the wrong approach, to view it as a totality thing, as opposed to a tool that is available to try to resolve key areas of a problem?

I do not think it was wrong, necessarily. As I say, it was a way of saying, “These are our five priorities, and that is what we are going to put our energy behind delivering,” which was then reflected in the spending review process, and ultimately what Departments are being asked to do.

The challenge with missions coming into Government after an election is that in theory they are constant, but we all know from being in Government that things change and move a lot . Y our priorities or your key deliverables might change within and between elections, and so you probably ought to be careful to not exclude responding to other things by just being so resolutely focused on the priorities that you set at election time.

Q90 Is that where the plan for change came in? Of course you already had your five missions, and then an additional list of things—that interacted with those missions somewhat—was brought in as short-term targets.

Again, I was only involved in the plan for change in terms of what it meant fiscally, but my understanding of it was that it was trying to translate the political missions into an operational plan for Whitehall . A gain, I am fine with that , so long as they are embedded in clear KPIs and performance-related pay and accountability from the system.

Q91 Just to scoop up some of the things that I am not sure if we have covered in much detail ; how were the mission boards themselves constituted? Could you take me through the life cycle of one of these mission boards? How frequently did it meet, and who decided who sat on it, for example?

They were set up from No. 10 and the Cabinet Office, and Pat McFadden, the CDL , was the lead Minister and sat as deputy chair on each of them . T he chair, of course, being the lead Department for the mission. The Cabinet Office then hosted the secretariat function to drive the work that those mission boards decided to take forward. I do not know how often they met; I do not know whether the Government have published any information about that.
Q92 What was the role of the Secretary of State for the relevant Departments that the mission covered?

W hen Yvette Cooper was Home Secretary for example, she would chair the mission board and Pat, as CDL, would be the deputy chair. Then the c ommittee would have Secretaries or Ministers of State from other Departments who had to sign up to the plan for delivering against the objective.
Q93 It would meet at the point where the budgets were being distributed. Did it meet again at periods after that?

Yes, they definitely met around the spending process, so they would meet quite frequently in the first year. As Chief Secretary to the Treasury, I was not a standing member of them, for which I am partly grateful.
Q94 Did you have any influence over their operation or who sat on them?

No, I did not when I was at the Treasury. It would have been a time challenge for me to be able to go to all five of them all the time, so that is why I say I was grateful to not be asked. I wanted to make sure that the spending process was mission-led as that was the direction we had from the Prime Minister. That is why I asked them to meet specifically around their bid into the spending review.

That drove some good work ; it got them to think on a cross-Departmental basis: what does each Department have to contribute to deliver this outcome, how would we measure that, and what do we think the cost of that is? There was some hope that the mission boards would just get extra money on top of the money the Departments also wanted . O bviously there is only so much money to go around, so that is why it did not quite work in that way.
Q95 Did it just meet at the point where the money was being distributed and that decision was being made? Did the mission boards not see the mission through?
No, they met frequently, but they had additional meetings to think about their bid into the spending process.

Q96 You have described how, once the money made its way into the Departments, the mission itself maybe became less of the motivator, but many of the missions you have described were Department-specific. I appreciate you did not want to mention any names earlier on and point blame at anybody, but were there any Departments that were particularly good at the mission approach? Any that you think were worthy of acknowledging that the culture of a Department maybe got on board with the mission approach?

I do not know is the answer ; that is not because I am trying to dodge the question, but certainly from my perspective they all just seemed to operate as you would expect them to operate. Culturally , for it to be optimal you needed a team approach. If you were in a scenario where the lead Department that chaired the board used it as a mechanism for wagging its finger at other Departments and telling them, “You need to do what I want you to do,” that culturally leads to a low performance atmosphere. What you really want from them, and this is the same for other forms whether they are taskforces or otherwise, is a shared sense of purpose and collective responsibility, as opposed to another hierarchy.

Q97 I remember reading the stories about the fights during the Blair and Brown years between No. 10 and the Treasury. Some people will just view this as another story in that history of Departments fighting with each other over power: the recreation of a delivery unit, the centralisation of power around the Cabinet Office and No. 10. Some may even have viewed this as the undermining of individual Departments. How would you respond to anybody who pushed that charge at you?

I do not recognise that at all. Departments have a million things that they also need to get on with every day. There is lots of business-as-usual operational work that they need to get on with. The structure in the centre should only really be focused on the kind of top-tier political priorities of the Prime Minister and the Cabinet of the day. Departments need to be allowed to get on with doing the rest of their business-as-usual job without the centre trying to run the Departments for them. You just would not have the capacity to do that. That is why prioritisation is so important, both in the centre but also for the Departments to know that these are the four or five things that they are going to be held to account for.

Q98 Is that easy to reconcile? Is this not one of the criticisms of the old No. 10 D elivery U nit model? P eople wrote books about centralisation, that KPI model. There is one called “The Whitehall Effect” by John Seddon, which is quite critical of that approach ; that it does not necessarily deliver the outputs. Is that easy to reconcile?

I would ask the author what the alternative is. I am not wedded to it at the exclusion of all other ideas, but the centre needs to know whether the political priorities of the Cabinet are being delivered or not. You cannot just send a letter to a permanent secretary and Secretary of State and come back in five years and hope for the best. The system of incentives and accountability around prioritised KPIs feels to me to be a sensible thing to do. If there are better options, I am all ears, really.

Q99 It is interesting that the work you have done is now developing further with the strengthening of the No. 10 operation and the creation of No. 10 North as well. Thinking about how we reconcile missions for central Government, how do you think it sits with the new plans for devolution, where we are actually trying to push some of this decision making to regional Government, even if some of the objectives sound as if they are national. Do you think that is compatible with the approach that was taken through mission g overnment?

It can be compatible ; you just need to be clear about what it is you are asking a combined authority to deliver. My two observations on that are I do not really mind whether the decision is taken in Whitehall or in a combined authority, so long as it is a good decision. If you have bad decisions being taken, in the centre or elsewhere, they are still bad decisions. I want to be assured that the policy analysis and effective delivery is being done in a combined authority. Then there is a question for combined authorities about what skillset workforce capabilities they have. I am totally fine with the idea of devolution.
If you delegate them, those bad decisions are their bad decisions, they are not the centre’s.
Yes, but that is not good enough, really. They are still bad decisions.
Q100 It is not devolution, is it?

It depends on how you set the question. What I mean by a bad decision is, for example, are you spending a lot of money and not achieving any real outcomes for people? What the Government mean by devolution—I think— is, “We will give you more authority to deliver your local transport projects.” I am not sure if where you decide to put your train stations in your city region is what is meant by a good or a bad decision. It is totally fine that that is decided locally, but I do not want mini HS2s in lots of combined authorities across the country; that is a poor performance around delivery and accountability.

To go to my point on accountability for combined authorities, I question whether the current accountability of the mayors is sufficient if we are going to give them much more money and power. They are currently held to account by the local authorities, and maybe that is fine, but do they have the same support and resource that committees of the House of Commons or the National Audit Office have? I do not think so. Then, what role is there for Parliament in holding mayors to account? Much like my point on the Cabinet Secretary and senior civil servants, if we are going to put much more public money and decision-making authority into mayors, the question that Parliament and the Government need to answer is, how do you have sufficient accountability around that?
Q101 Are you saying not just accountability to No. 10, but accountability to M embers of Parliament as well?
Yes, absolutely.

Q102 Good morning, Darren. I appreciate your honesty and candour this morning. You paint a very bleak picture of how the civil service works and how powerless we are, perhaps. I was smiling when you talked earlier about when you were sometimes asked to do things you were told were against the constitution. I remember my time as a Minister asking to do something and the official telling me it was against the law for me to try to do what I was going to do. I asked them to tell me which bit of the law I was going to be breaching, they went away and came back and they could not actually tell me which bit of the law I was going to be breaking. It shows the sort of culture that is there to push back whenever anything outside the ordinary was being suggested.

One of my biggest frustrations was coming across fellow Ministers who were just too accepting of what officials said. I know we discussed earlier about whether the way you rectify that is by providing better training, but surely it is actually about making sure the people who are appointed in the first place have the skills. I know from my previous work life, people who did not have the skills did not get promoted and were not given the job. Surely the job of the Prime Minister or the Chief Whip, whoever it is and whatever party that is making these appointments , need to make sure in the first instance that the Minister actually has the skill set, albeit with some training, to ensure Government are delivering?

I agree. If all the political parties and maybe Parliament can come to some consensus about what support, training, insight and mentorship we provide to Members of Parliament, that can only be a good thing. We have brilliant universities and think tanks, and lots of people who have been in Government and experienced these things. At the moment , none of that is really channelled to help the next generation of political leaders. Surely there is an answer there that we can come up with that is better than what we have now?

Q103 Going back to the mission-led Government in particular , the Government appointed 27 Labour MPs as mission champions. Can you explain what their role was supposed to be, and is that continuing, or has that been stopped?

No, that has stopped. Mission champions were a function of the p arliamentary Labour p arty, I think, as opposed to Government, and essentially their job was to, similar to a PPS, be a voice within the PLP on that particular policy area for Members of Parliament who were interested and wanted to engage with what was happening.
Q104 Was it more, as you say, a PPS type role, the link between the mission board and the parliamentary party, as opposed to anything more formal than that?
As I understand it, yes.

Q105 With No. 10 North being established, how is that going to fit in with ensuring the civil service is moving in the same direction and delivering Government objectives? Is it going to help, hinder, or just dilute the whole accountability even further?

I do not know. No. 10 North, as I understand it, is its own business unit within the Cabinet Office. No. 10 is obviously its own business unit , No. 10 North is its own business unit, and then you have the wider Cabinet Office around it.

I would be interested to see how the Government continue to roll out the creation of the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. I want it to be more than just a name change; how are you integrating those teams so that you have political appointees and civil servants, whether they are in No. 10 Downing Street, Manchester, 70 Whitehall or elsewhere, all focused around delivering the same set of objectives? If that results in a more integrated team serving the Prime Minister and Cabinet, then that is a great thing.
Q106 I have two quick questions — whether they will be quick answers, I do not know. What is your assessment of the t est, l earn, and g row initiative?

As a set of pilots they were doing some important work. The next question is, how is that evidence integrated into the mainstream delivery of services in Departments? That is a question for the current Government to answer.
Q107 I n terms of the underpinning ethos of them, which is do not be risk averse and learn from failure, d o you think that still has a useful role to play in delivering change?
Yes. Innovative approaches to delivering public services differently, with a very customer-centric view, is the way in which we should be building public services in the future.

Q108 Drawing on your Treasury and Cabinet Office experience, I just wondered what your assessment, evaluation , might be on the future of outsourcing. I n relatively recent memory w e obviously had the collapse of Carillion. We have Capita failing lamentably, vis-à-vis civil service and other agents. If we look back, the underpinning principle was that suddenly a very dynamic marketplace of lots of people trying to compete for a share of the g overnment cake would be created. That has not happened; we have a concentration of a few large players. Where do you think it goes? Are we on the cusp of a dramatic insourcing agenda?

I would distinguish between core services and where it is useful to bring in the private sector as a partner. By core services I mean such things as running a pension scheme, or front-of-house staff, where we made a commitment in our final few weeks in Government to bring our front-of-house staff back in-house as part of the Cabinet Office.

The n ational s chool of g overnment was the largest insourcing announcement that the Government made in the last two years, where outsourced contracts were not delivering the type of outcome s we really wanted. For those functions I am a supporter of insourcing them as you get better outcomes for your money.

I would distinguish that though in relation to technology adoption in the civil service, for example. The Government digital service is excellent and has led really well , but Government really do need a better approach to digital transformation because at the moment it is incremental. We can only really do that if we continue to reform our procurement rules to make it easier for particularly British technology companies to help us deliver better public services for the public. I do not think it is an end to outsourcing in the context of working in partnership with the private sector, but for core services the idea that the market is providing better options than actually just treating our people better has been shown to not be the case.

Q109 In answer to a number of questions you have mentioned time pressures, really : the ability to draw breath, think and reflect. I am sure it is something we will return to when the First Secretary of State appears before us, and indeed the Cabinet Secretary, but just fill in a little gap in certainly my knowledge, colleagues are probably much better briefed than I am on this. Let us say, for example, meteorologists are currently predicting a very significant El Niño, both wintertime and summer. That is going to present challenges in terms of food security, energy security, transport resilience, operation of the health service, kids sitting exams in schools in extreme heat, care for the elderly and so on and so forth. What, if any, processes exist within the Cabinet Office to say, “Look, this is looming, how can we be proactive rather than just react to events?” How can we better prepare our resilience, our staffing, and so on? Or is it a case of it is happening, and when it is happening, how do we respond?

On these issues, the COBRA team and the National Security team really are very excellent. In all my experience with those two teams, they have always been ahead of the curve, and they have always been extremely helpful in helping Ministers to understand the risk and what you might do about it.

COBRA and the National Security team are obviously in the Cabinet office, and you can use COBRA meetings or other Cabinet meeting formats to bring the right people together to look at the projection. I would be teased a bit for giving Cabinet weather updates when I was CDL, but it was really important because for example in the extreme heat this summer, thousands of people died who would not have died had it not been for the heat. We saw the impact on economic infrastructure and public services. I actually feel that that part of the system is really strong and very competent, and it is therefore more about what Government do in response to the information that they are being provided with.

Thank you very much, Darren. Thank you for availing yourself of the opportunity to come and talk to us. You have provided us with a lot of food for thought, and we are very grateful to you for finding the time so to do. Thank you .
Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee
Oral evidence: Modernising Elections , HC 43
Tuesday 20 October 2026

Witnesses: Florence Eshalomi MP and Stuart Ison .
Q193 Good morning and welcome to the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee. I will ask the witnesses to introduce themselve s—t hey are very unfamiliar to me !

Florence Eshalomi : Good morning, Chair. I am Florence Eshalomi . I am the Member of Parliament for Vauxhall and Camberwell Green and the Minister for Homelessness, Democracy, Communities and Faith, and formerly of the said parish Select Committee.
Good morning. I am Stuart Ison. I am the Director for Elections in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
I will ask Committee members to also introduce themselves.
Good morning. My name is Andrew Cooper and I am the Member of Parliament for Mid Cheshire.
Ashley Dalton, Member of Parliament for West Lancashire.
Will Forster, MP for Woking.
Lee Dillon, Member of Parliament for Newbury.
Lewis Cocking, Member of Parliament for Broxbourne.
Gagan Mohindra, MP for South West Hertfordshire.

Q194 As the Minister will know very well, this Committee launched an inquiry in March this year to examine the significant changes to elections policy in the Representation of the People Bill as well as to point out areas where we think the Government might go further. Over the course of this inquiry, the Committee has considered a number of proposals for the Government: voter registration, voter ID and the implementation of votes at 16. We have also ask ed what more the Government can do to protect our democracy in an increasingly complex online information environment, so we will come to these issues today with the Minister. During this inquiry, the Minister will remember that Philip Rycroft published his significant review into foreign financial interference in our politics, making some important recommendations for Government , and I know that the Prime Minister is also very interested in this area. This is a topic that we will cover this morning.

Minister, thank you for being here . B efore I turn to the Government proposals, on behalf of the Committee I want to refer everyone to the financial register of interests. All our declarations are publicly available, so I ask everyone in the room and online to check our register of interests.
I will begin by asking you this: how confident are you that the reforms to the political finance system will address the risk of interference in our democracy as identified by Philip Rycroft?

Florence Eshalomi : Thank you, Chair, and thank you for the invitation to address the Committee this morning. What we are seeing through the Representation of the People Bill is one of the most significant changes in looking at political finance for decades . The recommendation led by Sir Philip Rycroft looked at the forms of keeping foreign and illicit money out of our politics, making sure that any money coming into UK politics is transparent, traceable and from permissible donors. We are also working with the independent Electoral Commission on strengthening any additional regulation that we need on that , looking at any additional fines that the Electoral Commission can impose, strengthening the way in which political parties, individual donors and campaigners register their donations and a range of measures looking at how individual companies donate.

In response to your main question about foreign interference, we know that there are examples of where foreign actors are trying to influence UK politics. I think it is very important for us to be loud and clear that UK politics is not for sale , and it is so important to make sure that any money coming into UK politics is traceable. I think it is fair to say there is no appetite for public funding for political parties but the reality is that politics, elections and candidates all cost money. It is about how you make sure that any money coming into UK politics is through a transparent measure, that we know who is donating to political parties and candidates.

We are looking at making sure we are strengthening the know-your-donor framework, making sure all of us as candidates and political campaigners know there are additional risk assessments for donations over £11,180, which is the current threshold that is permissible from the Electoral Commission, making sure that any illicit ways to subvert campaigns and donations is traceable. That is why we are being very clear about the use of cryptocurrency, which is a new form of payment. This is not about saying that cryptocurrency is bad but it is about saying how do we trace where cryptocurrencies are originating . It is about looking at an annual cap placed on donations from overseas electors.
We feel that a number of these measures will help to trace and ensure that there is no illicit money coming into UK politics.

Q195 Thanks for that, Minister. It is good to hear the Government confirm they are supporting Rycroft and the Electoral Commission is working with the Government. You mentioned that the Government are looking to implement the know-your-donor framework, essentially requiring political parties to carry out a risk framework for funds. Will some sort of guidance be given to political parties? Each political party will measure what its risk is very differently. How would that be fairly measured and guidance given to political parties so that they know what they need to report?

Florence Eshalomi : It is very clear that during election campaigns you have paid party staff and many people who are volunteers with political parties. It is about ensuring that the rules are clear. It is working with all political parties and their co-operation is really important on this, making sure that all political parties are aware of those changes before any major elections happen, as we have done and successive Governments have done as well. You will be aware, Chair, that the Speaker’s Committee on the Electoral Commission also takes a keen interest in this, with representatives from all the major political parties in Parliament fee d ing into that. Ultimately, it is about how we clarify existing rules on donations and ensure that the parties are fully up to date with how any new changes are implemented for elections going forward.

Q196 That is very helpful. If political parties are required to make risk assessments, they need to be given some sort of framework so they know what they are required to do. The Government have said that they are accepting Rycroft’s recommendation — and you have just confirmed it now — to put in place a moratorium on crypto donations. My understanding is that the amendment added at Commons Report does not place the mechanism for lifting the moratorium on the face of this Bill. Why are the Government not making that explicit?

Florence Eshalomi : Just to reconfirm, the Government accepted all the recommendations from the Rycroft review, including the moratorium on crypto donations. Once we have a system in place where the Electoral Commission can work with Parliament to outline a proper mechanism for regulating and identifying cryptocurrency, that will help with protecting the integrity of a donation. The Government’s immediate priority is having that ban in place , and it is about continuing to engage with the EC and other organisations to look at a regulatory framework that w ill help identify cryptocurrencies in the future. It is also about being clear to say that not all cryptocurrency is bad. A number of people operate in cryptocurrency; it is a new form of payment. It is about getting a better understanding of where the funding is coming from.

As it is now in place, any requirement to lift that ban will require primary legislation , and I think it is right that the Government will come back to the House seeking views and comments, not just from this Committee but from Members right across the House, giving Parliament and wider stakeholders an opportunity to scrutinise that. Given the risk that the Government feel that cryptocurrency currently poses, they wish to keep the moratorium in place until we have a better understanding.

Q197 Minister, welcome back. On company donations, the Government accepted Rycroft’s recommendation to apply a profit test rather than revenue. However, companies will still be able to donate their profit many times over. Why have the Government chosen not to apply the donation limit to a company’s total political donations in a year, as recommended by the Electoral Commission?

Florence Eshalomi : One of the key things, which I am sure many of us see in our role as constituency MPs, is that many small and medium - sized companies want to donate. That does not mean that they are part of a political party , but they support individual candidates, individual MPs and individual councillors. We also know that for many companies there are periods where they are not making a good profit ; there will be peaks, repaying of loans, difficulties and challenges. We think striking the right balance in looking at the post-tax profit over a longer period will help in capturing the permissibility of a company’s finances. It is about closing a loophole for people who are setting up unincorporated companies, shell companies where they can in some cases—and there have been examples—funnel money into the political parties. It is about how we have a political regime and a political finance regime that is robust and able to respond to some of those challenges and make sure that any illicit or foreign money is not coming through.

We have listened to some of the stakeholders and taken on board the comments from the Rycroft review. We feel that by having a longer period looking at actual profits as opposed to a smaller period of two years, a five-year window would help in giving a company credibility and the opportunity to show that they are based in the UK, paying UK taxes, employing UK staff, and making sure that the viability of the company exists as well. I think that on the face of it we have struck the right balance to ensure that there is genuine economic activity in the UK to support genuine donations to candidates, political parties or campaigners.

Q198 While I applaud the Government’s efforts to make sure we are not creating fake companies and creating turnover and donating off the back of it, the point I was trying to make was about using the same profit level multiple times. To me, that feels like a bit of a loophole around this because if you have a successful company, what is to stop that profit being distributed many times?

That is a very good point . That is one of the reasons why we are reflecting very carefully on this and we will be looking to bring forward proposals in the House of Lords to address the challenges that you have just disclosed.
On the timeframes, in the previous answer you justified why it is five years rather than two. I am fine.

Q199 It is good to see you again, Minister. My question is about the regulated period. For the benefit of the viewers at home, the regulated period happens in the 365 days before an election. As you know, Minister, there are spending limits for the short campaign and the long campaign but political activity happens all year round, whether that is campaigning or donations. Philip Rycroft acknowledged this in his review. The chief executive of the Electoral Commission has talked about the need to set up a regulatory regime that covers the period between regulated periods, not least because foreign interference does not worry too much about when the regulated period is. It happens all the time. Does the Minister consider the current distinction between regulated and unregulated periods remains appropriate in an era of continuous campaigning?

Florence Eshalomi : There are two parts in response to that , Mr Cooper. The regulated period is quite important because it helps with providing transparency around the campaigning period. Many of us in this room know when the short campaign kicks in, when spending limits kick in, but there are also periods where it may feel that a campaign is going on but essentially we have seen over the last few years that there is a lot of activity during the periods outside of a formal election cycle. It is important for us to come back to why some of the key measures in the Representation of the People Bill are outlined. It is about how we ensure that those trying to influence and unduly target UK politics do not have a loophole, do not have a period where they can do that. It is about looking at accountability during the long periods where people may feel that there is not any campaigning going on.

Equally, we must also be careful about not overburdening campaigners. I mentioned that a number of campaigners are volunteers. They are not paid staff. They are doing it because they support political parties or no parties or independent parties. They are doing it because they have an interest in politics. It is about how we make sure that the regulations don’t put off those genuine people and that anyone coming into politics, anyone participating is not hampered or put off by that.

Looking at the current framework set out, we believe that it is the right balance for ensuring that the rules remain fit for purpose. We are looking at how we deliver recommendation 4 in the Rycroft review about the transparency of candidates’ donations in the lead-up to an election outside of the regulated period. There is still a lot more work to be done in that area and that is one of the areas that I think we will definitely come back to in due course.
Q200 Is there a risk that if we don’t get this right we will just end up displacing activity into an unregulated period, in particular from foreign influence?

Florence Eshalomi : On balance, that is one of the things we would want to test with the Electoral Commission. A number of different political parties or people who don’t even see themselves as political candidates are fundraising now. I know that if you go on some pages you will see a donate button. Would that count as election spend? When do you start valuing and quantifying that money? These are all areas that I think we need the Electoral Commission to be a lot clearer on as the independent body that will regulate the funding and donations received by individuals and political parties.

Q201 Indeed. As I said at the beginning, the chief executive of the Electoral Commission said in his letter to the Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy that it was keen to start that work, it was keen to get going on it. Have the Government asked it to start that work? Do you know if any work has commenced at the Electoral Commission?

It is a really important area. As we described in the opening moments of this Committee, there is a huge amount of work going on with the Electoral Commission in a number of areas. We are working with the Electoral Commission on issues like guidance for all of the things that the Chair described at the start of this meeting. There is a huge body of work ongoing. We are talking to them about the regulated period, which of course has a number of different strands. We will request that work as quickly as possible but, as the Minister has said, for the time being we believe that the current arrangement for the regulated period strikes an important and fine balance between not overburdening campaigning organisations and parties but also provi ding the right level of transparency. We will continue to keep it under review and of course we welcome the views of this Committee.

Q202 Thank you, Minister and Mr Ison. I want to be absolutely clear . You said that there is work going on with the Electoral Commission and that you are talking to the Electoral Commission about this issue. Just for the avoidance of doubt, have you asked the Electoral Commission to do some work specifically on this, as it has said it need s to?

We have begun conversations with them on the regulated period. As I said, there is a huge amount of work ongoing by the Electoral Commission i n a range of different areas. We will be looking to progress those discussions over the course of the coming months. I don’t believe they have a specific strand of work on that. They have got enough to do at the moment , but it is very important and we will address it very quickly.
Q203 Do you have an idea when that work might begin?
Not at this time , but we will keep the Committee updated.
Thank you.

Q204 Stuart, you said that the Electoral Commission is working on a number of different guidance documents , based on the Chair’s opening statement. One would assume that there is a work plan for those guides, for example to come to you for checking before final publication or for feedback. Are you able to share that timetable with this Committee so we can see th e schedule of work that you said is in progress now?

Yes. I am sure the Electoral Commission w on’t mind me saying that we have spent many joyful afternoons in the last few weeks working through some of the issues. On the timetable, I would be happy to share something with the Committee in due course. I don’t have it to hand but I am happy to share it.
It would help us to be able to feed in at the opportune moments. Thank you.

Q205 I want to ask a follow-up question. I think it is good that the Electoral Commission is doing work on this. We know that foreign interference is a global matter. Have you been looking at other countries to see what they are doing on this, to see if there are best practices that we could be doing in the UK?

I am happy to come in on this, if that is helpful. The answer is yes. There is a very wide range of different practices taken forward by countries across the world. We have regular dialogues in particular with countries like Australia, Canada and New Zealand, who are addressing similar challenges. Likewise, we talk with our European partners about some of these issues. We had a recent event that the Foreign Office helped to organise with a range of different countries looking at some of these challenges. The answer is yes but, of course, each country faces slightly different issues and there are varying different approaches. There is a lot to learn and it is a very important area.

Florence Eshalomi : I think, Chair, in your formal role , the Defending Democracy Taskforce is not just Ministers from MHCLG but Ministers from MOJ, Home Office, DSIT, DCMS, all those key areas of online safety and finances coming together to look at additional threats. It is a whole G overnment approach to looking at foreign interference.

Q206 I am a bit concerned about the unregulated period. I feel that a lot of work is being done on the regulated period but it will just mean so much will be done during that period that we won’t be monitoring that w ill be damaging to democracy. That is why I was asking about what conversations you have had with other countries to see if there are areas we can strengthen in the unregulated period , because that is what I can see slipping through the net.
Florence Eshalomi : That is something I will definitely take back to colleagues on the Defending Democracy Taskforce and the Speaker’s Electoral Commission Committee.

Q207 Welcome, both of you. Minister, earlier you touched on the issue of overseas voters and donors. Recent cases have demonstrated significant legal complexities associated with trying to target donations caps specifically to overseas voters. Can you tell us how and if the new task and finish team will be considering universal donations caps as a potential solution?

Florence Eshalomi : Thank you, Ms Dalton. The Government are still in the process of writing the formal terms of reference and key areas that will be discussed in the task and finish team, but it will be looking at the issue of foreign donations and the loopholes there. I talked about the know-your-donor rules to look at that assessment and risk assessment. There are also the additional measures of the residency test for people coming back to the UK. We understand that many people don’t spend a large proportion of time in the UK. They are overseas, which is fine, but from the day they come back to the UK, are they then donating large amounts to relevant political parties or independent parties ?

It is about how we make sure, following on from the Rycroft recommendations and in line with the £100,000 cap, which was the lowest threshold recommendation in the Rycroft review, it is designed to identify any immediate risks. It is making sure that when people come back to the UK they can demonstrate that they have spent the preceding 365 days in the UK before they can donate. Some of these additional measures will help with looking at the donations from people going through. A blanket cap on overseas donors would cause problems with tracing the source of the funding. It is about how we make sure we have measures in place to target some of the larger donations that we see coming into politics such as through cryptocurrencies.

T he new task group, which will be chaired by the Secretary of State and the Lord Chancellor, will identify a number of these areas , test out possible scenarios and come back with recommendations to me as the Minister and ultimately back to Parliament.

Q208 Thanks for that. You mentioned that the terms of reference for that task and finish group are still being developed. Do you have a timescale for when those terms of reference will be complete and the group will be able to start?

Florence Eshalomi : There is a lot going on at the moment , Ms Dalton, but because this is a key priority for both me and the Prime Minister, we are pushing colleagues to give us some information on that. As soon as we have any additional information, we will be happy to share it with the Committee.

Q209 Thank you. You talked about what the donations cap might look like and you mentioned the £100,000 lower recommended cap. Some of the witnesses at the Committee, who I am sure you will be aware of, have previously recommended donations caps as high as £1 million to ensure that additional state funding of political parties is not required. Do you have concerns with that approach or any thoughts on that?

Florence Eshalomi : I think it is how we get the right balance and the right funding coming into funding elections. Many of us in this room will hold different fundraisers, events to raise money for our individual campaigns. I think it is testing the level of appetite for public funding in political parties. That appetite is very low at the moment when we look at the situation that the Government and the country are dealing with in funding for key services, public services, key areas. The rationale for a concern about £1 million cap, which seems quite high—I feel that the current threshold is not just in line with the recommendation from Rycroft but it strikes the right balance.

Ultimately it is looking at some of the issues we have talked about with donations coming in during the unregulated periods. A lot more scrutiny of what money is coming in, of companies ’ and individual donations and where the funding is coming from will help , but the debate is around where should we put this figure, how much is enough, when you make comparisons to other countries where there are continuous political adverts and no caps or spending limits . T he last time the spending limit was increased was under the former Conservative Administration , whe n the cap was increased to about £1 million I think. We have a healthy balance in the UK , but the questions around the limits will continue to be debated.

Q210 Obviously that limit does continue to be debated. The Secretary of State has asked the Electoral Commission to recommend a lower spending limit. The Committee on Standards in Public Life made a recommendation in 2021. What is the rationale for another review to make a decision ?

Florence Eshalomi : The Committee on Standards in Public Life reported in 2021 , and a lot has changed in those five years. We are seeing new forms of funding coming into political parties. We are seeing new forms of campaigning, online campaigning taking off. We are seeing new parties form. It is not the traditional two-party politics. We are seeing an appetite for how politics are delivered. It is not a process that we take lightly. I think it is right that any major changes are led by proper consultation with all views being fed in. It is right that the independent Electoral Commission and other expert stakeholders come to a conclusion and an outline that we, as the Government, can then take forward.
Thank you.

Q211 Welcome, Minister, and congratulations on your appointment. I want to talk about automatic voting registration. Will this be done across the whole country for everyone who is eligible to be automatically registered to vote before the next general election?

Florence Eshalomi : Thank you for that, Mr Cocking. We have been very clear that across the country there are about 7 million or 8 million people who are either incorrectly registered or not registered to vote at all. Over the next two years we are hoping to work on creating a new automated voter registration system to ensure that more people can participate in our democracy. To help support that, we are hoping to have different methods tested in different parts of the country to look at a form of an automated system, looking at how we work on existing technology, new technology, to help improve that , and how any permanent changes will be supported by robust evidence. The Bill as it stands now is hoping to help roll that out across the country. I think the Government have been very clear that we are hopeful and trying to move towards an automatic voting system before the next general election. As we all know in this room, Mr Cocking, we do not know when the next general election is. If we are working on the cycle of the current Parliament, the next general election will have to be held before August 2029. We are working with local authorities and the Electoral Commission to have a system in place, hopefully before that date.
Q212 If this Parliament goes the full term until 2029, can you guarantee then that the whole country will be automatically registered or not?
Florence Eshalomi : We are working towards the ambition as set out in the last Labour manifesto of having a system of automated voter registration across the country before the next general election.

Q213 You do not envision having a general election where some people have been automatically registered to vote and other people have not. If that does become the situation, can you not see how the public could perceive that as being unfair?

I completely understand your question and your concern. For a bit of context, taking a step back on this a little bit, first, arrangements for automated voter registration are incredibly complex. If you look back at the Australian example, in the context of a compulsory voting system it took them over a decade to introduce an automated voter registration system.

What we are trying to do is to build towards that and take some important steps to improve voter registrations for the reasons the Minister has set out, the very high levels of either incorrect or no registration at all. Your concern is very much one about doing it in certain areas and not others, which I understand. That is why we want to test automated registration in a range of different areas, different demographics, different geographies, different locations, different types, testing rural and urban, and so on. We will try to ensure that we protect these arrangements, and to inform outreach with local authorities who may want to pilot, is to develop a set of criteria with the Electoral Commission to ensure that when we do this, it is done in a fair and balanced way.

We also want to talk to political parties about this because we understand the concerns that you have raised, Mr Cocking . They are entirely understood. We will be working with the Political Parties Panel, which the Electoral Commission chairs, to make sure that we are listening to the political parties as this is rolled out. There is a lot of work to do. There is some uncertainty about it in the sense that we are trying to use data in very innovative ways, pooling data from across Government to make this happen. There is a lot of work still to do.

To finish, there is also a lot that can be done within local authorities already. We are conscious that people will move frequently within local authorities, sometimes in the same authority, and there is data that is held there where people have already registered at one address and then have moved, and therefore their registration is not valid any more . We think there is more that can be done within local authorities to address that as well. Forgive me, a lot there, but there is a huge amount of work going on.

Q214 You are not answering my question, and you do not give me any comfort that we could not have a general election where some people are automatically registered and some people are not. When you speak about the pilots specifically, are they for local elections? Are they for constituency elections to elect MPs? What do you envisage those demonstrations to be?

This has all got to be worked through. As I said, as and when these pilots take place, we will be working with the Electoral Commission on those criteria to ensure we have the right balance for where these pilots are taking place and in what areas. We also want to work with the political parties for the reasons I have described, to make sure that there is an ability for political parties to feed into that process as well. The point I am trying to make is that it will take a while to get this running. We need to make sure it works. We are protecting the electoral register here. It is important we get this right.

Q215 For complete clarity then, if we have the next general election in 2029 and half the people, so half of that 8 million, let us say 4 million, have been automatically registered and 4 million have not, would you perceive the result of that general election as fair or unfair?

As I said, what we are trying to do is to make sure that, over time, we are building and improving the way in which voters are registered. I simply cannot comment specifically on the question you have asked, but the process will be there, and we will be engaging with you and with colleagues, and indeed with this Committee, to make sure that you understand and are fed into the way in which those pilots are taking place.

Florence Eshalomi : I think one of the other issues is that some of us will speak to people on polling day who say, “Yes, I do want to vote”, but then they will find out that they are not on the electoral register. You have a situation where some voters rightly feel that they can register there and then to vote. How do we make it easier for people to be automatically on their electoral register? That is the main aim. It is not a case of the aim being to look at areas to have more people on the electoral register; it is how we get a fair balance across the country .

As an example, we have a new initiative starting this month where, for anyone renewing their driving licence, as you are filling out the DVLA form, there is a box that will say, “Do you want to be added on to the electoral register?”

How do we make it easier for people to be automatically registered to vote? In answer to your specific question, what we are doing at the moment is inviting local authority areas to be part of the pilots and to come forward. We will be working with the Electoral Commission, making sure that there is a fair spread, a geographical spread across the country—coastal areas, rural areas, urban areas—so that we can get a better understanding of how we can make sure that this automatic voter registration works in practice before we then roll it out across the country.

Q216 Just for luck, one more, if that is okay, Chair. To labour the point, I want to make you understand that even doing it by local authorities can cause issues. My constituency of Broxbourne is across two district councils, both of which have electoral registration responsibilities. One of those could be part of the pilot, and one of those could not. I could end up facing a general election in my constituency where some of my voters have been automatically registered, and some have not. Unless you are going to do everyone at the same time for a general election, you must understand that it could be perceived—it could cause lots of challenges, between knocking i n one street saying that people there are automatically registered and can go down to vote , and knocking in the street next door to say they are not, if that makes sense. I just want to make sure you understand that point.

Florence Eshalomi : I think that is a valid observation and something that we will definitely be taking back. As this process for automatic voter registration develops, that is something that we will definitely be feeding in to look at. We look at any unintended consequences.

Q217 I have two follow-up questions, and then I will bring in Andrew, Lee and Ashley. The Welsh Government have already carried out automatic voter registration. There are examples there of best practices, what will work and what will not work. We are keen to hear from you what work is being done to engage with the Welsh Government to speed up the process, particularly for the general election. I wanted to touch on an answer that Stuart gave to Lewis. You mentioned approaching local authorities that might want to pilot this. I may have misunderstood this. So that I can understand this better, will the Government go to local authorities and ask, “Do you want to carry out the pilot?” I am struggling to understand the rationale behind that, particularly if you are looking for different demographics, how are you going to make sure that those demographics are the ones that you are correctly piloting? Personally, I just do not understand why there is such a delay.

Florence Eshalomi : On your last poin t about the delay, you will appreciate, Chair, that some authorities are going through local government reorganisation. You will also appreciate that a number of local authorities are facing quite difficult financial challenges. This is a key priority for the Government, so we are still inviting and writing to local authorities.

We are also working with the Electoral Commission and the Association of Electoral Administrators, which, again as you will know, Chair, administer all the elections across the country, and different civil societ y organisations in working on this automatic voter registration. The other key group that we need to engage with are the political parties themselves , around automated voter registration. It is not a case of us telling local authorities to respond to this. It is a whole range of different organisations as well. I think that will help us in making sure there is a good geographical spread across the country, that we are taking in different structures, different sizes, different demographics across the country, because we know that voting patterns in urban areas will be very different from maybe coastal areas, for example. On working with other devolved A dministrations—

Shall I come in on that? In Wales, the important distinction here is that for the Senedd elections , when an individual is registering to vote, they do not need to prove their nationality. There is an increased complexity here for the way in which we want to register people for parliamentary elections in the UK. There is a distinction there that is important. The Welsh register is about residents, not about nationality. There is a much greater focus on nationality in registering to vote for UK parliamentary elections, which is an important distinction. In gathering the data, that increases the complexity and makes it more challenging. That is the first point.

Coming back to your question about engaging with local authorities, what we have been doing over the course of the last year or so, we ran some flexible voting pilots—rather than automated voting registrations—in four areas last year. We are looking to continue that moving into 2027. We have been reaching out to local authorities to garner interest in that.

On automated voter registration, I want to be clear that we will be guided by the Electoral Commission, by conversations through the Political Parties Panel and by conversations and views from this Committee to guide us to the right approach to reach out to local authorities based on the balance of the issues that the Minister has raised. That will have to happen after the Bill has received Royal Assent, when we are talking about automated voter registration or improving voter registration. What we are doing at the moment , just to be clear, is testing flexible voting. Last year we saw voting in a hub in a shopping centre in Milton Keynes and some early voting pilots in north Hertfordshire and Cambridge and another place I cannot remember off the top of my head. Next year, we will be looking to extend that to do further testing of those flexible voting pilots. Improving voter registration or automated voter registration will come after the Bill has received Royal Assent.

Q218 You have partly pre-empted my question, Chair. I was going to ask about the pilot in Wales. We took evidence from an electoral registration officer from Powys, I think, which was one of the pilot areas. What I took from it was that quite a lot of the work that they had to do was around data cleansing of existing council systems. I think they found that they had some systems where it would be helpful if they recorded other fields about people that they do not currently store, which would help them join together various different datasets that they had. What all this comes around to is that the council needed resources to be able to do that. They needed a significant uplift in resources in job roles that you would not necessarily have expected, essentially data scientist-type roles, people who are used to digging into data and cleansing it. When this ultimately gets rolled out, how are you going to ensure that councils are appropriately resourced to make sure that they are able to undertake this work in an accurate way and in a way that is consistent, so we have a standard offer across the country with this?

Florence Eshalomi : That is a valid question, Mr Cooper. It is o ne of the changing natures of modern democracy and modern elections . T here was a by-election in my constituency two weeks ago, and one of the voters was very angry saying, “Why have we not introduced electronic voting?” , after which we had a very long debate. It is about how we work with electoral returning officers and electoral teams within individual councils — in some cases in many councils those teams have been dilapidated. They are carrying out an important function. It is about ensuring that when there are changes going on with local government reorganisations, those teams are protected, valued and are important. It is about outlining the roles, especially where we will see new changes in political finance, of election agents and people outside of that. I think, ultimately, it is about making sure that conversations are happening with my colleague, the Minister who holds the purse strings on this, making sure that when discussions from the Local Government Association are happening, I will be there to support them when they are making those bids to Minister McMahon for additional funding , to ensure that this is a key priority.

If we are honest about defending democracy and making sure that there is a lot more transparency and a lot more clean money going into politics, it is important to fund the very people we are asking to carry out elections, who do this weekly—everyone focuses on the general election , but there are elections being held up and down the country every week. There are dedicated small teams getting on with that work, so it is important that they are funded adequately.

Q219 On Lewis’s last comment, Minister, could you give us an assurance that you will not run a pilot where a constituency could have two sets of approaches or election law in a general election contest, so that a constituency like Lewis’s could never be part of that trial? It feels unfair that you would run a constituency with two different approaches, basically, unless his neighbouring authority is also signed up to it.
Florence Eshalomi : I think that is something that will definitely feed back to the Electoral Commission.

Q220 Will the work on this consider the potential impact, positive or negative, or consequences, of having a mixed platform of voter registration? Will it consider what might be the case if we have a variety of ways of people registering to vote, not one blanket way?
Florence Eshalomi : In terms of—

We may have automatic voter registration happen , as Lewis has mentioned, in some places, but it might not happen in others. I suppose what springs to my mind is that there is an opportunity there to consider what might be the issue — are there issues there? What are those issues? Is it possible to have a mixed platform of voter registration, depending on what works best for different people, for different geographies, for different environments, or are we looking specifically at having one blanket way of registering to vote for everybody?

Florence Eshalomi : I think that is one of the things that we want to test by having the pilots that will help tease out some of those key areas. Why do people not register to vote? Some people feel that you have to do it in person. You can do it online, you can do it on your smartphone. Some people feel that you can only register at your town hall; you can be in the comfort of your own house. It is a case of some people have never considered registering to vote because they feel that maybe they are not eligible to vote. In looking at different methods, looking at different options, these are all things that we would want to test out during those pilots. I think it has been very clear that any permanent changes to the registration process have to be based on robust evidence and research, because essentially we do not want to create a system that makes it harder and defeats the actual aim of registration.

As Stuart highlighted, the key issue we have in England is around access to data and data sharing. We need people to be UK citizens to be able to register to vote in the UK. The Home Office keeps that data, and trying to get things from the Home Office can be very difficult at times. When you are looking at the changes that we are bringing in for enfranchising 16 and 17-year-olds, we also need to ensure that they are UK citizens. The Department for Education does not have that data. It sits with the Home Office. Again, you can see a whole series of data challenges and complexities, but essentially it is around testing different methods to make the voting process a lot easier. This is why the pilots will be invaluable.

Q221 Thank you. Moving on slightly now to voter ID rather than registration, the witnesses to the inquiry have previously criticised the decision to add bank cards as an accepted form of identification. Could you tell us why the Government are prioritising bank cards over digital forms of ID?

Florence Eshalomi : I do not think it is the case that we are prioritising bank cards over digital. The reality is digital ID only came in a few years ago. For many years we were voting without any form of photographic ID, and elections went very well. We had very low periods of election fraud. I am trying to remember, but I think there were only about four cases of voter impersonation in the past that went to trial, so very low impersonation without the use of photographic evidence.

By introducing bank cards, we are responding to some of the concerns from campaigners, disability groups and other groups . A gain, we are trying to increase voter participation. The introduction of UK-only bank cards, being very clear that it has to be a UK-issued bank card, which again go through quite a number of rigorous tests before you can have a physical UK bank card in this country, and having that as a form of permissible ID at the polling station on polling day will help a number of key people in voting. We look at key workers, shift workers, young people who may not have a photographic ID on them but always have their bank cards on them. Again, how do we make sure that more people are ultimately exercising their right to vote as opposed to turning up at the polling station without a photographic ID and being turned away? Thee data shows that in many cases where people turn up without a photographic ID they do not return to the polling station.

Q222 I understand that , because obviously a digital voter ID is not currently being used. We have heard that making digital voter authority certificates available in the run-up to election day would particularly help young voters. Are we looking at making that available? Going back to the banking cards, the Financial Conduct Authority has pointed out that when we are talking particularly about people from disadvantaged socioeconomic groups and ethnic minority communities, they are more likely to be unbanked and not have a bank card, in addition to not having a photographic ID. Is there a risk that introducing bank cards replicates existing inequalities ? What are we doing to tackle that wide range of inequalities and look at how we can further develop that digital voter authority certificate that young people particularly are keen to have?

Florence Eshalomi : I think you raise some valid questions and some valid concerns, especially from some of the disadvantaged groups that may be disproportionately impacted by this. The main aim of widening the scope of permissible forms of voter ID is to ensure that legitimate voters are not turned away and that we are capturing more people at the polling station.

Opinions may be different, but the initial voter ID introduction was quite restrictive as a form of policy, and the Government feel that the bank cards are a form of ID held by the majority of electorates. I appreciate the point that you have raised about some people not having access to banks, but we feel that the majority of the population who are eligible to vote and eligible to participate in elections will have a basic form of a current account with a card that can be used as a sensible form of voter ID at the polling station.

It is also recognised in the fact that polling staff, since the introduction of photographic ID, have been challenged at the polling station through no fault of their own. By widening the scope of the range of ID that is permissible at polling stations, hopefully this will d e fuse some of the intimidation that we have heard reported back from the Association of Electoral Administrators, where hard - working staff are just trying to carry out their function and are being blamed for a policy that they had no say in introducing. Again, going back to a bank card with a named individual, a physical card should be a better way of enfranchising more people to vote.
Q223 Coming back to that digital voter authority certificate—which we know a lot of people were keen on, particularly young people—do we have any idea when they might be available for people to use?

Individuals can still apply for the voter authority certificate. The demand for it has not been hugely significant. I have not seen the data on young people showing a particular interest in it. I would be very keen to see that. We have not scrapped it; we have just paused it for the time being, and it is under review. To come back to what the Minister said, what we are trying to do here is to tackle the key 4% that the Electoral Commission has identified as the gap where they do not hold an eligible piece of ID. We need to create new arrangements that balance ensuring that the hard - working staff at polling stations, which the Minister has described, are not overwhelmed by a plethora of new bits of ID that they need to understand. At the same time, we are expanding the range of IDs that people can use in a workable way. I completely accept your points, Ms Dalton, that it will not capture everybody. What we are trying to do is balance that keenness to increase voter turnout and engagement with the democratic process against overwhelming staff at polling stations and making it unworkable. We think this is the right, balanced approach.

Q224 Presumably there is a chain of thought there that says if we can widen the acceptability of stuff that people already have, rather than requiring people to make more and more applications for more and more bits of things, you are more likely to actually widen participation.

Florence Eshalomi : I think a good way of widening that is looking at the fact that, for veterans, they already have a veteran card, and the Government have also pushed for the digital ID card for veterans as a permissible form. Veterans already have that, so instead of asking them to apply for yet another piece of ID to be able to vote—it is about taking a sensible measure and recognising that the digital and online world is ever changing, fast moving and fast paced. How do we ensure that the technology is there to secure and protect any forms of impersonation? I think, on balance, the bank cards will help to capture that small group that were caught out by the introduction of photo ID, and we will also look at other ways of ensuring that people can vote.

Q225 I sit here a bit bemused, Minister. You started the answer by saying that there is not a problem, that there has been a handful of—you said four occasions where there has been electoral fraud based on ID. However, you are also downgrading the type of ID required, so it is no longer photographic.
Florence Eshalomi : You can still use photographic ID.

Q226 You can, but you are accepting a non-form of photographic ID in a bank card. Why not just scrap all ID needed for elections? Why does Andy Burnham, as the Prime Minister, being a common-sense Prime Minister, not add this into his basket, along with headphones on trains and rogue parking firms? It sounds like a common-sense approach that you could just scrap it.
Florence Eshalomi : It is passed by Government, and it is a case of a lot of people feel that having a form of photographic ID helps. I think we have been very clear.
Q227 It does not help the polling staff. It does not encourage people to turn out , because it is another barrier. Your own evidence has said there is not actually an issue to be solved.
Florence Eshalomi : It is, but I think there are other things in the Representation of the People Bill that we should be looking at and focusing on. That is what we will be pursuing.
Q228 Not just deleting something so you have more time to focus on it rather than come up with loads of different ways for other types of ID. That would be the clearest headspace, would it not?

Florence Eshalomi : This is a key issue that was raised by campaigners for widening the scope of permissible ID, and that is one of the key things that was on the face of the Bill. We are delivering that.
Q229 I want to clarify. You referred to a requirement that it was a physical bank card.
Florence Eshalomi : A card.

The Bill does not actually require a physical bank card. The Bill refers to a payment card. It does not specify whether it is physical or not. In the Bill, it says, “A document referred to in paragraph 1H that is issued to the holder and produced in digital form is a specified document only if a person can form a reasonable view about whether it is a specified document by means of visual inspection alone”. That would suggest to me that a virtual bank card in your Google Wallet, as long as it showed your name, would meet the requirements specified in the Bill. That is not your view. Your view is that it needs to be a physical bank card. Is that correct?
Florence Eshalomi : That is correct.
Okay.

Q230 Minister, the Government have said that votes at 16 will be in place in time for the start of the next general election. What considerations are you taking into account in setting that start date?

Florence Eshalomi : One of the things we are looking at is how we ensure that we build the foundations of working towards votes at 16. We are still working with the timeframe of having this in place before the next scheduled poll, which again, for obvious reasons I have set out, I do not have the magic date but working on the current Parliament it would be before the summer of 2029.

We are working to make sure that that process is as easy as possible. We are working with the Electoral Commission and the different civic society groups. We are also looking at how we can work on the crucial education and engagement element to prepare young people from the age of 14 upwards, so that they are more involved in the political process, understanding elections in the UK. There is a D emocratic E ngagement F und being rolled out across England, which will help different schools, youth groups, civic society groups to engage young people in that civic process. Organisations across the UK will be able to apply for grants for up to £25,000, and projects will run next year from March through to October to help target groups of young people from as young as five years old.

Many of us visit schools in our constituencies, and we see interest in politics and democracy from very young people , and it is always a joy to see young people coming to visit Parliament, sitting in the mock Chamber. That fund has been targeted to engage young people, so that will help us have a process in place to support the Government’s ambition to enfranchise 16 and 17-year-olds by the next general election.

Q231 I have three follow-up questions. Minister, when you were on this Committee we heard from electoral officials who expressed concern that there might not be sufficient time in the run-up to an election to get young people registered. What are the Government doing to tackle that issue to assure the electoral administrators we met?

You have been very careful with your language about a scheduled poll.
