I think you are quite right to do that , but do we take that as if there was an election this year or early next year, votes at 16 would not happen but if there were a normal election in a four or five-year Parliament, we would have votes at 16? Is that the view?
Finally, if automatic voter registration is not in place when votes at 16 are introduced, what alternative measures do the Government have under consideration or rolled out to tackle this issue?

Florence Eshalomi : On the significant timeframe to get this right, we are rolling out the funding for the Democratic Engagement Fund so that that work can start in earnest. I mentioned that the projects will run from next March right through to October. Again, this is based on the cycle of 2029 in preparing and identifying those young people.

I also mentioned working with other Departments. Working with the Department for Education is very crucial and key to this in identifying, looking at how we raise awareness and how we make sure that we are working with different youth groups. Not all young people will be at school so how do we make sure that we are engaging with them in their relevant settings, working with charities and organisations, and looking at how we can roll out and identify that there is a big campaign around this change coming?

I mentioned that one of the things that we did on this Committee when I was here was the call for evidence. I know that you probably had a session with groups of young people on engaging them. These are key areas where we will be working with them and with the electoral administrators.

On your question about timetabling, these are questions way above my pay grade. I am keen to work on the basis of a five-year parliamentary cycle so that this can come into place before the next general election. We think that based on the current framework and the work going on currently, we have enough time for this to become a reality by the next general election.

On your third question, if this is in place would AVR be in place, as we outlined earlier, AVR would come in after the next general election, because we would need the Electoral Commission and other agencies to confirm which system would be best placed for the UK automatically registering people.

Those are really good questions. Building on what the Minister said, we are working very closely with the Department for Education on its review of the curriculum. There is a focus in the curriculum review on adapting the citizenship education that takes place in secondary schools, in particular trying to foster the enthusiasm from young people for democracy and the electoral system.

On the role of electoral administrators, we speak weekly to the Association of Electoral Administrators, and I have a series of stakeholder groups with people who are working on the ground in electoral teams. We will be supporting them through this process. We are used to working very closely with electoral administrators on a range of different policy changes. We have really good forums for making that happen and making sure that we are hearing from them about what is working and what is not working. I am really confident that we can make this work ahead of the roll-out of votes at 16, the extension of the franchise.

Of course you are right that there is a link here, as the Minister said, with improving voter registration and how we move towards automation. We are talking to the Department for Education about how we can support that in central government. Coming back to Mr Cooper’s point earlier, what we really want to do is not just us throwing something over the fence for local authorities to implement. This is about seeing what data we can harness from within central government to support teams and local authorities to make this a reality, both votes at 16 and improving voter registration. There is a lot of work to do, but we have some really good structures to support that work moving forward.

Q232 Thank you both. Minister, you and I and everyone around the table are probably going to be a candidate at the next election. It highlights the challenge that we face that we do not know when the election will be or who the electorate will be, even if there is an election this year. We have no idea, because you cannot rule in or out if 16 or 17-year-olds will be voting. That highlights how much our democracy is up in the air at the moment . Moving to the education side—

Sorry to interrupt you. The Democratic Engagement Fund that is being rolled out will be given to civil society to carry out. How will that be effectively measured to make sure that by the time it is votes at 16, we have reached as many people as possible?

Also, it was reported in September that potentially the UK Youth Parliament might be scrapped. I know it is on the DCMS. I just feel like that is moving backwards if we are looking to get more people, particularly young people, to vote at 16. I urge the Government to relook at that, so if you can indicate whether that is definitely happening . Sorry to cut you off there.

The Democratic Engagement Fund will run a very careful evaluation of how those pilots run. Bids have now come in. We are assessing them at the moment . We expect an average bid to be around the £20,000 to £25,000 mark. It might be slightly bigger or lower, depending on the type of organisation we are dealing with. You are absolutely right , Chair. We are talking to a range of different civil society organisations and others about how these can really make a difference.

Florence Eshalomi : Just adding to that, Chair, with the funding applications that have gone out, we are hoping to target organisations that are supporting young people aged five to 25. We are looking at ethnic minority groups, people who are homeless, regular movers, disabled young people and a range of young people from low socioeconomic backgrounds. We are ensuring that we are targeting some of the most disadvantaged young people, young people who may not feel that voting is for them, young people who are not already involved in the democratic process. The funds and resources are specifically targeted on those groups.

Q233 What I am worried about is measuring to make sure it is cutting through to those people. I worry about pots of money being given to civil society organisations and we do not know if it is reaching the people who we need to make sure are part of the democratic process. If I am quite frank , trust of politicians is quite low. We have a lot of work to cut through. I worry about how that is being measured in the outputs.

Florence Eshalomi : I think you are quite right, Chair. I just want to reassure the Committee that hopefully no MP will be running any of those projects in turning young people away. A number of those organisations are already trusted by young people, but it is highlighting some new ones that are experts in this field to do that detailed piece of work.

Q234 It was in your manifesto. It was in my manifesto to have votes at 16. We have heard on this Committee that for votes at 16 to be a success, we need additional funding and we need curriculum time to ensure that young people are properly prepared to have that franchise extended. What is MHCLG doing with the Department for Education to ensure that support is rolled out?

I will come in on this one. It is a good question . We are very much alive to those challenges. There are a couple of things to highlight. First, we have been talking to the Department for Education—we collectively as a Department —to influence and shape how the curriculum review is being taken forward, which is really important in helping to shape the educational basis for secondary school children.

The second really important thing is that we have begun conversations now with the Electoral Commission about their communications plans to help support this process as well. It is very much the remit of the Electoral Commission to communicate about these types of things with electors for obvious reasons of impartiality and independence. They have some innovative and important plans for their comms, which I think are looking to tie in very much to when votes at 16 have progressed through the Representation of the People Bill. I do not want to put poor Vijay on the spot, but I am sure he would be happy to talk in more detail about this and we would be happy to talk about those plans in due course. They are not quite ready yet, but they will be ready shortly.

Florence Eshalomi : Again, not to talk for colleagues in the Department for Education, but my understanding is that the reform of the curriculum is happening and that assessment will continue in alignment with what we are trying to do in enfranchising young people. That consultation on the proposals in the assessment will come in due course.

Another key area is the citizenship syllabus in the national curriculum, which, as you know, comes in at key stages 3 and 4. It currently covers a range of areas, including democracy, Parliament, voting rights and human rights and expanding the scope of that to look at stuff around media, judiciary and personal financing, in line with some of the changes we are seeing in elections. It is not just a case of, “These are your candidates, you go and vote”. It is about making sure that young people have a broad range of knowledge about how democracy and politics are changing. The review will recommend that all young people are taught citizenship content from an earlier age, a primary age, which I think is really important , and also looking at legislation, media and financial literacy.

Hopefully, once all those changes are in place, our young people will be better equipped and have a better understanding of not just the need to vote but why it is important to be part of civic engagement.

Q235 Minister, you highlighted the engagement funds that you are about to make some decisions on , and they will run from March to October. I assume that no one is thinking that will be enough to ensure that young people are equipped to be able to vote. Is that correct? We know that is not everything; that is a start. Is that right?

Florence Eshalomi : That is a start because that is the theory. In practice, we then need to make sure that once they are equipped with all of that, they actually go out and vote. Hence the work with the civic society and the youth groups is vitally important as well.

Q236 The engagement fund work will run from March to October. Hence I am saying that if there is an early election 16 and 17-year-olds cannot vote, but I assume that engagement programme will not run in every school and it will not run every year. Are we saying that engagement fund is a start but it is not good enough?

Florence Eshalomi : Mr Fo r ster, you will be aware that I do go asking the Treasury for additional funding every so often, but because this is a key area that the Government intend to bring forward, we need that upfront funding. I think it is right that we try to ensure that there is continuous funding basis to continue to engage and educate younger people coming forward, because we know that it is more likely that when people start to vote at an earlier age, they will continue to vote throughout their adulthood. It is important that we are not just doing this for the first cohort of 16 to 17-year-olds but that there is a system in place to continue to improve citizenship education. That will obviously require additional funding in years to come.

Q237 I agree with you. The engagement fund is not there to ensure all young people are equipped to vote when we lower the voting age. When the curriculum, which will change next September, comes into effect, is that meant to ensure that young people are equipped to properly vote and cope with the political challenges we will give them?

Florence Eshalomi : It is a case of you cannot say just one change will equip young people, because in 10 or 15 years the voting system may have changed. In 10 or 15 years, financial donations and caps may have changed. I am just speaking hypothetically. This is an area that will continue to evolve and it is important that we have the flexibility within the curriculum and in the funding keeping pace to equip young people to continue to vote.

Q238 I am mindful of time, so I will ask just one more question. Research shows that only around half of young people feel confident about identifying misinformation online. What steps are the Government taking to increase this proportion? I keep on highlighting that I want votes at 16 but I think we need to equip young people first. What steps are the Government going to take to ensure that young people can identify misinformation before we lower the voter age and before it is implemented?

Florence Eshalomi : The Online Safety Act, which was introduced in the last Parliament, takes us into that area and is enforceable by Ofcom. It is responsible for proportional steps in reducing and highlighting some of the misinformation, illegal information and harmful content currently online, including some of the stuff around AI-generated deep fakes and images. The current legal framework is there to tackle some of that misinformation and that sits within the 2023 Online Safety Act.

I think it is fair to say that we all recognise that the online world continues to change almost daily and it is how we ensure that Governments, not just in this country but Governments of all different political persuasions, Governments across the world, continue to keep up with the pace of that. The online environment continues to change at a rapid pace. We are working with colleagues in DCMS who are responsible for that, and also importantly working with colleagues in the Home Office on the dangerous nature of some of this content. This is something that we will continue to do in responding to those challenges.

However, going back to your main question, as part of the curriculum we will focus on looking at online safety, misinformation, disinformation. I think that is how we continue to feed in any concerns in that area to young people.

Q239 That is helpful. The new curriculum comes in in September. If I said that after one year it would make sense for young people to vote at 16 and 17, having spent a year teaching them and supporting them, do you think that makes sense? Would you think we should have more support for them or less support for them?

Florence Eshalomi : I think it is about continuous support for young people because the online world continues to evolve and change. We cannot legislate our way out of any harm. It is about keeping up and making sure that any policy or regulation we have adapts to some of the changes we will see in the online world.

I mentioned that as one of the members of the Defending Democracy Taskforce, chaired by Minister Dan Jarvis. This is a key area that we will continue to look at, reporting back to Parliament as well. There are many areas where it is important for us to have robust legislation to support some of the framework, but equally have the flexibility in the framework to adapt to some of the changes and threats that, if we are honest, today we are still not aware of, changes and threats that in some cases some of the young people will identify before the policymakers because of the way that online safety works.

However, looking at the bodies that are responsible for this is important. There is the Joint Election Security and Preparedness Unit, which looks at this both inside and outside of an election period, bringing together Government Departments, the Electoral Commission, the law enforcement agencies, intelligence services, all monitoring that area to ensure that the curriculum is fit for purpose, to ensure that youth groups or youth settings or non-traditional settings where young people are getting their content and information from. We need to ensure that the social media companies are engaged in this area as well because most of that information will be viewed on their platforms. This is not just a role for Government. It is not just a role for Government saying that we will legislate to change this. It is about making sure that there is flexibility to keep up with the pace and change to ensure that young people and the content they are consuming is of the highest accuracy and if there is any inaccurate information, how that content or misinformation is dealt with and taken down.

Q240 Thank you Minister. Where you have finished with Will Forster is a good place for me to pick up , because I want to talk about online disinformation but in the realm of electoral integrity . I appreciate that the Online Safety Bill sits with DCMS but the Government and I think most political parties have identified online disinformation as a real threat to democracy. Why were key election offences not priority 1 offences under that Act?
Florence Eshalomi : I do not know if there is anything you would want to add on that, Stuart.

Also on the Online Safety Act, but linking into your comment about Governments across the world, we have had representation that the Online Safety Act should include a duty on social media companies to mitigate risks to electoral integrity and the EU’s Digital Services Act specifically calls that out. Are your Government considering doing something similar to what the EU has done around that Digital Services Act?

We will have to take some of these questions back to DCMS. However, it is worth saying a couple of things. First, I know that colleagues in DCMS are looking very carefully at the sets of issues you have just described that order the application of the Online Safety Act , but also new and emerging threats through the social media space. I know they are very alive to those challenges. I will be happy to feed the questions you have asked back to DCMS and respond to the Committee in due course.

A couple of things to build on what the Minister has said in this context. As the Chair will know very well from her time in Government, the Joint Election Security and Preparedness Unit plays an important role in helping to support Departments in tackling and monitoring online misinformation and disinformation, the use of deep fakes and the like. It does this in two ways but at a macro level, first bringing together and co-ordinating work across government support, including through the Defending Democracy Taskforce, making sure that we are building and have a consistent and coherent set of approaches across all the relevant agencies that you can imagine. The police, the security agencies, the Home Office, DCMS and so on all have a part to play in this.

Then, importantly, during electoral events the team in the Joint Election Security and Preparedness Unit sets up or establishes an election cell, which in real time brings together all of those parties to make sure that where there are particular instances of misinformation and disinformation we are taking a co-ordinated approach across G overnment to tackle them and speaking to the social media companies and the like. There is a very comprehensive infrastructure within government to tackle these things but we will take back the points that you raised, Mr Dillon.

Q241 Thank you for that answer Stuart. The Prime Minister announced the new National Centre for Information Defence. Does some of this end up sitting under that new body when it is formally created and allocated to a ministerial Department?
The Prime Minister has said that the new centre that he has set up will work collaboratively with the other leaders of the parties. Is that correct?
That is my understanding.
Florence Eshalomi : I believe so , yes.
Q242 How will that work? Do you want to write to me?
Florence Eshalomi : Yes, we can come back to you on that.

Q243 My final question now. The Electoral Commission and the Speaker’s Co nference have called for section 106 of the 1983 Representation of the People Act to be updated. You referenced the Online Safety Act but the Elections Act is silent on making clear that the offence covers digitally manipulated false statements and deep fakes. What is your view, Minister, on whether that is necessarily specifically called out?
Florence Eshalomi : This is an area that we are discussing with the Electoral Commission, with the chief executive, and it is one of the many on my very long list.

Section 106 is one of those areas where we all need to make a judgment about whether or not it actually adds anything to the Government’s armoury in tackling these issues. I do not think that the case has quite been made yet but we are keeping it under review, as the Minister has said, and we will pick up those conversations in due course.

Florence Eshalomi : Another area that I would like to pursue is discussions with some of the big social media platforms that rightly say that they add a lot of value but there are some concerns that many people have raised. I think that a lot of them should be taking a lot more responsibility for the information shared on their respective platforms.

Q244 I agree with that, Minister. That is why I was questioning whether you would follow the EU’s Digital Services Act, which targets those companies and makes a requirement for them whereas our Online Safety Act does not. The Electoral Commission and the Speaker’s Conference have called for section 106 to reflect that. While you might be in ongoing conversations, the view is quite clear from the cross-party Speaker’s Conference and the Electoral Commission that change is needed.

Florence Eshalomi : That is something that we will continue to discuss with colleagues in DCMS as well. We all meet at the Defending Democracy Taskforce and I will be sure to raise this feedback from this Committee.
While I have the floor, in a month’s time it is Parliament Week from 23 to 29 November and I think that is a great way to engage with younger people as well.

Q245 I will follow on from Lee’s point. It is good that we have the leadership from the Prime Minister in recognising disinformation and the threats we face, particularly with misinformation, and that he has identified electoral disinformation as one of his priorities. It links with what Lee has mentioned. What are the Government going to do about placing additional requirements on social media platforms to tackle this threat, looking at what other countries are doing, particularly the Five Eyes, to work collaboratively to address this growing threat?

Florence Eshalomi : Those conversations, Chair, continue, making sure that is being addressed at the highest level. Where you see the Prime Minister’s commitment on that is in appointing a Minister with responsibility for AI sitting at the heart of Cabinet now, sharing the areas of misinformation, disinformation, AI and the changes happening at that level. I think that shows that the Government are committed to ensuring that we are doing a deeper dive into this.

On work with social media companies, I know that the Secretary Of State and Ministers in DCMS continue to engage regularly through the Defending Democracy Taskforce. I will be feeding any electoral concerns directly to them, so that they can take this jointly to them. I feel that if there are areas where we need to be a bit firmer, outline any explicit concerns, we will do that jointly as Ministers with responsibility on that. I think it is about being very clear that the Government will legislate in certain areas, but essentially we need the social media companies to also play their part in transparency, access to information, access to blocking harmful content, especially when we are talking about looking at the social media ban for young people. Sadly, we have seen some young people take their own lives and die by suicide because of harmful content.

This is about how to eliminate the risk on the online world and how we also recognise that the online world plays a big role in some of the technological advancements and changes we are seeing now. It is about responsible social media companies working with the UK Government to ensure that our elections are free and fair and free from foreign interference. That is an ongoing discussion and it is something that I will definitely be pushing very hard with colleagues in DCMS and the Home Office.

Q246 A recommendation was made by the Electoral Commission to address some of this, particularly on standards in public life. I want to explore where the Government’s appetite is on this. It is essentially about recommending social media companies to take more action, particularly when maintaining political advertising libraries. It is something I remember looking at quite a number of years ago and unless we actually mandate social media companies to do it, they are not going to do it on their own back. Do the Government intend to legislate them to do this?

Florence Eshalomi : This is not about saying that all social media companies are bad. There are some that are doing some good work, working with and co-operating with the Government and the Electoral Commission. For example, Meta and Google now have a publicly available and accessible political adverts library where for that transparency you can see where the ads are going. To answer your question, Chair, the Government have no plans to introduce a database at this time, but I think these are ongoing areas that we will continue to discuss with the relevant social media companies.

Q247 It is about recommending social media companies have an advertising library. I think it is good. Anecdotally, voluntarily some companies are doing this media literacy. We have a massive battle to face because the closest I have seen to people really understanding the risks is “The Wargame” on Sky. I do not know if anyone has seen that. Looking at the data, particularly in Ofcom’s annual survey, so many young people, particularly those people we are looking to target for votes at 16, get most of their information on social media. That is the first point that people go to, so it would be good if the Government could consider putting a media literacy requirement on these platforms. I don’t know where you are in exploring that.

Florence Eshalomi : This is about how we improve on social media literacy in and around elections and outside election times. We are building on the growing up in the online world consultation, looking at expanding support, not just for children but for parents and carers as well. It is important that they are able to recognise some of the risks being posed. This is around some of the new resources on AI safety, which again I know that the Minister will be looking at. It is about continuing these conversations and recognising that they need to happen not just in the classroom, which is a good place to start, but outside as well where young people are getting their information. It is working with the Electoral Commission and other groups to make sure that the media literacy and online safety programme is developed in a way that young people can identify any potential risks and deep fakes.

Q248 My next set of questions are about electoral law, which is complex, voluminous and fragmented. The Electoral Commission has said that there are over 100 pieces of electoral legislation now. There are differences in reporting requirements between different types of elections, a difference in statutory time limits on when you need to do expense returns, for example, between town and parish council elections and borough elections. It is a complete nightmare for agents and electoral administrators.

When we have introduced new elected roles, such as police and crime commissioners and things like that, quite often what previous Governments have done is just copy and paste the 1983 Act, so we end up duplicate legislation on the statute book. Now the Electoral Commission has called for a piece of work to begin the process of consolidating electoral law. Do you accept that that is necessary, and can you commit to it?

Florence Eshalomi : Mr Cooper, my in-tray as the new Minister has been very busy. What I am keen to do in this new role is ensuring that the major manifesto commitments as set up by the Government on votes at 16 and some of the other changes from the back of the independent Rycroft review are enacted as soon as possible. That is one of the key things that I am focusing on.

I think you are correct about the very complicated system we have in UK electoral law, running into millions of pages. If we are honest, a full-scale review and consolidation will take a very long time. It is something that will require major legislation and cross-party support, and an in-depth review. Based on my knowledge of this piece of legislation, I think it may also require more than one Parliament to change electoral law. My ultimate role at the moment is to ensure that the current Representation of the People Bill is in place, that we enfranchise young people before the next general election, and looking at some of the stuff in the Rycroft review before we open the can of worms that is UK electoral law.

Q249 Thank you, Minister. I completely understand that you need to prioritise, and certainly you need to prioritise what is in our manifesto. Do you agree that with 12 pieces of primary legislation and 15 pieces of secondary legislation for the 2026 local elections, that might risk resilience at a time when it is needed most? I also wonder if this is not a piece of work that the Law Commission was made for. Where we have had complex areas like this in other areas that the MHCLG are looking at, in particular around some of the stuff under Minister Pennycook’s purview, he has asked the Law Commission to take it away and come back in a few years with a Bill that can be presented to the Lords. Is this not a prime candidate for that treatment, given that what we are talking about is lots of duplicate legislation that just needs to be consolidated?

It is a conversation we have frequently with the Electoral Commission on this particular issue , and so we are very alive to the challenges. I completely take the point about the number of pieces of legislation. What we have tried to do over the course of at least the time that I have been in this post is to make sure that the guidance that is provided to agents and political parties is as clear as possible in helping to guide people through the respective pieces of legislation.

The Minister is completely right. This is an incredibly complex piece of work that would take a great deal of time to take forward. I take your point, Mr Cooper, about the role of the Law Commission. I respectfully say that I think this is an even more complex piece of work that would take many years to take forward. All I can say for now is that we have heard the concerns that people have raised in a number of different areas. We will keep it under very close review, and there is strength to the argument that this should be looked at in due course.
Q250 I would gently caution you against saying it is more complicated than leasehold in the presence of the Law Commissioners working on it . Each to their own domain of expertise.

A final question from me. The previous Government increased the amount that the Electoral Commission could spend on awareness-raising activity following the passage of the Elections Act 2022. We are significantly expanding the franchise by introducing votes at 16. Are you planning on similar measures following the passage of the Representation of the People Bill?
Florence Eshalomi : Yes, we have.
We are giving that very careful consideration to exactly the points you just raised.

Thank you for that. I have some follow-up actions, which I would like you to write to the Committee on. We asked some questions on automatic voter registration, particularly where it has been piloted in Wales. I wanted to know a bit more about what has come out of that and a bit more information about the pilot work that you will be looking to do.

Lewis Cocking and Lee Dillon also discussed the constituency, and if the pilot was done in one borough, how it may impact another borough with the outcome and also the capacity of local authorities. If you could reassure us that this is being looked into , please.
You also said you will take back the questions raised about the Online Safety Act, because some of that work overlaps with DCMS. If you could write to us about that, please.

I am particularly interested in a bit more information about the National Centre for Information, which was announced in September. How will that work and how can we as a Committee play a role in this? I know that Opposition leaders have been invited to this, but if we are going to be scrutinising elements of what MHCLG is doing, it is important that we know what is going on behind the scenes, so we can add to it through the scrutiny work that we are doing.

Also, timescales about some of the stuff that the Electoral Commission is doing, particularly on donations. We know that a piece of work has been given to the Electoral Commission to do on the unregulated and regulated periods. I think you said you would get back to us on timescales in that.
I do not think I have missed anything else. Thank you so much for coming. We are looking forward to seeing you regularly. Is it going to be monthly? Thanks for that.

segs.tx: Public Services Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Children’s social care
Wednesday 1 4 October 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Bradley (The Chair) ; Lord Barber of Chittlehampton ; Lord Faulkner of Worcester; Baroness Hollins; Lord Johnson of Marylebone; Lord Mohammed of Tinsley; Lord Mott; Baroness Nichols of Selby; Baroness Pidgeon; Baroness Redfern; Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson; Baroness Watkins of Tavistock .
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 – 2 5
Witnesses

Helen Waite OBE, Director, Children's Social Care: System & Strategy, Department for Education; Shazia Hussain CBE, Director, Children's Social Care: Help, Protection and Social Work, Department for Education .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Helen Waite and Shazia Hussain .

Q1 ​​​​​​ The Chair: Good morning. Welcome to the first oral session of the inquiry into children’s social care, particularly looked-after children in the system. I am Keith Bradley, Lord Bradley, chair of the committee. This is being live streamed; I just make you aware of that before we start.

I welcome you both, Helen Waite and Shazia Hussain, who will be answering our questions today. They will briefly introduce themselves at the beginning. Also, as you can see, we have three members joining us remotely, so that you can catch them as well. Thank you again for your attendance and we will hand over: is it Helen who is going to speak first?

I was going to speak first, if that is okay. I will start with the introductions. Hi, everyone. I am Shazia Hussain. I am one of the directors in children’s social care in the Department for Education. I cover the earlier bit of the system, help protection and the social work workforce.

I am Helen Waite, also a director of children’s social care in the Department for Education. I cover the care end of the system. Together we should have all angles of children’s social care covered today.

Q2 Good morning. Good to see you both. Thanks for coming in. I want to start with a question about outcomes for children. How well is the children’s social care system meeting the needs of children in care currently? How should we define a good outcome for a child in care? What evidence do we have that the system is delivering good outcomes, and how do we measure that over time?

I will start, but we will probably go at this one together, if that is okay. We are on a significant journey of reform in children’s social care. Much of this has stemmed from the independent review of children’s social care, which was led by Minister MacAlister, who is the current Minister for Children and Families, which presented numerous recommendations in relation to the way that the system was currently not working, frankly, and the outcomes for children are not good enough. We are on that journey of reform at the moment.

To get those outcomes in a much better place, you have to start at the start in relation to prevention and the investment that we are putting in that space; we can talk a little bit more about that as we go through. In terms of the current outcomes, we know that children are much more likely to not be in education or employment. The Milburn report that is due out is obviously very relevant for us, and we have been inputting into that in relation to the support that care leavers receive. We know that stability is a crucial factor: children being in homes or foster care, where they are persistently moved, where they are not placed within their communities, means that they have not got stable lives, they have not got the relationships around them to support them to thrive. They may not have stable educational attendance, which also impacts on their educational outcomes. The outcomes are not good enough at the moment.

We have a package of reforms that we would love to talk to you about today that would address some of that stuff. This summer, some of you will have seen that we published a review of care leaver deaths—a tragic and hard read—which really spotlighted the fact that if you are a care leaver, you are more likely to die sooner. That also presented some opportunities for us to think about transitions and how the system operates as children come through the system.
I wanted, though, a definition of a good outcome.

Sorry. A definition of a good outcome is that outcomes for those children should be as equal as they are for other children who are not in the care system. I think government, through its corporate parenting duties, has a responsibility to ensure that children ideally are supported not to come into the system and are supported to stay with their families and thrive. Where they do come into the system, we should look after them, support them and invest in them through all agencies and public services which should wrap around them to provide the advocacy and support to get better outcomes.

Outcomes need to be delivered within a budget and in the context of constraints in public spending. Children’s social care now accounts for 27% of local authority spending, up from 18% in 2011-12. We have heard that spending has risen much faster than the number of children needing care, and the average cost per child in care has risen by a third in real terms since 2015-16. Could you help us understand what is driving this increase in costs, and how can we judge whether local authorities are getting value for money from this expenditure? Finally, how do you define value for money and what is the baseline and counterfactual that you are using to measure that from?

Should I start? As you said, the overall number of children that are receiving social care services has remained broadly stable over the last decade, but the number of children entering care has risen, and that is where a lot of the cost in the system is. A child going into care incurs foster care costs and residential care costs, and in particular, the costs of residential care have been rising. That is in part due to the complexity of the children that now present. Children are presenting at a much older age than they would have done, as a result of prevention spending over the last 10 to 15 years declining because local authorities sought to protect their statutory spend. Following the care review, we have made a £2.4 billion investment in prevention so that we can build back some of those preventive services. We have our Families First pathfinder, now a national programme, trying to get to children earlier. A key part of our strategy is to keep families together. We think that is a key outcome of some of the reforms that we are doing; where they cannot do that, it is to stay within their family networks. That is both better for some of the outcomes we were talking about earlier, but will also help reduce the flow in. I do not know if you want to touch on some of the measures around the care system.
How do you measure VFM? What is an acceptable amount for a local authority to spend to achieve a good outcome for a child in care?

It comes back to what we invest in prevention. We saw local authorities whose preventive services had frankly all but disappeared. Therefore, if children are reaching the care part of the system and coming into care, as Shazia has said, with much more complex problems, not having the right wraparound support around them from Health, from Justice, from other agencies, means it is much more difficult to achieve an outcome when a child arrives in that position. By bringing support up front, we have a much better chance of ensuring they come out with a better education, better support and more stability.
I am not sure I am hearing you explain how you evaluate VFM in the context of achieving a good outcome. What is a reasonable amount for a local authority to be spending in a given circumstance?

I do not think we have put a number figure on that. The way that we are evaluating the Families First programme is that we expect to see a reduction in the number of children entering care. That is through additional preventive support and we are also diverting numbers into residential care through a much greater focus on kinship and a much greater focus on fostering and increasing the number of foster care places available. Children that do come into the care system are more likely to get a better outcome if they are in a family environment.
Can I just check, Lord Johnson, that you have no interests to declare?
No, no interests.

Q3 I apologise to the committee for arriving late. I wondered if you could just push a little bit on the preventive measures. I am particularly interested, following Lord Johnson’s themes about value for money, on whether we know what works if you are a local authority and you want to invest in preventive measures. You mentioned Health wraparound and Justice wraparound, but what evidence is there, for a local authority, about where the best place is to put your marginal pound and what support makes the biggest difference? Or does that evidence not exist?

We have got pretty good evidence on the preventive end of the system: evaluated program me s on specific issues. The Supporting Families programme is one of the main ones, which showed that, for every pound spent, you get £ 2.4 0 back. That described the practice that works with families: having a key worker that can help you navigate all of the wider public services that you might need. That is a key plank of what we are now saying that local authorities need to do in practice, which we have codified in our programme guide that we tell them to follow. There are a number of other similar kind s of What Works evaluated program me s. We are managing it as a g overnment major programme. We say , “H ere are all of the things that have an evidence base ” . They are a mix of interventions: if this family has a specific issue, try this type of intervention , and general practices of working with local authorities. That is codified in a programme guide. We have quarterly monitoring with every local authority in the country—how they are performing against those things . W here we are worried about local authority performance or practice , w e have support mechanisms in place with experts that can go and help them transform their services. It is a richer area of understanding what works. I would say less so than in the care system. We have got a decent evidence base.

I would add that, on the £ 2.4 billion that we have injected into the system over th e period of th is spending review, we have put it in through the local government funding settlement and have ring - fenced it. A l though ring - fencing fell away in the past , it has broadly been welcomed by directors of children’s services , who have struggled in more recent years to hold funding in the prevention end of the system. As we have learned over time, when prevention spend falls, statutory spend goes up exponentially , s o we are injecting this cash. We are effectively having to dual - run slightly in this rebalancing : we are having to put more money into prevention until we can bend the curve to improve the outcomes we are looking to see in the reduction in numbers of children going into care.

On w here we have built the evidence base , w e have worked with foundations —they are our equivalent of a What Works o rganisation —and this is focused on different aspects of support for parents. I n designing the programme , we worked with 10 pathfinder areas, which were 10 local authorities around the country. W e required co-design with not just the local authority ; we required health and police to be at the table. H ow do you design services that are fit for a local community? What are their needs ? Y es, you take on national evidence, but how do you make it bespoke in a way that meets the needs of those particular families around th at set of schools in that particular locality? H ow do you support a family to navigate it ? A s Shazia alluded to there, we have a family he lp worker who will co - ordinate everything —t he multi-agency response that is required around that family . A multi-agency person will stay with that family as needs ebb and flow , s o families do not have to persistently come back in and tell their story time and time again, become frustrated or feel stigmatised. W e want to remove the stigma so that prevention really make s a difference.

I have one final point: the place where we have the strongest evidence base is on family group decision - making. F or every £1 , I think you get a return on investment of £3.8 0 back , but it is also proven to reduce entry into care. W e therefore legislated for that, a nd we have put quite a lot of prescription around how local authorities do that , because we are so confident in the evidence base.
Can I just again confirm that you have no interests?
I have no interest to declare.

Q4 I have no interest to declare , either. But I am very concerned and was shocked to read that , two years after leaving care, nearly a third of care leavers are homeless. I understand this focus on prevention at the beginning of life, but what can we do to improve that urgently? W e know that, once people are homeless, all the data shows us what a disaster i t is.

Yes. T hrough the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools A ct , w e legislated to ensure that local authorities are publicising the support that is available for care leavers, but of course that is not enough. Again, w e start slightly in front of a child becoming a care leaver , with all the things we can do in advance of that . W e published a paper called the E nduring R elationships document, which is really designed to think about children in care and how we build those really important relationships with people that will stay with them when they leave the care system and become adults. T hat is not about just being the personal adviser at the local authority , who obviously should help the individual to navigate whatever support they nee d, b ut how they keep contact with the ir auntie or cousin —with the people in their community who will stay with them and provide that safety net , effectively , around them . It is really centring around enduring relationships .

On support for care leavers , local authorities should absolutely be publishing their offer. The Act also intends to expand corporate parenting responsibilities significantly , with a ll agencies across government, all schools and the health service having corporate responsibilities and duties to ensure that those in care and care leavers are supported. T hat is an expansion of the current arrangements.

W e are also going to be rolling out Staying Close, which we legislated for: that is targeted support for those most likely to be at risk of homelessness. It provides supported housing and the wraparound care that stabilises the individual in that housing , supports them to live independently and secures ongoing tenancies b eyond that . We will be rolling it out across every local authority across this spending review period. W e have been working with 47 local authorities so far. We have slightly refined our expectations based on what we are learning of what works. W e are going out to another 15 local authorities at the moment , a nd we will expand to all areas after that.

I can hear the optimism, and I am really hoping that it is prove n to be right. But I am aware that there are people of 20 who have been in care who go to A&E s across the country and report that they have nowhere to live while they are being dealt with for whatever they have gone to A&E for. W ill the statutory duty then be on hospitals to ensure that they do not go back on the street after that attendance? I can hear how you are working with local authorities ; I am frustrated with the other end — and I am , by background , a mental health nurse, just to declare that.

There is probably more to do in the way that the broader system comes around an individual , in taking those corporate responsibilities seriously and acting locally to bring about change. W e see a lot of variation in the way that housing teams within local authorities interact with the care leaving teams — you would think that would be an obvious connect , but it can be disparate. There is more to do there. The Prime Minister has stood up and clearly said that rough sleeping is top of the agenda , a nd we are working really closely with MHCLG to improve action on rough sleeping and homelessness more general ly , with a focus on care leavers.

Q5 Thank you for coming. I , too , have nothing to declare. My question is regarding Staying Close support, as you have just mentioned . T he main source s of support for carers often hardly kn o w the young person and are often unaware of the young person’s history and context. I wonder how that can be improved.

That is interesting. That finding came through in the care leaver deaths review , titled You Really Are on Your Own . It really shone a light on the fact that too many care leavers really are on their own , that t hey do not have the support and that p eople do not understand them. There are those transitions, particularly on health, if I am honest, around moving from children’s support, where they may have finally got some mental health support ; w e had cases where children had diabetes and died because their support was not transferred over into the adult system. There is m uch more to do to make sure that those transition arrangements are right — but right from a multi-agency perspective, not just rel iant on a n individual within a local authority.

W e are definitely in the foothills of what we are learning o n Staying Close. W e have redefined the model so that it is much more about the home itself and the support that comes with it. When we initially set off on the Staying Close journey, we were a bit more fluid about what might work for an individual, and we have realised we need to be tighter to get the outcomes and support that are needed.

The only other thing I would add is that, at every step, we are trying to get a further step back : on working with children when they are in care and making sure that you are finding the people who can build that network around them . A s Helen said , t hat sort of ambition is set out in the enduring relationship s strategy . O nce you have lost those opportunities , it is really hard to build people up to have a good transition out. Those things need to happen together , because it is quite difficult to find relationships for a 20 year-old : they are less likely to be engaged with their personal advise r and the local authority. Y ou need to be starting that much earlier in their care journey.
Would you think it is about building trust?

Yes, but it is also about preparing them for the fact that the professionals will not be there for ever. W e have had such a focus on building relationships with social workers and personal advisers , b ut , at some point, those people disappear. T he shift in focus that Minister M a cAlister has driven is towards find ing the people who are in their wider networks — the people who they grew up with and around them who are safe— who will support them through that , so that , as professionals step away, they have a wider kind of family to be part of.

On the reform journey, that is almost question number one when local authorities are engaging with a family. When there are early signals that things are starting to go wrong, one of the early questions is, “Who’s your support network as a family? Do your neighbours help? Have you got an auntie around the corner?” If you route in right from the beginning that you need a network around the whole family, and if things then go wrong, that network has already been contacted. They are already aware, so it is not a crisis phone call at the point at which a child may be going into care.

Q6 Chair, I also do not have any interests to declare. I want to talk about another area of outcomes, or the lack of them: NEETs. What sort of interventions do you think we need to do? Clearly, that cohort of young people, when they leave us as corporate parents, are more likely to be NEET than your average young person. What sort of things can we look at pushing to ensure that they get the best start in adult life?

These children, more often than not, have been through something fairly traumatic, so we should ensure that they get the right support at the right time. As we have said, stability is critical, but we see too many cases of children being moved placements—sometimes moved around the country, sometimes even to the other end of the country—so it is difficult. It would be unsettling for any of us to be doing that on a regular basis, but this breaks schooling arrangements and does not support children to have great attendance and therefore get a better education, which gives them the best shot at going on to further or higher education or into employment.

We have the virtual school head network. Every local authority in the country now has to have what is called a virtual school head. It is a bit of an odd name, but their job is to support all children in the locality who are looked after. They might be at a range of schools, but it is about making sure what is going on with their attendance and whether there is anything they need—again, being a sort of parental advocate to step in and see whether there are additional needs in place.

Children in care have a higher propensity to have special educational needs. Again, there is something in tandem with the reforms that are going on around special educational needs to ensure that this group of children, who do not always have the parental advocacy to push for the right support early enough, are seen, and that that support is put in place more quickly.

Coming back to your question, it is about supporting those children to thrive by creating as much stability as you can in the circumstances that exist. Wherever possible, that should be in a family environment. We are aiming for a massive expansion in fostering so that children do not have to go into residential homes but can be supported in a family environment. Those arrangements should be close to home so they can keep those enduring relationships and their schooling. Then, as they come into the care leaver system, we should ensure that we have great arrangements with DWP and that support is available for them to look for work.

Can I press you on the support? There are a number of initiatives, such as the job guarantee, but the issue is that you have to have been unemployed for 18 months. That is quite a long time for a young person. Do you think there is an argument for looking at some of those national programmes and specific issues. Why can we not guarantee that on day one for people leaving care, knowing that they are going to be the ones who are likely to have all these other complex issues? “Why wait 18 months?” would be my argument.

For some programmes that the DWP runs, there are arrangements that care leavers can access earlier. I know you are from Sheffield, and it is interesting that the South Yorkshire combined mayoral authority is running a programme with DWP at the moment that is really focusing in on NEETs, and a specific piece of their work is about care leavers. It will be interesting to see what we can learn from that and whether we can spread that learning.

The Alan Milburn review is under way at the moment, and he has made reference in the interim report already to the need to focus more on care leavers. The point that we have added to that is that, yes, we need to think about care leavers, but again we need to come back to children still in care. If you are going to push careers advice, work experience or whatever, how do we make sure that children in care are at the top of the pile for that sort of support to further reduce their risks of becoming NEET?

I have a couple of things to add. We talked earlier about Staying Close. Stable housing is almost a precursor to being able to get a job and stay in that job. These things are complementary and we definitely hope that, if someone has somewhere to live, they are not worried about being kicked out of their tenancy and they are being supported to maintain that tenancy, they will be able to secure a job, keep the job and so on. We have examples of that, both through our Care Leaver covenant, where other employers can pledge work experience, internships and so on, and through public sector internships. The Civil Service internship scheme recently reached 1,000 care leavers having been through that scheme. So there is a combination of things, but your point about the mainstream is, as Helen says, one that we have been pushing at.

Q7 I have a slight interest here, as in my other role I represent people working in the social care sector and have done for about 40 years. I was a bit anxious about the value-for-money element of this. For me, it is about how we can change young people’s lives, often from some really bad starts. Obviously society has changed over the years, and the needs of these young people are much more complex. We have to get to the bottom of that. The value-for-money element for me is in changing their lives, making them not go into shops and shoplifting but giving them employment so that they can then have a normal life. It is about support, I think. At one time, all care leavers were guaranteed an apprenticeship with my local authority, and that was a start. It went a bit haywire when the Future Jobs Fund was scrapped and now we have got the apprentices levy, but I do not think we use that as much. I do not know whether there is something that you can maybe tie in with that. My authority was a forerunner with the No Wrong Door programme, where it does not matter what complex needs you have because there is someone in these multi-agency teams now who can deal with everything for a family, rather than having four or five social workers or care co-ordinators going in to do that for them. Regarding value for money, if we support people and give them a good start in life, the health service will not need to give them as much support. Some of the issues for me have been about budget constraints over the years for local authorities and the move away from the looked-after bit and on to the foster carers. I worry that, because there are more complex needs, people cannot cope in their own homes. Those are all the things, for me, that we need to be sorting and being part of to make that better, because, if their lives are better, the lives of everybody around them will be better as well—and for the families.
Yes, it is about the right support at the right time from the right professional and then working together, rather than families being left to navigate.

We are doing a piece of work to think about the purpose of residential care. We believe that the vast majority of children who come into the care system should be in a family setting. That is why today we have launched our first ever fostering national campaign. We are aiming to get 10,000 more foster places by 2029. That is pretty ambitious, but we feel that children are better supported within the family environment, and obviously that comes with the need for us to think about support for those foster carers with, as you say, a changing cohort of children who come in with differing needs. How we support those foster carers is one huge plank of our work in that space.

The other is that some children will still need residential care, so what is the purpose of that residential care? Who are the specific children who require that level of support? In providing that, and accepting that there is always going to be a cost to that, how do we make sure that we get the best value for money by providing the right wraparound support? That will often require complete integration with health services.

Again, we have just announced—we have lots of announcements at the moment—the Home Again programme. Our new regional care co-operatives, working with ICBs, will specifically target those children who are on the edge of a deprivation of liberty order due to their welfare needs, or indeed who already have a deprivation of liberty order against them. Those are the children who are most high cost and most at risk, who often are not in appropriate accommodation or getting support, and nor indeed are their families. How do you support the child but, importantly, support the family as well in order to navigate that child out of residential and ideally back to a family environment, be that their own family or a fostering environment?

Q8 You have mentioned increasing complexity, and I wondered if you had an idea about the range of needs that children are displaying now. Sorry, I should say that I have no interests to declare, but I was a child psychiatrist and had a specialism in learning disability and autism for many years before I retired. I am interested in the range of different therapeutic support that children with complex needs might need, and whether the system is sufficiently joined up to enable that to happen. There is also the question of their continuing needs at 18, because a lot of these children are not going to be able to live independent lives. You spoke about fostering; should we be thinking about adult fostering? I am thinking about how complexity affects the picture that you are painting for us.

We can talk a bit about rising demand and where we are seeing the shifts in that, which Shazia can talk about in a second. When it comes to complex needs, through the Home Again programme we have commissioned a specific tool to assess the needs of a child much more effectively, with medical support, which then drives the right action, often medically related, around the child, with the anticipation that that could mean medium-term or long-term support and intervention that stays with the child whenever they are in residential care, but also backs out of the system once they go back to families. I do not know if Shazia wants to say a bit more about that.

I said at the beginning that over the last 10 to 15 years, because of the reduction in prevention activity, we have seen children presenting later, so the harm has been happening over a long period of time. We have not got in early enough when they are five, six or even younger, so that, by the time they eventually present, those needs, both in the family and for the child, are quite entrenched, and it is a much harder and therefore more expensive type of placement to do the right kind of work with the child and their family.

We have to shore up the family environment so that the child can return, which is important, but we have also seen a change in the harms that children experience. The change in age range is also linked to a rise in extrafamilial harm—not just online but grooming gangs, county lines and so on, so we have not really had to deal before with the things that we are dealing with.

Helen talked about us having to redefine the purpose of residential care. We have had a system that was designed to deal with children who struggled to stay in foster care. The next step was residential care. Things like the Home Again pilot are really starting to do exactly what you are asking: what are the needs? How many of those are mental health needs? How many of those are SEND/autism related? What is it about the environment? When we have really expensive placements, the ones that cost half a million pounds a year, that is because we do not yet know what the right treatment is, and we have high staff ratios to contain children because we have not quite worked out what the prescription is. That is what the pilots are designed to do.

Yes, we have pilots doing that, and the review on the purpose of residential is under way. We are trying to home in on which cohorts of children are best supported in that environment and what training and support the workforce should have in residential; it is a workforce that has not been reviewed for many years. So this is a real opportunity, a moment in time, for us to understand what we want from our residential system and change the way it operates.

Q9 I do not have any interests to declare. It is interesting hearing you talk about the work on prevention and what you are doing in that space. You have touched on the issue of residential care. Clearly, that sort of care is the right intervention in some circumstances, and it is important to recognise that. It is not always safe for some children and young people to be at their home. You have also talked about complexity and older children, and I think that is something we will want to explore further. Could you expand for me on what assessment you have made of the residential care market?

You have mentioned regional care co-operatives, which, I have to say, before preparing for this meeting, I had not particularly heard of. Could you expand a bit more on that and what role you think they will be playing in this area?

We honestly think that the market is not functioning in the way that it needs to. It is no secret that expanding costs mean that the system has moved to the point where about 83% of it is private sector and the rest is public sector and not-for-profit, and there is significant geographical variation in relation to supply and demand. One-quarter of our provision is in the north-west, but one-quarter of the children who need that provision are not in the north-west. We do not have enough provision in London or the south-west. That is why we end up in a situation where local authorities are scrabbling around for the nearest provision and seeing if it is good enough? Does it meet the needs, potentially on a Friday afternoon, when they are trying to find an urgent placement for a child with complex needs, where their existing placement has broken down or the child is at significant risk at that point in time? Crisis decisions are being made where ideally you would not make them in those circumstances.

To go back to the outcomes point, in no world is it good if a child is living in London but gets sent off to the north-west. That is nothing against the north-west; you want children to stay in and around their communities to be supported. Stability is really important.

So we are rolling out regional care co-operatives. They are designed to provide some economies of scale around local authorities and to improve commissioning arrangements. Often, we find that local authorities are doing spot purchasing when they are in those crisis situations. They do not have the economies of scale themselves to be able to drive a market that is shifting significantly at the moment.

We are seeing new private providers coming in all the time. Again, some of those will be brilliant and some of them will not when it comes to their ability to decipher what good looks like in terms of cost, value for money and, importantly, quality when it comes to the changing dynamic of that cohort. For the regional care co-operatives we have had two pathfinders, one in Greater Manchester, operating across the Greater Manchester combined authority footprint, and then one in the south-east. They are still fairly fledgling in terms of what we are learning from them. What we are doing a lot of at the moment is refining what we want those organisations to achieve. About two weeks ago we announced five more regional care co-operatives across the country, so we will be covering more than 100 local authorities, with an expectation that ICBs are signed up. They have signed up to the application process. We need health to be much more part of the story and the commissioning arrangements. Those boards must be chaired by an equivalent chief executive-type role, someone with seniority who is able to drive the sorts of budgets that exist in this space. There should be an expert in public commercial arrangements in order to drive the commercial arrangements that we want to see. Those are the headlines regarding the regional care co-operatives.

That is theoretical at this point. There are the two pathfinders you mentioned, but that is very early days, and then there are the five new care co-operatives. When is this going to be rolled out across the whole country, and when do you expect to see serious changes to the commissioning, hopefully driving down the costs of these placements in residential care?

I would expect that we will start within a year, and hopefully sooner. First and foremost, the new five are bringing into place their chief executives and their board at the moment. T hey are doing a thorough review of sufficiency across the local authorities in which they are operating , really understanding cohort and current supply , d emand and cost arrangements. O nce they have done that analysis , it will enable them to prioritise where they would go to try to achieve a better commissioned arrangement , where we might have particular issues with complex needs, and where we need health to step in and potentially support further . W e have announced two of our Home Again programmes , which I mentioned just now , so far: one is in Merseyside and Cheshire, and the other is in the West Midlands. T hey will work through the RCC arrangement.

Okay, b ut we do not have evidence yet , a nd there are concerns about the boundaries of these and how they link with ICB s—although, frankly, we do not know what ICB boundaries are coming; from the debate yesterday, their boundaries seem to be in a state of flux as well . I f you want to get ICBs involved, how will that work if t here are not clear boundaries ?

There is no doubt that it is a challenge. I have talked to my team about there being a kaleidoscope of boundaries across all public services at the moment, which makes it difficult. That is , frankly, what makes it difficult n ow for a local authority . It is the same again with the regional care co - operative i n some places . W herever we can , w e are trying to align around strategic mayoral authority footprints, be that one footprint or sister footprints — as we have with Merseyside and Cheshire — so that we can try to keep step with where we are with wider public sector boundaries a t the moment. We think the relationships between those organisations are critical.

Q10 Thank you. Finally, the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act h ad several measures in it aimed at managing the social care market. W hat will be the impact of the market management measures , and how will you be assessing this and on what sort of timescale ?

W e put a number of measures into the Act — a huge number related to children’s social care — but , in relation to the market, I suppose the biggest one that people are focused on is the profit cap. W e have put that in as a backstop measure , so that we are able to bring it forward at a point we think is necessary. We do not have the information yet to be able to apply a profit cap. T herefore , we need to take a number of steps to learn more about how the market is working and , ultimately , to decide whether that is necessary. R egional care co - operatives are gripping sufficiency and those commercial arrangements : value for money, cost and quality. We are rolling out a data platform. A t the moment , we have no national picture for cost and quality that enables us to take more informed decisions. W e think stuff will be better done regionally ; t here may be a question about what we learn from that data and whether there are some thing s you might do nationally — if you have a very slim cohort of children, for example . T hat is to be learned from and worked throug h. T hat will be rolled out by the middle of 2027. O ur regional care co - operatives will hopefully have also made good progress by then. I would like to think that, by the end of 2027, we will have a much richer picture of the market and the way it is operating.

If I can quickly say so, we are investing over £500,000- worth of capital. W e are doing this in our secure provision , building two new secure homes in London and the West Midlands because they have no provision for secure homes at the moment , and w e are refurbishing other secure homes and doing some rebuild s. This is to make sure that , where children are in secure provision , it is right and fit for purpose and provides the support that it needs for when they leave that environment. W e are also investing in what we call open children’s homes — normal children’s homes —a nd that investment is targeted at children with complex needs. W e have awarded those local authorities that have sufficiency issues and are committed to providing additional capacity for complex needs. There is a bit of market reshaping there in the way the G overnment are stepping in and making some market adjustments.

There is s o much going on , from what you have said , in this space , a nd it is really exciting to hear. Here is w hat I would lik e, probably in writing to u s. S ome of these will take a few years to be able to be assess ed, b ut how will you measure success? What are the different metrics that you are using to measure the performance of each of these interventions? I f you were able to write to us with that, that would be really helpful.

On a point of clarification, as I may have misheard what you said , is t he intention to have the RCCs on all the mayoral footprints, even if they do not match with ICBs, and n ot the other way a roun d?

T his is a decision still to be taken by Ministers. T he way we have designed the current ones is to try where we can , and where we know mayoral authority exists , to align with that footprint, whic h, in most cases but not all , ha s a match up to ICBs — I mean, it is quite live , with the movement of boundaries . We would want to align where we can , not create additional random boundaries.

Q11 Do you see RC Cs taking on specific responsibilities and functions from local authorities? W here RCCs exist, are you thinking that there is a set of activities that will no longer be done at local authority level but will be done at a regional level ? I f so, could you set out precisely what they are? I f not , and it is more about the RCC providing additional capacity to support the local authority in their functions , could you clarify exactly what that capacity will be? I am very interested in Baroness Pidgeon’s question of h ow we are going to monitor whether this additional capacity actually supports outcomes .

At the moment, the statutory responsibility will remain with the local authority , a nd that is our expectatio n. Again, there are lively conversations at the moment about devolution and how things will operate , b ut , at the moment , we expect that local authorities will continue to have the responsibility to place the child , and in a relevant setting . T he regional care co - operatives will have some capacity, and there is an expectation that funding will be p ooled from local authorities so that they can optimise the available budget to negotiate better prices and quality and to better meet the needs of that group of local authorities. That is not easy either ; i t is challenging.
You said that there is an expectation of funding being p ooled . Is that saying, “W e are going to make this happen ” or just, “We hope it happens”?

In the legislation, we have set out that we can require local authorities to be part of a regional care co - operative : there is an arrangement there where we can make that expectation clear. Obviously , the big case for local authorities is that the care market is not working as it stands at the moment ; by having specialist support, including specialist commercial support in place , you will hopefully have a better menu of support in front of you for the children that present to you — on a Friday afternoon or whenever it is —and be able to place them in something more suitable and closer to home.

I am so sorry, because it is obvious that I am missing something . L ocal authorities will be required to give some money to the RCCs so that the RCCs can do collective purchasing on their behalf —i s that right or wrong?

It is right that they are expected to pool their budget . T hese budgets are huge , a nd the regional care co - operative would be expected to commission the placements and go into the commissioning arrangements. I think it is still to be determined and worked through w hether a local authority then chips in at that point and provides enough money for 15 places or whatever it might be, or whether they put their money in up fron t.
How much money is also to be determined and worked through?

As part of setup arrangements for an RCC, what they are doing at the moment is determining what their local sufficiency arrangements are . I f they have 10 local authorities in their patch, how much are they currently spending on residential —w hat type of places and provider s? How i s the fit across the local area? Do they have the right support in the right place ? W hat does that tell them about the gap analysis and , therefore , what needs to be purchased in the future? W hich supplier would they not want to use in the future because the quality is not good enough or it is not meeting the demand in a certain place ?

Q12 I want to clarify a point. I can understand this regional devolution, but one thing that has worked well in the health service over the last decade is specialist purchasing for really rare conditions, so that you do not have 12 different commissioners trying to argue the toss. B ecause you need really expensive equipment in some of those centres, everybody ha s accepted it, b ecause you cannot have 20 of something for a relatively small population. I just cannot understand why, for those with really significant needs, we are not looking at something for England around defining the requirements, working with CAMHS and others, and saying, “This is what we wan t”. It just seems to me that we are getting eight or 10 teams to do something that, for that very high-level need, could be defined centrally. Could you comment on that?
