That is something we would be happy to explore as we learn more from regional care co-operatives and as they understand what those gaps are. It is no secret that, working with MHCLG, we have looked, and will be looking again, at those half-a-million-pound or even half-a-billion-pound placements and what those placements are paying for. Are they providing the right support? What is the integration like with health? Where is Health doing direct commissioning itself? Is that working well or not, and how can they combine locally?
Thank you for that answer. I think it is constructive.

Q13 I am concerned about the idea that some children just have to be in residential care. There is a big move to try to develop small supports in local communities, close to families, to help children and adults to have more ordinary lives, rather than making this financial investment in residential care, which is often going to be a long way away. When we know that people do better in small groups that provide permanent settings for them, I do not understand why the investment is not in small local support instead. I know it is more complex and requires good interpersonal skills, relationships, therapy and so on, but why this, at this stage of a young person’s life?

I do not think we disagree with that at all. That is why we are doing the work on what the purpose is of residential and which children it could support, and that might be for a very short period of time while needs are stabilised and the right support is put around them. However, the vast majority are much better supported by their families or in fostering care with the right support around them, again with the right health support needs around them as well.

Q14 I will ask the next question—I have no interests to declare—and it is about unregistered homes. Accepting that you are undertaking a lot of activity at the moment, over what timescale do you hope to stop the use of unregistered homes? What steps are you taking to ensure that they are not still part of the system in a timely way?

Obviously, the use of unregistered is illegal, but we know it is a practice that still happens. In combination with Ofsted, we are looking closely at this at the moment. Through the Act, we have introduced powers for Ofsted to be able to fine providers that are operating in this way. We have undertaken a deep dive with 15 local authorities around the country to get under the skin of why they are using this provision, getting them to talk us through the cases in their area and tell us what has happened. Very often, it is that spot purchasing arrangement on a Friday afternoon when there is a crisis and there is no provision available, so unregistered is used, maybe for 24 to 72 hours. Again, that is not acceptable, but it is what happens: a need is presented and that need must be met.

It might be for slightly longer where a particular organisation is seen to be able to support a child very specifically with their needs but they are not registered with Ofsted—or indeed they are in the queue to be registered, since one of the other issues that we have is that the queue is ever-growing, with more people trying to enter the market. We have done some work with Ofsted to better sift the queue so that we bring to the front of the queue provision that is being paid for by the department, by government capital investment, making sure that that is brought onstream as quickly as it is built.

There is also the question of geographical location. Where we have sufficiency problems, we have to make sure that those areas are able to register relevant provision as quickly as possible. There is also more to do when it comes to the portability of registered managers. If a registered manager moves to a different home because the organisation is set up and it might be something that is outstanding, that provision cannot be registered until it is sat in the queue and gone through the system.

It is an area we are taking seriously. We will have our first ever set of DfE data on the unregistered published in November. That gives us a proper baseline of placements in the unregistered system that we can work from. At the moment, Ofsted does an annual review, but it is a bit of a snapshot in time. We hope that this first set of evidence will give us more insight and allow us to target our support through our regions group that operates within the department.

I am slightly worried that the current system is that you are sifting through to put who is at the top of the queue and who is at the bottom of the queue when the intention, I hope, is to not have that queue because we should not be using unregistered. Do you have a timeframe in which you want to completely negate the use of unregistered homes?

We have not set a deadline on that. As I say, we are working really closely with Ofsted, which also looks at this within their inspection arrangements to again understand that, while it is illegal that these homes are used, what are the circumstances in which the provision was used? Was there an alternative available at that particular moment for that particular child? The data will tell us if we are starting to have an impact on the use of that provision. Again, for regional care co-operatives, this is absolutely going to also be on them in terms of understanding sufficiency needs in their area. If they have a local authority that is using unregistered provision, there is obviously an immediate question about what the regional care co-operative might be able to do to support them to back out of that circumstance.
But you have not set any time frame for resolving that problem.
As quickly as possible, but we have not set a deadline.

Q15 The average cost of an unregistered placement last year was £10,500 per week, according to our briefing—roughly half a million or £546,000 annually. Apparently, there were 36 children in placements that each had a cost of more than £1 million a year. Does the department have the data to establish whether these extraordinary costs might be justified in any way by the complexity of the care needs of the children in question? Related to that, what objective criteria would you use to set a profit cap so that you did not inadvertently penalise providers providing high-quality care to children with very complex needs?

We have not got the richness of data on those high-cost placements. We have worked with MHCLG, we have run some surveys in the past with them and, and the Local Government Association, to try to find out more about those placements. Again, I know we sound like we are going to be relying a lot on the regional care co-operatives. We are expecting a lot from them in relation to their assessment of sufficiency, which should also include a review of individual costs of placements, which again will provide an opportunity to see, of the highest-cost placements in a locality, what are the services that it is providing? What are the needs of those children? Can you get to a position where you might have a price-banding arrangement where it is legitimate that very high-cost placements will exist for the very highest needs of certain cohorts of children? That in itself will also inform more about cost breakdowns and how providers are behaving. We have also introduced a financial oversight scheme within the department that is doing a deep dive on the cost analysis of the top 40 providers of children’s social care. We have just stood that up; it is another form of data that will be coming to us during the course of the year. That, combined with the data collection that we will be doing nationally on placements and the intel that we will receive from regional care co-operatives, will start to give us a richer picture on costs.

I think it is very challenging for the department to work out what the right level of profit is in this space. Not least, that is because we have 83% private sector-led providers. I need to check the number, but I think it is about 20% of that number that are private equity. There is a risk that, as soon as we start chasing profit, we start chasing our tails around people’s accountants and how many can be moved aroun d. We need to go in with our eyes open in terms of building that data picture first on the richness of costs, the costs for particular cohorts of children, before determining whether a price-banding system or a profit-cap arrangement is the right thing to do.

We a re conscious of the fragility of the market as well : in moving to that too quickly, there is a risk that those providers disappear. We cannot afford for that to happen either , because we have children living in homes that need to be there .
Are there circumstances in which a £1 million annual cost could be justified ?

Yes, potentially— I would need to look at that. W ith very high - cost health needs, where you have round - the - clock support from potentially multiple carers, you can imagine that becomes more costly.
Yes—or high staff ratios with rotating teams so there is round - the - clock care.
Yes— for the individual ’s safety and the safety of others.

Q16 This is an important area of the discussion , and I very much appreciate the quality of the debate so far. Chair , following your question, on the face of it, if you step back from the detail that we are discussing, we are saying that there is a whole range of provision —which is costing a lot of money — that is illegal and routinely used . Y ou begin to wonder whether the English language has a meaning for “ illegal ” when we have that. I t is not an acceptable solution. I appreciate th at DfE colleagues are talking about solving it , b ut I just want to say th is, based on something I worked on for a long time in Punjab , Pakistan . T he moment a provider receives state funding — Lord Johnson has described just how much that funding sometimes is — that provider should be subject to all the regulatory provision, including Ofsted inspection , that goes with receiving state funding. We cannot have a situation where the state funds something that it knows to be illegal and does not even provide any quality assurance arrangements. I have not heard the DfE colleagues , who are answering very well , answer that point at all.
We will now get an answer.

Very often, these providers are waiting to be assessed by Ofsted, which then brings them into the regime. I appreciate that that should potentially be the other way a round. Directors of children’s services , who make these decisions locally , are assuring themselves as to whether that is an appropriate arrangement given the circumstances that are in front of them at that particular moment. T hey will look at the staff who are in place and whether the locality of the house or the home is suitable — albeit these are decision s that , ordinarily , they would not want to be tak ing at all.
We are allowing directors of children’s service s to commit an illegal act every time they do that —i s that what you are saying?
That is what happens, yes.
Lord Barber of Chittlehampton : I rest my case.
We will follow up. Thank you, Lord Barber. Lord Nichols—I mean Baroness Nichols.

Q17 Thank you, Lord Bradley—I will see you in the office later. O n the points we are raising about the costs , if we have to wait until the new bodies are set up, most of us could probably find an example , currently or in the past , where a local authority has spent that kind of money on a child ; I wonder whether you could look at some of that in the interim , rather than wait ing while these new bodies are set up. I am c ertainly aware of one : in my area , there was a threat to take the health board to court because it would not cough up half of the costs , and it needed to — I am talking of £ 2.4 million there. M aybe you could look at some of those in the interim and find out . I do not know whether I would ever believe that a cost around that would come to £ 2. 4 million , b ut there were very complex needs. I n another area , the staffing ratio for one child was 6:1 because of the complexity , and the needs were still not being met. T here is some information out there that you could maybe have a look at , a nd I am sure we would appreciate having that information on a confidential basis — we do not need to know who or where they are ; whether those costs were inflated, if you like , is the bit we would all like to see .

We can certainly take that away and come back with a couple of examples. I should say that , where I have pointed out the work we are doing with regional care co - operatives , we are obviously continu ing to work with local authorities alongside that : we have done that deep dive I mentioned on the 15 local authorities in relation to unregistered homes . T hat work continues whil e, at the same time , we set up for future arrangements.

Q18 Can I go back to this point about unregistered children’s homes? I assume— naively perhaps, but , I think , rightly — that no director of children’s services is sitting there wanting to use an unregistered children’s home. It is when you are faced with the position where, in an evening, you do not have an alternative , a nd so , at that moment in time , that is the best option for the child — I think that that is likely to be the case. I wonder if you could help us with this thought experiment : if we said collectively , or Parliament or Ministers decided , that we want to stop this and will give ourselves a month, two months or six weeks to stop the use of unregistered children’s homes , w hat would that require in practical terms? E xploring that , we may discover that it is just not possible to do in one, two or six months —b ut what would need to be built and commissioned? Do you have a sense of the scale of financial commitment it would take? How could we end this problem?

I think that is right. A s part of the deep dive that we undertook with directors of children’s services , their going through the list in itself has prompted some action around how quickly they can move a child if they are unregistered — it was the right decision at the time, but have they moved them on quickly enough , and w as it temporary enough? T here are some cases like that. W e spoke to a director of children’s services over the summer , who talked about the arrangements that he had made by going through that list and making sure people were moved on. There was , interestingly, one case where he still felt it was the right decision : i t was a rural location , t he child was in a very safe environment , t he provision around them was absolutely right , and i t would have disrupted their schooling if they had been moved to a different locality. T here can be some very specific circumstances where it is still the right thing to do. The importance there, of course, is in making sure that that provision gets registered as quickly as possible.

Sorry—just to chip in again on this , t hat exchange totally makes sense. I f they are necessary at certain moments, do we not need to change the law to make it legal and change the regulatory processes so that these people are brought within them rather than continuing to act in illegal ways?
That is something we certainly need to look at and Ofsted is pursuing at the moment.
Maybe it would be better to get them registered more quickly.

Q19 One thing that has struck me in this conversation is this: we are looking at our own problems and we acknowledge them , b ut have we looked in any way at international comparisons? For example, w hen I speak to people in New Zealand and Australia, I do not have any evidence from the people I have spoken to that they would be in this scenario. A re we in a really awful place compared with , say, European countries that I do not know as well as the two I have mentioned , o r do we not even look at what other people are doing?

I do not know specifically on residential care , but I know more broadly. Some of our family network reforms are based on the fact that some of the countries that you mention have always prioritised keeping children with families within their broader communities. T hat is a thing we have in common, including using foster car e. W e hav e definitely seen a growth in the use of residential. I do not know whether that is out of step internationally, or whether you know that. Certainly, our famil y reforms have more in common with others.

Thank you. That is very helpful. My gut reaction is we should be making some observation about the research that needs to be done for the long term. I know we cannot do that in three months, but it does seem quite important to me.

We understand that the provision in Denmark is very good , a nd there is an arrangement : as part of our review s on workforce and on the purpose of residential , w e will be looking at Denmark specifically .
Q20 Helen , you mentioned about growing the number of foster placements by 10,000. Could you break that down into full - time and part - time foster carers?
I cannot, if I am honest. We want 10,000 additional places for children , and, as part of that, w e want all sorts of different arrangements.
I wondered whether one was growing more popular than the other.

Oh , I see. A s part of this campaign , we want to be able to reach a group of people who have perhaps pondered foster caring and thought that it is not for them because they work or do not own their own house — they have ruled themselves out before t hey have ruled themselves in to explore whether it will be appropriate for them. S omeone in my team fosters, but he does w eekend respite foster caring for a family to give them respite periodically. T here are all sorts of different arrangements. What we want to do, through our first national campaign ever , is really open people’s eyes to what they can do. Of course, we need full - time foster carers as well — we really need them. But , in having that mix of type s of foster carers, we are aiming not just to have lots more foster care placements available but to include some choice . T hat will provide local authorities with not a “ panic match ” but being able to ask which will be the best family —a re they in the right locality for the school , with the health services support that they are receiving , so that we can really support th e transition i f a child needs to come out of the family home and into care ?

If there are part - time carers, the y might be more interested , in certain c ircumstances , in saying , “ I think we can do some full - time fostering ”. Do you know what I mean? It is to encourage.

Yes, definitely. S ometimes , people who might initially come in part time and test whether it works for them m ay then move towards full time. A longside the kind of recruitment , we need to think and are thinking about retention as well. How do we provide the support around that family? What does that look like? How do we meet their needs? T hat might be matching between a full - time foster carer and somebody who does some weekend foster caring , so that you can provide that support.
Is there a need for support for kinship carers if they need —I do not know— extra accommodation and that kind of support ?

Specifically on fostering, in relation to accommodation, we are rolling out something called Room Makers . This is about existing foster carers who are brilliant and would love to have another child in their home but do not have the space. T hat is a capital program me where we will convert the loft or garage and create some more space for the family.
Is there extra funding for that, w hen is it made available , and how much is it ?
Yes, there is: it is available from now in our foster hub locations around the country, and it is £25 million across the spending review period .

For broader family networks, within our Families First Partnership program me, which we talked about, where we are investing £ 2.4 billion , there is provision within there to do family network support packages. I f you have had a family group decision - making meeting, or if you have not and have identified a way of shoring up the wider family network, money can be spent via that program me i f the thing that you need is some adaptation to the house or whatever it might be. W e are seeing local authorities not use that provision as much . W e are currently on our second iteration of our program me guide : we have learned from the first year and said, “H ere i s a set of things that you might want to do ” . W e are trying to encourage more local authorities to make use of some of that provision.

T he only other thing to say on foster care is this: one of the misconceptions has been that you always have to make a lifelong commitment . T hat is maybe true , but it should be true in fewer cases. We have a big focus , through the prevention work but also in fostering, in trying to get reunification with the family, particularly where the family circumstances may be , for example, domestic abuse while the mother sor t s her housing arrangements, et cetera , or there is mental ill health in the family and that passes. W e are always trying , where it is safe and there is not abuse in the home, to have foster carers that have that as a route out as well.
There is the affordability issue for foster carers as well, is there not?
They are definitely cheaper than residential care.

Yes, they are significantly cheaper. A local authority would , obviously , for all sorts of reasons, select foster care over residential if it is appropriate and the right match. Foster carers obviously get paid a fee through the local authority as well , a nd some local authorities will band the level of fees that they pay a family depending on the complexity of need of the child or the arrangements that they have in place. There are various arrangements that local authorities have , from deductions on council tax in some cases through to accessing leisure passes or f ree swimming at the weekend —w hatever it might be t o really help the foster carer financially.

Q21 I want to turn to the subject of the people who are obviously pivotal in delivering this for families and children : the workforce. I n the report we have in front of us , in 20 23 - 24 , the department identified that social work capacity was at highest risk, but that was removed in 2025 because turnover rates had improved . A number of local authorities are reporting that that has now moved backward s, and that is probably about workload capacity and the complexity that people have to deal with. W hat do you think? What assessment have you made recently of the state of the children’s social care workforce ?

It was in 2022 that we escalated this to a set of people who are responsible for our department’s top - tier risks : the performance and risk committee , which looks at the things that are most serious. A t that point, we were incredibly worried about sufficiency . T hat was manifested in the overall number of social workers we had and in the workload statistics — how many cases each person was dealing with.

We were worried about the level of agency use. I t is incredibly expensive ; l ocal authorities have all sorts of constraints , and w e have spent quite a long time talking about some of the things that drive their costs, but agency costs were part of that problem . Also, those workers cycle in and out ; when we want stability for children, it is not brilliant to have turnover in that way. W e were also worried about people leaving the profession with burnout due to workload .

I t is worth saying that, in de-escalating the risk, it is not that we do not think that those things are a problem, but we have more confidence in the program me s we have in place and have certainty that, certainly for the rest of the spending review, those program me s will be in place , and w e have two to three years of improving data. I was not let off the hook the first time I went to the performance and risk committee — which was a year earlier —and said , “ I think this is ready to de-escalate ” . They said, “N o, you need to wait for another year of data ” .

Of t he program me s we have in place, a set of them are about recruitment — attracting people into the profession. The department supports a certain number , and w e ha ve modelled a continuation of those. Those are people from within local authorities who want to switch careers , as well as graduates. T hat is making a difference to sufficiency. I n the latest numbers that I have , in 2025, we were at 36,200, which is the highest we have had since 2017, the first point at which we started recording. Vacancies are down 17% fro m 2024—we saw a huge improvement in 2025. Agency social work is down 17% from 2024 too, turnover has improved, et cetera. A cross every metric that the department monitors, we saw a significant improvement .

As well as our workforce entry programmes, we took action on agency social work. We have talked quite a bit about some of the work we are doing on regional carers, which is much more complex, difficult and slightly more fledgling.

On agency, w e did not use the la w— we have now taken a power to put some of the work that we have done on a statutory basis — but worked to establish regional memorandums. Q uite a lot of what was pushing the price of social workers up was that people were competing for them. W ithin localities , t here are regionally agreed price caps ; r egions are required to report to us on a quarterly basis on whether anyone is breaking those. There are arrangements about p ost-qualifying experience : y ou cannot graduate into the workforce as an agency worker ; you have to have three years ’ post-qualifying experience in a local authority before you can move out to an agency. You cannot leave a local authority one day and appear in a neighbouring local authority a s a social worker ; you have to have a three - month wai t. This is a set of things to constrain the agency workforce. At the time, the market that operates agency worker s said that we would lose all these people , who would leave the profession. They have not : we have seen them return to the permanent workforce. W e are much more confident in the supply side .

O n development , we have talked quite a lot about the complexity that social workers are now dealing with . W e are investing heavily in professional development. F or quite a long time, we have had an early career program me , which is for a year , and we have just launched —well, we have just procured somebody to develop the curriculum materials for — a two - year early - career support program me for lead child protection practitioners. W e are saying that, if you go into child protection, i t is much more skilled and generic standards are not enough to do it, so t his is how we will support you in developing that aspect of your career. There are other strands for people who are leading family help teams, et cetera , which will come on board later. It is worth saying that we did quite a lot of work with ADCS and LGA workforce committees on the things they were telling us social workers needed, such as more CPD, more support, more group supervision, et cetera .

T he final thing on workload is this. W e are doing two things. W hen I talked about the F amilies F irst programme and the evidence - based program me s that we are putting into prevention, quite a lot of th em told us that , sometimes , the intervention works best when it is not with the social worker. T he social workers carry statutory responsibilities and t here is a lot of stig ma and fear : f amilies do not always want to engage , because they feel that that is quite serious. T he earlier , preventive bit of the system, building on things such as the S upporting F amilies P rogramme and the family group decision - making model, all of which used non-statutory workforces, is investing in building up a multidisciplinary workforce. We do not yet have a rich picture of what that looks like ; we have only just started collecting data on what sorts of workforces local authorities are building up . They might have a huge issue with domestic abuse or a particular clinical mental health thing , and t hey will have freedom to spend that money on a multidisciplinary workforce that sits within the local authority . T hat reduces the social worker workload —and they are not equipped to deal with those cases , s o they were carrying cases and thinking, “ I do n’t have the skills to deal with all this variety and complexity ” .

Those are just some of the things we are doing. The national professional development offer will come on board later in 2027 — I cannot quite remember the date. W e have just concluded the procurement , w e will be making an announcement very shortly as to the lead supplier , a nd then the suppliers will start developing materials so that local authorities can get their staff on to those offers.

Q22 I have a quick question: d o you think a region’s workforce vacancy rate is heavily linked to the performance of its individual councils, where they require improvement or a re judge d inadequate by Ofsted?

Shazia Hussain : Yes, definitely, but i t is incredibly complicated . W e know that you are more likely to be inadequate , as judged by Ofsted , if you are in a more deprived area , as there is more strain both on local authority finances and on their families. T here is a perfect storm : it is really hard to be good in those places, which is why particular parts of our country have more performance challenges , and then , if you are judged inadequate, you see an exit of the workforce. T hat is where we would see people — I was going to say “from Bradford ” because that is where I am from, but I know others in the room are , too , so I will say A and B — leaving a place and going to a neighbouring authority because it has a better judgment. S ome of the things we talked about earlier , about constraining that movement , are quite important . I do not believe people turn up to do a bad job —that is rare. T here are contextual factors , and those might be external to the local authority or might be about broader corporate leadership . W e have an intervention and improvement function in the department that is delivered through our regions group , who work with us on understanding which places the department needs to wrap around. To go back to workforce slightly, we are no longer a top - tier national departmental risk ; we are monitoring every local authority, looking at what is happening to the numbers that I talked about . I f , alongside our other set of numbers, we start to worry , w e are supporting individual places alongside the national program me s that I mentione d, whatever the specific prescription might be in that area.

Q23 I ha ve the last question , and I will make it slightly longer . W hat is the department’s assessment of how effectively Ofsted is regulating and inspecting the children’s social care sector ? S econdly, as we discussed before you came in , is CQC ever working together with it for residential care? D oes that provide an opportunity or a problem — does one go and then the other goes separately? W e wonder whether you think there should be an inspectorate for just this , which could be fast and rapid rather than designed in the current system.

The ILACS framework looks at the local authority children’s social care function overall — not the settings , which it also inspects separately. W e are currently working with them to align the intervention framework with the direction of reform. It is quite tricky, is it not ? We have set out a new agenda and are saying that these things now matter : w e want to see local authorities prioritising family , with this sort of practice , and doing these sorts of things when making residential care decisions or whatever it might be . W e are working quite hard with them to align the two , and I think we have good alignment. They have consulted on their changes now that our changes are law. F rom next year, we will have an inspection framework that is lined up to what the Government think good looks like in policy and legal terms , a nd then they will go through a period of piloting those inspections to see how they are going to work , because t here will be some changes around that. I t is definitely worth saying that, until quite recently , we in the department placed — I think rightly — a substantial weight on an Ofsted judgment in the action that the department takes. I f a local authority was inadequate , w e would tak e quite heavy action; if it was good, we would not. We have just moved into a slightly more nuanced place than that, because it can be a number of years before something is reinspected. We are now monitoring what we call a key set of system health data alongside that. This come s into the department on a quarterly basis . W e are using both —we have the Ofsted judgment, including monitoring visits , and our own data —and w e make a judgment as to whether we want to find out what is going on and perhaps provide some support earlier. Helen, d o you want to cover SCCIF ?
We are also looking at the inspection of children’s homes, which is called SCCIF. Ofsted do es joint targeted inspections with CQC and the police inspector —
That is HMICFRS .
Yes—the far - too - long acronym . These inspections do not happen that frequently.
They tend to be thematic, such as on neglect or sexual abuse .

I think it is legitimate for us to think about what more we could do in the future as we begin to look at the purpose of residential and therefore what the inspection arrangements look like , but Ofsted is in lockstep with us in the reform journey. Its consultation, which covered SCCIF and ILACS , closed in September , so we expect it to be coming out with its response to the consultation, and the changes that will be coming into effect , in the next couple of months.
I think I have heard that you might want something more tailor - made for the care home s— or is that a misinterpretation?
No, it is not a misinterpretation. W e have an ambition to work much more closely with H ealth across the whole of the children’s social care system.

Q24 I was struck when reading into this area myself —and I have learn ed a lot again this morning — by the gap between the outcomes , which are pretty poor for all kinds of reasons , for which I am not blaming anybody , a nd the Ofsted judgments , which seem to think that children’s homes are generally rather good. There is a kind of disconnect. It made me wonder what Ofsted actually do es when it does an inspection.

That is a really fair comment. I t is interesting, is it not ? I do not know whether you meant educational outcomes, lifelong outcomes, et cetera . The new SCCIF will be different, but it has essentially looked at what is in the gift of the children’s home —whether it is providing safe care and all the right professionals are there — and ha s not looked beyond that , because it would consider someone’s educational outcomes to be out of the control of the home. S ome of the changes that we are hoping to make are through the inspection framework but also through the direction that the Government ha ve set that, if you are in a parenting role, we are definitely concerned about the overall outcomes.

It is interesting, because , in the schools area, Ofsted start s with the outcomes and then , sometimes , when the outcomes are good , does not even bother with any inspection — but this is the reverse. I think ther e is something fundamentally flawed in the way this is happening.

Yes, there is the system join - up — really thinking about the child’s journey through the system. We design ed the F amil ies F irst program me through a co-design arrangement with those local authorities, and we thought about how education, health and police supported the family . I think we are into that space now with care : enduring relationships is a hook for us to get into who the people are around the child and, importantl y , how is the school amplifying the support needs of that child? If attendance is not in the right place and where it needs to be, what is the expectation on the children’s home, frankly ? I think we are getting towards that , but we are not there yet.

I will be really quick. T hinking about the outcomes , m aybe we need something such as payment by results : you may be keeping the child safe in the setting, but, if you are not preparing that child or young person for the world beyond, are we getting value for money? As we spoke about earlier , there is £500,000 to £1 million - worth. Maybe they may not be the people ready to go to work, but there might be an argument for payment by results here i f a substantial amount of money has been invested, and , as corporate parents, it is our responsibility and we are not getting it. That is just a comment.

Q25 I have a final question on Ofsted. Providers are required to notify Ofsted of serious incidents. R ecently — I think between April 2024 and March 2025— they received 42,500 notifications, of which 57% were recorded as “O ther ” . Are you satisfied that Ofsted and the department understand what “O ther ” means?
No.
Would you look into that and write to us about what “O ther ” is?
Yes.

Are there a ny further questions from the c ommittee? No. Well, t hank you very much for your time this morning and for being as informative as you can in a very shifting scene of care. I will officially close the session .
