National Resilience Committee
C orrected oral evidence
Th urs day 11 June 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Coussins (The Chair); Baroness Curran; Lord Farmer; Baroness Helic; Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch; Lord Marland; Baroness Mobarik ; Baroness Northover; Lord Oates; Lord Peach; Baroness Winterton of Doncaster.
Evidence Session No. 1 1 Heard in Public Questions 104 - 115
Witnesses
Prof essor Lee Miles, Professor of Crisis and Disaster Management, Bournemouth University Disaster Management Centre; Nihal Newman, Director for Resilience and Cybersecurity, Ofcom .
Examination of witnesses
Professor Lee Miles and Nihal Newman .

Q104 Good morning, welcome, and thank you very much for your time and for coming to help us with our very challenging inquiry into national preparedness and resilience. We are very grateful for your time . W e have you for about an hour . I remind you that this is a public session , which is being broadcast live. You will receive a transcript in a couple of days . I f there are any minor inaccuracies or if you spot any gaps where you suddenly remember something you might have said that you did not, we always welcome supplementary evidence in writing if you would like to do that.

We have a number of questions to ask you both. W hen you give your first answer, please begin by introducing yourself briefly , s o that we have that on the record as well. I will start with the first question, if I may , to set the scene. To what extent do you estimate that the public currently ha ve awareness of interconnected national and international risks ? Obviously, that includ es the ones relating to communications networks , where your special expertise is important for us to hear about . What is the level of awareness of risks in those areas ?

Thank you. I am the director of security and resilience policy at Ofcom. Communications infrastructure underpins our society and economy and our everyday lives. Ofcom’s role as a regulator is to enforce the relevant frameworks and legal frameworks that we have, and we monitor industry’s compliance against those frameworks. Therefore, Ofcom’s engagement is predominantly with the industry—with those organisations that we regulate—and there is limited direct engagement with the general public. However, there are some examples of where we do engage with the public and where we do communicate the risks that the telecommunications sector faces, such as our Connected Nations report. That is an annual publication where we set out the risks that the sector faces, plus what we are doing in that space. We also provide guidance and information for consumers. When we think about legacy networks such as the PSTN, we set out in our guidance the sorts of questions that consumers should be asking their operators to help prepare them for that transition, including for scams and fraud—practical tips for people to take; that is information that we make available on our website.

The more indirect engagement that we have with the public is through our compliance frameworks. When we consult on our guidance or policy proposals, that information is made available to the public. In those documents, we set out the risks that the sector faces. When there are some critical risks and we communicate with our sector, at that point we publish some of that correspondence on our website to raise awareness and to remind the sector of its obligations. For instance, in April, when there was quite a bit of media coverage around Mythos and the AI frontier models, we published that letter on our website.
Thank you. Just before I move on to Professor Miles, could I just follow up something you said? One of your functions, you said, is to monitor industry compliance. How compliant is it?

At the moment we have two separate frameworks for the telecoms security sector. We have the Telecommunications (Security) Act. We set out the various measures that operators need to follow. It is a journey, and the threat landscape is evolving. We provide a report to the Secretary of State, and aspects of that have been published by DSIT . We are seeing steps that industry is taking, and they are implementing the measures that we expect them to take in the sector.

Hello there. I am a professor of crisis and disaster management at Bournemouth University Disaster Management Centre, which has been around since 2001. I have worked on many aspects of resilience across the world, including in the UK. I am also A ssociate D ean for R esearch, I nnovation and E nterprise at Bournemouth University in the business school and the Faculty of Business and Law—so I come from the business side. I am also a director of the recent EM-PREPARE project funded by Innovate UK, which was on empowering everyday and household resilience and preparedness for it. It was a UK household study, a public study about levels of UK resilience in that space. Those are the three domains that I am here for.

I will answer the question by turning it to look particularly at the recipient of this, which is the public. You asked me the question, “How far is the public aware?” “Not very far at all” would be my immediate response to that. I think it is because, when we look at most of the data avai lable in terms of awareness, there is low awareness data among the public, particularly households, about specific types of risks and hazards . I shall give you an example. In the 2025 study that we did, something like 52% of households were aware of all the hazards that they faced in their households, but something like 21% did not think they had or were aware of any risk s at all. That is an illustration of awareness . The first thing is low awareness, which may be part of the argument. The second is what you might call disconnected priorities—the messaging around resilience coming from the resilience action plan, the national security strategy, the industry strategy and around the ‘ whole of society ’ approach .

What the data shows is that households, as well as the public in particular, see resilience in a very localised setting, often in their own personal dimension. In the survey study that I was involved in, something like the highest level of perceived threat were accidents at home (35%) , and the lowest level, at only 4%, was terrorism, and 5% on conflict and war. You see this disconnect ion of priorities. That is an important point. In effect, that leads to limited action. Something like 75% of households that we looked at in the study indicated that they took no specific action at all in relation to climate change, for example, and those kinds of elements. There is a communication deficit here in relation to the sending and receiving of information matters.

My final point would be that, with the Iran war and so forth, there is a rising awareness of what you might call ‘ cascading effects ’ . The public and households have become very much aware that geopolitics leads to higher energy prices, with implications for their standards of living. That is a causal economic relationship, which is wound up in hybrid resilience rather than necessarily different. There is a different interpretation about what is going on in Ukraine, which is seen as much more distant as a threat or a wider dimension when compared with other impacts. So that is the point I am trying to make here.
You have highlighted the disconnect between those figures and the whole-of-society approach, but would you say that those figures were an accurate perception by the public of risks that they face?

That is a very good point to make, because there is often a difference between awareness, if you like, which is perception, action— which can be seen as preparedness—and, if you like, delivery or outcomes. If you try to follow those aspects through, because of the personalised nature of hazards and threats, there is always going to be a level of perception as to what affects people’s regional or community locality and is personal to them. That means that there is always going to be a disconnect between aspects of that. There is also a very strong regional difference between urban communities and rural communities, about how they would perceive communication around awareness of interconnected hybrid threats.

Q105 Slightly following on from Lord Oates, I suppose that, in fact, accidents in the home, especially with little children, would be high on the agenda and are most likely, so maybe that conclusion that people are coming to appears to be logical. But that then leads on to how we address what we are talking about here and therefore how the Government can communicate to the public in relation to this wider resilience challenge. With a fragmented media landscape, with audiences receiving information from different places, platforms, formats, and that changing as well and being likely to continue to change, how do you get the resilience or preparedness message across in that circumstance? Professor Miles?

It is an important point that you are making; it is very strong. Just to be very clear about the first obvious point: we have to recognise that households and the public are rational actors, for the most part. They are being perfectly rational in deciding what are the threats and hazards for them in their local community—in that dimension. There is always going to be a disconnect between the localisation of that and national strategy. There is always going to be a communication—if you like, a translation—point.

Basically, we need to focus on the concept of everyday resilience; in other words, what is the notion of everyday resilience that it has sufficient pertinence that takes on national priorities and makes them have resonance in the domestic and household landscape? Usually, I think there are four parts to that—the four Es of everyday resilience , if you like. The first E is what you might call ‘ enlightened context ’ , which is making it clear in government communications why that context is important for the public and the households, to take on th e resilience domain. That is the why, if you like—why be involved in resilience and what the concept of resilience is.

The second element, after that enlightenment, is what you might call ‘ empowerment of choices ’ . T he important thing there is delivering communications that translate to and for people in their communities and households . R esilience is a choice about what they want to do and what they want to invest in . Do they want to invest in flooding measures for their houses, new technology, fire alarms or whatever, in relation to those kind s of elements? T hat is important for communication.

The third element is what you might call the ‘ enabling of actions ’ . Y ou can give people choice , but you also have to facilitate the ir actions. T hat might mean incentivis ation schemes , so that i f they undertake resilience actions or buy different types of new technologies , t he y might see an insurance discount , reduced premium and/ or g overnment scheme that might help with that.
The fourth and final element you might call the ‘ evaluation of outcomes ’ to show that doing this a ctually leads to an outcome of better resilience.
Those four Es—enlightenment, empowerment, enablement and evaluatio n—provide the way in which you can communicate the message.

How do you do that, given that people are getting information from different place s ? I n particular, as we heard in the previous session, 15 to 25 year - olds will be getting their information not from g overnment or broadcasters and so on but from social media platforms. People may be getting their information in WhatsApp groups from their friends and relations and so on. Following up on your four Es, h ow do you get information over that is reliable , in our view , i n th ose circumstance s?

I would advocate a hub - and - spoke communications strategy . In effect, t he hub is where you are providing a common agreement a bout what the communication of the threat should be —in other words, what the context should be. T he spokes are the delivery across the various platforms according to the different audiences. There is an argument that we often use for our traditional information campaigns. We use websites as static places where the interested will go to find out more information. We have large elements of society in households that are not interested or engaged, and the platforms from which they gain information are anything from TikTok all the way through to Facebook and other social media, and anecdotal information, which might be the local community or family. T he important thing to realise is that you need bespoke formats and delivery platforms to be able to achieve th is . That means that communication on resilience, to put it bluntly, is not a cheap endeavour. It is quite sophisticated and requires a lot of resourcing to get the communication right.

The only thing I would add is that Ofcom carries out consumer research, and there is one , specifically Media Nations , which, i f the c ommittee is interested , I can follow up and provide the information from , if it will be helpful.
That would be very helpful, thank you. Lady Hunter.

Q106 Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch: T hank you very much for bringing your knowledge and expertise to our c ommittee. I do not want us to focus only on you, P rofessor Miles, but i n the international context , I know that you have had dealings with Sweden . We heard from the Nordic countries on their communication s strategies. I know that you have also been in Africa and the Caribbea n. I wonder what you could bring to the UK : w hat experience have you seen out there that might be effective back here?

As a point of context, I was a professor in Sweden for 13 years . I worked in the resilience domain , on societal resilience aspects. There is a lot of emphasis on learning from international comparators , and we must do that ; it is effective. O f course, the Nordic countries , including Sweden , are good places to start doing that .

H owever, it is important also to recognise that they have very good techniques because , in terms of the overall security and societal framework in which they operate, there has been a total defence strategy, the legacy of non-alignment and neutrality and a high level of cultural and societal trust in the workings of g overnment . That allows for strategies like hard - copy pamphlet templates , such as the famous In Case of Crisis or War p iece from 2018, u pdated in 2024 . That provide s basic c ontextual information to the public about why and what they should know about these threats.

The other important point alongside that is that we can learn from places such as Sweden because they have also provided standards and incentivi s ation schemes to allow both households and communities to develop and move forward with various aspects . That includes everything from health service provisions in health trusts all the way through schemes for local communities. T hey are building on the foundational strength of a rather wholesome society, if I can put it that way , w ith a very strong cultural identity around a particular type of policy. If you look there, it is often the case that citi zen allegiance and trust in g overnment are much higher than they would be in the UK context. We learn from that perspective, but we also have to recognise that the environmental c onditions in the UK are very different. We are talking about a society that is not so wholesome at this point in time.

I will just add that Japan has an emergency alert system, and there is a similar facility in the UK , where we have our cell broadcast , which was launched in early 2003. It was tested and exercised in early 2024 when the Plymouth bomb evacuation needed to happen. I agree that there is a lot more to be done, but we do have some examples over here. The alert system is led by the Cabinet Office.
Baroness Hunter of Auchenreoch: How do they do it i n Africa, whe re there have been all these floods and climate situations ? How do they do it in the Caribbean , with their hurricanes?

I have been a professor working on disaster management, so I worked a lot in Sierra Leone, before, during and after the Ebola crisis in 2014- 16. I worked very closely on many projects of that nature , such as AFRICAB and EVALDIS . The important thing to recognise is that when we build resilience and talk about using examples from other countries, we often go to European countries , where they might be investing in high - technology solutions to make sure that they have redundancy situations for cyber for communities . T hey have a lot of technological advantages in terms of satellite phones , satellite redundancy situations and mobile networks th ey can call on , or mas t s , if they are damaged. You do not have that in the African context.

The African context shows that there is also a very strong reliance on low - tech solutions. As we become more digitalised, the question of single points of failure and redundancy becomes really quite challenging . W here we would have used analogue phones, for example, for a digital breakdown in the UK, we may be moving away from having an analogue telecommunication s system as it once was. T hat in itself creates challenges. O ften you find that the strength is in having local communities that might have hailer systems, for example, and communication agreements about how to communicate and do i t in the local setting. There are often low - tech solutions there. A s part of building resilience, we should not forget that we do not just need to go high ; we need to create redundancy which is lower , particularly in the parts of our communities that are rural and may be outside the communication s networks.
That answer leads logically on to L ord Farmer’s question .

Q107 Yes, i t answers part of it. P erhaps it could be for M s Newman. We heard in the last panel , as well as here, that all the information we are getting is dependent on internet communication. W e have not really looked at th e scenario of a total blackout in which it is lost for several days. In 2034 , the digital terrestrial television signals will be switched off. W hat effect might that have on the ability to transmit emergency messaging to the whole population i f there was a cyber attack causing a communications blackout ? It is an extreme situation, but we need to look at what happens when we do not have any communications coming in.

From the planning and preparedness side, I would like to break it down to what we currently have, and then talk about restoring the service. T he planning and preparation and the work that Ofcom does in this space refer s back to the resilience guidance we set for the operators. I n there , we say to avoid single points of failure : build your infrastructure and architecture in a way that there is an aspect of redundancy ; recognis e the challenges with that ; and, a s part of that, hav e business continuity plans and disaster recovery plans. But within those plans , we say to be very clear what those processes are because often the processes can be there, but they are not understood and they are not tested. W e make it clear that we expect the operators to do that. We also expect that there is power resilience. W here are the key sites that the operators should have the power backup ? T o build on that , for g overnment , i n the event of a national emergency situation, we have the Emergency Services Network. The Home Office is investing in this across the UK, and it is looking to further harde n that network. There are also the satellite communication services available to the UK Government in the event of a national emergency . Our military has access to that, as Professor Miles was referring to.

With regards to what is available now when there is an incident and what the telecom operators can already do, they can deploy mobile cell sites. Where there is either a specific incident, an outage or damage to a subsea cable, they can deploy an interim mobile coverage solution for that area. They also have generators on wheels, so they can deploy generators in the areas that need it. Alongside that, we expect the operators to be transparent with the services that they offer and the processes that they use. Many operators publish this on their website. For example, BT publishes very comprehensive set of steps that it takes so that there is an awareness of what it does in the event of an emergency.

There is action that individuals can also take. Currently, in the event of an emergency, individuals can roam on to different networks to make an emergency call. There are also satellite communication offerings now, with technology evolution that helps. We are getting a layer of resilience coming in—direct-to-device capability is there. In certain communities, such as the Shetland Islands, we are also seeing investment in satellite terminals that are available to the community. Again, when we talk about specific solutions available in certain communities, that is a great example where those localised opportunities need to be taken into account.

What we have seen, though, is that we can plan and prepare—we can have the solutions that we currently have—but to restore the power very swiftly is also very important. Ofcom has been working very closely with the energy sector and industry to establish how communication can improve when there is an incident. How can the telecommunications sector and energy sector engineers communicate and co-ordinate on the ground to ensure the services are restored very swiftly? That work still continues, but we are learning from what happened in Spain and Portugal, because that is a clear example that it is not if an incident such as that will happen but when. We are planning already and looking at those scenarios. But it is very important to not just work within our sector. It is a cross-sectoral challenge and there is interdependency with the energy sector.
If we had some satellite disruption—satellite warfare, for example—and all the satellites were destroyed, how does that leave us? You mentioned using various different networks.
The point is how wide, because it is a tiered level of resilience.

What is available in the fixed network? What is available in mobile? What is available in satellite? That is where the Government then step in from a national resilience perspective, rather than looking at it from a specific sectoral perspective. That is the role the Cabinet Office plays in this area.

To follow on from that, what proportion of the UK’s emergency communications capability is dependent on commercial telecommunications and satellite networks? What sovereign alternatives exist, should those networks fail? You mentioned the Shetland Islands but are there other examples? What kind of proportions are there?

On the facts about proportion s , I am happy to come back on that point. Sovereignty is a very interesting point and a discussion that is pretty alive at the moment. It comes down to what we mean by sovereignty. Are we talking about trusted partners and nations, or are we looking at just working within the jurisdiction of the nation? That dialogue is continuing at this moment, but we are seeing that in the UK we are building those layers of resilience for ourselves. We are building those necessary partnerships that the UK requires, which is the key thing for us.

Q108 Has Ofcom game-planned the possibility of a war situation, if we were attacked and it was a very serious attack on our communications ? Do you have emergencies for that kind of extreme situation?

That takes place with in g overnment . DSIT is the policy owner for telecommunications and carries out the cross-sectoral risk scenario that you are describing. We join those conversations with DSIT and participate.
Have you done that? Has that been done?
We work with them in that space , including with the Cabinet Office and industry. We also work with the industry bodies that play a part in that. So, yes, we do engage in those conversations.
This partly alludes to the previous question about international comparators. I fully support what Nihal is saying, but there are two important points we need to think about in terms of evidencing.

The first is about how long the outage would be. There are very good examples in the Caribbean of hurricanes that have knocked out entire communications networks for two weeks at a time. In the case of Cuba after Irma and Maria, there was a power outage for 80% of the island for eight months. One would have to talk about the extent to which there is a resourcing question. It comes down to the prioritising and resourcing of those two elements.

The other element in that is the expectations of the public—in my case, gleaned through household research—as to how long it is acceptable to be without communications, either by mobile phone or the internet. For many people—SMEs, the business community, local communities and households—the internet is not optional; it is a way of life and an essential service. We need to be very clear about treating the length of disruption to an essential service as something that requires management of expectations, both nationally and for our service providers.

The final point is to reiterate that in the resilience world, the vast majority of our recovery and response is delivered by private sector providers. It is often the case that 80% of recovery is provided by the private sector. The arrangements between those providers is important, not just over the short-term response phase but the longer-term recovery phase, because there are costs that have to be met commercially if those services are to continue to be provided beyond MoUs. Those are some of the issues that we need to think about.

Q109 This is primarily for Professor Miles. Could you share your views about the role that the education sector, at all levels, should play in promoting preparedness and resilience to a wide audience?

Not surprisingly, I am going to say that it is essential that the education sector plays a fundamental role. I am not just saying that because I come from that background, but because it is essential both strategically and for implementation at all levels. For example, if we look at the school level, there are lots of initiatives and work on smart schools, in which the idea is to build resilience—understanding resilience, basic resilience, response ideas and how to do things—into the curriculum. That is very common in places such as the Caribbean where there is a continual threat. As we move towards many of our threats and hazards becoming business as usual rather than extraordinary matters, it becomes part of the citizenship training element.

There is a very important point behind that. Education provides not just good citizens and our expectations of the state; it is the influencer. We are generating the resilience managers of the future, and it often has an important impact at home, in the household, where resilience influencers are in the teenage group. From a school perspective, we need to understand that 14 to 25 year-olds—if I may use that age bracket, which is beyond full school age— since these are the future volunteers on whom resilience will be based.

The FE level has a substantial role in widening access. What I mean by that is that FE colleges and provision do not just teach key subjects such as geography, where things such as hurricanes and earthquakes are part of the normal curriculum. Think about the access and competence courses that are provided, from boot camps to widening-access courses. There is a very strong market, particularly among the, say, 55 to 70 generation, who are interested in those resilience courses. It might also be the place where you find first-aid courses and basic issues to do with training, competencies and skills.
To use an analogy, the school element is often where you might enlighten the contexts; the FE sector is where you might empower the choices for people in terms of what they do and what they know.

At university level, it is absolutely essential, because our role is providing research about resilience and how it is evaluated in that piece. It is about building the knowledge and thinking. I am also a professor at a disaster management centre who trains emergency planners across the world. Universities have a fundamental role in training emergency planners, having resilience degrees and providing the context and the cohorts of specialist experts of the future. That is important.

The final point is about the impact on resilience agendas through that research—working, as I do, with companies including SMEs through to large multinationals, on resilience projects where the public-private partnerships are critical in providing the knowledge with commercial opportunities to deliver the competencies, skills, toolkits and markets of the future. It is important to recognise that resilience is a market, not just an education. Therefore, the societal impact role is largely on the part of universities.
M s Newman, do you want to add anything to that ?
No, I have nothing further to add on education.
We will move on to Lord Peach’s question.

Q110 If we turn to cybersecurity , on which the Government are proud of their efforts, do you agree that they should be? How does the telecommunications industry look? You have raised a couple of times what I might call exercising at the national level. Is that frequent enough and are the scenarios tough enough?

I would break this down into the telecommunications sector and the digital infrastructure sector—the internet infrastructure—because there are two different legal frameworks that we work to, and different levels of expectations that we place on the sectors. In the telecoms sector, we are proud of the Telecommunications (Security) Act because it is a key, comprehensive framework that we have in place. It was introduced in 2021 and came about off the back of a risk assessment and a threat assessment carried out by the National Cyber Security Centre.

A comprehensive exercise was carried out across the telecoms space by the UK’s technical authority to establish what threats the UK faces in that sector , and therefore what measures and steps nee d to be implemented. That was then baked into a legal framework . Ofcom has a key role in that space . W e monitor industry compliance and report to the Secretary of State in D SIT on how the sector is performing. One thing that is important with that framework is that it is proportionate . The code of practice i s not applicable to everybody , because there are large communication providers with turnovers greater than £1 billion, and much smaller operators as well. Th e UK Government segmented the market and said that the code of practice would be applicable to the large and medium - sized operators, because the risks they face are much larger and therefore the re are different measures that they need to take and timetable s that they need to follow.

That framework is already there and we have been monitoring it . What we are observing with those operators is a level of commitment to investing in the requirements that they have to follow. It is a journey —th e risk landscape evolve s and change s —and we have to ensure that any framework we put in place m ove s with the threat landscape.

T he code of practice was consulted on by the Government recently and will be published imminently as an update . We set out in a transparent way how we will monitor industry compliance and exercise our responsibilities in that area. O n top of that, we have our own resilience guidance , which I mentioned earl ier.

There are also high - risk vendors. T he UK Government now ha ve powers to deal with high - risk vendors —they have designated a vendor —but Ofcom does not have a very big role in that space . The enforcement sits with D SIT. W e monitor how the sector is doing and provide that report to the Government , who carry out the necessary enforcement steps.

L ook ing at the critical national infrastructure across the UK, we have the network and i nformation s ystems regulations , which are currently being strengthened on the point s about where cybersecurity is, how we are p reparing ourselves for the evolving risk landscape and how technology is evolving, not only thinking about the hardening of the frameworks within each sector but across the sector.

We welcome the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill , currently making its way through Parliament . Ofcom is responsible for the digital infrastructure sector . We are e xpecting data centres to come in, and th ey will be a key part of th at value chain . W hen we think about communications, we think about subsea cables, satellite communications, terrestrial networks and, now, d ata centres , as they come in. What is important when we think about cybersecurity is that there needs to be a baseline expectation as well . That is o ne of the things being proposed in the cyber B ill —a ll the sectors will need to work to an aspect of baseline , then the sectors can come and implement something specific to their sector.

We work very closely with other regulators . In the energy sector , w ith Ofgem , we work with the Information Commissioner’s Office . W e work with the CAA in the aviation sector . N ationally , we are working across the board , and we also work with international partners. L ate last year, we convened Five Eyes countries , where we shar e d our learnings and what each other is doing. I was involved earlier this year in international cyber regulation conversations at Wilton Park. Again, that is a great learning opportunity for us. We cannot operate in a silo, so we need to learn and hear what other nations are doing and what our partners are doing in other countries , while working very closely with the Government . U ltimately, it is a collective challenge that we need to work on and it is a team sport . W e need to make sure we are evolving and moving with time.

Q111 Ba roness Winterton of Doncaster: This is absolutely fascinating. You have mentioned the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill , which is, as you say, going through Parliament. It will be coming to the Lords fairly shortly, I imagine. You have just given a very good description of everything already covered by legislation. You talked about data centres. It is not quite clear to me why a data centre needs to be in legislation , b ut you might expand on that a little. Do either of you have reflections on that B ill ? C rucially , what extras will it bring? Is the requirement for everybody to reach a certain baseline in legislation ? Y ou described guidelines before that . Is there anything more that should be in this legislation , particularly in light of the international experience you just referred to ?

P rofessor Miles , you mentioned the training that you are already doing for the emergency planners and so on. I s there anything else that could be done to encourage skills development and engagement at senior level, given what you have already said about the extensive training that is there?

I will pick up the data centre point first. The data infrastructure sector was designated as critical national infrastructure. It is pivotal for us in the UK when we think about AI and our AI growth and ambitions in that space. So, h aving an aspect of security and resilience oversight is important for us.
It is the oversight that is in the legislation.
It is the oversight that has been proposed in the legislation. Ofcom is named as the regulator in the legislation. I will give you three specific examples of what is different.

The first is supply chain risks. We are seeing supply chains and the compromise of our supply chains filtering through all different industries. T hat is one aspect coming through in the Cyber S ecurity and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) B ill . W e are not just thinking about critical supplie r s within our sectors but also across the sectors. At the moment , we look at our supplie r s within our sectors. T he B ill looks at not only the risks within your sector and your critical suppliers, but also across the sectors. What does that mean? Where are the interdependencies?
Is i t regulation or monitoring that is in the Bill?

The detail will come in secondary legislation . T he proposals at this moment involve looking at the risks around supply chains. The Government’s ambition is dealin g with those risks. T hey are also looking at the specific requirements . W here the B ill reflects on existing frameworks , t he National Cyber Security Centre has the C yber A ssessment F ramework , which is peppered throughout the cyber B ill. It has been in the ambition, the policy responses and the B ill proposals. Again, once those proposals start making their way through Parliament , we will see what the detail is. But we are seeing that, at this moment in time , the Government’s ambition is to strengthen cyber resilience in the UK .

F inally , learning from other countries , i ncident reporting is important. If we do not have the data in a timely fashion, we do not have that evidence and we do not know where our risks are. T hat is another proposal that the Government have put in the Bill.

Q112 I believe you said that your focus is on the security of the larger telecoms providers, but we have heard that there is an increasing level of threat to SMEs. Are you looking at that? How are you proposing to strengthen that?

The Telecommunications (Security) Act is applicable to all telecoms operators . Our focus is on those operators that have a turnover greater than £50 million, because the code of practice is designed for that size of operations. But at the same time , where there are opportunities , w e engage with the smaller operators, even through industry bodies, and encourage them to look at the code of practice. T here is also quite a bit of information and guidance for smaller operators, which the NCS C publish es on its website. When there is an issue , concern or incident, we engage with the smaller operators as well. I spoke to the smaller operators at an industry round table last week, to see what guidance we can give them. So, it is not that we do not engage with them at all. The focus is mainly on the major operators where the code of practice is concerned but, where the opportunity arises, we also engage with the smaller ones. I spoke to the smaller operators at an industry round table last week, to see what guidance we can give them. So, it is not that we do not engage with them at all. The focus is mainly on the major operators where the code of practice is concerned but, where the opportunity arises, we also engage with the smaller ones.

I have two points, which might be the next step after this , from my role as a professor, where I look at these kind s of things . T he Bill is encouraging in having baseline expectations and creating sector standards, which are very important — and inter - sector standards, which is the implication of what is being talked about . T he important thing to also recognise is that th e codes of practice that follow need to be agile enough to take into account that the sector itself is moving at great pace, particularly around AI and other domains. For example, I was struck that most recent data shows that 60 % to 70% of SMEs in the UK have experienc ed a cyberattack , b ut I looked at the IBM threat intelligence report, and there is a massive increase of something like 44% in AI - accelerated attacks or attacks that do not even involve passwords, where the AI systems or the cybersecurity is about not just defence but maintenance. T he codes of practice are really important in h aving that agility and flexibility . F rom my perspective at the Bournemouth University Disaster Management Centre, we train around those codes of practice and build simulations and exercises to be able to test the adherence to plans and workarounds in this agile space. I n answer to the question put forward about the strategic value for senior policymakers, there is a big piece of work not just about how we train or exercise the Bill and its implications but about educating our senior management teams in the strategic value of investment beyond the regulation. That is very important.

Q113 That was on my question about what else could be done. A slight worry is developing in me: if we are waiting for all this secondary legislation , and if training will not start until the secondary legislation is there , I am a bit anxious as to whether that becomes a delay. Is there any danger in that ? Y ou have described what you feel could be done almost now, but then you say it has to be geared to the code s of practice. That is a little worry that you might like to comment on.

The framework that is proposed, and is peppered into the CS RB, is the C yber A ssessment F ramework . We already appl y th at framework, so we are already setting those expectations in the way we are engaging with our sector, and other sectors are adopting th e framework , because NCSC developed it a couple of years ago. W e want to make sure that these frameworks are put on a legal footing, but that does not mean we have not been using them. That is the key difference. It has already started to be applied. The other thing I want to pick up on is technology evolution , specifically AI, and ensuring that we keep an eye on our regime. T his is where Ofcom is on the front foot. We recently published our approach to AI, and in there is a piece of work that we are doing around looking at our existing regimes to ensure that we are not creating inadvertent barriers around the adoption of AI as defensive tools. W e are doing that piece of work this year. A gain, we are always proactive and ensuring we are on the front foot to say, “O kay, that technology is coming. What can we do to ensure that we are not creating inadvertent barriers? ”.

It is not a case of it having not started; i t i s already going all the time , because cybersecurity threats are a constant aspect in relation to that . Of course , as the legislation moves forward , this creates new environments and new expectations , s o it is about raising that game. But I also think that, from this perspective, it is about the linkage between what you might call resilience management — training managers in the industry of the value of cybersecurity and the investment — alongside the operational aspects of defending and operationalising it.
Do you think you can get the two tracks running together?

They have to run together. A t Bournemouth University, if I may use my own example, we have the Disaster Management Centre and the Cyber Competence Centre, and we plan and run operational and strategic courses where we build scenarios that go up and down the management chain to understand that investment and value opportunity.

Q114 Thank you. B efore I turn to Baroness Helic to ask a final question, I think there is time for me to squeeze in one of my own, which I ha ve been wanting to ask . May I ask you both whether you think that this plan to switch off digital terrestrial television in a few years ’ time is sensible or completely undesirable, given the concern expressed that it would reduce universal access to information and have a particularly disproportionate adverse impact on certain vulnerable communities or groups of people, such as older people who do not necessarily know what to do with broadband and or do not have very good internet connections ? I s this a sensible thing? Are we past the point of no return on the proposal? Is it reversible , and s hould it be? I would like v ery quick answers, please.

From my perspective as a professor of crisis and disaster management, I am always interested in two aspects. One is the communication of resilience and, therefore, as we talked about, a bespoke approach of using different landscapes and different formats to reach and hit different audiences. There is, no doubt, a challenge if you remove that terrestrial facility, which is used by a large demographic of society ; we would need to have very clear assurances as to what it would be replaced with as an effective strategy for resilience. However, I go back to this as my second point : if you want resilience to work, it has to be resilience every day. There are many communication channels, which affect rural communities and local communities, where you have dead spots and issues to do with digital delivery . W e would have to considerably raise our expectations around a 24/7 delivery or a delivery of core services that is robust enough to provide redundancy if that system is taken out.

To add to the professor’s points, I would say that there are two things. Technology is evolving , and that is the key thing : we need to look at how it is, what the opportunities are and how we can harness those. The second , I agree, is around ensuring the resilience of whatever we roll out , l ooking at what the different areas and communities require and targeting any additional enhanced resilience requirements for those as well.
Q115 With the wealth of all your experience, if there were one recommendation that you could make to the Government on resilience and preparedness, what would th a t be?

From my perspective, with the evolving threat landscape , the complexity of the risks we are facing and the sense of urgency, as I mentioned earlier, resilience is a team sport. We cannot work within our silos. We need to continue to work across the sector , and with communities , industry and academia. M y recommendation would be that w e need to be clear what we mean by the whole - society approach and we need to bring everybody around the table to work together.

My recommendation would be that, if we want a whole-of-society approach to work and be effective, we have to deal with the question of building trust , which is central to this. W hat I mean by that is , effectively , that we have a society that has issues of trust in messaging and communication from our institutions . W e need to invest and understand what we mean by everyday resilience t hat makes sense to the households and the publics of our country and, o n the basis of that, most importantly, can build trust. W ithout trust, there is no point in looking at states such as Sweden or others. We need to understand how a whole - of - society approach can work in a society that may not necessarily be whole.

That is a great and important point to end on, and a great challenge to us in coming up with our recommendations to government. Thank you both very much indeed for your time this morning. It has been really enlightening and extremely helpful .

Thursday 15 October 2026
Watch the meeting
Members present: Lord Newby (The Chair) ; Lord Carrington of Fulham; Lord Leigh of Hurley; Baroness Wheatcroft.
Evidence Session No. 2 Heard in Public Questions 7 – 1 9
Witnesses
Antonia Stokes, Senior Manager, Low Incomes Tax Reform Group; Adam Craggs, Partner/Head of Tax, Investigations and Financial Crime, Reynolds Porter Chamberlain LLP.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Antonia Stokes and Adam Craggs.

Q7 Good morning . I am Dick Newby, chairing this session of the sub- c ommittee looking at aspects of tax administration in the Budget. We are particularly looking at the requirement to correct, which HMRC is seeking to introduce in this year’s Finance Bill. We have two witnesses in this session: Antonia Stokes, the senior manager at Low Incomes Tax Reform Group, who is with us in person, and Adam Craggs, who will shortly be joining us virtually. He is partner and head of tax investigations and financial crime at Reynolds Porter Chamberlain LLP. We are going to start in his absence.

I will ask Antonia the question that, when Adam appears, I will also ask him: how important do you think this new requirement to correct will be in terms of how errors are dealt with under self-assessment?

Thank you for having me. This is a significant proposal that is being brought in. As you all know, i t includes two key measures: first, the requirement for taxpayers to correct, and secondly, the introduction of new customer correction notices. The Low Incomes Tax Reform Group is part of the CIOT: we would echo its support for a general need to fill the gap in civil law in terms of correcting errors in tax returns and other such documents. However, we are concerned that this requirement is particularly heavy-handed. We represent the interests of taxpayers who cannot afford professional advice: such advice is a very important part of this. Since this measure is designed to tackle high-volume but low-value errors across the tax system, it has to be a process that works for people who cannot afford to pay for tax advice. There are concerns that it is difficult for people to navigate if they do not have advice.

Moving the penalties potentially at stake from being careless to deliberate is particularly concerning, especially if the original error was made despite taking reasonable care. If the person does not understand the new obligations in terms of having to correct, it seems very harsh that they could potentially face a deliberate penalty for the original error. From what we can see, there is no method of appeal by claiming that there was a reason they were not able to meet that obligation to correct, and that is particularly concerning. In terms of the way this has been constructed, the taxpayer has to do that correction within HMRC’s assessment time limits; they have to understand whether HMRC would in theory be in time to do an assessment on this error, whether they are still within that time frame, what that means and what their next steps are. We are very concerned that for many taxpayers that is going to be way beyond their capabilities without professional advice.

Can I ask you a question that I have been asking others? Given that you are talking about people who are not going to have tax advice—the amount of tax involved will be relatively small—do you think there should be a de minimis limit below which this process should not operate?

Yes: in principle, we would like to see a de minimis built in. The only reservation I have is that this seems to be driven by low - value, high - volume errors; HMRC might say, “That defeats the point of why we’re doing this” . Personally, and as part of the CIOT, we would like to see that, but whether HMRC would go for it is another question.

Q8 We are presumably talking about people who are largely self-employed—genuinely self-employed and not caught under IR35—and who would have an income that would not justify employing a tax accountant to do their affairs. Say you are a successful plumber, earning £70,000 a year; if you make an error in your tax return, it is likely to be £1,000 or £2,000 at the most, or something of that order. If there is no de minimis—in any case you would not know what the de minimis should be until you looked at the error—then HMRC will go after you, presumably not because it knows there has been an error, but because it suspects there might be one. Chasing small amounts of money that are going to be pretty hard to recover in any case seems an extremely heavy-handed way of operating. Is there something completely wrong about the way HMRC is approaching people who are self-employed?

I would absolutely agree that it seems heavy-handed. It is also hard to see how HMRC would know that this person made the error that they failed to disclose. I am talking about issues here outside customer correction notices, where the taxpayer learns they have made an error. Do customers know about these rules and know what action they have to take? It feels as if HMRC is trying to force people into action with the threat of higher penalties, in the hope that they will comply so that HMRC does not have to get involved. It remains to be seen how that will play out in practice, and whether it will increase voluntary compliance. Much of the success of this measure will come from easy disclosure facilities. The current digital disclosure facilities are hard—nigh on impossible—for people to navigate without an adviser. HMRC needs to improve its disclosure facilities and guidance in relation to all the forms where these corrections can be possible. At the moment, it is not straightforward for people to deal with historic issues.
In terms of HMRC’s internal costs, do we have any idea of the cost of implementing this?

No. In the policy paper that accompanied the draft legislation the summary of impact in terms of costings was entirely silent on this, which was disappointing. There is no indication of the potential yield, how much it will cost HMRC to implement, and what it thinks will be the ultimate upside result.

Presumably, it would be very hard to automate this. There would need to be an officer inside HMRC who would look at the individual case and take a judgment as to whether the response—assuming there is a response—is acceptable or not. There are going to be several hours, if not days, of work on one individual. I do not know what HMRC’s overhead cost charge is, or its employees ’ hourly rate, but my guess is that it will lose money.

I obviously cannot say whether it would automate. We are in a new world where automation is more possible than it was before; HMRC might plan to keep this largely a hands-off method. We would hope that the process would still include human intervention to ensure that taxpayer safeguards are in place. We do not want HMRC firing out customer correction notices without having tried to verify that there is a reasonable expectation that tax has been lost in some way.
Is the problem a cultural problem inside HMRC? Is the HMRC organisation moving away from looking after its client base—taxpayers—to being antagonistic towards them?

Resourcing seems to have moved away from the personal approach of HMRC of old . We have lost the tax offices; everything is now being moved to self-service, digital first and so on. Noise about the tax gap has become ever louder in recent years; HMRC realises that it has to be seen to be taking action and chipping away at that gap. It is trying to move towards increased compliance and forcing compliance as far as possible, while still managing resources as best as it can.
Q9 Are there any safeguards that should be included that are not at the moment? If so, what would they be?

At the moment, the safeguards seem very weak. On a basic level, what time frames are we talking about? The legislation does not include any explanation as to what it means to become aware of an error. How long does a person have to act on that error? If they are entitled to get tax advice before coming forward, is there a reasonable time frame in which they are allowed to do that? All this information is missing, and that is very problematic. We definitely think that safeguards should be put in place for vulnerable people. In general, people who are unrepresented should have a manual review to help them understand if they require extra support. HMRC has an extra support team to help people who are vulnerable or going through any difficulties that might prevent them from being able to represent themselves effectively.
That would play into Lord Carrington’s argument about the cost - effectiveness ratio straight away.

Exactly. Obviously, it would not be appropriate for the extra support team to help every unrepresented taxpayer, but for those who are at the most risk of not being able to correctly represent themselves in these situations, it is particularly important. That also applies in the case of reckless untrue statements ; the two marry together.
What about a de minimis requirement?
As I said before, we are certainly supportive of that. My only concern is that HMRC would say that it goes against the whole premise; but it is logical that there must be a de minimis.

Q10 Could you say a bit more about the extra support team? It is potentially significant if HMRC is able to provide support. How does it work? If the extra support team is part of HMRC, is it potentially advising the taxpayer against the rest of HMRC? Or are external people brought in independently? Are there enough members of the team? There might be a lot of takers.

It is unreasonable to expect that the extra support team is going to be able to assess every single unrepresented taxpayer to see if they would qualify for assistance. It is more the case that the taxpayer has to be aware that if they are struggling, if they are frozen with fear and cannot see a way forward, they may qualify for help from the extra support team to navigate the issue. To answer your question, the extra support team is not separate from HMRC; it is very much a part of HMRC’s customer service team. The team members are specially trained to deal with people in vulnerable circumstances, and they do a wonderful job. We are very supportive of HMRC’s extra support team and what it does for taxpayers. It is brilliant.

There are also other organisations that can help, such as TaxAid , an external charity that supports unrepresented taxpayers who have problems. As a result of these new measures, its resources will undoubtedly be put under strain by people coming forward saying, “I’ve have received this notice, I don’t know what to do” , or, “I’ve heard about this new rule to do with correcting errors, and I’m worried” .
Do you have any idea how many cases the extra support team helps?
No, I do not; I might be able to find that data and let you know.
That would be helpful.

From what you said, they would not help my plumber, who is clearly quite capable of doing plumbing work, but is not able to cope with a tax return. What you are saying is that they are going to deal with people who are challenged because of disabilities, age or whatever.
I suspect your plumber would not qualify and would need to consider if he needs to take advice for this particular issue.
Taking advice might cost him £5 , 000.

Our position is that most people should be able to navigate the tax system without having to pay for an adviser; that is an important principle. It is problematic if we are getting to a stage where people feel they have no choice but to pay for advice. HMRC could also help by ensuring—as I have already said—that its guidance is clear and its processes are straightforward. It also needs to be prepared to have call handlers available to answer questions because those will undoubtedly result. I know that it is trying to push people away from calling on the phone towards digital self-service, but with a measure such as this, it has to expect that people want reassurance. Often, they might be the worried well, but it should not assume that such people are not legitimately making a phone call. That person should still be able to get reassurance, if that is what they need to be able to sleep at night.
Q11 On the other side of things , we should never forget that Al Capone was only brought to justice because his tax affairs were incorrectly submitted.

There is a huge tax gap: we can argue about its size, but we need to do something about it. One would have thought that with the current state of technology, one could create AI and algorithms showing that a person is living well above their declared lifestyle, including indicators of expensive holidays and so on that do not match income. Should we not be encouraging HMRC to be much more sophisticated and to go down this route of doing a wealth assessment—it used to be called a balance - sheet assessment—of individuals from one period to another? Or do you have a better idea of how we should attack the tax gap?

It would not be appropriate to use customer correction notices in circumstances where HMRC run the AI on somebody and it appears that they are living above their means, or there are red flags on the system. That situation has to be dealt with through good old-fashioned inquiry: if HMRC has something it wants to dig into, it will have to do it that way. We have to be clear: a customer correction notice must be based on a reasonable, defined suspicion that there is something wrong, not a broad, vague unease. That is important.

Another thing HMRC could do about the tax gap is to identify patterns in errors; in due course this could feed into possible customer correction notices. For instance, in recent years there have been high - value repayment agents—essentially bad actors—in the tax advice market, who reel in customers on social media, saying, “We’ll claim back all your working expenses, your uniform, and things such as that” . A lot of the claims are hugely inflated and without evidence. The taxpayer clicks a button and goes along with it. We have heard from HMRC recently that high - value repayment agents have spiked instances of high - volume, low - value errors in the tax system. If HMRC is able to spot a pattern such as people over-claiming expenses incorrectly, it can use that as a way to tackle it from the other side, to look at these agents and their end-to-end processes and shut down incidents, rather than going directly after the taxpayer. That would potentially be an effective way to tackle the tax gap.

To push you a little, there are communities and trades that are very cash focused and do all sorts of business with each other. It is commendable going after dodgy advisers but , at the end of the day, this is the taxpayer’s responsibility. I do not see why you think it is down to HMRC to investigate whether a person is living above their income; surely, it is down to HMRC to push the taxpayer to explain.

Yes, I agree. Having these additional measures in place—particularly the requirement for the taxpayer to correct outside a customer correction notice—will hopefully prompt more people to come forward and decide to rectify previous errors. In some ways that will undoubtedly be the case. But the majority of people are honest about their tax affairs and want to get things right. They might make a mistake because they cannot afford advice, or because they are not quite sure about it, or they feel nervous. Those people should be the priority in terms of not losing out as part of this measure.
To confirm, you think these measures will lead to an increase in revenue by adjusting behaviour.

Yes, there is a strong argument that it will. However, when you look at taxpayer behaviour in the context of reckless untrue statements , which we are coming on to next , there is a worry. On the one side you have this draft legislation that is pushing people to correct errors and do so promptly or risk getting much higher penalties. On the other side, you have these proposed measures where HMRC is saying—perhaps with regard to the correction of errors—“If we find out you’ve made an error, and we think it was reckless, you could be on the hook for criminal prosecution” . There are these two competing pressures, and we are worried that they could cause huge anxiety for taxpayers. It could diminish trust in the tax system; the impression is no longer being given that, “HMRC is supporting you to get it right, and if you get it wrong, don’t worry, we’ll help you” . With these two measures as they stand, that whole ethos is out of the window.

Q12 Can we come on to the issue of recklessness? The overarching question that we have been asking others is that, given the existing civil and criminal penalties that are available to HMRC, is the addition of a “ reckless ” provision necessary?

We have not been convinced by the case that it is. The consultation on reckless untrue statements has yet to set out why it is felt to be necessary. What is the reason? What are these cases where HMRC would have liked to have prosecuted but could not quite prove dishonesty? For what reason does it now want to bring people who are perhaps careless—and at the borderline upper end of careless—into a criminal prosecution? This could ruin people’s lives; it could ruin their livelihoods and careers and make them white-collar criminals. Is that fair, when dishonesty cannot be proven? We feel strongly that if HMRC is going to go down this route, it should remain within the realms of dishonesty beyond all reasonable doubt.

This comes back again to the culture in HMRC. Is that something that can be changed? Or is it something that has gone beyond the point of no return? If so, then the legislative attitude towards HMRC ought to change as well. Is that a fair statement?

HMRC is a large organisation and it is fair to say that it does not have only one personality. Without a doubt, it is under pressure to close the tax gap. It is also trying to do its best to support taxpayers where it can, but it feels that it cannot sit on errors and unpaid tax—and other issues such as low-value debts—any longer. It wants to take action but it would be a shame for it to push forward with these measures without bearing in mind that customer trust is important; it needs to be a living, breathing part of its charter and how it operates.

If I understand you correctly, the driver behind a lot of this is that HMRC is being pushed on the tax gap. How confident is anyone that the tax gap is real, or at least of the size that it is claimed to be?

I have seen the workings and I know that a scientific approach is taken. As I understand it, the scene is quite robust, but I am not an expert on the tax gap and its methodologies so I will not pass comment.

Q13 We are delighted to be joined by Adam Craggs. We might come back to where we were, but I would like to start again with a reprise of the questions we have been asking Antonia . The first was: in terms of identifying errors and raising additional revenue, what is your assessment of how significant a change this new requirement to correct will be?
Could I clarify whether we are discussing the proposed criminal offence, or the proposals to correct errors?

We were talking about the criminal offence when you came on the call, but that was because we had dealt with the first issue already: I am go ing back to that. I would like your view on the question about correcting errors to start with.

It is a fundamental change. There is some uncertainty among the tax adviser profession as to whether there is an existing obligation to correct an error once one has submitted a tax return or a claim for relief to HMRC. There are grey areas: the view of some professionals is that , if it was accurate when it was submitted , it is very much for HMRC to be proactive and contact the taxpayer or the adviser if it feels there is an error or a mistake , and that i t is not for the taxpayer to correct it. I f this ends up on the statute books, it will certainly clarify the position ; in practice, it might have a lot of unforeseen consequences. HMRC may be inundated with questions from overcautious taxpayers and their advisers —an abundance of caution— especially as there may be a new offence of making a reckless, inaccurate statement. That links to the second issue. I would also imagine that there will be a huge increase in compliance, which is fine for those taxpayers who are able to pay professionals to advise and assist; the vast majority of taxpayers, however, are not in that position and they deal with their own tax affairs.
Lord Carrington, that has been an issue that has been very much in your mind.
Q14 Yes. If you are somebody who does not employ a tax adviser and you get something wrong, how clear is the advice on what you have to do to make a correction?

At the moment, it is not clear. I often talk to friends and family who are not involved in either the legal or accounting profession: they find tax and the whole UK system hugely complex and rely very much on HMRC telling them how to fill in a tax return and so on. I cannot imagine that many taxpayers would, in good faith, be aware of errors when they filled in their tax return, so it is difficult to see a scenario where they would realise that there was a mistake at a later date. One example that springs to mind relates to changes in case law: there is an argument that, if you filled in your tax return as of 15 October 2026 and the law changes or is interpreted differently by the tax tribunal, then there is an inaccuracy that needs to be corrected. I cannot imagine many taxpayers spend their time reading law reports published by the tax tribunal.

In that case, presumably, HMRC would contact the taxpayer and say, “We think there is an error” , and would issue a notice to correct. For the taxpayer who does not have an adviser, would there be a requirement for HMRC to say what the correction should be?

There ought to be. It should justify and explain the basis for that decision, although in practice that may not help the taxpayer. I suspect most taxpayers who are not fortunate enough to be able to pay for professional representation would accept HMRC’s own interpretation of the law. As any tax lawyer will tell you, there is more than one way to interpret either a statutory provision or indeed a decision, but most taxpayers would simply accept HMRC’s view.

Can I ask you the question that I asked Antonia about the cost to HMRC of chasing small errors in individual tax returns? I assume we are talking about people who are self-employed: most other people’s tax returns are relatively straightforward, particularly if they are paid through PAYE and earn a certain amount of dividend interest or dividend income or whatever. I gave an example of a self-employed plumber who maybe earns £70,000 a year and makes some error that is likely to be worth at most several thousand pounds. They would not understand how to correct it. What is the cost to HMRC of challenging that, identifying the error and responding to the individual taxpayer? How much would it cost HMRC in administration costs to recover, say, £2,000?

I would not be able to quantify that but it would be disproportionate. One would hope that HMRC would concentrate on larger errors and mistakes; it may well be that there should be a de minimis stipulation, a calculation of value for taxpayer’s money to enforce and take compliance action against taxpayers. As you say in your example, pursuing a plumber for a few thousand pounds would almost certainly cost HMRC more than the amount of tax it was pursuing.
Q15 This measure is aimed, we are told, at catching low-value, high-volume errors. Can you think of a more effective way of doing that?

HMRC has a number of tools available at the moment. Its one-to-many letters—they used to be called nudge letters—are very effective in my experience: they point out to the recipient, “There may be an issue, and you need to look at your affairs” . Most honest, law-abiding taxpayers either look at their affairs themselves and double-check to see whether there is an issue, or they ask their tax adviser.
A s far as you are concerned, this is not necessary to accomplish what HMRC says is needed.
You are correct; that is my view.

Q16 You gave the example of someone who submitted a tax return in good faith: the case law then changed, or there was a case law judgment that meant extra tax was due that had not been declared at that time. In those circumstances, you said, an adviser may or may not choose to disclose that to HMRC. Does that reach someone who, for example, discovers a source of income that he or she had forgotten about, or who makes a loan to someone and that person decides to repay it with interest, or other cash events? Are you saying that some advisers would not suggest that an extra disclosure is made to HMRC, ex post facto?

No. All reputable, honest advisers in that scenario would say to the client, “You’ve been paid interest on that loan, it’s income, and it has to be included on your tax return” . Depending on your personal circumstances, of course, income tax will be due on that.
Are there currently any penalties for advisers who do not do that?

This is obviously a big issue, and an important one. As the c ommittee will be aware, an obligatory registration system is being implemented as we speak to wield out the less reputable advisers. Prior to that, anyone could call themselves a tax adviser: they did not need to be regulated or have any qualifications, which to my mind is shocking. Hopefully, the unreputable advisers out there will be weeded out by having to register with HMRC. There are also professionals who are regulated by their professional bodies and there are codes of conduct. I know that in appropriate circumstances HMRC will report an adviser to their regulatory body and so on, so there are mechanisms that are already in existence.

Q17 When you joined the session, we were already on to the second issue: the proposed criminal offence of making reckless, untrue statements or declarations. I will ask you what we have already asked Antonia; to what extent do you think there is a gap here that needs to be filled? Given HMRC’s existing powers, do you think there is still an area that needs to be covered, or are those powers already extensive?

I do not think there is a need. I know HMRC has said, “We have this for indirect tax, and it has been on the statute books for many years” , but my understanding is that there have been very few—if any—prosecutions for reckless statements. I am certainly not aware of any, either when I was a member of the old Inland Revenue—when I dealt with prosecutions—or in private practice, so I am not convinced. Superficially, it sounds attractive: if you have it for VAT and indirect taxation, why not also for direct taxation? But in practice, it is not used. HMRC has a record of being given new criminal powers: for instance, the Criminal Finance s Act 2017, which addressed the failure to prevent tax evasion. Only one prosecution commenced last year , which was against an accountancy firm , so that suggests that this particular provision was not required. I am certainly not convinced that anything is needed here. I also have serious reservations about criminalising taxpayers who make a reckless, incorrect statement to HMRC. That is not a road that we want to go down. It should be limited to deliberate, dishonest statements.

You make the observation that a lack of prosecutions implies that legislation was not required; the counterargument is that it implies that the legislation has worked and it has not been necessary to prosecute, or alternatively that HMRC is not doing its job properly.
Perhaps all those possibilities apply.

Q18 We have been told that a lot of this is driven by pressure on HMRC to close the tax gap and collect large numbers of small amounts of money that it believes have previously not been paid —very much small parcels, if I can put it like that . If this is all being driven by a political desire to close the tax gap, how confident are we that the tax gap is the size that it is claimed to be? How confident are we that the tax gap lies where HMRC thinks it lies?

That is a very good question. I caught Antonia’s answer as I was joining ; I am in the same position. I do not know what data or criteria HMRC use s when calculating the tax gap. I would imagine that, by definition, it has to be very much a finger in the air. HMRC is not aware of the size of the black economy—people who are being paid in cash and not declaring it—so I would have thought the estimate is very rough and ready. T o be honest, I am not qualified to comment.

My worry is that these changes are being driven by a political agenda. I am an old cynic who believes that politicians are always looking for easy headline answers to difficult problems: the tax gap sounds like that to me : “L et us say we have a problem and let us then produce legislation to fix the problem that we have dreamed up ” . It is not something that can be defined accurately, and therefore you cannot design legislation to address it accurately.

I have looked at the tax gap figures and how those are split. From memory, about 6% of the tax gap is made up of tax avoidance—a relatively small amount—and criminal activity is about 15%. One could be forgiven for thinking that the tax gap is almost exclusively a consequence of tax avoidance arrangements. Irrespective of one’s view about the morality of entering into arrangements to minimise your tax, that might be the dragon that has been created so that it can be slain. In reality, the amount of revenue that is lost to the Exchequer as a consequence of tax avoidance arrangements is relatively small, yet a huge amount of legislation in the last 10 years has gone into tackling tax avoidance.

Q19 There is a feeling of inevitability that the Government want to bring in this “ reckless ” proposal and legislate for it. If that is the case, are there any safeguards that should be built in to protect taxpayers from a potentially heavy penalty? As Antonia said, they could lose their jobs ; they could lose everything.

I deal with clients who are accused of criminal offences under the existing regime ; the effect on innocent people cannot be overemphasised. The decision to prosecute is taken by the CPS, not HMRC, so thankfully there is an independent body that reviews the evidence. Some clients are not prosecuted, but others go to court; even if they are found not guilty, the consequences are huge. My clients are often on medication for stress, their marriages end up in ruins, their businesses and employees are affected; it affects their working life and family life. If we are going to criminalise reckless behaviour rather than deliberate, dishonest behaviour, there needs to be the safeguard of a statutory definition of what recklessness means. That is crucial so that people are not put through the criminal process for innocent mistakes, no matter how foolish or stupid or negligent they might have been. We should not criminalise stupid mistakes unless there is dishonesty involved.
Antonia, do you think it is possible to define reckless?

It is very difficult. The response from ourselves and other professional bodies across the board is that the examples included in HMRC’s consultation represent careless but not reckless behaviour. If it is going to plough forward with this, that definition needs to be tightly drawn.

In terms of other safeguards, we think it is important that there should be explicit exclusions for reasonable reliance on another person. If you have taken advice and you honestly believe that it was correct—even if they knew they were leading you up the garden path—then that should be excluded. Tax issues are rarely black and white; there are judgment cases and instances of legitimate uncertainty which very much need to remain part of this. Behaviour that is already being adequately dealt with under the civil penalty regime should not be criminalised.

As a final safeguard, we suggest that there should be senior approval for anything being pushed forward into a criminal prosecution; there should be an appropriate independent oversight, not one rogue HMRC inspector deciding that it is the route they are going down. There need to be processes in place to ensure people are protected.

In general, the scope needs to be initially limited to higher - value and higher - risk cases. HMRC need s to test and learn and assess how it is going.
