Q828 There is a certain framework that can be acting inside—because that is not what we have heard from offshore energy operators who consistently ask me, “I do not know who to phone if I see that”.
They should phone me.

Q829 I will pass on your number. That specific question has been raised numerous times and no one has been able to give me an answer, and that has been different Ministers over the last few years frankly because I have been raising this numerous times. You are the first Secretary of State to say there is a clear framework. Whose decision is it; is it yours or is it the Secretary for Defence?

If there is a specific threat it will go to C obra , but the point is we have the architecture that sits underneath that so we are working in co-ordination. If there are particular companies or organisations that are worried, come to me.
Q830 Is the kind of scenario I have outlined tested regularly?

Yes, there is a contingency framework in place and there is a cross-government team that brings in all the agencies that you would imagine, that are constantly reviewing and testing that and also reporting to Ministers so that we are alive to any issues.

Q831 You are comfortable that should that incident happen and something happens near UK offshore energy generation it will be dealt with quickly enough in a way that would not presumably disrupt UK electricity supplies?
I think we have robust structures in order to that. Until structures are tested we cannot say definitively, but we have robust structures to deal with that.

Clearly the context has changed. You saw the speech from the Director General of MI5 and so we are very alive to that. We are working across Government on a series of risks, including cyber risk as well. There is a whole programme of work looking at the security of our offshore assets. We cannot give all the details of that here but there is a great deal of work making sure that we understand that risk and we respond to it.
Q832 Do you think the public would benefit from some of that information being published in some way and discussed more openly?

There is a balance. What the public need to know is that we have the structures in place, we have the contingency plans in place, and that we are working across Government so that everyone that needs to be part of a process to respond is there and responding. That is the thing that I can give assurance about.
I think the Defence Secretary has talked about some of these issues in Parliament.

Q833 It was me who asked the question, both of Secretary of State for Defence and of junior Defence Ministers, and their answer was not as clear as the answer that you have given there, Secretary of State. I hope that is something that is being progressed. If I can develop that a little bit onto a cyber - attack point as well. We have raised these questions with Ofgem and others who gave limited reassurance. I think it was a session with yourself in your previous role. I understand you do not want to present your opponents with all of your preparation but some of the discussion with Ofgem and NESO around what is in place to prevent or to deter a cyber - attack had not necessarily been worked out. There was talk of co-ordination bodies but no one being clear about how that is being done, how that works with NCSC and others. Do we know where the pinch points are? We know that our adversaries are very keen to use energy as a weapon. With winter approaching the energy system is more under stress at those points and they will know that. Can you tell us a little bit more—as you have on physical security—about cyber - security and how that operates?

There is a cross-government process that has been co-ordinated with the Cabinet Office to look at our resilience across the piece for cyber - security. From a DESNZ perspective we are doing all the planning, we are putting in place the infrastructure, we are making sure that we have the relationships and information flows with different parts of the system to be able to respond. We are very alive to this and we are building our infrastructure. The threat is new and it is real, so we are constantly having to adapt and improve, but there is a clear mandate and requirement from the centre that we get our house in order and that is what we are doing.

Q834 There was discussion this week from the AI Minister that he felt the UK could be under AI attack in the future. Do the plans on cyber - security take into account what initially begins as low level AI attacks that can escalate very quickly and they can be sustained over a very long period of time?

That is absolutely in the thinking between DESNZ, NCSC, and my old organisation, Ofgem. We are Joint Competent Authority with Ofgem. We are taking the industry on a journey. In my previous job, with successive Secretaries of State from the Department, we have been very clear with the industry that they need to move to respond to this risk, and we have made significant progress. The other thing that is happening, which I am pleased about, is that we have the legislation in the House on firming up those powers and broadening the supply chain that we look at. All of this will need to continue to evolve as the risk evolves. We work very closely to make sure that we are aware of all the emerging risks. But, as ever, we are dealing with an old system and we will have to make sure that old system remains robust.
Q835 With that in mind, can you give the public the same reassurance you gave earlier on that you are 100% sure that there would not be difficulties with the energy system over this winter?
Driven by—
Driven by cyber - attacks. Do you feel the resilience is at that level?

I think the system is resilience but I also think that the nature and sophistication of the attacks are changing all the time. What I am confident about is that we have structures in place and we are testing it and working in the way that we need to. Candidly, the fact that the system remains robust should give people some confidence, but you will understand while I will not say that with 100% certainty because the nature of it is changing every day.
But we are doing incredible amounts of work to make sure the system is increasing its resilience and we continue to do that.

Q836 I will move on because I am conscious of time and I can feel the Chair’s eyes drilling into the side of my head. We heard from Offshore Energies UK that their offshore gas fields and wind turbines and other things that we know about are not designated as critical national infrastructure. Is that something you think is the correct position? Is it something you would look to amend in the future?
Is this in reference to cyber - security or more generally?

Q837 Just generally. It generally surprised me that we designate other energy generation as critical national infrastructure, which helps them secure support, but we do not do that with any offshore assets, whether it is renewable or oil and gas.

As you probably know, the decisions on ultimately what is CNI are taken through a separate process so I will have to come back on that. The measures we put in place on security and cyber - security are expected to go beyond CNI, and that is why that new legislation is important.
Q838 Your view is they are protected enough, that being designated CNI would not add value; you feel it is already enough?
I have to come back on the specifics , but our security strategy goes well beyond that.
Thank you very much. Thank you, Chair.

Q839 Thank you. We may ask you to follow up in writing on some of these resilience points. It is hugely important to get clarity, especially given what Graeme has had from defence Ministers previously in comparison to what you were saying, Secretary of State, to make sure we have it absolutely clear. As far as you are able to, obviously.
The caveat is : if it falls within the energy system , it comes to me. That is possibly why defence colleagues were not as robust.
That is helpful but if you can give us what you are able to publicly on both physical and cyber resilience that is important, thank you. Melanie, I think you have a follow up question.

Q840 I have been listening carefully to your responses and I heard lots of references to bottlenecks and defence of some of the quangos and agencies that the Department relies upon to deliver our future energy system in all of its parts, whether it is understanding and accepting that there are workforce issues, or whether it is very difficult to get the materials or to get the planning in place. Given we have had a change in Secretary of State after two years—and I wish you a long career in this role— were it to change again, unless there is some robustness behind the conversations that are happening, are we not at risk of the Government being led by all of these other organisations, holding their hands up and saying, “There is nothing we can do because we are waiting for them to get on and do it”?

I do not believe that there is nothing we can do and our job is to get on with it. It is not necessarily defence of the system but a recognition that different parties are working within a system that is candidly not fit for purpose and that we need to reform. DESNZ needs to take responsibility and Secretaries of States that have preceded me also need to take responsibility for that, but we are robust. In the end no one will forgive us if we do not deliver on affordability, no one will forgive us if we do not deliver the clean power ambitions we have that will translate into jobs in industry. We are very clear about the imperative. We will put a lot of pressure on the system, but I do that with some humility because I also think in the end it is the job of Government to design it and for 40 years Government have not designed it in the way it needs to and we now have an opportunity to get that right.
I hear you say we need to reform the system and I think that sounds like it will take a very long time. Thanks, Chair.
Thank you. That might be something else we ask you put in writing, what does reform look like. I will not ask you to answer all of it now. Final word goes to Mike Reader.

Q841 Thank you, Chair. Picking up on Torcuil’s question, I recognise you cannot make a comment specifically on Jackdaw and Rosebank but the Committee has heard—including when we went to Aberdeen—that consenting is directly linked to taxation, and the industry needs to enter the energy profit levy to make those fields viable. Does that consideration come into how you make a decision on those?
No.
Q842 Do you have to consider viability of those consents when you make a decision on consenting?

It is a planning application so the viability of the project is part of that process, but ultimately tax decisions are out with that consenting decision. That is something for the Chancellor. The framework that I have to make the decision by is pretty clear. There is obviously an environmental consideration and the requirement to take in scope 3 emissions has made that tighter. It has to be compatible with our climate obligations and our delivery of common budgets. Then there are other considerations such as security of supply, and economic considerations such as jobs. You have to weight those in order to come to a final decision. Ultimately that is out with tax decisions that the Chancellor needs to make.
Secretary of State, Permanent Secretary, thank you very much for your evidence this afternoon. That is the end of our session.

sessions.w: Sandy Bhogal (The Law Society of England and Wales); Reuben Duffy (The Law Society of Scotland); Margaret Curran (Chartered Institute of Taxation (CIOT))

segs.tx: Economic Affairs Committee
Finance Bill Sub-Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Draft Finance Bill 2026-27
Thursday 15 October 2026
Watch the meeting
Members present: Lord Newby (The Chair) ; Lord Carrington of Fulham; Lord Leigh of Hurley; Baroness Wheatcroft.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 – 6
Witnesses

Sandy Bhogal, Co-Chair, Tax Law Committee, Law Society of England and Wales; Reuben Duffy, Policy Executive, Law Society of Scotland; Margaret Curran, Technical Officer, Chartered Institute of Taxation.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Sandy Bhogal, Reuben Duffy and Margaret Curran.

Q1 Good morning. My name is Dick Newby, and I am chairing today’s session of the Finance Bill Sub-Committee of the Economic Affairs Committee of the House of Lords. We are hearing evidence today on various aspects of the Finance Bill 2026-27 legislation. We are very pleased to have three guests who will be giving evidence: Sandy Bhogal, co-chair of the Tax Law Committee of the Law Society of England and Wales , who is with us virtually; Margaret Curran, technical officer of the Chartered Institute of Taxation; and Reuben Duffy, policy executive of the Law Society of Scotland. I have a particular sense of affinity with the Law Society of Scotland because, when I was a Minister doing financial services legislation, it produced the most detailed examination of the legislation of any body. I do not know whether this tradition has continued; it is very impressive.

I will ask the first question and then we will go round the room. We are discussing the new requirement to correct, which the Government are introducing in this Finance Bill. They say this new requirement is about making explicit the obligation on taxpayers to correct errors. Do you think this is necessary? To what extent is the current legislative framework deficient in giving powers to HMRC to pursue taxpayers who fail to correct errors on their returns?

Both the Law Society and I take the view that further statutory compliance powers should only be introduced where a clear policy requirement has been identified. My starting point is that I do not believe that to be the case here. While it is right to say that, under the current UK tax rules, there is no general standalone statutory duty obliging a taxpayer to voluntarily notify HMRC upon discovering an error in a previously filed return, failing to correct an error can expose the taxpayer to penalties , and potentially larger penalties if that behaviour is treated as careless or deliberate. That should be enough. I f you were to expand th at beyond where it currently lie s from a statutory framework perspective, you would think that would have to be conclusively demonstrated.

We have a system of self-assessment, where a taxpayer has to take reasonable steps to ensure they file accurate returns. Sufficient burden is placed on taxpayers at that point in the cycle without them having to further police what happens post filing those returns while HMRC consider the submitted returns and any ancillary evidence or documents required to substantiate them. I can potentially see the value in HMRC being able to issue something akin to a correction notice, but I also query how different that is in practical terms to the existing powers it has . If it look s at a return filed by a taxpayer and is not sure about something, it can open an inquiry and ask for further details. There is a potential danger in taxpayers having to self-police post filing and the consequences of that being potentially deemed deliberate behaviour. Given not just this power but others that HMRC is looking to introduce, is this proportionate to what it is trying to target in terms of behaviour and closing the tax gap? I struggle to see how this power potentially helps with those objectives. In summary, that would be my take on where I see the need or indeed the justification for this measure.

I disagree because the CIOT consider this to be necessary. We have advocated for it in consultation responses made to HMRC in the last few years, when various other compliance interventions were suggested. There is a strong policy rationale for encouraging taxpayers to correct errors once they become aware of them; it is reasonable to expect taxpayers to do that. This is all with the caveat that it is clear what people need to do, which we will come on to later. We take that position for a number of reasons. We think it will help improve compliance, encourage more voluntary disclosures, and it should reduce the need for HMRC to make active interventions, which is all for the good, given the resources it has to hand.

Very importantly, the measure has the potential to reduce the tax gap. Latest figures show that error, or taxpayer mistake, accounted for more than half of the latest tax gap figures. In terms of the exact figures, failure to take reasonable care was £20.8 billion, and error was £9.3 billion, so we are talking about significant amounts of tax that are due to taxpayer mistake. If this policy drives behavioural change and encourages more taxpayers to correct errors once they become aware of them, that should hopefully impact those figures.

Additionally, it would reinforce the requirement on tax advisers that currently exists in professional conduct in relation to taxation, or PCRT, to which CIOT is one of seven signatories. It is basically our professional rules, and in them there is a requirement on tax advisers to encourage and assist their clients to correct errors once they become aware of them. Having an overarching statutory duty to correct will support those professional rules and help tax advisers in those sometimes difficult discussions they may have with clients when an error is identified in discussing what to do about it and how much additional tax might be payable.

Sandy mentioned there are already consequences in legislation if you do not correct once you become aware of an error. There is an implicit duty under criminal law to rectify errors — for example, the offence of cheating the public revenue — but, as far as we are aware, HMRC’s prosecution policy seems to indicate that it would not prosecute most cases under that offence. There is also the requirement in penalty legislation that, if you discover an error and fail to correct it, and the error was not originally careless or deliberate, then it will be deemed to be careless. That legislation is already there. In the new draft legislation, we see a step up from that; it will be treated as deliberate. If you report an error later, it is more likely to be prompted, so there will be higher penalties. There are already consequences, but this just puts things under a statutory umbrella. So long as there is sufficient awareness raising and education, so taxpayers actually know what they have to do, then we support it.

The Law Society of Scotland will take perhaps a middling tack as compared to the Law Society of England and Wales and CIOT . We certainly understand the policy aim behind this legislation. In principle, we are supportive of it, but we have a couple of reservations regarding the specificity of some terms, which in general need further guidance in order to properly work through this legislation. I specifically point out two unclear terms : “ r easonable steps”, in terms of steps taken and w hen the taxpayer “ becomes aware” of the inaccuracy. These are two terms that we highlighted in our written evidence as well, that we believe could do with further guidance from HMRC to specify what exactly they mean. Building off what CIOT just said, making this legislation work will depend greatly on taxpayer understanding of their obligations, and that will require clear guidance.

We are supportive in general of HMRC cracking down on the tax gap, but we also note that the last couple of years have been a fairly busy period for legislation on tax conduct. We wish for consideration to be given to how this properly fits within that overall framework. We highlight particularly the recent introduction of mandatory registration for tax advisers. The obligation to comply is on the taxpayer but they will take advice from tax advisers. We will come on to that in a little while, but there needs to be further consideration of how exactly this impacts tax advisers and their professional obligations under the legislation.

Can I just press you on the point, which I have sympathy with, about defining reasonable steps? It seems to me that is quite difficult. What form of guidance would you look for? Would it be examples of what is and what is not reasonable? As you say, reasonable is a subjective term; we find what people consider to be reasonable or common sense varies very much.

In terms of reasonable steps, in particular we picked up the lack of a deadline for the correction. A clear timeline outlined in guidance would help taxpayers and tax advisers understand their obligations and at what speed they should move to correct errors. I could not speak to a specific example, but I can get back to you in writing when I have spoken to our tax law sub - committee; it can perhaps provide more detail on that.

Thank you very much. I have a supplementary question, which is principally addressed to Sandy. Given that you are not keen on what the Government are doing, if this is not the way you would do it, do you have any other suggestions as to how HMRC might improve taxpayer behaviour around correction of errors? Or, as you slightly implied, do you think HMRC already ha s the powers to deal with errors anyway?

If I may, I will start with the second point first. Sufficient powers do exist and with further resourcing, HMRC could probably take better advantage of them. I appreciate that it is a hard job and therefore sometimes the easy solution seems to be to increase the scope of powers and hope that creates more of a deterrent in terms of dealing with errant taxpayer behaviour.

In terms of alternatives, I would come back to what Margaret correctly identified earlier when pointing to the biggest component of the tax gap. I am using HMRC’s own statistics here. What it call s failure to take reasonable care is 35% of the tax gap, and then errors—mistakes that a taxpayer makes despite taking reasonable care— are a further 16%. Together, that takes you to over half of the tax gap. The question is, does that arise because taxpayers are not behaving appropriately, or is there something else going on?

Typically, a lot of the tax gap comes from the small business sector. I am quoting the latest tax gap figures for 2024-25, but that trend has been replicated in the tax gap statistics for a number of years. That tells me that the tax code is too complicated and , as a result, compliance with it is problematic. If we really want to make a significant dent in the tax gap, we need to look at the existing tax laws and find a way to make compliance easier for the taxpayer.

When you look at careless or negligent behaviour by taxpayers, I am not convinced—certainly my professional experience does not tell me—that it comes from bad behaviour by taxpayers. It is more of an issue of people struggling to understand obligations and the scope of the laws they need to comply with. Tax is inherently complicated and uncertain. Therefore, enhancing powers, which have the premise that the taxpayer is somehow at fault and their behaviour is what is driving the difficulty, is my key concern. My alternative would be a fresh look at how we legislate in the UK to consider whether there are areas of the tax code where the tax gap is wide and things can be done to address that.

Do the three of you think that the main focus of additional HMRC efforts as a result of this provision will be towards small businesses rather than individuals, if that is where the bulk of the tax gap is found?
I do not know. HMRC ha s not said, as far as I am aware. But, at the moment, other things are happening that target small business in terms of guidance, so it would make sense.

I agree with CIOT there. We are not entirely sure where the focus will be, but I echo the earlier point of the Law Society of England and Wales that resourcing is key. Wherever HMRC target s , it need s to make sure that it has adequate resources and do es not give itself more powers without the resource to back it up.

Q2 We have probably already touched on what I am trying to get at, but there will be some taxpayers, particularly very small businesses or indeed individual taxpayers, who do not have professional advisers. Others, particularly small businesses, will have professional advisers who—how can I put it ? — do a cheap and cheerful procedure for their client because that is all the business can afford. How difficult will it be for a non-specialist, an individual or a small business owner to get their taxes correct? More importantly, when a customer correction notice comes through, how easy will it be for them to respond to that without incurring unreasonable costs?

You mentioned the notice. It feels to me that this correction measure is more understandable when you think of it in terms of HMRC sending a prompt to someone to make them aware that they may have made an error; but obviously they will need to check. The explanation in the notice needs to be very clear about the error that HMRC suspect s has occurred and what the taxpayer should do about it. There should be an easy process to either let HMRC know, “Actually, no, I haven’t made an error”; or, “I have”, and this is how to tell HMRC. There needs to be very clear guidance especially to somebody who does not have access to professional advice.

There will be a cohort of people who may struggle with this. If you have a professional adviser, they will be there to give advice. Of course, one concern is that we do not know how HMRC intend s to use correction notices. Obviously, these will be new. We would hope, expect and advocate for them to be used only in cases where HMRC is pretty certain there has been an error — for example, that a source of PAYE income has been omitted. Otherwise, if they are used for broader things, taxpayers could be put to a lot of unnecessary work and cost in trying to deal with them when maybe there is no error.

Could I just come back on that quickly? I have to say, my experience of HMRC is it goes fishing. It send s out a general notice saying, “We don’t think this is correct”. This is largely driven, particularly in the corporate sector, by possibly AI or a system-generated comparison between previous years’ figures. It says effectively, “We don’t understand why this is different. Explain it and justify it”. Is it not going to do exactly the same with these notices? Is it not just going to say, “We have looked at your tax return from last year and your tax return this year. There is a difference. Go into detail as to why that is different”?
We would strongly advocate that it does not use them for that.
That is what it does at the moment.
It uses other prompts.
A CCN.
It do es , do es it not?
Yes, but that is not a CCN; that is a nudge letter.

That is also a prompt. If this measure comes in, at that stage, the taxpayer may be aware that they might have made an error. They then have to do some work to investigate it, and take professional advice if they do not already have an adviser. Ultimately, if it is unfounded, as it does now, that will create a lot of unnecessary costs and work. With this measure, the stakes are higher because if you do not correct, and it is an error, HMRC come s back , decide s it is an error and issue s a deliberate penalty; then you are into new elements of risk.
Do you think there ought to be a clear definition as to what the taxpayer has to do to satisfy the correction notice?
Oh, definitely, yes.
Is there not at the moment?

The measures are new. The consultation around the correction notice is less mature than it is around the overarching duty of error correction. There should be further consultation on how these notices are going to work, what they will look like, how they are to be issued and what for and what information they will contain. That is really important. HMRC has said it will continue to engage with us during that process, which we welcome.

Can I interrupt on that? My understanding was the CCN was going to be specific and say, “You’ve forgotten that bank account; you’ve forgotten that source of income”, whereas the nudge letters are open-ended, and you sit there worrying, “What on earth have I forgotten about?” Can we be clear on this? Will the CCN specifically say what the error is that needs reporting and be limited to that?

At the moment, we do not know because obviously they are new, but these are the sorts of things we would advocate for. Another risk of a CCN is it picks up HMRC’s spot that a taxpayer has omitted one source of income from their tax return, but actually the taxpayer did the same thing last year or the year before, or perhaps there are other errors. Another risk is that a taxpayer could make an incomplete disclosure. They should be disclosing all their errors at the same time, and there are routes to do that. Just responding to a notice that identifies one error may leave them exposed if there are other errors that they do not correct at the same time. That is a risk of these notices. It needs to be clear that they will also nudge to consider whether the taxpayer has made other errors.

Just to go back to Lord Carrington’s question about taxpayers who do not have professional advice, earlier this year, in HMRC’s consultation on the reform of behavioural penalties, we considered that generally when it comes to penalties HMRC should not just take a black and white approach; it should consider, for example, the size and scale of the instance and look at the size of the tax loss here. Building off what Margaret just said, the frequency of errors is a key point. Is this a first offence? Is this a one-off or a pattern? What was the intent? As Lord Carrington asked, was professional advice received? If not, that also builds the case for clear and coherent guidance with examples, so taxpayers can be made to understand their duties under the legislation.

Tax is complex; we all know this. There are people who will say, “Well, I won’t need professional advice; I’m going to do it on my own”. I believe that will, sadly, result in errors. Guidance is key but also HMRC discretion in making this work and building confidence in the system that HMRC is not simply punishing taxpayers for modest errors.

I hate to come back on this all the time, but you have a view that HMRC will assist the people who it challenge s . Is that realistic? Do es HMRC really operate that way? I can tell you, that has not always been my experience.
I cannot speak to that, but I certainly hope that HMRC would work to that. That should be its aim; that would be the position of the Law Society of Scotland.

I hope with Sandy that it simplif ies the tax system, but experience suggests that the opposite will happen. I suspect that, if it has the power to just demand, it will just demand rather than assist.
Just to be clear, what ha s HMRC said so far about the extent to which it will explain what it is looking for?
That is key because if you receive—
Has it said it will do it? You may think it is key, but does it acknowledge it to be so?

I hope so. It is something that we will continue to press for. HMRC ha s already piloted that with some of its nudge letters—these can be really vague—by stating the source of income it thinks someone may have omitted from their tax return. The feedback from taxpayers is that is really helpful because people need guidance. If you get a correction notice from HMRC, you need to know what it is concerned about, otherwise you will be put to a lot of time trying to work out what it may or may not think the error is.
Sandy, you were a bit sceptical about the whole process. Do you think HMRC will use it correctly?

I am not sure I can answer that question. HMRC is an enormous organisation; it is very difficult to say that, as an organisation, it will behave in a particular way. I would say—this is both a Law Society position and my own personal view—in order to ensure that we have rule of law in the UK, state bodies need to have very clear scope of their powers. There should be limited discretion that should be appropriate and proportionate, certainly in the context of this particular proposal.

I agree with a number of the concerns that have been raised. It is my understanding from the original consultation document that the threshold for HMRC and CCNs will be a reason to suspect, which is an inappropriate threshold for something such as this. The bar should be higher, particularly to your point about ensuring that legislation is appropriately used. It may well be the case that, when further draft legislation is published, the rules are tighter and these things are clarified. I would also advocate that HMRC is put on a very clear statutory footing in terms of its powers, and that we do not put too much in the discretionary guidance about what HMRC can and cannot do, for the very reasons that you have identified.

Lastly, I go back to what HMRC want s to achieve. Reuben rightly pointed to the idea that legislation should hope for best behaviour by parties; but it should also cater for the potential worst behaviour, both on the side of the state as well as the taxpayer. In order for a measure such as this to be proportionate, it should be very clear about the type of behaviour it looks to target. If it is bad taxpayer behaviour, then it should be clear, and the rules should be tightened accordingly. If it looks to create a broader deterrent for all taxpayers, it is reasonable to ask whether it will provide the appropriate deterrent or simply add yet more cost and administrative burden on taxpayers, who are already trying very hard to comply.

Q3 Going back to Lord Carrington’s point, there seems to be an assumption on HMRC’s behalf—and underlying some answers we have had here—that most people have access to professional advisers at one stage or another. The self-assessment net is now so wide that this simply cannot be the case. My concern is that receiving a CCN would instil sheer panic in quite a lot of taxpayers, who are perfectly innocent in what they have done. Do you share that fear? Do es HMRC have powers enough already? It can send out one-to-many letters, what you refer to as nudge letters, and probably need s to draft them more tightly rather than go on fishing expeditions. Is there a risk this will to add to the fear factor among a lot of taxpayers, who already choose not to open letters from the taxman? Is it necessary? That is really the point. Margaret, you thought it was when we started out on this session.

There is the overall statutory duty. Correction notices are just a way HMRC ha s thought up—perhaps a more effective nudge than a one-to-many letter—to get people to correct what HMRC think s are errors. If it is to use them at high volume, there will need to be a lot of thought about how this is done because, as you say, a lot of people, maybe the majority, will not have an agent. Some may not respond to customer correction notices and , of course, not responding means you could end up with a penalty even if you have not made a mistake. What is HMRC going to do about people who do not respond? Some people will think, “Oh, actually, I need to go and get advice”, which they would not otherwise have done, to just protect themselves. You can see there will be more paperwork and more obligation on people.

At the same time, the notice will act more as a prompt. We talked about becoming aware of an error. It is more understandable when you receive a prompt from HMRC. That is a point at which you become aware. The problem is if you do not receive a prompt from HMRC; how will anyone know or be able to prove that they might have become aware of an error?
That surely is only effective, as you suggested before, if the prompt is fairly specific.
Yes.

If it is general, the panic factor will be quite large. In the end, do es HMRC need to tier the way it deal s with taxpayers far more than it does at the moment? Should people who are liable for very little tax get one particular form, so it is graduated that way and it does not waste too much effort on the small things?

I certainly think there ought to be some kind of de minimis threshold. Is it going to send a notice to someone because it think s they have omitted £50-worth of income? If you have an adviser, you certainly do not want to be spending a lot on fees that would end up being totally disproportionate to the actual tax that you have underpaid. At the same time, these notices should not be used for technical areas of uncertainty; they should be for obvious, spelled - out errors, nothing that is complicated, for example, if someone is a UK resident or domiciled. They should be kept to the simple, straightforward, obvious mistakes.
Sandy, you talked about simplification. Do you have any thoughts related specifically to this issue?

Simplification is a difficult overall objective; there will always be an element of complexity in tax laws. With this particular measure, if notice had to be introduced—again, for the reasons I mentioned previously, I am not sure it does—I would probably drop the first element of it and say that once the taxpayer does what they are supposed to do, which is to take all reasonable care to ensure that they file an accurate return, they have done their duty; then it moves to HMRC to take that forward as part of the normal compliance lifecycle. If HMRC feel s that customer correction notices would be a useful additional tool in ensuring compliance but also assisting taxpayers in terms of getting things right, even though it is post filing, as long as they are appropriately and tightly defined, I see how that could work. It would be another arsenal in HMRC’s compliance powers, which is pretty close to what it has already.

I question whether, in isolation, it is much different to contacting a taxpayer and opening an inquiry into an existing return. As Margaret rightly says, if you are talking about something where it is very clear there has been an error, then quite rightly, the threshold we were talking about earlier about reason to suspect can, by definition, be much higher. Therefore, as a result of tightening the scope of this legislation, you can hopefully simplify it by ensuring that it only applies in very limited circumstances. Off the top of my head, that is probably the best I can think of in terms of simplifying the measure.
Reuben, would that in any way fit with your thinking?

I would refer back to the answer I gave to Lord Carrington regarding the degrees of behaviour we see. The Law Society of Scotland thinks that is key, which is why we responded to HMRC’s consultation on the broader reform of behavioural penalties. We need to understand things are not black and white when it comes to tax, even though the legislation often is in terms of behaviours. Sandy touched on the key point of complexity. Tax law is complex, and some areas are more complex than others. If people, as you allude to, are not using professional advice, then, as I said earlier, there will be mistakes. HMRC need s to take that into account when utilising this, which is why we are supportive in principle of this legislation, but there are practical difficulties that need to be worked out before implementing it.

Q4 To disclose for the record, I am a member by qualification of the CIOT, admittedly in 1985 when it was a bit simpler, but none the less . Can we talk about safeguards? Just to scope the matter, the CIOT said in its submissions that this policy will be effected through the TMA. Can you explain which taxes it does and does not affect? Can you also explain the difference between the proposed and the current system? It must now have a system whereby it discover s undeclared income and it does something about it. What is the difference in the two routes? Sorry, there are a lot of questions.

I will take the first question about which taxes it will impact. The draft legislation is making amendments to s chedule 24 to the Finance Act 2007, which is error penalty legislation. That applies to all taxes, so all the main taxes and a lot of the more minor ones such as income tax, capital gains tax, corporation tax, VAT, stamp duty, land tax, et cetera.
Does it also apply to i nheritance tax?

Yes. My understanding is it applies to all taxes. There is an amendment to section 118 of the TMA, which generally only applies to income tax, capital gains tax and , I think, corporation tax. It is unclear whether any other amendments are required in other statutes in order to tie any loose ends together. We can put that question to HMRC, but until we see the Finance Bill we will not know whether there are further amendments. What was your other question?
HMRC must have had something prior that was comparable, so what is the change?

The change is that it will be a statutory duty to correct, and the consequences of not correcting, once you become aware, are that your behaviour will be treated as deliberate for penalty purposes; whereas currently it would be treated as careless.

You have covered the matter for everyone. I move on to the issue of safeguarding. As we discussed earlier, in circumstances, particularly with inheritance tax, where the people making the submissions are not responsible for the asset collation, what protections and safeguards should be built into the CCN legislation?
Do you mean in terms of advisers?
I mean particularly executors, who pay the tax but do not necessarily have the information that a taxpayer would.

That is a good question, and it touches on something we have also considered. The focus of the legislation is very much: you make a mistake, you do something about it, and if you do not do something about it, you are going get a higher penalty — that is the main focus —w hereas there is a gap , which we think should be included in the legislation , around people who are unsure whether they have made an error or whether they have forgotten something they ought to disclose. People may not have, or cannot access, all the information they need to establish whether an error has been made.

There are lots of examples where HMRC thinks an error has been made but the person disagrees. What do they do? It could be a very complex area of law. HMRC may not have all the facts. The escalation in risk around the consequences of not correcting an error could place a lot more responsibility on taxpayers, their advisers and others to make absolutely sure that they do their research, get all their evidence together and, if necessary, take advice or even get a second opinion. It ups the ante because the consequences of getting things wrong are higher.

Specifically in terms of executors, I echo Margaret and say that is a good question. I can ask our trusts and successions sub - committee at the Law Society of Scotland to come back to you with a more detailed answer, as they will have more knowledge in regard to IHT. Picking up on Margaret’s point that this applies to all taxes, I would highlight that Scotland now has numerous devolved taxes that are outwith HMRC’s remit and are managed by Revenue Scotland. Consideration needs to come into play about how these two potentially divergent systems will operate alongside one another. Our most notable one is, of course, the land and buildings transactions tax.

The Law Society of Scotland’s main concern about safeguards is around advisers. It is not clear to us what obligations there are when advisers identify or suspect an error on a taxpayer’s behalf. For example, one of our members asked, “What if you advise a client that there is an error in their return, and the client says, ‘I disagree’”? Is there an obligation on the solicitor to secure a correction on that? At what point does it become sanctionable conduct? This is a very pertinent and timely question, given the recent introduction of the framework around mandatory registration that I mentioned earlier. We query whether HMRC would deem it as misconduct if a tax adviser was unable to secure a correction to a client’s return. How far are we going with this? What are their obligations under the legislation? That is quite an important question from the tax advice perspective, particularly for solicitors.

I would like to come on to reckless behaviour in just one second, but I first want to pick up a point Margaret made at the start. She said it was absolutely crucial that HMRC took steps to ensure that taxpayers understood that this was happening. If you were them, how would you do that? This is a question to everybody.

There needs to be comprehensive guidance with examples, which need to be not just obvious errors but also difficult ones around things such as : what if there is a change in HMRC’s guidance? What if there is a court or precedent decision that changes everyone’s understanding of what the tax position is? There needs to be extensive communication. It will be easier to communicate with agents. The real problem is those people without agents, the unrepresented. How is the message going to get to them? If HMRC issue s a correction notice, that should comprehensively explain what the position is. But, absent a prompt or a notice, how is HMRC going to reach those people? It is a good question. It tries using social media, YouTube videos, those sorts of things. It generally get s quite good viewing numbers, so there are various options available to it , but I still think it is going to be quite challenging.
And whistleblowers, of course.
Presumably, a sentence could be added to the letter you get with your tax code to say the new provision is there, linked to wherever the details are. Are there any other thoughts, quickly?
I have nothing in addition to what Margaret said. I just echo that it is important that appropriate resource is put behind public awareness of this.

Q5 The Chair: . Can we come on to the proposed criminal offence of making reckless untrue statements or declaration? The overarching question here is, given that we have an existing framework of both criminal and civil sanctions, is it necessary to introduce this new category of behaviour that could lead to this sort of sanction? Who would like to start? Sandy, you are the sceptic.

Both the Law Society of England and Wales and I would have concerns if this was introduced. There is a lot to this, but I will be as concise as I can. There are probably five reasons why we should be careful with something such as this. First, recklessness is not particularly well defined from a legal perspective, and there is potential to confuse taxpayers, tax advisers and indeed HMRC officers. W e would advocate caution there. There has not been much in the way of real consideration by the courts in tax cases on the concept of recklessness, and certainly in the case of indirect taxes, this is a not often used power.

To elaborate on the differences in taxation, direct taxes can frequently be qualitatively different in scope, complexity and application from indirect taxes in terms of everything from timing and regularity of collection and filing to just the nature of the way that the taxpayer has a relationship with that tax. For example, with VAT, oftentimes the taxpayer is also in the position of the tax collector because of the way it works as a cascade tax. There are various differences that do not necessarily mean that the powers should align for consistency’s sake. That distinction should be borne in mind.

It will inevitably raise concerns around the rule of law and access to justice because taxpayers may lack sufficient certainty as to how to comply with the law, and it is obviously hugely important for that to be clear in the context of criminal liability.

You also have to potentially think about the way that legislation might impact taxpayer behaviour. What could be the impact on voluntary disclosures by compliant taxpayers in a situation where they are concerned about the possibility of a criminal offence? Even HMRC acknowledge s that voluntary disclosure processes have worked well and are getting better and better all the time.

I would reiterate my earlier point: with the powers it currently ha s , what is it exactly about this escalation of existing powers that the Government feel will have a significant impact on the tax gap, either by encouraging compliance or deterring non-compliance? Again, I do not think the case is clear there.

To build on that, the Law Society of Scotland point out that HMRC’s investigative policy states that, for cases where it need s to send a deterrent and deem s a criminal sanction necessary, the examples are money laundering, fraud, theft and organised crime. We query then : does this policy need to be revisited in light of this? To the actual offence itself, we take no firm position on it, for or against. I would not want to pre-empt our criminal law committee’s consideration of it, but Sandy has raised numerous points that bear careful consideration.

I would also point out that in Scotland there is only one public prosecutor, the Crown Office, and the way this legislation is drafted, it is not necessarily clear that it understands that particular role. I believe there is a reference to independent prosecutorial authority or some such other thing. Those are the two points that the Law Society of Scotland wish to raise in reference to that.

On this occasion, I am going to come over a bit stronger than Sandy and disagree with this policy. The CIOT takes the position that we do not support it, particularly as it is currently proposed. It is far too uncertain what recklessness actually means. It is supposed to sit between carelessness and deliberate behaviour, but the boundaries seem really blurred. The examples that HMRC used in its consultation document did not help at all; in fact, they just muddied the waters. It was very difficult—and very worrying, actually—to see some of the examples of behaviour it would consider to be reckless. A lot of people would think, “Actually, that is probably careless, not reckless”. The boundaries are going to be really difficult to establish. It will make giving advice potentially quite difficult, especially in complex areas. As Sandy said, direct tax is different from indirect tax in that it is less transactional; there is more nuance and difficult technical positions that might need to be worked through.

Another reason we do not support it is that there seems to be little evidence, or a little evidential basis, on which HMRC was suggesting it needed this offence. It is already in place for some indirect taxes, but as far as we could find out, it has been rarely used.
As in possibly never?
I do not know. I saw somewhere there might have been one case.
That is always a problem.
It seemed an assumption that Angela Rayner had been reckless because she did not take professional advice. Would that be a defence against recklessness , to come to people such as you?
It would be a good thing if you can prove that you took appropriate advice from a qualified professional.

Q6 We looked at R&D tax credits a little while ago. From the examples given, making an R&D tax credit, where you think, “It might be right, it might not, but I will stick it in anyway” , which happens , would be considered reckless now, would it not?
Maybe, especially if you did not take advice from a suitably qualified professional, although some taxpayers might find it difficult to judge whether someone is suitably qualified or not.

That is the point. That is what we discovered, that the advisers for R&D tax credits were not professionally qualified at all. Do you think HMRC is doing this to try to catch that area of tax? I t is an enormous sum of money.

I do not know. One reason for introducing it is because it is a lower threshold than trying to prove dishonesty. I do not know because we have not been shown any evidence, but maybe there are certain cases that are at the back of HMRC’s mind, where it is thinking, “Actually, we could use this offence for those”.

It is not clear to me from the consultation document and process that followed exactly what HMRC is trying to target. I agree with Margaret that it is looking to catch behaviour that sits somewhere between carelessness and deliberate or dishonest. But the scope of recklessness is unclear in this context, as indeed it is in various other parts of the law of the land. That is one of our concerns, the idea that you cannot necessarily appropriately define the type of behaviour that you are looking to criminalise. It should be something that we take very seriously as a country. If someone is going to be potentially criminally liable, it should be very clear what the scope of that legislation is.

As far as you are aware, is there a hard case that has led to HMRC wanting to do this? It is quite a significant proposal. If it does not use this provision for indirect taxes, one wonders why—other than a bureaucratic desire for tidiness— it has decided to introduce it. Are you aware of anything specific?
We are not, which is part of the problem. If there was some reason for it that could be explained, we may have a better understanding of why it wants to introduce it.

This is a pattern of behaviour. Treasury and Whitehall consistently bring in mountains of legislation, and HMRC never implement s it. It never, or hardly ever, go es after anyone. It is some civil servant justifying their existence, which is fine, and it may be good, but there is no good if HMRC do es not actually implement legislation. Is that your experience? Your words might be slightly less pejorative than mine, but is it your experience that there is a lot of legislation that HMRC ha s but do es not use?
Absolutely, yes.
I agree there are a number of powers that HMRC ha s that it does not use. Exactly why that is the case could be for any number of reasons, my Lord.
Could it be because it already ha s too many?

As tax rules develop, it can be difficult to have the appropriate opportunity to holistically consider whether HMRC’s compliance powers remain fit for purpose. Particularly with the way business evolves, the nature of cross-border business and how that is transacted, there could be any number of reasons why the tax code, particularly the compliance aspects of it, are always playing catch up. There are various difficulties in a democracy in there being the appropriate opportunity to re-think how these powers should be both legislated and enforced.

I have a bit of sympathy with the way that the jigsaw is at the moment, and I am not necessarily sure that is HMRC’s fault. If it is being pushed to close the tax gap, it may well be it is being asked to consider things that would potentially up the ante in a way that would deter or otherwise impact taxpayer behaviour so that it helps with closing the tax gap. The difficulty I face when I look at these proposals is that, if it is not clear exactly what it is trying to do, it is difficult to be helpful in terms of better targeting the proposal. All you can do is raise concerns.

You have done so extremely clearly, and it has been extremely helpful to us. Thank you very much. We have learned a lot, and you have given us a lot to think about and to ask future witnesses, not least the Minister when he comes later in this inquiry. Many thanks.

sessions.iT: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
sessions.w: Brett Ryan (Hydrogen UK); Kisha Couchman (Energy UK); Martin Lambert (The Oxford Institute for Energy Studies)

segs.tx: Environment and Climate Change Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
Wednesday 14 October 2026
1 0 am

Members present: Baroness Sheehan (The Chair); Lord Ashcombe; Baroness Coffey; Lord Jay of Ewelme; Lord Krebs; Lord Lennie; Baroness McIntosh of Pickering; Baroness R afferty; Lord Redwood; Lord Rooker; Earl Russell; Lord Trees; Baroness Whitaker.
Evidence Session No. 2 Heard in Public Questions 22 - 30
Witnesses
Brett Ryan, Policy Director, Hydrogen UK; Kisha Couchman , Deputy Director for Policy, Energy UK; Martin Lambert, Senior Research Fellow, Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Brett Ryan, Kisha Couchman and Martin Lambert .

Q22 Good morning and welcome to the Lords Committee on the Environment and Climate Change. Today is the second session of our inquiry into the impact of Dunkelflaute weather events and the challenges they present to the Government’s ambition to deliver the Clean Power Action Plan by 2030.

Before we start, I remind everyone that the session is webcast live and that a transcript will be taken and made public. Witnesses will have an opportunity to review the transcript and, if necessary, make very minor amendments. Members are reminded that they should declare any relevant interests the first time they speak and this of course applies equally to all witnesses. I will take the opportunity here to say that I am a director of Peers for the Planet.

On to today’s business : w e are very grateful to our panel of expert witnesses for making the time to be with us today. Before we proceed any further, I will ask each of our witnesses to introduce themselves. We will start with Martin Lambert.

I spent much of my career, 30 years or more, working for Shell, mainly in the natural gas and liquefied natural gas, LNG, business. I retired from Shell nine years ago and I do consultancy in the gas area. Today I am representing the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies , where I am a senior research fellow . I set up the hydrogen programme about five years ago.

Good morning, everyone. I am from Energy UK , which is the trade body for the sector. We represent the breadth of the energy sector in the UK , from power generation through to networks , and also the retail supply part of the business.

Good morning. I am the policy director for Hydrogen UK , which is the largest trade association representing the smallest and largest companies looking to deliver hydrogen within the UK. We cover hydrogen production, transport and storage infrastructure and all the various end use applications. Probably very importantly for today’s session, our members are either leading or active in the vast majority of projects that are run through the Government’s various support schemes.

Q23 Thank you. You are very warmly welcome today. The purpose of today’s session is to understand low - carbon molecular storage technologies, namely hydrogen, biomethane and gas storage with carbon capture and storage. I will start by asking each of you to give your perspective of molecular storage technologies and their potential to help mitigate the risk of intermittency during a Dunkelflaute event as the grid decarbonises. Who would like to start?

I am happy to start. First, it is important to recognise that there is not a single solution to a Dunkelflaute. They will range in duration , so it is important for us to have a portfolio of flexible technologies to be able to respond to the system requirements. The UK is already developing a range of technologies. We have batteries, pump storage and interconnectors. We are developing consumer-led flexibility, which is how we shift consumption on the demand side. Ofgem has also just announced its cap and floor regime, which will bring forward investment for long - duration energy storage projects. That will be quite fundamental to how we deal with periods of low wind going forward.

However, in a prolonged period of low output , it is not just the number of gigawatts that you have installed on your system that will be important, but the number of terawatt hours or gigawatt hours that can sustain the system for a multi-day or multi-week period. That is where molecular storage is particularly useful. Today we have natural gas , which provides a significant source of stored chemical energy and it is also dispatchable generation. The challenge for us is to find the low - carbon alternatives to that source that we use today.
Can you say what dispatchable generation is?
Of course. Dispatchable generation is where you burn a fuel to generate electricity. Today that is predominantly natural gas and there are gas-fired generation power stations.
It is immediate generation?

Yes. Hydrogen, as you mentioned, is one of the options that we are looking at as an alternative to burning gas , because hydrogen can be produced during periods where there is excess or surplus renewable electricity. We have the benefit of a very large offshore wind fleet , so we have the opportunity to harness some of that renewable electricity to produce hydrogen. That can be stored in very large quantities and transported to a hydrogen-fired power station, which can then generate electricity. That is one option.

We have natural gas with CCS and that is where you attach carbon capture technology to capture carbon emissions. That is particularly useful because it has the benefit of lowering carbon emissions and it also has useful applications in the industrial sector.

The third option is biomethane, which offers a complementary role and potentially a more near-term option , because it is chemically very similar to natural gas. You can use the existing gas infrastructure without major modifications . The industry is quite confident that that can be scaled up in relatively short order, subject to gas quality checks and sustainable f ood stock s .

The thing to underscore is that it requires a range of different solutions. There will not be a silver bullet . T he core objective is trying to build a resilient portfolio and ensuring that we have the market frameworks and the policy frameworks to bring forward the investment that is required to value each of the technologies that will have a different role i n the system.
Each technology has a role and it depends on incentives to bring those technologies to markets.
Exactly.

I will ask you a little bit about the sources of biomethane. You said that it has great potential. Of course it is methane like natural gas, fossil gas, so modification to the existing infrastructure will be minimal, but where does the biomethane come from?
It tends to come from agricultural sources predominantly. I would be happy to follow up in writing with some more specific details on the sources of sustainable f ood stocks and biomethane.
Is it land that we currently grow food on?
Yes.
I just wanted to be clear about biomethane, the scaled-up production of biomethane. Martin, you wanted to come in.

Yes. I can complement what Kisha has said. I fully agree on the portfolio approach, with a range of different options available , because there is no one single answer. That is definitely a key takeaway.

Molecular storage is essential for covering Dunkelflaute because the energy density of molecular storage is so much more. Batteries can do so much , but if you tr ied to cover a 10-day Dunkelflaute with batteries, you would need to cover a large chunk of the country with batteries to be able to do that. That is clearly not practical or sensible. Kisha has outlined the three types of molecular storage pretty well, but I will add a couple of points. We store a fair bit of natural gas today , but a key point for natural gas is that it flows as well as being stored. What I mean is that we get natural gas from Norway. We can import it as LNG , then we store some in the Rough gas field offshore of north-east England and we store gas in LNG terminals. There is a buffer , but the storage is just a buffer to smooth out the flows that we are bringing in from elsewhere.
Biomethane and hydrogen both need to be manufactured , so you have a different approach. You manufacture the product and then you can use it.
You manufacture it and store it?

Indeed. To answer your question on biomethane, just to be clear for everyone, you start with stuff called biogas. On a farm , you effectively anaerobically digest biowaste and you produce a mix of methane and CO 2 called biogas. To make biomethane, you separate the methane and the CO 2 and that gives you grid - quality biomethane that you can then inject, with certain constraints, into the grid. You are right that there is a limitation on it , but various studies that we and others have done show that probably you could—currently we produce pretty small amounts of biomethane — increase it to about 10% of current natural gas consumption. That would still be sustainable because when you produce food you produce waste as well, but if you produce too much, you are right, you start to affect agricultural land and so there are constraints. W e could do more with biomethane but there are limits on how far it can go.

To finish off, hydrogen has to be manufactured. There are two types of hydrogen, loosely called blue and green. You can make b lue hydrogen by taking natural gas, using carbon capture and storage, and then you make hydrogen that can be stored. Green hydrogen is when you have renewable power , you can put it into a thing called an electroly s er and you can make hydrogen that way by breaking water down into hydrogen and oxygen. The problem with making hydrogen, storing it and making it back to electricity again is the round - trip efficiency. If you put in electricity, you make it into hydrogen, you store it, then make it back into electricity again, that is quite low round - trip efficiency. You can make it when you have very cheap electricity, surplus wind you do not need, but if you make too much of it, it becomes quite inefficient , h ence the need for a portfolio approach. I will stop there and let you follow up.
Can you explain when you make too much of it and it becomes inefficient?

Yes. On a very windy, sunny day in the future energy system, it is quite likely that the instantaneous wind and solar production will be more than the normal demand for electricity because we have built lots of wind farms, lots of solar farms and there will be more potential production than we need.
There is free energy available for electrolysis.

At that point you can use th e effectively free electricity for making electrolysis. A complex modelling question that is quite hard to answer is how many hours a year you will be in that position, and that depends on many factors. When you have free electricity to make use of the available wind power, making green hydrogen and storing it is a good thing to do, but then you have to add the cost of the electroly s er, which may not run for that many hours, and that affects the economics as well.
The economics of electroly s ers could be of interest. I would be very grateful if you c ould send us further information on that. Many thanks.

I will pick up on some of the points on hydrogen , but first I want to echo Kisha and Martin’s points. We need a portfolio approach to ensure resilience in the future energy system. When we talk about hydrogen’s role in the ability to mitigate the impacts of a Dunkelflaute, it needs several components linked together to make that happen. Of course the first is the storage element itself. When we are talking about the scale that we need to be delivering sustained power generation over the days, weeks and months that we are talking about for a Dunkelflaute scenario, you are really looking at—
Months? I think we have heard that two weeks is the longest possible , or 11 days. It is the first time I have heard of Dunkelflaute events of months.

I was talking about the ability of the hydrogen storage system to be able to provide that power. Technically y ou can do it over weeks and months, whether or not the Dunkelflaute weather event itself persists.
Sorry, I misunderstood you there.

We are looking at large-scale geological formations, depleted oil and gas fields, salt caverns and limed rock caverns. They are all technically feasible and some are already being used for hydrogen storage. Martin has pointed out that you need hydrogen production upstream of that to create those molecules in the first place. The UK has a twin-frac approach, as it is called at the moment, following electrolytic production and CCS-enabled production.
Could you go through those again?

Yes, sorry. Electrolytic production is commonly called green hydrogen , which us es electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. T here are a number of different pathways for CCS-enabled production, but effectively they are using a fossil fuel as a feedstock to split out the hydrogen and carbon. Once you have produced it, you then need to transport it to th e geological formations, because they are in fixed locations. You cannot just put them where it is handy, so you will pipe the hydrogen to the storage facility.

When the Dunkelflaute conditions arrive and you have low renewable output , but still have high electricity demand in the system, you withdraw the hydrogen molecules and run them through a hydrogen-to-power unit—in the industry we shorten it to HTP—that can range in size and technology. You can have fuel cells, gas engines or combined heat and power units , all the way up to grid-scale combined-scale gas turbines. They can be from tens to hundreds of megawatts in generation capacity. Once you have all of those elements combined, that allows hydrogen in molecular storage and low-carbon dispatchable technology to help mitigate the Dunkelflaute.

H ydrogen has the unique advantage of solving a problem at both ends. You are taking the excess renewable generation from the clean power buildout and absorbing some of the excess generation capacity, converting it into hydrogen, storing it for when you need it later and bringing it back online when the renewable output is low but your electricity demand is still high.
Excellent , t hank you. Lord Ashcombe, your question.

Q24 Good morning. I think this leads on from what you were saying, Brett. Does the UK have sufficient hydrogen storage to meet the energy demand in a multi-day, multi-week Dunkelflaute, bearing in mind that we have information here that people seem to think the amounts are fairly different? Secondly, I believe that in a Dunkelflaute , very often we are not going to have the interconnectors producing what they will because it is highly likely it will happen in northern Europe at the same time.

There are various numbers in the public domain o n the technical potential for hydrogen storage capacity within geological formations. There are all sorts of characteristics of the individual geological formations that will decide whether it is technically or economically feasible to develop a site into storage. The specific references will be in our written submission. A number of reports put the technical potential as 1,000 terawatt hours of storage capacity within those geological formations , but once you start looking at the site characteristics — access ; whether or not you would get a planning consent on those sites ; whether the formation has the technical integrity to store hydrogen in great volumes over long durations —of course that number comes down.

What the system needs is still up in the air at the moment. There are various models out there. T he CCC’s seventh carbon budget says that the system requires in the order of nine terawatt hours of hydrogen storage by 2050. NESO’s future energy scenarios have a similar figure by 2050. There is a strong expectation that of the 1,000 kilowatt hours of potential storage we can feasibly deliver around 10 terawatt hours technically and commercially.
Thank you. I should have declared that I work for an insurance broker that does a lot of work with hydrogen.
So “What do we have today?” is m y first question . The next is : h ow easy is it and is it realistically possible to repurpose natural gas storage for hydrogen? I know you can do it for biomethane.

We have very little today. Some small salt caverns have been used on Teesside since the 1970s. They have about 25 gigawatt hours of storage capacity , but one thing to note is that because they have been used to support the chemical industry, they have not been subject to the vast injection and withdrawal rates that we would expect for supporting the power sector. The cavern itself is proving its technical integrity and ability to store hydrogen over long durations , but it has not gone through the same injection and withdrawal rates that we would expect for future use.

That being said, the technology is being proven elsewhere at the moment. One of our members is supporting the ACES Delta p roject in America . They have two salt caverns storing hydrogen, each one with about 150 gigawatt hours of capacity , and they are using it to feed grid-scale gas turbines. They are blending the hydrogen with natural gas at about 30% . T hey are proving the technical ability to store hydrogen in salt caverns and withdraw it for the power sector. Sorry, forgive me, what was the second half of the question?
The repurposing.

Absolutely , it is technically feasible , and there are two aspects to it. One is converting a cavern, the subsurface itself. That is absolutely technically feasible. Similarly, you have to address the topside equipment. You will have compressors and gas - conditioning equipment, things like seals on your pipework. They are all very well - known and all technically possible. It comes down to the commercial frameworks to be able to do that economically.
Would we be able to use the Rough field? The biggest one we have is the Rough.

You are right. Rough, the offshore gas field, is bigger than most of the caverns that we are looking to use onshore. Centrica absolutely has a plan to be able to repurpose that for storing hydrogen , as long as it has the right investment signals and certainty that will be required. It is doing a lot of technical feasibility work to ensure that that is possible.

I can add a couple of points on that. It is important to distinguish between hydrogen storage in salt caverns and hydrogen storage in depleted hydrocarbon fields. Storage in salt caverns has been proven for years. ICI did it, when ICI still existed, in Teesside. Hydrogen storage in salt caverns is an absolutely proven technology and there is no issue with doing that. The other comment on salt caverns is that in the UK we are very blessed with lots of structures . We have several existing and we have a lot of potential for more salt caverns in the UK.
They would need developing?

Some of the current salt caverns have been used for hydrogen in the past. Many of them are being used for storing methane today , but they could be relatively easily converted back to storing hydrogen. I do not have a figure on how much they could store , but they could be converted.

Storing hydrogen in depleted hydrocarbon fields is a quite different proposition altogether. There is some testing being done in Austria. RAG Austria is doing some tests for that at the moment , but if you think about it, the issue is that you put the expensive hydrogen you have produced in a hydrocarbon field and you are not quite sure what will come back out again. From conversations with the people in Austria, they get back some hydrogen but it is mixed , so it needs to be treated when it comes out again. To be honest, given we are so blessed with salt structures in the UK, I think we should explore that fully first and give converting hydrocarbon fields a second order priority.

Bearing in mind we have heard about moving stored carbon from A to B, how easy is it to move the hydrogen from A to B? Do we have a network that does that to get it to the right places? We know that we have a problem with getting power around the grid at the moment.

You can move hydrogen in pipelines. That has been done for ages. There are existing hydrogen pipelines, fairly small scale , but hydrogen pipelines exist in the US and north-west Europe — Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany. The harder bit is you cannot automatically convert a natural gas pipeline to hydrogen. You can eventually convert it normally , but it depends on the metal used in making the pipeline, the seals and the valves, so it requires a fair bit of expenditure to upgrade a former gas pipeline to make it suitable for hydrogen. National Gas has Project Union , which is doing quite a lot of work on looking at what would be required to convert the pipelines for hydrogen. It could be done but it is not an overnight switch. You need to put in some investment to make the transition.

The Government have set up the developing hydrogen transport and storage business models with the intention that they will be rolled out together as a network. There was a commitment with the first regional hydrogen transport and storage network that the allocation would launch later this year and ideally would target commercial operations by 31 December 2033. That is due to the long lead times for such major infrastructure. There are plans to do that , but unfortunately the industry has seen a bit of a slowdown in the development of those business models and the launch of that first allocation. That is a key thing for our members , because we have members developing plans in various parts of the country with different options for what the first regional network could be, but it brings together the storage and the transportation by pipeline , which deserves to get a mention.

I agree with what the others have said. One thing to add is that repurposing gas salt caverns for hydrogen, while technically possible, would be economically challenging and would need to be done case by case. Our members have suggested that it would probably make more sense to develop the salt caverns specifically for hydrogen rather than trying to repurpose. That is also because you need to plan whether you need the gas in the cavern for system resilience . I f it is still useful in the system, that needs to be co-ordinated before we start to repurpose it for something else.

The other thing is just to reiterate the point about the entire hydrogen value chain. It is very difficult to develop storage without a clear view of having sufficient volumes of hydrogen production , and producers also need the confidence that there will be demand. That needs to be done in co-ordination with developing the hydrogen-fired power stations that will ultimately produce or use the hydrogen to generate electricity . T here are lots of different things and it ends up in a sort of chicken-and-egg situation . The business models that Brett mentioned are key to this and are what is required for the development in order to allow that investment to come forward.

I f I may, I have one final question. If we need to make new salt caverns, and the washing process is not a short process to open them up , h ow long is that going to take to get to a sufficient volume, whatever I mean by that?

It takes roughly six to 10 years to develop a hydrogen salt cavern , so the lead times are very long and those investment decisions need to be made as soon as possible. We would suggest that we make those decisions ahead of need. There are obviously various useful indications about the range of hydrogen that we could have on the system . N E SO ’ s future energy scenario pathway , which was published last year , suggests three terawatt hours by 2035.
How many, sorry?

Three terawatt hours by 2035 . T he Climate Change Committee ’ s balance d pathway is three terawatt hours by 2040 , so there is a slight difference in those two scenarios.
