I guess the key thing — because they are not policy targets, just scenarios —is how we turn those scenarios into investable frameworks in order to facilitate the investment that is needed , because 2035 is not that far away . If it takes 10 years to develop , we need to be making those decisions now.
That was going to be my final point , t hank you.

My question follows directly from what you were just saying, Kisha, about both the timescale and the scale of hydrogen storage that might be needed . I wonder whether either you or maybe Brett can shed a bit of light on this , because the National Grid say s we need between 12 and 51 terawatt hours of hydrogen by 2050. The Royal Society concluded we need between 60 and 100 terawatt hours by 2050. The National Infrastructure Commission say s we need 25 terawatt hours by 2040 and , as you have just said , the CCC say s we need three terawatt hours by 2040, so it is pretty confusing. There are orders of magnitude of difference .

G iven what you have just told us about the timescale to develop this, if we are thinking comfortably that three terawatt hours is what we need by 2040 , but actually the number is 10 times that, we are going to be completely off-track. C an you explain why we get these vastly different estimates of how much is needed ? Ei ther Kisha or Brett.

I am happy to go first. F rom an industry perspective , we tend to use the Climate Change Committee and the N E SO scenarios as our main barometers of how much is likely to be required. W hat is also very important — back to th e portfolio point — is that the amount of hydrogen that we are going to need on the system will very much be dictated by the future generation mix . I t does also depend on the extent to which we have managed to scale batteries, long - duration energy storage, pumped storage, biomethane and interconnectors, because that will all have implications for the amount of hydrogen that we need on the system. We would tend to err on the slightly more modest end .

T hat is one of the things we have been calling on the G overnment to do: set out their view on how they see the role of hydrogen in the future system , being very clear about where it adds most value in the system and where the end uses are likely to be, because it depends on how much of it will be used by industry or other sectors, and the extent to which we have electrified across the economy. It is worth taking that sort of whole - systems view.

T o build on what Kisha is saying, you are absolutely right . S ome of the studies that you mentioned there , with some of the targets, are possibly a little bit outdated . S ome of the thinking about how far electrification can go will have changed . S ome of the thinking around which sectors hydrogen could and should be used in have also changed . That has a big impact on the volume or the capacity of hydrogen storage that the system will require. To Kisha’ s point, some of the models that are out there from the Climate Change Committee — and even within NESO’ s f uture e nergy s cenarios m odelling — are pessimistic, shall we say, around the role that hydrogen will play . T hey certainly show a non-zero requirement for hydrogen storage .

When you look at the trajectory that is needed and the long development times to be able to get these projects off the ground, even the first allocation the G overnment are planning to do for the hydrogen storage business model does not set a specific target . I t just has a minimum criterion of 50 gigawatt hours of storage capacity , which would come online in 2033 . To get from 2033 at 50 gigawatt hours — it may be more, but if they just go the minimum — anywhere close to three terawatt hours by 2050 is a huge curve.

This is an interesting avenue of i nquiry . W e would be very grateful for further information about the underlying assumptions and robustness of the targets for hydrogen storage that the G overnment are working to .

I will move on in short order to Lord Jay ’ s question, but can I just probe a little bit further about salt caverns ? I think it is very important that we understand the challenges there. Once salt caverns are created — there is a six to 10- year lead time, I understand — how long do they last?
A very long time. I do not have the exact number, but I think they have a very long operating life.
W e could store very large volumes of hydrogen in there. Are they in the right positions geographically, the locations, to work with existing transmission infrastructure?

O nce they are created , they can last pretty much indefinitely because they are in the geology and so do not wear out. I mentioned the existing ones that ICI created . I am guessing slightly, but it might be 40 years ago they were created and they are still going strong.
H ow many do we need? How many salt caverns do we need to supply i nfinite amounts of hydrogen ?

To give you some context, each cavern will be different and will have a different capacity. It is down to the physical size of that cavern itself ; it is down to the pressures that it can withstand in terms of being able to compress and inject th e hydrogen into it. I think there was a study earlier this year that we will reference in our written submissions, which assumes an individual cavern ’s storage capacity of in the region of 20 to 50 gigawatt hours per cavern. Now, e ach facility may have multiple caverns to make up an individual facility. I f we look at SSE ’ s planned Al dbrough hydrogen storage project, that first cavern is in the order of 20 gigawatt hours of storage capacity, but there are nine caverns within that development that could take that total storage capacity to in the order of 300 gigawatt hours.

Thank you. Again, any further information on salt caverns and how they can help us meet this challenge would be much appreciated. Before we move on again, I am very interested in specialist tanks and storage vessels for hydrogen. Are they expensive and how big can we make them? W here would they fit into that chain that we need to deliver a sensible hydrogen strategy?

Are you talking about pressurised storage containers? Okay . Apologies , I do not have the numbers off the top of my head here, but it is not expected they would give the scale that is needed that we are talking about for supporting and mitigating a Dunkelflaute event. I am aware of one developer that is looking to try to deploy effectively high-pressure storage cylinders buried below the surface, but that is still to be proven at the commercial scale.
T hey would be useful for delivering hydrogen to areas where energy was—
W here there are no geological formations .
Yes.
Absolutely, that is a possibility.
We must move on. P lease do write to us if there is something that the committee needs to hear about. I am going to move on to Lord Jay ’ s question.

Q25 Thank you very much. I want to turn the attention back to gas, if I may. Existing gas plants in the UK are ageing and many, as I understand it, are due to reach the end of life in the early 2030s. However, gas is expected to remain on the grid until the 2040s or thereabouts, even at a rather lower scale than at present. This is a question about costs . Could you say anything about the cost of retaining and upgrading existing gas - fired power stations, or indeed of building new ones ? Most important is how those costs compare with the cost of other potential solutions, such as developing hydrogen storage and hydrogen to power or indeed of using biomethane. Who would like to go first on that?

I am happy to go first. It is very important that we plan for the capacity that the system requires , rather than assuming that the current gas fleet will remain in operation through the 2030s or that it will retire ahead of that time. DESNZ, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, did a piece of analysis that was published earlier this year , which recognised that much of the fleet could potentially continue to remain in operation throughout the 2030s. However, what is key is that owners and operators of those assets need to have early visibility of what is actually required and how much of that capacity needs to be retained so that they can make investment decisions about whether to invest in maintaining, upgrading, extending the life or repowering those assets. There are also substantial lead times for those decisions as well, so those decisions need to be made urgently.
What sort of lead time s are we talking about?

There are significant supply chain constraints currently for certain parts, including turbines and transformers, and there are some estimates of around seven years to wait for those parts. A gain, these are decisions that need to be made with some urgency.

On cost, I think extending the life of the current fleet is generally seen to be the lower - cost option, rather than building new gas generation. Just to give you some ballpark figures, it is thought that it would cost around £ 140 million to extend the life of a CCGT by about five years. To repower a site is about £ 900 million, and that is where you replace m any of the existing key parts of the equipment. A new CCGT, which is about 1,700 megawatts, would be somewhere in the realm of £1 billion to £1.5 billion, so significantly more expensive.

Both will have advantages . E xtending the life of a current gas-fired plant would be quicker and cheaper, particularly where there is already a gas connection, gas infrastructure and operating arrangements . The benefits of a new build would obviously be modern equipment that would run more efficiently and would have a longer operational life, but that needs to be assessed plant by plant. Fundamentally, all the options require significant up - front capital costs, and given supply chain constraints internationally, those decisions would need to be made as soon as possible.

Ultimately , there needs to be a clear transition plan from the G overnment . T hat is certainly one of the things we have been asking for : that they set out how much capacity they anticipate will be required, based on the pace and scale of development of those low-carbon alternatives that will be coming through to replace our current dependence on gas for electricity g eneration.

What about the cost of alternatives? T hat is very helpful , what you said about the cost of extending the life of existing plants and the difference between extending the life and building new ones. That is very clear . C an you give any sense of how that would compare with other solutions?

Yes . A t the power station level, the turbines that are used for gas power stations and hydrogen power stations are broadly similar. I think they are expected to be at a similar price point, although there is an expectation that there could be a modest cost premium for a turbine that operates 100 % hydrogen-ready . It will also be subject to reliability and efficiency standards and so on, which may mean a slight increase in cost. However, I think the non-fuel operating and maintenance costs are broadly the same. I think the biggest difference is the fact that the hydrogen value chain is where you need to consider the total system costs, because it requires production in sufficient volumes. It requires storage — those salt caverns that we talked about — so you need to take into consideration that cost. It requires transporting and that transport and storage network also needs to be accounted for. I t is the entire value chain that needs to be considered when you are comparing those costs.
Any other views?

I will come in very quickly . To put some data on it, B a ringa did some analysis on behalf of DESNZ around hydrogen-to-power costs, and it put that premium for new-build 100% hydrogen turbines at less than 10%. We can provide that data point within the evidence. Similarly, with some of the new-build plants that are built hydrogen-ready, you are looking at approximately 5% of your total capex to be able to retrofit later down the line to be able to handle hydrogen.

To Kisha’ s point , you have to take account of the upstream infrastructure as well, the hydrogen production and the transport and storage infrastructure. With the T & S infrastructure, some of those costs will be borne by other users of the system as well. The power sector will not be the only user of that infrastructure. You will have heavy industry and other e-fuels produc ers using the system for capital cost recovery.

On the hydrogen production aspect, one of the things that we have been working with DESNZ on very much recently is improving hydrogen producers ’ ability to access low-cost renewable power when the system is operating with excess generation. It is not something that the market allows for at the moment in the business models, so we are looking to improve that so that you can materially bring down the cost of hydrogen that will be used to generate power further down the line.

Just to add to Kisha’s point, keeping existing natural gas-fired generation going through the 2030s is certainly going to be the lowest-cost option. There will clearly be some carbon emissions when it i s running, but we are not yet at the net - zero target. T hrough 2030 to 20 40, natural gas has to be the lowest - cost way of keeping it going, and it is probably the only realistic option in that timescale. E stimates I have seen suggest that perhaps around 35 gigawatts of gas-fired capacity will be required through the 2030s, and for that gas is the only option.

In terms of costs, I ha ve some numbers. With the current , rather high cost of gas after the war in the Strait of Hormuz issue , we are currently looking at gas prices of about £ 65 per megawatt hour. If you go back a year, it was more like £ 35 per megawatt hour.
We hope it will go back.

Hopefully. If we can sort out the Strait of Hormuz crisis, then in fact it could go even lower , because , looking at the global gas market, there is a glut of natural gas coming . The US is building LNG export very rapidly, so there are expectations that gas prices on the world market will go quite low. In the medium term, we think gas prices will be low, assuming the Strait of Hormuz gets sorted.

Indeed. I n that economic scenario, are you building in the cost of carbon capture and storage and abated gas ? B ecause we are looking here at low-carbon solutions to meet the clean power action plan of 2030 . P rojecting ahead from where we are today, assuming no changes, is not really what we are after. What we are looking for is the alternatives and the production of abated gas as a transition fuel.
Well, exactly. We are on a transition pathway, but it takes time to scale up the alternatives , so I think just on the cost and scale of things —
Time is of the essence —s ix to 10 years if we are going to scale up some basic hydrogen infrastructure and put in place market incentives.

Hydrogen storage we could do, but we also need to scale up hydrogen production . The Government ha ve a target of 10 gigawatts of electrolysed capacity by 2030. That is clearly not going to happen. If you are very lucky, it might get to 1 gigawatt. T he first hydrogen allocation round, which has gone through, awarded 125 megawatts. The second round, which seems to have gone into limbo, would be taking it up to 1 gigawatt. I t is rather small compared with the 10-gigawatt target. S caling up hydrogen production is a real challenge and will take time, which is why I said that through the 2030s there is no realistic option apart from gas.

In parallel, you can do two things. You can scale up biomethane production, which will lower the carbon footprint of the methane that you use, and you can scale up CCS. On that transition pathway, you want to go as fast as you can with all of those routes , so scale up biomethane, scale up CCS, but as an insurance policy, do not throw away the gas power plants yet.

I accept that there would be low efficiency if you use d electricity to create hydrogen and then burn ed the hydrogen in the power station to create electricity. Can you just give a number on how much loss there would be from the original electrical power, and how does that compare with the inefficiencies of burning direct gas in a conventional gas power station?

If you start with renewable power, turning it into hydrogen has an efficiency of about 75%, and then putting it into a combined cycle gas turbine is probably about 55% or 60%. O verall, if you multiply those two together, you are a bit below 40% efficiency , roughly.

T here is absolutely no getting away from the physics of that ; there is a limitation . W hat I would say is that it is very important where you draw the boundary for measuring efficiency and system cost. There are a number of studies out there — again, we will reference those in our written submission — that show that the integration of hydrogen long-duration storage and dispatchable power generation alongside renewable generation and gas delivers the lowest total system cost. Y es, there is an efficiency point, but the total system efficiency and cost is the important factor, particularly for these Dunkelflaute events , where you do not have other options available to you.
Q26 Our molecular storage options have quite a lot of international ramifications, so how vulnerable are they to international supply issues? Who would like to begin?

I am happy to go first. As I mentioned earlier, the trump card for hydrogen as a molecular storage option is that you are using domestically produced renewable electricity to produce that hydrogen in the first place, so it is reducing your exposure to some of those international markets for gas and power.
We do not do that enough yet.

Not at the moment, no. The renewable generation buildout is happening . I am glad you asked that now . At the moment we are curtailing a lot of the renewable generation because we do not have either the demand or the transmission infrastructure to be able to handle that excess generation capacity. If we start rolling out electroly s ers in strategic locations to be able to absorb that, we can start maximising the use of our renewable generation assets. As s ome of NESO’ s modelling has pointed to , curtailment could reach 10% of total renewable generation by the mid-2030s, so something in the order of 35 to 40 terawatt hours per year. A lot of that could go into electrolytic hydrogen production that could be transported and stored and used again later.

In terms of the physical assets, so the hydrogen to power, the turbines and the compressors, of course the UK is still exposed to international supply chain pressures. Kish a has already given some indication that there is competition within that market already, even within traditional gas turbine and gas equipment, and we are expecting to see that also for hydrogen equipment.
On that, h ow high would you rate grid insufficiency? Is that one of the priorities?
In terms of electricity grid insufficiency ?
Yes.
I t is very high.
Very high?

It is obviously one of the key priorities for NESO, DESNZ and Ofgem at the moment. Another positive for the use of hydrogen is that you can move more energy cheaply via hydrogen pipelines than the equivalent energy capacity through power cables. I think it was a study by Martin ’ s organisation — and it is backed up by a similar study done by academics in the United States — that for a given energy output, you can move it more cheaply via pipeline than you can via electricity wires, so it can help alleviate some of that cost and pressure.
Could you give us a reference to the American work?
We absolutely will.
T hank you very much. Do you have a nything to add?

Yes. I do not think we should assume that hydrogen imports will be reliable in the sufficient volumes that we would probably need if we were to assume that it would be a significant part of the future system. Very few countries are currently producing sufficient quantities where there is a buoyant export market. There was some work published by the International Energy Agency this year that found that less than 8% of announced hydrogen export volumes had reached operation or committed investment, so it is worth just bearing that in mind.

I would just reiterate the point that Brett made, which is that we have the opportunity to produce hydrogen domestically, so before thinking about which countries we might want to consider as a reliable source of supply, we should absolutely think about exploiting our own domestic production abilities first and try to get as much value out of the current renewable generation fleet that we have available to us. So, yes, I am underscoring the point about resilient portfolios and not wanting to replace our current import dependency on gas with an import dependency on hydrogen.
That is good. Could we have the I E A reference too, please?
Yes, of course.
Do you have a nything to add?

I will add a couple of things. N atural gas is a globally traded commodity . E ven with the Hormuz crisis this year, there is still a lot of gas flowing around the world and there will continue to be, so in terms of security, natural gas provides that security, but with the caveat of needing to add on carbon capture and storage. In terms of domestic production, biomethane is a good source of secure domestic production based on local production from farms in the UK , so that is worth looking at as well.

On hydrogen, I have a couple of points to add. One is that transporting hydrogen over long distances is challenging and expensive. I said before that pipelines have been proven at a fairly small scale. Transporting hydrogen by ship has been tried, but that is very difficult. It is perhaps worth noting that i n the UK, we already produce about 13 terawatt hours of hydrogen. It is all high-carbon hydrogen, so in refineries and petrochemical plants, but we do produce a lot of hydrogen and it is nearly all used pretty much adjacent to where it is produced. T here is an evolution that could happen to migrate from current high-carbon hydrogen to lower-carbon hydrogen and that is something that could also kick-start the industry in some way. On hydrogen, we are talking about it for Dunkelflaute today, but there is a wider angle on looking at it from an entire energy system perspective.

May I interject here on that point about hydrogen interconnectors? Purpose-built hydrogen interconnectors , how robust are they and resilient to the historic issues around transporting hydrogen in older infrastructure such as gas pipes? Are they much more resilient and robust if they are purpose - built to deliver hydrogen?
I am not sure I understand the question.

The pipewor k—and w e are talking about interconnectors, intercontinental interconnectors —is it up to the job? We hear quite a lot about the way hydrogen can escape, the way hydrogen can cause brittleness in some of existing pipework. Is that an issue in purpose-built interconnectors transporting hydrogen?

There are not any long-distance interconnectors today. There are cross-border hydrogen pipelines between Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, but they are fairly small - scale. Technically they are robust. Politically they are exposed, I guess, to terrorist acts against them, so there is that security sense. P erhaps the bigger question is whether they are commercially and economically justifiable . That is still an open question, I think. The answer may well be that you are better off making hydrogen and using it locally. I do not see a global network of interconnectors like there is for gas currently.

I have one supplement ary . If nevertheless we do have to import some — and I quite take the point that it is better if we do not have to—t here is something , we are told , called the European Hydrogen Backbone, a collaborative initiative by 33 energy infrastructure operators which want to sort out a hydrogen infrastructure throughout Europe. Is that any use or is there anywhere else? We are also told about e astern Europe as a source of hydrogen. Is there a ny point in looking at that?

I believe there are certain feasibility studies that have been carried out on whether the UK or GB should and could connect to the European Hydrogen Backbone . S ome of those projects have applied for funding through what is called the IPCE I .
Please could you send us the reference to that . Thank you very much.

Yes. Those are projects of common interest within the EU. It very much depends on where the expected production and demand of hydrogen will fall as to where those cross-border — particularly interconnector s from UK to Europe —pipelines would arrive. Of course , Europe has some pretty ambitious targets for hydrogen consumption in order to be able to wean itself off Russian ga s. We could be producing more hydrogen than we need domestically , with the opportunity to sell into Europe , rather than the other way around , using Europe as a source for input.
That sounds nice. Okay , t hank you very much.

Thank you. Just before we finish this section, can I ask that you send us some further information on Project Union, as well as the NESO projection that a new 1.4-gigawatt interconnector with Germany will be in place by 2030 ? I have a reference for that : i t is the Resource Adequacy in the 2030s report. Thank you. Lord Lenn ie .

Q27 Thanks. Carbon capture and storage technology is part of the G overnment ’ s solution for the decarbonisation pathway to 2050. What progress has been made to date? Are there barriers to d eployment ? If so, what are they? The researchers have found that technol ogical immaturity, high capital intensity and historical policy inconsistency in G overnments are features of CCUS. It seems to me it is always in its infancy rather than at any point of maturity.

Yes , you are right. CCUS has moved from the policy development stage into the early construction phase. The G overnment ’ s initial programme is supporting two t rack 1 clusters. There is the E ast C oast Cluster in Teesside, and then there is the HyNet cluster in the north - east. That is currently backed by £21.7 billion worth of funding over a 25-year period. Construction has started on those projects and they are expected to be in operation in 2030 , I think, b ut I can come back and confirm those numbers for you. That includes the associated transport and storage infrastructure that is also required to enable that.

Some of the barriers are quite similar to what we have heard in hydrogen, where there is a need for supporting and enabling infrastructure in order for these projects to be in operation. The power station is only one part of the project. You can build the power station with the carbon capture technology on it, but you also need to build the CO ₂ transport network to transport that captured CO ₂ out into the depleted North Sea oil and gas field . That requires permits, commercial arrangements , and so on. It also needs to demonstrate reliability at scale, which it has not done in the UK in the power sector so far , so we need to take account of that. There are two other projects that the G overnment are considering or are the process of developing : the Acorn project in Scotland and Viking in the Humber.

T hings are moving in the right direction, but that is not to say that those projects have reached financial investment decision s . There is still a lot of negotiation and , as you have mentioned, these are very capital-intensive projects that also require a lot of co - ordination. T hose are the key barriers that we see. I think the key priority for us is to turn this from what is a first-of-a-kind technology for us in the UK into something that is scalable, and to move it from that nascent market into something that is slightly more mature, which requires less government de-risking to enable that private sector capital to come forward.

I will build on that a little bit. One thing to remember is that with the CCS projects, they are at a huge scale. If we compare , EET Hydrogen ’ s HPP1 project within HyNet is looking to develop in the order of 300 megawatts of hydrogen production from that one facility. As Martin mentioned, the total capacity that has been approved through HA R 1 for electrolytic hydrogen is only 125 megawatts , so it is at a very different scale in terms of being able to get a single project. As Kisha mentioned , co - ordinated execution is needed. You have the capture project itself, then you have the CO ₂ pi pelines, you have the stores and you have the commercial contracts that all have to hang off each other and be delivered in parallel. T here is progress, but it is a difficult task, for sure.

C arbon capture and storage, as I say, is essential for reaching our net - zero target so we need to make it work if we are going to achieve net zero , but it does need to scale up a lot. The UK track 1 projects are a great step forward for doing that b ecause we need to try it out : does it work as expected ? Much of the technology is proven . C apturing carbon is fine , w e know that works well , but if you look around the world at where it is been tried , Norway has been successfully storing carbon in the Sleipner and Snøhvit fields for a very long time —a great success. In Australia, by contrast, the environmental permit for the Gorgon project there said for its environmental permit that it would capture 4 million tonnes of CO ₂ per year and inject it. It has had loads of technical issues on the storage side , a nd I think at best it stores about 1.5 million tonnes a year. With CCS, we need to make it work. Technically it should be okay, but it is not without its challenges.

In order to make it work — and we have not talked much about the carbon price today — for a CCS project in the UK, it needs a carbon price a round £ 150 to £ 200 per tonne of CO ₂ . The last time I looked, the current market carbon price is about £ 60 or £ 70 a tonne , so we need to raise the carbon price and incentivise more CCS projects.
What causes the difference between the Norwegian success and the Australian lack of success?

I think it is geology. If you are injecting CO ₂ into a known disused hydrocarbon field, the geology is understood and you can inject it and you understand how it will work. In the Gorgon case, they inject it into an aquifer ; that is, where there is water stored under the ground . T hey intended that the water would get displaced as they pumped CO ₂ in , b ut the reality was that the pressure built up. T hey had to drill some additional wells to relieve the pressure and let the water out, and it gets very technical.
Do we have geology on our side ?
Geology is the short answer, I think.
We have that on our side.
I think so. I do not know enough about the particular projects, but we have a lot of disused hydrocarbon fields. W e should be okay, but we need to scale it up.
Your c olleagues are nodding.
Q28 Good morning and welcome. I remind the committee I have small interests in my portfolio in National Grid, BP and Shell.

The purpose of the i nquiry is to look at alternatives where the wind does not blow and the sun does not shine, but which are low - carbon. I n an earlier answer, Mr Lambert, you alluded to the fact that there will be carbon emissions from the conversion of hydrogen. H ow decarbonising , potentially , is this ?

Yes. I spoke about blue hydrogen. Current hydrogen production in the UK is done largely in refineries and petrochemical works from fossil fuels, and that emits carbon , as a rough number, at 10 tonnes of carbon per tonne of hydrogen that you produce. However, with the so-called blue hydrogen, you can capture most of, not all, the CO ₂ that you emit in making hydrogen. Y ou can capture that carbon and you can then, with CCS, store it , so t here are ways to mitigate that. I n general with CCS, even direct use of CCS in power generation, it is important to note that CCS can capture a large majority of the CO ₂ but not all of it. T here will always be some residual carbon emissions , which, if we are to achieve net zero, would need to be mitigated in some other way with carbon removals or something.
But you are using more energy to do that.
Correct.
There is a cost.
Yes , d ecarbonising is not going to be cheap.

I would like to refer to the 2023 report to Parliament from the Climate Change Committee, which stated that 12 to 20 gigawatts of low - carbon dispatchable capacity will be needed to replace unabated gas by 203 5 . It recommended that the G overnment should develop a portfolio-based strategy that includes hydrogen and gas with CCS . B ut then the Royal Society ’ s report on large-scale electricity storage , published in September 2023 , expressed reservations about the use of gas with carbon capture and storage and went on to say that it would lead to unacceptable emissions of CO ₂ and methane and also to higher costs .

Do you see hydrogen to power being able to compete with gas with CCS , abated gas, as the decarbonised dispatchable power source for 2040 and beyond or could both technologies play different roles? Shall I start with you , Mr Ryan?

I am happy to start. They will play different roles. We already mentioned at the start the portfolio of options that are needed to be able to provide true resilience across the differ ent timescales of how long you need that dispatchable power on the system. Even some recent modelling by the UK Energy Research Centre , which came out only in the last couple of months —i t will be in our written submission — shows that you need both technologies : power CCS and hydrogen to power. The point where hydrogen to power comes in is that 100 hours - plus duration of generation. I think that is where they have started to coin the term “ ultra - long - duration energy storage ” .

Kisha mentioned earlier the Ofgem cap and floor long - duration energy storage . T hat maxed out at about 22 hours of generation duration . Th e work by the UK ER C is looking at 100 hours - plus. It is taking it into days , weeks and longer , so it is not an either / or in terms of these technologies. The gas CCS will run at higher load factors , where as it is expected that hydrogen to power over 12 months will be running at single - figure or low - teens in terms of the load figure across the year.

Yes, I would agree. It is worth also consulting the most recent C limate C hange C ommittee ’ s s eventh c arbon b udget and its balanced pathway , which includes 15 gigawatts of low - carbon dispatchable power by 2040 . That is a combination of gas with CCS and hydrogen to power. I would agree that these technologies are not competing , that they are definitely serving different purposes and system requirements.

The really important thing is that there needs to be a clear plan from the G overnment on how they intend to facilitate the investment in these technologies and how we are going to bring them on to the system. The key challenge is that without that clarity , there is a risk that we are not able to invest in the current gas fleet , which is providing much of that system support at the moment , in terms of both security of supply and system operability . We would end up either prematurely retiring the gas plants that we have or investing in gas , further unabated gas , without a clear pathway of how that gas fleet decarbonise s . I would say that it is not an either / or choice . A gain , we support a portfolio of technologies that will each have different characteristics and system requirements , but the key thing is we need a really clear transition plan of how we get to that point.
One last question on that point . It cannot be the case that householders or taxpayers take the risk . By w hat means can you see that this will be commercially viable?
T here is certainly a question in here on what market mechanisms should look like to facilitate that investment.
We are coming on to that.
I am happy to answer that.
Thank you. Earl Russell , your question.

Q29 Good morning. Thank you for your evidence. I think everybody agrees that we need long - term and ultra-long-term energy storage as part of our energy mix and that is regardless of the Dunkelflaute. However, my question is about market mechanisms and what can be done to help improve them to support these emerging technologies and the particular issues. You have all talked about the need for market certainty in terms of investment and obviously these are new technologies, they are high - risk.

There are obviously different problems between long - term and ultra-long-term storage. In June we had an announcement of 7.6 gigawatts for LDS and the cap and floor mechanism. I think Energy UK has been critical to limitations of cap and floor. A s we move to ultra - long-term storage, those problems compound. W hat more can and should we be doing to help improve the market mechanisms for investment to bring these technologies to fruition ? Kisha , perhaps you would like to start.

Yes, I can kick off us off. It is important that markets are able to adequately value the services that these assets provide , even if they are running infrequently. F or the low - carbon alternatives such as hydrogen to power and power CCUS , the expectation is that they are not going to be providing a significant amount of power generation. They are going to be used in those Dunkelflaute periods where there is low renewable output. The capacity market , which is the primary mechanism through which we procure capacity for security of supply , is a key part of that framework.

The G overnment did consider something like a strategic reserve under their review of electricity market arrangements programme , and that involved considering whether to take gas capacity out of the electricity market and contracting it on a long-term basis to provide system back - up. We would be very cautious about taking gas generators out of the market because of the fact that we still rely on them so heavily for security of supply currently. They still provide over a third of our electricity in the system , so we are not at that point of considering something like a strategic reserve.

T he other thing to consider , though , is electricity capacity and gas storage being two very different things when you are thinking about strategic reserves. For example , a power station can provide electricity for as long as there is fuel available . We have already said that the UK benefits from quite a diverse supply of gas around the world , but declining domestic gas means that we should be stress - testing how resilient the system is in more extreme scenarios . There is potentially a case to be made about whether the G overnment could look at what market mechanisms should be shaped in order to support strategic energy infrastructure that is used infrequently but which provides insurance in those periods where it is highly valuable during an extended period of system stress.

This is something that the G overnment are looking at currently in their gas systems transition work . They published a consultation last year , which we responded to and suggested that they should look at making a targeted intervention where the market does not currently value that sort of insurance that it provides. They published an interim response over the summer , which suggested that they were looking at this , and we look forward to the full response.

The easy answer is that to encourage investment you need to give investors enough revenue confidence to make the investment . T here are different ways that policy can do that . There are a couple of examples relevant to this . W e talked before about the European H ydrogen B ackbone . The only part of that that progressed anywhere is in Germany , where they are building the Kernnetz, their core network , which is backed by the German f ederal G overnment . There are arguments about whether it is worth doing or not and it is quite expensive for g overnment to do .

T he trade-off clearly is the exten t to which g overnment back s it directly and fund s it or whether you pass it on consumers , but you need to find a way to give investors confidence . In the UK , with contracts for difference for renewable power , we have achieved that fairly well . A gain , I am not pushing b io methane too strongly , but if you wanted to encourage more bio methane , that would be where another contract for difference approach could work , because right now the current support scheme is ending and there is no confidence in what will proceed .

S imilarly , for uncertain carbon pricing , Germany has introduced a carbon contract for difference . T hat gives revenue certainty . T hat could work quite well as well . T hinking of ways you give revenue certainty is the answer , but there are many ways to skin that cat .

Are you confident that contracts for difference are capable of helping to meet the challenges of picking technologies and investing in ultra-long - duration energy storage or are there particular problems there that need other market mechanisms ? I guess the other side to that is : are the G overnment doing enough in terms of the actual market system they are providing for the ultimate development of ultra-long-term energy or is there more thinking the G overnment need to do in that space ?

I think it depends on the design of the contract for difference and the auction . There is always a danger in g overnment trying to pick winners , so it needs to be a market mechanism whereby the industry and technology can then choose the answer . That is not quite an accurate answer your question .
No, but I understand that complex relationship between markets, government, subsidy and technology.

Also u nknown technology , so finding a mechanism that can promote development of technology , but we do not try to pick winners when the technology might evolve . T hat is something that needs further work .

It is a complex dance. F rom H ydrogen UK , I do not know whether you want to comment on long - duration and ultra-long-term market mechanisms and where hydrogen fits into that financial sort of relationship .

I would echo the point that Kisha made right at the start of this question . It is about being able to adequately value the service that that storage is providing . As I mentioned earlier , the power sector is but one use of the hydrogen storage . T hose storage developers will have options to be using hydrogen to be stored for other sectors such as industry , so there has to be a market mechanism that values not just the megawatt generation capacity and the duration that it can do , but the availability , the guarantee that it will be there when it is needed and not used for anything else . There still needs to be further work on defining exactly how that happens within the support mechanisms .

T his is an ongoing and evolving space between technology , industry , G overnment and financial mechanisms . Kisha , going back to your point on the RAV on gas , when I saw that proposal , that was also about dispatchable power and gas . The unit price is the dispatchable power , so that is technology , but it is also the market mechanisms and transcending price from that unit that set s dispatchable power , I guess . That is two slightly different arguments coming together .

Yes. There is dispatchable power and then there is energy storable fuels . O ur perspective is that we are not at that place where we can credibly consider taking gas generation or dispatchable power out of the electricity market because it plays such a fundamental role currently , given that it produces over a third of our electricity generation today . W hen we get to a point in the 2030s where we have a clear er view of the of the pace and deployment of low -carbon alternatives and how much that has come to market and a clear review of the decarbonisation pathways for gas generators , then we can have that conversation . However, I think the capacity market remains a very efficient use and plays an important role.
They would be quite complex market changes . I guess they would take some time to prepare, if we chose to go down that route .
We know that the G overnment are currently considering reforms to the capacity market , so we would be very keen to understand what they have in mind.

Thank you . We are at 11.29 am and we have one further question . I just want to ask our panellists whether they are okay to stay with us a little bit over time. Thank you very much. Lord Trees , your question.

Q30 Thank you very much . T his session is about molecular storage , hydrogen , natural gas and bio methane. We have said very little about biomethane. I will come to hydrogen strategy in a minute, but , Martin, you have mentioned biomethane several times in a relatively positive way. That would be derived from crops, right, but is there a potential at scale from capturing from animals? We have millions of cows in Britain and they are housed all winter . I know work is going on in some places about that. Is that at all a feasible contribution to the issue of storage?

Yes. Biogas becomes biomethane . L andfill gas is one source of it. Farm waste, agricultural waste , is another. Sewage in the broader sense, so whether it be human sewage or animal waste, is also a source . All of that can be put into the digester and can produce biogas , so it does come from a range of different sources.
What about capturing from live animals in houses ? Most dairy cattle are put in houses all winter.

I am not sure , t o be honest . I will check on that and get back to you with a written answer, but I think that may be too dilute to make it significant at scale . Like everything in the energy system, getting things to enough scale is a key challenge. We can do more in biomethane in the UK and keep it sustainable . A question for g overnment is indeed what policy there should be to promote biomethane , but without getting it too much, so you get beyond that sustainable level. T here is more we can do in that space.
In g rowing crops, we would deprive us of food , so there are trade-offs.

No, because it should be biowaste. Y ou grow the crops for crops. You grow sweetcorn, for exampl e. Y ou eat the sweetcorn, but the green stuff that goes around it you do not want, so you can put that into a digester , so it is a waste that comes along with growing crops. What you want to avoid is repurposing land that otherwise would grow food , for growing energy crops. That is not the idea.

Can I just interject here, Lord Tre e s ? I will come back to you . In terms of low-carbon biomethane sources, we need BECCS alongside that. How well developed is bioenergy and carbon capture storage?
BECCS is different. BECCS is you grow the bioenergy —
It is methane you are burning. You will still generate carbon dioxide. You need to capture and store that carbon dioxide . How do you do that?

If you do that, you get negative emissions. BECCS is a way to get negative emissions, because with biomethane, the carbon in it is “ good carbon ” , I would call it, because it has been captured more recently.
Finally , the hydrogen strategy : the G overnment have suggested that t hey are going to produce one in due course. Do we know when that is and what do you expect from a hydrogen strategy?
Do you want to go first?

I want to very quickly say , just on the biomethane point, that we are also very positive about biomethane, and we think that it does also have the potential to scale. There was a report by the Green Gas Group, which has some estimates of biomethane producing around 120 terawatt hours per year by 2050. T hat is a high-end estimate, but we think it is worth exploring. I will hand over to you on hydrogen and then I will come back.

When do we think the strategy will be released? We would love for it to be a surprise announcement this afternoon, but we carry on waiting. There are a few things here. Our members have been waiting quite patiently on a number of funding and allocation updates that can happen without the strategy itself. I mportantly, the second allocation of the electrolytic hydrogen production projects has been stalled since early last year. Those projects need to go through to what we call the invitation to offer stage, so that the developers and the investors know that there is still confidence that the UK and the G overnment are still serious about hydrogen. Similarly with the transport and storage, that first regional network, there was a £500 million commitment that came through in the last spending review in the industrial strategy. That is great, but we need to see that actually launch, and then a timeline and plan for when future networks will be allocated.

As we talked about today, most of the salt caverns that we are going to be relying on for ultra-long - duration energy storage are located near clusters , s o there is a regional network buildout required to go with it , a credible pathway for production projects beyond those current HAR 1 and HAR2 allocations and , importantly, the launch of the hydrogen to power business model. As I said earlier, you need production, infrastructure and the power generation for this all to work. Those are the absolute minimums we would need to see from a strategy or announcements beforehand.

Yes, I think I would agree with that. I would add what I mentioned earlier around clarifying the role of hydrogen and setting out where g overnment think s that it adds the most value so that we can understand where it fits in the broader picture of that portfolio of flexible technology. R esolving some of the outstanding market questions, particularly around how hydrogen might play in the capacity market, is crucial for investors to understand what routes to market look like.

Y es, the question o f when it is coming —it would be good if DESNZ gave us some indication of what its thinking is, because it was expected earlier this year . It has been very silent and we do not understand why. Similarly , with h ydrogen a llocation r ound 2 , there was a shortlisting done — if I remember right ly—in April 2025, so well over a year ago. We would expect that to have been confirmed this year. Again, there has been radio silen ce from DESNZ and we are not quite sure why. Perhaps you should ask it.

On t he other thing you mentioned, in 2026 there was going to be a decision about the role of hydrogen in home heating. I think it is pretty widely recognised, unless Brett refutes me, that hydrogen home heating is not going to happen because of the inefficiency issue. Heat pumps for home heating, or district heating, are clearly the route to go but not hydrogen heating. Similarly, electric cars have come a long way since 2021, so EVs for transport, not hydrogen for transport, that has to be the answer. However, for aviation and maritime, there is a clear role for e-fuels derived from low-carbon hydrogen. I think the new strategy needs to be clear where the priorities are and what the pathway is to get there . H aving that would be a real help to investors and moving everything forward.
That is very helpful, thank you.

T hank you. We are at 11.37 am. T here are several colleagues who are bursting to ask further questions. I want to give them a chance, but we have run out of time in this forum. If those colleagues could please email their questions to Lily and Al a stair, we will make sure that the panel has an opportunity to address them. I apologise to colleagues, but I think that is probably the fairest way to proceed.

Thank you very much to our expert panel . It has been fascinating to hear your perspectives . I remind you that the written evidence that you have already committed to send to us would be very much appreciated . If you could bear with us and answer further questions from colleagues, that would be much appreciated also. With that, I bring today ’ s public session to a close and the committee will now move into private session.

Health and Social Care Committee m embers present: Layla Moran (Chair); Jen Craft; Josh Fenton-Glynn; Andrew George; Joe Robertson; Gregory Stafford .
Education Committee members present: Helen Hayes (Chair); Sureena Brackenridge; Jodie Gosling; Darren Paffey; Mark Sewards; Peter Swallow; Caroline Voaden .
Layla Moran took the Chair.

Witnesses

I : Professor Peter Fonagy, Chair, Independent Review into Mental Health Conditions, ADHD and Autism; Professor Gillian Baird, Vice-Chair, Independent Review into Mental Health Conditions, ADHD and Autism.
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Professor Gillian Baird and Professor Peter Fonagy .

Q221 Welcome to this joint session of the Health and Social Care and Education S elect Committee s. This is the fourth session of our inquiry into young people and children’s mental health services. It is a delight to have with us today Professor Peter Fonagy and Professor Gillian Baird of the now infamous Fonagy r eview. I t has been a week since it has come out, and it has been very widely reported.

Can I start by asking a very simple question ? How d id you come to be the one to be asked to do this review? What is your background , so that those who may be less familiar with it understand the expertise that you bring to bear on this area ?

Thank you for asking , and thank you for having us here. We are really pleased to be able to present to you. By background, I am a clinical psychologist . I have been working in child mental health for four decades, which is quite a long time. Since 2011, I have been senior clinical adviser to NHS England in the child mental health policy team. I have really enjoyed it. That is probably the reason why I was asked — I was familiar with the system and had clinical experience that seemed appropriate to the task.

I was asked to be co- v ice c hair with Professor Sir Simon Wessely , who is not with us today but who m I suspect many of you know. By way of background, I am a paediatrician . I specialised in p a ediatric neurodisability and was a consultant running a large service at Guy ’ s and St Thomas’ for rather more years than Peter has been. I was also much involved in NIC E and various guidelines and research into areas relevant to this review.

Q222 People can read the over - 600-page report too, if they want to, but , Professor Fonagy, could you very briefly outline the top recommendations that you made? While you do that, could you underline the recommendations that you think are the low-hanging fruit , and which ones you think might be more challenging to implement?

The low-hanging fruit will be a little bit challenging , but I will try. The review proposes a radically different model of managing children’s mental health. It is a shift from a diagnosis - led system , where people have to wait to get a diagnosis in order to get support, to a system where , as soon as they present with a need, that need get s addressed and they are then prioritised for a diagnosis if needed, but in the hope that in many instances it will not be. Th is means that they would receive support earlier in relation to what they actually need, because , surprisingly, diagnosis does not tell you what people need. After you have a diagnosis, it still needs to be figured out what it is that you require. That seemed to us illogical. I emphasise that diagnostic assessment and specialist services remain essential in this system. We are not trying to downgrade the service. It needs to be protected and strengthened.

We called for a number of other changes, which are perhaps ambitious . A stronger focus on prevention, a public health approach to wellbeing, and tackling the social and environmental drivers that we identified for the increasing prevalence of common mental disorders, particularly in children and young people but across all ages, seemed to us to be important .

We also identified that the current system was incompatible with delivering effective prevention. The system that we are proposing is far more aligned to a system where targeted prevention is aligned with offering support at the point when people present with need. We argued that we need to create conditions for people to stay well rather than relying predominantly on specialist services.

There are j ust a couple more things that are really essential to our logic. This has been recommended because of the very high level of co- occurrence of neurodevelopmental disorders and common mental disorders.
Q223 What do you mean specifically by that ? Just break it down for a non-clinician like me.

For a non-clinician , i t is that a person who is diagnosed with ADHD or a utism is likely , in the majority of cases , to also have common mental disorders of anxiety, depression or self-harm , or an eating disorder. T hat means that , in order to deal effectively with both common mental disorders that carry with them traits of autism and other neurodevelopmental problems such as ADHD, it is essential that the assessments occur as part of a single system. That does not m ean it is the same assessment or a single assessment, but it does mean that it is an integrated assessment.

At the moment, people get put on one of three pathways, as I am sure you know. That is an inefficient system . That sometimes requires people to be assessed a number of times and wait on a number of wait ing lists before they acquire a diagnosis.
There are other things that we recommended that we will perhaps come around to being able to talk about.

T hank you for that . I have a constituent who has been on a CAMHS waiting list for an autism diagnosis for seven years. They are now 15. The time has passed to help them in their schooling. I am sure every MP here and many listening will relate to that.

Q224 One of the experiences we all have as local MPs is exactly as Layla describes there, hearing from families who are very distressed that their young people are not getting the support that they need.

A nother thing that we will all be familiar with is others telling us that it is all down to the snowflake generation, and that the mental health crisis we are seeing in our young people is because they just are not resilient enough. Your report rejects that idea. Could you perhaps just explain why you reached that conclusion and the evidence that lies behind that ?

You asked two questions. I will answer the second one and maybe turn to Professor Baird to answer the first . The “ snowflake generation ” is an insult to young people . I challenge all of you here to cope with the pressures that young people are under and to sustain the quality of childhood and young adulthood that you all were privileged to experience .

You did not have two major categories of pressures. One is increased stress . I can go into detail in relation to this, but increased stress is financial; that is well known. It is about insecure work, unaffordable rents and so on . Also, there is increased stress in terms of social media and social comparisons that are incessant, and educational pressures. We have evidence for that. Again, I can go into that, but it seems that young people are less well protected and less well supported . That is the second category of issues.

It is recorded that they have a lower sense of belonging to their schools. They do not feel that they belong, but it is not just schools. There has been a 73% reduction in youth services that are funded by local authorities since 2011. They do not have other young people to go to.

Finally, in terms of the lack of protection, I want to mention what we found particularly important, which is the opportunity for recovery, which is unstructured play. That is not just about youth clubs, but just being able to sleep. If you have social media that keeps you awake , stops you from sleeping and reduces face-to-face interactions, you will have less capacity to cope.

When you and I were young, we had friends . W e went to see friends when we were in trouble. If that is taken away and replaced by mobile phones, they have greater stress and less support. I would reject the idea that it is a snowflake generation .
The other question was particularly a bout waiting lists .
That was more of a flavour to get into the question. We will come back to that.
We will be coming back to waiting lists. Fear not.

Q225 I do not want to steal anyone else’s thunder on that question. R eally , I just wanted to follow up on a very helpful answer about this idea of a snowflake generation being an insulting narrative. Why do you think it has gained such traction despite the lack of evidence for it? How do we combat it?

I am going outside the report slightly and now expressing my personal views. This is not so much about me, because I am on the other side of this, but looking at you, most of you are of a generation that was brought up believing that you r future would be better than your parents ’ . The current generation are convinced , and rightly so, that they will not have the opportunities that their parents had.

That sense of hopelessness has been demonstrated . This is an empirical fact. T hat is part of their beliefs, but it is also part of our beliefs about them . It is an enormously powerful influence , b ut it also makes us feel somewhat guilty in relation to them. T herefore, it is much easier for us to say they are a snowfla ke generation than for us to say, “ Actually, we have really messed it up for them, and it is our fault . ”

If you think back, c ovid was the first time that I can remember when our generation , the adult generation , brought in a way of adjusting to a major health crisis that advantaged adults and disadvantaged children and young people. Mostly, the priority is given to the new generation , but for whatever reason — I am not here to blame anyone — we decided that our health was more important than theirs .
Q226 T hat is a profoundly challenging answer. It is challenging to all of us here. I just briefly reflect that, with AI coming down the track as well, it is not at risk of getting easier .

The other prevailing narrative that we hear a lot is that the rise in need reflects better diagnosis and identification of mental ill health by practitioners. That is perhaps slightly less of a pernicious myth, but nevertheless it is one that you also rejected in your report. Could you again just say a little about how you came to that conclusion?

T he first thing to say is that there is no evidence of overdiagnosis . We did not find evidence. To some extent, the studies have not been done. Nobody has take n a very large number of people with one diagnosis and had another group of people then examine them to see whether they would come to the same conclusion. That would be the obvious way to answer this question. Despite a huge amount of anecdote, report and opinion, there was no evidence, and this is a highly evidence-based review.

We did find evidence of misdiagnosis , where somebody would have a diagnosis of one condition and another condition was not recognised that might better explain their difficulties. This comes back to the co-occurrence, which is a central feature of the review.

The obvious examples are with eating disorders; only more recently are people recognising that many of those affected have autism as well, which has an influence on the management of the condition. You could be diagnosed with autism when somebody else might think that your major problem was ADHD or anxiety or another mental health problem. The way in which services are so often organised as single-diagnosis pathways means that you go for an assessment where the answer is, “Yes you do have this, ” or “ N o , you do not , ” and then you may have to rejoin a completely different pathway for an integrated assessment of what the main problems might be.

The other thing is that , when we looked at the number of people with a common mental disorder such as anxiety or depression, you might think the first thing would be that perhaps people have much milder problems these days. That is not what the evidence found . The evidence found that the level of impairment was as high or sometimes higher. The symptoms were causing greater impairment, so it is not a milder problem.

There are various other possible explanations for why the number of people with a diagnosis of ADHD or autism might be rising. I am happy to go into those, but there may be some other questions about those. There is a broader understanding of some of these difficulties. There have been diagnostic criteria changes. Of course, while the underlying traits, features and symptoms of neurodevelopmental conditions are heavily genetically influenced, the impairment that people experience is a result of the interaction of genetic predisposition with environment.

Q227 I would now like to talk a little bit about the drivers of mental distress that you refer to in the report. You talked about several things including emotional pressure, social media, economic uncertainty and reduced social connectedness . I notice, Professor Fonagy, that you have already talked about social media . You refer quite a lot to sleep in the report . W e know that sleep is really important to good health . Being on phones late at night is a real barrier to good sleep.

Is it possible for you to quantify the extent to which each of these pressures is driving demand , where you think the main focus should be , and where the priority should be in the Government’s response ?

T hat i s a brilliant question . As with all brilliant questions, I cannot answer it. There is an honest reason why I cannot answer it, which is that they are interacting. I f influences interact , it is very hard to see which came first: the egg or the chicken.

There are three things that I can say with confidence. One is that, as I have already said, they are not making it up, but the language has changed. A wareness of mental disorder has changed so that it has become a psychological language. The same level of distress that a person might feel today is more likely to drive them towards getting mental health support than it used to. That may seem like a negative, but it is actually a positive because we can help these people.

In terms of the drivers, there is a lot of negative content on social media and I do not want to minimise that. I do not want to be an apologist for social media, but it displaces things that are protect ive rather than simply causing harm.

I am mentioning that because of the second part of your question , about what the Government can do. B y banning social media broadly, we can not achieve quite as much , because the same distress that drives people towards social media and to seek answers from social media will still be there even if you ban it, except with less support.

It is really important that the good things that it displaces can be encouraged and supported. For example, if social media displaces physical exercise, we can encourage it. If social media displaces face-to-face interactions, we can create situations where they are enhanced. If it causes problems with sleep, we can have good ways of dealing with sleep problems. You cannot force people to go to sleep, but you can put on an alarm clock and make them wake up, which is a very simple measure of dealing with sleep disorder that we have used for a number of years.

I have one final thing, which touches on the earlier point that I made. One thing that we could all do in relation to discouraging children from overusing social media is to use our own social media less. The number of people who are engaged with their cell phones rather than face-to-face interactions over meals is appalling. Of course, it sets a model for young people because they are there to learn from us. H uman beings learn by looking at adults and seeing what they do. If we set an appalling model, can we be surprised that they do appalling things?

Q228 T here is quite a movement now for delaying the purchase of smartphones for children g oing in to secondary school , and not having one at 11, but pushing it back. Do you think that just not having a device until young people are older would perhaps make them more resilient?

Young people are very resilient , remarkably so, but at the same time I want to emphasise that they are also shrewd. A ny attempt at some kind of G overnment injunction to deprive them of something that they feel that they need is less likely to be successful than we hope. We can do a great deal to change social norms and expectations on them, and to emphasise, as I said, activities that are displaced by social media.

I do a lot of advising parents about how they should bring up their children, and there is one piece of advice that I give above all: stop criticising your child and notice when they do something that you want them to do ; r einforce and e ncourage that . We need to be less spiteful and less depriving in our approach to young people, and far more encouraging. T hat is a general shift that your advice to Government could probably take forward.
Q229 Last, I have a private M embers ’ B ill about outdoor education .
Thank you for that .

I believe that getting children outside is a very cheap way of improving children’s mental health, sense of belonging, wellbeing and all of that. C ould you tell us how important you think it is for children to be outside more and to be in nature?
The reduction of green space correlates positively with the increase in mental health issues for young people and the decrease in wellbeing. I am sure you are very familiar with those statistics.

Obviously, being outside is an opportunity. This is irrelevant, but my father, in order to enhance my resilience, made me wear short trousers throughout winter. T hat was in Hungary , in a continental climate. I do not think it made me more resilient. It is not about being exposed; it is the opportunities that it brings with it, which is communication with other young people.

F rom age 8 through to age 11 or 12 , there is a shift in the interest s of young people from their parents as the primary influence to other young people being the primary influence . If we deprive them of having that opportunity, we deprive them of the major way that their genes have enabled them to integrate with modern culture. You are doing God’s work.

Q230 Thank you for the evidence so far . It has been quite difficult for me because in one breath I agree with everything you say , and then you say something else that I fundamentally disagree with . It has been interesting, but I totally agree with you on the c ovid point. Locking our children away was probably the worst thing we did, and we should never do that again .

Before I go on to my main questions, I want to clarify something you seem to be suggesting , which I have not heard before. You seem to be suggesting that a number of societal factors are having a significant impact on diagnoses of people’s mental health. This then begs the question that, if those societal factors are removed or improved , are you saying that people who have been diagnosed with ADHD could, for want of a better phrase, get better?

As Professor Baird very eloquently explained , any neurodevelopmental disorder such as ADHD is a combination of biological predisposition and environmental pressures. If you live in an environment that is stressful, it will bring forth traits that you h ave that you were born with.

Q231 I f I can drill down into that, for example, I am someone with light skin and red hair —well, it used to be red. I have a genetic predisposition to skin cancer because of those factors, but if I do not go out in the sun or I put factor 50 on all the time, I am less likely to get skin cancer.

Am I being very reductive in this? Are you saying that you might have a predisposition to ADHD but , if the societal factors are vastly improved, not in every case but in some cases, you would not develop ADHD ? I am using non-medical language here. I t is not a disease; it is a condition. It is a multifactor i al condition. I am trying to understand what you are saying here.

I am saying that it is a continuum . It is not something that you either have or do not have. I will turn to the local expert here to answer the question, but let me just emphasise one thing . Maybe you could give one of your favourite examples on this.

“A ttention deficit ” is actually a misnomer ; i t is attention regulation that is the problem . Hyperactivity is a way that people with ADHD cope with the problem of attention regulation. For example, the subjective inner restlessness they feel is reduced by hyperactivity. It is a continuum, as indeed most disorders are, between environmental and situational demand. When the disadvantages in mental abilities become disabling, it is more difficult to cope with the demands of modern life, and you struggle more . That moves you over to a threshold that is, ultimately, arbitrarily defined.

Q232 Yes , and I am not in any way trying to suggest that the condition does not exist . I fully accept that it absolutely does. As we would do with anything , I am trying to look at how we prevent and cure. We have talked a lot about how we diagnose and how we deal with that diagnosis, but we do not seem to talk , in these areas , about prevention and cure. Maybe that is for another time.
There is a very good example that Professor Baird can give.

I will certainly try to move that forward slightly , because it is helpful to consider a dynamic interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental circumstances. For ADHD particularly, the demands for attention and the demands on the executive function will make more manifest.

First of all, here is a figure. I f you have a common mental disorder and are aged 16 to 24 — that is anxiety or depression — 60% will screen positive for a utism traits and for inattention or traits of ADHD. That brings up the likelihood that the dynamic interaction with the environment will occur, that the problems will become more manifest, and that you will probably come into a diagnostic category.

The example that Peter was referring to that is sometimes a helpful way to think about this is with t ype 2 diabetes . Type 2 diabetes is a well-described medical condition with a genetic predisposition . I f a combination of the genetic predisposition , lifestyle and particular features , such as being overweight , all come together, your blood sugar is in difficulties because of the insulin resistance. T he diagnosis of diabetes becomes manifest . If you reduce the lifestyle factors and the obesity, the diabetes can disappear, but if you have that combination of problems for long enough, you get secondary effects, so you will get a cumulative impact that then has secondary effects that are much more difficult to diminis h. Is that helpful?
Q233 That is certainly an interesting example . I have some other questions on the paper that I am going to go into, but perhaps we can come back to it at another point.
I hope that was a sufficient example of the sort of principle that one could apply. It is a hypothesis, but it has some merit.

Q234 Thank you very much . Moving on to some of your recommendations , in recommendation 5 , you essentially looked at a complete overhaul of the commissioning, funding, oversight of the system, et cetera. What change s do you propose to improve the ADHD and autism diagnostic and treatment pathways? Specifically, which change do you think would have the greatest impact on improving the waiting times ?

The most important is to integrate the mental health and neurodevelopmental disorder assessment so that , if you have problems and y o u come in for assessment, you will be having an assessment of all the possible contributory factors. If you have one problem, you are so much more likely to have another. To miss that then has a huge impact on the level and appropriateness of support that you are likely to achieve.

That is going to be one of the most important things that we can do, rather than these separate pathways. A huge amount of duplication is currently going on . P eople have an assessment in one place, then in another. There is a lot of duplication. Integration , both of assessment and then of services following that , is one of the most important recommendations that will help.

Q235 I n terms of that balance , are you suggesting that changing how the support is accessed and delivered is a greater priority , for example, than just increasing capacity overall ? They are both important, but that is your view.

Yes, a bsolutely . I f all you did was to increase capacity, you would not do a very good job at all. The system as it stands at the moment is not the right one for meeting people’s needs early and then providing appropriate and comprehensive assessment.
Q236 W hat do the Government or the NHS need to do to provide this “no wrong door” access? What are the practical steps?

T here are several . The first one that should be emphasised is changing the sequence from a sequence that is , “ W ait, assess, diagnose, support , ” to something that is , “ R ecognise need, then understand need , then begin support, then establish diagnosis where it changes, and then review and adapt as needed . ”

This is a radical change that has been implemented in a number of places. As we cite in our review, we try to seem original, but we are not. This has been discovered. It only works though, as is also documented in the review, if it is sufficiently well supported. To have a needs-based system without adequate support creates a problem rather than solving one.

We are asking for two things. One is further resources to support that needs-based system. The second is a reorganisation that is more efficient than anything that is in place now. The combination of the two will ultimately lead to a reduction in cost because of earlier intervention.

At the moment, we have a system where you gatekeep in order to be able not to treat. With children and young people particularly, if you wait long enough, the treatments that we have are not helpful. It is setting thresholds at a level where you can no longer intervene effectively. It is a particularly mindless thing to do . I t is understandable, but all the evidence is that moving support earlier makes the treatments that we have far more effective. If you wait even for two weeks, the likelihood of a condition getting worse is something like 20% ; i f y o u wait for six months, it is 75%. Reducing waiting lists is really a key part of what we are recommending.

Q237 This is a really specific question. On the CQC regulation recommendation, what is your reasoning behind the thought of banning public advertising for NHS-funded assessment ? Where is the evidence there?

It is very simple . You have a system where people are incentiv i sed by the number of diagnoses they do, and y o u enable them to drive up demand through advertising, which the NHS has to pay for. That is an avoidable problem.
Demand is driven up , but previously you said that levels of diagnosis had not gone up.
We are going to come back to this.
K eep that thought, and I will leave it there. Thank you very much.
Josh Fenton-Glynn might well go down this rabbit hole. Thank you for setting it up.

Q238 Before I pick up on that particular rabbit hole, I want to go back to a rabbit hole that you had at the start of your conversation with Greg. It was quite interesting talking about how culture and education culture has probably led to a rise in diagnosis.
