I thought I was back in an A-Level psychology class talking about the social model of disability again, but I wonder if there is a factor that , since Michael Gove, education has been more focused on a specific, strict type of education while society has moved in a different direction in terms of the education economy , and whether that has led to more people being likely to present with ADHD symptoms in an education environment?

Yes is the answer . The changes meant that people felt that the only way that they could get support was through diagnosis . The number of EHCPs—the education, health and care plans — just went up like that after 2014 .

Also, diagnoses changed; that is the other interesting feature. We have talked a little bit about co-occurrence and the importance of not just thinking about things in terms of single diagnoses. In 2016, for example, the proportion of people with a special educational need who had a learning disability was something like 15%. That halved by 2025, whereas the autism has gone like that. It is not only the number going up, but the contents.
Q239 Just to clarify, what would a classic learning disability be as compared to autism?

A general learning disability means having intellectual disability across the board. The number of pupils diagnosed with that has gone down , whereas other diagnoses have gone up. The main answer to your question is that after 2014 there was a change.
Q240 T hat was in terms of both the classification of what got support and the way that the general education system works .
Sheer numbers and the classification, ye s.

Q241 I t seems to be the case that people just do not feel they can get support another way. If I look at my local ICB , West Yorkshire , the cost of the neurodiversity service has risen from £3 million in 2022-23 to £25 million in 20 25 - 26 , which is clearly unsustainable. Do you think that the model that you suggest , having support before diagnosis , would make a significant difference to that ?

W e would not have suggested it if we did not think it did . People ask us sometimes if we are optimistic about change and whether some of this is going to be implemented. Our response to that is that, unless there is change, we are going to have such a catastrophic set of problems that change is inevitable.

The question is how we can change . What we are suggesting here is a feasible, practical pathway that has been tested and shown to work, which is early intervention linked to prevention. The costs are so high and the processes involved are so frequently bidirectional that the solutions that we propose actually cause the problems later down the line .

I cannot mention the person, but in one of the media encounters that we have had recently since the release , a person presenting to me said, “ I just had my child assessed . It was privately done . I t was a 20-minute assessment of the child, a one-hour assessment of us as parents, we got the diagnosis of autism and that was it. Now what do we do? ”

Q242 Fundamentally, that is what this comes down to. There is a lot of problematising lots of people going through these assessments , as if they are the problem, but at the centre of that is usually a parent who is worried that their kid is not getting the support they need for education.
Yes, a bsolutely .

Q243 U ltimately, that is where it i s falling down . I wonder if you think a rising tide would lift all boats in some of this. If we assessed need rather than disability, would that not be better for all children going through an education system, not simply those children who happen to cross the line into neurodivergence ?

Yes, a bsolutely. A t the moment, we are in a system that def i nes children and young people in terms of their limitations. We should be in a system that describes them in terms of their potential . If that change was made systematically across the board, instead of problems, there would be opportunities for enhancing an individual’s capacity.
That means focusing on their functioning, which is linked to need. You meet them where the limitations in their function are. You support them, and suddenly the problem changes.
Q244 T hat comes back to the earlier discussion about whether society disable s them. Of course it does, because it focuses on what they cannot do.
I can give you a nice clinical example at some point, but maybe we do not have time for that.

Q245 T he R ight to C hoose assessment is something that every Member of Parliament with an inbox has come across. Th is is the idea that people have a right to choose to have a private assessment after a certain time. I n West Yorkshire , there is a two -year minimum wait for that . I use that example just because it is my local ICB so it is closer to me. T hat is over 10% of someone’s educational experience. Is R ight to C hoose working as a model?

I t is important to say that w e did not recommend aboli shing R ight to C hoose , but we did recommend prioritisation. At the moment, as Professor Baird said, there is a major issue in relation to the population changing for those who meet criteria. Pare n ts are not looking for a label; parents are looking to help their child to deal with the challenges that the child face s . If we change the system so that what it offers is support for the parents, R ight to C hoose becomes an irrelevance except for in the cases where it is not.

You will be familiar with this from your own ICBs . In terms of the proportion of the ir resource that is currently going to R ight to C hoose , the costs of that are far higher than perhaps the NHS cost would be. It then means that there is nothing available to support the families afterwards.

Y ou cannot possibly blame parents . They are doing the right thing for their child. They want a diagnosis. They think it will help . Of course, they are going to do whatever they possibly can in order to get that, but it is not followed by anything. You can find that, “I have my diagnosis. My child has autism and may be non-verbal. What is going to follow?” They fall into a hole. That is not the way to manage these situations.

Q246 A lot of the private providers have an incentive to find people who have those issues. Do you think more needs to be done to regulate the private providers to make sure that they are coming out with good results ? I think I know the answer to this.

That is a major recommendation that we hav e. It needs to be something that is probably developed by NICE and then implemented with CQC oversight . It is a very simple thing. It applies to most conditions. Why not this one?
I suspect that will be in this Committee’s recommendations as well.

Q247 This is a very brief supplementary. I declare an interest as the chair of the a ll - p arty p arliamentary g roup on l earning d isability. I was fascinated to hear that learning disability diagnoses have halved. Do you think part of that could potentially play into the misdiagnosis , around autism particularly? M aybe people are seeing that as the route to go through to get support for their child, and that is , in fact , perhaps obscuring an underlying learning disability

Yes, I do . I t is also probably obscuring underlying difficulties of a variety of sorts, such as speech and language impairment and other specific learning difficulties such as dyslexia. There are a number of conditions that co-exist. If you do not look for them, they can be overlooked. Of course, our report was particularly about the combination of common mental disorders, severe anxiety and the neurodevelopmental disorders. They are all interlinked.

Q248 Thank you. That sets me up very well for the questions I want to ask . I might give you a slight break, Professor Fonagy, and direct them at Professor Baird , because they are about data and the underlying data about misdiagnosis, overdiagnosis and so on. You touched on it earlier.

In your report, you talk about how the balance of risks of underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing. You then say that you need more evidence to be able to determine whether or not and how this is changing over time. From your perspective, what should we be recommending to Government that they do now as a matter of course to make su re that that evidence base exists for where we are now? What needs to happen moving forwards so that we can check whether these interventions or any others are working?

First of all, we have some good evidence, which the report refers to, in the A dult P sychiatric M orbidity S urvey, which was done relatively recently , in 2024. When it came to conditions such as autism and ADHD, there is no recent population survey in England , which was the geographic area that was the focus of our report, since 2017. W e are relying, therefore , for information on population prevalence , on rather old data.

Q249 Is that because it did not happen due to c ovid , or is it just that it is ad hoc commissioned by Government ? Is this something that just needs to be commissioned more regularly on a rolling basis? I wanted to understand.
That is absolutely right ; it is the latter. There have been attempts to do so. It is a recommendation. That would make a huge difference if we had that regularly, yes.
Q250 W hat would need to happen? I t simply needs commissioning and money, presumably.
Commissioning, yes , and a certain amount of money , but not a vast amount. People are ready , willing and just waiting and very much hoping that that is going to follow.

Q251 Y ou have answered most of this , but I just want to make sure we have not missed any points. You say that misdiagnosis can particularly do harm . Professor Fonagy, you nodded most emphatically. Can you describe what harm it is that we are potentially doing with misdiagnoses ? What would stop misdiagnoses from happening?

I magine a young person who does not want to go to school , wakes up in the morning already exhausted, and complains about attention problems but also complains of an overwhelming experience they have in social contexts in school.

The p arents are obviously out of their mind with anxiety. They go and the child gets referred, because of complaining of attention problems, to the ADHD pathway for assessment. That child, while waiting on the pathway, gets more anxious and the problems get worse.

If we intervened in terms of addressing the attention problems by getting that child to sit closer to the teacher, to get written instructions, and to have the available, simple anxiety reduction that mental health support teams can deliver, it may we l l be that the attention problems would quieten, and that you would not have that difficulty.

The harm that it does is that the problems that are most likely to be resolvable are not addressed in a timely manner ; they get worse as a consequence of waiting. That is very simple. Misdiagnosis is not simply making a mistake; it is missing an opportunity for effective intervention.
Q252 That is b ecause o f the delay , primarily .

It is b ecause of the delay . If the child gets put on, say, stimulant medication because the anxiety reduction treatment did not deal with it , you are still in a situation where you have put many of the ways of addressing that child’s problem already in place , so you are more likely to be successful. M issing the diagnosis of anxiety in that case is a major problem, and that probably happens quite a bit, as Professor Baird explained, because of the way that mental health problems can drive it.

Q253 In that example, is that not underdiagnosis , because there is a condition that has not been diagnosed as part of it, or is that a misdiagnosis because , in fact , that child does not have ADHD ? You say that they are co-occurrent, but I am trying to pin it down for the sake of the parents watching who are now worried that their child who is on medication, for example, may not need to be. Can you try to unpick it for their sake?

If they were put on medication , I am not saying that that is unlikely. All the evidence that we have suggests that people put on medication and diagnosed now have problems as profound as they ever did, as Professor Baird mentioned.

I am saying that there may be others for whom, as Professor Baird described, we are missing the opportunity to intervene in a dynamic interaction between environmental pressures and genetic predisposition , in a way that may be able to afford the possibility of dealing with the problem before medication and diagnosis.

Q254 What do you say to parents who want a diagnosis to better understand how to help their children ? I have had many in my own surgery who say, “I do not know if my child is or is not, but I want the diagnosis because that will give me a toolkit to better help them . ” Is that a good thing to do or a bad thing to do , or both?

It is a wonderful thing to do , but there are two things. I can tell that Professor Baird is dying to come in here but , if I can just say one thing , t he toolkit should not be sitting behind a diagnosis; the toolkit should be there , delivered by the NHS. That is one of our recommendations. It is not just about an awareness toolkit , but an action-oriented toolkit should be there.

Y ou mentioned twice, particularly in recommendations 2 and 3 , AI-enabled shared needs assessments and priority frameworks. Then again , in recommendation 3 , you mention digitally enabled mental health and neurodevelopment assessments and support. A s a Committee , we are taking a particular interest in that digital strand of the NHS. I wondered if you could point us at good practice where this is happening. My concern was that you said this because AI will solve all problems. You are evidence-based, so I am confident that that is not what happened, but could you point us to the best practice so that we can help the NHS to do this further and faster ?

There are three quite different jobs that digital, more broadly, could do. The first is, as we were touching on, information and support that is more specific. Parents do this already. T hey go to ChatGPT and say, “How do I deal with this?”, and sometimes ChatGPT answers in a sensible way; sometimes it does not. The NHS could do a much better job of giv ing better advice in that way.
Second ly , digital tools are very helpful in assessing people’s needs more efficiently. We are very clear about it : AI de s cribes; the clinician decides. There is a clinician sitting behind that.
Q255 D oes this model already exist , or is this a model that you are hoping will exist one day ?
It needs to be vastly improved .
Q256 W ho is doing it?
We are not .
Q257 ChatGPT is one end of the spectrum.
T here are some examples .
Q258 Are they from other countries ?
Ye s. There are some examples, particularly in different places. A far more integrated system is required . A lot of places are using digital in some areas.
Q259 I s that i n the UK?

Yes, i n the UK. There are some in s outh London, for example. We had a fantastic look around the Maudsley Hospital. I believe the Scottish Government are looking for exactly this. Of course, they have the possibility of then extending it across the whole of Scotland. There are a number of different places where it is in part , but insufficiently. We are suggesting that the information section should be a nationwide system.

Q260 Joe Robertson: Professor Fonagy, you say that there is no evidence of a substantial overdiagnosis in conditions such as ADHD and autism, yet your own report identifies a population prevalence of autism in young people of about 1.2%, but a diagnosis that has increased to over 4%. That does not include waiting lists. How is that anything other than evidence of overdiagnosis, based just on your figures?
Professor Fonagy: What we said was that we have no evidence of overdiagnosis at scale.

Q261 Joe Robertson: You identify that the population prevalence of autism in young people is 1.2%, but the diagnosis rate is over 4% , which is increasing further with a big waiting list. That seems to me evidence of overdiagnosis, when nearly four times as many young people are being diagnosed as the population prevalence.

Professor Fonagy: This is a really important point, and I am really grateful for you raising it. Overdiagnosis implies that there is nothing wrong with that person: that the diagnosis is applied, but there is nothing wrong with them. We find absolutely no evidence of that.

We find that it may be that some of those 4% are misdiagnosed, as Professor Baird has already pointed out. We find no evidence that there is a group of people who are presenting and there is nothing wrong with them. “Overdiagnosis” is a very unfortunate pejorative term that indicates that people are presenting with problems that they do not have. All the evidence that we have is that the risk of misdiagnosis is increased, which your example covers, but at the moment there no evidence for overdiagnosis.

What we do point out is that there is a warning sign in the figures that we present. Unless the system is changed, it is almost inevitable that the problem of overdiagnosis will arise. For example, with young people in the adolescent age group, the prevalence of ADHD has reached the level at which all the figures that we have available suggest the population prevalence should be, at which point the administrative prevalence, the number of diagnoses, should have levelled off.

Q262 Joe Robertson: It has not levelled off. If the population prevalence of autism in young people is 1.2% and diagnosis rates have climbed above 4%, it seems a problem if it cannot be asserted—it can be disputed—that that is an overdiagnosis. It could be re-explained as a misdiagnosis, but for autism itself those are the figures. I cannot see how that can be anything other than an overdiagnosis. What support is then required for people who are being overdiagnosed is a separate and very valid conversation, but you seem to be asserting a lack of overdiagnosis when your figures say something different.

Professor Baird: There are several things about your proposition, which is a very good one. The first thing to say is exactly my response to Layla’s question, which is that there simply has not been a recent population prevalence study.
Q263 Joe Robertson: You quoted data from 2017.

Professor Baird: Yes, 2017 was the last one. We do not know whether the population prevalence has changed. You may have thought that it would be impossible, if it was a substantially genetically predisposed condition, that it would rise, but that is not the case. You could have a rise for the reasons that I outlined earlier. We do not know what the population prevalence is. We are making a comparison between now, in 2025-26, with figures that were available probably just before 2017. That is one thing.

The second thing is—I will turn to ADHD because we have rather better figures about that, and exactly the same situation pertains to ADHD—the population prevalence is, again, from 2017. We have projected forwards from the previous figures to a possible population prevalence of 3.8%, but diagnosis in some groups of children and adolescents is already at that level or a little bit higher.

We know that when the DSM-5—the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders , the classification system that we all rely on for diagnosis—was rewritten and published in 2013, there were changes in the conceptualisation of ADHD. There were specific changes for ADHD that raised the possible population prevalence by 2% in adults and 3% in children. The way in which people are understanding these conditions has changed. You are using a population prevalence in this country of 2017 on a slightly changing base.

In autism, we do not have quite the same detailed figures to give you about what happened when the changes were made in the DSM-5, but there has been far greater recognition in girls and women and the numbers of diagnoses have then increased.
Q264 Joe Robertson: That does help, although I notice that the data up until 2017 allows you to conclude that there has been no substantial change in the prevalence up until that point.
Professor Baird: That is perfectly correct for the data up until 2017.

Q265 Joe Robertson: Can I ask about support for those with these sorts of conditions? Support is given through education, health and welfare. I will put a proposition to you. There has been an oversupply of money to deal with an issue particularly in welfare, rather than the therapeutic health or educational support. Is that your view? Does it at least need to be explored whether the right support is being given and whether there may have been an overemphasis on money to families rather than health and educational support in community environments?
Professor Baird: I am not quite sure where the vast amount of money came from, Mr Robertson.
Q266 Joe Robertson: I am sorry. I will spell it out. I mean money being provided via the welfare system, through PIP and DLA, rather than community health support or appropriate support in schools.

Professor Baird: There are varying levels of support that are required at different stages of a child’s life. The most important thing we want to emphasise is that there is a developmental accumulation of problems, if you do not deal with something early enough. Putting in money for early support is absolutely vital. Yes, we also need more focused support for the particular therapeutic approaches that we have outlined in the report, for which there is a good evidence base.

With regard to your later question about PIP and so on and so forth, that is not what our study was about at all. We were looking at prevalence, what evidence we had for interventions, what works and what does not work.

Q267 Darren Paffey: If, as you suggest and as a lot of the reviews around the SEND system in education are proposing, we should be moving to much earlier intervention and having a support-first system instead of a diagnosis-first system, what should that support look like? Is it the same kinds of interventions that typically currently have to wait until after diagnosis? Is it different or lower-level interventions?

Lots of the parents who I have spoken to fear that, if they are going to get support first, it is going to be going on a course or it is going to be online or sporadic rather than feeling that, if they get a diagnosis, they will get a robust package of interventions. What do you see as being the difference, if we make that shift?

Professor Fonagy: That was a concern that was expressed to us by lived experience partners, and it is a concern that we share. The important qualification is that we know what works. In this country, we have a remarkably good system for identifying the best health interventions that can be applied. That is defined by NICE. I know of no other country in the western world where that is available.

We are very clear that there is a real gap at the moment between what NICE recommends and what is offered even after a diagnosis. The gap can be eye-watering. Yes, you could probably reduce the intensity of the intervention, if it were applied earlier, but this cannot be something that is not tested and recommended by NICE.

However, we also recommend that we should be contemplating a set of interventions that is broader than health. It is partly education, partly welfare and partly youth justice and MOJ. This needs to be a cross-Government initiative that has early intervention and prevention of increased problems at its heart.

If I can plead for one thing for your wonderful cross-departmental Select Committee to recommend, it would be to broaden it even further. It should not just be education and health; it should extend to welfare. These systems need to work in an integrated and aligned way to achieve the objectives that we know need to be achieved, much of which is really not rocket science.

Education, I am really pleased to say, is moving towards that. We need to align health with education and the recommendations that education is coming up with in terms of SEND reforms. Education is coming up with one set of understanding about what need is and one language for what need is; health comes up with another set of definitions of what need is. Unless we align health and education, we will be back in the same catastrophic position. If you can persuade these Government Departments to work together to arrive at a single definition of need, you will have done something useful.
If that is aligned with welfare, which already works in principle, not in terms of diagnosis but in terms of need, that would be the ideal. I hope your joint Select Committee can achieve that.

Q268 Darren Paffey: If I am hearing you right, your suggestion is that NICE has to stay in control of what the interventions are. We have a process at the moment whereby schools are going to be reimagined as much more inclusive and need s will be met in mainstream for many, preserving specialists for the most complex needs. NICE and health need to be involved in designing what those educational environments and interventions are. Is that right?

Professor Fonagy: The way we put it is that health is the steward. If you are the steward for anything, you do not define, but you oversee and ensure that good practice is implemented. I hope that is possible. The NICE ADHD guidelines already make many recommendations that are to do with education, except education feels that they need not be followed because they have been made by NICE and they are all to do with health.

Q269 Jodie Gosling: We have talked a lot about the harm that is being done on current waiting lists. You described it as a mindless thing to do, making people wait for that threshold while complexity increases and the chance of irreversible issues increases. What safeguards are needed to ensure that any move to needs-based support does not weaken access to specialist support, reasonable adjustments and statutory entitlements?
Professor Baird: It is certainly a concern and one that has been very well articulated to us, as Peter says.

There are several levels to that. The way in which it is organised will also make a very big difference. For example, we have been talking about integrating services. If you can integrate support services as close to home as possible—to a large extent, this fits with the devolution agenda of the present Government—if you have them there and people can see that they are actually working for them, that dissipates a great deal of the concern.

There is a job of work to be done about enhancing parental trust in how the education system is going to manage that. They are very well aware of that because at the moment—you have articulated this—parents generally feel like they are not going to get anywhere without a diagnosis. Equally, parents understand that diagnosis alone is not working for them. It is not getting them the support that they require.

One example is ADHD. The opportunity to move from a diagnosis of ADHD to implementing a very specific treatment, first of all a psychosocial intervention, which is the number-one treatment, and, secondly, a medication intervention, has halved since covid . There is no follow-through at the moment. It is going to be in the doing of it and how the doing is organised that it is going to work best.
Q270 Jodie Gosling: Are there any interventions that you feel are inappropriate before a diagnosis?
Professor Fonagy: I would say medication.
Professor Baird: Medication before diagnosis, yes. Indeed, yes.
Q271 Jodie Gosling: To what extent do you think that people with co-occurring conditions require different support and different pathways rather than those presenting with a single condition?

Professor Baird: The vast majority have more than one condition. Half of the people with a common mental disorder are going to have two or more conditions. It is the rule rather than the exception. It is a question of finding what the co-occurring condition is and treating it appropriately.

To go back to one of the earlier points, in the discussion about how the dynamic environmental interaction is making things more obvious, I definitely do not want to ever suggest that people do not have very significant problems with each of these individual diagnoses. People have very significant autism and very significant learning difficulties, but it is the combination; it is when they come together.

About 4% of young people will have combined difficulties with lifelong impact. Whatever you do, it will go on affecting them. They and their families need a very particular form of support. In general, that has been less available to them because of the huge waiting lists. They just have to join a waiting list like everybody else. It is one of the reasons why we have proposed a very careful prioritisation based on complexity and risk.
Q272 Jodie Gosling: Should services be designed around individual diagnosis criteria or categories or the wider pattern of needs?

Professor Fonagy: One of the difficulties with the current system and indeed with NICE, which I very strongly support as an arm of the health service, is that it is based on single diagnoses. That needs to be changed. It needs to change because of what Professor Baird said about the prevalence of co-occurrence. Single diagnostic pathways are probably unhelpful in general.

That does not mean single problems cannot or should not be dealt with in turn, but it needs to be a multidisciplinary team. The team around the child should represent the appropriate addressing of the problem of co-occurrence. I would very much hope that in those new neighbourhood services that Professor Baird was talking about we will have mental health and physical health co-represented because of the co-occurrence of physical health problems in many children, which at the moment is completely separate.

Q273 Jodie Gosling: You have touched on the breadth of experience in the services that need to be involved, but who should be responsible for co-ordinating the support for individuals with complex and overlapping needs? Moving past school into employment, what does that look like for employers?
Professor Fonagy: Who should be in charge matters less than somebody being in charge. We have problems where there is dissipation of responsibility.

It is not a problem for the system to be organised in a way that can be specific to a local system. It does not need to be a national model that is implemented. It can fit that local system and the prevalence that occurs within that system, which widely varies because of a whole range of social factors. It is appropriate to a locality, but at the same time it is integrated and coherently organised.

All the parts are there in the current system. What we are recommending is co-ordinating them in a more efficient way. The co-ordination should come locally, but that means leadership. If there is no leadership, the service will fail.

Q274 Jodie Gosling: Of course, one of the aims is to increase participation of work, especially for people with multiple conditions. What support are employers going to need from Government and that leadership in order to make that effective?

Professor Fonagy: The same principles apply. At the moment we have a system, which you are well familiar with, that in a way incentivises disability. We need to have a system where employers are supported in enabling and supporting, rather than simply signing off. The same thing needs to apply. At the moment, doctors do not give advice to employers about what can be done with this person that might help them. They give advice that they are unfit to work. That is a limited way of dealing with it.
The principle that we are recommending for education applies equally to employment. It should be focused on need and supporting that need. Employers need to be supported in supporting needs.

Professor Baird: That means understanding the barriers to perhaps being able to participate. Coming back to your original question about single diagnosis, that is where understanding a particular diagnosis can have an impact.

For example, somebody with autism may have a very marked reaction to the sensory environment. Although anxiety may be mixed in with it, that is different from simply feeling anxious and thus avoidant. For the sensory environment, if it is effortful to manage that, you might need longer periods of recovery rather than the avoidance that might come with an anxiety. There are subtleties that need to be borne in mind.

In school, it is very helpful to understand the particular profiles that people present and understand, therefore, how their particular difficulties impact. In autism, you might have learning difficulties, extreme anxiety associated with it or a demand avoidance profile. There are a variety of different ways in which children interact with the environment that need to be understood and then they can be helped individually.

Q275 Can I quickly pick up on the point about a demand avoidance profile? We have had a question from a clinician, Professor Baird, who wrote to you about this. Are we talking about the same thing? Is PDA the same thing?
Yes.

Q276 I believe that the report says that the evidence for PDA is clinically contested. This professional said to us that, at the same time, the 2021 NICE guidance, which she believes you were in fact involved in drafting, specifically says that PDA is a subset of autism. Her concern was that this is a mixed message to clinicians, who are looking at the report and trying to do the best they can for the families who are coming to their door. It feels to her slightly at odds with the fact that NICE says that PDA does exist and is not clinically contested. Could you clear that up for the clinician who wrote to us, please?

Professor Baird: Yes. The way in which most clinicians work is to follow the international classification systems, particularly the diagnostic statistical manual, called the DSM, or the ICD international classifications by the WHO. They have particular diagnoses.

When we were compiling this particular report, we were using the standard classification systems for different diagnoses. That is in chapter 9. There are a number of situations that are clinically very important but do not necessarily come into the DSM or the ICD. Challenging behaviour is one of them. This is a common problem in young people. They have a combination of severe learning difficulties, often autism as well, and challenging behaviour. Challenging behaviour is not a diagnosis in itself.

We separated, therefore, a list of conditions that are important but not in the classification systems. That is where PDA comes into our report. As a recognised way of behaving, yes, clinicians will be familiar with it and NICE guidelines can be followed. I hope that is helpful.
I am sure we will be told if not.

Q277 Sureena Brackenridge: My questions will be around schools and family support. We have heard time and again—it has come through clearly in the report—that there very much needs to be a needs-led system rather than young people with their parents facing excruciating waits and feeling like they are in an abyss or a void when they are trying to get the support that they need.
What is the role of a school in terms of ensuring that needs are identified as early as possible so that they are addressed appropriately before waiting for that rubber stamp or label of a diagnosis?

Professor Fonagy: That is excellent. I am really pleased to be able to say that the current SEND reforms are very much in line with developing those strategies. Many of the things that we know work for neurodevelopmental conditions are not clinical but are best implemented in the context of education.

There is a very well-known study, the OxWell Student Survey, that asks young people, “What is helpful in your mental health need?” They prioritise family and friends, but immediately afterwards they put school. Way down the line comes child and adolescent mental health services. That really underscores the importance of how much schools can do.

Importantly, there are limitations, and I just want to underscore those. Special educational needs, particularly EHCPs, in terms of looking at the evidence, have not quite delivered in the way that people had hoped. The outcomes, even despite greater investment, have not improved. It is hard to assess, but we know that the major influence of mental health prevalence are things such as school climate.

You have vast differences between two schools in the same demographic area in terms of mental health prevalence. That is understandable in terms of the climate of that school. For example, we know that teacher distress generates pupil distress. It is important that we address that.
Children also often mask their discomfort at school. Many children who I have worked with, who are regarded by their teachers as doing just fine, are really difficult at home.
What we need to do is integrate a sensitivity to a child’s problems with education far better. Mental health support teams, which I had something to do with establishing, is a step in that direction.

Q278 Sureena Brackenridge: As a former school leader, I recognise a lot of what you have just shared. What more can mental health support teams do? Dedicated and caring teachers and wider school staff, the whole pastoral team, et cetera, cannot and should not replace the specialist health teams that are there. What more can mental health support teams do in schools?

Professor Fonagy: Again, you would do us an enormous favour if you were to agree with us that increasing the competence and increasing the complexity of problems that mental health support teams can deal with is a major way of dealing with the group of children who do not meet criteria for specialist intervention but exceed the current capacity of mental health support teams. It is sometimes called the “missing middle”.

If you can empower mental health support teams, which you could do, to deliver the interventions that we know work in a timely way in the context of schools, you would improve the outcome of schools quite broadly. At the moment, even though mental health support teams are being rolled out, they are somewhat underpowered. They do not deal with the missing middle.

Q279 Sureena Brackenridge: That goes back to the point that you made earlier about how the Education Department is sometimes working in a silo away from with the Health Department. They are at different positions on that journey. They are heading in the same direction, but greater collaboration is needed. Professor Baird, is there anything you wish to add?

Professor Baird: I totally agree. You have it absolutely right. There are a number of interventions that at small scale are shown to be very effective and could be increased. There are specific treatments for anxiety in school. Noticing earlier and instituting those would make a huge difference in the avoidance of school and people not wanting to go to school.
We are also concerned—no doubt the Education Department is too—about the 1.5% of children who are not attending school for a whole variety of reasons. There is much to be done.

It is one reason why we have been very supportive of neighbourhood hubs, which bring together the people who could further support in school. This is the expert at hand, as the education reforms have it. These could be mental health professionals who could help run behaviour programmes for parents, help with the anxiety inputs and so on.

They would also have specialisms in autism, just as they have specialisms in being deaf, visually impaired and so on. It would all be co-located in neighbourhood sections, which would enhance very considerably this integration that we think is absolutely vital.

Q280 Sureena Brackenridge: You have just answered my follow-on question, which was about mental health not stopping at the school gate and what more could be done to support families to access the support that they need. Neighbourhood hubs with specialist support is key.
Professor Baird: That is absolutely right.

Q281 Jen Craft: I am now going to turn to look at the proposed SEND reforms a little more widely. I noted with interest that your recommendations seem to focus quite a lot on taking a more holistic approach to these common conditions and perhaps not seeing things in silos. For example, I noticed that you warned that the SEND reforms will fail if the health and education services do not develop a shared approach, particularly around the language for assessing need. Would you be okay to speak a little bit further on that? Particularly, how could the health services see their role not just in terms of medical interventions?

Professor Fonagy: We raised four conditions that are required in order for the SEND reforms to succeed. One is shared language. Investment is another one. That touches on what you are raising. We also need to have specialist advice and we need to have parental confidence in the system.
What is required, most of us would agree, is a model where parents can be confident that their child is not being deprived of the support that they need in order to thrive in that school.
Q282 Jen Craft: Should things be seen through a lens of educational attainment or wellbeing or should we be looking at something else entirely?

Professor Fonagy: One of the things that we are very hopeful will be adopted is a common metric for understanding benefit from services. At the moment, health measures symptoms at the same time as education measures educational attainment. Believe it or not, there are some people who do very well in education who are quite unhappy.

You need to have an alignment of objectives based around what we call participation. Participation is when people feel like they belong to the school. It is as much a wellbeing issue as much as anything else. In education, sadly, young people less and less feel that they belong, but that is not an issue that schools are assessed on.

Q283 Jen Craft: I noticed this in your review. You said that education itself can contribute to distress through factors such as the lack of belonging. We have been talking a little bit around the social model of disability as well. In their current guise, can schools be a risk factor for people who are predisposed to ADHD and autism?

Professor Fonagy: Can I just be very clear about this? Although children link their unhappiness to school, that is not necessarily a development that has occurred recently. There have been children who have linked their unhappiness to school since time immemorial. It is really an easy mistake to make to blame schools.

As Professor Baird mentioned, there have been some changes in schools, but the focus has moved to performance in a particular modality that may indeed create pressures on a particular population of children. To me, broadening that is a no-brainer. Schools are trying to do their best. I would be very unhappy if any part of our report was read as trying to blame schools for the problems.

There are problems that could be changed. There are aspects of schools that could be changed that would reduce the problems, but that is in relation to broadening the parameters that are used to evaluate education in this country.

Q284 Jen Craft: Professor Baird, perhaps I can turn to you on a similar vein. I do not necessarily mean that schools are to blame as such, but you mentioned some of the changes to the way that the education system is set up. To use your analogy earlier, for people who are predisposed to autism or ADHD, could the way that schools focus on particular things, such as certain types of educational attainment or attendance metrics, be exacerbating some of these issues?
Professor Baird: There is no doubt that, when we look at the evidence, around exam time people’s anxiety rises, but then generally it comes down again. There are certainly those specific aspects.

The important thing is that people need to feel they are succeeding, do they not? They need to feel that there is something in which they are being successful. Schools have a really difficult job, but, given the range of what people are able to experience and engage in, they need to have something that people are good at and can do. Those positivities are extremely helpful and necessary.

People do comment on various aspects of school, which some of them have struggled with, but I totally concur with Peter. Overall, people have always found some things very difficult about school. Adolescence is a time when people are really trying to discover themselves. That sense of belonging and the opportunities for the rest and recovery that Peter has emphasised throughout the report are really the most important factors in learning how to manage social relationships and the interactions with the outside world. That is really some of the job that needs to be enhanced.

Q285 Jen Craft: I do not envy anyone for being a teenage girl; I hated it. If we move on to the wider SEND reviews and proposals—we touched on this a little bit—one of the key things that we have taken quite a lot of evidence on is the lack of health representation around the table when it comes to either planning individual educational health and care plans or commissioning SEND services. Time and again, we have taken evidence that they are just not there; they do not play their part. It is a systemic issue rather than a variation in any particular regional area.
How should we ensure that that changes? How do we make sure that health see their role as being more than just, “We need to improve our diagnostic time frame”?

This is very interesting, but I note that the focus of my local area seems to be on improving the delay in diagnostics rather than maybe holistically looking at how they support the wider system. How do we get them to do that?

Professor Baird: The model that we propose of local neighbourhoods, using examples where it is already happening, would be really very helpful indeed. The next is commissioning and having integrated commissioning, so that people are organised and that that is their job. Again, it should be as close to home as possible. Those would be the main two drivers that you have going forward.

Professor Fonagy: Can I add two others to it on either end? First, we should be commissioning for outcomes, rather than commissioning for the performance of actions that may or may not be successful. We need to commission for outcome, where “outcome” is defined as participation.

The other, which touches on what Gillian mentioned, is understanding that health is responsible for improving understanding. I cannot think of a better example than understanding behavioural problems. Health has a better understanding of why behavioural problems emerge in children than education does, which has to deal with it much more in terms of the core class. If health was at the table, it could provide better ways of managing problem behaviours in children, either via help supporting parents, which I personally believe is the most effective mode, or, as we know, supporting teachers and teaching assistants in managing behaviour better.

To take one example, we developed the model of a family school—Pears Family School at the Anna Freud Centre —where we bring parents into the school to observe how to manage their child’s behaviour better from teachers and from assistant teachers. Embedded in that are supporters of the teachers to manage the child’s behaviour. This is children with diagnoses of autism or severe OCD. These are children who have been excluded from other schools. Integrating the wisdom is the answer.
Q286 Jen Craft: Do health services see that as part of their role? Do they embrace that?
Professor Fonagy: They are not commissioned to. They are not commissioned to, so why would they see it as part of their role?
Q287 Jen Craft: They do have a duty on prevention and public health.
Professor Fonagy: They do not. I do not believe that they do. That is not a CAMHS—

Q288 Jen Craft: It seems that you are saying that there is definitely something that could be done centrally in terms of articulating that health does have this role in prevention, increasing knowledge and increasing education for both teachers and parents.
Professor Fonagy: Yes.

Q289 Jen Craft: You will be aware that the statutory responsibility for the delivery of education, health and care plans currently falls solely on local authorities. We have taken some evidence about putting a similar duty on health bodies.

Indeed, I tabled an amendment that was supported by both of our Committees to the recent Health Bill to place an equivalent duty on ICBs or health trusts to deliver that health plan to give them that real onus and owning of the issue. Is that something that would be helpful?
Professor Fonagy: It could not be otherwise.
Jen Craft: On that very helpful note, I will go back to the Chair.
That is really helpful.
Q290 Helen Hayes: I would like to push you a little bit on some of the practicalities of delivery, building on the questions that Jen has asked already.

The conversation that we have had today will be enormously frustrating for many of the stakeholders that my Committee works with within education. Some of the things that you have said imply that schools can just do things. If you are working in the education sector as it is at the moment, they are under a whole range of pressures that stem from their own accountabilities and what they are tasked with doing that would make it very difficult for them to do things. It is hard to overstate the extent to which both the education sector and local authorities are tearing their hair out with the health system.

We can all look—and we do on our Committees—at examples of good practice, who is doing things well, how things should be and what we can learn from, but this will boil down to accountability. It boils down to what people are measured against and what they are required to do. We do not have that for health at the moment in relation to the delivery of support for neurodivergent children and children with mental health difficulties in schools.

We have been talking about this agenda for 25 years. We have been talking about co-commissioning. We have ICBs, which are supposed to have local authorities at the table, though their voice is extremely weak. They are supposed to do joint commissioning. These things are supposed to happen, and yet they do not.

I would just make a plea that we move the conversation on from how things should be and hypothetically can be, and indeed are in some circumstances where things are done well, to how we arrange the system in its fundamental accountabilities to deliver the things that we know children need in education because that is the thing that is not happening at the moment.

Professor Fonagy: I believe that is beyond our remit. I believe the Government are responsible for doing that. We can and we do recommend a commissioning system that is mindful of exactly those things. An integrated system is the only system that could possibly work and meet the mental health crisis that we see in young people at the moment. We could not agree with you more.

I would not want to in any way underestimate the pressures that schools are under. I hope that I have not tried to shift the blame, but I would not want to underestimate the pressure that those working in child and adolescent mental health care are under either. When you have two bodies that talk poorly to each other, it is very easy to blame the other for not doing their job properly.

The conversation needs to change. It needs to start with a common language around the needs of families, children and young people and shared responsibility for those needs being met. Unless you do that and you invest sufficient resources for that to be delivered in a timely way, when it is needed, as soon as the problems present, you will not deal with this problem.
Professor Baird: It is co-location. Co-location as local as possible would make a big difference.

Q291 Helen Hayes: My second practicality is around expertise. We would agree with you—this inquiry has heard a significant amount of evidence on this—about the missing middle who are in education, whose mental health needs are not currently met through mental health support teams. That requires a change in the expertise within mental health support teams, because their current remit is mild to moderate mental health needs. The children who we describe as being within the missing middle have a more severe need stopping short of requiring CAMHS interventions.
Can you say what you think is needed in terms of the level of expertise in mental health support teams and perhaps what that might look like in terms of a change in the workforce required?

Professor Fonagy: We are quite explicit about that in the review, but let me just set the record straight. Although they are supposed to do mild to moderate mental health support teams, the objective reality is that they do moderate to severe and they deal with the co-occurrence. Most of the children referred have a diagnosis of neurodevelopmental conditions in addition to mental health conditions. All the other data that we have supports that.

Mental health support teams at the moment do more than what they were originally designed to do. The system needs to change for there to be better training in cognitive behavioural therapy, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder and a whole range of systems. This is something that personally, with a different hat, I recommended three or four years ago. It has not been possible so far. If you can add your voice to this, maybe jointly we will be successful.

At the moment, the initiative has been to spread this to all schools and include all schools. We have been successful at that. In the case of anxiety, mental health support teams are remarkably successful. They may not be dealing with everything that you want to deal with, but those who meet clinical levels of anxiety are dealt with successfully over 50% of the time. That is from a study that we recently published on 23,000 children, if I remember correctly. It does deliver, but it could do a hell of a lot better.

Q292 Helen Hayes: I have a final question. My Committee has had a lot to say about how we think that prevalence in the classroom at the moment is about 20%. We think that about four or five children in every classroom, in every school right across the country, have some type of neurodivergence, special educational need or disability, and yet our education system is fundamentally not designed for those children.

We know the Government want to shift towards inclusive mainstream schools that can better meet the needs of all the children who are in the classroom. We want all children to thrive in education. There should not be any conflict between high standards and meeting the needs of children who have neurodivergence in the classroom because those children are a part of our population of people whose needs we are seeking to serve.
What does an inclusive mainstream system look like from the perspective of your expertise? How should the Government be defining that as they seek to implement their SEND reforms?

Professor Baird: It does slightly depend on the age group of the children. Let us start with the preschool and the way in which it is possible to integrate and have inclusion at that stage while also defining the problems that the children are going to experience as they move on.

It is not that any system has shown that you can accurately screen everybody and expect to get 100% sensitivity and specificity. You cannot. By the time children are starting at five or six, you can have a very good idea of some of the biggest problems that they are going to get and they should already be in a system of parental support. You will know about the success of Sure Start and how one really needs to get back into having early support hubs and bringing families with you.

By the time you get into primary school, different problems may become manifest. That is the time when inclusion should be possible, if you make the modifications that, again, an understanding of the individual pupil will bring.

I totally support your aim of trying to insist that local hubs have expertise that is able, from health as well as education, to investigate such children and support the school with an understanding of what they need or do not need.

The next cliff edge tends to be entering into secondary school. Again, we do not have really good properly integrated systems of planning for individual children who are likely to need additional support as they move from that stage to secondary and then on to further education. Peter, I am sure, has other visions.

Professor Fonagy: I just want to put in a word for higher education, universities. Universities are also facing pressure in accommodating people who now increasingly come with neurodiverse conditions. The sad fact is that, as far as we can tell, the accommodations that universities offer are totally without value.
Please go slightly further into that statement.

Professor Fonagy: These accommodations do not effectively deal with the issues. The problem seems to be that universities fall into an accountability vacuum. You are absolutely right that in schools, right up to university, there is scrutiny, but there is no proper exploration of university provision.

There is no input of the kind that Gillian was talking about from health into universities. Universities try to manage as best they can. You would not expect a university to deal with brain scans. They do not install a scanner so that they can deal with possible brain damage, but they are expected to deal with neurodiversity and t hey are not well equipped to do so. If you could point to that, that would be helpful.

Q293 We are about to lose quorum, but I have one extremely fast final question. I appreciate that this is asking you to pick among your children. This review comes as a whole, but, if there were one single most impactful recommendation that these two Committees could make together to help to implement your review, what would it be, Professor Fonagy?

Professor Fonagy: I have written mine out; I could send it to you. It is bringing services together around the needs of children, young people and families. That reduces fragmentation and makes support easier to access.
Q294 Do you agree with that?
Professor Baird: I totally agree.

Professor Fonagy: Family hubs come into that. We need neighbourhood family hubs and integrated models. It is something that enables us to overcome the fragmentation that has stopped us from delivering what ensures mental health, which are three simple things: people, place and purpose. You need relationships with people, places where you can benefit from that social support, and purpose in your life. Education is a major purpose. Let us hope that we can do better for children and young people than we have been able to do over the past 20 years.
That is a good place to stop. Thank you very much.

sessions.w: British Retail Consortium; Food and Drink Federation; Harry Metcalfe (Harry's Farm)

segs.tx: Public Accounts Committee
Oral evidence: Resilience of the UK ’ s food supply to disruptions, HC 717
Monday 12 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 12 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown (Chair); Mr Clive Betts; Rachel Gilmour; Rupert Lowe; Blake Stephenson; Matt Turmaine.

Gareth Davies, Comptroller and Auditor General, National Audit Office, Rich Sullivan-Jones , Director, National Audit Office, and Marnya Jain , Alternate Treasury Officer of Accounts, HM Treasury, were in attendance.
Questions 1-6 0
Witnesses

I : Harry Metcalfe, Farmer and YouTuber (Harry’s Farm), Oxfordshire, Jim Bligh, Corporate Affairs Director, British Retail Consortium, and Balwinder Dhoot, Director of Sustainability and Growth, Food and Drink Federation .

I I : Professor Neil Ward, Professor of Rural and Regional Development, University of East Anglia, and Professor Tim Lang, Emeritus Professor of Food Policy, City University London’s Centre for Food Policy.
Report by the Comptroller and Auditor General
Resilience of the food supply chain to disruptions (HC 587)
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Jim Bligh, Balwinder Dhoot and Harry Metcalfe.

Welcome to the Public Accounts Committee on Monday 12 October 2026. Today marks the start of our farming week, in which we take the unusual step of dedicating two separate evidence sessions to examining the resilience of the UK’s food supply to disruption, in order to highlight the significance of the issue.

Disruptions to the food supply chain can have a significant impact on consumers, businesses and Government. Overall, food availability has been maintained in the UK food supply chain during recent disruptions, such as the covid-19 pandemic, and the wars in Iran and Ukraine, but the risks are increasing. Today’s sitting is split between two panels, comprising a cast of witnesses with a huge wealth of knowledge and experience of working in this area. On Thursday, we will hear from senior Government officials about the Government’s point of view on the issue.

This afternoon, we look to hear from our witnesses on a variety of topics, including the Government’s ability to maintain our food supply, the preparedness of the farming sector for major disruption, and the Government’s engagement with food retailers, manufacturers and farmers about food supply resilience. I will now do my usual and ask each of you please to introduce yourselves briefly and perhaps to say what your history is on this subject. Jim, will you start by introducing yourself, please?

I am Jim Bligh. I am director of corporate affairs and food policy at the British Retail Consortium. Before joining the BRC in January, I worked for the Food and Drink Federation and before that for PepsiCo, so I have a range of experience in the food industry.
Good to have you, thank you very much for coming. Harry, of course, we all know you—you may not know us, but we know you.

I am very grateful to be here, Chair. My background: agriculture college, 1981 came out of there; grain buyer, but wanted to get into farming; started in farming in my own right in 1984, first harvest ’85; and it has gone from there. Currently, I have a farm in the Cotswolds, 300 acres, 120 acres rented, and I am next door to Mr Clarkson, whom you might also know in the Cotswolds.
Thank you very much, Harry. Bal, please.

I am Bal Dhoot. I am the director for sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation. I have been there for three and a half years. Before that, I was a civil servant in DEFRA, where I worked on some previous crises and shocks to hit the food system.

Q1 Thank you very much. I will start with the first question, but before I do, I should declare an interest as a practising farmer and as a chartered surveyor. Everyone take that into account when I ask my questions. My first question is, I think, to all three of you. What are the biggest challenges that farmers currently face?

Thank you for the question, and for the excellent Report from the Auditor General’s team at the NAO, which sets the scene really well. Resilience is absolutely critical to retailers. A resilient supply chain is what we require to be able to operate all around the UK. The vast majority of the food that we sell through retail is produced in the UK, but too much of that comes in as imports from overseas, and all of us as retailers have a priority to increase domestic production.

Clearly, there are challenges for farmers, for manufacturers and for us. We have been through a number of shocks over the years, and the NAO Report identifies them very well. They range from covid to Ukraine, the Iran crisis this year and the ensuing problems with fuel, fertiliser, diesel, and so on. What they show is that we have a remarkably resilient system but that that system , as the NAO says, is reliant on the private sector to be able to co - ordinate itself and to move at the right pace so that we do not end up with, for example, a lack of availability in stores and empty shelves , which for us are a mark of serious failure.

There are probably five groups of risks. I won’t go into too much detail in this answer, but they are climate ; energy and water ; cyber - security ; regulation and Government policy and the constant chopping and changing there ; and the geopolitical and trade risks that we all face as well. But specifically on your question about farmers , Mr Chairman, what is abundantly clear to us is that farmers are struggling to get planning permission — struggling to be able to put in , for example, above - ground reservoirs, which should then be able to water field - grade crops. E very farmer I talk to says, “W e can ’t get the approvals from Government quickly enough ,” or, “We’re restricted from being able to put a reservoir on our land. ”

At the same time, energy costs have gone up enormously. If you are in protected horticulture or in poultry, it is extremely difficult to fund the energy costs , given where they are. Given that food is a critical national infrastructure industry, it is surprising that Government ha ve not taken any steps on energy to reduce costs for those particular industries, whereas it has for other industries around the place. A nswering specifically on farmers, I think those things are among the challenges .

For us as retailers, our tax cost has gone up by 20% in the last two years —since the 2024 B udget . We now pay an effective tax rate of 73.5% . The increase in costs is from employment costs , business rates , packaging costs—the full range . It is about £8 billion a year since the election. I f there is one thing that worries us about resilience, it is the huge costs that have been piled into the system since 2024 —and, to be fair, in the years before that as well , but this has been particularly pronounced recently . It limits our capacity to invest and the capacity of the system to make money ; and ultimately, profit is a good thing. Profit in the food system is the only way we will create the investment and the conditions to grow and to change , g iven all the circumstances that we face and those risks that we face.
Q2 Thank you very much ; that is a really good opening statement from you .
I will now go to Harry for the farming point of view. Farmers have had a pretty difficult year with the drought.

Well, you say that. Farming is interesting because it is so variable. The definition of a farmer is a food producer, but you can go from a chicken farm to a pig farm , a L akeland sheep farmer, a Scottish farmer or my sector, which is arable farming mainly —that is more concentrated in southern England. We have all had certain struggles in different ways , but if you are asking me about our ability to maintain our food supply while keeping food affordable, the challenge right now is this. As an arable farmer, I have had four of the five worst harvests since 2020 , and 2026 is the smallest harvest of all since records began—people started keeping records in 1984, when I started farming . The frustration from a farming point of view is that the small harvest is all down to climate change , or climate events , as you would term it. We have had it go from flooding to then not being able to establish a good crop and then get to harvest. This year, for example, it was like someone pressed a switch at the end of June and it just went out. You thought it was going to be a really good harvest and you put the combine in —and it’s not there. So the challenge at the moment for farming in my area is , “What on earth is happening? How can I still grow food? Do I have to grow earlier crops or something to take advantage of the climate change that we ’ve got? ”

I ought to just mention here that the Scottish farms have done really well this year , because they did not suffer that extreme climate ; they have had a good year. The only dilemma I have in talking on farming is that it does vary , depending on where in the country you are growing food.
Q3 I have just c ome back from the north of Scotland—I have never seen so much grass in all my life. Mind you, they were still trying to harvest oats in October, so there is always a downside.
Yes, they are very keen on their grain dryers up in Scotland, but then in the Lake district, they have had a fantastic year.
Q4 Indeed. Bal?

I agree with a lot of what Jim has said about how the sector has been incredibly resilient over the last six or seven years. It has been through some exceptional shocks. Our sector is very reliant on farming. They produce the ingredients that go into our products, and we are a massive customer for domestically produced agricultural production. Having talked about those shocks that have played out over the last seven or eight years, my concern would be, “Would we manage them the same over the next seven or eight years?” I see resilience around domestic production slowly being eroded. It is a bit like a slow puncture, in some ways.

We published some trade data recently, which showed that in the first half of this year, the gap between our imports and exports was one of the highest it has been in the last 25 years. That is not an exception. That is a trend that has been happening over the last decade. If you look into that, I think it suggests that production is moving overseas more. That could be because people are sourcing more. It could be from overseas for their inputs here. It could be because factories are being relocated overseas. When a factory relocates, it is not going to be buying British produce; it is going to buy produce from the country where the factory is. It is kind of a signal around what is happening. At the moment, it is probably manageable. The question is: if that trend continues for the next five to 10 years, would we be able to manage the shocks that the food system has experienced in the same way that we have got through the last six or seven years?
Q5 What is the answer to that question?

I think it would be a lot more challenging. The other thing I would add is that we know there will be more volatility and more shocks. We consider what we have experienced in the last six or seven years to be the new normal, whether it is geopolitics, climate or other events. We should be preparing for the same again, if not worse. We should be thinking about that long-term resilience piece. It is important to think about how we react to specific shocks in the moment or prepare for those, but long-term resilience is the key.
Q6 Would you like to give us any specific examples of how you think we could increase our resilience?

Resilience comes down to investment. In the same way that Jim talked about being able to make profit, if you cannot make money in this country, you will stop farming, you will move your factory and so on. How do you have a system that gets the market to invest in production, but also in the things around resilience, such as stronger supply chains, de-risking energy costs and cyber-security? All those things require investment. How do we have a system that allows and encourages that investment? Alternatively, you can have a system that encourages you to import or shift production overseas. I would add that we are not anti-trade. Having a mix of domestic production and trade is really important for food security. The question is the balance, and the trend is signalling where we are heading, which could become problematic over the next decade.

Q7 I will hand over to Rupert Lowe in a minute, but Harry, from your point of view, not only do you have resilience in the farming field, but you have to look at resilience in the food chain. Have you any suggestions for us, looking forward five or 10 years, about what we ought to be doing?

My concerns with the food chain are really about whether they understand how we farm, how we have to take a risk on putting a crop in a ground, and this long-term wait until we can actually give them what they have requested. For an arable farm, I have already committed my 2027 harvest. I know precisely what I am harvesting. It is all in the ground. I have already incurred 74% of the cost. There is nothing I can do once it is fixed. I am then reliant on the weather to behave and can then supply to the food chain. Right now, growing food seems to be an incredibly risky business . I am not sure what we do to encourage me to grow more food at the moment, because currently, it is very high risk —t hat is proven by the fact that four of the worst harvests have happened since 2020. Why would I continue to grow food when it is such a high-risk activity ?

I am also doing it on the back of those four harvests . As I said in a recent video, 2025 was my worst harvest since 1984 , by a country mile , so although ’ 26 was okay, all it actually did was make up what I lost in 2025. I need ’ 27 to come along before I can put investment into the farm , or into anything . C ash flow is a disaster for farms in my region. The challenge for cereal-growing farmers at the moment is cash flow — they just have not got the cash. What I have learnt recently is that the withdrawal of the basic payment scheme has exposed all farmers to the realities of trying to farm at world prices. That has been a real wake - up call for some, especially when you throw a weather wobbly into it as well. That is the real challenge. As I say, livestock farming and Scotland have not suffered this , as it is regional in this country, but a very big region of the UK has suffered this year.

Q8 You already mentioned the SFI debacle a week ago. Is there anything more the Government can do—not necessarily monetarily, but in terms of longer-term pronouncements—to give you some confidence that what you have done in planting those crops will actually produce a result?

As far as I know, the Government cannot control the weather, so they cannot really control the big lever for what the yield will be. I am sure we will come on to SFI and the schemes that are currently there. I am a bit of a fan of those, but none of them actually encourages me to grow food at the moment. That is what I would love to see come out of the debate this week: how will DEFRA encourage me to grow food in the very high-risk environment we have at the moment? To be perfectly honest, I do not have the answer, but I do know that taking away the safety cushion of the area payments has exposed farmers to the reality.

I am also very concerned about the tenanted sector of farming. If you have cash-flow struggles, the last thing you can afford is next year’s rent for your landlords. I can see that being a major challenge. I am also a British taxpayer, as I have other businesses, so I do not want to see money being wasted in terms of how we pay our taxes and where they should go, but food security is a really big one and we ought to be concerned. Right now, as a farmer, I am doing everything I can to not grow food. That is just wrong.
Q9 That is very helpful. Jim, before I bring Rupert Lowe in, do you have any thoughts, five or 10 years out, about what we should concentrate on with the food supply chain?

The first thing, reflecting on where Harry and Bal are as well, is long-term investments. We are seeing a lot more supermarkets having long-term partnerships with farmers and manufacturers. Those enable them to weather the storm, as it were, to create the long-term conditions to invest. If we are asking for tens of millions of pounds of investment in new agricultural machinery or new infrastructure on a farm, there has to be some kind of payback over a period of time. That means that you have to guarantee to farmers that the financing will be there over a long time for stability.

As industry and as the major buyers, we can do quite a lot of that—the challenge comes with Government. I will not make a political point, but we are now on our third Environment Secretary since the last election. I have lost count of the number of discussions I have had about food strategies and cycles—honestly, I am a little lost as to what the strategy in the Department is. Then there is the question of policy priorities. Farmers, manufacturers and retailers are in the middle of a global storm. The Government are saying, “You’ve got to fix the roof,” but the sun is not shining. How do we do that in a way that is affordable, enables us to meet our goals, and supports farmers and manufacturers to adapt and be resilient? It is really tricky.

In terms of what the ask is, we can provide long-term investment against a long-term, certain backdrop, but that means the Department needs to provide a clearer steer on what its long-term strategy is. Risk mitigation for the big buckets of risk that we face needs to fit in as part of that: if the climate goes one particular way or we have serious cyber-security incidents, how will we respond to that in practice? That is where the Department has not provided adequate clarity yet and it could be a lot more strategic about how it does that in the decades to come. We know this storm is going to continue; it will not get easier.
Thank you for all your opening remarks.
Q10 I should disclose that I have an 865 acre farm in the Cotswolds where, like you, Harry, we farm arable land and we have some sheep.

I take your point about the variability of farming across the country, but that has always been the case. Very often up north they cannot harvest their crops because they get too much rain and even the dryers cannot cope with wheat at 25%.

As to what concerns me, it was quite instructive that paragraph 10 of the NAO Report said DEFRA is “less confident about the ability of businesses” in the food supply chain “to withstand shocks without government intervention in the next five to 10 years.” Frankly, the last thing we need is Government intervention, but why do they need to say that? The answer is that they have created that situation: we watched them increase taxes on employment; taxes are about to come in with this UK carbon border adjustment mechanism, which is going to put another tax on fertiliser; and the net zero agenda means that energy is more expensive than in any other country in the world. They basically are doing absolutely everything in their power to dissuade people, to Harry’s point, from planting crops.

I am fortunate that I do not have any debt, but like you, Harry, when you drill crops, pay 700 quid a tonne for nitrogen and have expensive wheat seed, you are effectively drilling your grain into the ground knowing that you are going to make a loss. You are effectively speculating on two things: No. 1 is that the price is going to go up, and No. 2 is that we are not going to get a catastrophic harvest like we did this year, last year and the year before.

On an overcrowded island, I think we should be prioritising growing crops and feeding ourselves. We account for a relatively low percentage of our food. With rewilding and all the other sorts of schemes—I have recently stopped development on grade 1 arable land in my Great Yarmouth constituency—the Government are doing everything they can to score an own goal and then wondering why farmers are going bust and the supply chain is falling apart.
We have got quite a lot—
