We should be thinking , “How did that work, and what made that work so well?” because we need change of that magnitude over the next 25 years to cope with the need for resilience to climate change.
I agree with that completely. There is a case for imagination in Governmen t.

Q52 Is there a sense that, in the 1940s and 50s, the memories of the s econd w orld w ar were very fresh? People could remember almost running out of food, whereas now they think we have got food running out of our ears, which is not necessarily the case.

Consumer culture assumes that food is there 364 days a year, 24 hours a day. Look at resilience planning , the sort of meetings I have just been in — twice this week —and the shock when phones go down. One of the points my report made was that we do not know how a culture that thinks food is available in that way will respond if there is major disruption.

There is a bit of complacency about saying, “ W e were great in c ovid, weren't we?” Actually, Government w ere terrible in c ovid. They closed the hospitality sector when it was close to where people are. It needed to be better organised and used. It was people from outside Government who went to the then Government and said, “ Don’t you think we ought to actually be looking at food, because you are closing down some of the workers who are in the food system?” That is why the Food Industry Resilience Forum was set up, and it was closed down. No notes were even taken about how it should be resurrected. That is complacency, to be hard about it.

We need that direction to deal with crises in the short term , but the long-term change that Neil and I am referring to requires a bit of political courage : “Dear British public, we are now in a new era. Things aren’t going to be the same. Here ’s the options for what we could do.” The food industry broadly thinks like this. Talk to people privately and the stories will come out about how close things are to being completely broken up.

Q53 Isn’t part of the answer to your question about why the City is not investing in food security and farming is that successive Governments keep changing the policy ? I nvestors need stability and certainty, and they are not getting that from their Governments.

If that is true for the supply side, think how true that is for the demand side. Consumers want to have security. At one level, they have it—through their phones, or through walking in and seeing full shelves—but that is very easy to knock. We know—indeed, the food industry tells me of its experiences—how easily disrupted that is, and people go from confidence to panic very quickly.

I do not think we can turn to DEFRA to do that sort of work, but there are some of us in academia who are interested in it. To be nice to Government, having been quite critical, there is actually a really interesting bubbling up in the Resilience Academy in the Cabinet Office, as well as the two units now in DEFRA itself, where they are realising that the public are not that myth from world war two—the compliant, knowledgeable, skilled and thrifty shopper. That is not the modern shopper.

Q54 Our previous panel suggested that you would be able to provide some good answers to this question, so I am looking forward to them. Can you give us some examples of other countries that have a really good approach to food resilience? What can we learn from them?

I will get in first and then Tim can expand, because he will have more to say on this than me. For a start, it is really good that people are asking this question, because a lot of discussions about agricultural policy and food policy in the UK are quite parochial. It is really useful to be thinking, “What can we learn from elsewhere?”

Finland comes up very prominently, so I would suggest you look at Finland. There is all sorts of interesting institutional architecture there, but I think it is largely a function of the geography of that country and the Russian threat in the north. Singapore, the Netherlands, Japan and Israel—there are lots of countries that have active and assertive approaches to the resilience of their food systems. They have different types of concerns, and they will have different complexions to their strategies, but there is plenty to be learned from other countries. I am sure Tim will be able to say much more.

I think you have given that breadth. Different countries have different strategies, and their motivations are different. If you go to the Netherlands, which I did for my report, it is a small country that had experience of famine in world war two. Welfare and health policy are really important in the Netherlands because of the 1944-45 famine, and you can still measure the life expectancy of Dutch women by the preconceptual care of their grandmothers—it is quite extraordinary. The threat of famine has had a very big impact, and a bit like how Finland decided to specialise in ceramics and glass, post second world war, the Netherlands chose to invest in those very fertile soils beneath the sea level. It built a culture within Government of taking food production very seriously, while Britain’s approach has been much more about avoidance.

I agree that Finland is also very good. In my experience, the closer to Russia you get, the more seriously they take this. I agree that Singapore is interesting as a city state, because it has decided to double its own production, even though it is a city state, not a big landed sovereignty. I was personally very impressed in France by how—not in the name of resilience, but in the name of rebuilding urban-rural connections—they had done some very interesting work to diversify food systems in the name of agri-food regionalism. Now that work has been of great interest and support to the French Government in the name of resilience.

At the sub-national level, I was particularly taken by the French-speaking part of Belgium: Wallonie or Wallonia , depending on what your language is. There is a city called Liège —it is like Sheffield, because it is a deindustrialised coal and steel town—and 15 years ago they essentially started to say, “What is the point of Liège ?” They said, “Well, let’s run with food as a purpose. People in Liège eat food,” and they basically built a new culture. They have a big annual food festival, and they have started a new programme of regional horticultural enterprises around it.

What I did in my report was look at countries, which is why Neil was turning to me, and there are lessons we can learn from them. For me, the No. 1 is actually Sweden, which I was hinting at earlier. It has done the most astute national review of resilience and what it want s from its land . Norway is doing something very similar , so I think we can learn from the Baltics. Latvia was very interesting to me. It looked at, “ What do we do if Russia rides all over us? Well, probably the Government will have collapsed , so we need to go down the levels and think about hyper - local community food resilience. ” My answer to your question is : don’t just look at national Governments. We need to look below national Governments at the regional —or the sub - national , to be pompous —and at cities down to the very local.

To go back to the question Sir Geoffrey asked a quarter of an hour ago , one reason why I think Neil and I were both saying that you do need the Government to set new frameworks is that one weakness of DEFRA and the British Government system is that they do not apply food and environment strategies to the sub - national. It is all assumed to be done from Whitehall , until you go to Wales.

In Wales, there is a really interesting movement going on. It has created and appointed a food security adviser and a food strategy adviser , but it also has 22 local food partnerships covering the whole of Wales. County councils are doing interesting things in Wales. It is much more multi - level. Do not just look at what we can learn from other countries ; we need to look at who is dealing with the multi - level - ness of food security resilience well . The short answer to that is , no one is doing it perfectly , but there are wonderful lessons we can draw for different levels from different countries.

To wrap that up and to try to be practical , one of the things my report suggested was that English mayors get powers . The Devolution Act needs to do for England what it has done rather unequally and differently for Scotland and Wales. We need to unleash imagination and change to be a more resilient food system . Giving mayors and unitary authorities responsibilities and powers— people like me have been arguing that that needs to come but for resilience . If you are just planning for bombs going off , shocks , disasters , floods and droughts, you in voke the Civil Contingencies Act . Call it a “ resilience Act ”; you would want food to be in there, in which case we need to be giving powers to different levels for different capacities. I think the metro mayors would be up for that in England, and certainly the devolved Administrations in Wales and Scotland would; Northern Ireland is slightly different.

To answer your question in one sentence, there is lots that we can learn from lots of other people, but no one has it perfect because we are all having to rethink what we have done in the last 70 years. We have created a more vulnerable food system that is more prone to shocks . We are now all having to think, what do we want for the next 30 years? We will need to look at that multi-level -ness very seriously.
Tim, thank you. We are up against the clock now. We want to finish by 6 pm .
It was a big question—forgive me.
I want short questions and short answers, please.

Q55 Tim, you just mentioned the issue of critical national infrastructure and the database, from which food is of course missing at present. I think you just said to us that that is an issue in itself , but that a lot more can be done as well. Should the food supply chains be part of the critical national infrastructure database , and should more be done in addition ?

Clive, I am going to answer you frankly: is the Pope a Catholic? Of course. It is absurd . If we make food a critical national infrastructure — which we have , and rightly so —then come a shock , within three days , you need some food. Well, actually, you can do without food for 30 days — it depends where you are —but you need water. We have things like water, electricity and food as CNIs . It clearly ought to be in the database. The NAO—I defer to your colleagues here with you, the NAO team—has that excellent bit of the Report saying that DEFRA has the database , has a benchmark and has dashboards , but they are weak ; they are not enough. But should they be there? Absolutely. That is why we need clearer guidance from the Government about what we want from the food system—or, as I put it, “What’s food for?”
That would then lead on to what elements should be in the database.

Precisely. As I put it very clearly in my “Just in Case” report, I would like that to be not just supply or targets for production; it has to be availability, confidence and trust measures—consumer-ish measures. Again, that takes me back to the thinking behind the food Bill proposal; it is all about that. Keeping the confidence of consumers is a key indicator.

I would just add a point—which is inspired by Tim’s work, actually. I do not know whether this is because of the rules, but a lot of the discussion about critical national infrastructure seems to focus on distribution centres and the cold chain—the hard, technical kit, the science and the big capital stuff. You were also told about the NFU list, which talked about abattoirs as well, which you could add, but there is institutional infrastructure as well.

There are local food groups and food partnerships; Tim mentioned 22 local food partnerships in Wales. There are organisations where people come together regularly to talk and think about this stuff. That is part of the critical national infrastructure for food. It is the institutions and food partnerships that help to distribute food, and promote growing food as well, that will play a part in the resilience of the food system in a crisis.
They are kept out of it at the moment. They are operating as civil society, but they need to be in the overarching framework.

Q56 Is there a responsibility, presumably for the Government, to start educating the public so that they understand some of these challenges and difficulties, and the fact that food is not just going to be there automatically? We do see some national politicians questioning whether climate change is actually a problem that needs addressing; perhaps that sometimes confuses the public on social media, when these are big issues that ought to be part of any understanding.

They are. As you will probably remember, Clive, on the day that the election was called, 22 May 2024, the Government of the day launched the Prepare website . People like me were glad that it had been launched, but it is weak. Telling the 20% of the population who cannot afford to eat well, or even adequately, that they now have to spend about 500 quid preparing for shocks was not helpful. We can do better.

Shortly, the Government will launch a revision to the Prepare website. I think that is good, and we should encourage that, but just having a website is not engaging with the public. It is not—going back to Neil’s point an hour ago—involving the public or representatives of the public in DEFRA committees. We need more public involvement at the heart of what DEFRA is trying to do, or not do, with food.

It is a big question, but Neil is right: it is partly an institutional failure. We do not have a council of food and national food security; we should do. If we had something equivalent to the Climate Change Committee , we would have something giving clear, strategic, central advice to the Government. We have a few bolt-on committees that come along one moment and seem to fade a bit, but we need something put on a better footing. When you look at other countries—to go back to the earlier question—the ones that are doing interesting things for resilience and security have better institutional structures. Ours are out of date.

One of the recommendations in “ The Roadmap for Resilience ” is that we have a co-ordinating board or committee that sits above DEFRA, perhaps through the Cabinet Office and reporting to the Prime Minister. It is easy to make these sorts of machinery of government recommendations in these sorts of reports, but I think this is a case where you have a major and complex challenge that crosses Government Departments and does not really get the co-ordinated focus that it warrants. This is an occasion where it would be quite good to have a bit of machinery of government change.
Or else why have food as one of 13 CNIs? I mean, we either take it seriously or we don’t. The public take it very seriously—they want their food; but it might be different food in crises.

Q57 This is the last question. Both of you have previously touched on elements of what I am about to ask. You just said, and I think you are right, that a Government setting up a website saying this, that and the other is not enough; you are not drilling down as much as you need to, whether that is into local resilience forums or otherwise. And out of that falls another question: how can you ensure that vulnerable people would have access to food during a severe disruption? And out of that then falls another question: how much should be left to individual households, in terms of preparedness? So there are three tiers, if you could wrap it up, please.

I am glad that Mr Turmaine pressed my button pressed earlier about different levels. This applies to consumer confidence. One of the big holes—the NAO Report did not go into this for whatever reason—is storage.

If you look at the Prepare website and, I think, from the hints that we are getting, at the replacement that will be announced shortly—Get Ready, or Play Your Part, or whatever it is called—we know that the onus is going to be on households to protect themselves. But when we interview consumers, we know that it is actually about neighbourliness and community. If we go to the community level, we know that we need something slightly bigger than that.

That is why, in answer to Mr Turmaine, I pointed to the Swedish report. The Swedes were very Swedish and said, “We cannot just say to consumers any more than, ‘Well, it is all just up to the central state to have storage.’” You have got to have different levels of storage, of different things and at different levels if you want to be serious about maintaining trust and confidence that the food will be there.

It is back to this challenge of multi-levelness and encouraging the creativity of the British public. They are amazing; British civil society is fantastic. However, as Neil was alluding to earlier, it does not have the support or indeed recognition. It is not being included enough in central Government thinking about what we want from food. That is where they told me loud and clear, for my report: “Look, we are doing sticking plaster work in food banks. What would it take for them to become community food stores?” What a thought!

What would it take for cities or towns to have town plans for which neighbourhoods can help each other? What skills would we need to spread in the population to enable better access to land? I speak to those of you who are farmers. At what point would you allow 10 acres to become an allotment? Seriously. I talked to landowners who said, “We are up for that. Why not?”
Q58 Why not, Rupes?
There you go; you can have this internal discussion.
I don’t think they’d grow very much—

I talked to very big landowners who said, “We’d be up for that.” We need better access. You look at other cultures, to go back to Mr Turmaine’s question to me, such as the Netherlands, Sweden or France, and you see that access to land is totally different. Go to Russia—old-style Russia—and the allotments kept people alive.

The “Roadmap for Resilience” report talks about three core transformations in making production more resilient, particularly to climate change but also to shocks, and to be smarter about land use. That is my point about better mapping the productive capacity of our agricultural resource to our needs better, and making healthy food more accessible and affordable. You have to do those three things together.

I do not think that we do the accessible and affordable very well, irrespective of the resilience challenge. However, if thinking about the resilience of the food system is becoming more high-profile and more prominent, that might be a way in which we can start to get a food system that delivers more broadly across the population. The Food Foundation has done really interesting work. It shows that to afford a healthy diet among the poorest families takes up 85% of their total income, just on food.

We have a problem around access to healthy food among a part of the population. Community initiatives around food—these local food partnerships—can be a vehicle to bring in all sorts of other social wellbeing improvements and deal with a range of social problems beyond the food system. It is really important to think about people on more modest incomes and more vulnerable groups.

Q59 It strikes me, as somebody who represents very strong communities, that we don’t have to just talk about food resilience; you can talk about communities in terms of resilience generally. I very often say our community will probably be the last thing we have.

In my report, the Treasury very kindly gave me the figures on how little money is spent on the British population for civil defence. I was interested—following the Sweden, Latvia and Finland example—in getting the population engaged in general food resilience. I asked them to show me. They said in Britain we spend less than £1 per person on civil defence, out of £55 billion for the MOD.

Apply that to DEFRA’s thinking and you can say there is no civil food defence. If we put a hard, military lens into our glasses, you would say, “Well, you would want more than that.” You would want some serious money to go into helping people to protect themselves to protect the nation, if you took that framework.
The NAO Report went into that in a roundabout way, on the question of how much money we are prepared to spend on that sort of infrastructure. At the moment it is not much.

It is quite interesting because it is very comfortable for people to say that the first function of a Government should be defence of the people—you hear people say that—and no one challenges it and says, “Hang on a minute, I think there should be less government.” That is very comfortable, but having a well-fed population ought to be pretty close to that.

That is where I called it; I said we have to dust down the 1930s notion of food defence. It changes the whole discourse. If you start looking at the complexity of the food systems that Neil and I and many colleagues have worked on for the last 30 or 40 years, these are acutely vulnerable chokepoints from very big powerful industries. They are vulnerable to attack.

How can we protect them? The answer is to create a slightly different food system. You go from single supplies to networks. That requires a very different economics. The notion of civil food defence is really interesting, and it is being applied by some groups in Wales now as part of the movement that is going on—with the approval of the county council. What would we do at a community level to protect ourselves?

Q60 I want to finish on that theme. I have a question for Neil. I want to quote paragraph 25 of your evidence back to you: “Responsibility for resilience should sit at the lowest effective level, while responsibility for systemic risks should sit at the national level. Major disruption exposed the limits of purely commercial approaches. Resilience should therefore be treated as a public good requiring a long-term partnership between g overnment, industry and civil society.” What did you actually have in mind there?

I have done a lot of work on trying to make sense of how we have the agriculture and food system and land use system that we have. We take for granted its current pattern and structure, but it has actually evolved quite a lot. You can look over 200 years and there have been huge shifts, but in living memory—since the second world war—it has been through quite a profound set of changes. The changes were relatively highly planned and orchestrated by the national state, with an architecture of county agricultural committees that oversaw what constituted good farming practice in different counties. Farmers could be told to pull their socks up and sort out the rabbits, the nettles or whatever— [Interruption.] And plough more, yes. And they were graded A, B, C—it was quite interventionist.

But in that period it was a partnership between the farmers and the state and the agribusiness companies and science and technology interests in the agribusiness companies. I think we need to revisit that idea of a national system—it could even be thought of as a patriotic mission around making our food system secure and resilient. I think we need the scale of ambition for change that was evident in the post-war period.

The “public good” terminology is to appeal to the very doctrinaire economic orthodoxy about the limits of government, but I do believe that the resilience of the food system is a public good. You can’t get away from that.
I agree.
Good. I was going to give you 10 seconds, but as you agree—
Geoffrey, can I just—

No, time is up. I thank our witnesses very much indeed. You are both very busy people, and we have benefited a lot from your evidence this afternoon. We will be having officials in on Thursday and we will no doubt use some of the information and knowledge that you have given us to further probe their intentions, so thank you very much indeed.

Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Henry de Zoete, Cat Little and Alexandra Jones.

Q153 Welcome to this final panel in today’s hearings on AI safety and security. Thank you very much indeed to our witnesses for joining us today. Cat Little, congratulations to you on your new role in His Majesty’s Government.
Cat Little, can I start with you? Was yesterday’s announcement an important announcement of G overnment policy ?

Cat Little: In relation to the announcement that Minister Narayan made, yes. Ultimately, it is setting out the approach to safety and cyber-security , and the importance of working with our partners to protect the British public.

Q154 I know you will have memorised section 9.1 of the m inisterial c ode, but, if you have not, let me read it to you : “When Parliament is in session, the most important announcements of government policy should be made in the first instance in Parliament . ” Why was it briefed to the Telegraph on Sunday?

Cat Little: Our Ministers take their responsibilities very seriously. I am aware that there was some trailing in advance. I will report back to the Minister your concerns about his compliance with the code. I will support him and give him some advice on how best to respond to that.
Ultimately, it is an important part of the overall work that we are doing on AI. I hope that we will be able to give you more information today at this hearing.
Q155 Why was there not an oral statement in the House?
Cat Little: I will need to come back to you on that. This was an important thing that Ministers wanted to talk about very quickly upon the closure of recess.
Q156 B ut not in the House of Commons.
Cat Little: Clearly, that i s not the case —yes .

Q157 The announcement, which was confirmed in Minister Narayan’s letter at 10.31 pm last night, reiterates merely the contents of the written ministerial statement. It says that the Government are offering consideration but not commitments: no new regulatory powers, no timetable for amendments to the C yber S ecurity Bill and no binding duties on AI developers. Is that true? Have I understood the announcement correctly?

Cat Little: As the Minister set out, there are a number of different actions that we are taking to make sure that we both manage the risks and promote the opportunities of AI. There is a combination of things that we are working on. Part of it is regulation; part of it is the standards, the principles, the approach and the work that we are taking globally at the G20, which the Prime Minister has already spoken about; and, of course, there is the work of AISI. It is up to Ministers to set out the full timetable. I am confident that that will happen in due course.
Q158 I ncident reporting remains undecided and, from my reading of the letter, it could place the obligations on affected essential services rather than the AI companies responsible. Is that true?
Cat Little: I am very sorry. What are you reading from?
Q159 Is the Government’s approach to mandatory incident reporting undecided?

Cat Little: It is one of the things that we are looking at. I know that in your previous panels you have been talking to industry about how this will work. Transparency, reporting, the standards, the regulation and the opportunities that we have to manage AI safety are part of the work that is under way. This is policy under development.
Q160 It is under development. The Minister says that systems should not be released if the risks cannot be controlled. Should the Government therefore make that requirement enforceable?

Cat Little: To the extent that we can, yes. Everything that we are doing has to have real-world delivery bite. A lot of the work that we are doing at the moment is on a voluntary basis in partnership with industry, but, for all the reasons that you have just discussed with your previous panels, that is exactly why we are doing further work on standards, principles, guardrails and regulation , and using our convening power to make sure that we are taking all the action that is necessary.
Q161 Today, UK testing still depends on voluntary co-operation from both the companies and foreign Governments. That is the case.
Cat Little: Yes.
Q162 Should that change?

Cat Little: At the moment, if you look at the evidence—Henry might want to add to this—we have a really good track record of working on a voluntary basis. We cannot guarantee it, but the success of the work that we are doing particularly with AISI is dependent on having access to models. We have really good relationships and a good track record of that being the case. We are very fortunate to have AISI as part of the package of levers that we have within the UK to manage risk.

Q163 Let us compare the Government’s approach to AI with its approach to, say, aviation, financial services, pharmaceuticals and food safety. In aviation, financial services, pharmaceuticals and food safety, you have proactive risk monitoring, independently set safety standards, authorisation of market entry, post-market monitoring, an independent regulator with enforcement powers, accountability measures, routes to redress , and transparency and reporting requirements that are mandatory. I cannot quite understand why the Government are not proposing to align the AI safety regime with the approach that we take in aviation, financial services, pharmaceuticals and food safety.

Cat Little: Th e Committee will be aware that our approach to the regulation of general technology is to regulate within context. One of the big policy questions at the moment is whether that continues to be enough. Given the pace at which the frontier models are moving and the level of risk that we are seeing, yes, regulation has a really important part to play. Ministers have made it very clear that we will see regulation where we think it is enforceable, useful and will have an impact.

That has to be part of a total framework that includes the work that we do in pre-testing deployment, the convening power that we have with other countries and the work that we do with the labs, and it also has to be part of the guardrails that can be enforced on a day-to-day basis. The pace at which these risks are potentially manifesting needs an urgent and comprehensive response. Regulation is part of the answer, but it is not everything.
Q164 G iven the urgency that you have underlined, can we expect amendments to the C yber S ecurity Bill by the time that it gets to the Commons?

Cat Little: I do not know whether Alex might want to add to this. It is probably worth explaining our different roles. I am here as the Permanent Secretary of the Cabinet Office, which is responsible for AISI. Alex Jones is the director general responsible for AI policy in my new Department, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade .

Alexandra Jones: DCMS is responsible for the Bill, but we are proposing, in the speech that the Minister made yesterday, to use the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill to consider changes to improve preparedness for AI cyber and loss - of - control risks , and to look at how serious incidents and near misses are identified and reported , and how AI - driven disruption across the organisations is contained.

Q165 Alex, just to interrupt, you cannot consider something in a Bill. You have to legislate for something in a Bill. Given the urgency that Cat Little has just underlined, by the time the C yber S ecurity Bill hits the Commons , will there be G overnment amendments to deal with some of the risks that we have identified?
Alexandra Jones: The consideration is that we are looking at that live — developing the policy to look at whether we use the cyber Bill to do that.
Q166 “ We ’ re thinking about it . ”
Alexandra Jones: We are developing the policy very rapidly, given the pace at which the technology is developing.
Q167 Charlie Maynard: To whoever would like to answer, if AISI decides that a model is too dangerous to deploy or should be withdrawn, what plan do the Government have to effect that?
Cat Little: Henry, do you want to explain what happens when we do our testing and how we work with laboratories?
Charlie Maynard: Importantly, if you say no, so you do not approve it—that is what I am asking—and they carry on, what do we do?
Cat Little: That is what Henry is going to explain for us.

Henry de Zoete: I will try. Chair, if you do not mind, I want to say at the start that I owe an apology to all the M embers. We were bad at getting back to your letters. It slipped between my predecessor and m e , with the change of Government.
We call it the change of Administration.
Well, it was the machinery of government change. I would like to apologise to everybody for that.
That is understood. We are grateful.
As I said in my letter, I am keen to invite everybody into the security institute so we c an do an afternoon or a day to talk about all these things in depth.

We had better break this to you now. The Committee has just agreed an ongoing inquiry into the UK’s AI safety regime , which will unfold from today over the course of the next 12 months , with its first report in the months ahead.
Henry de Zoete: It is hugely welcome to hear that. We are keen to help as much as we can and to provide whatever you need for it.

On th e specific question, right at the start it is worth saying what AISI is and what it is not. It is a part of the Cabinet Office. It is a directorate there. It is a research organisation that is not making policy.

What are we doing when we test models? When an AI company says, “We want you to test a model , ” we say to it , “How powerful is it?” We need some information about it. We will not test every single model that is out there. It is not worth our time or resources to test some of the less powerful ones. We will then go through a process of testing that model—I can talk in depth about that—and then we will write back to the company with what we have found . Then the company will take actions to improve things, depending on what we have done.
What we are not doing is kitemarking. We are not saying yes or no to any model. That is not what we are doing in our role.

Q168 Charlie Maynard: Let us say you write back saying, “We are absolutely terrified about what this model is . ” You are relying entirely on their good graces to say, “We agree with you . ” Let us say that they do not agree with you and they proceed. I am worried about that model then being put out into the public domain, the world. Your job and our job is to protect 70 million UK citizens. How do we protect them?
Cat Little: If I could just add to what Henry has said, it is really important to understand that AISI is not a regulator.
I am clear on that.

Of course, the research, evaluation and testing that is undertaken is publicly and transparently reported. If we look back at the incident that happened in July, we very quickly reported the evaluation and what we had found.

Ultimately, we are not just reliant on voluntary good will. A really important part of it is transparency, so that everyone can see what we have found and what the risks are. Ultimately, like many products, this is about making sure that people are informed and aware of what risks are there.

Q169 The challenge we have is that Ken McCallum has warned this afternoon about low-capability terrorists being given a capability uplift using AI to develop bioweapons. Mr Maynard is asking what powers are available to stop that technology entering the UK market. What is the answer to that, Mr de Zoete?

Henry de Zoete: Specifically on that biosecurity, I will give an example of the work we have done with an AI company. Last year, before OpenAI released GPT-5, we did our testing. We found 12 biosecurity vulnerabilities.
Q170 Say that again. You found 12 biosecurity vulnerabilities ?

Henry de Zoete: We have talked about this publicly. We found 12 biosecurity vulnerabilities in GPT-5 before it was released in our pre-deployment testing. That also included a universal jailbreak, which is where you can remove all the safeguards very easily. We took that back to OpenAI . It made a whole bunch of changes to the model and publicly praised the work that it did with AISI to make those changes. That is a real example of how we have made the world safer.

Q171 Charlie Maynard: There are a whole load of Chinese models too, for which you do not have these agreements in place. You might be looking at the US and they might do everything that you want them to do, but the Chinese do not and the people with those Chinese models do not. The key question is, “What controls do we have?”

By the way, I am not saying that there is an easy answer or that I have the answer. I am not. I am worried; I am scared. What can we do, as a country, to protect ourselves against a very dangerous model? Is there a plan? Maybe that is the first question : i s there a plan?

Yes, and Alex should add to this. I must come back to what the Prime Minister and Ministers have already said. Fundamentally, this is about working with international partners and using our convening power, especially at the G20 during our presidency year, to tackle this issue. This is not something that the UK alone can lead on. We have to work with all of our foreign colleagues and industry partners to make the most effective response to exactly your question. The work that goes into the G20 is very much under way, but, Alex, you should add to that.

Building on that, and also on your specific issues around biosecurity, for example, we have the UK biological security strategy, which is all about making sure that we are resilient to a whole range of biological risks. The Ministry of Defence announced an investment of £115 million earlier this year to make sure that we are raising our defences against AI. That includes using AI to improve our biological security.

AI clearly has real opportunities in relation to developing drugs, but also massive challenges. The MOD investment is about improving biological security and mitigating some of the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, and that is alongside investments in biosecurity centres. I know that that does not respond to all those risks, but there is definitely a particular plan.

Q172 We might as well nail this down, just so that we all know where everything is. We have had a pretty stark warning from Ken McCallum this afternoon. We have heard a range of views today from AI companies on statutory regulation and the role of international conventions. The truth, though, Henry de Zoete, is that we do not have the power to stop dangerous AI models becoming available to bad actors in this country, do we?
AISI is a research org. It is up to Ministers what they want to do with—
Q173 I just want to clarify where we are right now. We do not have the power to stop bad actors getting hold of dangerous technology.
The truth is that there are lots of factors at play here. There is not one single thing that is a silver bullet to answering your question.
Q174 I know that. I am just trying to establish a single view of the truth, which is that we do not have the power to stop that dangerous technology becoming available to bad actors. Mr de Zoete?

With open-weight models, I do not think that anybody necessarily has that power. There is a bunch of things to think about here. These companies, which are either American or Chinese, are building at the frontier the stuff that is the most powerful. There is only so much that we, as the UK, can do in that context. We are doing extremely good work at the AI Security Institute and in diplomatic engagement to try to move things in the right direction on it.

At AISI, that is not just pre-deployment testing of the models, but post-deployment testing of the models. We are doing research. We are publishing things to move the field onwards. We have built six or seven tools that we have open-sourced to carry out evaluations, which all the AI companies are currently using. The US AISI equivalent uses it. The South Korean equivalent uses it. Japan uses it. The EU uses it. We are at the heart of the international network of AI security institutes. The UK is doing a hell of a lot to try to move things in the right direction.
Q175 Yes, without doubt, but it is on a voluntary basis.

At the moment, yes, it is, but the implicit point that you are making goes to the question of whether that is adequate. That is exactly why we are using our unique position, as Henry has just set out, to make sure that we really tackle and address that question.

Q176 I am sure that we will return to that , but let me move on briefly to some slightly more positive potential for artificial intelligence . Ministers have talked a lot about how we could deploy it to improve the economy and support public services. I just wonder how we can get the balance right. If we are going to train these models and to work collaboratively, as we have heard, what do we have to bear in mind when we consider that there is still going to be a risk there, but we know that there are lots of benefits that we could achieve?

Cat, you may wish to comment, but, Henry, perhaps from the institute’s perspective, how can we make sure that we are not just being completely permissive and that we still have some safeguards, so that, when we are deploying this in public services, hopefully to great effect, we do have that confidence?
Do you mind if I start?
Of course — that ’ s fine.

I know that Henry will want to give an AISI perspective, but your question is primarily a policy question about how we manage the very best opportunities that come from AI while balancing that with the risks. The simple answer is that AI is the defining opportunity and the biggest challenge of our generation. There is absolutely no doubt about it. We should not be forced to choose between the opportunity for progress, productivity and prosperity, and safety. They are totally intertwined, and I do not believe that we can deliver the benefits of AI if we do not also have trust and safety at the heart of our agenda. We know that we have to be able to do both. It is not a decision between the two.

Q177 Thank you. Henry, can you add some flavour to that? We have just had quite a debate i n this Committee about whether that is even possible, whether there is that trust, and whether we can deploy those things. I know that we want all the good things from it, but we are all now starting to panic slightly about the bad things that come from it. Are we sure about that deployment, particularly in public services?

I am not clear, for example, on why we need to train them on everything in the world entirely, to be perfectly frank. If we are going to deploy them in the public sector, are we going to be looking at models that are looking at very specific tasks? That would be a much easier way, surely, to contain what they do and how they do it.
Yes, absolutely. If you do not mind me saying so , the question is probably less for AISI and possibly more for Alex and me. AISI does not do the sort of policy balance that you are pointing to.

It is testing the frontier models. If you look across the economy, most people are not using frontier models. They are using different models. One of the things that we are trying to do to increase resilience, but also to make sure that we are looking at the opportunities, is to have a diverse set of models and think about how to apply them and what to use them for. We are helping people to trust those models. We have been introducing, as the Minister said yesterday, some more AI assurance around how you make sure that the models are doing the things that you think they should be, and how you can test that and have some tools available.

As we deploy it, it is about trying to get that domestic capability, but not at the frontier. In some businesses and in public services, y ou do not always need the frontier ; y ou need tailored models. It is about trying to get that resilience, making sure we have that AI assurance so that we can trust it and test it in the businesses, while still testing and understanding the frontier models and making sure we have access to them where we need to, which is not going to be across the spectrum. All of that also needs to be done with workers and people, and the opportunities that it creates, in mind.
Q178 Is that differential between AI models and frontier models clear in terms of how Ministers are talking about the benefits to the economy, to public services and the like?
Yes, absolutely.

Q179 Perhaps you can enlighten us on how they are going to approach that, because we are not quite clear on whether we are going to be taking the upcoming opportunity of the Cyber S ecurity and Resilience Bill to regulate .

There is that very clear distinction. Our experience of adoption so far, particularly in the public sector, is that our real challenge is scaling and adopting to get the benefits of productivity, efficiency and service outcomes for the public, using very openly available AI tools. We have ambitions to use AI right in the frontline of public services just to boost productivity in the way that we know it is capable of.

There is brilliant work under way that is nowhere near using some of these frontier models for the work that we do. Part of our job in the public sector, when we are looking at adopting AI, is to know which technological tools are best suited in our value streams for delivering the productivity and service improvements that we are looking for. Frontier models are not necessarily always the best tool for the sorts of service outcomes that we are looking for.
Q180 What have you learned about your testing processes after the breach in July? Do you trust your environment?

That is a very good and important question. The thing to be clear on about our incident, which was an incident, i s that there was no security breach. It was not like some of the other incidents that we have heard about, where the models have worked out an exploit to get out of their sandbox and to go and do bad things.

When we set up our evaluation, we connected the models to the internet. We did that on purpose because we wanted to see what the models’ capabilities would be to go out there. Bad people are going to connect these things to the internet, so there is a very fine line between doing testing in a simulated environment and connecting it to the real world and seeing what is going on.

What the model then went and did was definitely bad behaviour. When we became aware of it, we shut it down within an hour, and published a full report on it within a week. I could talk through the things that we have changed. Essentially, we reviewed when we give internet access to the models to make sure that we know when we are doing it. We have made our sandboxes harder anyway, even though there was not a security breach. We have improved our monitorability, creating a synchronous monitor that looks at what the AI is doing.

F rankly, the speed and change of the capabilities caught us off guard at that point, because we did not think that the model would have the capabilities to go out and do the kinds of things that it went and did. On reflection, we should not have connected it to the internet, but these things are judgment calls. Previously, we had done that and things had not gone wrong, and we learned lots of important things. It is very important to test in real-life situations in order to see what is happening, but we have improved the simulated environments. The speed of improvement across these models is quite something to behold.

Q181 Is there any other environment in which you would try something in a live environment when you did not know how it worked? The way that we are trying to evaluate these models is just so dangerous.

This is a nascent science. Evaluation of these models is very new. It started only in the last two or three years, and we are learning all the time. The kinds of things that we are doing now include creating very detailed cyber - ranges, where we simulate a computer network for a model to attack. This time last year, the models were able to do very simple, narrow cyber tasks of a certain nature. We have now created cyber - ranges that involve 32 steps, covering everything from reconnaissance to exploit identification, lateral movement inside the system, and then data exfiltration. These take a human 20 hours to do. We found in April this year that the models were able to do these autonomously, and now they can all do it.

We are having to build more and more difficult cyber - ranges, and doing lots more difficult tasks to get them. We have one that is called the cooling tower. It is a harder task, but it involves the models making things happen in the real world physically. That is also a cyber - range that has now been completed by the models, so we are having to use all our resources and talent to keep building these simulated things in order to keep on top of the speed of the capabilities of the models.
Q182 Are you faster than Anthropic, OpenAI and everybody else?

My team is great. We are very lucky. We have 240 staff, with brilliant civil servants and a brilliant technical team who are taking pay cuts to be involved in AISI, because they believe in the mission and want to work with G overnment on all of this stuff. We now do four times as many tests as we did back in 2024. When we tested a model, it used to be a whole team exercise that would take a month, or even two, to do, and we could run only one model test at a time. We are now able to run multiple tests of models at the same time and get results within days, so we are speeding up as hard as we can.
All of that is laudable, but you are chasing people who are chasing a $2 trillion IPO.
Q183 AISI has no statutory powers to regulate AI. Given what we have heard this afternoon, can that be right? Would you like statutory powers?
We are a research body.

This comes back to the question of what should be regulated and what we need more powers for. That is ultimately part of the policy work that is under development. If Ministers decide to have more regulation, and if Parliament legislates, the question of who does that is a really important one, but, right now, AISI is not a regulator. It is here to do really valuable work. If you do not mind me saying so , it is doing fantastic work. You have heard today from many people just how important it is to the overall regime globally. We are very lucky to have it.
Q184 It is inevitable, though, is it not, that it is going to need a statutory basis?
That is a matter for Parliament.
Q185 You are going to be the lead architect on the policy framework. You are going to supply the policy advice to the Secretary of State and to the Minister of State.

I repeat what Ministers have said. Ultimately, we are setting out the whole framework. We are looking at a comprehensive package. If Ministers look at that analysis and say, “Yes, we really do need to put in place further regulation , ” that is absolutely on the table.
Q186 In your own mind, do you know what you will recommend?
We are doing the work now. By the way, I have not even started to take up office yet in my new role , but —
I know that you have been thinking about it very hard.

T his is very live in terms of the work that we are doing. To assure this Committee, it is comprehensive and very thoughtful analysis that is not just about the UK ; i t is about how we work in a really collaborative, open way with our counterparts internationally.

Q187 We do not have our own sovereign AI frontier model. Google DeepMind is based in London but is US-owned. We are seeing and have heard today that we are having more and more powerful frontier models, and there is a relative rather than an absolute view of safety among those developing them. What role can a country such as the UK play in preventing a global race to the bottom in safety standards?

I come back to the very unique strengths that the UK has. We have unique convening power. It is fortunate that we have the G20 presidency next year. That is a really important moment for us to put AI at the heart of the global agenda. We are very fortunate to have AISI. From an economic perspective, we have thousands of AI businesses here. We are underpinned by world-class research and fantastic tech talent, which puts the UK in a good position to convene and to lead this agenda in a respected and trusted way, and that is absolutely our intention.
You might have seen that, yesterday, AISI published its approach on best practices. This was following the Prime Minister’s discussion on standards for safety and security and what could be done.

Specifically on your question of preventing a global race on safety standards, we are engaging with industry along these lines, and working with our brilliant partners in Government, such as the National Cyber S ecurity Centre, on what the next step for standards and best practices could be, such as monitoring or preserving oversight over these systems.

We have laid out eight areas that we want to get into. I feel quite strongly about monitoring, and I can talk about that if you would like me to. Working with industry, working with brilliant people in Government, and working across Government in this area, the technical capability that we have in this Government to write these standards and best practices is genuinely quite unique in the world. That is what we are going to try to do, with other people’s help.

There are also some examples of sector regulations. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Authority regulates not AI but medical devices. It is running a sandbox to check whether there are AI-specific questions. It has been accepting recommendations from the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare to make sure that we monitor those devices throughout their lives. There are a number of sector-specific sandboxes and regulations coming into play where they are not regulating AI specifically, but regulating within. That is true for the Financial Conduct Authority as well. We are looking across the piece and asking, “Is that enough? Is that effective enough? How is that working?”, but there are a number of sector examples that are useful too.

Q188 Superintelligent AI poses a different but similar-level existential threat to climate change. The UK legislated on climate change in the Climate Change Act 2008 , seven years before the Paris agreement, which is a global agreement. As you say, we have convening power. AISI is the first one to have been established. Would the UK legislating not create momentum towards a global agreement in the same way that the Climate Change Act did?
That is, of course, a matter for Parliament and for Ministers, but that is exactly the sort of work that is under way as we go across all of the things that we have just discussed.

The clock is against us, so I am sorry that that session was cut slightly short, but we will aim to generate a special report from today’s session in order to help inform Parliament ahead of potential G overnment amendments to the Cyber S ecurity Bill once it reaches the Commons. A new inquiry on AI safety and security has been launched today by the Committee, which will help us contribute to this debate over the course of the next year. For now, thank you very much indeed for your evidence. Henry, we look forward to coming to visit you sometime soon on a mutually convenient date, but, for now, that is it.

Joint Committee on Human Rights member present: Alex Sobel .
Science and Technology Committee member present: Martin Wrigley.

Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Lord Booth-Smith, Tom Duff Gordon, Owen Larter and Rob Sherman .

Q36 Welcome to today ’ s second panel on AI safety and governance. Thank you very much indeed to our witnesses for joining us today. I know that the parliamentarians among you will need no reminding, but to give false, misleading or incomplete evidence to a C ommittee is, on the face of it, a contempt of the House.

Let me start with some of the warnings that we have received from the leaders of your organisations. Mr Altman told the US Senate in 2023 , “My worst fears are that we…cause significant harm to the world . ” The leader of Anthropic went on the record in 2025 to say, “I think there ’ s a 25% chance that things go really, really badly . ” Mr Zuckerberg said in 2024 that individual bad actors may be able to use the intelligence of AI models to fabricate entirely new harms. Demis Hassabis has said that advances on the frontier are now outpacing our understanding of the technology.

Nobody in the world knows for sure what is going to happen from here. C an you assure the C ommittee today that your models can do no harm to people or businesses in our country and will do no harm in the years ahead?

Good afternoon, Chair. Good afternoon, members of the Committee. We take safety incredibly seriously at OpenAI. We listened very carefully to the previous panel. Our position at the moment is that we should not progress with AI as fast as we can make it and develop it ; w e should progress AI as fast as we can keep it safe. Those are not just words; they are also deeds. During the summer, after the Hugging Face incident, we paused the training and reinforcement learning of our most advanced model. Just recently, we held back a model—Astra 6.1—that we were due to release. We say that we want to move at the speed where we can make sure that capabilities are not outstripping safety, and we are matching that with what we do . We have very significant processes internally to ensure that we manage risks. We have a preparedness framework.

Q37 Tom, that is great, but it is no t the question I asked you . The question I asked you was whether you can guarantee that today your model is not capable of being used to cause harm to people or businesses in this country.

Yes, I can reassure you that we are confident in the processes that we have internally to ensure that we manage frontier risks, particularly risks with regard to cyber, bio and loss of control. We have a preparedness framework and will not deploy a model unless it has passed that framework. I can assure you that our deployed models are safe and do not pose a risk to the UK.
Q38 Lord Booth-Smith, can you give the same assurance for Anthropic?

Lord Booth-Smith : We have rigorous safety processes in place. We were founded as an AI safety research company. Alongside those safety processes, we also believe that we need to pace the frontier. We consider deployed models safe. They have mitigations in place.

It is also worth pointing out that we are learning a lot as we go about how these models are used. It would be wrong not to say that. As new issues emerge, that is something that we believe should be publicly shared and debated. We factor that into all our future thinking about safety research.
Q39 You think that harms could be caused .

Lord Booth-Smith : We have seen in the last six months some instances where models have done things that we would not have wanted them to do. Safety is stratified, as to how one would determine that, but we have seen models do things that we would not have wanted them to do. I believe that it is entirely plausible that we have the mitigations in place to deal with those. As models become more capable, we need to make sure that the safeguards in those models are in place to deal with the additional capabilities that we see as the models improve.

Q40 The question was whether you can guarantee that the models are currently safe. You started off by saying yes, but then said that there have been some problems in the past and , no, you cannot absolutely guarantee that model development will be safe in the future.

Lord Booth-Smith : I am confident that the models on the market right now are safe. I am confident in the processes we have around them. I am just saying that, given the testimony we heard earlier and our own research, we know that, if models become ever more capable, we will need to have testing and evaluation that can keep pace, but also safety mitigations that can match up to the capability of the model. That is why a few months ago the CEO of the company called for a pacing of the frontier, including embedding evaluators, which is something that we have already done.
Q41 The capability of the models may be proceeding so fast that we may not currently have the systems in place to keep the model s safe.

Lord Booth-Smith : That is a genuine concern. One reason why we should pace the frontier is that, if we are able to pace the frontier properly, we will buy ourselves time and space to do two things. The first is to make sure that the testing and evaluation processes and frameworks that we have in place are adequate to the capabilities of the model. Secondly , we will create the time and space for policymakers, elected representatives and G overnments to think through what the appropriate governance framework for these models is , both pre and post ‑ release.
Q42 The technology is moving faster than our ability to keep it safe, and therefore we need to slow down the speed with which the technology is proceeding.

Lord Booth-Smith : It is more about where we see the technology going. It is exponential. It is a trajectory. If one assumes that it continues progressing at an ever more rapid pace, then , yes, the current testing and evaluation framework does not meet some of the future risks that may appear. We want to be confident that that matches up properly , and you can only achieve that by pacing the frontier of the technology.

Q43 Our concern is that many technology bosses at the moment appear to be behaving almost like the Dr Frankenstein of the 21st century. They are seeking a freedom to deploy powers beyond our ability to control the harms that might arise. You think that that is a risk, and therefore legislators need time to develop stronger safeguards.

Lord Booth-Smith : We have consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough. We have been very consistent about that for a number of years. The industry and the technology should be subject to G overnment rule setting.
Q44 Mr Larter, what is the commitment that you can give on behalf of Google DeepMind as to whether the model is today safe for people in this country?

Thank you, Chair and members of the Committee. This is a very important conversation at an important time. We at Google DeepMind have been doing AI research in the UK for over 15 years now. We think that there is an enormous amount of opportunity around the technology. It is fantastic to see the way in which people right across the UK, whether scientific researchers, teachers or tradespeople, are now using this technology. It is absolutely fundamental that we do this in a way that is safe, secure and responsible.

Alongside the work that we do to advance AI capabilities, we invest in our internal governance processes. We have a frontier safety framework internally that tests our most advanced systems for misuse risks, so the idea that a bad actor could weaponise an advanced model for a cyber-attack or create a bioweapon, and issues of alignment, making sure that advanced models are following instructions.

At the core of this safety framework is a critical capability level. We make sure that we are not putting models out there on to the market that are beyond a certain risk level. We test them rigorously internally to assess that. We then apply mitigations. We have those mitigations red - teamed by both internal experts and, critically, third parties. They give us good confidence that the models we are then putting out there for people to use are not breaching these critical capability levels.
Q45 Can you give the commitment today that the model you have available is not capable of causing harm to people or business?
Yes. The whole point of the frontier safety framework is that we would not put something out there unless we were very confident that risks had been mitigated to an appropriate level.
Q46 Do you think that the potential risks of your model in the future are containable under the current safety regime we have available?

This is powerful technology that will have all kinds of incredible opportunities and all kinds of applications in scientific research and healthcare, but we should take AI capabilities seriously and continue to invest in safety science and matur e—
Q47 T hat sounds like no .

If I could just finish the answer, please, Chair, a fundamental aspect of this AI governance debate is how quickly it is moving. The AI continues to become more capable. We are also learning a lot more about how the AI performs and how to mature our governance processes. We have had our frontier safety framework in place for two years. We have updated it four times to iterate to improve it. We have to keep investing in that safety science so that we are able to keep speed with the capabilities of the technology as well. That is a fundamental.
Q48 D o you think we have the right regime for keeping these models safe?

We have to continue to invest in the scientific study of AI safety, mature these best practices and work with others. This will be a partnership as well. There are institutions such as the UK AI Security Institute, which is world leading, and its equivalent in the US. They have an enormous amount of technical expertise as well. If we can pool that knowledge and expertise and build these best practices, we must find a way to keep pace with the capabilities of technology.
Q49 Given what we have learned about the incidents this year, why should we trust you to do that?
This is fundamental to the systems that we have put together.
Q50 Sure , b ut why should we trust you?

A fundamental part of what we do is to perform our internal testing and apply mitigations, but then also, critically, work with third parties to have that verified. I would draw us back to the AI Security Institute, which is a crown jewel that we have here in the UK. There are a lot of research collaborations and pre-release testing that we do with organisations such as this. The AI Security Institute mission, which is to make sure that Governments have an understanding of advancing capabilities, is very important as we seek to continue to mature this best practice that I am talking about.

Q51 It does not have compulsory access to models. It does not have access to the early testing regime that it needs. It does not have a kill switch. It does not have the ability to stop models coming on to the market. It does not have any of the tools that could help guarantee to us, as legislators, that it has the power to keep us safe.

There is a really important conversation about the role of the AI Security Institute, which has been right at the forefront of maturing AI safety science over the last few years. One benefit of the AI Security Institute is that it is not a regulator, so it has open discussions with the labs. We do testing with it and learn from it. We share knowledge. We do research collaborations as well. It is really important in terms of maturing the science.

If you turn it into a regulator, you are going to completely change the dynamic with which we engage with the AISI. I think you might lose a lot of that ability to have the open, collaborative discussion that is maturing the science at a rapid lick, which is what we need.
Q52 T hat brings us back to a position of basically trusting your good intentions.

I do not think that it is a case of trusting our good intentions. It is also important to understand that we have a good body of regulation in the UK to start from. It is interesting hearing the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum talking about the existing law that applies. Alongside that, we need to continue to invest in this ability to test, understand and mitigate risks. It is interesting hearing the contributions of the Governor of the Bank of England recently, looking at what AISI put in its blog and focusing in on this safety science and maturing things as quickly as possible as the place for us all to be focusing.

Q53 Let us come back to some of those questions. Rob Sherman, what is the assurance that you can give to the Committee that Meta systems are not capable of harming either people or businesses in this country?

Chair, thank you so much . Thanks to the C ommittee for the opportunity to be here and for this important conversation. We are sitting at a critical moment in the development of this technology , and thinking about how to build it safely is critical. When we think about how we should approach building AI safely, we think about the appreciable benefits of the technology. Our particular approach is on a concept called personal superintelligence, which is around taking this technology and making it available to help individual people reach their potential. W e reali s e that we are only going to do that if we build technology that is safe and trusted. O ur approach is to use multiple layers of safeguards, including both internal and external ones , in order to make sure that we are shipping models and products that are safe.
Q54 Your conclusion is that your model today is what — safe, risky or dangerous?

We have what we call a scaling framework, which talks about the standards that we use for evaluating our models as we are building them and deploying them. That looks at three different areas: cyber-security , chemical and biological weapons , and loss of control. In each of those areas, we evaluate our models as we are developing them and before release to see what the level of risk is. If we concluded that it was not safe to ship a model, we would not release it.
Q55 To be clear, the commitment you are giving to the Committee this afternoon is that the models that you have available are safe.
Correct. If we felt that a model was not safe to release, we would not release it.

Q56 Over the summer, we learned that OpenAI systems had engaged in a pretty serious hacking attack at Hugging Face. Anthropic identified three incidents affecting three different organisations where the evaluator allowed internet access when normal safeguards were absent. A t Meta, there was a testing company, Irregular, that gave a model access to the internet and a real website to target. In May 2026, a Gemini system gained unauthorised access to systems affecting three real companies. Those incidents are known. Are there other incidents affecting cyber-security or other misbehaviour that is not in the public domain , that you are aware of and that the Committee should know about today?

Lord Booth-Smith : We published a blog post on Friday that detailed nine incidents that affected US entities, and they were informed. As part of what happened over the summer in terms of misbehaviour of models, we just began a process internally to review a huge number of transcripts, covering many months of different testing environments, to identify whether there had been any incidents or misbehaviour in the models. The nine that we released last week were surfaced as a result of that process. That process is still ongoing. Obviously, as and when the process is complete, we will update and report to the affected entities any incidents we uncover.
Q57 At this stage , you cannot assure us that there are not more to come.

Lord Booth-Smith : I am not close to the technical process and it would be wrong to suggest that I can give you that assurance. I cannot. We are going through the process right now. One reason why it takes longer than we would like is that, as part of that process, there is a human verification element to it. As we put more people on to do it, it takes time to get through.
Q58 T here may be more incidents reported.
Lord Booth-Smith : Yes. I cannot give you an assurance that there are not.
Q59 Okay. Tom .
It is a similar answer , but first of all, a t OpenAI we certainly apologise if our agents access G overnment websites in ways that are unexpected or ways that we do not direct them to .
I am sure that everyone will be reassured to hear that .

Similarly, after the Hugging Face incident, which occurred in July, we launched a very extensive look - back investigation, looking at our models that were pre-deployment in training to see whether they had gone and visited other websites. You are probably aware of what happened in Australia and other places. There is a very deep, ongoing investigation.

There was also a report in the press recently in the UK that one of our agents had accessed statistics from a UK Government website. To be absolutely crystal clear to the Committee, this was publicly available data and the Government said that there had not been a breach of their cyber-defence s. Nevertheless, we notified. Our commitment is to notify whenever there are incidents such as that.

I will say that sometimes, when these agents go to the website, if they are acting in a way that we do not expect, we do not think it is necessarily on us to disclose that publicly. It is on the recipient, because there is potentially a vulnerability in that website. From a security perspective, it is almost incumbent on the Government to say, “We have had these reports . ” It is incumbent on us to report them, but I do not think that it would be responsible for us to say immediately, “We found this kind of credential on the internet that allowed an agent to do X , ” because we think that that opens the door to bad actors. Our commitment is to be very transparent through that investigation and to make sure that the Government know as soon as we know that there has been activity that we have not expected.
Q60 Are we fully aware of any other major incidents that may have occurred, or is there still news that may come?

Hugging Face was by far and away the most significant incident that we have seen. I do not want to trivialise them, but all the other incidents, or most of them, have been data retrieval, so an agent has gone to a G overnment website to get information.
Q61 Do you think that there are more to come, or can you assure us that that is it?

I cannot assure the Committee or you, Chair, that that is it. There are a handful of others that I am aware of that we have notified and there may be more to come as we go through what my colleague was saying, similar to us, is a very substantial amount of information. We are going through that as fast as we can. As soon as we identify that, we will notify the Government. There is a handful of others, but there may be more.
Q62 Mr Larter , what assurance can you give us?

There are a few important pieces here. With our frontier safety framework, we talked about the importance of testing, identifying risk and mitigating it. The other part of it is having the utmost security across the lab at all stages of the process. This is where we, as Google DeepMind, benefit from being part of Google, which has almost 30 years ’ experience of securing information across various different services . With our latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, which is forthcoming, we have very secure sandboxes that we are using whenever we are doing any high-risk training or testing.
Q63 Are you happy that we are not going to learn about more incidents, or major incidents, in the weeks ahead?

I would distinguish the one incident that you mentioned in relation to Google DeepMind, which was in connection with a testing partner. The system slowed down and stopped before it was able to do any harm. It did not break out of a secure sandbox.
Q64 You do not think there will be more news of incidents to come. This is your opportunity to let us know that there are other problems.
I am not aware of any other incidents.
Q65 Okay. Mr Sherman.

When we develop and test our models , it is important for us to have a range of safeguards in the way that we build them . An example of this is in the M use system, which we recently released in the US and hope to bring to the UK soon. There is an additional AI - driven Sentinel system, as it is called, which looks across the behaviour of the M use model , evaluates whether it is taking actions that are not expected and independently oversees it. That is one example of many safeguards that we should have in place as models are running so that there are checks and balances to make sure that models do not behave in unpredictable ways. I t is incumbent on us at Meta, and all the companies on the panel , to adopt safeguards in the way that we build.
Q66 The assurance we are seeking is whether you can assure us now that there are not major incidents that your models have been engaged in and that you are aware of but we are not.
The major incident that I am aware of is the one that you mentioned.
Q67 Are there any more to come ?
My expertise is in building governance systems , and I have to operate on the assumption that we should be looking for things happen ing that we do not want to happen. I am not aware of any.
Q68 You are not aware of them, but you cannot necessarily swear on behalf of the company.

I am not aware, and the company is not aware, of similar instances to the one that you described, but it is important, if we are acting responsibly, to have safeguards to look for those and guard against them.
Let us get into some of the detail , then.

Q69 I have a follow-up to Tom. GPT-6 .1 Astra was due to be released late last month. That release did not occur and it was reported that that was due to high levels of deception after alignment tests and that the model failed to accurately disclose actions it did or did not take. We know that today ’ s models are the least capable models we will see going forward. Can you tell us why GPT-6 .1 Astra was not released? What did it show that concerned you so much that you did not release it?

Thank you for the question. You are absolutely right. We decided not to release it because it did not score high enough on our alignment tests. It did not refuse enough when we were testing certain things and we were not comfortable that it had progressed in terms of alignment from 6.0. We actually saw a regression in the alignment of that model.

Now, 6.0 was our most aligned model, and much more aligned than 5.6. While 6.1 is still an aligned model and it was going in the right direction, we noticed a regression in alignment and because of that we decided not to deploy it. That is evidence that OpenAI takes safety really seriously. We are not racing to the bottom. We are not deploying models that we do not think are safe , and we are pausing training where we see significant incidents such as the H ugging F ace incident.
Q70 In plain English, what do regression and alignment mean?
It means that it was not as good as the previous model in doing its tasks in a way that we would want ethically, based on human values.

Q71 Tom, specifically on the incident with Australia, our report says that you guys discovered that in mid-August, but Australia was not notified until 10 September. Coupled with what you just said about not notifying Governments when your agents do things that they are not expected to do, to me as a legislator, that is really concerning. I want to understand why there was such a significant gap, but also who has decided that legislators should not be made aware when agents are doing things that they should not be doing with G overnment data . I feel like that is a really big decision to take as a company.

We apologised.
