Tuesday 1 3 Octob er 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Keeley (Chair); Baroness Caine of Kentish Town; Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay; Baroness Fleet; Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate; Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge; Lord Storey; Lord Tarassenko.
Evidence Session No. 3 Heard in Public Questions 52 - 72
Witnesses

Andy Burrows, Chief Executive Officer, Molly Rose Foundation; Katie Freeman- Tayler , Policy and Research Director, Internet Matters; Professor Sonia Livingstone, Professor of Social Psychology, London School of Economics and Political Science .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Andy Burrows, Katie Freeman- Tayler and Professor Sonia Livingstone .

Q52 ​​ The Chair: ​ Good afternoon and welcome to this meeting of the Communications and Digital Committee, where we are continuing our inquiry into the Online Safety Act. We will focus today on the measures in the Act that aim to protect children online. We are very grateful to our three panellists for coming to speak to us today. C ould I ask each of you to introduce yourself and your role, and then we will go into questions ? ​​
Professor Sonia Livingstone: ​ I work at the London School of Economics, and I lead the Digital Futures for C hildren centre with the 5 Rights Foundation.
​​ Andy Burrows: ​ I am the chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation.
​​ Katie Freeman- Tayler : ​ I am the policy and research director at Internet Matters, a UK not - for - profit that exists to make the online world safer for children and young people.

Q53 The Chair: ​ You are all very welcome. Let me start with the first question. To what extent have the risks children face online changed since the Online Safety Act was passed? I am sure you all have something to say on that. Can I start with you, Andy?

​​ Andy Burrows: ​ Thank you for the opportunity to give evidence. The risks have continued to grow and evolve since the Online Safety Act was passed . P articularly in respect of suicide and self-harm content, which the foundation focuses on , those risks have been inadequately addressed by the regulatory regime so far. The nature and complexity of the risks have continued to evolve quite s ignificantly and disturbingly .

I n particular, I draw the c ommittee’s attention to the risk being posed by com groups , which are a new group - based type of grooming. We are all familiar with grooming for sexual purposes or so-called sextortion , where there is a financial motivation. What we are seeing are radicalised , mostly young men i n competitive groups that are driven by sadistic motivations to groom young girls , who are being identified and targeted on gaming sites in particular and then coerced into appalling acts of violence, including , in the worst extremes , live - stream ed suicide , suicide attempts , peer - on - peer sexual abuse and animal torture . T he thread throughout all this offending, which has been growing rapidly , is that this is being driven by sadistic motivations. This is an area where , frankly, Ofcom has been asleep at the wheel when it comes to understanding the nature of the threat. There has been a problem in terms of Ofcom keeping up to date with new and evolving threats.

Frankly , this is not a tangential or small issue. Sky N ews ha s done some incredible reporting on this . F igures from the National Crime Agency supplied to Sky News point to almost 1 , 500 referrals in the 11 months to September and about 35 com - related referrals a month. T his also points to some quite significant issues with not just Ofcom’s application of the regime but the design of the A ct itself. One of the most striking things about these new threats as they pertain to suicide and s elf-harm is that we are no longer looking at a threat that sits in an individual silo as a child - abuse problem , a suicide problem or a terrorism problem. These threats are now hybrid in nature, and that is a major structural problem for the legislation, which was designed at a point when , by and large, we had the luxury to be able to think in those silos.

T he risks continue to grow. I have to say that they are probably as severe as I have seen them in my decade of working on these issues, and they are surfacing some very significant issues around the design of the A ct.

​​ Professor Sonia Livingstone: ​ Sadly, I agree with everything that Andy just said. In the research world, we think about the risks that the A ct is designed to address in terms of the content, contact, conduct and commercial risks. I n the academic world we try to keep track of how those are developing and , hopefully , reducing. W e find repeatedly that they are increasing across the board. W e can measure that over several years and, indeed, before and after the A ct came into effect. It is an interesting question how rapidly one expects to see the benefit to children in their everyday lives once an A ct has come into effect.

We see a multiplicity of risks. Some of the risks are new and some are still ther e. C hildren still report exposure to inappropriate or sexual content ; t hey still talk a lot about bullying and cyber bullying . The familiar problems do not go away as the new ones arise ; indeed, they get increasingly interconnected. One way in which they get interconnected is that they especially focus on the children who are already vulnerable. I n surveys, we interview lots of children who say, “ I can cope. It ’s fine. I’ve got a handle on it ” . But the children who are vulnerable or marginalised in some way will report a whole array of risks and harms, and the impact on them will be the longest lasting.

We have just surveyed children in 19 European countries, although unfortunately not this one, which has given us a very good measure of how children’s reporting of the risks of seeing self-harm , violent content and inappropriate sexual content have doubled in the past five years . P erhaps the last thing to say is that Ofcom’s own statistics show no difference in children’s exposure to risk before and after the A ct.
Q54 ​​​ The Chair: ​ Which figures have doubled ?
​​ Professor Sonia Livingstone: ​ The European research showed a doubling in children’s exposure to self-harm content, pro-suicide content, violent and sexual content and to being bullied.

​​ Katie Freeman- Tayler : ​ ​ I agree with the points around harm remaining high , which I can talk about later. In terms of the new harms that we are seeing , a clear one is AI chatbots . T hey present some similar risks to those that we see with other services, such as surfacing harmful content, but how they work is fundamentally different in how children engage with them . The responsive and conversational tone presents a new range of risks for children and young people , who are going to AI chatbots for advice and emotional support. They are changing how young people think about relationships and where they go for reliable information.

Research we did last year showed that children in the UK are using AI chatbots in this way . A round a quarter of children said they were already using them for advice , and 40% trusted the advice that they were getting from AI chatbot s. A further 36% were unsure whether they should be concerned about the advice they were getting. This is really important . As we know, around two - thirds of UK children aged nine to 17 are already using AI chatbots, and I am sure this figure has also grown in that time as well.

Fortunately, some elements of AI chatbots come under the Online Safety Act, but not all elements. As we know, that focus es more on th e harmful content side rather than some of those other risks that AI chatbots can have, which relate to the design of the services themselves.

Another risk that is increasing is AI - generated content. This comes with many different risks, but I want to focus in particular on the use of it for the creation of n ude deepfakes or sexually explicit images. Our research on this is a little old, but two years ago it showed that around half a million UK children had encountered a n ude deepfake , w hether by being shown one or whether it was an image created of them or of someone they knew. The latest data from the IW F, published last week , shows that AI - generated CSAM is increasing. M ost shockingly , it is being used more in sextortion cases. This intersects with existing risks. F or example , visible lists of children’s followers or friends can be used alongside AI - generated content to cause harm to a child through sextortion.

A longside those existing risks, something that is less well addressed in the current online safety framework is the design of the platforms themselves. Again , we focus on that harmful content, but we hear regularly from parents , children and young people that their top concern is the amount of time that children and young people are spending online and the impact that that is having on well - being, sleep and offline relationships.

Q55 Thanks , y ou have gone into quite some detail there. I have a follow-up question that you have already touched on, so perhaps we can just summarise it. W hich of the new or emerging harms, technologies or patterns of behaviour are the most concerning? Andy, you might want to talk to us about the com groups again. In particular, is there anything you wish to say about how Ofcom has approached this and what it could have done? That would be helpful.

Yes, absolutely. What the response to com groups has shown is the shortcomings in the way that Ofcom has implemented the Act, as well as some of the inherent structural weaknesses in it that I mentioned earlier.

If we go back to 2024, that is when we first started to see com groups emerge as a significant threat. At that point, we had the first of two warnings from the FBI. We have subsequently had warnings from the National Crime Agency, Europol, the Australian Federal Police and many others.

During that time, we saw a substantial lag before Ofcom updated its r egister of risks. We have seen measures proposed in respect of livestreaming in the Additional Safety Measures Consultation , on which I think Ofcom will publish its final decisions relatively shortly. But there is a substantial gap between a rapidly growing problem and the codes of practice containing the measures that are needed and are commensurate to deal with a problem of this magnitude.

I do not exaggerate when I say that this is the worst threat that I have ever seen. It is , in effect, a melting pot of some of the most egregious harms online . W e are seeing radicalised boys with fluid ideologies , very much what we saw in Southport with Axel R udakubana but taking place online with organised groups every day , and the regulatory response is falling short.

One of the areas that I think I mentioned was about the hybrid nature of the threat . T he A ct deals with silos and with measures being built into codes of practice only where there is evidence that measures will work. We have a situation where , when new harms grow, there is a disincentive for platforms to be invested in safety by d esign to tackle them, because that will in turn add to the regulatory burden. We a re effectively doing this the wrong way round.

We a re looking at a regime that fails to place duties on platforms to co - operate with each other on the nature of the threat . W hen you think about com group s, this is grooming that starts on gaming platforms such as Roblox , very often in plain sight. It will then move to the likes of D iscord, where the groups will operate , or the likes of encrypted site s such as Telegram . T he reality is that no one platform can see the jigsaw because they only have individual pieces of it. In the absence of clear duties on platforms to have to work together on the threat and being outcome - focused —so that the test is : is enough reasonably being done to tackle the threat ?—we are seeing a regime that is at best introducing very belated , specific , ad hoc measures , rather than th e comprehensive, cohesive set of duties that we really need.

Q56 Thank you. Katie, and Professor Livingstone, I have another supplementary question. Which of the risks that children face today is the current regulatory framework least well equipped to address , and why? Andy, you have just given us one example . Katie, you talked about chatbots. Do you want to talk a bout that?

Katie Freeman- Tayler : It broadly comes back to the fact that the OSA and particularly the protection of children’s codes and illegal harms codes are focused on content , and content that is harmful to children , but that is not the only way that harm occurs. It can be down to the design of platforms and services. W e see that with AI chatbots , where harmful content is an important consideration but it is also about continued use, misplaced trusts and the blurred lines between a trusted source of information and online and offline relationships. In that circumstance it is very much about the design of these platforms , and that is something that the OSA is least well equipped to address.

S imilarly, when it comes to impacts on children’s well - being, we know that more time online lead s to higher rates of harm but also impacts on how children feel after they have been online , and on sleep. Those impacts are, a gain, not necessarily because of the content they are seeing, although that can contribute ; it is often down to those platforms that are keeping children engaged for longer through mechanisms such as recommender systems and notifications.
Q57 Professor Livingstone, is there anything you want to tell us about this?

Yes, the evidence is mounting now very fast that the chatbots are beyond regulation at the moment and causing a whole range of problems for children, from misinformation to inappropriate advice and advice not to tell their parents of a problem that they are worrying about , and indeed, building those relationships that can themselves be so dangerous. B ecause these are not user - to - user services , it is difficult for the A ct to address.

A really crucial problem is the personalisation of the feed that children are getting , which is often weaponised against them and tailored to their particular vulnerabilities . I t is very hard for anyone else to know what is being fed to an individual, because we all get a very personal and very different feed. We could look over the shoulder , and we should probably do that more , b ut some of the avatar studies that show what comes to a 13 year - old girl, for example, is so different from anything that will ever come to me that it is a stretch and is hard to measure and get that broad picture.

Lastly, just to echo something that Andy said, I hear from children over and over again that someone says, “L ook at this YouTube ” , and it is not the YouTube but the comments below the YouTube that t ake them to a D iscord server and that then take them somewhere and eventually they get to a D ropbox and see something terrible. I t is across the services that are falling through the gaps of the A ct at the moment .
That is really helpful . I will come to you, Lord Storey.

Q58 Good afternoon. I find your answers very depressing, to be honest . I t is almost as though we are playing catch - up. M y question will now sound a bit trite a fter what you have said in your opening comments to question 1 . We all thought and hoped when we were dealing with the Online Safety Bill that we were going to be able to make a real improvement to the safety of children online. From what you have been saying, that clearly is not the case. My question was going to be: w hat changes have online services made to protect children in response to the Online Safety Act, and how effective have they been? It is almost like you cut off one head and another head or tentacle grows up. I do not really know what to say. Sonia, perhaps you can help me.

I will have a go. The position is not entirely depressing . At our centre, we have been trying to track what changes platforms are making as a result of the Act. Of course, the Act came in at the same time as, and hard on the heels of, the age-appropriate design code, as part of our data protection regulation , and at a similar time to the E U ’s Digital Services Act. So the platforms are responding to a number of different regulatory changes all at once. When the Act first came in, we saw a number of efforts to change services by design and by default . Some steps were taken towards the safety by d esign that I think many of us would advocate. But that is tailing off . W e s aw less of that in our last effort to look at this.

My colleague Steve Wood has looked at 70 services and how they have responded to the A ct , and what we see is increasing provision of user guidance , p are ntal tools and age assurance. So there are some greater efforts to keep children away from services that the Act says they should not be using and some greater tools in the hands of parents and children. What we do not see so much is efforts to stop the problem arising in the first place as a matter of by-design and by-default provision.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : Just to build on that, we did research with UK families after the protection of children codes came into force and, similarly, found that children, young people and parents reported that there were more reporting tools and features on platforms, such as age checks and parental controls, and that there were limitations on features on platforms.

However, unfortunately, that has not led to the step change in children’s well-being and safety that we expected. In the same study, we asked children whether they had experienced a list of harms in the months after the protection of children codes came into force, and we found that around 50% of children had experienced at least one type of harm. This included seeing violent content, content promoting unrealistic body types and hate speech, which should all be prohibited under the protection of children codes. Examples that were given in focus groups included children seeing the video of the assassination of Charlie Kirk—not seeking it out but it just appearing in their newsfeed—through to localised examples of violence, maybe a fight or weapons in their local area, coming up on their feed as well.

Similarly, in the same research, we heard children and young people talking about how much they were struggling with disengaging from online spaces and the impact that that was having on their well-being.

If we focus on age checks as an example or microcosm of where a change on a platform is not delivering on the intended outcome, around 50% of children had been through an age check in the two months after the protection of children codes came into force. That might have been on an existing platform or a new platform. However, around the same number of children thought that age checks were easy to bypass and a third of children had actually circumvented an age check. Obviously, that is significant because, if that is what is being used to protect children online and to reliably understand their age, it cannot deliver the protections that are needed for children and young people.

We also see this with the fact that so many young people under the age of 13 are on platforms, despite many platforms’ terms of service having 13 as the minimum age. Children are accessing platforms that are not designed for them.
We see that kind of disconnect not just with age checks but also with reporting—more reporting features but the same levels of reporting.

Katie teases out an important point, which is that so many of Ofcom’s measures feel like they have been outputs rather than being rooted in delivering outcomes. Where measures have been adopted into codes of practice, they are not translating into the change that civil society and Members of both Houses would have expected when the Bill was passed.

At the Molly Rose Foundation, we always had a very simple yardstick for the Act: would it do everything that was reasonably possible to prevent further deaths in circumstances such as Molly’s? Unambiguously, the Act has so far failed in that regard. Our research, which we undertook immediately prior to the Act coming into force and then again earlier this year, shows that there has been no change in the proportion of teenagers seeing harmful suicide, self-harm, intense depression and eating disorder content. Some 48% of girls had seen that content, which we would expect to be classified as either primary priority or priority content under the Act and therefore either restricted or throttled. That has dropped by only one percentage point compared to the data from before the Act took effect—so, no real change.

One in five girls who see content that actively promotes suicide sees it 10 times or more per week. That is exactly the type of cumulative harm that led to Molly’s death. Of the algorithms recommending large volumes of content, on about 60% of the occasions, on each of the platforms we surveyed where young people were seeing this content, it was because of algorithmic exposure. It is a failure to tackle those systems and processes. The measure that are built into Ofcom’s code are not translating into results.

For me, one of the things that is most frustrating is that that data has shown that, on TikTok, young people are three times more likely than on the next platform to see this type of content. As a civil society organisation, I do not know what more evidence we could produce to prompt Ofcom to open an investigation into the algorithmic failings of a platform such as TikTok. It is frankly exasperating that we have seen the European Commission reach provisional findings on an investigation into the same thing , a nd Ofcom, with the evidence being provided to it, has still not acted.

Q59 It is almost like Ofcom is playing catch-up all the time. Ofcom itself says that it has seen no significant reduction in overall exposure to harmful content among 11 to 17 year - olds. I t reminds me of something that the Child ren’s Commissioner said when she came to speak to us : the platforms themselves have a duty of care. Well, if they do , you would expect them to be proactive — not waiting for the latest piece of legislation to come down the track but to do something about it straight away. I wonder whether we are perhaps not dealing with it in the right sort of way and whether, all the time , we will be faced with the new way of exposing young children to harmful content.

That is probably one of the major structural issues with the Act: what was originally intended as being an overarching duty of care, analogous perhaps to health and safety legislation — where the objective is that you have to deliver outcomes and t he defence is that you can reasonably point to having taken steps to tackle identified risks — is not what we have ended up with. I nstead , we have ended up with a set of safety duties that are operationalised by codes , a nd then the measures are set so low —in conjunction with the safe harbours, which I imagine we may go on to —that it means that we end up with a regime that is , effectively , capturing the status quo at best.
That leads into our next question, from Lord Kirkhope .

Q60 Thank you for coming. I want to ask you some specifics. I n doing so , I refer quickly to the reference made to the GDPR, which I had something to do with preparing and drafting when I was in Brussels. I t was always going to be an umbrella, if you like, which was going to rely on further legislation of a more individualised natur e and particular ly on regulators , which would have adequate powers to be able to find the redress and the actions that were necessary. I n that context , let me ask you about a specific point : in Section 1 of the Act, as you know , the whole point is that regulated services must be safe by design —t hat is stated very clearly. I know that the Molly Rose Foundation in particular has expressed concerns about that, around its nebulous nature or the difficulty regarding it. I would like to know your views : i n this context, do you think the regulator , Ofcom , has enough s cope or powers to enforce changes in service design when it is clearly shown to be inappropriate or unhelpful? Could you answer that one for me first?

Sure. I think many of us anticipated this. As you said, the online safety objectives are there , right at the beginning of the Act , and the wording around safety by design is unambiguously clear, but I think Ofcom has expressed that it does not feel that it has the powers in the Act to then be able to operationalise that. I am not sure that I understand those arguments , so I will not try to explain them on Ofcom’s behalf, but I think there is a substantial gap between what we thought the Act would do and the way in which Ofcom’s lawyers have interpreted it. T he other part of this is that , where Ofcom has the scope in its codes of practice to introduce safety - by - design measures — for example, relating to the algorithmic recommendation of content —t hose are then developed in a way that hamstr i ng s their overall effectiveness. T he way Ofcom has interpreted this is that provisions have to be clear , detailed and technically feasible , and there has to be an evidentiary threshold to show that they are proportionate . W hen those things are built in , i t means that , even where measures are being built into codes, their potential efficacy is likely to be very low , because they are just being constantly chipped away at to the point that it becomes , effectively , a tick - box exercise.

I have also been thinking about what Ofcom has been doing. I know there is considerable frustration among civil society groups, as you will have heard, about the piecemeal and one - by - one ways in which it takes some actions. T his year , Ofcom looked into how Snap had allocated its risk levels for Snapchat and found that it had not identified as high risk t he fact that adult strangers are able to contact children. Ofcom intervened here and got Snap to agree that it would now stop adult strangers contacting children. T o many sitting outside, it is just mind - blowing that this was not done the minute the Act came into force , nor indeed under the 20 years of self-regulation that we have all lived through, where probably the public’s No. 1 anxiety is that adult strangers can contact children. Y et this was just this year —and t hen we go back into the waiting game. Will it happen? Will it be followed through? How will it be checked? How will we be sure that they do not roll back on this promise, given that their business model is expanding content and contacts ? H ow will we be sure that children are safe as a result? A lot of the questions about evidence cut both ways. It is very hard in civil society to see what indicators we could get from how platforms operate to see whether they are indeed acting as they said they would — or as they should — and to see that those improvements, if they exist, continue.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : The only thing I would add is on the pace of change or recognition of challenges. P latforms continue to roll out new features —t hey add in things such as AI , or new types of messaging or image sharing —a nd , for some reason , that is not being picked up before those are released , s o there is none of that safety by design from the beginning. A n example is the new feature that has been added to one of Meta’s platforms . An investigation has been opened into it, b ut that is after it has been out for around six months. There is also a question around why Ofcom is not addressing these safety - by - design issues at the outset.

Q61 I will put two things to you, if I may, and ask for your comments. One is safe harbour, which in itself some people have suggested should be done away with. T here are criticisms of Ofcom having a tick - box mentality regarding it. I would like your comments on that. T he other thing is the question of proactive technologies.
That is another question.
Oh, it is; I am so sorry. I shall leave that to my colleague —i n which case , I would like your comments on safe harbour, please.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : I will leave that one mostly to Andy. F rom our perspective, any measures that could improve the safety and well-being of children and young people should absolutely be acted upon.

We would support the removal of safe harbours. They can be an effective part of a regulatory regim e, but , in reality, the way that Ofcom has developed the codes means that the total measures that platforms have to deliver are barely capturing the status quo , a nd then the safe harbour means that platforms do not have to go any further. T hey should go. E ven if we were to wave a magic wand and Ofcom were suddenly much more ambitious and assertive than it has been to date , w e obviously now have thousands of pages of Ofcom decisions saying that it is not proportionate to do X , Y and Z, s o I am not sure that this is merely a step change in ambition ; t he safe harbours need to go.

It was plausible at the time, when the Act came into force, that there would be the safe harbour to get the platforms to play ball and t ake the steps that they could , a nd then there would be a further assessment and we would see whether that was sufficient and whether the expectations should be raised . S ince the platforms have not done what was expected at the start —and t he sense is that the safe harbour is setting a ceiling for what they might do, rather than a floor from which they would progress and do more to keep children safe — I would agree . T he comparison with Europe’s Digital Services Act is striking: it does not offer that safe harbour , and they are now pushing for safety by design in a more ambitious way.

Q62 Lord Kirkhope has been proactive in flagging my question, which I welcome. The word “proactive” often appears in your submissions. I want to focus on proactive technologies—for example, tools that analyse the content, such as hash-matching tools or even automated classifiers. AI could really have a role to play in that before it even reaches the children. Interestingly, when Ofcom came to see us, they said they would want to see wider use of these technologies to protect children, but their written evidence also said that the OSA limits their ability to require the use of these proactive technologies. If we had OSA 2.0, would you welcome that—legislation that would make it easier for Ofcom to require the use of these proactive technologies? Or can you think of anything else in terms of these tools, or similar ones, that would make a real difference?

I am thinking about the GDPR and wondering what the barrier might be; I assume it is going to be something about data protection and privacy. There is a serious issue in which that kind of proactive AI-led analysis could involve privacy risks if it were done in a way that was not transparent or open to scrutiny by independent researchers or civil society, or indeed the regulator. That would allow the platforms to conduct all kinds of analysis that at the moment data protection precisely restricts on the grounds of privacy. We would need to be convinced of the benefits that that was proportionate and that people’s data protection rights were protected in the process. At the moment , that would take a lot of trust in the way that platforms operate, since they are so black-boxed that they give us little in terms of their risk assessments and their mode of operation, and the data that was always offered to independent researchers has never materialised. In short, it is very hard to know how we would have any checks and balances that what they were doing was appropriate and effective.
Q63 To take a simple example, which was mentioned by Andy, could you not proactively look for suicide content and prevent it from reaching that young teenage girl?
Andy, you were going to talk about suicide.

Crudely, if we rely only on content moderation, then we are acting after the event and after harmful content has already started to be distributed, and we know that it can be distributed at scale very quickly. So proactive technologies absolutely play a role. Right now the regime does not incentivise the use of proactive technology. This comes back to what Sonia described a moment ago, with Ofcom developing codes of practice that act as a floor rather than a ceiling. There is much more that we could do with proactive technology to identify and remove, or prevent the distribution of, harmful content; to do that to a high standard; and to share signals between platforms of harmful content that is being shared, in respect of com groups and the behavioural nature of risks. That is something that we should see. Right now, we see the industry doing that itself on a voluntary basis—albeit with no meaningful transparency about whether those measures are effective—and that is over and above what Ofcom as the regulator requires. So there is a role for proactive technology, and Ofcom’s remarks were very interesting.

My fear is that if we had a clause added into the Act that broadly allowed for proactive technology, we could find ourselves in the same situation where, regardless of the policy intent, Ofcom’s lawyers then chipped away at its usefulness until we ended up with measures that were there but not terrifically effective. We should look much more structurally at how we can have an outcome-based regime with an overarching duty of care that says, “Your job is to make sure that the platform is safe”. Then, by implication, proactive technologies would be one route to achieve that. We have been badly burned by Ofcom’s risk aversion and, frankly, the lawyers chipping away at something until there is not much left.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : Obviously we would support the proactive use of technology if it was effective and privacy-preserving. What I am cautious about is that it might be an either/or, where we say, “We are using this measure now so we don’t have to use those measures”. Children’s online safety is always going to need a layered approach. You need a number of different measures working on top of each other to produce good outcomes, and that needs to be kept in mind. We should not say, for example, “If we’re using this technology then we don’t need to look regularly at how recommender feeds surface content”. That would be my only caution.

Q64 I think I know what your answers will be on this from all your comments on Ofcom, but I would like to ask the question in any case to get a clear, straightforward answer. Ofcom has described its approach to supervision and enforcement to date as strategic, saying that it is learning to walk before it runs. Is that a fair characterisation of what it has done ? Has it set the right threshold for when to take formal action?

The regulator has been far too risk averse, and it has been far too slow to act against the largest companies. Ofcom has set out that it has chosen to focus on certain harms, particularly around pornography and Section 5 of the Act. However, that has been at the expense of the focus on large tech companies. It is striking that we are now seeing investigations being opened into TikTok and Meta. The investigation into Meta is very welcome but it is essentially a procedural slap on the wrist. We have not seen investigations going for the high-risk design features, the algorithms and the fundamental design choices that we know are the drivers of harm and that result in problematic use and problematic experiences.

I make the comparison between Ofcom’s approach and that of the European Commission, which came out of the blocks very quickly to enforce the DSA by opening investigations into TikTok, Instagram and Meta. It made very clear that it had the powers and that it intended to use them. From my engagement with the companies, if you ask if they are complying with the OSA then you generally get a bit of a shrug, but if you talk about the DSA then they sit up and take notice. There are lessons to be learned there.

The other striking example that we have all been paying attention to this year is the litigation happening in the US, especially in California but also from the attorneys-general, particularly against Meta but against others too. There again, we see a focus that is especially concerned with safety by design, with advance warning and with knowing what the risks are on a platform and then being held to account for not having informed children and parents that the risks exist, and we see a focus on the features. That is where, both in Europe and in the US, there is a move away from saying that a platform is good or bad and instead looking at where it is designed with particular features that are available and carry a high risk—live streaming might be a good example, or having open profiles that strangers can contact. It is not hard, and a list of features is now emerging. This approach has not come from here, from the actions of Ofcom and the OSA, but it has become an international consensus that that is the direction of travel and we really hope to see that happening here as well.

As a rider—maybe this is more of a political point—from the platforms’ perspective, there is power in numbers: hearing the same message coming from multiple states and big markets has power. In that sense, it feels to me that it would be effective if Ofcom acted in tandem with what is happening in other countries so that the big companies get the idea that the consensus is that change is expected now.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : The slow enforcement has created a gap between expectations and reality. T hat is what has led, particularly from the public, for a push for more protections for children online . P arents did not think the online world was getting safer — they were not seeing differences , and so they were driving for more changes. W e will continue to see that unless we focus, as Andy and Sonia have pointed out, on outcomes — what are we trying to achieve? Compliance is useful only if it drives those outcomes ; i t is not useful for compliance ’s sake.

Q65 Focusing specifically on Ofcom’s investigation of the US - based suicide forum that we all saw , c ould you tell us more about the limits of Ofcom’s enforcement powers under the Online Safety Act? Would you like to start , Sonia ?

I will probably defer to Andy on this one, but , generally , we see a difficulty in transparency and in understanding how platforms are operating , and a l ack of public risk assessments , so that it is very hard to know what is in fact happening. On t his particular cas e , w ould you like to answer , Andy?

Sure. This forum is absolutely appalling. We know that more than 160 lives have been lost because of it , and the true figure is likely to be substantially greater. This forum exists to promote and encourage suicide, and in particular to promote a suicide method which is then sold through the site and related marketplaces . I t has been allowed to exist in plain sight for far too long.

There are limitations in the Act, but this has also not been an example where Ofcom has covered itself in glory. The Lords amended the Act to give Ofcom powers specifically to regulate small but high - harm sites, which Ofcom then recommended to the Secretary of State should not be enacted , which is a decision I find inexplicable to this day. I t has then taken Ofcom a tortu r ously long time to determine that this forum was breaching a whole catalogue of safety duties — frankly, I think many of us could have taken a look and decided that in the course of an afternoon and arrived at a watertight set of conclusions . T hat has been incredibly retraumatising for bereaved families who have been campaigning for Ofcom to take action on this and have been desperately affected by the failure to grasp the urgency of this ; we certainly know of lives that were lost while Ofcom’s investigation interminably dragged on.

O n the point about the limits of Ofcom’s powers, which I think have been surfaced, there are three that I would really highlight. One is around issues of scope and jurisdiction. This is a forum that has played a cat - and - mouse game of voluntarily geo - blocking itself when the heat comes on it in jurisdictions. That voluntary geo - block means that Ofcom has then said that no further action can be taken against it. We should instead be amending the Act so that action can be taken where there is a significant risk to UK users , s o we can shortcut this kind of complicated issue around scope . I f it can be accessed in the UK and we know that it can and it is causing harm, then Ofcom should be able to intervene.

Secondly , I think Ofcom has felt that it was not possible to apply for an interim service disruption order. Ideally , it could do that where there is an imminent risk , as this case has clearly demonstrated , whil e an investigation is ongoing . I f there is a public safety risk that justifies an immediate service disruption order, Ofcom should have the ability to go to the courts and apply for that. There is also a case for service disruption orders where, for example, a platform does not pay a fine : y ou have a situation right now where the fine that has been levied against this forum is there with very little chance that it will be recovered.

T he third gap is around criminal sanctions. W e should be looking at how they can play a much more expansive role in the regime , broadly ; on this forum specifically, we know who its operators are — they operate this forum and the world’s largest incel forum , and t hey are fundamentally bad actors responsible for truly appalling, egregious harm —and we should have criminal sanctions that could apply. I n practice, what does that mean? I guess that, if they want to try to leave the United States, then there is an Interpol notice on them. There are a range of ways that the Act could be amended so that we really start to bite on some truly appalling individuals and the truly appalling harm that they cause.

Q66 Thank you, Andy. W e have touched on the second part of my question ; just to conclude it nicely before moving on to Katie , w ould you say that that would make the biggest practical difference in this case and any future cases to ensure that we capture services that refuse to comply?

Yes, absolutely. I would really encourage Ofcom to be working with the Secretary of State at pace to identify what lessons need to be learned here. T he reality is that , if other , similar sites appear , which they will , then , right now , the Act has proven that it is limited in its scope to protect some of our most vulnerable.
Q67 Katie, would you like to add anything?

Katie Freeman- Tayler : There is nothing I could add to that—it was v ery powerful —but w e would also support changes that prevented further harm from happening, particularly when an investigation is already under way.
Thank you so much.

Q68 Just to complete a question that Lord Kirkhope asked you earlier , I think y ou all said that safe harbour should go. Is there something it should be replaced with, or is it as Professor Livingstone was saying —it was maybe needed to start with, but let us look at the situation and say that it has not worked h aving it and that it is getting in the way ?

The alternative would be to have a more articulated and developed code around safety by design —which is now emerging in a number of countries — and, t o be crystal clear, what that includes and the standards that we would expect it to live up to. F or example, age assurance would be part of safety by design , b ut a lot of age assurance , as it is being implemented , is not privacy - respecting and does not draw on the existing standards that are being used . I could say the same for parental control tools, for example. But, on pre-emptive actions — I will go back to that list of features and functionalities of platforms — having a risk assessment attached to those and then ensuring that those are embedded in a code, which it is then mandatory for platforms to live to , is probably where the EU kids Act is also going to go , building on the DSA.

Q69 Do you have a nything to add , Andy or Katie? No? I will move on then. The n ext question is about the potential benefits and risks of preventing under - 16 s from using social media — a ban, effectively . H ow do you see those restrictions interacting with the Online Safety Act? Andy, can I start with you?

Sure. The Molly Rose Foundation has been concerned that a ban means that we move from an Online Safety Act that has not worked effectively to a measure that is well intentioned but where we have question marks about whether it will work as intended and designed . I spoke earlier about how we have not seen the Online Safety Act deliver a meaningful change in platform s. T hey are simply not complying. If we are going to introduce a ban with the same incentive structure in place as the Act, I do not see how we should expect materially different results. I f that is the case , then my fear is that we will be looking at compliance that is broadly similar to what we have seen in Australia, Indonesia and other countries that have brought in a ban so far.

Our big fear there is that in that situation—and this is being borne out by the data we have seen from the eSafety Commissioner in Australia—we will see a disconnect between parents who think their children are no longer on these platforms and the children themselves, who are there in significant numbers. In that case, our fear is about the safeguarding risks. We have spent 10 to 15 years trying to build an approach to online safety based on relationships of trust between parents, professionals and children, but we risk putting a barrier in the way while the harms are still there and are being tackled. The real risk, now that we are moving forward with a ban, has to be thought about carefully to ensure that we do not see unintended consequences.

There is one more point here. You mentioned the interplay with the Act. There are some very big unresolved questions about the interplay between a social media ban and the children’s codes under the Online Safety Act. Essentially, this is about whether a form of double jeopardy can apply. If the ban is introduced to a similar level of compliance to what we have seen in Australia, where somewhere between 60% and 85% of children are still viewing content on these platforms, then can a platform be allowed to roll back its measures under the children’s code for under-16s? Can it be held accountable if children are then navigating the ban and accessing content with perhaps even fewer protections than now? I have not yet heard a clear position about what that interplay looks like. The fear is that we could end up with a situation where we have a ban in name only and children continuing to use services with even fewer protections than now. There is an opportunity to surface what that interplay looks like so that we can draft the regulations to avoid that risk, because clearly it is not what anyone, whether they are pro or against the ban, wants to see. We still have that ambiguity, and that ambiguity is worrying me. We need to understand that to make sure that the regulations that will be brought forward in a matter of weeks can adequately deal with those dynamics.

I absolutely agree about the uncertainty and what it will mean for the implementation of the Act, and indeed what it will mean for the actions of platforms, if children are banned below a certain age. How will the platforms then provide, on the assumption that everyone there is an adult? How will we and Ofcom respond when it turns out that of course children are still using those services but the platforms have been given a licence to withdraw their safety efforts because they will have been told there will not be children there?

As I understand it, one key reason why the Australian ban is failing is that the platforms are not implementing age assurance effectively. There is of course a wider debate to be had about whether age assurance can be implemented effectively in a way that is privacy-preserving and will get the trust of the population. It is not that there is a simple technology that they are failing to use; there is a genuine debate, especially in the privacy community, about whether there can be such a thing.

We need to find a good age-assurance solution, whether we want to ban or whether we want age-appropriate safety by design. Do we have it today? Not necessarily, but a crucial point is that one might begin to wonder in this conversation why on earth children want to go on social media at all, given all the horrors that we have been elaborating. No one wants children to be in a deeply unsafe space, and neither do children themselves, but they want to be part of a digital world. They want the opportunity to chat with their friends, meet others, participate, express their views, join groups, share culture and so forth. All of those are their rights. In the holistic sense of how we bring up children to live in this digital world, our task is to enable those rights safely rather than, as it were, wrapping them up in cotton wool and keeping them away from everything. That is why there are some real concerns about a high age limit that is, I suggest, too high for children who need to be in touch with people, to get help and to go online to the sources of help, support, belonging, information and action. That is what they often tell us about.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : I think there are some positives to a ban. We find that children experience a significant number of harms on social media platforms; around 85% of the harms that children experience happen on social media, according to our data. We also see that some of the platforms that have personalised feeds based on the child can have really negative impacts on children’s well-being as well. The potential of the ban is that we reduce the amount of harm that children experience and improve their well-being, but these opportunities can only be realised if age assurance is implemented effectively, as both other witnesses have touched on. What we have seen in Australia is that to date that has not been the case. We also need to look at how children may circumvent some of these measures. Unless that piece of the puzzle is solved then a ban is unlikely to deliver those positive outcomes.

However, there are a lot of risks that come with a ban. Harm does not just occur on social media; it happens across a range of platforms, such as messaging services, gaming platforms and AI chatbots—smaller platforms that we might not think about just yet. It is unlikely that harm will disappear; it will probably just be displaced to other platforms, and we need to be cognisant of that.

As Andy touched on, there is a danger of a false sense of security for families. The online safety landscape is difficult already for parents. There are a number of age checks, and that is only going to become more complicated with a ban as it is likely that children may fall through the gaps. Parents may think they are safe, but they are not. Children of different ages will have different protections. It is important that we support families in that period to understand how children are safe online, with media and digital literacy skills and guidance around that.

To touch on Sonia’s point, children want to be in these spaces. They create community connection, and they help them to learn and stay informed. Some children rely on these spaces more than others, particularly those with additional needs, and they will acutely feel that loss. How do we support their well-being from that perspective?

On the question of how it intersects with the Online Safety Act, one of the strengths of the OSA is that it is platform agnostic, so we need to not let it take a back foot; we need to continue to keep pressure on the Online Safety Act to keep children safe in those spaces, like gaming platforms, for example. It also covers 16 and 17 year-olds, and one criticism has been that a ban might create a cliff edge for children and young people rather than preparing them for a digital world.

Q70 You touched on this in earlier responses, but would the approaches being considered in Canada and the EU, which place more responsibility on services to demonstrate that they are safe for children, address all the drawbacks to the under-16 ban?

Katie Freeman- Tayler : That would be an improved approach. The safety-by-design element would serve some of the benefits that we have just talked about. It would probably be less complicated for families, hopefully, and it would stop that cliff edge. Most importantly, when we ask parents about whether they supported a ban or other alternatives, safety by design was a popular alternative. More parents supported alternatives than a ban itself in our research.

Both Canada and the EU have strong outline approaches. Canada in particular effectively views a ban as a means to an end; it is a means to incentivise safety-by-design requirements. That is an approach that Ministers have signalled in recent weeks they are looking at in terms of whether there should be off-ramps. That addresses some of the strong disincentives to comply with an outright platform ban. It means that we could be looking at a model where there are stretching targets that are not fixed in aspic but can be amended. If a platform earns an exemption then that is only as good as continuing to invest in safety by design.

In terms of seeing compliance, there is a path here for the UK, Canada and the EU to come together as middle powers, with an approach that is broadly similar and focused on safety by design, with a ban as a means to an end.
Even compared to back in June, when the then Prime Minister announced the ban, the Australian approach already looks like an increasingly lonelier and harder road than it did just a few months ago.

The principle sounds great. It resonates with many people that you do not let a product on to the market, especially for children, until you have proven it safe. There are some serious practical problems—I can imagine the lawfare that is going to result as companies start suing because they are not allowed into the marketplace—so we are going to need some very strong regulation if that is the direction.

One difficulty that we are currently facing is that we have had a race to the bottom in the way in which social media platforms have provided for the public, so we do not have a diversified market in which we can already say, “This one is safe, this one is child friendly and this one is aspiring to do the right thing”. That comes back to the question of incentives and how we get a more diversified market so that parents and children can make choices and know what to avoid, what could suit them and what could keep them safe.

Q71 Thank you so much for all your stimulating evidence. I have the last question, which you might recognise if you have read the previous contributions, which I think you have from some of the evidence that you have been giving: if you had to prioritise, what are the key recommendations that this committee should make to improve children’s safety online, and why? I am going to ask you for two priorities each.

Oh dear. That is a zero-sum game, is it not? I might start with making age assurance effective because, until we know who is a child online , we cannot treat them as a child. Finding a trusted mechanism that meets privacy-preserving standards and so forth is critical.

Secondly, I will mention something that has not really come up yet: an issue of reporting. I work with a child-rights approach, and children need remedy. When something goes wrong, nothing works for children, so can we make something that works? Can we really put some effort into the reporting services that platforms operate, which do not work and which children do not trust, or other services? Can they report to Ofcom? That could perhaps be a helpful change. At the moment , when there is a problem, children have nowhere to go.

Katie Freeman- Tayler : An important part of online safety is not just regulation but education, supporting media literacy and supporting parents. Just last week, the Molly Rose Foundation and Internet Matters wrote a joint letter signed by 70 organisations calling on the Government to make media literacy a national priority. That is not just about protecting children and young people online, particularly from new risks; it is also really important for democracy, social cohesion and growth. As this committee knows more than anyone, it is a shared responsibility: there needs to be action at the government level but platforms can be made safe by design. We need support for teachers to teach media literacy confidently in the classroom, and support for parents who we know are children’s main source of information about online safety. That would be my first one.

My second is a focus on outcomes. We cannot just be thinking about compliance. We have to think about what outcome and vision we want for children and young people in the UK. How do we want them to benefit from online spaces and thrive online, and how do we get there?
Thank you. As you are aware, this committee has done a report on media literacy. It is something that is very dear to our hearts, so joining up on that agenda is something we will be looking at.

I am conscious that I have been very pessimistic in my answers, so I will say that we are dealing with preventable harm and issues of product safety here. We should not accept that tech products are somehow exceptional and different; we know how to do this in every other part of the economy, so it is just a matter of will and fixing the things that have not been learned.

I would like to see the Government commit to a third-Session Bill, and for that to be ambitious in its scope to fix and build on the Act that we have right now. There are two key elements to that. First, we should move back towards an overarching duty of care, which is what many of us envisaged when discussions around online safety legislation first started, very clear outcomes and learning the lessons of what has worked. I mentioned health and safety legislation, which went on to the statute book in 1974 and is as good today as it was back then.

The second is a focus on incentives. I would look at what has worked well in financial services regulation, where we have seen huge companies but with a focus on criminal sanctions and conduct measures, which we know has brought about fundamental change in, for example, retail banking. We should be looking at those lessons because, frankly, with some of the most cash-rich companies in the world, we have seen that fines will not work and there are strong incentives not to comply. Let us learn the lessons from financial services.

Q72 One issue that you have all touched upon variously is the hybrid nature now of how things are developing and morphing. Do you have any thoughts on what a regulator could do to manage that within the kind of constructs that you have been talking about? You have talked about a duty for people to collaborate, but how would you enshrine that in a legal response?

At every stage of the process, whether risk assessment, risk mitigation or showing that you have discharged a duty of care, this is about recognising that there are harms that just do not exist in silos, so you should be co-operating with other platforms to understand the threat. You should be developing appropriate structures, as seen in respect of child sexual abuse and terrorism, to work together to identify, to signal-share, to respond and to mitigate threats. There should be co-operation on what proactive technology looks like and how we can ensure that that meets sensible safeguards. It is about embedding it throughout.
Like the word “Blackpool” through a stick of rock—an expectation all the way through. Maybe that was a bad analogy.

We need to finish now because we have run over a bit. Thank you for sticking with us for a slightly longer session. On behalf of the committee, thanks for all the work that you do—not just your presentations to us today, which have been very helpful, but the difficult work you do navigating all this. We know it is difficult and horrible but it is vital work. We all want to protect children but you are on the front line doing it, so thank you.

Witnesses

II : Ashley Broadley, Chair, Sports Journalists ’ Association; Leon Mann, Founder, Black Collective of Media in Sport (BCOMS); and Barbara Slater, f ormer Director, BBC Sport.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Flo Lloyd-Hughes, Natalie Pirks and Fiona Tomas .

Chair : G ood afternoon and welcome to the Women and Equalities Committee . This is my first evidence session as C hair , so I would like to say a huge thank you to my predecessor , Sarah Owen , for her phenomenal service and fantastic leadership of this Committee . S he will be missed , but I am extremely excited to be stepping into her shoes.

Today we are holding a session for our inquiry on routes into non-participatory roles in sport for girls and women . I n the evidence we have heard so far , we can see that women are underrepresented in those roles , fac e many barriers and sometimes overt discrimination . W e are really looking forward to hearing from our first panel today . W e will hear from Flo Lloyd-Hughes , who is a footb all broadcaster and founder of T he Cutback ; Natalie Pirks , who is a former BBC S port correspondent ; and Fiona Tomas, women’s sport reporter at t he Telegraph . Thank you so much , all of you , for coming . W e are really grateful to you for giving up your time , and we look forward to asking you questions this afternoon.
Q164 Rachel Taylor : Flo , w hat is your assessment about the accessibility of sports media roles today for young women looking to break into the profession?

Flo Lloyd-Hughes : I t is very different , depending on what landscape you look at . I f you look at legacy media in the broadest sense, so print and newspapers, there are no strong ro u t e s in . I t is predominantly older white male terrain , and that is probably represented in press boxes and in big awards recognising and acknowledging the achievements of those in the sports press . I f you were to walk into many newsrooms , you would also see that . T here is that reality of numbers , but there is also a perception that impacts the wider interest in those roles . A s someone who chat s to young people, go es into schools , deliver s workshops and talk s to them about the jobs in this landscape they might be interested in, a lot is focused on content creation in the digital world and not necessarily traditional media roles . T here is obviously huge opportunity in the growing digital world that we live in , in terms of how you can be part of the wider sports media conversation and get jobs that way . B ut when you look at traditional media , young people probably do not see it as a landscape for them anymore.

Fiona Tomas : I would very much echo what Flo has said. For women in the industry who cover women’s sport on a regular basis , they are probably mixing with press p acks that are very much more gender diverse than press p acks that solely cover men’s sport . I t is getting harder , not just for women but for young people in general , to break into the sports media industry because of the rise of AI , and lots of people are masquerading as journalists these days but in reality they are content creators on social media.
Q165 Rachel Taylor : Natalie, do you feel that is true ? D o you think it is also true in technical roles , such as camera operators or producers?

Natalie Pirks : I am obviously a lot older than Fiona and Fl o, and my experience of working in sports broadcasting lasts two decades. W hen I started , I was very much one of one, maybe one of two, in a press box or press room. You have to be a certain type of woman to rub along with this very male press pack. Now there is a landscape, certainly in print journalism, where they are losing headcount rather than adding people , so it becomes a lot harder to break into those traditional legacy media roles . T here are now a lot more women in press boxes . I will go into a press box or a press conference and there will be maybe five or six women. We all know each other . We all talk . T hat feels more positive . W hen you go to events , there are a lot more of us , and that does feel like a step forward .

E qually , when it comes to what type of women are now getting those roles and what type of women are coming in , that feel s like a bit of a step back because journalism itself is not quite what it was . For example, if you a re a woman taking a journalism degree and you want to work in sport , the advice I would give to women now is very different from the advice I would have give n a decade ago , such as getting your journalism degree , working really hard , going into a print room and doing your work experience . I t is just not the same anymore ; i t has become better and harder at the same time.
Q166 Rachel Taylor : Do you think there has been a change with the rise in the viewing of women’s sport? Do you think that ha s changed the routes in for people?
Natalie Pirks : I do not work exclusively in women’s sport . Y ou two work a bit more in that world, what do you think?

Fiona Tomas : To a certain extent , y es . T here has been a small uptick in the number of women-specific roles when it comes to digital and print . I would argue that everyone talks about this broadcast boom , but there has been a print lag when it comes to the coverage of women’s sport and how much it gets these days . You can pick up any newspaper on the shelves today, flick through the back pages , and I guarantee that there are a couple of female bylines , if that . T hat has been the same for quite a while now.

Flo Lloyd-Hughes : I would say that , in the last four years , you have seen a huge shift . P robably before the women’s E uros in 2022 , we were not at a stage where there was a national correspondent for women’s football at every single newspaper. W e have now got to that stage and s ome newspapers even have two , so that is huge progress , but it does not necessarily filter out across the board . A s Fiona mentioned, men’s P remier L eague football still dictates the vast majority of coverage .

T he W omen’s S port T rust released its most recent visibility report last week. It is constantly crunching the numbers on how much coverage women’s sport is actually getting , whether that is newspaper or viewing figures . S o much of that relies on how the market i s looking . O bviously , a lot of legacy media have to shift their focus to a more digital element and therefore sometimes women’s sport or more women get ting into those roles might suffer . T here is sometimes a n unfortunate assumption that women’s sport and women working within women’s sport and media roles are the same . I w ill not speak for the others on the panel , but sometimes you feel like you are fighting th e assumption and they often go hand in hand , but they are separate in that there are lots of women who work predominantly in the men’s game . T hat was the case for me , probably up until the women’s E uros , whe n it shifted because there was more media spend going towards women’s football . U p until then, pretty much all my work was in the men’s game.

Q167 Rachel Taylor : How important are mentors and networks within the industry for young women who a re aspiring sports journalists to navigate through their careers ? D o you think there are enough of them?

Natalie Pirks : They are hugely important. I belong to WIF, Women in Football, and that is an invaluable network of women . It started out as a few women in a pub who were just fed up and had a conversation ; it has now grown to thousands of women who work in sport .

W e have to talk about the importance of male allies as well because sometimes it can perhaps come across that men are difficult , or men are the barriers . I have obviously experienced that in my 25 years , but I have also experienced brilliant male allies, men who absolutely want to make a difference . T hey know there is a need to employ more women and bring more women through . W e have to acknowledge that as well.

Going back to what you were saying , there is a saying in news : “I f it bleeds , it leads ”. W hen it comes to sport , it is Premier League football and it often leaves very little space for anything else . W omen’s sport certainly get s a bit of a raw deal when it comes to coverage . U nless they are winning or doing something exceptional , it is probably not going to get on . T hat is the reality . W hen it comes to this digital space that we are now living in , if people are not clicking on it , it is perceived as people not being interested in it so it gets pushed down the agenda.

Fiona Tomas : O n that point, women’s sport is now at the stage where coverage tends to spike around major events . It is true for football, rugby and cricket . I t is not too dissimilar from Olympic coverage really . I t is very hard to sustain a consistent cut - through during regular seasons because leagues such as the Premier League are still so dominant . F ootball is king , it always will be . I know from a domestic perspective at t he Telegraph that we cover women’s sport on a weekly basis from the ru n- of - the - mill season , but it is very difficult to cut through during regular months when there is not a World Cup o r Euros happening.

Q168 Chair : Flo, I was really interested in the point you made that you have to fight against this assumption , just because there is more interest in women’s sport , that it is going to mean there are more women in sports roles . I invite the panel to say some thing further about that . W hy do you think that might be ? W hy would you not see an increasing number of women working in sport if there has also been that expansi on of interest in women’s sport?

Flo Lloyd-Hughes : A lot of it comes down to the realit y of the econom y of the media landscape . O bviously , we are witnessing huge cost cutting at the BBC at present , and changes are being made in relation to that . W omen’s sport, and minority sports in general , often bear the brunt of that , and that is the unfortunate reality of the ecosystem . For example, e ven the BBC ’ s coverage around the WSL has a s hort window of pre-match and a short window of post-match . I t is not necessarily always guaranteed to be on BBC1 or BBC2 , and that over time takes its toll on the number of eyeballs that are going to see it, and o bviously things around the number of contracts that can be awarded to pundits to be on that coverage and so on . T hat is all operating within the challenges of the wider media landscape that we are seeing , and the reality is that very few major sports in this country , apart from the Premier League , have the opportunity to be as aggressive in the media market . E veryone else is fighting for eyeballs , whether that is men’s cricket or r ugby , against that beast . T here is not always a run - off , and that wider digital view on things means that it has , in a way , been democratised because you can jump in and tell those stories , but it has probably removed the allowance of the legacy media to do that.

Natalie Pirks : The only thing I would add is that , from my perspective as a broadcaster , I do not think you have to be a woman to cover women’s sports , and this is industry - wide ; I am not speaking j ust as a former BBC person . I ndustry-wide , you would put your woman on it . I t is lovely to be able to go and cover women’s sport , and I have done it my whole career and it is brilliant , but you may be slightly doing it a disservice if you do not put your sports editor on a wom e n’s story if it is big enough . W hy are you not putting a man on it as well ? I t does not have to be the woman you have in that day, a nd I have seen that happen across the industry . I would say there is that element to it as well . A s much as we want women to be covering these stories , it does not have to be .

Fiona Tomas : I joined t he Telegraph seven years ago , and it was a newly created role called women’s sports reporter . I was one of two . W e still have two at the paper but , over time , I have morphed into all sport . W hile it was my big break , per se , because I came from local news , at the time it felt really novel . H aving written for a national for seven years now , there is this strongly held belief that women can only cover women’s sport . T hey have their expertise questioned more when they are sent out to men’s sport . O bviously , there are exceptions . A s Natalie touched on earlier , there are probably a handful of women who are regularly covering Premier League football , from a print perspective anyway — i t is different for digital and broadcast . T hat has a knock-on effect further up the food chain. There are fewer women in editor roles and fewer women commissioners on sports desks . T hat ultimately means that , historically , fewer female issues are covered by the mainstream media. I am fortunate enough to have been mentored by some brilliant women in sports journalism such as Anna Kessel . She is always pushing the female sport science take , such as how athletic performance is impacted by the contraceptive pill or when a woman is on their period .

G oing back to the male allyship angle that Natalie touched on , I have been fortunate enough to have some quite eye-opening , brilliant conversations with male colleagues who want to know more about how these female - specific issues are relevant to sport . If they come to you for advice because they are a bit underconfident on how to approach these subjects, that is totally fine by me . I t is not to say they can’t, but there has historically been a belief that women can only cover women’s sport and it is just not true.

Q169 Nadia Whittome : The Committee has heard previously , and from the three of you today , about how women in sports media roles are still facing gender bias , such as having their expertise and credibility questioned and undermined . W e heard previously from academics at Nottingham Trent University that men are often seen as an automatic authority on sports and sports journalism , whereas women are having to prove themselves just to get a seat at the table . H ow far , in your experience , does gender bias shape women’s careers in sports media roles?

We have already spoken about some of that, especially around expertise and being pigeonhol ed based on your gender. For me, personally, a huge angle is around social media safety. That is something that is very much gender - specific in sport , especially football , but is also probably something that impacts a lot of minorities, whether that is people from different races or ethnicities, different religions, sexualities and anyone trans working in football especially. That is something I have experienced massively. It is obviously not something that is exclusive to sport or football , but it is something that I have experienced and is common when you have a more public - facing role within journalism. How you are treated on social media is a huge barrier to wanting to work in sport and media.

Given my experiences, I am not sure what I would say to the next generation. I say to them, “You need to go in eyes wide open about the realities of existing on X, Instagram or TikTok in this society that we live in and how people are going to view your opinions on football, your analysis or anything really , because that is one of the things you have to deal with, the realities of working in this industry. From the minor things to the more extreme end of the scale, which is certainly stuff that I have experienced where you are having to get police or lawyers involved because of those experiences.” There are lots of people in our field who have experienced very similar things.
I am very sorry that you have had those experiences. I just want to express my solidarity with you. It is absolutely disgraceful.

I am very fortunate. I have never had anything like that because I have worked in news for the majority of my career, which meant I was not giving my opinion. I now have a podcast where I give my opinion—
I listen to it.

Thank you. Boy, do people like to tell me I am wrong. Even if I have expressed an opinion that is exactly the same as my male co-star, I will be told that I am the one in the wrong, especially when we did an episode on women’s football; that was enlightening! It is not something I have experienced badly. I have had all the usual misogyny but never anything like that , t hankfully.
Q170 Nadia Whittome : I bet you are told you are wrong by men who never watch the women’s game and do not like the women’s game .

Natalie Pirks : O ften , if I have done a live broadcast about something , someone say s that it was not good or whatever . That must be what it is like to be a footballer when someone who ha s never played the game is telling them they are very bad at their job . I am sorry , but until you do live broadcasting to millions of people in a stadium where you cannot hear yourself think , do n ot come back to me .
Nadia Whittome : Yes, it is very “ I would have got that penalty ” kind of energy, isn’t it ?

Flo Lloyd-Hughes : T he fact that Natalie is saying , “ t he usual misogyny ” , shows that we normalise it so much because we see it as part of the job . I am sure there are lots of young people who are now so exposed to some of the darker side of social media that they , too , may see it as part of the reality of existing on the internet , whatever field they are in . I t is a challenge that does not necessarily have an answer , w hether that is the work that W omen in F ootball have tried to do or the Online S afety Act and things such as that . W e have normalised it so much now as part of our jobs.
Q171 Nadia Whittome : Fiona , you have already spoken about this quite a bit , but is there anything you want to add?

Fiona Tomas : The reality is you need a thick skin to work in this industry and not be affected by th e issues we have just talked about . I am quite fortunate , like Natalie , not to have experienced the scale of abuse that F lo referred to . U nfortunately , it is symptomatic of the world we live in . I n terms of young people trying to break into this industry , a s we have already touched on , it is unfortunately shrinking . J obs are being cut left , right and centre . It puts pressure on you to push your own brand as a journalist . T he role of a traditional print journalist has had to change so much to adapt to the boom in social media .

A n up side from a women’s sport coverage perspective , to counter all this negative chat , is the fact that we are seeing a lot more athlete-led storytelling , which has been crucial to the rise in women’s sport coverage . T he bottom line is you need a thick skin.
Q172 Nadia Whittome : I n your experience , are there differences between the culture in sports journalism and other areas of journalism?
