That is really fundamental. What is the problem you are trying to solve? What is it that you are trying to understand?
Kicking it into the long grass is usually the answer to that.
Kicking into the long grass ?
It is a typical answer, is it not? You set up an inquiry with a clear idea as to what the outcome is going to be and then someone else will have to deal with it down the line.
That serves no one.
Yet it is what people in ministerial role s say at the time.
I know , but you and we need to make it different.
I advocated a public inquiry , because r oyal c ommission s take a hell of a long time and do not do very much — I was going to say something quite rude.
There are international examples where countries have been really swift, nimble and clear. Not us. There are lessons from that.
A review of inquiries.

Q137 Cindy, you are the IPA for England and Wales. I know you are visiting Scotland soon, which is very welcome. How can any system best take account of the role played by the devolved E xecutives and legislatures, particularly in major incidents that occur across the borders?

I am not the independent public advocate for England, Scotland and Wales. I am still visiting Scotland , but I am the IPA for England and Wales. Actually , I am due to be in Wales in December hopefully. What is really important for me in my role is to understand the particular structures, needs and infrastructure that exist in Wales. Some will be similar to England; some will be different. What is important for me is to understand the systems, structures, responses, individuals and communities, again learning from past incidents that happened in Wales. I have been talking to families who have been so terribly impacted by Aberfan.

For me , it is about really understanding the Welsh system and building those relationships in Wales. At some stage I will be recruiting additional advocates. The legislation allows for mini-mes, if you like, a pool of people who can be deployed. I am absolutely sure that I will need somebody who knows and understands Wales. I intend to make sure that one of those additional advocates knows and understands Wales so that I can be as effective in Wales as I am in England .

The other thing to note is that trauma and its effect on victims, families and the bereaved do not know any boundaries. We know with the Manchester Arena attack, for example, that people travelled from across the country to attend that concert. It is not always easily mappable, if you like, across geographical areas. I am very conscious of it and want to make sure that my team and I do not forget that we represent England and Wales.

Q138 In Scotland, many victims of infected blood and their families are still seeking justice and answers. There is not the same provision , but do you feel that you could work with the Scottish Government and agencies in Scotland in those inquiries?
Yes.

Q139 You gave evidence on the Hillsborough l aw. As it stands , how important is that legislation in changing the culture to one that is less defensive and more willing to learn lessons from where things have gone wrong?

It is hugely important. It is such a seminal bit of legislation that has the real potential to deal with the issues that families, survivors and the bereaved talk to me about all the time. They are having to deal with defensiveness, delay, not getting the answers, being shifted and moved around from pillar to post and , in the case of Hillsborough , being blamed for the loss of their loved ones. It has real potential to deal with that issue of truth-telling, which is at the heart of the Public Office (Accountability) Bill, as well as being able to deal with what we know is an inequality of arms between families and the state and state institutions . T here will be greater parity in terms of legal representation.

It is absolutely fundamental , but it will not bring about change in and of itself. The culture of institutions, the leaders within those institutions, the framework, leadership and values that sit around the Bill are equally if not even more important. The IPA of course is not mentioned in the Bill, which is a huge mistake. I see the duty of candour—making people tell the truth—as the flip side of my role, which is ensuring that they do, at least in terms of major incidents of course — we know the Bill is bigger than that.

It is a really poor decision not to make sure there is greater coherence between the Victims and Prisoners Act 2024, which gave birth to my role, and the Public Office (Accountability) Bill. There is still time to change that , because it matters. Making sure that institutions have a duty to tell the truth and act with candour in their dealings with me is important and is an important safeguard for the public.
Q140 Why do we as a Committee not undertake to write to the Bill Minister to ask if it is a deliberate decision , or possibly an oversight that could be rectified?

Without being cheeky , you might want to apprise yourself of the discussions and debates that have been going on in the other place , because I have managed to get good cross- d epartmental support. In fact Theresa May introduced her amendment yesterday. She was not there physically , but it is her amendment. Apprise yourself of all that is going on , and then fight for it.

Sometimes , if a Minister knows they are getting it from both ends , as it were , then it helps to concentrate the mind. I have just realised the potential for misinterpretation of that phrase , so I apologise unreservedly if anybody got the wrong end of the stick, not least the Ministers themselves. Luke, was there anything else you wanted to ask?
No, thank you. That was very helpful.

Thank you for your time and for taking our questions. More importantly, in what is a complicated and under-resourced role, thank you for stepping up to the plate to fulfil it. We are very grateful to you for your time this morning.

sessions.iT: The impact of serious and organised crime on local neighbourhoods
sessions.w: Dr Kate Tudor (Durham University); Robyn Munt (National Farmers Union); Dr Kreseda Smith (Harper Adams University)

segs.tx: Home Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The impact of serious and organised crime on local neighbourhoods , HC 36
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Dame Karen Bradley (Chair); Ben Maguire; Robbie Moore; Dr Peter Prinsley; Bell Ribeiro-Addy.
Questions 143-1 89
Witnesses

I : Dr Kate Tudor, Associate Professor in Criminology, Department of Sociology at Durham University ; Robyn Munt, Vice President at National Farmers ’ Union ; Dr Kreseda Smith, Associate Professor of Rural Criminology and Social Science at Harper Adams University .

II : David Allen, Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner for Cumbria and Association of Police and Crime Commissioners Joint Lead for Serious and Organised Crime ; Donna Jones, Police and Crime Commissioner at Hampshire and Isle of Wight ; Andrew Huddleston KPM, Head of the National Rural Crime Unit, NPCC Tactical L ead for Rural Crime .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Kate Tudor, Robyn Munt and Dr Kreseda Smith.

Q143 I welcome our first panel in this evidence session as part of our inquiry on the impact of serious and organised crime on local neighbourhoods, with a focus today on rural crime—which, as an MP representing a rural constituency, I am very interested in. We have had some really interesting evidence sessions so far and learned about the way that organised criminality is invading the high street, and how the high street is being used to allow for a multitude of criminal activity behind blocked-out windows and behind counters. It has been very interesting, and we are really keen to hear about the impact of rural crime. I am going to let the first set of panellists introduce themselves, and then we will go into questions.
I am Dr Kreseda Smith, associate professor in rural criminology and social science at Harper Adams University.
I am Robyn Munt , vice-president of the National Farmers ’ Union, representing 42,000 farming members. I am also a farmer myself on the Isle of Wight and in Worcestershire.
I am Dr Kate Tudor, an associate professor of criminology at Durham University.
Thank you so much. We will start with another MP from a rural constituency, Ben Maguire.

Q144 Thanks, Chair, and thanks to the panel for coming in to see us today. First, I want to get some context and background. How has the scale and extent of rural, and particularly organised, crime changed in recent years? Have you seen any trends or patterns?

I will just give a very broad overview of how farmers feel about this. It is about the recognition of rural crime having a serious impact on their farming businesses, which I hope we will get the chance to talk more about. It is a range of criminal activity—everything from theft through to waste crime and hare coursing. All of these things cause immense disruption to our farmers and their businesses.

I would probably draw attention to the fact that it is incredibly difficult to get an accurate picture of what is actually happening for a number of reasons. If we take the concept of rural crime, we do not have reliable statistics on rural crime for a number of reasons. The first reason is the problems associated with policing statistics. Rural crimes are not generally separated from other crimes, so it is very difficult to ascertain how much rural crime even takes place in one police force area, and added to that is the fact that national figures are not currently collated.

For that reason, when we talk about how much rural crime is going on, we usually see people make reference to the NFU Mutual claims data—that is really where the debate is at the moment. There is some really good work going on under the National Rural Crime Unit to try to clean up that picture and get a more detailed picture of what is actually going on.

On the second point that you raised in relation to organised crime, it is very difficult to understand what percentage of rural crime would be considered organised crime for a number of reasons. Again, it relates to how we define it and then how we impose that definition in order to come to some kind of statistical measurement—but that does not happen, so we do not have clear statistics.

The research that I have carried out into organised crime in rural areas indicates that a significant proportion of criminality that takes place in rural areas would be considered organised criminality, according to a number of different measures. Whether we take the UN definition or the NPCC definition, all of those definitions can be imposed on to the kind of criminality that takes place within rural settings. But if, for example, you looked at traditional measurements of how many organised crime groups we have operating within rural areas, that data would not give you insight into that, because the groups that are engaged in rural organised criminality have not been defined as organised crime groups.

I just want to come back to what Kate mentioned about the NFU Mutual data, which is really the tip of the iceberg in terms of what we know about rural crime. That is insurance claims, so it is focused very much on acquisitive theft and damage—theft of property. But we know from various research sources that rural serious and organised crime extends far beyond that particular element. There is modern slavery and human trafficking; cyber-dependent and cyber-enabled crime, which is very much a concern in rural communities; drug trafficking; wildlife crime; food fraud and adulteration; agrochemical counterfeiting—the list goes on.

While NFU Mutual gives us something—£41.5 million from its last report earlier this year—that is the tip of the iceberg. I did some rough calculations with a lot of assumptions included, but that brought my figures to approximately £1 billion in terms of just potential insurance claims. Again, that does not go into other criminality that would be considered organised within the rural space.

Just to reiterate, NFU Mutual is our partner insurance organisation. That is the data from only one insurance company. As has been said, this does relate to the loss of equipment or the loss of assets, so it also relates to the impact of livestock theft, but it is not covering everybody. It does not talk to the full cost of the impact of all these things. There is also an issue around reporting, and that fundamentally is down to the relationship between farmers and their local police forces. That varies massively across the country, and how these crimes are recorded is a fundamental piece, as Kate said.

Q145 Anecdotally, as the MP for North Cornwall, I get lots of constituents who have had farming thefts and other rural crimes telling me that they do not bother reporting them any more because there is no follow-up or further investigation. That is not a criticism of the local police because they are massively under-resourced. We heard from the Home Secretary in one of our previous sessions that the rural crime unit that Dr Tudor mentioned has, on average, about £8,000 per police force if you spread it out across all of them. Not all of them are rural forces, but even so, it shows you how little resourcing is going into this.

The National Rural Crime Unit is actually a separate entity that is largely funded by the industry. NFU Mutual makes a considerable contribution towards the cost of the running of that unit, whereas those designated teams within rural forces are a separate issue. We find that there are not always designated people who are able to stay in those positions. Again, that undermines the ability of our members to build relationships with their local policing teams.

Q146 Can I pick up on a point that Dr Tudor made earlier about the statistics not being recorded by police? What would best practice in that space be? We have heard about the evidence we have in terms of NFU Mutual’s statistics, but how can we tackle that?

There is a piece of work going on at the moment with the national rural crime co-ordinator. That is trying to identify best practice in forces nationally to come up with some advice to try to implement across all force areas. Again, that knowledge can be developed and disseminated , but the forces that we are asking to improve their practice need the financial input to facilitate that . Really, we are asking someone to do a huge piece of work collating figures within each force area.

The National Rural Crime Network had a 10- point plan recently, and one of their recommendations was for each force to have a rural crime co - ordinator, because that is a role that we see as vital to improving things like statistics, intelligence collation and intelligence sharing, and improving the knowledge a bout rural crime. T here are things that can be done, but they need investment to facilitate them.
Q147 It will be more than £8,000 per police force.
Yes, absolutely.
Q148 What examples of best practice in tackling serious and organised rural crime c an you point to that you have seen , perhaps in other parts of the country?

There is some really good practice, but it is not on an even playing field. If we take TVP — Thames Valley p olice — for example, they have a really exceptional rural crime taskforce. They have huge numbers of personnel on that taskforce and they have taken the serious and organised element of their rural crime problem very seriously. That is probably a bit of luck , in the sense that they have a chief officer and a PCC heavily invested in this reality, but they have also a very unfortunate history that has made them prioritise rural crime and the more serious element of that —in the light of PC Andrew Harper.

That is an exceptional example for all those reasons . What they do is incredibly impressive. They are really, really good at collating intelligence and creating operational outcomes on the back of that intelligence , using quite sophisticated S O C tactics within the rural arena. That is very rare nationally , because of all the problems that we see around funding .

R ural crime teams, if they exist, do not have the resources, knowledge or capabilities to take on jobs like that. In a situation where they do not have those capabilities, they could, traditionally, escalate that to R OCUs—r egional organised crime units — to draw on their specialist capabilities in order to help them out with that. What I have found , looking nationally, is that a lot of these jobs are far too big for rural crime teams to take on , because they are very complex and very serious. They often involve crossover with high - level drug supply. They can have a national element ; they can have an international element .

If you have one or two people on a rural crime team, they simply do not have the investigative capacity to take on a job like that. But when they are thinking about escalating it to a regional organised crime unit, that becomes problematic because they might not reach the threshold of threat, harm and risk to justify th at intervention , because they are competing with things like child sexual exploitation, drugs t rafficking , firearms, terrorism and so on. W hat I have found is that quite often the organised criminals who are operating in rural areas are able to act with impunity, because the y slip through the cracks of policing . They are too large for local forces and too small for ROCUs, so—
We have some questions specifically on ROCUs later.

There is a piece about recognising the full breadth of the impact . Particularly when I visit members and when I talk with members who are affected by rural crime, I see the full breadth of the impact . This is not just about their businesses ; it is also about their homes. You have members telling you that they do n’t feel that it is safe to let their children play outside because of intimidation that they have suffered from criminal behaviour .

There is also the disruption that i s caused by the theft of machinery. Yes, there is an immediate piece about th e particular item, but that has a knock - on effect on being able to vaccinate livestock for their health, to put crops in the ground or to manage crops. That is all very time sensitive. The loss of equipment for that process has an impact through the whole business and on the general food production of our country.
That machinery is very expensive compared with the kind of stuff that might be stolen on a driveway or something like that.

There is a key thing that we need to take into account in terms of the activities of organised criminal groups in a rural space. Research recognises that serious and organised crime is a violence enhancer. With these threats, intimidation tactics and other violent incidents, if you think about communities that are socially and geographically isolated where there is not a general police presence, they further enhance this issue of the threats of violence towards these communities.

Q149 That is a really interesting point. I think Dr Tudor alluded to that—how criminals are exploiting that in those remote areas. Before I move on to neighbourhood policing, do the three of you feel that police leaders are taking this seriously enough? Do they recognise the issues that you have just highlighted?

There is a full-chain piece here about knowledge, because our members find that even when making the first call to a call centre, the people in the call centre do not always appreciate what is being reported to them and its level of impact. We do a lot of work at a county level with our teams and members going into call centres to highlight this to the people who are in those call centres. That is again about those relationships, but it is also about navigating that piece between urban and rural, and ultimately making sure that farmers are not limited or impacted by a postcode lottery of where they live. These communities are just as important, and it is about making sure that is recognised. The fragmented nature of where they live and the way in which we operate our businesses in those settings gets a bit lost in translation some of the time.

I think that things are a bit patchy with police leadership. As Kate has alluded to, there are some really good practices. I have also spoken to Thames Valley, and what they do is great. There are other forces out there that are really taking these issues seriously, but at the other end of the scale, there are police and crime commissioners who do not even recognise that rural crime is a thing.

I have heard that from my own police and crime commissioner in public fora; he said that there is no such thing as rural crime. That is not a great thing for rural communities to be hearing. But then in the next breath, you have some good responses; they have been working in partnership with the NFU locally to get experts in to talk to their call handlers. This kind of gives a mixed message to our rural communities about how these issues are being seen by the police and appreciated in terms of the extent of the impact it is having on them.

I think it is a mixed bag. It is very dependent on who is in place at any given time, but over the last few years, we have seen a kind of material and ideological withdrawal from rural policing generally. We have seen rural crime teams disbanded and reduced in size. That is not good enough, because of all the things that Robyn mentioned earlier around the frontline experiences of trying to contact the police. For rural communities, it is really important that the people they contact have that specialist knowledge, not only so rural communities feel heard and seen, but so the people they contact have the actual capabilities to deal with those crimes satisfactorily. Yes, we have seen rural crime teams disbanded, but we have not seen other frontline staff being trained with the specialist knowledge that is required to deal with this kind of criminality.

Q150 I wanted to briefly touch on neighbourhood policing. How important is neighbourhood policing in tackling crimes? Local officers in my constituency have the very large Bodmin moor to police, and with the best will in the world, I cannot imagine the Home Secretary suddenly announcing loads of money for lots of new rural crime officers. They have talked about things like drone technology, ATVs and other kinds of tech solutions, even wildlife cameras in some cases. What kinds of things could be improved in the neighbourhood policing space to tackle some of this?

You referenced the cameras, and we have heard from talking to members in York East that they have been really effectively used in that area to give more presence in a virtual space. Absolutely, the use of technology has to be the case, but we see some patches where they do not even have a 4x4 vehicle in order to access the sites they are dealing with. Again, it is about seeing more consistency across the country in how engagement is happening.

I think farmers would welcome being recognised in that neighbourhood space, because it shows focus. When I met a roundtable in Essex—again thinking about things that work in other neighbourhood settings—there are roll-overs you can do and more targeted programmes to deal with crime. As Dr Tudor said, there is a real piece here about farmers being heard and part of the conversation. Neighbourhood Watch schemes, WhatsApp groups and all these things contribute to building a framework of partnership that helps us to address these issues.

An NPT definitely has an important part to play. You are quite right that it is possibly unrealistic to think that we will have 43 wonderful rural crime teams properly funded, but the NPT has to receive training. That has to be institutionalised through the college, or whatever will replace the college post reform. It has to be not just CPD or simply at the introductory level; it has to be part of the centralised neighbourhood policing offer.

I would also agree that tech has a large part to play, but generally speaking across the country, the advancements in that area tend to have been funded by really insecure funding revenue streams, things like Home Office grants and so on, which inevitably run out. We have to think about much more permanent ways of funding those improvements, because if we take the National Rural Crime Unit, as has been alluded to, it was predominantly funded through private industry. The NPCC has to take its responsibility seriously to fund improvements in rural policing and not rely on those adjunct funding streams.

I completely agree that neighbourhood policing teams have a really important part to play. They should be seen as almost the community policing face. Getting to know rural communities is a really important part of what the police need to be doing to gather the information they can then use to generate the intelligence that will lead their policing strategy. The problem we have at the moment—I allude again to the community confidence survey in my force area, which suggests 80% confidence in the police among communities—is that when I replicated that survey with rural communities, it is 50 points lower. There is a huge imbalance between rural communities’ experience of the neighbourhood policing approach, compared with that of urban or suburban areas.
Q151 I have a final question. How do you think we improve that relationship, particularly with farmers, as Robyn alluded to—building that trust between farmers, others and the police force?

Again, it is about improving and sharing best practice. We have some really good examples of where those relationships function well and where the sharing of information works to deal with the problem. Ultimately, farmers need to see results, because that builds their confidence to continue to contribute to the conversation and the reporting piece, as you started out with. Farmers will report if they feel that the problem is going to be dealt with; if they feel that they are not going to be heard, then they will not engage, and I think we can appreciate why. As we have talked about, there is knowledge, training and making sure that the people they deal with have a full appreciation of the impact, because it can just feel like things are not taken seriously enough. Having farmers feel that they are heard in those conversations will help to build trust.

Familiarity is obviously a major thing. We have had the guarantee that we would have a named officer for every community, which is fine, but they also need to be competent. By competent, I mean they have to have the requisite skills relating specifically to rural crime. That is really important. We also need to give them the tools to make them credible. There has been a lot of research on the role of WhatsApp across rural communities. If police officers are allowed to join those groups and engage in conversations with the community within that forum, again the impression of the police is greatly improved and the outcomes are improved.
We have heard that in previous evidence.

I think we can add to that. We have a cycle. If farmers do not see a satisfactory—in their consideration—response to a report of a crime, they are less likely to report future crimes. That means that police do not know that these things are going on. They do not have the information, they cannot create the intelligence mapping and they therefore cannot request the resources to be able to tackle those issues. That means that police are not visible. Farmers and rural communities do not see the police, and the cycle continues. It is a self-defeating issue if there is not a visible presence.

We know that police presence itself does not deter crime, but it is not necessarily about that; it is about building community confidence. I am not saying, “Let’s go back to having a village bobby,” because we know that that is just not feasible, but it is about being able to know who to contact and how to contact them if there is an issue. As Robyn pointed out, farmers, in particular, cannot separate home and work, which puts an added pressure on the farming community to protect their livelihoods and their homes adequately, and to try to deter being targeted in the first place.

Q152 The Staffordshire constabulary has invested in a rural crime unit, so I want to reassure people in Staffordshire. The reality is that a third of my constituency is in the Peak District national park. Trying to have a named officer covering an enormous amount of countryside and an enormous area that will take hours to cover is a logistical problem. How quickly could that named officer actually get to where they need to be if something happens? Is there a role for first responders? I know people normally think of first responders from a medical point of view, but they are there in the villages. Can we use them more effectively?

That is a really interesting idea. Initially, my thought is that it would be great to have somebody within the community. I would caveat that a little bit by saying that sometimes people are reticent to get involved from that perspective, whether in a volunteer role, as a warranted officer, as a PCSO or whatever it would look like, because they might be seen as a snitch or a grass. It has been talked about in research internationally that some communities will not talk to that person, so it defeats the object. I think it is something worth exploring if it is done in the right way and the community is on board. I do not think it can be imposed on a community necessarily.

It must be the right solution for each community. We cannot have a one-size-fits-all approach, because every community will have different needs and different types of farming. My area is dairy farming predominantly, with livestock. We do not have arable. There will be areas with arable that will have different needs.

The severity of crime also varies; that is something else to bear in mind. Some areas suffer more from some crimes than others. Unfortunately, everywhere suffers from too much, but the type of crime does vary, which means, as you say, that the response also needs to vary. It is probably more about strategy than anything else. In the modern age, presence is a very different thing from what it was with a village bobby. We make an active effort to invite police forces to our farm safety and county events, just so they can build that connection. It has to be about relationships.

Q153 I am Peter Prinsley, the MP for Bury St Edmonds and Stowmarket. It also has a big rural district, although we have some small towns. Do you think visible police stations in rural areas are important, in the same way that we have, say, visible fire stations? We have retained fire officers in some small, rural locations. They obviously need to be there because if there is a fire they need to get there quickly. Do you think we could have a model that looks a bit like that for police stations?

I think it might have symbolic power, but beyond that, it is largely irrelevant to achieving outcomes. You need investigative capacity . T he seriousness of the offenders involved in that type of crime is often lost in debate. W e are talking about first responders ; you could use th em for reassurance and familiarity, but certainly not in relation to any kind of response to criminality. T hat symbolic gesture may be advantageous, but in achieving outcomes it is largely irrelevant, because we are talking here about incredibly serious offenders. I have interviewed quite a few as part of my research and I have looked at the ir offending histories. They are not to be messed with, and they really are the preserve of regional organised crime units. Some of them are from abroad and involved in international drug supply rings. For tackling the organised nature of rural offending, it would not do much.
We will move on to drugs and county lines with Bell Ribeiro-Addy.
Q154 How are county lines operating in rural areas, and what impact do you think drug crime is having there generally?

We have seen a real transformation of county lines in recent years. Traditionally, they were conceived of as drug lines coming out of major hubs such as Birmingham, London and so on , running to more rural areas, the idea being that they could operate with impunity and not be noticed so much. They could also expand their territory and market share. However, in recent years we have seen a real contraction of county lines, so they are no longer as frequently running across those large geographical areas; they have significantly shortened. We do still see them running into rural areas, but we tend to see them within a force area. C ounty lines do remain an issue within rural areas, but in other ways than you might traditionally think.

I did some analysis of wildlife offenders within a couple of force areas, and when we looked at the nominals involved in those offences, such as badger baiting, hare coursing, poaching and so on, a lot of those nominals were county lines-affiliated OCG members from other force areas. W hen we are thinking about rural offending, it is not just the direct presence of a county line within a particular rural area; it can also be the nominals involved in those drugs networks coming to rural areas to engage in those other types of crime.

We have been alluding to the kinds of acquisitive offences that we traditionally relate to organised crime activity , but actually when we are thinking about things like poaching, hare coursing, badger baiting and so on , they are the offences that rural communities really worry about , because they tend to be associated with much higher levels of violence, intimidation and aggression, over a sustained period.

Violence during a particular act of theft is very rare, because the offenders do not want to engage in that — they want to get in and get out. However, in relation to those other types of crime, the people involved in county lines who are involved in poaching, hare coursing and other wildlife offences engage in much more sustained aggression towards rural communities and business owners.

Y ou have two elements there to think about. County lines are relevant to any community. It is no longer just rural communities, seaside communities, local towns and so on . It is a huge problem, but it has changed quantitatively and qualitatively in recent years. You also have that other link between traditional rural offences and county lines OCGs.
Q155 How do policing strategies to tackle county lines differ in rural areas?

It is amazing. Actually, I think the county lines model is worthy of consideration in relation to rural crime. I work with the National County Lines Coordination Centre, which does some absolutely brilliant work. It has regional county lines co-ordinators for each ROCU, who act as a point of contact for the forces within those regional areas. To replicate that with rural crime co-ordinators would be a massive step forward, both in the dissemination of best practice that we talked about earlier and in intelligence collation and creating those jobs for some kind of regional-level force operational outcomes as well. T here is a lot of best practice that sits in the world of county lines that could be replicated within this arena.

It is important to recognise that, from a farming perspective, when we talk about wildlife crime, the impact starts to get a bit lost in translation. As Dr Tudor said, the intimidation and violence that our members experience as a result of these crimes is a big part of it. That is what makes them feel very unsafe in rural settings. We tend to find that once a group has found a soft patch, as it were, for this kind of crime, they keep coming back. We have members who have unfortunately faced repeated instances of this, and it just gets worse. Our members have suffered some awful instances of assault. If you put that in an urban setting, there would be a much different response to it. It is important to recognise that impact piece.

Our members also feel that if there is a push down on these crimes, they move somewhere else. How the intelligence is shared between forces means that it sometimes feels like you are starting from scratch again in a different space—it is that falling through the cracks piece. From an impact point of view, as well as intimidation, there is disruption and damage. With hare coursing, we rightly focus on the welfare of the animals involved, but there is also a lot of damage to fields, crops and food production, as well as issues with being able to access fields, because you have individuals there. It is not just happening at night time; this happens in broad daylight.

We need to consider the information that is being provided to Government about the role of county lines and the impact it has on our rural communities. The 2020 report from His Majesty’s inspectorate of constabulary only mentioned rural once, and that was in relation to rural being an importing area—the drugs coming in. A 2025 evaluation report of the county lines programme did not mention rural at all. We need to consider that rural is no longer just an importing area. It should be seen as an exporting area in some places . There are plenty of locations in rural communities where drugs factories or drugs farms can be set up under the radar—abandoned barns or buildings. That is changing what drug production and trafficking looks like from a rural perspective. That needs to be recognised.
Q156 What about the effectiveness of initiatives like the national intensification week? Have you found them productive?

County lines policing is a contentious issue, because it is dominated by a strong Home Office-driven vision of what constitutes success, which is based around the number of lines that are closed. If we think about the harms associated with county lines, we are thinking about serious forms of child criminal exploitation, so we should really be looking to measure the outcomes around safeguarding as well. Yes, we can say that the taskforces that have been set up have been a massive success in terms of line closures, but that has not done anything to chip away at the broader networks of drug supply. It certainly has not done anything to protect the children who are exploited within them.

Q157 You touched on the issues of people using fields, abandoned places and so on, but obviously some places are legally allowed to grow cannabis under special licence from the Home Office. How do you think this impacts the issue of tackling county lines overall?

That is an interesting point, and it is something that Harper Adams investigated. We wanted to do some research using cannabis, and we decided not to apply for the licence to do that, because of the potential threat of criminalisation and criminal activity that it could bring. From a criminal perspective, i t is difficult to separate those licensed locations. They are still locations that they could target. If it is not something that is appropriately protected, they are just going to infiltrate it. Having those legal, licensed locations is great , as long as there is a reason for them. We decided against that approach and changed tack in our research. In terms of criminal thought processes, they will find anywhere and they just do not care, essentially.

Q158 Thank you for being in front of us, everyone. I am keen to focus on rural organised crime units. I know they have been touched on, but I would like to delve a bit deeper. They are made up of various organisations, covering a wide spectrum. I want to understand, from each of you, how effective you think they are.
Can you just clarify—
How effective do you feel that rural organised crime units—
Regional organised crime units.
Sorry. How effective are regional organised crime units at attacking organised crime in rural areas?

Regional organised crime units do not generally take on jobs. They offer specialist capabilities to forces that need support because a job would be too big for them. Generally speaking, they do not dip their toe into rural organised crime very often. The reason for that is essentially the scarcity of resources. When they are thinking about their capacity to take on jobs, they have to take on the jobs that have the highest threat, harm and risk. They are therefore oriented towards terrorism and all the things that were outlined earlier on.

When I looked, as a kind of dip test at a particular time, the NCA had something in the region of 3,500 to 4,000 OCGs mapped, 22 of which, at that time, had a primary threat associated with rural criminality. When we think about which rural organised crime groups might be mapped or addressed by regional organised crime units, it is the groups that tend to be pushed up over the threat, harm, risk threshold, such as people who are stealing telehandlers to rip out ATMs and people who are using explosives in that context. It could be related to the volume of their offending, or to the networks that they are involved in, potentially involving trans-national drug supply and so on. Generally speaking, rural organised crime groups do not feature on ROCU radars very often, but when they do, it tends to be at that end of the spectrum.

That mapping piece is really important. Mapping and monitoring to get to the bottom of the cause and effect is surely where we can see most positive change. Ultimately, as the National Farmers’ Union, we want to see delivery on the ground and members feeling like there is change, but this all ties together. I made a point earlier about reporting. If farmers do not feel like they are going to get an action, they do not report it. If they do not report it, you do not have the data. That all drives back into the picture about where resource is targeted. We have to ensure that resource is placed where it needs to be, but if the impact of rural crime is not properly recognised, that is not where the resource lands. The full breadth of that impact is not currently being seen. Kate made a point about recognising that if the thing happening here that looks small was tackled, it could have a much bigger effect elsewhere. That has to be properly addressed.

Can I add one more thing? I looked at the groups involved in rural criminality across the UK: they look like an OCG, they act like an OCG and they are involved in organised criminality. They are committing cross-border criminality for material gain involving networks that are regional, national and international. They are also involved in multiple forms of poly-criminality involving really serious forms of serious organised crime. Just because they have not been mapped, as Robyn says, that does not mean that they are qualitatively different from the groups that have been. We have a huge problem that is not captured in the data.
Okay, that has been raised.

I also think that ROCUs not being involved or having a part in policing or the oversight of rural serious and organised crime is missing the picture. For a lot of the NCA and Home Office priorities that ROCUs are dealing with, those crimes are happening in rural areas. Modern slavery and human trafficking, fraud, cyber-enabled crime, serious violence and drug trafficking—these offences are happening in the rural and, as Kate rightly points out, they are being committed by offenders who are not just offending in the rural space; they are offending anywhere. It is a business model, and geographical space does not underpin it. They can commit the crime regardless of the space.

Q159 Are there any drawbacks to the regional model? Do you feel that intelligence sharing and data collection, where it exists and can be captured, can be better distributed and shared from an intelligence point of view?

Again, it comes back to the resources available and the interactions between the local force and the regional units. I have talked to various members of ROCUs, and they would love to get their mitts on some of these crimes that are happening in the rural space, but there are just not enough people to do that as well as deal with child sexual exploitation and the terrorist offences, which they really are focused on because of the high level of threat, harm and risk, as has been pointed out.

Intelligence sharing is a huge part of the problem. A central part of offenders’ modus operandi is to exploit the weaknesses in policing that exist around intelligence sharing. They know fine well that if they travel further afield, they may not be known because the information may not necessarily be shared between police forces. I said earlier that they are involved in crime series; they commit multiple crimes. You have talked about retail crime, and it is a similar model. They will disperse that criminality across multiple forces, so the extent and nature of the crime series is not necessarily immediately obvious to policing, because there is a failure to share that information.

There is a huge improvement piece that has to go on around intelligence sharing. There is some really good work taking place under the National Rural Crime Unit around the introduction of T eams channels to facilitate that, and that should be supported and developed much further. Intelligence sharing has to get better, because that is the fundamental weakness that criminals are currently exploiting.

Q160 I want to ask some questions about police reform. Before we get on to that—this maybe picks up some of the answers that you gave to previous questions—I want to talk about where data exists and the confidence associated with how rural crime is being dealt with. Do you feel that there is a correlation between the confidence in how police forces are dealing with rural crime and the way the local police force’s police and crime plan and strategy refers to dealing with rural crime?

I suppose the point I am getting at is this. I represent a constituency in West Yorkshire that is predominantly urban, although there are huge rural crime challenges on the periphery—the boundaries—but the neighbouring police forces naturally focus on rural crime, given that bigger, more rural communities are encompassed by those constabularies. Does the data that exists show a correlation between confidence levels and the police force’s reference to dealing with rural crime?

Both my colleagues will probably be able to talk about the data. Certainly, the feeling from members is that if their issue is not going to be taken seriously, they do not report it next time. We have to get out of that. Dr Smith called it a vicious cycle, and I think that is absolutely right: it is perpetuating a problem. Farmers must feel that they have been heard and that their issue has been properly recognised and taken seriously. We have incidents where people report, “We’ve got your crime number. What more do you want?” Functionally, that deals with an insurance claim, but it doesn’t address the problem. You find that these crimes often happen on a repeat basis because, again, criminals know where to exploit weakness. They have an awareness of the triggers that result in other teams being dispatched. Our members need a response; that comes back in some of the confidence data that we have seen.

For me, it is more operational matters than strategic matters that would influence public confidence. The police need investment, real outcomes, investigative capabilities and people with specialist knowledge. From my experience, I do not think that strategic-level conversations would influence their perspectives too much.

I have spoken to farmers a lot about what is affecting their confidence and trust in the police. More often than not, the response I get is that the police just do not know what rural crime is. This comes back to a definitional piece; we do not really have a good working strategic definition at a national level of what rural crime looks like. It is more than just the acquisitive theft, as we have all talked about this afternoon.

If a farmer or rural resident reports a crime and somebody comes out to them who does not have the first idea of what they are dealing with—again, this comes back to the importance of knowledge and training—the confidence that something is going to happen, and that there will be a positive outcome and that the report will not just be “no-crimed” and closed, is not great.

I will just make one more point here, because I think that the response I just gave you was very short-sighted. The operational outcomes are what will influence perceptions on the ground, but to facilitate better operational outcomes, you need the strategic investment that will begin in those crime plans. The people at the top making the decisions have to understand the reality of those on-the-ground experiences and provide the resources to improve them. So, it is both—operational and strategic.

Also, language is a fundamental underpinning of this, because the term “wildlife crime” does not give enough of the picture of the impact of that crime, just as “livestock worrying” really does not convey the impact of a farmer coming out to a field of animals that have been mauled by a dog.

Q161 The Government’s police reform White Paper has committed to significantly reducing the number of police forces. What do you feel could be the impact of moving to fewer larger forces and what would be the effect on their addressing rural crime?

In a general sense, we have contributed to the conversation around the White Paper, particularly around funding—making sure that those fragmented communities are properly represented with the resource needed to deal with the crimes in those areas.

Our concern has always been that we really want to get away from this postcode lottery of provision, whether in terms of operational delivery or resource, because farmers in a rural area who are suffering from the consequences of rural crime should not be disadvantaged in what is available to them to access from police forces on the basis of poor calculations of resource allocation.
Q162 Does the NFU have a position at the moment on the White Paper? I know that you objected initially to the direction that it was going in.

I would be really happy to share with the Committee the full paper that we submitted, because it goes into all the available things, and probably in a far better way than I can convey in a couple of minutes. I think it would be very helpful if we sent that into you.
Okay, fine.

I think it can go either way; it provides both a beautiful opportunity and a real risk to rural communities. All the same arguments that we are having around current police provision are applicable in that context. We could build in rural perspectives, rural safety and taking the organised crime picture very seriously into the institutions and the organisations that we build, post reform. However, that will take police leaders, Government and the Home Office, and so on, taking the reality of organised crime in rural areas seriously, and building that knowledge into the actual institutions that we choose to create.

It is not that it is automatically a bad thing for rural communities. There is a real danger that the creation of the larger forces draws resources away from rural communities to the high-demand areas, for sure, but that is not an axiomatic outcome of this agenda. If those of us sitting in this room take the knowledge around the seriousness of this form of criminality, and you build it into the institutions that you decide to create, it could be a wonderful opportunity and could mean that we start to take this type of crime seriously.

I probably agree with that. I have had the joy of reading the 96-page document in detail, and my initial thought was, “Where is the detail?” I know it is a White Paper, so IT will not provide the detail, but I got the feeling that they are not taking rural serious and organised crime seriously. To echo Dr Tudor’s comments, if we can collectively put that position forward, this is the opportunity to make the change for rural. As it stands, the only mention of rural in the White Paper and its associated documents is in relation to response times to category 1 calls. I still do not have a clue where the figure of a 20-minute response time for rural areas came from, given that some villages in Ceredigion are a 40-minute drive from the nearest police station—I am sure it is the same in Devon and Cornwall.
And in Staffordshire and Staffordshire Moorlands.

Absolutely. I do not know where these figures have come from. On the neighbourhood policing guarantee, which is one of the documents associated with the White Paper, introducing 13,000 new neighbourhood police staff would not introduce 13,000 new people—the majority of those people will be redeployed from other areas. Rural crime teams have a significant problem with that abstraction and the redeployment to other policing priorities of their staff, who then do not come back.

On going forward with the reforms, the Government need to honour their commitment, as stated in 2025 and 2026, to rural-proof all policy. At this point in time, with the proposed policing reforms, I do not see that happening. If we have to work with this proposed system for the next 50 years, we cannot overlook the rural voice in these reforms.

Fundamentally, where we have seen positive change and good best practice, the last thing we want is regression. Some really good measures are being implemented in certain parts of the country, and rural teams are supporting rural communities, but that needs to be done more widely. The last thing we want from reform is backward steps.
We have overrun slightly, but I want to finish on this, so Ben Maguire will come in a quick supplementary.

Q163 One of the really big problems in North Cornwall, and in Cornwall more generally, is the county lines drug gangs. We see some horrible practices, such as the cuckooing of vulnerable adults and children, and, recently, the grooming of children to get them involved. One selling point of this police reform is that, by definition, larger forces will be able to co-ordinate literally across county lines, as you have mentioned. Devon and Cornwall recently led Operation Scorpion and worked with regional forces across the south-west, which was really effective. In your view, Dr Tudor, is it a case of carrying on doing that, rather than expanding the geography of police forces?

That is an interesting point. We see some really good practice with forces working together. In the north, Operation Hawkeye meets something like every two weeks to share intelligence and to identify nominals of interest who work across the region, not just within the area of a particular force. We also see that in the south-west, and in a number of other examples. That is really good practice that needs to be extended and facilitated more.

In relation to rural crime, a really interesting part of the reform agenda is the potential creation of the National Police Service, particularly the more organised element of it. That is because of all the issues around intelligence sharing and facilitating cross-border jobs within policing that we are talking about. That potentially offers policing an important opportunity to get the policing of organised crime in rural areas right. However, the resources of ROCUs, the NCA and everything we have talked about are drawn towards high harm. It is about writing rural interests and the reality of the organised crime picture into the operating model during the creation of the National Police Service, and that needs to be done from the very beginning. These operations are really good and do help to tackle cross-border offending, but beyond the forces that are working together, there is still a border. We definitely need a much more joined-up, coherent approach.

Before I draw things to a close, I have to comment that, as the MP for a place called Three Shires Head, where Cheshire, Derbyshire and Staffordshire meet, the idea that the east midlands, north-west and west midlands services will be able to understand what is going on there fills me with horror and deep cynicism, so I am yet to be convinced about the need for police reform. I appreciate everything you have said and the time you have spent with us today. I am sorry that we slightly overran, but it is a fascinating area. I bring this panel to a close.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: David Allen, Donna Jones and Andrew Huddleston.

Q164 Welcome to our second panel in this evidence session for our inquiry on the impact of serious and organised crime on neighbourhoods, in particular rural crime today. Could the panellists introduce themselves?

I am David Allen. I am the police, fire and crime commissioner for Cumbria. I am also the APCC joint lead on serious and organised crime. I spent 30 years in law enforcement, finishing up as the head of Interpol, Europol and the Schengen information bureau in the NCA.

Hello, my name is Donna Jones. I am the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, the sixth largest police force in the country and a very large rural police force, as well as having big urban areas. I was the Association of Police and Crime Commissioners lead for serious and organised crime for two years prior to Mr Allen taking it on.
Yours is probably one of the only forces that has a sea between parts of the area it covers.
Sadly, yes—it is causing me much consternation at the moment.
Good afternoon, Chair. I am Andy Huddleston. I am head of the National Rural Crime Unit and the National Police Chiefs’ Council tactical lead.
I think you heard quite a lot of what was said on the first panel. There will be some repetition, but any additional things you want to bring in will be appreciated.

Q165 Hello, I am Peter Prinsley, and I am the MP for Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket in Suffolk, which is very rural, as you know. We have a lot of sugar beet and other things. I have a couple of questions for you. Can you prioritise rural crime effectively within the national policing policies, and what types of rural crime present the biggest challenges?

That is a good question. This is probably an area that needs work, certainly within national strategy, and I would like to see the rural crime strategy come forward and be developed, which it has not been yet.

In terms of rural crime, as part of my police, fire and crime plan I have consulted local people. Rural crime is a priority within Cumbria police—it is one of the four main priorities—as you would expect within Cumbria, which is a massive rural area; we have big urban centres in terms of our population, but rural crime impacts on us disproportionately. Part of it is making sure you have a local response and invest in that local response, but I would like to see a stronger regional and national approach to rural crime as well.

It is an excellent question. As you will be aware, the Home Secretary sets the national policing priorities, of which there are six as of the last two years; there were five for many years before that. As police and crime commissioners and mayors, we set the local policing priorities. In my first term in office from 2021 to 2024, I was not able to give the focus on rural crime because we had so few police officers in my police force area, so my priorities lay in a different area at that point.

From 2024 onwards, it has become one of my top three priorities. Rural communities are disproportionately affected by serious and organised crime. There is the competing challenge of the urban threat versus the rural threat for police forces—particularly those such as mine and yours, which are trying to police hundreds of square miles and keep communities safe in them.

The really key thing for me around serious and organised crime is that it poses a significant, evolving threat to communities. Criminal gangs are highly adaptable. They are absolutely financially motivated. On that, I want to pause for a moment. Crime types, as we know, fall into three main classifications: they are either sexually motivated, violence-led or dishonesty-led. What we know about serious and organised criminal gangs is that they are motivated by money—that is exactly what they are doing it for. It might be black market gambling with hare coursing or plant and machinery theft, but the violence often comes in off the back of that, so those are the two main crime drivers. Modern-day slavery then plays out, and there are a whole host of other things that I am sure we will get into.

Back in 2024, I made rural crime a priority for my chief constable. I have funded a rural crime taskforce . I put local bobbies into every rural community in January 2024 . We have now got dedicated detectives in my force. I have paid for people to work in our police intel unit just to be developing leads from our rural communities. We have also got analysts developing those leads too. A whole lot of investment has gone in from me, which has driven up our charge rates, but we still have a way to go.

To summarise , we have 43 different ways of doing this. You are hearing from two PCCs who represent two rural forces that do it very well , but in terms of prioritisation, we have the National Police Chiefs ’ Council strategic priorities and we have a strategy that is there for all 43 forces to work to. You are hearing that variation that we have across the country of forces where it does work very well, but equally, there are forces where that strategy has not been implemented as well. The strategies and priorities are there ; it is about how they are followed in those 43 different ways. If you take nothing else away from today, the point I want you to take away is that rural crime is not green grass , taking a hare or rabbit. Rural crime is serious organised crime , and I will give you examples this afternoon where international organised crime groups are specifically targeting our rural areas to commit crime because it is advantageous for them to do that.

Q166 There is a sense that rural districts are relatively under - protected by the police , as opposed to urban areas where there are very many more police. Is this question also about balancing organised crime in rural and urban areas and how you prioritise that ?

It is very easy to make the statement that rural areas are not p oliced as well. Look at the size of Northumberland : it is twice the size of Luxembourg. You are never going to get the police officer footprint per square mile as you would for the City of London or anywhere else. We have to be realistic around what the policing model is that fits for that area. In my experience as the national lead for the last eight years , there is a correlation between a PCC’ s priorities , a chief constable ’ s priorities and crucially the investment in delivery. What you have heard about Thames Valley earlier this afternoon is absolutely right, and that works very well. There are large areas where we have got a good policing footprint, but there are others where it is just not prioritised in terms of commitment on the ground.

Q167 There is the question about whether the priority is something determined locally or nationally . Andrew, if you were to be given a whole lot more resources — suppose I had a chequebook here — what would you do with them ?

To repeat, the strategy is set. We have got the priorities ; we know what we need to be looking at. There are numerous examples that we could give of where organised crime groups are operating, and we would look for the assistance of the RO C U s— the regional organised crime units — to help deliver. When that has not been forthcoming, we have had to find other ways of doing it.

If you look at the two international crime groups that have been committing the vast majority of the GPS theft s across the country, they were international groups that have actually not been taken out by the RO CUs; they were taken out through co - ordination of the national rural crime unit, working with the regional forces. Eighteen months ago , it was Cumbria and the west coast. In the last two months , it has been the south - east of England. Eight forces have been affected , and there have been multi-million - pound thefts. It was the work of those rural crime teams that actually caught the offenders and put them in prison.
Q168 So that problem is solved.

It is like anything. It is often referred to as the whac k- a - mole game : we deal with one group , but we know that it is a lucrative market. You heard from Rob y n from the NFU this afternoon. You have heard from the PCC as well that there i s a lot of money at stake here —millions of pounds . As soon as we take a team out, it is just a matter of time before the next team is sent. It is a constant recurring thing ; we are focusing on following where the intelligence takes us and being able to be fleet of foot to be able to deal with it as quickly as possible. That is why the NFU Mutual ’ s figures will show an 80% reduction for 2025 in GPS thefts. That is not down to luck; that is down to a lot of hard work by some very good officers and staff.

We are never , unless we close significant public services across the country, going to have enough police officers to be able to have Dixon of Dock Green stood on the corner of every village green. This is about working smarter, not harder. Where policing in England and Wales has been a bit slow to the table is in exploiting technology in rural communities .

In the bigger rural forces that are really getting into this, led by Andy and the team, you can really see the difference. For example, in rural communities, you have very willing participants . The people who live there are much more willing to work with the police as a group of local residents than you get perhaps in some of our urban areas.

What I have done in my patch, for example, is invest in rural CCTV—mobile, deployable CCTV—that we can lend to the farmers, landowners and gamekeepers who are being targeted by poachers. We know when the season is about to start and when they are going to be more vulnerable. I have invested in rural drones. I launched the first rural drone pilot in the country last month.

I will give you an example from 18 days ago, when someone was catapulting livestock on a farm in Hampshire. A 999 call came in and, through the EyesOn app that I have launched, the police control room sent out a notification to everyone in that area registered as rural drone pilot s to say, “We need to get a drone up in this area.” I have paid for those drones; they are tools owned by the police but given to local communities to use.

The drone was up within five minutes. That meant that the police control room was able to see straight to what was going on through that drone, live, because it is all linked up. We were able to evidence-capture from that. We were then able to get another drone up a couple of miles away, so that, as the poacher was driving away, we could follow. The number plate was tracked to an address in Southampton. It is a live investigation. The person was arrested and is someone who already happens to be a person of interest to the Hampshire and Isle of Wight c onstabulary for similar linked offences .

So we cannot have hundreds of police officers policing our rural communities on the off-chance that something might happen, but through working with willing communities, gamekeepers, farmers and landowners, we need to be exploiting technology so much more to give communities the tools that they need to make them safer.

In rural Cumbria, most of our rural crime in the north and east comes from Durham, unfortunately. We work with our farmers and locals in Kirkby Stephen. We regularly have joint operations with Durham, North Yorkshire and Northumbria, and Andy’s team as well.

We also co-opt the locals. They all have radios and are very active with their WhatsApp groups as soon as anything is seen, especially when we have the days of action, and we have many of those during the course of the year. That has reduced quad-bike theft by almost 50% in the last year, because we are working with the locals. As Donna said, there is a willingness in rural areas that you do not get in the urban centres. They know that the individuals are coming in from elsewhere to take their livelihoods and property away; they feel very strongly about that, and they are willing to work closely with us to tackle it.

Technology is vital. Drones are the next thing coming along. We do not have an infinite number of police officers, and the areas that we are covering are massive, so drones are absolutely vital going forward.

While I would always take money from you—it is always helpful, and there is an element of that—we would actually have a greater ask in terms of support. This is not just about policing. This is not, as you have heard from many of my colleagues in the past, just about arresting our way out of this. This is also about the fact that there are many factors that make rural crime the problem that it is.

To take it from the very beginning, I will give the example that you have heard this afternoon of cash machine rip-outs. We had a figure at one point where, of 17 cash machine rip-outs across the country that were done using farm machinery—telehandlers and things like that—14 were done using machinery stolen from a farm. The reason for that is that, in the vast majority of times that we go on to farms, we will find keys left in the machines. I say that publicly because the criminals already know that.

This is absolutely not about blaming farmers, because we work very well with them and everybody has a role, including ourselves, but there is an element of this that goes from farmers leaving keys in machines through to manufacturers. It is absolutely wrong that you can buy a £100,000 or £200,000 tractor today and a single key will start every single machine that that brand makes. It is the same with quad bikes too. There are elements of that that need to be addressed.

On legislation, my ask would be about the likes of the Equipment Theft (Prevention) Act 2023. Three years later, we still do not have what we were asking for, which was assistance to help make farm machinery and construction machinery more secure. Again, as you have heard today, this is not about one criminal who just picks on a rural area; this is about people who are targeting construction equipment as well. That is why our team, which is only eight people, is actually funded by the industry, rather than, as it was historically, by the Government as well. My ask would therefore be to say to the Commons and MPs, “Look, you could help us to better support what we do by giving us those powers.”

Again, I would also like to think that the new power regarding searches with an inspector’s authorisation—which is in legislation now; we are just waiting for it to be pushed out—will be a game changer in helping us to recover stolen equipment.
Q169 Did I hear that correctly, that there is one key that operates all the tractors that are manufactured?

I will be very clear on this because some manufacturers will be watching very closely what I say. Some manufacturers have machinery that is very secure. It has immobilisation and digital keypads, but there are manufacturers out there where one key will start every single machine in the range that they make. If you look at quad bikes as well, not every manufacturer, but for some manufacturers it is one key starts all. From a policing perspective, this should not just be about policing.
It is easier for the user, because you just need the one key, but it is not safe.
In fact, for most quad bikes you just need a screwdriver.
That is heard very loud and clear in this Committee. Thank you for that. I would say that the television programme most relevant is probably “Heartbeat”, not “Dixon of Dock Green”.
That is a good point: I stand corrected.

Q170 I am from the North Yorkshire moors, so I know a bit about that. The police chief constable that I met in my district told me about domestic violence and how it is very under-reported in rural districts. I can believe that, not just on farms, but in villages as well. What would be your answer to that problem?

Domestic violence is under-reported across the country, not just in rural communities, so I do not see a profile that stands out for me particularly about rural communities. If you were talking to me about some ethnic minority communities, I would say yes, because they try and keep things much more insular, but not particularly the farming community as a cohort, or rural communities. It is a problem across the whole country. It is the largest reported crime in every police force in England and Wales. It is not the largest committed crime; it is the largest reported crime. But we know it is very under-reported, particularly with male victims of domestic violence, too.

I would agree with Donna in a lot of those respects. It accounts for 25% of all calls into the police control room, so it is the largest scale of offences reported, but what we find in the isolated communities—we have very isolated communities in Cumbria—is a husband and wife farming team who work together. It is very difficult if one of you is a victim of domestic abuse. How do you report that? That could be the livelihood of the farm gone—you have broken up the family unit and the farm. We do know that it is considerably under-reported. There have been many, many instances of domestic abuse before it is reported. That is in the national stats, anyway, but more so in a rural setting is what we found from local experience.

Q171 Finally, I think the point about domestic violence perpetrated on men is also very much under-reported. In my constituency surgery last week a mother came in to tell me about her son who had been murdered by a partner who is now in prison. He had failed to report it. I think it is a big problem. I think it is a rural problem, actually.

Yes. A new rule is coming in from I think 26 October, which is the domestic violence death review. Currently when someone dies in a domestic setting, it falls to the local council to lead the review. In some cases it is a very small district council. Some of them have community safety partnerships—CSPs—and some do not. For some of them this will be the first domestic violence homicide review that they have done in 10 years, and I do not believe that that is the right place for domestic violence homicide reviews to sit. Where you have a mayor, it could sit in the mayor’s office or as part of the command authority work. It probably should sit with your upper-tier council or your adult and children’s social care teams as opposed to—I would have said with police and crime commissioners, but as we are a finite commodity, clearly that would not be the place to put that now.

I would agree with Donna on that. Evidence from Cumbria is that about a third of the cases are of male domestic violence that we are now seeing reported. We invest locally in help in that area with the domestic violence co-ordinators and victim support, etc. It is an area of concern. It is massively under-reported. There is no doubt about that.

Q172 Picking up on one of Peter’s earlier points, this is probably for Mr Allen and Ms Jones. This is about prioritising. You both have urban areas where it is probably easier to get a crime solved than it might be in a rural area. I understand that, but how do you, with your competing priorities, make sure that rural crime is properly prioritised? What is your technique for doing that?

It is very difficult. I will be very honest: in my first three years, 2021 to 2024—in my first term of office—it was not one of my top priorities. I had come into a police force that had cut its frontline police officers . Hampshire and Cleveland were two forces that still had not recovered their 2010 policing numbers 18 months ago. It is a very large police force, as you said, with urban and rural push and pull, and competing demands.

I have 360 parish councils across the 2.2 million people I represent. I spent years going around and saying to them, “I promise you that I am going to get to you, but at the moment we have people being killed, gun exploitation, drug exploitation, sexual violence and prostitution. We have a lot of things going on in the cities of Portsmouth and Southampton and some of our big urban areas. I need to make sure the chief constable has enough police officers, and I need to fund that to enable him or her”—I had a her at that point—“to do the job I am paying them to do.”

In 2024, I was then able to have that reset. In the last two years, I have reopened 10 new police stations—particularly in rural communities—that my predecessor had closed. Giving people a front counter not only gives them the ability to come in and speak to the police when they need to, but provides reassurance. The people sitting on the front counters are not just sitting there waiting for someone to come in, but are processing all the online crime reports as well.
Q173 So you have administrative staff doing this?

Absolutely. They are doing that to help police officers. The key thing for me has been having a visible presence and giving people back their local bobbies. In January 2024, I brought back a named local police officer for every single community, so every village and every hamlet has one. Those local bobbies are never abstracted to deal with 999 calls; they are proactive only. They should know the local headteacher, barber and hairdresser. They should really be a part of their communities, and that is what I have been striving to do.

Investing in the rural crime taskforce was a significant investment on my part. That was about my priorities, but also about my representing a large swathe of rural communities across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. If you do not have buy-in from your mayor or PCC, it is incredibly difficult, because a chief constable will always have a greater threat and harm assessment in other areas. If it is not led by people like us, it is probably not happening, to be honest.
Q174 I was particularly interested in your point about the front desk. Have you seen an uptick in reporting of crime since that was reopened?

Yes, we have, but the great impact has been something else. I will use the market town of Petersfield, which is in Damian Hinds’s constituency, as an example. In June last year, I opened a police station there for the first time in 10 years—it had been closed 10 years ago by my predecessor. We have seen a 19% reduction in crime in that market town, not so much because people are going in and reporting crime but because there is a more visible policing presence. I have both 999 responders and neighbourhood policing teams working from there, and that has been a visual deterrent—so prevention is better than cure. That has been really key, and we need it for rural communities too.

That is really interesting. In my rural community in North Cornwall, Launceston has been trying to get a front desk for a long time, and our PCC Alison Hernandez has refused to do that. I agree that it would increase confidence in policing, not necessarily from increasing the number of police officers, but from having the access to the police to report crime, and from having confidence and trust.

Q175 The view of the professor from the first panel was that, if you had a pot of money, it would best be spent on investigations and zapping up your investigative capacity.
