segs.tx: International Agreements Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO)
Monday 12 Octob er 2026
Watch the meeting
Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair) ; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord Stevenson of Balmacara .
Evidence Session No. 3 Heard in Public Questions 15 – 22
Witness
Rt Hon Sir Andrew Mitchell MP, former Secretary of State for International Development .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witness
Sir Andrew Mitchell .

Q15 ​​ The Chair: ​ Good afternoon and w elcome back from Recess. I am extremely pleased that we have managed to accommodate the diary of Sir Andrew Mitchell and are having our meeting on a Monday. I am very grateful to those colleagues able to join us today. As you know, we are undertaking a public evidence session and a general inquiry into our decision as a country to join the United Nations Industrial Development Organi z ation. We are fortunate enough to know the individual who decided we should leave UNIDO in the first place. We have had one full evidence session already , at which we heard from the department, the F CDO and other witnesses.

Sir Andrew, thank you very much for being with us. We could not be more fortunate than to have you explain to us why we left in 20 10—well, t he decision was taken in 2010 , and w e eventually left in 2012. Your views on our rejoining would also be very helpful , and then we will have questions from the rest of my colleagues. That is a good place to kick off ; we appreciate you r coming to speak to us.

​​ ​ Thank you very much, Chair . I am obviously both honoured and privileged to be invited to give you this evidence, which I do with great pleasure. I would like to give you a slightly lengthy answer about why we left , if that is all right .

W hen we came into g overnment in 2010 , i nternational d evelopment had the very strong support of not only the Prime Minister but the opposition parties. I have always been very keen to make it clear that it was a British policy, not a Labour or Conservative one. We knew then that Britain was an international development leader. That was a time when we really mattered and we set the agenda. During the course of that Parliament, the House of Commons agree d—I think only four people vot ed agains t—that we should spend 0.7% of our gross national income on international development , not only because it was the right thing to do but because it was, if you like, the other side of the coin to defence . It was money that was always spent , or should always be spent , in our national interest, and it was about enhancing our security and prosperity as much as that of th e very poor countries in which we worked.

But we knew that if we were to spend 0.7% of GN I we would have to satisfy the public that the money was being really well spent. T hat was why we set up the multilateral aid review and the bilateral aid review . T he multilateral aid review put all 43 —I think—UN agencies through their paces to see whether they merited UK taxpayer support. The criteria against which we measured what they were doing w ere whether they were pursuing UK interests and whether they were delivering value for money for the UK taxpayer. Many of th o se agencie s had never been looked at. The UN w as aghast that we were doing it and did not really believe that we would . The process was founded in our absolute belief in the importance of results, which was then copied in many other countries around the world. We put all our conclusions into the public domain , w e had a peer review by experts about those decision s and I announced the results of the multilateral aid review on 1 March 2011.

W e basically divided the 43 agencies into three groups. First , we looked at the ones that were really successful against our criteria , such as UNICEF, which looks after children . We were so impressed by what it was doing that w e doubled its core grant and gave it an extra £10 million. Secondly were those that were critical to Britain’s interests, such as the Commonwealth Secretariat, which needed to improve . Thirdly were th e agencies to which we gave nine final warnings . Finally, there were four on which we decided we could not justify spending British taxpayers ’ money any longer , one of which was UNIDO.

W e thought that it had no impact on global poverty, that it lacked a country - level presence in the countries it was working on and, in terms of its significance, that there were more effective development actors with greater impact on the ground. Key elements of what UNIDO was doing in those days were done better by the UNDP. Your Lordship s will remember Lord Malloch- B rown, who was a n important presence in your H ouse . He ran UNDP and was responsible for it doing so well. T he key weaknesses identified at UNIDO were a lack of transparency, weak financial management and weak financial reporting. W e decided to withdraw over two years, saving £7 million a year , but we continue d to fund specific projects .

For example, while we did not leave the IOM , which dealt with migration, we cut back what we were doing, but subsequently the IOM was engaged in specific project issues that were very important to Britain’s interests. I remember a particularly tricky and worrying occasion during the Libyan crisis when we had thousands of refugees s itting on the coast at Misrata. W e provided funding for the IOM to go in and lift them off the side of the wharf; the people who did that were very brave. We could always still fund projects if a specific necessity arose, but we decided we would not give it any more annual funding .

It was fully in the public domain, but there was an occasion when I was rung up by Downing Street because they thought that the Prime Minister was concerned about whether we had got UNIDO right ; someone had had lunch with someone batting for UNIDO. I explained to No. 10 why we were doing it and they were entirely satisfied . I t was a well thought - through and careful decision.

Q16 ​​ The Chair: ​ Thank you very much. I have a follow-up question, and my colleagues have questions as well . We heard that we are already contributing a substantial amount of the UNIDO’s development budget. I cannot remember how much; is it £ 200 million ?
​​ ​ Now or then?

​​ ​ At the moment . I d o not know whether that is a new initiative from the new Government or whether it was going on towards the end of the last Co nservative Government , b ut what would you say would be the benefits of rejoining, assuming we are already channelling money through UNIDO? I am still not 100% sure why you thought it was bad value for us to be a member. Can you vaguely remember how much we were spending?

​​ ​ I cannot, but I will let the committee know . I think I have set out quite clearly the reasons why we did not continue to give it core funding , and that is included in a very good document that was published at the time o f the multilateral aid review. I think your c ommittee wondered whether it had come across my desk during my last iteration in Government between 2022 and 20 24.
​ Yes .

​ The answer is that there was no discussion , in my time , about rejoining UNIDO. We may have had far too much else to do. W e certainly had an awful lot to do because the vaporising of DfID by Prime Minister Johnson was an absolute disaster . T he F CDO had no clue how to deal with many of these issues , and t he talent that DfID had so splendidly managed to accumulate was all leaching out of the door. But I certainly did not make any decision to rejoin. There was no Foreign Office funding for UNIDO at all in the last five years. Any UK funding was being done by other departments, in particular DESNZ . I m ight have announced some funding in part of a package at C OP, but it was not from my budget. As you know, Chair , the O DA budget, although held by the Foreign Office, is distributed in some cases by other departments. I believe I met the d irector -g eneral of UNIDO during my time, but the Foreign Office ha s not been able to locate a note of that meeting.
​​ ​ T hat is very helpful ; t hank you very much indeed.

Q17 ​​ Baroness Anelay of St Johns: ​ Thank you, Sir Andrew, for joining us today. I was interested in what you just said . It sound ed as though you were categorically not planning to rejoin UNIDO during that last period , when you were the Minister responsible , but, in the earl ier iteration , you had clearly gone into great depth , with the multilateral aid review. Now that the current Government ha ve decided to engage and join and the agreement is in operation , c ould you give us an idea as to why you think the UK would do that? Is it related to some of the reforms carried out by the director - general, who has now been there for about three or four years ? Is it now morphing, in a sense, into the kind of animal that you would have been happy to see resuscitated and deliver ing proper assistance to those in poverty around the world ? Sorry for the rather long question.

​​ ​ Thank you very much, Lady Anelay . I think you are basically asking me whether there are tangible benefits over and above the informal engagement and voluntary amounts that we make. T here are arguments for going back in , but they have to be tested against the current —and very different from my time in g overnment —constraints on the development spend. The development challenge debate and the era have changed , and developing countries need industrial capacity. There is a change now in that there is very little grant aid money but there is money for investment , so “ investment ”, not “ grant aid ”, is the word of the day —although it is important to remember that, in a very poor country , that investment will not be successful unless you have an educated and healthy workforce. T echnology, reliable energy and access to market s all help create jobs and increase incomes. T here is no doubt that there is a stronger focus on that by UNIDO today.

Secondly, over the last five years, a more intense project relationship has developed between the British Government and UNIDO. It is not a result, but I will take for example a project in Brazil, where £15 million of UK taxpayers ’ money unlocked £250 million of development finance money and , allegedly , some £2 billion in private investment. That is anticipated and not verified, and I am sure that the c ommittee will be as interested as I will be to see whether that is indeed how it transpire s .

T he third argument is the “ seat at the table ” argument, which , on the whole , I rejected when I was Secretary of State for International Development because Britain was such a dominant force in development. At the time , virtually all the developed countries in the world came to London to talk to my officials about what we were doing on the multilateral aid review, and many of them copied it, including America , Germany and the Scandinavian countries. T he “ seat at the table ” argument may be more relevant now, but it should always be heavily tested. It is always much enjoyed by officials, but it should be very heavily tested by those with responsibility for UK taxpayers ’ money.

​​ ​ Thank you very much for that exposition of how matters have developed since we left UNIDO, now that we are in the position of joining. You mentioned having a seat at the table and taking part in governance . T hat, of course , involve s decision - making. Would it be your concern that , if we were in the minority on the governance board , that would bring the UK a not very good reputation , shall we say, given the background that you laid out from 2010 , whe n we were carrying out the multilateral aid review, which, as you said, was very much recommended and copied by other countries ?

​​ ​ I think Lady Anelay is asking me whether the “ seat at the table ” argument implicates us in the decisions made by UNIDO. Of course it does to some extent, although people understand that these things are not always unanimous. But if you go back before then and look at the weaknesses —I think, Chair, that you asked me whether I thought that it had addressed the weaknesses, so perhaps I could come back to tha t—
​​ ​ I think that is the next question .

​​ ​ Okay. I t is for the Government to justify , Lady An e l ay, that your concerns are not the case. We know perfectly well that Britain is better in some international organisations today at providing leadership and defending British interests than it is in others.

Q18 ​​ The Chair: ​ We have a supplementary , Sir Andrew, which follow s on from what you were just saying . W e heard from UNIDO officials that significant reforms had been made , a nd I wonder whether you fe el that that i s true. I do not know whether you could expand a bit on your original answer as to why you withdrew but—I am obviously sensitive about how I ask this questio n—there were concerns about how the organisation itself was run and the leadership, and there were other political views. Quite a few others left at the same time, alongside us.

There is a new leader ; I think he is a German ex-F oreign Minister or D efence Minister. Forgive me for not knowing his previous role but he was a senior German politician , as I understand it , who has come in and is now running it. We a re given the impression that it is significantly better at measuring outcomes and doing all the things you said. Can you comment on whether you think that is actually the case and give us your thoughts on what you thought was wrong with the management of the organisation when you withdrew?

First, about whether UNIDO has rectified the weakness, as Evelyn Waugh said in Scoop in 1938, “U p to a point, Lord C opper ”. T here have been three important developments since my first iteration in development in g overnment. T he first of those is that there is undoubtedly a more focused industrial and climate agenda. There is much greater emphasis on industrial decarbonisation, clean energy, green industrialisation and sustainable supply chains. In all those things, you will find that UNIDO is taking a much greater interest and the UK Government , as I think may be eviden t to you, my Lord , ha ve noted that international co - ordination al technical standards and investment are very important and are better.

Secondly, there is clearly better oversight and transparency. I am advised that the Government think UNIDO is smaller and more efficient than when we looked at it before , has a proper independent evaluation unit and has much greater openness on the effectiveness of their programmes. I am giving a précis , but I think that was the burden of the evidence on 15 September this year.

T hirdly , we have developed program mes w ithin UNIDO rather than pay a membership subscription . T hose programmes , l ooking back over what Britain has sought to influence , are on clean technology , i ndustrial decarbonisation and work on clean industrial markets. T h at has clearly increased the Government’s happiness with what UNIDO is doing.

In terms of the problems, I think I mentioned that if you look at the MAR report you can see that we were very worried about its impact on global poverty and abo ut the spread of UNIDO’s assets around the world. I think I made t he point about Lord Malloch- B rown and UNDP —if you look at the work of UNDP and the work of UNIDO in those days, you can see that there were others who were much better at doing UNIDO’s core job than UNIDO. At the time, my officials noted the weak financial management and lack of transparency. T hat is why we took the decision that we could spend our £7 million better elsewhere , and we withdrew over two years.

Q19 Andrew, you have spoken about your own thoughts on the Government’s decision to rejoin UNIDO. I got the sense during our evidence sessions that many people were very sceptical of joining a big organisation involving all the money, particularly given that there were parts of the world that did not have clean running water and had clear needs to be met that would be better met by private sector investment and focused project management such as you promoted, as you have outlined. Coupled with your other aims, these were aims that you pursued. They have not happened everywhere. We heard from a couple of Peers about their experiences in Africa and India, where these things are lacking. What is to guarantee that joining UNIDO, another big organisation where the members—I think there are 53—meet every two years, and which is run by a secretariat, would be any better, despite the reforms, at achieving the three aims you had: efficiency, private sector investment and tackling corruption? Are we not better to do that on our own, with specific focus and keeping an eye on our prime aim in the UK of tackling the problem of migration? I think in your view it would be through development at home.

That is an extremely interesting question, your Ladyship. First of all , in order to do a number of those things, you need a bilateral programme on the ground in the countries where people are working, which of course gives the Government direct eyes on what is happening. You will have seen that although I, in the last year of the Conservative Government, doubled the bilateral programme across the countries in Africa that we worked in, because of the inexplicable decision by Keir Starmer to cut development even further from 0.5% to 0.3%, that sort of involvement does not exist and the bilateral programme in Africa has been cut to ribbons. But the real question is : how should the Government keep an eye on what is happening now that it is rejoining , to see whether it meets British requirements?

T he questions I would bear in mind when looking at UNIDO’s work, and I hope t here will be proper evaluation of it, are fourfold . First, is membership necessary ? If we are already funding projects for and with UNIDO , w hat are the additional benefits for the UK taxpayer?

Secondly, what is the opportunity cost of spending this extra money through having a seat at the table at UNIDO? I ha ve already spoken of the very stressed budget that we now have, and it needs to be measured against the myriad of very good calls on that budget. Is this one of them? Are we missing an opportunity here to do something else?

Thirdly, w e need to make sure that UNIDO is kept up to the mark. We do that by the very British results agenda a nd holding their feet to the fire on the promised improvements ; something you always have to do with these agencies , because when they want the money they are quick to say that they will make these improvements , but when they have the money they sometimes get distracted . I t is very important that Britain does all that , particularly if we are going to be on the board of UNIDO, as it were.

Fourthly and finally, go back to the multilateral aid review criteria, of which development impact, value for money, additionality, governance and sustainability are explicit criteria that could lead to us leaving once again. The Government are proposing a 2029 review. The original MAR provides the enduring guidelines to that.

I will just play devil’s advocate. You talked about feet on the ground and bilateral arrangements, so that we have people who will conduct the projects. You had various projects on the ground. Some of them may have lasted, some may not. I do not know what happened to your own projects in Sierra Leone and Rwanda. Those were focused programmes and you had feet on the ground. I presume there are agencies with which you work and you wanted to bring in investment from your background as an investment person. Why can that not continue to be done , including by agreements or funding to specific agencies, if you need them, that you are confident are on the ground, or other bodies? Then the task is not to find the boots on the ground but rather, having identified the projects, to fund those, rather than just joining yet another UN commitment to have a seat on a table of 52 members and a secretariat that will, in the end, decide the agenda.

That is a most interesting point. We currently work with UNIDO on projects and in areas where we think it is presumably value for money and in the British taxpayers ’ and British national interest . The question is whether or not by being on the board, as it were, we are able to help fashion which areas UNIDO goes to, rather than just having to say, “That looks a rather good project, I think we will support that”.
I do not know whether you are going to ask me whether I support the decision or not, my Lord—
I think we are.

I have obviously thought about it. All those decisions are much more difficult now because the funding is so constrained. Also, never forget that the cutting of the funds is one thing, but then there is the vaporising of the expertise which was respected around the world. Indeed, I would go so far as to say, my Lord, that the only area of British international leadership which has been accepted in the past without qualification has been on international development. You saw this respect on all sides of the United Nations, and today I am afraid we are in a very difficult and different circumstance when it comes to British interests and British effectiveness in the way I have described.

Are you saying that, because of these cuts and this change, we now need to work more through organisations like UNIDO, and one of the reasons why you withdrew was because you felt we could do it better ourselves?

I felt we could use taxpayers’ money better ourselves. The very limited taxpayers’ money that is available today—much of which of course is going to fund the first year of an asylum seeker’s time in Britain; that is in accordance with the rules governing the overseas aid budget—leaves very little indeed. Therefore we have to approach being careful with the way we spend this money in a very different way from when, with all-party agreement, the money was far greater and our reach and effectiveness were far greater. We must always remember, of course, that the first call that the British public expect us to make on this budget is on humanitarian expenditure. The committee will be well aware of the disaster that is going on in Darfur at the moment . Quite apart from being an area of previous British historical interest, that is obviously also an area that cries to the heart of a generous British public in supporting these people there who have been, and are, in desperate peril.
Thank you very much. I just ask for a small clarification. When you talk about £7 million cost, that is not money that goes into development; that is the administrative—
Sorry, the 0.7% or the £7 million I mentioned in respect of UNIDO?
Yes, the £7 million.
The £7 million I mentioned in respect of UNIDO was the annual cost of being a member of the board.
It is a fee to manage—
Yes, it is the fee for joining, which is at the heart of your inquiry, because the Government have decided to change what we agreed and go back to doing that.

Sorry, I have asked this question, so I am repeating myself slightly, but that is a very small amount in relation to the money that we were channelling through UNIDO, which would be hundreds of millions of pounds.
You mentioned £200 million, my Lord, which is more than I remember it, but I would have to go back and consult the papers.
I think that is the current contribution that we are working through UNIDO. Have I got that right? Am I way off? Oh, it is £125 million, but I think it is going up to £200 million.

That money is not being spent by the Foreign Office. It is doubtless from the ODA budget—the development budget—but I think it is being spent mainly by DESNZ, because, of course, within the Government, they have the lead on many of these climate issues. I gave an example where £15 million of British taxpayers’ money was being spent in Brazil, but if—if—it brings in not only the development finance money from multilateral organisations but also the additional private sector money, it would look to be very good value indeed. But you have to wait and see what the evaluation says.

Q20 We will have to wait and see what happens in the Brazilian election too. Thank you very much for coming along; it is hugely valuable to the committee to have a former Secretary of State of your effectiveness—which I would certainly bear testimony to—coming here to tell us why it was you withdrew and to answer our questions. That is very good.

I would like to pick up one point that you made at the beginning. You instanced UNICEF, where you had greatly increased our contribution, because it was a very good organisation which was spending the money in an effective way. That is a very important point. When I was responsible in New York for these matters, one of the weaknesses then was the position we are in now, which is that whenever we went to subject a UN organisation to a rigorous inquiry, they would say to us, “And if we can satisfy you, will we get more money?” The answer in the early 1990s, when Baroness Chalker was the Minister, was, “Sorry, it won’t make any difference to the amount of money you can get”. That is a hopeless position to be in because there is no leverage for improvement there. Thank you for reminding us that, when you were in charge, you were able to increase that sum.

Could I ask you a double question, really? It is entirely about the desirability, and the nature, of subjecting the decision which the Government has now reached to rejoin UNIDO to a review of some sort or another, probably in a specified period of time, to make sure that the UN is not—as I think you yourself suggested; sometimes UN organisations do this—slipping back again into funding largely its own running costs and not the objects that the organisation is set up to do. The double question is this. First of all , do you think that the decision that is being taken should be subjected to some form of review to ensure that there has not been backsliding on the elements that the Government considers have demonstrated that UNIDO is doing better in recent years? I am sorry, I am just jumping to the assumption that it will be taken, that it has been taken, and that it will be sustained. Do you think that there should be a review? The second part of the question is: if there is going to be a review of the decision to rejoin after, let us say, three or five years, do you think that should be subject to any kind of parliamentary process in either House of Parliament, of the sort that we are having at the moment here on this decision?

That is a very interesting question. On UNICEF, I completely agree with your Lordship, because it was something important to show. As I said, the UN were aghast that we were doing this. They did not believe we would do it—and that speaks to the complacency of an organisation which you know far better than any of us do. With UNICEF, we were showing that it was not an exercise in cutting. Often people immediately would cynically think, “They are only doing this to cut away”, but we only cut away four of the organisations, and UNICEF are an example of one where we looked at the results they were achieving. We saw what they were doing for children in impossibly awful situations around the world and how they were ameliorating that. Following a very stringent analysis, we were able—with some pleasure—to double the core grant, which I think was £10 million a year at that point. We were very pleased to do that.

On the subject of a proper assessment of this decision and the nature of whether it should be a parliamentary inquiry or not, I think your committee, my Lord, has shown the right way to do this. I note that the Government has, I think, promised that there will be an evaluation in 2029, and I hope very much that this committee will hold the Government’s feet to the fire on that. Certainly, the International Development Select Committee in the House of Commons should look at that report and establish whether it is both helpful and justified and that it agrees with its conclusions. If it does not agree with its conclusions, I hope that both it and you will set about the Government to hold them accountable for the decisions that they have made.
I think your Lordship is also asking me whether I think it is a good idea to go back, so would it be helpful if I—
Yes, please. Your direction on that would be very useful.

I start by saying that the ODA budget is under unprecedented stress, and therefore you have to be clear that this is not just a “nice to have”. Because of the stress on the budget, it needs to be something that will really do good. I have mentioned a number of ways in which it could really do good—in particular, helping with the very important climate change agenda.

But there are issues that remain. There are two that I will mention to the committee. One is UNIDO’s own review and independent evaluation of its results-based management, which looked at the performance of UNIDO between 2018 and 2025. That was some time after we had given UNIDO the shock of leaving and, and as you said, my Lord, other countries had copied our lead. The formal systems and frameworks, according to the 2018 to 2025 review, are much improved. But it made clear that results management was not well implemented across the whole of UNIDO. That is incredibly important because, if you cannot show the results, you cannot justify to taxpayers the money that you are spending.

Secondly, the report identified weak accountability and controls below senior management levels. This included fragmented data systems, incomplete baselines and shortcomings in measuring outcomes across their activities—the results agenda that I have repeatedly mentioned. This really matters because better systems and a more attractive strategy are not the same thing as demonstrating those results.

My conclusion is that UNIDO has changed in ways that are important since we reviewed them in the multilateral aid review after 2010, but they have not fully overcome the original MAR concerns. When I was in the Foreign Office, my department was not spending money on UNIDO, and it has not done so for at least five years. So, in a way, the question of justifying rejoining, where I think the jury could be argued to be out, needs to be put to DESNZ, and a lot of attention paid to 2029 when the next review takes place.

Thank you very much. I am delighted that , when you read the transcript of the evidence that we took from officials, you got the impression that they committed themselves to a parliamentary procedure with this committee when they reviewed. I have to say that , having sat in the room and watched them doing so, I was left feeling a little way short of certainty that that was actually going to happen. Of course, they will have another opportunity to do so if we decide to raise this matter in our report, because it will come up in the debate that the House has. I would hope that we would get a more full-throated commitment to that.

One of the reasons for that is because—and I would like you to comment on this last part of my question—a parliamentary dimension to this is of benefit to our negotiators when they are talking to UNIDO, because they are able to say, “Look, you understand that we’re going to have to go before a parliamentary committee and tell them that the money that you, UNIDO, is spending is good money for our taxpayers, and to do that we’re going to need some very convincing arguments. Here are three, four or five of them”. This is a weapon in our hands rather than something we should be flinching from. Is that your view?

Yes, your Lordship is entirely correct. My observation would be that the International Development Select Committee in the other place is highly respected. Certainly, officials both in my second time in government, between 2010 and 2013, and my third and final time, between 2022 and 2024, were very wary of Select Committees, because their job in representing the taxpayer and our constituents is to get to the bottom of all these matters. It is a very good system for holding G overnment to account, and the International Development Select Committee is extremely good at doing it.
I hope I said, because my notes here say, that the Government are proposing a 2029 review. Perhaps in your future discussions you might wish to turn that proposition into a commitment.

We definitely need to do that. I do not think it was a firm commitment; it was more that we always have a check after however many years. Lord Stevenson, do you have any supplementary questions before we come to a conclusion ?

Q21 Yes, could I ask one question? We are very grateful to you for the comments you have made, Andrew. You have broadened the debate and enlightened us on a number of issues that we were concerned about.

I was just reflecting on what you said about the MA review, which was obviously groundbreaking and you should take credit for attacking something that most people within the system would have thought impossible. But if we are going to have a review in 2029, which I hope we will and I think we should say so in our report, is the MA review as you originally described it relevant? “Relevant” is perhaps too strong ; of course it is relevant. But would it be the right model to use in the sense that we are comparing the time when you launched it, when, as you say, our development work was world-class and top of the league, and now we are way down near the bottom? We might be seen to be trying to do something rather ridiculous—straining at a gnat—because we are no longer experts. Do you agree with that?

The truth is that the agglomeration of skills that rested in D f ID, when it was a department of state for international development, was quite extraordinary. If I, as Secretary of State, wanted to know how research was going in developing a climate-resistant seed to grow in very arid soil in the poorest parts of the world where there was huge food constraint and I raised the question, I would probably have six PhDs outside my door in the department to answer that question by lunchtime. That skill has been greatly mitigated, although there are still some quite extraordinary people in the Foreign Office, led by Nick Dyer, the Permanent Secretary responsible for international development, but they are now few and far between.
On the other hand, we were able to engage externally with a number of experts in think tanks and universities. I would hope that some of that would be able to be brought into play again.

The six points I gave about the MAR, which will be in your records, are the six key questions, and I would hope that they would be asked in any review undertaken by this committee or the International Development Select Committee.

Although t he bilateral aid review , which is of course not relevant today , was not about saving money at all, it led to us reducing from, I think, 42 or 43 to 26 the number of countries we worked in, because we did not feel that spending British taxpayers’ money on continuing bilateral programmes in those countries could be justified.

Q22 Thank you very much for coming. Everybody has found this very helpful. Looking at the review, which Lord Hannay and others have mentioned, and with us all perhaps looking forward to a commitment, what kind of people should be doing the review? How would you ensure that you have truly independent people doing a review, rather than it being something to rubber-stamp membership post-2029?

Of course, he who pays the piper calls the tune. We have to be wary of that. But the department—the Foreign Office—which has not been spending this money , would commission the experts from the areas I described to make that assessment. Although there would undoubtedly be official involvement in that, one would hope that external independent resources would be involved in drawing up the details and judgments from which officials would be able to make a proper decision.
And the terms of reference?
Well, again, I think they could do worse than look back at the multilateral aid review of 2010.
A classic approach, which I am sure will be used as a template for the future too. Do any of my colleagues have any further questions? No?

Sir Andrew, thank you so much for being with us. I do not know whether you gave us an equivocal answer in a binary—join or not rejoin—sense, but your caveats are extremely relevant. I am very grateful to you for drawing our attention to the 2029 review point and the fact that the world has changed since we left and, it would seem, we will have to rely more on third-party agencies than perhaps we did, even though the principles you outlined in your original MA review still have to be coherent and adhered to , otherwise we will end up wasting money. Do you have any final comments you wish to make?
No . T hank you very much for giving me the opportunity to answer your questions.
It was greatly appreciated. Thank you very much indeed.
Backbench Business Committee
Representations: Backbench Debates
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Bob Blackman (Chair); Mr Lee Dillon; Mary Glindon ; Martin Vickers.
Questions 1-1 0
Representations made
I: Scott Arthur and Clive Jones
II: Scott Arthur and Julie Minns
III: Olivia Bailey
Scott Arthur and Clive Jones made representations.

Q1 Welcome to this meeting of the Backbench Business Committee, where we will be considering applications from colleagues for debates in the main Chamber and Westminster Hall on Tuesday morning s and Thursday afternoons. Our first application is from Scott Arthur, for a debate in the Chamber on the future of cancer research in the UK. I will declare my interest as a strong supporter of Cancer Research UK and chairman of the all-party parliamentary group on smoking and health.

Thank you, Chair. I am sure that all of us have interests in this area, so you will not be alone in that. Although you have a formal conflict of interest, I am sure that we all have an interest in this subject.

This debate is about looking at how we can progress cancer research in the UK faster and further. Fundamentally, it is about holding the Government to account, but also thinking about not just the health benefits of working in this area, but the economic benefits. The UK has a world-leading record on cancer research, and breakthroughs have transformed the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of cancers in my lifetime—although, I have to say, I am in my 50s actually . But there is a feeling that, while progress is faster than in the past, it is perhaps starting to slow a little.

We have the national cancer plan, which was published earlier this year, but we have had a few personnel changes in that Department since then. This is a challenge, really, just to keep them on their toes. Although this is not a DHSC debate, it is a chance to shine some light on the progress that has been made.

This is extremely timely; there are several pressing issues, principally delays in setting up clinical trials, which mean that promising treatments are reaching patients more slowly than they should. I want to give two examples. I have a constituent called Faye Robertson . She is a clinician, and she has just won £70 million to research glioblastoma with the University of Edinburgh and NHS Lothian in my constituency, which is fantastic. However, were she here, she would say that, if she had chosen to go to the States, she would have started the work a year earlier, such are the delays in the UK.

Yesterday evening, we had a meeting with universities that want the Government to invest around £500 million in science infrastructure to progress treatments both for cancer and other conditions. There was a pharmaceutical company there that is investing alongside Cancer Research UK, and it was asked, “If this new research institute develops intellectual property, would that stay in the UK?” It said, “Well, that can’t be guaranteed, because it can be more attractive to do the work overseas than in the UK.”

That is something that we have to address. It is not just about giving people access to treatments; it is about giving them access to really good clinical trials that mean that they have more support as they go through their cancer journey. It is also about ensuring that we are investing in the UK economy and bringing those jobs and that investment to the UK. I would therefore say that this is very timely indeed.

We have broad support from within my own party along with Liberal Democrat—Clive is always a fantastic supporter of everything in this field—Conservative, SNP, Plaid Cymru and DUP Members. I want to stress that the MPs signed up did not sign up because I approached them in the Tea Room or Division Lobby with a piece of paper to sign; these MPs have signed up because their constituents have contacted them and made the case. Every single one of those constituents has either lost a family member, has cancer right now or is a survivor of cancer. That is what makes this application a little different as well. It comes from the grassroots.

Thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak in favour of the application, Chair. Cancer is going to touch one in two of us, meaning that we all know somebody who is affected by cancer. As Scott said earlier, it remains the leading cause of death in the UK. I have experienced at first hand what it is like to go through a diagnosis, and I know the importance of effective treatment. The treatment I had, 18 years ago, had not changed for 40 years—but it was successful. These days I would not have to go through so much difficulty. It was something that was pretty hard to cope with.

Survival rates have doubled since the 1970s, but have started to slow a bit recently. We in the UK have a proud history of world-leading cancer research. In the discussions that I have with a lot of cancer charities I hear that we could be doing so much more. We could be back to a leading position in the world, and we have slipped away from that recently.

This debate is definitely needed . It has lots of cross-party support, and the Government’s recent national cancer plan has set a target of three in four people surviving for five years or more by 2035. To be able to do that—and it is a goal that nearly all of us would say we need to reach—we have to improve the research and the development of treatment.
I hope very much that you are going to say yes, and let us have this debate.
Q2 Mary Glindon : My late husband benefited from being on a trial and I know what a difference it makes to cancer patients to be able to partake in trials. I am glad that Scott mentioned that.
Is there a particular special date that you would like this debate to coincide with?

I understand that November is the national awareness month for lung, pancreatic, oral and gastric cancer. I know that November seems quite close, but that would seem timely. Obviously, I am in your hands.

As you say, it is a very well-supported application. I am not sure whether you could prevail upon the Leader of the House to give us plenty of time in November. At the moment , we are not getting time in the Chamber at all, for one reason or another—other than the odd day. We also have the Budget coming up, which means that debating time will be on the Budget. Then we have the short recess that comes up at the beginning of November. We will do what we can to get you a proper date. The Clerks will be in touch with you in due course.
Scott A r thur and Julie Minns made representations.

Q3 We now come to Dr Arthur’s second application. It regards the impact of the illegal use of e-bikes and conversion kits on communities. Once again, it is for a debate in the Chamber. I have to say, this is one of those things that I am sure all MPs are getting plenty of correspondence on.

One of the questions I am worried you might ask me is which of these two debates I might prefer. Certainly, this issue is the one that I get emails from my constituents about. If I had police officers from my constituency here, they would say that this is the No. 1 issue that people are raising with them right now in my constituency. Obviously, cancer care is a separate issue, and a really important one as well, but is very different.

I have a good friend who goes to my church. She is in her 70s and recently bought an e-bike. It has transformed her life. Her boldness in using it is incredible. However, the flip side of the positivity that has come with e-bikes is the use of illegal e-bikes , and kits that are used to convert legal bikes to illegal e-bikes. I see this right across my constituency. One of the hotspots is right outside my constituency office, which is a little embarrassing at times for me : people are able to point to it and ask me what I am doing about it.

The se bikes are big disruptors. We see them every day and they are a huge concern to the police. It is right across our country , whether we are living in an urban area or even some rural centres as well. We really do feel it. We have had past discussions about e-bikes in Westminster Hall, and I remember taking part in the debate. That focused on antisocial behaviour, and we are all aware of those implications.

This debate is focused on understanding the role that illegally modified and illegal e-bikes are playing and thinking about the import ing of them into the country and what steps the Government could be taking to deal with that. They are disruptors but , if we are all being honest, the Government have been too slow to respond. A consultation recently closed on the import of these devices, so there is a real chance to hold the Government to account and push them to do more.

It is not just about the safety issues that we see in our streets. I met with the London Fire Brigade recently in this building. They were talking about how they see a fire every two days caused by the batteries—including in the depot that the police use for confiscated bikes. They even catch on fire there. While the fireman was far too professional to be angry, he sounded angry about the inaction from the Government and all parliamentarians on this issue.

This is a serious issue, both in terms of the threats that we see on our streets, but also what our emergency services are dealing with. If debated, there will be broad support from our parliamentary colleagues, but I think also from the public as well. There is a chance that they might tune in and watch what we are doing in voicing their concerns in Parliament.

Thank you for the opportunity to address this issue and propose the debate. As Dr Arthur says, this is an issue that affects all our constituencies. We all see it in our postbag. We are all well versed in the criminal and safety aspects , along with the speeding that we see. Some of the less well-known aspects, which the debate would give us an opportunity to rehearse, include the impact that this is having on the legal market.

First, on the sale of legal e-bikes, in the UK, just 9% of bikes sold are e-bikes. If you go to Germany, it is 53%, and in Holland it is 61%. The debate would allow us to understand , or give us an opportunity to rehearse , why it is that the UK does not have similar sales of legal e-bikes. I would contend that it is because we have a very rife illegal market, which exactly as Dr Arthur said, is made up of these conversion kits and illegal e-bikes. The other impact is that they are undercutting legitimate businesses. For example , they are affecting the sale of low-powered motorbikes and mopeds. That market has seen a 20% decrease in Q1 this year alone , because why would you buy, license, insure and MOT a moped when you can buy an illegal kit that will get you to exactly the same speed?

The other aspect we want to look at in the debate is that, because there is a definition of a legal e-bike, if an e-bike is illegal, it becomes a motor vehicle. At that point, if you have an accident with an illegal e-bike and you are injured, you can go to the Motor Insurers’ Bureau and raise a claim because it is an uninsured motor vehicle. The Motor Insurers’ Bureau has seen a 73% increase in claims attributed to people now having accidents with these illegal bikes. So there are multiple aspects to this issue . It is not just the safety, the fires, the speeding or the criminality; it is having a financial impact on the legal sale of e-bikes and also mopeds.

The last thing I would say about the timing is that next year the Tour de France is coming to the UK—it is coming to my constituency and to Dr Arthur’s constituency. If we have this debate, let us push the Government to legislate to ban the sale of these illegal kits and illegal bikes. Incidentally, China has already done that, but where do these things come from? They are coming over from China. If we can get a ban in place, we can focus on the safety and enjoyability of cycling as we go into the Tour de France next year.
I always find it bizarre that the Tour de France comes to the UK, but that is another matter.

I chair the all-party parliamentary group on fire safety and rescue , and I recommend that you watch the video that the London Fire Brigade has produced about an e-bike in the vestibule of a block of flats going up in flames and how the smoke emanates right up the stairs. It is horrible ; you are absolutely right about the dangers.

Q4 We had a lithium battery fire in my constituency over recess that closed the Paddington line. I have just one question for you : y ou have requested a debate in the Chamber , but w ould you consider one in Westminster Hall on a Tuesday or Thursday if it could happen sooner?

Our preference would be the Chamber, because it is such a national issue. But as Dr Arthur has alluded to, the sooner we can push the Government to make a decision on this, the better, so if the only option was a Westminster Hall debate, we would happily take that.

Just so you know, we are still dealing with applications for the Chamber that we received in January this year. That is how long we are having to push people to. The Clerks will be in touch with you in due course. Certainly, if you are willing to take a Westminster Hall debate, you are more likely to get one sooner rather than later.

Our other applicants have decided not to turn up. There is one application for a debate on Black History Month. Our understanding is that the Government are going to organise a debate in Government time on the subject, so I suspect the proposer is not coming to us .
Olivia Bailey made representations.

Q5 This is a request for a debate on the legacy of the Jarrow Crusade, on the 90th anniversary. The application is in the name of Kate Osborne, but Olivia Bailey is presenting on her behalf. Olivia, please present your case.

Thank you, Chair, very much. I am presenting on behalf of Kate, who is the MP for Jarrow and who is very determined that there should be a debate to mark the 90 years since the Jarrow Crusade, when 200 men marched almost 300 miles to London to petition Parliament over devastating unemployment and industrial decline. T he anniversary is an important opportunity for the House to commemorate the march and reflect on the circumstances that led to the march and its lasting national significance. I ts legacy continues to resonate in debates about the dignity of work, regional in equality, and industrial communities and their relationship with Parliament. I t has significance far beyond Jarrow , a lthough of course it is very important to Kate in terms of her constituency connections.

Q6 Olivia, it is proposed that on the application that the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade is to respond , but the last time we had a debate on the Jarrow Crusade, the DWP responded. Are you aware of a particular reason that you have gone for Business?

No, not that I am aware of. I imagine the significance might relate to the Employment Rights Act 2025 and recent improvements in workers ’ rights legislation under this Government. T hat perhaps is one reason DBIST has been suggested.

Q7 Okay. We are suggesting , to try to coincide with Kate Osborne ’ s original request , to allocate the debate for 22 October —t hat is obviously next week — as the second debate. Is that acceptable? W e will need to know immediately , because we are allocating the time.

It is hard for me to say—I a m afraid I don’t have access to Kate's diary right now. I could say yes provisionally , and then I could very quickly correspond with you , Chair , following this meeting, if there is a particularly significant reason
Kate cannot make it.
Q8 Just so you are very clear, if she is not then able to do it—
I will do it.
The debate will s lip until November.
Okay.
Q9 Olivia just offered to lead the debate , i f Kate could not.
I could do, but I imagine Kate would prefer to do it .
Q10 Lovely. Thank you very much. We wi ll have correspondence if necessary, but the Clerks will contact you about the offer formally.
Thank you.
T hat brings the public proceedings of the Committee to an end. The Committee will now retire to consider the applications in private and allocate time accordingly.

Oral evidence: The work of the Secretary of State for Defence, HC 73
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026 .
Watch the m eeting
Members present: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi (Chair); Alex Baker; Lincoln Jopp; Mike Martin; Jesse Norman; Ian Roome; Michelle Scrogham; Fred Thomas; Derek Twigg.
Questions 1- 81
Witnesses
I : Rt Hon Wes Streeting MP, Secretary of State for Defence; Jeremy Pocklington CB, Permanent Secretary, MOD; and Air Marshal Tim Jones CBE, Deputy Chief of the Defence Staff (Force Development) .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Wes Streeting, Jeremy Pocklington and Air Marshal Tim Jones .

Q1 I call to order today’s House of Commons Defence Committee evidence session with the new Secretary of State. It is an absolute delight to have the right hon. Wes Streeting MP, the Secretary of State for Defence, for his first outing at the Defence Committee. It is a pleasure to have back with us Jeremy Pocklington, the permanent secretary at the Ministry of Defence. I also welcome back Air Marshal Tim Jones , who is the Deputy Chief of the Defence Staff (Force Development) .

Secretary of State, thank you very much for appearing before the Defence Committee. Formally, on behalf of the Committee, congratulations on your new post—it is not quite as new now as when you took charge.
It feels like a long time ago now.
A long time ago, back in July. You have now been in post for nearly three months. What is your initial assessment of the main challenges facing UK defence?

Fundamentally, this country and our allies in NATO face a threat of a kind we have not seen since the end of the cold war. I come into a Ministry of Defence that is well positioned to meet that challenge, because of the work that John Healey did on defence reform to modernise the shape of the Ministry of Defence and because of the way the national security strategy spells out very clearly for us what the threat environment is. The strategic defence review sets out how we need to respond to it and the defence investment plan sets out how we then make that happen. I have come in and inherited a Department with the right focus, moving in the right direction.

Where is my focus? What am I most worried about? First and foremost, spelling out my priorities is simple because, fundamentally, they are to make sure that this country can deter our enemies and, should deterrence fail, be able to fight and win. That means that to meet the challenge set out for us by NATO we need to strengthen our capability; strengthen our defence industrial base, effectively making sure that we can out-produce and out-innovate our adversaries; and strengthen our alliances.

In that context, we have the right plan and the right strategy, and we’ve got very capable people. One of the great privileges of being in this post is that I get to peer behind the classification curtain and see just how extraordinary those people and much of our capability really are. It is important to say that against a backdrop in which talking our country down is something of a national pastime, and that we can be self-confident enough in what we can do but also self-aware enough to know we need to step up several gears.

That brings me to my final point, which is about how the country—the Ministry of Defence, Government, industry and the public—need to be thinking. NATO says we need to be able to fight and win a war against our adversaries by 2030. That is not because NATO wants a war—quite the opposite. We do not seek conflict with Russia. We do not seek escalation. We do not seek to provoke Russia. But we know that every single day Russia is testing us and testing our allies.

We know—I feel very strongly about this personally—that the term “hybrid threats” offers a sanitised description of what are acts of sabotage, targeted assassinations and, effectively, state-backed terrorism. That is the world in which we live today : it is extremely uncertain. If we are serious, and if we set as our organising principle warfighting readiness, that means making some whole-of-Government and whole-of-society choices to make sure that we invest in our defence sufficiently, modernise our capability and are ready to fight the next war and not the last one. It also means thinking not just about broadening and deepening our defence industrial base but about strengthening resilience across British industry, so that we are in a place where we could sustain and win a war.

Finally, on alliances, we are extremely fortunate that we sit at the centre of one of the most successful alliances in the history of the world: the NATO alliance. That is important at a time when multilateralism has somewhat gone out of fashion, but one of our challenges as a country is to make sure that the same unity of purpose that we see driven through NATO on defence is read across to other areas, like economic co-operation.

These are interesting times, and it is a great privilege to be asked to take on this job. For all the challenges, I think there has never been a better time to join Defence, in terms of the investment, opportunity, innovation and opportunities for careers in defence in the broadest sense, but there are significant challenges and we have to be honest about them.

Q2 Secretary of State, I wanted to give you a couple of minutes to set the scene and explain the importance of your role to the wider public, because you are our Defence Secretary at a critical juncture in history, so how you communicate to the wider public, particularly via the national conversation that we have talked about, will be very important. On behalf of the Committee, I also place on the record my thanks to you for the secret and classified briefings, and to the wider Ministry of Defence team for their co-operation.
You talked about modernisation; can you explain any immediate changes that you have managed to implement since taking charge at the MOD?

When you come in as someone new, you want to make your mark, and there is always the temptation to come in and upend everything, but actually, I have inherited defence reform at an advanced stage, in terms of how the Ministry of Defence is modernising.

But there are things that we need to do, and that we are doing, to cohere the four strands of the Ministry of Defence and to make sure that we have joined-up leadership at the top of the organisation. The NAD group is absolutely central to dealing with the issues that have historically plagued the Ministry of Defence and its reputation: value for money, productivity, procurement, buying the right things, and distinguishing between the exquisite capabilities that we need to design and procure and the stuff that we can get off the shelf. That is one of the most important parts of defence reform, so it is about seeing that through.

If I may say, the one thing I have personally brought and will continue to bring to the Ministry of Defence is the focus on value for money, productivity and making sure that we spend taxpayers’ money wisely. There are lots of similarities and lots of differences between being Defence Secretary and being Health Secretary, but there is one fundamental difference. When I was Health Secretary, I was constantly asked why we were “just throwing more money at the health service,” and I constantly had to prove that we were modernising, innovating, balancing the books—which we did in the NHS for the first time in a decade—and focusing on productivity, where we smashed our targets.

In defence, the entire media conversation, and a lot of the conversation we have on the Floor of the House of Commons, is—not to put too fine a point on it—about asking for more money. That is really important, and long may it continue, I might say, ahead of the Budget and the spending review—I’m never going to complain about people batting for the Ministry of Defence—but I have to bring the focus on to making sure that the money going in is well spent, because I am acutely aware of the choices and trade-offs that imposes on other Government Departments and on the taxpayer.

I am also really convinced that, when you look at the Prime Minister’s overall vision for the country and some of his key priorities around reindustrialisation and opportunities for the next generation, the Ministry of Defence, led correctly, can also be a Ministry for growth and opportunity that can serve the economic and social benefits and impacts that the country needs, so that we are not just able to fight for our county but can build a country worth fighting for.

Q3 You touched on a range of issues in relation to defence spending. You will find Defence Committee members calling for not just more defence spending but making sure we have value for money. As you rightly pointed out, we want to ensure that defence reform addresses the capability gaps. In due course, Committee members will be drilling into the various facets, but I want to come in on value for money. As you rightly said when you took office, when you were Health Secretary you embarked on a bold programme of reform and modernisation, which is why you want to tackle wasteful procurement practices. In defence, we have unfortunately had perennial procurement problems. Can you give me any specific examples of where you have cut waste or are looking to do so to ensure value for money for the British taxpayer?

Some of it is held at a higher classification. Obviously, I have been in for a few months, so the first thing I will say is that I am not going to pretend that I have completely overhauled the way the Ministry of Defence approaches these things in the first few months; I will not claim credit for other people’s work. What I definitely want to do this afternoon is a bit of naming and praising, but I also want to take some responsibility for some decisions I have made since coming in.

On naming and praising—obviously, some of this is held at a higher classification—the way in which the Defence Nuclear Enterprise has organised itself to drive real productivity gains, working with industry as a good partner, but also challenging industry to make sure it delivers on time and with good value, has shown what is possible when you have the right leadership and the right focus on those things. What we are seeing in DNE is the most important part of what we are doing, in terms of our capability and industry partnership, and I think we will see more of that come through with the NAD group as well.

In terms of decisions that I have taken, and have taken some flack for, when I came in the finances for this fiscal year were off track, and we needed to make some savings to bring them into line and balance the books. I have taken decisions to stop doing some things this year. In some cases, they have been higher profile, and we have taken some criticism. I have taken those decisions unapologetically, mindful of the impact—I am not indifferent to it, by the way—because it was important for me to signal very early on that we cannot have a culture of overspending in the Ministry of Defence.

We are receiving more money. It has gone up significantly since Labour came into office. We are delivering the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war, with more to come at the Budget and in the spending review, but that is not an excuse for overspending and overcommitting. I hope that some of the decisions I have taken, although they are not entirely popular—stopping doing things is never popular—have sent the right signal throughout the organisation and the armed forces that we will get greater resource and support, but that we also have a responsibility to live within our means.

Q4 You mentioned the Defence Nuclear Enterprise; I put it on the record on the Floor of the House that the Defence Committee unfortunately does not have sight of it, which is a major gap in parliamentary scrutiny. Your predecessors were talking about establishing a Committee to look at that, with linkages to the Defence Committee, and I hope you will take some steps on that very soon.

Yes, I can absolutely give you the assurance that I have been engaging with the Prime Minister on making sure we have appropriate parliamentary scrutiny of the DNE, given how important it is to the country. We can get this right. The Intelligence and Security Committee shows that there are ways of having effective democratic oversight of highly secretive and sensitive work.
Q5 Good. We look forward to that taking shape very soon, because, as you rightly said, value for money is key.
Q6 Thank you all for coming. Secretary of State, what personally would you like to achieve over the next year?

To gear-shift from strategising to delivery mode. For lots of reasons we are all familiar with, because it was highly visible, the necessary work around developing both the SDR and, particularly, the defence investment plan that followed took far longer than anyone involved in that process would have liked. It has meant that for some time—although, to be fair to my predecessors, there has been lots of really positive work going on, lots more money going into defence and lots more activity as a result—it has inevitably been the case that, when you are focusing on something as fundamental as a strategic defence review and then wrangling over the defence investment plan, that has consumed a lot of oxygen and focus.

For me, shifting into the implementation of the DIP is the most important thing. I pay particular tribute to my immediate predecessor Dan Jarvis for the heavy lifting he did to get the DIP over the line. But we need to shift from saying to doing.
Q7 So it is about the implementation of the DIP. Are there any metrics you would like to put on that to judge yourself by over the next year?

The DIP sets it out. We have got just shy of £300 billion over the next four years. We need to show that that money is being well spent, that programmes are running to time and that, at the same time as we are doing all of that work domestically, we are also strengthening international alliances.

A personal priority for me, as well as for the Government, is supporting Ukraine. In the short time I have been in office, I have done a lot through the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, which I co-chair with Boris Pistorius of Germany, to mobilise support for Ukraine ahead of this winter. We have another UDCG shortly, in November. It is of critical importance to this country, as well as to Ukraine and our wider allies in Europe, that we see Ukraine through what will be a very difficult winter and make sure they can build on the extraordinary progress they have made this year.

Q8 As you know, the DIP is in two parts: there is the bit covered by the current spending review, and then another spending review is slated for next autumn, which will do the bit from 2030. You will also know that two thirds of the money in the DIP is in that bit beyond 2030. Can you speak a bit about your personal ambitions for that second bit of the DIP, which is currently unfunded?
This is one of the tensions, to go back to what I was just saying about strategising and planning versus delivery and doing. Obviously, it is my responsibility—
It is a huge bit of strategy.

It is, yes. It is my responsibility. Without walking straight into the set of inevitable questions I am about to get around the spending review, it is my responsibility to put the best possible case forward to the Treasury for the spending review, to make sure that we make it as easy as possible for the Chancellor to say yes.

This goes back to the point I was making with you, Chair, about sending the right signals internally very early on. It would be very easy—and, indeed, extremely complacent and irresponsible—to assume that we can just send John Healey’s resignation letter into the spending review process as our submission and say, “Well, this is what you said and this is what we expect you to fund.” We know the Chancellor wants to spend more on defence. We know that is one of the big reasons why the Prime Minister appointed him. We none the less have to put forward the best possible case to justify that investment and to make sure we are well on our way on the path to 3.5%, which the Chancellor will set out.
Derek Twigg is going to come on to all these issues in terms of defence spending.

Q9 Sorry to bring this up , because you are only just in post, but you mention ed resignations. If the second bit of the DIP is not fully funded as per the document in the DIP, will you be offering your resignation?

I am not sure if there is a precedent for this in British politics, but I managed to achieve front pages in my first week setting out the conditions in which I would resign from the job I had just been given. I would rather not repeat those front pages today, but suffice it to say that I stand by everything I have said previously. One of the reasons I said what I said in my first week so confidently is that I have absolutely no doubt about this Prime Minister and this Chancellor’s commitment to funding defence and to making sure we get what we need when we need it, but I also have a responsibility to make sure that I make it as easy as possible for them to say yes.

Q10 To follow on from that and clarify your position exactly, John Healey’s resignation letter said that the DIP funding settlement was insufficient. You posted: “Every word of warning here needs to be heeded.” Do you still think it is insufficient?
To be fair—this goes back to the point I made about Dan Jarvis, who did a lot of heavy lifting to get the DIP over the line and unlocked extra resource—
You can tell us it is going to take us to 2.7% by 2030. We have not committed to anything above that at the moment.
It takes us to 2.7% next year.
Q11 Where is the commitment after 2.7%?
That will be set out at the spending review.
That is what I am saying—there is no commitment currently.

But to be fair, Derek, if we go back through, Dan got the DIP over the line and got it out the door. There was a £4.7 billion gap, which needs to be plugged at this Budget for the immediate term. John—sorry, I am being far too familiar—the Chancellor has already said that he will plug that gap at the Budget and he has indicated that there will be more to come at the spending review. I understand what you are saying, which is that, so far, we can only see a line of sight to 2.7% next year, but given that it was 2.3% when Labour came to office and by next year it will be 2.7%, we can see a really clear trajectory that puts us well on the way to 3% and on the way to 3.5%.

Q12 Well, we don’t, because we have not got any commitment or confirmation yet. If you can point me to a commitment or confirmation that it will be at 3% by 2030, please share it with the Committee now.
But we would not normally, and we do not normally, set out ahead of spending reviews what the control totals will be.
That is my point. There is not any commitment as of today of getting to 3% by 2030. Unless you can share something we have not seen with us today, I fail to see where that is.

My argument would be that, from the choices that Labour has already made in Government through to how strongly the Chancellor felt about this as a matter of principle and through to the public statements of commitment that there will be more to come at the Budget and more to come at the spending review, I feel confident that we will get there, but I am not complacent and we need to put our best foot forward.
Q13 So we are relying on your confidence at the moment. You are on record that you are confident we will be at minimum 3% by 2030. Is that what you are saying?

I am looking for a mutual defence pact with this Committee. You can rely on my confidence, but I also rely on your advocacy, and I rely on colleagues across Parliament and the public. Honestly, Derek, I genuinely think that we will get to where we need to be, but we have to put our best foot forward as well. It is not reasonable to expect the Chancellor to make big spending commitments outside a fiscal event given where we have been as a country in the recent past, where the economy has tanked and the borrowing costs have gone up as a result.

Q14 We have heard similar commitments previously and we have not got there. I am pleased that you feel you are confident. Let’s hope that proves right. I am not going to ask about the spending review because you will just say, “It’s not for me, it’s for the Chancellor”, but I am going to ask this question. The Financial Times reported in August that the Chancellor would not use the October Budget to commit to the 3%, but that the decisions about the future of defence spending will be deferred until next year’s spending review. Is that your understanding?
I don’t think the Chancellor was ever going to set out 3% in the Budget; it was always the spending review.

Q15 That’s fine; it was just to be clear. Again, you will come back to me and say, “We haven’t actually set a date for the spending review,” but the report is that it was going to be in the spring, but it will now be delayed to the autumn, which is around about a year’s time. Based on our and NATO’s intelligence, there will possibly be a Russian attack on NATO or a NATO country by 2030. Do you think that year’s gap is showing sufficient speed to up defence spending to meet that threatened potential attack by Russia in 2030?

Given that we are already experiencing increased investment in defence, and we are on the upward trajectory, it does not stop us from doing anything now. This in some ways comes back to the line of questioning or the tension I identified in response to Mike, which is that we absolutely need to plan for the medium term. We have to make the case at the spending review and win the resources that we need, but we also have to crack on with delivering now. This is part of my anxiety in a way about the debate always being about what is going to happen at the spending review. We also have to focus on making sure that we spend what we already have.

Q16 John Healey said in his resignation letter: “ The extra support is backloaded when the pressure of operations and imperative to speed up readiness to fight is in the first two year s and it rises to just 2.68% of GDP ”—it is obviously 2.7%—“in 2030.” What do you make of that comment, given what you have just said?
Extra funding was won by Dan Jarvis during the DIP process, and we will be getting—
But it is still backloaded.
We will get the £4.7 billion at the Budget. I will bring in the permanent secretary, because he was party to those discussions.
Q17 So are you saying that it is no longer backloaded? I missed that, if that is the case.
The specific point about—
Is it backloaded or not?
The additional resource—
Sorry, can I interrupt, because I want to get a straight answer for the Committee. Is it backloaded or not?
Additional resource DEL was given to the Department between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis settling the DIP.
Q18 Can you remind the Committee how much that was?

That included a £500 million modernisation fund and additional changes to our spending power that gave the Ministry of Defence more RDEL than previously. I am in an unusual—the first position in time—
Before we get into RDEL and CDEL, Mr Twigg is asking a question about backloading. It would be good to get an answer to that, please.
The overall departmental spending is on a rising profile, so by the end of this Parliament it will be 27% higher in real terms than at the start—
We have very limited time—we have only two hours to drill into these facts. Can we get the answer to Mr Twigg’s question?
Q19 Is it backloaded? Can you tell the Committee?
I am keen to help the Committee. I can read out what our spending totals are for each year—
Q20 I am asking a specific question: is it backloaded?
I am not sure I understand the definition—
Well, your previous Secretary of State said it was.
What I am saying is—
It is in his letter.

We received additional support between the time between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis that meant that the spending power of the Department has actually increased by £15 billion. It was a lower amount at the time that John Healey resigned. We do have additional support, including, in particular, additional support for RDEL for readiness—
Q21 I will ask you one final time, Mr Pocklington. Do you agree with your previous Secretary of State that it is backloaded?
I think the settlement had changed. There is not more that I can give to the Committee. The settlement had changed after John Healey resigned and Dan Jarvis—

Q22 Time is running out, so can I go to another question for the Secretary of State? Do you think that it is acceptable that we have to wait until possibly next autumn, assuming your confidence is borne out, for the decision on reaching the 3% to be taken? Is that acceptable given the urgency of the need for us to become war-ready, rearm, increase our capabilities and fund the armed forces in a better way? Given the threat, do you think it is okay to wait until next autumn?

First, it doesn’t stop us doing things now, it does not stop us doing things next year and it does not stop us planning, with some assumptions that defence spending will continue to rise. I do not think it needs to slow us down or stop us from doing anything. I do not know when the spending review is going to be.
Q23 Are you going to be spending money you have not got, then?
No, because we know what we have got for this year. We know what we will get for the next year—

You are missing the point. The spending review may be in autumn, although it could be spring; let us say that is in the autumn. You are telling us that you will not know exactly what you have got to spend up to 2030 until then.
The Budget will set out—
Q24 Is it acceptable to wait for nearly a year for that decision to be taken? It is a simple question. Yes or no?

I think we can live with that. We can absolutely live with that. We have got the resources we need for this year.
