Q52 Welcome to the Administration Committee’s hearing as part of our general election planning inquiry. Thank you to our witnesses for coming to this second session of our inquiry. We welcome our witnesses, whom I will invite to introduce themselves in a few moments. We are grateful to each former Member of Parliament for coming to the Committee today to speak to us about their experiences of leaving Parliament.

The Administration Committee in the last Parliament looked at the quality of services provided to MPs when they leave the House. As part of our inquiry, we want to look at whether the support put in place after the last general election was effective in helping MPs to transition to a life after Parliament. Can you please introduce yourselves?
I am Nigel Mills; I was MP for Amber Valley from 2010 to 2024.
I am Charles Walker, MP for Broxbourne from 2005 to 2024.
I am Thangam Debbonaire, MP for Bristol West from 2015 to 2024.

Q53 Sir Charles, you were Chair of the previous Administration Committee when it conducted its work on supporting Members when they leave the House. You called that work “Smoothing the cliff edge”, and it acknowledged that departure is a difficult time. Did the support that was put in place after the 2024 election live up to your expectations?

Chair, for the sake of brevity, it did live up to my expectations. I would argue and give evidence that more needs to be done, and we constantly need to be improving, but I was very impressed by the performance of the House service. Although I am now on the board of IPSA, I am here in my own capacity. IPSA also came through with the pledges it made. You cannot give 10 out of 10, but I would give nine and a half out of 10.
I see a future on “Strictly Come Dancing” for you. Thanks for that very succinct answer.
Q54 This is primarily a question for Nigel and Thangam. Reflecting on your experience of leaving the House, how well prepared were you, and what, if anything, came as an unexpected difficulty?

Shall I take that first? I kind of expected it—you could see the opinion polls and you could see what was happening. It was not like I walked into the count and got a shock, but there is not much you can do to prepare. You cannot apply for jobs in an election campaign—imagine if it got out. I knew what I would try to do, but until it happens, you do not really know how big a shock it is or how different it is on the Friday morning—going into the office to start winding up versus planning for another term. It takes a while to get your head into it.

I rush to everything—I was cancelling everything on that Friday morning. That may or may not have been the right thing to do, but I was very determined that, at two months, I wanted it done. Until near the end of the last Parliament, it was the case that you had two months to wind everything up, so that is what I got everything set up for. That is what I stuck to. I am not sure I would recommend rushing at things in quite that way, but I knew that that is what would work for me in other situations. I like to get out of the place—it is finished; move on to the next thing. I do not want to be hanging around.
Q55 Was the experience very different for colleagues who were not expecting to lose? I know some people lost by very small majorities.

Yes, for some people, I suppose. If you have a complete shock that you were not expecting, and you do not have any plan for what you have to do or how you are going to go about it, I imagine it would be a lot worse. Maybe Thangam is a better bet for that.

Any therapeutic model of trauma identifies loss of job as a form of trauma. When you lose your job on TV in front of your friends and family—although I told my mum not to come; I did not want her to see—knowing that your colleagues are watching across the country, and that you are a 58-year-old unemployed women and are making your staff redundant, I don’t know how you are supposed to prepare for that, especially as, like Nigel says, you fight to win. Even if you know you are going to lose, you have to fight to win. You cannot start buffing up your CV, and I honestly don’t know when you would have the time. I was campaigning 16 hours a day for six weeks. You have to put out a face that says, “I’m going to win”.

It is not just that it is a form of trauma to get to the end of that; it is also slightly mentally deranging, because in my case, my party was going to win. That was part of the problem for me, having to be positive about that—which I was; I was very pleased that my party was going to win. I had some preparedness in that it is that sort of seat—the seat I represented is the sort of seat that always votes against the Government, and it likes to give the Government a good kicking—but how well prepared are you to make yourself redundant at 4 o’clock in the morning? I honestly don’t know how you are supposed to prepare for that.

I mean, I did prepare. I was prepared in the sense that I had prepared my staff via and with my office manager to make sure that they all had CVs. We worked out the emails of which MPs we knew were going to win and we had jobs for most of my constituency staff very quickly. That was a preparedness thing. We did that at six weeks out under a veil of secrecy and said, “You don’t speak about this, I’m afraid, because you can’t let anyone in the constituency know that you think you’re going to lose”. So we just did it to be “prepared”, but being prepared personally? We will probably come back to that, but calling anything an unexpected difficulty about that is just a real exercise in understatement. It is traumatic. Your entire way of life is suddenly changed, and very publicly as well—in a very big and public way. But the biggest trauma for me was making my staff redundant.
Thank you, Baroness Debbonaire . I am pleased to say we have been joined by Sir Nigel Evans.
Mr Nigel Evans. Thank you for the promotion!
Q56 My mistake; excuse me. Nigel, Bambos was asking the panel to reflect on your experiences of leaving the House. How well prepared were you? What, if anything, came as an unexpected difficulty?

What was unexpected was losing the general election in my seat. It has been Tory forever, since the seat was invented. It was only towards the end—we knew the Tories weren’t going to win—that I then started to go, “Hmm, if the swing is much bigger, it could involve even seats like mine that were rock-solid Tory”, with a majority of over 18,000. So I had never done any forward planning, and I was mildly surprised and pleased by the way that people like me were looked after. I think in the past it has been a bit of a disaster, a bit of a cliff edge, and this was not a cliff edge.

We were given adequate time to sort out our affairs as far as our flats, apartments and housing were concerned. Clearing the office has got to be a bit of a rush, that has to be the priority, so actually having somewhere within London to put all the stuff from the office is really useful. I had 32 years of memories, or “tat” as Colonel Bob Stewart would refer to it—it is now sitting in his garage, God bless him. Having that ability to get all your stuff out to somewhere and then plan for the future was good. To be greeted by a number of people on the day you got back was excellent, talking you through the pension arrangements, the redundancy and all of that. There again, my mind was never on the pension, redundancy or leaving Parliament. I think that four months of coming to terms with everything— still seeing your friends and colleagues as well, because 251 Conservatives lost their seats that day—meant that it wasn’t such a shock. It wasn’t as brutal as it clearly has been in the past. So from my viewpoint, I was really grateful there were no surprises.

Q57 I want to touch on the winding-up period. What was your experience of it, and how realistic were the deadlines and arrangements for closing down your parliamentary affairs? Did you feel you had the support you needed, and how did you support your staff? What more can the House or IPSA do generally?

First, thanks to Charles and other colleagues in the last Parliament, and the parliamentary staff, a lot of things that could have been much worse were not, as Nigel has already touched on. Colleagues who have lost in previous general elections said that some things were literally a cliff edge, so I will always be grateful.

Primarily, on my staff and the deadlines, it helped to have been pretty sure that we were going to move room at least, because I had packed up my office. The arrangements would have been a lot harder if I had not done that, because your pass stops working very quickly—within days. Within seven days, your pass stops working and your car parking is removed, so it is pretty quick. The three-month deadline made a huge difference. We could not get a two-month notice period on my office, so I knew all along that if it stuck to two months, I would have to pay for the other month, and that was common in Bristol—we could not get any flexibility. That was really helpful and saved me money.

Did I have the support? I think emotional support is different from practical support. On practical support, we will come on to arrangements for the reception centre, which I do have some comments on, and my staff have given me various bits of feedback that come under lower questions. I think three months is realistic. It may have just been me being sensitive, but I felt that there was pressure on me to make sure my staff were out the door and no longer getting paid. But that may have just been me misinterpreting, because I would not judge anything on how I was emotionally during that period. As I said, three of my staff were employed by the end of the weekend, so that was great, but that is because we had prepared. We had no help with that from anybody, but I did not need any, so maybe it doesn’t matter. For everyone else it was harder. I will come on to why later.

Without the work that Charles did—sorry, Charles; I feel quite emotional about this—and I know this from comparing notes with colleagues who have lost in previous years, what was a devastating experience probably would have been catastrophic for me and my staff. And we were in the winning party. That has both pluses and minuses. The minus is that people come up to you in the street and say, “Congratulations on winning.” I go, “No, you voted to get rid of me, remember?” and they go, “Oh no, we thought you’d still be our MP.” How does that work? Do I have to explain democracy to you? It is comical. Similarly, my staff were all supposed to be in this happy shiny thing and they were looking for jobs. The grace period we were given was really helpful. My office manager had already retired from paid work originally and I had brought her back into employment. That helped, because she wasn’t rushing off looking for a job, so she could do everything and we could concentrate on the staff. That was my main concern.

I have some practical suggestions later on. I did not have warning—well, it was complicated, but I had enough sense to get myself a private therapist from February of that year. Without the private therapy, the careers coaching would have been less effective, but without the careers coaching, the therapy would have been less effective. I do not think that getting any sort of therapeutic support through Parliament really works at that time. It had to be private for a range of reasons, and I would encourage anybody to do it. I say that because I want people to know it is a good idea anyway.

I am going to be very brief. I stand by the statement I made in the House and in the report that you should be planning for your last day in Parliament on your first day in Parliament. It is a vocation, not a career. Most people—not all—will leave here as the result of their electorate deciding they would prefer to put someone else in office. Some have the luxury of retiring, as I did, but it is extremely difficult when you leave this place. We have some success stories here, but for most colleagues, the money runs out long before the jobs arrive, and that is even with the improved package that IPSA offered.

If the House is going to be a serious employer—I know that we are not employees—it has to look at ongoing career development, professional development and qualifications, with all the skills that we have, accredited by a top-flight university. We have many in London, such as King’s, UCL and LSE. There are also organisations like Deloitte, which runs the Deloitte academy, for example. That helps people prepare for executive positions. We need to get much more serious about how we prepare colleagues to leave this place, and they need to be responsible to themselves and their families by recognising, on day one, that there is a time expiry on all our presences in Parliament.

On staff, the nearest Conservative MP to me is probably an hour and a half’s drive away, so there was no prospect of my staff getting a job doing the same thing. I remember the excitement in my office when they found that it was a four-month period rather than two months, and they all assumed that meant they would get four months’ pay. I was like, “No, that’s actually a limit, not a target.” In all my election campaigns, the casework really dried up. There is not much work left for your staff to do other than literally empty the office. A few of them didn’t really get on with their job searching, because they thought, “I’ve got four months, so I can do nothing for the first month,” and then they slowly started to realise that it was a bit harder than they expected.

There should be some clarity on whether that four-month period is standard, and every departing MP can give their staff four months’ pay regardless of if there is any work for them to do; whether we can do that only for enough staff to justify whatever the workload is; or whether it really is an exception and we should be sticking to the notice periods in their contracts. I was never quite clear whether I was allowed to give four months’ pay. I closed my office after two months; I think I paid them all for three as a kind of compromise.

The redundancy process is a bit strange. They know there is no job. You get your guidance that you have to have a consultation meeting. You have to give written notice of a week, so you come down here, you get your advice, you then go back, you issue these template letters with an appointment for a week later and then you have a meeting where you say, “Well, there’s no job—sorry.” There is not much else you can say. You then have to give the formal redundancy letter, so you burn two or three weeks before actually starting a process. It felt a bit odd, to tell you the truth. I do not know how you fix that with employment law. I do not know how it felt for a member of staff—maybe they got three weeks’ extra pay so they were a bit happy, but it did not feel, to me, a very helpful process.

You are right about the support for staff to get jobs in different sectors. They did not really have access to the CV preparation or interview training that ex-MPs got, which was really helpful. Maybe there is a bit more we could do on supporting staff. Mine all got jobs before the end of their three months, so it all worked out, but I think it was probably worse for them in some ways.

Can I back up what the other Nigel just said? I felt a bit guilty about my staff. My getting a P45 at 66 is different from an MP getting a P45 at 36, particularly if they have two kids, a mortgage and all that sort of stuff—it is very different. I did not have a mortgage. All the cushion that has been put in for Members is absolutely superb. The staff do not get that. Nigel is right: it is sort of suggested that, unless you have meaningful work for them, you should really dismiss them immediately. When 251 Tories lose, and you have, let’s say, three staff on average, that is 600 people chasing maybe 30 jobs. The reality for them is brutal.

I do not know if you remember the time when MPs could push in front of their staff to grab a cup of coffee and all that sort of stuff—that was soon elbowed out. My being treated preferentially to my staff is completely wrong; I think that they should be in exactly the same place as me. They, by dint of the job, tend to be in their 20s or maybe their early 30s, and they deserve exactly the same sort of cushion. My staff did not expect to lose. It was all right for me; I did not go into the jobs market like they did. Some of them must have found it very difficult indeed. The one thing I would emphasise is that we look at the people that are with us. I know that, out in the country, we are not going to get too many violins playing by the stories we are telling—I understand that—but maybe we will get a few violins for our staff.

Charles is right to say that it is not a career and that it could end at any time. I looked at it a few years ago and the average duration is about eight years. We know that averages hide all sorts of extremes. I was an MP for 32 years, but there are people who were elected in 2024 and will get their P45 at the next general election—a lot of them, if the opinion polls are to be believed. As Thangam said, it could be a mixture, and some people who you expected to stay will go—like the former MP for Blackburn . That constituency had been Labour for generations and I never expected it be anything other than Labour. I was shocked when I got the result from Blackburn. That MP would certainly not have been expecting what she was faced with.

There is one more reason why a soft landing for staff matters: you do not want all your staff resigning six months before an election, because then you cannot do your job. They can read the opinion polls as well as MPs do. I had one member of staff resign during the election campaign. She was very upset about it, but she said, “I just cannot risk you losing, and not having a job and not being able to pay my rent. I have found an offer, and I have to take it.” There is a benefit for the workings of Parliament in parliamentary staff knowing that they have a soft landing in case something goes wrong.

Q58 Following on from those points, how clear was the guidance that you received from the House, IPSA and your own political parties about the steps that you and your staff had to take during Dissolution and winding up? Did you have all the clarity that you needed?

I find it really hard to answer that question. I had been through Dissolution before, so I did at least understand Dissolution. Winding up is just so hard to comment on. From my memory—which could be faulty, but I have tried to triangulate it with my former office manager—I think that the House guidance was good, and the IPSA guidance was good, by and large. There were things about pressure, which, as I said, could be in my own head. But I am now hearing from the Nigels that it was not imaginary; it was, “If you did not have anything for your staff to do, we cannot pay them.” They do not get a redundancy package, and they certainly do not get careers advice. To me, the guidance was not clear on that, but I think that is a different question.

For my office manager, there were various practical things that she was more than capable of doing. She was a highly experienced woman who had worked in a multinational company as a very senior manager. This was a doddle to her, but she was not sure that everyone would have found it a doddle. There was good guidance, but it would have been useful to have things such as a clear toolkit for office managers—something really clear on how to destroy data and which data to destroy; on recycling computers; on ensuring that all computers are registered before Dissolution or during Dissolution; and on whether staff can carry on doing casework to close things down during Dissolution. My office manager said she would have appreciated a bit of guidance on that.
Q59 A toolkit that takes you along the timeline?

There was assistance on those things, and parliamentary staff were really helpful, so this is definitely not a criticism, but my office manager’s point was that it could be something really clear, particularly about casework. Former constituents contact me even now. One has emailed me this morning about his case notes, and I do not know how many times I have to say to this guy, “I do not have them, and for good reason”. A way of resolving some of those open cases sometime during Dissolution might have helped. It is more than it would help constituents and my former staff; it probably would not make any difference to me. My memory is that the guidance was mostly pretty good.

I thought the guidance was really useful. The thing that distressed me most was seeing my seven-year-old IBM printer being hauled off by the House of Commons to be put into a skip somewhere or into landfill. I do not understand why I could not be given the option to buy something that could print loads of pieces of paper and CVs.

I think one thing that the House did really well —I did not access it, but I have heard this from colleagues— was outplacement . It funded and did outplacement advice — I hope that continues. My own party also did some career coaching through Mark Prisk. He could reach 30 colleagues; that was what we had funding for. I do not know whether you are going to take evidence from Mark or the outplacement company, but they did some really useful work. The Committee might find it helpful to know how that went and some of the feedback they got .
We can ask him . Thank you.

Disposal of the kit is a big deal . I t really annoyed us that we could tell that it was being taken off us to be put in a skip. The way that my iPad was removed from me was particularly and unnecessarily humiliating. I said, “You are just putting it in a skip, though . W hy are we doing this? I would buy it, yet you are humiliating me.” It was okay, but i t was a waste.
Very quickly, Chair, Mark Prisk gave evidence for my “Smoothing the cliff edge” report, so he has sort of seen the continuum through.

I think the guidance was very good ; I came down for the sessions on the Monday morning, I think. Dealing with the staff and getting the legal stuff right was the challenge. I remember that they gave me an A3 piece of paper with the notice periods, redundancy pay and whatever else on it , which y ou then had to transcribe into a standard letter and get the right thing for the right person. Then they worked out that, if you gave them two months’ notice, they would cross into another year of service , and you had to go and change all the numbers.

On that stuff around employment , I wonder whether there is a way that they could just give you the pack of letters, so that you do not risk messing those up. There was no issue for me —t here was not going to be any legal dispute over it — but you could see a situation in which you could slightly mess that up and create a problem.

The rest of it was fine. I booked the IT collection nice and early . T hen, on the day, they did not turn up. They rang and said, “ Yeah, we ’ve got another one in the south, so the driver thought he ’d go there first and miss the Friday traffic.” “ Well, my office is closing at lunch time ; I’ll leave it on the street outside if you want.” T hings like that were a bit aggravating, rather than a problem. The support for what you needed to do by when worked pretty well . E ven the IPSA stuff was fine. I think they returned some papers with typos at one stage, or something like that, but other than that it was pretty smooth.

Mr Nigel Evans: Richmond House had everything sorted when I went in with a couple of my staff. They were appropriately sombre, apologetic and sympathetic, with handkerchiefs on hand and all that. I f heaven had the same sort of arrangement when the deceased come , I feel that it would base it roughly base on the model I saw in Richmond House.

I thought that everything was explained to me. You had opportunities to ask all sorts of questions. Listen, you have to get out of your office , because 650 other people are now eager to establish themselves , and y ou have to lose your parking space , o therwise where are they going to park? You understand the urgency of all that. But everything else — the cliff - edge work that Charles and his colleagues have helped to bring about — has been absolutely superb.

The one thing that I would suggest — other than all the stuff that the others have mentioned — is to do with email. Losing your parliamentary email is a bit brutal, to say the least. People do not know how to get in touch with you. M y one suggestion is that you then shunt everything over to a new email address, such as nigel . evans.ex mp @parliament.uk , or something like that. Then everybody will know that, if they need to get in touch with you, there is a standard format and they can just put “ex” in front of “MP” .

T hat is the cliff edge , I can tell you now. You are told, “Oh yes, transfer everything over,” and all that sort of stuff . Wel l, you do not get through it all. Just think, after 32 years, how many emails were floating around . I just think that that would be a lot easier. It would also make it eas ier for ex- MPs to get in touch with other ex-MPs. T hat is the one solid suggestion I will make to you.

Q60 Thank you very much for being here . It is slightly terrifying for some of us, and probably for staff who are watching, but your insight is really helpful. We need to be mindful that other people in the country lose their jobs at a moment’s notice. I am thinking about Jaguar Land Rover, for example, and its employees. We need to remember other staff, but equally, it is a very special situation here.

On handing over to incoming MPs, one thing that did not work particularly smoothly for me as an incoming MP was casework handover. I understand that all former Members were offered advice on handing over casework within the restrictions of data management and confidentiality. Do you feel that that worked well? It may well have worked well for you, but would you have benefited from anything else when handing over?

I got my successor in as soon as she arrived. I sat down with her and offered everything she wanted. I was more than happy to give her anything. The ex-MP email thing might have helped if she needed to get in touch about any casework. The door was absolutely wide open—and still happens to be if she needs to get in touch on any issue.

As I said, by the time we got to polling day, most casework had been dealt with. A few outstanding replies came in, which we dealt with. In some cases, we went back to the constituent and said, “Do you want us to send it back to you? Or do you want to give us consent to send it to the new MP?” Generally, people were quite happy for it to be handed over, but there were not that many cases. It is not that easy when you have just lost and your staff are being made redundant for them to be in touch with the people who are replacing them in the job they quite liked. That is not a natural situation. We did it and it worked pretty well, but we did not actually have to hand over a large number of cases.

There were, I think, two—or a few, but not many—long-running cases that I briefed my successor on. He had worked for me in my office when he was 16 or 17 on work placement, which made me feel very old. Mostly, when the election was called, we were getting legacy cases coming in from ministerial offices, which we just passed back to the constituent. Our constituents do not appreciate that when a general election is called, we cease to be a Member of Parliament. As far as my constituents were concerned, I was the Member of Parliament for Broxbourne until the point my successor was elected—then for a few weeks afterwards. We very politely suggested that they wait a few weeks, unless it was really urgent, and then we did some triage. I said, “Wait a few weeks and get in touch with whoever my successor is, and I am sure he or she will be delighted to hear from you.” And that is what they did.

I probably do not have anything much to add. Incoming MPs who have beaten another MP are probably not aware that any casework that anyone is going to die over is not being handed over—it will have been dealt with. Therefore, the assumption should be that they start from scratch. Similarly to others, we had worked really hard to make sure that things were resolved for constituents—in our case, I am not sure whether the incoming MP understood that—but we also provided the information about how constituents could get in touch with the incoming MP. I think that that is adequate.

On the confidentiality guidelines, I think we had some good support. I would have been grateful for some advice on how to dispose of confidential waste. We worked it out—it was fine—and we worked out what to say to the constituents. I think we had some help with that.

May I just answer Marie’s observations? I was probably about as tight with public money as I could be, and I agree, actually, we should not put MPs in a different place from where a good employer would put people. That would be my default situation.

A good employer, when making people redundant, does try to support them into the next stage of their lives. The support that MPs got on CVs, interview prep and all that stuff, I think a good employer would do. There is a secondary point, though, about if you want to attract the brightest and the best to be MPs. If you said to me, “Look back to when you were 35. Had you known you would get married, have two kids and be out of work at 50, would you take the risk?” I think it is quite difficult in that situation to think that that is a very good idea.

If you want Parliament to function and you want the best people here, showing that there is a soft landing and that you will not struggle to pay your mortgage is really important. If you make it too tight and play too much to the TaxPayers’ Alliance lobby on this, it will do real damage. I say that as somebody who said to you, “Be clear whether you mean to give all staff four months’ pay when they have one month’s notice.” What do you really mean? That is a challenge. Why are we paying people far more than they were legally entitled to? We should think that through. I would just be cautious that playing to that lobby is quite dangerous and will do damage.

Q61 I would like to dig into that a bit. This is a public session and there will be people watching this who say, “Hang on a minute. I just lost my job. I had no notice. I went into this knowing that it might not be a job for life, but I probably expected that I might have a bit longer. And it was a bit of a shock to me and probably I had even less notice because something suddenly happened.” I mean no disrespect to the House staff, and I completely agree with you. I would love to be able to pay my staff more. They work incredibly long hours. The office is run by young people a lot of the time. I know some people have more experienced staff, but that is not always the case because we do not pay enough to have really experienced staff a lot of the time. I have huge respect for what they do.

It is just about getting the balance right between what the rest of the country experiences, what MPs experience, and what MPs’ staff experience. We need to make sure to get that balance absolutely right and offer what we can along the way in terms of support, career progression and development and stuff. We have talked before about the potential for some staff to be employed by the House so that they can move around a bit more and have more security. What might you think about that?
Funnily enough, Sir Charles Walker was a former staffer of mine. Not only did I not put him off becoming a staffer, but he then became a Member of Parliament and did much better than I did.

I am with Nigel on this. I do appreciate where you are coming from. Among a lot of people out there, as I said, there will be no violins for the MPs, but hopefully they will have for some of our staff who still face that cliff edge. My staff never thought I was going to lose my seat. I get Nigel’s point that you want to attract good people to come and do the work for MPs. If we are going to get our P45s— The changes that have happened since elections in the past should be reflected on the staff as well. Why should they be treated any differently to the Members of Parliament? I really would stress that if we want the very best working here and they are going to be booted out rather suddenly and publicly in the way that it is done, and they have no prospect of getting another job in politics, they should be treated in exactly the same way.
Okay. That’s great. Thanks, everybody. I have to nudge you. We have four questions to get through, so will have to move it up a gear. Mary, you’re next.

Q62 This one seems a bit cruel after what we have heard. What we learned during the inquiry was that new Members would appreciate a Member buddy in addition to a House staff buddy just to listen to what your situation was when you lost your seat or retired. Would you have been willing to return to Parliament to support a new Member in getting to grips with parliamentary life and offer them advice on their office? Do you have any thoughts on how such an offer could work in practice?

I will answer that—absolutely not. We had left Parliament. The last thing that Lewis Cocking, my successor, wanted to see was me running around the House of Commons. We have an election, people are defeated, they leave and new people come in.

Also, there is a general view. I did a lot of things for a lot of people for no money after I left this place. Luckily, I could take my pension early at great cost to myself and my family, because it is very difficult to get a job. And let me just say that if you want better MPs, treat MPs better. But the idea that I would come back to the House of Commons and do anything for free is nonsense—just nonsense. I am sorry, but it is a cruel question. I really advise all of you to not lose your seat , because no matter how good you think you are, you are not that good. Nigel Mills here did very well, but many of my former colleagues are still struggling to find meaningful work. If you want better MPs, treat MPs better.

The last place I wanted to be was here. I came down on the Sunday, emptied my office, did the session on the Monday morning and handed the keys back—this is the first time I have been back since. I am afraid the idea that I would be of any use to a new MP is for the birds.

I do not think the new MPs, especially those in the winning party, wanted to see us four losers—I think we were seen as contagious. Coming in on the Monday morning is pretty humiliating anyway, as everyone else is happy and shiny.

It sounds like tough love, but learn the job and get the skills. If you do not know how to do a Bill, go on a Bill Committee to learn how to do it. If you do not know where your office is, ask a Doorkeeper. You have been elected as MPs to be leaders. This is not an old mill owner thing, but if you have been elected to be a leader, do you really need an old MP who is trying to get a job as a buddy? Learn your job. There are ways to learn the job of being an MP, and part of it comes with a certain amount of humility. You need first to recognise that you have a lot to learn; secondly, to recognise that, as Charles said, you will also lose eventually; and thirdly, to make yourself work hard to learn the skills and your way around Parliament—learn what it takes to be a legislator.
Most of us need to be paid when we leave here, so we need to get a job.

Yes—we were unemployed. I have to say, what I wrote down here was, “Are you kidding?” I was a 58-year-old unemployed woman, and there is no such thing as an ex-MP—you have no idea. I am not asking for sympathy and do not feel sorry for myself—I served in a democracy and am very proud to have done that—but you do have to pay your bills. I hope we have made ourselves clear: the answer is no.
I still see a lot of wisdom here.

Q63 On career transition, which some of you have touched on, how prepared were you for working life beyond Parliament? Did you use the career transition service, and if so, how did you find it? Also, how important was the emotional support, which Thangam touched on, in the career transition?

The two things are separate. I used the career transition service, and there was not a single day when I did not mentally thank Charles Walker. It is a valuable investment in making use of the skills we have gained, but I would not see it as anything other than saying, “This is useful to the world.” Some of us were able to retire, but some of us could not, and some of us will rightly have to work for another 15 years. We wanted to make use of our skills and needed a bit of technical help with wiggling around and thinking, “What are my skills? How do I work them?” You really should not—although maybe some did—be looking for a job until after you lose.

It would be great if the careers transition service was offered to our staff, because I felt quite guilty. I still use my careers transition person; I pay her privately. That was not for emotional support, and it is really important that the two things are separate. Personally, I am glad that I paid for private therapy. Others may think that that ought to be paid for by the House services, but I do not. I would have liked a bit of advice from the House services on how to get a private therapist, but my therapist was invaluable to making the careers service work, and vice versa. It was brilliant.
If nobody else wants to come in on this, we will move to Marie.
Q64 The departing Members’ area was mentioned earlier. Did its location and atmosphere, and how it was brought together, work well for you?
Yes.

Yes, it was excellent. Everything was there, it was cleverly organised to get you around all the various topics and they were suitably sympathetic. It is not an easy day—mine was the first working day. It was handled very well.
It is a bit like speed dating—not that I have done that! You sit for 10 minutes and then you move on to the next one. It is a Disneyland conveyor belt for the politically deceased.

I agree with everything that was just said, but the one issue was location. Again, this may have been because of my mood, as I was a losing MP when my party had won, but you walked in to see a gazillion new, shiny, excited MPs going up to the bright, sparkly rooms of PCH, while we were escorted down to a basement. Once you got to the basement—maybe it was not a basement; it just felt like one—the service was excellent and the staff were brilliant. It was like speed dating, but in a least-bad way.
Q65 Obviously, you made way for another MP from your party, Sir Charles. Did he take on any of your existing staff?

No. Many of my existing staff had been with me for 13, 15 or 16 years. To be perfectly honest, one of them was my wife, and although they love each other dearly and have known each other for a long time, I am sure that he would not have wanted to employ her. There was no transfer.
Q66 Are any of you still in touch with your ex-staff?
Yes—with all of them.
Q67 Have they managed to get new jobs and careers outside of your employment?

I am in touch with all my staff, and I continue to be a lifelong careers coach for some of them. The pledge I made to the ones that were still with me at the end was that they will have me for life, and they have continued to use me. I am very proud of that, and I am very proud of them.
Q68 Have they got jobs?

You missed when I spoke about this, Bob, but we had prepared my constituency staff early on, so my office manager and I got them jobs fairly quickly. My office manager had come out of retirement to work for me anyway, so that was fine. Weirdly, it was harder for my parliamentary staff—you would think that with an incoming Labour Government, that would have been easier, but it was not. That was partly because two of my staff were working not for the taxpayer but for the Labour party, because they were my advisers. I dealt with that, but I put on record that the way they were treated was suboptimal.

My staff got jobs. Our staff have hugely transferrable skills, without the baggage of having been a Member of Parliament, which is a great barrier to future employment. They do not carry that baggage. It was difficult for them, but they were very talented people and were snapped up pretty quickly.

My staff all had jobs within three months after the election. References are an interesting one: IPSA will give a reference saying, “They worked for Nigel Mills from 2022 to 2024 as an in-role caseworker,” but if an employer wants any more than that, they have to email my personal email address, which does not feel right. I gave them all a signed, headed-paper letter reference—I am not sure whether I was meant to use the headed paper after polling day, but I dated it as polling day—but how you handle that situation is quite fiddly. Obviously, the MP email does not work anymore, so they can only get to you via a personal one.

Fortunately, one had left me just before the election to join the Navy, as we have heard. He was very apologetic: he said, “I know there is an election coming,” but I said, “No—you have a lifetime opportunity here. Go join the Navy,” which, fortunately, he did. I am still in touch with the others. I remember looking across at them during this speed dating exercise, and they were whiter than I was, so I knew that they were concerned about what they would do next. Fortunately, they have all got employment outside of the House.
Thank you for your valuable feedback during this important session. I end this meeting by thanking you all for talking to us and answering our questions. That concludes this session.

Tuesday 15 September 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Liddle (The Chair); Baroness Alexander of Cleveden ; Lord Burns; Lord Carrington of Fulham; Lord Newby; Lord Petitgas; Lord Prentis of Leeds; Lord Razzall; Lord Reid of Cardowan ; Baroness Wheatcroft; Lord Young of Cookham.
Evidence Session No. 8 Heard in Public Questions 115 - 12 9
Witnesses
Howard Dawber OBE, Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth ; Lord Houchen of High Leven, Metro Mayor , Tees Valley.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Howard Dawber and Lord Houchen of High Leven.

Q115 Welcome to this meeting of the Lords Economic Affairs Select Committee, where we are looking at the very topical question of fiscal devolution. We have with us today two witnesses who are closely engaged o n this question, representing mayoralties from different parts of the country. First, Lord Houchen, c ould you introduce yourself ?

I thank the committee for inviting me. I am currently the M ayor of the Tees Valley . I was first elected in May 2017 as part of the first cohort of directly elected mayors under the northern power house reforms of George Osborne. It has been a significant journey over the p ast nine or 10 years — we were just saying outside that there is a lot of confusion around whether I am a lord mayor, a mayor, a Lord or some other qualification —with a lot of change .

There are different ways in which devolution has accelerated or decelerated, depending on the Administration and their buy-in . My being invited to this committee could not be more timely . The prioritisation of devolution, which has been on the radar of G overnments of both colours in recent years, has gone into the stratosphere with the new Prime Minister prioritising devolution. This conversation about fiscal devolution , including what it is and is not , will be particularly pertinent to members here and in the other place in terms of how those rules might come into force, how they could be managed and the accountability for them .

Good afternoon. Thank you very much for inviting us to take part. I bring apologies from my boss, the Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan. He could not be here because he is being introduced to the House of Lords this afternoon as Lord Khan of Tooting ; unfortunately , it clashed.

I am the Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth, covering the economy, business and skills. I chair London & Partners, which is our promotional agency. Prior to that, I spent 20 years working in the private sector at the Canary Wharf Group, where I worked with successive mayors on things such as the Elizabeth line, which is quite pertinent to today in terms of where fiscal responsibility sits. As Lord Houchen said, this is a perfect time. We have had the Cabinet paper signalling further fiscal devolution and we are in the run-up to the Budget , where some of that will be codified, so this is a very exciting moment.
Q116 The first question is a simple one : w ill fiscal devolution boost economic growth in your area ? I f so, how?

In short, yes, I think it will. I will give you a concrete example : Crossrail and the Elizabeth line. I worked on this from the private sector point of view . W e spent a long time campaigning for the line being supported by government in terms of both a route and how it would be funded ; t hat could all have been done a lot quicker if the Mayor of London had had more responsibility over some of the fiscal measures that we then needed to bring in to fund it.

When I was at Canary Wharf, we were campaigning for additional taxation on property companies because we could see the benefit that the line would bring to enable physical growth that would not be possible otherwise. We also made the case that London should pay more of the costs, that this should not be seen as a national project that happened to be in London and that , because of the very significant growth the line would deliver , Londoners and London businesses should pay a significant chunk of the money. However, the structures to do that were not in place.

Through legislation and working with successive G overnments, we managed to get a business rate supplement and the mayoral community infrastructure levy as mechanisms for capturing some of that growth in the economy to help pay for the line. The Elizabeth line has been a very successful railway line : it now carries, I understand, one in six of all rail passengers in the United Kingdom , and i t has certainly delivered significant growth around the stations of the line. It could have been done a lot more quickly , though, if the Mayor of London had had some of those powers up front to put that funding package together and drive that project.

T he overnight visitor levy, which is proposed new taxation and is not currently captured, is incrementally additional funding that could be used to support growth or for other things. The proposal to devolve some of the income tax would then enable, for example, mayors to borrow against that income tax ; they cannot currently borrow against the grant that is given to mayors to fund certain things. A mixture of control and new responsibility provides the context in which further fiscal devolution will support growth.

I come at this from a slightly different angle. We have to be clear what fiscal devolution is being proposed. As Howard rightly said, there are things such as SILs and TIFs, which have been available or not available to different parts of the country through devolution and are now coming into force in a more uniform way across the country. There is the overnight visitor levy, which is a single new tax being introduced by mayors who want to use it. W e have to be clear that the measures we are talking about and the fiscal devolution that the Prime Minister is talking about concern how combined authorities—mayoral combined authorities , by and large—are funded by central government.

Given how that works , fiscal devolution is a slight misnomer. It is not technically fiscal devolution. In terms of what the Government are doing — they have been pretty clear on this ; I will make up the numbers for the purpose of th is example to keep it simple —t he Tees Valley will get £1 billion , let us say, in grants and other moneys from central government over the next three years. The Government will calculate the amount of money that we currently get and say , “That’s the equivalent of ” —again, I will make it up — “ 3% on income tax, so w e’ ll allow you to retain 3% of income tax ” . The reality is that they are not giving us 3% of income tax. What they are doing is replacing a series of grants , with strings attached , with a single block grant : a Section 31 grant, which gives me , as the mayor , full autonomy on how to spend it. They are saying that that is the equivalent of 3% of income tax. To set up fiscal devolution properly , you are having to set up, in effect, mini - HMRCs, which is not the game. It is clear that it is then the responsibility of the mayor to provide an appropriate business case as a spending decision to justify the spend of that money. Government do not tell you at that point how to spend the grant, so , in reality , it is a movement of chairs ; it is not actually fiscal devolution.

The next outstanding question, on which I hope we will hear more , come the Budget, is : what is the level of that ? I f it is a like - for - like replacement of what we already have, we have already made significant spending commitments on infrastructure. Th is means that , if we get fiscal devolution that replaces the billion pounds - worth of grants with a £1 billion grant, all we are doing is substituting one grant with a single grant , and our spending commitments are already made. If fiscal devolution is additional money on top of that, it gives us more flexibility to look at pipelines of how we can invest in infrastructure, job creation and getting sites ready for investment. So w e have to be really clear about what fiscal devolution is and is not.

The second part is that, irrespective of what we call it, what the G overnment are proposing will help positively in two ways. First, it will help with flexibility because , with the strings attached over the p ast three or four years—it happened in the last two years of the previous G overnment and has certainly happened in the first two years of this G overnment—it was more decentralisation than devolution. We would get money but DWP or DfT would say, “You can only spend it on this and , of your budget on transport, only 10% can be spent on roads”. It was quite restrictive. Having full flexibility to say , “W e can spend it on what we like , but we still have to justify ourselves through a business case and a spending decision through the accountability framework ” , is a good thing because it means that we can manage our budgets. If certain projects are delayed for whatever reason, year and multi-year, we can move our accounts around : we can move money from transport to business , business to culture or whatever.

Secondly, it will give a long-term settlement. What the settlement will be is not a three-year transport settlement but a long 10, 15 or 20-year settlement to say , “Y ear in, year out, this is what you will get ” . That longer-term planning, particularly when you are looking at infrastructure, paired with flexibility , are two significant benefits of this reform. I just want to be clear that this is not fiscal devolution in the strictest sense, which you may or may not have heard when I have talked about tax rebates, because there is a misunderstanding around what the mechanism is and how you would go about doing something like that.

Apart from the benefits that you outlined in your answers, are there any other reasons why you think fiscal devolution is a good thing? D oes it improve local accountability? Will it make it easier for services to be run more efficiently than they are? How important is revenue certainty — Lord Houchen, you indicated that it is important — to the efficiency of your outputs as a local mayor?

There are two points to pick up from what Lord Houchen said. One is that , at the moment, as you said, quite a lot of our funding comes in the form of government grant s . I t is great that we have had a multiple - year grant and an integrated settlement in London, which enables us to move money around between different responsibilities with fewer strings attached. However, we cannot borrow against that grant because , obviously , a future G overnment could just decide not to give a grant at all , to give a smaller grant and so on. If the principles of the devolution of a piece of income tax are followed through, that would allow you to borrow against th e income tax because, as you said, it is a long-term, reliable source of income going into the future.

The second thing — you are absolutely right here—is that , if it is just swapping one grant for a grant by another name, that is one thing, but can you capture some of the increase by engendering and promoting growth in your area ? F or example, say income tax goes up and you are able to capture some of the increase , and there is an incentive there, that give s another incentive to local groups. It is a significant change in the power structure between regional government and national government.

T here is an accountability issue and a principle here : historically , we have had very strong city government in the United Kingdom, going back 1,000 years to the strength of the City of London in setting itself up as an alternative power base as compared to the Crown. Historically, we have had very strong city government , and most of our competitor countries around the world have very strong regional or city government , often within a federal structure. We have not had that in the UK and we have lost out because of it. There have been various attempts over the years to have a regional government structure —y ou may remember the Government Offices for the English Regions and the regional development agencies — then this new process , over the p ast 30 years , with the Mayor of London being created in 2000 , the Osborne city deals under the previous G overnment and new deals coming forward under this G overnment.

We are heading in the right direction , but we are a long way from where we need to be. In London, 93% of the tax raised goes to national government, t hen national government chooses how to spend that. Some of it comes back to the mayor and local authorities, but it is at the discretion of national G overnment Ministers. In New York, which we see as a strong competitor of London ’s , 50% goes nationally and 50% is retained by the mayor. In Tokyo , 80% is retained by the mayor , who is responsible for lots of things for which we are not responsible. T hat local accountability for local services delivered within London, at a mayoral level and at a local authority level, is important. Th is is why having more of those decisions taken at a regional or city level, as compared to at a national level and then coming down with strings attached , is a significant change — one that will , I think , drive greater accountability and engagement.

Q117 Ben, you have already made the point that what is on the table is simply using a different formula to allocate money from central government. I want to follow up on a point that Howard just made. He sees a key difference as being the ability to borrow against the future income tax flow in a way that you cannot borrow against government grants. I want to pursue that for a moment. At the moment, there are no restrictions on what a local authority can borrow. Under the 2001 Act, I think, it has to be prudential and sustainable. The Government can intervene if they think that you are going too far, and your borrowing is secured against the rates.

The argument that I think I heard was that the grants could suddenly be cut off, whereas the income tax stream is more reliable. The grant system changes all the time. Each time , there are floors and ceilings to prevent too much distortion in the amount of money a local authority gets. If you switch over to income tax, central government could cut income tax. I wonder to what extent this really is a more secure income stream against which to borrow than the system that we have at the moment. No G overnment are suddenly going to cut off local government grants; that would be unthinkable. Is the key factor the ability to borrow in a way you cannot at the moment?

By and large, for most mayors, yes . T here are lots of infrastructure projects where they have a level of grant , but some of the ir ambition around what they want to invest in — again , ultimately , this goes back to the accountability point : as a directly elected mayor , they must justify spend to local people — means that they want to accelerate a lot of the development. Having that long-term income stream in legislation , which might give more certainty than grants, is for people to discuss ; I do not have a strong view on that one way or the other. It would allow them to significantly borrow against that.

O ne thing I would say is that , at the minute , all combined authorities—I might be wrong, but we certainly do this; indeed, most combined authorities do—do not behave in the same way as a local authority. We do not have prudential borrowing in the same way that local authorities are completely uncapped. We have a hard cap. In each of the deals , there is a hard cap against a mayoralty. Even if I have a fantastic business case that has strong prudential borrowing and a strong income stream, if I have already borrowed, say, £500 million , and another £100 million takes me up to my cap, that is an absolute cap that I cannot borrow.
That is a different point. That is because there is a cap. It is about the source of the income.

That is absolutely true. T he reason why that was introduced is, first, because mayors were relatively new and , to some extent , immature as an infrastructure, so there was a safety net to try to cap that.

Through this, in terms of what the Government are proposing to do—I say this from speaking to Treasury officials , rather than Ministers , so there may be some divergence — I know that officials are looking at a version of a cap and a collar on income tax to negate the fluctuations that may happen, which we see in places such as Teesside. If you have a large employer that loses 4,000 jobs —take Jaguar Land Rover , for example —that will have a material impact on income. The Treasury is talking about compensating on the downside as well as the upside . I t is saying that, to some extent , if you are too successful , it might cap the upside to capture it in central government as well. These are just working philosophies —w e do not know what will come out in the coming weeks — but they are being discussed.

May I press Howard on the point that he made? Are you saying that , under the new regime , financial institutions will be more prepared to lend more money to mayoral strategic authorities because they now have their money coming from government through an income stream , rather than through a grant? Is that the argument?

They should be. Certainly, that is how we are looking at this in terms of both income tax and things such as the retention of business rates and the overnight visitor levy. All of those measures are tax - based and tax - backed. That is a different conversation with a financial organisation , as compared to, as Lord Houchen said, the government grant, which is fixed and capped at a certain level.

We have been very successful, given the size and strength of Transport for London and its historically good credit rating, at borrowing against, for example, future farebox on Crossrail ; t hat was part of the funding package for Crossrail. We are looking at that in terms of one of our current projects : the extension of the Docklands Light Railway to Thamesmead. U ntil now, nearly all the levers in the box have been held at a national government level. We have farebox but we did not control, for example, business rates. Off our own bat, without Treasury permission, we could not do a tax incremental financing deal, borrowing against business rates. These are all steps in the right direction to give mayors a bit more fiscal autonomy, but it is still a relatively small amount as compared to what other cities around the world have.

T o follow up on that and, I suppose, answer Lord Young’s question directly, the answer is demonstrably , “Y es, it will ” . If you go to any financial institution to leverage that money, they will look at the credit rating of the organisation. O ur combined authority does not have a credit rating, but they will use an evaluation mechanism that gives us an equivalent of X ; t hat is often strong enough.

What the G overnment are creating here is gainshare 2.0. When we were first established as mayors, all mayors got a 30-year income stream. T ake the Tees Valley, for instance : we got from the Government , as part of our deal , £15 million a year , guaranteed for 30 years. That is not index - linked; it is a flat amount. When it was set up in 2017—I know this to be true—that was done with the purpose that the G overnment wanted you to borrow against that income stream. They did that on purpose by not index - linking it, so you get more bang for your buck if you spend it up front, to try to incentivise growth.

If you say to an investor, whether it is M&G or Macquarie, “We want to borrow £200 million , but don’t worry, this is how our money works. This is the contract we have with government against that”, they will borrow against that all day long because , really , they are borrowing against government covenant strength, not your covenant strength. Having this income stream that is guaranteed in legislation will help to some extent.

There is an interesting academic question here ; i t depends on how financially prudent you want to be. Do you need the income stream from income tax? If you have a borrowing case because you have a piece of land and an investor, and if you had the ability to retain business rates, for instance, income tax could be slightly irrelevant because , if you can retain business rates — and if, for example, you own the land and you can get some rental income as well — there is a strong chance that , on their own, those investments stack up by themselves. We have seen this a lot in Teesside , which means that we do not have to rely on our gainshare. There is an argument that , by releasing the absolute cap on borrowing and leaning more heavily on the business case and the spending decision at a combined authority level, which is a Green Book spending decision, that should give confidence to go to the market and say, “I have an investment from what is, in effect, a BB- rated company. We have a parent company guarantee”.

I can give a specific example. We have landed SeAH Wind on Teesside. It is the largest single private investment ever from South Korea. It is a private company with a £1.4 billion investment. It built a 1.1 million - square - foot shed. It pays rent and business rates. Because of the deal we did with the G overnment in 2018, we retain the business rates on the whole site. With the business rates income, once that reaches practical completion, and our rental income, we went to Macquarie , which financed the whole project. It did not require us to get income tax from government ; the business rates and rental income allowed for the borrowing to build that project. Why did it do that? I t had a huge amount of support from UK Export Finance and some support from the South Korean Government. It had a parent company guarantee —i t is part - listed on the Korean Stock Exchange —so i t was a commercial deal that stacked up.

When you talk about borrowing, what lots of mayors are talking about — we have been part of this as well — is, “We want to build new train stations. We want to subsidise buses around franchising”. That will never be financeable in the market because it requires subsidy. Take Manchester ; I have talked about it a lot. The Bee Network costs the taxpayer £250 million net every year. Around £120 million comes directly from government through the bus service improvement plan — BSIP — and the rest comes from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. That is fine ; it is a spending decision . W hen Andy was mayor , he was re-elected, so local people must want that. There is a transparency and accountability to it. However, you are never going to be able to borrow on the markets because they will say, “Hang on, you want to borrow how much money , and you ’ re going to lose £250 million a year?” What a lot of the mayors want is to say, “It’s not about the business case. We ’ re just borrowing against the direct income stream from government , and we are leveraging the g overnment covenant to expose that risk to the market ” , but , ultimately , it is all backed off to government.

Q118 That was enlightening. If we abstract ourselves from whether the grant equals the proceeds of devolution and look just at the taxes that might be assigned or devolved, what , in your mind , would be the most efficient way of finding the right construct in terms of which taxes to devolve or assign to local government? We have talked about economic growth. We have talked about having skin in the game in terms of having some equity upside , depending on which projects you are backing. We have had other people come here ; we talked about size, efficiency, the quantum raised and so on. I n an ideal world , what would be the right construct of which ones to assign — all the way from the small ones to the big ones?

T here are probably four tests for which taxes are appropriate in looking at devolving to local areas. The first is economic growth. Is it a tax that grows when the local economy grows? This answers some of the points you were making. Are we investing in growth then capturing the benefits of that growth? Income tax, for example, does that. If income tax is devolved to London, London grows, the income tax rate goes up and , depending on how that deal is structured between the proportion that central government gets and the proportion that London gets, that will provide more money for the rest of the country, given that , last year, London ha d a fiscal net transfer of £49 billion to the rest of the UK economy, which we want to grow. We are comfortable with the idea that London should fund things outside of London, but we also think that you could invest more in London and grow that cake.

Secondly, is it stable? Is it a stable thing that we can potentially borrow against? Things that are very variable do not give you a stable income stream , which m ake s it very difficult to plan ahead or borrow against it. I s it a stable tax —that is , a tax that grows when the local economy grows ?

Ano ther important thing is the geographical remit. Can you point to where that tax is raised and spent? This is important. Again, if you are doing something like a transport project, it is important to see where the beneficiaries of that project are and , with the expenditure of the project , whether the project actually works.

Finally, it is about accountability. Can the public see the link between where the tax is raised, a decision taken by a mayor or a mayoral strategic authority, and the outcome? If it is clear that this tax came in, this was the decision taken on what to do with it and this is the outcome, the public can take a decision on whether the tax was right and the decision was right.

Given those tests, income tax and business rates make a lot of sense because you can tell where they are generated. With business rates, obviously , buildings do not move —they are physical — although new buildings can be built , generating new sources of business rates. VAT is quite difficult because, particularly with online expenditure and separating out income streams into retailers, it is sometimes difficult to see where the VAT is generated. A visitor levy is generated from hotels in a specific area ; a decision is then taken and it can be spent in that specific area. Those are the ones that make sense.

We are at the start of the conversation. We do not expect to get to where New York and Tokyo are overnight, but moving a little further in that direction , with appropriate discussion as we go , seeing how this current wave of fiscal devolution or more autonomy plays out , is very important.

I agree largely with what Howard said. The Government are concentrating on income tax and business rates because they are the easiest to follow, administer and manage. Start with the low-hanging fruit. There have been lots of tests up and down the country on business rate retention schemes as one-off, isolated examples. Howard gave a good example. We have a great example , which I have given already, at Teesworks on Teesside : SeAH . A huge amount of income is now being generated from business rates. Th is will mean that , over the next 15 to 20 years , it will net an extra £4 billion, which we can then put back into the local economy, so that works.

I know that we might come on to this but , with business rates—the Government are trying to tackle this—we have to be careful that we do not fall into the same position we fell into with local authorities. Sadly, in parts of the north of England , you have a business rate settlement with a local council, which works in the beginning, but , when you have post-industrial decline, large employers go bust and the business rate base falls, and you find that it creates a disincentive to the local authority to care any more . I have seen this at first hand . W e are trying to attract major investors to the UK and it is nigh on impossible to make the local authority interested in meet ing them or do ing anything about it. They are bringing, say, £1 billion - worth of investment and 1,000 jobs, but the reality is that local councils are trying to manage their budgets . T hey think , “E ven if we land this, because of the equalisation on business rates , we won’t see a penny of this investment. We have children and social services to deal with. We cannot dedicate the resource to it ” .

What the Government need to consider around business rate retention—to be fair to them , they are giving serious consideration to this ; I expect some protection in the model—is how to create a floor so that, five or 10 years down the line , mayoralties do not end up in the same place as local authorities : “We’re chasing investment but it’s not making a material difference to the local area because we ’ re playing catch-up on a drop ” . This is an important point on devolution full stop, never mind fiscal devolution . Teesside is , sadly , a good example of this. I can point you to lots of private investment that we have made in Teesside a nd talk to you in my press releases about the thousands of jobs that are being created . That is all true but , at the stroke of a pen, when national insurance goes up or electricity prices go up because of regulation, the macroeconomics for a place such as Teesside always drown out the micro that we can affect. Even with those guards, we have to be careful that we do not quickly fall into a deficit.

On the income tax point — to be fair , London , Howard and Sadiq have been very vocal and hugely supportive here— equalisation , as a result , will be important as well. If you look at income tax, 3% of income tax in the Tees Valley will be equivalent to about £170 million a year. I believe that, in London , it is about £2.3 billion. If there is no level of equalisation, you are baking in left - behind areas , and great cities and successful areas such as London will continue to march ahead , leaving everybody else behind. Again, with equalisation , you are potentially creating inertia in organisations . T hey say, “Even if we don’t achieve, the y’ ll just re-equalise it and we ’ ll get a bit more money”, which is where the business rate system is with local authorities. Although they are the easiest to pick off, there are some nuances and unintended consequences that might not happen today but could easily happen in five years’ time if we are not careful.

I am hugely supportive of it ; it is the right direction , and I agree with Howard that this is the start of a journey. People need to be aware — I believe this for lots of things around devolution — that , once you let that genie out of the bottle, it feels like a one - way street , politically speaking . It becomes difficult to take money away from local areas and take powers back. W e are at a precipice here. You could easily see a place in 10, 15 or 20 years’ time where we do see real fiscal devolution — and not just on those things we have talked about. You could create systems, particularly with emerging technologies , on local sales taxes, corporation tax and income — all those things — where the barrier to entry of establishing local HMRCs is much less than it is today. That will be the direction of travel. This is not just a decision about the legislation today : you are setting out a direction of travel that might look very different to the one you think you are setting out on today. That is open for debate, but you have to be careful that , if you do not want that, now is the time to consider it.
That leads on very well to Lord Prentis’s question.

Q119 M y question is about equalisation mechanisms. You have talked about the growth that comes from devolution, but , at the same time , the economic disparities between regions often lead to G overnments implementing equalisation mechanisms. My question is centred on that. If fiscal devolution is designed to reward success , as you are saying, how worried should we be that there may be corresponding costs to underperformance?

T he starting point here , on equalisation , should be that this is not a zero - sum game. The country does well when London does well, as well as the other way round. Our principle would be to equalise the starting point and start in neutral so that nowhere, including London, is any better or worse off on day one. L et places keep a meaningful share of the growth that they get for long enough that it makes a difference. If you equalise every penny away, you have reinvented the grant, just with extra steps to get to it . Things such as needs-based funding for core services — policing or the fire service — might be something that we look at separately , using a separate structure. Starting in neutral then incentivising growth , with a structure that prevents some of those core services being affected in the case of catastrophic downturn , is the right way to go. T he principle of devolution is giving the regions the opportunity to encourage and allow that growth.
How much equality do you think we need?

That is a very good question. This is one of those things where it is about equality of opportunity. I have seen previous measures where you disincentivise some areas from growing too much because there is no benefit to them to grow, as Lord Houchen said . This is also the sort of thing where , when new powers are introduced , you need a review period at some point to look at the impact before you take any further ones.

This is an essential question because that is the element of regulation with which Parliament should be concerned. By allowing for growth on the upside, you do one of two things. You could allow for the downside , so do the Government then take a view that areas are allowed not to fail , perhaps, but to suffer and lose income as a result ? I get the impression from decades of government policy that the Government are not going to do that.

Then the question becomes: what regulation are we putting in place to reduce the downside marginally in order to protect against failure but incentivise growth? Then you have to be very careful not to get into that cycle of there being areas that are not geared up to do this and say, “Actually, we ’ re quite happy with the equalisation from London. We ’ re getting more money. We don’t have to do anything. You know what? If we get a bit less money, ther e’ ll be a review in five years’ time , and we ’ ll get more of a top-up. What we ’ ll do” — we see this up and down the country in local authorities — “ is play politics and say that we have missed out and need more money because we have been left behind”.

To your second question, Howard has made his point , and London has always been very clear and supportive on this, but it depends on the philosophy. If you want to take a pure economic philosophy, as some in the Treasury and some pure economists do, you let each part of the country fail and succeed on its own terms. However, because of the intervention s from G overnments of both colours going back 50, 60 or 70 years, there have been unintended consequences i n different parts of the country. If we are a single nation and we want to go forward as such , for places such as Teesside , which have been left behind by G overnments of both colours in a post-industrial world — sadly , that is typical of the post-industrial story in the UK — there has to be a rebalancing, whether you call it levelling up, the northern powerhouse or whatever ; I am sure that Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, will come up with a term for it. We have to show that the powerhouse and the engine of London should not just help London succeed but provide support to the whole country. How do we provide opportunity in parts of the country that do not have it? As a great Prime Minister once said, talent is equally spread across the country , but opportunity is not. How can we use potential mechanisms through devolution to readdress that balance?

T hat goes to the crucial part of this and the whole debate on levelling up : if levelling up is about taking money from London and distributing it to the rest of the country, it will not work in the long term because London will lose out and London’s economic motor will cease to delive r that £49 billion of extra funding. It has to be an “and”; it has to be both. Allow regions to capture some of the benefits of growth but , at the same time , in London, for example, that growth will drive additional income for Treasury that can then be used to support projects in other parts of the country.

I am sorry to interrupt but the reality is that you have to look at the proposed fiscal devolution rules and the proposals that will come out in more detail in the coming weeks , in conjunction with the d evolution Act and the Infrastructure Act, which complement them . A big thing that can help with equalisation is the devolution of powers in regulation. We are now in a consultation period for other mayors to get the same call-in powers as the London Mayor for Housing and Infrastructure. The proposal from the consultation seems to be that some of those powers will come in on day one , while o thers will have to be earned once a spatial development strategy is in place.

For a place such as Teesside, that is a huge opportunity. It is not a financial mechanism, but we can build thousands of houses — not just houses : industrial estates and big developments , too— that have been blocked by local authorities and not been delivered for one reason or another . This will deliver jobs and economic growth for our area. We have to look at that fiscal devolution in line with the other powers.
