Either way, a bit of joint work between the FCDO and the MOD would be helpful in making these guys’ lives easier. Sometimes unnecessary paperwork, delays on the Polish border and nitty-gritty issues are holding up these convoys and demoralising the guys and girls a bit.

Making the process of these charities getting hold of old ambulances or fire trucks, or taking them from the Government estate, if they are no longer used, would be really helpful. We had a couple of meetings with an FCDO official, and then things slowed down a bit. It would be fantastic if we could pick it up again, perhaps jointly with an MOD official, so that we can make this work a bit better.
We will take that away and come back to you.

Q59 Through the Council of Europe I sit on the network for Ukrainian children, and our chair is a Ukrainian Member of Parliament. They were talking to me about the simple challenges that schools face. I was reflecting on your earlier point about the solidarity of the British public; as David has just said, we are seeing that in relation to Ukraine.

We want to explore together something as simple as linking schools—having partner schools so they can meet each other, have pen friends or fundraise. Is that the sort of thing that the Government could look at supporting, to help unlock the natural charity of the British public—people who want to give more but do not always know how or where, and who to be linked to?

I mentioned Save the Children in response to the question about development education. It has done some interesting work on piloting modern school twinning of the sort that lots of us grew up with. It is piloting how you do that in a digital age, and I have been very impressed by the results of that so far.

One of the questions from lots of colleagues who come from a development education background is about what role posts can have in facilitating that sort of link-up. That is something we can take away.

Q60 I think I can probably say that most of us in this room and across the House of Commons, if not all of us, were very pleased to see what the Foreign Secretary said about what is happening in Israel and about stopping trade with the illegal settlements.

I want to ask a rather hard-nosed question—I tried to ask this yesterday in the Chamber, but we did not get an answer. You may have seen the headline from back in April this year, “Foreign Office shuts unit tracking potential law breaches by Israel.” That refers to the IHL cell that deals with the middle east inside FCDO and the funding that went from it to the Centre for Information Resilience, which is a unit that had a massive database of all the dreadful things that have been going on. From that, how do you expect the Government’s change in approach on Israel to effect change? This is probably a good place to start, because if the Government are blind to what is going on there because funds have been cut from this cell and the Centre for Information Resilience, how will it be dealt with? This is so important. This is a very hard-nosed, specific question.
It was a cell that was specifically gathering data around potential war crimes.
There may be more to say on the Centre for Information Resilience in coming days, but I might defer to Nick on the size of the team in the cell.

Originally, that IHL cell was spun out of the export control joint unit. [1] We have an export control unit, and then we spun out the IHL cell specifically to track the Israel situation. It has now gone back into the export control unit, so it has not disappeared. The 21 staff are now working back in the export control unit. There is this misunderstanding that we have stopped doing the work—we have not. The work continues; we are still doing it—they are just sitting somewhere else in the structure.

On the Centre for Information Resilience, we still have access to its reports. We are not relying only on that source of information to make our judgments; we are relying on open-source information, NGO reports and feedback on the ground. There is a whole range of information that we are relying on, including that centre.
Q61 Nick, you said that we still have access to the reports—is that future reports or do we have access to the data that has already been collated?
We certainly have access to the data that has already been collated. Let me check on the other data—I will be surprised if we do not, but I will try.
I think that was the concern—about the historical data and our access to it.
I will check and come back to you on that.
Q62 Do you want to say anything else about how the Government’s change in approach on Israel will effect change?

It is very important to put on record—I think the Foreign Secretary has done likewise—the speed and professionalism with which the Department has responded to what is, by any measure, a very significant shift in policy. I am pleased to have you reflect that it has been welcomed so warmly by Parliament. Honestly, it is a really significant change in policy in terms of how we talk about the settlements and the legality of the occupation.

What remains unchanged is our humanitarian commitment to the Palestinian people. What I hope we have done is effect a policy change that means that that sort of commitment is enduring—as you will know, during the cuts, our aid for the Palestinian people is one of the things that was protected. As with so many conflicts, humanitarian aid is trying to deal with a problem that has a political cause and a political source, and it is trying to mitigate risks the origin of which lie elsewhere, so this change that we have effected is to try to keep the prospect of a two-state solution alive. That is really the only way we will get to a situation where the duty bearer to the Palestinian people is a Palestinian Government and they are not reliant on humanitarian funding and support in the way that they have been for so very long.

On a personal note, I went to Gaza before the more recent war, and conditions were completely intolerable then. I met Gazan children, and it was sort of mortifying to have them say, “We’re so pleased you’ve come because we thought the world had forgotten us.” The conditions that children were enduring were horrifying. This policy change is an attempt to keep the conditions alive for a future two-state settlement that means that this ceases to be the FCDO’s humanitarian priority, protected above others, because the duties will be borne by a functioning state.

Q63 Minister, can I just say, personally, how disappointing it is to hear it referred to as a policy change? The ICJ advisory ruling two years ago was very clear that Israel was occupying Palestine, and therefore we as a country had duties that were signed up to that. You rightly talk about the horrendous humanitarian situation in Gaza years ago—we have known about this for a long time. It surprises me that it is a surprise to the Department that it now needs to change to scale up to do what legally we should have been doing the whole way through.
I would not characterise it as a surprise to the Department. All I would say is that it is a really significant shift in UK policy—

Q64 That pains me, Minister. Our international credibility has been dented because we did not follow the very clear rules of law, particularly when it comes to protecting humanitarians. I hope that one of the big shifts that we will get with this change is being a lot more front-footed when it comes to honouring international law.
I think you will hear a lot more from the Foreign Secretary on precisely that.
We look forward to it.

Q65 As colleagues have said, a lot of people welcomed the announcement last week. However, 1.4 million people in Gaza are likely to face acute food insecurity leading up to December this year, yet the UK has reduced its funding to the World Food Programme by 78% since 2024. Can you explain why that makes sense?

It is important to restate that our humanitarian commitment to the Palestinian people is ongoing. I met with the interim executive director of the World Food Programme about our support to the programme more generally. The thing that he impressed upon me that I have been really wrestling with since the conversation is that we have a series of choices that are the stuff of nightmares. There are so many acute emergencies where lives are at stake right now, and there is a need to invest in ongoing resilience so that there are fewer such instances in the future. Now that we are past peak aid, these are the nightmare choices in front of every World Food Programme donor: does our money do more good, and is it more successful in building the world we want to see, if we are investing it in long-term resilience or if we are constantly responding to emergencies? I would welcome reflections and challenge from the Committee about whether we are getting the balance between those two things right, because this is the stuff of nightmares.

The issue in Gaza is not money; it is access. Averting famine cannot be a measure of success. We know exactly why there is not the access, and we know exactly why the dual-use goods are not being allowed into Gaza: it is purely because of the actions of the Israeli Government. We need more crossing points to be opened and more flexibility on what comes in, and we need Israel to live up to the commitments it made in the 20-point peace plan. I would not say that this is a money problem.
Q66 In short, the money is having to be spent elsewhere because we do not have the access.

Well, money can be spent—the needs are enormous inside Gaza. We are still funding UNRWA, despite what the Israeli Government is trying to do in terms of shutting it down, because we think it is incredibly important for the services of the Palestinian people. We are going to be, and are, supporting the Palestinian Authority itself. There are ways that you can provide and spend the money well, but ultimately, the scale of the resources going into Gaza needs to increase fundamentally.
We have 11 minutes of your time left, Minister, so we will go into quick-fire questions and we would be very grateful for quick-fire answers.
I will do my best.

Q67 I need to pick up on that point. The World Food Programme is very specific that this is about need, not access. I 100% agree with you on dual use, but we are the ninth largest donor to the World Food Programme, and we have cut funding by 78%. With respect, you can see the frustration when we say that there should be a pathway to 0.7% so that this is not the stuff of nightmares any more, but we are not hearing that pathway from the Government.

I will move on to Sudan. Talking of countries that think that we may have forgotten them, and the Government’s very welcome shift to adherence to international law and international humanitarian law and calling out our friends as well as our foes, will there be a shift in how the Government approaches Sudan?

I said last night that you should expect to hear more from us on Sudan in coming weeks and months. The volume of humanitarian assistance going into Sudan, and its being maintained, is important, but there has also been the track around the conflict more widely and making sure that we are straining absolutely every diplomatic sinew. Both I and the Foreign Secretary have sought and received briefings on Sudan from day one. I think we are going to be speaking in coming weeks and months to satisfy ourselves that we have strained absolutely every sinew to get an enduring settlement in Sudan that means that the humanitarian needs are not as great. I would expect to hear more from us in coming weeks and months.
Can you give us any indication of where that might go and what that means?
Monica, the Minister has answered.

Q68 The situation with Ebola in Africa is very serious and there continue to be grave concerns about the progress of Ebola across the continent. How is the UK supporting efforts in the region to make sure that we are containing it as best as possible?

I think you will have seen that I announced to Parliament two weeks ago extra funding. I spoke to Africa CDC and the African Union when I was in Ethiopia, and they both said that British money is fast and wise. We are spending it on the right things and disbursing fast. As you know, other donors have made commitments but have not moved as fast to disbursal. As I noted earlier, I am having a number of bilateral conversations with African Ministers, of which this is very much a feature. I am confident that we have stepped up to the plate and that all of our conversations for the Africa-led response are being had with the right African interlocutors.
Q69 How is the vaccination programme developing?

The first trial, which includes Oxford, has started on the vaccine for this particular Ebola strain. We will have to wait and see how that progresses. The bottom line is that this is now the second largest Ebola outbreak ever. We have been playing catch-up right from the beginning. Our support has been terrific and well-targeted, but this is a marathon, not a sprint. This thing is going to go on for two years.
While we are on the DRC, I put on record my gratitude for the commitment to the TFFF fund, but also my concern that it is a loan rather than a grant.

Q70 In the next 12 months, food supply systems are likely to come under considerable stress through war and climate events. Being an agricultural engineer, I will talk about the importance of soil and compost in improving moisture-holding capacity and preventing famine.
Briefly, please, Brian.
What priority are you placing on strengthening these systems and addressing malnutrition?

A huge priority. As you will have heard me say at the outset, food security is a huge issue for me. One of the changes we need to effect—it is not about a reprioritisation, and it is certainly not about the allocations—is that organisationally, at the moment, food and the food system sit in our corporate mind in humanitarian, and I think they need to sit alongside climate, health and economic security and human security. They are so cross-cutting. Of the five securities, food security and the pressure on the international food system is the thing that keeps me awake most at night. I will be very keen to continue these conversations with you, because I think we are both expressing a similar level of alarm.

Q71 My question is about women, peace and security—sorry, it is a very large topic. We were told previously by the Minister that they would be reviewing the current commitments in relation to conflict prevention and resolution as part of the NAP. When will that be published, and when will the planning, monitoring, evaluation and learning framework be published?

I cannot give you a date for when it will be published, but to reassure, I think there was some disquiet about whether a refresh was adequate and whether there needed to be a completely new plan and strategy, and having spoken to the colleagues working on it, I think they would want me to signal and telegraph that, actually, the fact that it is a refresh is a sign of how highly we prize it. We do not want the work to be slowed down. We want to crack on with the work and scale it, rather than restarting it from first principles. I cannot give you a publication date, but I will get back to you.

Q72 Thank you. We have heard a lot about mainstreaming of women and girls through specific programmes and commitments towards their inclusion. Is that still the direction of travel? Also, will the FCDO collate the data on how these projects have been engaging with women and girls, people with disabilities, the LGBT community and other minority groups?
Human rights and equalities, yes, will be an ongoing feature. Minister Elmore, as you know, is leading on all those, and I will be working with him very closely on that.

More widely, I think lots of feminists have a legitimate anxiety that mainstreaming is code for: “It will be everywhere, but potentially nowhere”. To give a very public undertaking, women and girls is absolutely central to everything that I want to achieve. I want held to account on it, and I want held to account for the agenda beyond VAWG, as I have said repeatedly in public. I need you all to hold me to it. Next week at UNGA, I will be doing some interventions on SRHR and a wider rights framework. As I say, VAWG is foundational, but it has to be the floor, not the ceiling.

Q73 Minister, may I reiterate the point that Tracy made? If we could, or you could, ask for a commitment to data collection, that seems to be the best way to hold people to account, because we are talking about structural inequality here, not access to resources. That seems to be the one way that we can make significant change.
Understood.

Q74 I want to ask you about children—I have heard you use the phrase today. UNICEF found that bilateral aid for child-focused programmes was cut by 57% from 2019 to 2023. It has obviously been cut even more deeply since then. We have heard evidence that when the previous Home Secretary made women and girls a priority, that made a material difference to the way that NGOs were writing their programmes and applications. Will you consider making children an explicit priority of Government, so that we can reverse the decline in child-focused funding?

I have received a number of very persuasive technical representations about the mechanisms—for example, about whether there should be a special envoy for children and young people, and how we do programme design. I have received a number of very helpful representations. I do not want to pre-empt where we are going to land, but I do want to underscore in public my level of ambition. I am not yet completely set on what the right mechanism is, but to reassure, I am taking advice from officials about how we do the organisational design piece right, to put children and young people at the heart. I can very happily reiterate my level of ambition, but I do not want to give you a commitment on the mechanism until I am sure that the mechanism is the right one—perhaps the next time I come.
I will just flag that I do not actually recognise that number.

Q75 Minister, talking of structural inequality, with UN80, the restructure that the UN is trying to do, the male Secretary-General put forward that the only two women-specific organisations, UN Women and UNFPA on sexual health, will be merged, even though they are very different. What is your view on that?

Minister Elmore holds the decision making on this. My understanding is that we are trying to balance two separate and competing progressive priorities here. We absolutely do not want to see a reopening of the mandate of either of those very important organisations, and we stand four-square behind the legitimacy and importance of the mandate. At the same time, we do think it is a progressive imperative to make the UN slimmer and more fit for purpose. We are balancing those two at the moment, but if I may, I will get Minister Elmore to come back to you on our current negotiating and voting position.
We would really appreciate that. We hear that the proposal is back on the table, which would effectively halve women’s bodies within the UN.
Q76 Minister, have the FCDO’s strategic priorities on climate and nature changed under the new leadership?
In terms of substantively what is on the agenda, I would not say so, but in terms of the level of primacy that this agenda has in all our diplomacy, I would say that it has rocketed up the agenda.
Q77 Great. How do you plan to deliver the UK’s international climate finance commitments effectively in an increasingly climate-affected world?

It will be a huge feature of everything that we do in the upcoming multilateral settings. The Foreign Secretary and I have a discussion tabled on financing tomorrow to address this and other questions. I will be delighted to come back to you after that, but I think the Foreign Secretary would want me to underscore just how committed he is to this and how happy he is to spend significant international political capital on it.
We will be tracking that £6 billion commitment over the next three years.
Q78 That is really appreciated. What reforms of those multilaterals are you looking at to increase the accessibility, volume and reach of climate finance flows?

I think this is something we will want to come back to the Committee on, not least because it is going to be such a huge part of our G20 agenda. With your forgiveness, Chair, perhaps we could table that and do a really chunky session on it, because it is going to be such a huge part of what we do.
That would be great.

Let me just say that we will be publishing our report on international climate finance on Thursday, and we really hope that it is a very practical tool for you. Basically, we need more data on what works and where you have spent, but the principles we absolutely stand behind. We look forward to you hopefully being able to use that.

Minister and Nick, it has been a real pleasure. It has been fascinating to learn your approach. Thank you for being so generous with your time and sharing your thoughts on all of this. We hope that this is a regular occurrence. We wish you well for the rest of your day. Committee, thank you very much.
[1] Correction requested by witness: *These figures refer to the number of Full-Time Equivalent Staff in the Export Control Joint Unit.

segs.tx: Environmental Audit Committee
Oral evidence: Air Pollution in England, HC 21
Monday 14 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 14 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Mr Toby Perkins (Chair); Julia Buckley; Jonathan Davies; Barry Gardiner; Sojan Joseph; Manuela Perteghella; Adrian Ramsay; Martin Rhodes; John Whitby.
Questions 221 - 2 62
Witnesses

I I : Emma Hardy MP, Minister of State, DEFRA; Bill Parish, Deputy Director for Noise, Agricultural and Industrial Pollution, DEFRA; Simon Lightwood MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State (Minister for Buses and Local Transport), DFT; and Jennifer Raynor, Deputy Director for Environment and Adaptation Strategy, DFT.
Written evidence from witnesses:
- Written submission from the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs, Department for Health and Social Care and Department for Transport (AIR0144)
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Emma Hardy, Bill Parish, Simon Lightwood and Jennifer Raynor.

Q221 Welcome, everyone, to the second panel of today’s Environmental Audit Committee evidence session on air quality. I am delighted to say that we are joined by Ministers and relevant experts from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Department for Transport. Ministers, I will start by asking you to introduce yourselves and the people who are supporting you.
Good afternoon, everyone. It is great to be here. My name is Simon Lightwood, and I am the Minister for B uses and L ocal T ransport. I am joined by Jennifer Raynor.
Hi, I am Jennifer Raynor. I am the deputy director for environment and adaptation strategy.
Hi, I am Emma Hardy. I am the Minister of State in DEFRA, and I am joined today by Bill Parish.
Good afternoon. I am Bill Parish, deputy director for agriculture and industrial pollution in DEFRA.

Q222 Minister Hardy, you have been newly promoted—congratulations . You have appeared regularly at the Environmental Audit Committee, and it is always a pleasure to have you with us. Previously, we discussed the cross-governmental aspect of air pollution—the number of different Departments responsible for areas that are impacted. Ahead of this meeting, we very helpfully had a document from your Department laying out the responsibilities across the various Departments, which the Committee is publishing today.

How successfully do you think the Government are working across different Departments in those other areas of responsibility? Can you explain some of the contradictory ways in which your desire to have better air pollution standards butts up against things that might be moving in the opposite direction?

Absolutely. I will start by acknowledging the work of campaigners. I particularly want to pay tribute to Rosamund, who I have had the pleasure of meeting on a number of occasions. I want to recognise her advocacy and how she has been instrumental in pushing things forward, along with many other campaigners . Rosamund and what she has done deserve particular recognition .

To answer your question on cross-Government working, it could be better. We are launching this new air strategy call for evidence. We have to do the air strategy in 2028, and we are bringing it forward to start a call for evidence this year. One of the things I want to look at is how we can improve cross-Government working because, in putting that document together for ourselves, we can see where the responsibilities lie.

Setting up a cross-Government group to meet formally and talk about air quality is a really good way forward. Since there has been a change in Prime Minister, it feels like now is a really good time to say, “There have been some changes at the top. Let’s see how we can all work more effectively together across Government on tackling air pollution.”

That is because you are right. We will be talking about what we can do in terms of air pollution, but we are obviously mindful that there are different perspectives on how it impacts the cost of industry or the cost of living, for example. It is something we could have done better, so I want to do some work on it. Creating a more formal cross-Government group, where we can openly and honestly discuss where there are trade-offs in achieving this, is a better way forward. We want to do that as part of this air quality strategy call for evidence.

Q223 We very much welcome that approach, and you will certainly have the Committee’s support. I said to the previous panel that we are very disappointed not to have a Minister here from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. It has a number of areas of responsibility, not least construction, planning and local government monitoring of air pollution, but it was not willing or able to send a Minister. From your perspective, is MHCLG a Department that recognises the role it plays, or can play, in improving air quality? What sort of conversations have you had with them?

We have not had a formal conversation at Minister-to-Minister level, but I know there are meetings at official level about different areas. One of the things we want to do through this air quality strategy call for evidence is look at things in a more straightforward and simple way that we can communicate to the public and also talk about cross-Government.

We have done it with themes. One of the themes is healthy schools. Thinking about how we make schools healthier for children includes school streets, which are obviously in DFT, but it also means the Department for Education when we think about ventilation. And that also means building regulations, which are in MHCLG. There are all these different aspects.

The worst government is when we are too siloed. I am not saying we have perfected this—it is absolutely a work in progress—but we are trying to think about it in terms of themes. How does this impact you and your children as a dad? You want healthy schools and some of our other themes: nature and the countryside, cleaner and safer communities, and healthy homes.

Rather than thinking in terms of this bit being DEFRA and that bit being MHCLG, we have tried to address it by thinking about how you as an individual interact with the air, and where. We then ask which Departments have something to do with healthy schools, and we bring those together.

It is very much the beginning of trying to work together. As I say, I feel like there have been some changes at the top. There is a new Prime Minister, so let us try to find a new way of doing this, because I openly admit that it has not been as good as I would have liked.
Agreed.

Q224 Welcome, Ministers. Minister Hardy, it was really reassuring to hear that you have been working so closely with Ella’s family. Turning to the central aims of Ella’s law, which are to ensure that everyone’s health is protected from air pollution regardless of where they live, can you tell us what consideration has been given to those core principles in terms of future legislation and any barriers that you have identified?

I absolutely support and share the ambition behind Ella’s law and what they are trying to achieve, and of course I completely understand the reasons why. What I am trying to think about from a DEFRA perspective is, “What is the most effective way we can improve air quality?” I am trying to think more practically about what we can do. Looking at that call for evidence about what we can do for schools, in homes and in the countryside, I am trying to think about it that way, about the targets where we need to focus work and about where we can see a difference.

There are two things that I think we could do better. One of them is about the targets we are setting. Some of them—I want to put this the right way—are not old-fashioned, but they recognise air pollutants from the past. They focus quite a lot on what we are doing about the ones created by soot, rather than the ones created more by modern air pollutants. I want to have a look at some of the things we are doing to make sure that we are actually measuring and focusing our time and energy on the main pollutants that we have in front of us, and I want us to do that through the call for evidence.

The other thing we have with the system at the moment is that once a local area reaches compliance with an air quality strategy, it is like, “Box ticked—done.” What I want to think about through the strategy and the call for evidence, and obviously working with everyone, is rather than just saying, “Right, you’ve met it—tick,” asking, “How about continuous improvement, then? Okay, so you’ve met it, but what more could be done? What could we do next? How could we take this further?”

There are two things there that I want to look at: are we measuring the pollutants that are of most concern, and are we setting a mindset and a culture of continuous improvement rather than just having a static target? That is what I am trying to think about.

Q225 That is really useful to hear. We wanted to ask how we move beyond that minimum compliance level. We heard earlier about how we have almost fallen behind EU targets, and we are worried that the gap will get bigger. Will any specific actions be taken, thinking about the population and the environment, that will look beyond just that minimum? What are the specifics?
Do you want to say a little about some of the other particles we are looking at measuring, Bill?

As an example of how we are trying to work beyond the simple limit value, we have set a long-term PM 2.5 reduction target, and the interim target was updated in the environmental improvement plan in December last year. We are aiming to achieve 10 micrograms across the whole of the country by 2030, which is level with the targets set out by the EU. We set a different target, a population exposure reduction target, and our aim is to reduce population exposure to PM 2.5 by 30%, based on the 2018 baseline, by 2030. That population exposure reduction target’s purpose is to continue driving down PM 2.5 exposure even if that 10 microgram basic limit has already been achieved. We are trying to look at it from an outcome focus rather than a simple concentration limit.

Q226 That is really interesting . Can I ask you a bit more about that? Obviously, Ella’s law is about making sure that everybody and every postcode is covered. You are talking about a 30% reduction, but we know that the current situation has really high inequalities. We often find in deprived areas, particularly urban settings, that those levels are much higher, so they should be areas that have a greater target for reduction. Is this 30% reduction an average across the UK, or do you have more targeted measures that take into account the impact of deprivation and inequality?

The PERT is a national target, but to measure our progress against that target, we are putting in a lot more PM 2.5 monitors. We need to place those monitors close to centres where the big population exposures are, and those will be big urban environments, including those more vulnerable communities. Since 2024, we have installed 65 new PM 2.5 monitors. Our monitoring network will be expanded to about 197 PM 2.5 monitors in total by the end of 2027. With a much more granular understanding of PM 2.5 concentrations close to those areas, we have a much better understanding of exposure. That is a mechanism by which we hold ourselves accountable for the progress we are making against that target.

However, when we drill down to another level of granularity—let’s say square kilometre grids—there are communities within communities, and some of them are much closer to busy roads or centres of industrialisation. We have been working closely with the UK Health Security Agency to pilot vulnerability maps. With UKHSA, we have developed maps that will help local authorities to identify, using existing criteria overlaid with concentration data and modelling, where deprived communities will be disproportionately exposed. That gives us real-life data to allow us to identify and home in on where the more deprived neighbourhoods that have been disproportionately exposed are.
The next step is, “Okay, now we have looked at it from an outcome point of view rather than just a simple concentration level. What action does the local authority need to focus on?”
Q227 What funding resources will be made available to those deprived communities so that they can tackle such issues?
That is probably one for MHCLG, because it will be funding for local authorities. Apologies, Chair and Julia.

Q228 Nitrogen pollution is a threat to public health, but also to our natural environment. It causes degradation of habitats and loss of biodiversity. Will DEFRA commit to a comprehensive national nitrogen strategy, and how would it integrate air quality, water, climate and biodiversity objectives?

Nitrogen is really complex . It goes across air quality, water quality, biodiversity, climate, agriculture—all of them. At the moment , rather than addressing it as a single stand-alone strategy—my gut feeling is that Government are good at doing strategies and maybe need to get better at doing—some of this is addressed through the various strategies we have already published. Some parts are addressed through the environmental improvement plan. There are some ways of dealing with it through the water White Paper and the farming road map. There are different ways of tackling nitrogen across existing frameworks and policies.

It is really challenging and really difficult because ammonia is the largest source of nitrogen, which is causing the difficulty. It is really hard to tackle ammonia. We are working across Government and with stakeholders, particularly farmers, to try to do that, but it is a very difficult challenge.
Q229 So you are not going to publish a national nitrogen strategy at the moment ?

We do not have plans to, but we are looking at how Scotland has done the nitrogen balance sheet. We do not currently have plans to publish a strategy, but we are looking at how the balance sheet is working in Scotland and whether it is effective.
Q230 To track progress across sectors?
Yes.
Q231 Are you working with other Departments like the DFT and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to ensure that you are at least coherent in your approach to reducing nitrogen emissions?

Yes, and the DFT is here. We are looking at how to tackle the different problems we face—water, air and soil—in a way that minimises the burden on farmers, and we are looking at how we are working across Government to do that. The short answer is yes, but it is a challenge, particularly with ammonia.

Q232 Are you drawing any lessons from countries other than the UK that have already implemented national nitrogen strategies, such as the Netherlands and Denmark? Are you looking at best practice there?

Yes, we are looking at best practice, and the reality is that Denmark and the Netherlands had to get quite brutal with their farming sectors. Now, Denmark and the Netherlands are embarking on compulsory buy-outs , whereby they are actually taking land out of agricultural production and paying farmers to stop being farmers: they are shutting farms down. That has been really difficult politically.

At this stage, we are proposing to work with the farming industry to reduce its pollution as much as it can while farmers can keep their farms. It is not an easy time for the cattle sector in particular to contemplate significant extra costs on its operations in order to adopt what needs to be done to reduce pollution.

There is no denying that the cattle sector itself is responsible for 46% of our national ammonia emissions. It is a sector in which ammonia emissions are currently unregulated. We committed in the farming road map and in the environmental improvement plan to consulting on how we will bring that sector into environmental permitting, because environmental permitting worked really well for the poultry and pig sectors. We are working up proposals for how we can introduce legislation for that sector and help it to respond to the challenge, put the infrastructure in place and reduce its contribution to ammonia emissions.

We are focused more on contemplating a regulatory approach for that sector, supported by grant funding, the technology fund and slurry infrastructure grants, but—put simply—we are adding a little more stick to the carrot and looking at how we can make faster progress on reducing emissions from those sectors.

Q233 You may have just answered some of this, but the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from some sectors has highlighted just how little emissions from agriculture have reduced over time, particularly ammonia emissions. The Chief Medical Officer also spoke about ammonia in the previous panel as something that we can and should address. We are aware that there are alternative ammonia-reducing practices out there, so, first, how are you supporting farmers to adopt those ammonia-reducing practices without undermining their viability? I think you have half answered this.
Secondly, will the Department commit to strict, mandated regulations around fertiliser use and storage, rather than relying on voluntary measures?

As Bill has mentioned, we are committed to consulting on measures to look at extending environmental permitting to beef and dairy. However, we really recognise that farming has been under real pressure: farmers have just had the worst drought in however many years, and the winter before last they had one of the worst floods that they have ever had. We are therefore trying to work with the industry. Yes, we want to move forward on what we can do around permitting, but we want to do that with the industry by working together.

The things that we are doing to support farmers include looking at more precise spreading and how they can use equipment in that way. The farming equipment and technology fund had £46.7 million available for farmers, growers, foresters and their contractors; £30 million was to help farmers invest in equipment to help them manage slurry in ways that reduce pollution, which obviously includes ammonia. I should say—well, it goes without saying, really—that whatever we do for ammonia often helps with water as well. It helps with both forms of pollution, so it is really effective . We have just put another £10 million into slurry management in 2026 as well, so we are putting the money in to try to support the farming community.

We were having regular meetings with the farming community around reducing water pollution, which obviously helps with ammonia and air pollution together. During the period of drought, the focus had to be on tackling the drought, but we will recommence those meetings on looking at water pollution and air pollution as soon as we can.
Q234 Y ou mentioned the Netherlands. What have we learned from countries like the Netherlands that have already implemented more stringent ammonia controls ?

We regularly look at what other countries are doing. W e mentioned what Scotland is doing on its nitrogen balanc e sheet . It is really useful to look at what other countries are doing . The Netherlands made quite a courageous move in paying farmers to stop farming . That is not something that the Government and I are looking at doing. We are looking instead to support our farming sector to be profitable and to continue to be successful, while at the same time looking at what they can do with agriculture. We have increased farm inspections . We have done all of that through the E A. We are looking at permitting. There are all these other things going on as well, but we have no current plans to adopt what has been done in the Netherlands.

Q235 May I pick you up on the use of the word “courageous”? That would generally be considered to be a good thing , but your subsequent answer suggest s that you thought the idea was bad . I am not sure whether it was a euphemism, but when you said “ courageous ” , did you do so because you think it is a good approach , or do you think it was reckless?

This reminds me of when I first became a Minister . I was commenting on the program me, “ Yes, Minister ”, in which everyone always agrees with the Minister . I said, “ When will I know when you actually disagree with me ? ”, and they said, “ Minister, it’s when we call you courageous. ” I am not going to criticise decisions made by another sovereign countr y; I will say only that we do not have plans to adopt them here.
That makes sense. Thank you for the clarification.

Q236 Minister Hardy , in August you announced the new opt - in scheme for people to sign up to get alerts on their phone if levels of five pollutants reach “ high ” or “ very high ” levels . Can you recall how many people had signed up to the scheme by the end of August ?
Is it about 2 , 500 - and - something ? I know I recently answered one of your written questions about it.
Well, the answer you gave to the parliamentary written question was 525 , actually, but there we are.
Ah, right. I do remember signing off that question.

Q237 What I really want to ask is why you do not do it in the same way as for heat waves or flood alert s by p ut ting it out on the weather channels or put ting it out to the Met Office , so that people do not have to opt in to get the information . W ith the best will in the world, you might reach 10,000 . Why not put it out there as public information in the way we do with heat waves and so on ? Then everybody will know.
The air quality alert is brand- new : it started on 30 July. It is super - new , so obviously any support the Committee could give in encouraging people to sign up would be great.
We have just publicised it for you.

Yes, you have just given it a plug. It is similar to the flood alert system , in that you have to opt in and sign up for it. Yes, it would be great if we could get a few more, but we have also got the APAC, the A ir P ollution A wareness C oalition, which I set up a number of months ago — I do not think it has been a year yet —and which is working with health and E NGO s . We have just got Enact Equality to be a member . It is looking at how we can communicate and raise awareness of air pollution , because they are experts.

I was listening with interest to the previous panel ’ s response to questions about what more we can do . The advice I have had from DEFRA is that public attitudes research says that people listen to professionals much more than to something I might say, for example. We are trying to get our message out on air pollution through the air pollution awareness campaign and through getting people to sign up to the new air quality alert system. It was only launched on 30 July, so it is brand-new .

Q238 I have your lovely rainbow tabulation for nitrogen dioxide and for PM 2.5 . W hat really struck me , looking at it, is that you have 10 grades from light green , which is low , to purple , which is very high , but all the nitrogen dioxide levels, from “ moderate ” to “ very high ”, are actually illegal in the UK. For PM 2.5 , even the third band of the “ low ” level is illegal in the UK. We are telling people that illegal air quality is “low” and “moderate”. This sounds like “Nineteen Eighty-Four”—we are just not using words properly when we are doing this sort of stuff, are we? It is illegal. Why do we not tell people that it is illegal, not that it is low?
Are you talking about the bands in how we set the levels for—

For PM 2.5 , the annual and 24-hour exposures are shown on the chart. The annual UK legal limit is 20 micrograms per cubic metre. It also shows the 2021 WHO guidelines and what you then call hourly mean concentrations. As I say, you are calling stuff that is illegal “low”. That seems quite extraordinary.
Bill, do you want to explain how we came to set the different bands?

The limit values that we have set in current legislation are based on long-term exposure. We are trying to reduce pollution below the legal limit all the time. If somebody is exposed to concentrations of a pollutant above that threshold day in, day out, they may expect to start experiencing some health impacts.

The DAQI—the daily air quality index, to which I think Mr Gardiner is referring—is a very different device. It was developed by the Committee on the Medical Effects of Air Pollutants, and it is about short-term exposure. Yes, the pollutants may on certain days, for a day or two, exceed the legal limits—the legal limits are average concentrations over the year—and we are warning people when the pollutants have exceeded certain limits on those days. The banding that we use for deciding whether it is medium, high or low is based on very short-term exposure. In other words, we are warning people that there could be acute spikes of air pollution because of weather conditions and so on. That is very different from the limit values that we set in legislation. We aim to keep long-term exposure below those limits.

Q239 The chart sets out the annual, 24-hour or one-hour exposures and sets the limits on each. The annual UK limit is 20 micrograms per cubic metre. The 2021 WHO guidelines are 5 micrograms per cubic metre for annual exposure and 15 micrograms per cubic metre within a 24-hour period. Against that, you are showing that 12 to 23 micrograms per cubic metre is low and 24 to 35 micrograms per cubic metre is low. You then have moderate, which goes up to 53 micrograms per cubic metre. This is a dog’s breakfast if you are trying to tell people what is going on in their life on any given day. These are supposed to be the daily air quality limits, and at the moment you are telling people that an illegal limit is perfectly acceptable.

I want to get on to ammonia, because you, Mr Parish and I had a conversation about that last week. I am deeply concerned about what you have just told the Committee. Ammonia reacts with other pollutants in the atmosphere to form secondary inorganic particles that contribute to PM 2.5 . You said that most of the achievements in the Netherlands and Denmark had been attained by basically shutting down farms. In fact, the Air Quality Expert Group highlighted the successful policies in the Netherlands, where regulatory controls of agricultural ammonia were responsible for around half of a 64% reduction in emissions between 1990 and 2016. That decrease was mostly due to measures implemented before 2010, such as changes in feed composition, the use of low-emission stables, the covering of manure silos and the direct incorporation of manure during application. Denmark reduced levels of ammonia by 40% between 1990 and 2016 by measures such as slurry-spreading technologies and building floor technologies. We are not talking about shutting down farms. In fact, the Air Quality Expert Group comments on the high stocking levels that these places had.

I am afraid that I feel that what you said earlier was rather misleading to the Committee. It chimes, I am afraid to say, with exactly the way this country has been negotiating at UNECE on ammonia. I mentioned to you last week the Swedish environmental organisations that—
Let’s come on to the question, if we can.

The UK has been arguing, against the rest of the parties, that you should de-stress and take away the importance of meeting the formal technical annexe that UNECE is putting forward. We are pretending that we are in the lead on this and that we are trying to do the right thing, but behind everybody’s back at the international negotiations, we are actually negotiating against that position.
I was just waiting for the question, but I will comment on what has been said.

Well, there are two questions. First, given what I have just said about your own Air Quality Expert Group’s analysis, do you feel that it was a fair comment to make to this Committee that in fact it was all achieved through closing down farms? Secondly, why is it that in the international negotiations the UK is an outlier seeking to water down the regulations? Those are the two very specific questions.
I do not believe that I did say that about the Netherlands. The Netherlands is one of our friends—
Mr Parish did.
I do not believe he did. Let us check the transcript, but I am sure that is not what was said.

The Netherlands is one of our friends and allies. It is a country that we work closely with and that we can learn a lot from. We are doing precision spreading and slurry management through grants. All those things are great examples. However, we would not go as far as the Netherlands in actually paying people to stop farming. I want to be completely clear on that, but in many other things it is a great example. We are good friends with the Netherlands and are working closely with it.
I am quite sure that I did not hear Bill say that, but do you want to comment, Bill?

I commented on what both Denmark and the Netherlands are contemplating now, because they are clearly finding it difficult to make further progress on reducing the impacts linked to cattle production. The Air Quality Expert Group is quite right: yes, you can make progress with measures on housing, precision spreading and slurry storage. That is exactly what we propose to introduce as measures through environmental permitting. Those measures are being encouraged now through grants. As I said earlier, we are now looking at how a regulatory mechanism can complement those grants to help to reduce pollution from the cattle sector, using exactly the mechanisms that the Air Quality Expert Group set out. It set out that it is possible to make reductions, and that is the direction in which we want to go.

Q240 Indeed, and the Netherlands made reductions of 64% by 2016 and Denmark of 40% by 2016. We had targets under the Gothenburg protocol to the convention on long-range transboundary air pollution and under the national emission ceilings regulations. That was to reduce ammonia emissions by 16%, compared with emissions in 2005, by 2030 . As things stand, in the past 21 years we have managed to reduce them by 9%, haven’t we?

There is more to do on ammonia. There is no doubt about that, but as I said, we have set up the farming equipment and technology fund, which helps people to invest in the right equipment, and we have the slurry infrastructure grant, which helps them to pay to manage slurry more effectively. We are looking at introducing permitting, which is a bit more stick—if we want to put it that way—but I am also, I have to say, acutely aware of the difficult summer that farming has had and of the really hard winter it had only a couple of years ago. Generally, as a politician, an individual and a Minister, I prefer to work with an industry to bring it with us, to take it along on this journey with us and to introduce things in partnership with it, which is why we are looking at how we can incentivise it with slurry stores through grants, and at how we can look at regulation, inspections and permitting. Both things need to be hand in hand, so that we are working with the industry.

Q241 Minister Hardy, I absolutely agree that farmers have been through a very tough period, and we want to do all that we possibly can to help them, but if you look at a 9% reduction versus 40% and 64% in the other two countries, I think you can agree that we could do a lot more, a lot more quickly. I will, however, change my direction of fire. Given that non-exhaust emissions are now the dominant source of particulate matter from road transport and will persist beyond electrification, what action is the Department taking to ensure that the regulation keeps pace? How will you implement the UN brake emissions regulations into UK law? Will that align fully with the Euro 7 regulations?
I think that was directed at me—
It was definitely directed at you. You have had an armchair ride up until now.

Good afternoon, Chair and colleagues. It is great to be here. I welcome the opportunity to talk to you as the newly minted Minister with responsibility for decarbonisation, sustainability and air quality within the Department for Transport when it comes to public transport. The transition to zero emission vehicles will significantly cut air pollution, by completely removing tailpipe emissions, but of course the Department absolutely recognises that zero emission vehicles will not solve the particular problem of brakes, tyres and road-surface wear. As transport continues to decarbonise, tackling those sources will be increasingly important. To support that, we recently consulted on adopting the Euro 7 standard in Great Britain. That will require us to regulate brake and tyre wear particles for the very first time, helping to reduce those emissions to clean up our air. We will publish the Government response to the consultation shortly.

Alongside the regulatory action, we have been investing in strengthening our evidence base, so that we have the most up-to-date data possible on tackling non-exhaust emissions through our four-year research programme, which completed in 2025. The programme’s findings have helped us to play a leading role in the development of common international limits for brake and tyre wear emissions. That work underpins the Euro 7 standard and provides the consistent framework for such emissions and for cutting those pollutants across international markets. The Department will continue to contribute to future development of the regulations at a UN level, including considering more stringent limits as technology continues to progress.

Q242 Minister, when can we expect to see binding standards in place? I know you said that you are out to consultation at the moment and that you are feeding into the UN brake emissions regulations, but we are keen to find out when we will know what the standards are going to be and when they will actually be operative.
We continue to work at an international level. In the consultation we proposed that new brake emission regulations will be introduced for all new cars and vans by 29 November 2027.

Q243 What recent assessment has been made of the contribution of maritime emissions to air pollution in UK coastal and port communities, and what steps is the Department taking to reduce associated health impacts through the clean maritime plan and subsequent policies?

This area is not normally my responsibility. I have prepared for this bit, but my colleague here might be able to chime in as well. The Department is committed to ensuring that we have cleaner air for our coastal communities and people living near ports while maintaining the vital role that ports and shipping play in supporting trade, jobs and economic growth.

We are taking action at the domestic level but also at the international level to reduce emissions from shipping, support the transition to cleaner fuels and technologies and work with ports to improve their environmental performance. There is already an established framework to address air pollutant emissions from shipping. At the international level, the International Maritime Organisation regulates emissions of sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter. We are continuing to make progress in this area. The recent adoption of the north Atlantic emission control area by the International Maritime Organisation will extend the highest tier of air pollution controls to all UK waters once it is fully effective from 2028. I don’t know if you want to expand on that, Jennifer?
The north Atlantic emission control area has recently been adopted, and, as the Minister said, the whole of the UK’s waters will be covered by the most stringent air pollution targets.

Q244 Can I ask about a specific port, which is not far from me? The Dover port on the English channel is one of our busiest waters, with so many ferries moving every 24 hours, and there are lorries parked on the motorway in my constituency every time there is disruption in the water. There is a quick solution to get better air and reduce that lorry movement: the channel tunnel runs at less than 50% of its capacity, so we basically need to move the lorries on to rail. That would be wonderful to reduce the air pollution caused by hundreds of thousands of lorries. Subsequent Governments have ignored this. Is there any thought on it from the Department? If it is an easy fix, why are we not doing that?

I turn to my colleague here, but on rail generally, you will see with the establishment of Great British Railways that our main focus is around passengers but also increasing freight on the rail network in order to achieve the very benefits you are talking about, including internationally.

We are looking at ways in which we can reduce the impact of ports and the emissions from ports on air quality. At the end of August, we published the Department’s “Net Zero Ports: Call for Evidence”. That really highlighted the vital role that ports can play in reducing emissions and the opportunities for them to improve air quality. We are focusing on championing what ports need in terms of their energy needs in wider Government. That will hopefully remove barriers to ports, for example, delivering shore power, where the ships can plug in rather than keep the engines running and increase air pollution that way.
Q245 What steps is the Department taking to address the gap between the ambitions of the clean maritime plan and the progress to date in reducing maritime-related air pollution?
I will have to turn to Jennifer on that one.

The clean maritime plan was published under a previous Government in 2019. This Government published the maritime decarbonisation strategy in 2025, and that set out our vision for decarbonising maritime and improving air quality and the wider environment. As the Minister set out, it sets out our domestic and international approach to that.
Q246 How is the Department for Transport quantifying the specific contribution of aviation to the air quality of local communities?
I will turn to you again, Jennifer .

We publish the statistics on emissions from across the economy, including aviation. The Government are committed to decarbonising aviation, helping us reach net zero, clean up our air and reduce air pollution.

Q247 What about the impact on particular communities , perhaps those that are near airports? How are we looking at that? How is the information that you are gathering at that higher level impacting different communities differently and how are you measuring that?

Local areas monitor their air quality, and they will have to have air quality action plans and management areas to do that. In specific hotspots, be that aviation or ports, there are specific measures to try to reduce emissions as much as possible. A lot of the air pollution coming from airports is surface access, so improving public transport and transitioning to electric vehicles will help in those areas.

Q248 Some things are relatively easy to attribute to that, in terms of the impact on local communities. If you are talking about the road transport coming in, it is very clear that is in a specific geographic area. What about the wider impact of aviation? How is the specific impact of that on the community measured, as opposed to the wider impact?
We might have to take that question away and write to the Committee about that.

Q249 We know that electrification alone will not remove all emissions associated with transport. Minister Lightwood, can you give us an overview of the steps that the Department is taking to reduce traffic volumes in the most polluted areas?

This Government are taking a balanced, whole-system approach, focused on improving services and infrastructure so that people have a real choice in how they travel. I draw the Committee’s attention to our “Better Connected” document, which is a fantastic read. We are looking to create a more joined-up, people-focused transport system that makes sustainable travel more attractive, convenient and affordable for everyday journeys. That will help accelerate that journey to low-emission travel.

Members will be aware of the affordability measures we have introduced: maintaining the £3 bus fare cap for the rest of 2026—the Prime Minister announced that, from January, it will reduce to £2 throughout 2027; free bus travel for children over the summer; freezing rail fares for the first time in 30 years; and announcing just the other week that we will remove the time limits for disabled travellers so that they can travel 24/7 from April 2027.

That has all been supported through the Bus Services Act, which I was pleased to lead through Parliament, and the Railways Bill. Alongside that critical investment in our public transport, we supported active travel through the third cycling and walking investment strategy, which was published in June. Something like £4.5 billion is projected to be invested into active travel up until 2030 from a wide range of funding streams, including £1.1 billion for Active Travel England to track the progress of active travel. We have set ambitious targets for something like 60% of children aged five to 16 to usually walk to school by 2035.
We want to move people away from cars by providing a wide menu of alternative, trusted, cleaner, greener, more sustainable, and affordable means for people to get about.

Q250 For many people in more rural areas, bus services are patchy or finish early at night. The Labour Rural Research Group has looked into that in its recent report—I will absolutely send you a copy, because there is some good stuff in there. An electric car may be a solution for those people. I know they are coming down in price, but the cost of affording one is still a barrier to people scrapping their ageing internal combustion engine cars. What work is the Department doing to address that inequality for people who cannot afford to buy EVs?

E nsuring a fair and inclusive transition to zero emission vehicles is a key priority for the Government. We recognise that the benefits and opportunities associated with electric vehicles must be accessible to all parts of society, not just those who are able to purchase a new vehicle or install a home c harge point. Up -f ront costs continue to be higher than for some conventional vehicles.

Overall, the cost of electric vehicles is falling. The second - hand market for electric vehicles is growing , and they can offer significantly lower running costs. According t o Auto tr ade r’s data from April , EVs were cheaper than petrol cars for the first time . I think that is a really interesting point . A broad and increasing range of EV models are now available o n the second - hand market for around £20,000 , w ith the average price of a three - and - a - half - year - old EV around £18,000.

C harging is really important as well. We want everybody to be able to charge an electric vehicle easily where they live , a nd that is why we are providing additional funding to councils to install cross - pa ve ment charging channels. W hil e local authorities may decide their own cross - pa ve ment arrangements , over 80% have applied for funding from the D epartment in this area , so we expect more installation soon . B ut I am very acutely aware of the cost differential between charging at home and using the public network. In fact, I charge d my EV on the way back from the Great North Run, which I ran yesterday — I wanted to get that in Hansard . Unfortunately, the Prime Minister beat me by over 20 minutes.

W e want to narrow th e cost difference between home cha r ging and public charging , an d we have commissioned an independent review of public charging costs , led by Philip New. T hat is examining what further measures we can introduce to reduce the prices that some drivers are facing , a nd it is going to be reporting in autumn of 2026.

Q251 F or people like me who do not have off - street parking , will it be cheaper to charge using the local council ’s provision ? O ne of the things that is hindering the shift is that people cannot realise the financial benefits if they have to charge at a supermarket or a service station.

We have made funding available for cross - pavement charging. E ssentially , it is like a channel in the pavement that the cable goes down. T hat enables people without off - street parking to take advantage of the much , much lower cost involved with at - home charging . But as I said, we are looking at how we can narrow th e gap between the cost of public charging —it is sometimes 10 times the cost, if not more — and the home charging costs , a nd that is exactly the work that Philip New is undertaking for the D epartment.

You mentioned the availability of public transport in rural areas. W hen it comes to the bus funding that we have given to local areas , we have added a rurality element for the very first time . In the past, it was almost like a “ Hunger Games ” style funding competition to get the money to improve bus services . T h e rurality element h as helped to narrow th e gap , but there is still a lot of work to be done to improve rural transport provision across the country.

Q252 You mentioned the second - hand car market. T here is a great electric car grant for new EVs , bu t has any consideration been given to applying any sort of incentive to the second - hand car market , to really kick on EV ownership?

No, because what you are already seeing is that , for the first time , a second-hand electric vehicle is cheaper than a petrol car, if you look at Autotrader . You are already seeing the market itself dictate. People are adopting EVs because of the lower running costs, and I think we will continue to see that narrowing of the gap.

Q253 We recently saw the Mayor of London celebrating the reduction in road-based air pollution as a result of his introduction of ULEZ. We have seen many other mayors fight shy of that, given some of the political pushback around ULEZ previously. What is the Government’s approach to ULEZ? Is it pretty much agnostic, or is the Department encouraging more mayors to introduce these things, which we are told by the Mayor of London have been tremendously successful?
I think it is for local areas to decide.
Q254 So you are broadly agnostic as a Department .

We are agnostic. It is really important that these types of decisions are made by local leaders, because they understand their communities best. They understand the social and economic drivers and the local conditions.

Q255 I understand that, but given that something like 5% of vehicles are responsible for something like 70% of exhaust emissions pollution, and recognising why some mayors might have resistance in their local areas to schemes like ULEZ, shouldn’t the Government and your Department at least do all they can to try and make it attractive for local mayors to introduce it in their communities, and also help with the messaging? Many people who are opposed to ULEZ do not realise that they will not actually be affected by it. Many people consider it to be a sort of congestion charge, but it is a high-polluting vehicle charge rather than a general congestion charge. I would challenge you on whether a policy of being agnostic means the Government are doing all they can to reduce emissions. Shouldn’t you, at the very least, while maybe accepting that mayors get to make the final decision, do all you can to make it attractive for them to reduce the number of polluting vehicles on our streets?

Local authorities play a key role in reducing transport pollution. As I said, they are best placed to decide on the priorities for their area. There is something like £21 billion of local transport funding across England over this spending period. We are backing local leaders with that long-term, simplified funding and giving them the certainty that they need in order to plan ahead to deliver and grow their economies. We set out in our local transport plan guidance the Department’s expectations on how funding can be used to reduce air pollution, but it is very much the case that local leaders should be able to decide. Is there anything extra you want to add, Jennifer?

Clean air zones have been introduced selectively by local authorities where the evidence shows that they are the quickest way to reduce the nitrogen dioxide exceedances in their area and where other options would not deliver the same results as quickly. DFT and DEFRA work really closely with local authorities and have provided £582 million of Government funding. Clean air zones do work. In the areas of cities that have them, between 2014 and 2019 nitrogen dioxide exceedances fell by between 18% and 46%. That is one option that a local authority has in dealing with its exceedances.

Q256 Minister Lightwood , on the more general move towards electric vehicles, hasn’t there been some confused messaging, particularly out of the Treasury? We have seen fuel duty under successive Governments remain at the same level for quite a long time. It has not remotely kept pace with inflation; it is significantly lower than it was 10 years ago. At the same time, the Government announced recently the intention to have a pay-per-mile tax on electric vehicles, which we know has had an impact on consumers choosing whether to move to electric vehicles. Shouldn’t the Government, more unmistakably in tax terms, try to drive forward that transition to electric vehicles, rather than, as I say, sending the somewhat mixed messages we are getting currently?

Even with those changes taken into consideration, EV sales remain really strong . In May, for the first time , over a quarter of new cars registered were EVs , with registrations up 34% compared with May 2025 . We c ommitted £7.5 billion to 2035 to support the transition to zero emission vehicles . That includes £2 billion for the electric car grant, which has been hugely successful , helping over 120 , 000 people to choose an EV , with grants of up to £3,750 for the most sustainably manufactured vehicles . It also includes £1 billion for vans and trucks and £600 million for charging infrastructure.

Q257 We have just a couple more questions for M inister Lightwood. I know you are on a time budget, Minister Hardy, so if you feel you need to go, go with our thanks. We will not keep Minister Lightwood much longer, but thank you very much for the evidence we have heard from you.

Minister Lightwood, you are absolutely right that the market for new electric vehicles has continued to be positive, primarily driven by the fleet sector. There have been positive measures in place under successive Governments to encourage the fleet sector to move. They have been very clear to us that the second - hand market remains difficult, in as much as the amount that they lose from buying a new car , compared with a second - hand vehicle , makes it challenging for them to continue. The British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association ha s spoken powerfully about the pressure on its members and the vital role that fleet plays. A necdotal evidence from the motor sector is that the interest of non - fleet customers in the second - hand market is very much driven by the price signals. W hat representations have you made to the Treasury about the importance of continu ing to send messages that encourage people to take those vehicles, when the Government are leaving fuel duty stagnan t—and celebrating doing so—a t the same time as introducing a new tax on electric vehicles ?
I have been doing this role for around two weeks , Chair , so I will pass over to my colleague to cover the conversations that happened before my time.

There is a three - pronged approach. Y ou have regulation in the form of the Z EV mandate , the electric car grant, which the Minister spoke about , and all the charging infrastructure provisions. As you say , given th at electric vehicle drivers do not pay fuel duty at the pump , t he Government are introducing a new add - on to vehicle excise duty so that all drivers contribute an appropriate share to use of the roads. R ates will be 3p per mile for electric cars , which is around half the average fuel duty equivalent rate . P lug - in hybrids will pay half that rate again, because they will continue to pay fuel duty on some of their mileage .

Q258 You are telling me what I already know . I appreciate that you are only two weeks into the role , Minister, s o we look forward to the forthcoming B udget to s how further progress . This country has done well on electric vehicles, but my worry is that the mood music is facing slightly in the wrong direction because we are hearing suggestions that the Z EV mandate will be watered down. Even some people on our side of the Chamber are suggesting that that should happen. As the Chancellor considers these difficult choices as he heads towards the B udget , will you make sure that he is considering the impact of his decisions on fuel duty and electric vehicle pay - per - mile charges on electric vehicle sales ?
As you know, Chair, taxation is a matter for HMT and the Chancellor . I am sure he w ill have heard loud and clear what you have said today.
Q259 If he has not, can you make sure that he does?

I am sure we will have those conversations , but it is important to put on record that we have gone out to consultation about the Z EV mandate. I want to emphasise that the phase-out dates are not changing. The Government’s overall ambition remains the same.

Again, EV sales have remained strong. As I said, in May, for the first time, over a quarter of new cars registered were EVs. Registrations were up 34%, compared with May 2025. The car grant has helped 120,000 people to make that transition. I hear exactly what you say about the taxation, however, and I am sure the Chancellor has too.

Q260 Before I bring in my colleague, on the issue of plug-in hybrids, have the Government done any assessment of how much they are actually using electricity, as opposed to just their fuel? Anecdotally, I hear from many people, particularly in the fleet sector, where drivers are probably not actually paying the bill themselves, because their companies are, that they continue to have plug-in hybrids, but that those are basically operating as emitting vehicles. Have you ever done any assessment of that? Can you tell us about it?
That is one I will come back to you on in writing, Chair, if that is okay. I do not have that to hand.
Of course. Finally, I bring in Barry Gardiner.

Q261 To follow up on the interesting discussion you had with Minister Lightwood, Chair, this is about the role of central Government. I understand, Minister, what you are saying about local mayors, local decisions and devolution, but often, certainly in the past, different areas have received different incentives from Government. Would it not be better if there were a national framework that each mayor and community could look at and say, “If we go down that route, we know what support we will get from Government to do this”? That is not trying to take the decision away from them, but giving them certainty about the support they would have if they did choose that route.

I can write to you with further details, if that would be useful. I hear exactly what you are saying. Fundamentally, in terms of direction of travel, the Government as a whole are about devolution and empowering local leaders. I think we do set a national framework, but with the flexibility to take into consideration local needs, local pressures and so on. But I will take that away and write back to you, if that is okay.
I appreciate that. Giving them certainty enables them to take the decision. At the moment , when they do not have that certainty, they think, “Well, it could be this or it could be that.”
Sure.

Q262 F inally, on that point, we all know about the political pressure against mayors introducing schemes that reduce emissions. The Government should at least be in the lead, saying, “Look, this is the benefit to your health. Don’t see this as, ‘Am I going to pay more for my travel?’”— 95% of drivers will not, and every single year the number of drivers who will pay ULEZ is going down —“ but as, ‘Am I going to be kept safer in the future? Are my children going to be safer?’” If we have that conversation, we might see the public demanding schemes, rather than pushing back. I will just leave you with the thought that, although I accept this is a local decision, rather than the Government being agnostic, it would be helpful if they were doing what they could to support mayors to do these things. Instead, they are saying, “This is a local decision” and basically leaving mayors swinging in the wind if they choose to do something we know will make a real difference.

I hear what you say, Chair, but when I spoke earlier, I talked about incentivising the transition to public transport by ensuring that we have high-quality, reliable and affordable public transport. Record funding is going into mayoral combined authorities across the country to support mayors to do exactly that—with bus franchising in Greater Manchester, we have seen 14% year-on-year growth in passenger numbers—to get more people out of their car and using public transport, and to ensure we have a more integrated transport system. The Department is doing a lot to support mayors, but I hear your overall message.
Thank you very much indeed. We appreciate your evidence, Minister, and that of Ms Raynor.
