It is an incredible amount of time, and the community has had a lot to put up with. One of the things that we will ask the new chief executive and the new chair is to really have a look at that timeframe and test, “What is the opportunity to improve on that?” Mark has set out his ranges—or bookends—of 2040-43, but we want a new chief executive to look at them.

We also want them to have the freedom, to be fair, to give us their honest views about the right time to deliver the various parts. The next few years are largely in the planning. The most important lesson we can learn is to get a really robust set of expectations around costs and around schedule before we move into delivery. We want the chief executive to have a really good run at that. What we will not do is put in an arbitrary date and say, “By next year you’ve got to have all this sorted,” because I think that you would fundamentally set them up to fail. We will give them some space.

We are also focused, with Network Rail and all the operators at the current station, on making sure there are benefits being delivered to improve the experience that passengers have going through Euston—today, this year, next year, every year—until we get the fully redeveloped station.

Q36 That is fine. My next question is about whether this is a mega-project or not. I am looking at your Government major projects portfolio. In April this year, the redevelopment of Euston conventional station was considered a Government major project, which is a mega-project. Have you answered this question already? It is now a mega-project, isn’t it? Is that correct?

It is not designated separately as a mega-project. It is part of the HS2 mega-project. To my mind, it feels like a slightly moot point at the moment, because it benefits from the flexibilities and integrated assurance that comes from HS2 being designated a mega-project. There is a discussion for us to have with NISTA and the Treasury about whether at some point it will be useful to designate it separately. But I think it is fair to say, Dean, that we do not see any constraints in it having a separate designation to being part of the HS2 designation at the moment.

The thing it must absolutely not do is create some kind of competitive incentive with HS2, because it is a core part of getting Mark’s ranges delivered. It needs to be properly integrated. The ideal solution would be to get the flexibilities and freedoms that come with mega-project status, without creating it as something entirely separate.

Q37 Apologies, but I am going to be very specific. The Government major projects portfolio, which lists the mega-projects, has them separately listed. It has HS2 phase 1 and then the redevelopment of the Euston conventional station. You are saying that they are actually the same thing. Is that correct, even though they are separately listed as two separate things?

Yes, they are separately listed. There is a genuine question that we need to work through with NISTA about how best to manage those two programmes together when there is such an interlink between them. It may be something that we phase, so that they may stay together for the next few years over planning, but as we get into delivery, we may change that. Our view is that we need to keep that under review.

Q38 I appreciate that it is also below the £10 billion threshold, at £8 billion. My last question is on paragraph 6.10, which says that you have begun early market engagement on the approach with the private sector. Without a defined plan, it is probably difficult to define what that might look like, but you are looking at some form of PFI or other arrangement. Are you learning from other Government projects, especially those in the nuclear industry and others where good contract arrangements might be important?

Yes. Let me hopefully give you some reassurance. One of the reasons why this takes a long time is that if we go into a commercial arrangement but we are unable to be really clear, or we have a lot of uncertainty, we will pay significantly more for that uncertainty. In terms of the support that we are getting, we have some external expertise coming in to support the programme, so the Department is not doing it on its own. We are working closely with the Treasury and with NISTA, and with external expertise, as I say.

We have had some early engagement with the market. We have had about 70 responses to that engagement and they are saying the things that you would expect them to say. Their concerns are: “How do we manage inflation and what protections are there around inflation?” There are also questions about how you manage the interfaces within Euston itself. If you are a private provider, you want to be able to control your own destiny and deliver that programme, so if there are lots of interfaces, how are we as the Department going to make sure that those are properly capped off and managed?

Those are things that we will need to work through, so that as and when we go out to a procurement, we will have those capped off so that we get the best deal for the taxpayer. I would also say that we will do a deal only if we can get the right deal for the taxpayer. Again, we will need to agree the thresholds for that with the Treasury before we take a view on it.

Q39 I want to ask a question from the point of view of future HS2 passengers about their route to and from the HS2 terminus at Euston. On the whole, they will not be stopping at Euston, but getting the tube, rail, HS1, buses—
Bikes.

Bikes—everybody always says bikes, which is good and fine, but not if people have luggage generally—taxis, private hire, or private pick-up and drop-off by friends and family. Who is making sure that all those different transport choices are integrated into the design at the early stages? We all know of infrastructure developments where passengers were not thought of. Walking distances are an issue for many. TfL, much as we love them, tend to work in silos themselves, and they have three, if not four, different business interests in terms of their public transport provision. Who is holding the ring on this and how will we make sure that the design and the thinking is built in at the start?

It is a really good and fair challenge. I talked about the concept design and the reason why we have all the dutyholders in the EDC, and it is for that reason. TfL have already been very clear about how we will manage taxis and the bus interchange. When I talk about a concept of operations, before we move even into concept design, one of my challenges to the EDC and the partnership is: “Have we got a plan that understands how we would operate this station at a high level, and have we got all the red lines from all those partners that will be managing passengers?” We know, for example, that one of TfL’s concerns is that if you have two stations—Euston Square and Euston—some passengers might need to tap in and tap out. All those issues need to be managed, and that is why we are bringing all the partners into the tent. As we sign off and move into concept design, the EDC will need to get approval from its board and from that strategy board at a political level that says, “Everybody now says we are content that all our requirements are being met.”

There is a challenge that we will have to manage, which will be ambition versus affordability, and part of the EDC will have to manage those trade-offs with the partners and with Ministers as we do that. To give you some reassurance, the thinking is happening now, as part of that planning. We will not enter concept design unless we are confident that all the partners are happy entering into this level of design. Are we equally mature for Euston as TfL would be if they were doing a station on their own? If we are not, there is more work to be done.
Q40 The point I am trying to make is that there are some of those transport choices that none of those partners see as their priority, but HS2 is moving this new group of passengers.

I should be clear that Andy Lord, the TfL commissioner, is very clear about the centrality of the redevelopment of Euston to the overall London transport system. Just as Mark, as chief exec of HS2, is very generous with his time to the Euston programme and the new Euston Delivery Company, so is Andy personally for TfL, because he represents all those different transport needs for those travelling through London.
Q41 Except those going to St Pancras for HS1 and other lines out of St Pancras.
Making sure that they can get there and that the flows work effectively, which is the work that Dean has described.

Q42 We noticed on the visit how close the Euston development is to existing and often long-standing communities. What steps are you taking to reduce the impact of building works and delay on the residents and businesses around Euston?

Going forwards, our expectation is that the EDC will co-ordinate that work to make sure that all the partners are joined up in the way that they interact and manage the community. Mark might want to talk a bit about this, but on HS2 we have some funding—about £2 million—that has gone into making sure that we can mitigate some of the challenges that we are creating for communities. I know that Camden has put in about £3.5 million as well, particularly to mitigate around noise.

There are some things that HS2 has been able to do over the last year that have made things much easier, including road movements and the removal of spoil from the site by rail as opposed to road. But we are very conscious that it has been a long time and this will carry on for a long time, so we will also look at maintaining the community funds that we have now for as long as they are needed.

It is a great question. The Drummond Street community, in particular, is one of a handful of communities on HS2 that has been very disrupted and suffered prolongation—in fact, it may be the most affected community with prolongation. I have spent a lot of my personal time with the community. As Dean said, one of the best things we have done in recent weeks is to get the spoil away by rail. We have one train a day that takes about 50 lorries off the road. But there are no two ways about it: the Drummond Street community, in particular, has been separated from the main effort.

We have to redouble our efforts to help the community. The Euston hub has been very successful for the community. The skills centre for Camden, for the construction teams, in the basement of our large development is very successful, and w e have just opened a skills yard within our site to try to get local employment in the construction industry. But there are no two ways about it: we need to stay focused on the needs of that community. They will remain very disrupted and, to be sure, it is top of the agenda for Dean and me when we deal with them. I have a lot of sympathy and empathy with what has happened.

Q43 Dean, I think this one’s for you—oh joy. In figure 12, we can see quite how much land, housing and whatever else HS2 or the DFT—HS2 was an agent, if I am reading it correctly, so whichever way you want to look at it—has purchased. It is a vast amount of property and many square miles of Britain. That no doubt enriched and put new wheels on the Bentleys of lots of lawyers through compulsory purchase orders and so on. The decision was made in October ’23 that we were not going to go ahead, so a lot of this land is now surplus to requirement. Why has it taken so long for it to be returned, and what is your strategy for doing so? Under the Crichel Down rule—if nobody has been there, it is a wonderful house down in Wiltshire—you are required to offer it to the landowner who has been disadvantaged as a result of the CPO. What is the plan? I think, having messed up people’s lives, it is incumbent on the state to put it right as quickly as possible.

There are four areas where we have property. There is phase 1, where we are closing our existing property. Mark and his team are doing that, and we continue to monitor them on their ability to close out properties at phase 1. There is phase 2a between Birmingham and Manchester, where we hold some permanent and some temporary land, and there are the small number of properties—about 200—that will be needed for NPR.

I think what you are talking about is the land on the east, which is the Leeds leg. That is about 500 properties that are no longer needed. We have an agent that will now take forward a strategy to dispose of those properties. It has taken a while because we needed to work out what the Government’s plan for that area was. As you say, we also needed a strategy. There are 500 properties, but only 300 of those will have the Crichel Down rule applied to them. The other 200 were bought by the Department, sometimes because the seller wanted to sell them to us—they were not necessarily compulsorily purchased.

On the next steps, an agent will provide us with a strategy in the autumn—we are expecting that to be by October. They will be testing and piloting that strategy with vacant properties over the next few weeks. We will then, in the new year, move into—I hope that we will have some properties on the market this year. The challenge we will have, and the balanced judgment we have to make, is that we want to get properties disposed of, but we do not want to flood the market and undermine the local housing markets for local residents, and we want to protect the taxpayer. There is a sensible sequencing that will need to come as part of that strategy.
Q44 Presumably, a lot of this is land as well as properties, because you bought the land.
Yes, it is a mixture of commercial and private residential.

Q45 But again, I could argue that given what has been happening with death taxes on farmland, farmland has come down. Equally, the economy is grinding to a halt, so you do not have the demand for housing. We are seeing house prices come down radically in London, and that is now starting to affect the rest of the country—we are told not Manchester, for some reason, but I do not believe that. At the end of the day, you are more vulnerable the longer you wait. As a matter of interest, why have you waited so long? Is it just because people have not been able to get their act together?

The picture is complicated, as Dean says, and it reflects the decisions that different Administrations have taken over a number of years—decisions on the full Y scheme moving back to phase 1, and the commitment of this new Administration ultimately to build a new line north from Birmingham to Manchester. That has meant, as Dean said, that we have needed to wait to understand and assess the consequences of the decisions to curtail the original HS1 programme for our future heavy rail infrastructure, and to make sure that we have the land and property strategy to deliver against. As with everything else, we are taking the decisions that we have in front of us and making sure that we best support all the communities and individuals affected, as well as securing best value.

Q46 But in the same way that Ruth was concerned about the local residents around Euston, I think we should be concerned about people who have had their lives turned upside down by a centrally planned statist failure, which has not only messed up their lives but now left them with uncertainty. In my view, we have a moral obligation to sort that out as quickly as possible.
Absolutely.
Q47 It is all very well to have ministerial decisions awaiting approval and everything else, but we need a plan.

I read in the R eport that you are retaining some land in case you decide to go further north. When I was on the board of the FA when they mothballed the national football centre, they ended up with a load of grass cutting. You cannot just leave tracts of land with nothing happening to it, because you disadvantage local farmers, you create weed banks and you do all sorts of damage to nature. What are you doing about that, because that is going to cost you money?

It is a very fair question. First of all, on the strategy, we will share that with the Committee when it has been agreed in the autumn. On the land that we are retaining, I know that one of the concerns is what happens with empty properties. The plan is that we will maintain properties. Some of those are listed, as well, so we need to maintain those in a state commensurate with their listed status.

Where we can, we will look to rent out properties, and, as with sales, they are rented out at market rates. Some of those require some capital investment to bring them up to standard. There is a value for money and balanced judgment about the extent to which you invest in those. Let us be honest: the Government does not want to get into the business of being a property developer or manager here, but where we are holding assets, we need to do it in a sensible and well-balanced way where we rent out as much as possible.

I think we are at about 60% rental of the properties that we have in that space. We will look to maximise that at market rates as far as possible, without fundamentally spending more taxpayer money than we absolutely need to.
Those principles apply to the agricultural land holdings just as much as to the residential properties.
Correct. In fact, in many cases, the previous owners are still using that land under lease from us.

Q48 Can you assure the Committee that we are not wasting taxpayers’ money on this now? It looked to me like this new agent you have appointed is quite well remunerated for what they are doing. Again, it is rather like when I was on the board of the FA . I t was going to cost a million quid to cut the grass at the new national football centre, so I said, “I’ll buy some tractors and a topper and hire somebody, and I’ll do it for a quarter of a million a year,” at which point they changed it. Are the taxpayers being disadvantaged by this multitude of loose ends?

My view on this is very clear. We pay market rates, but we will look at this very closely . A s it goes on , o ne of the challenges that we have is that we have an income stream from properties that are rented and we have an opex to maintain those properties. That broadly evens out. Let us be really clear: we lose money on these schemes because we are required to invest in them. We have an incentive to keep properties in a good state, but where we can get rid of them, we are looking to get rid of them.

This is something we will look at very closely. It is also something very close to Ministers’ hearts. We have a KPI with HS2 around the management, disposal and completion of properties as well. Frankly, it is something that I am checked on by Ministers regularly. This has visibility at the highest level.
Q49 Finally—this is probably one for you as well, Mark—when are you going to start returning this unwanted land to people?
In terms of the temporary possessions?
Yes, in terms of temporarily possessed properties, which I think is still your responsibility.
The temporary land on the formerly known phase 2a is starting.
Q50 That is starting, is it?

Yes, it is starting. We are filling boreholes in. There are 450 boreholes on temporary land to fill in. They need to be remediated. That is under way now. We will have that completed in the next 18 months. Some of this land is under licence; some of it was actually purchased, but that process is under way. The permanent land requires a decision before—
Q51 So it is in hand and it is not going to be delayed by ministerial holidays or tardy decision making.
No, no. The temporary land is under way.

Q52 Finally—Jo, I think this is for you—I have been thinking about this following my question earlier. Would you commit to the Committee to doing an independent review of the cancellation costs ? I don’t think it is great that it is just HS2 and DFT; I would like some form of confirmation that that is independently verified. That is for you, I think .

Absolutely. As I said, we are very focused — I hope the Committee would support that —o n making sure all efforts are applied to the decision that has been made by the Government to complete the program me safely, at lowest reasonable cost and as fast as possible. We have made a judgment about the proportionality of the work. Th e decision has now been made to continue. Obviously, if it is something the Committee recommends , we will consider it with Ministers, but we made a proportionate assessment of the amount of work we wanted Mark and his team to put into assessing the cost of remediation. But we will of course consider—
Q53 With my taxpayer hat on, I think that would be desirable. That is my opinion ; the Chair—
We will consider recommendations from the Committee—
The C hairperson might overrule me !
Let’s wait and see what is in the recommendations, shall we?

Q54 M y final question follow s on from Rupert ’ s . Clearly, we now have some answers a bout some of the commercial and housing development. The NAO Report says : “The g overnment will also need to decide ”— I know you have answered this question before, but I just want to get a tiny bit more detail about whether this should be designated as a mega - project now . I know that it is below the threshold of £ 10 billion, but we are seeing increments and also commercial real estate and retail development here. The NAO assessment is that it does fit “ most of the characteristics of one ,” so are the Government going to recommend that , and what parameters will you need to utilise to get it to that point if you are going to ?

It is something we keep under review with the Treasury and the National I nfrastructure and Service Transformation Authority. It is not in my gift to designate it . It is a discussion that we will continue having within Government , and certainly the assurance the Committee can have from me and from Dean is that we will advocate for whatever we think gives the Euston programme, and the HS2 program me, the very best conditions for successful delivery, given the difficult history that ha s got us to this point.
At the moment , the Euston program me, because it is part of HS2 , does not lack any of the flexibilities that it would get as part of a mega - project.
Thank you very much.

Thank you. That brings our session to an end . Thank you all very much for appearing and particularly for the candour with which you have responded. It is obviously a project with a very troubled history, as everyone on this Committee knows, but it has been really useful and constructive to hear your most recent update , so thank you very much for that.

Witnesses: Cristina Nicolotti Squires and Glenn Preston .

Q107 Good morning and welcome to this meeting of the Scottish Affairs Committee . W e would like to discuss with our colleagues from Ofcom issues relating to STV and probably a little about Gaelic broadcasting as well. I am very grateful to you for coming along this morning and giving us your time. Could you just briefly introduce yourselves and say what your role is?

Thank you very much for having us , Chair. I am director of Ofcom Scotland and head of the Ofcom Scotland team , which is based up in our Edinburgh office . W e represent Ofcom right across our regulatory responsibilities and I am Ofcom’s senior leader in Scotland. We have about 130 colleagues based in Edinburgh now who do a whole range of jobs across Ofcom’s regulatory responsibilities.
I am the group director of Broadcasting and Media at Ofcom, so I lead the team that carries out our regulation. I joined Ofcom a couple of years ago , after 35 years in journalism.

Q108 Thank you both very much. I will just start by asking a couple of questions about Gaelic broadcasting. First, it appears to us that there are several bodies involved in Gaelic broadcasting between Ofcom, MG ALBA and the BBC , and the Scottish Government have an interest too , of course . To what extent does that complexity create governance challenges , or does it create governance challenges ? W ould there be a risk that , because that responsibility is shared among so many organisations , no single body has ownership of the long term future of broadcasting in Gaelic?

That is an interesting question. I was reflecting on the session that you did with MG ALBA and the BBC last week. I have been in this job for about 10 years so I find the clarity of roles and what we have to do relatively straightforward, but that might be a passage of time point rather than necessarily if you were looking at it from the outside when, as you say, you could understand that it is a fairly complicated picture. It runs pretty smoothly, to be honest with you. We would describe Ofcom’s duties as largely fiduciary in nature. You will likely already know that we make appointments, or we certainly make recommendations for appointments , to the MG ALBA board ; it is Scottish Ministers who take those recommendations and are formally responsible for the appointments.

We hold the Gaelic media fund : the grant in aid that is paid by the Scottish Government to MG ALBA comes via Ofcom, and MG ALBA then draw that down for both the operational and the content sides of their business. There is an MOU that exists between the Scottish Government and MG ALBA as a matter for them. We have no involvement in the preparation of that but we meet the MG ALBA executive quarterly just to look at performance issues and how it is performing against the obligations that the Scottish Government place on it under the MOU that it has . That all works relatively smoothly—it is quite well oiled—lots of the people involved have been doing it for a long time. Then obviously the UK Government and UK Parliament have the responsibility for the overarching framework.

That is where those kinds of questions that you were discussing in last week’s session around, for example, the adequacy of funding or the statutory nature of Gaelic broadcasting , sit. Those are not matters that we engage directly with as the regulator; we do not have responsibilities for MG ALBA funding decisions or its status on the statute book, for example, but it works relatively well for us .

Q109 That leads me on nicely to my second question , which is around the BBC operating licence . F rom the evidence we were given , w e understand that Gaelic broadcasting largely operates through that prism of the BBC operating licence , and I wonder whether you think that is sufficient from a regulatory and policy perspective?

Yes. I saw the comments that the chief executive made about the number of lines that MG ALBA or Gaelic broadcasting gets in our annual report on the BBC. That was a fair comment, but the whole point of what we do with our annual reporting on the BBC is it is a holistic view of how the BBC is performing against the specific conditions and the operating licence across all its services, and how it is fulfilling the mission and public purposes. We do not tend to do kind of deep dive stuff into individual services such as BBC ALBA as part of that: no service really gets particular treatment in the annual reports that we do.

It probably underplays the amount of work that we do with MG ALBA on questions of performance. We other analyses of developments in the market, for example we have just published our annual Media Nations Scotland report in the last few weeks. There are two or three different sections in that looking at what has happened in Gaelic broadcasting over the last year ; for example , there is a bit of analysis of the brilliant live free - to - air Gaelic language coverage of the Commonwealth Games that was done through the partnership. We look at all the first run origination data—the hours, spend and so on—and do some analysis of that. This year we had stuff in there about the quality of Gaelic podcasting that was going on, for example, including through Radio nan Gàidheal as well. You could look at that BBC annual report in isolation and legitimately say that there is not a huge amount in there; if you look at it set against the other things that we publish and all the other work that we do with the MG ALBA board and executive , there is a lot more going on there.

Q110 T he question really comes back to the point that BBC A LBA is not explicitly mentioned in the operating licence. Is th e current framework sufficient to give both visibility and proper regulation to the organisation and if not , what changes would you like to see in that framework?

I should say that the operating licence contains specific provisions about hours and spend, for example, that you would have to have on the BBC ALBA service. But you are right that that would be an assessment of the BBC’s performance against its mission and public purposes, and particularly the Public Purpose 4 , which is the one that would be relevant for BBC ALBA.

Whether the governance and operation of MG ALBA itself has that adequate scrutiny is actually an interesting question. We fulfil the fiduciary duties that are quite narrow in the Broadcasting Acts of 1990 and 1996 and the Communications Act 2003 , and we would say we are content with the way those are working. There is a legitimate question about what the scrutiny is of the MOU arrangements between the Scottish Government and MG A LBA , for example, which is something this Committee or the Culture Committee at Holyrood might be interested in. There does not tend to be an annual assessment, for example, of MG ALBA’s performance against things like that. It lay s its annual report and accounts, and that is actually something that has to come via Ofcom. It does that here and at Holyrood as well . W e notify the Ministers and the Parliaments that that is happening, so there is an opportunity there to look at the performance of MG ALBA specifically , through that lens.

Q111 We are now going to move on to Ofcom’s decision about the STV changes. As you know , Ofcom was due to announce its decision on STV’s proposals before Easter this year but it was delayed until after the Scottish Parliament elections . Y ou will understand this caused quite a bit of consternation , with the National Union of Journalists calling it “ a stonishing. ” Can you explain why that decision was taken , please?

Yes. This was a difficult decision to make and we wanted to give it full consideration. We had a lot of public response, quite a bit of it generated by AI, which was a novelty that, as a regulator, we are all getting used to, and so we needed to make sure we went through the consultation responses carefully and gave it the fullest consideration. There was no other reasoning behind the delay.
Q112 Did y ou not factor into the initial timescales that the proposals would generate a lot of responses due to the levels of concern?

We knew that there would be a lot of responses and we knew how people felt because a lot of it had been expressed, but we had to go through each individual consultation response. If I am right, it was the first time we had such a volume that had been generated by artificial intelligence, which again, was something we wanted to be very careful how we handled. We were very keen to make sure that this was a consideration that was given full deliberation and analysis, and we did not want to rush into it.

I am struck by the point you make about what the NUJ said. At the beginning of the process, which was about mid-October last year, we actually had representations from a number of organisations—including the NUJ—that we should not rush the decision because it was too important. Then, when we reached the point just before the election period where actually we would not typically publish anything that had any kind of political ramifications, we were told we were too slow. So at the beginning of the process we were being told to slow down, and then we were being told we were too slow towards the end of the process.

We might get into this in the questioning, but I would observe that we got our first submission from STV in mid-October, had engagement with it about that, then it sent us a second submission towards the end of November last year. We published the consultation before Christmas, 19 December, I think. The 16th was it? Thank you. I am being corrected by one of your members. That concluded in mid-February and we then published on 1 June. As Cristina was saying, we had never had an AI-assisted campaign response such as we did for that particular consultation, when 90% of the responses—just over 1,100—came to us through an AI-assisted tool.

There was a campaign called Save STV North, and people were able to pick from a menu of possible responses and send stuff to us. We had not had something like that before. It also included a free text capability for people that generated an email to Ofcom from an individual’s account, so it gave us all sorts of personal data for people as well, which we had to manage quite carefully. We undertook to go through all those 1,100 responses in addition to those that came individually, to make sure that we were not missing any of the free text responses and that there was a proper full analysis of the evidence available to us. That is what took us the additional time. We had wanted to conclude this prior to the Scottish election period so that there was certainty for STV about who, how, and where it would be broadcasting from but we were still going through those 1,100 responses during that period, which is why it took us that additional period of time.

Q113 On that point, MPs are well used to dealing with campaign emails so I appreciate the volume. However, the concerns about the time taken and the delay are well founded : people expected a quicker response, particularly given the level of concern. I am really struck by the point you just made, Mr Preston, that you would not publish anything that had political ramifications. Are we to take from that that the election, or the level of political opposition to the changes, influenced the timing of the decision?
No, you should not take that from it because Ofcom essentially does not do publications across its entire regulatory remit during an election period.
I rrespective of what they are .
Yes.

Q114 W e all know when the Scottish Parliamentary elections are, and you previously stated that you would publish before Easter. Why was that statement made if there was no intention to do it immediately before the election?
A t that point we did not have all those AI-assisted responses that came in to us , and it took us a long period of time to go through each individual response.
Before Easter was still in the lead up to a Scottish Parliamentary election.
Yes, absolutely.
Q115 Why was that timescale given if, as you have said, you would not normally put anything out before a Parliamentary election?

It was our hope that we would be able to conclude it by that period. What we had not accounted for is that large number of AI-assisted responses that required that particular type of consideration. It took us several weeks to go through those.

Q116 I understand that, but the point still remains that you initially said the decision would be out before Easter when that election was already on the calendar, so the two things do not really match up for me.

We hoped to publish before Easter. That was before we realised we would be getting that volume of AI-assisted responses. We publish our responses afterwards and, as Glenn said, we had to remove all the personal data. There was an awful lot and we had to go through each individual one. At the point when we said we would publish at Easter we did not know the volume and the manner in which the consultation responses would be delivered . As Glenn said, we do not actually publish anything across Ofcom during an election period because most things can be taken as an issue, so that is what the delay to that was.
Okay , the timescales do not marry up for me , but I will leave it at that.
Q117 Yes , and I plan to pursue that . W hat would you consider an election period to be?
It is the formal election period in the sense you get the dissolution of the P arliament for however many —four or five— weeks . It was towards was at the end of March.
It probably would be the end of March , I think Easter was in April this year.

Yes. So the point for us was that we closed our consultation in February and we had hoped to conclude the analysis of all the responses that we got between the period of closure and then when the election period would normally start. We did not know until closer to the time what the specific dates of the election period would be, but then in that window that we had we did not get through all the consultation responses.

Q118 To go back to Ms Sullivan’s point, Scottish elections are fixed. We know when they are and we know how long the election period is, we know when parliament will dissolve. I find it difficult to understand why, if you have a rule or a guidance that says you will not publish documents during an election period, that that calculation could not have been made. How many consultation responses were received in total? I think you said it was 90% were generated by AI.
That was 1 , 196 AI , that was about 90% . I think it was just over 1 , 300 in total.
Q119 Okay, so what weight were those AI - generated responses given in comparison to those that were not AI generated?
We do not work in that particular way . W e look at every individual response to make sure that we are doing a full analysis.
Yes, w e do we not do not say , “Oh, it’s AI, therefore it’s worth less or more.”
Yes.
That is reassuring.

This was a really interesting experience for us because it was not AI generated. The Save STV North campaign and website gave people a list of options that they could choose from in relation to the different areas of the consultation, as well as free text options. That is different from AI generation, which might be coming up with the arguments itself. It sent to us individual responses from named individuals — it could have been me or you — with named email addresses and so on. We treated them as individual responses. When we looked at them , people almost exclusively did not use the free text option , t hey only used the pre-generated list options . Y ou could start to look at it thematically, for example, but it was still necessary for us to go through each individual response.

Q120 Okay . A s M s Sullivan says , we are all well used to those kinds of campaigns so I do not think any of us would be surprised by that , but if this was new and unexpected , what mechanisms have you put in place to make sure that in future you are able to cope with those in the time frames that you have established?

We are doing quite a lot of work on this at the moment. We are not unique in this regard. As you say, MPs, local authorities, and other public bodies are increasingly seeing consultation responses and complaints, either through AI generation or AI-assisted tools.

We are looking at our own technology options to be able to filter through those sorts of numbers of responses that we are likely to be getting for consultations in the future as well. There are a few tools on the market at the moment that you can put these things through to allow you to be able to work out whether they have been AI generated or , as in this case, have been AI assisted but are still individual responses. We are confident that we will be in a better position if something like this happens again.
It might just be a slight irony that an organisation that is involved in broadcasting , which is a very technologically driven field , was surprised by the arrival of AI - generated responses .

Q121 You have slightly beaten me to the punch there, Chair. Having listened very carefully to both of your responses to these questions it seems quite clear that you dropped the ball with the phasing of your publication of the consultation , which I am sure you will dispute but it is nevertheless very clear . You clearly did not get the date and the phasing of that right. Then, apparently because you got 1,200 AI responses— that would not phase a single MP around this table and their staff of five or six people to process—it apparently put a spanner in the works of Ofcom . T he Office of Communications was caught on the hop by getting some AI responses. There is a vicious irony there that does not reflect well on your organisation, or am I being unfair?
I do not think we we re necessarily caught on the hop in terms of the volume and the feelings that the people were expressing because we did an extensive amount of stakeholder engagement.
Q122 You were surprised by the AI lobby, were you not ?

I would not say surprised. It was the first time that we had had such an enormous amount. Some 90% of the responses had been generated by AI, and it was the first time in all of our consultations that had happened. As an organisation we needed to work out not only how we do that but also the cleansing of that data by removing all the personal information, which was something that we had not had to do before.

Q123 That is process. You were late publishing because you were not expecting the volume of AI that you had to go through . H ave I misunderstood ; were you late processing because of the volume of AI?
It was the volume and the fact that it had been AI generated rather than generated by individuals without using AI , so there was a lot of data that had to be removed from it.
Q124 You only received 1,300 responses, so with the closure of broadcasting from the north of Scotland how many were you expecting?

I was not surprised by the sheer volume but it was the nature in which it was delivered that was the thing. Maybe we were over-ambitious when we said we would publish before Easter and maybe we should have been a bit more cautious in our timeline.
I do not think anyone’s ever accused Ofcom of being over - ambitious.
Q125 Douglas McAllister : Just on that point again about the over 1,000 AI - assisted individual responses , were these all published and treated as individual responses?

We have treated them as part of the analysis of the evidence as individual responses. There is a whole section in the statement that we have done on how we have handled all these sorts of things as part of this process. I will need to double check this for you, I am happy to come back on it, I do not know that we have published every individual response. That is partly because they have come to us with personal data on it as well, and people have not given us permission to publish that.
Q126 Douglas McAllister : Personal data can be removed . T here is a suggestion that these over 1,000 responses were treated as a single response . H ow many responses did you publish then?
I do not know the answer to that.
Q127 Douglas McAllister : Was it almost 100 ?
I actually do not know the answer.

Q128 Douglas McAllister : You do not know how many responses were published in relation to the consultation exercise . I f I was to suggest it was 1,300 responses received and you published less than 100 , would that be accurate?
I am sorry, I do not know.
Douglas McAllister : You do not know?
Q129 Would it be possible for you to write to us with that information please ? It would be helpful.
Yes, we can .
I assume that you have information about what has been published on the Ofcom website?
I assumed you had that information as well .
We will have it and we will give the Committee that information.

Q130 Douglas McAllister : My concern is that you have taken over 1,000 individual responses from members of the public , viewers , and you have published it effectively as a single response simply because it is AI assisted as if somehow that is not a response to a consultation.
That is not the way we treated it and that is the reason we took a stand over—
Douglas McAllister : You cannot say that because you cannot tell me the figures.
What I do know is that our teams have gone through every single individual response that we had to the consultation.
Q131 Douglas McAllister : How many did you publish?

How many were actually published on the website? I am afraid I do not know the number , I can write with that to the Committee . I t is important to weigh up how we responded to the consultation response. People a s individuals , whether the responses are generated by AI or assisted by AI , is part of our decision making and we use d a number of different factors including economic issues and impact assessments . S entiment and public opinion is a very important part of it but there are other measures as well that we have to weigh up when making decisions .
Q132 Douglas McAllister : In relation to the amount received , how many were in favour and how many were against?
We had very few against.
Q133 Douglas McAllister : You had v ery few against?
Yes.
Q134 Douglas McAllister : But you don’t know the figures?
I do not know the exact number , I have not brought those exact numbers with me today but I can , of course , give them to the Committee .

Q135 J ust to keep on with the AI - assisted responses , you have put quite a lot of weight on the fact that it was the volume of AI - assisted responses that delayed your self-imposed deadline of before Easter. W hat difference did an AI - assisted response ma k e in the consideration of the responses ? F or me , 1,300 responses in total is not a great number , given the importance of the subject . I would easily have anticipated at least that , if not more . I do not see why it takes longer to go through the AI - assisted ones as opposed to individual responses. Can you help me understand that?
I do not think that is the way that we treated it.

Q136 You placed a lot of weight on to the fact that the AI - assisted responses extended past the original Easter deadline , so I do not understand what additional complexity those added or why it took the whole process beyond that original deadline. Other than that, did you not expect to get at least 1,300 responses?

I do not think we knew how many we were going to get before the consultation closed. Clearly a significant proportion , 90% of them , came through that campaign tool. We read every single response , whether it was through that campaign tool or whether it was sent directly to us formally as part of the normal consultation method of just submitting to an Ofcom address. I t took us that period of time to go through all the responses , not just the 1,100 AI - assisted ones .
Q137 T he AI - assisted response in itself did not add any additional pressure , i t was more the volume of them ; i s that what you are saying?
It is a volume point , yes .

Q138 In which case you did not expect at least 1,300 responses , if not more , for changes that were so contentious. I say that as an MP who literally gets hundreds and hundreds of campaign emails on particular topics. None of this is unfamiliar to anyone sitting around the table. I struggle to understand why an organisation such as Ofcom could not deal with 1,300 responses within its self-imposed deadline.
With hindsight , which is a fantastic tool , the self-imposed deadline that we had se t was perhaps unrealistic.
Q139 Did you not anticipate that volume of responses?

As I said, we did not anticipate the handling ; with the AI thing , t here was a lot of data in there that would not normally be provided, as I understand i t, h ad people taken the more traditional route . I t was the treating of that data that was an issue.
Q140 W hen people put in responses to consultations do they not normally provide their name , address and personal data?

It differs. They are asked to , certainly , with the tools that they provide , b ut there is also then an opportunity for them to say whether they want the response to be published or they want personal data to be removed . N one of that happened with the AI - assisted tool because it had come directly via the website. An Ofcom pro forma would have your name and your email address , for example , and then an option as to whether it would be published or whether you wanted your personal data removed .
Which this did not.
N one of that happened with the AI - assisted responses.
Q141 Did you say it did not happen?

W hen people filled out their options from the site and it generated an email from them , there was nothing that was provided by the campaign tool that allowed them to say that they either wanted it to be published , not published , or that they wanted personal data to be removed.
Q142 What did you do? Did you go back to those individuals and ask them ?
We did not go back to them as individuals , no.
Q143 You would then make a decision about how it would be handled , in that scenario ?
Which was to read every single one of those responses.
I am not questioning that they were read , I am questioning how they were then dealt with. I am genuinely trying to understand why it took so long , but I am clearly not asking the right questions.

Q144 You seem to be reading my mind this morning , C hair . It is concerning that an organisation , Ofcom, has taken so long to read or deal with such a small number of responses to a consultation, given that in this digital age people are turning to other methods to share their views . I t is concerning that those with the campaign were not contacted to ask whether they were for or against. I find that really concerning. Am I right to be concerned?
I am not sure about the last point you were saying , about being contacted to ask about whether they were for or against ?
The Chair asked you about those AI responses , and you said that there was nothing within the campaign tool that suggested they were either for or against.
No, I do not think it was about that.
It was whether we could use their data or not , whether we could publish who they were and their data. It was not whether they were for or against it.
Q145 Right okay , but you did not contact them?
No , we did not go back to the individuals that had used the AI tool .
Q146 Those responses were not published as a single response?
No.

Q147 Douglas McAllister : J ust on this point again , the explanation that Ofcom gave for delaying the decision was that — correct me if I am wron g—you, “W anted time to engage with representations we ha d received throughout the process. ” That was the explanation given by Ofcom for the extension and the delay to allow you to publish in June . Y ou have now told the Committee that you did not engage with those representations.
No , that that is not what we said. W e said that we did not respond to the individuals who used the AI - assistive tool , but we did read every single representation.
What you mean by engaged was we were not engaged with the individuals ; we were engaging with what they had said and making sure that we had been across it all.

Q148 Douglas McAllister : How did you engage with the audiences during this consultation process? T o my mind , those over 1,000 would be the audience. How did you engage with the audience? You asked to continue publication to allow you to engage with representations received. You received over 1,100 from individual , I presume, audience members. You are telling us that you did not make any contact with them. How did you engage with audiences before reaching your decision?
Before reaching our decision we did a number of engagements directly with a wide range of different organisations from the newsrooms affected.
Q149 Douglas McAllister : And a udiences ?

In terms of audiences we did a large amount of research. From the amount of passion felt by this programme you would have expected it to have much larger audiences than it does. The actual figures show us that that programme has been in decline in terms of audience numbers over the last five years, which have gone down quite significantly. Last year it was a 14% share. This programme was not being watched by people and its audiences have been continually going down over the last five years , i n line with a lot of public service broadcasting news programmes — we know that audiences are going down. They are actually fragmenting and going in different ways.

We engage with audiences very much through a lot of research that we do that continues throughout the year. Glenn mentioned Media Nations, which was published a couple of weeks ago. We have our News Consumption Survey that comes out next week, which we can obviously make sure you all have copies of. It shows us that people are increasingly turning to social media and digital resources to get their news. That is not just a young people thing actually, older generations are turning to that as well.

If we look at what has happened in the six weeks since the changes were made to these programmes , the audiences have stayed roughly the same : t hey have not gone up or down. One of the reasons why we made this decision was so the STV would be able to make sure it was delivering the news where people were consuming it. The digital video views before these changes was about 64 million a month, and it has now gone up to about 80 million in the last couple of months. I t is really important to look at it in the context of, in terms of the audience, yes, there were a lot of people who felt very strongly about these changes but they were not watching the programme. The programme’s audiences were declining and continued to do so.

That is not because the programme or the content is no good, it is because audience habits are very much changing. We are seeing a fragmentation right across all public service broadcasters. People are consuming the ir news in different ways. When we made this decision we were very mindful of the fact that we had called public service broadcasters to make sure they were delivering news in the form that people are getting to it. I hope that gives you some sort of context in terms of how we engage with audiences in terms of our research, but also the evidence of the numbers of audiences that were watching the programmes and still are.

Q150 We are going to move on to another question but I will just make a slight comment , which is that it is making quite a sweeping assumption to assume that the 1,200, 1,300 people who responded were not part of the audience or not the audience. I would have thought they were.
I am sure they were.
You suggested they were not watching.
I was not talking about those individuals, but in terms of the population watching that programme over the last five years, fewer and fewer people have been watching that programme.
Q151 You actually said the people who responded were not the people who were watching.
I am sorry I am sorry if I misspoke. I do not know if the individuals who wrote to us in whichever way they communicated with us were actually viewers of the programme. I imagine they probably were.

Q152 While listening to that I was looking at the data : you had 1,340 responses but you actually seem to be using the data on the audience figures going down to make the decision . I guess a lot of people will be thinking , for the consultation, “What is the point?” W ith 1,340 responses the vast majority of them were against the changes that were proposed and the decision ha s been made anyway , so for future responses , is there any point in people actually submitting anything at all?

Absolutely there is. It is important to remember that, as part of all of this process we have moved STV from its original position. What we have ended up with is not what it originally proposed, so we were able to use that sentiment. As I said, audience and people’s response to our consultations is really important, but the y are among other factors. Again, it is important to take this in context. Public service broadcasting is struggling financially, as we have said publicly. STV’s revenue was published last week, and it has gone down by 27% over the last year. Channel 4 will be announcing a reorganisation this morning, or later on today, about which it is reported that a considerable number of jobs will be going. The BBC has another £500 million to save.

Public service broadcasting and regional, local, and national news is in a very difficult place. We were very mindful that we wanted to make sure that STV continues; we want it to flourish and thrive. I do not want to see STV not delivering to audiences at all and so we had to balance very carefully the sustainability of public service broadcasting in Scotland and the exact manner in which it is dealt.

I have been in journalism for 35 years ; I started in local news. I am passionate about news, that is why I have come to Ofcom: I want to preserve it and for people to be able to get accurate, impartial news wherever they are. I personally believe in that, but the long-term sustainability of that service was a factor in our decision making.

Q153 It still gets to , what was the point of the consultation ? Y ou have maybe 95 % , 96% or something of the people who have actually taken part in that consultation who have just simply been ignored . T hey will be thinking , “W hat is the point in future?”
They were not ignored ; all those responses were carefully read and considered and taken as part of the evidence.

One of the challenges, particularly through the large number that were generated online as well, is there was not as much engagement with the actual questions that were in the consultation, and there are these broader contextual issues that Cristina was just describing as well. People were really kind of countering the evidence that we have been presenting, that Cristina has just articulated. There is a real concern for us about waiting to a kind of point of crisis for having to have to act with ST V ; the situation is quite difficult for both the STV News at 6 pm , the numbers are quite similar across c entral and n orth . Sometimes we think about this only as an STV North licence issue ; it is not, it is an STV North and an STV Central one.
It is the same for c entral , yes.

Where we have seen that decline in linear across c entral and Scotland successively over five years with the share, as Cristina said, at 14%. That is concerning for us. We know that the costs of running the news service for STV are always likely to outweigh the amount of money that it is making, we said that in analysis back in 2022. I t is a very precarious position, not just for STV but the other public service broadcasters in the provision of news, and we would not want to be sitting here in a year’s time, for example, and you saying to us, “You ’ ve been asleep at the wheel and not been making changes that should have been made.”

G oing back to your point about the consultation responses being ignored , the point of a consultation is not just to get people’s sentiment but it is also to look at evidence . I t was clear in the consultation responses that nobody had come up with different evidence that changed the story . T here was sentiment and feeling but there was no actual evidence , and w e have to make decisions based on evidence.
Douglas McAllister : Ofcom said it was minded to approve STV’s proposals even before the consultation began.
Mr McAllister , we are moving on.

Q154 T he supplementaries have obviously raised wide-ranging response s from yourselves , but does Ofcom accept that STV’s new service will be a weaker offering than the one that i s currently available?

I do not, but you would expect me to say that. As I said, if you only judge it through the narrow lens of a 6 pm programme then I would not say it was weaker, so far it seems to be over - indexing on the 30% of bespoke content for that particular area . It has increased its provision of news digitally, which is where people are getting their news from.

All I want is for people to get impartial, accurate news where they are consuming it . Y es, it would be fantastic if they did not have to make any financial savings, nobody had to make any cuts and we could continue, but people are getting their news in different ways. I will be honest ; the work we did with STV was to make sure that it was delivering the news digitally. I met a very nice woman in Aberdeen who said to me, “I ’ m a journalist, I want to carry on being a journalist. I do not want to move to Glasgow and I want to be able to deliver the news. A s well as on the linear programme I want to be able to do more digital stuff.” She actually said that to me, and that has enabled her to do it. I do not think it is a weaker proposition, it is a different proposition and I wish STV well in continuing to do this.

We will be very carefully making sure that it stick s to the requirements we have given for this and, as I said, the numbers speak for themselves. The linear audiences have not gone down, so people obviously feel that it is worth watching, and the digital engagement has gone up. The evidence shows that no one is getting anything weaker.

Q155 We have heard a number of times how many communications MPs get from their constituents and, as elected representatives of those constituents, the First Minister and MSPs from several parties opposed the changes. How did Ofcom consider these views and take them into account as part of the decision?

We have treated them all the same. We have gone through every individual response that we have had , and the collective ones , including the one that you have just articulated, and that is part of that broader evidential picture that Cristina has just been describing.
In terms of engagement, we went and gave evidence in Holyrood ; when was that?
January.

In January. Since the decision was published I have been to meet the Culture Minister in Holyrood to try to explain and unpack a bit of the thinking behind it and, as I said, give a bit more context to the decision we had made.

We also had quite extensive engagement with the previous Culture Secretary and the Scottish Government prior to the election period, so Cristina , our c hief e xecutive and ourselves have met them. We meet Scottish Government officials regularly just to talk through what we are proposing to do.

As Cristina was mentioning earlier, during the consultation period we were in Dundee and Aberdeen. We were particularly interested to hear from STV’s own staff, so we saw the newsroom in Dundee, Cristina and other colleagues saw the newsroom in Aberdeen and there was engagement actually online, not in person, with the newsroom in Inverness. It is worth saying about that that the licence obligations that STV are now under, post the changes that we announced in June, still require that kind of regional diversification and, critically, they still require it to have physical news resource in those sites in the north and central Scotland .

Yes, the news gathering resource has not been affected by this. There were no compulsory redundancies and we very explicitly said that the reporters and journalists still have to be there. There are as many of them there now as there w ere before, they are just delivering the news in a different way.
Q156 Is Ofcom confident that the decision is sustainable, given the apparent opposition from the political spectrum?

I accept that it is a decision that politically people have not supported and, as was said to me when I was in Edinburgh a few weeks ago, it was a decision that we made that people do not agree with. The decision was made because it is really important that STV is able to continue to exist, frankly, and it is really important that Scottish audiences have a commercial PSB, as well as the BBC. ITV, which STV is not a part of, feels it cannot survive and it wants to be bought by Sky. I want to be able to do everything I can to ensure the long-term existence of STV and its provision of news to audiences right across Scotland, wherever and whoever they are and however they consume their news. It was a politically unpalatable decision, I get that, but we had to make a decision that was the best for audiences wherever they are and however they consume their news, and for the long-term sustainability and future of STV. The test of that will be whether it is still around in 2034 when its licence runs out . I very much hope so.

Q157 The centralisation of services and the provision of less good services for people in rural Scotland is my number one issue. Yesterday, I got a memo from someone in the BBC outlining the cuts in Inverness and Stornoway; I do not know if you know about that. My concern is that we are seeing a centralisation of news services that disadvantages the highlands. As an amendment—you may know about this better than me—I believe that the Westminster Government give funding to the regional press in England, but no such funding is available in Scotland, which disadvantages the rural press. Do you have any comment on those two things?

Questions of funding from the Westminster Government are for the Westminster Government and not for us. I do not know the details of further BBC cuts—those have not been communicated to us—but the BBC, as I have said, has £500 million worth of cuts to make.

You talk about the word centralisation. I would not necessarily say that is what has happened with STV: yes, the production of the programme has gone to a single place in Glasgow, but the journalists who are news gathering, talking to communities and telling their stories—whether online, through an Instagram post or in a package for the 6 o’clock news—are still there. To my knowledge, STV is not being centralised: I would be aware if that happened. The Aberdeen newsroom is still open, and people are still working in it, they are just delivering news in a different way. Production—the physical place from where the programme is transmitted—has been centralised, but I would not characterise the content going into it as having been centralised.

In terms of your question about the BBC, I do not know what its long-term plans are; I have read some speculation in the press, but I cannot add any more. That is for the BBC to answer, rather than us.
Q158 If the BBC closed Inverness on the same basis the STV are closing it , which is not a proposal , presumably that would be a very big issue for you.
The closure of any newsroom is an issue.
Q159 If they reduce their staff significantly, is n’t that also an issue for you?

There would have to be a regulatory process for any such decisions and we would look at it as we do all these things, but I do not want to speculate on something that has not actually come to us yet. Journalism is more important now than it has ever been; reducing the amount of people doing the job is always difficult.

I would add one quick supplemental: it is STV specific but goes to your point about centralisation. Ahead of coming today, I watched both editions of n orth and c entral news last night just to get a feel for how they looked after the changes. There were two stories in particular—on the Eljamel inquiry and an announcement on Spaceport funding for SaxaVord— that were run from both licences, so you could watch them on c entral as well as n orth last night. There was incredibly high - quality journalism—from staff in the n orth region, as I understand it—presented across the whole of Scotland because of the national interest.

When they did the more local stuff, again there was some brilliant quality journalism from the n orth; one of the stories was specific to Dundee but had a broader application because, ironically, it was about the use of AI in the creative sector. It has not been long, and we are going to have to assess STV’s performance over the course of next year, but at the moment the evidence is positive. It is important to emphasise that quick shift to digital news that Cristina mentioned.

STV seem s to be over-indexing on the regional news online, but substantially more people are engaging with its regional news online, according to year-on-year comparisons: there have been a third more even in the last handful of months. T here are some positive moves about regional news having more eyeballs on it than it had previously.

That is what Ofcom wants to see; we want people to get access to accurate, impartial and trusted news. We know that people who engage with local and regional news and the nation’s news have stronger links to democracy and feel more supportive of their institutions.

I am not being negative about people who do not watch the regional news or the 6 o’clock programme anymore, for whatever reason. Their ability to get that news— wherever they are consuming it—is really important, and this decision has made that possible. It is early days, but we made very clear to STV that we would be on at it about this. The evidence so far is that the viewing figures have not gone down for these programmes but have stayed the same ; more high - quality content is being consumed, but in a different format.

Q160 I am concerned with two things. First, the public sector broadcasting licence was issued to STV on the basis that it provided this service; it then came to you and said, “We can no longer economically provide this service.” You said, “We’ll need to have a consultation in order to find out how we go forward.” Everybody across the entire political spectrum in Scotland—very little unites them—is against this. Everybody who is affected by it is against it. Everybody who works there was against it: incidentally, if your job moves 150 miles away from where you live, your letter might not mention compulsory redundancy but in effect that is what it is. The vast majority of people who responded to your consultation were against this, and yet it went ahead anyway. If something similar was to happen to a broadcast region in England, what would be the point of engaging with Ofcom’s consultation, when it is just going to do what the broadcaster says anyway?

It is important to make the point that in this particular case, we did not do what the broadcasters initially suggested. We told STV that we would not approve its original submission, and where we landed has given more than was originally proposed. We are evidence-based, and that is evidence that we absolutely do not automatically do what broadcasters tell us. If ITV decided to approach us, again we would consult. We do not ignore the consultations. We look for new evidence. That is the point of a consultation , for people to bring up new evidence that we have not perhaps considered or were not aware of. I would say to anybody, “P lease indulge in the consultation process, that is what it is there for; we want to hear from you. We do not ignore it and we do not make decisions in advance; we look for new evidence. ”
Q161 What changed as a result of the consultation?
We did not accept the initial proposal from STV. Nothing changed after the consultation because, as we said, nobody had given different evidence.

You talked about the financial situation. We did an assessment of the sustainability of the news provisions for Channel 3 licence holders back in 2022, which we have to do under statute. Even at that point we thought it would likely result in a net cost for STV. That has come to pass, and if anything that net cost has been higher as programming costs have gone up over the course of the last few years. That is a driver for STV to come to us and say, “You’ve already recognised that this was going to come at a net cost to us; it’s coming at a greater net cost and that’s why we want to talk about changing the obligations in the licence.”

It is really important to stress that when it sent us the first case for change—we have published both—it proposed 100% worth of sharing; there would be no regional distinction at all between the n orth and c entral licences. We could not read the licences in that way, so we went back to it and explicitly said, “That isn’t going to work with your licence commitments; you need to come up with an alternative that still allows us to see that regional distinction between the two places.” It has done that, and the early signs are that it has been done to a good standard.

Another point that people were specific about in the consultation responses—we have touched on this in the other questions—was the requirement to have journalistic resource still located in particular places in the n orth licence: Inverness, Aberdeen and Dundee. That is a licence obligation for STV as well, so it has been written in in part as a result of the consultation responses.
I am not aware of anyone who has been asked to commute 150 miles. I do not think people have been relocated unless they particularly asked for that.

We are going to move on to something else, but can I just leave you with a point that perhaps you can come back to before the end of this session ? I would imagine you expect people taking part in a consultation to be predominantly members of the public. How does Ofcom expect members of the public to come up with new evidence that counters the evidence given to it by a large broadcaster? I will leave you to think about that until the end of the meeting and we can then come back to it. I am going to go on to Lillian Jones.
Q162 STV revised its original proposal before Ofcom made its decision. How significant were the differences between the two proposals?

They have both been published. As I mentioned, STV sent us its initial submission and suggestion for 100% of new s sharing in the middle of October last year. We were not happy that that would be compliant with the licences, so we asked it to rethink; it came back to us in November. When we published the consultation in December, we published both of STV’s submissions to us alongside that, to give people the evidence they would need to respond to the consultation.
There was no 30% in the original submission. STV was going to do only one programme with totally shared content and no bespoke content from the northern belt at all.
That is detailed in our final statement and in the consultation that we published in December. STV came back with the revised proposal of a 70:30 split.
In the original submission there was no mention of any digital strategy and no mention of increasing the delivery of digital news.

One more point I would make—it is not recency bias from watching the n orth and c entral programmes last night—is that this does not stop STV using stories from the north that might be of national interest or particular interest to people in Scotland, on the c entral programme. The two examples I just gave you on the Eljamel inquiry and the SaxaVord Spaceport funding last night are a really good example of the type of content we are seeing that is both particular to the north but also has a wider Scotland-level application.
Q163 Did Ofcom work with STV to come up with the revised set of proposals?

No. We talked to it about the first thing it submitted; we said, “We want you to go away and think internally within STV about what it is you think would actually meet the obligations in the licence that require that regional distinction.” It came back to us in November with the one that we published alongside the consultation three or four weeks ago.
We didn’t tell it how to do it. As a former journalist I was tempted to draw up a plan, but , at the end of the day, editorial plans are down to the broadcaster.
Q164 Did you not work with STV on its proposals?

It depends on how you define “work with” . We did not create the submission, but we told it the first one was not good enough: there was no digital news plan and we wanted more bespoke content in the north than it was proposing.
Q165 Did you suggest anything that it should include within the proposals?

When it submitted the first one—this is all publicly available—we said, “This doesn’t meet the licence obligations around regional distinctiveness. We need you to come back with a proposition that specifically demonstrates that you’re still able to do things that are particular to the c entral region and the n orth region.” That is what it did. It was an internal process; it is not for us as the regulator to make an editorial choice about how news is delivered. STV worked on that and came back to us with the revised proposal.
Ms Squires stated five minutes ago that Ofcom would not have approved the original proposal from STV.
Q166 Can I ask a supplementary on that point? Before the consultation process, did Ofcom state publicly that it was minded to approve the revised proposals?

The consultation that we put out had a minded to approve proposal in it, predominantly because it met the conditions that were in the licence for that regional distinctiveness that I was talking about, and we were getting additional commitments—as I said, those came out in the consultation responses—that journalistic resource would be retained, particularly in the n orth licence.
Q167 Was the minded to approve statement issued by Ofcom before the consultation?
It was at the consultation.
It was when the consultation went out.

Across all our different types of consultation , it is common for Ofcom to give people a steer on what we are thinking in relation to the evidence. As Cristina says, if we then get evidence that counters it—we may come back to your question, Chair, about that—of course we will consider that.
Q168 Did you give evidence to the Scottish Parliament during the consultation process?
We did.
Q169 Was that in January?
It was, yes.
Q170 How did you describe the proposal to the Scottish Parliament during the consultation process?

We described it in the same way. The consultation had been published prior to our evidence session at Holyrood in January; they had the published consultation that included the minded to approve proposal plus the two STV submissions that had been sent to us in October and November.

Q171 Looking at the timescales around this decision making, Ofcom renewed all 15 licences, including for STV, for a 10-year term starting 1 January 2025. Just nine or 10 months later, STV asked for that to be looked at again and tried to change the terms of the licence. Do es Ofcom feel duped that STV signed up to the new licence and then almost immediately tried to change things?

I would not characterise it as feeling duped. I cannot think what the timescale was, but there were a lot of conversations with STV before we got a firm proposal that it wanted to vary the licence. That was well after the licence had been agreed by us. I do not think Ofcom would ever want to turn around and say, “We’re not going to grant this licence because we don’t think you’re financially sustainable.” At the time, we were happy that STV had the finances to continue delivering on its licence obligations, but changes in audience and the other things we have mentioned probably moved faster than we thought. STV’s financial position has changed quite considerably, and that has been a recent thing. Glenn know s more about the timescale of the actual awarding of the licences because the decision was made long before the licence.

It was made several years before. I have already referred to this, but in answer to your question it is probably worth repeating. There is a statutory obligation on Ofcom before the 10-year licence period ends to give advice to the UK Government about the sustainability of the licences. The UK Government then have to make decisions about whether the framework needs to be changed. That process went back to ‘21-22.

As I have mentioned, our financial sustainability testing had already identified that there were likely to be net costs for STV in running its two licences in Scotland in 2022.
