That was the basis on which the Secretary of State made the decision that the licence would be renewed on the same terms. That meant there were three and a half years between the original financial assessment, the Secretary of State’s decision, and the issuing of the new 10-year licence. As Cristina says, the picture changed dramatically during that period of time : for example, the cost of production, including the cost of news production, went up quite dramatically, higher than we—or even some broadcasters—anticipated. Part of the case that STV brought to us was that those likely net costs we had identified three or four years before were higher still; in consequence it would be very difficult to deliver a sustainable news service.

The other thing I would say is that there is nothing to stop any broadcaster, whether STV, ITV or the BBC, coming to us at any point to say, “We would like to change the conditions in our licence.” It might be because of financial sustainability or something else, but it is always possible for them to come to us and say that.
Indeed, it can be handed back. There is no obligation on STV; it could turn around and say, “We have the licence until 2034, but we don’t want to continue with it.”
Q172 When STV looked for the licence to be changed, did you consider putting it back out to the tender process, or was there no consideration of that at all?
What do you mean by the tender process?
Q173 I mean, making it reapply for the licence with the new information about what it would deliver, which had obviously changed since the licence was granted.

The important point about the process is that we give advice to the UK Government or the Secretary of State about the sustainability of the licence. They then have to make the decision about whether there should be changes to the licence terms for Channel 3 operators. That decision dated back three or four years prior to STV coming to talk to us about these changes. We can only reissue the licence on the basis that has been agreed by following the advice we have given to the Secretary of State. Once that process has been completed, there is no option to go back and say, “We think it should be different”.

Q174 If it is granted and then changed very soon after, does that not set a precedent for anyone else to say, “Hold on, I want to do something different, I don’t want to deliver on what I’ve promised, I want to change the rules?”
I completely get the meaning behind your question. It is perfectly possible that STV or any other broadcaster could come to us at any point.
Anyone could come to us and say, “We can’t do what we said we were going to, and we want to apply for a licence variation.”
Q175 Has anyone else asked for that?
Not that I am aware of.
That has not happened with the Channel 3 licences, but it is not uncommon for a broadcaster to come to us from time to time and potentially ask for changes to their licences.

When it was granted the licences, STV said, “We welcome the renewal of our licences, which provide us with the certainty to continue to invest in our business for the long term while ensuring continued delivery of valued public service broadcasting.” A few months later, it wanted to renege on the licence.

Q176 This will be a quick question, as we have covered it to a large extent and are less than halfway through our list of questions. As we have discussed, STV says that it will maintain news gathering resources across all its bases. What do you think that means in practice? How many journalists did it have, and how many does it have now? Coming back to the BBC, do you have an idea of how many journalists it has, and do you keep a track of that number?

I have experienced huge changes in journalism. When I first started in local news, there would be four— sometimes five—journalists doing a story for TV. Now a regional news organisation will very often send one person to do it all. The number of people has changed as technology has changed. I will not go into whether that is good or bad, but the creation of journalism has become much more efficient. I do not know if it is about hard numbers; as I said, there were no compulsory redundancies in STV North as far as I am aware, and there are still the same number of journalists. I s the person who operates the vision mixer in the production gallery a journalist? In pure terms, no, because they are not going out and telling people stories. As I understand it, the number of journalists going out and doing news gathering and telling stories has not changed.

The answer to your question is that we do not track the number of journalists ; w e see that as a strategic or editorial choice for the broadcasters themselves to decide who they need to have where. With STV, we have provisions in the licence that require it to have journalistic resource, but decisions about the shape of that and the number of people is rightly for it to make. I certainly do not think we want that to be a regulatory choice for a commercial business. STV announced that the total number of jobs it was looking to reduce as part of its wider savings package, was—I think—60. What I am not sure about is how many of those classed as news journalists were included in that number. It was certainly a smaller proportion, as I understand it.

Q177 You can see where I am coming from: I am worried that the north and west are losing their journalists. I touched on the fact that Westminster is giving money to help the regional press, but that is not happening in Scotland, as far as I am aware. Does that bother you?
I would not know about that because we do not regulate the press, we only regulate the broadcast media. I am not aware of whether it applies to Scotland or not.
I do not know the answer about funding.
One would have thought the funding might be devolved to the Scottish Government.

That is potentially the case, but the one thing we know about—you probably do also, Mr MacDonald—is that there was a pot for local democracy reporters that was essentially funded through the BBC, which had numbers of people. The point was to embed a regional representation piece along with local regional news providers, including some from the press.
It has not been very successful.
I do not know what the status of that is, nor—in the context of charter reform—whether it will be a feature of the conversation about the BBC’s obligations.
It is actually being discussed as part of charter reform.
Q178 Following on from my colleagues’ previous questions, how did Ofcom assess the impact of these changes on the representation of different communities and cultures across Scotland?

We are statutorily obligated to do impact assessments, and we published those alongside the consultation. The probable standout was a recognition—this goes to your question also, Mr MacDonald—that it was possible that areas with older viewers, which are skewed towards rural areas, would be detrimentally affected by having less local news available on the linear STV News at 6 service. We countered that with the increasing availability of things such as fixed broadband, fixed wireless broadband and so on, where it is possible for people to be able to access regional news digitally and online. The early evidence we have seen from STV over the course of the last couple of months is that even those older audiences are beginning to shift to accessing regional news online, but we need to continue to look at that and see whether it is a continuing trend.
Q179 It would be a concern for people who do not have that access, but are you saying that you are going to give that support going forward?

It bleeds into a wider conversation about other things for which Ofcom is responsible: for example, promoting more competition and the availability and take up of internet access, whether that is through fixed broadband, mobile or satellite and so on . We publish the specific numbers for Scotland separately, and I am happy to share them with the Committee if that would be useful. There is a positive upward trajectory here; as a consequence, you can see audience behaviour begin to change as older audiences access more news and other content online. It looks like this is travelling in the right direction, but you are right to ask the question. We need to continue to look at it and make sure that we do not have a group of older or more vulnerable consumers who are left behind.
Q180 Is STV unusual in seeking changes to the scale of regional news services, or is it an outlier? Is there something going wrong at STV that is not happening at other channels?

I do not know about that. I am not going to comment on how it manages its finances and business strategy; that is down to STV. Going back to the broader picture, the financial pressures are hard on all these public service broadcasters. ITV is in discussions to sell half of its business to Sky because it feels that would be more sustainable like that . As I said, the BBC is facing big cuts, and Channel 4 is cutting roles as well. Is STV an outlier? I do not know. We have not had any other proposals and no one else has come to us yet. In the past, the BBC has asked for various operating licence changes; at the moment, ITV is focused on the acquisition, so I do not know its plans for the future. There are real pressures on public service broadcasters.
Q181 I understand there are pressures, but I am confused as to why only STV has actually requested a change.

ITV are the holders of the Channel 3 licences across the rest of the UK, including in Northern Ireland and Wales. Cristina mentioned the BBC; over the last two or three years, we have made licence changes for the BBC specifically in relation to its news provision in Scotland. You will know that it had the centrepiece 9 o’clock news on the BBC Scotland service; it came to us because it was not getting the audiences it had hoped for. It asked to do a 7 o’clock half hour to reduce the amount of news that was on that service, and we agreed. That is an example of the BBC having to do something similar over the last couple of years.
Q182 If STV comes back asking for further changes that will reduce local news content, can Ofcom give any assurance that those will not be allowed?

I cannot imagine a situation where we would agree to that, but I do not want to say never; STV has the right to come back to us at any point. I can certainly say that we would not accept a proposal without very serious consideration, consultation, and evidence from stakeholders. As I said, STV could turn around next week and say, “We do not want to have a licence to the north anymore , ” and hand it back. We cannot prevent that. I cannot sit here and categorically say that we will not accept anything it proposes to us, but I really hope that does not happen. Again, the reason why we made our decision and ended up with STV doing more than it originally wanted to do, was to make sure that it was sustainable and able to continue to deliver for audiences across Scotland in whatever manner they consume their news.

Q183 We know that viewing habits are changing ; we have referenced that already. Is there a risk that an increased focus on digital news could disadvantage some viewers? You mentioned evidence that older people are perhaps beginning to catch up, but technology continues to move on. Is that problematic for you, going forward?

At the end of the day, we are here to make sure that all audiences get the content that they need and want. We are seeing changes in the way content is delivered across the Ofcom remit, and we do not want to leave any audiences behind. There is a risk I suppose; we need to make sure that the 20% of the population who do not get their news from social media are catered for and supplied with good quality information. We are very cognisant of that and of making sure that everyone has access.
Q184 Can I ask you about that 20% figure you mentioned? I am conscious that I still watch the news most days—
I do too.
I also get content from social media; i s that 20% people who exclusively get their content from other sources ?

Our research figures show that 80% of people get their news mainly from social media; one assumes that the other 20% do not. That is my explanation. A lot of people get it from both, but as the numbers show, fewer people are choosing to watch a linear news programme.

The other thing to acknowledge is the current consultation by the UK Government on their Green Paper, which specifically covers your question in a lot of detail. Some decisions for the UK Government in response to these issues—for example, about the prominence of public service broadcast news on particular platforms—might manifest in our regulatory duties.
Q185 For the past seven years, STV News at 6 has been Scotland’s most watched news programme. How important was that as a factor when you considered STV’s proposals?
Do you mean that it is more watched than the BBC? There are two, are there not?
Q186 It is the most watched: it is the one that most people in Scotland turn to. Was that considered as evidence?

It is a fact, without a doubt, but the bottom line is that the number of viewers has still gone down considerably in the last five years. It may be the most watched, but fewer people are watching it than five years ago. That has not changed.

That audience share point is quite important. As you rightly say, the percentage suggests that the numbers watching it could be high, but they are not. They have been declining successively year on year, over five, possibly even more than five years now. The issue for us is that the numbers are rapidly going down.
Q187 In reaching your decision, did you consider the overall provision of regional and local news available to audiences, including news provided by the BBC? Did you look at the mix?

This decision was about STV’s licence obligations and news provision, rather than balancing them out with other organisations. There are lots of very good organisations in Scotland that provide news. Unless I have misunderstood your point, t he BBC does not do separate programmes; it does one programme, so we did not use that as evidence when we came to making this decision.

The other important thing is that the STV commitment was to push more regional news to the digital platforms where audiences were going to be watching or viewing and able to access it. Cristina mentioned the fact that we asked it to come back with a more well thought-through digital strategy for how it would deal with this, making sure that the regional news provision was still available to people, not just in the n orth, but in the c entral licence region as well. There is some evidence now that this is working, though it is too soon to say that definitively.
It has been six weeks.

STV formally started the news sharing provisions on 13 July, but there are encouraging early signs that its regional news is performing better than it has ever done, and we want to see that trend continue. We will report against that when STV reaches the end of its licence year next summer.
Q188 I s i t fair to say that you are taking a narrow view of your remit in purely looking at STV’s obligations ?
T hat is what we are obligated to do u nder our regulatory duties.

Q189 Can you see that there is a wider concern for the audience that perhaps they are not getting the regional news service they deserve? Communities in rural areas already feel left behind: news and services are often focused on areas with larger populations. Would you agree that there is a wider context here?

There is, and we recognised that in the consultation for STV. Yesterday we updated our Transmission Critical public report, which is looking at the sustainability of public service broadcasters and the public service media more generally. It absolutely highlights the issues you have just asked about. As an exercise, we are required to consider STV’s licence changes against its obligations, but that is not our only ongoing work. In the Green Paper that I have already mentioned, the Government are doing work on things such as regional news that might result in further legislative changes that we would have to implement.
Q190 Did you say that you recognised the wider context as part of the consultation?
The whole sustainability of public service media was a feature of the consultation.
Q191 It was not a feature in the decision, so you can understand why people feel frustrated: they gave their views, but those were not taken into account in the decision.
I do not agree that it was not considered as part of the decision. For us, the point was to ensure that STV was able to continue to sustainably provide news and regional news—
O f high quality.

That is in the wider context of the serious financial headwinds it is facing. We have reached a balanced position that still requires STV to have distinctive news in the two licence areas and journalistic resource in those areas as well, but which gives it sufficient financial headroom so that it can sustainably continue to function in the next few years.

I do not know whether this helps or not, but when we were discussing the differences, we were quite surprised that the audiences for the n orth programme and for the c entral programme were not hugely different. I naively assumed that the audience would be much bigger in one or the other, but they were actually very similar. The proportion of people in the northern belt who were watching a programme was not very different from the proportion of people who were watching it in the central belt, which I thought was quite interesting.
Q192 Do you accept that those audiences might have different needs?
That is exactly why we have written regional distinctiveness into the revised licences and required STV to retain journalistic resource.
It is to make sure those needs are catered for.
Q193 How important was STV’s digital strategy to Ofcom’s decision to approve the changes?

It is important; as we said publicly in our Transmission Critical report last year, broadcasters need to take public service content—news content in particular—to where audiences are. I have worked in a number of newsrooms over the last few years, and they all had digital strategies and were pivoting to become digital-first newsrooms. It was really important that STV had a clearer path to making digital news available because that is how people are consuming it.
Q194 To what extent did the expected growth in digital news consumption influence your assessment?
It was one of a number of factors. I cannot give you a mathematical formula but making sure that people get good high-quality news wherever they are was really important.
Q195 To what extent can social media and digital news services replace locally produced television news?

The digital content is locally produced. The journalist making a piece for the 6 o’clock news audience is the same person producing the Instagram reel or the written content. It is still locally produced journalism and it is still telling people stories from the areas where they are based.

Q196 As someone who lives in Aberdeen, I miss the STV North news programme. I kn o w many of the STV North team: something that really sticks in their throats is that STV has been pleading poverty and that is why it cannot produce the regional news as it has done in the past, yet at the same time they see STV spend half a million pounds for example , on setting up a radio station. Quite rightly, they feel hacked off by that. Did you work with STV to look at other ways in which it could save money instead of that money coming from the local regional news?
STV’s obligation is to deliver the news to its audiences; it is down to STV how it does that.
Q197 That is not really the case: it operate s under a licence.

In broad terms STV has created a radio station , which was not terribly expensive and is doing quite well , so people are getting news in a different way. As a regulator I would not want to sit down with any organisation and be involved in working out how they finance things; that is down to the individual organisations themselves.
Q198 You mentioned earlier that you are looking at a sustainable future.

We look at sustainability in the round, but exactly how they spend their money and how they run their businesses—not only the editorial freedoms but the financial decisions they make—are not part of our regulatory framework.
Q199 I f STV comes to you and says, “We don’t want to spend money on regional news, we want to spend it on all these other things,” that is a commercial decision for it to make.
No. It has an obligation to provide regional news and therefore—
Q200 You have allowed it to break that obligation.

We have allowed it to change the way it delivers the 6 o’clock news on weekdays; it has been sharing content at weekends for many years. Originally STV wanted to have completely shared content across the entire week, but we landed at some bespoke content from Monday to Friday and none at weekends. We have not stopped STV doing regional news: we have allowed it to deliver that in a different way and to vary the licence in that respect. In terms of the other obligations, we are not saying that it can do whatever it wants.

It is important to pick up on the point just made that STV said it was going to spend half a million pounds on the creation of a new radio station and that meant it would stop spending money on news. That is not a conversation that we would have with any broadcaster. We do not say, “You have to spend this amount on the production of news.” We say, “These are the licence conditions that require you to deliver this proportion of news on—in this case—the weekly show.” We have inserted that or kept that regional distinctiveness between the two licences. How much the broadcaster spends on doing that is for it to decide.
Q201 But you have allowed STV to change.
We have allowed it to change the proportion of sharing between the two shows.

We have not allowed it to close Aberdeen ; we have not allowed it to close Inverness; we have insisted it keeps those resources. What we have allowed it to do is to extend the sharing of a proportion of content.
Q202 You seem to suggest that this is because STV was not financially sustainable going forward, but at the same time it is spending half a million pounds on a radio station.

It has a financial challenge overall, and the cost of news is going up. Whether it starts a different service—the radio station delivers news and is doing quite well—or has a proposal that it wants to do, that will not come to us for regulatory approval. As Glenn said, how STV spends its money is entirely up to STV . If it had not created the radio station, would that have enabled it to have 100% content instead of 30%? I do not know.

As Cristina says, it could have chosen to split the money however it wanted to. We could not stop it from creating a radio station: that is a revenue generating opportunity. It is a little odd to think of a modern media organisation that is not working across platforms and trying to create alternative sources of income.
Q203 I understand you cannot stop it having a radio station, but you can stop it changing its obligations and the licence it agreed to just a year beforehand.

I understand the point you are making. What we are saying is that over the longer term the cost of news is going up dramatically, and the way in which people are consuming it is completely different. As a consequence it was reasonable for STV to come to us and say, “We think we’re going to have to change the provision of our news because we don’t think we’re going to be able to do this for the whole duration of the 10-year licence.”

Q204 My point is that it seems to be spending a lot of money elsewhere. It is spending half a million pounds on a radio station, half a million pounds on a chief executive, but it cannot afford to spend money on regional news. For me, that seems wrong.
That is for STV.
That is a question for it to answer .
Q205 But you are allowing it to do that.
We have allowed it to change the specific obligations in relation to the 6 o’clock news programme on STV, that is correct.
Q206 Just to clarify, you have no responsibility for its wider decision making?
No.
No.
Q207 Following on from my colleague’s point, do you think that cuts to regional news provision are viewed as an easier way to make savings, and a quick win?
I do not think it has been easy.
Q208 Perhaps easy is not the right word. Do you think it is one of the first things that broadcasters are reaching for when they realise they have to make savings?
I do not know. I have only seen one example of it and that was this one.
I was just asking for your opinion.
My job is to not let that happen.

I have mentioned already that the STV savings or efficiencies programme was across the entirety of the business. I do not think it was unique to news; it included areas such as studios and other operations. There were 60 jobs in total due to go across the business. I do not know what the final number is, but as I understand it the smaller proportion of that was from news; other parts of the business were cut more significantly than the news provision.

Again, we will see what happens. The BBC has said it needs to make £500 million worth of cuts. We do not know where those will land, but I do not think that it is politically easy for anyone to be cutting regional news.
We heard previously about investment in a commercial radio station occurring at the same time as cuts and reductions being made in regional news production; that is quite a stark contrast.

Q209 That brings us to the end of our formal questioning session. I mentioned earlier on that I was intrigued by the idea that—from what you were saying—there seemed to be an expectation that people responding to the consultation would bring new evidence that would refute the evidence given by STV and therefore influence your decision making. I am genuinely intrigued to know how you think members of the public would be able to do that.

We take responses from everybody. The First Minister’s response is as relevant as that of a viewer from the Hebrides. There was the ability for a lot of people to bring us evidence to show that this was the wrong decision, or not the right decision, and it was not only members of the public who could have done that; no one came to us with evidence. I take your point about what we expect of members of the public, but if you do not mind me saying, evidence is probably not what we expect from members of the public. We welcome consultation responses from everybody in whatever guise, whether they are responding on behalf of a Chamber of Commerce or Aberdeen Council, or as individuals.

I do not think there is an expectation that individual members of the public would provide evidence, but if they have it , that is great. It is a principle across all regulation: people might unearth something that we have not considered or were not aware of.

The First Minister would probably be quite concerned that his response was characterised as not giving any new evidence, but we will leave that to him to argue. Thank you both very much. That has been very helpful to us today.

Thank you for having us and giving us the opportunity to explain the thinking behind what was a difficult decision. I did not come to Ofcom to stop people getting regional news, and I am here to make sure they continue to get it in the way that they are getting it, so thank you for your time.
I am sure we can agree that it should not be an easy decision. Thank you.

segs.tx: Science and Technology Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA)
Tuesday 8 September 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Mair (The Chair); Lord Booth; Lord Drayson; Lord Duncan of Springbank ; Baroness Jones of Whitchurch; Baroness Nicholson of Winterbourne; Lord Patel; Lord Ranger of Northwood; Lord Stern of Brentford; Lord Willis of Knaresborough; Baroness Willis of Summertown; Lord Winston.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 - 15
Witness
Dr Kathleen Fisher, Chief Executive Officer, Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA).
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witness
Dr Kathleen Fisher.

Q1 Welcome to this morning’s meeting of the Science and Technology Select Committee. We are very pleased to have as our witness Dr Kathleen Fisher, who is the CEO of ARIA, the Advanced Research and Invention Agency. Dr Fisher, we are very happy to have you here. I will ask the first question. You took over as CEO of ARIA in February of this year. By way of an opening statement, could you set out for us your key priorities for the role and how you think your approach will differ as ARIA matures as an organisation?

Thank you very much for the question and the opportunity to meet with you today. I am Kathleen Fisher, as you said. I am the CEO of ARIA and I have been in post since February. When my predecessor, Ilan, met with you, ARIA was in its infancy. At this point, ARIA is starting to deliver on its promise, which is exciting. We have more than 300 creators who are working on various projects across 15 different programmes and we are starting to see exciting results coming out of those programmes that I am happy to talk to you about in more detail throughout the time that we have together.

My time as CEO will be marked by growth and execution. We will be getting the flywheel of ARIA spinning at full velocity to deliver on the mission and promise of ARIA. We will spend the full £1.2 billion of the money allocated to ARIA in the most recent spending review to deliver on the next cohort of programme directors, the next cohort of activation partners and multiple opportunity seeds, as well as seeing the cohort 1 and cohort 2 programmes to possible extensions and many exciting results.

Of course, ARIA’s success is not measured by things like the number of creators under contract or amount of money spent but on results. It will take a while to get the results that ARIA is set up to achieve, the decadal results that DARPA is famous for. The things that ARIA will be measured for are three different impacts. The first is scientific breakthroughs, scientific miracles that change the way we think about different concepts, breakthroughs that change the conversation. Of course, many of our programmes will fall short of the North Star aspirations that we have for the programme. By setting those aspirations high, we often are able to drive work further than ever anticipated. However, if we fall short, we still can achieve amazing things in falling short. No matter what, we will advance the cause of science. Sometimes the fastest pace to a breakthrough is by a well-understood failure.

The second impact is societal impact or economic impact. That is some of ARIA’s most important work, crossing the valley of death, which is of course hard anywhere and in any time. We take that extremely seriously and we plan for it from the very beginning. When we start thinking about a programme and the scientific impact that we are hoping for, we think about what happens if we get this scientific impact, how this will translate into societal impact and what we need to do to make that societal impact happen as quickly and as expeditiously as possible so that we do not have to wait 50 years for that impact. To that end, we have just created the post and hired a chief translation officer, so there is someone on the executive team whose full-time job is focusing on crossing the valley of death.

The third impact is a change in mindset. ARIA is a beacon of hope in a time that is somewhat filled with pessimism. Part of the reason why I wanted to come to ARIA was because I saw it as such a beacon of hope. The creation of ARIA represented a commitment by the UK Government to commit not to simply reacting to the future but driving the future and helping to shape it.

I spent seven years at DARPA, three years as a programme manager and four years as office leadership, spending time doing the high-risk, high-reward, programme-director, manager-driven projects, each of which had a very ambitious North Star goal. I have seen how effective that style of research can be. I was impressed, blown away, by the audacious way that the UK set up ARIA to succeed in a very similar style and I was honoured and delighted to be chosen to be ARIA’s CEO. Part of the reason was because I have seen and know how strong the UK science and technology research base is. It has the core to be able to drive similar success.

Everything that I have seen at ARIA since coming in as CEO only reaffirms that base, that ARIA is on track to deliver that same success for the UK and the world, if left with the same authority and funding that it has seen to date. Thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to come here and talk to you today. I look forward to your questions.

The Chair: Thank you very much. Before we move on to other questions, could you set out for us some of the existing programmes that excite you most? We are interested in the cross-cutting work that ARIA does with its activation partners, its innovator circles and the AI in science programme generally. Would you pick a few that excite you most?

I would be delighted to. It is hard to choose. I love all my children but in the course of today I hope to be able to talk about many of them. I will start by talking about the forecasting tipping points programme because it allows me to make a couple of different points at the same time, but I am happy to follow up and talk about any of them.

The forecasting tipping points programme is exploring, using and developing sensor technology, low-cost distributed technology and models to look at tipping points in climate change, specifically the AMOC current in the North Atlantic and glacial melt in Greenland, to hopefully develop an early warning system about possible climate change that could have substantial impact on the climate of the UK. Whether or not that North Star comes true, part of what they are developing is low-cost sensors, one of which is a small company in Plymouth called Oshen, which is developing autonomous solar and wind-driven robots called C- Stars . Instead of having one big ship that monitors the ocean current, a whole fleet of them could be deployed at very low cost. Oshen originally had one of these C-S tars. They have now deployed five and the plan is that in a year they would have 50 of them to be able to be deployed and monitor the subpolar gyre. They are now deployed and able to receive, on a minute basis, instructions that are being derived by the models on where to go and what measurements to retrieve to send back to inform those models.

That company was subsequently contracted by NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration of the United States, and asked if they were willing to try to monitor a hurricane to get the conditions of the eyewall of the hurricane. The CEO of that company, Anahita Laverack, thought about whether we want to do this. It is super high-risk, trying to deploy these metre-big vehicles during a hurricane, and the odds of failure are pretty high . However, she is amazing and said, “Let’s go for it, that is worth the risk”. They deployed their C-S tars during it, and it was not just any hurricane. It turned out to be category 5 Hurricane Humberto. They succeeded at monitoring and transmitting back the conditions during that category 5 hurricane. They subsequently have contracts with five different Governments to monitor various sea-state conditions.

This is an example of the way ARIA works and the benefits it can deliver. Even if the forecasting tipping points programme falls short of its North Star—and we are still on track to potentially deliver the North Star of the programme—this type of small company could grow and deliver enormous technology for monitoring ocean conditions for different applications. It is an ancillary benefit.

You asked about the ecosystem. One of the ecosystems that we have is activation partners. ARIA does not give funding to our creators and then sit back and watch. We actively monitor the progress and work to remove friction throughout the process of scientific discovery through to hopefully massive economic benefit. One of our activation partners is Amodo Design, which is a small company in Sheffield. It came to us and said, “You do not know this yet, but one of the frictions that your scientists will run into is that they need bespoke engineering”. It was right that we need bespoke engineering and it is now providing bespoke engineering to more than 35 of our creators. [1]

One of our creators was , again, on the forecasting tipping points. It turns out it needed batteries that work in Greenland where temperatures go down to negative 50 degrees; normal battery technology does not work at negative 50 degrees. Those creators talked about the normal process that they would use, which is applying to a funding agency for a grant to pay for bespoke battery technology. That process would take six months. If they got that grant, they would go and put out an RFP to find a company that could do engineering for them and they would iterate with that company to create a battery. They estimated that the whole process at best would take 18 months. Instead, they had a conversation with Amodo Design. It iterated three times and it produced a modular battery pack that would work in negative 50 degrees Celsius, in three months. That removed a massive amount of friction from their effort. It also works for all the other teams that are working on low-cost sensors for Greenland. There are potentially 11 other teams that benefited from that same effort. That is an example of an activation partner and the synergies that we are seeing.
I have already taken up too much of my time, so I will defer talking about other children who I love in ARIA to other questions.
The Chair: Those are two very interesting examples. Thank you very much.

Q2 Good morning. I am already enthused by your examples. My question is about how you define success. To start with, how do you track progress on your projects when dealing with this incredibly expansive portfolio? Three years is a very short interval of time, so how do you manage to do that in a light but effective way?

We track progress in lots of different ways. The first one starts with the programme directors themselves and the programme creation process. When we design the programme, we design in what we think the measures of success will look like, milestones or metrics, and what we think success should look like. This is programme by programme because what success looks like in forecasting tipping points, in an AI safety programme and in a precision neurotechnologies programme are all completely different, so it is programme by programme. When we design the programme, we set up milestones or metrics of what we think it will look like.

Then the programme directors meet with the creators quarterly, so they are saying to them all the time, “How are you doing on the science? How are you doing on translation?” It is stacked, so you first do the science and then you do the translation, but you are thinking about both all the time. We track red, amber, green on how we are doing towards those. Sometimes the science might not come out exactly the way you expect, but you can pivot the science—you can change the science a little bit and change red to amber or amber to green as you are going. We do not say that if the science is not doing exactly what they said out of the proposal, that is a failure. We are well aware that we are doing very hard science and you cannot predict exactly what will happen, so there is room for manoeuvre. The programme director is constantly monitoring what is happening and working with the creators to shift as appropriate while keeping the North Star goal of the programme in mind.

At an annual cadence, the programme director reports to ARIA where the programme is on track for its metrics and milestones. At that point, we bring in outside experts on the science and translation side, who look over the programme materials and provide guidance to the agency, to me, the chief science officer and the chief translation officer on whether this is still worth doing or we should be pivoting. The programme directors have been quite proactive and I have been pleased to see, coming in from DARPA, that programme directors have been terminating projects that are not on track. The agency has been either adding resources or repurposing resources that are not on track. The safeguarded AI programme, for example, determined that one of the tracks of the programme, which was about verifying AI itself—statistical AI—would not be possible, given how fast AI is moving, and repurposed that part of the funds towards using a combination of AI and formal methods to verify infrastructure instead, which is a good repurposing of those funds. We are regularly looking at the work that we are doing to make sure that the funding is appropriately allocated.

Baroness Willis of Summertown: Thank you. That sounds very robust. Can I just ask a junk question? It was going to come up later but I will bring it in now. When you get the external reviews or the reviews outside of that, are they also checking about overlap with what other people are doing? How do you ensure that this remains unique to and going for the blue-sky thinking rather than existing work?

One of the questions we always ask at the very beginning is whether this work is distinct. How does it fit with the ecosystem? Would this work happen without ARIA doing it or not? That is key. If this work would happen without ARIA, it is not work that ARIA should do. We ask that question during programme formulation and the outside experts on the panel at that point. We ask them again during programme review. This is one of the questions that always gets asked.

It is a question that requires a good deal of context to be able to answer, because if there is no work going on in an area, ARIA cannot fund the work either, because you need to have a creator base that is working in the space. If there is a lot of work going on, it is totally not appropriate. Therefore, you need to split this needle. There is a needle that you have to thread. If there is nothing going on, there is no one who can do the work. If there is a lot of work going on, it is not appropriate. I remember when I was a programme manager at DARPA and having to thread exactly this needle and being frustrated by the person who was poking me, saying, “First you say I cannot do it because there is no work and now you say I cannot do it because there is too much work”.

Baroness Willis of Summertown: Thank you. Overall as a whole, what does success look like for the portfolio? When we had Matt Clifford here, he said that the one success in a sense will be the success of the overall programme, whereas a number will fail, by the very nature of the work. Do you share that vision?

Mostly, yes, although I have a slightly more nuanced take on it. Over a 60 or 70-year period, like DARPA, there will be punctuated massive successes—the power law, where every 20 years or so there will be, in US terms, a grand slam, a programme that is so incredibly impactful that it easily pays the budget for ARIA for a 20-year period. However, in the meantime it will not be that there will be zero successes but they will be smaller. The Oshen example by itself is probably not a grand slam but it produces really useful technology that is profitable. There are similar examples that change our understanding of science, are good advancements, create useful companies and industry that may be not of the same, “Oh my God, it changed everything”, but are still very worthwhile and probably pay the bills. They just do not have the same type of impact.
Baroness Willis of Summertown: Yes, I get that. I think that you do share that vision, but I understand where you are coming from.

The third question is that the length of grant is very short—three years. First, is that, in your view, long enough? I was thinking about my own research and within three years you are barely off the starting blocks. Do you follow it up? Are there follow-on grants and how do you choose what you will follow? It could take something 10 years, for example. Take nuclear fusion, for example. If we had not had the government support, that would have stopped years ago. How do you balance that?

It is three to five years; it is not always three years. What is useful about that is that it does not continue by default. It stops by default and then you can continue it. An illustrative example, again from DARPA, is that DARPA invested in artificial intelligence for 60 years, but it did not set out to invest in AI for 60 years. It invested in AI for 60 years because over and over and over again different people continued to decide that investing in AI was a good choice, even though for most of that time there were not massive returns on AI.

ARIA has mechanisms to decide to double-down, to add investment, to reinvest in areas, but those reinvestments are decisions that this is still a good area for ARIA to invest in, still something that would not happen without ARIA’s investment, that other funding agencies, other sources of funding, would not pick up the ball and run with it. Therefore, what is important is that the funding does not continue by default. It stops by default and ARIA has to make a proactive decision to continue the funding.

Two or three weeks ago I was at Newcastle talking with a researcher who was working on forecasting tipping point s . He had a sensor that could detect moisture, which he originally was using to detect moisture for farms but was repurposing to detect glacier melt in Greenland. He originally wrote the proposal for ARIA, thinking that it would take three years. He has accomplished in a year what he had planned to do for three years. Part of that was because he originally planned to work 20% time, but ARIA asked him, “Can you only work 20% time? If we could fund you, can you work 80% time?” He said, “Sure, I would love to work 80% time”. We talked to his university and his university was fine with him working 80% time. Therefore, working for ARIA can compress the amount of time. Like the example that I talked about with Amodo and the bespoke engineering and pooling the resources, you can go faster. Part of it is that we are working at a sprint.
Baroness Willis of Summertown: Let us say that he has gone to 80%. Does that mean that his funding only lasts for one year?
No, his funding is extended. He can go further.

Baroness Willis of Summertown: He can go further. My other question is that you said you will continue the funding of a subject area, but what about the people? If you have someone who is an absolute star, does that stop or can you carry on funding the same person?

It would depend on what they wanted to do with their research and whether that aligned with ARIA’s purpose. ARIA does not have a long enough track record to know, but there is a synergy that happens where people find ways to continue working and get funded for a long period with DARPA. DARPA is larger, so it is easier at DARPA than at ARIA, but in the fullness of time I could imagine that happening at ARIA as well.

Q3 Lord Duncan of Springbank : Following up on Baroness Wil lis’s point, if you find that a project is not going where you thought it was going but it has done a lot of useful stuff, how do you influence a pivot point within the project that says, “It will not get to where we thought it was, but we still think it has enough—we would like it to pivot”? Is there a mechanism within your structure that says, “We can guide you further to a different destination in real time”?

Absolutely. This is why the relationship of the programme directors with the creators is so important and why the programme directors are constantly meeting with the creators. The programme directors and the creators are talking all the time about what they are doing and how the science is coming out and where it is going. If the original vector is not turning out to be promising but a related vector is turning out to be promising and it is still in the direction of interest to ARIA—hopefully in the direction of the North Star of the programme—that is a perfectly fine pivot.

One of the lessons that we are learning is that originally our contracts were very specific and some of those pivots would need to be adjusted in the contract, which is overhead. We are learning to write contracts that are more flexible in the terms so that we can do those pivots without having to rewrite a contract, where it is still specific about the work that is being done but the milestones are tracked separately. They do not need to be tracked in the contract per se, which is a best practice from DARPA, for example.
Lord Duncan of Springbank : That would not interfere with how you measure the success?
Yes, we can measure success not in the contract. Measuring success independent from the contract is a best practice that we are adopting.

Q4 Thank you very much indeed for coming this morning. What you are saying to us is very interesting. Could you give us a view of the selection of programme directors—obviously they are critical to the aims—to give them as much latitude and freedom as possible? As you recruit your third cohort very soon, what are the things that you have learned about the qualities of the directors that you find most important? Do you think that will change during the course of your current approach to appointing them? Finally, has this been influenced greatly by seeing the existing progress of the projects they are doing?

Thank you for the question. We are in the middle of recruiting cohort 3. It is important that we recruit programme directors regularly because they are term-limited, so they will leave and ARIA will be always recruiting. The vision is that we will be recruiting cohorts every two years. One of the important lessons is that we recruit an entire cohort, because that will give us balance across our opportunity spaces. One of the exciting things about how ARIA recruits programme directors is as a cohort so that we can view a whole class of candidates at the same time, which is different to how DARPA does it. DARPA recruits one at a time, which means that you are making a decision about whether this person is above the bar, whether this person above the bar, and you have a very small pool at any one time to be considering for a particular post.

At ARIA the current class deadline is 28 September and we have more than 1,200 applicants right now. In the last round we had 400 applicants. This is a testimony to how well ARIA is perceived here in the UK and abroad, which is really exciting , because the quality of the programme director is important for the success of the agency and the programmes.

On your question about the qualities that we are looking for in a programme director, they are multiple. One of them is technical depth. They are managing science breakthroughs and they need to understand good science and what good science looks like. They also need to be technically broad, because all of our programmes are interdisciplinary, so you need to have an appreciation not just of one particular discipline but be able to talk across disciplines. You also need to have good technical judgment, because people will come to you and try to sell you stuff. You need to be able to appreciate whether that sales pitch is well grounded or it is snake oil. It is technical depth, technical breadth and technical judgment.

You also need to have an entrepreneurial spirit, because ARIA is not in science for science’s sake. Just getting a scientific breakthrough is not enough. ARIA’s mission is to make the UK and the world a better place through scientific breakthroughs. Making the world a better place requires getting across the valley of death, so our programme directors have to have that entrepreneurial spark. We are looking for that in some way. You need to have good communication skills because, as the programme director, you do not do the technical work yourself. You explain and convince and cajole other people to do the technical work, and that requires good communication skills. Similarly with leadership skills, because you have to have the hard conversations with the scientific teams that, “You are not doing what you need to be doing”. You have to be able to fire people and to motivate people to do the work. That requires good leadership skills.

You also have to have good resilience, because you have to go around the UK and the world to explain what you are trying to do and get told by people that it is stupid or that it is really exciting . It is like doing a PhD. The first time you put together a programme—that process—even if people tell you you are doing a good job, you do not believe it. When doing a PhD, you do not believe it until you are all the way through the process, so you have to be resilient.

Nobody comes to ARIA or to DARPA with all of those skills, which is probably not surprising given the list of things I have just told you. Therefore, you also have to be able to take feedback well, because if you do not take feedback, the time it takes to learn all those skills is too long because you only have a three-year appointment plus one or two years of renewal. People who are able to learn on the job faster by listening to people who are working hard to coach you to get up to that set faster will make a bigger difference faster. Those are the set of skills that we are looking for. We found them in the first two cohorts and I am convinced that we will find them in this cohort as well.

On some of the learnings, the first cohort was heavily academic and the second cohort was heavily entrepreneurial. We are looking in the third cohort for a balance of both academic and entrepreneurial. In the first cohort we allowed people to be 80% time, to accommodate academics. The second cohort we made 100% time at ARIA. The third cohort will go back to letting people be 80% time to allow people to be academics. That is partly because academics often have PhD students who they do not want to abandon. I have seen at DARPA that it is definitely doable to be an academic on 80% time and be effective as an ARIA or a DARPA programme manager.

The Chair: To intervene for a second, on the 1,200 applicants who you have just mentioned, do you have, off the top of your head, what proportion of those would be academics and what proportion would be from outside academia?
I do not know. I am sure that there is a healthy mix, but I can get you statistics.
Lord Winston: It would be useful to know.
The Chair: Yes, it would be helpful to know.
Lord Winston: Is that possible?

We can get you the statistics. Maybe wait until the 28 September deadline so that we can get you the statistics of the full pool. We have been going on a tour around the world and the UK to highlight the positions and to explain working with ARIA.
Lord Patel: Does it matter for your programme whether it is academics or those who come from industry?

The people matter a huge amount. I think that both academics and industry people can be hugely successful as programme directors. Having a mix in the cohort is valuable because a bonding happens between the programme directors. They talk to each other a lot, so having some of each is a good combination. At this point we have a good mix of academics and entrepreneurs across the two cohorts. We would like to see that replicated within the third cohort.

Lord Winston: Could I come back with my last question? Your previous CEO suggested to us that the ideal projects were the ones where there was violent disagreement, where half the people looking at it thought that it was a fantastic project and the other half thought that it was complete rubbish. What do you feel about that? Do you feel that you can make those decisions to find the projects where there is very considerable disagreement in the panel that is looking at it?

I do not know that I would be as strong as Ilan was, that what you are shooting for is 50:50. I think that zero people is a bad sign and 100% is a bad sign—it is somewhere in between. I do not think that you should be going for 100% of people who think that this is a good idea. If you are there, it is probably too settled and probably a case where the field is already going to go there. If nobody thinks that it is a good idea, you probably should not be doing it either.
Lord Winston: That is a pretty sane answer. Thank you very much.
The Chair: Lord Willis, would you like to come in online? Oh, I am sorry, we are not getting Lord Willis; we cannot hear you. Lord Winston, would you like to ask the question for Lord Willis?

Q5 Very quickly, because it follows up on what we have been discussing already. Programme directors retain a great deal of autonomy. How do they allocate their funding with that autonomy, what approaches have been taken to allocate that funding and what is your view of how the research is best performed?
I did not hear the last part of your question. Can you repeat it?
Lord Winston: What approach have your directors of projects taken to allocate the funding that they get? What is your view as to where the research is best performed?

There are lots of different programme structures that can work and the right programme structure depends on what the programme is trying to accomplish. One structure is that you allocate all of the money up front and you then actively manage as the programme goes along, cutting the teams that are not effective. Sometimes you overallocate at the beginning because you assume that you will cut certain teams. The programmable plants programme, for example, took the first strategy there because plants, it turns out, grow really slowly, so they anticipated that, no matter what, it would take a long time for the plants to grow and doing something faster was not going to be helpful.

In the enduring atmospheric platforms programme, where the teams have a relatively expensive cost to send various vehicles up into the stratosphere to set up communications, the programme director wanted to take the approach where we invest in a whole bunch of different approaches, overcommitting at the beginning and then cutting the teams—the ones that show the least promise—which allows you to put more shots on goal. That is an advantage of that approach but it means that the teams know that they are actively competing against each other for a smaller pot, so they will not be working with each other because they know that they will get cut. Some of them will have to get cut because the programme does not have enough budget to continue all of them forward.

The forecasting tipping points programme set up a structure where they were not sure what approaches would work. Therefore, they set up a two-phase programme where they ran the first phase for 18 months and they will send out a second solicitation in the next month or two to set up the second phase of the programme. That was appropriate because they knew that they would be able to iterate and get information in the first 18 months that would dramatically affect what they wanted to do in the second part of the programme.

The trust everything, everywhere programme that Alex is running is running a competition because he wanted to see what was out there. That space is moving so fast and there are so many players and it did not seem that he would be able to get all of the people on contract that he wanted to be able to try out. By running a competition, you can throw it out there and see who will come to play. The challenge of a competition is that it is extremely challenging to get the rules exactly right so that you are rewarding what you want to be measuring and not inadvertently rewarding something else. You need to be very careful about setting it up so that the players cannot cheat in a way that you do not want them to be cheating. Those are all interesting different structures.

We recently hired a chief science and technology officer, who comes from spending significant time at DARPA and has had a large amount of his career working on different programme structures, to help particularly cohort 3 be very sophisticated in programme structures. One thing that he will be particularly looking at is setting up; I talked about phased structure and funding structure. Another interesting structure is the technical area structure. ARIA has done quite a bit on a social impact structure and an adoption structure of how this technology will be received, which has been interesting.

Another technical area that is very common at DARPA is an evaluation team, because often how you evaluate cutting-edge science is itself a research area and it provides programme directors with an interesting lever arm. If you are creating challenge problems, you can make challenge problems more or less difficult and you can choose challenge problems to facilitate translation or adoption. Having a separate technical area that is responsible for managing evaluation gives the programme director another lever arm to move. The new chief science and technology officer, who will be starting on 1 October, has deep expertise in these structure choices and he will be working with cohort 3 in those choices.

Q6 Good morning, Dr Fisher. My questions will focus on ARIA’s approach to bringing economic benefit specifically to the United Kingdom. When we spoke to Matt Clifford, he said that ARIA has been designed very explicitly as a value-creation mechanism rather than a value-capture one. However, ARIA has a mandate that says it needs to bring economic benefit to the UK specifically. How is ARIA doing that?

Thank you for the question. I appreciate that ARIA has indeed a mandate to bring economic benefit to the UK. I think that ARIA is a value-creation agency primarily, but it also has a value-capture role. ARIA’s value-creation mechanism by itself will bring tremendous economic benefit to the UK. For example, the precision neurotechnologies effort that Jacques Carolan is bringing is working on creating technology to address neurological disorders and neuropsychiatric disorders that currently afflict one in six citizens of the UK and cost the National Health Service £4.1 billion a year. If that programme delivers technology that could treat those patients in a much more economic way, that will deliver enormous economic benefit to the UK without having any profit associated with it. Therefore, value creation can be economically impactful by not costing the NHS an enormous amount of money and by returning the people who are currently suffering from those ailments to the productive workforce.

That said, I agree that value capture is also an important part of what we are doing. That is part of the reason why we created the chief translation officer, whose job is to work with programme directors to identify what the impact path is. Every time we create a programme, we also think about what the path is for translation of this programme, what the path is for social or economic impact. Some of them are things like climate change, but some of them are creating companies and driving those companies to cross the valley of death and commercialisation and how they can deliver that benefit to the UK.

Our IP terms are designed to maximise that. We have chosen not to take intellectual property. We think that the best way to drive economic benefit for the UK is to have the creator themselves maintain the IP rights so that when the creator goes to start a company, their cap table is clean and they have the best terms to go to the venture capital companies and get funding. They will be maximally incentivised to go and do that process. We have, with multiple activation partners, worked to create a climate to incentivise an entrepreneurial spirit to go and drive the commercialisation through those mechanisms. I can say more, but I will stop there for now.

Lord Drayson: Your example, Dr Fisher, is a great example of how the programme would bring economic and societal benefit to the UK, but not specifically to the UK. Those issues that you highlighted are common globally. It is the economic benefit to the UK specifically that I want to drill down into, rather than a spreading of progress globally. When we spoke to ARIA’s leadership back in 2024, they very clearly expressed the view that any attempt to capture value for the UK specifically could jeopardise the success of the project attracting investment. Do you agree with that?

Crossing the valley of death is really hard and crossing it successfully needs to be the first priority . If we can successfully cross the valley of death, we need to think about how to make sure we cross it in a way that maximises benefit to the UK. ARIA is working to create an environment that makes crossing the valley of death in the UK as maximally attractive as possible. That is why we are doing things like the venture café with the activation partner in London, Manchester and Edinburgh to create a climate where entrepreneurs know that they are not alone—that there are tons of entrepreneurs in the UK.

One of the things that I have been asked by creators who are thinking about becoming an entrepreneur is, “What if I create a start-up and it fails?” with the implicit notion that having a failed start-up is like a kiss of death and your career is over, versus the mindset in Silicon Valley where a failed start-up is a perfectly good thing to have on your resumé. It gives you credibility to start another start-up. The creator communities, the Venture Café , are creating the mindset that if you do not try, that is a failure. Trying and failing is a perfectly reasonable thing to do. It is why we have the activation partner, Fifty Years, which is one of the world’s best deep-tech venture capital companies, working with us to run the 50 50 partner, to work with scientists on how to create a pitch deck and how to be an entrepreneur—to create a population who will become entrepreneurs who decide that they want to create a great company and want to stay in the UK and do value capture here.

Lord Drayson: Dr Fisher, you have highlighted the important role of activation partners in crossing the valley of death, as you describe it. Why are some of your activation partners not based in the United Kingdom?

When we made the agreements with the world-class, deep-tech investors who know how to convert science into world-class companies, the terms of the agreement required them to establish UK operations and to invest all of the money in the UK. Yes, they are US companies, but they are focusing these efforts on the UK. That is a good thing for the UK because they are bringing their expertise. They know how to do this but they are bringing them to the UK.

Lord Drayson: Yes, but as multiple inquiries have shown, the UK does not have a problem in attracting investment. The UK has a problem in commercialising the breakthroughs that are made here in the UK to generate economic growth from the UK. Is there a case to be made, when it comes to selecting investors to help commercialise ARIA’s discoveries, that ARIA should prefer UK investment partners?

ARIA’s role is producing companies that have world-class technology and world-class teams and want to stay in the UK. If there are UK investment organisations that want at that point to fund the organisations, that would be fantastic. If there are not UK investment companies at that point that want to invest and there are US investment companies that want to invest and keep the company in the UK, that would be fantastic. The most important thing is that the company decides that it wants to stay in the UK, whether the funding comes from the US or the UK. The most important thing is that the company does not die.

Lord Drayson: Unfortunately, Dr Fisher, from this committee’s previous inquiry, in our Bleeding to Death report we have catalogued thoroughly the tendency of promising UK technology start-ups to leave the UK. Therefore, my concern is the risk that the activation partners become acquisition partners facilitating the cream of ARIA’s IP to ultimately benefit global investors outside of the UK rather than creating wealth and economic growth in the UK. Do you see this as a risk? If you do, what will you do about it?

I do not see that as a huge risk. I see the huge upside of leveraging their knowledge and expertise to produce world-class companies that maximise the chance of crossing the valley of death, and therefore getting the benefits of the value creation no matter what, and maximising the chance of having companies that will in the long run decide to stay. It is not only ARIA’s responsibility to make it so that these organisations decide they want to stay in the UK. Our remit is producing the selection of companies and, as an entire ecosystem, we have the opportunity to create the conditions in which they will want to stay. We are doing our part to contribute to that ecosystem to make it attractive for those companies to want to stay.

Lord Drayson: You have already in your earlier answer touched on the issue of intellectual property. ARIA is unusual in that ARIA projects do not have the IP generated retained by ARIA. There was some explanation by Ilan Gur and Matt Clifford in their previous evidence to us that there are some royalty payment arrangements that come back to the UK, but you will be aware of the significant concern that has been raised on this issue. Have you considered or are you considering changing ARIA’s approach to intellectual property to help ensure that these breakthroughs do stay in the UK and do generate economic growth here?
We are always reviewing our policies, and if we come across a policy that we think would serve ARIA’s mission better, we would be happy to adopt it.
Lord Drayson: I am afraid, Dr Fisher, that that is a very politician-like answer, a bit surprising from the CEO of ARIA.
It happens to be true.
Lord Drayson: Are you reviewing this policy now?

We are constantly—we are looking at our IP policies, but our current assessment is that the policy that Ilan talked about last year is the correct policy. ARIA’s best way of making the world and the UK a better place and producing economic return for the UK is through value creation. To do that value creation, we have to cross the valley of death, and that means getting the technology out. Our analysis to date is that the best way to do that is to put the IP in the hands of the creators. Most of the creators are in the UK and that intellectual property is, therefore, in the UK. If the intellectual property is licensed or assigned or sold outside of the UK, there is a royalty fee due to the UK. They are the same conditions that Ilan talked about last year. If we come across a better policy, we will implement a better policy. However, again our primary goal is the value creation and crossing the valley of death.
Lord Drayson: I think I understand that you are saying that you have everything under constant review, but you have not considered changing ARIA’s approach to IP.
We have talked about changing ARIA’s approach to IP, but those conversations to date have concluded that our current policy is the best policy for accomplishing ARIA’s mission.
Lord Drayson: Thank you for that clarity. Thanks very much.

Q7 Thank you for your time today. I am following on from Lord Drayson’s questioning about economic benefit to the UK. As someone who spent most of my time in the private sector, I am very supportive of collaboration between industry and government when we are at the cutting edge of science and technology. There was an announcement last week where the chair of ARIA, who has resigned now, was moving on to a global US firm, Anthropic, but was going to retain his position as chair of ARIA. That led to quite a bit of dismay in the UK, as we are talking about UK economic benefit and UK businesses—particularly now in the AI industry, where growth, development and investment is such a hotbed and we are competing in that global race. There was confusion that somebody who had been so close to the UK’s AI strategy, not only the AI Safety Institute and the AI action plan but the architect of the AI action plan, would remain in position as chair of ARIA and take up such a critical role. I say this, I should declare, as a co-founder of the Business AI Alliance, which has several hundred UK AI start-ups in it, as vice-chair of the AI APPG and an adviser to some UK AI businesses. I heard this and it was felt and it was in the press, and there was a genuine anger and I think that it united the political spectrum as well as industry in questioning how this decision had come about. I know that yesterday Matt Clifford announced that he was resigning as chair, but I would like to understand what the thinking was within ARIA before that resignation in allowing that role to continue.
It was not ARIA’s decision. It was up to BIST to decide on the mitigations in place. ARIA did not have a role in that decision.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: Did the executive team and you not have any consideration about how that may impact ARIA’s perception, the people involved in ARIA or the broader industry?
It was a conversation between Matt and BIST. The appointment of the chair of the board is under BIST not under ARIA’s purview. Therefore, no, we were not involved in that conversation.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: Did you receive any feedback once that announcement came out about how it was being received?
Yes.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: Would you like to share what feedback that was, without any—
The feedback that I received was much along the lines of what you have reported.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: What was your view on that? How would you communicate a response to that feedback?
The decisions and so on were conversations between BIST and Matt, and it is up to them to decide what they needed to do.

Lord Ranger of Northwood: The reason I am asking this, as I think you will understand, is about confidence in UK AI businesses and the relationship between such a significant funding body that is so strategically critical to decisions that the UK will take and its relationship with large international businesses such as Anthropic, and this was seen as a huge conflict. The concern is there that, yes, okay, the decision may sit with BIST, but what was ARIA itself thinking and what was its executive team thinking as this decision was being made? That has raised a lot of concern in the industry. Do you accept that point?
I understand the concern, and ARIA was not consulted.

Lord Patel: Following on from that, do you think that there are lessons learned from this episode that occurred—that it is important that the future chair of ARIA does not have conflict of interests that may in some way end up not harming necessarily but impeding the work of ARIA in any way?

I think that it is essential that the chair of ARIA does not have conflict of interests that impede the agency. It is important to acknowledge that we choose board members for their expertise in science and technology and translation. It is not uncommon that board members have interests that overlap with ARIA. Board members declare their interests and those interests are published on the website and are routinely monitored and updated, and we have mitigations that are put in place. ARIA has a code of conduct that is in line with the code of conduct for board members of public bodies and we monitor and put in place those mitigations regularly. You do not want board members who know nothing about the industry or the topics, so there is a judgment call about the expertise and the experience and the degree of conflicts.
The Chair: The point you are making is one of 100% transparency.
Indeed.
The Chair: We understand. Thank you.

Q8 Good morning, Dr Fisher. My question will come as no surprise in that I am calling in from my home in Cornwall. ARIA has been criticised in the past for the percentage of funding that goes on projects in the golden triangle of London, the east of England and greater south-east. In 2025 your corporate plan said that you would set diversity metrics based on gender and geography to drive a more diverse discovery process. However, in 2025-26, 67% of ARIA funding was spent in the golden triangle, and that was much unchanged from the previous year at 66%. Given the Government’s focus on regional economic development through research and development, what steps is ARIA taking that funds opportunity across the United Kingdom?

I have talked about how ARIA’s mission is to make the UK and the world a better place through scientific breakthroughs. That mission on a per-programme basis requires a science miracle and then a crossing the valley of death miracle. That is a daunting mission and it requires working with the absolute best scientists. We know that the best scientists are spread out across the entire UK. I have talked about Oshen, which is in Plymouth. I have talked about Amodo Design, which is not a creator but an activation partner, in Sheffield. I have not mentioned Touchpoint, which is a small company that is on our robot dexterity programme in Sheffield. [2] I mentioned the creator I talked to in Newcastle the other day. We have worked with fantastic creators.

Those are just four that I have mentioned not across the golden triangle, but we are not where we want to be. The golden triangle has a dense concentration of world-class scientists, so it is not surprising that they are well represented in our portfolio. However, as I said, we are not where we want to be. That is why we have put in place the requirement that our programme directors must do their discovery process. When a programme director sets up a programme, they kick the tyres on their thesis by going and talking to scientists all over the world, not just the UK. We now have a process of taking their programme thesis and identifying the science and technology that underlies that, cross-referencing that with the scientists across the countries and regions of the UK and figuring out where they are and requiring the programme directors to talk to a representative sample across all the countries and regions of the UK.

I just got back from meeting with the DCSA [3] of Scotland and the DCSA of Northern Ireland, and I am scheduled to go to meet with the same in Wales. The DCSA of Scotland and the DCSA of Northern Ireland agreed to work with ARIA to make sure that in that process they would help us identify the scientists in Northern Ireland and Scotland that we should be talking to. Part of the challenge is that the way ARIA works is very distinct from the way the traditional funding agencies work. We do not have a call that comes out on a fixed deadline; for example, it is November, so the deadline comes out now. Our calls come out when the programme director has finished the discovery process and there is a relatively short period to when the proposals are due. The people who are in the know have been following the thesis publication or the discovery process to know that the proposal is coming and have already been talking to the programme director.
