That is why I went to Newcastle a few weeks ago, Scotland two weeks ago and Northern Ireland last week to meet with faculty at University of Strathclyde, University of Glasgow, Edinburgh University, Ulster University and so on to communicate this. This is so that people across all the countries and regions of the UK know how to work with us so that we can pick the best scientists across all the countries and regions of the UK and at the same time distribute the funding more equitably across the countries and regions.

The programme directors are required to do this discovery across the UK and in proportion to the scientists in the areas of their programme. They cannot get the programme approved until they have demonstrated that they have done so. We had one programme director a couple of months ago say, “I got all but one”. “Okay, well, we will delay your programme approval meeting until you are done.” Then they say okay and get that one scheduled. We are taking that seriously. It is important for ARIA to deliver on our mission, and the best way of doing that is reaching the best talent throughout the entire UK, and we are committed to doing so. The same thing applies with gender as well.

Baroness Jones of Whitchurch: I am listening intently to what you are saying, and it is good to hear that you are doing that regional engagement. The reality is that the consequences of this are not having a great deal of impact. The statistics are not changing. The money is still going to the golden triangle, the south-east, and so on. It is all very well talking to people, but that is very different from putting your money where your mouth is and funding the projects with a much broader distribution. You will know that the new incoming Government are focused on regional development, and I am sure that there will be pressure on you to be able to demonstrate in practical terms how that distribution of investment is happening on a broader scale. Do you recognise that there is a lot more work to be done here? Engagement is one thing, but you need to go out and find new talent in places that you would not normally find it to bring it into your funding structure. Please reassure me that that is happening, because otherwise you will talk to lots of people, but the bids for the projects will still come from the usual suspects.

That is what the engagement has set out to do—to find those people. Another thing we are doing is refining our data collection. Right now our data collection is only at the prime level. The primes are the people who have contracts directly with ARIA. In fact, primes have contracts with subs that are spread out, so prime contracts do not do a very good job of tracking where ARIA’s funding is going. We are working on refining our data collection so that we have a much better sense of where ARIA’s funding is actually going, tracking not just the people who receive ARIA funding but the people who apply for ARIA funding, at both the prime and the sub level, so that we can get a better sense of whether the problem is people not applying or people not getting funding.

When I went to the meeting in Newcastle, one of the comments that I heard in the audience was that they are serious about wanting to work with us. Part of the challenge is people not believing that ARIA wants to work with people outside of the golden triangle. Some of the engagement is extremely important from the point of view that we do not just care about the usual suspects; we care about working with the best people wherever they are. ARIA’s funding model of covering 100% of the costs and not just 80% means that universities do not have to pony up some of their own money and universities that are not so well funded are not at a disadvantage in applying for ARIA’s funding. The messaging is an important part of delivering in the long term. I want to try those mechanisms as the next step, which is a significant step up from what we have been doing, because I do not want to sacrifice ARIA’s prime mission, which is super important for the UK and the world.

Baroness Jones of Whitchurch: Going back to the discussion that we were having earlier, the latest stats show that 15% of your investment goes outside of the UK. Is that being reviewed? To what extent can we focus it? Fifteen percent is more than some of our regions, for example. Therefore, we are putting more money outside of the UK than in some of the regions that could have and do have very good research capacity. Are you reviewing that?

We definitely think about that, but the freedom to invest there is important. When we choose to start a programme, we kick the tyres on whether the science hypothesis is plausible. Is it at a place where it has the potential of a breakthrough? If the science breakthrough comes, is the potential for societal impact enormous? If ARIA does not do this, is it unlikely to happen? Those are some of the questions. Another key question that we ask is: does the UK have enormous scientific potential in this area? If we put out the funding call, will we get really strong proposals so that we can run the majority of the science and research with UK technology? It is unlikely that all the science and technology capability to give the programme the maximum chance of succeeding exists in the UK.

We reserve the potential to fund up to 20% of the research outside of the UK. When we get the proposals in, every proposal that gets funded outside of the UK has to cross a high bar—that this is a capability that is not in the UK and will enormously contribute to the likelihood that the UK part of the programme will succeed and cross the threshold, the scientific barrier, the valley of death, do that value creation and produce the promise of the North Star of the programme. All the non-UK funding has to cross a much higher bar and have a case that it will add enormous value. Sometimes non-UK contracts cause the non-UK companies to relocate to the UK. For example, Normal Computing, one of the creators on the Nature Computes Better programme, moved to London and subsequently invested 150% of their ARIA funding because the talent it has found in the UK and London has been so strong. There are sometimes upsides to that non-UK funding as well.

Q9 Thank you very much for coming and for your very thoughtful answers. I want to take forward some of the discussion that has already begun on your understanding of and relationship with the research landscape across the UK. We have just discussed the regional part of that, so I will not ask you to repeat that. In response to Baroness Willis, you emphasised that if nobody is doing something, there may be a reason for that, and that may not be a good place for you to do your ploughing, as it were. If everybody is doing that, maybe you are not needed, and you did not want to stick with a number in the middle but somewhere in that spectrum, which will depend presumably on the subject matter.

Could you say something more about how your programme directors understand that research landscape? You have said that you are out there and you are trying to convince people that you are serious, and it sounds as if they are responding to that. This has to be done at a fairly granular level and the programme director has to understand what is going on where in quite a detailed way. How do they go about doing that?

The programme director has some initial idea about what they are interested in doing. They read a lot of literature, and they use AI a ton, which is common practice these days. They then talk to a ton of people. It turns out, as with DARPA, if you are an ARIA programme director and you call people, they answer the phone or the email and spend time. I was talking to a programme director the other day and, “Wow, fancy, people answer the phone when you talk to them”. They talk to various people to refine the hypothesis. They go on what we call discovery tours. Ivan, who is the programme director for the materials science programme, went to talk to people in every country and region of the UK. In the process, they refine the programme thesis.

At some point, when they have kicked the tyres to their satisfaction, they publish the programme thesis, which is both a short statement and a multi-page document, outlining their beliefs and observations and what they think that says, to get open feedback. This statement is informed by all the conversations that they have had. At some point, either before or after the workshop—it depends a little on the programme; some have done it before and some after—they run a workshop, which is by invitation. They invite people who they have talked to or who have been named in the process. In this discovery process, you talk to one person and ask who else you should talk to, and that goes on. One of the termination criteria mentioned by a programme director was when that process does not discover any more names, they feel they have reached the conclusion.

The discovery workshop often ends up with three or four different scientific disciplines that do not normally talk to each other, and they are facilitated so that you get those people talking to each other and finding out what you can discover if you apply this technology to that problem. Often one of the other programme directors in the precision mitochondria programme was talking about how at the beginning they wondered, “Why am I here? Why are they here?”, and then on the morning of the second day, they realised, “Oh my God, we can do this, and we can do that”—a discovery process. After ingesting that information from the discovery process, publishing the thesis and getting open comments from the workshop, the programme director writes a programme approval document, which is presented to a panel at ARIA, including the chief technical officer, the chief translation officer, the CEO and outside experts for approval.
Lord Stern of Brentford: Those workshops would include also people from outside the UK, and their view of what is going on in the UK is of real value.

Yes, for sure. The workshops often include the world’s experts on certain topics. There are many people from the UK, but the workshops vary in size depending on the programme. Some have multiple smaller workshops and some have a larger workshop, but there are many people from the UK and there are also people from outside the UK.
Lord Stern of Brentford: On tipping points, which is a subject that concerns a number of us in this group, you would obviously want to bring in people like the Potsdam Institute, PIK, and so on.
There are definitely world experts on the panel. It is not just people in the UK.

Q10 Very good. Thank you very much for that. I would like to ask now about how you compare ARIA and DARPA. You are particularly well placed to answer that question. You have brought DARPA examples up during this discussion. Could you give us a broad-picture view of how you see ARIA and DARPA as similar or different, and how ARIA learns from DARPA, can learn from DARPA and so on?

They are both high-risk, high-reward, programme director-driven, project-based agencies. The mission is different. DARPA’s mission is national security; ARIA’s mission is making the UK and the world a better place through breakthrough science. DARPA does a lot of classified work, which adds a ton of friction that ARIA does not have to deal with. DARPA’s budget is a lot bigger. DARPA is a lot older and has a proven track record that means it does not have to prove its existence, while ARIA still has to prove its existence.

DARPA has the Department of Defense as a customer and I think it is overblown that people talk about how DARPA has a built-in customer. Having been the director of the Information Innovation Office, DARPA’s computer science office that just got renamed IPTO, there was nobody in the Pentagon who was eagerly awaiting the products of IPTO or I2O. I spent a lot of my time as the director of I2O strategising about how to take the results of our successful programme and subversively getting them to be translated into the Pentagon. I think that translates very well into ARIA, where we have to figure out how to engineer translation.

I mentioned earlier about the hiring process, how DARPA hires on a one-off basis, and ARIA hires more in cohorts. ARIA will still have to hire sometimes in individual cases; I had a lot of experience of hiring individual programme managers at DARPA, which will be helpful in the cases where we have to hire programme directors at ARIA individually. DARPA has another level of hierarchy that ARIA does not have because the scale of ARIA is smaller. The scale of ARIA is roughly the size of the office that I managed at DARPA. ARIA’s scope is all of science, roughly the way that DARPA’s scale is all of science, but the financial size of the office and the number of programme directors at ARIA is roughly the size of the office that I managed at DARPA, so a significantly smaller budget.

Lord Stern of Brentford: Thank you very much. I want to follow up on the public procurement side, because DARPA, being associated with national security, would have a customer in defence for a lot of what it did, although perhaps not the stuff that you were doing. The public procurement issue is still important for the UK because crossing the valley of death, as you have emphasised a number of times, depends on the market and potential customers—that is the first question in crossing the valley of death. Do you think there is scope for a more active link between public procurement in the UK and what ARIA does? If so, how could that happen?

There definitely is, and I have talked to our chief translation officer about this. Every programme director has what we call an impact mechanisation plan: assuming your science pans out, what is your strategy for crossing the valley of death; or, as not every programme is doing commercialisation as their strategy, what is your strategy for impact? Some programmes have a strategy in place, but the science is very early, so they are mostly thinking about what they would do if the science panned out. Others are further along and may have an entrepreneur in residence working with the creators to put together business cases and teaching them that a pitch deck for a VC is not 17 slides about how cool the science is and one slide for “Give me money”; it is more like 17 slides on what the market is and one slide on “Give me money”. If they get further than that, it is all hands on deck. On some of the cases may need us to create a market, so how do we create a market, and how do we co‑ordinate with government to do that?

Advance market commitments could be very helpful in creating a market. For example, the Scaling Inference Lab, a programme in the AI hardware space, started with creating novel hardware because of the end of Moore’s law and Dennard scaling. Perhaps the end of Moore’s law is overblown, but we are now having to create more unusual kinds of hardware and co‑ordinate different kinds of hardware to be able to continue producing more and faster hardware. That programme funded the creation of different kinds of hardware, which has been very successful so far: “This piece of funky hardware is doing things much faster”. But the end user does not care about funky pieces of individual hardware; you have to put them together into a system that delivers overall system performance. Therefore, we stood up the Scaling Inference Lab, which is actual rack compute that delivers performance an end user can measure, and we are partnering with the Government; they are providing a commitment to buy it.

That is an example of ARIA doing exactly what you were talking about, and that is what our chief translation officer works on with programme directors when they reach the point where they need all hands on deck, all parts of the Government who might be potentially helpful in doing that kind of translation.

Q11 Clearly, you need the other side of the partnership. To push the question a little bit further, do you think BIST and the Treasury should do more to encourage government departments to have a closer relationship with ARIA so that these possibilities of procurement are explored as early as possible? That also would, of course, be a way of responding in part to the question that Lord Drayson was emphasising about benefit in the UK.

It depends on a programme-by-programme basis. So far when we have reached out we have met with partners across the Government who have been very enthusiastic and helpful in working with us on what is needed for the particular programme in a way that continues to preserve ARIA’s independence. I would welcome those continued kinds of engagement across the Government as we get particular programmes in particular locations in particular stages where that kind of engagement would be helpful.

Lord Stern of Brentford: I want to go on to something else, but to remark on that, it is one thing you reaching out to them; it is another for them to have an active role in getting all parts of Government to reach out to you.

Indeed, and it is tricky because before we are ready, we do not want premature engagement but when we are ready, we absolutely want to be actively engaged with the appropriate parts of the Government.

Q12 My last question is about UKRI and the way in which the UK research and innovation landscape is changing—and it is changing for good reason. In that process, do you think there are major lessons from ARIA that can help inform the strategies being followed to recast those structures?

I will start by saying that a healthy UKRI ecosystem is absolutely essential for ARIA to be able to do its job well. Part of the discovery process that I was talking about, or the basis of confidence for whether the science in a given area is mature enough or is at a point where an ARIA investment makes sense, relies on there being a science and technology base that is suitable for ARIA to build on top of. Part of the reason why I was excited to come to ARIA as a CEO is because in many indices about research and engineering in the world, the UK is around third, and per capita it is number one in the world. That is on the back of UKRI’s investment. You cannot have an agency like ARIA if there is no agency like UKRI doing the blue-sky research.

The funding for the long-term scientific infrastructure that ARIA pulls upon comes from UKRI. ARIA does projects; we go in and we do three-to-five-year funding, or maybe we do it for a long time, in successive funding chunks. We do not do the long-term commitment that UKRI does that sustains a healthy ecosystem of scientists. You cannot have a healthy ARIA if you do not have a healthy UKRI. It is extremely important for ARIA that there is a healthy long-term agency like UKRI.

The way ARIA funds is programme-based. We go in and we do a sprint in a particular area to say we think we can accelerate the progress in that area. UKRI does the important work of building the path forward, brick by brick. They are very complementary models. I think before ARIA was established, the UK was missing an important modality of doing research. With ARIA’s establishment, it has become an ecosystem that has a lot more promise.

I am not sure that I have a lot to say on lessons learned because I am not an expert in the UKRI. I was a researcher for many years. I was a professor for seven years, department chair for five in the NSF ecosystem in the US, which is only somewhat analogous to the UKRI analysis. I do not want to overstep my areas of expertise.

Lord Stern of Brentford: Is that something you would bear in mind? You are learning a lot about how to get research done and about the research environment in the UK. Do you see openings or value added in sharing that in a direct way with UKRI?

Sure. I have already met with Ian Chapman multiple times, and I have met with the heads of all the UKRI organisations multiple times as well. We have a lot to learn from talking to each other, and certainly at the scientific level, there are many things to learn.

Lord Stern of Brentford: Before I hand back to Baroness Willis, I cannot resist just one observation, which is that—and I say this as a university professor—the UK’s deep strengths in science come from, in large measure, a few hundred years of first-class universities before UKRI came along. Our strengths, I hope, and we all hope, are enhanced by UKRI, but there is a deeper source there, which is, as many of us know, under some threat at the moment on the financial side. That is not a question; that is an observation. It is prompted by not overdoing the link between the strength of the UK science base and UKRI, although we all hope and encourage UKRI to do its best to make the most of that.
I appreciate the information regarding both UKRI and the universities.

Q13 One more question, coming back to how you ensure there is not overlap in the subject areas that you are working on compared to those being funded by other trusts and foundations. I have sat in workshops—I am not going to name the foundations but they are not in this country—for the very role that you mentioned of having international experts come in. I found in the two that I have done in the last couple of years that I was the lone voice in there; the rest of the people were scientists from that country with incredible levels of self-interest regarding what the areas should be going forwards. In some ways, that plays against the blue-sky nature, because you want the expertise but there is a balance in there.

Is there another way, with all your background and expertise from DARPA and your AI knowledge, that we should be moving away from workshops? What is your view on this? Are there alternative ways to work out what the new areas of research are? My second question is: how do you manage to avoid overlap? One criticism I have heard of ARIA is that some of the programmes directly overlap those being funded by other large trusts and foundations in other countries.

We are experimenting with using AI extensively. This was the summer of AI, and “everyone is a dev” was one of the projects this summer. We have been experimenting extensively with using cutting-edge AI to kick the tyres and read the literature and challenge our assumptions. I personally have been using AI a lot, certainly not for making decisions, but it is incredibly good at reading a large volume of literature. I have an AI Gem, or whatever they are called—and I actually use multiple of them—and I have told it to not be sycophantic at all. I do not need it to suck up to me at all. I want it to challenge the assumptions, kick the tyres and always give me the sources to go back to. The programme directors do the same thing and are very sceptical of all these things. These are the kinds of tools that the programme directors and the leadership at ARIA are hungry for. We use those tools to supplement the workshops.

The workshops and the discovery are helpful, not just for being sceptical. I appreciate your point that there is a little bit of a conflict of interest because the people in the workshops are also possible funding recipients. The workshops are also mechanisms to recruit the creator base, so you need to do them as advertising but you also need to do them to gather information. The people who serve as experts on the review panels are expressly conflicted from ever receiving any funding in the programme, so they do not have a conflict of interest. We are doing our best to get unbiased opinions throughout the pipeline, even if the workshop feedback is not always unbiased.

On the point about other foundations potentially funding the same thing: we do ask the question about being differentiated among the experts who are on the panels and are conflicted from receiving funding, and we weigh that consideration strongly. Sometimes it may seem similar but not be that similar when you pull up the hood—the digital olfaction programme that we just approved is a good example. There was an article, maybe in Wired , about digital olfaction that came out shortly after the announcement. If you dig into the article, it was very much about specialised olfaction for a particular application, as opposed to a general-purpose e-nose. The question becomes whether you want 15 different electronic noses or one, and the game-changing nature of having one versus 15 or 70 as you go on. When I asked the programme director about the particular article , she had already talked to all the people quoted in the article. If we discover something that contradicts a particular part of the thesis, or the whole thesis, we pivot and shut down part of the programme or all of it.

Baroness Willis of Summertown: Taking the olfaction example, how would you react in your capacity as CEO if you found that the Gates Foundation, for example, had an almost identical call coming out at the same time?

We would talk to them, and in fact we have been talking to the Gates Foundation, so I am comfortable on that particular point . We would talk to them and do a deeper discovery to figure out how much they overlap, who the creators being funded are, how much technical risk there is in that area, and how much creator population there is. It could be that funding two efforts in parallel might be perfectly reasonable, or it might be that there is not that much depth and it would be the same people involved, so double funding would not be appropriate. We would need to look at it and figure out the appropriate response.
Baroness Willis of Summertown: There is a network of other foundations, such as the Simonian Foundation, that talk to each other.
Yes.

Q14 My question is slightly tangential, but maybe it is part of it. ARIA seems to be focused mostly on technological advances that may occur. One of the key pillars of UK economic activity or economic growth is the life sciences sector, which is quite strong. Part of the government plans now are that UK life sciences are the engine, and the fuel is the huge amount of NHS data, dirty and fragmented in most part. The challenge is—and the UK is now beginning to invest in it—to streamline this data and curate the data in a format that is accessible, the NHS being a cradle-to-grave organisation. Do you have a view about where you think ARIA may focus on this area or be able to help? There has also been a criticism that because it is data, if it is given to outside organisations, it could be—how should I say?— put to different kinds of usage.

Indeed. ARIA does have life science programmes. We have the precision neurotechnologies opportunity space, with two programmes in that area looking at neurological and neuropsychological disorders, with more than £100 million invested. We also have the programmable physiology opportunity space, which has a programme on viral resistance and a programme on precision mitochondria, amounting to roughly a £100 million investment. ARIA does do things in the life sciences. That said, ARIA has £ 1.2 billion to invest across all of science in the spending review period. Although £ 1.2 billion sounds like a huge amount of money, when spread across all of science, it is not very much, and ARIA can only do things where we have programme directors. The unit of energy or deployment is programme directors.

I experienced this viscerally at DARPA, where I wanted to do a programme on shutting down rogue AI—which seems extremely relevant these days—but I could not find a programme manager to hire who had the expertise and wanted to work in that space. It took me two years to recruit a programme manager for it. For ARIA to do work in a particular space, you have to hire a programme director in that space. The question of data and the protections around data is always important, and you have to be careful about who has the data and who has access to data. We take that very seriously. We always have the ethics, social responsibility and the normal procedures and practices about how you ethically and responsibly do work in a particular area. If we stood up a programme dealing with big data in a medical area, we would follow those practices and potentially conduct research on how to do that work even better.

Q15 Dr Fisher, you have very helpfully answered many of our questions. I have just two final questions for you. You mentioned, and it is very welcome news, that ARIA has been funded through the recent spending review, so you will have, we hope, quite a long time to go as CEO. What will be your top priorities for ARIA during your tenure and what would you most like to look back on and say you have achieved with ARIA?

My top priorities are delivering on many of the things I have talked to you about: the science miracles, the translation miracles and the shining beacon of hope. What I most want to accomplish is delivering on those things. ARIA’s long-term success is creating one of those breakthrough technologies, along the lines of the internet for DARPA, that establishes ARIA firmly in the minds of the UK and the world. That will take a while, and it is unpredictable when that might actually happen . In the meantime, we will deliver a steady progress of important breakthroughs and meaningful translation that will benefit the UK, both through value creation and value capture.

Another important contribution will be ARIA’s growth from a small start-up to a well-run organisation that is at full capacity, where programmes are ending at the same rate that programmes are being born. We are not quite at steady state at this point, but we are almost there. An organisation of 10 people who all fit around a table at the British Library operates very differently from one where everybody no longer fits around a table. Getting through that growth period is another important contribution.

ARIA is a place where people love to come, and I want to maintain that. I want people to come not because it is the new shiny thing but because it is a place where people know they can make a tremendous difference in the world and have a massive lever arm to change it for the better. Building and maintaining that is important. The people are critically important. I highlight that the people ARIA has attracted across the board are fantastic, and that is true of the operational teams, the communications teams, the finance team and the procurement team, in addition to the programme directors and their support staff.

Let me highlight one of the programme directors, Brian Wang, who, before coming to ARIA, started a company to create medication in advance of the next pandemic—hopefully not in the immediate future. He came to ARIA with the idea of new technology to address the same challenge, leveraging the innate immune system instead of the adaptive immune system. The challenge with the adaptive immune system is that vaccines have to be specially crafted for the particular virus , which is why we have to get a flu vaccine every year and why it does not always work. You have to predict what the particular manifestation of the flu will be, and if that prediction is not exactly right, the vaccine does not work. A little while ago, however, our understanding of the innate immune system advanced, and it is now possible that we might be able to sculpt and control the innate immune system more effectively.

One of the advantages of the innate immune system is that it is more general purpose, so it would be able to respond to all variations of the flu and not just be targeted to a specific version. Brian Wang’s goal is for that protection to last approximately three months at a time. That is what he came to ARIA to do, and that is the North Star goal of his particular programme . If successful, it would have enormous economic benefit. Among other things, it would finally provide a cure for the common cold, so that parents would not have to miss work when their kids are sick and we would not miss work when we were sick. We would, of course, want to commercialise that in a way that benefited the UK financially, not just in value creation but value capture. If it is successful, it would also provide an off-the-shelf treatment, most likely for the next pandemic, and so would have a national security application as well, delivering on ARIA’s mission of making the UK and the world a better place through breakthrough science.
The Chair: A cure for the common cold is a great ambition.
Of course, it is high risk, high reward. It most likely will not work exactly as envisioned, but no matter what, it will advance science.

The Chair: Indeed. Dr Fisher, thank you very much. You have answered our many questions and have been very helpful and informative. We wish you every success in your tenure as CEO of ARIA, and we will keep in constant touch with what ARIA is doing. Thank you very much for coming to talk to us this morning. That concludes this session.
[1] The witness has clarified that this refers to 35 projects across 25 Creator teams.
[2] This should refer to Touchlab in Edinburgh.
[3] Devolved Administration Chief Scientific Adviser.
