Councillor Lucy Nethsingha, Vice - Chair, County Councils Network; C ouncillor Eamonn O’Brien, Chair, Local Government Association ; Jonathan Stephenson, National Chief Executive Lead, Local Councils Network .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Lucy Nethsingha, Eamonn O’Brien and Jonathan Stephenson .

Q96 The Chair: Welcome to this meeting of the Economic Affairs Committee . W e have some distinguished guests from local g overnment who , we hope , will illuminate the problems of fiscal devolution, which is the subject of our inquiry. Please c ould you briefly introduce yourselves, then I will ask the first question.
​ Eamonn O ’ Brien: ​ I am the chair of the Local Government Association and the leader of Bury Council in Greater Manchester.
​ Lucy Nethsingha: I am the leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, and I am here as the representative from the County Councils Network.
​ ​ I am the chief exec of Brentwood Borough Council and Rochford District Council in South Essex, but also the chair of the c hief e xec utives’ g roup in the L ocal C ouncil s N etwork.
Q97 ​ ​ Thank you. The first question is about fiscal devolution . Do you think it will boost economic growth in your area a nd , if so, how ?

Eamonn O ’ Brien: ​ Thank you very much for inviting us. It i s an important topic, and timely. T his is central to the case for fiscal devolution : it can unlock not just economic growth but good economic growth, inclusive economic growth, however you want to describe it . I t puts local councils and strategic authorities in a position to more adequately address local needs, deliver on local priorities and exploit local opportunities.

F rom my experience in Greater Manchester , I do not think it is a coincidence that the area with the most progressed and strongest devolution arrangements is also now the fastest growing, in relation to both GDP per head and p roductivity. So there i s a growing body of evidence to support this. A piece of work by the OECD , done about 10 years ago now, provides a more theoretical argument in favour of this.

T he reason why I think it will unlock more economic growth is that it is a possible solution to a range of other issues facing local g overnment, the first of which is clearly the financial challenge and difficult ies facing many, many councils. We are in a position where money is tight , which is taking capacity and focus away from potential opportunities to deliver more economic growth . It is , effectively , forcing the conversation and all the time and energy , as well as a lot of the capacity , around managing demand - led complex services , such as social care and housing.

I f fiscal devolution can be an answer to those wider problems — I am sure we can develop our arguments further in this discussion — it will open up far more avenues to deliver projects that d eliver economic growth. As I said , that is good economic growth , which looks at people ’ s skills and education, health and well-being , housing, transport and a whole host of other areas. W e are confident , from both theory and practice , that we can stand behind fiscal devolution as a means to economic growth . C rucially, I think it has answers to other problems as well.

​ ​ I agree with most, if not all , of what Eamonn has just said. T here i s really strong evidence. My area is another area where we have a mayoral combined authority ; w e a re one of relatively few rural areas that have one . Our mayoral combined authority is not in a s advanced a state and has had significant problems on the way , b ut even in our area there is clear evidence of how devolution is driving growth in complicated but interesting ways, one of which is to do with our public transport and bus services. I am happy to talk about that at length later if anyone wants me to.

There i s a really important message from the C ounty C ouncils N etwork that I heavily endorse : devolution needs to be delivering for rural England as much as it is for city regions. At the moment , rural England is getting left behind in the devolution race , as it were. T hat is a real problem . F iscal devolution needs to think about how it is going to work for widely different areas across the country.

Rural England represents about half of England ’ s population and almost half of England ’ s businesses. It i s not quite half of England ’ s GVA , but if we are not delivering growth in rural England then the rest of England will not grow as fast as it could. T hinking about how fiscal devolution works in rural areas as well will be critical in this conversation.

​ ​ I agree with the points made. We definitely need a reset of fiscal devolution w ith regard to local councils . As an organisation , we represent 170 councils across very diverse communities. The challenge is the resources that we currently have and demand. We very much have Amazon Prime expectations on public services with a corner shop level of resource . That is a really difficult challenge for us to have in local g overnment.

There is also the challenge of the parent - child relationship with Governments — not just this Government —around funding opportunities and devolving those powers down . W here we have had opportunities we have definitely made a difference. L ocal place policies with those institutions that know the local postcodes and the local people have really made a difference to outcomes , whether during Covid, with UK shared prosperity funds or business improvement districts. Those are examples of a range of things where devolved powers have really started to make an impact at a local level o n the growth agenda.

​ ​ You a re saying that growth is the main motivation, but it also sounds as though better local g overnment is also your motivation —that growth is not the sole driver of this desire for devolution .

​ Eamonn O ’ Brien: ​ Absolutely. There i s always a debate about having more resources but even just having greater flexibility over existing resources will allow us to accelerate public service reform in a really meaningful way far better than we currently can. W hat I mean by that is moving the areas of spend away from very costly, reactive , crisis areas , such as social care and housing , and shifting resources into more prevention and early intervention areas . At the moment, many councils are struggling to do that , and many are taking money away from that just to fund and keep the lights on in some of those other areas.
G reater fiscal devolution and greater flexibility around that money are a means to an end. I do not think it is an achievement in and of itself ; it is about what it unlocks for local g overnment.
T he Chair: I hear your enthusiasm. Do you accept that , in this move to fiscal devolution, there are trade - offs? I f so, what have you thought th ose trade-offs to be?

​ Eamonn O ’ Brien: ​ I am happy to start, but there will inevitabl y be discussion around where some of th i s devolved mon ey go es to or get s decided upon. There is clearly a debate here about what you might call a “ vertical argument ” in relation to where this all sits. T hen there i s the debate about where you spread those resources ; t hat is maybe the horizontal argument for how you utilise these resources.

That is an inevitable challenge with any system. It is not something to shy away from. I think we can design systems that are mature enough to reflect different priorities, and that different areas will look and feel differently in how they distribute and make decisions about fiscal devolution.

T here are clearly challenges around where we are starting from. We are starting from a point of real financial challenge for local government. This is not a silver bullet to solve all those problems. This inevitably is going to take some time to effectively rebuild and get local government back to where it ought to be. I have described it to other people in a way in which it feels like we are driving around in first gear at the moment, and we are going to have to try and get out of that as quickly as possible. But you cannot go from first gear to fifth or sixth gear straight away. There is going to have to be an expectation that this is a process rather than an event.

I do not disagree with that. Can I also come back to your previous question about it being about not just growth but better local government? There is an important point about democracy and people being able to see where their taxes go. At the moment, there is quite a mismatch between what people feel council tax is being spent on and what it is actually being spent on. The majority of the public think that council tax goes on local services: roads, street lighting, libraries and things that they can see. In fact, the vast majority of council tax goes on social care, which they tend to think is national government spending. It is not.

That mismatch causes real problems for local government, in that it means that we are constantly being held to account for the fact that people are paying more and perceive that they are getting less for their money. That mismatch is a problem for local government but is actually a problem for our democracy because there is a mismatch between where people think their money is going, what they think their money is being spent on and what it is actually being spent on. Fiscal devolution and allowing local authorities more ability to spend money on the things that are the priorities for their residents can potentially increase the faith that people have in how their money is being spent. At the moment, they do not see that connection. There is also the important thing about local areas having a clear understanding of what the needs and desires are in their place. There is also a question about accountability but we can come back to that.

I am hearing two arguments. One simply says that there are insufficient resources and we should have more taxes and more spending. The second argument is that if we had control over a larger part of the pot, we could allocate the money better and get more out of it. I get nervous about the first of those arguments, as that goes into other territory in terms of where it leaves national government. But I am interested in the second and the extent to which you think you can do better with the money that you have that is allocated to those services you talk about and how you could spend it in a better way.

Meaningful devolution must be delivered at local as well as regional level. We are definitely looking at that. It is not just looking at local government as well but looking at strategic authorities and definitely taking a holistic approach. It is not about just passing funding down, even though we cannot just pass responsibilities down without resources; it is actually about having the opportunity to be innovative and creative around those resources, and the ways in which to think about income streams and spending. At the moment, lots of those are under the tight control of the Government.

I mentioned the parent-child relationship earlier. It is very much like a parent and a child with no pocket money, and they are telling them that actually they cannot go out to work either. That is the challenge we very much have with government restrictions on some of that. Having that local decision-making will make it a lot easier for us to think about new income streams, new ways of working and where local pressures can allow us to look to build local income and local resources.

I share a nervousness in saying that the answer is just more taxes. A paper by the LGA and WPI Economics about four years ago looked at a range of possible new revenue raisers. For instance, an e-commerce levy or devolving elements of sales tax may offer some flexibility around that. Of course, that is an option. The LGA does not have a position that says, “You have to pick one of those”. But I agree with you. There is a huge amount of existing spend that could easily, in theory, be moved around the system. You would start by looking at how much the NHS spends. To be honest, even just moving 1% of the total spend is billions. We are spending nearly £3 billion a year on temporary accommodation and that is going up significantly year on year. There is a cost to not getting this right. You then run out of options and have to look at what you can do quickly.

There is also a huge amount about the utilisation of things like business rates. In Greater Manchester, for instance, we retain 100% of our business rates. That allows us to take long-term decisions about growth because you can see it, whether that is borrowing against those business rates receipts or spending up front on infrastructure and bringing in private sector investment off the back of it. This idea of devolving income tax or a portion of it could potentially incentivise pushing more projects towards greater employment. So there are ways in which you can do this that are not simply going back to the tax and spend lever, although that is an option. There are a range of options that our work has set out could be done, and a degree of preference around which of those would be better. But that is not the only solution.

Q98 You all agreed that the progress we have made on devolution so far has been beneficial. We heard it is driving growth and we heard about Manchester. Can we just focus on the proposition that the Government have now put before us, which is that for the mayoral strategic authorities, instead of the current grant system, they are going to, on a fiscally neutral basis, switch it to another grant system—namely, a percentage of the local income tax that is generated. Looking at that and putting aside some of the other things about growth, what is it that local authorities will be able to do if you change the system that they cannot do at the moment?

I will give you a practical example of some money that was given that has been devolved to Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority, which is to do with the skills budget. I am the chair of the skills committee there. That money previously would have been going through the Department for Education directly to colleges. It is now coming through our mayoral combined authority and the level of the detail and the work that we are doing in collaboration with local employers is at a much more granular level and is far more carefully calibrated to what our local economy needs than it could have been otherwise.
Is that not a function of the decision to devolve the responsibility for skills, rather than the mechanism through which the Government pass the money?

Yes, that example is. On the issue about the mechanism through which the Government pass the money, I imagine that one of the reasons that they would want to do that is to incentivise growth in places. I am not sure that income tax is necessarily going to do that. The problem with income tax is that some areas will benefit and others will not. That is something that the Government are going to have to address. In the case of the business growth currently devolved to Manchester, there is an incentive for areas to grow faster, whereby they get to retain some of that growth, and that would be beneficial and helpful for local places to see how that connection works for them.

That would not solve the problem that Councillor O’Brien referred to about the pressure on local government. As Lord Burns implied, that is a separate issue with how much the resources go through. It is not quite clear to me if there is anything practical that authorities will be able to do that they cannot do at the moment under the current regime.
Under the grants regime?
Yes . The same amount of money is coming through; it is just coming through a different channel. What difference of itself does that make?

There is an element of looking at devolution and looking at conditions around the devolution of funding, resource and responsibility. As an example, recently the Government changed the business rate multiplier to look at pubs and live music venues, reduce the business rates on those venues and increase the level of business rates on vaping shops, which, at a local level, is a really good idea. We never had the powers locally to do those. That would be a good idea and on a local, more place-based, level, you could trial those things, rather than always on a national level. Having that fiscal devolution of responsibility can be tested on a local area and really make a difference. It is about not just the funds but the responsibility and the conditions that come with the funds. Because if we say, “Here’s the funds, here’s the responsibility, but these are the conditions and you cannot move outside those parameters”, we will not be able to test things.

As I understand it, t he responsibilities are not in and of themselves going to change —just the channel through which the money comes. That is the proposition. I s j ust channelling the money in a different way really fiscal devolution? Is that what you regard as devolving real power to local authorities : the power to raise their own revenue , apart from overreliance on council tax and business rates?

Eamonn O ’ Brien: T here is sometimes confusion around what you might call fiscal decentralisation and devolution. Explicit in devolution has to be far greater flexibility around how you spend the amount of money , but there is also the question of your ability potentially to raise more yourself. The overnight visitor levy is a good example of that : some places will embrace the opportunity to raise that income while others will not. The ability to do that is devolution.

If the Government simply said, “We’re going to raise it nationally and we’re going to give you a chunk of that money , but here are the 10 conditions and the areas you have to spend it on ”, that would be more decentralisation than devolution. Until now, the journey has been , by and large , one of decentralisation rather than genuine devolution.
May I ask a final yes/no question ? Is the continuation of council tax capping consistent with fiscal devolution?
Eamonn O ’ Brien: The LGA’s position is no.
No.
No.

Q99 C an we look at which taxes should be devolved or assigned ? What guiding principles should be applied when deciding which of those should be devolved? You mentioned business rates earlier, but do you have a set of principles or any idea of which issues would make one approach more successful than another in terms of either particular taxes or some of the charges that you mentioned ?

Eamonn O ’ Brien: As I mentioned earlier, w e did a piece of work back in 2022 ; if colleagues have not had a chance to have a look at it , we would be happy to make sure that it gets shared. It set out a series of principles by which you could analyse a variety of potential revenue streams .

The principles beg i n with sufficiency : d oes this address the point I started with? Does this help us get to a point? However, as Lord Young alluded to earlier, just moving money and paying for it in a different way does not deal with the issue of sufficiency.

The second principle is buoyancy : in g oing up and down, there is a risk associated with having greater fiscal devolution. If money can go up, it can also go down , potentially. So there is a question mark around p rotecting against that dynamic, especially when our demand certainly is not going down. The other principles included fairness, efficiency, predictability, transparency and incentives.

What the paper outlined , against all those principles , is what we would argue theoretically meets them. The thing that was highest up there was the devolution of income tax , as well as an e-commerce levy. T he paper set out what that could theoretically raise and how it could potentially be distributed. It balanced that against areas that we did not think were as appropriate for fiscal devolution.

So there is a body of work there. We stopped short of saying, “The LGA’s position, therefore, is that the Government must do X, Y or Z”, but the report set out a pretty detailed argument across a range of options. As I say, the devolution of income tax and an e-commerce levy were the two top ones that came out of that process.

The CCN ’s position is that it is important to recognise that areas are different . What works in one area may not be appropriate in another area. It may be helpful, therefore, to look at a range of options for fiscal devolution so that areas get some choice over the bits that they have . Clearly, if you are in a n area of high business growth , as I am, the retention of business rates is really helpful because we have high growth anyway . In other areas, the tourism levy might be really helpful , but there will potentially be parts of the country for which neither of those options is particularly useful ; indeed, they may even be detrimental. H aving a range of options will be really important in how you look at this.

T o go back to the previous question slightly , there is also the business about people wanting to see how their taxes make a difference to their local area , regardless of which tax it is . Even if all you are doing is passporting income tax, if people can see how some of that income tax is being spent in their local area, and that is visible and accountable locally , you may at least get some slightly different outcomes from what you would have had otherwise.

Financial stability requires diversified r evenue streams. In local government, we have very few revenue streams. We have four of them: council tax , business rates , fees and charges , and limited grant funding. We had commercial income , which has changed in terms of the approach we can take.

The LCN’s position is that, where costs are local, revenue should be local. I have a good example of that. We talk ed about tourism . Oxford has massive amounts of tourism, which is fantastic, but that has a cost as well. For a population of 160,000 people , 7 million visitors to the city is fantastic, but that obviously has an impact on the public realm and on open spaces, as well as on street cleansing and environmental impacts. As a test, Oxford was looking at whether put ting £2 per visitor in would help it achieve £2.5 million of income. However, at present , it cannot do that without the local powers to do that. A gain, it is a bit handcuffed in terms of the income streams it could achieve, but visitors who visit Oxford would probably be very happy to pay £2 as a visitor levy to come into Oxford.

I go back to my first category around whether this was high er taxes or reallocating spending. Of the things you mentioned, the e-commerce levy , the visitor levy and keeping all business rates are all cases of more taxes . The only one that I would describe as the devolution of existing taxes is income tax , of course, but you are happy to sell this on the basis that , because they are called charges or levies , they somehow or other do not go under the heading of taxes.
Eamonn O ’ Brien: I am not a cynic ; I would not be as cynical as that. I will leave that to you to decide.

To be clear about this, the alternative is that people are going to pay more in taxes anyway if we do not get this right, and they are going to pay significantly more in taxes because council tax is going up every year . As Lucy was saying, people are paying more and getting less. That is breaking an element of the social contract in places where people are feeling hard done by because of this situation. There is a massive debate around what to do about council tax but, in the meantime, it is continually going up. Nowadays, it is a deeply regressive and unfair tax .

The alternative here is not a low tax nirvana . We are still going to be in a situation where we are spending more money on failure , with an inability to deal with some really tricky issues. There has to be an honest discussion , if we are serious about fixing these problems, around new levies or taxes potentially being part of th e solution. As I said earlier, there is a huge amount that could be done with the existing amount of money if we were given more control over it and had more influence to spend it in different ways. I could give endless examples , from health and social care to housing and children’s services, of where we can demonstrate that . T he problem we have at the moment is our inability to do both things at the same time.

If you have devolution, it is not necessarily always about putting up taxes. Taxes rarely go down ; t hey are sometimes held steady. In Cambridgeshire and Peterborough , under the previous mayor , we had a mayoral precept for bus passes for young people. We now have a C onservative mayor. He has decided not to raise that tax , so there is a ve ry tight squeeze on how much money can be spent on buses. That is about local accountability. T here is a clear choice for the local population between whether to vote for a mayor who raises taxes and get better bus services or to have one who keeps them static , meaning that the bus services must be managed so that they stay within the budget. There is at least clarity about it and there is local accountability. P eople can see that our bus services have got better since we had the mayoral precept , but they are now being squeezed again. But it is about accountability and being able to see if your £36 a year goes on this. If it does not go up , we do not get as much of it.

I want to follow up on the question of which taxes, on Lord Young’s point about council tax capping and Jonathan ’s point about having a bit more flexibility over business rate design . It feels like the taxes that we think of as local are quite centrally controlled, but something that is not often raised is devolving control over how those taxes are calculated —whether that is more flexibility over council tax or on how business rates work. I just want to know whether that would be part of the mix , in terms of which taxes or fiscal devolution.

For the last 15 years, we have been capped on council tax . Think about the commercial world : in different areas , there is a different requirement on resources and on spend , so having 2.99% without going out for a referendum is a real challenge for local authorities . If they have a democratic mandate and have been elected , they should make decisions . C entral g overnment makes decisions at central g overnment level ; the Government will make decisions on income tax or national insurance without having to go back out for another referendum. A t the moment, the tools to do that are really challenging and very difficult for democratic accountability. The leaders and politicians have been voted in , but they can raise council tax only up to a certain level. If they want to go further, they have to go out to a referendum. Not many politicians are going to ask people, “Would you like to pay more taxes? ” So that control is not really helpful .

D ifferent areas have different requirements. In some areas, such as buses, as has been said , politicians will say, “We would like to put more into bus service s” or “W e would like to put more into open spaces ”. The public, through consultation, will actually say, “We would like to see that”, for some areas . So they should have the powers to increase council tax if they want to and they have that buy - in locally. That is a real challenge.

We see across the country, in the commercial sector, that the same supermarkets charge different fees at different places , because the demand , need , cost of service and resources are different. So why can local g overnment not have that sort of flexibility as well ? There is a difference but, at the moment , we are all treated the same with regard to council tax. I am just u sing that as an example, because it was highlighted.

Your point about which taxes local government has any control over is a good one. We have very little control over anything , in terms of what we are allowed to raise money for. This means that we increasingly have to raise money from the very small number of things over which we do have control : car parking is an obvious example. It is one of relatively few areas where local councils are able to put taxes up—in effect, they are taxes on parking —and mostly they do. S ome places choose not to , because they choose to prioritise bringing people into their high streets in response. T here is a massive debate going on in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough about where we do that and where not to .

That example also brings out the much greater opportunities in some areas than others. So the opportunity to charge for car parking in the centre of Cambridge is completely disproportionate from what it is in some of our market towns. W hen you allow flexibility, you also need to recognise that those flexibilities are likely to benefit some areas more than others. T here are questions there about how you make sure that any flexibilities do not just benefit areas with potential for growth and visitor income , but think about how other areas can benefit as well.

Q100 The car parking example was quite good for me and my question, which is about equalisation. One of the things that always comes up when we talk about fiscal devolution —not decentralisation , in your sense, but devolution —is the fact that some places have more opportunities to raise money than others. E qualisation is something that central g overnment already spends a large amount of time worrying about and no doubt will again .

B efore I come on to asking you whether you think this is a major problem , I am interested to know whether you think that current equalisation works anyway. There is a certain tendency to talk as though we have an equalisation system at the moment that is just fine , but now we are heading off into the badlands. M aybe that is true, but I would be interested to know whether you think that the current approach , in which you have a limited number of income streams all of which are tightly controlled, is delivering something that could be seen as fairly equalised or whether that is not the case.

It is not the case, I think. The vast majority of rural councils would say that they do not get a fair deal from the current system. If you look at the per - head spending in an area such as Cambridgeshire in comparison with some of our more urban areas, particularly London, it is far, far lower. That is even more the case if you look across education and health , as well as local government. It does not feel fair to lots of places.

There will always be a debate about what is fair and fair funding, and what drives need. In the last 15 years , we have seen a move away from deprivation and a move towards deprivation in how health funding is largely determined . It is a complex thing , and we would be kid ding ourselves if we said that there was an exact answer that was completely perfect, unless we had twice as much money to deal with, when it would not really matter. T here will always be a debate about how you distribute the money.

A t the moment , we have a fairly obscure and difficult - to - understand system of tariffs and redistribution that many people in local g overnment feel they have no ability to influence . M oving away from something like that and having a more local discussion and debate about how resources are shared is a far better way of dealing with it. T hat has certainly been my experience from devolution : we get certain pots of money at a Greater Manchester level, and sometimes my council benefits and sometimes it does not. Sometimes we get our fair share and sometimes we do not , but I would rather have that.

This goes back to Lord Young’s point: you are being given a pot of money with more freedom to do what you like with it . C an I push you a bit further on that ? What if we move d to a system that was more like car parking or hotel and tourism taxes, in which local governments, presumably at many different levels, have different powers to raise taxes and can make different decisions about whether they want to have a bus precept or not ? I am putting words in your mouth, but would that be any worse from what we have at the moment ? If it would , w hat would be your preferred method to make sure that things did not get too unequal?

We have to accept that, in any sort of localism agenda , local areas will make different decisions that look and feel different. I do not think it can be too stark , but it would not be unreasonable for Greater Manchester to choose to take the overnight visitor levy when the Liverpool City R egion does not. I do not think that that would be a major problem ; it is something the country can be quite relaxed about.

The question is who gets to determine what a sufficient level is . It come s back to the point that Lucy made earlier about accountability that, if we get it wrong in a local area and put too much resource into certain areas and not others, we should be accountable for that back to the electorate. This idea of saying , “T he only way that we can ensure that there is no postcode lottery and complete equality across the country is by containing and restraining everything in the centre ”, I would argue , has not worked. W e should embrace the differences and say that there is probably not a perfect position in all this, but it should be guided by a series of principles and what you perhaps might call an accountability framework on outcomes. We are moving towards a sense that , if we achieve the outcomes, we can be pretty relaxed about the means by which it is done .

You also need to recognise that different places will probably end up with different outcomes, and that that might be a choice , but that is okay. A ctually, if some places choose to have more street lighting and more nightlife , and other places choose to have less street lighting and less nightlife, that is okay. Places should be different. T here should be differences even in how our market towns feel, but the current system does not seem to allow much flexibility for that at all.

There is disparity around the funding but also around regions. In the east of England, as I am sure my colleagues would agree, we get very little funding compared with other parts of the country. There is a real opportunity for accountability and local ownership, and the opportunity to decide and be accountable for those decisions locally, at the lowest point at council level. Doing so gives us a longer-term view on a place; at the moment it is piecemeal and day-to-day. We are trying to plan long term, but when political and funding cycles come together they create very short-term thinking. That creates difficult issues where we cannot plan for the future of both the people and those places.

Q101 I understand and accept the argument about local decision-making leading to different outcomes. To what extent, however, do you think you still need a national minimum in terms of standards? Suppose you had a council that decided it was going to do something very radical, which meant that you were getting deep cuts in provision, and in some cases it was possibly very costly. How do you cope with that? Do you accept that if you have considerably more local decision-making, you can get not only the sunlit uplands of more growth but also the sloughs where things go wrong—I mean “sloughs” without a capital S.

This is absolutely a dynamic of the debate, and it must be had because it is important. When you look at a range of the services that we are talking about, you would still have national standards on housing, for instance—on housing quality, social housing and the regulator. You would still have national standards on education, children’s social care and adult social care. There would still be the national audit system for local government, although that is in itself going through some difficulties at the moment. There is always the provision, too, of some form of intervention from the Government, which is a potential check on some. You gave a good example; there are other examples at the moment where there is active intervention in councils that have taken too much risk, perhaps, or that have made some reckless decisions. They are however probably the exception where councils are concerned. It goes back to an element of trust but with a framework of accountability. There is a pretty strong framework of accountability for the types of services that we offer.

There is also an element of understanding shared outcomes; I mentioned this earlier. If we can agree a sense of shared outcomes between national and local, and hold ourselves to account over those in that relationship, then we should feel confident to let go of the reins more than we currently do and say, “We will give you the opportunity to prove yourself against a shared set of outcomes”. That is effectively what we have now in Greater Manchester. It has not had time to really show its results yet, but that is a fair way of working. It is probably a stepping stone towards what it ought to be because, of course, in many other countries around the world this would be a fairly alien discussion. We should acknowledge that, too: that other countries would be surprised that this is even a debate. It is not how most countries operate. It is fair to say that we could look at using that existing framework, but also at some form of shared accountability of outcomes. I do not think we should be afraid of saying places will look and feel different, and that there will be different outcomes at the same time.

The current framework in which local government operates feels pretty crazy at times. If you think about the legal requirements that we have to provide special educational needs services—which we cannot provide because there are not enough educational psychologists available to provide them, and yet we are held legally accountable for that—we are bleeding money out in a crazy way. There are no standards however about what our roads or street lighting need to look like. At the moment, we have a structure within which local government is attempting to operate, with very tight and sometimes completely undeliverable legal expectations in some areas and almost no legal expectation in others. That is the position that we are currently trying to navigate. A slightly more rational accountability framework might be welcomed by a lot of people, but it should not be overly prescriptive.

Q102 During the discussions prior to today, and indeed after today, I have not been able to understand how equalisation would work. Put simply, the distribution of more equality is largely determined—not exclusively but largely—by the Treasury. This may be fair or unfair, but that is the present system. The more that fiscal devolution occurs, the less power and quantity the Treasury will have in determining equalisation. On the other hand, if success through local autonomy is to be rewarded, it is a natural concomitant that there will be failures. There will be a need, perhaps a greater need, for some form of equalisation. At the moment, as you said, it is very complex, and yet it is centrally decided. How will equalisation work structurally to overcome some of the disadvantages and the lack of success in areas after fiscal devolution? Do you have a formula or a structure for that, or do you just think that this is a matter for future discussion?

I will not go directly into the formula, but we have gone from a place of the Treasury being the controlled decision-maker to being an assurance role , and then to the powers and funding being passed down to local government. There is a big piece around the culture change of local government and the transactional relationship between local and central government. There can be many formulas, but central and local government working differently to deliver these outcomes will be a massive cultural change in government. There needs to be a reset; there needs to be engagement; and there needs to be discussion on how we can work together and not continue with the current parent-child relationship. The formulas can come with that: we must have a framework, whether it is a local, national or regional framework, for public service and public life, while giving wider parameters for doing things locally. That is the risk of failure, but accountability locally means that if there is failure, it is local accountability with assurance at Government level as well. I do not know if I have fully answered the question.
That is a slightly different issue. When you say assurance, it means that the Treasury will still be the treasurer of last resort for failure.
Yes, as Government.

That also has implications for fiscal rules and so on, as presently constituted. You can imagine that there will be all sorts of problems if the Treasury is landed with bills of a significant nature; recent local government suggests that it might be. What I am asking is not about the relationship between the parent and the child; it is between the siblings. Once you pass the power down, a proportionate passing down of power means a proportionate decrease in the central capacity to equalise. That means an increased responsibility to find a way for the siblings to compromise. Do you have a plan, or a formula or an idea of how that might occur, given that you accept that if success is rewarded then failure is going to be penalised?
The short answer is that we do not. That is something that needs to be worked on through this process .
That is why I did not understand it; it does not exist at the moment.

We have a set of principles on which a system could be developed. That is probably our starting point. The first is that we should aim, as much as is possible, for a fiscal or fiscally neutral starting point, and a floor at which we allow for devolution to be built upon. I will give an example. If you had a large employer in your area that went bust, and that was a very significant hit to your business rates, or if there was some form of natural disaster—say, flooding—and that had a big hit on your local area, then the question would be about who steps in to equalise in that situation. This would contrast with another scenario where you borrow recklessly, your commercial investments go sour and you are left with a very significant gap. I think there are two versions of failure — or maybe underperformance —that might merit different types of responses and interventions. I t starts with understanding the principles through which you would interven e, should there be underperformance. I t is fair to say that I cannot point to a formula at this stage that says exactly how it will work.

Q103 I will take the siblings analogy one step further. N ever mind whether somebody makes a mistake and they borrow money they should not have for a f oolish project —o ne sibling is likely to be more attractive than the other. C ar parking charges and visitor levies will bring in a huge amount more for an attractive town than for the really unattractive town that does not get m any visitors —it might have the odd business travelle r. It simply does not have the same advantages. I s that something that you would hope to compensate for, or is that just the luck of the draw?

As local government, we do that all the time in certain places. We have lots of market towns , and lots of other towns and cities, and we — members and officers — have to do that equalisation all the time . T here will be one that is more affluent and another that is more deprived and needs more resource. W e work with the public on that justification. Some are very keen to see the more prominent town or city being invested in more , because of the ripple effect out into the countrysid e . T here is a lot of work , and e ven though we have not got the full details of a framework, there are definitely principles that we already apply to local g overnment life .
How do you think it might work under the fiscal devolution that is now being discussed?

I will try to answer that and the previous point. These are my thoughts and not those of CCN, j ust to be clear. We talk about the Treasury having to pick up the tab for local g overnment failure, but actually quite often the people who have been picking up the tab are the local council tax payers. T hat is painful for them and for the councils that take over from the ones that have caused problems —and t here have been a number of those .

I n a number of cases, if you had asked neighbouring councils whether they knew things were likely to be going wrong, they probably would have done. T here are quite a lot of situations where the councils in a surrounding area can see and understand —and hear rumours about — what is happening, but they have no capacity or mechanism for saying , “T his council in my patch is heading in a bad route ” . So , if you are looking at fiscal devolution and looking at where that accountability sits, some of it can sit nationally but some of it could also sit at a regional level , p otentially at a slightly higher level than the mayoral combined authority level.

C oming back to the point that was made before about siblings and local g overnment also supporting the less attractive towns , that sharing across regions and the stronger areas supporting the weaker areas are things that happen. It could certainly be incentivised within the way in which fiscal devolution happens. T he more you look across broader regions, the more you are able to think, “I f we are judging the growth of a whole , larger region and incentivising that , you then have to bring everywhere up to some extent ” . So there are ways in which you could look at regions and look at responsibility and accountability being not just at a very local level or at the T reasury level but at some levels in between , so that people have more control over what their neighbours are doing, which we do not have at the moment.

There is also work that the LGA does with its peer improvement programme and scrutiny . S ome of that could be helpful in mitigating the potential for disasters. It does not necessarily answer the equality point, but it does answer t he question of w ho might be responsible for failure .

On that point, there is an opportunity to grow on some of the things we have had in local g overnment , such as the duty to co-operate, the duty to support and the duty to collaborate. Y ou could look at that in regional areas and strengthen it; you could build it with local and central g overnment to create that insurance piece. The sibling probably know s more about the other child than the parents , s o those siblings need to work together to make it work.

It all exists in a context where we have a mechanism for equalisation at the moment, b ut would we all say it is working? We have the Barnett formula for the devolved nations, is that working? There are international equivalents , such as reunification in Germany ; equalisation between e ast and w est was constitutionally required. There is an argument that we should ask: is that working ? T here are formulas and mechanisms —
The answers o n the whole are not positive.

On the whole, I think the argument is that they are better than not having them . But the question is: c an we get to a point where we start from a pure position of equality? I do not think we can do so . How we make sure people do not fall too far behind is an important part of that , b ut I also believe that that should not mean that we hold people back at the same time.

Q104 We now come to a series of questions about who makes the decisions in a greater devolution system. First, I will ask you about a specific point. The Prime Minister, as you know, has announced that mayors will be given new powers to override local councils ’ planning decisions. I s this a positive development or is it actually a step away from localised decision - making and , hence , from the very spirit of devolution?

The LGA’s position is that there is a great deal of concern about these types of proposals, because it is certainly our belief that local councils represent their local communities and residents and their needs and are accountable back to those people for that. T herefore, anything that potentially takes away from that would undermin e that position on localism. U ltimately, it will depend on your perspective of what is local and what is appropriate at a local level. The argument, I suppose, from the Government is that economic growth cannot be purely a local matter ; there has to be an element of regional consideration of local growth. I t is a debate that will continue to go around.

W hat we are keen to do at the LGA is to express those concerns, and also to highlight where it is already working quite well. I t actually be comes less about powers and intervention and much more about relationships and co - operation, which are far better way s of establishing a system than purely one of hard - edged powers and intervention.

There are a couple of things in your question that are really worth thinking about. First, local authorities frequently already have their decisions overturned by the n ational Planning Inspectorate or by Ministers. I f that decision is coming to mayoral combined authorities , it is probably at least slightly closer and more accountable than if it is being done by the Planning Inspectorate or a Minister. A s with all these discussions, it slightly depends on whether you are moving powers down or up.

W hen the Prime Minister talks about moving powers to mayors, I am constantly concerned about whether he means mayors very specifically —namely, one person — or whether he means a mayoral strategic authority. I would be enormously worried about significant planning decisions resting with one individual, because the potential for corruption in that particular circumstance is vast , and h e should be really nervous about it.

We at the LCN support strategic planning , but we feel it im portant that local accountability for planning decisions must remain with councils. Thinking about the decision - making piece , 90% of applications are decided at the local council level. Some 1.5 million properties have already had planning approval. T he decision - making level is important , but decision - making is actually happening. We need to look at how we take a holistic approach to large schemes and long - term growth, because it is challenging at a local level to make those big decisions , while also not hav ing support around sustainable infrastructure. T hat probably needs a more strategic, holistic view tailored to a place. T hose local decisions on the place and the environment need to be made in the local area. There is definitely a role for strategic planning, but local accountability and decision-making should be at the local council level.

Q105 ​ ​ C ontinuing on from that theme but broadening it out , w hat powers and responsibilities should rest in your opinion with the different tiers and types of g overnment as outlined in the English d evolution Act ? A lot of the focus that we have had so far from this new A dministration is on the strategic authorities and mayors. ​ Lucy Nethsingha: ​ M y experience of working in a sometimes dysfunctional and sometimes more functional strategic authority is that the really important thing that a strategic authority can do is try and build local consensus and a shared vision across the place. I f you get that shared vision, that is when you get a real driver of growth and a real sense that everybody i s working in the same direction.

W h at we have had wh en we have been dysfunctional is one direction set by one mayor , t hen another mayor com ing in and completely chang ing the direction . An enormous amount of time and money is wasted on mayor number one c ommissioning X reports, which then get put in the bin , then number two commission ing another set of reports.

The crucial thing is about making sure that everybody is incentivised to work together and that you do not end up with a system where it is very easy for people to veto other people’s ideas, or go off in a direction where they do not have the support of the broader area.

W hen you are thinking about the structures, the most important thing is that the structures support each other to build consensus, not necessarily giving this power to this person and that power to that person. Does that answer your question?
​ Does what is being put in place through the d evolution Act and this Government’s plans do that ? Do they provide the structure for building consensus across those areas?

​ ​ I do not think it is clear. It comes back to this question : when the Government are talking about mayors, are they talking about individuals or strategic authorities? If they are talking about strategic authorities, then it probably does build that consensus because you have to have the buy - in . It i s clear that , whoever the mayor is, they have to work with their partner authorities and they cannot do things on their own.

But a lot of the way it is expressed is that it is about an individual . P utting all that emphasis on an individual is not helpful in relation to building that consensus. If you are going to get growth, you have to have long - term visions that will survive more than one individual. T hat is what happened in Manchester before and after Andy Burnham .

​ Eamonn O'Brien: I cannot complain about anything in Greater Manchester. I think the powers broadly set out make sense . S trategic authorities are well - placed to look at things like labour markets, travel - to - work areas, skills, housing markets —and t ransport would certainly be in that category.

But i t has to be a relationship of mutual respect and of mutualism, I suppose. Both have to exist together ; you need the sort of symbiotic nature between local authorities and strategic authorities. I think you could easily compare the set - up and the way in which we work in a place like Greater Manchester —and it would be true for other place s—with , say, London , where there is not quite the same relationship between the mayor , the mayor’s powers and role , and the 30 - odd authorities across London .

T he Prime Minister, before he had his current role, used to describe himself as the captain of the football team. It was helpful because there were 11 of us . W e were all equal players but he was the person who brought us together around those objectives. B y and large, that worked. In the time of the combined authority in Manchester, we have only had two votes at combined authority meetings. One of those was on the position on Brexit and the other was on bus franchising.

By and large, it has forged consensus across different political parties and different political leaders. So when it works , when it is founded on mutual respect and a sense of mutualism, then it works very well and it can work very well in those areas. But it has to be a partnership and it has to be a partnership of equals.
The risk in all of this is that we somehow recreate a two - tier system of g overnment where one is the poor relation to the other. I think that is a risk ; I do not think it is an inevitability.

​ Jonathan Stephenson: ​ The o nly point to add there is to make sure that it is complementary w ith the strategic authorities and the local council. It needs to be a partnership . M oving forward , d evolution does not stop at that. Strategic authority has to go down. T h e relationship is key to making that work. It might look different in different parts of the country with the functions and services. S ome of those discussions will happen and i t will be the right solution for that place.

I hope so. That does not necessarily mean that I think it will, but I hope so.

There is no getting around it: an absolutely necessary part of making devolution work is a clear , understandable and coherent map on which you can put devolved arrangements. I suppose that, if there is an irony in the devolution debate, while the criticisms of local government reorganisation are that it potentially lifts levels of governance away from communities , the argument we would all make is that we need to find ways of bringing services much closer to people , communities and neighbourhoods, and to work with public services around people rather than processes. So there is still a battle to be fought around structures.

Clearly , yesterday’s decision will prolong that , but missing in that debate is that , regardless of the details of that structure —and there needs to be a structure —we need to find a way of making public services much more engaged and responsive to people , communities and neighbourhoods . W e are not spending as much time talking about that , because it is difficult and complex , as we are about the size of new councils , what level they should be , what we should call them and whether there should be a mayor or not . In every postcode ?

In an ideal world, yes. There are a lot of moving parts in local government but, after yesterday, there are now lots more. Some parts have stopped moving.

Moving forward, in trying to get there, we should definitely aim for that blueprint. That should be the case . On whether everybody gets there at the same time , that is what we need to work through. If you try to get everybody in that box together, you will leave a few people; they will pop out at the same time as you bring some in. Create the blueprint, create the ambition, create the vision, get some delivery and use some good practice . H opefully , others will then follow. I have one very short question. Does that mean that you would accept an incremental application of devolution, rather than a big bang?
We have to, I think.

We have just seen 21 county areas go through LGR— local government reorgani sa tion —which has been a huge challenge for the sector. We are talking about 60% or 70% of local government at once. That is a huge challenge, especially when most of us are in a very difficult space. We would love to be in that R&D space and looking at the future, but most of us are in the A&E space and looking at trying to keep people alive ; I mean that metaphorically.

Incremental steps towards that are also really important because a combined authority or a strategic authority does no t immediately come into existence fully staffed and with all of its finances u p and running. You have to start in an incremental way. What has happened in Manchester has happened over 20 years, not just in the short term . In Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, where we were starting from scratch , it has taken us at least eight years to get to a position where we have enough staff to be able to run trailblazer schemes and things .

There is the question of how you will pay for it and the question of how you will get the right capacity. The Government’s announcement, which suggested moving people out of Whitehall and into strategic authorities, is a start. One way in which you could do that would be to move people away from the centre and put them into places. The vast majority of what was the apprenticeship levy is not being spent by local councils ; it is being shipped back to the Treasury. Much more flexibility was needed around how that could be used so that we could solve some of these challenges.

The other way of looking at this is that we need to have a pretty flexible relationship between strategic authorities and local authorities. There is a risk that, if you set up a lot of strategic authorities overnight, they will simply take from an existing small pool. We, the Local Government Association, are going to help manage that risk by looking at training and development courses. It will then take some extra resource to lift that new talent —the new generation—coming through. W e could be looking at more secondments and, again, more flexibility in the short term, but this is going to take years to turn around. It i s going to take years to build that capacity. You cannot just click your fingers and get people into social care or into the highest positions in planning authorities. This will take a really concerted effort .

I look at the opportunities within that. I see great opportunities for a new generation of people to come into these organisations and p rovide lots of new perspectives, new energy and new ways of working . However, that can be done only if we sort the finances out. That is where it will always go back to in local government: do we have a sufficient level of resource to do all of this work? At the moment, we do not.
That is the crunch question. I wonder whether the LGA has put a figure on how much it would take to get local g overnment on a sound footing before devolution and all these wonderful visions.
The figure at the moment is £7 billion.

I will just touch on your point about the calibre of people in local government. M y experience of recruiting into the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority is that , because it is now seen as a n exciting and functional organisation and as an exciting place to work, when we recruit people, we get high - calibre applicants . L ots of people really want to work in their local place ; t hey want their local place to be successful and to achieve. On the other hand, trying to recruit into Cambridgeshire County Council , with LGR hanging over us , is not easy at all , because it is very difficult for people to know what the long - term future of the council will be—and it will be e ven more difficult after yesterday ’s announcement . T he uncertainty is really hard, but if you provide certainty and a sense that this will be an exciting place to work, people will come.

Q113 I want to return to the question of building a framework as a basis for devolution. H aving heard your evidence today, I think you three are absolutely ideal to do that. D o you feel you are being properly consulted? I f this c ommittee were to recommend a mechanism for building the framework, what should it be?
We are probably not being properly consulted. It has very much felt as though devolution is being done to local government and has been a very top-down process and not very collaborative.

On how that framework ought to look , I think that the CCN, the Local Councils Network and the LGA would be absolutely keen to be involved in looking at what a framework ought to look like and how it can be more collaborative. As you will have noticed, many of us think about it quite a lot. T here would be enormous willingness to collaborate on what that framework should look like. Probably the sensible thing to do would be to build on what has happened and look at what has been successful already in terms of steps towards Manchester or London, rather than saying that everywhere needs to start from there , because you need to build the capacity and that takes time.

I have a similar point on how we might frame what we say. Y ou started off by pointing out that one of the things you are facing at the moment is a legal obligation to provide services that you simply do not have the resources to provide. To p ick up on Baroness Wheatcroft ’s point , if we are going to start down a road of greater devolution, it will be very difficult for any local authority or strategic authority to succeed if it starts from that position. M y question is quite straightforward. If you took special education and social care out of the equation, would you then feel that you were in a position to start delivering in a more accountable, efficient and creative way? Are they the two key things?

I have worked across unitary, district and borough councils. When I was in a unitary council, adult and children’s services wa s the priority when we balance d the budget. N ine times out of 10, some of the place - making opportunities are the things that are taken off the table. It is challenging to do some of the things that we need to do as a place to stimulate growth , because they sometimes come off the list . A child in care or a vulnerable adult has to come first. T hat is a real burden. That is part of our role in the public sector, but it mean s that some of those other things that we need to help stimulate local growth , and to help with GDP at a g overnment level , get taken off the table. W e are really limited on that.

I started in local g overnment in areas where 50% of the budget was for adults and children ; now it is 80% or 90 % in some of those councils. They are left with about 10% to do that place work , or they have to be very creative with financial opportunities to look at investment. A gain, you can be creative , b ut with some of those parameters that I talked about earlier , it is really difficult to move some of those things on.

There will be a lot of debate about this in the Casey review into adult social care, b ut I remain of the opinion that there is a lot that local authorities should do around adult social care that we are currently not able to do . T he cost of that has been picked up elsewhere in the system — for instance, by the NHS. P otentially , you could take it all out and create a national care service, and maybe it could even be merged with the NHS ; y ou c ould have ICBs and NHS bodies dealing with it. However, I think that that would be quite a backwards step, because the solution is not a bureaucratic one ; the solution is purely to ask whether we are spending the money in the right places —and we are not.

H ow do you deal with a problem like the £7 billion gap, which is growing? How do you deal with the demand in housing, which is growing ? These are big, serious issues , a nd they will need big, serious , radical changes. W ithout that, the risk is that devolution flops a little bit , because the constituent parts of strategic authorities — the councils — are just far too busy and taken up with dealing with that crisis. It will be like driving around in first gear all the time. It will feel like we could maybe get there, but it is going to be slow , sluggish , irritating and poor , compared with an alternative that we can se e but we cannot quite do.

We have not mentioned it yet, but I think No. 10 North is an interesting innovation in this space—this idea that it can become a sort of engine room to deliver this rewiring. This is a new dynamic in the system, and I am really looking forward, as the LGA—not just because the commute will be shorter for me—to working with No. 10 North and the officials there to try to improve the consultation and engagement, which has been underwhelming so far . So there is an opportunity in that to correct some of the mistakes of the past few years.

Q114 I am going to move from first gear to 33,000 feet, as we come to an end. Obviously you have an immense amount of experience and have been thinking about this a lot. That is very impressive. We are also looking for thematics and the top questions to ask as this d evolution framework is being put in place. Top of mind —I am asking each of you : what are the top three questions that should be answered and that one should really be thinking about to get this right ? It could be about governance, equalisation, structures of local government, et cetera .

A really important question is: where do the public think their taxes go and what do they think they pay for? How can you better align the way in which people feel their taxes are going out of their pockets with what they feel is being delivered in their local area ? We need to increase the accountability and responsibility between those things. At the moment, it feels as if there is an absolutely incomprehensible gulf between what people see going out of their pay packet s and what they receive. There is no way of joining up the levers. P art of that is because all of it goes into the Treasury, goes through some completely incomprehensible formula and comes out the other end in a way that even we do not understand.

Does it provide sufficient resources to meet our commitments and deliver on our commitments —our local priorities , our legal obligations and our public services? Does it provide an avenue for greater efficiency? So you might see sufficiency as the first one and efficiency as the second. Does it provide an avenue to make more efficient public services work better together, more collaboratively, reduce the silo working and potentially even merge budgets together ?

Then the third one would be accountability : how do we create a system that is coherent and accountable enough that it gives confidence to the Treasury , civil servants generally and G overnments to say, “We can let go of the reins because the system will take care of itself ”? It would be on rare occasions that we need to intervene when there are particular points of failure. So you need accountability downwards to the residents , but at this stage it is fair to say that, if we are to get to a position where everyone i s on board with this, there needs to be an understanding of accountability back up , as well.

We need to be partners in devolution . We picked up earl ier words about consultation ; we need to be properly engaged. It is not consultation at the end of a solution when someone says, “What do you think of this? ” W e cannot be bystanders in this ; we need to be properly engaged. C entral and local g overnment need that relationship, and both parties need to play ball in that space.

Meaningful devolution must be local as well as regional. I mentioned that earlier, but we really need to think about that , so that it is not just coming down on strategic authorities but is local. W e need to think about the framework to do that. We need to make sure that they focus on the key outcomes : a dults and children , and health and well - being are key outcomes in our places. The h ealthier people are , the more prosperous places will be, so we need to work in that space together.

We need to be really careful just to create structures. Society is challenging out there. How do we change society or societal behaviours? At the moment, people in society think that I or the council drop litter. They think that the police cause crime. They think that Health is there to repair them when they have been injured. Actually, it is the other way round : society has dropped litter , s omeone in society has caused the crime and someone else has injured themselves , not the NHS. H ow do we get people thinking different ly ? T he only way to do that is to have a stronger contract between local and central g overnment to focus on those things together. That societal change is huge .

We can structure things. You can merge two commercial organisations , but you have to look at the human side and the behaviours of those workforces coming together . It is the same with this : we can put new structures in place , but how do we look at society and see their roles? They need to be accountable , as well as us, the public sector. T hey want to be.

T here is an element , at the moment, of a lot of people on the street say ing , “We don’t want the council telling us what to do, but we also want the council to do everything for us ” . That is a really odd situation that we need to get better at. On the transfer of resources with responsibility, we are happy to find solutions together that are not just about passing money down saying , “Over to you to deliver ” . We should be able to reduce cost and put funding into that R&D space that I mentioned earlier, rather than firefighting in a non - prevention way . Otherwise, it is just a race to the bottom.
I found that very enlightening. It helped to clarify a lot of this in my mind and we owe the three of you a lot of thanks for that. On that basis, I close the public part of our meeting.

sessions.w: Commission for Victims and Survivors for Northern Ireland

segs.tx: Northern Ireland Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Reconciliation , HC 185
Wednesday 9 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 9 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Tonia Antoniazzi (Chair) ; Chris Bloore; Sorcha Eastwood ; Simon Hoare ; Mike Kane ; Katrina Murray; Gavin Robinson ; David Smith ; Robin Swann .
Questions 3 1 - 6 9
Witnesses
I : Sandra Peake, Chief Executive Officer, Wave Trauma Centre; Kenny Donaldson, Director, South East Fermanagh Foundation ; Mark Thompson, C hief Executive Officer, Relatives for Justice .
II : Joe McVey OBE, Commissioner , Commission for Victims and Survivors for Northern Ireland .
Examination of witness es
Witness es : Sandra Peake, Kenny Donaldson and Mark Thompson .

Q31 Welcome to the Northern Ireland Affairs Select Committee session on reconciliation. For panel one, we have Kenny Donaldson, the director of SEF F, who is joining us online ; Sandra Peake, chief executive officer of the Wave Trauma Centre —welcome, Sandra — and Mark Thompson, chief executive officer of Relatives for Justice.
I will ask Sandra first because you are in the room. What does reconciliation look like from the perspective of victims and survivors?

Reconciliation varies considerably in relation to how people would define it. I will share one piece of feedback from a lady who was brave. She said, “R econciliation means to me healing, moving forward and growth, being able to face the past openly and honestly like Operation Kenova” — which she came through — “ and understanding that to heal does not mean forgetting .”

F undamentally , all people would define reconciliation as an understanding that their loved one’s life mattered and what happened to them mattered, and we need to acknowledge that. We need to ensure that it is not a bout forgetting the past ; i t is acknowledging the past and ensuring that we do not repeat it . T hat is really the drive of many people who give very freely, who work very freely and who are courageous in the name of trying to create a better society.

Yes, I have similar views to what Sandra ha s expressed. W ith reconciliation, in many ways we feel like this language has almost become part of the stumbling block. It is a quarter of a century old at this stage. In many ways, peace and reconciliation, when it comes together, is often attributable to resourcing and grant aid . T hat is unfortunate.

We would always say that it is about good neighbourliness . If you are a good neighbour to someone, you will have their back. You will watch out for them. You will ensure that their rights are protected and enshrined . What you demand for yourself you also demand for others. That is how we break it down.

For reconciliation to be possible for victims and survivors, accountability is a critical component part. I have heard many over the years almost put that pressure point on to the shoulders of victims and survivors : “Y ou must forgive . Y ou are the impediment to peace ” . The truth is that victims and survivors , with the grace that they have shown over the last quarter of a century, are the living embodiment of peace.
T hat has often been misunderstood . P eople have not been given the due respect that they should have had.
I would not disagree with anything that Sandra or Kenny have said. It is similar. There is a personal reconciliation in terms of people and how they reconcile themselves with what has happened.

For more general societal reconciliation, the prerequisite is dealing with the past. A t times , it is putting the cart before the horse. Sometimes politically it is nice to tie things up in a bow and have it nicely presented as reconciliation —“Everybody is happy and move s on ” . The truth is that society will not move on until we deal comprehensively with the past. T hat has been the stumbling block.

There is also an emphasis of enforced reconciliation on the victims. Kenny picked up on that a little bit . T he emphasis is on the victims to reconcile , and if they do not , th at responsibility on them i s a negative connotation.

Generally, I think reconciliation is the by-product of getting everything else right. That is where the hard work needs to be done. It is reconciliation between communities, within communities and between countries . It is within this P arliament that you are in today , the P arliament in Ireland and the A ssembly. There is responsibility everywhere. It is incumbent upon everyone to deal with the past b ecause getting that right means the path to reconciliation is much easier.

Q32 B oth of you have brought up the unfair burden being placed —you use the word “ enforced ”— on victims and survivors by expecting them to deliver reconciliation. Can you expand on those concerns and the consequences of that, Mark?

W hen people in society talk about reconciliation , t he general expectation that we all need to move on creates pressures. I t sometimes silences people who want to speak up . S ometimes the people who I speak to say, “ I do not need to make reconciliation. People have to reconcile with me for what has happened to me, my experience and the harm that has been visited upon me . When I speak about addressing that publicly, whether by using the law or human rights to address that, somehow or other, people talk about reconciliation , and I am a barrier to that ” .

There is an emphasis placed on that . It can be disingenuous and it can be carefully choreographed and juxtaposed to portray victims as toxic or in a negative light. We hear that quite a lot. That is part of the condition for silencing people too.

If I give an example, the Legacy Act had the word “ reconciliation ” within it, camouflaging the true intent of what was in that B ill , from immunity provisions right through to not being compliant with the law . I n challenging that you were some how challeng ing reconciliation . T hat was deeply offensive.

W e have used l anguage that almost two Northern Irelands have grown up as a consequence of 1998 and the Belfast a greement. In 19 9 8, for those who were not directly touched by the violence, the violence certainly receded, if not stopped . At that particular juncture, many people were clapping others on the back and saying, “T hank you for stopping . Now we are committing to a new agenda ”.

Even the impression across the water was that at that stage we had realised peace and reconciliation was going to follow naturally . T hat was an absolute misjudg m ent , because the truth is that many of the cohort of people who were directly impacted by the violence have never received any account for what they have endured. They have watched some parts of Northern Ireland and some communities move forward at pace , and they are left in this space of almost being portrayed as backw ar ds people who somehow cannot move forward with this new agenda.

That is deeply troubling ; i t is grossly unfair. If you think about it, many of those individuals lived life by strong values. They were opposed , and always had been opposed, to the use of violence from whatever quarter it came. They lived their lives in that manner. They were good neighbours to others. Yet they are the people who are left now in the shadows. They are no longer part of the mainstream. They are almost part of the fringes. That is what needs to be addressed in all this.

To pick up on Mark’s point , in putting reconciliation into the legislation , the last Government placed an onus that, in some ways, victims and survivors were holding us back. That could not be further from the truth.
