At home, basically, the schemes we were in got a roll-over. We have not had to move into any other schemes. I would add that, from experience, you tend to find that they come and have a look at your land, find something magnificent like an orchid and decide, “Right, let’s fence that off.” The reason the orchid is there is because it is suited to the way it is being managed. Everybody has to be mindful of that. It is how it is because of the way it has previously been managed and has been for generations, so do not go in, bulldoze and make a mess, because you create a total imbalance.

Q68 I think you are right. There is a danger that, in trying to achieve good things with the environment, we end up pitting the farmers against it. They need to make money and operate as a business while respecting the heritage that we have. If we had the Government in front of us, what would be the one takeaway for which you would say, “Do this and it will make life much easier”?

A universal offer so that all farmers are not having to stop-start. This is what we used to have under HLS. You applied monthly. People were not in a panic. It was not like buying a Taylor Swift concert ticket—literally, it feels like that. The people we work with, and who Adam works with, are very busy. They are running businesses on a fine margin. They are under a lot of stress and do not have the capacity necessarily to be there on 22 September and then panic that, by 28 September, there is no money left in the pot.

If I were sat in front of the Government—this goes back to the Chair asking, “Are you being heard?”—I would mention how SFI feeds into nature recovery. I hear frustration from many farmers that they would like to work more closely with Natural England officers. They would like to have officers on the ground—on the farm. They would like to show them the good bits of the farm that they are proud of, where there is biodiversity and good things happening, but that is not happening to any great extent.

Also, I talk to many farmers who would like to have that nature knowledge from organisations—conservation organisations, per se—to help them learn those greater skills. There is a frustration that that is not happening. When we talk about nature recovery, very often, as Lisa just said, there is a focus on one thing. That leads to frustration, especially if you are on a really hard hill farm where you need your hay fields to make your winter crop, but you are being advised that you need to plant trees on there or turn them back to nature, or there may be a hay meadow scheme but you cannot cut your hay until the middle of August.

The point is this: we need proper co-design. In a lot of schemes, it says, “This is co-designed, working with farmers.” Very often, it is not. It is farmers being told, “These are your options. Pick your favourite.” Genuine co-design will recognise farmers saying, “This is what I’ve got for nature that is good on my farm, but hey, I am a farmer, and I am here to produce food. I want to farm this land, and I need to farm this land.” That co-design is a bit of give and take on both sides, but we have to find that sweet spot. We are not finding that in many cases at the minute.

There could be more people on the ground. There are 2,800 members of staff, and 53% of SSSIs are in the uplands. We could have a significant number of staff there. There are some excellent Natural England people locally in Cumbria and other areas. This is not about the individual staff. We are saying to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and its executive agencies and arm’s length bodies collectively: “We could deliver so much more by putting people in the right place.” We run training courses. On 24 September, 12 Natural England staff members are coming, and we will be training them with two farmers, who will teach them how to draft sheep, how to dose them, how to do some dry-stone walling and how to understand the economics. They are often coming from quite a low base level. We had an accountant giving a talk about farm economics in this training course, and a Natural England staff member quite innocently said, “Why does a farmer need an accountant?” We are starting at a low baseline—there is no such thing as a silly question.

We would love to work with more Natural England staff, and I know Natural England staff would like to be able to spend more time doing it. A Natural England staff member said to me that when she visits a farm, she has to report back on the visit through three different computer systems and portals. Is that the best use of precious civil servant time?

I know. We will shortly come back to Natural England, but as you said, every farmer knows their farm incredibly well, and we need to have greater integration. During the summer, across South Northamptonshire, where I am, there was a worry about all the fires that were coming. A lot of my farmers were saying that they wanted to cut down some of the vegetation but that they would be penalised if they did, so the fuel was left there. It is that balance. It is a real strain for them.
We will also come back to that. We now move on to future funding.

Q69 We have had the farming road map, which focuses, until 2030, on improving the application process and, as you said, preventing it from becoming like a Taylor Swift concert and providing more stability. From 2030 onwards, there is an ambition to move towards a model where the Government pay for public goods, with that being more of an emphasis in ELM schemes as a whole. Can we focus on the term “public goods”? When we think about designing future schemes, should we be considering what makes up those words and what should be included in them that is not currently?

It is a very strict economic use. I trained as an environmental economist. If something is paid for at the till, it is not considered a public good. That is where we have got a bit trapped, and it could definitely be broader. We know, and the Joint Intelligence Committee has said, that nature and biodiversity are absolutely at the heart of future national security. This is a matter of what is in our national interest. It is in our national interest that most people wish to eat three times a day, and therefore, providing food is really essential. We need to have a stable landscape, we need to have enough water, and we need to have climate resilience. Nature and our biodiversity are at the heart of that.

There is a matter of what we include in that, but there is also the quantum. I have noticed over the last 30 years of working as a land agent that the quantum is about the same. We have had this magic £2 billion figure, and that is now worth perhaps less than half of what it did. I think a group of environmental NGOs wrote to the Government only yesterday and said that they need at least an extra £2 billion a year—an extra £30 billion in total. Yes, let us broaden the term “public goods”. I suppose what you are trying to get at is whether food is a public good, and should we be expanding it? That is a leading question, and I should not be asking the questions.
It is your evidence.
Fill your boots.

It is about producing the right food in the right place and making sure that we have a balanced land production system and a land use framework. I am also a commissioner of the F ood , F arming and Countryside Commission and am really pro a land use framework. As Adam says, it is not either / or ; it is both. W e can produce lots of nature in a farmed setting with a resilient landscape that ensures communities are healthy, thriving and protected from climate change.

And it must be sensitive to the local environment. To go back to Adam’s point, we do not want people to go back to piling as much fertiliser on the ground as possible. We are not looking to have pedigree Charolais or Limousin herds in upland moorland, but there are breeds that are sensitive and appropriate for areas like yours, which is ultimately good for nature recovery.
Q70 Lisa and Adam, I am curious how you view this term, and whether there has been a narrowing of what is included in it.

The road map was welcome. I think the farming community probably hoped for far more than it actually delivered. It centres on a direction, but that direction has been to a series of tunnels that are not lit. There is not enough in the road map to allow any forward-thinking farmers and farm businesses to say where they are going to be in 10 years. Farmers do not business-plan for next year necessarily or the year after; it is a much longer-term commitment, especially if you want our land to be managed correctly. So it has given us a direction of travel but, my goodness me, we need a heck of a lot more information.

We must not get away from the fact that nearly every farmer I know in this agricultural county wants to produce food, wants to farm livestock, is proud to do that and believes that they are delivering an essential public good. I have heard people say, “Well, yes, but not much of your hill stock goes for prime,” but we are here now in Cumbria at the time of year when we are having our big autumn sheep sales. Here, this week, next week and next month, farmers from Cornwall to Caithness are coming to Cumbria to buy replacement stock that has been bred from our hill sheep and our hill suckler cows—a tradition that has gone on for generations. The stratified sheep industry is the backbone of farming, and it is so important. Although we struggle and we want to embrace farming and enhance nature in our environments, it should not be a crime. Farmers should not be castigated for wanting to be farmers and food producers.

We need clarity on the future and a set of guidelines with which farmers will be comfortable. We have not used the most important word, which is “trust”. There is not a lot of trust out there at the minute. Yes, a road map is welcome, but we need a heck of a lot more clarity in the future.

I totally agree with what Adam says. I am a farmer and we are a hill farm; we cannot change anything really in what we do because of the way our landscape is. As Adam says, we produce breeding stock, rather than prime stock, to go down country. That is what we do.
You take pride in what you do.

Yes. My partner has been busy for the last fortnight doing what they call a mule gimmer—which is a Swaledale x Leicester that goes on for future breeding—up ready for the sales. It is a case where everybody will judge you when you go with them. There is so much pride in taking things to the livestock markets and in what the end product actually is.
That sounds like a public good.
Q71 Do you feel like the Government have lost sight of that cultural heritage?
Totally, yes.

Cultural heritage is a public good. Going back to the example of cathedrals—this is an intangible cultural heritage. You are here in the Lake District world heritage site and that is recognised by UNESCO. Nobody is going to say that Westminster Abbey does not have value. We are talking about a landscape that has enormous value and has been recognised as such. The very system that Lisa uses—and which 3,900 commoners across England use—is part of our cultural heritage. We risk it at our peril.

Like Adam, I was really pleased to see the road map published but I had two concerns. First, it was a little bit warm words and cold comfort, because how does it help you day to day? Secondly, there was a hint there that, as a nation, we are looking to corporations to fund the delivery of public goods. The clue is in the name: public money for public goods. Why would a private corporation wish to finance a public good, because they cannot capture it for their shareholders’ benefit? We are really proud in this country of our national health service, our public education system and our libraries, and we do not expect private companies to fund those.
The private finance issue is one on which we are sighted; we will come to that again in a few minutes.

Q72 Lisa, c an I just ask about the length of the contracts — three or five years ? On the ground, i n terms of the delivery of these schemes, do you feel that that is a sufficient length of time to be able to do what you do best?

No, not really. You need longer to actually see and deliver that change. For example , a lot of years ago, they brought in the ESA scheme, and a lot of farmers around here delved into that. Historically, what you did to farm was that your sheep were in the meadow , so b asically they took what would be classed as the first cut, and then you would traditionally spread it with 20-10 -10 fertiliser, because that is what you did. Natural England came and looked at the meadows and saw all the flowers and grasses that it wanted ; 10 years later, once the scheme had ended, it went back and revisited the site , and a ll that had gone. That is what I mean about how you can create change that does not —things are there because of how it has been done.
Q73 Do you think there is a loss of focus on outcomes rather than processes ? I see you nodding, Adam.

I absolutely believe that is the case. Looking at the outcomes of the schemes as they are now, I question whether due diligence has actually taken place. In other forums, I have managed to talk to people at a high level in D EFRA, and i t was clear to me that those outcomes were not under consideration.

We are talking about the trade in sheep and cattle that we have at this time of year . A s we lose more and more sheep from the hills for various reasons, predominantly through the schemes, what effect is that having on the local economy and the community? Behind every farmer, you can count 40 other businesses that support that farm business to a greater or lesser extent. Of the money that farmers like Lisa will reinvest in their businesses when they have sold their lambs this autumn, probably 80% will be spent within 20 miles of the farm. That is the ethos, the essence, of the local circular rural economy.

I do not think th at due diligence is being done to work out what the effect will be if we take 50% of the sheep off that fell, 25% off that fell, or, in some cases, entire flocks. What is the knock-on effect of that on the community and the economy? I do not think that that due diligence is being undertaken. We are focusing entirely on the outcomes for nature , and, hopefully, possibly a bit on the farm business , but what is happening more widely to communities?

If you go on a website like Rightmove at the minute, there are valleys in this county where you will see four or five farmhouses on the market for £800,000, £900,000 or £1 million. The land is being taken back in hand by the estates ; i t is being planted with trees, rewilded or rewetted —i t is in schemes —and t he house is on the market. There are numerous examples of th at taking place right now. Is that an acceptable outcome of an environmental scheme or a tree-planting scheme? I do not think that is being taken into account enough , and particularly the effect that it is having on the local community, some of whom class themselves as the indigenous people.

It is about trust, but it is also about power. Cumbria is not as feudal as some upland counties, but a lot of the uplands are very feudal and remain so. Power can be used by many people in different ways. There are some brilliant landowners, and then there are other landowners, whether corporate or private, who are using the opportunity that has been provided through public money for public benefits to say that they do not require tenants any more in order to extract a rent from the Government.

There was an article recently in The Guardian , “T he business of rewilding ” by Patrick Barkham on Nattergal and Boothby , where investors had bought an arable farm for £13.8 million ; it is no longer being farmed b ut it is a business. I know that that is not in the uplands, but we are finding similar things in the uplands, where boutique land agency advisers will tell you how to maximise your return from purchasing something like that . That is different from—t here is a range. Clearly, we have an open free market for property, thank goodness, but at the same time, where is the incentive from Government, potentially leading to unintended consequences?

May I just go back to the issue about time? It is really important that agreements are long enough to deliver change, so three years is very short. I know the idea was to help tenants, but there are other ways to do that. The other thing about the new CS in the uplands is that a lot will be 10-year agreements, yet I do not know whether the Committee is aware of the unilateral, one-way six-month break clause, so that the Government can at any time just give six months’ notice. You might have committed to plant pasture, to change your whole system and perhaps to buy a herd of Luing cattle—to have native breeds there—but suddenly, in two and a half years’ time, you could find you have your notice served, and that is that.

Under the landscape recovery scheme—we have some good new landscape recovery schemes coming forward; this is not universal, but there are some good examples—the Government, or DEFRA, have increased the break clause. It was one year and is now two years, but still, when talking about landscape-scale change, the length of certainty for farmers is two years. That makes it really hard to plan their business. Farmers have said that to me. One commons in the south of the county, the DSTC from around Coniston, have done an amazing scheme on their 4,000 hectares. They put in 600 hectares of wood pasture a few years ago, but they said that they would have done more had it been a 20 or 25-year scheme, because they knew that they could have committed for a generation. You do not want that after 10 years, having trees that are half grown. What do you do with the fences? Where is the income coming from? Collectively, therefore—this is what you were saying about co-creation, isn’t it, Adam?—if we can have that co-creation, we can collectively deliver more at better value.

Leading on from Julia’s point, I am having conversations right now with farmers in the Lake District who are being persuaded to go into schemes, and commons agreements as well. They make the point that even at 10 years—although I think probably most would settle for 10—there is a lack of trust in the longevity of this situation. The farmers are saying to me, “What happens in 10 years’ time? If I am down to 25%, 30% or 40% of the sheep that I used to have, what happens if the public money runs out? Where do I go? I will not have a farming business in 10 years. My kids are small now, but I’d like to think they would have the opportunity in future. What is going to be left for them?” That trust in the longevity of the schemes is not there, and that is a barrier.

I am notoriously bad at keeping the Committee to time, but we have time pressures today, because you need to be back judging. I am not going to get on the wrong side of the show committee. Henry, as you are done with that, we will move on with Charlie. We are at the point where the rubber hits the road on the role of regulators and regulation.

Q74 Natural England has been mentioned a couple of times already, so perhaps it is worth exploring that theme a little further. The Tenant Farmers Association has described Natural England as anti-farming, and it was mentioned constantly in the responses to our calls for evidence. Adam, I will start with you. In your experience, how transparent are the processes by which Natural England makes decisions on stocking rates, site conditions, scheme access and so on?

That is a crucial point. There is huge frustration among hill farmers, not just in Cumbria but further afield. We have discussed co-design, and farmers are really frustrated that negotiation with Natural England is not happening. Even in this part of the world, Natural England has produced its idea of a set stocking rate of 0.05 livestock units per hectare, or half an AU per hectare or something like that, and in some parts of Cumbria, in the most challenging areas of the Lake District—where Lisa farms—that might be right. But in other areas of the Lake District, in higher, drier fell areas, the farmers believe that land can carry far more stock, but they are not getting that message through. The co-design does not seem to be there. Even peer-reviewed projects that have stated that no scientific evidence can be found to say that a set stocking rate will be universally effective have been immediately challenged by Natural England.

Where is the red line? Where does it stop? At what point does somebody somewhere say , “A ctually , on this common ”—or in this area —“ enough sheep have gone ”? There are no red lines , and this is a huge concern for farmers and a very great frustration. Where does it stop? When are we happy that we have got rid of enough stock and we are doing enough for nature? It is a real worry for many farmers that I know.

I should declare , just for the record, that I was on the board of Natural England from 2014 to 2019 and I chaired the u plands c ommittee. I have a lot of time for a lot of people in Natural England, but we are finding that there is a gap between what they are seeking to achieve and what is happening on the ground. Part of that is, as we have said, about the staffing constraints among local teams, and there is not enough time , but I think it is partly about how these schemes are constructed. It goes back to something Henry was saying : what is the breadth of public goods we are looking for? If you are looking only for particular vegetation outcomes, you w ill inevitably go down that line.

In the document that Adam is referring to , the 0.05 livestock units per hectare is a n average. It is true that if you are looking for ecological outcomes, you rarely get them above 0.06 , but what we are saying is that we are looking to conserve and sustain a system of farming : the cultural heritage and the natural heritage . The issue is a lack of attention to the whole.

One of the reasons why c ommons are so highly designated — seven times more designated for nature than enclosed land — is that they have these multiple outcomes. That means that you do not have one person who has only got a single agenda. We feel that it is really important to maintain that. Sometimes you can do things—on Bampton common, they want to have 500 hectares of planting. So you can have a bit more intensive grazing here , and then you have areas that are fenced off.

If Natural England had the staff on the ground and we as a nation committed to supporting farmers to develop schemes that really work locally —I think Natural England staff would be really happy to have more people there. I know that , as a community, we would be very pleased to have that . In my work in private practice as a land agent , I have been doing some of these schemes and working with these farmers for 30 years , yet with the numbers of staff changes that we are seeing , the continuity —it is really hard for staff when they are changing regularly.

You are in Cumbria, but if you do n’t mind , I will take us to Dartmoor, where 23 c ommons agreements are due to run out in the next year —mostly in the next year and a lot of them in the next six months. N atural England do es not have enough staff there. There is work through the Dartmoor Land Use Management Group, and w e are finding that people are attending meetings, but are people collectively really working for a common good? Rather than people feeling defensive, what we are seeing at the moment is — farmers are feeling their identity as farmers is threatened, and ecologists have a strong and equal passion towards delivering for ecology , and we are seeing a diversion rather than a coming together.

Q75 The staffing thing is very interesting because the annual report shows they have 427 senior manage rs; 15% of their entire workforce is senior management. They have a chief exec who gets paid more than the P rime Minister. You are saying they are completely under-resourced on the ground. That view is shared by a number of people who ha ve responded to th e call for evidence. W e are saying either that Natural England need to get a grip on their structures, or would they be better off back in-house , in D EFRA , where we woul d have better political oversight?

It is also worth remembering that the headcount of core DEFRA has gone up by 3.7 times since 2016 . In 2016 DEFRA had about 1 , 600 core staff and the re are now over 7 , 000 . I have added together all the staff at DEFRA and all the A LB s , and th ere is one civil servant for every five farmers in this country now. I don’t think it really matters whe re they sit. I personally am in favour of a statutory conservation agency. I am in favour of Natural England being a separate , independent body , because I think nature is really important —t he Joint Intelligence Committee says it is. H aving that independence is important.

But at the same time, it is always about the “ how ” as well as the “ what ” , is n’t it ? We are not seeing delivery on the ground. It is not for me to tell Natural England how to organise their staff count. All I can talk about is what we see in terms of how commons are managed and the risk to the future of common land and the most precious places. Whether you are on the tors of Dartmoor, in the New Forest, on Ingleborough and the Yorkshire Three Peaks, or on the North York Moors, these are the places that lift the soul; when you want to take a weekend break, those are the places you go to. You are not going to go to the cauliflower fields of Lincolnshire, however wonderful, are you? I love cauliflower cheese—it is my favourite food, I hasten to add—and I love Lincolnshire for producing that.

It is also really important that there are well-rewarded staff. The pay for Natural England staff at the lower end is shockingly poor, and that has been the case for many, many years. I know that from talking to staff; I know lots of people who work for Natural England. We have not got it quite right yet.

We need to ensure that there are lots of staff. To give an example, at home my mother farmed—it is now a charity and there is no financial interest. The first time we went into a stewardship scheme, a Natural England member of staff spent the whole day on the farm. We gave him lunch. He ate our home-made shepherd’s pie made with our own lamb. It was a great day. He gave us wonderful recommendations, and we fenced off all sorts of rivers. Ten years later, Natural England came round and they did not leave the kitchen. They did not walk a single field. They said they did not have the time. They were giving us £21,000 a year to do more for nature, and not a single field was visited, because they are under pressure. Think what more could have been done if they had the staff on the ground.
We really need to keep things short.
Q76 Do you have anything to add from your experience, Lisa?

From my experience, when they came to do a site visit at the farm, they did spend the day outside looking at everything and did a tremendous report. But Kentmere Dale Head Common came out of the scheme. It had been in for 10 years. We had had to heavily reduce stock to get it in for that 10 years. It was up for renewal, and we went back, but they wanted to halve the stock yet again. They came and looked at it. Their assessment was that, on the top of the fell, there had been no regeneration of anything. It’s 2,000 feet high; sheep don’t tend to graze up on the top there. They never came to the people who farm it and understand it to have a joined-up conversation about what is actually going on. They basically give you a bit of paper and say, “Right, these are the stocking numbers.” So it has not gone back in. Any good that was possibly done will have been undone. Yet all the neighbouring farmers have put their inside land into schemes and planted trees. So all the sheep that were in the allotments, as we call them, are now back out on the fell.
Chair, I could go on all day.

Q77 Let me bring it down to one question. My experience across Government is that the relationship between the regulated and the regulators works when it is a relationship of trust and respect. Do you feel you have that relationship with the regulators, particularly Natural England?
No.
Okay. I suspected that that might be the case, but I felt it was worth getting it on the record.

It does vary; it varies a lot from place to place. We have some really good schemes with really good staff. There is good practice, and we would like to have more good practice consistently across the country, and also to enable it. It is quite a complex relationship. Who makes the rules? Between DEFRA, Natural England and the RPA, this is not about anybody getting at anybody. It is about collectively having a scheme that enables Natural England, the Rural Payments Agency and DEFRA to do their job better.
I am hearing that there is room for improvement. We are going to move on to protected sites and landscapes. Sarah, you are going to start, and Ben will follow.

Q78 Covering about 24% of land in England, protected landscapes status allows quite a lot of opportunities. Here in the Lake District, the national park authority has supported 302 FiPL-funded projects, distributing approximately £5.9 million in grant funding. Obviously, there are those additional restrictions as wel l. For example, Friends of the Lake District said that designations have had “a significant impact on decision-making, land management and outcomes. However, this is not always the positive impact one would expect or desire.” To what extent do these designations affect the ability of farmers and landowners to operate viable businesses?

For instance, if you have to reduce your stocking numbers on the fell, if you have not got as many, and you have not got as many lambs, you have not got as much to sell. It reduces your income. Yet because of the heafing imbalance, we have twice as much area that we have to cover to do the same job, basically.

There are lots of forms of designations, as you are probably aware. There are the sites of special scientific interest. Only 8% of England is in a site of special scientific interest , but we have a huge proportion of that in Cumbria and the uplands. As I said, common land is highly designated. I think it is about 1 million hectares of England.

This could be an opportunity, if we can get the schemes working well. I would like to be “ cup half full ” about this. A designation can be a fantastic opportunity. Where the charity that I am a trustee of farms, we are not in a protected landscape. It is very beautiful in the Eden valley. We have no access to FiPL. It is actually quite hard. There are pluses and minuses to being in a protected landscape. FiPL has been great, but it does not give revenue. People have done lots of hedging schemes, they have done up their barns and they have done other things, but it is not helping farm businesses’ income on a regular basis.

I am really in favour of designating areas for nature. I am really in favour of protected landscapes. I think the Glover review was fantastic. Some things have been implemented, but more could be done. But we need to support people, and we need to say that this is a collective endeavour. At the moment, we do not charge anybody to come to our protected landscapes. That means we need to invest sufficiently. We know that national parks and national landscapes are run pretty much on a shoestring. My view is that this is actually a really good source of wellbeing for the nation.

To go back to that £2 billion figure, that is 0.2% of Government expenditure. You will probably know more than I do, but the Government spend roughly £1.3 trillion a year, and that £2 billion is 0.2%—and that is for all food, not just for the uplands; this is for 70% of England. If we are saying that it is part of our national security to have healthy biodiversity, a resilient landscape and good-quality food production to have a healthy public, then I would suggest that 0.2% is very much on the low side.

As a farmer support organisation, we have close relationships with the national parks and the protected landscapes areas, and FiPL has been really good. It has been one of the successes for many of the farmers I know. It is proceeding now, and hopefully for another two years after this one as well. It has done some good for sure.

We also have to remember that a lot of farmers fall through the cracks. If they are not in those protected landscapes, there is very little for them. We support various cluster groups of farmers who do fall through the cracks.

There is a willingness to work and to embrace, but—it comes back to the same old thing—as long as there is recognition that farmers want to farm that land as well. There will have to be a little bit of give and take on both sides.

Q79 To what extent do you think those existing designations, whether they be national parks, national landscapes or SSSIs, are achieving their intended environmental objectives in the uplands? What do you think the conflicts are, and how can they be resolved?

If we go back to the Dower report, which underpinned the National Parks Act—John Dower produced a report, and then there was the Hobhouse report—it was rather broader. I think there has perhaps been a bit of a shift and a bit of goalpost moving around what our national parks and national landscapes are for.

The Dower report was very much about having places for the whole nation in terms of wellbeing. We had just had world war two, and they were landscapes of beauty. That word “beauty” is perhaps not used enough. Clearly, underpinning that beauty is our natural environment. Over the last few years, Governments have very much led with the 30 by 30 target , on top of that 24%. I would suggest that we can deliver 30 by 30 —to remind, that is for 30% of the country to managed for nature by 2030. I would suggest that that should be a national target so that we can have farming with nature across the whole nation, not simply say, “These are the pockets.”

It is land sparing or land sharing, and in a highly populated country such as England, a land-sharing approach is more appropriate, particularly in such precious landscapes as the Lake District and the Yorkshire dales where we are looking at that cultural heritage.

I would like to go back to the roots of our national parks and landscapes in the 1949 Act. It is not either/or; it is both/and. It is both nature and culture and food and recreation. They are places where the 60 million to 70 million people in this country can go and learn about farming and our cultural heritage, enjoy squishing around in the sphagnum moss, and relish the orchids that are there. We need to do much more to connect people with food, with nature and with place.
Q80 Adam, do you want to add to Julia’s comments? I saw you nodding.

I was nodding in total agreement. I hope you enjoy the landscapes that you see around you here in Cumbria as much as us locals and the 20 million visitors to the county every year—they make 40 million visits in what is upwards of a £4 billion visitor economy. It would be good to accept that those landscapes are predominantly predicated around the work that farmers and their livestock do. We are proud of that, and as a county we should be proud of that.

These are managed landscapes. Can they be managed better? Yes, of course they can, and our farmers are up for that challenge. But is Cumbria, which is a large county but a relatively small area, the right place to start thinking about large landscape change, when a lot of livestock would be taken off those areas? Nobody knows because the data is not there and the science has not been done. The projects are being looked at now, but it is about achieving balance. We cannot get away from the fact that we need managed landscapes in this county.

It is optimising those numbers. There is quite a lot of work done. There was a whole system in common law called l evancy and couchancy . It is a medieval term, and the idea was that the number of stock you had on the fell was the number you could hold at home in the winter. As Adam said, we went through intensification with the post-world war two drive for increased production, beyond what were probably the limits of some of the upland areas. We are now in a system where farmers need support. In the old days, someone from the Min of Ag sat in your kitchen and supported you doing that. That is what I would love to happen. I am delighted for DEFRA and its family to have so many staff, but let’s get them on the farm rather than in the office.

Q81 Farmers are the proud custodians of some of the most beautiful parts of the country, whether it is up here in Cumbria or down in the Somerset levels and moors. Being in that protected landscape should not mean choosing between nature and livelihoods. That has been very much outlined already today.

So often, farmers are left to absorb the cost of public good. What can be done to improve the balance of incentives and the current constraints between supporting farm businesses producing food and delivering environmental improvements?

You need schemes that have delivering multiple outcomes as their targets. A challenge for Natural England staff, many of whom do appreciate the cultural heritage of these areas, is that they are being asked to deliver a nature-only focus. Nature is really important and climate resilience is really important. We have heard from the Copernicus report how hot Britain has been. We must absolutely ensure we address climate resilience and climate change. People here in Cumbria have huge opportunities to do that, but let’s have cultural heritage going alongside it . At the moment, people just try to sneak it in. Natural England staff often do their best within a system that does not allow them, and is not empowering them, to pay for hefted flocks and a system of intangible cultural heritage.
Q82 Do you think there is enough emphasis around food production? Do you think we have the balance right?

I think that we need the right food being produced in the right place. We are brilliant at producing red meat; that is our area. We particularly need grass-fed meat. I am personally an advocate for Pasture for Life, and we are Pasture for Life-certified at home. There are opportunities to have lower input systems that are more resilient to geopolitical shocks.

Producing good-quality, nutrient-dense food off the fells is something we can support farmers to do more often. The Farmer Network does brilliant work in peer-to-peer learning and site visits, and fantastic work is done among its members to support farmers to look at optimising the efficiency of their agricultural production business, and we need to do a lot more of that. But is it really up to Adam and his small team of part-time people to transform the rural economy of Northumberland, Cumbria and Yorkshire? Perhaps some of the many thousands of people in the civil service could be seconded. I think that some people will be seconded from DEFRA to the Cumbria combined authority, which is very exciting to hear. We are looking forward to that.
Q83 Do you think we have the balance right between nature and food production?

Not at all, at this moment in time. I would maybe go a bit further than Julia has, because we have had many of these conversations over the years. Julia is right that it is about the quality of food and how we do that—I do not want to use the R-word, because it means different things to different people—in a regenerative way, but I absolutely believe that we need intensive agriculture as well.

When you understand the true effects of climate change and how that will play out over 20 or 30 years across the globe; that we have a rising population—we are about 67 million now, and we will be 75 million or 76 million by 2050, which will go in the blink of an eye; and the pressures that will be on this country and others, you realise that we will have to produce a lot more food. Low-input and low-output systems are brilliant in the right environment, but farmers will have to produce a lot more food quite intensively in other areas if we want to feed ourselves in the future. Food security needs to be on the agenda.
I absolutely agree with that.
Ben, do you want to pick up some of this and then move on to private finance?

Q84 I am happy to move on to private finance. One thing that stuck out to me is what you said early on, Adam, about the farming road map. I am paraphrasing here, but your quote was roughly that we have a road map that leads to a series of tunnels that are not lit, and that really stuck with me.

One thing that was in the farming road map and the land use framework, with much fanfare from DEFRA, was the idea that private finance can start plugging the gaps and providing more support to the farming industry. I am interested in your opinion, Adam. How mature and accessible are natural capital markets for upland farmers and land managers?

I cannot speak with any authority on that at all. I can say that the Farmer Network’s strapline is, “Whatever the challenge, whatever the opportunity.” We always say to farmers, “Look at the opportunities. You may or may not decide to go down that route, but you have to have knowledge of the opportunity.”

In terms of future green finance, a lot of farmers are sceptical at the minute about where that will lead them—the tunnel that will take them down, if you like—and what will be in it for them, as well as about the longevity of that funding. A lot of farmers I know are pretty sceptical about putting land into long-term schemes like 30 by 30, and nutrient neutrality, which is longer than that. There is quite a lot of scepticism at the minute and not a lot of trust in the system from many farmers I know in this part of the world. I always say to farmers, “Make sure you understand it and use the knowledge. If there is anything there that will be of benefit to you, your business or your family in future, we can help you embrace that.”

Q85 Lisa, obviously you are the one who is working the land. You are one of the people who is expected to be able to access these private finance markets. Is that something that you feel is actually achievable?
I will be honest: we have never been approached with any of that, so at this time—

Q86 That is quite telling in itself. Do you think that is just because there has been no support from central Government to make you aware of these schemes, or do you think that it is too much of a wild west, where the private companies are allowed to set the rules of the game?

From my experience, what I would possibly say is: have a lot of them been cherry-picked as to where they are focusing it, and that is why I know nothing about it? We have neighbours who have gone into a scheme to improve water quality. Surely all our tributaries flow into the same river, but we never got the opportunity.

Larger estates find it easier to access this, I think it would be fair to say. I am involved in a really good landscape recovery scheme: I am on the interim board of the Resilient Glenderamackin, which is led by the Rivers Trust. They were really confident about trying to get private finance. I am sure you are all aware that it is the pinnacle of the ELM 20-year schemes. DEFRA was hoping that maybe it would be an 80:20 split, or 75% public and 25% private money. I think they have managed to get maybe 2% to 3% of private money going in, and that has been really, really hard to get. They might get, over 20 years—say the budget is £120 million—£3 million or £4 million. Those are people who are working incredibly hard. The Rivers Trust nationally have access to all sorts. For an individual farmer, it is very, very difficult.

It is not only the regulatory framework, but also whether there is a demand. That will depend on accounting standards, and often international accounting standards. I do not want to pick on any particular corporation, but if you are a large corporation and you have to internalise those externalities—sorry; this is a bit of economic speak—if you are producing fast food, or running a mining company or an airline, you produce these externalities and then effectively you are buying in carbon credits or biodiversity net gain. Actually, if regulation is not requiring you to do that, then why would you? This is a global market, and there have been quite a lot of changes across the pond in terms of attitudes towards environmental requirements. You only need to have an announcement over in Washington DC and the market changes dramatically in the UK in terms of people’s expectations.

Q87 Lisa, some of the written evidence that we have received over time has highlighted a concern, especially up here, about private finance actually taking land out of being accessible to people like yourself. We had evidence from Friends of the Lake District, which said: “A further tension relates to farmland in the uplands and upland fringes being sold off by landowners for carbon credits”. We had the Lake District national park authority saying: “Green finance is also increasing pressure on land values”. We had the Campaign to Protect Rural England again saying that it was another risk. Is it something that you fear as well?
When you actually travel and leave Cumbria—a lot of farmers don’t necessarily do that very often, do they?
Well, why would you?

Yes. When you do, you then appreciate what we actually have here. As a farmer, I personally want to share that with people, as long as they come and leave it how they found it, and do not destroy it. That is a bit of a challenge of all these people coming. I am going to talk in technical terms, but when you take the sheep off the fells, etc, we have loads of footpaths. Now when you go to gather the fells, etc, the easiest place to walk is on a sheep trod. If you go off the sheep trod, it is hard terrain. People want to come and walk, and we want to share it with them. We do not want it to be closed. The majority of them do respect what we have here and look after it, and I think we should share it. Nobody wants to see the last of anything, do they? It is a balance.

It is. In terms of changes, I can think of one valley in the middle of the Lake District, Thirlmere Valley, where there used to be six farmers. I am an administrator for the common; there are about 2,500 hectares of common land there. There were four farmers around 10 years ago, and we are now down to one; that one farmer has been served a notice to quit on their farm. It is a matter under arbitration, but it is really tough. There is a plan and there is already a website talking about resilient Thirlmere and rewilding the whole valley. We know that there will be more flexibility for that landowner in terms of what they do, but that family is facing professional costs of a quarter of a million pounds to try to contest that. These cases are always complex—nothing is ever straightforward—but the intention behind that is not to have better farming on that site, because the other three farms they have back in hand have not been re-let.

I know exactly the area and farm that you are referring to. I was talking to a farmer just last week further down that range of fells, and he said to me, “If you look up at that fell there, Adam, my sheep are up there”—he is not in any commons agreement at the minute—“and my great pleasure in life is to walk up there every day. I see my sheep, and they are in great condition. There is plenty for them to eat, there is plenty of nature up there and I genuinely believe that I have got the balance right. If I want to go into a commons agreement, the first thing I will be told is, ‘You’ll have to downsize your sheep flock.’ But I think I have the balance right.” I do not think we are paying enough attention to those farmers who think that they have the balance right.

In terms of tenant farmers—he is a tenant farmer—there is pressure from some estates that are taking some or all of the land back in hand when they can. Farm business tenancies are always for a fixed term if they are not on an Agricultural Holdings Act tenancy . That pressure is definitely rising, not only in Cumbria but across other northern counties. That is a result of schemes and the possibilities, perhaps in the future, of forms of green finance. It is another pressure on farmers.

There is a strong incentive for landlords to do this. This is effectively what the ELMS do, but it is inadvertent, I would say, and unintentional. There are some great estates—good estates doing good things. The National Trust has 90 farms and a nature-led farming policy; it wants farms there. There are some really good examples of where we can do both, and we need to do more of that.

That needs to be encouraged through Government policy. One thing we absolutely know from world war two onwards is that farmers are very agile and responsible to the signals sent by Government through support. If we can get that right and build trust, which is hard won and easily lost, and have consistency and ensure that people can access schemes, farmers will be the first to deliver a balanced approach to delivering these designated landscapes.
Q88 My final question on this—a yes or no answer from each of our panellists, if you don’t mind—is: do you agree that private finance will deliver public good?
No.
I need to think about that, but my immediate go-to is no.
My immediate go-to would be no.

Julia, you have been remarkably adept at bringing common land and tenancies into just about everything, but we have a few specific questions. Terry, you will be mopping up anything that Julia has not already covered, and then we will move on to wildfires.

Q89 As a Committee, we are very conscious that farming looks and feels different in different parts of the country. That is essentially why we are here; we have made a real effort to get out and about around the UK. The fields are green here—they are not in Norfolk where I am from, so that is a very strong difference at the moment. But even here there are more variances between owner-occupiers, tenant farmers and commoners. If I am feeling charitable, I do feel sorry for DEFRA sometimes, writing a policy that covers all of those different challenges.

Adam, you mentioned the word “co-design” a couple of times today. I think that is absolutely crucial. We are not going to write DEFRA’s policy today, but what does it look like around recognising the differences between owner-occupiers and tenant farmers, and how does that get captured in a policy? I will start with you, Julia, because this is your area of expertise.
I would put commoners in there as well.
Yes, commoners too—absolutely.

We have been working on this at the Foundation for Common Land since 2012-13, first in “Better Outcomes on Upland Commons” and then in “Our Upland Commons”, and we work with 25 partners, including Government, national landscapes and national parks. What we found is that if we have a facilitator, we have these ingredients of success—trust, integrity, valuing local knowledge, consistency: those areas—and also the stepping stones to get there.

The first of those is that social relationships are at the heart of all change. If you have strong social relationships within a community—if you have them between landlords and tenants, within a commons association, with Natural England, with the protected landscapes, with Friends of the Lake District and with other bodies—we are much more likely to deliver change.

The next stepping stone—these are prerequisites—is that the farm business must be thriving. That is an absolute prerequisite. If that is happening, we can deliver those environmental outcomes. We have roughly 86,000 commercial farmers in England. If we recognise that they are farm businesses, then they need to make a living—whether it is part time or with 20 members of staff—and they need to be solvent. Let’s look at this through that lens. We know that they can deliver in spades for the environment if we work with them and encourage that co-working.

Where we see really good practice, we deliver great outcomes, and that does happen. We have examples from really good work that we are doing—there is some good work in the Buttermere Fells that we have been doing for many years; there is good work on Kinniside . There are areas where we know that all these partners can work well together.
Q90 I often say that farmers are the best conservationists. If they are making a profit, most of them would invest back into the environment anyway.

Yes, and commons are complex. When you have a contract between the commons association and DEFRA, below that you have something called an internal agreement, which is a management agreement between all the parties—the landowners and all the commoners. In the forest of Dartmoor, they have 380 people signed into that agreement. These are complex agreements—it is my role to make that work with solicitors on the quasi-legal, economic side of things—but we really need Natural England at the heart of that.

If we go back a couple of hundred years, we had these things called manorial courts. A lot of tenancies and commons were managed through manorial courts, through the steward. We then lost that—it was all to do with universal suffrage, a rather good thing, coming in—but we then ended up in a rather chaotic position for the management of commons.

We now have some very good governance systems available. Elinor Ostrom was the first woman to win the Nobel prize for economics, and her initial work was based on managing commons in Switzerland. We know that if we can get it right on commons, we can get it right at a landscape scale, across estates and on the new landscape recovery systems.

There is a lot of good practice. Sometimes DEFRA can be a little frightened of entering wholeheartedly into that process—they go, “Oh, that’s nothing to do with us. If you give all the money to Terry to go to The Bahamas, that’s fine by us, as long as you deliver the outcomes.” But this is public money and we should be really clear about who is keeping it. We unfortunately see some really bad practice, where either one or two commoners, or one or two landowners, use their power to lever a larger sum of that money. Managing money is really important. Public money should be well spent, and my view is that DEFRA has a responsibility to make sure that the split between landlord and tenant, or between commoners and landowners, should be better managed, with more scrutiny placed on that.

Q91 Adam, with the work that you do, taking a broad look at the difference between owner-occupiers, commoners and tenant farmers, do you see similarities, or are there particular challenges for different groups?

There are particular challenges for different groups, but it is a huge frustration. We have talked a lot about the polarity between farming and conservation, which is pretty manifest in Cumbria at this moment in time, and it does mask the good work that is going on. But i n real terms, taking what Julia has been talking about —down to grassroots, sitting round the kitchen table—in an ideal world what should happen is that the Natural England field person should sit at Lisa’s table and start the conversation with, “What’s important to you on this farm? What do you need to do on this farm for your farm production business?” Then, when that trust is built, they should walk round the farm, looking at features and whatever it might be, with advice being given, where trust builds up.

Instead, in certain circumstances, it is almost like a “them and us” scenario. That is never going to work. We have to build trust and we have to pull people together. Our ecologists and conservationists must learn about the farm business and know exactly what that is. That in turn will help our farmers to understand better practices in terms of nature, biodiversity and everything else. It is doable. It is not difficult, but it is being made very difficult.

Q92 Adam has just described what a good system would look like. Lisa, if the Government came out with a new grant scheme tomorrow, what would go through your head? What are the challenges for you to access that money? What is your immediate reaction about how it would work on the ground? Do you go, “Yes!” or do you go, “Oh God, not another form to fill in”?
No, we’d get somebody else to fill in the form. [ Laughter. ]

You would go through it. We all want to work with nature; we all want to see everything there. So, if it is for the benefit of the good of the environment and the benefit of the good of our cash flow, you go with it. Nobody wants to see the last of anything and we want to protect what we have. For instance, in the Lake District, there are a lot of stone walls, etc. If somebody came and said, “You need to be planting hedges to get harvest mice, etc, to come back,” you would be keen to give it a go, as long as it did not go right through the best of your hay meadows. You would have to have a balance somewhere as to where you put it. That is what it is about. It is a bit of what Adam says—a kitchen conversation with everybody there is what it needs, and it all needs to be done on an individual basis, rather than a scattergun approach that fits everybody.
Q93 Do you think that tenant farmers have fair access to Government funding at the moment?

I think we have equal access, as everybody else has really. It is there for us; it is just about getting the correct advice about where to go to move into it. We are actually National Trust tenants, so we might see it from a different point of view. A private—
Q94 Equal entitlement, rather than necessarily equal access?
Yes.

The National Trust have lots of staff who help their tenants go into things, but sometimes what we find is land being taken back in hand and let on shorter tenancies, or the landlord enters into the SFI and charges a rent. I can think of one example of a farm over on Shap. The farmer retired completely. No pressure or anything; he retired. The landlord kept the farm in hand. Previously, the rent had been £30,000; it was a large farm. Then they went into countryside stewardship—the old countryside stewardship—and the income was £300,000 per annum. They are expecting under landscape recovery to get £700,000 per annum; the landlords will get that and they will charge conservation graziers to graze that land.

That just shows where public money is flowing, and that £700,000—yes, it is a big farm, but it could be spread among a lot of things. This is the problem—there is no plan for this money. It is like these Taylor Swift concerts; if you want to buy 20 tickets, you can buy 20 tickets.

I know of an example of a farm that was in private ownership that just recently has been rented. Basically, the landlord has gone and said, “If you get more payments than this, we want it.” He has capped how much they can actually take, and it is not a big farm. That is when it is unfair, but as I said, we are on a National Trust farm; we have not seen that.

Q95 Good. Lastly, Julia, the Government have tried to make access fairer by putting the 100k cap on SFI for example. Even so, it is a race to access that before the money runs out, because it will never be enough to cover all of the need. Do you think that approach has helped tenant farmers and commoners, or does it still need to evolve and change?

It is a very simplistic approach. If Brant Fell, which is 2,700 hectares, want to open up and go into a scheme, they would not be able to put their common into an SFI scheme because they would be above the £100,000 cap. That just shows that the system does not necessarily work, although it is well intentioned. We have written to DEFRA to ask them to please lift the £100,000 cap for commons. There are 23 active farmers on that common, so their share is less than £100,000. It varies a lot. A lot of farms will be going for only £5,000 or £10,000. A blog produced last week said what the average claim was under SFI—was it about £7,000 or something?

It is going in the right direction. This is nothing against Norfolk, but we have seen quite a lot of BPS money from Cumbria flow to winter bird food mix agreements in Norfolk. I know Norfolk farmers, who tell me that their average earning per hectare is over £560, while in Cumbria you are stuck on £80 for HLS. There are good payments available, as you can see in the column here—£164 for moorland under CSI tier—but you can’t actually get them at the moment. That is the problem. On paper, there is equal access, but in practice there is not.

Q96 Buckle up—I have a few questions on grazing and moorland management. We touched on this at the start, Adam. Julia, I want to come to you, because you have touched on this a few times already. Quite a lot of the evidence that we have received has been characterised as saying that Natural England often defaults to reducing stocking rates. As a farmer, do you feel that alternative management options are being given sufficient consideration?

I would not feel that they are. For instance, with the system that we were looking at, it was a bit of a case that they were not willing to come back to the table, negotiate and meet in the middle; their figures had to be stuck to, but they weren’t prepared to go out and do a walk of the fell to see what there is and how it was beforehand. It was a case of, “No, we need to reduce it further to this.”

Q97 On the subject of the fell and livestock, if you are foolish enough to spend any time on Twitter—I really would not recommend it—you will see some fairly extravagant claims made about levels of mortality and animal welfare. Talk me though how you see it and how you manage your stock in upland areas, sheep in particular.
Sheep?
Q98 Do you allow them to go lame?

No, you treat them if they go lame. A lot of the reason why sheep now go lame is that everybody is encouraged to take them off the fells and winter them in the lowlands. The cows in the lowlands tend to have dermatitis in their feet, so when the sheep come back to the fells they fetch that with them from the lowlands. That is a bit of what happens. If they are up on the fell and they get foot rot, the flies are attracted to their feet. Basically, they have them under their body and they get maggots, and you can’t treat them on the fell. But you tend not to get as much of that on the fell as you do in the fields because it is colder up there and the flies don’t tend to thrive.

The welfare of the stock is in every farmer’s interest—for them to be looked after and tret right. Everybody can miss something in the field. Something can be taken ill after you have been round, but you treat it as soon as you find it. For farmers to sell their stock at the auction, they must either have a VAN number, which says that you have had a vet inspection to say that your husbandry is up to requirement, or they must be in Red Tractor or FABBL. It is displayed on the board that you are in those schemes. Some companies will not buy your products if you are not in them. They see it as a premium—that you are looking after things correctly.
Q99 We spoke earlier about the pride that you have as an upland farmer working in a traditional low-impact system. Is that reflected in the way that you treat your stock?
Not at all; you just look after stock. You are basically a stock person, and that is what you want—you want the best of everything. It is an embarrassment if something is not right.
You may be referring to an article that was in The Spectator . There has also been quite a lot of publicity, hasn’t there?
Q100 There has been a degree of comment, but I do not want to get into that, because there is other stuff that I want to stick on.

Just very briefly, I think that what is important is that this is very unhelpful without going into the detail. Anything that polarises farmers from nature conservation is deeply unhelpful. Leaving aside the whole personal nature of that particular article, which I think is very unfortunate, all the work that we at the Foundation for Common Land are trying to do, and that I know that Adam at The Farmer Network is too, is about building trust and bringing people together. That sort of article, which was in The Spectator , makes our job 10 times harder. Why, as a farmer, would you want to come to the table to discuss nature conservation?
Q101 If that was how you were going to be met when you got there. Lovely point, well made.
Lisa, if I can come back to you, we have heard that constant reductions in stocking levels are now posing a threat to the system of hefted stock—which you work with, I think, if that is right?
Yes.
How important is that hefted system for the whole farming community and the cultural heritage, and the way that you farm here?

To start with the cultural heritage, you traditionally have what they call joint gathers, whereby on that particular fell you could have four different hefts owned by four different people. They all come together on a day—it has to be a clear day, when there is no mist on the top and the weather has to be correct—and they all gather them in and then, at the sheep end, sort off their own, and then they all go their separate ways. It is just so frustrating when you have to go so much further to gather your own heft, and it is the same for everybody.

I am hearing this constantly from upland farmers in the Lake District and the Pennines as well. Those sheep reductions—in some cases whole flocks, side by side by side on the top of a fell—are having a major impact in some areas. The shepherds are telling me that they are having to go miles and miles past the original traditional heft into other areas or other valleys. They are telling me that the bracken creep as a result of the reducing sheep numbers is making it impossible to gather the sheep hiding in the bracken. They and the dogs are worked to death. I have had farmers almost in tears, sitting in my office, telling me about this. It is the impact of the loss of the sheep on the remaining shepherds that is an equally important pressure that is building in some areas of the Lake District.
Q102 It comes to this whole idea of community. These gatherings in uplands, they are not just individual shepherds and farmers on their own; it is a community effort, isn’t it?

It absolutely is. That gather is a skill in itself. You cannot just set 10 people off on a hill and say, “Go there, go there and go there, and bring all the sheep with your dog.” Those shepherds and those families, some of whom are intergenerational, know every area of that fell. They know where the sheep will be hiding, because the sheep will teach their next generation that that is where they go. This is what hefting is: it’s acclimatisation. It’s mothers, ewes, teaching their young stock where they need to be on the fell. It’s so important and so valuable.
Q103 It strikes me that it is not just the sheep that are hefted; it is the farmers and the shepherds as well.
There was an excellent article in the Financial Times , just last week or the week before, about this, explaining how it works.
Q104 You are hearing that all the time, Adam.
All the time.
Q105 Why are Government and Government agencies not hearing it, do you think?

I would like you to ask that question to them, because there seems to be a stumbling block. We have said it frequently, there is this huge frustration. Farmers are trying to have that conversation and, invariably, habitat recovery seems to always be predicated on “Reduce the sheep”. I would like to know about that question.
Q106 Do you feel that there is sufficient transparency in the way that Natural England assesses moorland condition and what it sees as being appropriate management interventions?

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, isn’t it? Many upland farmers say to me that there are areas of the fells that they know they understand—they know better than anybody what is up there—and they do not seem to be able to get that message across. How that plays out in future , we will have to see. There is huge frustration that farmers are trying to say, “We know what is good on here and we know what could be done better.”

As a farmer and a stock person, when you put your sheep out on to the fell, if they don’t come back in in the condition that you have hoped, you know that you have put too many out. It is about a balance. You have that understanding of a fell.

Q107 Then there are other, wider consequences for the way in which you manage moorland. This summer, we have seen quite dramatic scenes across upland communities and other moorland communities. Adam, I think you touched on this earlier. Do you feel that we have the balance right in terms of managing the land to mitigate the wildfire risk?

Not at all, and that is not me saying that; that is farmers saying that. Frankly, in Cumbria this year, we have dodged a bullet. There are areas—not all, but many areas—across the uplands in Cumbria that farmers say have been under-grazed for some time, and the burden of dead grasses and the build-up of combustible dry, dead vegetation—white grass, as we call it up here—is ever-increasing. There is real concern in the farming community across this county that at some stage one of the major fells is going to go, and when it goes, it will not stop. There is real concern about that.

Farmers can do a lot to help. In Dartmoor, my member of staff down there worked with 30 of the 34 commons associations to put together wildfire action plans. What do we do in the case of a fire? It is about ensuring farmers are trained. They can use their quad bikes. There are lots of ways that they can work with the fire service. It is a combination of things, such as being proactive in terms of fire breaks. It is making sure that we work collectively. We know that summers are likely to continue to get hotter, so how do we collectively ensure mitigations against fires happening in the first place?
Q108 Farmers can do a lot, but they have to be there in order to do it. Just a few minutes ago, you were talking about land being taken out of production.

Totally, and then they are not going to be there, and that is a real concern. Dartmoor and Exmoor and the Quantocks are further south. Sarah will know from her neck of the woods that there is more pressure in terms of the climate down there. There was a big fire in the New Forest, which is a common as well. We know that farmers could have been better integrated there.
We are running up against time now. We have spoken a lot today about social value and the community impact. Sarah has a few questions on that to round off our evidence session.

Q109 You said earlier that the Government seem to have lost sight of cultural heritage being a public good, and do risk losing skills. On the way here, we saw all the dry stone walling, which is absolutely beautiful. We have talked a lot about hefting. Is our key message back to the Government that we should not lose sight of that, and to make sure that there is support there?

Yes. Let’s have an integrated approach. You came to that event we did in 2019, where Adam and I said we wanted a culture-rich, nature-rich Lake District. We have the new Lake District partnership plan. It is not either/or. We can do both/and, but we have to support farmers to be there. We would like to have the same number of commoners there.

Going back to my analogy, if you are a choir in a cathedral, the back row only has one bass on each side; suddenly, you are not getting a great voice from that. What we want to have is healthy younger people and the back line of the choir—the commoners of all ages being there. If we can encourage that through public payments for the public good, and ensure that nature recovery and climate resilience are working alongside cultural heritage together, then it is through working together and valuing each other that we will get better outcomes.

May I add to that? I think it is absolutely imperative, and this is a plea to Government, that any and all impacts of schemes must be recognised. It is not good enough to say that nature recovery trumps everything else. Any and all impacts need to be assessed.

Basically, just don’t take the finger off the pulse on the next generation; they’re the future. It’s all right us in our generation doing all this good, but it’s the next ones following on who can continue it.

Q110 What might be the implications for rural communities if nature markets become a major source of upland income? For example, peatland restoration looks very different in Cumbria than it does down in Somerset, but both regions face a fundamental question of how we support farmers and land managers to deliver climate and water benefits without undermining their businesses’ viability. On that basis, how will that change impact rural communities?

You are talking about communities disappearing, because large corporations like to have simple transaction costs, which means it is much easier to deal with one person rather than 21 people on a common. So, commons are not really very attractive for this.

What we are finding is that our communities are literally disappearing. They are at risk of that because it is not financially viable for them to continue. You will not get the next generation coming through.

We need to ensure that there is a living wage, if people’s sons and daughters wish to come into a farming business, but the figures I gave you show that the risk is that farming really will not produce a living wage. Yes, we need peatland restoration, but alongside other things. Again, anything that is single-agenda has significant risks for rural communities.

Absolutely. We have already talked about the fact that there are a number of estates that are taking land back in hand and embracing every scheme that there is with relish. The knock-on effect, as we said earlier, is happening now. Communities are having pressure placed upon them. We have farmhouses now on the market as separate entities, with people buying them for second homes or for Airbnbs. This is happening now and communities in Cumbria are starting to feel that pressure already. Also, there is that circular rural economy to consider, because if that land is no longer being farmed, that farm is no longer buying goods and services from other people that support that farm business. It’s happening now.

I find myself wishing that we had started at 9 am instead of 10 am, because I could run this for the rest of the day. However, Adam, you have important duties elsewhere in the show field, and we are up against time.

Can I thank you? I said at the start that this was about making sure that people felt that they were being heard. I hope that, in small measure, people in a community like this today will perhaps feel that they are being heard, and that that might be a better direction of travel in the future as this conversation develops.
I thank you for your attendance, for your engagement and for your enormously important evidence, but for the moment, I am afraid that we are beaten by the clock.

segs.tx: Justice Committee
Oral evidence: Children and Young Adults in the Secure Estate , HC 190
Tuesday 8 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 8 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Tessa Munt (Acting Chair) ; Janet Daby; Sir Ashley Fox; Warinder Juss; and Sarah Russell .
Questions 96 to 15 4
Witnesses
I : Laura Cooper, Youth Justice Lawyer, Youth Justice Legal Centre; and Steph Roberts-Bibby, Chief Executive, Youth Justice Board for England and Wales.
II : Dame Rachel de Souza, Children’s Commissioner for England.
Written evidence from witnesses:
Youth Justice Board for England and Wales [CYA0061]
Children’s Commissioner for England [CYA0064]
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Laura Cooper and Steph Roberts-Bibby.

Q96 Welcome to this session of the Justice Committee. This is the second session of our youth justice inquiry, with a focus on sentencing in youth justice cases, and community-based alternatives to custody. For our second panel we will hear from the Children’s Commissioner, but first we will hear from the Youth Justice Board and the Youth Justice Legal Centre. Before we begin our questioning, the m embers of the Committee will need briefly to make declarations of interest.
Good afternoon. I am Ashley Fox, the Member for Bridgwater. I am a former solicitor and my interests are on the register.

I am Tessa Munt. I am acting Chair this afternoon, until we elect our Chair for the next session of Parliament. I am the Member of Parliament for Wells and Mendip Hills, which is in Somerset. I am a director and the vice-chair of WhistleblowersUK, which is a not-for-profit organisation, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on penal affairs.

Hello. I am Sarah Russell, the Member for Congleton. My interests are as on the register, but I am a member of various trade unions, I chair the all-party parliamentary group on access to justice and I am a solicitor.
Good afternoon. Good to see you both. I am Janet Daby, the Member of Parliament for Lewisham East, and my declarations of interest are on the register.

Good afternoon. I am Warinder Juss, the Member of Parliament for Wolverhampton West. I am a solicitor, although not practising, and a member of the GMB trade union executive council. I am also an officer and member of various APPGs , including the one on penal affairs.
Q97 Thank you. Can I ask you briefly to introduce yourselves and the work of your organisations?

I am Laura Cooper. I am a director of the Youth Justice Legal Centre. I am a specialist youth justice lawyer. The Youth Justice Legal Centre is a centre of excellence and innovation in youth justice, law and practice. We support professionals to get better outcomes for children, with the aim that that benefits the wider community and society.

Hi, everyone. I am Steph Roberts-Bibby. I am the chief exec of the Youth Justice Board. We are an arm’s length body of government, sponsored by the Ministry of Justice. We have a number of statutory functions that come out of the Crime and Disorder Act—namely to provide advice to Ministers on how best to prevent children from offending. We have a number of other functions relating to overseeing the system, exchanging information and publishing data, sharing best practice , and commissioning and undertaking research on the cohort of children in the system.
Q98 Thank you very much. Could you provide an overview of the youth sentencing framework, and explain how it differs from the one that applies to adults?

The sentencing framework is, rightly, intended to be extremely different from the adult framework. It is important to start with the child, and not go to the adult guidelines. A number of guiding principles must be considered and followed in relation to children. There is an entirely different approach. You have to look at a number of different key principles. Under section 37 of the Crime and Disorder Act there is the statutory aim of preventing offending. You must have regard to the welfare of the child and their best interest s , under the UNCRC. Obviously, these are all reflected in the Sentencing Council guidelines for children and young people. There has to be a very individualised approach.
