One would be proper use of titles and n ot allowing regulated professionals under the GMC to call themselves miscellaneous names such as “ cosmetic surgeon ” . You have to stick to your regulated title , and t hat would clear up some misunderstanding from the general public ’s perspective , and t hen there is the consequence.

The second would be if there w ere legislation behind people who act outside their scope of training and practice —f or example if they we re a completely different specialty or not a specialised doctor — then you c ould have a consequence from a licensing perspective. Without legislation to back it, it is going to be very difficult for the GMC to do anything. The latest GMC consultation has suggested removing the specialist register altogether and coming out with something called enhancements to identify a specialist going forward ; none of us is entirely clear what that will mean . It certainly will not help the current situation.

I agree completely with what Nora ha s just said . To your point around whether there will be an underground operation , p robably ; t here will always be people who operate under the radar. The important thing would be that if legislation w ere in place people would have the tools and resources to identify what is and is not illegal. People who are then n amed by these people who may have unknowingly fallen into unsafe hands will have a means to access justice for what they have been through . At the moment there is no justice available to these people.

It is currently not illegal for someone non-medical to inject dermal filler , so it is very hard to get a comeback when you do not have the legislation to back it. While you would probably get an underground industry, at least there w ould be a consequence as opposed to now when there is actually no legal standard to hold them to.
That is an interesting point that will probably shock a lot of people : it is not illegal to perform it.

Q29 It is lovely to meet you both. I do not think I was here at the last session so t his is a whole new world for me and not necessarily in a good way. Thinking about social media and advertising, Ashton said something about irresponsible marketing and advertising. Do you think that social media platforms are doing enough to prevent the promotion of these high-risk cosmetic procedures to under 18s in particular ?

No. Social media companies are wholly to blame really for why these treatments are so popular . There are so many unscrupulous providers operating out there , e specially for younger people whereby social media has become a research tool for these treatments. Because o f that it has trivialised them to the point where they think that they are akin to having your nails done. We did a survey with VICE a few years ago and 41,000 young people responded. Some 59% of those people said that they thought that dermal fillers and Botox were akin to having your nails done and there was no risk involved.

Social media companies enable practitioners to post about Botox and fillers freely. You cannot advertise those treatments via a paid - for post but you can create an organic post without being paid or sponsored and use the word Botox. There are 25 million posts with the hashtag # Botox that they could filter out. They filter out medical and reproductive things such as uterus and periods ; y ou cannot post about that without them filtering it out. Yet you can use the hashtag # Botox and it is ubiquitous. For young people especially it is extremely toxic and dangerous.

It is not just Botox , fillers and all those things ; i t is harmful skincare ingredients that are now being targeted to children as young as eight who are wanting to go out and buy things such as retinols and acids , which are causing damage to their skin. Social media has a lot to answer for .

Ashton has covered the main points , but I would say we are now also seeing AI searches playing into it as well as social media. I would say the vast majority of people start their research by doing an online search or looking on social media. All the findings of a search are subject to what is out there. If what is out there is poor quality then their research is going to be poor quality. That is how people look for things nowadays and how the vast majority of people seeking aesthetic treatment start their research. They start online, whether it is a Google o r AI search or Instagram, Facebook or TikTok , and the glossy platforms with lots of followers draw them in.

It is partly the standard of advertising and partly the use of filters, not standardised photographs. They are not even seeing a true picture of what is being done. It is glamo u rised , and it is as if it is a lunchtime procedure with no downside. There is a way of doing these things educationally and t here is a way that is just pure marketing and exploitation. That is where we are at right now.

Q30 A quick thing that just struck me is that we are talking about effectively invasive procedures , but some are injections and injectables. Injectables generally are becoming a much more common thing across society ; I am not just thinking of weight loss jabs but this very grey and black area around peptides and steroids more generally. That is a cross gender as well. With this big growth and concern around these injectable peptides is there a link between all these things? Is all this being done by the same sets of people or are there different marketplaces for these different types of product s ?

It is part of the same problem , y et by and large it is the same sort of people who are responsible for these things. Social media enables people to set themselves up very quickly and easily as practitioners or sellers of these products and allows them equally to operate like ghosts. You can use spurious names , cause harm, disappear and reappear just as easily as anything else with different, equally spurious names. The amount of fake and unlicensed products — peptides, fat dissolvers, weight loss medications and Botox — that is now being sold and proliferated on social media is unfathomable. They are not doing enough to clamp down on it.

This is a very fast-moving side of medicine. I am calling it medicine deliberately because these are medical products with medical consequences. If we are talking about regulation, there also has to be some c apacity to categorise new developments so that you do not bring out legislation and it is almost immediately out of date. There has to be some mechanism to categorise the procedures so that new procedures that come along would automatically fall under some level or section of the regulation. We have to think about that aspect in terms of bringing in regulation as well : n ot just what is out there now but w hat might come along , its level of invasiveness and risk and who should be doing it.

Q31 That feels as though we are playing catch-up in two worlds that move very quickly : the online world and , from what you are saying, the cosmetic procedures world as well , which is doubly difficult. On that note , ha ve the Government done enough to educate the public about the risks of cosmetic procedures , and particularly the cosmetic tourism that Rosie talked about? If you do not think they have done enough, what more would you like to see them do?

While the Government have done awareness campaigns in the past they have been very fleeting. They tend to be one-off and run for very short periods of time , w hereas this is something that needs an ongoing commitment. For us the biggest frustration is that whenever they are asked to comment on the back of a horror story in the news it is always, “Do your research ; find an appropriate practitioner ,” whereby the public do not know how to do that. If you are sat in front of somebody unscrupulous you can ask all the sensible questions that you want but they will tell you whatever to get your money.

We operate a G overnment -backed, Professional Standards Authority- accredited register whereby we inspect every single practitioner in every single clinic and take them through really robust assessment processes. Therefore I find it unfathomable why the Government do not direct the public to these registers to make safe and informed choices whereby if something go es wrong they have access to redress and complaints processes . For example if they were asked to comment on a gas safety issue, they would not just say , “Find a suitable gas enginee r;” t hey would say , “Go to the Gas Safe Register . ” There are lots of things that they could be doing now that would make such a meaningful and tangible difference to the people seeking these treatments.

I agree with what Ashton has said. In addition , from a cosmetic surgery tourism point of view, we know the countries that are most commonly involved , so t hey could work with the corresponding health and G overnment D epartments in those countries as well. I know there has been work in the past , but I have not heard anything recently about progress. This needs to be something that is ongoing as well as public education. It needs to be multi-pronged and not a one-off campaign. This is something that you have to repeat over and over and over and a lmost have a long-running campaign or just a background constant campaign. One-off campaigns are fine at the time but the impact will wane and it will start up again. It has to be a sustained effort.
Q32 It sounds as though you think there should be more public awareness raising and an ongoing piece of work around that l ed by the Government.
Nora Nugent : Yes
If and when they bring in legislation it is useless without public awareness , so i t would be beneficial for everybody.

Q33 Thank you both for giving your time and expertise today. If the Government were to publish their consultation tomorrow , what are the key changes that they must implement if patient safety is to improve?

From our perspective the urgency around restricting who can and cannot do these high-risk procedures is paramount. Had they listened to our calls for action in 2023, Alice Webb would still be alive. We cannot be in a situation where lay people are able to pick up scalpels and dissect people’s faces in living rooms ; t hat is completely unacceptable and needs to be addressed as a matter of priority.

Ashton i s absolutely right . The two key things are who can do what and where they can do it. It is n ot just about who is doing it but they have to do these procedures in a healthcare facility — whether it is a hospital or clinic depending on the level of procedure — in the right environment and with the right emergency processes and equipment available should the worst happen .

These procedures carry risks in qualified hands as well as unqualified hands. We would hope the risks are lower in qualified hands , and the ability to treat the risk is there as well. You have to be able to plan and be prepared for complications if you are going to do these treatments in the first place. I t is not just about doing the treatment ; i t is about being able to have a backup plan and handle it if something goes wrong , regardless of who is doing it.

The best place to handle a complication is in a healthcare environment, not a beauty salon, hotel room, living room or a random building. You need emergency equipment available for things such as allergic reactions and someone who is able to prescribe for infections or dissolve fillers. All these things need to be in a healthcare environment. It is about w ho is doing it and where they are doing it and making sure that people are not going beyond their knowledge and skill levels.
Q34 Not to necessarily go over anything you have said already , but what would success look like in two years ’ time in an ideal world?
That these procedures are off the high street and in healthcare environments , done by healthcare practitioners.

I sound like a broken record , and I am sure policymakers are sick of me saying this , but f or the last 10 years I have been begging for the establishment of a dedicated taskforce . Oftentimes complaints involving these types of procedures are complex and require input from a vast array of different regulatory authorities, whether that be National Trading Standards , the MHRA, the statutory regulators, the ASA or wh at ever it might be.

Currently these people operate in silos. As I said , they do not take these complaints as seriously as they ought to, which means that current legislation is underpoliced and underenforced. I would like there to be much more accountability around the regulators that are responsible for policing and enforcing this legislation.
Q35 I do not want to end on too negative a note , but on the converse, w hat would concern you most if no legislation were passed before the end of this Parliament ?

That we are still in the same situation and we have another death or more than one death. We have already had one on the non-surgical side and w e have had surgical deaths. How many more do we need? Basically my concern is that the status quo continues.

Exactly that. My fear is that with every day that passes somebody else is going to lose their life at the hands of one of these unscrupulous people. Even in the case of Alice Webb, that police inquiry struggled to bring about charges in a timely fashion because of the lack of legislation surrounding these things.
That is very clear and articulate. Thank you very much indeed.
That concludes the inquiry for today. Thank you both very much for coming along.

sessions.iT: Pre-appointment hearing: Chair of the Care Quality Commission

segs.tx: Health and Social Care Committee
Oral evidence: Pre-appointment hearing: Chair of the Care Quality Commission , HC 656
Wednesday 9 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 9 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Layla Moran (Chair); Danny Beales; Jen Craft; Josh Fenton-Glynn; Andrew George; Joe Robertson.
Questions 1- 5 6
Witness
I : Baroness Julia Neuberger DBE .
Examination of Witness
Witness: Baroness Neuberger.

Q1 Welcome to this one-off session of the Health and Social Care Committee, a pre-appointment hearing for the chair of the Care Quality Commission. It is very much my pleasure to welcome Baroness Julia Neuberger DBE, the Government’s preferred candidate. Thank you so much for joining us this morning.

May I start with a bit of a preface? Ever since this Committee has been meeting, and indeed before that, it is fair to say that the CQC has received significant criticism on its performance. We have had numerous hearings with it over the years, at times feeling slightly more hopeful than not, but I must be honest: I start this appointment hearing feeling relatively down in the dumps about the fact that we have not got further than we have. Could you explain to us and the public why you want to take on this role right now?
You are questioning my sanity, I think.
Maybe.

Okay. Let me start by saying that I am not sure I really wanted it in that sense. I am still, for the next couple of weeks, chairing two NHS trusts: UCLH, which is a foundation trust, and Whittington Health, which is not. I therefore have experience of the CQC from the user end—organisations that are inspected by the CQC—and the experience has been singularly mixed.

The thing I feel most strongly about—this is, I suppose, a public service point—is that we have to have a really effective, trusted and respected regulator in health and social care. It does not have to be loved, but it has to be respected and its inspectors have to be respected. That is not the case at the moment. It is better than it was, I have to say—certainly better than it was a year or 18 months ago—but it still has an awfully long way to go.
Q2 Can you pinpoint how it has lost respect? What is it that you would seek to turn around?

It is not one thing. CQC began not to do nearly enough inspections, so it had a huge backlog, and a huge backlog of registrations as well. Then there was a sense within the service—whether or not it was fair I cannot judge—that it was trying to catch up, so that it was not doing them as thoroughly as it might have. Also, the reports of inspections were coming back incredibly late. People were finding that they got two different judgments at the same time. It just felt chaotic. I think if it feels chaotic, you do not have respect.

But I think it goes deeper than that. I think that is the question you are asking me, but I am not there yet; you will decide whether I will be. However, I think CQC has become quite demoralised as an organisation. Demoralised organisations—I do have experience of those—do not function terribly well and do not have confidence. So when they do an inspection, they do not have the confidence that they might have had if the organisation itself had felt held together—or felt held, actually. That is at the bottom of all the rest of it.

I think losing Julian Hartley very quickly after his appointment was a real problem, and Mike Richards’ resignation was another. CQC felt unstable and the staff felt that they had not had the kind of leadership that would make them feel they were respected by their leaders and were held, while also being told when it is just not up to scratch. That is at the bottom of a lot of it, but the symptoms are delays, inadequate performance and feeling a bit of a mess and a bit sad.

Q3 It is worth saying that many people working in the CQC will be very interested in this hearing. When we criticise, it is not individuals who work below the executive team level that we are aiming at, but it is important that we have a fair and frank discussion about the turnaround. Would you agree that this is a turnaround job?
I think this is a turnaround job, and that is why I want to do it.
Q4 What experience do you have of turning around organisations at this level of turnaround need—to put it mildly—and of size?

Not of its size, but of need, yes. I can give you two examples. I arrived at the King’s Fund as chief executive, not chair, a long time ago—this was 1997—when it had lost a lot of money and had to reduce its size by half. It had to look closely at what its purpose would be. The King’s Fund is a small organisation, and smaller now than it was then, but it did have to be a complete turnaround, and we did it. It got its confidence back and I hope—I think—it did some remarkable things once it had got its confidence back.
Q5 What did you learn from that experience? What will you bring to this turnaround that you learned from that one?

The first thing we need to do is meet the people who work within the organisation and meet the people who are the users of the organisation. There is a huge amount of listening to do. I know that Emily Miles, who is coming in as chief exec, also believes that the first thing we need to do is a huge amount of listening. We need to give the people within the organisation and the people who use it or are inspected by it—and the public, as the public after all have to trust the CQC—the confidence that we are listening and that then we will take some actions.

Many of those actions have actually already been taken. I want to say that Kay Boycott as acting chair, with her team, has done a remarkable job in quite difficult circumstances since Mike and Julian have gone. The performance is significantly better than it was. I have not gone in, but I am told that staff morale is on the up.

Q6 In your replies to our questionnaire, you said that you “ hope to help the CQC get back to that position of trust and respect ” . I worked for another regulator before I came to this place and have been the head of a social care department, so I have been regulated by the CQC. “Trust” and “respect” were not the words that came to my head thinking of the CQC. What are we going to do to get that back?

As I said before, a lot of listening, but also—this is more the chief exec than me—really thinking through how inspections are done, who carries out the inspections and whether we can use more inspectors from different areas across the country, and doing something to make people feel that it is fair. I have a daughter who is a psychiatric social worker, so she too is regulated by the CQC. I think it is that: people need to feel that it is fair. If they feel that it is fair and if they meet the inspectors and have some respect for them, I think you grow the respect.

Q7 From my perspective, looking in from the outside, I noted two problematic things about the CQC. One was the internal relationships and internal structures; the other was how it interacted with those it regulates. I would posit that the former is quite tricky to deal with, but is much more within your gift than the latter. You talked about transparency. What else might you be able to do to build confidence with those you regulate?

I think it is about the nature of the inspections. You have been inspected. I have not yet been out on an inspection, but that is one of the things I will do. You do not have to be there for the whole inspection, but you have to see it in progress. I have only been on the other side.
Q8 How did you find being on the other side?

I was not directly in the room on the other side. In fact, UCLH is being inspected at the moment and I am recusing myself for obvious reasons, which is a bit of a shame; I would have quite liked to be on the other side, but I do not think it is right. From what I hear, it is mixed. You have a combination of people saying that they had a very good discussion with inspectors and, while I would not say it was a benign process, that it felt like a fair process.
Q9 I imagine that it is a collaborative process at its best.
Yes. It was collaborative trying to find things out. Then you get the report and can send back things that you do not think are right, and all of that. That feels quite positive.

Equally, I have heard of the CQC picking up on something very minor but missing something very major, including—this applies to the internal stuff within the CQC—where the atmosphere in a particular department is quite tricky or even hostile.

Q10 Any inspector will have trouble with those they inspect, because there is a lot of anxiety. You will have seen that the Government have done quite a lot to change the way Ofsted works, because of the detrimental impact it was having on headteachers and so forth. One thing it did was move away from the single-word assessments of schools. Does it make sense from a policy point of view that, at the same time that Ofsted moved away from single-word assessments because it did not think they properly summarised what a department or school was like, the CQC moved in the opposite direction and brought in a single assessment framework for local authorities?

I do not think I can comment on that yet. However, I have to declare that my son is a headteacher regulated by Ofsted, so I hear quite a lot about Ofsted. I need to look at how it works before I can comment on that. In plain policy terms it looks a bit odd, but I would have to look at it. I cannot comment on that yet.

Q11 One thing the Dash review found was that there is limited information available for providers and users, so they do not know what good care looks like under all the ratings. You have had so many roles around health and care. Can you say at this point, going in with confidence, that you know what good care looks like and what the different ratings would look like?

I cannot say that I know with confidence exactly what they would look like. I think I know from experience of chairing health organisations that you can feel what a good institution feels like. Sometimes people say—I think I even share this view, and it is certainly true in social care—that you can do it by smell. I know that sounds absurd, but it is true.
I know. I have walked into care homes when I was a cabinet member for social care in my authority.

There are various things that you get a sense of. For example, you get a sense of the confidence of staff to speak out. Those things are part of what good looks like, but I cannot say, “This is good. This requires improvement.” I need to look at that in much greater detail with the new chief exec. We will do some thinking about that, but the first thing I want to do is restore some confidence.
Q12 Do you think it is altogether obvious enough to the public what the different ratings will look like?

The public find it easier to understand the single assessment rating than people working in the service, because the closer you are to something, the more nuanced it always is. The public probably does not have as much of a problem with “good” or “requires improvement” as we do.

Q13 We have talked about the complexity of turning around the organisation, which has seemed in freefall , and the length of time that might take. You mentioned the conveyor belt of leadership , which has been destabilising. It all points to the need for stability and long-term effort. How long do you envision th at task tak ing ? How long do you envisage yourself in the role of chair? Is it the length of time needed ? Do you have t he ability to commit t o it?

I am old, so I will clearly not do it forever, nor do you expect me to. We will know whether we are on the right track within a year, and I would commit to doing at least one term. By then, I will be really quite old, and I had always thought that I would be out before I was 80. That probably remains the case, but let us see. We will know within a year whether it has stabilised, and its performance has considerably improved, which it is already doing, so that is quite important.
Q14 Are you indicating that a year is a check-in point for you or the executive team?
For everybody. For you, for that matter.
Q15 Do you think that 12 months and then potentially further change is helpful?

I do not think it requires further change—I would rather hope not—but you can get a sense within an organisation if it is going in the right direction, usually within 12 months. It might be 18, but it would be that kind of time. It takes a long time for staff to feel really confident in leadership, and they need to do that to do their job better. That will help confidence in the regulated community and will ultimately increase public confidence, I hope, but I would have thought we would know the direction of travel within a year.

Q16 There is an old adage that you need to give a new football manager some time; you might lose a few games initially, and it might not be the best first season. For people in business and MPs, it takes a year to get to know just the fundamentals of an organisation—the rules, the business and compliance practices. Is it realistic to expect to see the organisational change in a year, bearing in mind the journey it has gone through? To challenge you again, does a leadership team or an executive team not need a significant number of years to turn it around from where it is to being—not to avoid a single-word judgment—a good organisation?

I did not say it would be a good organisation within a year . I said that within a year you would be able to feel whether the direction of travel was going the right way. I cannot do the football analogy because I am no good on the football stuff, and I still get lost in the House of Lords even though I have been there over 20 years . I absolutely accept that it takes ages , but when people start to feel better about the feel of an organisation, you can tell , and you can then say, “ It ’ s going to take us another two, three, four , five years to become the good or the excellent organisation. ” You can talk to school s’ leadership about that as well , but you do know quite quickly whether it is feeling better. You can feel it in your fingertips before the performance indicators show you.

Q17 I agree on holding the senior leadership team to account to deliver that journey of change over five years . My challenge to you is whether you are committing to do that over that period of time? From a board and governance perspective, having constant change in the chair and the board can undermine holding the executive team to account on deliver y .

Baroness Neuberger : I completely agree . I will definitely do one term. I will be quite old , as I said. The point is, how much longer would they want with the old bat , and how much longer would it be useful for me to do the job ? I will definitely do one term , and if it seems right, I will continue , let us say for a year or two, but I do not think it is right to be in a position where they want you to go . I have been extended twice at UCL H; they have wanted me to stay. I have got to go now. I do agree with you that stability is good for an organisation. Stability of leadership is good for an organisation , so I would definitely give it three years whatever happened .
Q18 Who tapped you on the shoulder to do this?
The Department.
Q19 Who?
The permanent secretary.
Q20 Okay. Did you know the perm sec before?
Very slightly. I had met her once.
Q21 What was the approach? What did she say to butter you up?
Let me say that I did not say yes first time.

Q22 The delay of four months in the recruitment of the chief exec in particular, has been pretty appalling. Did you discuss that with the Department? Are you any the wiser as to why they could not sign off any recruitment ?
I have not discussed that in detail, but I was involved at that stage as an independent i n the appointment of Emily.
Q23 So you have met Emily Miles?
Not yet. In fact, we are going to have a coffee after this. But I was on her appointment panel.
Q24 I understand. Did you know her from before?
No.
Q25 Okay. What is your style of chairing? Are you a very involved chair? Are you a daily check-in kind of chair, or are you a hands-off come-to-me-if-you-have-a-problem chair?
Not quite any of those, really.
Q26 Those are the two extremes. You are welcome to land yourself on the spectrum.

I think I am quite collaborative. I have always had in any organisation I have chaired , or the other way round when I have been the chief exec and I have had a chair , a very good working relationship with the chair , or the chief exe c—whichever it happens to be . In some cases , they have become my friends after I have no longer been in the position. I do not think you want to have a close friendship because it is a working relationship where you are holding somebody to account.

I am very collaborative. I like chairing organisations. I like pulling a team of directors together. I like the feeling that you make decisions together, but then different members of the board actually carry them out or are responsible for ensuring that they are carried out. I suppose I try to be a kind of supportive friend to the organisation as chair. In my time as chair of the two NHS trusts, I do a lot of walking around and meeting staff, and I think that is quite valuable so that they feel that , should they need to, they can come and talk to me and I have an open door.

Q27 How far into the weeds of the detail do you like to get? I ask because this is not a full-time role. It is more or less a half-time role. Do you think that will be enough time, given that you do not have regulatory experience and you will have a lot to learn? How are you going to balance the fact that, at the beginning, maybe it will not be a half-time role?

It won’t be half-time at the beginning, clearly. Apart from anything else, if you are going to go around and meet people and talk to them, although there is a lot of remote working and a lot will be online, it will not be half-time at the beginning. It will be probably quite a lot less as it goes on, but it will not be half-time at the beginning. I am well aware of that and up for it because this really needs to be done. We really must have a regulator that works and is respected. I would expect to do three and a half or four days, certainly at the beginning. I would expect to work very closely with the chief exec at the beginning and work out who is going to do what, how much we are doing together, how much we do separately and all of that. I think it will be a lot of time at the beginning. I am sure that Kay Boycott, who has been acting as chair, has been doing more than two and a half or three days a week.

Q28 I would like to put a challenge to you, if I may, and invite a response. In your questionnaire, and indeed in the session today, you have effectively acknowledged that you have relatively little regulatory experience. Does that present a problem? If so, how are you addressing it?

I don’t think it presents a problem, as such. I will learn. I think you can learn that quite quickly. The chief exec is a regulator, so I come, if you like, with the service experience and she comes with the regulatory experience. That should be quite a good match, actually. Of course I will learn. My last proper regulatory experience was in the GMC very many years ago. Regulating doctors individually is very different from what the CQC does, but I have been within the service and know a fair bit. I have also seen quite a lot of regulation within the care sector. Seeing it from the other end helps you to understand a bit of how it works. I will have to learn the detail and technicalities of regulation, but that should be all right.

Q29 Are there any other gaps that would require you to do some learning—potentially even some gaps that are not covered by the combination of you and the chief executive? Are there any other areas that you would like to reflect on?

There are some things the CQC absolutely needs, like a really good IT system. I have not talked to Emily about this, so I do not know what her expertise in IT is, but mine is not great. We will need to have serious expertise in IT on the board and we need to think about that very hard. That is particularly true with AI and all the things that are happening there. We need somebody on the board who is absolutely up to speed in all that. Emily and I, and the board as we have it now, do not have all the expertise that we would need.

Q30 Finally, social care and the vital role that local authorities play in it is often treated as second class to NHS and healthcare across the whole sphere of policymaking and spending. Do you see any issues within the way the CQC operates that fail to elevate the importance given to social care and the way it is regulated?

I am not inside the organisation yet, so there are some things that I cannot comment on, but oddly enough, most people I have talked to externally find the inspection in the social care area more satisfactory than in the health area. That part of the work seems to have greater trust. Although I think quite a lot of social care providers find it quite irritating, there is quite a lot of respect there. By the way, I ought to say that wearing a different hat—a private hat—I am quite involved in some work to up the status of care workers within the social care sector. I am a trustee of the Rayne Foundation, and we are doing this thing called “Better Careers for Better Care”, which I am deeply involved in. I see quite a lot of social care at the moment. I will stop doing that in December anyway.
Q31 W e briefly touched on the Dash review , but I wanted to bring you back to the Dash and Richards review s . What lessons do you take from them?

Both were pretty thorough looks. Of course, the Richards review was done before he became chair . I ought to say that Mike Richards is one of my closest friends —he is a very old friend ; w e go back to our student days. W hat would I say? W hat you learn is that when an outsider who is not a complete outsider looks at an organisation, they can identify some things that people within the organisation do not seem to be able to see — I think that is often the case, by the way. In both cases , they did some very useful things on detail but a s I said before , I cannot comment yet . O n the HSSIB point, which I think that you very much take to heart , w ould I have started from here? No. I don’t think that I would necessarily have gone with the recommendation of HSSIB going into the CQC, but that is where we are.
We might come to that.
Yes, we are going to come to that.

T hat recommendation comes out o f t he D ash review, which is one of the reasons why I raise it now. I think that you look at the review and what you can learn from it. Did they spot things that the organisation itself cannot spot? Y es, almost certainly so. What do you do with it? I am very happy to talk further about HSSIB.
Q32 You are right, it identifies quite a lot of significant issues. Do you come away from them with any sense of priority? Do you think, “I must do this on day one. This is top of my list ”?

Not from the reviews. I think it is much more from what I have learned from being in two health organisations, and from talking to people in care organisations, which I ha ve been doing quite a lot because of the Rayne Foundation work . It is much more from the people that have experienced inspection and also from the public and publicity generally about the CQC and inspection and standards.

Q33 I know we will come to that issue in a bit, but there has been a widening of scope of the role of CQC at the same time as existing challenges in delivering its responsibilities. Do y ou have a sense of where the balance and priority should be ? Should it be doing new things better or focusing on the fundamentals of the existing responsibilities and backlogs?

Of course you have to do that. You must get the basics right before you can take on the new, in my view. Wes Streeting, when he was Secretary of State , said that that the CQC would not be taking on HSSIB until it was r eady . I agree ; I think that is right. There is a difficult point in judging when that time is right — that is the point that that you made —b ut as I said before, I think you can sense the direction of travel within a year.

A ssuming that the legislation goes through and the decision remains that HSSIB goes into the CQC, we would make it work . B ut I would hope that the C QC would be given enough time under m ine and Emily’s leadership to stabilise the ship and to get those basics , as you describe them , right and begin to get the respect back. I am thinking about the early days of the C QC and when Mike Richards was chief inspector of hospitals. The CQC was very much respected. It was somewhat feared, but it was very much respected , and I want to get that back.

Q34 I think it has been said that the C QC is “ not fit for purpose ”—t hose words have been used. A re you confident that it can be saved and that i t can be turned around and be a respected, well-performing organisation ?

I think so. I am not inside, and I will very deliberately not be inside until you confirm me or otherwise. Do I think that it can be turned around? Yes. The evidence is that its performance is getting better. Kay and Arun have provided that leadership. The team have provided that leadership and we can see performance improving. Do I think it is possible? Almost certainly yes. I will be able to tell you a bit more when I am there. But do I think it is possible? Yes. It is going to be quite a big job though.

Q35 As well as providing assurance about the quality of care, there are, unfortunately, instances of quite serious failure of providers of different sorts. Unfortunately, we have seen them far too frequently. The Committee is looking at St Andrews in relation to mental health. I think we are going to come to maternity later . There will be more questions specifically about that. Does it worry you that in all of those instances the CQC has actually been there at different points? People have been harmed. There has been serious failure.
Yes. Of course.

Q36 What do you think the CQC’s role in action should be? How quickly should it act? Should there be quicker intervention from the regulatory state when concerns like this are evident? In a number of instances, it feels that it is many years before national inquiries are eventually called, but the regulators, the people who should be assuring people’s safety, have often been there right from the start.

I agree. I expect a regulator to flag stuff up. You are not always going to be able to do it. Obviously, regulators are not always going to see where there are problems. Very often you need an inquiry for a particular thing, but if the regulator has found things that are of serious concern, I would expect that to be flagged quite quickly.

Q37 You said that you believe there are signs of improvement. On culture specifically, I think recent surveys have indicated a decline in staff confidence. That might not fully reflect more recent leadership changes due to time periods and lagging, but it identified concern about being supported by leaders and not being listened to enough. You talked a lot about listening being a priority and concerns not being acted on. What is your view of the organisational culture and staff morale?

I am not there yet, but from what I hear it has been quite low. I suspect that there is probably a bit of a lag with the staff survey, but that is one of the first things I would want to address with Emily. You need to have staff morale up to get the confidence back. It is absolutely essential.
Q38 Are there particular actions that can be taken to do that?

The first action is simply to get to know people. I know that sounds ridiculous, but it is true. One of the things that I have done a lot of in my time chairing both NHS organisations is going to see people at work and also saying thank you a lot. Some of those things are quite basic, and I suspect we need to do quite a lot of that.
Q39 Do you think the previous chair and board or leadership team were not doing that? They were not saying thank you.

I think they probably were, but it all felt chaotic and then Julian left very quickly. Do not forget that Julian Hartley instituted quite a lot of changes, brought a lot of people in and then left very suddenly. That is really hard for an organisation. They do not feel held any more. I think the fact that Emily and I will come in at roughly the same time—I am a couple of weeks earlier—is quite helpful. We will both be there and both be listening. We will probably listen in different ways and speak to different people, but we will both be there. That is quite important.
Q40 Finally, how will you know when the organisation’s culture has changed? How will you be confident that the morale and confidence has turned around?

As I said, you can feel quite a lot of it. Of course, there is the staff survey, although it will lag. At UCLH, we always do incredibly well in the staff survey, and that tells you something about the culture of the organisation. T hat is important. I believe that organisations function well when staff feel supported and feel you are fair. Sometimes you will not necessarily agree with them or you will think that some people are not doing a particularly good job — but you will be fair.

Q41 In answer to that last question , you referred again to your emphasis on feeling —the feel matters, and you can smell whether an organisation is up to scratch. Is there not a risk that, without some objective means of measuring that, you fall into using the mores and metropolitan club b ability of the people you meet? You talk about your friendship with Mike Richards . I s there not a risk that you are working within a bubble of smell and feel , and are not sufficiently self-reflective to see what is really going on ?

No, I do n’t think I am saying that. Y ou need the rigour of metrics. T he staff survey is one way of getting a metric on how the staff are feeling. But, as I said, there is a lag, so you can usually pick up a change before you can see it in the metrics. Equally, with a hospital or care home, the inspection inspects against standards, which are objective , so y ou can tell the direction of travel from that. But again, you can usually g et the feel of it before you get the metric. That is all I am saying. On the metropolitan bubble , it is probably fair to say that, although Mike Richards is one of my closest friends, I do not think that he thought it was a great idea to become chair of the CQC. I am not sure it was a wholly happy experience for him. I am doing it because it needs to be done .

Can I offer another smell or feel, which is on the ground where I live and operate in w est Cornwall ? P eople there do not feel confident that the CQC is doing its job or undertaking sufficient inspections . The impression is that if people are going looking for a suitable care home for their loved one, they have no confidence that the CQC has provided them with satisfactory information. T he smell and feel out there is not a good one, whereas you are getting the impression that it is improving.

No, not yet, but I am getting the impression— which may be wrong—that there is less dissatisfaction with the inspection regime on the social care side than on the health one . That is all I am saying. I f there is dissatisfaction with how the CQC inspects care homes, that is something we should take extremely seriously. A ssuming I am in post, along with Emily and the people in charge of inspection of social care, I will look at that. I do not think I would take anything for granted.

Q42 On Emily—who I am aware is present—there has been some observation that she does not come from a health and social care background ; I think she currently holds a DEFRA role. How confident are you that it is appropriate to have a chief executive without that background experience? D o you think that she can realistically get up to speed with the nature and complexity of the sector in which she will be asked to operate?

Yes, I think she can. She is a regulator, which I think we absolutely need , and she has experience of that, and I come with the health and social care experience. We also have a board with health and social care experience—actually, it is a board that does not have enough regulatory experience, in my view. The board has quite a lot of health and social care expertise, and specific individuals who are the leaders for particular areas of inspection and who are experts themselves. I think that is fine.

Q43 Returning to the subject of HSSIB, which you raised, and the appropriateness of bringing an investigatory body into a regulatory body, that merger has been subject to significant comment and criticism. HSSIB is admittedly a relatively young organisation, but it has a good reputation and is much admired by people within the sector as a harbour to which they can report matters of concern. How satisfied are you, looking at it as someone coming in from the outside, that it is a wise move to take that risk?
Would I have done it in the first place? No, but we are where we are and so we will make it work.
Q44 The Lords could still save us if they chose to.
I cannot comment on that, can I?
Maybe they will .

Yes, but let me say, assuming that it goes ahead, which to be honest is probably likely, we would have to make it work. That means having Chinese walls and making sure that the CQC is itself in a better place than it is now before it happens. That is all I can say.

To me, it seems that they are different kinds of bodies . In that sense, would I necessarily have done it? No. But that is the Government ’s decision and if that is what happens, the CQC will make it work. But I think we would want some time before that even happened.
Q45 I am encouraged by the approach that you are taking, and I would not necessarily say that you should express the view publicly in more trenchant terms, although I would like it.
We are in public.

We are, absolutely. Do you not think that it is appropriate that, on coming in, you should be able to express your view very bluntly to the new Secretary of State and that where you feel uncomfortable about such a merger, that view should pertain as well, even during the passage of the Health Bill?
I could not possibly comment, but I am talking to the Secretary of State.

Q46 That is very helpful. You talk about Chinese walls, but there is also the risk of Chinese whispers. The problem that a lot of those in the sector are worried about is that HSSIB provides a safe space for clinicians to raise concerns without fear of getting into complex litigation. That seems to be a very attractive option and one that would advance patient safety. I cannot believe that those within the CQC would be prepared to take the risk of going into a world where there is a lot of uncertainty about whether it is going to work through the merger.

To some extent, they may have to, so let us see where that goes. Assuming I do this role, I am happy to come back when we know exactly how it is going to work. I think I agree with you; it is the safe space bit and how you keep that completely separate that bothers me. I think we would make it work, but as an outsider at this stage, I cannot say exactly how. That is something that Emily and I will want to talk about very quickly along with Kay.

Q47 I would like to turn to maternity services. Y ou will be aware that Baroness Amos told this Committee that in her review of maternity services , she found “ significant regional variation in the way that the CQC operates ” and often “ insufficient expertise ” to adequately inspect maternity services. W hat steps will you take to make sure that the organisation is able and has the right expertise in place to regulate these vital services? C rucially , how will you make sure that the public have confidence in the CQC’s ability to do so?

Let me say that what has been going on with maternity is one of the reasons that convinced me in the end to say yes , b ecause I am so worried about it. I am d eeply concerned about what Baroness Amos has said, what Donna Ockenden has said and what we are hearing. V ery early on, I want to sit down with Emily and the team and look at that in great detail.

I suspect — but I may not be right —that if you looked at other areas of practice, you would also find situations where there was no t adequate expertise always among the inspectors. T hat is something that we need to look at very closely and work out how we make sure that there is adequate expertise and that the group being regulated — the maternity department, wherever they happen to be — feels that that is being done fairly.

The other thing that is happening at the moment — I speak as the chair of two providers — is that the maternity departments themselves are now incredibly worried , scared and all over the place, and midwives particularly. It is becoming increasingly difficult to recruit midwives. It is a huge issue . We have to look at how maternity is regulated, but we have to look at how everything is regulated , look at the expertise and then make sure that those who are being regulated feel that it is — that awful phrase — firm but fair. T hen I think the public will begin to get their confidence back , but we will look at it very quickly.

Q48 I know that you are still an outsider. Do you think there is potentially a cultural issue in the way that inspections are carried out? Do you think inspectors have the right frame of mind as to why they are there and what they are doing? For example, in adult social care, care agencies can be inspected and given a rating by the CQC without anyone actually ever visiting any of the sites in which they operate. I am confused as to how you would be able to visit a nondescript office , carry out an inspection and say, “T his care agency is good ,” or even more. Do you think there is an issue in the way that those inspections are carried out , and d o you think the inspectors themselves have the right attitude and understand what they are there to do and why ?

I am not there, as you rightly said. I suspect people would not be inspectors unless they had the right attitude and the right underpinning desire to make sure it is working well and , to some extent , to make sure it improves.

But there is something that worries me considerably , a nd that is the extent to which the user voice is heard . That is a much more general point than about the CQC . I started in all of this as chair of the Patients Association a million years ago. I do not think the CQC is good enough at listening to the user voice. In maternity , the sort of thing that you might expect is scanning Mumsnet or something like that. Y ou would expect more of a scanning of what is going on outside, to inform the culture of inspection. That is one thing.
T he other thing is that I think there is a general lack of user voice . I n fact, in terms of social care, often it is family and carer voice. T hat is something that needs to be looked at.

Q49 Thank you ; that is really helpful. Just to clarify, is it currently the case that a maternity unit would be able to get a “ good ” overall rating if they were rated as “ require s improvement ” on safety ?
I cannot comment on that. I am not aware that it is, but it may be. I do not think so.

Q50 For context , t hat came from my trust. Oxford University H ospitals trust’s maternity unit became part of the Amos review because there were a large number of failures . V ocal groups had written to the CQC over a number of years with their personal stories and nothing happened .
T he personal stories that are not being taken seriously is the bit that worries me .
T hey will have been heartened to hear about your approach.

Q51 In terms of putting the user voice front and centr e, how would you look to do tha t? How would you make sure that everyone who works for the CQC is a ware that that has to be part of their focus , as well as everything else that they are looking at ?
That is part of the culture change, and it is part of the leadership that I would hope that Emily and I would provide.

Q52 I am very grateful for your answers on maternity in particular. The lag between inspections was something else that came out of our experience in Oxford. The unit was rated as “ requires improvement ”. It made improvements quite rapidly , but then there was no planned reinspection for a very long time. Meanwhile, the community was saying , “It’s not safe to have your baby there. ” I had to beg by all means possible for the CQC to come to r einspect , and now the unit is “ good ” again , but the parents point out that there are still some concerns around safety , so I urge you to look at that. I know that that is reflected in other areas , where too often the CQC is too late ; t he trusts have already identified problems —in fact, NHS England quite often comes in to sort it out — and then a year later the CQC comes to inspect. H ow do you intend to sort out those sorts of issues? D o you recognise what I am saying ?

I absolutely recognise what you are saying. I come from the provider side —I a bsolutely r ecognise what you are saying, but the detail of how we try to sort that out is not for me to comment on yet. That is something that Emily and I and the team will talk about, but I completely agree.
Q53 O bviously , this role is not just chairing the CQC ; it is also co-chair ing the beefed - up n ational q uality b oard. Do you know Penny Dash ? Have you worked with her before?
I know her very slightly.

Q54 In this broader landscape , where do you see the role of the CQC? You have read the D ash review, but you are the chair of a provider. What role could the CQC play now , but also in a future where it is up and running properly , in that safety and quality landscape?

If we got it completely right , and that will take some time , it could provide a lot of the assurance to the system more widely — the quality board a nd beyond — that t here is proper inspection , that issues that are flagged are dealt with, that the public are listened to and their concerns are acted upon , a nd that it ultimately has the confidence of both the broader sector of health and social care and the public. T o some extent, it would be the provider arm of quality assurance for the quality board. That is how I assume it would work a t best . I t is going to take quite a while to get there, but that is what I think it should do.
Q55 S econd to last , I just need to ask , beyond what you have told us on your questionnaire, are there any other conflicts of interest that are important for us to know about?
Not that I can think of , otherwise I would have put them down.
Q56 Fair enough —t hat is what we assumed , b ut it is worth asking , just in case another had emerged in between.

This is my final question . You have mentioned a year a number of times and have said that we will be seeing significant progress in a year’s time . L et ’ s fast - forward , and I appreciate that you are not there, but play with me. I f we were to have a session like this in a year’s time , maybe also with Emily, what sort of metrics should we be looking at to start to see that success? What would you hope to be able to bring to our Committee to show that that direction of travel is not just starting, but starting to take hold in the organisation ?

I would hope that you would see the improved performance that you are already seeing vastly increased. I would hope that you would see a staff survey that is considerably improved, although , given the lag, that may be more difficult. I would hope that you would hear less concern from the public, although again, there will be a lag in that. I hope you would hear from provider organisations —a nd we would probably want to measure that in some way —t hat they are more content with both the frequency and the manner of inspection. I would have thought that you could measure some of that within the year.
Let’s see . M aybe we shall have you back , b ut for now, that brings us to the end of our questions. T hank you for joining the Committee this morning. We must now be left to d eliberate.
