John Slinger made representations.

Q18 Next up is John Slinger, applying for a debate on a subject in which we all have a vested interest: the role of an MP. It is a request for a Westminster Hall debate on either a Tuesday or a Thursday.

It is good to be back before this Committee. I seek this debate because I regard the role of an MP as absolutely critical to our democracy. I will talk you through the reasoning. The role has evolved organically over time. It has never been truly gripped, defined or properly assessed in this place, though it has been outside, and as far as I can tell there have been no debates on the role of an MP. There are strengths to that organic growth and some deficiencies, including there being no job description— [ Laughter. ] I note the laughter of hon. Members.

Each MP determines the role as best they can. The public often do not understand our role—how could they—nor do organisations. Nor, quite often, do we. Certainly I do not understand it on occasion. As hon. Members will know, we are under no obligation to ever visit our constituency—although I live in mine so I visit it every week—nor to come to this House, save to swear the oath of allegiance. That is frankly preposterous, I think we can all agree.

There is a grey area both nationally and locally: there are very few formal powers and they apply pretty much only nationally. They are the legislative powers to vote on and to amend legislation, and the powers to question Ministers, to initiate debates or to scrutinise. Of course, we have immense power at certain moments. We may have noticed that when we—those of us in the PLP, at least—determined who the Prime Minister is. That is an enormous power and privilege but the other powers are heavily constrained by whipping.

Locally, no public or private organisation that provides services to our constituents is under any statutory obligation ever to meet us, consult us or respond to us. Of course, they do because they know our status but they are not under any obligation—not even councils are; it is incredible. We have no formal executive power locally to direct policy; we have no resources. Local councillors, for example, do have resources to deploy on issues that they care about. In my area, Rugby borough council is just about to bring in a £3,000 fund for each councillor and councillors on Warwickshire county council each have £8,000 per year to distribute to good causes and to make things happen in their constituency. We have the power of influence, convening, writing, talking and cajoling and that is not insignificant, but it is not enough. That is within the context that we face, which is vital.

If we look at local Government reorganisation and devolution, we are seen as the most senior politician in our areas and yet we hear little else of metro mayors in the current debate. People assume that we have the power and the budget to deploy locally when we know that we do not. People assume that we can improve their area and local services. Of course we can, but the route to doing so is of course highly complex.

As Members of Parliament we end up being held accountable for almost everything that happens in our area. We pick up the pieces of often broken or failing local and national public services, and much more besides. Of course, if I could be so bold, due to our nature as democratically elected politicians, we are incentivised to maximise the appearance of power and minimise the absence of it, which is slightly ironic.

I am seeking a debate to discuss this perhaps most vital role in our democracy, and most importantly to give hon. Members across the House the opportunity to make their suggestions and discuss these issues. They can take it wherever they want: they can talk about the logistics of being an MP, our formal powers, our informal powers and the support we receive; maybe even pay and our package, security and the wider context, as I have mentioned. I want the debate to be about not complaints or moaning but improving the situation, focused on solutions and constructive ideas.

MPs are vital to our democracy, and I believe that our status, power and authority need to be enhanced—not for our benefit, but for the benefit of our constituents and the democracy of this country. MPs must have more opportunities to speak out, and I want this debate to be part of a much wider discussion here in this place, among the various Committees, with academia and others, about revitalising our democracy. Rewiring the state must include improving and revising the role, status and powers of MPs. When I mentioned my application to colleagues, they were very interested. I think the debate would be well supported from across the House, and it is an important and timely one.

Thank you. I would add to your observations that, for those of us who have served in executive roles in local authorities, becoming an MP changes your position from one of making decisions that affect people in the places they live to one of, “Can I bring influence to bear to make a decision?”. It is very frustrating, I agree.
Q19 Thank you for bringing this debate forward, John. Would you want it to coincide with any particular time, or to happen as soon as possible?
As soon as possible, Will—I am not supposed to call you Will, am I?
I called you John, so I started it.
Thank you, Will.
Any other questions? I think we all have an interest in this.

Q20 I do. Thank you for bringing this application, John. I describe myself as a combination of the Terminator and a fairy godmother. That is how I think my constituents see me, but of course, as you say, the reality is completely different. I cannot believe that we have never debated this—is that right, Chair, to your knowledge?
We did check, and I did not find anything, although there may have been some debates that I have not found.
I am sure that if it is accepted, it will be oversubscribed, because you know we MPs love talking about ourselves!

There probably were discussions about this during the expenses scandals, when IPSA was set up, because there is obviously a rationale for that. The Standards Commissioner clearly has an interest in this—as we know, he tried to inflict certain things on MPs—and I think IPSA would have a say on what happens. But you are absolutely right: we have no contract of employment; we have no job description; we set up a small business; we employ our staff, albeit to contracts and within a budget; and there are examples of people who arrived in this place and sworn their oath of allegiance, but who have never been to their constituency or done anything for their constituents, and somehow they managed to get re-elected.
It is extraordinary.
It is. Anyway, the Clerks will be in touch with you in due course about a potential date. Thank you, John.
Liz Jarvis made representations.

Q21 Our final application is from Liz Jarvis. It is an application for a Tuesday morning Westminster Hall debate on improving post-diagnostic support for people living with dementia. Liz, please present your case.
Or a Tuesday afternoon.
We get to allocate only Tuesday mornings and Thursday afternoons in Westminster Hall.
Okay. I am sure that many of us have been impacted by dementia or will know constituents who have been impacted by dementia.

Without wishing to bring everybody down, one in three of us will develop dementia. It is obviously the defining health and social care challenge of our time. Later this year the Government’s modern service framework for frailty and dementia and the first publication of the Casey commission is expected. This would be a timely debate looking at what happens after diagnosis. At the moment, in far too many cases, people are told that they have dementia, and then they get sent home and are left to get on with it. They have to do their own research and find out about everything themselves. However, research shows that if properly supported, they can live a reasonably productive and active life for as long as possible. That is really important.

This debate has cross-party support and would give Members the chance to talk about experiences in their constituencies and to put the case forward for ensuring that everybody in the UK has access to the post-diagnostic support that they need.
Thank you.
Q22 Thank you for bringing this application, Liz. Would you consider a debate on a Thursday in Westminster Hall in order for it to happen in October or November as requested?
Yes, we would consider it, but the ideal would obviously not be either of those.
Q23 But you would consider it?
We would.
Q24 What would be the answering Department? Is it Health and Social Care or is there a different Department?
It is Health and Social Care. I am trying to think who the Minister is now because the last time I spoke about dementia it was Stephen Kinnock, but it is not him anymore.
They have all changed.
Yes.

The only reason I ask is that because if it is a Tuesday morning it has to fit within when Health and Social Care are answering. Thursday afternoon is different and anyone can answer; it is basically a free for all.
Thank you very much. The Clerks will be in touch with you shortly.

Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Grace Carrington and Dr Rakib Ehsan.

Q1 Good morning. In this session of the Foreign Affairs Committee , we will look at the forthcoming Commonwealth H eads of Government meeting in November. I should start by saying that I am in the C hair today because our C hair, Emily Thornberry, is unable to be with us . O ne of our previously advertised witnesses, Professor Onslow, is also unable to be here. I welcome our two witnesses on the first panel . Will they introduce themselves?

I am Grace Carrington, an honorary research fellow at the UCL Institute of the Americas. I specialise in politics and decolonisation in the Caribbean. My last book looked at non-independent states, including the British overseas territories . M y current book project looks more at the relationship with the monarchy, campaigns for republics and debates around reparations in the Caribbean.

My name is Dr Rakib Ehsan . I am a senior fellow at the Policy Exchange think - tank. I was the author of the Policy Exchange report , “ One Family : Harnessing the Strategic Potential of the Commonwealth ” .
Q2 Can I start with the obvious question : does the Commonwealth still matter? Is it still something we should devote attention to? D oes it still have a relevance in today ’ s world?

I n my view, in recent times , the Commonwealth has drifted to the margins of international relations. There is a growing foreign policy tendency in the UK to say that the Commonwealth is somewhat outdated , irrelevant and not necessarily an international arena where British national interests can be amplified

The big thing with the “O ne F amily ” report I authored for Policy E xchange was that it dismissed that view ; rather, it offer ed a blueprint for providing the Commonwealth with a renewed sense of purpose and for the UK playing a leadership role in that. I certainly think that it will be able to achieve that in certain areas, especially educational co - operation. E nvironmental sustainability is a big area, especially when we are looking at small state development across the Commonwealth.

But t hose are the softer , comfort - zone policy areas —t he one thing I really wanted to achieve with the report is to say that we need a Commonwealth that has more teet h. We suggested the creation of a security and defence co - operation forum within the Commonwealth . T hat would help to support member states , such as Guyana, which in my view has faced considerable political aggression from neighbouring Venezuela, especially over the oil - rich Essequibo region. W e are talking about the idea of member states having the potential to have collective military exercises and increased naval co - operation.

T here are certain areas where we traditionally look at traditional alliances, such as NATO , b ut if the Commonwealth wants to have increased relevance within the international system, that will be very difficult to achieve without deepening co - operation between member states, especially in the areas of security and defence.

That is not just about military and naval co-operation; it is also about looking at what forms of modern co - operation we can have, especially in terms of cyber - security. M ember states such as Namibia, Cameroon and Tanzania are exceptionally vulnerable and have very weak cyber - security infrastructure , and t he UK has a sophisticated, Commonwealth - leading cyber - security capability. We are not just looking at those traditional military and naval alliances ; we are also looking to deepen cyber - security . That is essential if we want to allow underdeveloped countries across the Commonwealth to grow and prosper over time.

I agree. A real challenge is to make sure that the Commonwealth seems relevant to the 21st century. The imperial legacies are something that could pose a challenge to making it seem like a modern partnership for the modern age. The UK has a key role: if the UK approaches the Commonwealth from the perspective of leadership, the issue is that that seems much more like the traditional dynamics, whereas if the UK approaches the Commonwealth from the perspective of partnership, collaboration and coalition building, the scope is for a much more modern partnership, with the UK reinforcing that.

One key opportunity for the Commonwealth is to do with climate, coalition building on climate issues and the environment, particularly given the timing of CHOGM, with COP31 just a few days afterwards. That is a real opportunity for the Commonwealth to be a useful forum feeding into COP31.

Q3 Dr Ehsan, can we have the defence co-operation you talked about given the very different views among members of the Commonwealth about who the enemy might be or about particular conflicts and threats?

Absolutely, that is a very important question to ask. Without doubt, as we have seen in recent times, China is looking not just to gain an economic foothold—especially in the African Commonwealth member states—but to develop a military and policing presence, especially in the sensitive Indo-Pacific region. That is where the UK has to be realistic about its role, especially its leadership role, which has to be done in partnership with other countries. India is a critical strategic ally in that sense, as is working closely with countries such as Nigeria, which has considerable potential—youthful potential. Russia making military and defence investments is also an issue, especially in African member states.

It is not necessarily easy—the UK will have to work on it over time. The critical point to make is about the need for a cultural shift. As I said, there is a foreign policy tendency to look at the Commonwealth as irrelevant, but I do not think that we should give up because China has gained such a foothold somewhere, or Russia has made certain investments in military and defence developments. In response to that, as a counterbalance, we need to look to deepen our defence and security co-operation over time. That will not happen overnight, but we should work towards it.

Critically, we should do that with countries that have traditionally been strong diplomatic allies in the Commonwealth. Australia definitely has a role to play—it is also in the Australian national interest—especially with China looking to make developments, contributing to the social and institutional development of Pacific island countries. Recently, China tried to interact with Fiji—it has a policing agreement with Fiji, although I think that Fiji has taken a step back from it. There is also a history of China having that pact with the Solomon Islands in critical areas. The key is for the UK to work with like-minded allies in the Commonwealth to make the Commonwealth over time a counterbalance to growing Chinese and Russian involvement and influence in the international system.

Q4 Dr Carrington, we talked about whether we think that the Commonwealth matters, but what is the view of the rest of the Commonwealth? Do they regard it as important? The heads of the leading members did not turn up to the last meeting.

I think it depends. Looking specifically at the Caribbean, the Commonwealth can be a real opportunity for states to mobilise on vulnerable island states and climate, particularly on adaptation and resilience. It can be a forum for building co-operation and coalitions outside Russian, US and Chinese influence, but it depends, and I think that there is a challenge there to ensure that it continues to be a useful forum. As I said, climate is one issue, given the timing of CHOGM and COP31, where it can be a really useful point of international co-operation, particularly for small and vulnerable states in the Caribbean.

I will just add a quick point. The Chagos islands are very relevant: that was almost a result of the UK, in my view, failing to nurture, build and pay attention to quite important relationships within the Commonwealth. That is very much a gift for countries such as China and Russia.

I agree that China and Russia have made certain developments in terms of gaining a foothold, especially in certain public policy areas and in relation to other Commonwealth member countries. The solution to that is not for the UK to row back, but to actually lean in more to the Commonwealth, see it as a key pillar in its foreign policy interests and try, over time, to cultivate an environment in the Commonwealth that acts as a counterbalance to those growing forms of Chinese and Russian influence in the international system.

Q5 I want to expand a bit on the Chair’s question. I am interested in how relevant the Commonwealth is to the members, given how many members there are and how different all those countries are. Dr Carrington, you have identified that there are shared interests around climate with some countries and shared interests around security in the Caribbean. Dr Ehsan, you mentioned that there are some states where we might deepen our military co-operation. But in every instance, you are dividing up the Commonwealth based on our particular interests in a particular thing or where we have shared values. Those are all effectively separate multilateral groups that you are talking about setting up, so how relevant is the Commonwealth as a collective, given what you have already said?

I think there are certain areas where it is easier to cultivate collaboration and deepen that co-operation across Commonwealth member states. In terms of increasing its relevance, you have to look at the key member states. I will take India, for example: when you look at healthcare there, there are still very significant problems in terms of a lack of healthcare infrastructure in certain parts of India, especially in poorer eastern states. The areas that the Commonwealth could really build on include disease prevention and control—that is a critical area where co-operation could be deepened.

Naturally, female economic empowerment is a very important pillar of the economic development strategy of many developing countries, so the UK can definitely contribute to that by making it an important goal for the Commonwealth. When you look at defence and security, as I said before with, for example, Venezuelan aggression towards Guyana, you have to be very selective about where there are realistic prospects of defence and security co-operation. I am very much of the view that, without any attempts to deepen co-operation in those more controversial areas, I just don’t see the Commonwealth really commanding that relevance and respect within the international system—unless it branches out from those more traditional areas of education and trade and investment.

That is not to undermine the importance of trade and investment; I think that the Commonwealth advantage should be built upon. Having that asset of a shared official language, common legal systems and familiar administrative frameworks is something to really build on. That is a golden aspect of the Commonwealth, but without defence and security, I think it would be very difficult for it to have that relevance.

Q6 I take your point. I guess the UK has a certain romantic attachment to the idea of the Commonwealth, and I am trying to understand whether the Commonwealth has the same attachment. I get that there are areas where we can deepen relationships or work on particular issues, but how relevant is the Commonwealth as a collective to its members?

I think that question depends on whether you are talking about national Governments or the publics across the Commonwealth. The five-country polling I did for the “One Family” report on behalf of Policy Exchange had a very interesting item. It asked survey respondents, “Do you believe the UK does more good than harm in the world?” and the lowest level of approval was among the UK public. It was especially high among the Indian and Nigerian publics, so I think there is a great deal of good will and affection towards the UK among Commonwealth publics. If you are talking about soft power, that is an amazing asset to have. Of course, there could be a difference between the opinion of the Government of the day in those countries and the broader population.

In my view, there has been a growing culture of self-flagellation in the UK, where we have a lack of confidence in what we have contributed to the world, in terms of human advancement and, in general, our moral obligations. I think we have fared quite well on an international level, and we need to make the most of the good will and affection that does exist. India and Nigeria are two huge, very important populations in the context of the strategic future of the Commonwealth, and the UK should build on that and work towards really making the most of and maximising the potential of that good will.

I agree. You mentioned particularly that there are unifying issues for particular regions or countries, but I think that that is the case with any major international organisation. It is the same with, say, the United Nations. With the Commonwealth, there are opportunities for particular regions or groups of countries to unify around key issues and build coalitions. With any major issue, there will always be tensions with other major powers, say, on climate perhaps with countries that are less on board with supporting vulnerable states with climate resilience. But I think that the Commonwealth has a degree of uniqueness by not having, say, Russia, the US and China in it. It offers a unique forum.

As for the attachment, or the particular fondness, that the UK might have for the Commonwealth or the sense of the Commonwealth, it is crucial, for the Commonwealth moving forward, to have a shift in mindset around that and not to focus on the sense of a fondness for the Commonwealth and the shared history. That can often lead to colonial dynamics. It is about seeing this as a useful forum moving forward, perhaps separate from the history.

Q7 I was able to visit Guyana earlier this year with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. It was a fascinating visit; we met President Ali there. My experience of visiting the Commonwealth countries has always been that their desire is to deepen and build more strategic relationships with the UK—I agree with everything you said, Dr Ehsan, about the possibilities for the relationship with the Commonwealth. Have you looked at perhaps how the Commonwealth could figure in a more strategic relationship around critical minerals and diversifying supply chains for the UK?

That is something that we considered to a degree in the report. On critical minerals, one thing that we talked about was leveraging the blue economy—blue economic instruments—including looking at blue carbon. What we want to do, in my view, is support emerging markets, so small state islands, and help with their development. Naturally, they have a very small land mass but they have considerable ocean resources.

The UK should work towards leveraging its expertise, especially through the City, and work towards blue carbon, blue bonds and coastal resilience insurance—those are the kind of things that we should really move forward with, especially if we are serious about small state island development. I think that would bring the UK to the fore. The last CHOGM was in Samoa and the forthcoming one is in Antigua and Barbuda. If the UK can really feed into that agenda on small state island development, that will heighten its reputation in the Commonwealth, for sure.
Q8 What is your assessment of how well or badly the FCDO is currently doing at building—

It is hopeless. In my view, there is a situation whereby it is seen as an outdated, moribund organisation, and I don’t think that is specific to the FCDO. Many of our public institutions are seen as some sort of outdated imperial relic. I look at the Commonwealth very differently. I think the smooth transition spearheaded by Her late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, from having imperial control to the voluntary association of nations, really was one of her finest achievements. That is not something we should neglect.

The reality is that we have attracted new member states such as Togo and Gabon —former French colonies—and I think that that is a real feather in our cap, if I am being honest. The fact that we have Mozambique—a former Portuguese colony—and Rwanda, a former Belgian colony, already in the Commonwealth shows, in a way, that outside former parts of the British empire there is an admiration for the UK in that after decolonisation, more than any other former European colonial power, it has really made an effort to rebuild relationships with former parts of its empire. I think that we should really build on that. You talked about soft power, and that is a critical element of it. I know that other people have a very different view and see it as some kind of outdated imperial relic, but I completely disagree with that.
Do you want to add anything, Dr Carrington?
I have nothing to add on that.

Q9 I want to talk about human rights violations. I know that Commonwealth members sign up to the charter and various declarations, but many members have been suspended or removed as a result of violations in their countries. Do you think that the Commonwealth takes that seriously, or is it superficial in nature? I will come to you first, Dr Carrington.

That is a really good question. I think that it reveals one of the real issues within not just the Commonwealth but international organisations generally. It can be a great opportunity to build consensus around issues, but when it comes to enforcement, particularly around human rights and democracy, it reveals the weakness of the Commonwealth. From a UK perspective, it is important to have a consistent approach and look at how it and the Commonwealth can support earlier monitoring around democracy, elections and human rights issues, as well as early intervention and looking at clearer follow-ups when there are, say, human rights violations. But I think that with international organisations, there is always that issue around enforcement, which reveals a flaw in those kinds of organisations.

There are definitely some enforcement issues. In an incredibly diverse association—I think there are 56 member states now—there will be cases where we feel that there are human rights issues across a number of those member countries. But expulsion is very much a last resort, and engaging with those countries in terms of flagging those issues has to be done in the spirit of the Commonwealth charter, which is ultimately that the members are free and equal nations. Adopting a heavy-handed approach there would not necessarily work—if anything, that could be alienating. It is a very difficult balance to strike, and I think that the UK would be best served looking at those issues, especially female empowerment, across member states. That would be helpful in terms of the economic development of lesser-developed member states.

There are issues in certain member countries in terms of the persecution of religious minorities, and the UK should be a critical friend when it comes to those issues. That has been a concern even when it comes to India, to be perfectly honest. But again, it is a difficult balance to strike because without a strong strategic partnership with India, I do not think that the Commonwealth can move forward very much. In terms of the UK’s position on some of those human rights violations, I think that flagrant violations do need to be flagged, but there has to be a sense that there are countries with certain local cultural customs whose perception of human rights might be different from the liberal, western understanding of human rights. That is very difficult in terms of striking a uniform view on all human rights issues.

The one area that the UK could really work on through the Commonwealth observer groups is the creation of more robust procedures over time in terms of the monitoring of elections—the democratic integrity of those member states. I think that is where you could find the UK exerting a decent level of influence. In terms of flagging every single human rights issue of the 56 member countries, which have very different cultural and social environments, that is a bit more difficult.

Q10 It is a challenge. Coming on to specific cases, if a country is deemed to be more acceptable and has allegedly met the requirements to be readmitted, as in the case of Zimbabwe, what do you think the procedure there should be? Should they be readmitted quite readily, or should caveats be in place?

I think with the case of Zimbabwe, the UK should support long-term readmittance if conditions are met, looking specifically at the Commonwealth charter and making sure that all conditions around elections and democracy are met. More broadly, not just with readmitting but with admitting new states, I think if states can show they do meet those requirements, the UK should support them being admitted or readmitted.

Q11 Dr Ehsan, if I can use another case study, I am contacted quite frequently by constituents in relation to the incarceration of Imran Khan in Pakistan. Do you feel that the Commonwealth could play a stronger role in relation to that? You have referenced the importance of democracy and democratic procedures. Could the Commonwealth have a stronger position in relation to the incarceration of Imran Khan, or is that something you think it should perhaps stay away from?

I think there is potential, if the UK Government feel passionate enough about that particular case. I would maybe stay away from certain individual cases and look more broadly at the overall human rights environment in certain member states and across the Commonwealth more generally. I think there will be many people who would consider that particular case to be a grave injustice, and it has attracted a great deal of interest within the British Pakistani population here in the UK. If the argument is about whether the UK should try to strike alliances across the Commonwealth and ultimately work towards the release of Imran Khan, I am not sure the Commonwealth is necessarily the right arena for that. I think that, over time, if we were to adopt that kind of approach, that could be incredibly alienating for Pakistan.

Overall, I think this is a case where there are very serious issues in terms of the imprisonment of Imran Khan. But at the same time, I think if the UK were to adopt an approach of, “Let’s band together with lots of other countries and try to exert pressure on Pakistan to release him from his imprisonment,” that would do more harm than good over time, especially in terms of Pakistan’s place in the Commonwealth.

Q12 I have questions about four different areas, so they are more quick-fire questions. I would like to ascertain how successful the Commonwealth, and particularly CHOGM, has been in advancing all four areas. If you were writing the leaders’ declaration, would you put these issues in it? Also, what is the strength of the Commonwealth—but particularly the CHOGM meeting—to take action on them?

The four areas are: violence against women and girls; sustainable finance; climate finance; and marine protection. First, violence against women and girls has been a subject of previous CHOGMs, and is a focus for the Commonwealth, but have they been at all effective in tackling some real differences between the countries and raising awareness of and action on that issue?

Violence against women and girls is definitely something the Commonwealth has traditionally focused on a great deal. I think in terms of action, it is difficult to achieve certain goals across the board within the Commonwealth, but there have been certain improvements.

In terms of the UK’s focus on sustainable finance and climate finance, I think these are very important areas. The reality is that the Commonwealth is an international association which is not vested with considerable financial resources, but the argument made in the “One Family” report for Policy Exchange is that it should be a powerful convening agent. Ultimately what the Commonwealth should do here, in terms of these areas, especially finance-related ones, is act as a switchboard. Ultimately, if member states want to access sustainable or climate finance, the reality is that cannot be drawn from some kind of Commonwealth centralised pot. But what the Commonwealth can do is offer that top-tier technical guidance in terms of connecting member states with certain organisations and international associations that do have those financial pots available.

One could be the World Health Organisation, for example. Being a gold-standard example of a convening international asset is the future of the Commonwealth, and the reality of having a budget that is not necessarily large means it needs to lean more in that direction. There has been considerable focus on climate finance within the Commonwealth, but naturally, it has to use that convening potential to do more. If we are looking at small state island development, much of that will ultimately come down to the climate resilience of those member countries. What was the fourth theme?

Q13 I will come on to that now. Dr Carrington, you mentioned that climate was the focus—it absolutely is, especially given that the meeting is being held on small islands. Can you give an assessment of whether the Apia Commonwealth ocean declaration, which was introduced at a previous meeting, has been useful? What is the likelihood of there being further and better marine protection, especially given that we are about to have COP31 and the world conference on marine biodiversity in Belgium later that same month, as well as the fact that the first marine COP is coming up? In the context of those, will the declaration in CHOGM further that, and was it a successful part of the declaration last time?

I think the Commonwealth is a really good forum for tackling issues and building coalitions in all four areas, including on climate issues and on violence towards women and girls. I would not comment specifically on the success of previous actions, but given that CHOGM is going to be held in Antigua and Barbuda, the blue economy and marine conservation is going to be one of the key issues. Again, that will be feeding into COP, so there is a real opportunity to build consensus. One of the key things will be whether it is a case of having discussions and building a general consensus, but there being nothing that forms direct action. A real challenge for climate issues in particular will be developing something that creates direct action, rather than just further discussion.

Q14 Would that be a Caribbean climate fund? Do you need to see an actual pot to take it from being a talking shop to something that can deliver? Is it an actual fund or finance mechanism that makes the difference?

I think it could be, and that would be really crucial. As I said, it has been done in the past. If we look at 2015 and the timing of CHOGM in Malta and then COP21 in Paris, we see that that worked really well in getting direct action on climate issues. Something like that could definitely happen.

Q15 I wanted to ask about reparations. Ahead of CHOGM in 2024, the UK Government made it quite clear that reparations were off the table, which I must say is a position that I probably agree with. How did that land with Commonwealth members? Is there a way of discussing reparations and the legacy of slavery with them, given that the UK has such a clear position but many Commonwealth neighbours have the opposite position?
I think there definitely needs to be a shift in position.
A shift in position by who?

By the UK. I think there needs to be a shift from maintaining the position in Samoa of not discussing anything, with no apology or movement there, to a listening position. If you look at the CARICOM 10-point plan on reparations, you will see that there is a really broad range of issues in the way that the legacies of slavery have impacted the Caribbean. The UK Government could work across various issues, including public health, education, debt cancellation and climate, to show that they are listening to the Caribbean.

Momentum has certainly built up this year. The meeting in June in Accra between African and Caribbean Governments really built a global framework on reparatory justice, and you then had the CARICOM delegation in London in July. It has put out a new manifesto, which again includes climate reparations, so that has been included in the conversation around reparatory justice. Yesterday, the Jamaican Government put a petition to the King, with three questions for the Privy Council specifically about the legality of issues relating to slavery in Jamaica. A real momentum has built up and there has been greater co-operation between African and Caribbean countries, so it is not something that the UK can switch off from and ignore.

If you look at the recent UK-Caribbean discussions in March, you will see that there was a degree of more openness in the UK position. The UK committed to funding and supporting the digitisation of documents relating to transatlantic slavery. With things like that, the UK can show an openness to having that conversation.

Q16 I suppose there is a difference between openness to working on the history, documents and health programmes, which we might have been doing anyway through our aid programmes, and debt cancellation and large amounts of reparations. Is it more about reframing what we are doing, or would the UK have to go a lot further with financial commitments to satisfy some of these demands?

Long term, I would say yes, but if you are talking more broadly about engagement in organisations such as the Commonwealth and engaging with Caribbean Governments, and if you look at the narrative behind discussions about reparations, it is all about a shift in power and perspective. If the UK is coming from a position of power and leadership, that needs to shift to one of partnership and co-operation.

I would have to offer a slightly different view. If we really wanted to get into the nitty-gritty of it in terms of slavery, we would look at the very origins of the supply chain. There is no doubt there were incredibly wealthy and powerful African kingdoms that benefited a great deal from the slave trade.

I find it peculiar that we have Governments, such as those in Ghana and Nigeria, being as pro-reparations as they are, given that Asante and Yoruba elites in modern-day Ghana and Nigeria respectively benefited a great deal in terms of slave trading operations.

There is no doubt that in its imperial era the UK was a major player in the transatlantic slave trade. It was also responsible for atrocities such as the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar in Punjab. There was also a very brutal crackdown of the Mau Mau uprising in Kenya. But the truth is that we have to provide a broader picture.

The reality is that the UK also played a pioneering humanitarian role in suppressing the slave trade at considerable human and financial cost, especially to the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron. You have to look at that particular era when the Royal Navy was competing with slave ships that were far more sophisticated, dynamic and well-resourced. Some people might argue, “Where are the reparations for the fallen sailors who made the ultimate sacrifice in suppressing the slave trade?”

Reducing the debate on slavery to reparations does not serve the UK very well. The UK should be firm that, in the spirit of equality and partnership, we are very willing to play a leadership role in terms of deepening co-operation, educational development and female economic empowerment, and we will work towards building the Commonwealth advantage in terms of trade and investment.

We are also looking at environmental sustainability. On the point made about climate finance, the UK could play a critical role in mobilising private capital in terms of helping countries towards their green energy transition. We could do that through the City and also co-operate with major financial centres across the Commonwealth, especially Mumbai in India, Lagos in Nigeria and Singapore. Singapore does not get talked about very much at all when it comes to the financial potential of the Commonwealth, which I find quite baffling.

In my view, if I am being absolutely honest, some of the cases in the debate on reparations are ultimately designed as a form of resentment and almost as a way of bankrupting the UK. I do not buy into those arguments at all. I think what the Commonwealth should be is not so much about looking in the past. If people really do want to look in the past, we should obviously consider the role of those wealthy and powerful African kingdoms, whether the Yoruba elites, the Asante elites or the kings of Dahomey in current -day Benin . It would be foolish for anyone to suggest that Benin should now pay any form of reparations in terms of the Dahomey kingdom’s role in the slave trade. What I would really support is a future-oriented Commonwealth that ultimately operates in the spirit of equality and partnership, and the UK should remain very firm in that view.

Q17 F ollowing up on that — because you clearly have slightly different views on this subject —t he last CHOGM was, to some extent, dominated by discussion of this, and it led to the communiqué at the end sa ying that everyone “agreed that t he time has come for a meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation” . Has that actually happened? Has there been any progress? Is there a risk that we are just going to have a repetition of the whole argument all over again at this year’s CHOGM?

Yes, I think there is a risk of that. That is why I would say that, in terms of reparations, the UK needs to shift that position and have more of a listening approach. A wider understanding can also be quite useful in feeding into these conversations, not just in terms of reparations but around the climate.

It is often mentioned that Caribbean countries—small island states in the region—are among the most vulnerable globally to extreme weather events and climate-related loss and damage. A crucial aspect is that that has been exacerbated by the experience of plantation slavery in the region — for example , through cutting down sustainable forests and replacing them with monoculture s . Another legacy is that populations were displaced and concentrated in coastal areas, so then, whenever you have an extreme weather event, loss and damage are much higher.

F actoring in th ose histories is important for really understanding present-day challenges. But to circle back to your question, I think it is a real issue , and t here needs to be a shift in approach for it not just to be a replay of Samoa two years ago.
Dr Ehsan, y our view is probably closer to that expressed by the UK Government last time, but do you think that we can move beyond just having the same argument again?

Before moving beyond, I think that the UK should lean confidently into those discussions in terms of its own role in ultimately suppressing the slave trade and being at the heart of abolitionist campaigning at the global level in that era. I am not saying that the UK should ignore these debates or just put them aside ; I think that it needs to engage with them very critically, but have the self-confidence to say, “ Well, a ctually, we played a pioneering humanitarian role in suppressing the slave trade. We acknowledge the atrocities that were committed under the British empire , and the fact that it was a major player in terms of slave trading operations, but we also acknowledge that , ultimately, it did play a role in really trying to suppress the slave trade.” As I said before, the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron made a considerable financial and human sacrifice towards that goal .

Very clearly, you do not want to antagonise fellow member countries within the Commonwealth, but the reality is that there were African kingdoms that benefited a great deal at the very origins of the supply chain . Ghana also brought forward a United Nations General Assembly resolution on th is matter of reparations, which I find quite baffling. I think , i n some ways, it is a deflection tactic by certain countries to try to take attention away from their own role s in slave trade activities.

The reality is that what we should be promoting is a future-oriented Commonwealth. That is the key here: free and equal nations. I would also make the point that, if the UK caves on reparations, it will lose respect in other parts of the Commonwealth. I am not sure that many Indian citizens , who think that Britain has done more good than harm in the world and for humankind , will find it very impressive that the UK has caved on reparations, if truth be told. Of course, there is obviously an appetite to make this a critical pillar of the Commonwealth agenda, but I do see it as a major distraction.
Q18 Finally, we are about to hear from the officials responsible for preparing for the UK’s presence at CHOGM. In your view, what should they be aiming for the UK to get out of the meeting?

A key focus should be around some of the more traditional issues where the Commonwealth has had success. Issues around women and girls, and looking at education, have been mentioned. As I mentioned, climate is really crucial, as are trade and investment. Given that CHOGM is going to be held in Antigua and Barbuda, there should be a focus on vulnerable states, and real support and action on climate finance—not just further discussions, but some actual delivery—and on the reform of the Commonwealth more broadly. There have been efforts to look at that over the past few years, and it is something else the UK should support.

To give an example of a potential shift in position, the UK has traditionally looked at education in terms of scholarships, but there are examples of more recent partnerships and set-ups that show a more modern perspective. For example, the University of Glasgow has a partnership with the University of the West Indies, which is much more about shared courses and shared knowledge, rather than a more extractive model of offering scholarships in the UK and in some way perhaps contributing to brain drain from countries that are offered scholarships. There is an opportunity for things around education in that respect.

I really want to see a very strong focus on deepening trade and investment relations. I think the best way to overcome the focus on reparations is to say, “We want a future-oriented Commonwealth. We want to build on the existing Commonwealth advantage that we have in place and to deepen trade and investment relations.” That could be done through the striking of innovative partnerships. There was a proposal in the Policy Exchange “One Family” report to strike partnerships based on digital finance, for example, between London, Mumbai and Lagos—across different continents. I want to see something more innovative that really attracts attention and shows that the Commonwealth wants to be a serious player on the international stage.

Dr Carrington mentioned the traditional issues such as the deepening of educational co-operation. I would like to see more in terms of pro-youth mobility schemes across the Commonwealth, with a particular focus on girls and young women. That would be very important. I think it would be asking for too much to say there should be a strong focus on defence and security on this occasion in Antigua and Barbuda, but that is something the UK can work towards further down the line.

Environmental sustainability is very important. As I said before, especially given the UK’s technical expertise in the City, the reality is that it is not so much about looking at public money and Government funding, but about looking at how we can mobilise private capital to help countries to progress towards their green energy transition and to leverage blue econom ic instruments such as blue carbon and coastal resilience insurance.

It is about looking at how we can develop small state island development. That will benefit the UK, because if those emerging markets grow over time economically, that could present opportunities for British companies and firms as well. I think there should be a very strong focus on trade and investment. I know that Antigua and Barbuda wants to have a strong emphasis on economic prosperity as well, so it would fit in quite nicely if the UK was to take that approach.

Thank you both for appearing this morning; it has been very helpful. If you have any further thoughts you would like us to consider, please feel free to send them in. Thank you very much. We will suspend for a couple of minutes while we change over witnesses.
Sitting suspended.
On resuming—

We had been intending to hold this morning’s second panel session with officials from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office to discuss the preparations for this year’s CHOGM, but as our panel members have not appeared in time, we will have to suspend the sitting and look to pursue them through other means.

Evidence Session No. 22 Heard in Public Questions 194 – 20 4
Witnesses

Alex Davies-Jones MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Ministry of Justice; Florence Eshalomi MP, Minister for Homelessness, Democracy, Communities and Faith, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; Josh MacAlister OBE MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State (Minister for Children and Families), Department for Education.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Alex Davies-Jones, Florence Eshalomi and Josh MacAlister .

Q194 Can I welcome everyone to this session on the Domestic Abuse Act 2021? This piece of legislation was passed five years ago and today we are conducting post-legislative scrutiny to see how the legislation has worked. While this is not done with all legislation, this particular Act has involved changes at many different levels so we want to look at whether it is truly effective and achieving its intended aims.

Let me welcome the expert team of witnesses that we have here today. Sitting there to the left in red is Florence Eshalomi MP, the Minister for Homelessness, Democracy, Communities and Faith. Appointed Minister of State in July of this year , her responsibilities include community, green spaces, social cohesion, faith, homelessness and supported accommodation for domestic abuse victims. That last point is clearly the key issue for us today. She was previously the co-chair of the APPG, the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Ending Homelessness , so it is going to be a big challenge given the priority the Prime Minister is giving to this. We are very concerned to ensure that domestic abuse victims remain a high priority within that category.

Then I would like to welcome Alex Davi e s-Jones, who is the Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Victims, Violence Against Women and Girls and International Justice at the Ministry of Justice. Also appointed in July, she is a new and important arrival. Her responsibilities include criminal law, victims, witnesses and vulnerabilities, rape and serious sexual offences, the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority and miscarriages of justice. That is going to keep her very busy I am sure. We are glad to see her here today.
We also have Jo hn MacAlister —
Sorry—

It is Josh—forgive me. We have Josh MacAlister , who is the Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Children and Families at the Department for Education. He was actually in post before, in September 2025, and reappointed in July of this year. He has given real priority to the position of children and that is one of the issues we want to address today.

I want to start the session by asking : how are responsibilities for the different provisions of the Act divided in practice? One common problem we have is that responsibilities can fall between ministries; how do you maintain cohesion , and who is accountable for ensuring that the Act actually works coherently? I see a nod from Alex.

I can happily explain to the committee how we have set up and developed the strategy for tackling violence against women and girls across government. I am responsible for this, alongside my counterpart in the Home Office, Minister Kaur, who succeeded Minister Phillips.

To ensure collaboration, we have developed a cross-government ministerial board. This board reviews everything within the tackling violence against women and girls ’ strategy that the Government published in December last year, which includes the Domestic Abuse Act. We welcome attendance at that board from Ministers in other government departments to look at how best to deliver both the Act and the strategy. The board really pushes accountability and delivery and implementation on all violence against women and girls ’ issues across all other government departments. Minister Kaur and I chair this board together.
Can you spell his or her surname for me?
Her surname is K, A, U, R.
Do you have a regular meeting pattern?

We did; we are yet to meet since the forming of the new Administration, but we previously met regularly every six weeks across government. Attendance was a three-line whip from every government department that had a stake within this. We were also joined by a representative from the devolved Government of Wales given the cross-nation situation , because a number of the provisions such as health, housing, social care and local government are devolved to Wales. Therefore collaboration was needed in order to deliver on the aims, means and priorities of both the violence against women and girls ’ strategy and the Act.
Who deals with it at Cabinet level?

At Cabinet level, i t is primarily led by the Home Secretary, but under the previous Administration , before Andy Burnham became Prime Minister, we also held high-level Cabinet meetings. At the time, Minister Phillips and I would attend these sessions alongside then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer. While these meetings have yet to be reconvened under Andy Burnham, my understanding is that it will be imminently.
We are expecting to have a voice in Cabinet then?
Yes.

We heard from Jess Phillips, al though she was no longer Minister, and we heard from the Minister at that time. What was quite revelatory about the evidence we had from Jess Phillips was the extent to which she felt that resource should be coming from more than one space—because these are H ealth issues , and they also fall under other ministries—and where there could be some greater complementarity, particularly around resourcing. She also felt there was still a sense of silo around these issues; it was not spreading across the ministries well enough. I do not want us to go into this in any more detail, but I want you to take this message away with you: there is a strong sense in which this should not be falling between ministries and we want to see cross-ministerial collaboration to ensure it works , as that is the only way this issue will be well addressed.

I totally agree with you on that point and we noticed that the departments that did step up to the plate , not just in meeting their obligations but prioritising the implementation of the Act and the strategy, were ones where there was ministerial direction and prioritisation for this. Where there was a Minister in post that saw this as a priority, that is where it got driven.

She told us something that very few of us knew—certainly I did not—which was that she received assistance from the Department of Health and Social Care and that some resource of the Department of Health and Social Care actually went in her direction, which brought about a great deal of loyalty from her to the Secretary of State at the time. All I would say is that this seems to be a rather good example of a Cabinet Minister recognising that this is a subject that falls on everybody ’ s plate.

Totally. Just on that point, victim support is one of my policy areas that I lead on for victims within the criminal justice system. However—I am sure the committee will be very well aware—victim support is very, very broad; particularly when you are discussing health concerns by long-term health conditions. M ental health support, provisions for children — all this comes from the Ministry of Justice victim support fund. Before we set up the inter-ministerial board on tackling domestic abuse and violence against women and girls, there was no contribution from the H ealth department. That changed following direction from the then Secretary of State, Wes Streeting, to fund the Steps to Safety programme for GPs to have a set direction to point survivors and victims of domestic abuse through the right pathways and then make sure that that was supported and funded along the way. We also introduced the Child House model across England. Previously, there was only one funded model in existence. The commitment to fund this model, and to grow and increase the number of them for child victims of sexual abuse, now comes directly from the Department of Health and Social Care.

It is very helpful to hear you speaking with such familiarity about all this. One of the repeated pieces of evidence we have had on this committee has been about people going to their GP and somehow it never filtering onwards or not getting the advice that they, looking back, feel would have assisted them greatly. She is not here today but we have a GP who sits on this committee so we have been very mindful of that and we would like to see that progressed with the new Administration.
Can I add two reflections? First, Government are awash with inter-ministerial groups.
That is one of the problems.

They are not all that effective; I do not think that will be a bombshell to m embers, but the work that Jess and Alex have led with the VAWG inter-ministerial group is unusual in both its effectiveness and its degree of accountability. The fact that there is a clear action plan, with a strategy driven by very effective Ministers, has been a large part of the ability to bring across-government commitments together, including at the Department for Education. If part of your work is looking at Government ’ s ability to work across departments, there is definitely more to be done, but this is probably one of the areas where it has been more effective than others.

Secondly, most departments will have an insight into the same group of families we are concerned about when we are talking about domestic abuse. These are families where there is a mental health concern, families where there may be substance abuse issues, housing problems or child poverty. We often find ourselves coming at the problem through the perspective of our own system. In my world that is children ’ s social care and how we make sure social workers are effective and equipped to respond to significant harm and abuse. I chair the keeping children safe board alongside Jess and health colleagues, where domestic abuse is a massive feature of the discussions that we are having.

There are moments where we step back as Ministers and realise we are talking about the same group of families. We are all trying to crowd in investment and changes to systems with a common aim; it does not necessarily mean they all fit into the same spreadsheet of tracked actions called the VAWG strategy. As a point of reassurance I am happy to elaborate later on in this session on some of the changes we are making.

There are specific things that, of course, we are wanting to hear from you about, but it is very interesting that you have mentioned children. We have some questions for you, particularly around the special way in which this piece of legislation really homed in on the fact that children inside families where there is domestic abuse between the adults suffer enormously, with a long-term impact on their lives. That is something that we have to have to the fore in all this because of the cost to the lives of people and to society as a whole. Thank you, Josh, for that. Florence, is there anything you would like to add at this stage?
I echo comments from both Alex and Josh in that it is cross-departmental including a big role that MHCLG play in this because—

Now li sten, I have to remind you about acronyms simply because we have people who listen in who do not know them. If we could tell people what we are talking about, at least in the first instance, that would be great.

The Ministry of Housing , Communities and Local Government plays a key role in this and attends the inter-ministerial board. Obviously for MHCLG —Housing, Communities and Local Government— the key areas are around looking at the homelessness provision and rough sleeping element: when you look at the issues that women and men fleeing domestic abuse are facing, it comes down to where they lay their heads, in terms of safe, secure accommodation. We have heard many examples of some challenges many local authorities are facing when people present themselves as homeless. This is a key area that we are looking at in terms of working with the other departments and making sure that the housing element is treated as crucial.

As Josh mentioned, it is not just the women and the men fleeing domestic abuse, it is also the children and the impact on them. We know that a number of them are still very sadly caught up in temporary accommodation, and many are caught up in unsuitable B&B accommodation exceeding the six weeks ’ limit. These are key areas that we are really trying to address to ensure that councils remember and implement their duty to act. That is a key area that I am keen to explore with the committee later on.

Yes, there is research that statistically shows that young people who are rough sleeping have often come from backgrounds where they have experienced domestic abuse with their parents. I will move to Lord Russell, please.

Q195 You might want to get your pen and paper because this question has three parts and you might wish to remember which they are and in which order. This is to do with the experience of victim-survivors.

I would just say as a preface that we have focused quite a lot during our inquiry on trying to find examples of best practice in a variety of areas around the country, and they are many. What they almost all have in common is a bottom-up strategy: they look at the experience the victims are having and they work their way up to see what can be done regardless of financial boundaries, departmental boundaries, or whatever, because it is victim focused.

First, in your particular department, what do you consider to be the principal barriers that victim-survivors are having problems with? Secondly, what plans do you have to improve their experience? Thirdly, much more specific, we have heard a lot of evidence about the value brought by IDVAs — independent domestic violence adv isers ; there are a lot of acronyms here—to improving victim-survivor experience , including specialist IDVAs such as criminal justice IDVAs, child IDVAs, and housing IDVAs. What plans do you have, if any, to increase the number of IDVAs available in your department to help victim-survivors? C ould I start with you, Alex, please ?

I would say the biggest challenge that victims are dealing with is the criminal justice system at the moment, given the incredible backlogs in court delays. The issue of victim support and the capacity problems we have across the system are proving incredibly challenging. You will all be aware of the issues surrounding the entire criminal justice system at the moment: prisons at capacity; courts with severe delays; rape victims waiting three or four years for their trials to get to court; victim support is very patchy across England and Wales, particularly for child victims who—as you quite rightly pointed out, Chair—were recognised for the first time as victims in their own right as part of this Act, yet services and support for them are still very limited.

All this has been recognised, not just by the Ministry of Justice but by the cross-government working group to tackle the problem. We have funded record levels of court sitting days. We have funded record levels of victim support services—over half a billion pounds , and made that funding available for three years, which is something that the sector primarily told us was needed in order to put that sustainability and continuity in place.

However, it is not enough. It is not enough in terms of the court sitting days ; it is not enough in terms of victim support services. So w e really need to get to the heart of tackling prevention, looking at what more we can do. Specialist domestic abuse courts — problem-solving courts — are doing really great transformative work. This is where the judge follows the victim and perpetrator through the entire journey, bringing in positive requirement trainings. We are trialling d omestic a buse p rotection o rders, again introduced in the Act, across specific areas in England and Wales at the moment, but they are truly life - saving so we are committed to rolling them out as quickly as possible. There are issues with them because they do not cover children, so family courts are choosing not to use them. However, we have recognised this and are seeking to address it.

In terms of IDVA provision, with the record funding for police and crime commissioners, which is devolved to them, we have ring-fenced the violence against women and girls ’ pot that we give to them to ensure that they are able to fund more IDVAs and child IDVAs where necessary. We know, because victims have told us, the huge impact that they make. In the Courts and Tribunals Bill that is currently making its way through the Commons, we have made a provision for IDVAs to sit as a trusted person in the courtroom with victims as well, so that will be a new measure that we are introducing to improve victim experience in court. We are getting rid of so-called bad character/good character evidence in the court as well, which can be used to showcase perpetrators in specific lights , which is not helpful , and to discredit victims and survivors of domestic abuse as well.

We are also ensuring that trauma-informed training is rolled out across every part of the criminal justice system. That is essential in terms of how victims and survivors are treated within the system. We are working with the judiciary, who are of course independent but who recognise that domestic abuse—particularly coercive and controlling behaviour—needs to be better identified in the courtrooms; the Judicial College are working on training packages. The Judicial College has been working with Women ’ s Aid to develop this and I am looking forward to actually seeing for the first time ever this training being rolled out. The Judicial College and the judiciary have invited me in to witness this, which is a first, and I am very much looking forward to that too.
That is terrific because there was a time when I raised the idea of us getting women ’ s organisations to be the trainers of the judiciary and it was seen as the wildest idea possible, so I am glad—
The training is still being done by the Judicial College, but the training has been developed in partnership with women ’ s organisations.
That is a step forward; that is terrific.
Just a very brief follow-up on the PCC point; obviously they are on the way out in 2028. Do you have clear plans on how you are going to ensure that IDVAs are properly funded?

Yes, just to reassure you and the sector that might be listening to this: one of my key priorities now in post is looking at how we can reform the victim support funding model post the abolishment of the police and crime commissioners. We are working to address systemic issues such as postcode lotteries and ensuring we have good service provision while maintaining the violence against women and girls ’ funding because we know how crucial that is.
Lord Russell, I saw that you were anxious to come back in.
Liz asked exactly the same follow-up question I was going to; great minds follow other greater minds. Josh, over to you please.

The biggest barrier for parents and adults in terms of the children ’ s social care response is that we have a children ’ s social care system that, over a number of years, has become increasingly skewed towards late-stage crisis intervention. It is now spending about £15 billion a year. While that spending has gone up hugely above inflation every year, it has been driven by a rise in the number of children in care, particularly those in residential care , where costs have escalated. We are in a cycle where more and more of the overall spending goes towards that late - stage, costly and often poorer - outcome resulting service, which has squeezed what was already a very limited amount of support for families in the first place.

The Government ’ s plan—following my independent review of children ’ s social care that was published under the previous Government in 2022—now has a £2.4 billion reset package over the next three years. We are currently in the first full year of that rollout across England. That is money going into local authorities that is conditional upon those areas building up a multidisciplinary family help service: it is not just social workers; it is made up of other practitioners—including those that work in domestic abuse fields—who can do more intensive work to help change family circumstances before the crisis escalates into a child protection or care concern for the child.

I can say a lot more about that but essentially the main system obstacle is finite resource to help families because of the doom loop of late-stage crisis interventions. That is being addressed at the moment through a massive programme of change that is about funding and legislation.

Specifically for children, if you are a practitioner at the moment the biggest barrier is there is no UK-based, evidence-based intervention of what works to respond to children as victims of domestic abuse. That is staggering because it is one of the most prevalent causes for state intervention in family life. We are feeling around in the dark for what to do that is effective for these children. If this was any other public health area, for years we would have had randomised control trials, impact evaluations in the field identifying what works and what does not. That is not just a UK problem ; that is a worldwide issue of an evidence gap.

Before being elected here, I was the executive chair of Foundations, which is the What Works Centre for Children and Families. We began a programme of building up the evidence around the most promising interventions; two are currently now in evaluation, Bounce Back 4 Kids and For Baby ’ s Sake, and I believe the committee has heard from the organisations behind those. Both have been through, or are in, a randomised control trial as a pilot. One of them is now in a full randomised control trial. That matters so much for the Department for Education and the work that we are doing , because establishing a proven model of intervention that changes outcomes for children who are victims of domestic abuse allows me, as a Minister, to set practice guidance that can then be inspected against; so the system follows scientific rigorous evidence of efficacy rather than spending lots of money on people trying to do their best, which can sometimes cause more harm than good. A good example of this is some evidence showing that doing group work with perpetrators can result in it not only being ineffective, but it can actually be counterproductive to the effort. There is a specific problem to overcome with regard to what works and there is a broader system dynamic at play, which we are addressing.
Where are we in terms of timing? When will you be able to sit where you are and say, “This is now happening”?

The Families First Partnership programme, the £2.4 billion, is money being spent this year; so over £800 million is this year, over £800 million is next year. That programme needs to be fully implemented by every local authority by March next year, so that is six months from now. I guarantee you, there will be lots of problems with the efficacy of the implementation of that reform. However, on a quarterly basis, I am monitoring local authority implementation and we will take intervention action with councils that prevaricate, delay or do not implement those changes. It is absolutely essential.

By the end of financial year 2027-28, they will have had the full funding for the Families First and the system should be seeing more money going from the late-stage crisis costs end of the system—hundreds of millions and then eventually billions—towards more intensive help for families. The work of building up the evidence base will take as long as it takes to do randomised control trials. It is worth saying that we have not kind of left that to chance: Government are behind Foundations and the organisations that are doing that work.

From a housing perspective, the biggest barrier is definitely access to secure, safe, affordable, social housing. There simply is not enough accommodation for women and children fleeing domestic abuse.

If you look at the situation across England, the majority of councils are currently facing major financial challenges. In my former role as the C hair of the Housing, Communities and Local Government Select Committee, one of the key areas we looked at was temporary accommodation and its impact on women and children. That report highlighted that, because of the situation with housing, some councils are sadly sending women fleeing domestic abuse into shared accommodation with men who have just been released from prison. There are women sharing accommodation where they are having to use mixed facilities—such as kitchens and bathrooms—with men and known abusers.

You also have situations where children are being placed outside their home borough, meaning families are travelling up to two hours just to get to school every morning, and we see the impact that is having on those children. You have a situation where, because of this pressure, a number of councils are placing families and women fleeing domestic abuse in hotels with no cooking facilities and no proper washing facilities. The impact this is having on women who are fleeing horrific circumstances is just adding an additional burden on them.

The key area that we are looking at from MHCLG is how we are working with local authorities to bring down the temporary accommodation bill. A number of councils across England have been given exceptional financial support to stop them going into bankruptcy. However, that is not a permanent solution. In essence, we do not want councils relying on what has been described across the sector as an overdraft facility from the Government. We need to look at how we fix the long-term issues.

That will only happen if we build the homes. That will not happen overnight. The Government ’ s key ambition is making sure we build 1.5 million new homes before the end of this Parliament, and what I am really keen to see is that a number of those homes are affordable homes that will be able to address this specific issue. There are things that we can be doing in the interim to look at areas where we can help.

First is making sure councils are remembering their duty. We regularly inspect and help councils on that. Second is funding for the Women ’ s Aid project, No Woman Turned Away, so that when women and children are presenting before their local councils for emergency accommodation they are not being turned away. Third is working with housing associations and private housing providers around what more they could be doing in terms of that duty. There are some really good plans around no - fault evictions in the Renters ’ Rights Act 2025, where we are securing tenancies for women. Before this, the threat of being evicted by a landlord for no good reason was hanging over their head: you have finally been able to secure somewhere only to face the threat of being evicted just because a landlord changed their mind. That is a monumental piece of legislation that will help many women in terms of having a base and having roots.

In the Social Housing Bill that is going through now, there will be additional changes to protect tenancies. We are finding that whenever there is an issue around domestic abuse, it is the women and children that have to leave the property. Why should they? In most cases, the abuser stays in the property. We want to ensure we are addressing that through legislation so women and children have a safe space to lay their head, while recognising that there is a lot more to do on that.

IDVAs are generally supported by M o J funding. For housing IDVAs, it is a local decision from the councils in how they allocate that funding. Again, we are working with the Local Government Association and other councils, ensuring that money is being spent in the right areas. There is a lot being done, but rightly there is a lot more that needs to be done to address this area.
Thank you. Now we move on to training . Baroness Neate?

Q196 Just to say, I am really heartened actually from everything you have all said about addressing some real systemic issues that lie behind. In my professional experience I have seen them all, so I am heartened by that.

My question is about the here and now really. One of the things that we have heard repeatedly in the evidence, which I have personally seen, is just the lack of understanding of domestic abuse right now and the dynamics of domestic abuse in many of the professions that victim-survivors and their children come into contact with on a daily basis. There is also a lack of understanding and knowledge of the responsibilities that some statutory agencies hold in relation to domestic abuse, and specifically the interplay between those statutory duties and the dynamics behind domestic abuse so that you really know when you should be applying those duties in the first place.

One way to address this could be mandatory or improved training. Training is not a panacea, I absolutely get that, but it could be one way to address this knowledge gap. This is a kind of short-term issue and it has been going on for a long time.
