Witnesses: John Morrison, Donald Campbell, Margaret Mary Murray and Luke McCullough.
Good morning and welcome to our second panel. May I ask you all briefly to say who you are and what you do ?
M adainn mhath —good morning. I am Luke McCullough , the corporate affairs director for nations at the BBC.
I am Margaret Mary Murray. I look after the BBC’s Gaelic - language services, BBC ALBA, which we operate in partnership with MG ALBA, and BBC Radio nan Gàidheal .
I am John Morrison, the chair of MG ALBA.
M adainn mhath . I am Donald Campbell, the chief executive of MG ALBA.
Q58 Thank you very much, and welcome—welcome back to some of you, as we have had you here before on at least one occasion, or perhaps more in your case, Mr McCullough.

My first question is for Mr Morrison. MG ALBA has called for parity with S4C in funding and in its statutory recognition. In practical terms, what would that look like for Gaelic broadcasting, and what specific changes would be needed to make that happen?

In terms of parity, we look for an equivalence of treatment. I do not think that we are in the position where we are looking for the same budget that Welsh has , but we would like to see, for example, when documents come out relating to broadcasting from DCMS, a couple of additional words in Welsh and Gaelic . That would be very welcome because sometimes, as we have seen even recently, Gaelic is not mentioned in very important documents that are looking forward to the BBC charter.

We were happy to see the Green Paper mention the sustainability of MG ALBA. Sustainability is key for us, as I am sure the Committee is aware. I notice that you have actually used some of our own words, that we are in real jeopardy, and that cannot be overstated . Our budget was frozen for 10 years, so its value has dropped by about 45%. That trajectory is unsustainable for any organisation or company. We are looking for equivalence in both legal terms and in the treatment of Gaelic and Welsh. Obviously, we are also looking for an increased budget.
Q59 And how would that help you to improve what you deliver for broadcasting?

It would be transformational, because one of the first things we did when I came in was get EY to have a look—Ernst & Young, in old-fashioned language. EY did an analysis that showed that, effectively, our budget should be double what it was at the time because it had fallen so far behind. It said that, if we had kept up with inflation, we would have created an additional 300 or 350 jobs. Most of the jobs we have created as a result of production have been in the h ighlands and i slands, which badly need jobs. For example, we have a media centre in Stornoway that is now one of the biggest employers in the whole of the Western Isles.

The demographics of that are fantastic , because you see young people who have gone away to college or university, and they come back because they can have careers. Trevor mentioned the importance of sustaining communities, and that is vital. So we do all that. Then, in terms of broadcasting, it allows us to do the ordinary things that every other TV channel does. We are now down to new content every week of just over 20%—21 %, or is it 23 %?— which is not a TV channel . If we slip below that, we can see audiences go away, particularly young audiences because , like everybody else, they are consuming Netflix and Apple TV . With BBC ALBA , u nless we have new content, they go away. We can see that in the weekly figures.

For example, one big thing that we did, and would like to do more of — I am sure you will ask us about the risks associated with spending all our drama budget on one big production; the board sat with the image of eggs in a basket — is that we took a calculated gamble that a big production in Gaelic could actually raise the profile of the channel and the language. We are delighted that happened, because “An t-Eilean ” was watched by 2 million people—more than 2 million now , because of the iPlayer. However, it also won best drama in public sector regional television in Europe, and also best programme in regional television in Europe, which shows you that there is no dearth of talent nor of storytelling ability. W e would love to do more high-profile drama.

If you think about it, we spent our entire budget for a year on a four-part series, and we would love to do more of that. In other programming, one of the previous contributors spoke about big gaps. There are big gaps in our schedule as well. We would love to do more programming. We would love to do more digital because, as we heard earlier, that is where the youth audience is going.

F or example, with our LearnGaelic and SpeakGaelic , which have been hugely important and have been welcomed by audiences and learners of the language, we now have nearly 50,000 people signed up to Facebook and learning Gaelic online. We can see that they are staying with us for over 20 minutes, which shows they are actually savouring the content. On Instagram, we are heading towards 110,000 followers, again showing the way that young people are consuming the content. We would love to do so much more than that.

In terms of finance, there was a figure that emerged in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords that said that MG ALBA spent £420 per G aelic speaker while S4C spent £260 per Welsh speaker. Honestly, we looked at that figure and were bemused by it . W hen you look at the budget that Wales ha s and the budget that we ha ve , how do you slice and dice th o se figures to come up with that figure ? W ho has done that ?

W hat we found was that if you add all the sums that go into Gaelic broadcasting and then take the lowest number of speakers, which is those who are totally fluent in Gaelic — 69, 000 or 70,000 — then you get that figure. T he latest census showed that the number of speakers of Gaelic had actu ally gone up to 130,000, which is a doubling in ten years. BBC ALBA has played a critical role in that alongside Gaelic - medium education.

Also, i f you are going to do that calculation, that is the least helpful figure for us , because every week 360 , 000 people in Scotland tune in to BBC ALBA— 360,000. Then you look at the figures. I seriously ask the Committee to look at that figure with a fairly jaundiced eye, because we think it is flawed.

Q60 I was going to ask you a little bit more about the issue of parity and the numbers of speakers but, t aking your point about that particular figure, was it calculated in the same way for S4C, or do you think it ha s been calculated differently?

I do not know. We do not know, unless you have depth of knowledge, Donald. C ertainly , if you take S4 C’s budget and MG ALBA’s budget — even when you add the BBC — it is very difficult to calculate how you can get to that figure. I think it is by taking the lowest number of speakers, the highest amount of money , i f you add the money that we receive at MG ALBA, and then add ing in the BBC contribution . T hen you get a figure divided by the lowest number of speakers. But the lowest number is people who use the language daily. We then have the same number again who are learners , a lot of whom are approaching fluency now and have shown by their interest that they want to continue.

T hen you add in the 360,000 people who tune in every week. I f you look at when we do the really high - end productions , which we would like to do more of, more than 2 million people watched “An t-Eilean ” . I do not know exactly how it was calculated.
Q61 What is the annual budget? What i s the actual figure? I can see the figure for the Welsh and Irish.
W e were working with £ 13.4 million , a nd it was stuck there for about ten years. L ast year , we got an uplift of about £ 2 million , so o ur annual budget is £ 15 million now.
Q62 Where does that come from?

That comes from the Scottish Ministers. T he way I ha ve described us previously is that we are like the orphan child of British broadcasting because everybody loves us ; w e were set up by Westminster ; w e are regulated by Ofcom ; w e have a very valuable and productive partnership with the BBC ; we ar e funded by Scottish Ministers , b ut somehow, somewhere , we fall between the stools . W e need somebody to take charge of where we are going and mak e sure that we have a proper settlement.

Q63 Mr McCullo ugh, S4 C currently has a multi - year funding settlement and TG4 is also hoping to secure multi - year funding. W hat would the benefits be of multi - year funding for MG ALBA and BBC ALBA ?

I t is interesting to go to that question on the basis of what Mr Morrison has just been saying because, of course, we have both MG ALBA funded by the Scottish Government and BBC ALBA—t he BBC ’s channel — which is funded by MG ALBA and by the BBC through the licence fee. T here i s the funding that MG ALBA brings to the channel, and there i s the funding that the licence fee brings to the channel. When the channel started in 2007-08, as the Chair will remember from her previous life, the BBC invested £4 million of licence fee funding and there was investment through MG ALBA from the Scottish Government, which, as the Committee has just heard, has got stuck for some period of time .

In that same period of time , despite the BBC’s revenue decreasing in real terms by over £1 billion, investment from the BBC in BBC ALBA has gone up by more than inflation. If you applied the inflation rate to that £4 million original investment, you would get something like £7.5 million. We now spend £10 million on BBC ALBA and then further investment on Radio nan Gàidheal , BBC Online and so on.

There is no less certainty of the BBC’s investment in the channel than there is in any other BBC service. We treat our investment in BBC ALBA exactly the same as we would BBC One, BBC Radio 2, Radio Scotland and Radio nan Gàidheal . There is the certainty of licence fee funding for all that we do, to an extent, but, as Mr Doogan was saying in the previous session, there is a real challenge and a threat to that licence fee, which probably impacts multi-year anything.

The licence fee settlement as it is at the moment ends in August 2028. We are in the slightly strange position where 93% of the population of the United Kingdom use the BBC every month, but only 78% of households are paying for it. There is a large and growing gap between the number of people who are paying for their public service media, including BBC ALBA and BBC Radio nan Gàidheal , and the costs of providing them. The real threat is around the sustainability of funding generally to all the BBC’s services and no service is exempt from that. I would say that the BBC’s contribution to BBC ALBA has been more than steady. It has been growing. However, we entered that as a partnership model, and it is vital that the partnership as a whole continues to grow and have some certainty.
Q64 Mr Morrison, can you give any specific examples of projects or investments that would be easier to pursue if MG ALBA operated within a multi-year funding framework?

If you take “An t-Eilean ”, the high-level drama, for example, that rarely fits neatly within a financial year. Therefore, it would be easier to plan ahead for high-level drama. The other important element for our viewers is that we like to think of ourselves as the home of women’s football. At BBC ALBA, we show a lot of women’s football and it has been fantastic for the game and very good for the channel as well. However, sports rights are negotiated over a three or four-year period. This comes very high up the risk register for the board when we have to say, “Do we commit to this?” The answer is, “Yes, we want to commit to it, but we have no guarantee that we can fulfil that commitment without the multi-year.”

There is a risk there. It would bring security for us, but it is not just for MG ALBA; it is for the people who work for us. It is the jobs that are involved in showing these games on TV. Women’s football is one of the fastest growing sports in the world. In Scotland, BBC ALBA’s coverage of it has contributed to that, but it is not helped by not having a multi-year deal.

Q65 Mr McCullough, since 2017 BBC ALBA has been regulated through the BBC’s wider operating licence rather than a distinct service-specific framework. Has the move to a broader BBC-wide regulatory model strengthened or weakened protections for Gaelic-language broadcasting?

Ofcom’s operating licence for the BBC is as strong a regulatory footing as any. BBC ALBA is regulated in exactly the same way as BBC One, Radio Scotland, BBC Radio Wales or any of the other linear services we have. The operating licence makes a number of clear provisions for Gaelic, which I think are really helpful . In terms of BBC ALBA, it determines that there will be a weekday evening news programme that is provided entirely from licence fee funds. It is broadcast live from Inverness every evening in the studios there. The operating licence also provides for a news review programme at the weekend and, beyond the BBC ALBA conditions, for learning in Gaelic.

Our learning provision, yes, exists on BBC ALBA, but also in our partnership SpeakGaelic and the Bitesize service that we offer for children and learners. There is provision for regular news on Radio nan Gàidheal through the day and for Gaelic content on the BBC website, particularly the news content, which again operates primarily out of Inverness, Stornoway, Portree and Glasgow, although also through journalists based in the Scottish Parliament.

The regulatory system therefore underpins all that, but it also allows creative freedom for us and those who co-commission with us. Margaret Mary will be able to talk about our content decisions but, working with our partners, in the licence we need a bit of freedom to stay where the audience is. If you get too prescriptive and have very specific licence conditions, you end up moving quite quickly away from perhaps what was the intention at the time that the licence was set. If you look at the charter 20 years ago, for example, which came into force in about 2007, it did not envisage BBC ALBA or iPlayer, and yet within about 18 months, both those things existed and became absolutely part of the weft and weave of the culture of Scotland and the UK.

I think you need a framework that not only sets the minimum requirements—particularly around how we serve as journalism and tell the story of Scotland to itself—but allows for creative freedom and the ability to make editorial decisions that move with the times.
Q66 What opportunities does the BBC charter review present to update and strengthen the long-term sustainability of Gaelic-language broadcasting?

In our BBC response to the UK Government’s Green Paper, we said how important the languages that the BBC operates in remain and how important we see them remaining in the future. Obviously, like everything else, that requires sustainable funding for public broadcasting and for the BBC as we move into the future, but I would expect the charter to underpin the fact that we have services in Welsh and in Gaelic, with that freedom to respond at the speed that the audience needs, and perhaps also to give a nod to the other languages that we work with.

I know that this morning the Committee has heard about Gaelic Irish in the Republic of Ireland, and about Welsh. The BBC also works with the Northern Ireland Screen broadcast fund, which the witnesses earlier mentioned, to produce content—Government-funded via Northern Ireland Screen—in Ulster Scots and in the Irish language, in Northern Ireland, sometimes working in Irish in partnership with TG4, who you heard from earlier.
In Cornwall, we are working—again in a partnership model—with Cornwall council. They have helped us invest in a “Learn Cornish” podcast , and we present the news in Cornish on BBC Radio Cornwall.

We also have a partnership with Manx Radio in the Isle of Man, where we help support learning in Manx with some Manx output. The charter needs to allow the BBC to continue to evolve that provision in a way that future-proofs it and does not tie it to one particular model and—provided that sustainable funding is found—gives a way for those language services to grow and flourish as the future demands.
Q67 Mr Morrison, what are the implications for Gaelic-language broadcasting if the charter review does not result in more stable funding and a statutory framework?

I would not be overstating it by saying it would be catastrophic for us. If you were running any sort of private company and the value of your turnover had reduced by 45% over a decade, that trajectory would be very concerning indeed. The most important thing for us is that it is not just about MG ALBA or BBC ALBA itself, but about the whole language and the importance of the language to the increasing number of young people who are learning it now and who are embracing it.

As we heard from earlier speakers, it is important that we are no longer just a linear TV channel; we are having to work on multi-platforms. Again, colleagues in the Celtic countries got serious support—millions of pounds—to help them diversify in the dash to digital, as we call it, but we got no money to support us with that. If that continues, we would be in a serious place and so would the language, because we are the most visible representation of Gaelic that exists anywhere in the world. Where would all the young people who are going through Gaelic-medium education go and watch sport, music, drama and television in their own language? We cannot continue on this trajectory.
Q68 Do you see the fates of both as quite closely intertwined?

They are absolutely linked. We would like to say that since MG ALBA has existed and BBC ALBA came on to screens, we have seen a doubling of the number of people with ability in the language. There are two key factors in that, and they are Gaelic-medium education and BBC ALBA.

There is another thing we do. I have spoken to a lot of musicians about the explosion in traditional music and the number of traditional bands playing Gaelic music, and they are now exporting that all over the world. The first platform they had for this was Gaelic radio and television, and you are now looking at potentially hundreds of people earning a living from music. Again, would they have done this anyway? Maybe they would have, but we gave them the platform that allowed them the confidence to express themselves on stage and on television, and to export this music.

Q69 Looking to 2028, what would you say matters most for the future of Gaelic broadcasting: statutory recognition in the UK’s public service broadcasting framework or guaranteed long-term funding? Or do you see them as equally important?
Can I be greedy and say both?
I thought that might be the answer.
I will say both, and the reason for that is, if you have statutory status, it makes it easier to make the arguments for funding. I would have to say that we need both.

It is important to say as well that, on your Committee website, the word “jeopardy” is used. There is another side to that, because if the Government make the right decision with the charter, you are creating a huge opportunity. In terms of finance, there is not far to go between jeopardy and the sort of catastrophic outcome I am telling you about here, and creating a world of opportunity where we create hundreds of jobs in rural areas and communities, strengthen communities, and use the Gaelic language.
Q70 How do you see long-term funding being linked to statutory recognition?

That is one for the politicians, isn’t it? This is maybe where I diverge slightly from BBC colleagues: we really do not care where the money comes from, whether it is BBC or elsewhere. Looking at the programme for Government and the rationalisation that has been planned for in Scotland, our money is not going to double overnight, but this is our road for the Committee to recommend to DCMS how you would go about doing it.

The EY report said that if our money had kept pace with inflation, we would be sitting at around £30 million now, rather than £15 million, so we are talking about £15 million to get us back to where I think we should be. Is that enough? Compared to the other Celtic countries, we would still be way behind, but it would make a big change for us, as well as creating digital content, sustaining the language and all the kids coming out of Gaelic-medium education, and creating jobs in communities.
Q71 You said that you did not mind, in a sense, where the money came from, but how important in reality is the contribution from the BBC in supporting the work that BBC ALBA does?

The BBC has been very important. When you look historically, the BBC has been broadcasting in Gaelic for 100 years. I think that without the BBC, Gaelic broadcasting probably would not exist—there might be small pockets here and there—and the language would be in a much worse condition that it currently is. The BBC has been hugely important. Mr McCullough has explained that the contributions from the BBC have increased above the level of inflation, so we welcome that. The BBC still has a cachet, and the three letters are very important for us.

Q72 Chair, can I ask a question on that point? From the evidence we have heard this morning, the BBC funding has increased every year. It was originally £4 million and it has gone up to £10 million, so the BBC is increasing funding in line with inflation, if not higher than inflation. The problem seems to be your core funding from the Scottish Government. From what I can see and have heard in the evidence today, that has largely flatlined since the inception at roughly £13 million, with just a small increase in 2025. The problem lies with the Scottish Government flatlining your budget, does it not?

I suppose the facts speak for themselves. The funding was frozen for 10 years and, like anything that is frozen for 10 years, broadcasting inflation tends to run above inflation elsewhere. They were not our figures; we brought in experts to do the analysis.

Yes, that is right. The BBC contribution has been valuable. It has given us the news and current affairs. We do “New Year’s C eilidh ”, which is probably the best new year’s show on television—it is a straightforward party, and it is good. But we cannot get away from the freezing of the funding for 10 years. It has been very bad for our income.
Q73 Ms Murray, beyond BBC ALBA, what role does the BBC play in supporting Gaelic-language broadcasting, and how significant are those contributions to the language?

As Mr Morrison said just now, the BBC has been broadcasting in Gaelic since 1923, and we have grown and developed our services over that time. We have a portfolio of services including BBC ALBA, but also critically BBC Radio nan Gàidheal , which is an audio service that can be heard throughout the world via BBC.com. You can hear the service live on a daily basis , but also enjoy a variety of podcasts, from learning to entertainment to the more recent addition of world cup content, which followed Scotland’s journey during those fateful weeks.

We offer a window or a door to the Gaelic language and culture through BBC ALBA. We also deliver a language-rich daily service for Gaelic speakers through Radio nan Gàidheal . We also have BBC Bitesize, which supports young people through their learning journey, from school all the way through to the latter stages of their education. We also partner with the BBC brands CBeebies and CBBC to deliver a daily schedule of children’s programmes. That has been the backbone of BBC ALBA, but it is also really attractive from an iPlayer point of view.

In terms of core public service genres, we have a new service that broadcasts hourly on Radio nan Gàidheal . Every evening it provides a live heartbeat for the TV channel. Increasingly, our news is being consumed via social and digital media, so we have seen a real growth in the consumption of our news on our recently added accounts on Instagram, Facebook and X. The BBC support Gaelic in a variety of ways through the core public service genres of news, current affairs, learning and children’s.

Recently, the partnership model has been reviewed in order to make sure that our partnership with MG ALBA is future facing. We are really ambitious for Gaelic broadcasting and the Gaelic language. That review of our partnership looked to drive digital growth, to invest more in content of high impact and to support the growth of the language, which we do through partnership services such as SpeakGaelic , which has undergone really impressive growth since its inception during the lockdown years. That is how the BBC supports the Gaelic language.

If I could just add, that renegotiation of the partnership, which was voluntary and entered into by both parties, ended up really strengthening the service. If I could also just add a little bit to my answer to you, Mr McAllister, we were frozen for 10 years. We have to give the former Deputy First Minister, Kate Forbes , credit: she found us an extra £2 million, which came in at the time that we were looking for funding for the second series of “ An t-Eilean ”, so that was—
A one-off?
A second-off of a drama; it was a one-off, but I think it’s—
It’s not annual core funding.
It’s not annual core funding.
It is now.
That bit is locked in, but we do not have a multi-year deal, so we do not know what we will get. We have not met the new Gaelic Minister yet, so we look forward to that meeting.

Q74 Some of us had the opportunity to visit the CBeebies set at the BBC, which I have to say was really fun . Mr McCullough, we have talked a lot today about parity between Welsh and Gaelic-language broadcasting. How significant is the BBC’s in-kind contribution to S4C in comparison?

It is different, but they are not like-for-like services. As I think your witnesses from S4C were saying earlier, it is a service that runs from 6 or 7 in the morning till midnight. BBC ALBA is a service that runs from 5 in the evening, when we start with the children’s content that Margaret Mary was just speaking about, and also runs till around midnight. In terms of the proportion of hours of broadcast, they are reasonably similar, but the model is different. The BBC is obviously making content in Gaelic for a BBC service. There is a lot of history of the BBC making content for S4C in Welsh that predates the channel’s existence.

They are different models and different systems, and there are different models for the other languages I was talking about earlier. A lot of the time people compare Welsh with Gaelic, but they are two different models with two different systems. Here is a partnership model on a BBC service; S4C is a different model, with different lengths of broadcast.

Our contribution to Cornish is very different again. Where the news in Cornish is broadcast once a week, in Gaelic we are broadcasting the news every hour. The number of speakers of Cornish is obviously lower, but it is not insignificant. Again, we are investing there to help more people learn.

We need to grow these partnerships and move at the right speed for the audience. I don’t think things should be the same—I don’t think anyone is saying they should be the same—but they should probably be broadly proportionate. I think the BBC’s contribution to BBC ALBA is broadly proportionate, but there are always opportunities to grow.
Q75 Luke, it has been reported that there are financial pressures on BBC Scotland. Is the cash for BBC ALBA protected in any way?

Nothing is protected at BBC Scotland at the moment , but we are not expecting our investment in BBC ALBA to change, particularly in the current financial year. BBC Scotland’s budget is under a lot of pressure, and we are on record as saying that, across the savings we are trying to deliver at the moment , we are trying to save around £10 million.

I know that if you look at £10 million in an S4C context, you would think that it is not enough. The entirety of our spend on BBC ALBA is also the equivalent of what we are looking to save in other areas of BBC Scotland at the moment , so we are under real pressure. The Committee will have seen some of that recently. We expect around 60 roles to close in BBC Scotland out of our headcount this year, and across the UK we are looking at around 2,000 people out of our workforce leaving the BBC over the next couple of years. These are really serious savings challenges.

However, over the 15 years that we have just come through—where, as I was saying to the Committee earlier, the licence fee income has dropped by over £1 billion in real terms—we have increased our investment in Gaelic, precisely because we know how important it is that the BBC is there to support speakers of minority languages. That is not least because, as Mr Morrison was saying, there are not many other people who are making that investment.

We are very grateful to have the partner to do that with, and we see the economic impact of that all around Scotland. We would not move away from that lightly, but I cannot stress enough that we are in really difficult times financially because of that growing gap between users and payers. You are seeing a real impact on our English-language services now. There are a number of Scottish titles that are not coming back for a second or third series, and a number of other titles that are coming back for shorter runs.

The coverage of this place—the politics programme on a Wednesday—will cease, so there will no longer be a Scottish Prime Minister’s questions programme on the basis that you can watch Prime Minister’s questions somewhere else. We are looking at shrinking the length of some of our radio news output. These are real, difficult decisions, but with less money, there will be less that we can do.
Q76 Ms Murray, at a time when the BBC is facing pressure about its own future, how can it ensure that investment in Gaelic broadcasting is protected?

The BBC’s investment in Gaelic broadcasting demonstrates real value for money in terms of the way we operate in partnership. With that investment, we can demonstrate that we operate a very lean structure. The content that we make and the models that we use to deliver content are also innovative. Recently, the BBC funded coverage of our Commonwealth Games, and we did that in a very innovative way, which offers the BBC some lessons and some learning in terms of how best to ensure that its investment goes as far as possible.
Q77 What assessment has been made of the potential consequences for BBC ALBA, Gaelic content production and the wider Gaelic media sector if further BBC savings are required?

The investment that we have is tight for the services that we deliver. However, that does not diminish the ambition that we have for the growth of the language. It is about recognising the value in that investment and how that value is demonstrated across the sector in jobs and in communities across Scotland.

Can I add a wee word there? I was with the BBC for many years. Because we are in this partnership, the partnership actually gives value to the BBC that is immeasurable in many ways, because of the diversity and the role of the BBC in representing all our communities. MG ALBA and BBC ALBA work together to represent some of the areas of the highlands and islands that are probably under-represented when you look across the whole of broadcasting. It is valuable and it helps the BBC deliver on its core purpose as well.

On the practical day-to-day side, all the Gaelic-speaking reporters that they employ also speak English, so if they end up doing a story they will often double up and do something for “Reporting Scotland”. In fact, one of the main contributors to “Reporting Scotland” for many years was from Inverness and was bilingual, and they did Gaelic and English broadcasting, so it is real value for money.
Mr Campbell, did you want to add something to that?

Yes, please. The discussion is dealing with the obvious deficits with Gaelic broadcasting at the moment . Those are laid out in our submissions here and elsewhere. Gaelic broadcasting is more than BBC ALBA; it is more than the BBC regulatory framework governing it. BBC ALBA is not just a portfolio channel within the BBC. BBC ALBA is the UK’s only Gaelic - language service, and it is delivered in a partnership between MG ALBA and the BBC. It fulfils the UK’s policy promise and its acceptance of the European charter for regional or minority languages that says there should be a Gaelic service.

The deficit that we have—and I think this will be apparent in what is coming— is that there is no mechanism that says, “This is what the licence fee will contribute, and this is what Scottish Ministers will contribute.” There is no compact that says clearly why that is important or how much it is going to be. That, in a nutshell, is what we are proposing. When we look at the discrepancies between the situation of Gaelic and that of Irish and Welsh, we see that, predominantly, they have that certainty as to why it is important, who is going to deliver it and how much resource is going to be allocated.

In some ways, one of the solutions is what S4C has, which is an allocation from the licence fee. If there was an allocation from the licence fee, that would answer the question about how funding could be protected. We are not looking for special protections, to be honest, because we realise that funding is tight in many ways. If there is a set of priorities that the UK Government and Parliament have in relation to Gaelic broadcasting, and those are shared by the Scottish Government and the Scottish Parliament, they should be provided for by both partners. It is our contention—or my contention, at least—that that should be brought out of the realm of management decision making. It should be policy-led decision making. I hope that is clear.
That is helpful. Thank you.

Q78 I am going to go on to tax relief and credits, which we discussed with the earlier panel. Margaret Mary , what tangible benefits has the UK Government’s audio-visual expenditure credit scheme delivered for Gaelic broadcasting?

I am delighted to say that Gaelic broadcasting and BBC ALBA have benefited from the tax credit, including on children’s content. Through the BBC’s delivery of children’s programmes, the tax credit has been applied, and that, in turn, delivers benefit and allows us to commission more original content. In the independent sector, again, children’s programmes, successful documentary programmes and drama programmes for children that have been part of the EBU scheme have also benefited from tax credit and partnership funding from Screen Scotland. I guess that the biggest area of benefit is in drama, where the first and second series of “An t-Eilean” benefited from the tax credit, which supplements the budget to a significant degree. It is a really valuable part of that funding cocktail for content.
Q79 Can you give us some sort of idea of how much it is worth, percentage-wise ?

In very rough terms, the threshold of £1 million an hour needs to be met for high-end AVEC or tax credit. Practically speaking, we need to find the funding for £800,000 of that, and the tax credits take it up to £1 million. The question that was addressed in the previous session was about those kinds of credits being more accessible and the financial limits or thresholds being set at a more reasonable level, particularly for minority-language content. The figure of £1 million an hour is a very high threshold for us to reach. We can do it only very occasionally, as with “An t-Eilean”, but if the threshold was much lower, as it is in Ireland, many more productions would qualify and the benefit to the economy and to the rural economy, where a lot of our business comes from, could be considerably greater.
Q80 Would that be your biggest ask of the UK Government just now—to reduce that threshold to a lot lower than £1 million?

Yes. There is a lot of interest looking for that to happen. The challenge is if it is set by the Treasury, it needs to wash its face in terms of bringing money in from the outside. It is there as a financial incentive to drive inward investment primarily, so it needs to pay for itself. When you reduce the thresholds too low and apply that to a lot of programming, the dividend needs to be as much about the cultural return or the investment in future economic growth as about immediate return through taxes, VAT and suchlike.
Q81 How many programmes have you had that have benefited from that? Is it just the one that we were speaking about earlier?

Some of the children’s programming benefits because there is no threshold; it is just kind of a test—and that is through the BBC’s arrangements. There have probably been five or six smaller dramas, with the European Broadcasting Union scheme, as well as series 1 and 2 of “ An t-Eilean ”—so very few.

In terms of the circular economy, the budget for “ An t-Eilean ” series 1 was £1 million per episode, so £4 million. Tax credits made up for roughly 20% of that. When we did some analysis on the spend, nearly £1 million of the £4 million was spent directly on hotels, bed and breakfasts, food suppliers in the Western Isles. Had we not done that, that £1 million would not have happened. That was for five weeks of filming. Series 2 has just finished filming. That was seven weeks, so we would expect to surpass the £1 million. You can actively see the money that has come to us for creating programmes, and then part of it—a quarter, roughly—being directly injected into economy.
Q82 John, are there any more schemes you would like to see to boost Gaelic broadcasting?

Oh, lots of schemes. But partnerships are the way forward. We have the partnership with the BBC, but MG ALBA is not prevented from seeking partnerships with other broadcasters—any of the streamers, for example—but we would need to have skin in the game and the money to put skin in the game in order to deliver a partnership. You can see that some of them—Netflix and the big streamers—are filming in Spain, but money will be coming in to make a contribution to that.

Q83 On that point about partnership funding, could the argument not be made that you deserve additional funding from other external agencies such as Creative Scotland and Scottish Enterprise if you are creating these programmes? You have demonstrated to us the vast economic benefit gained by the community in the highlands and islands. Surely funding should be coming from other sources.
Yes, and we did that for series 2. Do you want to break that down, Donald?

Yes. In series 2 of “ An t-Eilean ”, for example, the local authority and Highlands and Islands Enterprise both contributed to effectively ensure that it happened on that patch, because of the vast economic benefits. I think there is a wider point around this. Earlier in my job, I was tasked not just with spending money wisely, but with ensuring that every £1 received would generate a lot more value and other income. Last year, we had almost £5 million of additional investment into content that we were funding. It was not money into MG ALBA but it was money into the projects that we had initiated, such as “ An t-Eilean ” and documentaries.

Scotland represents a vast opportunity and a huge talent pool, if the funding is there to further support strategising —for international documentary making, for example. That is part of question in relation to the benefits of multi-annual funding. What would that permit you to do that you cannot currently do? One thing that it would permit would be a stepped approach to ensure that our documentary producers in the Gaelic language have the marketing, networking, idea development, and partnering opportunities to work in European and worldwide networks to originate ideas that broadcaster and agencies in other countries will support.

A very good example of is a Gaelic programme based out of South Uist , from a number of years ago. There were 14 partners, and 13 of them were agencies, Governments and broadcasters from the Baltic nations. We were a minority funder; it was a programme for BBC ALBA and for the Scandinavian and Baltic channels. I t is a documentary series with three episodes, about the art of yoiking —a very interesting show, by the way . That represents an example of the opportunity we have in Scotland, and Gaelic broadcasting and media are one of the catalysts for enabling that to happen. The skills are there, but what is not there is the stepped approach of “Let us invest over five years to try to get economic and cultural dividend out of this.”

It is also having the ability to do the investment. If you have 13 partners, that is a complex partnership that needs a legal framework. Another point I came across recently is that tourism organisations are aware of a phenomenon called set-jetting, which is when people come to the country to visit sets. It is usually those used by the high-profile, international sales, but Shetland has seen the benefit of that because of the seven or eight series there, and we hope that “An t-Eilean” will be similar. It is too early to judge the impact on the Western Isles, but it is very difficult to get a bed in Stornoway these days.

Those partnerships and the economic benefits apply to pretty much everything we make in Scotland, both in Gaelic and in English. As this Committee has heard before, in our English-language content, we are increasingly requiring partners to be able to make stuff of the scale and to the level that the audience expects. When Louise Thornton appeared as a witness before the Committee, she shared the fact that the BBC drama “The Ridge” had been funded by BBC Scotland, yes, but also by Sky New Zealand, and ended up being filmed in both Scotland and New Zealand as a result of that partnership.

We have also discussed at length the investment of the BBC in “The Traitors” with this Committee. We commissioned an economic impact report on that and, as Mr Morrison has said, when you talk to people at VisitScotland or Trainline, you can see the absolute impact on requests about journeys to the highlands and Inverness. We think that the first three series of that added about £22 million of GVA to the highland economy, so there is a definitive impact of having public investment in content filmed in Scotland, in Gaelic and in English, on tourism, economic development and jobs. We can see that tangibly, with everything that we produce.

Q84 That is very interesting. Mr Morrison, the Media Act 2024 modernised the statutory remit of S4C. If the statutory remit of MG ALBA were updated in a similar way, would that be enough to make a difference to its future sustainability, or do we need to do something structural as well?

Sustainability usually takes you back to budget; that is probably what will deliver sustainability. Legislation is important, and being mentioned and getting parity in legislation would be hugely important—not just for BBC ALBA and MG ALBA, but for the language and the confidence of language speakers—but sustainability usually goes back to budget.
Q85 If we take out the financial side, do other structural things need to be done, as well as looking for an updated remit?

Absolutely. Our position is that the BBC charter should address Gaelic specifically, not as a subset of the BBC’s nations and regions. As I said before, Gaelic broadcasting is a matter of UK policy and is delivered in partnership, so is not solely a BBC concern. There is a regulatory framework point. At the moment , it is entirely through the prism of the BBC operating licence. For example, last year, Ofcom’s review of the performance of the BBC was 74 pages long, with six lines dedicated to BBC ALBA. My question is whether that is enough about the contribution of BBC ALBA for there to be in the public domain—other than what we say in MG ALBA’s annual report, which is quite full. Is it enough for the regulator and UK public policy to say, “That was a good job—well done,” “That was a poor job,” “Could you do better here?” and so on?

The lack of structural provision means that we rely, sometimes quite beneficially, on the BBC remembering that there is a Gaelic priority among the other thousand and one priorities that it currently has. A special statutory or charter designation for the partnership that delivers Gaelic broadcasting would give Gaelic a seat at the table beside S4C, STV, the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5. As John alluded to, the Green Paper that was published a short while ago by DCMS was very inclusive of Welsh language, but there was not a mention of Gaelic language, and that is because the structural provision is not there. We rely on people to remember that it is there.
That is very interesting. Thank you.

Q86 Mr McCullough, drawing on your experience with S4C, what are the most important features of the Welsh - language broadcasting model that are currently absent from the BBC ALBA framework? Which, if any, do you think would have the greatest impact on the long-term sustainability of Gaelic broadcasting if applied to BBC ALBA?

Again, I think the models are different. In Wales, the BBC provides two radio stations in Welsh—Radio Cymru and Radio Cymru 2 ­ —as part of the way that that service has grown and evolved over time. Those are obviously BBC services, and alongside that you have an independent broadcaster, S4C, which is presenting the content that your witnesses described to you earlier. In some ways, I would say that there is more of an opportunity to share content services and, as Margaret Mary was saying earlier, to maximise value for money in a model in which we are working in close partnership in everything we do, compared with models in which you have multiple players. The histories of the two languages and the broadcast services of the two languages are very different.

It is likewise with the other languages that we are working in. We have been on a journey with Ulster Scots and the Irish language in Northern Ireland through the Northern Ireland Screen broadcast fund. Again, it is a very different model. We are commissioning both audio and video content within the BBC portfolio but also with partners from time to time. With Cornish, we work with the local authority in Cornwall to try to drive uptake of the language, which itself will hopefully generate further content in due course.

I do not feel that one model is better than another. It is important that the public broadcaster of the United Kingdom can work in an appropriate way with the languages. We said in our Green Paper response that we know how important the language services that the BBC provides are. We are absolutely committed to them but, at the risk of sounding slightly like a broken record, it is subject to sustainable funding for the BBC. Your witnesses from S4C said that earlier about their contributions from the BBC. They recognise the jeopardy around the funding of public broadcasting at the moment .
Q87 John, how important has showing Italian football been to promoting the Gaelic language?
Very important. As I said earlier, we see ourselves as the home of women’s football in Scotland. It has been good for the channel, and it has also been very good for the women’s game in Scotland.

If I were to sum up the board’s philosophy and strategy, I suppose it is basically to be brave. We need to be noticed and to try to make as much of an impact as we can with the budget. Pre the run-up to the world cup, we managed to get eight games from Serie A involving the Scottish stars playing in Italy. That was fantastic. It drew in an audience. To go back to the figures that I was explaining to the Chair, it brought in football fans—Gaelic speakers and non-Gaelic speakers—and it was really good with the youth audience. We saw a real spike in new content—fresh, interesting and probably surprising content—on BBC ALBA. That has been really important .

Looking ahead, Serie A came to us to ask whether we want to continue doing that. We again have a partnership, this time with BBC Sport on the iPlayer. We will do 19 games on BBC ALBA, and BBC Sport will do 19 games on Serie A.

Sport is hugely important for us, as is music, and so is drama, because all these things have an interest that transcends any linguistic barriers that exist. The barriers exist, but football is slightly different. The technology is improving, and we will get subtitles with live commentary—that technology is not far away. With football, you see the sport, and if you are a football fan, you want to watch.

Q88 I am trying to understand the driver behind it. Is it about trying to increase the numbers, even though it is not really promoting the Gaelic language? Or is it about promoting the Gaelic language?

It is absolutely about promoting the Gaelic language. Part of our drive is to take the Gaelic language to new audiences and to increase interest in it, so that when people watch things they think, “Actually, I’d quite like to learn this language. Why can’t I learn it?” That is shown in the huge increase in the number of people who are logging into SpeakGaelic , our language series, which is one of the most successful things we do. All these things are interlinked.

Why do we do sport? Because lots of people are interested in it. We saw a deal and we went for it. Similarly, the Commonwealth G ames were in the English language behind a paywall; we came in and did the sport in Gaelic. Again, the audience on the iPlayer was fantastic, and on the channel it was really good as well. We did not have studio content; we just focused entirely on the sport, because we thought that was what people want to see. If they are watching live sport, there is less of a linguistic barrier.
Q89 If you were watching that on iPlayer, for example, could you choose the commentary in different languages? How did that work? Was it just in Gaelic?

The commentary in English was from TNT—Warner Bros.—and in Gaelic we were free-to-air. The only place you could see it free-to- air was with us. S4C had a deal for coverage in the Welsh language, but we could not do anything in English.
Q90 In terms of the percentage of your budget, how much are you spending on, for example, Italian football?

I need to do the arithmetic in my head. The way we work is that we are not spending an awful lot on rights per se. We are spending money on rights, obviously, but it is a very small amount, relatively speaking. The cost of these things is usually in production, so that is part of the balance that we have to work out. If, for example, we take a package for Scottish women’s football, the SPFL, rugby or Serie A, that means we are not just able to show those games but, quite often, we have got to show those games. We then have to find the producer who is going to produce that.

The way we budget out is that we have one of these multi-year deals that we have been talking about with a sports provider—just extended for a couple of years—and that gives us security of what we are going to be paying. Within that, there is a portfolio of a lot of different ways that the thing could shape out. We have to move things around to make sure—to do Italian football, we have to do a little less of something else.

We can work out the cost of it. At MG ALBA we spend roughly a quarter of our content budget on sport, and that delivers about 60% of our audience on a weekly basis, so the return by audience is really good . As you will know, sport is on the up and up and up. You just cannot get enough sport with broadcasters now, and live, event-based television is really important .

One of the things it does for us, as a minority language broadcaster, is that not only are Gaelic speakers, users or learners interested in sport the same way as anyone else is interested in it, but there is a normalisation effect of the language. People are not necessarily saying, “Gosh, it’s a bit strange that BBC ALBA’s covering Italian sport.” But our response to that would be, “Well, the English language handles Italian sport and the Welsh language handles Italian sport. Why shouldn’t the Gaelic language handle Italian sport?” What distinctions are people drawing in their minds that would say, “Oh no, Gaelic broadcasting is only for a certain number of things,” or, “The Gaelic language is only for a certain number of things”?

It is a very deep part of the language revitalisation strategy that Gaelic is just normalised. It is a normal thing. It is just a language people speak. It has the right to cover whatever territory it wants, provided that it finds an appreciative audience for it, and in our context we can demonstrate that it is value for money.

It is so important for the confidence of young people to be speaking the language, and to be speaking it on a daily basis when they can say to people, “Did you see the Italian football on BBC ALBA last night?” It is hugely important. We do not see any barrier to doing any aspect of the world in Gaelic. The only barrier is usually—

Q91 You mentioned 360,000 viewers. My only concern is that with some of these sports things, people perhaps are not really engaging in Gaelic or learning it, and they are really about boosting the viewing figures—that is one thing, which is great—to justify extra funding later on . If I were to put that to you, would you say it is completely wrong?

I would never say it is completely wrong, but what I would say is that we have to do what is of interest to our audience. A lot of research goes into that, and the percentages that Donald just described show that our audience love sport, and we want to provide sport for them. And how do you make the language relevant to the lives of people and increase their interest in it? By giving them what they want in that language.

It is about overall audience access to sport as well, at a time when sports rights and broadcaster access to them have come under a huge amount of pressure. The ability of MG ALBA and indeed the BBC, who acquired the Commonwealth Games rights in Gaelic, as Margaret Mary was saying, to get that content to the audience in Scotland is vital. The sports rights market in English has more than doubled in cost since 2010, at a time when—we went through the history earlier—the licence fee has been either flat or just going up with inflation. During a period when BBC resources have been really tight , our ability to get rights in English to serve the audience has been extremely constrained.

We have been able to open up the market in Gaelic rights and put that in front of all our audiences, not just those who are speaking the language, because it is a BBC service and it appears on the “ N ew & T rending” rail when you open up iPlayer and people think, “Oh, there’s some live sport on there. Oh, it’s in Gaelic; that’s fine, I’ll watch that.” You could see that with a number of the sports that we were covering. We were not able to do that with the Commonwealth G ames , in terms of “N ew & T rending ” , for various other rights reasons, but generally speaking you can bring Gaelic sport to the prominence of English - language sport, and we find the audience generally will come.
Q92 So could it be a lot cheaper to show it in Gaelic as opposed to English? Is that how the licensing works?

I will not get into specifics, but you are in a market, and I suspect that the market for Welsh - language rights, Gaelic - language rights, and Manx and Cornish rights for sport would be of lower value than the English - language rights, not least because of global markets who will come to English.

I do not think you are going to see the English premiership on BBC ALBA any time soon. We have, as you correctly pointed out, to look for that balance between audience, value for money, interest and growth of the language. We balance all those things, and we thought, because of the number of Scottish players playing in Italy right now, that that would be of interest to our audience. When we say “our audience”, we mean Gaelic speakers, Gaelic learners and everybody else who is interested in football.

We see with SpeakGaelic that the people who are logging in and then going on to additional courses in learning the language have usually come in because they have heard the language through either music or sport. We also do a lot of shinty, which seems like a very natural game for us to do, and the number of young Gaelic speakers coming through the teams—all the teams, male and female—has increased over the over the years as well. There is a language growth there. That figure of 69,000 Gaelic speakers increased to 130,000 in the decade up to 2022. BBC ALBA undoubtedly played a big part in that, and sport and music are key, because they attract young people.

Sport opens the door to public media for a lot of the audience who might not find it otherwise. When Hayley Valentine, the director of BBC Scotland, was before this Committee, she talked about the fact that the BBC had reacquired the men’s international football rights after a long period when they were not on the BBC. We know that a good chunk of the people who came to iPlayer to watch, for example, Scotland versus Denmark, had not been to iPlayer at all for months beforehand, and within a couple of weeks of watching the Scotland-Denmark match they came back for something else because they had found other public content that they had either forgotten about or had not engaged with. It opens the door to people consuming public service content that they might not otherwise find.

If I could just add one thing, the point that you raise is important about how this is not about chasing numbers for us. It is not about even the BBC’s objectives in terms of serving its audiences. For us, it is a minority Gaelic - language service. We are looking to create opportunities for people to encounter the language. Those have to be widespread. It is not the numbers that any of us are chasing. It is the difference that it can make from having an encounter and bringing people in, opening up a pathway towards language awareness, language participation, and being a creator in language, perhaps as a parent or whatever putting the children through a Gaelic-medium education and learning the language. Those are the important steps. That is a different perspective from English - language broadcasting. There is a purpose to what we are doing, which is quite different in that sense. In some ways it is the same and in that way it is different.

Can I add a tiny wee thing and say that yes, we like numbers as well? We look at the numbers for “ An t-Eilean ” , and over 2 million people have watched it. It is hugely reassuring for us as creators that this is something that is so attractive that it brought in 2 million people to watch it. They loved it. The feedback has been huge. Nobody cared whether it was in the English language because we are all consuming content now on our phones or on our laptops or iPads with subtitles. But it is in Gaelic. It raised the profile of the language, and we would like to do more of it.

Q93 I guess when you look at drama there are other benefits: as we have mentioned, there is tourism and the jobs that it brings to the area. When you look at investing in Italian football, there is none of that.

There is—there is interest. You cannot just do one thing with that scripted drama, and then you have sport. You do not have a TV channel that just does drama. It probably exists somewhere in the digital sphere, but we need to provide a balance of programmes.

Thank you. That concludes our question session for this morning. Thank you all for coming along today. It is always very interesting to hear what is happening and to look forward to the future. I am certainly looking forward to the new Serie A, which will be great fun. Thank you all very much indeed.

sessions.w: The National Education Union (NEU); National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT); Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL); NASUWT - The Teachers' Union

segs.tx: Education Committee
Oral evidence: ‘ Every Child Achieving and Thriving ’ White Paper , HC 430
Tuesday 1 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 1 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Helen Hayes (Chair); Jess Asato; Sureena Brackenridge; Manuela Perteghella; Mark Sewards; Peter Swallow; Caroline Voaden.
Questions 1-3 3
Witnesses
I : Alun Francis OBE, Chair, Social Mobility Commission , Daniel Lilley, Head of Youth, Centre for Social Justice and Julie McCulloch, Chief Executive, The Education Policy Institute .

II : James Bowen, Assistant General Secretary, National Association of Head Teachers , Mrs Julia Harnden, Deputy Director of Policy, Association of School and College Leaders , Daniel Kebede, General Secretary, The National Education Union and Darren Northcott, National Official, NASUWT .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Alun Francis, Daniel Lille y and J ulie McCulloch.

I welcome everybody to this oral evidence session of the Education Committee, and I welcome colleagues back from summer recess. This is the first evidence session in our new inquiry in which we are scrutinising the Government’s White Paper entitled “Every child achieving and thriving” ahead of what we believe will be legislation coming forward later in the autumn or early in the new year. We are also scrutinising the White Paper in the light of some subsequent policy announcements that the new Administration has been making over the summer.
I would like to thank our witnesses for joining us today. I will invite each of you to introduce yourselves, but before I do, I invite Committee members to make any declarations of interest.

I declare that I am the chair of the all-party parliamentary group for schools, learning and assessment, the secretariat of which is the NEU. We have just produced a report on votes at 16, which might be relevant today.
I declare that I am a former member of ASCL.
Now we will go to introductions from our witnesses.
My name is Daniel Lilley. I am the head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.
Good afternoon, everyone. I am Julie McCulloch, chief executive of the Education Policy Institute. Thank you very much for enabling me to join this session remotely.

Hello, everybody, and thank you very much for also allowing me to join remotely. My name is Alun Francis. I am the chair of the Social Mobility Commission and I am the chief executive of Blackpool and The Fylde College, which also includes Furness College in Barrow.

Q1 I will lead off our questioning with a question about some of the changes in policy. We have the White Paper, which is the Government’s formal statement of current policy, but over the summer the new Prime Minister announced further changes to policy specifically around technical pathways and the delivery of technical and vocational education in secondary schools, as well as plans for devolution. I would like to ask, first, for your understanding of how the new announcements have an impact on the existing White Paper and the impact that they will have on schools seeking to navigate one policy change and then a further evolution and iteration of the policy that has come subsequently.

My opening comment is that it is probably not entirely clear yet how much of the White Paper the new Prime Minister and Secretary of State remain entirely committed to and how much they want to change or align with different priorities. So this is my best understanding as things stand.

In terms of the new changes that we are expecting, our view as an organisation is that there is a lot to admire about England’s education, but we think there continue to be some significant challenges. We think it is a system that works very well for some children and young people in some ways but much less well for those from disadvantaged backgrounds, which is one of our major areas of focus, and those with SEND, and also in promoting pupil engagement and strong mental health for all children and young people. So we definitely think there is a case for delivering on many of the proposals that are in the White Paper as it stands but also for thinking whether there is more that we can do in those areas.

We think there are things that need to change. We definitely think that improved technical education, as the Prime Minister is now proposing, should be one of those changes. It feels to us as if the system is still very much one in which the default assumption is that young people will follow an academic pathway, with options for those who want to follow a more technical or vocational pathway being both fewer and much more complicated to navigate. We are pleased to see those changes, but the challenge—as you are alluding to in this question, Chair—is how the system can navigate and understand both the direction of travel set out in the White Paper and what changes we might see now.

In terms of those newer changes, it is important that they are done carefully, drawing on relevant evidence and not undermining the academic improvements that we have seen over the past decade, and that they recognise many of the reasons for the disadvantage gap and the shocking number of young people not in education, employment or training. Many of the ways that we tackle those challenges sit within education, but many more sit outside it, in the labour market, health, social care and welfare. In summary, we are warm to the changes in the White Paper and to those that the new Administration is hoping to bring in, but there is a lot of devil in the detail in how those two slightly separate visions at the moment are brought together and how we make sure that both are delivered in a really clear and evidence-informed way.

That was a really coherent summary of some of the areas where we are clear and not clear. To pick up first on the technical pathways, obviously that is my specialism and my day job, and something we in the Social Mobility Commission are keen on. We have been keen to see a much stronger technical pathway alongside the university pathway. It is clearly the case that over a long period of time, one has had much more attention and funding than the other.

I will make a couple of observations about the whole academic or technical debate, though. The first point to make is that everybody has some of both at some point in their career. We all start off with general academic education, in primary and most of secondary. There is then a question mark about when we move over to some more technical training. Some people do that at 16, particularly things like craft trades, construction and so forth. Others do it at 18, particularly higher and degree apprenticeships, which now allow you to start your degree a little bit earlier, in the workplace. Others start their technical vocational training after they have completed their degree—the typical examples would be medicine, law and teaching—so I think we have to be careful not to set them up as opposites. They are very much complementary and have a large degree of overlap.

That leads me to a second point, which is that we must not confuse technical education as an alternative to academic learning, because actually there is so much overlap between them. The best technical education requires really strong academic skills. You can see that in the way that, for example, T-levels have been constructed, and in apprenticeships, which frequently require good English and good maths. We must avoid the idea that they are somehow alternatives to each other.

That being said, there is a great deal about attraction. Some people find the applied learning of an apprenticeship or a technical course more appealing and motivating than they find academic study. I do not think that is necessarily reflective of academic ability; I just think it is about motivation and interest. The question we then have to ask ourselves is, at what point do we allow people to make that transition? The notion of having clearer pathways from 14 is a really good one in the sense that it is very helpful for young people—this comes out of the research on NEETs and various other sources—to have a clear line of sight to work, to understand how the qualifications they are studying can help them to move in the direction of the career that they want to go into. Whether that means that we need to start to think about a 14-to-16 technical curriculum in schools involves some really hard questions that we have to ask.

The first point to make is that, when we taught technical education in schools before, we did it really badly. We ended up devaluing the qualifications and actually encouraging young people to take courses that schools were very keen for them to take, because they improved league table performance, but in all honesty, the young people would arrive at college not ready for the workplace or to progress, and they would have to resit quite a bit of work that they had done. That was the work that the Wolf review challenged in vocational qualifications becoming less valuable.

We will also need to think about whether young people are ready, at 14, to make those choices, which can be quite weighty. As you probably know, in Europe the system works differently—but it is the whole system that works differently, as well as the labour market. We need to bear that in mind. That being said, my college currently delivers a 14-to-16 programme for a group of local schools; under the right circumstances, with the right, skilled tutors, the right kit and equipment, and the right facilities, such programmes can be powerful additions to the general curriculum.

My final point is that there is potentially a role for strategic authorities and mayors to think about how they can broker that kind of provision, as long as it is of high quality and an actual choice for the student that sits alongside their other choices, and as long as students have a clear line of sight to work and it is not presented as, “Well, we just want to get you out of class and into something else because we do not know what to do with you.”

If the provision is brokered in that way, groups of schools working with colleges could be productive in thinking what a 14-to-16 pathway might look like. The broader Manchester baccalaureate philosophy—thinking about careers and groups of choices that lead to careers—definitely does not always mean changing the curriculum; it just means helping young people to get the right work experience and so on. There are some really productive ideas to be brought in that regard. I will stop there.

A lot of ground was covered there, so I will just make two short comments. The first interesting thing is that the White Paper—broadly speaking and zooming out—emphasised continuity in synthesising what had come before. It is not yet clear that the implication of this announcement has been that it will emphasise discontinuity from what has come before.

At the Centre for Social Justice, we are cautiously optimistic about the idea of technical education at 14. We have advocated for it and worked with the now Prime Minister on it while he was Mayor of Greater Manchester. But we really think that it should sit within the continuity framework of the White Paper. Some things will need relitigating in terms of how we look at the EBacc, Attainment 8 and Progress 8. If the policy is to function well and not look second rate, those things have to be relitigated. But in general we would really like it to be integrated within that continuity document, which we think synthesises a lot of really good work.

Q2 There is some concern, based on past experience in this country, about technical education; as Alun said, it has not always been delivered very well. The concern is about the risk of a technical pathway from 14 resulting essentially in a limitation of the academic aspirations of some children and proving to be a constraint on social mobility for children from some backgrounds.

Briefly, what policies, mechanisms and checks and balances need to be built into the new system—each of you has broadly welcomed the intention—that would guard against the risk of its becoming a limiting factor on some children’s aspirations, rather than a broadening of aspirations and outcomes?

There are three points in particular. The first is about what the policy is seeking to achieve. It will go wrong if it is designed as something for children who are failing in education; that would be incompatible with parity of esteem. There has to be an aim for high-performing children to be taking this technical pathway. What problem are we trying to fix? I think it is a lack of technical excellence in the system.

The second thing to make the policy work is that it needs to latch on to something at 16. Look at the issues with T-levels—in many ways, the children who have done them have been very successful, but T-levels have had very low take-up because they have been somewhat incongruous; there has not been a runway up to them. This is an opportunity for embedding such a runway into the system.

The third thing somewhat repeats my previous answer. The policy needs to be integrated into the accountability frameworks. For it to have the same esteem, it needs to have the same rules and sharp edges as the academic framework. It needs to sit in things like Attainment 8 and Progress 8, and potentially even some sort of EBacc/TBacc-style thing.

I agree with all of those comments. I would also add that I think it needs to be a high-quality qualification. It needs to be a clear choice that involves the young person and their parents so that it does not become an option that is imposed on people. Where young people are struggling with their English and maths, in particular, it has to be a condition that the English and maths continue to be a high priority because we cannot ignore those challenges.

I also think it needs to be carefully managed in the relationship between schools, colleges and strategic authorities, as the scale of this for employers could be overwhelming because of the number of people looking for work placements and so forth. That is where the brokerage role of the strategic authorities could be quite productive. Keeping that balance between the school and the college on expertise is, I think, very important.

I also agree with both of those points, so I will just add a couple of extra thoughts. One is about teachers. I take on board Alun’s really good points about how we can have schools and colleges working together more closely, but to deliver this vision we will have to look at the skills, knowledge, backgrounds and expertise of teachers in schools as well as colleges, particularly if we are looking to extend some slightly different options down to 14. We need to look really closely at what we need from the teaching workforce to deliver that.

The other point that I would make is that we need to be really cautious—I do not think that this is where we are, but there is a danger that we could go there—about thinking that this solves all the issues, particularly those around disengagement and disadvantage. We know that whatever route children and young people take, disadvantaged students need more focused support than many of their peers and than is often currently possible in our tightly funded schools and colleges, whatever route they take.

Let’s make sure that we are looking really carefully at having the right teachers in place and the right wider support to sit alongside the broadening of the curriculum that I think we are looking at.

Q3 I think we have covered this extensively, but I want to ask one brief question, perhaps to Julie. There is sometimes a risk in having this conversation that we fall into the trap of thinking that vocational subjects are the only place where students develop skills, whereas the reality is that skills are taught across the curriculum. Are you concerned about that and what do we need to do to ensure that the academic side of the curriculum is also better at delivering and articulating the skills that it is teaching our young people?

That is absolutely right. Too often, as a system, we have fallen into that slightly tiresome debate between knowledge and skills. We know that both knowledge and skills are essential and both are developed through a range of different pathways, approaches and routes that children and young people take.

What is really important, and what is implied in your question, is that we should essentially make sure that the policy pendulum does not swing too far away from the significant benefits we have seen in academic knowledge and skills over the past few years. There is no reason why it should or why it needs to; with intelligent policy design we can keep what has been beneficial about that focus on academic skills, particularly for disadvantaged children, that we have seen recently while recognising some of the challenges of that to curriculum breadth, engagement and opening up different routes. It is about ensuring that we do that at a national policy design level and about how, as this plays out in individual schools and colleges, we do it in a really mindful way and recognise the potential benefits and the challenges.

Q4 The Government’s White Paper sets several ambitions, and I want to ask about one. It says that, on average, by 2040 children will leave school achieving a grade 5 or higher across their GCSEs. There was obviously a slight fall this year, but there are 14 years to go yet. In your view, what steps need to be taken to achieve the necessary changes within the timeframe set out? It would be helpful if you could touch on whether you think any changes need to be made to the curriculum and assessment.
Could I confirm whether you are asking about the specific ambition for achievements in English and maths?
The ambition is that, on average, “children will leave school achieving a grade 5 or higher across their GCSEs”, so not just in English and Maths.

Okay. The great strength of an ambition like that is also the great weakness of it—it is a bit like GDP. It compresses and condenses so much information and so many different factors into something that gives you a really clear sense of system health in one number. That is extremely helpful for understanding what is going on in the education system, but very difficult for understanding what specifically contributes to it and what specifically is causing different movements that we see in the number, which then makes your question very difficult to answer. That is one of the cautions that we have to exercise when we chase the really big numbers, as it were. It is the same with halving the disadvantage gap—the same thing would be true.
I will come on to that.

To try to give a specific answer, the strategy has to match the metric, and it has to be a broader system health strategy, as opposed to something specific. Attendance would be a different example, where you have a very specific number that you can then have a specific strategy for, whereas this is a very general number that compresses lots. Really, the strategy should be, “Make the system function as well as you can”, and that number should move.
Thank you—I appreciate that.

It is hard to disaggregate an answer to the question about the attainment ambition and the ambition on closing the gap, but I will try to focus on attainment and then perhaps we will come on to the disadvantage gap afterwards.
