Absolutely. In our study, like I say, only 53% of people had had all their adjustments put in place. I think that people in large organisations were much more likely to have them, and in the qualitative interviews, when we asked who had paid for them, people in large organisations were much more likely to say, “Actually, my employer paid for them.” An interesting thing about the National Audit Office report was that it said that some of the support provided should be given by employers.

That is another thing: it is about educating employers about what they should be providing and what Access to Work can pick up. Of course, we cannot expect Access to Work to supply everything. We have talked about universal design, and there is a responsibility, if you are employing someone, to make the workplace inclusive and ensure that it works for that person. But, of course, Access to Work has a role in picking up that kind of surplus. As you say, SMEs sometimes do not have the funding to provide some of the higher-cost adjustments that are needed.

Q71 I think your commitment to co-designing and bringing in the voices of disabled people and their organisations is extremely laudable and correct, but I am sure that you have opinions yourself. In particular, what changes and redesign options would you really want to see for Access to Work to make it sustainable in the long term?

I can’t speak to sustainability, apart from the inefficiencies that I have just mentioned, but it must be redesigned so that it is needs-led. At the moment, it is demand-led—people apply for funding—but not needs-led. We can see that just from the fact that people’s awards have been cut, but they are still disabled; they have not told anybody, “My health has improved,” or, “My impairment has disappeared,” yet their support is being cut. That is definitely not needs-led. Of course, making it needs-led will require further investment. One of the greatest cuts has been to support worker hours, which has left a lot of people in deep distress and unable to fulfil their function at work.

I think strides have been made to make it easier to transfer awards from job to job, but people are still saying that it is a bit difficult. That should be made easier, because we do not want people having to reapply when they want to take on a new job, either to move into better work or different work. Otherwise, that will put employers off, if they know that there will be a delay.

The delays are another issue because they are making people anxious, and people are losing job offers because they are having to wait for so long. Somebody was talking about this on LinkedIn: they had spoken to an Access to Work adviser this month and were told, “Well, we’re still working through October’s applications.” We are now in September.

Imagine an employer who has two people, where everything else is equal —both brilliant candidates—but one of them is waiting on an Access to Work order; it is awful, isn’t it? But some people will be in that situation, where they are losing jobs.
I have a few comments on how to improve the scheme. We submitted separate written evidence to the Access to Work inquiry, and we outlined several things.

The first is to improve the accessibility of the application processes, including the online portal, which is not hugely accessible. That builds on some of the points that Paula made about how the process works in terms of the practices that are engaged with—phone calls, written signatures and all those things. Streamlining that process would massively enhance the accessibility of the process, but it would also make it more efficient.

Secondly, we suggest using AI-supported triage to reduce waiting lists and ease the caseload on caseworkers. One of the things that the investigation that Paula mentioned uncovered is that the retention rate for caseworkers is really low. You have caseworkers going off on long-term illness; you have caseworkers who may themselves be disabled; you have caseworkers who are leaving their jobs. That creates more gaps and inefficiencies in the system. Keeping hold of those caseworkers and keeping them healthy is really important. Looking at ways of taking some of those initial, basic, preliminary tasks and using things like AI and automation tools to support that makes sense.

The next thing is enhanced training and support for caseworkers to provide more of a menu of options. There is almost an underlying assumption that people need to know what they need. People don’t know what they need. If someone has recently become disabled, they will not know what they need. If a new assistive technology becomes available, how will they know about that? Again, the onus on the individual is too great. Providing a better menu of options would support better outcomes and probably also increase efficiency, because it would help with matching what people need to what is available.

Awareness campaigns are really important. Interestingly, the Government are worried about the costs of the scheme, but it is not actually used that much. In our study, we had several people refer to it as a secret Government fund that they felt they did not know about; they only heard through other disabled people they engaged with that it was available. I suggest that in the short term the fund actually needs more investment.

As Paula mentioned, the return on investment evidences that the scheme is generating a beneficial outcome—it is generating more benefit than cost—so it should not be seen as financially unsustainable. Any other Government investment that generates more benefit than cost would surely not be seen as financially unsustainable. Investing more in the scheme and getting more disabled people into employment and supporting them in employment is surely the positive way forward for this scheme.

Can I add one more thing? Leading on from what Dan said, we really need a proper evaluation. We know the return on investment is sound, but we need to evaluate its impact on disabled people’s employment and health and their income, on the disability employment gap and the disability pay gap, and on NHS and welfare spending. We need a full, holistic evaluation.
Q72 It has never had a comprehensive evaluation?
Not to that degree, no.

Q73 Professor Wheatley, you have mentioned AI and how that can be useful. To what extent can assistive technologies, including those driven by AI, help increase flexible working opportunities for disabled people?

In our study, AI-EMPOWERED, we highlighted the huge potential of AI in this arena. We found that AI supports much greater personalisation and flexibility in people’s jobs, both through assistive technologies that are powered by AI and through the AI that disabled people use as an assistive technology; often, those are quite off-the-shelf generative AI tools—household names—that they adapt to their own needs. In combination, we found that AI allows people to fill gaps in capabilities and to create space for them to utilise the expertise and talent they have more effectively.

AI assistive technology has progressed massively in recent years. Things like computer vision technology, auto-transcription tools and audio description tools have all improved hugely. Some of that development, including things like auto-transcription and audio description developments, happened throughout the pandemic, with remote and hybrid working, but AI has powered a lot of them to progress and improve, and the accuracy of these tools—screen readers and things like that—has improved significantly. That is really important for disabled people because, coming back to some of the entrenched perceptions around disabled people, with respect to productivity levels and things like that, if we can use digital technologies as a tool to support productivity, that will hopefully, over time, dissolve some of those perceptions and evidence that, given the right resources and tools to do the job, disabled people can be just as productive as any other worker.

In our study, we identified really mixed levels of awareness and engagement with AI, and significant variation in adoption levels. Large organisations, of course, have been quite early and quite heavy AI adopters, driven by their resource, dedicated IT functions and so on. SMEs are an interesting case: a lot of very small organisations have been quick to adopt AI because they see it as a way of leveraging a competitive advantage in the market; they can pull in AI tools and make them more efficient and agile. It is in medium-sized organisations where there seems to be a big gap in AI capabilities. Those organisations, as we have already discussed in terms of SMEs and the situation for disabled people anyway, are where more support is needed in understanding how AI can be deployed in a way that can support disabled people. Again, we are talking about both assistive technologies and more off-the-shelf AI tools that disabled people can use as assistive technologies and personalise to their needs.
Q74 Even where employers have adopted AI, do you think they are as aware as they could be of the potential for supporting disabled people into work?

Not in a lot of cases. A lot of organisations are adopting AI in quite piecemeal ways. They are taking off-the-shelf AI tools, and some of them are developing much more advanced, bespoke tools, but often for very specific purposes or, at the flip end of that, with no real strategic focus; they are just doing it because everyone else is doing it. In either case, the discussion is not always around how it can help different groups of workers. Bringing disabled people into that conversation—making sure that you have disabled representation within organisations and that there are governance systems—is hugely important. This includes a role for central Government in promoting the use of AI and helping organisations upskill in terms of how AI can be used and deployed, in many cases, as a form of reasonable adjustment and a way of supporting disabled people to work to their best.
Q75 How concerned should we be about the risks of AI-based recruitment processes to disabled people’s employment opportunities? Should the Government take action on that?

I want to talk a little more broadly about the impact of AI on the labour market. It is still early days. ChatGPT was released only a few years ago. We are seeing predictions of what will happen to the labour market—we saw one by Bill Gates just the other day—and we are seeing some of the evidence coming out now. We have seen that AI has huge potential for enhancing productivity, and if that productivity gain is distributed across the population, we could really come to a utopian labour market where people have more time and are able to really focus on wellbeing and so on. But we are seeing that it is also increasing the destruction of jobs and increasing competition for jobs. A lot of people are losing jobs—especially young entrants to the graduate market but elsewhere as well—and the people who remain are having their jobs intensified or having lots of issues around that.

In addition, we are seeing differences in the population with regard to access to AI equipment, because obviously some of this technology—especially the more advanced AI technology—incurs costs. As you mentioned, there are the recruitment processes as well. We have seen evidence of the ideal worker norm that we spoke about earlier in the hearing—this able-bodied and work-devoted person without any responsibilities outside of work—being used in recruitment processes or AI tools without even the employers themselves understanding it. It is embedded in the systems, which will discriminate not only against disabled workers but against workers with caring responsibilities and so on. That could potentially enhance the gap, but it is still early days and, again, this is one of those areas that we need more evidence on and we need to look into a bit more.

I have spoken to a couple of organisations that provide these automated recruitment tools, and the important thing to recognise is that what you put into it is what you get out of it, as is often the case with technology. If you put in biases, you will get out biases. If you put in flags for gaps in CVs, or non-standard educational or employment backgrounds, as things that you do not want, that will necessarily discriminate against people who have those things present on their CVs.

If you put in place good rules and inputs—again, there is a kind of educational component to this that is central—these systems can actually reduce bias and discrimination. The massive risk, as Heejung just said, is that they perpetuate existing biases in society. In an increasingly competitive labour market, where employers will put up a job advertisement and get thousands of applications literally within seconds because AI tools apply for jobs for candidates, the risk is that anyone who does not have a typical CV—anyone who is atypical in any way—will be screened out of the process at the very early stages.

Evidence-based research needs to be done on the impact of automated tools being used in recruitment processes. The impact on the labour market could be massive, but it is really not known; it is very anecdotal at the minute.

The other thing is that there are companies selling these tools—not necessarily intentionally—with these inherent biases, but a lot of companies using them do not necessarily even understand what is embedded in them.

The other side of it is that now we are hearing from employers who, because online job markets are generating just too many applications, are going back to network-based job recruitment processes, which again will limit certain people, including disabled people, who do not have the social networks and social capital to rely on. Again, that can increase inequality patterns.
The Business and Trade Committee have been running an inquiry on AI in the workforce. I believe they were interested in detrimental impacts of recruitment, so that might be worth cross-referencing.
Thank you very much. Unless anybody has anything else to add or to ask, that concludes the session. Thank you very much to our witnesses for coming along today.

sessions.iT: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement
sessions.w: GMB London Region; BusinessLDN; British Chambers of Commerce

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement , HC 482
Wednesday 2 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 2 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Steff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Daniel Francis; Olly Glover; Alex Mayer.
Environmental Audit Committee member present: Barry Gardiner.
Questions 56 – 11 1
Witnesses
I I : Perry Phillips, Aviation Officer, GMB London Region, Kate Shoesmith, Director of Policy and Insights, British Chambers of Commerce, and John Dickie, Chief Executive at BusinessLDN.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– GMB London Region
– British Chambers of Commerce
– BusinessLDN
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Perry Phillips, John Dickie and Kate Shoesmith.
Welcome to our second panel. Could you please introduce yourselves?

My name is John Dickie and I am the chief executive of BusinessLDN. We are a business membership organisation representing a couple of hundred or so large businesses headquartered in or with substantial operations in London.
My name is Perry Phillips. I am the GMB union regional officer with membership responsibilities for our members at Heathrow airport. I am also the aviation officer for the GMB London region.
Hello and thank you for the invitation. I am Kate Shoesmith and I am the director of policy and insights at the British Chambers of Commerce.
Q56 Thank you very much. Before we go on, some of us need to note our interests. I am a member of the GMB.
I am a GMB member, and I should also declare a donation.
I am also a GMB member.
I am also a member, and received a donation that was not registrable because it was under the threshold.
Barry?
I don’t think I have had a donation yet, so if there is anything—

Q57 Right. Thank you very much. A lot has changed since the last airports NPS was designated in 2018: we have had expansion approved at other airports, changes in business travel habits, growing geopolitical uncertainty, legal compliance with net zero and so on. Do you think any of these changes have affected the potential benefits of more hub airport capacity in London?

The changes that you listed, Chair, and some of the other geopolitical factors over the past few years, have of course moved demand up and down. If you look at Heathrow now, we see quite a strong rebound in long-haul business travel but not quite such a strong rebound in short-haul business travel, which is kind of what you would expect, given that it is easier to do what one might describe as casual meetings online and over Zoom—that is the experience of the pandemic. So the case, as it were, moves up and down, but we do know that Heathrow is operating at about 5% above its pre-pandemic peak. That level of operation puts all kinds of stresses on the way the airport works. The airport is a bit less resilient than one might like it to be because it has so many flights leaving across its two runways.

We also know that there is still, as of today, huge unmet demand for capacity at Heathrow, due to the inability to get more aeroplanes in and out of the airport. That is why pairs of slots at Heathrow can be sold for very large sums of money—much more than at virtually any other international airport. That means two things. One is that we are continuing to lose out on the direct benefits of the economic activity at Heathrow. For the rest of the UK economy, outside of aviation, and certainly for the London economy, what really matters is the connectivity that we are losing out on to the rest of the world.

I think Heathrow is still the world’s best-connected airport, although there are people snapping at its heels; it is, I think, no longer the busiest airport in Europe, having lost that crown to Istanbul over the summer. We are losing out on the connectivity that that brings. If you are, as London is, an international business centre on an island, connectivity really matters for the growth of your professional and services economy in particular. It also matters to the whole of the country, because we know from other airports and from other regions that people in those regions value the ability to transfer via Heathrow rather than having to transfer via Schiphol or middle east airports to go on their full journeys.
Q58 Have you done an analysis of the economic cost of the difference between somebody changing planes at Heathrow, Schiphol, Charles de Gaulle or Dubai?

I have not done such an analysis, although people on your previous panel may have done—I am sure there is a lot of analysis out there—but we do know it to be what people think, and we do know it to be what representative organisations in the rest of the country believe they want.

From a union perspective—from a GMB perspective—Heathrow at the moment is at its full capacity. Obviously, we are losing out on connectivity to Istanbul and other airports across Europe, such as Charles de Gaulle and Schiphol airports. Because of the full capacity, we are losing out on those connections, and business and flights are choosing other airports. We are getting left behind—Heathrow is getting left behind—while a decision is being made on the future of the third runway.

From a British Chambers of Commerce perspective, we have been looking at the case for Heathrow expansion for a number of years, and it is felt that there is a lack of capacity and that to expand Heathrow is the right way forward. It is the only UK option as a hub airport and, as my colleagues said, that is important—otherwise, we lose out to the international competition out there.

When we look at what will create growth in the UK economy, we know that trade is one of the fastest routes to that. British Chambers of Commerce has a long, proud heritage of supporting businesses to trade more effectively, and when we looked at international trade opportunities and how we grow exports as a UK economy, if we had grown exports last year by just 2%, it would have added 0.6% to UK GDP, which is a significant amount in the current economic climate.
Q59 To what extent is connectivity an element of that growth, or of that lack of or constraint on growth?
Not from economic analysis, but from our case studies, we believe that is a point to—
Has anyone done economic analysis?
No—
Of the benefit or cost of connectivity, as opposed to the benefit of trade—we all know that.

No. From our perspective, we look across our member businesses—the 60,000 member businesses in the network of chambers—and talk to the chambers locally about what they get from being part of a supply chain, working with Heathrow, and what trade capacity does for their local economies.
Thank you. Let us now do a bit more on assessing the benefits and costs, with Olly.

Q60 We explored with our previous panel the often very technical appraisal and economic modelling that underpins the draft policy statement, but there may well be things that conventional appraisals of economic benefits cannot consider. What potential economic and employment benefits are not captured by the usual tools that are used for appraisal and economic modelling? Who would like to start?

Shall I pick up where I left off, thinking about supply chains and the work of different chambers? A number of chambers of commerce submitted evidence to the Select Committee. They articulate why there is a benefit in them working with Heathrow. In the north-east, about 19 suppliers locally in that area work with Heathrow. That adds £3.5 million to their work. If they can increase their capacity, if they can trade more effectively and if they can enable that work through Heathrow expansion, they believe that there is a gain to be made there.
These are businesses that are using belly or hold freight at Heathrow.

Absolutely. Whether they are part of logistics or exporting a capacity, they are a whole part of the supply chain. They might also work in construction. A number of different organisations submitted evidence to say that they could benefit advantageously from Heathrow expansion. I mentioned the north-east, but there is also the north-west. Our chamber that covers north Wales and west Cheshire has 61 suppliers working with Heathrow right now, and they think that they could grow that number.

I listened to the earlier session and heard the great complexity of different approaches to economic modelling. It is worth remembering that the DFT’s methodology is fundamentally about how to get the best value from scarce public capital when investing in transport projects. At Heathrow, we are referring to a scheme that will attract something of the order of just under £50 billion of likely inward investment to the UK’s infrastructure. Quite how that benefit is captured by the modelling seems to me to be important, and so too—I think you talked a little about this at the end of the previous session—is the dynamic effect of improved access to international markets.

Frontier Economics did some modelling that is now quite old— I think it was in 2011—about the benefits of direct as opposed to indirect connectivity to markets. Back then, they estimated that well over £1 billion of trade was being lost to the UK because of the lack of connectivity through viable air routes . The air routes were not viable because there was not the capacity at Heathrow. There are some broader issues that it would be useful to build into the appraisal on the benefits side, as well as some of the costs you have talked about.
Is there anything you would like to add, Mr Phillips?

Yes . To reiterate what my colleagues have said, the modelling misses the export and import of cargo into Heathrow. That misses the important contribution that cargo freight coming in and out of London makes to the UK economy.

Q61 On cargo, we have had witnesses from the logistics industry saying that the growth of capacity in passenger airports is not enabling them to grow their business, because dedicated cargo is squeezed out and there are virtually no dedicated cargo flights at Heathrow. Is the issue whether cargo should be going through Heathrow in greater capacity if runway 3 goes ahead, or should there be more dedicated cargo capacity? Manston airport is lobbying for reopening as a dedicated cargo airport. To what extent is runway 3 logistics and cargo expansion a key factor, or are there other wider issues in air freight? Has that been included in the analysis to an adequate extent?

Let me take part of that. There is a definite proportion of the value of air freight that is going via Heathrow and air freight more generally that we think could be expanded. Obviously, the vast majority of freight does not go via airports for all sorts of reasons.
By volume, no, but the value does.
Yes, and the costs and so on. However, it is important that we continue to have that capacity and that we can grow it. That is the key thing that we hear all the time, to export—
Any capacity growth is a good thing in your view.
Exactly.

I very much agree. It is difficult to see a world where it is somehow bad for exporters across Britain that there is more capacity and, over time, cheaper capacity at Heathrow, given its interconnectivity.

I can see there is a bit of complexity about where that might lead to a reduction in demand too. I would have thought it was, on the face of it, likely to be a good thing for those businesses trying to export. The Scottish Chambers of Commerce described the expansion of Heathrow as a “huge opportunity” for Scotland, in part because of the impact it would have on the ability of Scottish businesses to export goods through Heathrow. Notwithstanding the conversation I just heard about gold going through Heathrow, I am told that Scottish smoked salmon is its biggest export by weight. I am not sure how that stacks up with gold, but one way or another it is obviously a big export.

Q62 I want to pick up on something you just said, John, which was that the likely benefits to the UK were £50 billion, but the HEAR confirms that the upper bound of the range is £40 billion. Our other witness, Alex Chapman, said there is an element of cherry-picking figures. Could you clarify? Are we talking about apples and pears, or the same thing ?

I think so. The numbers I gave earlier—£49 billion to be precise—are a combination of the investment that Heathrow will make in delivering the third runway, coupled with the modernisation programme associated with that at the airport. That is the amount of aggregate inward investment that investors in Heathrow will make in the airport and its environs.
Q63 Is Heathrow expansion important for the principle of business confidence, and, in your view, is there a cost to business confidence from proceeding or not proceeding?

I started the evidence today by saying how long we have spoken about Heathrow expansion. I can find the British Chambers of Commerce talking about Heathrow expansion right back to the early 2000s. We have produced something called a quarterly economic survey for the last 40 years that gets 5,000 businesses—largely SMEs—to respond every quarter. We know from looking at our data that business confidence is critical to future productivity, investment and growth. That is what we find.

We are now in a situation where many businesses say that the lack of a decision is causing them to take pause for thought and not know whether to invest. Only around 17% of businesses responding to our survey in the last quarter said that they are looking to invest and grow in terms of their plant machinery operational equipment. That is significantly low, and we have seen that lack of business confidence play through into investment and the private sector.

Q64 But is your view that the main cause of holding back investment is a lack of decision, as opposed to their not investing because there is not the capacity at Heathrow and that is directly holding back their businesses?
They are definitely two sides to the same coin.
Q65 Which is bigger?

The lack of a decision is the significant one. The reason for saying that is that it is not just on this critical infrastructure project; we see it across the board. Whenever we are out and about talking to members about what is happening, whether we talk about roads, rail or air freight—across the piece—they really hold back because of the lack of decisions.

Q66 So, John, is this just a vibes-based thing that is to do with Government’s commitment to seeing things through, or is there a specific reason why business confidence is being affected by the decision?

As Kate said, 2003 was the first time a British Government said that we should expand and create a third runway at Heathrow, and here we are in 2026. Who knows? At some point in the next decade, all the paperwork may be done, and you can start digging for a third runway—or not. That undermines global confidence in Britain as a place to invest, because, not just in transport but in commercial development and a whole range of areas, if you start the process of investing, you do not really know how long it will take and what the deadweight costs of preparing for that are. Whereas, if you want to build a data centre in Iowa, you kind of know how long that will take. That debilitates the UK’s competitiveness globally in attracting capital. That is definitely a thing.

There is then an issue with confidence about Government commitment to growth. Governments talk a good game on growth but do not always deliver behind that. I think that, not least because the previous Chancellor of the Exchequer in particular made such a strong commitment about Government support for expanding Heathrow because it would drive growth, not doing that will have an effect on confidence in investing in Britain. It would suggest that even that level of support cannot be relied on to deliver projects, if that were to happen.

As you say, there is a third impact, which is that people are not flying directly to parts of Asia in particular and parts of America because there aren’t flights. There aren’t flights because there is not the capacity at the hub airport, and that is holding business growth back. It is impossible to quantify that. I fear that this may be one of those areas where, depending on what answer you would like to get, your assumptions will get you there, but it is a common-sense statement that it must be the case that it is holding back growth for Britain.

Q67 Well, that was the subject of much of the deliberation with our first panel. Thank you. Lastly, Perry, I suppose you look at it from a slightly different perspective, but do you have a view on what the impacts of continued uncertainty about the third runway are on your workforce?

From my perspective, I have spent 16 or 17 years representing members down at Heathrow airport, and there is uncertainty as the years go on about what businesses need to do. From the perspective of airlines down at Heathrow, having spoken to a lot of people, companies and airlines, there is uncertainty because they need to have the green light for the expansion.

There is a danger if we do not give the green light to the third runway. What will these airlines do? Already at Heathrow, they are looking at better connections, so what will they do if we do not get the expansion? They will be looking at other airports for new routes across Europe, into Asia and China. India and China are emerging markets that obviously need connectivity. Just to reiterate what I said before, we are getting left behind. The uncertainty is that we may lose what we have already.

Q68 Perry, could I just pick you up on that? Heathrow is obviously the UK’s major airport with 480,000 ATMs every year. Where is the evidence that business will move away from Heathrow if runway 3 does not go ahead? I have not seen any.
It is just the perception—
Q69 So it is a perception? There is no background to that statement?
It is just the worry about them expanding to—

Q70 How many of your members who currently work at Heathrow fear that their jobs are at risk? I guess you mean among all the employers at Heathrow, not just Heathrow Airport Holdings Ltd. How many of your members who are there now fear that their jobs are at risk if runway 3 does not go ahead?
To be quite honest, Chair, it has not been a big factor. It is just the uncertainty.
Q71 Could you give me an example? What sort of uncertainty do you mean? What risk is there for people or businesses operating at Heathrow now?

It is those businesses that are operating now and want to expand, but have the option of other hub airports that they can take advantage of with their capacity. Like I said, Chair, it is obviously not a statistical point of view; it is just that uncertainty and pessimism about what happens if we do not get the third runway. Will these airports—
Q72 I understand the emotional question. I am just wondering where the evidence that any airlines are considering moving away is.

To reiterate, Ruth, it is just about looking into the future. If we don’t get the Heathrow expansion, what will these businesses and airlines do when they suddenly realise that the extra capacity that the third runway will bring is not there? They see Dubai and emerging airports such as Istanbul building capacity. Will they be looking at that business, and will it have a big effect on Heathrow if it does not move with the times?

Q73 All those businesses will be making forecasts for their business and for investment, and it is steady state or expansion. I am happy to be corrected, but are any of them looking at a third option of retraction if runway 3 does not go ahead? I have not been made aware of anything like that.

There are two parts to this. One is that there are airlines—a Chinese regional airline, for example—looking to have a base in Europe to get adequate capacity to do what it hopes to do over time: grow its business. It is very difficult to do that at Heathrow, for all the reasons that we know about with capacity constraint. That is a loss of jobs at Heathrow—well, it is a loss of increase in jobs.
Q74 It is a loss of increase in jobs. Will there be any loss of existing jobs at Heathrow if runway 3 does not go ahead?
Heathrow will be able to give you better answers than I can.
We will ask them.

If you are a Chinese airline that has one slot at Heathrow and you want to expand, you might decide that it is cheaper and that you will have greater growth options if you sell that slot and invest in a base of your own at, say, Schiphol or Frankfurt, at which point you will leave Heathrow. And that does happen.
Q75 But because of the demand, others will fill it.
Someone else will fill it—indeed. In the short term other people will fill that demand, but not necessarily in the long term.

Q76 I have a question for you, Perry. Do you think the draft HENPS strikes the right balance between the interests of those who may benefit directly from new jobs and opportunities, which we have just been discussing, and people who may bear the negative impacts of expansion and who will not be able to access those benefits? In particular, I am thinking about many of your members and other people working at Heathrow who live in the areas that are going to be affected by the third runway being built.

The HENPS is a balanced proposal, and it is balanced in its assessment. Our caution is different, as the benefit it describes cannot simply be assumed; it must be built in. The draft weighs economic, community and environmental questions together in one framework, which is the honest way to do it, rather than treating them as rival cases.

Q77 Many of your members—many of our constituents—do not fly in and out of Heathrow, as they cannot afford it, and the levels of deprivation around Heathrow have also been increasing in recent years, which has been confirmed by all the local authorities around. Why do you think that is the case? Why do you think runway 3 will make a difference?

I come from a union perspective, and I have been working down there for practically 16 or 17 years and speaking to thousands and thousands of workers, our members and staff, who range from aircraft cleaners to ground handlers and terminal cleaners—it is a massive employment workplace. I have spoken to a lot of our members who are obviously raising concerns, and they say, “Perry, when is the third runway going to go ahead?” The opportunities for the local areas around Heathrow and beyond—
Q78 Why do you think the local areas have not benefited from the expansion of passengers at Heathrow to date? Why do you think deprivation is increasing around Heathrow, rather than decreasing?

There is a case to say that the third runway will offer massive opportunities through thousands of jobs and apprenticeships. To go back to the fundamental basics, you have school leavers who will have the opportunity to go into apprenticeships.

Q79 That goes without saying, but we were made those promises with terminal 5. However, they did not materialise, and we have not seen the benefits that we were promised then, so I am trying to understand from you and other panel members why that was the case.
The expansion will create thousands of jobs, and we expect them to be well-paid jobs.

Q80 Heathrow itself and its direct contracts did commit to the London living wage for a short while. I do not know whether we are back at that now, because that was dropped during covid. How many of the new staff will be at the national minimum wage and London living wage levels?

That is a very good point; part of our support for the Heathrow expansion is based on jobs with well-paid, liveable wages, pensions and proper contracts of employment, rather than casual hours or zero-hour contracts.
Q81 Are you saying the latter is the reality at the moment? Are casual hours, zero hours and the minimum wage what the bulk of your members are on?
No, not at the moment, because through the years—
You have negotiated.

Yes. As you know, Chair, through the years, we have worked with Heathrow on employment status and low wages, and we managed to achieve liveable wages, specifically in the direct supply chain. There is an ongoing commitment from Heathrow that the jobs and apprentices hips created by the expansion will be good, well-paid and unionised jobs with pensions, and that is our expectation with the third runway .

Q82 Thank you. I would like to ask the other two witnesses about the range of negative health and environmental impacts that are going to come about with runway 3 . Obviously , the Government have to weigh those up against the benefits. How will those environmental and health impacts affect businesses and employees around Heathrow?

W e think the framework is the right framework in terms of looking at the four tests and making sure that there i s equitable treatment across them , and that is really important in terms of this scrutiny from the Committee and across the board. In terms of our membership, which includes Heathrow, one of the things that we are very aware of is that Heathrow , as well as the aviation industry more broadly , has established good working relationships and good collective agreements with unions. It recognise s the unions. That has been part and parcel of its modelling over the p ast few years. It is really important that each and every one of these tests is taken into proper consideration , and we would expect that to happen going forward.

As Kate has said, the work Heathrow airport has done to try to make sure that its spend goes through small and medium-sized enterprises in London and across Britain has been formidable. It seems to me that the economic test of the four tests is overwhelmingly and clearly met. The other tests do require serious regulatory oversight, both by the London government and by the national Government , but we have already seen considerable progress.

A lot of the issues are not really to do with the airport as a place with lots of planes coming in and taking off ; it is to do with the ancillary activities. We have seen something like a fall of a third in N O x around Heathrow airport since 2019, partly because of ULEZ , as well as the work TfL has done, for example, on modal shift. There is a whole range of interventions that can be made, and we have already seen substantial fruit around Heathrow that could meet the local environmental impact aspect of the test. There is a great deal of regulatory and other intervention s that can be made to make sure that the planes that fly into Heathrow are modern planes that emit less and that produce less noise.

There is also work on carbon, which I think it is important that the Government do , and on creating a strong framework for sustainable aviation fuels. I think I am right in saying that there are some short-haul flights that , over time, might very well be made using batteries and electricity . We do not know quite where that will go , but it is plausible. It is difficult to see there being a world where batteries power long - haul flights , so I think getting the UK’s SAF capacity up is a really important part of the mix over the next decade of making sure those tests can be met.

Q83 Kate , in your written evidence you said that the British Chamber s of Commerce would not support Heathrow expansion at any cost. What are your red lines , and what would you like to see reflected in the national policy statement ?

Obviously, Heathrow is an ecosystem. We have spoken about its supply chain in terms of wider distribution across the whole of the UK and about how it works with SME businesses . It works with a number of businesses on site at the minute. It is really important that the views of those businesses, which are well - established , highly regarded and profitable UK businesses , are taken into consideration. We need to ensure that there is clear analysis of the costs and the expected return on investment. There are a number of organisations—I know you are taking evidence from some of the airlines in the coming weeks—that have a set of assessments of what they think should be a fair price on this and why they need that look across the long-term consequences for them.

Q84 Perry, in your evidence you said, “The benefits of expansion cannot simply be assumed, they must be built in.” We have just had a conversation about pay and conditions, and I suppose that will be something that you will also consider as you go further. Can you explain what you meant by that and is there anything else that you think should be reflected in the policy statement?

I think it was reflected to the Chair previously that we expect that to be built in. Over the years, the GMB have done a lot of work on liveable wage salaries. Many years ago, a lot of our members were working there on a wage that was not acceptable. We worked on a collaborative approach to reach the levels in the direct supply chain that are happening now, where a liveable wage and beyond are being paid.

Going back to the statement, we expect the commitment to be built in when the Heathrow expansion gets the green light. We expect decent pensions, decent employment contracts and a liveable wage. Our expectation is that they are built in with a commitment to the Heathrow expansion.
Q85 John, are there any gaps in the national policy statement that need to be filled? That question is open to anybody if you think there is anything that needs to be included.

The national policy statement as it stands is pretty well balanced. There is more, as we heard earlier, around the economic benefits of Heathrow that could be built in. But the local environmental tests on noise and pollution, as they are currently set out, are sensible. The importance of making sure that the economic benefits are well distributed is sensible too.

As I said previously, the only thing I would add would be about the carbon implications. It is always worth remembering that there may be more flights taking off from Heathrow but that may mean there are fewer flights taking off from Schiphol to go to Sydney or wherever. We need to think about how the Government can play their part in building the UK’s sustainable aviation fuel capacity at pace across the aviation sector.

To pick up on what John said, we were very clear in the submission that the nationwide benefits need to be secured moving forward. We have heard from different chambers in our membership and their organisations about why they work with Heathrow and why they think it is important to their future capacity. We need to ensure that there is a broad base across the UK.

In particular, we would argue that the SME supply chain needs to be considered. We know from direct investment from the public sector that not enough SMEs get access to those opportunities. We need to secure it here.

Q86 Under the economic tests set out in the policy statement, promoters will have to demonstrate how their scheme will deliver economic growth nationally, regionally and locally. What kind of evidence should they be required to provide?

We would like them to take evidence from across a broad base. The British Chambers of Commerce has 51 accredited chambers across the UK. Each and every one of them will have a perspective on how they can operate and work with a hub airport. It will be important to take account of their views.

I said at the beginning what I think the principle local benefits are. It is good to do economic modelling to test and assess those benefits, but as we have just seen, economic modelling is heavily contested. It takes you as far as it takes you.

It seems to me that for London, the economic benefits of being a professional services global centre on an island of greater connectivity speaks for itself. We are talking about an investment that is being made by the private sector, not the public.
Q87 A quick supplementary: if the expansion resulted in labour being reallocated to different places rather than additional jobs being created, would that affect your view of its impact?
Different places around the UK? Is that the question?
Yes.

I think there is a wider benefit. Shall we go back to our Scottish salmon example? We know that 44% of it goes through Heathrow, and we know that premium food and drink is a growing market globally right now; we know that there are key areas of the world looking to benefit from the UK’s reputation in terms of that premium food and drink. We think that there are jobs to be created in other areas as well, which can come from this.

Q88 How important is the ultimate affordability of services through Heathrow airport to realising the benefits of expansion and how do you think that that should be approached? I will start with you, John.
Are you thinking of the cost of using the airport for airlines?
Q89 Absolutely, because clearly—depending on the analysis—that cost might change.

It is absolutely right that a regulated airport—the only regulated airport in the UK—is scrutinised carefully by the CAA, and that the CAA has the resources and capabilities to scrutinise carefully Heathrow’s expansion plans, the cost of those plans, the effectiveness of the delivery of those plans and the effect that all that will have on landing charges for airlines. However, I do not think that landing charges for airlines will constrain demand for Heathrow.

I think it is important that expansion is done as efficiently and as effectively as possible, but I really think it is important that it’s done. It is the increase in capacity that London and Britain need at their hub airport. The lower the cost of doing that, the better. But it is not the cost that is the barrier to growth; it is the lack of capacity.
Q90 You represent London, so do you have a view on the impact that expansion might have on other London airports, because obviously changing costs at one airport might impact another?

It may well do so. If there are concerns about the impact on other airports, then of course costs at Heathrow going up make it more attractive to go to other airports, rather than less attractive. But in the round I am strongly in favour of competition and choice. You can have effective competition between different airports with different catchment areas, different assets and features, and different strengths and weaknesses, but you cannot have effective competition between those airports if capacity is constrained at one and there is no competition.
Q91 Perry, do you have views on the original question?
Apologies—I am not an economics expert. But obviously I see the point of view that my colleagues have just put to you.

Q92 Would your members or you as a union have views, given that, depending on those costs, it might mean that there are additional routes, but it might also mean that some routes no longer exist? Has the union considered those points?
We have not considered those points, so it would be difficult for me to give you a proper direct answer.
Q93 Okay. Kate, do you have any view on the original question?

I fully agree with John’s point of view, in that is really important that there is a regulated environment for this. That is why the CAA needs to have a strong voice in terms of looking at this. And the airlines need to be fully involved in the decisions that are made next.
Q94 How important is increased domestic connectivity to realising the benefits of Heathrow expansion for businesses around the country?
Is there anything you want to add that you have not already covered on that issue? Kate?

The thing that we have not necessarily spoken about is surface transport options. It is obviously essential that they are part and parcel of this, because if we are going to realise the benefits they need to be part of the scheme and understood from the outset. I think that it is super-important that that aspect is considered, too.
Q95 So you do not necessarily think that we need more domestic flights going into Heathrow from other parts of the country, and you would be just as happy with people coming to Heathrow by rail?

I do not know enough about it. What we do know is that a huge number of passengers go via Heathrow who are domestic travellers using it as that hub airport, and it is the only option we have for that right now. What we have heard from our membership is that they think that increasing capacity will allow them to do more of the travel that will enable them to grow their businesses.
Anyone else got anything to add?

A very substantial increase in the capacity at Heathrow will make it more viable for there to be more flights from UK airports to Heathrow than is the case now, and that will support wider hubbing through Heathrow. All the arguments we know. There are important modal shift issues about how you get to Heathrow. That is particularly true for people coming to Heathrow from relatively short distances. So things like the expansion of Southern rail—
We are going to come on to surface access.

Long-distance surface. I think Manchester is one of the busiest routes in the UK going into and out of Heathrow. One way to get modal shift there is to improve the rail service between London and Manchester, which would make a lot of people in both London and Manchester very happy. My view is that we should be thinking about modal shift by making trains more attractive to passengers, rather than saying you cannot fly, because all that does is hobble people’s ability to go on holiday or do business.
Q96 Do you think that the requirements of the NPS put enough duties on the promoter to safeguard and expand domestic routes?

I think it is complicated is the simple answer. We might get on to this on local surface access. What you really need is good institutional co-operation between Network Rail, the Highways Agency, Transport for London and the GLA and Heathrow. We need to make sure we have a framework that encourages and supports that co-operation. In the case of Heathrow, it links into the way in which they are regulated, because fundamentally the contributions they can make to local public transport or national public transport are a function of that regulatory model.

Q97 In terms of more domestic flights in and out of Heathrow, we had evidence that the growth at Heathrow could mainly end up going to wide-bodied long-haul flights, and regional flights might not be able to afford to take the additional capacity and get into Heathrow. They would be priced out or squeezed out. As I say, do you think the NPS should put a duty on the promoter to safeguard those routes? If so, how would that be done and paid for?

I do not know the answer in enough detail, so we can come back to you. In terms of the economic analysis, the consideration was across the piece in terms of that nationwide benefit, and domestic routes were part and parcel of that. That is definitely the strong pull that we have had from the membership in terms of thinking about it. Across the sector and across the economy, what they are particularly interested in is how this allows them to grow locally but also have access. They do not have the capacity right now.
Q98 Does that growth in capacity that you say they want have to be protected in some way because it might not happen?

That is a really fair question in working out the balance of this. From our perspective, we are looking at how it allows all boats to rise. I am thinking about a UK-wide perspective, so I think it is worth considering.

Q99 When your members get to Heathrow, they get on a big plane that goes far away. Is that the key thing? Or is it just as important that they can get from wherever they are in England to Heathrow? Which bit are they most worried about? They are going on a big plane far away, but there is not enough of that.

They are worried about three things. They are worried about the domesticity and being able to go on a short-haul flight. They are worried about the long-haul opportunities and what that allows them to do. And they are worried about cargo and freight and how that allows them to export goods.
Okay. Thank you. Is there anything still to be asked about freight stuff?
I was going to ask about the benefit to businesses and jobs of what seems to be uncalculated increases in cargo capacity. Are there any views on that?
Witnesses indicated dissent.
Right. Now we will move to surface access. Olly is next.

Q100 As you will be aware, the ground transport links, particularly the prospective rail from Heathrow, are pretty dismal compared with European competitors. It is great in the London direction, but apart from that it is nothing compared to the Amsterdam Schiphol direct intercity train to basically everywhere in Netherlands. Frankfurt Flughafen is similar, as is Paris CDG.
Okay, you’ve been to all those places.

I just want to emphasise the point, Chair, because we say we want Heathrow to be a globally leading airport, yet we have persistently neglected all that stuff. A lot of business organisations have emphasised to us in their evidence that improved surface access is really important for realising the airport’s benefits. That would also be important for people who work there and commute to it. Are you reassured by what the draft policy statement says on this front?
I am reassured, but I return to the point from right at the beginning that it is over 20 years since the Government first said we should have a third runway at Heathrow.

Q101 Can I correct you on that? In 2003 Heathrow airport changed their minds and said, “We do want a third runway.” The then Government proceeded with that. This time around, it was not Heathrow that started the conversation; it was the Chancellor who said we need a third runway, and the DFT and Heathrow are now working up the plans.
It depends when you believe that conversation started, but shall we agree that we have been talking about this very seriously for over 20 years?
I would definitely agree with you on that.

The question is really about delivery capability. As I said a minute ago, that requires a properly joined-up conversation approach, plan and funding model across Transport for London and Network Rail, in particular. We have been talking about the western rail link and Heathrow Southern Railway for a similar amount of time—possibly even longer than we have been talking about expanding Heathrow—and it would be great if we could just crack on and do it. There is a distributional question of whether that is paid for by the taxpayer or by people flying through Heathrow. Those are your options.
Q102 Where would your members be on that question?
We would be in favour of the model that maximised the efficiency of who was paying. That is an empirical question that will need to be studied as part of this process.

That is very fair. The other part of that is being extremely clear in terms of the respective roles—the Government, the actors that John spoke about, and the promoter of the scheme and their ownership. Which parties are involved in this, and are they very clear on their respective roles? Local transport is a frustration. It is absolutely important that it is factored into all these considerations and addressed properly. We put this in our evidence—just on a national level, over 60% of businesses are unsatisfied with local transport options because they are not good enough.
Q103 Are you are talking about now?

Yes—right now. It is not enabling people to get to their place of work properly. We hear this over and over again. There is a series of examples of how it stops people being able to do the work they need to do.
Q104 Perry, to what extent does the transport infrastructure at the moment impact your members? What are you calling for in terms of surface access changes?

A lot of our members had travelling problems getting to work and with the cost of parking at Heathrow. We have quite a few members who do unsociable shifts. We have a lot of members with caring responsibilities, like a husband and wife sharing caring responsibilities in terms of dropping children off at school, at nannies and things like that, so they work around each other. A lot of the time, they cannot rely on public transport to get to work. From the perspective of an employee getting to work, the cost of parking at Heathrow is still a concern. A lot of companies subsidise staff car parking. A lot of employers do not. It is a concern that the cost of our members going to work is considerable. That is a main concern from our point of view.
Q105 Do delays and congestion impact on staff arriving at work on time?
Do you mean currently, Chair?
Yes.

That is not a big problem. We have a lot of members that live in Hampshire and Berkshire—not just in the surrounding areas of Hounslow, Southall, Ealing and Heston. We have a considerable number of members that live quite far from the airport. With their connectivity, using the M25 and the M4 for those connections, there has not been much of a concern coming to us as a trade union at this current time.
Q106 But Kate, your members have raised issues of congestion around Heathrow.

It is the availability of the transport options, rather than the congestion. I do not know about congestion specifically, but we can ask. It is the availability and the unreliability of those transport options that is particularly problematic. It is coming into London and leaving London that is the particular issue.

Q107 I only found out later, but apparently, the M25 was closed completely in one direction near Heathrow yesterday, which must have caused some problems. John, do you have issues from your members? Is there a cost of congestion at the moment?

In general, we are favour of London-wide congestion charging so that journeys become more predictable and all the externalities of lots of idling vehicles are reduced. It would be a good thing if we could improve the surface transit reliability from central London to Heathrow, but of course, it is also a good thing that we continue, as the Mayor’s transport strategy is doing, to drive up modal shift, getting more people to Heathrow using public transport. Again, we are in favour of an expansion in those options, particularly for commuters coming in from outside London, where there is now quite robust connectivity.
Q108 Would you like to see the HENPS strengthened in the area of surface access?

I would particularly like to see the roles of each of the participants in the scheme outlined so that there is a clear articulation of what each party is doing and what Government’s involvement is in the funding going forward.
Q109 Great. I will ask the final question. Is there anything else that we have not covered today that you would like to see amended in the final version of the HENPS?
Some of the economic benefits of expansion, which we have talked about.

I would reiterate our position as a union. I have been with the workers for so many years, and I would just like to give an example. From my position, it is jobs, jobs, jobs—good jobs. With the Heathrow expansion, there is an opportunity to grow the UK. I was across at Heathrow a couple of weeks ago, and that hit home to me. I am passionate about the airport. I have been working for so many years down there. I was talking to a couple of ground handlers about the Heathrow expansion. They were giving me a history of how they came into the airport—guaranteed jobs. A lot of people have been there 30, 40 or 50 years. They have spent their whole working lives there. They are like me—I came out of school when I was 15 or 16. I went straight into an apprenticeship, when manufacturing was massive back in the late ‘70s and early ‘80s—it has obviously declined a lot now. As an engineering apprentice, I had that opportunity, just like thousands of people. Young people leaving school will have the opportunity to gain experience in aviation. Talking to these guys, they were saying, “We would like our children, our grandchildren and our great-grandchildren to benefit from the economic value and job opportunities that we knew would come our way and would give better prospects for a lot of people.”

Q110 I absolutely agree with you, but I think there is a much wider debate, which this Government are picking up, about the need to do far more for young people to get them into the kind of work that you have described—a proper apprenticeship.

It is a massive opportunity for these young people leaving school. A lot of the boroughs have high employment rates. It is a massive opportunity, whether they take apprenticeships or trade skills, or whether they go into a job position that is vacant for them. When you look at aviation, you look at so many job positions. We can say to young people leaving school, “There is a massive opportunity for you.”
Obviously, I am aware that the airport provides many of those opportunities. The colleges are tied in and so on.
I was just singing from my heart, Ruth—that’s all.
Q111 I know many people who, similarly, have worked all their working life at Heathrow. Is there anything else that we have not covered?

The role of the Committee is essential in making sure we get to a clear articulation of what the next steps are. The prolonged uncertainty has created a situation that we would like to see move on now.

Many people have made that point. Thank you very much for your evidence and for the time you have spent writing your evidence and preparing for today. If there is anything that you feel you did not get to cover, please feel free to write to us. That concludes today’s meeting.

sessions.iT: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement
sessions.w: New Economics Foundation; Peak Economics; Department for Transport; Frontier Economics

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement , HC 482
Wednesday 2 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 2 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Steff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Daniel Francis; Olly Glover; Alex Mayer.
Environmental Audit Committee member present: Barry Gardiner.
Questions 1 – 55
Witnesses

I : Matt Shepherd, Director, Frontier Economics, Dr James Laird, Peer reviewer of the S -CGE modelling, Peak Economics, Dr Alex Chapman, Head of Economic and Environmental Policy, New Economics Foundation, and Ian Mulheirn, Chief Analyst and Chief Economist, Department for Transport.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Alex Chapman, Dr James Laird, Ian Mulheirn and Matt Shepherd.

Welcome to the first evidence session in the Transport Committee’s scrutiny of the Government’s draft Heathrow expansion national policy statement, which will be the policy basis against which a decision on whether to grant planning permission for a third runway at Heathrow airport will be made.

The Liaison Committee has granted us the right to scrutinise the draft Heathrow expansion NPS, including the extent to which it provides clear guidance on how to assess the proposed runway scheme and the robustness of the assumptions and requirements in the NPS and its associated documents. This session is very important, given that the former Chancellor used economic growth as the reason for moving ahead with Government policy to support runway 3.

I welcome Barry Gardiner , who is joining us as a guest from the Environmental Audit Committee. We look forward to Barry or a colleague joining us for future evidence sessions in this inquiry. I also thank all the people who have been advising us and the core team on the work for this inquiry. Although it concerns a single piece of infrastructure, it is the most extensive inquiry I have been involved with in all the time I have been on the Transport Committee. It has so many different aspects that require an awful lot of work and support, so I thank both our core Transport Committee team and all the additional people who have come in to help and advise us on the inquiry.

We have two panels today. During our first panel we will hear about the economic case for a Heathrow expansion, and in our second panel we will hear about the business and employment case for Heathrow expansion. First, I will ask our witnesses to introduce themselves.
Good morning, Chair. I am Ian Mulheirn. I am chief analyst at the Department for Transport.

Good morning, Chair. I am James Laird, director of Peak Economics, which is my own company, and also a visiting research fellow for the Institute for Transport Studies at the University of Leeds, although I am based in the north of Scotland, in Inverness.
Good morning, Chair. I am Matt Shepherd, a director at Frontier Economics.
Good morning. I am Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at the New Economics Foundation. We are a charitable think-tank based in London.

Q1 Chair : We have limited time this morning and an awful lot to cover, so if our witnesses find themselves being drawn into a lot of detail on something, they should please bear it in mind that they are more than welcome to follow up on the detail in writing afterwards. I also remind our Members to keep their questions brief.

We have an initial question for you, Ian Mulheirn, because you were able to send us a correction last night. Thank you for drawing attention in your letter to a technical correction to the Department’s analysis. We have published that correction. Would you briefly explain the significance of it?

Essentially, the expansion of Heathrow has effects on other airports, and there are terminal capacity constraints and runway constraints. With some of the changes we have made, terminal capacity constraints at some other airports become more important, and some of the benefits from the expansion of Heathrow actually occur at those airports because it relieves pressure on them. We have found that there is a significant chunk of benefits at Gatwick airport because those constraints are relieved by the expansion of Heathrow. That was not captured in the initial analysis, because we have had to fundamentally change some things in how the analysis is done for this exercise. Apologies for missing that. We still have not finalised exactly the scale of that, but we hope to do so in the coming days. We will write to you about the scale.
Q2 That would be my next question: we would like an indication of the order of magnitude of the correction. Is it billions or millions?
It is likely to be billions; it is a material change, but we are fairly certain at this stage that it does not change any of the qualitative conclusions of the economic case.
Q3 Does the analysis have any other outstanding issues that the Department is aware of?
We are not aware of any other issues with the analysis at this point.

Q4 Thank you very much. Let us get back to the main questions. The first is to each of you in turn, in the same order in which you introduced yourselves, please. The draft HENPS states that analysis shows the Heathrow expansion “could add up to 0.05% to GDP in 2056”. Has the economic case for a third runway at Heathrow diminished in the time since the Airports Commission reported ? If yes, why?

In order to consider whether the economic case has deteriorated, we have to consider both the GDP modelling and the appraisal, which takes into account welfare — the full set of things that people might value, not just the GDP bit. I t is fair to say that there have been significant changes since the last decade , when we looked at this most closely , t hat have made the case somewhat different to what we looked at then.

Most obviously, there i s significantly greater capacity in the rest of the s outh - east. We also have a more graduated expansion plan here from Heathrow ; i t takes a number of years before the full programme is delivered , and t hat means capacity comes on stream slower. A third issue is that business travel is significantly lower as a proportion of passenger flights than it was back in 2018 , pre covid . T he final thing that weighs i n the economic case overall is that how we , as Government , value carbon emissions has changed since 2021 , and we now place a higher value on carbon emissions. T hat is not an underlying change in the case, but how we look at it is significantly different.

One way to think about this is that the airport system in the south - east eventually fill s up and by the 2040s and ’ 50s you are really starting to see benefits coming through . So there i s a question , in a sense , about when things will fill up , as much as the re is about whether the economic case has deteriorated i n absolute terms .
Q5 James, I should explain that you are the peer reviewer of the Frontier Economics work that was commissioned by the DFT.

That is correct. Obviously, the Frontier Economics work did not look historically at the previous work. The previous S - CGE work was done by PwC 10 years ago, and the modelling set-up was completely different. I also peer reviewed that.

What I would say first — you introduced it by talking about the 0.05% of GDP —is that that is actually quite a material and significant impact from a transport project. I am estimating that that is equivalent to about a 4.8% real rate of return. To take a Government gilt , s tripping out inflation , that c ompares to about 2%. F or a transport project, 0.05% of G DP is actually really quite lar ge. It i s not as large as what the PwC model found 10 years ago, but Adolf Stroombergen and I conducted the peer review and we were highly critical of what they did.

Other than for the reasons that Ian has given , which I will not repeat, I will not say that the case has been diminishing. It was possibly overstated before in terms of the S - CG E work , not the welfare analysis . A 4.8% real return is still high for a mature economy that is very well connected already. A gain, we would probably want to look at that . I am sure we are going to come on to that further.
In the interests of brevity, I agree with the comments James and Ian have made and do not have anything to add.
Scott, you wanted to come in.
Q6 James, thanks for putting that 0.05% in context, but you compared it to transport projects—
Sorry. I forgot to bring in Alex Chapman—sorry, Alex.
I am happy to wait for the Member’s question, if preferred.

You compared the 0.05% to other transport projects, but normally when I think about transport projects, they are delivered by the Government. That is a different context. This will not be a Government-funded project, will it? It is a private investment. I know it is a transport project, but is that the correct comparator in this context?

There is an economic literature that looks at capital investment in transport, whether it is privately or publicly funded. The mechanism of funding is irrelevant. It is to do with whether we are increasing the stock of transport in the system.

We would expect different returns from public and private investment in transport : we invest in transport as a Government because it is a public good, not necessarily because we want to get a return from it.
There are multiple reasons for investing in transport—
Q7 So what is the comparator?

Part of the overarching process within Government is that we are looking at it from a wellbeing or quality perspective, which is the economic case. There is also an interest in the economic performance of the nation as a consequence of the infrastructure, so we look at that as well. Generally speaking, transport is something that contributes across the piece to quality of life and to the economy, so we would always expect the rate of return on a transport investment to be lower than something that was maybe purely focused on business.
Thank you. Back to Alex Chapman.

I personally think the primary driver is this decline in business passenger demand. Just for context, back at the time of the Airports Commission assessments, the DFT was forecasting something like 93 million business passengers in the UK aviation system in 2050. That has now dropped to somewhere around 50 million, which is essentially implying more or less no growth between now and 2050 in business passenger demand. That feeds both into the welfare assessment and the ticket fare savings that drive the appraisal and the GDP assessment. That is a fundamental change in our expectations about the future.

I would just add that what we need to investigate here is not just whether there is a beneficial GDP impact, but whether that impact is worth while relative to the costs of the scheme, social and otherwise. There have been some material changes in the way that we look at those costs. Even looking back, for example, to the period since the jet zero strategy, the Government ha ve now changed their position such that they are expecting residual emissions from aviation of 41 million tonnes in 2050 instead of previously— only a few years ago — 15 million tonnes.

Why is that relevant to today? Under a net zero legal obligation, the plan is to pay to capture those emissions. That is a cost of this intervention. The scheme will be responsible for expanding the envelope of the number of emissions that will have to be paid for and bought back, potentially by the state or otherwise. W e do not have any kind of mechanism to secure that.

I n the appraisal , we have a recognition of that loss, which is why there is such a negative overall appraisal assessment here, because there is no way of dealing with that future cost. However, that needs to be weighed against the scheme. That is something that we did not have, partly because we did not have the net zero commitment back in 2017, alongside the other changes that we have seen, including things such as the use of remote communication technologies, Brexit and all the rest of it. That is a material consideration here.
Thank you. We will now move to the economic test.

Q8 Thank you for inviting me to join today, Chair. Dr Chapman, tell us about the economic growth test that is specified in the draft national policy statement —a re you content with how that is specified?

To put it simply, for me it is not specified. The reality of the test is that, to be able to judge, you would need to have some sort of benchmarking of what would be an acceptable level of beneficial impact relative to the costs of the scheme, economic , environmental , social and otherwise .

T he thing that I find most shocking about the way that it is currently written is that, at two points—paragraphs 5.92 and 5.99—the test asks the applicant to assess beneficial effects. It mentions at one point a “ breakdown of wider benefits ” and, at another point, about information on “ expected benefits ” without reference to costs, which sort of suggests that the intention is to ask the applicant to provide essentially a puff piece or propaganda piece about their own scheme, which does not actually appraise the full system.

Q9 Who would have guessed it? Did you hunt through for some numerical values to be attached? Were you surprised, as I was, not to find them? Do you think that requires some real offsetting against costs?

Clearly it does. But you can refer to what we have seen recently with the Luton and Gatwick decisions, whereby initial recommendation opportunity was given to the Planning Inspectorate to make their recommendation. In both cases, their initial recommendation was that the economic benefits were not sufficient to outweigh the environmental costs. But the Government later overturned those recommendations anyway. Essentially, that leads to some scepticism about what the value of that process really is. The Government have set their intention here. It has asked the Government, the provider, to present their benefits. Whatever level those may be, it seems likely that they will be deemed acceptable or overturned if they are not.
Q10 So it was a conclusion looking for a justification? Is that what you are telling us?
Perhaps you could say so, hence why it is so important today that we scrutinise the Government’s own impact assessment and appraisal.

Q11 Let us look at the Green Book cost analysis. That concludes that the scheme has a net present value of between negative £23.4 billion and negative £62.5 billion over 60 years. What do you make of that?

It is also important to note that the figures you quoted are only for the UK-side impacts . There is a subsequent assessment further down that identifies, I think, around minus £80 billion to minus £120 billion when considering the global impacts here. We are not a society in the habit of considering only impacts that occur within the domain of our borders. I would like to think that we are better than that.

I am interested to hear from the DFT on this, but I would not be surprised to hear that that is potentially the worst net present value appraisal outcome that a Government scheme has ever delivered in history, although I cannot prove that point. It is quite extraordinary. As I say, it reflects a number of different factors, particularly the inadequate policy infrastructure in place to deal with the climate emissions and climate damage of the scheme.

Q12 You also did some analysis of jobs created.
